*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age up to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscripts, corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so. An edition of the greatest accuracy and easily preferable to all others when one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reissued works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—unified, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.*

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in every branch of ecclesiastical learning.

[**EXPOSITION OF PSALM 118.**]

## [Column 1193]

# Prefatory Notice on the Exposition of Psalm 118

[Column 1193]

From the entire sequence of this work we plainly understand that blessed Ambrose, when he resolved to equip the Christians entrusted to his care with the precepts necessary for the fullest attainment of the perfection proper to their condition, considered nothing more useful for that purpose than to expound for them the most beautiful of all the psalms, and one especially rich in moral teaching (Preface). Accordingly, since the holy Doctor had undertaken so noble a subject, he applied to its illumination the whole force of his intellect and every capacity divinely granted to him. Whatever eloquence, whatever ardor, modesty, humility, and learning it contained—all of this shines forth with such brilliance in this commentary that, by the common judgment of the most learned men, including even heterodox scholars, it is numbered among the outstanding works of our Ambrose.

At the beginning he offers a brief preface, as though playing a preliminary theme, in which he explains in summary everything that generally pertains to this psalm. He then proceeds to an exposition of the groups of eight verses, at the threshold of each of which he analyzes the Hebrew letters. According to his own testimony, these letters are like the titles of the verses written under them (Sermon 14). It is worth observing that the holy Bishop openly declares that the very things which David transmits here under each individual element of the Hebrew alphabet are also described under those same elements by Jeremiah in his Lamentations. Yet before the eighth sermon he does not disclose this correspondence; thereafter he pursues it most carefully to the end of the work. Only in this latter section does he explain the meaning of those letters at greater length.

After explaining each of the elements, he proceeds to interpret the text and examines, in their proper order, each of the eight verses contained under each element, treating some at greater length and others more briefly. First he sets out the actual words of each verse; and whenever any variation occurs—whether in the Greek or Latin copies, or even among different interpreters—he presents it to his readers with great learning (Sermons 4, 10, 12, and elsewhere). He points out, as it were with his finger, the sources of such differences, attributing them sometimes to disagreements among interpreters, but more often to the fault of copyists who corrupted Scripture through ignorance or carelessness (Sermons 4, 5, and elsewhere). He also candidly states his opinion concerning the various versions of Scripture (Sermons 9, 17, 20, and 22), and teaches (Sermon 13) that at that time the interpretation of the Seventy—namely, the Septuagint—held the principal authority in the Church. Nevertheless, he himself more readily used his own Greek copy (Sermon 17), although he by no means neglected to consult other copies from time to time or to propose different interpretations of the text that seemed defensible on some grounds.

Although from the outset of this work (Sermon 1), as in his other writings (*On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 4, section 23; Preface to Luke; and elsewhere), he recognizes three senses of Scripture—the natural or historical, the mystical, and the moral—he does not follow the first here, passes over the second rather lightly, and devotes himself entirely to carving out and illuminating the third. The reasons that led Saint Ambrose to adopt this course are not difficult to identify, since he repeatedly affirmed (Sermons 1, 13, and elsewhere) that although the mystical sense is more acute, the moral sense is much sweeter and more acceptable to the people (Sermon 13), who recognized that it offered them a richer harvest of practical benefit. He therefore directed all the strength of his intellect toward this sense and taught Christians by what means they could attain the highest degree of perfection. There, with incredible fervor of spirit, he attacks the principal and most widespread vices of his time. Nor does he spare the ministers of the sacred altar: indeed, he wished those guilty of offenses that did not seem particularly grave to be removed from their position and dignity (Sermon 2 and elsewhere), while condemning both the excessive indulgence of those who showed themselves too lenient toward sinners and the no less excessive severity of those who were lax toward themselves but exercised a harsher judgment against others (Sermons 4 and 5). In the same place he also attacks the Jews and, above all, heretics and Arians, demonstrating (Sermon 22) that their heresy arose from their having followed the subtleties and quibbling of philosophers, especially Aristotelians. Finally, he refutes here as well the falsehood—elsewhere more than once opposed by him—that writers of our faith were guilty of plagiarism because they had compiled the finest portions of their books from the works of philosophers (*On Abraham the Patriarch* and the following works).

Into all this he interweaves a very large part of the Song of Songs, whose mysteries he chiefly interprets, as he had said elsewhere (*On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 4, section 17), with reference to the Church. Yet he does not pursue this exposition with great precision. Apart from omitting it entirely in several sermons, he follows the order of that sacred book only near its beginning and end. In the remaining portions he cites testimonies taken here and there from various chapters solely to establish the matter under discussion by their authority. Consequently, he has no hesitation in citing the same passages a second and even a third time. Since he had asserted that the consummation of Christian perfection is contained in this same psalm (Sermons 13 and 21), he concludes this work (Sermon 22) by expounding the final portion of the Song of Songs, in which the spiritual marriage of the Word with his Bride, as well as their intimate union—the reality that constitutes complete and perfect perfection—is described. No nobler crown could have been placed upon so distinguished a work.

Dallaeus acknowledges the excellence of this book (*On the Use of the Fathers*, p. 248), where he says: “A work otherwise outstanding, filled with sound doctrine and eloquence, and exceedingly worthy of being read.” Nevertheless, elsewhere [Col. 1195] he dares to brand it as erroneous, asserting (ibid., p. 270) that Ambrose here follows Hilary in teaching that all the saints must be purified by flames before they enjoy the sight of God. He adds (ibid., p. 248) that Ambrose’s license in playing with allegorical interpretations is insufficiently modest. Finally, he says that in explaining the Hebrew letters Ambrose tells his readers mere dreams (ibid., p. 244).

But in these three matters he is equally unjust. As to the first, there may be those who say that he has not spoken consistently, since he plainly professed that the work was filled with sound doctrine. We have already explained what the holy man’s own view was on this subject. For the rest, if Dallaeus finds nothing displeasing in this work apart from the error just mentioned, we earnestly beg him and others of the same communion to believe and profess concerning our sacred mysteries—and especially concerning the most holy Eucharist (Sermons 8, 14, 15, 16, and 18)—the same things as our Doctor. Only then would it surely come to pass that, once the wall of division had been broken down, we might be joined together in the same faith.

As to the second accusation, we admit, with Gregory of Nazianzus, that excess in allegorical interpretation ought to be condemned. But we maintain that scarcely any work of Ambrose is less liable than this one to such an accusation. This is perfectly clear from the fact that nowhere else, as has already been said, does the holy Bishop range so widely in moral exposition, while he touches upon the mystical or allegorical sense only in passing. Indeed, from the very Song of Songs he draws the most beautiful precepts for the formation of morals.

Finally, as to the objection concerning the interpretation of the Hebrew elements, we shall demonstrate, under the letter Aleph, that it rests on no firmer foundation.

That this book consists of sermons which Ambrose delivered to the people of Milan is by no means obscure. This is proved by the style of his diction itself, by the citations from both Testaments read in the assemblies on those same days (Sermon 3 and frequently elsewhere), and finally by the most explicit words of our Bishop (Sermon 14). It will be more difficult to determine whether each group of eight verses comprises a single sermon. If we compare the length of some with the brevity of others, and take into account both the diversity of subjects and the various interruptions and resumptions, we shall readily agree with those who think that some of the groups of eight were treated in more than one sermon. But since all the manuscripts and the old editions consistently present the sermons divided according to the elements of the Hebrew alphabet, and since it is therefore very likely that Ambrose himself arranged this commentary in that order when he wrote it down, we have wished to change nothing in this respect.

It must, however, be said that the preface to this work, which is certainly too brief to contain a sermon by itself, was either delivered together with the explanation of the first group of eight verses, or was later added by Ambrose himself to the beginning of another sermon.

We must now inquire when the holy Bishop delivered these sermons to the people. There is no doubt that this occurred before he wrote the book *On Isaac and the Soul*, cited above (chapter 4, section 17); we have established that this book was published around the year 387 (*Prefatory Notice to On Isaac and the Soul*). Moreover, his commentaries on the Gospel of Luke seem to be cited here (Sermon 14), and the more probable opinion assigns those commentaries to the year 386. In addition, mention is made (Sermon 6) of the annual feast of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, whose sacred relics were discovered around the year 385 or shortly thereafter. From this one may conclude that this distinguished work appeared at approximately the same time.

The same conclusion also seems confirmed by the holy man’s ardent expression of his desire for martyrdom in words (Sermon 21) indicating that the period was still one in which the crown of martyrdom could be attained—an expression that may appropriately and suitably be referred to the persecution of Justina, who was raging against him, that is, to the year 385 or thereabouts.

It is nevertheless highly credible that these sermons were delivered neither in one continuous series nor in one and the same year. We see that Ambrose sometimes preached when the annual feasts of Gervasius and Protasius recurred, as we have said; these feasts probably fell on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July. At other times he preached when the day sacred to Sebastian was being celebrated (Sermon 20), which was likewise then customarily observed on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February. We also observe that this holy man preached sometimes on days of fasting and sometimes on other days.

Finally, throughout the entire work we find nothing pertaining to catechumens; rather, everything appears to have been spoken to people already initiated into the Christian rites and consequently thoroughly instructed in all our mysteries. It is established that he was accustomed to preach to such people not every day, but only on Sundays and other more solemn occasions. For he did not abandon the subject he had begun in order to speak about the feast; instead, he was sometimes content to touch upon it briefly by way of digression, as has been observed above.

We have established this exposition according to the authority of many codices, if not the most ancient, at least written by hand with the greatest elegance and accuracy. In all the printed editions, both older and more recent, not only had many errors crept in, but frequent unauthorized interpolations had also been inserted. Some of these we excised; others, when we hesitated to remove them, we indicated among the variant readings. Finally, we restored the work’s proper title, supported not only by the testimony of written codices and ancient editions, but also by the approval of the Church of Lyon (*On Maintaining the Truth of Scripture*, volume IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 426) and of ancient authors who mention it.

# Exposition of Psalm 118 by Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan (C)

## Prologue

[Column 1197A]

971

### 1.

[Note: [Col. 1197B] Some manuscripts: “Although also the mystical things.” Some: “Although also the mystical thing,” with the old edition. Others, and finally the Roman edition, as in the text. To shed some light upon it, we should note that the words “in it” ought to be referred to the mystical things, as though by the sound of a trumpet—that is, through the sweetness of the song and the delight of chanting—as Saint Ambrose immediately explains.]

Although the prophet David has sounded forth every mystical truth as if with the blast of a trumpet, the supreme teacher of moral matters declares, by the excellence of this psalm, how greatly ethical teaching excels within it. For although all moral instruction is sweet, it especially delights the ears and charms the soul through the sweetness of its song and the pleasure of chanting. And rightly, in many places, he spreads abroad the moral teachings of the psalms like the lights of stars, which shine and gleam [Note: [Col. 1197B] Roman edition: “and flash forth in the world, the holy Prophet spreads them abroad.”] throughout the world. But Psalm 118 he establishes, as it were, at the mature age of a book, like the sun of full light burning with the heat of midday, [Note: [Col. 1197C] Some manuscripts: “in the progress of the book, as though he constituted its full maturity.” Others and the editions agree among themselves, except that a few read *in advanced age* instead of *in the progress*; the Roman edition has *imperfect*.] so that neither the half-complete beginnings of the morning’s rising nor some aged decline of the evening’s setting [Note: [Col. 1197C] Roman edition: “would take anything away from the perfect splendor of its brightness.”] might detract anything from the brightness of its perfected splendor. He arranged it according to the individual letters of the Hebrews, so that, just as the minds of children become accustomed to the practice of learning through the first elements of letters [Note: [Col. 1197C] Roman edition: “learn the practice of reading; so we also, through such elements,”] so we too might learn through such elements the practice of living.

[Column 1198A] 972

### 2.

He assigned eight verses to each letter, so that he might teach both unity [Note: [Col. 1197C] The old edition and not a few manuscripts add the word *not*: “to teach not plurality.”]—for unity restrains and governs all things, and all things are subject to it—and the purification of legitimate sanctification [Note: [Col. 1197C] The Roman edition adds after the word *sanctification* the verb “he might establish.”] For the solemn purification is on the eighth day [Note: [Col. 1197C] The same Roman edition reads: “Purification according to the Law is on the eighth day, and on the eighth day … it was established, because the whole …”] either according to the Law (Leviticus 12:3–4), because the solemnity of circumcision was appointed to be fulfilled on the eighth day, or because the whole world had been defiled by our sins and polluted throughout those seven days.

But when the day of resurrection arrived, we were made alive together with the Lord Jesus, rose with him, and were raised up, bearing the grace of cleansing in the newness of life. Rightly, therefore, we offer firstborn animals in the figure of the firstborn Son of God—a spiritual sacrifice acceptable to God—not on the fourth or fifth day, lest the sacrifice be unclean or incomplete, but on the eighth day, when in Christ’s resurrection we were all not only raised again but also established.

Thus, although complete purification is immediately present in baptism, nevertheless, because the baptized person ought to understand the meaning of that washing and sacrifice, [Note: [Col. 1197C] It is not easy to find among the ancients what that sacrifice was, or why the baptized person did not offer it until he had entered the eighth day. The difficulty is increased by the certainty that in former times the Eucharist was customarily administered to the initiated immediately after baptism. Nevertheless, since Ambrose here speaks not of simple communion but of sacrifice, this point of ecclesiastical discipline—perhaps observed only at Milan—may be explained as follows: the neophyte was indeed given the divine sacrament immediately after emerging from the sacred font, but it may have been taken from the little tower erected upon the altar, or from a golden or silver dove placed there or suspended in the baptistery, in which the sacrament was formerly kept. Many have observed this practice from the life of Saint Basil written by Amphilochius, from the petition presented by Antiochene clerics and monks in the fifth session of the Council of Constantinople held under Menna, and likewise from Paulinus, Gregory of Tours, and others. Meanwhile, however, they abstained from the sacrifice for seven days, while they were being more fully instructed in knowledge of the mysteries. Certainly that the ancient bishops took special care to instruct the newly baptized in the doctrine of the mysteries previously concealed from them is attested not only by the homilies of the Greek Fathers delivered during the days of Easter and by several sermons of Augustine—namely, 127, 129, 260, and 262—but also made clear by Ambrose himself in the book *On the Mysteries*, which consists of sermons delivered for this very reason: “Now,” he says, “the time urges us to speak about the mysteries and to disclose the meaning of the sacraments themselves. If we had thought this should be explained before baptism to those not yet initiated, we would be judged to have betrayed rather than disclosed it.” The books *On the Sacraments*, which are acknowledged to be either by Ambrose or at least by an author of the same age, also prove that they were delivered to the flock of neophytes. This is shown by the following passage from book 5, chapter 3: “The Church rejoices in the redemption of many, and rejoices with spiritual exultation that a family clothed in white stands before her.” Once they had finally become better instructed, it is credible that they customarily brought their offering—namely, the bread to be consecrated by the priest—to the altars. For that it was customary for each person to offer the bread of which he was going to partake is sufficiently demonstrated both by the miracle reported in the life of Gregory the Great concerning a woman who did not believe in Christ’s presence in the sacrament and by a passage from the book *On the Seven Orders of the Church*, which says plainly: “As consecration belongs to the priest, so the disposition of the sacrament belongs to the minister. The former sanctifies what has been offered; the latter distributes what has been sanctified.” Moreover, that neophytes were not accustomed to be present at the sacrifice seems confirmed by the fact that Ambrose and Augustine, in the passages cited, say that they saw the sacrament on the altar but are entirely silent about the sacrifice. Add that it is beyond doubt that they were not joined to the community of the other faithful until they had removed the white robe.]

he does not offer the sacrifice until he enters the eighth day [Col. 1199A] [Note: [Col. 1199D] Roman edition: “enters into the day, so that you may indicate that, once instructed …”] so that, instructed in the knowledge of the heavenly sacraments, he may then offer his gift to the sacred altars not as an unformed beginner but as one capable of understanding—once he has begun to be better instructed—lest the ignorance of the offerer contaminate the mystery of the offering. 973

### 3.

The title of the psalm is *Alleluia*, that is, “Praise God.” For God is truly praised in those hymns in which there is forgiveness of sins. Indeed, in the preceding psalm the Lord’s Passion was set forth beforehand; it washes away this world and makes peoples worthy to praise God with an immaculate mouth.

The very elements of the letters, like all Hebrew names, are not without rational interpretation or meaning; we shall explain their significations in their proper places.

[Column 1199B] [Note: [Col. 1199D] The Roman edition reads: “Psalm 110 … and Psalm 111 are arranged by these …” Here it evidently wished to restore the proper numerical order. But it is clear that Ambrose placed first what he believed certain, and second what was not so certain.]

Psalm 111 is arranged in Hebrew by these letters at the beginnings of its verses, and it is wholly ethical; and Psalm 110 seems to me to have been written in this manner. In the end, they have twenty-two verses, and each verse unfolds a separate thought. Hence they are also said to have been written in meters.

# First Sermon: Aleph

### 1.

[Note: [Col. 1200C] Dallaeus writes in his book *On the Use of the Fathers*, p. 244: “Ambrose tells his readers mere dreams … in Psalm 118, when he explains the names of the Hebrew elements from which the verses of each group of eight begin, and so forth.” We have already shown more than once that our Doctor was occasionally less successful in extracting the meanings of Hebrew names. Yet this must be attributed to the age in which he lived, when knowledge of the Hebrew language was not so widespread; nor should he be mocked, since he consulted the writers who were available to him on the subject. It would indeed have been desirable for him to have encountered less corrupt sources, since perhaps he found none other than Philo’s *Etymologies*. Jerome teaches that these were so full of countless errors that he himself was moved to undertake their correction. Moreover, Dallaeus was not unaware how easy it is to go astray when explaining words so fertile in meanings. This consideration ought surely to have made him somewhat more modest toward a Father of such authority.]

The first letter is called *Aleph*, whose interpretation is “doctrine.” Therefore, attentive listener, you ought to expect that the verses which follow are full of doctrine.

### 2. (Verses 1–2)

“Blessed are the immaculate,” he says, “in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who scrutinize his testimonies; they seek him with their whole heart.”

What a beautiful order, how full of doctrine and grace! He did not first say, “Those who scrutinize his testimonies”—although that could have suited the literal sense—but first: “Blessed are the immaculate in the way.” For life must be sought before doctrine. A good life, even without doctrine, possesses grace; doctrine without a good life does not possess integrity. For wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul. Therefore Scripture says: “The wicked will seek me and will not find me” (Proverbs 1:28), because the eye of the mind is blinded by wickedness; and when iniquity has darkened it, it cannot discover profound mysteries.

The warfare of life must therefore first be practiced, and one’s morals corrected. When we have set these in order along the proper course, so that there may be correction from offense and the grace of purity, then let us come in due order and along the proper way to the studies by which knowledge is received. Moral matters therefore come first, mystical matters second. In the former there is life; in the latter, knowledge. Thus, if you seek perfection, there must be neither life without knowledge nor knowledge without life: each must support the other.

Therefore Scripture says: “Sow for yourselves unto righteousness; reap for the fruit of life; enlighten for yourselves the light of knowledge” (Hosea 10:12). It does not say “Enlighten” first, but “Sow”; nor merely “Sow first unto righteousness,” but also, it says, “Reap for the fruit of life.” Then “enlighten the light of knowledge,” 974 so that perfection may be demonstrated not only by what has been sown but also by the fruits that have been gathered.

In the first psalm as well he maintained this order: he first taught that one must walk in the way, and then meditate on the Law. One who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly has certainly not departed from the way of piety or the path of righteousness. Rightly, therefore, one who walks in the way is pronounced blessed; and by practicing meditation on the Law day and night he possesses the grace of blessedness.

### 3.

Following this instruction, Solomon wrote the book of Proverbs, in which he expressed moral teaching more fully; natural teaching in Ecclesiastes; and mystical teaching in the Song of Songs. Yet if you examine carefully, you will find many mystical things in Proverbs and the sweetness of moral teaching in the Song of Songs. For this is certainly mystical: “Wisdom built herself a house and set up seven pillars; she slaughtered her victims,” and so forth (Proverbs 9:1). [Note: [Col. 1200D] Most manuscripts and the old edition: “And this shines forth in the Song of Songs, although it is both mystical and moral.” The Roman edition: “And this shines forth in the Song of Songs, both mystical and moral.” We reproduce the reading of the Remigius, Vienne, Theodore, Navarre, and Aud manuscripts.]

This too shines forth in the Song of Songs as both mystical and moral, in which the sweetness of endearments and the affection of the lover are expressed: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth; for your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices” (Song of Songs 1:1).

### 4.

Imagine, then, a betrothed virgin who has waited a long time and burns with a just love; who has learned through the testimony of trustworthy witnesses of the beloved’s many proven works; who, with her desires suspended, has often been delayed and can no longer endure postponement; who has done everything so that she might see the bridegroom; and who, at last attaining her wishes and disturbed with joy by the bridegroom’s unexpected arrival, does not seek the beginnings of a greeting or an exchange of words but immediately demands what she has desired.

So too the holy Church, betrothed at the beginning of the world in paradise, prefigured in the flood, announced through the Law, and called through the prophets, had long awaited the redemption of humanity, the beauty of the Gospel, and the coming of the beloved. Impatient with delay, she rushes to his kisses, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Delighted by the kisses, she adds: “For your breasts are better than wine.”

### 5.

And to speak in a more moral sense, understand by this the flesh that had been moistened in Adam with the serpent’s poison; that languished in the stench of crimes; that went forth among the daughters of Zion with an exalted neck and darting eyes, dragging their tunics along the path and playing with their feet, making itself all the more shameful by its curled hair, arranged faces, ribbons, and every affected adornment.

Yet this same flesh, taught by many oracles that the one who would exclude the serpent’s allurements and pour forth the grace of the Holy Spirit was coming, so that all flesh might see the salvation of God and all flesh might come to God, had begun to burn with desire. But it feared that it might displease him as impatient, wanton, luxurious, or complaining, as it had been before; and it was shaken by the expectation of the Lord’s coming, delayed longer than it could now endure. 975 Nevertheless, it did not murmur or transgress, but lifted up pure hands everywhere without anger or disputation, adorning itself in modest and sober dress—not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but with those things that suit the grace of chastity and good conduct—and prayed, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth; for your breasts are better than wine.”

The flesh already wished to cling to Christ; it was already hastening to marry him, so that it might become one spirit, and that flesh which had formerly been a harlot’s might become the flesh of Christ.

“Let him kiss me,” she says. (The Word of God kisses us when the spirit of knowledge illuminates our understanding.) And as though scorning all her pleasures and delights, desiring to cling to heavenly commandments, she says: “For the excellent precepts of your covenants are better than every appetite of the flesh and pleasure of the world.”

For she remembered that she had previously fallen in Eve in this very way, when she preferred bodily pleasure to heavenly commandments. She says: “Your name is oil poured out” (ibid., 2). That is, the whole world had reeked of the unclean impurities of various crimes; now the sweetness of modesty, the ointment of faith, and the flower of integrity breathe everywhere.

And from mortal things she comes to mystical things, saying: “The King brought me into his chamber; let us exult and rejoice in you; let us love your breasts more than wine” (ibid., 3). For the kiss is simple, but the secret of the chamber is full of activity.

### 6.

In the Gospel itself there is also a most beautiful passage on moral matters, teaching each person to cleanse his vessel. The Lord says: “Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and dish, so that what is outside may also become clean” (Matthew 23:26).

For unless each person cleanses himself inwardly, even if he appears outwardly beautiful and righteous, he will be like whitewashed tombs: outwardly he may appear righteous, but inwardly he is foul. Such is doctrine without innocence of life. But doctrine itself cannot receive a reward where it does not possess the grace of innocence. For God says to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteousness?” (Psalm 49:16).

But let us return to the psalm under discussion.

### 7.

“Blessed are the immaculate,” he says, “in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who scrutinize his testimonies; they seek him with their whole heart.”

The first verse is moral, the second mystical. Who says this? The prophet, certainly, [Note: [Col. 1201D] That is, he who spoke as though in the place and under the name of the flesh.] who was speaking on behalf of the flesh, and he says this after the psalm in which the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ was described.

When, therefore, the divine sacraments had been revealed, and he had put on the joy of the Lord’s resurrection and tasted the grace of the Passion, he saw the assemblies of the righteous, [Note: [Col. 1201D] Roman edition: “the redemption of the peoples.”] the peoples who had been redeemed, the salvation of the lost, the resurrection of the dead, and the sanctification [Col. 1202C] of the sacraments; and he cried out, saying:

“Blessed are the immaculate in the way”—that is: Behold, the earth that had been cursed in Adam has begun to possess blessedness, provided that it does not abandon the law of the Lord. Behold, the human being who had previously been polluted is immaculate.

How precious it is to keep the Lord’s commandment! How precious also to know the mystery of the commandment itself!

8. But who is spotless? Certainly not one who walks along just any road, but one who walks in Christ. For he himself said: “I am the way” (John 14:6). Whoever walks on this way knows no error—provided that he never turns away from this way. There is also the way of the Law; and [Note: [Col. 1202D] The Roman edition reads: “and therefore, while the one who walks in the law of the Lord is spotless, nor [let him] walk . . . . seeking the things that are before.”] therefore, since he is spotless, let him walk in the law of the Lord; nor let him cease walking on this way, lest he cease to be spotless. Let him not turn aside to the right or to the left, stumble, resist, or hold back; but let him walk, forgetting what is higher and seeking what is prior, pursuing the goal, hastening toward the prize, pressing on to the end—for Christ is the end of the Law. Many wish to walk on the way, but not all the way to its end. The Jews do not walk all the way to the end, because they do not walk as far as Christ. The Manichaean does not walk on the way, because he rejects the Law; but true faith walks on it, both receiving the Law and recognizing the fullness of the Law.

9. If anyone, then, walks on the way, let him search out the Lord’s testimonies. Although they are mystical, they also contain moral instruction, since one who searches the Lord’s testimonies can walk better on the way. For suppose that an utterly intemperate man, seized by the heat of adulterous desire and overcome by lust, or one who gives himself over to shameful acts and is unwilling to resist the desire of his flesh, turns this way and that; if perhaps he sees no one, he rushes into crime. [Note: [Col. 1203D] All printed editions read, “if he sees no witness of his shameful act, he rushes into crime”; all manuscripts, “if he sees no one, he rushes into crime.”] Yet even when he finds an opportunity ready for satisfying his desire, he carefully investigates everything, repeatedly turning his eyes in different directions—careless of justice, but anxious about his reputation. He is ashamed of the testimony to his error, though he is not ashamed of the error itself. And if he happens to recognize someone watching his crime, shame restrains his intemperance. Even though, with a maidservant or an ordinary prostitute, he is contriving the beginnings of lust where there is no danger of being caught, he nevertheless abandons what he has begun out of shame. [Note: [Col. 1203D] Compare this passage with what is related above in Book 1, On Abraham, chapter 7, no. 59; and also with the note appended to chapter 4 of that same book, col. 289.] How much more, then, if someone lifts the eyes of his mind and considers that everything is full of angels—the air, the earth, the sea, and the churches over which angels preside! For the Lord sends his angels for the defense of those who are to become heirs of the heavenly promises. By such reflection he can renounce the sin he has conceived.

Where, then, does this crowd of innocent people come from, if not from those sinners? The nature of all is the same, but their discipline is different. Circumcision is nothing, and paganism is nothing; but obedience to God’s commandments increases the grace of nature itself. He changes a person’s merits who says: “Darkness surrounds me, and walls cover me; the Most High will not remember my sins” (Ecclesiasticus 23:26).

[Col. 1203C] 10. Would you not have respected the presence of angels if you believed that they were present? Would you not have feared—not merely to do, but even to say or think—what is evil, if divine Scripture had taught you that God is the judge of thoughts and the truthful witness of hidden things, as he himself says: “You are my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and my servant whom I have chosen” (Isaiah 43:10)? You fear a human being who is present, but do not fear the presence of God the Father and the Son? But you do not want to believe, lest you be able to take precautions; you do not want to listen when it is read that God knows the secrets of human beings, lest you begin to know what you ought to fear, and to fear lest you sin.

Listen, then, to divine Scripture, so that you may turn away from a crooked and evil way. Do not be like a person blind in bodily eyes, or like a deaf person who, because he cannot see or hear those present, believes himself to be alone. In the midst of a crowd, thinking that no one is present, he begins to perpetrate what he supposes to be secret. For one who does not see cannot see those who do see. Likewise, you, blinded in the eyes of your mind, must not suppose that you sin without a witness merely because you have been able to avoid the presence of human beings. There are more who can rebuke you than there are people from whom you have been able to hide.

You cannot flee from yourself, your own accuser, whom your conscience brings before the tribunal. [Note: [Col. 1204D] “Brings before the tribunal” is a phrase from the marketplace; that is, conscience prosecutes him in judgment.] Even if you deny it to others, you do not deny it to yourself. Even if you disavow it before a human being, you confess it to God. And even if you wish to deny it, your own thoughts convict you.

11. Angels attended Elisha, and he saw them; therefore he was not afraid of the armies of the enemy. But his servant was afraid, because he did not see the angels. At the prophet’s word, the grace of God opened his eyes; he saw the armies of angels and believed that those who previously, because he did not see them, had seemed absent were present (2 Kings 6:16–17). You too should read the prophet, so that you may see; read, so that he may open your eyes. Let not the hostile legion terrify you, and do not think yourself besieged when you are free and fortified by spiritual troops—provided that you do not abandon the prophet.

When the prophet speaks to you, because God has said, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24); when the prophet tells you that “there are more with us” (2 Kings 6:16), because angels are all around us—lift up the eyes of your mind, and you will see not only angels but also God, who says to you: “Open to me, my sister, my close companion” (Song of Songs 5:2). He knocks at the door even while you sleep; but if, once awakened, you wake fully, or, when called, open the door of your heart, he will enter.

But if you flee prophetic reading, if you do not read at home and refuse to listen in church, are you not like someone who closes his eyes and blinks away from what he could see, or like those who, in a fit of rage, have put their hands over their eyes so as not to look at something they have the power to see? In the same way, you first turn away through evasive dissimulation rather than through open resistance. For when you come to church and claim to be a Christian, you appear sound; you open your eyes so that you can see. But when you pretend not to hear what is read, you close them so that you will not see for yourself, even if you appear to see for the sake of others. You also place certain hands of unbelief and intemperance over the eyes of your soul, bringing blindness upon your heart—what is worse, a voluntary blindness—so that, though seeing, you do not see, and, though hearing, you do not hear.

12. Do you think you are alone when you commit fornication, and do you not remember that the eyes of the Lord behold the whole earth? Do you not hear him saying: “Behold, the hour is coming . . . when you will be scattered, each one to his own, and you will leave me alone; but I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32)? The Father is therefore present, and the Son of God is present; his ministers are present; the Cherubim and Seraphim are present, saying: “Holy, holy, holy; the earth is full of your majesty.” The world is full of holy powers, because it is full of wickedness. The whole earth is full of remedies, because it is full of snares.

Do you think that Christ does not see you in a brothel, when he sees you entering the brothel? Do you think that he does not catch you in adultery, when he sees you thinking about adultery? Does he flee from walls, though he watches your errors? Does he turn away from the secrecy of the crime, though he observes the scene of the crime? Or do you think that you enter the brothel for the first time [Col. 1205A] [Note: [Col. 1205D] One manuscript of Navarra reads meretricatorium, “belonging to a prostitute”; but meritorium should be retained. Understand here a lodging-house or inn; for such places were once called, as Tertullian puts it, “meeting places of public lust.” Hence some wish prostitutes to have been called prostibulae or prostibulae, because they stood pro stabulo, that is, “before the lodging-house.” Meritorium, however, is derived from mereri, “to earn,” because it earns—that is, produces—profit for its owner. In this sense Horace says in the Art of Poetry: “Here the freeborn boy earns money for the Sosii.” From this, too, prostitutes and meritorii boys received their name, although meritorium sometimes signifies an honorable lodging-house.] when you enter the prostitute’s brothel? You entered it already when the prostitute entered your thoughts. You entered it already when, in your mind, you entered in order to satisfy the desire for the prostitute. You knocked at the doors of the brothel when you opened the eyes of your mind to desire the woman’s beauty.

And if you wish to hear the truth, how could Christ not see you in the brothel? He saw you, because, by committing adultery in your heart, you made yourself a brothel. Indeed, the Lord Jesus himself says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). How, then, can someone be considered so religious in reputation when he is so disgraceful in his crime?

13. But let me grant you that Jesus does not wish to see you, does not wish to convict you, and does not wish to accuse you; let the angels also not wish to see you. Yet the devil sees you. He entered with you—or rather, he brought you in. His ministers see you; they surrounded you so that you would not see the angels of God. Belial saw you; the legion saw you; they drove you on so that no one might call you back and no one might restrain you.

Do not think that the one who wishes to share punishment with you offers you the collusion of silence. [Note: [Col. 1206D] Colludium, or collusio, signifies simulation and fraud. Those who appear to contend or quarrel with one another are said to collude when they do so merely as a pretense, one of them deliberately allowing himself to be defeated in court. This fraud, however, also occurs outside the courtroom.] He seeks to see many like himself, and he counts it as his glory that he has made many people lost. He is the instigator, the accuser; he entered into Judas; he drove him to betrayal; he sent him to the noose.

How many will say against him on that day: “You deceived us; you drove us on” (Genesis 3:13)! Do you seek an example? Hear Eve saying that the serpent was the author of her transgression. But although she implicated him, she did not absolve herself. To her the Lord replied: “Had I not commanded you not to taste only of the tree that is in the middle of paradise?” (ibid., 11). Truth will therefore reply also to many others: “You listened to the devil when he advised what was harmful, but you were unable to listen to me when I commanded what gives life.”

14. (Verses 3, 4, 5, 6.) And therefore let us practice righteousness: “For those who practice iniquity have not walked in his ways. You commanded that your commandments be kept with great care. Would that my ways be directed toward keeping your ordinances! Then I shall not be put to shame when I examine all your commandments.”

“You not only commanded,” he says, “that your commandments be kept, but that they be kept with great care.” When did he command this? In paradise he certainly commanded Adam to keep the commandments. But perhaps he had not commanded him to keep them with the utmost care. That is why Adam fell; that is why he was bent aside by the voice of his wife; that is why he was deceived by the serpent, thinking that if he departed from the commandment in some respect, he would not go completely astray. But because he had once withdrawn from the path of the commandments, he abandoned the whole way and stripped himself of everything, leaving himself naked.

Therefore the Lord, because Adam had fallen—he who had been in paradise—later admonished you through the Law, through the Prophets, through the Gospel, and through the Apostles to keep the commandments of the Lord your God with the greatest care. “Every idle word,” he says (Matthew 12:36), “that you have spoken, you will give an account for.” Do not dissimulate: not one iota or one stroke of any commandment passes away. Do not leave the way. If, while walking on the way, you are scarcely safe from a robber, what will you do if he finds you wandering outside the way? Let your steps be directed; and, lest you be too weak to direct them, pray that the Lord may direct your ways.

15. Here he says: “Would that my ways be directed!” Elsewhere he says: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he heard me . . . . and he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Psalm 39:2–3). You too should pray that the Lord direct the footsteps of your mind, so that you may keep the Lord’s ordinances. You will not be put to shame when you look upon all his commandments.

For previously you were put to shame in Adam and Eve. You became naked; you covered yourself with leaves because you were ashamed. You hid yourself from the sight of God because you were embarrassed, so that God said to you: “Adam, where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). When he says this to Adam, he says it to you, for Adam in Latin interpretation means “human being”: “Human being, where are you?” And Adam answered: “Because I was afraid, since I was naked, and entirely ashamed in my mind, I did not dare come before your sight” (ibid., 10).

Therefore, so that we may not be put to shame, let us keep the Lord’s commandments—and let us keep them all. For if someone keeps one commandment but transgresses another, it does him no good. Someone may have guarded himself from bloodshed but not from adultery; once convicted in the one matter, he is certainly punished also by the laws of this world. Abstinence from one crime does not benefit him if he is caught in another.

16. (Verses 7, 8.) “I shall confess to you, Lord, in uprightness of heart”—you see which ways he directs—“when I have learned the judgments of your righteousness. I shall keep your ordinances; do not abandon me completely.”

In this passage he testifies that he wishes to know the mystical meaning more fully, so that he may enter the inner chambers of the heavenly mysteries and that the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ may be opened to him. Hence Solomon also says: “Draw us after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments. The King has brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs 1:3). And perhaps what he said above, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (ibid., 1), signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon her, just as the angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

[Note: [Col. 1206D] Several manuscripts read: “When he has brought her in . . . . the compunction [of the side] is declared.” Whoever accepts this reading should understand it as though it said: “When the Church is read as having been brought in, the time of the Passion is thereby declared.”]

When the King brings her into his chamber, the time of the Passion is indicated by the piercing of the side, the outpouring of blood, the ointment of burial, and the mystery of the resurrection. Thus she has received the kiss as a bride; and the Church has been brought into Christ’s chamber, no longer merely betrothed but also as a wife. She has entered not only the bridal chamber but also received the lawful tokens of the marriage bond.

Therefore, as though situated in the bridal chamber, she says: “My brother is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will rest between my breasts” (Song of Songs 1:12). But if we ask where the chamber is, let him himself teach us, for he says: “When you pray, enter your room; and after shutting the door, pray to your Father in secret” (Matthew 6:6). The chamber of the Church is the body of Christ.

The King brought her into all the innermost mysteries and gave her the keys, so that she might open for herself the treasures of the knowledge of the mysteries, throw open doors that had previously been closed, and know the grace of the one who rests, the sleep of the dead, and the power of the resurrection. [Note: [Col. 1207D] All printed editions read “the grace of the one who rests,” whereas nearly all manuscripts read “the grace of rest.” Again, the Roman edition alone reads “the power of the one who rises”; the others, together with all the manuscripts, read “the power of the resurrection.”]

17. In that chamber the bride found the righteous acts of the Lord Jesus. What are those righteous acts? They are certainly the mysteries of baptism, as we read: When John said to Jesus as he came to baptism, “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” Jesus answered: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:14–15).

In that chamber she learned the Lord’s ordinances and came to know the counsel of God, as it is written: “All the people who heard, and the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John; but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the counsel of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him” (Luke 7:29–30). What they rejected, let us choose, and let us follow the counsel of God, than which nothing can be more sublime; for this is divine, and through it the forgiveness of sins is accomplished.

When she has learned the Lord’s righteous acts, she will not be put to shame because she fears God. Thus Paul also says: “In nothing shall I be put to shame” (Philippians 1:20).

18. And because no one can be perfect or secure without God’s favor, he ought to pray that God not abandon him completely. Above, David prayed not to be abandoned, saying: “Do not abandon me, Lord my God” (Psalm 37:22). Here he says: “Do not abandon me completely,” that is, “to a great degree.”

Previously, perhaps as one still imperfect and placed amid great disturbances, he feared being abandoned. Here, however, being stronger, he does not fear being abandoned for the sake of testing; rather, he asks not to be abandoned completely. For God often abandons those whom he wishes to have tested; but he abandons completely those whom he forsakes.

He completely abandoned Judas. He did not abandon holy Job, into whose possessions and body he gave the devil power (Job 2:6), but not over his soul. For if he had given him power over his soul, he would have abandoned him completely. Was Job not abandoned for this reason: so that, having been left, he might be tested, and, having been tested, crowned?

He therefore abandoned Judas, to whom he said: “What you are going to do, do quickly” (John 13:27). He completely abandoned the one whom he permitted to carry his crime into effect. [Note: [Col. 1208D] All manuscripts read “permitted to carry into effect”; the printed editions read “permitted to bring about,” and some Paris editions “to the emotion.” He did not, however, abandon the other apostles, whom he saw troubled.] But when he saw the other apostles troubled because he had said, “Where I am going, you cannot come” (ibid., 33), he added: “Let not your heart be troubled” (John 14:1). And later: “I shall come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, there you also may be” (ibid., 3).

Finally, Peter, troubled because he feared being abandoned, said: “Lord, where are you going?” (John 13:36). The Lord saw him troubled and answered him: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but afterward you will follow” (Matthew 14:30–31). So too, when Peter was wavering on the sea, he cried out to Christ, and Christ extended his right hand to him, lest, completely abandoned, he perish.

19. No one should be puffed up because he is never abandoned, or grieve because he is sometimes abandoned, since the Son himself says that he was abandoned, as you have it: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you abandoned me?” (Psalm 21:1).

Yet he was never abandoned by the Father, with whom the Father is always present. For it is written: “Behold, the hour is coming when you will be scattered, each one to his own, and you will leave me alone; but I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32). But this voice came forth according to the body in which he was handed over to suffering, because we seem to be abandoned when we are placed in danger.

Hence Paul also says of God the Father: “He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32). He seems to have abandoned him because he did not spare him, but handed him over to death; yet he did not abandon him completely, for it is said to him: “You will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15:10).

## SECOND SERMON. Beth

1. (Verse 9.) “By what means does a younger man correct his way?” Our discussion of the preceding eight verses was not unreasonable; therefore we have been eager to pursue what follows as well. First, we must consider the interpretation of the second letter, that is, Beth, which, translated into Latin, signifies “confusion.” But the one who corrects his way will not be put to shame.

Since the one who corrects his way was previously in error—for how can something be corrected unless it first turned away from the truth?—he is, in effect, situated in a fall. Captivated by the luxury of adolescence and by the allurements of a wanton age, when, having advanced toward the threshold of youth, he comes to his senses with a sober mind, he turns the matter over within himself for a long time. As one confused in spirit, he considers how he may lay aside what ought to cause shame and assume what is full of virtue. Torn by conflicting thoughts, he weighs and examines how he may correct his way, forgetting what is higher and seeking what is prior, and how he may cover over the offense of his younger years with the serious face of youth.

Therefore, lest such a person remain long in doubt and cling to uncertainty, the Prophet gives counsel, as though deliberating with him himself. For we consider counsels more beneficial when they appear to have been examined through more earnest reflection. Yet the very process of deliberation is marked out by a learned formulation, so that he removes the clash of conflicting thoughts by asking: “By what means does a younger man correct his way?” This is the conclusion of the one deliberating: how he may correct his way.

2. And he answered: “By keeping your words.” Properly, turning toward the Lord, he answered the one who was deliberating, as though, through prayer and supplication, he had found this counsel by the inspiration of the Lord, so that the remedy might be understood to come not from human presumption but from divine favor.

Our mind, sprinkled with the seeds of heavenly words, which previously produced degenerate growths, begins to yield better cultivation and bear fruit. Let us therefore make our paths straight, and let us not follow the winding coils of the crooked serpent. The ways of the Lord are straight, but the ways of those who go astray are crooked; of them it is said: “O you who have abandoned straight paths” (Proverbs 2:13)!

A flourishing crop extends in ordered rows, and vineyards are planted in a kind of regular line. The course of deer is straighter; that of the fox is winding. Therefore it is said of Herod: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke 13:32), because he had turned away from the straight way and had not corrected his path in his youth—worthy of the lament of Jeremiah, by which sinners are mourned, those who refused to take up the yoke of the word in their youth.

Therefore they were led away captive; therefore they are lamented as though dead, because they did not know the paths of life and did not turn away from deeds worthy of the funeral pyre of corpses. [Note: [Col. 1209D] This refers to the custom of the Greeks and Romans of burning corpses. Such punishment is said to be deserved by grave sins.]

Thus Jeremiah, mourning the perpetual death of the Jews, says: “It is good for a man when he bears the yoke in his youth; he will sit alone and keep silent, because he has placed it upon himself” (Lamentations 3:27–28).

3. We must take up not only the yoke of the word, but take it up in youth. For if we take it up late, we begin to possess rather the repentance of earlier things than to retain grace. Let us therefore anticipate the years of youth with appropriate correction, so that each of us may say rather: “God, who has fed me from my youth” (Genesis 48:15), than, remembering our fall, lament and say: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Psalm 24:7).

The former is a remedy for weakness; the latter, the strength of salvation. Medicine for salvation is sought for the wound; grace for health. Therefore he says: “It is good for a man when he bears the yoke in his youth” (Lamentations 3:27).

For the one who takes up the yoke after the years of youth have run their course does not immediately possess perfect goodness. His sins goad him, the habit of sinning harasses his conscience, and his experience of error makes him unstable. Such a man must struggle for a long time in order to eradicate the long-standing and enduring practices formed in youth. [Note: [Col. 1209D] All printed editions and some manuscripts read “so that he may eradicate what has become old,” while several more numerous and better manuscripts read “so that he may eradicate what has become old, formed in youth,” that is, so that he may erase the habits acquired throughout youth, a period in which childhood and adolescence are included here.] For the former, the matter is dangerous; for the latter, it is beneficial.

4. Finally, he will sit alone, as one who easily finds no equal, endowed with exceptional rewards. He will sit in silence, peaceful and released from every interruption of worldly anxiety and pleasure. He will devote himself to divine oracles, which are accustomed to being revealed to those who sit alone, as to holy David, who says: “For you alone have established me in hope” (Psalm 4:10).

David did not sit alone in secret, since he ruled over peoples; nevertheless, he excelled through a unique grace. Elijah sat alone when he was fed by an angel—or even by ravens bringing him food (1 Kings 17:6; 19:7). He was alone not merely because he was separated from crowds, but also because he was set apart from the merits of the many. Finally, divine revelations shone upon him, and he received the fruit of that gift as his reward, because he had considered that the yoke of the word should be taken up from his youth and that sins should not be dragged along any longer by a long rope.

5. This younger man, who did what was good by taking up the yoke of the word in youth, may be understood as not yet perfect, because he is still young. Yet he separates himself from the conversations of his peers, which often corrupt good morals, and willingly flees the contagion of sinners. In this way he may be understood to sit and remain silent alone, lest he fall through the recklessness of an inexperienced age. But he attends to the instructions of elders, the oracles of the prophets, and the teachings of the apostles. He is worthy of praise because he wishes to learn what must be said before putting forth what he thinks; before learning to speak, he fears contracting sin through excessive speech.

Hence I think that that philosopher Pythagoras, as an imitator of this prophetic young man, also founded his school, so that his disciples, remaining silent for five years, might learn to speak through such silence. [Note: [Col. 1209D] Everyone knows that a distinctive feature of Pythagorean discipline lay in silence. This had two aspects. First, what they called ἐχεμυθία (*echemythia*), “restraint of speech,” was sometimes imposed on disciples for two years and more often for five. The second was that they kept their mysteries from the profane; this was called παντελές (*panteles*), “complete” or “perfect.” That he could have learned much from the writings of David and Isaiah is not chronologically impossible: David lived 536 years before Pythagoras, and Isaiah 246 years before him. The authority of Flavius Josephus, Origen, and Clement of Alexandria also supports the point. On this matter, consult Johann Gerhard Vossius, *On the Sects of the Philosophers*, chapter 6, § 5. See also what we observed in Book 2, *On Abraham*, chapter 11, no. 20, and at the end of the *Admonition* in the book *On the Good of Death*.]

For David certainly lived earlier than Pythagoras, and he says: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.’ I set a guard over my mouth” (Psalm 38:2). And because he may at some point have spoken something carelessly, he later asked God to set a guard over his mouth.

Who does not know that Isaiah also lived before Pythagoras? When he heard, “Cry out” (Isaiah 40:6), he did not cry out before he had heard what he ought to cry. He answered: “What shall I cry?” (ibid.). Therefore it was said to him: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers and its flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (ibid., 6–8). Then he cried out with a prophetic voice.

6. Both young men, then, deserve praise: the one was late, but the other cautious; the former content with himself, yet never alone; the latter adopting a beautiful discipline of silence for a slippery age, not yet self-sufficient, but afraid to entrust himself to others. Nevertheless, from youth he sought to gather what would benefit both himself and his neighbors in old age, lest it be said to him: “What you did not gather in youth, how will you find in old age?” (Ecclesiasticus 25:5). Therefore, if he sits in the council of elders, he will place his hand over his mouth, so that, by listening to their judgments, he may gather what he can preserve for a more mature age.

So did Mary, when she heard Christ’s words, “keep all these things, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:51). So did John, when he reclined his head upon the breast of the Lord Jesus (John 13:25): he drank in the deep secrets of wisdom. [Note: [Col. 1211D] To remove the obscurity of this passage, observe that in the first part the one who returned late to good conduct is contrasted with the one who took up the Lord’s yoke from adolescence. In the second part, the two are compared with one another: both submitted their necks to the same yoke, but, as was mentioned above, not in the same manner.]

7. Here you have a young man who corrected his way in youth. He was a fisherman with his brother. He saw the Lord Jesus while he was folding his nets and heard him say: “Come . . . I will make you fishers of human beings.” And leaving his nets and his father, he followed him (Matthew 4:19–20).

He had begun to run along the way of the world; but when he heard Christ’s commands, he abandoned the life of the world and followed Christ. He proved that “a younger man corrects his way” when he keeps Christ’s words, saying to him: “We shall love your breasts more than wine” (Song of Songs 1:1). Yet he drank in such a way that he was not overwhelmed by wine; he imbibed its grace as joy of heart, rather than staggering through bodily drunkenness.

Finally, while drinking this wine, he opened his eyes and saw the straight way. He abandoned the winding paths, saying: “Equity has loved you” (ibid., 3)—that is, you do not follow crooked roads; only the path of righteousness can reach you. For whoever loves righteousness does not turn away from Christ. How could an innocent conscience fear the arbiter of righteousness and the rewarder of merits?

8. Therefore, as we contemplate this young man correcting his way, behold great mysteries, which holy Solomon, filled with the Spirit of the Lord, proclaimed in the Song of Songs. Picture the Lord Jesus reclining at a banquet, with John reclining upon his breast. Let the others marvel that a servant should recline upon his Lord, that sinful flesh should recline upon the temple of the Word, and that a soul bound to the chains of flesh should investigate the palace of divine fullness.

Then John’s soul answered those who were marveling: “I am dark but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song of Songs 1:4): dark through guilt, beautiful through grace. The flesh also says: “I am dark but beautiful”—dark with the worldly dust that I gathered in struggle, but beautiful through the spiritual oil with which I wiped away the dust and grime of this world. Dark through vice, but now beautiful through the bath that washes away every sin. “I am dark because I sinned; beautiful because Christ now loves me.” What he had banished in Eve, he received from the Virgin; he took it up from Mary. [Note: [Col. 1212D] Some manuscripts read “beautiful in the spiritual eye.”]

9. The Synagogue also speaks, whose mysteries many believe are expressed in this passage. When it saw that it was already being rejected because of the impiety of the entire people, it nevertheless consoled itself because it saw Christ himself coming from its people, along with Peter, John, and James, clinging to Christ, who possessed the divine utterances entrusted to him. Therefore it said: “I am dark but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem”—dark through unbelief, beautiful through the Law; dark through my fall, beautiful because the sun has loved me, and I became the first assembly of God.

“Do not reject me because I am dark. I am dark because the sun of righteousness, which once used to illuminate me, has left me. I have lost the color of my face; the sharpness of my eyes, with which I formerly saw the sun, has become dull. I walk in darkness because I do not know the day of Christ. Yet do not despise me, because the one who left me can look upon me again and have mercy once more. He is accustomed to gathering the scattered, seeking the abandoned, and collecting the forsaken.

“All the tribes of Israel, come together; look upon me, beautiful, once beloved. [Note: [Col. 1212D] Eight manuscripts read, “look upon me, beautiful before [I was] abandoned.” Two—namely the first Navarra manuscript and St. Aud.—read, “. . . beautiful before my sins,” which is not displeasing. The rest, however, agree with the printed editions as in the text; consequently either a conjunction has dropped out, or the second adjective is used substantively.] Do not look upon me, for I am darkened” (ibid., 5)—that is, do not look upon me merely because I am darkened. The sun has not looked upon me, and therefore I am darkened.

“But the sun shines upon the righteous and the unrighteous: upon the righteous through grace, upon the unrighteous through mercy. To the former it gives the reward of their merits; to the latter it grants forgiveness of sins. It did not shine upon the nations before, but now it shines upon them. Now it rises for those upon whom the one who used to rise for me was rising. The one who forgave them will also forgive me.

“Do not suppose that, because I am darkened, the sun has abandoned me entirely and no longer looks upon me; do not suppose that it does not seek the one who is sick. It has hidden itself from me because I did not keep its commandments; it will be reconciled when it sees repentance for my sins. The sun did not see me because I did not receive the one who came; I did not open the windows so that the light of life might enter. When I open them, he who came to illuminate the whole world will illuminate my eyes also, so that even those who do not see may see.”

[Note: [Col. 1212D] The Roman edition reads, “nor revisit the dark one. He has hidden his grace from me.” The older edition reads, “does not seek me, and has hidden his grace from me.” The manuscripts, however, strongly confirm our reading, except for two, which have “revisits” in place of “seeks.”]

### 10

The sons of my mother fought against me; they appointed me as keeper of the vineyards. I did not keep my own vineyard. Some think this is said of those who constrain the Synagogue to the precepts of the Law, so that it might observe the Law and protect its own vineyard, which it was unable to keep. Indeed, it kept watch in order to produce grapes, but it produced thorns. David comes to testify to us what this vineyard is, saying: “You brought a vine out of Egypt, You drove out the nations, and planted it” (Psalm 79:9).

The apostles too may be the sons of his mother, who truly fought against the Synagogue, saying: “Behold, we are turning to the nations” (Acts 13:46), and began to sow the word of God among the Gentiles. The prophets too may be understood, for by admonishing and warning they accomplished nothing when they urged the Synagogue to keep its vineyard. For it produced the thorns of wickedness, though it ought to have borne the abundant fruits of virtue. Therefore she confesses that she was unable to keep her people; and rightly, though late, she seeks to hold the one whom, while holding him, she lost. She is very different from the one who says: “I found him whom my soul loves; I held him, and I will not let him go” (Song of Songs 3:4).

### 11

Finally, that woman invites the Bridegroom into her garden; but this one, asking where he feeds, says to him: “Tell me, you whom my soul has loved” (Song of Songs 1:6). Why do you say “whom my soul has loved,” and not “whom it loves”? Why did you let go of the one whom you were holding?

[Note: Four manuscripts read: “You lost the faith of the fathers; you lost belief: you were holding him, etc.”]

You loved him through the faith of the fathers, but lost him through unbelief; you held him with the bonds of love, but lost him through the long rope of faithlessness. Therefore you do not know where he feeds or where he rests; for if you knew, you would not ask. You say: “Where do you feed? Where do you rest at midday?” (Ibid.).

You know that midday is the Church, which holds Christ; and are you seeking him at night? Say to me, he says, O Christ: answer me, at least because you were once dear and beloved to me. Even though I have lost the privilege of such love, still, as the merciful one, answer me: Where do you feed? Where do you rest?

You left me and went to the nations; you withdrew far from me and became nearer to those from whom you had been far away. But you became near to them because they believed in your blood. You withdrew from me because I did not receive your cross as the redemption of the world, but as the condemnation of a guilty man.

Those who received you, Lord, as the author of salvation are in the light of midday. For them you shine; for them you gleam; for them your grace is warm, like midday. You were morning to me when I still believed, but I did not believe fully, because I was not found at midday, like Joseph with his brothers, who were dining at midday.

You became midday for those who are fed by your riches and hope in you. Therefore, as David said: “You will bring forth their righteousness like the light, and their judgment like midday” (Psalm 36:6).

### 12

You seek, as though they were strangers, those who were near; as though you were poor, though you had been rich. You wish to follow those whom you formerly preceded—and would that you might at least follow those whom you ought to have preceded! You desire to be a hired woman, though formerly you gathered the hired workers.

This is surely the voice of a hired woman who says: “Lest I become like one who is veiled among the flocks of your companions” (Song of Songs 1:6). Formerly you received proselytes from the nations; now you yourself wish to be received among the nations in place of proselytes and to be gathered in as a stranger.

### 13

Jesus answered: “Unless you know yourself to be beautiful among women” (Ibid. 7).

What is it to know oneself, unless each person understands that he has been made a human being in the image and likeness of God, capable of reason? Such a person ought to cultivate his own land like a good farmer, with a kind of plow and the sickle of wisdom, so that hard things may be split open and luxuriant growth cut back; and he ought to govern the lower part of himself by the rule of the soul.

Therefore it is also written in the Law: “Take heed to yourself, lest there be a hidden word in your heart” (Deuteronomy 15:9). “Take heed to yourself,” he says—not to your money, not to your possessions, not to the strength of your body, but to your soul and your mind, from which all counsels, deeds, and thoughts flow. Take heed to yourself, therefore, there where you know yourself to be superior.

[Note: Thus the old edition and a far larger number of manuscripts. Some manuscripts, however, and the Roman edition read: “Unless you know yourself, O beautiful one,” etc. This reading is supported not only by the Septuagint, where ἡ καλή is read consistently, but also by Ambrose himself, *On Isaac and the Soul*, book 4, chapter 4, §15. Although there too he seems to indicate our reading when he writes: “Unless you know yourself, because you are beautiful,” etc.

Many attribute this saying to Chilon the Lacedaemonian, as do the author of the homily on the Song of Songs preserved among Origen’s works, Jerome in Homily 2, and others. Among them Ausonius writes in the seventh book of his *Seven Sages*:

“Γνῶθι σεαυτόν”—that is, “Know yourself.” Many think this belonged to the Lacedaemonian Chilon. But perhaps the same saying had been attributed by some to Apollo, since it was read, by order of the Amphictyons, inscribed on the column of the Delphic temple, as Plato states in the *Charmides*. Ausonius also records this in what follows:

“Marked by the brevity in which we Lacedaemonians excel, I commend our ‘Γνῶθι σεαυτόν—Know yourself,’ which now stands upon the Delphic column.”

Chilon flourished 950 years after Moses and 615 after Solomon. Others too have been regarded as authors of this maxim; Elias Vinetus discusses them in his commentary on Ausonius. More may also be found in Erasmus’ *Adages*, book 1, century 6, adage 95. It is fitting to add here what that same poet laments, in *Edyllion* 31, that this saying is too greatly neglected:

“Although it is difficult to know oneself—‘Γνῶθι σεαυτόν’—as quickly as we read it, so quickly we neglect it.”]

“Know yourself,” which pagan writers attribute to the Pythian Apollo, as though he himself had been the author of this saying. They take what was borrowed from our writings and transfer it to their own, although Moses, who wrote the book of Deuteronomy, lived long before the philosophers who invented such things.

### 14

For this reason Solomon too, following the divine oracle, wrote in the Song of Songs: “Unless you know yourself to be beautiful among women” (Song of Songs 1:7). That is: unless you recognize yourself as mortal and rational, and confess your sins; unless you quickly declare your transgressions so that you may be justified; unless you turn back and first accuse your own offenses, the day of death will come, and there will no longer be any remedy of conversion: you will be overtaken while you are not thinking.

[Note: All printed editions have this reading. The manuscripts, however, do not recognize the negation. Some have: “You should forestall it while you are thinking”; one has: “Forestall it while you are thinking; kindle the torch,” and so forth. Although these readings are not without meaning in their own way, the reading of the editions nevertheless seems preferable.]

Kindle your lamp before the Bridegroom’s door is closed to you; he does not usually wait long for the negligent. “Unless you know yourself,” he says, “to be beautiful among women,” and say: “I am dark but beautiful” (Song of Songs 1:4). I am dark because I have sinned, but beautiful because I am loved, because I am a descendant of Abraham, an elect race, beloved by God.

The favor shown to your fathers will profit you nothing, for God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones. Elsewhere in the Gospel you read (Luke 13:11–13) that the devil had bound a daughter of Abraham with the bonds of his wickedness, but the Lord released her on the Sabbath day.

Unless, therefore, you know yourself, nothing will profit you. And if you say, “I am a daughter of Abraham”—though you do not believe and do not correct your error—Abraham is indeed saved, but the nobility of your ancestry will not help you unless faith preserves you.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “unless you preserve the faith.”]

Let not the promise made to your fathers deceive you. I do not accept a person’s status; I do not accept the privilege of ancestry unless I see a nobility of conduct corresponding to the nobility of the race, so that the election of the righteous race may be realized.

### 15

But if you know yourself and acknowledge that you are subject to sin, you must go out in the footsteps of the flocks. Go out, then, barefoot, and feed your young goats in the shepherds’ tents (Song of Songs 1:7).

The one who is without sin feeds lambs and sheep. But the one who is subject to sin feeds young goats, which are on the left; for she cannot be on the right hand of the good shepherd.
