Rather, let her follow the one who says to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:33). By following, Peter deserved to be placed on the right; therefore it is said to him: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:16).

But hear where she is to go out: “To the shepherds’ tents,” he says—that is, to the nations, to the dispersion. Therefore he said: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7), so that the whole earth might be filled with Christ’s flock. This signifies that the Synagogue will then be saved when she too joins herself to this dispersion, which has filled the world; for the shepherds’ tents are the kingdoms of the earth.

Therefore the prophet David, announcing that the nations would believe, says: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God” (Psalm 67:33). Let the younger one, then, know herself, so that she may correct her way.

### 16

But you say: Who can know the way of the younger one, so that she may correct it, when the prophet says: “There are three things impossible for me to understand, and a fourth that I do not know: the track of an eagle flying, the way of a serpent on a rock, the paths of a ship sailing, and the ways of a man in his youth” (Proverbs 30:18–19)?

If Solomon confesses that he does not know the ways of a man in his youth, how can the younger one know them?

The answer is that the ways of a man in his youth are not known when they resemble the ways of a serpent on a rock, the paths of a ship tossed by waves, and the track of a flying eagle, which has rough talons, encloses its prey, flies above the clouds, wanders through the air, and kills a fish in the sea. Yet this fourth thing is not impossible in the way the other three are; for “the Lord knows those who are his,” and he wishes each person to know himself, and the people of God to know themselves.

[Note: “Encloses its prey” is absent from the ancient edition and most manuscripts; in some manuscripts one finds: “does not enclose its prey.”]

### 17

But suppose that the ways of those who wander are not known, as the Lord says: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27). The younger one who can correct her way may perhaps be young in age, but not in character. She may possess, in the first flower of youth, an understanding mature with age, concerning which it is said: “Old age is understanding among human beings” (Wisdom 4:8)—that is, those who possess mature counsel and gravity.

Therefore it is also said to Jeremiah: “Do not say, ‘I am young’” (Jeremiah 1:7). He was certainly young in age, but the one who possessed more mature prudence forbade him to call himself young.

When Daniel was still a boy, he received the spirit by which he was considered worthy of the first fruits of old age. Thus he himself, though not advanced in years, rebuked the elders—not by longevity, but by grace. For in him the age of old age was an unblemished life (Daniel 13:45). To him the saying of David aptly applies: “I have understood more than the elders” (below, verse 100).

Therefore, as though concerning a man of seasoned counsel and mature knowledge, the divine oracle declared: “Who is wiser than Daniel?” (Ezekiel 28:3).

### 18

Let us now consider whether it is possible for the younger one to correct her way or not. If it is not possible, then the prophet is lying; but since he is not lying, it is possible.

It is possible, however, in such a way that what appears impossible becomes possible: if the younger one keeps the words of God; but if she does not keep them, it is impossible.

Hence the Gospel saying: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:24). We understand this book likewise to have said that it is impossible, yet impossible because the rich do not keep God’s commandments. If they keep them, what seemed impossible becomes possible.

This is the camel that enters by the narrow way. The way that previously could not contain him because he desired things now contains him because he keeps the divine commandments.

[Note: The ancient edition and several manuscripts read: “But he chose Moses, as an elder, who kept the divine words, because he kept them.” The Roman edition removed the words “because he kept them” together with the following punctuation. Several other manuscripts read: “But he chose Moses, as an elder.” From this it is scarcely possible to elicit any proper sense. The readings of the Regius and Remigius manuscripts, as given in the text, are therefore preferable. What is said—“because he keeps them”—means the same as if it were written: “for no other reason but that he keeps the divine commandments.”]

But he chose Moses, as an elder, who kept the words of God (Exodus 7:1). Even now, those to whom this duty is entrusted by the Spirit of God—namely, to choose elder men—undoubtedly choose among the elders a young person who corrects her way by keeping the words of God.

And if they choose a man advanced in age, they have not chosen him merely because he has lived long, but because he keeps the words of God. If this is found in a younger person, he too must certainly be chosen.

It is therefore clear from these things that what is chosen is not longevity of old age, but the keeping of God’s words. Indeed, Moses himself approved Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb, young men, above the others; and he himself followed their counsel in choosing the land, and God preferred it to the counsel of many elders (Numbers 14:6–7).

### 19

Hence also what we said above concerning Jacob: “The God who has fed me from my youth” (Genesis 48:15). This reveals that it was said of one who bore the yoke of the word in his youth (Lamentations 3:27–28), and who, withdrawing from Esau and those like him, sat alone, awaiting within himself the time when he could bring forth speech with discipline. For this reason he was endowed with spiritual nourishment: still young in age, yet a veteran in counsel.

For it is not fitting to believe that so great a patriarch spoke of bodily food when he said: “The God who has fed me from my youth.” He did not even desire bodily bread when he said: “If the Lord God is with me, so that he gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear … of all that you give me I will give a tenth to you” (Genesis 28:20–22).

For if our fathers ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink, how much more was holy Jacob fed with spiritual nourishment!

### 20

Another understanding is also available here, and it is not foreign to the truth: the younger people are that nation gathered from the Gentiles, which, before it believed in Christ, wandered along a crooked and winding path. It corrects its way because it kept the words of God, which the Jewish people refused to keep; and for this reason that people could not find the way of salvation.

Let us consider the following verse as well.

### 21

**Verse 10.** “With my whole heart I have sought you; do not reject me from your commandments.”

If God rejects each person whom he judges ought to be rejected, let us see whether he thereby gives an excuse to one who wished to follow God but was rejected. First, how does the good God reject one who follows him, unless that person himself deserves rejection?

As the Lord himself says: “Foxes have dens” (Matthew 8:28); therefore he rejects him as though he were a fox. Elsewhere he says: “To everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matthew 25:29).

To whom does he add this, except to the one who seeks him with his whole heart, so that what is lacking by nature may be acquired through God’s work and grace? Thus Solomon, seeking God with his whole heart, asked for wisdom. Because he requested not royal wealth but the gift of divine grace, he deserved to receive the discipline of wisdom; he was filled with the Spirit of the Lord so that he might know all the commandments (1 Kings 3:11–12).

But whoever does not possess the will to seek the Lord in his heart and performs God’s work negligently is subject to the curse, as we read: “Cursed is everyone who performs the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah 48:10). He is rightly rejected, because he deserves the curse, because he pollutes and obstructs the work he undertakes negligently.

### 22

Let us therefore consider whether it is good for the negligent person to be rejected from the work, or whether he should instead be retained. Let us take an image of this from other arts.

A physician treats a sick person, but negligently, and through the physician’s indolence the poison of the wound spreads deeply.

How much better, then, is it to remove such a physician, who wastes time while the wounded person experiences no improvement, so that the duty of treatment may be transferred to a physician who can more promptly help the sick person through his diligence! Is not the one who rejects a person who accomplishes nothing more merciful than the one who retains him to the peril of the patient?

Suppose that someone has been placed in charge of builders, or even of weavers, and ought to supervise the whole work. Would you not judge him more favorably if he applied himself diligently to the task and, whenever he noticed someone careless among those working to construct a house, rejected him, rightly judging that it was better not to build than to have what was built collapse through gaping cracks—and placed someone else in his position who would build diligently?

Likewise, would you not approve a supervisor of a weaving shop who rejected the negligent and substituted diligent workers, lest prolonged carelessness ruin the workshop, more than one who allowed the idle to persist in their negligence?

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read: “but through the negligence and indolence of the physician, the poison of the wound spreads.”]

### 23

Now pass to those who build up the commandments, weave together the Law, and have received the soul of each person to heal.

If one of them builds God’s house with justice, weaves a garment with diligence, and heals a soul with grace, does he not perform a good work? But if some careless and negligent person occupies the place of a builder, weaver, or spiritual physician—as high priest, presbyter, or minister of the sacred altar—is it not more advantageous that no one undertake a duty he cannot fulfill than that, having undertaken it, he should not perform the duty entrusted to him with vigor and deprive another of the place which he could energetically maintain?

What is more, this also benefits the negligent person himself when he is rejected, so that he does not accumulate greater offense.

### 24

Let us consider what it means to be rejected. For it is written: “Like the wounded who sleep in tombs, whom you remember no longer; indeed, they have been rejected from your hand” (Psalm 87:5).

Let us therefore observe whom he rejects as wounded and cast into tombs, whom he will remember no longer. These are those who are rejected from the commandments of God.

But God said to the sinner: “Why do you recite my statutes?” (Psalm 49:16). And because they are rejected from God’s commandments, they are certainly rejected from God’s hand.

Yet he wisely took care that no one should appear to be snatched from the hand of God, since no one can snatch anyone from God’s hand. Therefore the person deprived of the office or grace he had undertaken is not snatched away but cast out.

Thus the Lord Jesus said to Jerusalem: “How often I wanted to gather your children … and you were unwilling! Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:37–38).

He took away from them sanctification, the altar of incense, the sanctuary of prayer, the mercy seat, the altar of sacrifices, and the ministries of priests and Levites. Yet when all these things had been removed from them, which they possessed according to the commandments of the Law, the Apostle said: “Has God rejected his inheritance? … Certainly not. Rather, he confined all things in unbelief so that he might have mercy on all” (Romans 11:1–2, 32).

### 25

There are therefore those who, for a time, are rejected from the commandments for the sake of mercy, just as those who are vomited out are also thereby helped.

For just as what must be vomited out becomes more sour while it remains in the body, so the person who ought to be expelled, if retained and not corrected, ulcerates the whole body.

Rightly, therefore, the faithful and true witness says to the angel of Laodicea: “I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 3:15–16).

He openly condemns negligence with a more severe judgment than ignorance. The one who does not know the faith is cold; the one inflamed by the fervor of the Holy Spirit is hot. Therefore, one who does not have the warmth of faith would have been more tolerable had he never received faith than if he had neglected it.

The lukewarm person is worse than the cold person, like the Jew who seems to himself to possess a faith that he does not possess.

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read: “worse than the cold, deceiving between the two” or “deceiving the nature of both.”]

How much more tolerable is the case of a Gentile who can say, “I did not know the Law; I did not hear the prophets; therefore I did not believe,” than that of one who read everything from which he ought to have believed that Jesus would come, and yet did not believe!

Neither is excused: neither the one who read nor the one who refused to read. But the one who denied what he had read sins more greatly than the one who did not perform works whose necessity he did not know.

How great, then, is the grace of faith and righteousness, that the one who holds the faith and practices righteousness should be in the mouth of God! And how much does the one whom the Lord Jesus vomits from his mouth and casts out from his own inward parts lose!

Yet how merciful he is: he holds the righteous in his mouth, and does not vomit out the unrighteous before announcing that they are to be vomited out, so that, converted by this warning, they may accomplish something worthy and not be vomited out.

Now let us consider the third verse.

### 26

**Verse 11.** “In my heart,” he says, “I have hidden your utterances, so that I may not sin against you.”

Therefore the good mystery of the King is to hide it; for the person who thinks that the mysteries entrusted to him should be proclaimed to the unworthy sins against God.

There is danger, therefore, not only in speaking falsehoods, but also in speaking truths if someone discloses them to those to whom they ought not be disclosed. This fault has four forms: flattery, greed, boasting, and careless talk.

When someone wishes to flatter the person to whom he is speaking, he pours out the mystery. Some, driven by the desire for profit, pursue the payment received for betrayal, selling by their speech what ought to be covered in silence. Others, so that they may seem to know more and boast of their knowledge, reveal what they ought to conceal. Many, speaking without judgment, utter a word that they cannot recall.

Therefore a man who speaks later is praised, and not without reason. Such a man concealed his words, like the Apostle Paul, who knew what to say to each person and when he ought to say it.

Thus he says to the Corinthians: “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able to receive it. Indeed, even now you are not able” (1 Corinthians 3:2). Therefore he sees them only in passing; but he remains among the Ephesians, because a great door had been opened to him, so that he might make known to the Gentiles the mystery of Christ (1 Corinthians 16:8–9).

For this reason Solomon too teaches that there is “a time to be silent and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes 3:7).

### 27

Above all, the Lord Jesus declares this in his Gospel, saying that “the kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field” (Matthew 13:44).

[Note: Some written manuscripts read: “The kingdom of heaven cannot be bought with gold, silver, or money.” Here, however, “bought” signifies comparison, not acquisition.]

Certainly the kingdom of heaven cannot be bought with gold, silver, or money. Rather, it is acquired through the utterances of the Lord—utterances that are pure silver, tested by fire.

When a person finds this treasure of wisdom and knowledge hidden in the field where the words of the heavenly Scriptures have been planted, he hides it in his heart and does not make it public, knowing that if he reveals God’s treasure to the Babylonians, he will incur great offense. Thus the prophetic word says to him: “From your offspring they will take, and they will make eunuchs in the house of the king” (Isaiah 39:7).

This signifies that the person who betrays the divine mysteries cannot have descendants of his soul or a seedbed of merits.

### 28

Beware, therefore, of revealing your riches to the faithless. Even if they pretend friendship, do not open to them the inner chambers of your house. Do not unlock the royal treasures, which the Babylonians ought not to know, lest they come and capture your descendants and cut off the seedbed of virtue.

This is what the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7:6).

Therefore the person who hides the Lord’s utterances in his heart does well, as the prophet David hid them, and as Mary did, who kept all the words of the Lord Jesus in her heart (Luke 2:51).

If it is good for a man to hide his words, how much more ought we to cover and hide the word of God in the embrace of our heart!

### 29

**Verse 12.** In the fourth verse he says: “Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your justifications.”

For not everyone who says, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of God.

Therefore this person, who has corrected his way from his youth, kept God’s words with his whole heart, sought the Lord his God, was not rejected from God’s commandments, and was judged worthy to be entrusted with the secrets of wisdom, has hidden them in his heart so that he would not sin against God.

As one who possesses the utterances of God, he gives thanks, saying: “Blessed are you, Lord.” He desires to have God himself as his teacher, wishing to know the secrets of the Law and how it should be interpreted—for example: “If you buy a Hebrew slave, and he serves you for six years” (Exodus 21:2), and the rest. These are the justifications he proposes to learn before the children of Israel. He seeks from the Lord to learn what human beings could not teach unless God had first taught them.

After the apostles learned these things from Christ, the Church says: “The King brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs 1:3)—that is, into his secret place, in which are the treasures of his knowledge and understanding.

Therefore it is said to you: “When you pray, enter into your chamber” (Matthew 6:6), which signifies the secret place of the mind and soul. Into this chamber the Bride asked to be led, after she had run forth following the fragrance of the ointment, which always flows and never fails.

### 30

**Verse 13.** Therefore, as one taught the justifications, the prophet says in the fifth verse: “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth.”

And how does he say elsewhere: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7)? How does the Apostle say: “O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11:33–34).

If his judgments are unsearchable, how then are they judgments? How does the prophet say, “I have declared all the judgments of your mouth”?

Perhaps the judgments of God are not the same as the judgments of his mouth. If they are different, it is rightly said: “Who will be like your thoughts?” (Psalm 39:6). His judgments are therefore unsearchable because “we know in part and we prophesy in part.”

But if no one except Christ says this—Christ who can say, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)—

### 31

Let us nevertheless distinguish the matter, and not fear that venerable Scripture contradicts itself as though by opposing statements.

For observe that it did not say, “The judgments of his mouth are like a great abyss,” but “Your judgments.” Nor did the Apostle say, “The judgments of his mouth are unsearchable,” but “His judgments.”

We can understand the judgments of God as those which he has not disclosed to us because they are hidden; but the judgments of his mouth as those which he has announced, since he spoke through the mouths of the prophets.

The prophet is understood to be the mouth of God, to whom it is said: “Cry out!” And he replies: “What shall I cry?” Then he is inspired to say: “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6). In speaking this, he certainly performed the office of God’s mouth, because he spoke God’s judgment.

Therefore the prophetic oracles are no longer merely like an abyss; they too are an abyss, because no one in heaven or on earth was able to open the book except Christ.

Let us now come to the sixth verse.

### 32

**Verse 14.** “I have rejoiced,” he says, “in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches.”

Some delight in gold, others in silver, others in clothing; some in possessions, vineyards, olive groves, and fields; others in works of painting and marble. In short, individuals have their pleasures in different things.

The spiritual person delights in the way of the heavenly testimonies, as though possessing an entire inheritance and being rich in all things, as the Apostle says: “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you were enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1:4–5).

The Corinthians advanced so far in the Apostle’s teaching that, though previously they could drink only milk like children, afterward they abounded in all the riches of knowledge and speech.

David therefore delighted in all the riches of knowledge, understanding, wisdom, and every practice of good works. If someone now, attentive to divine things, drinks deeply of that threefold discipline of wisdom—θεωρητικήν (*theoretikēn*, contemplative), πρακτικήν (*praktikēn*, practical), λογικήν (*logikēn*, rational)—he will be good in his zeal to acquire knowledge and more beautiful by possessing the grace of carrying out rational and moral teaching.

Whoever, with the Spirit of God revealing them, understands the prophetic riddles of God, comprehends the depth of the Gospel in works and counsels, and perceives the moral teaching of apostolic speech—that person, as rich in all things, will receive abundant delight.

### 33

And because bodily pleasure is sweet, it is not compared with spiritual things as though equal in kind; rather, it is summoned as a testimony to sweetness.

The Apostle teaches that God’s invisible and eternal things are understood by us through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20).

In the Song of Songs we also read: “I have compared you, my neighbor, to my mare among Pharaoh’s chariots.” In this passage, while the Church is compared to the running of swift horses, her rich grace is indicated.

Do not therefore understand a single mare belonging to a wealthy king, but understand the term absolutely as referring to a whole cavalry, as we have often said that “sheep” may refer to a flock of sheep.

Pharaoh, therefore, as a most powerful king, possessed very strong and exceedingly rich horses, as Scripture says: “the chariots of Pharaoh”—a most powerful force for use in war and support in battle. Indeed, with these chariots Pharaoh easily overtook the fleeing Hebrews.

Just as joined horses draw a chariot harmoniously, patiently accept the yoke, carry it with fitting grace, and are tamed by bearing that yoke, so the congregation of the nations formerly vaunted itself as untamed in its ways. But when it accepted the yoke of the one who said, “Take my yoke … for it is light, and my burden … is sweet” (Matthew 11:29–30), the Bride of Christ began to be exalted through the harmony and gentleness of the peoples.

Carried throughout the whole world like a chariot drawn by swift horses, she mounted above the world and ascended to the Bridegroom.

### 34

Finally, in a later passage of the Song of Songs he says: “I have set you as the chariot of Amminadab” (Song of Songs 6:12).

The Church contains many chariots, all of which the Lord governs with spiritual reins. One soul too has many thoughts, which the Lord’s rein restrains and turns back, lest our chariot at some time be driven over a precipice.

Amminadab is interpreted as “father of favor.” His son is read about in Numbers as Naasson, leader of the people (Numbers 2:3), who is to be understood by interpretation as “serpentine.” You recognize this if you recall that he who redeemed you hung upon the wood like a serpent.

### 35

The soul, therefore, is God’s chariot, so that its anger, lust, fear, and all worldly desires may be restrained.

The Church too is God’s chariot, and must be governed by Christ’s reins, lest the movements and disagreements of different peoples disturb her.

Naasson may also rightly be understood as Christ, because Aaron’s rod, when it was changed into a serpent, devoured those Egyptian serpents (Exodus 7:12).

Let us possess these riches and delight in them, so that rational horses may run for us and we may remain in their commandments.

### 36

**Verse 15.** Therefore he says: “I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways.”

For the person who exercises himself in the words of the apostles recognizes the commandments of Jesus the Lord and considers his ways, whose end is Christ, who says: “I am the way” (John 14:6).

### 37

**Verse 16.** “And I will meditate on your justifications; I will not forget your words.”

This passage admonishes us to remember the Scriptures and to meditate on his justifications not only in speech but also by imitating them in our works. For it is not those who discuss the Law and do not do what belongs to the Law, but those who practice the Law, who are justified.

## THIRD SERMON. Gimel

### 1

The third letter among the Hebrews is *Gimel*, which in Latin is called “retribution.” This is immediately shown in the first verse.

### 2

**Verse 17.** “Requite your servant,” he says.

How is it that David himself said above: “Do not deal with us according to our sins, nor requite us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 102:10), while here he asks for retribution?

The former appears to be the voice of a sinner, while this is the voice of one conscious of doing well, who asks for the rewards of good work.

Accordingly, we can also understand that this psalm is formed from the person of the one who, born of the Virgin for the redemption of the whole world, presumes to sit at the right hand of the Father, as he himself says: “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power” (Matthew 26:64).

3. Yet it is not inappropriate or arrogant if David also asks recompense from the Lord his God for his outstanding labors. It is a prerogative of faith and righteousness to claim a reward from the Lord’s favor. Thus Peter is reproved (Matt. XIV, 31), because, while walking upon the waves, he doubted more from human weakness than he ventured with apostolic authority. In the Gospel also we are taught to have faith (Luke XVII, 6) and not to hesitate over doing things that exceed human capacity. Therefore David rightly, in the earlier passage, as though still imperfect, refuses and declines to have recompense made to him according to his sins; but in this later psalm [Col. 1223C] (Ps. CII, 10), as though established through progress in virtue, he entreats that he be recompensed according to the struggles of his faith and work. Indeed, Paul too, who had earlier said, “I am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. XV, 9), later says: “There is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing” (2 Tim. IV, 8). The Apostle makes a promise there, whereas here he still prays more modestly. To ask a wage from the one whom one has served is certainly not insolent arrogance, but the conscience of an innocent person; for despair is an occasion of sluggishness, whereas hope is an incentive to labor.

4. Ask confidently, then, if your merits support you, so that by asking such things you may strive more diligently and become more worthy of that request. What athlete, if he despaired of the crown, would enter the stadium—or, if he asked for it after victory, would give offense? Testing produces hope, and hope produces confidence. Such, then, is the prayer of the righteous: the Lord takes pleasure in such supplication, so that you may exercise authority on the basis of a pure conscience.

5. Nevertheless, so that the request might appear less arrogant, he rightly added, “to your servant” (1 Cor. VII, 22): in this there is both the grace of humility and the reward of servitude. For whoever has been called as a servant in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman, bought at so precious a price—the blood of Christ. “It is a great thing for you to be called my boy,” as though this were said to a servant. If anyone, then, is a servant and serves the Lord well, doing nothing as a servant of sin, but says, “I am an unprofitable servant; I have done what I ought to do,” he rightly says, “Recompense your servant.”

6. Glorious is the servitude by which Christ also served on our behalf.  
[Note: [Col. 1223D] The manuscripts omit “Blessed is the servitude by which you also serve.” Yet these words do not seem useless for completing the sense.]

Blessed is the servitude by which you also serve—but only if the adversary can claim nothing from your service for himself. Christ therefore loves the freedom of a good little servant. Thus he says in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful your cheeks have become, like those of a turtledove, your neck like strings of jewels” (Song I, 9)! The face is freer where there is the consciousness of chastity;  
[Note: [Col. 1223D] Several manuscripts have “the consciousness of charity”; one has “the consciousness of chastity and charity.”]

and bearing Christ’s yoke is gentle if you consider the ornaments of your neck to be adornments, not burdens. Therefore always lift your eyes toward the Lord your God and seek God in order to find him. Raise your neck: you wear ornaments, not bonds. Many animals too delight in ornaments, and seem to prefer being decked out  
[Note: [Col. 1223D] All editions and fourteen manuscripts read “rather than being stripped.” The Reg. manuscript reads “rather than being burdened,” somewhat better. Best of all, the Vat. manuscript has “rather than being bound.” On this word, consult Cangius’s Glossary.]

rather than being bound. Let cheeks like those of a turtledove display the emblems of modesty; let the ornaments of the neck raise the confidence of freedom. For Christ’s yoke is light, and therefore the neck is not weighed down by it, but lifted up.

7. “We will make likenesses of gold for you, with settings of silver, until the King is in his repose” (ibid., 10). For those who are from the Law and the prophets had previously believed only moderately in the glory of the Lord Jesus; but his inheritance, spread among the peoples, was proved all the more thoroughly the more frequently it was tested. For the frequent persecutions of the Church have produced for us the titles of the righteous  
[Note: [Col. 1223D] Quite a few manuscripts give “the titles of martyrdom”; some have “the titles of martyrs”—“for victories.”]

and the victories of martyrdom. Thus, like good gold, when the Church is burned she suffers no loss, but her splendor is increased, until Christ comes into his kingdom and reclines his head upon the faith of the Church. When he came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, he had nowhere to recline his head; but now faith already gives forth its fragrance. Therefore the Church says: “My nard gave forth its fragrance” (ibid., 11). And she says this confidently, awaiting recompense.

8. The ointment of grace gives off its fragrance, from which the Virgin gave birth and the Lord Jesus assumed the mystery of the Incarnation. “A bundle of stacte is my cousin to me; a cluster of Cyprus is my brother; he rests between my breasts” (ibid., 12). For in assuming a body, the Lord Jesus bound himself with the cords of love; and he bound himself not only to our limbs and natural sufferings, but also to the cross. Therefore, like a cluster of grapes in the faith of the Church, he rests in moral grace.

“My nard of Cyprus, my cousin, in the vineyards of Engaddi” (Song I, 13). If we are looking for a place, Engaddi is the name of a place in a certain region of Judea, where opobalsamum is produced; if we are looking for an interpretation, Engaddi signifies “temptation” in Latin. In those vineyards, then, there is a tree which, if someone punctures it, releases an ointment: this is the fruit of the tree. If the tree is not cut, it does not give off such fragrance and scent; but when it has been punctured by the hand of a skilled worker, it drips a tear. So too Christ, crucified on that tree of temptation, wept for the people in order to wash away our sins, and poured forth ointment from the depths of his mercy, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). Then he was pierced upon the tree by a lance, and blood and water came forth from him, sweeter than any ointment, a sacrifice accepted by God that spread the fragrance of sanctification throughout the whole world; and, like balsam coming from a tree, power came forth from his body. Hence he says: “I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke VIII, 46).

Therefore opobalsamum is called an “extraction,” because through the puncturing of the tree the balsam bursts forth through the cavity of the puncture.  
[Note: [Col. 1225D] Most manuscripts and all editions read “opobalsamum is more expressly called” (some manuscripts, “is called expressly”). Several others, and better ones, read “opobalsamum is called an extraction.” How this extraction is made is described next. The same matter is explained still more clearly by the writer commonly called Hegesippus. For he says: “There opobalsamum is produced. We have indicated this with the addition because the cultivators cut the twigs in which the balsam is produced only through the bark, so that the moisture, gradually dripping through those openings, may collect; an opening is called ὀπή [opē] in Greek.” Others, however, prefer to derive the name from ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀποῦ [apo tou opou], which means “from sap” or “juice.” J. Gerard Vossius says much about this matter in his Etymological Dictionary under the word “balsam.”]

Thus Jesus, pierced, poured forth the fragrance of the remission of sins and of redemption (Luke XXIII, 11). For the Word was also bound when he had become human; and he became poor although he was rich, so that we might be enriched by his poverty. He was powerful, yet presented himself as one to be despised, so that Herod scorned and mocked him. He shook the earth, yet hung upon the tree; he clothed the heavens in darkness and crucified the world, and yet he was crucified. He bowed his head, and the Word went forth; he had emptied himself, and filled all things. God descended, man ascended. The Word became flesh so that flesh might claim for itself the throne of the Word at God’s right hand. A wound had been inflicted, and ointment flowed; a scarab was heard, and God was recognized.

9. Christ also replied: “Behold, you are beautiful, my near one; behold, you are beautiful” (Song I, 14). Because the Church had understood the mystery and proclaimed the Lord Jesus crucified for the redemption of the whole world, she deserved to hear: “Behold, you are beautiful”—you who call me good are yourself good; you who saw the beauty of my glory are yourself good and beautiful. What does it mean, however, for Christ to say, “You are good,” or “You are beautiful,” except the Gospel saying: “Take courage, daughter; your sins are forgiven” (Matt. IX, 22)?

[Col. 1225D] 10. (Verse 17.) Therefore the one whose sins Christ has forgiven rightly says: “Recompense your servant, that I may live and keep your words.” He has no reason for despair in the matter of recompense, because the Lord Jesus came to save the world, not to destroy it. Therefore he is mindful of grace and forgetful of injury, as he himself testifies in the prophetic book, saying: “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will remember them no more; but you, remember, and let us be judged. Speak your iniquities first, so that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII, 25–26). Whoever therefore declares his iniquities to God is justified; and whoever is justified does not fear recompense, but asks for it. Whoever does not fear recompense will live.

11. But why did he say, “I may live,” and not, “I live”? Because this life is not the place of reward, since it is in the place of death. The Prophet grieves that he has been brought down into the dust of death (Ps. XXI, 16); the Apostle longs to be freed from this body of death (Rom. VII, 24); and are we to think that the Prophet takes comfort in this life? Everything here is full of death. Death enters through the window; it enters through the door—unless the Lord sets a guard at your door. Indeed, sin arises from excessive speech. Read the commands of the Law, and you will find it written: “Whoever, while alive, touches a dead person is defiled” (Num. XIX, 11). How many dead people do we touch? Among how many dead do we live? Therefore the Author of life says to you: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII, 22). Therefore elsewhere it is said to you: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead” (Eph. V, 14). How could it be said to you, “Rise from the dead,” unless you were living among the dead? Let us suppose that you are clean from dead works and from the filth of sin. How are you clean when you are in the body of death, when you live among the tombs of the dead?  
[Note: [Col. 1226D] The Roman edition alone reads, “It was necessary first to speak to the dead.” This is less satisfactory, since there is a clear allusion to 1 Pet. IV, 6: “For this reason the Gospel was preached even to the dead.” Anyone who compares the beginning of that chapter with this entire passage of Ambrose will readily understand.]

It was necessary for Peter to speak to the dead, so that they might come forth from their tombs.

[Col. 1226C] 12. We therefore need purification, because we have touched the dead (Num. XIX, 1). The Law commands us to be cleansed; who is so great as to be above the Law? It declares even the holy Nazirite of God unclean if he touches a dead person (Num. VI, 9). Therefore he shaves his head and removes his hair as though it were no longer holy; and he prays again to be heard, although previously he could not plead because he had touched the dead. He counted his days as irrational, because he had approached an irrational thing. Therefore he removes the dead and superfluous things from his head in order to be reconciled to Christ. If, then, the Nazirite is purified, we too must be purified.

13. We have all touched the dead. For who will boast that he has a pure heart, or who will dare to say that he is clean from sins? Perhaps there is someone who has not sinned in speech—though such a person is rare—of whom God says, as he says of holy Job: “He did not sin with his lips” (Job XXII, 10). Yet he could not always have pure thoughts in his heart, since the devil thrusts himself into the human heart. Suppose that someone has surrounded his heart with ever-ready and watchful protection; nevertheless, he lives among sinners and must himself also be purified. Hence Isaiah, after saying, “Woe is me, for I have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips” (Isa. VI, 5, 7), immediately says that one of the Seraphim came down and touched his lips with a coal, in order to cleanse his unclean lips.

14. Baptism is not one alone. There is the one that the Church administers here, through water and the Holy Spirit, by which catechumens must be baptized. There is also another baptism, of which the Lord Jesus says: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, which you do not know” (Luke XII, 10). He had already been baptized in the Jordan, as the preceding passages make clear (Matt. III, 13); but let this be the baptism of suffering, by which each person is also cleansed through his own blood. There is also a baptism at the entrance to paradise, which did not exist previously; but after the sinner was excluded, the fiery sword that God placed there began to exist (Gen. III, 24)—a sword that had not existed before, when there was no sin. Guilt began, and baptism began: baptism by which those who wished to return to paradise might be purified, so that after returning they might say: “We passed through fire and water” (Ps. LXV, 12). Here, through water; there, through fire. Through water, so that sins may be washed away; through fire, so that they may be burned up. But what is more serious is that here too we endure fire, and there as well.

[Note: [Col. 1227D] We have already noted that Ambrose borrowed from Origen the opinion that the righteous are purified by fire on the day of the final judgment. Here we add only that a clear distinction is established below, in §17, between this fire and the fire in which the Devil and the reprobate will burn; yet Origen is emphatically denied to have made this distinction.]

15. Who is it who baptizes in this fire? Not a presbyter, not a bishop, not John, who said, “I baptize you for repentance” (Matt. III, 11); not an Angel, not an Archangel, not Dominions, not Powers, but the one of whom John says: “He who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry; he himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire. He has his winnowing fork in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor; he will gather his wheat into his barn, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (ibid., 11–12). The Lord himself testifies that this does not refer to the baptism administered by the priests of the Church (Matt. XIII, 49–50). For after the consummation of the age, when angels are sent to separate the good from the evil, this baptism will take place: when in the furnace of fire iniquity is burned away, so that the righteous may shine in the kingdom of God like the sun itself in the kingdom of their Father.

And even if someone is a saint like Peter or like John, he is baptized in this fire. Therefore the great Baptist will come—for this is what I call him, as Gabriel called him when he said, “He will be great” (Luke I, 15). He will see many standing before the entrance to paradise; he will brandish the revolving sword and say to those on his right, who do not have serious sins: “Enter, you who are confident, who do not fear the fire. For I foretold to you: ‘Behold, I come like fire’” (Isa. LXVI, 15); and through Ezekiel I said: “Behold, I will go forth against Jerusalem and blow upon you with the fire of my wrath, so that you may melt away like lead and iron” (Ezek. XXII, 20).

[Col. 1228A] 16. Let the consuming fire come, then; let it burn away in us the lead of iniquity and the iron of sin, and make us pure gold. Let it burn my kidneys and my heart, so that I may think good thoughts and desire the things that belong to chastity. But because one who has been purified here must again be purified there, there too let that fire purify us, when the Lord says: “Enter into my rest.” Thus each of us, scorched but not burned up by that flaming sword, may enter the loveliness of paradise and give thanks to his Lord, saying: “You brought us into a place of refreshment” (Ps. LXV, 12). Whoever therefore passes through fire enters into rest. He passes from material and worldly things to those that are incorruptible and everlasting.

17. This is one fire, by which sins that are not voluntary but accidental are burned away; the Lord Jesus prepared it for his little servants, so that he might cleanse them from this dwelling-place, which is mixed with the dead. That other fire is the one he appointed for the Devil and his angels, concerning which he says: “Enter into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41)—the fire in which the rich man was burning, who asked that moisture be dripped onto him from Lazarus’s finger. But Lazarus, reclining in Abraham’s bosom (Luke XVI, 24), was enjoying eternal life, which the Prophet promises himself when he says: “I will live and keep your words.” “I will live,” he says, as though he were not yet living; for here we live in shadow.

18. Therefore this life in the body is a shadow and image of life, not its reality. Indeed, man walks in an image, and we dwell in a land of the shadow of death. But if someone directs the eyes of his mind not toward earthly things but raises them toward spiritual things, so that he can say, “Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face,” he will be worthy to say, “We shall live in his shadow” (Lam. IV, 20). For Christ is life; and therefore whoever lives in Christ’s shadow is in the shadow of life. Thus elsewhere the Lord’s holy one says: “Protect me in the shadow of your wings” (Ps. XVI, 8). Therefore all the saints too are in shadow as long as they are in the body: they do not see perfectly; they know not perfectly, but in part. Paul himself says: “For we know in part” (1 Cor. XIII, 9). That chosen Vessel, to whom Christ restored his sight and whom he illumined by his grace, saw not face to face but through a mirror. And David asks that his eyes be unveiled (below, verse 18), so that the shadow that obstructed the full sight of his eyes might be removed.

Who would doubt that this region is the region of the dead, when the holy one himself says: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV, 9)? For no one can please perfectly here; even if it were possible for someone to have no sins of his own, nevertheless, by living in the very region of the dead, he needs purification to free him from the contagion of this region.

19. Therefore here we live in shadow, and for that reason in shadow we keep the words of God. To use an example: formerly they were certainly under the shadow of the Law, when people kept the Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come; so too today the Jews, who do not see the true Sabbath, serve the likeness and the shadow. We too, living now according to the Gospel, follow the shadow of God’s words. Nathanael is seen beneath a fig tree (John I, 48); David says that he hopes in the shadow of the wings of the Lord Jesus (Ps. XVI, 8); Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree in order to see Christ (Luke XIX, 4). Jesus has also spread out his hands over us, so that he might overshadow the whole world.

How are we not in shadow, when we are protected by the covering of his cross? How are we not in shadow, when the crucified one defends us from the wickedness of the world and the heat of the body? Do we not know that the Word of God, coming into this world, did not come as the Word was—what he was in the beginning, what he was with God—but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant? He came in a light cloud; and although he was the power of the Most High, he overshadowed Mary, so that he might transform the body of our humiliation and make it conformable to the body of his glory.

Therefore, just as he changed his form when he was born from the Virgin, so the sayings of God also appear transformed to us when they are read in the Gospel, when their appearance is seen in the Scriptures as through a mirror, because the whole truth cannot be grasped here. But when that which is perfect has come, they will no longer shine through a descent, nor through an appearance as though transformed, but with complete and manifest truth.

20. Nor should it trouble you that he says: “I will keep many words.” Whoever has understood one Word has understood many words. For in the one there are many, and in the many there is one. We must therefore demonstrate how one Word is many words and many words are one Word. It is not difficult to teach this, since the Apostle says that he is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, in whom all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers; all things were created through him and in him” (Col. I, 15–16).

There is therefore one Word that works in each individual; and when it works in each individual, it works all things in all. This one Word, present with the Father, spread itself into many, because “from his fullness we have all received.” Therefore, if you look at each individual thing that has been created in him, you will see in each one the one Word of all things, of which we partake according to our capacity.

In me there is a human word,  
[Note: [Col. 1229D] The words “but the Apostle … I too have the Spirit of God,” which were missing from the editions, have been restored on the authority of nine manuscripts, among them one Reg., two Sorb., Vind., Fisc., and others.]

but let the Apostle come to my aid and say: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. VII, 10). In another there is a heavenly word, and in many there is the word of angels. There are those who possess the word of Dominions and Powers, the word of righteousness, the word of chastity, the word of prudence, the word of piety, and even the word of power. Thus one Word is many, and many words are one. Nor is this difficult to estimate, since we read that the Spirit of wisdom can do all things.

21. Thus, just as to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing in one Spirit, to another the working of powers, to another the spirit of knowledge, to another the spirit of fuller counsel, to another the spirit of strength, to another the spirit of piety—yet in all there is one and the same Spirit, dividing to each as he wills.

There is the spirit of the prophets and the spirit of the apostles. There is also the spirit of craftsmen, as in the case of Bezalel and Oholiab, whom the Lord filled with the divine Spirit of wisdom and knowledge and every craft, so that they might make the vestment, the Tabernacle, and the altar according to the understanding God had given them (Exod. XXXV, 30 ff.); and also so that the other wise men might understand and perform all the works according to everything the Lord commanded. Thus they did things they had neither learned nor seen, according to what the Spirit showed them.

Many think that the spirit of the apostles is one, the spirit of the prophets another, and that the spirit in each is different. But it is not different; it is one Spirit, dividing different kinds of virtues. Therefore it should not seem doubtful if to some is given the apostolic word, to others the prophetic word,  
[Note: [Col. 1229D] Quite a few manuscripts, and manuscripts of no inferior quality, add “to others the angelic word.”]

to others the evangelical word, and to others the operative word; yet it is one Word, dividing itself among individuals according to our capacity or according to its own voluntary generosity.

This Word, then, which is the head of all things, I see here through a mirror; and therefore here I cannot keep the words. But when I see his glory with unveiled face, then I shall live, and, living in life, I shall also keep the divine words.

22. (Verse 18.) Therefore in the second verse he says: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law.” Whoever asks that his eyes be opened certainly recognizes that they are burdened. For no one asks a physician unless he is seeking a remedy for his illness. This man therefore says to the physician who comes from heaven: “Open my eyes.” If the eye is inflamed, all pain is easily calmed with an eye-salve; but if its sharpness is obscured by an influx of moisture, greater remedies are sought.  
[Note: [Col. 1229D] “Collyrium” especially denotes a medicine for the eyes. Hence Erasmus’s proverb, “to cure all eyes with one collyrium” (Chil. 4, Cent. 8, Adage 21). Yet the word is also used for other purposes; indeed, among the ancients it also denoted a kind of bread. Such medicines were made either from dry substances and were called ξηροκολλούρια [xēro-kollouria], or from moist substances and were called ὑγροκολλούρια [hygro-kollouria]. Their shape was rounded and approached the likeness of a mouse’s truncated tail; hence some derive collyrium from ἀπὸ κολοβῆς οὐρᾶς [apo kolobēs ouras], “from a shortened tail.” Other etymologies and meanings of the same word may be read in Brissonius, *De Verborum Juris Significatione*, book III, and in Vossius’s *Etymologicon Linguae Latinae* under the same word.]

There is therefore in the eyes of the body, and likewise in the eyes of the soul, a certain condition of this kind that must grow worse unless the good physician removes that covering and a certain cloud of congealed moisture which, it is thought, prevents—or rather covers—the mind’s vision from seeing what it used to see.

Illness entered through old leaven, because when we first came to the Church we did not strip off either the Gentile or the Jewish obscurity. We did not hear the instruction of the good physician, saying: “Strip off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him” (Col. III, 9–10). Someone has therefore clothed himself over rather than stripped himself off. The illness grows more severe; a lasting covering weighs down the eyes. No one can remove it—not an Angel, not Powers, not Dominions, not Authorities. That covering remains; it obstructs reading and darkens vision. “Which is not unveiled,” the Apostle says (2 Cor. III, 14)—that is, by anyone else—“unless it has been abolished in Christ.” But when such a person has turned to the Lord, the covering will be taken away.

23. You have therefore learned how to remove the covering that remains over the eyes of your heart. Turn to the Lord, and the covering will fall. Paul turned at the blessing of Ananias; scales fell from his eyes, and he saw who previously had not seen for three days (Acts IX, 18). The eye of the body and the eye of the soul are healed together, because that physician from heaven had shown him the remedy, concerning whom it is written: “He sent his Word and healed them, and delivered them from all their infirmities” (Ps. CVI, 20).

This is not an earthly physician, who heals every sickness and heals whole peoples.  
[Note: [Col. 1231D] This reading occurs only in the same edition: “healing whole peoples.” Perhaps it was altered lest Ambrose seem to teach that Christ healed peoples who were already whole. For *integer* sometimes has that meaning, especially when the subject is the health of the soul. Here, however, understand “whole” as “entire” or “all,” so that it does not refer to the words “from all infirmities,” but to “he healed them … he delivered them,” which have broad and indefinite meanings.]

Send this physician, then, Father; let your Word come and open my eyes. The eyes of the Apostles were also closed unless Jesus opened them. Thus, when two of them were going to a village called Emmaus, while he interpreted the Scriptures and blessed them, “their eyes were opened,” he says, “and they recognized him” (Luke XXIV, 31). Therefore unless Jesus had opened our eyes, no one would have seen; unless Jesus had lifted the covering, the grace of the Gospel would have shone upon no one.

Peter had closed eyes; John had closed eyes; James had closed eyes. Indeed, on the mountain they were weighed down by sleep, but when awakened by the splendor of the divine majesty, they opened the eyes of their hearts. And because, being situated in the body, they could not see fully, a cloud overshadowed them (Matt. XXVII, 5), lest the radiance of heavenly glory dazzle the eyes of the body.

24. Who, then, is so great as to open the eyes and see the mysteries of the Law, unless Christ shows them to him? Moses was not so great. Thus, at the Lord’s command, he threw down his staff, and it became a serpent, and he fled from it; he grasped the serpent by the tail, and it became a staff again (Exod. IV, 3–4). Yet he still did not understand the mystery by which it was declared that the Lord Jesus would descend to earth—he who, after emptying himself, allowed himself to be laid upon the cross and thrown into the tomb, becoming like a serpent from a staff because he was thrown into the tomb,  
[Note: [Col. 1232D] The manuscripts of Gaul omit the words “as a serpent made from the staff, because he was thrown into the tomb.” Nevertheless, they seem to contribute somewhat to clarity.]

from which, rising according to the oracles of the Law into the glory of God and the royal fellowship of the divine throne, he would return from the serpent.

Let us therefore also grasp the tail of that crucified serpent, so that we may recognize his royal power. And the woman who placed ointment upon his feet held him. Moses therefore grasped the serpent by the tail, and its mouth was opened. He would not have spoken about him, therefore, unless the Lord himself had opened his mouth.

25. Here David asks that his eyes be opened, and earlier he said: “Who shows us good things?” (Ps. IV, 6). He had been raised under the Law; he knew that the Law contains a shadow of future good things. He now desired to see those good things not through a shadow but with open eyes (Heb. X, 1). He knew that those who served according to the Law of Moses served a likeness and shadow of heavenly mysteries. He wished to grasp the very truth of divine worship; therefore, in order to scatter the covering from his eyes, he turned to the Lord and prayed, saying: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law.” He truly understood that there was a heavenly warfare which anyone could know from the Law, provided that the Lord revealed it to him. For who could ascend by human steps from earthly things to heavenly things, from shadow to brightness, from the likeness to the inner chambers of truth, without divine guidance?

[Col. 1232C] 26. Who can contemplate that heavenly altar and the true temple, the priests and Levites—not those according to the duties of the flesh, but those according to the grace of the spirit? Thus David desired this grace alone above all others, saying: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may see the delight of the Lord and contemplate his temple” (Ps. XXVI, 4).

Who could know that the rich man should offer a great gift according to what his hand could afford, so that his sin might be forgiven? Who could understand this, if he did not possess it? Who could offer, for example, a ram, since his sin was not forgiven by that offering? Who could perceive what those impurities were that were removed not by the Law that the Jews imagine, but by the spiritual law that Paul recognized?

Who could see the true remission of sins, whose likeness is in the Law but whose truth is in the Gospel, when the Lord Jesus says: “Your sins are forgiven” (Luke VII, 48)—not through the blood of goats, but through the sacrifice of his own body?

That rich man in the Law, therefore, who by confessing the fullness of perfect majesty in Christ and, as it were, offering it with the hands of faith upon that heavenly altar, has removed his sin—that man sees the true Priest. Whoever sees the Prince of priests sees the true Priest; whoever hears him saying, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19), contemplates the true temple. A great temple, from which power went forth and healed everyone. That altar was wondrous, upon which the sacrifice of one lamb took away the sins of the world. That man was the most excellent Levite, who came not to demand service but to offer everyone the service of his suffering; whose portion was God, since he possessed nothing here in order to possess all things.

27. What shall I say, moreover, about the Hebrew, whom the Law commands to serve for only six years and to go free in the seventh year (Exod. XXI, 2)? Who is this Hebrew servant? Which Hebrew could be understood to be free? Who is so great that, holding eternal years in mind, he sees the true Hebrew, who does not remain a slave forever but, having performed the service of a slave for six years, attains the grace of freedom in the seventh year?

The patriarch Isaac seems not to have been ignorant of the mystery of servitude and freedom, when he says: “You shall serve your brother, and it shall be that when you have laid it aside and loosed his yoke from your neck” (Gen. XXVII, 40),  
[Note: [Col. 1233D] Several manuscripts read “signifying the time … who, after these days,” perhaps indicating the time … “who from these days,” and so forth.]

signifying that a time would come when, even if someone served his brother while placed here, nevertheless, after the years had been completed—years gathered from those six days and from those months that we spend here—he would remove from his neck the yoke that is removed in the seventh year of remission.

We may conjecture the type of the true Hebrew in Joseph, who bore the yoke of servitude; but guilt did not seize him, prison did not confine him, and Egypt did not discolor him. We may also conjecture it in Peter, John, and James, who, created and instructed under the yoke of the Law, nevertheless laid aside the Jewish yoke of their brother when the appointed time of rest arrived, when the remission of sins shone upon them. Yet even this was still enacted here in shadow, in comparison with heavenly things.

28. How great that rest is which is inferred from the Law and revealed in the Gospel, and which is still preserved in its fullness, when the Lord Jesus says: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24)!  
[Note: [Col. 1233D] “And it is still preserved in its fullness.” These words are absent from all editions and from some manuscripts; nevertheless, they occur in seven manuscripts of no inferior quality.]

How blessed is the one who there can earn the fruit of that dwelling and participation in that rest! Then he will understand what it means to have opened his eyes in order to see the wonders of God’s law.

29. The reading from the Gospel that has just been proclaimed gave a fitting warning: there the leper was healed who said, “If you will, you can cleanse me” (Luke 5:12), placing the effect of power in the Lord’s will. He answered him in like manner: “I will; be cleansed” (ibid., 13). The mercy of the will came first; the authority of power followed. Jesus says to all, “I will,” to one who does not wish to be sin. [Note: Seven manuscripts read: “who does not wish to be a sinner.”] Christ’s willing is common to all; being cleansed belongs to the faith of the one who believes in Christ. “And he touched him.” He touches those by whose faith he is touched. Hence he says: “Someone touched me; for I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:46). [Col. 1234A] Here you have the working of the undefiled body; here you have the forgiveness of the Godhead.

30. But so that he might be healed more completely, he opened his eyes, saying: “Go, show yourself to the priest” (Luke 5:14). The Synagogue had many priests; but the one who opens the eyes does not see false priests—he looks upon the true one. Who is the true priest except the one who is priest forever? Therefore the Father said to him: “You are a priest forever” (Psalm 109:4). Thus he opened his eyes, and the man saw and understood what offering he ought to make for his cleansing. Blessed is the one who hears these things; how much more blessed is the one who sees, who can truly show himself to the Priest, so that there is nothing in him that he need fear being seen, because he first looks upon himself with unveiled face! For unless he has first seen himself, he will not dare to show himself—just as Adam wished to hide himself because he did not recognize himself. But let us now also consider what follows.

31. “I am a sojourner upon the earth; do not hide your commandments from me” (verse 19). This is not the voice of just anyone, but of one who has renounced earthly pleasures and stripped himself of every inclination toward worldly desire. He is a sojourner upon this earth who can say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20); who has his portion in the Lord; who can grieve that he lives longer upon earth; who is wearied by the length of this life; to whom the prolongation of this dwelling is burdensome, which the holy man turns away from and says: “Woe to those who dwell upon the earth” (Revelation 8:13)! He does not fear being dissolved; and if he is released, he confidently expects to be with Christ. He is truly a pilgrim upon earth, because he is “a fellow citizen with the saints and a member of God’s household,” and stores up treasure for himself in heaven.

He certainly does not desire, after leaving Egypt, to return to this intelligible Egypt; nor does he fear the borders of old age and death, once old age has been laid aside; nor does he build barns for storing harvests, intending now to live for ages that belong to others. [Note: The manuscripts read thus; the editions, however, have: “which neither old age can give back to him as lost, nor death,” etc. But the wording not found in the manuscripts is an interpolated gloss.] Rather, rich only in the fruitfulness of virtues, he gathers those things which even death cannot take away from him.

32. And rightly he says: “My soul has desired to long for your judgments at all times” (verse 20). This is done only by one who is free from bonds—not merely from the bonds of worldly anxiety, but also from the bonds of human affection. There are many bonds in this world: the desires of living are bonds; the allurements of pleasures are bonds; honors are bonds; marriage is a bond. Accordingly, the good Teacher says to you: “Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (1 Corinthians 7:27). Yet the one who takes a wife does not thereby sin; but he binds the bonds of his mind upon himself, because he is concerned with how to please his wife. He would be happier if he desired to please God alone. [Note: Eight manuscripts read: “But he is bound by the bonds of the flesh, who does not have authority over his own body,” etc. Others, with the editions, read as in the text.]

You see, then, that the one who does not have authority over his own body is bound. Therefore, since God’s commandment—drawn from the utterance of the Law and from apostolic teaching (Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 10:37)—is that no one should prefer a wife, riches, honor, or family ties to God, and since the one who prefers them becomes liable to God’s judgments, he first asked that God not hide his commandments from him. For the one who knows and keeps God’s commandments does not flee divine judgments but desires them; and so, as though the commandments had been revealed to him, he says: “I have desired to long for your judgments at all times.”

33. He did not say, “I have desired your judgments,” but, “I have desired to long for them.” For just as “to live life” is more than merely “to live”—since living is common even to this present life, whereas living life belongs to the blessed—so to long that we may desire God’s judgments is more than merely desiring those judgments. We desire to desire them, as though the desire itself were not within our power but were a grace of God.

When the Lord sees us taking delight in the desire for his judgments, he increases this sober affection. But when we sin, we do not desire to long for God’s judgments. An ill person does not desire to be burned or cut, so that he may recover health. One who is more gravely ill recoils from being burned, cut, or bound, and refuses to abstain from food. But the person in sound health approaches the physician without fear.

Therefore the Lord also says, not without purpose: “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke 22:15)—not merely desiring it, but, with a doubled desire, longing to bestow the remission of sins. Let us therefore also desire to long for God’s judgments. A good conscience is approved when it is examined. And let us desire to long for them at all times, so that no moment of our goodness may pass empty of desire.

[Col. 1235C] 34. “You have rebuked the proud: cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments” (verse 21). Since the Lord Jesus redeemed the human race through obedience and restored righteousness, while the serpent introduced sin through disobedience, we can judge from this what evil pride is, whose author is the devil—the one whom the Prophet portrays as saying: “I will set my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14).

Although he was utterly wicked because he failed to give honor to the Lord our God, he nevertheless taught disciples who were worse. He exalted himself so far as to wish to be equal and like the Most High; but his disciple is signified by the Apostle as one who would resent being considered equal and like God. For it is written: “When the man of lawlessness and the son of destruction is revealed, he who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God” (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4). The teacher presumes himself to be like God; this one presumes himself superior. Therefore the Lord also said to his disciples: “You will do greater things than these” (John 14:12), so that Christ might grant those from whom the serpent had taken more than he himself had lost the ability to do greater things than Christ himself had done on earth. In himself he wished to deceive the prince of this world; in his disciples he wished to triumph over him.

35. Therefore, wishing to free the human race from so great a crime, he brought the Pharisee and the publican into the temple to pray (Luke 18:10 and following). He taught that, even if one possesses other good qualities, the proud man gives greater offense than the humble man who has no virtue to support him; for the devil strives to trip up those intent upon good works.

How much that Pharisee labored not to seize what belonged to another, not to be unjust, not to commit adultery! How much he labored not to sin, as the publican had sinned! How much he labored to fast twice a week! How much he labored to give a tenth of everything he acquired! Which of us does these things? How many possess estates, lie upon their produce, and store their harvests only for themselves!

The devil noticed this and covered him with a grievous ulcer, so that, inflated in the mind of his flesh, he could not hold his head upright; and in the very matter in which he was thought likely to be praiseworthy, he was judged more blameworthy. For he gave thanks to God that he was not a robber, adulterer, or unjust. How disastrously the serpent struggled against him, binding him with its heavy coils! It made him superior so that it might throw him down from a higher place; it presented itself as inferior so that it might overthrow the loftier man with a more grievous fall. Evil is the downfall of arrogance, which has stolen away the one who seemed superior. Evil is this struggle of the serpent, by which it twists itself through so many winding coils.

36. He also wanted to inflate Paul. Which Paul? Certainly the apostle who was not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 12:7–8). He almost deceived him, so that Paul asked for the thorn of his flesh—which humbled him—to be taken away. But the good Lord, who wished to make Paul stronger through weaknesses, assigned to him an angel of Satan, so that the devil might be conquered by his own arts.

The Pharisee was not lying; indeed, he was speaking the truth. But everyone who exalts himself, even if he speaks the truth, gives offense (Luke 18:14). In fact, the Pharisee entered the temple apparently more commendably than the publican; yet he left condemned. What a great crime pride is, if even adulteries are preferred to it!

37. Finally, the Lord, who gives to others but resists the proud, as though he engaged those who exalt themselves in combat, claims this contest for himself. He who has compassion on others rebukes the arrogant, because nothing is more grievous than that we should look down upon our poor brothers with a proud eye, reject those like ourselves with intolerable disgust, and judge them unworthy of our favor because they are needy. For poverty is more readily acceptable to God than a treasure. [Note: “More readily”—that is, “more acceptable”—is connected with the preceding phrase; it is a pleonasm, such as is not uncommon in Latin authors.]

[Col. 1236D] 38. “Cursed,” he says, “are those who turn aside from your commandments.” Above he had said: “Do not hide your commandments from me.” Therefore, as one who knows the commandments once they have been revealed to him, he condemns those who have turned aside from the heavenly commandments. And he rightly said, “who turn aside”; for the commandment is straight, and therefore no one should deviate from it.

39. Yet the question arises why he says here: “Do not hide your commandments from me.” What is hidden becomes obscure and concealed, whereas above he said: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm 18:9). If the commandment is clear, how is it hidden, since no one puts a lamp under a bushel? Unless, perhaps, one commandment is clear, while many commandments are hidden. For he says: “Your judgments are like the great abyss” (Psalm 35:7). It is not “judgment” in the singular that is called an abyss, but “judgments” in the plural.

40. Observe the order. Above he said: “Do not drive me away from your commandments.” In what follows he says: “Do not hide your commandments from me.” Here he says: “Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments.” Truly cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments, although they ought to have returned thanks: first, because they were not driven away; second, because they were not denied the merit of having the divine commandments revealed to them. Thus someone turns aside from what he desired.

41. “Remove reproach and contempt from me, for I have sought your testimonies” (verse 22). If contempt is regarded as a form of reproach, how is it written: “God chose the contemptible things of this world” (1 Corinthians 1:28)? Consider, however, that he said “the contemptible things of the world,” not “of God.” What is contemptible in this world is precious before God. Thus humility is despised in this world, but approved by God’s judgment. And if the publican humbles himself, he is exalted. [Note: The editions read: “Hear whom God does not regard as nothing.” Several manuscripts omit “not,” incorrectly. Others, in greater number, read as in the text.]

Hear whom God loves and does not regard as nothing. Whoever is holy, lives without blemish, keeps the truth, and has not coveted his neighbor—“the wicked man has been reduced to nothing in his sight; he has rejected all that belongs to evil” (Psalm 14:2–4)—such a person, even if he is highborn, is approved by God because of his devotion in humility. But the proud, like the Pharisee, are regarded by him as nothing because of their arrogance. In the end, noble birth does not endure, but devotion remains forever.

Therefore take care not to become a reproach to Christ. I do not want anyone to curse me and despise me as though I were a sinner; how grave it would be if Christ judged me worthy of reproach! “Woe to you,” he says, “Chorazin and Bethsaida” (Luke 10:13). They are condemned because they did not repent of their offenses. Let us therefore act so that reproach may be removed from us.

Who, however, is not worthy of reproach? The one who has sought the Lord’s testimonies. There are many who wish to bring reproach upon your servants, but they themselves are more reproachable, because to suffer reproach for your name is glorious.

42. Therefore he says: “For princes also sat and slandered me” (verse 23). This is the voice of a martyr who, brought before the judgment of persecutors and compelled to sacrifice to idols, resisted steadfastly. The judges sat upon their tribunals, surrounded by their officials, indignant that their commands were not obeyed, and deliberated what punishment they should consider appropriate. But the martyr stood fearless and said: “Princes sat and slandered me.”

This is also the voice of the Lord, when the assembly of the people’s presbytery, the chief priests and the scribes, had gathered, and he had been brought before the council of the Jews, who said: “What further need do we have of witnesses? We have heard it from his own mouth” (Matthew 26:65). When he stood before the governor and was led to the cross, what more beautiful words could he have spoken than: “Princes sat and slandered me”—that is, “while I stood, the princes sat”?

And because they were raised high upon the supports of their tribunals, they did not see the Lord. They sat; they were at the height of princely authority, yet they did not consider the Prince of princes.

But this is little enough. “They slandered me,” he says. I, their Redeemer, had come; I had come to cleanse the sins of all, to recover the lost, to restore to holy Jacob the inheritance of paradise—and they slandered me. Therefore, my imitators, my disciples, do not be ashamed of suffering insult if you stand before princes for my name, since I stood for your salvation.

43. Finally, when Peter and the other apostles had been handed over to custody and on the following day were brought before the council, he said steadfastly: “Rulers of the people and elders of Israel, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a sick man, by which this man has been saved, let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, this man stands here before you healthy” (Acts 4:8, 10). That is: You are the ones who crucified Christ; we regard this insult as a matter of glory, because we are accused on account of the healing of a sick man. The Savior of all left this inheritance to his servants.

But they conferred among themselves, saying: “What shall we do with these men?” (ibid., 16). And they released them. Peter therefore rejoiced, and each of the apostles rejoiced, because they had been considered worthy to endure insult for Christ’s name. Rightly, then, each of them could say at that time: “For princes also sat and slandered me.”

44. Princes sat against Isaiah and deliberated that he should be cut in pieces. But he did not fear them when he said: “Hear, princes of Sodom” (Isaiah 1:10). They sat against Jeremiah so that he might be thrown into a pit. They sat against Zechariah, who was killed between the temple and the altar. They sat against Susanna and judged against the woman of chastity.
