But to show that the counsel of princes is not good, the Lord stirred up the spirit of a boy; and the woman whom the princes had pronounced guilty of death was acquitted by the prophet of every accusation as wholly innocent.

45. There are also other princes who slander us, of whom it is said: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12). These sit and examine who is just in this age, who serves God attentively as a Christian, devoted to good work and conduct.

They slander him, saying: “Let us lie in wait for him; let us hinder him; let us prevent him from accomplishing what he desires; let us crush his mind; let us break his courage through repeated and sudden adversities. And if he is approved by God because of his righteousness, let us ask that his temptations be given to us.”

For they could not have been granted power over so great a prophet and over the many temptations that he endured unless the Lord had allowed it for the testing of his soldier, so that he might crown him with greater glory. [Note: The Roman edition has in the text, and the old edition in the margin: “had given an opportunity for testing his soldier.” The old edition has in the text, together with some manuscripts: “had given a cause.” Other manuscripts of better quality read: “had given the cause.” This is best, since the power over his temptations must be understood here; it is expressed in the preceding clause.]

[Note: The Vienna manuscript reads: “Who, then, stirred up the force of an evil spirit in King Saul against him?”] Who, then, stirred up King Saul against him except the evil spirit, as we read—the spirit that grieved at being excluded whenever David, by the sound of his harp or by the strings and chords of good counsel and good works, soothed the king’s mind and spirit (1 Samuel 16:23)? Who stirred up the wickedness of Doeg the Syrian, so that he would betray the holy man and bring hospitable kindness into danger for the priest (2 Samuel 22:9–10)? Who inflamed Ammon’s passion so that he violated the prophetic household and grieved his father’s spirit, one by an incestuous desire, the other by the outrage—and so that the man who prophesied for others could not foresee the evils of his own household (2 Samuel 13:14)? Who armed Absalom’s fury so that he excluded his father from his house and pursued him in a parricidal war (2 Samuel 15:14)?

But when the holy man was already nearly inferior in the strength of his kingdom, he extinguished the darts of the devil that had been kindled against him by this one act: although his son sought his father’s death, he nevertheless, moved by paternal affection, commanded the safety of his son.

46. Therefore the princes of the people—Ahithophel and the other commanders of the warriors—sat (2 Samuel 18:5). The princes of the people deliberated with Absalom against the Prophet (2 Samuel 15:31). Hence he says: “For princes also sat and slandered me; but your servant was occupied with your justifications.”

We recognize the weapons of the righteous man, with which he repels every assault of his adversaries. Elsewhere he says: “They surrounded me and attacked me without cause; instead of loving me, they slandered me, but I prayed” (Psalm 108:3–4). Here he says that his youthful energy was devoted neither to the practice of military arts nor to any cunning of heart for deceiving an adversary, so that he might overcome the one whom he saw; rather, he fought against those whom he did not see. In him piety fought more powerfully than bodily strength.

Thus he was occupied with God’s justifications, so that by an opposing blow he might wound the devil. The devil tried to draw him away from his purpose of righteousness and his devotion to divine worship through military occupations; but the righteous man occupied himself even more with meditation upon divine work and worship. Therefore the Lord protected the one who hoped in him, with whom he spoke, and to whom he clung with his whole affection.

For the righteous man either speaks with God in prayer or speaks of divine works in praise; and he always speaks of God’s works, so that his mouth may not speak of human works. The righteous man speaks nothing earthly and does nothing mortal.

47. Therefore he says: “For your testimonies are my meditation, and your justifications are my counsels” (verse 24). Do you see what he teaches—that these ought to be the counsels of the righteous person: to meditate on God’s commandments, to exercise himself in God’s praises and oracles, and always to justify the Lord?

Whoever does what God commands and what he believes pleases God justifies God. We can understand this from the reading of the Gospel (Luke 7:30), where the Evangelist says that the Pharisees rejected God’s counsel, not having been baptized with John’s baptism. In another book, however, you find: “They did not justify God, because they refused to be baptized.” Therefore, when John said to the Lord, “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me,” he answered: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:14–15).

Whoever, then, does God’s commandments justifies God, because he performs his righteousness. And it is good that human counsels should follow God’s counsel, because God’s counsel is always certain, whereas our counsels are generally uncertain and are tested by the outcome of events.

SERMON FOUR. Daleth

1. The fourth letter according to the Hebrews, Daleth, signifies “fear” in Latin or, as we find elsewhere, “birth.” Both meanings can agree and suit the sense. Birth belongs to those things that are generated in this age; by it we understand corporeal and material things, which are transient, and therefore it is not far removed from fear. For fear arises from corporeal and material things. What, indeed, is earthly birth except fear?

2. Thus the verse begins: “My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word” (verse 25). By “pavement” we understand earth, and by earth, material things. To the sinner it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Genesis 3:19), because he did not think he should cling to the divine commandments but turned aside toward material and corporeal things, upon whom the pleasure of this worldly life had left its imprint.

Thus, expelled from paradise—that is, from that lofty and heavenly place to which Paul was caught up, whether in the body or outside the body he did not know—Adam, cast down from that elevated place onto the earth, laments, saying: “My soul has clung to the pavement,” just as he says elsewhere: “My soul has been humbled into the dust, and my belly has clung to the earth” (Psalm 43:25).

These are the words of one doing penance, who remembered that he had clung to God and had not known, nor been able to discern—as Paul also did not discern—whether he was in the body or outside the body (2 Corinthians 12:2). He scarcely felt the weakness and sluggishness of the body, because the Lord’s presence clung to him. Thus the prophetic Spirit, which expressed the grief, or the Lord, who took upon himself Adam’s weakness, represents Adam’s person and assumes his state of feeling.

[Note: Wherever Ambrose speaks of Adam’s expulsion from paradise or of Paul’s being caught up into paradise, he appears to indicate that they are one and the same place, as may be understood from chapter 1 of the book *On Paradise*, section 1, and other passages. Hence, as Sixtus of Siena says in book 5 of his *Bibliotheca*, annotation 35, some have concluded that Ambrose departs from the received theological opinion in two respects. First, they say, he places paradise in the third heaven; second, he reduces the whole account to mere allegories.

As to the first point, we admit that it is difficult to interpret his words in another sense. Yet in such a matter the error is not especially dangerous, particularly since Augustine states concerning paradise in book 8, chapter 21, of *On Genesis*: “It must be believed that the place of paradise is exceedingly remote from human knowledge.”

As to the second point, we maintain that Ambrose says in several passages things that presuppose the historical truth of the account according to its natural meaning. Thus, in chapter 1, section 5, of *On Paradise*, he says: “Understand also that it was not the man who is according to the image of God, but the man according to the body; for an incorporeal being is not in a place.” Consider also many other passages of the same book, especially chapter 10, sections 47–48, and chapter 12, sections 59–60. From these you will undoubtedly understand that the holy Doctor did not doubt the historical reality of the earthly paradise.

But when, in chapter 2, section 11, of the aforementioned book, he leaves the entire account intact so that those who wish may interpret the whole history allegorically, he does so by a kind of concession, as those words clearly show: “lest,” he says, “they seem to be offended by our speech.” Everything preceding those words in the same chapter strongly confirms this.

Moreover, since Augustine praised this book in his work against Julian to support the doctrine of original sin, it is manifest that it is free from the error of one who in a remarkable way favored the Pelagians. We have already touched somewhat upon this matter in connection with the same passage, and perhaps we shall add something further in the letter to Sabinus.]

3. Let Adam therefore speak: “My soul has clung to the pavement.” The man who earlier, supremely blessed, breathed the ethereal air and knew nothing of the cares and weariness of this life is now bent down by concern for the world, devotion to luxury, and desire for money, inserting himself like a fox into earthly holes and hiding places.

Rightly did he cling to the dust, since he could not raise himself unless Christ lifted him above his cross. Rightly did he cling to the pavement, since he was hiding himself from Christ. He does not cling to the pavement to whom Jesus says: “Follow me” (John 1:43). He does not cling to the pavement who hears and follows the Law when it says: “You shall walk after the Lord your God and cling to him” (Deuteronomy 10:20).

4. To understand how one person clings to the pavement and another to God, hear the words: “Whoever clings to a prostitute is one body … but whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:16–17).

This earth that we bear captures us by certain enticements of a prostitute and smears upon us, as it were, certain faces of pleasures with the cosmetics of bodily delights, so that the truth may be concealed within them and, by a kind of marketplace appearance, they may deceive those who approach. [Note: All editions and several manuscripts read: “deceives by a certain marketplace appearance.” Others more correctly read: “they deceive,” referring to the faces of pleasures. Here “marketplace appearance” does not simply mean an exterior appearance that is visible outwardly, but one arranged after the fashion of wares customarily displayed in the marketplace so as to attract the eyes of passersby.]

But once they have temporarily obscured the inner eye of the mind, the dust of such pleasures is eventually shaken off, and it is easily recognized how empty is the grace of this age or of the body.

5. It is good, therefore, to cling to the Lord and not to hold one’s neck bent beneath the yoke of the world. Hence Wisdom says to the Church, or to the courageous soul: “Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built in Thalpioth; a thousand doors hang upon it, all the weapons of the mighty” (Song of Songs 4:4). [Note: The old edition, together with most and better manuscripts, reads as in the text. The Roman edition, together with others, reads: “a thousand shields hang upon it.” The Septuagint has χίλιοι θυρεοὶ κρέμανται ἐπ’ αὐτόν (“a thousand shields hang upon it”). The variation arose because θυρεοί can signify both doors and shields.]

A neck raised upright toward God and suited to Christ’s yoke, not bent by any inclination toward earthly enticements, is like Christ’s royal tower, upon which Nebuchadnezzar cannot impose his yoke. David—“the strong-handed”—built that tower and raised lofty structures above the walls, so that it might serve both as protection and as an ornament: as protection, because it foresees and repels the enemy; as an ornament, because it rises above not only lowly things but even lofty ones.

Yet it serves as protection or ornament only if it contains the teachings of the Word like ornaments of a harness, and also the weapons of the mighty prophets—arrows directed by certain arms of faith against every height that exalts itself.

6. Therefore do not bring your soul down into the dust of death, since the Lord has also granted it natural height and the vigor by which it may rouse and raise itself. Hence these words may aptly be understood also of the union of soul and body: in the mystery of our natural life, the soul joined to the body crawls, as it were, along the ground and clings to the pavement, partly because of this earthly dwelling and partly because this body is from the earth.

The lodging of the region and the very material of our body alike support this interpretation. Therefore the Apostle rightly desires to be freed from this body of death (Romans 7:24), because we are shut up in a kind of prison and, dwelling in a sort of den of luxury, are wrapped in the darkness of sins.

7. Let us therefore walk according to the will of God, so that we may be said to cling to God. Whoever lives according to the desire of the body is flesh; whoever lives according to God’s commandments is spirit.

Let our soul therefore not become flesh—that is, let us not be called flesh like those who perished in the flood, of whom it was said: “Because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3). Rather, let our flesh, obedient to the guidance of the soul, become soul and deserve to be called by that name, just as the household of the patriarch Jacob and his holy descendants were so called.

For it is written: “These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel his daughter, and she bore these to Jacob: seven souls.” And elsewhere: “All the souls who entered Egypt with Jacob, who came forth from his loins”—apart from the wives of his sons—“were sixty-six” (Genesis 46:25–26). And at the beginning of Exodus we read: “All the souls of Jacob were seventy-five who were with Jacob” (Exodus 1:5). [Note: Most manuscripts read: “and she bore these to Jacob; all the souls were seven.” The old edition reads: “and she bore these,” etc. The Roman edition does likewise, except that, together with some manuscripts, it omits the word “all.”]

Therefore those who dwelt with Joseph and came out of Egypt were souls—seventy in number. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “they came out, seventy souls.”]

8. But those who, although they were angels of God—that is, who imitated the grace of angels through the uprightness of their lives—for those who do not take wives, and those who do not marry, will be like the angels in heaven—those, then, who seemed to be angels but were captivated by feminine beauty, are flesh, as the Lord God said: “My spirit will not remain in these human beings forever, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3).

And rightly those who are free from lust are compared with angels: they are not flesh in the flesh but in the spirit, like those who followed the apostolic teacher, to whom he said: “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit” (Romans 8:9). But those who are captivated by bodily lust for women are flesh. Would that they were flesh only and not also like neighing horses, since it says: “They neighed after the wife of their neighbor” (Jeremiah 5:8)!

[Note: Here Ambrose appears to follow the opinion of those who understand the beginning of Genesis 6 as referring to the sons of Seth, although he himself frequently interprets it as referring to sexual intercourse between angels and women, as we have shown in the note on chapter 4, section 9, of *On Noah and the Ark*, and also below in Sermon 8, verse 64. Moreover, he clearly teaches elsewhere that angels were cast down from heaven because of the sin of pride: below, Sermon 7, verse 51, and Sermon 16, verse 122, of this work.]

9. The one who feels his soul’s descent, bent all the way down to the pavement, therefore asks that he be given life according to God’s word—the word that draws souls to itself and, in its mercy, wishing to raise them, leads them away from earthly things.

The soul is given life when it walks in Christ’s ways: dead to sin, it lives for God, so that thereafter the death of sin can no longer exercise dominion over it, once it has been buried with Christ and justified from sin. But the one who wishes to be justified must first declare his own ways.

10. (Verse 26.) Therefore in the second verse he says: “I have declared my ways, and you have heard me; teach me your ordinances.” He rightly thinks that one must reach God’s ordinances in a proper order [Col. 1244A]: first, one must confess one’s sins. Thus we are taught elsewhere also: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26).

We must therefore understand what it means for a person to walk in his own ways and in the ways of God. Whoever does the desires of the flesh and lives according to the lust of this world walks in his own ways, in which he delights and rejoices. But whoever comes to do the will of his Father who is in heaven, whose food is to complete God’s commandment; whoever does not seek what is pleasurable to himself but what pleases God—he proceeds along the Lord’s way, that way which says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). You see, then, that the person who walks in Christ’s way lives according to the word of God.

The Lord God himself also teaches in Deuteronomy how one should walk in his ways, saying: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in his ways, love him, and serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep his commandments and his ordinances” (Deut. 10:12–13)? It is therefore clear that some ways belong to the flesh and others to God; and if anyone wishes to walk in God’s ways, he should know that the ways of the flesh, the body, and worldly wisdom must first be abandoned.

11. Having therefore left them, David declares them and does not remain silent before God. He confesses his errors [Note: A considerable number of manuscripts read “he does not deny his falls.”]; he does not conceal his falls. He said something similar: “I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord” (Ps. 31:5).

For if a righteous person accuses himself, he silences the voice of the ready accuser, who is accustomed to aggravate sins and magnify everyone’s crimes. He therefore closes the accuser’s mouth who has first confessed against himself, and he forestalls [Note: Some manuscripts read “the pardon of the confessor’s modesty.” “The shame of the deed excuses him; it accuses the author.”] the pardon of the one who confesses. Shame excuses the guilty person; his own modesty accuses the author [Note: It is sufficiently clear from what follows that “the author,” or instigator, here means the devil.]. For whoever has not concealed his own offenses seems to have grieved over what he did in himself, and to have exposed in the devil what the devil had persuaded him to do.

Therefore Scripture says: “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17). Whoever accuses himself, although he is a sinner, begins to be righteous, because he neither spares himself nor fails to confess God’s ordinances, believing that nothing can be hidden from him.

Would that Adam had wished first to accuse himself rather than conceal himself! But it is not enough for us to confess our error: if we truly wish to be corrected, let us also ask the Lord to teach us his ordinances, so that afterward we may not be able to err. He therefore asks to be taught by the Lord, because there is one teacher of us all, as Christ says (Matt. 23:8). Nor does he ask this pointlessly; for the person whom a human being teaches is not blessed, but the one whom you instruct, O Lord.

12. (Verse 27.) He remembers himself everywhere and does not think it sufficient that the Lord our God should teach him his ordinances; rather, he adds: “Make known to me the way of your ordinances, and I shall exercise myself in your wonders.”

Observe the order. First, we must learn the Lord’s ordinances; then we must understand the stages and order of those ordinances—what ought to come first and what should follow. For knowing what to do, while not knowing the order in which it should be done, is not perfect knowledge; things done out of order generally give offense.

Thus the righteous person is the one who accuses himself at the beginning of his speech; but the unrighteous person is the one who confesses what he had previously denied. The former finds the grace of modesty; the latter incurs the mark of shamelessness. In this way ignorance of order confuses the nature of affairs and the character of merits.

But the person who has first learned the mysteries of God and then the order of the mysteries exercises himself in God’s wonders.

13. The Greek has ἀδολεσχησῷ [Note: For variants concerning this word and other interpretations of it, see *On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 1, section 1, and also below, Sermon 11, verse 83. On this word, see also Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, book 1, question 69.], which the Latin renders, “I shall hallucinate.” There appears to be some difficulty of expression here according to ordinary usage, because ἀδολεσχῆσαι is commonly understood either as “to hallucinate” or “to say more than one ought,” and to seem superfluous—something tiresome to the listener. It also seems to be out of order when the order of events itself appears to produce weariness: for example, if you wished to recount some case and maintained the order of events, while the listener hurried toward the outcome and grew tired of what came before.

Yet no one can be fully instructed unless he has understood everything in its proper order. From this one perceives not only what happened, but also the weight of what happened and the disposition of the person who acted. Therefore David, as a good judge and arbiter of himself, wishes to be taught almost to the point of weariness, and to linger for an apparently excessive length of time, rather than pass over the necessary order.

[Note: For ἀδολεσχία, many manuscripts correctly read ἀδολεσχήσεια.]

For ἀδολεσχία [Col. 1245C]—or “hallucination”—seems to be a certain lengthy meditation and a deliberate concentration of the mind; from this it is not far removed from exercise, whether of the spirit or of the body. For just as the person who exercises his limbs in the wrestling school exercises them for a longer time in order to strengthen them, so the person who exercises his mind in the divine Scriptures or in counsels ought to exercise it for a longer time.

14. “Isaac went out into the field” (Gen. 24:63). The Greek says ἀδολεσχῆσαι; the Latin, “to walk about” or “to exercise oneself.” Rebecca was coming; in her the type of the Church was prefigured; a marriage was being prepared in which there would be a great sacrament.

Seeing those mysteries, the patriarch went out into the field, spreading abroad the keenness of his mind and walking in the innocence of his heart. He exercised his spirit with various thoughts and delighted in the wondrous mysteries. Wishing to become his imitator, the holy prophet yearned to be taught God’s ordinances and to know the way of the heavenly ordinances, so that his soul might not sleep the sleep of this age [Col. 1246A], nor, captivated by the allurements of worldly vanity, slacken its pursuit of truth.

15. (Verse 28.) He then explains in what manner he wishes to be taught, saying: “My soul has dripped away from weariness; strengthen me in your words.”

Some manuscripts read “has grown drowsy,” because ἐνύσταξεν and ἔσταξεν differ by two letters. The translator or an ancient copyist may have made a mistake here: νυστάζειν means “to sleep,” while στάζειν means “to drip.” The perfect person who directs his mind toward the divine mysteries does not grow drowsy.

Thus he himself says elsewhere: “If I give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids” (Ps. 132:4). But he is always vigilant; and even if the flesh sleeps, the heart keeps watch. Therefore the person who was thinking of building a temple for the Lord—not by constructing stones, but by building up heavenly words—was not sleeping.

The word of God drives away weariness [Col. 1246B]; by it the sleep of the soul and the slumber of the mind are excluded. For sleep creeps in through sadness and anxiety over worldly matters. But whoever clings to God, fleeing cares, takes pleasure in the knowledge of eternity and fears no change in worldly affairs there.

16. Those, therefore, who use the easier shortcuts accept “he grew drowsy”; but Origen, who carefully examined the interpretations of many with painstaking inquiry, followed “he dripped,” because the soul of the perfect person, being well composed and strengthened, does not drip—like the roofs of buildings that are well covered and protected. Unfitted structures, on the other hand, quickly drip.

Hence the expression: “The drip from the roof drives a person out of his house on a winter day” (Prov. 27:15) [Note: All printed editions and a few manuscripts read “in which severity of cold”; a larger number of manuscripts read “in which,” and so forth. The latter is better, since it refers to the preceding words, “on a winter day.” Again, shortly afterward, where all manuscripts and the old editions read “For the tested,” the Roman edition had substituted “For the prepared,” and so forth.], when we are tested by the severity of the cold and by frequent changes of weather.

Therefore we are taught to take care that our flight not occur in winter or on the Sabbath (Matt. 24:20). The day—whether of judgment or of death—ought to find us already tested, lest death find us stripped of the greenery of prosperity and wholly deprived of every flower of successful circumstances.

17. Let us therefore beware lest any one of us be driven from the state of his mind and from its natural dwelling, if the dwellings have openings through which dripping water, flowing as though from the foundations, may bring down a person who has no firm foundation of wisdom.

Therefore the prophet says: “My son, do not flow away” (Prov. 3:21). Our soul must accordingly be strengthened so that it does not drip, and it must be solidified by an unbroken structure of virtues, so that it may be able to preserve the mystery of the eternal King.

Otherwise, whoever is loose in speech, as though full of cracks, flowing out here and there, empties his interior and is flooded by outward passions, unable either to cover himself or to retain the word he has received—like holy Mary, who “kept all these words in her heart” (Luke 2:51), lest anything should flow from her [Note: All printed editions read “flow from her mouth.” All manuscripts read “flow from her heart.”] heart.

18. With such a defense of virtues the Church speaks, so that she may appear worthy to be the dwelling into which the Bridegroom, when invited, may enter. She first presumes that she will be pleasing if Christ sees her well covered and faithfully keeping silence.

“Behold,” she says, “you are beautiful, my cousin, and indeed lovely; our resting place is shaded, the beams of our houses are cedars, our ceilings are cypresses” (Song 1:15–16).

The Church praises the beauty of the Bridegroom, whom each person praises all the more with silent affection, and whom the faithful interpreter of the mysteries proclaims all the more by silence. For whoever divulges secrets diminishes Christ’s beauty. Therefore let no one cast his pearls before swine, lest he cause precious ornaments to be trampled.

Christ therefore does not incline his head in the tabernacle of the talkative and chattering—for sin is admitted through many words—but in that of the serious man who is sparing in speech, not intemperate in conversation, and who avoids the drunkenness of talkativeness through sobriety of words.

19. It is rightly called a shaded resting place, because in those established in the Church the virtue of the Most High casts its shadow. David asked to be protected by this shadow, lest the sun burn him by day or the moon by night (Ps. 121:6). Spiritual grace supplies this shadow to those fleeing the scorching summer of this age and world.

The resting place of Christ and the Church is therefore shaded, and the eternal rest of God the Father breathes upon it. Let us therefore rest in this shadow, wearied by the heat of our sins. If lust has scorched some, let the Lord’s cross refresh them, upon which he reclined himself in order to receive our sins. If guilt has exhausted others, let Jesus receive them into his bosom and cherish them in a gentle embrace.

Hence I dare to say that the flesh of Christ is the resting place of the Church.

20. “The beams of our houses are cedars.” Under the appearance of cedars, the glory of the ancestors who were righteous is declared; for “the righteous will flourish like a palm tree and multiply like the cedar that is in Lebanon.” Just as the cedar does not decay, so the glory of the ancestors is not corrupted by any old age.

21. “Our ceilings are cypresses.” This kind of tree never loses its greenness. In winter, spring, and summer alike it nourishes its foliage, and it does not change into a different color. Of all trees, this alone the wind never strips of its proper dignity; it alone is never stripped of its old covering or clothed in a new bloom.

So apostolic grace also knows no decline, but flourishes through its age. The soul, therefore, cannot be corrupted when, vigorous in its flourishing merits, it continually supports the heights of righteousness and of the other virtues with patient courage. Thus it neither flows away nor fails, because there is in it nothing cracked or slack, nothing unstable, nothing slippery, nothing that could pour out of it through the fault of speech.

Therefore the Prophet asks to be strengthened in his words (Ps. 73:2), lest his feet be moved and his steps be poured out. If anyone is vigorous in an upright heart, he does not suffer this; rather, rooted and founded, he remains immovable against all the waves of the passions.

22. (Verse 29.) Strengthened, therefore, in his words, he says: “Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me according to your law.”

He did not say, “Remove me from the way of iniquity,” but “Remove the way of iniquity from me,” as though it were in us and appeared to dwell within us. For as long as we practice anything wicked, the way of iniquity remains within us and does not depart from us. Therefore let us act diligently to separate it from ourselves.

But because the inherited bond of iniquity has clung to human minds, the aid of the liberator is necessary. You too should pray and say: “Wretched man that I am, who will remove from me the way of iniquity?”—“The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” [Col. 1248B]. And he rightly called it the way of iniquity, not iniquity itself, since iniquity is not in us as something natural, but has been worn smooth by the footprints of our ancestors who ran after sins.

23. And rightly so, because the wound is great, old, and long spreading; it demands the remedies of a more perfect medicine. He implores that it be healed by the Lord’s lawful mercy. A wound that has not been healed according to the rule of medicine is quickly reopened; indeed, delayed treatment makes slower progress. Therefore, if the poison spreads into the interior, medicines applied externally do not reach it.

The nature of medicine therefore requires that it be treated either by cutting or by cauterizing. Unless the rotting parts are cut away or the useless moisture is boiled out, the physician’s hand is applied to the wounds in vain. Hence the good physician says that such a sick person must be treated according to due order, so that medicine may achieve its purpose.

He shows mercy according to the law who shows mercy with justice and wisdom, so that he may remit what he knows can rightly be remitted, lest, when he shows mercy to another, he make himself subject to the law. After Agag had been spared through mercy, he caused Saul to sin. Saul sinned in that very act of mercy, and therefore he sinned after receiving mercy.

24. Let us also consider whether we might make worse the very person whom we unjustly pity. Often not restraining offenders [Note: Thus the old edition and all manuscripts. The Roman edition, from the margin of a Vatican manuscript, reads “is an act of greater severity.” This is not unsuitable if the sense is considered. Yet since it is supported by no other authority, it must be said that the passage means that some people, when they pardon a crime in order to display their authority—for granting pardon belongs not to inferiors but to the ruler—harm the guilty more by the indulgence of impunity than if they had punished them severely.] is a greater exercise of authority than punishing them.

For all who have committed something dishonorable are handed over to disgraceful passions, and they receive no recompense for their guilt. Thus, concerning those who did not think that God knew their crimes and lived as though there were neither judge nor law, Scripture says: “God handed them over to a depraved mind” (Rom. 1:28), because they chose the way of iniquity and refused to choose the way of truth.

25. (Verse 30.) But the prophet, who wished to turn back with sincere affection, says: “I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments.”

The person who errs in doctrine cannot say this. The person who errs in doctrine cannot say this. An Arian cannot say it; a Sabellian cannot; a Manichaean cannot. The greedy person who desires worldly and material things cannot say it. The businessman cannot say it; for the pursuit of possessions and the desire to own are not the way of truth.

How can it be the way of truth when the rich man in this world cannot carry his wealth away with him and, after death, begins to be poorer than that beggar Lazarus? Worldly honor is not the way of truth; nor is worldly anxiety.

Thus the person who chose the way of truth says shortly afterward: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity” (below, verse 37). The temporality of worldly things is vanity; the eternal things are truth.

If, therefore, we wish to walk in the way of truth, let us be pilgrims in relation to the world rather than to God, and let us walk by faith. For whoever walks by faith is present with God; whoever walks by sight is present to the world and is a pilgrim away from the Lord. But the latter is quickly put to shame.

[Col. 1249B] 26. (Verse 31.) Therefore David, fleeing from such a person, says: “I have clung to your testimonies, O Lord; do not put me to shame.”

The person who clings to the Lord’s testimonies does not reject his commandments, does not forget his judgments, and does not indulge his pleasures. Whoever clings to the Lord’s testimonies renounces the world, forgets what lies behind, and presses toward what lies ahead, so that he may reach the prize, which is the distinction of victory.

The person whom the seductive things of this world have not captured is therefore not put to shame. Even if he has committed shameful acts, he is not put to shame if he asks Christ for the pardon of his sins. Therefore it is said to him: “Your sins are forgiven … go in peace” (Luke 7:48, 50).

But he is not put to shame in this way only if the remission of sins has worked in him so as to remove not only his sins but also his inclination to sin. Let justice remit iniquities, fortitude fear, and temperance impurities, so that the remission of sins may become not merely temporary but everlasting.

Let Christ enter your soul; let Jesus dwell in your minds, so that sin may have no place in the tabernacle of virtue.

27. (Verse 32.) “I ran in the way of your commandments,” he says, “when you enlarged my heart.”

For he could not have run in the way if his heart had been constricted by narrowness. Thus the Apostle says to those running in the Lord’s way: “Be enlarged yourselves, and do not be yoked together with unbelievers” (2 Cor. 6:13–14). And concerning himself he says: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged” (ibid., 11).

Therefore it is also said of Solomon: “The breadth of his heart was like the sand of the sea” (1 Kings 4:29). Observe the distinction: the way should be narrower, the heart broader, so that it may sustain the dwelling of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Otherwise the Word of God may come and knock, and, seeing the narrowness of the heart, disdain to dwell there.

Thus wisdom is sung at the entrance, while in the streets it acts with confidence. The streets are broad. Wisdom is therefore not sung in the ways but in the breadth of the heart. In this field of the inner person, then, we must run—not in the narrowness of the mind—so that we may attain. For it is written: “Run in such a way that you may all attain” (1 Cor. 9:24). The person who ran in such a way as to say, “I have finished the course” (2 Tim. 4:7), attained; for he ran like a good horse.

28. Indeed, Christ has his own horses, concerning which the prophet says: “You sent your horses into the sea, stirring up the many waters” (Hab. 3:15). The apostles, by preaching the Gospel, stirred the peoples of the nations, who move like many waters and rise like the waves of many waters, so that, rising from earthly idol rites, they might believe in Christ.

Above he also says: “I mounted your horses; your cavalry is salvation” (Hab. 3:8). O wondrous team of twelve pairs of good horses, whose bridles are peace and whose reins are love! They are bound together by the ties of concord and subjected to the yoke of faith. With the four wheels of the Gospel they carry the mystery to the ends of the whole world, bearing the good charioteer, the Word of God. By his whip the allurements of the world have been driven away, the ruler of this world has been destroyed, and the course of the righteous has been completed.

O great contest of rational horses! O wondrous mystery! A wheel was running within a wheel, and it was not hindered. The New Testament was in the Old Testament; it ran within it, through which it was announced. The wheels went in four directions and did not turn back, because the spirit of life was in them. They ran toward the four quarters of the entire world and ran without stumbling, because the good life of the horses was complete.

The horses therefore ran, because the one who had mounted the horses was not asleep.

29. Jesus is therefore the charioteer of our souls, and he also wishes us to mount our horses—that is, our bodies—but always to remain vigilant, lest it be said to us: “Those who mounted the horses have grown drowsy” (Ps. 76:7).

This sea must be crossed diligently. It can scarcely be crossed by the vigilant; but if anyone sleeps, he will not be able to cross it. Rather, he will be submerged like the Egyptian, whose soul and body alike perished: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exod. 15:1)—those who did not follow the law but persecuted it.

1018 **FIFTH SERMON. He**

1. The fifth letter, He, follows. In Latin it signifies “is,” or, as we find elsewhere, “I live.” Both interpretations suit one another: whoever is lives, and whoever lives is.

Thus the gentiles “are not,” and therefore they do not live but are dead. “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8). And whoever is lives: “As I live,” says the Lord God (Ezek. 33:11). For how can one who lives not be?

Jesus lives, and he also gives life to the dead and calls those things that are not as though they were. It is no wonder if nature yields to the Lord, so that the dead are given life and those who were not begin to be.

And since, according to him who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), the way is also life, let us seek the way so that we may deserve to have life. Let us therefore listen to the one who lives in Christ.

The person who says, “But we who live bless you, O Lord” (Ps. 115:18), lives; for in Christ Jesus even whoever has died lives.

2. (Verse 33.) Let us listen, I say, to what he said in order to live: “Establish a law for me, O Lord, the way of your ordinances, and I shall seek it always.”

A soldier who enters upon a journey does not arrange the order of travel for himself, nor does he choose a road according to his own judgment, nor does he seek pleasant shortcuts, lest he depart from the standards. Rather, he receives a travel order from the commander and keeps it; he advances according to the prescribed order; he walks with his weapons and completes the journey by the straight road, so that he may find provisions prepared.

If he travels by another route, he receives no rations and finds no prepared lodging, because the commander orders all these things to be prepared for those who follow him and do not turn either to the right or to the left from the prescribed route.

Rightly, then, the person who follows his commander does not fail. He walks at a measured pace, because the commander considers not what is useful to himself but what is possible for everyone. Therefore he also arranges stationary camps: the army marches for three days and rests on the fourth.

Cities are selected in which three days, four days, or more may be inserted, if they abound in water and are frequented by commerce. Thus the journey is completed without hardship until they reach the city chosen as almost royal, in which rest is provided for the weary armies.

[Note: Since many matters concerning ancient military service are treated here, we shall explain them briefly and in an orderly fashion for the benefit of readers. “From the standards”: properly speaking, these were solid images, such as eagles, wolves, and dragons; but here the term also denotes the banners, that is, the cloths suspended from a spear. Each legion and maniple had its own standards; anyone who withdrew farther from them than the distance at which the trumpet could be heard paid with his life. “Itinerary” means the same as the token given to announce the route. “He marches with weapons”: this was light work for those who carried weapons on their limbs, but in addition they usually carried grain and food, often for fifteen days, stakes, baggage, and other equipment. The word “lodging” was used in later Latin for the camp itself. “He arranges stationary camps”: understand “stations” or “lodgings,” so called from standing. Justus Lipsius denies that this is the name for a camp in which a soldier remains only a few days. But he had evidently not read this passage, since he nowhere mentions this intervening rest after every third day’s march. As for what Ambrose adds about a city in which rest is provided for exhausted armies, we believe he is designating the place selected for winter quarters. Finally, an “emperor” is not always the same as a king or ruler of the Roman world, although he may also be so called. The term may also denote one who undertakes to conduct a war under his own command and auspices, or one who has obtained this title of honor after killing the legally prescribed number of enemies in battle. Whoever desires more information about the whole subject should consult Lipsius himself, *On Roman Military Service*, book 5, dialogues 1, 9, 11, and 12.]

3. I would have you recognize that this is the prescribed law of marching, with Christ as leader, for the saints making their journey. For our fathers also set out from the land of Egypt across long stretches of territory; all their stationary camps and lodgings were recorded until they reached Kadesh, that is, the holy land.

These are the encampments of the children of Israel that Moses recorded at the Lord’s command. Let us therefore observe who arranged these lodgings and how the children of Israel ought to walk.

God went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, to cool those on the journey; by night, in a pillar of fire, to show the way to those walking and to drive away the darkness. The law of the ways was a pillar, both of fire and of cloud. Indeed, he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.

When he wished the army to rest from the labor of the journey, the pillar of fire did not move, nor did the cloud of light pass onward. But when he wished to move the army, the pillar of fire advanced at night, while the pillar of cloud advanced by day.

That pillar of cloud, in outward appearance, went before the children of Israel; in its mystery, however, it signified the Lord Jesus who would come in a light cloud, as Isaiah said (Isa. 19:1)—that is, in the Virgin Mary, who was a cloud according to Eve’s inheritance, but light according to the integrity of her virginity.

She was light because she did not seek to please a human being but the Lord. She was light because she had not conceived in iniquity, but gave birth when the Spirit came upon her; she bore not in sin but with grace.

4. This interpretation may also be understood in another way. Christ came in a light cloud into Egypt—that is, he came into this age by assuming a body. He came in a cloud, for the mist of the body overshadowed him; yet the flesh was light, since no sins of its own weighed it down.

How could he be weighed down by his own sins, who took away the sins of all peoples? “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

Yesterday it was read that Jesus was standing and wearing filthy garments; for he was carrying my sins. He took our garments upon himself so that he might clothe us in the splendor of immortality.

He came in a light cloud, like righteousness; for iniquity sits upon lead in the talent, whereas Christ is in the hearts of the righteous, in whom there were no sins [Note: The Roman edition reads, “in whom sins do not weigh heavily.” And so forth.].

Therefore it was rightly read today: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (Ps. 116:12). For our sake the Word assumed the weakness of the flesh; for our sake he hungered, was scourged, crucified, and died, so that for us—whose life had previously been held ignoble and degenerate—death might begin to be precious.

5. But let us return to the completion of the journey and the order of the lodgings. You too should follow spiritually this law of marching, so that you may go out from Egypt. Then, advancing from there, pitch your tabernacle at Succoth; let this be your first station.

Succoth is the first lodging, signifying a tabernacle. Therefore pitch the tabernacle that is within you and strengthen the station of your mind, so that you may remain rooted and founded in the faith of Christ.

The next lodging is at Marah, that is, in bitterness. Not all lodgings are equal. From there they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees. After bitterness, pleasant and fruitful things ought to follow, lest the people fail.

From there they came to Rephidim, which means “the praise of judgment.” Then Sinai follows, containing both the testing of the people and the promulgation of the Law.

The merits of the lodgings vary, because there can be no uninterrupted prosperity of life in this age. Thus the good commander supplied manna to the hungry people in one place; in another, by august providence, he commanded water to flow from the rock to quench the people’s thirst; elsewhere he gave the Law; elsewhere he granted triumphs, so that the army, strengthened by these benefits, might feel none of the hardship of its long journey.

6. Thus there was a type in that people, but in us there is the truth. Let us therefore entrust our journey to the leadership of the Lord Jesus, who first introduced the Law and earlier gave the promised land into the possession of his people through Jesus.

But even when Moses appeared to be the leader, Jesus was present with him. He was present, but not openly or visibly acting as the leader or ruler of the people; for he was waiting until Moses had completed his time. When that time was complete, Jesus succeeded him.

Therefore, if you consider the Scripture that says, “Their days will be one hundred and twenty years” (Gen. 6:3), you will see the mystery of the fullness of times [Note: The edition reads, “From the one hundred and twenty years.” The manuscripts agree with us.] and of the one hundred and twenty years, after which Moses rested on the mountain and Jesus openly assumed the leadership of the lodgings.

Then the people would no longer be under the fear of the Law, but, raised from the dead, would enjoy the fruit of eternal life. Let us therefore walk according to the teaching of the Law; let the Law of God be our way.

7. Walking this way, the Church says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys, like a lily among thorns” (Song 2:1). For the faith of the believing people has gone out into the whole earth, and Christ has planted his feet in a spacious place.

Therefore she rightly says that she is the flower of the field. Paul too was a flower, for he said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God” (2 Cor. 2:15). Truly he was a flower, since he could bring forth new and old things from the treasury of his heart.

The Church is also rightly called a lily. Just as a lily shines, so the works of the saints also shine. Most beautifully she is called the lily of the valleys, because grace shines forth more brightly in the humble.

But this lily is among thorns—that is, among Jews and heretics, and among the anxieties of this age, which prick the human mind and spirit. We may also understand it differently: just as a lily rises above thorns, so the Church of God shines above all assemblies.

8. It is also worth considering that this lily is surrounded by brightness, while what it contains within is red and itself has a good fragrance. This is because the flesh of Christ, surrounded as though by a wall of divine radiance [Note: Six manuscripts read “as though by the wall-like brightness of mortality.” Five read “as though by the wall-like brightness or splendor of divinity.” Others, with the edition, read “as though by the moral [brightness],” and so forth. The reading we have adopted is preferable, as the entire passage shows; Ambrose means nothing other than that Christ’s flesh was enclosed, as by a wall, by the splendor of divinity.] possessed the protection of heavenly grace.

Thus he says later: “My brother is white and red” (Song 5:10). White in divine radiance; red in the appearance of human color, which he assumed in the sacrament of the incarnation.

And rightly, what is red itself also smells good, because the flesh of Christ is without sin. The impious, when they handled it, defiled their hands; the saints, when they revered it, exhaled the fragrance of devotion.

9. The Lord Jesus received this fragrance from his fragrant Church and said: “Behold, my beloved is good” (Song 1:14–15). And the Church says to Christ: “Behold, my brother is good; behold, you are good … like an apple tree among the trees of the forest.”

Such an apple has a pleasing fragrance [Note: All editions read “it has a pleasant fragrance”; the manuscripts partly read “the grace of fragrance” or “of fragrances,” and partly read as we do in the text.], so that it surpasses the fragrance of all other fruits.

Christ, therefore, fastened to the wood, like an apple hanging on a tree, poured forth the good fragrance of the world’s redemption. He wiped away the foul stench of grievous sin and poured out the ointment of life-giving drink.

“Like an apple tree,” he says, “among the trees of the forest, so is my brother among the sons” (ibid.), because he softened the inmost hearts of human beings with the sweetness of his words, more than the prophets and apostles.

But an apple contains not only fragrance; it is also a pleasant food. Christ, therefore, is pleasant food.

10. “In his shadow I desired, and I sat” (Song of Songs II, 3). For he had received the Law, followed it, and ran along its path. Thus, resting in the Law, he rested in the shadow of Christ. A good shadow, which alone protects us from the heat of iniquity. Who could doubt that the Law of God is Christ’s shadow? What is the law of the feast day, of the new moon, and of the Sabbaths, except a shadow of things to come? What is the day according to the law of Moses—so that I may see six days, and then the seventh day, and thus the everlasting ages? What is the month according to the law of Moses—so that, knowing the month, I may know the new moon of the first of the month and the true holy offerings to be offered at the new moons? What is the year according to the law of Moses, which consists of those six days concerning which he says, “For six years a Hebrew shall serve, and in the seventh year he shall be released” (Deuteronomy XV, 12)—so that six years are found in which one works the land, but in the seventh year one shall remit it to resident aliens, the poor, and the beasts of the land? What is the seventh year, in which all debts owed to Hebrews are remitted? In this shadow rested the faith of the patriarchs and the holy devotion of the prophets.

[Note: [Col. 1253D] The edition and several manuscripts read, “which alone protects us from the sun of iniquity” [Col. 1254D]. Other manuscripts read in part, “protects us from heat and sun,” and in part, “protects us from heat.” Better are one Navarre manuscript and Laet.: “alone protects us from heat.”]

11. Thus the religious assembly, or the holy soul, says: “In his shadow I desired, and I sat” (Song of Songs II, 3). His shadow is the year of Jubilee. For who sees its mystery, so as to know face to face what was prescribed by the Law to be completed in the fiftieth year (Leviticus XXV)? A shadow are the feast days according to the Law, from the tenth day of the first month through the fourteenth, and from there through the twenty-first day of the month (Leviticus XXIII). What is that festival between the first and seventh months in that unnamed period?

[Note: [Col. 1254D] The old edition reads, “at that time, in the fiftieth year, which is called the Jubilee.” The Roman edition, with part of the manuscripts, rightly reads, “at that unnamed time”; for the time of that celebration is not expressly stated here. Moreover, the words “A shadow is sanctified freedom on the Sabbath” are absent from all the manuscripts; some of them connect the sequence of the sentence in this way: “At that time—is not the feast day a shadow?”]

A shadow is sanctified freedom on the Sabbath. A shadow is the feast day of the new moon of the seventh month, the memorial of trumpets of the seventh month, the tenth day, the Day of Atonement (Leviticus XXIII). You see that the first and the tenth are two feast days. Likewise, the fifteenth day is the Feast of Tabernacles for eight days. All these things are in shadow. In shadow are the first day called holy and the eighth day called holy, which are prescribed in the Feast of Booths according to the Law.

12. Imagine some believers from the circumcision, instructed in the Law, men careful in observance, and now enlightened by the knowledge of the Gospel and filled with spiritual grace. The Church, which sees Christ, receives the Bridegroom, and feeds upon his food, says in them: “In his shadow I desired, and I sat; and his fruit is sweet in my throat” (Song of Songs II, 3). What is his sweet fruit except the preaching of the Lord’s Passion, as he himself says: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb” (Psalm CXXVI, 3)? For what fruit could be sweeter in our throats than the remission of sins? And rightly the Church is a flower that announces the fruit—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—of whom it was said to Mary: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke I, 42).

13. Therefore, when she had tasted the fruit of sweetness, impatient, she hastens toward greater perfection, saying: “Bring me into the house of wine; establish love in me; strengthen me with perfumes; surround me with apples, for I am wounded by love. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field: if you awaken and restore love, until it wills” (Song of Songs II, 4–7). Rightly does she seek him, rightly does she desire him, because our Commander has ordered everything well along this course and journey. First of all, he judged that this tabernacle must be strengthened upon the foundation of faith. Then, if there is for us any harsh, arid, and precipitous dwelling-place, this commander nevertheless distinguishes what is confused, waters what is dry, and makes the desert fruitful. If there is any bitterness, temptation, or weakness, our leader both tempers what is bitter and softens what is troubling; he loosens what is hard and strengthens what is weak.

[Note: [Col. 1255D] Some manuscripts read, “this one distinguishes the encampments.”]

14. Thus, when the king of the earth wishes his army to rest, he chooses neither an obscure village, nor a place lacking provisions, nor a sandy and barren region, but a city distinguished by its buildings, well supplied and rich in resources; or a pleasant field green with pastures; or wooded and open country suitable for encampments. Therefore, if earthly kings know how to provide conveniences for those who follow them, how much more does God, who is good, know how to arrange what will benefit those who love him? And first, if an unknown route must be traversed, guides of the roads are chosen to precede the army. But these commanders consider this an insult to themselves; God, however, went before when the Hebrews were making their journey. Indeed, he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud. And so that you may know that he went before them: “God,” he says, “went before them on the way, showing them the road by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire; and the pillar of cloud did not fail by day” (Exodus XIII, 21–22).

15. The Church, following this preceding pillar of cloud, which did not fail, lest she herself fail, was refreshed by its shadow; and therefore she says: “In his shadow I desired, and I sat; and his fruit is sweet in my throat” (Song of Songs II, 3), because she was fed by the Lord, led into a place of pasture and to waters of refreshment. “Bring me into the house of wine” (Song of Songs II, 4). From there, with supplies prepared, she seeks to proceed to another dwelling-place in which she may receive the grace of mysteries and taste the sweetness of joy. Advancing from there along the true way, she says: “Establish love in me” (ibid.). Good is the encampment where there is the fullness of charity. “Strengthen me,” he says, “with perfumes; surround me with apples” (ibid., 3).

16. You have other dwelling-places to which the Church proceeds with delight. These dwelling-places are the cross of Christ and the tomb, in which the Church is wounded—but wounded by love. For the wound is what Christ received; but the ointment is what he poured out. The apple is what hung there. The Church tasted this apple and said: “And his fruit is sweet in my throat” (Song of Songs II, 3). And so that you may know that the Lord is the apple, you read above: “As an apple among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved” (ibid.).

We too acknowledge the wound when we preach Christ crucified; but we are a good fragrance to God, because the cross of Christ is a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks, but to us it is the power and wisdom of God. The Church is wounded by this wound when she proclaims the death of her Savior; but this wound is love. In the end, the one who does not believe denies, while the one who loves confesses. The Manichaean denies; the Christian confesses. Therefore it is written: “The wounds of a friend are beneficial, but the kisses of an enemy are voluntary” (Proverbs XXVII, 6). Beautifully, therefore, the Church says: “For I am wounded by love” (Song of Songs II, 5).

17. Let us bare our limbs to the good wound; let us bare them to the chosen arrow. This arrow is Christ, who says: “He made me like a chosen arrow” (Isaiah XLIX, 2). It is good, therefore, to be wounded by this arrow. This is no ordinary advance to a dwelling-place: not everyone can say that he has been wounded by love. The apostles said this when they were stoned for Christ’s sake and preached Christ. Paul said it when he was beaten three times with rods and argued day and night that Christ must be worshiped by the nations. The martyrs say this, those who are wounded for Christ; and because they have been found worthy to be wounded for his name, they love him more.

18. Coming, therefore, to this dwelling-place, to this advance, so as to offer her children for Christ and receive the wounds of love, the Church, as though finding good nourishment for faith and tasting the fruit of devotion herself, began to exhort the others, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet, like an apple” (Psalm XXXIII, 8). In the apple too there is a wound, but nevertheless it is sweet (Song of Songs II, 3).

Again she came to the valley of the grape-cluster and saw a grape of such great size that two could scarcely carry it: one to go ahead and another to follow. She tasted the mystery; she tasted it in Jesus son of Nave; she tasted it in Caleb, who said to the people: “We saw a land flowing with milk and honey” (Numbers XIII, 28). “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is.”

19. And the Church added these words: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field: if you awaken and restore love, until it wills” (Song of Songs II, 6–7). These too are dwelling-places along the royal road on which the Church proceeds. “There are many dwelling-places with my Father,” the Lord Jesus testifies (John XIV, 2); and: “Behold, I come, and I summon you” (ibid., 3).

Good is the dwelling-place of wisdom; and whether in his left hand or in his right, the dwelling-place is good, because it is the royal road. Therefore the wise messengers say: “We shall go by the royal road; we shall not turn aside to the right or to the left until we have passed beyond your boundaries” (Numbers XX, 17). The messengers sent by Moses said this to the king of Edom, that is, to the earthly king, because all earthly things, whether on the right or on the left, are evil.

Ignorance is an evil dwelling-place; lack of self-control is an evil dwelling-place. Therefore the Hebrew passes through these dwelling-places: he does not turn aside to them but passes through, so that he may arrive at the left and right of wisdom and remain there, where there are the riches of simplicity, glory, and length of life. “Length of life is in her right hand,” as Solomon says, “but in her left are riches and glory” (Proverbs III, 16). In the right hand is life; in the left is rest. Would that I might rest upon her left, so that I might not seek pillows. Woe to those who sew pillows, says Ezekiel (Ezekiel XIII, 18). The good leader prepares these dwelling-places for his Church and directs her journey along the paths of wisdom. Indeed, the Wise One praises her ways: “Her ways are good ways, and all her paths are peace” (Proverbs III, 17).

20. But because wisdom, goodness, and glory are perfect only if they possess love—for the fullness of the Law is love (Romans XIII, 10)—she wishes love to be awakened and restored: awakened in the Old Testament, restored in the New. Love is God, as we read (1 John IV, 8); love is Christ. He is awakened like a lion and a lion’s cub, so that the Lion of Judah may arise from the offspring. He is restored like one sleeping, like one reclining, because he was raised from the dead not by human majesty but by his own and the Father’s majesty. Hence Scripture says: “Who will awaken him?” (Genesis XLIX, 9). For neither an angel nor an alien power could awaken him, since he himself was awakening others.

Therefore, when he says here, “If you awaken or restore love until it wills” (Song of Songs II, 7), he is speaking of those who can fittingly preach his resurrection, so that they may kindle in their hearers the fervor of faith and devotion. Or Christ is awakened in those who approach him for the first time; he is restored in those who, after approaching, have fallen asleep. Christ therefore sleeps in the negligent and is awakened in the holy.

21. (Verse 33.) The Church therefore has paths by which she may walk; she has dwelling-places in which the saints rest. One of these says: “Establish for me, O Lord, a law, the way of your righteousness.” He rightly says, “Establish,” so that it may remain immovable and fixed in his breast and not be torn from his affection by any storm of the world; so that he himself may be a law to himself, having the work of the Law written in his heart.

21. “And I shall seek it,” he says, “always.” For what is sought is no small thing: the grace of paradise, the kingdom of God, the fellowship of angels, and the dwelling-place of immortality. It is not sought in one day, nor in two, nor in a few months; rather, it is always sought and sought in every way, so that many supports of merit may converge. The expression διὰ παντὸς signifies both all time and “throughout everything.” When, therefore, he says, “I shall seek always,” he says that it must be sought without end. But it is not enough to seek unless you understand what you seek.

22. (Verse 34.) Therefore he says: “Give me understanding, and I shall search out your Law, and I shall keep it with my whole heart.” First the whole mystery of the Law must be sought, then understood and searched out, and finally kept in the heart. Who can keep the Law of God unless he has received understanding? But whoever understands and searches it out is led, by searching, into the path of the commandments.

Here we should observe that the Law is righteousness and the commandment is judgment, as we also read in this passage. The way of the Law is to stand in the ways of the Law; there is also the way of righteousness, according to the first verse. There is therefore also a way of testimonies: “I delighted in the way of your testimonies.” And there is a way of commandments: “I ran along the way of your commandments.”

Let us therefore question these ways, so that it may be said to us: “Stand in the ways of the Law, and ask about the everlasting paths; see which is the better way, and walk in it” (Jeremiah VI, 16). When, therefore, we have all walked along the ways, we shall come to the end of all the ways, who says: “I am the way” (John XIV, 6). Christ, therefore, is the end of the ways; for he is “the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans X, 4). From this I dare to say that Christ is the end of righteousness, for he is righteousness; Christ is the end of the testimonies, of whom it was said: “Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord, and my servant whom I have chosen” (Isaiah XLIII, 10).

23. We therefore perceive how far we must walk in order to come to Christ. We must walk in the Law, because Christ is the end of the Law. Without the Law, therefore, one does not reach Christ. Hence it is clear that the heretics who do not accept the Law of the Old Testament, even if they say that they hold Christ, nevertheless cannot hold the end if they have not held the beginning. Jesus himself is the beginning and the end.

We must therefore walk according to the spiritual Law, so that we may come to the Lord Jesus, the end of the Law. We must follow the testimonies, so that we may be able to reach the great testimony, the Lord Jesus. We must also walk in the Lord’s precepts, so that we may reach the great commandment, concerning which you have read: “It was said to the ancients: You shall not kill … but I say to you” (Matthew V, 21–22)—that is, I speak above every commandment. Thus I shall not have said this presumptuously but truly: just as there is a Holy of Holies, so there is a Commandment of Commandments.

24. But so that we may be able to keep these things, let us ask the Lord for understanding. Let us understand what circumcision is. Jesus circumcised with stone knives and removed the reproach of Egypt from the children of Israel. The rock is Christ. May the Word of God circumcise you, and the sword of his mouth; then you will be free from the reproach of Egypt.

Circumcision must therefore be understood not of the body but of the heart. If you understand the Law, you will keep it in your heart. The Jew does not keep the Law in his heart; he recites the Law on his lips and does not know the Law. Indeed, he says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah XXIX, 13). How can one hold the Law who is far from the author of the Law? Let us consider what the third verse contains.

25. (Verse 35.) “Lead me into the path of your commandments, for I have desired it.” Who says this except the one who follows Christ? No one else can say this except the one who carries out what is written: “You shall walk after the Lord your God and cling to him, because he will lead you” (Deuteronomy XIII, 4). Hear how he will lead you: “Unless one takes up his cross and follows me, he is not worthy of me” (Matthew X, 38).

Christ therefore goes before, so that we may follow; the Word goes before. Christ is the beginning; therefore Wisdom says: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Proverbs VIII, 22). We perceive that Christ is both the beginning and the end of the ways.

I am not afraid that someone will say, “Then you assert that Christ was created?” I will answer: I say that he was created in the same way as I read that he was made—that is, made from a woman, made under the Law; in other words, created according to the assumption of flesh, according to the fact that he was born from a Virgin. He was created so that he might redeem creation; he became human so that he might free human beings from everlasting death. He was created so that he might show me the everlasting ways by which a human being can return to the kingdom of God.

Therefore, because he is the beginning of the ways of God, let us follow this beginning. He was the first to enter the way of the New Testament, so that he might make the road of devotion ready for us along this way. If we fast, he fasted before us; if for the Lord’s name we endure insults, he first endured them for our redemption. He offered his neck to the scourges and his cheeks to the palms of hands; he ascended the cross to teach that death is not to be feared. Indeed, as one going before, he said to Peter: “You follow me” (John XXI, 22). And therefore Peter completed the course, because he followed Christ.

26. (Verse 36.) The fourth verse follows: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice.” Some copies have “utility”; and I think it was changed because the utility of a good thing seems something to be sought rather than avoided. But because most people think that monetary profit is their advantage, if we read “utility,” we should understand that the Prophet is asking to turn away not from the soul’s benefit, but from monetary gain. The holy person does not know such profits; rather, he considers all these things loss, so that he may gain Christ.

And rightly so. For what we think is monetary profit is damage to the soul, because it is the loss of virtue. Therefore, according to those who have understood the passage in this way—that the Prophet wishes to incline his heart toward the testimonies and not toward avarice—we too agree. Would that, following the prayer of the holy man, we might pray what he prayed and imitate in our affections what we pray for.

What does it profit me if I pray that God turn my heart away from avarice, while I myself seek monetary gains day and night? If we pray with words, let us also share the prayer in our minds. Jesus hears our inner meaning too; and when he recognizes that the two do not agree—the speech and the desire—he does not answer the one who speaks. Therefore the one who wished to pray well said: “I shall pray with the spirit, and I shall pray with the mind; I shall sing psalms with the spirit, and I shall sing psalms with the mind” (1 Corinthians XIV, 15). He hears the one praying more readily if that person rejects avarice.

27. (Verse 37.) But because we are weak, and often, although we wish to turn our heart away from money, gold, or silver, we are captured by the sight of them, and when we see another’s field or building we desire it, the Prophet rightly added: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; give me life in your way.”

For whoever is in God’s way does not look upon vanities. Christ is the perfect way. Whoever, therefore, is in Christ—how can he look upon vanities, since Christ in his own flesh crucified all the vanities of this world? Let us therefore turn our eyes away from vanities, lest what the eye sees the soul desire.

For the moment, let us set aside the mystical interpretation. Would that by this interpretation we might recall those hastening toward the various spectacles of the circus games and the theater.

[Note: [Col. 1259D] The circus games consisted of various kinds of contests and were so called because they were held in the circus, that is, in a place of circular shape. The spectacles of the theaters included not only tragedies and comedies but also the dances of pantomimes. Lucian teaches in his *Dialogue on Dance* that these were dancers who represented a subject by gestures and signs without speech so naturally that the spectators seemed not only to see it but in some way to hear it. Hence Lucian says: “The spectator must understand a dance even though it is mute, and hear it although the dancer does not speak.” Cassiodorus likewise calls them in *Variarum* Book IV, final letter, “the most talkative hands of the dancers, their eloquent fingers, their clamorous silence, their silent exposition.” There is also this ancient epigram of uncertain authorship on the subject:

“Many tongues as there are limbs in the man—a wondrous art—  
which makes the joints speak while the mouth is silent.”

The same author, Cassiodorus, already cited, reports that this art was a part of music and was called by the ancients “mute”; see *Variarum* Book I, letter 20, and Book IV, final letter, as well as Fr. Juret’s annotation on the passage. Consult also Brissonius, *On the Meanings of Legal Words*, under the same term, and Vossius’s *Etymological Dictionary* under the word *mimus*. Moreover, since popular enthusiasm in Ambrose’s time burned for those empty spectacles, it is not surprising that he attacks this vice so frequently and shows himself in this matter inferior to neither Tertullian, Cyprian, Chrysostom, nor the others. Consult him in *The Flight from the World*, chapter 1, section 1, and below, Sermon 16, verses 59 and 64, but especially *On Duties*, Book II, chapter 30, and elsewhere.]

That is vanity which you see. You look at a pantomime: it is vanity. You look at wrestlers: it is vanity, because you see them wrestling for a green crown.

[Note: [Col. 1260D] Five manuscripts read, “wrestling with crowns of green leaves”; three, “with crowns of withered leaves”; one Vatican manuscript and the Roman edition, “wrestling for a cheap crown.” The true reading of the remaining manuscripts and editions is, “for a green crown.” At the Olympic games an olive crown was awarded; at the Isthmian games, a pine crown; and at the Nemean games, a crown of celery.]

For those are the true wrestlers who wrestle against the enticements of this age. Let not the arena of bodies seize your eyes. You look at running horses: it is vanity, because those who run are running in vain, since they cannot save the one who is ascending. Indeed, the very turning back teaches you that those run in vain who do not complete a straight course, forgetting what is above and desiring what is behind.

28. Christ is before us; before us is his prize, which he reached because he did not run uncertainly, nor turn back from his course, but pressed on. Direct your eyes toward him. Turn them away from spectacles; turn them away from every worldly display. Whenever you recognize the applause of the crowd, turn your eyes away from it; bend them down, lower them, and preserve them so that you may raise them to better things.

Raise them to heaven: by night, look upon the necklaces of the stars and the beautiful orb of the moon; by day, look upon the sun. Observe the sea; look around at the earth, so that every creature, made by divine workmanship, may nourish you. What beauty of form there is in the animals themselves! What magnificence in human beings! What beauty in birds! Look upon these things, and you will not see wickedness and contention in the city. Look upon these, and death will not enter through the windows of your eyes.

29. If you see a woman so as to desire her, death has entered through the window. If you see the property of a minor or a widow and desire to seize it, death has entered through the window. If you see another person’s necklaces, gold, or silver and desire to extort them, death has entered through the window.

Close this window, therefore, when you see the beauty of another man’s wife, so that death may not be able to enter. Let your eyes not see what belongs to another, lest your tongue speak perversely. Close your own window, therefore, lest it lie open to death as it enters. But beware also of another person’s window. For through the window of her own house the adulterous woman enters. She enters through her window when the wantonness of a shameless eye tempts someone.

Therefore block this window with the door of the word; do not be caught by the eyes of a prostitute or seized by her eyelids. But there is not only one window through which death habitually enters. There is also the window of words, through which the speeches of the prostitute pass. Therefore guard yourself from another man’s wife, lest she assault you with seductive words; for she enters through the window of her own house.

Death enters through kisses; therefore beware lest she bind you with the snares of her lips. Death enters if a prostitute kisses you. Death enters if you quickly consent to the one speaking.

[Note: [Col. 1261D] Some manuscripts read: “Death enters if you speak; death enters if you speak much.”]

Death enters if you speak much, for sin is incurred through excessive talk. Death enters even if you do not speak and are afraid to confess Christ. “For confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Romans X, 10). Death enters even through the openings of the ears; therefore the ears must be fenced with thorns, so that you may shut out the enticements of the prostitute’s speech. These are the moral interpretations.
