30. There are also mystical eyes that you must turn away from vanity. There is also a vanity of the senses which the eyes of your soul must not see, because those see it whom the Apostle condemns.

[Note: [Col. 1261D] After the words “whom the Apostle condemns,” the editions continued: “Learn what the vanity of the senses is, which your mystical eyes must not see.” But these words are found in none of the Gallic manuscripts and do not appear necessary to the sense.]

Let us therefore learn from the Apostle himself, as our authority, what the vanity is and what the eyes are (Ephesians IV, 17–18). For it is clear that there are many who have been darkened in their understanding by the vanity of their senses and alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their hearts.

[Note: [Col. 1262D] Ten manuscripts add: “and alienated from the life of God,” and so forth.]

Yet the Apostle calls those people Gentiles. Let that Gentile be ignorant of what he has not learned; let him be ignorant of what he has not believed. You, however, may not be ignorant of what you confess.

Christ did not come in vanity but in power.

[Note: [Col. 1262D] The editions add after “but in power”: “not in antiquity but in newness.” These words are absent from the manuscripts. Some, however, read “in truth” instead of “in power.”]

He did not inflate the human mind but gave it life; he did not produce blindness of heart but illumination of the mind. He inflamed your heart so that you might grasp the order of the heavenly commandments, the substance of the soul, the grace of the life to come, and what our condition will be after these things.

31. Raise your mind, therefore, and use your natural intelligence. You were made in the image of God so that you might look upon heavenly things and not seek earthly ones. Do not bend your neck to be weighed down by the burden of the world. Do not pant after gold and silver,

[Note: [Col. 1262D] Some manuscripts read: “lest you offer yourself to be bound to the world.” Several others read: “lest you offer yourself to be bound to moneybags.”]

lest you offer yourself to be bound by the chains of the age.

Therefore the Lord said: “Do not possess gold or silver” (Matthew X, 9), lest the greedy desire for gold and silver possess us. Do not insert your neck into the snares of the devil. Avarice strangles the poor person in this world; but the rich person is suffocated forever by his own snares. His understanding is in vanity; he walks in darkness, because he labors over things that cannot benefit him.

The anxiety of this life is vanity. Therefore we ought to place our delight not in revelry and drunkenness, nor in bodily pleasures, but in knowledge of the heavenly commandments. He runs in vanity who seems to himself to abound in worldly successes, which pass away like a shadow. Turn your eyes away, therefore, lest they see vanity.

32. But it is not enough for you to turn them away, lest perhaps you wish to do so but cannot, while the devil casts spectacles of vanities before you and inserts incentives to pleasure. Ask that the Lord turn your eyes away. This too is the grace of God and the Lord’s gift: that he turn the eyes of our soul away from the affairs of this world. For all blessedness comes from the Lord.

“Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord and who has not looked upon vanities and false madness” (Psalm XXXIX, 5). The one who does not look upon these things is blessed; the one who looks upon them is insane and mad. Therefore let each person recover his senses from the frenzy of worldly desires, which disturb the mind and soul so greatly that he can no longer remain master of himself.

33. If you are placed in a tossing ship, you turn your eyes away from the bilge, lest it provoke vomiting in you. If, walking through a city, you encounter something with a foul odor, you flee far away and turn aside. If something appears that horrifies your eye, it closes or turns away.

You are tossed upon the sea of this world; the bilge of vices pours in. In this ship of your body the surge of desires is stirred, yet you do not turn away the eyes of your soul, lest they see the bilge of lust, lest they look upon the filth of this world, lest an unclean stench fill the nostrils of your mind, in which the Holy Spirit is accustomed to dwell, so that you may be able to say: “The divine Spirit who is in my nostrils” (Job XXVII, 3).

Let the nostrils of your soul therefore be turned away from the stench of various crimes, for in them there is, as it were, a distinctive sign of judgment. Hence it is said to the Bride: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, looking toward the face of Damascus” (Song of Songs VII, 4). The ointment of the true Priest, which descends from the head into the beard—that is, the divine fragrance, the fragrance of spiritual grace that was in the Father, descended in Christ, and through the mystery of the Incarnation came down upon the earth so that all things might be filled with the ointment poured out—stands forth in the lofty power of judgment and fills the nostrils of the soul.

Thus it may distinguish what is kindly from what is foul: the sweet things of the saints, who can say, “For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians II, 15), from the foul things of sinners.

34. These are the nostrils like the lofty tower of Lebanon, raised above the world; and therefore they look toward the face of Damascus, that is, toward the Gentile people, smelling its faith, by whose grace the stench of its sins would be wiped away.

The face of Damascus, therefore, is the faith of the nations, shaded by no covering, concealed by no garment, naked and free, directed more toward heaven than toward earth. The nostrils of the Church watch and look upon it, gathering from it whatever is sweet and fragrant in its breath and grace. And rightly are its nostrils like the tower of Lebanon, because in the sacrifices there is the Church’s sweet fragrance, in which there is a victim of good odor, the remission of sins.

35. Take these nostrils, therefore, O human being, so that you may distinguish what is flower-bearing from what gives off a foul odor; and then the Lord will give you life. For when he perceives that you ask him to turn the eyes of your mind away from vanity, he cooperates with your soul: if it is captured by some outward appearance, or is not bent by harshness or weakness, he bends it by the yoke of the Word and governs it with his reins, so that by God’s will it may be led away from vices and receive the fragrance of eternal life.

For perfect life is not here; this life is in shadow. Therefore, so that the human being Christ Jesus might be born from a Virgin, the power of the Most High overshadowed the mother who was to give birth. He descended in shadow, beginning to work human salvation from the shadow, and bringing it to completion through the love of the eternal sun.

This life, therefore, is a shadow. Hasten to the sun, so that it may defend you from the cold of this shadow and pour summer heat upon you. Hence he urges us to pray that our flight not occur in winter or on the Sabbath (Matthew XXIV, 20), signifying not a time or a day but preventing us from growing cold in merits and from being barren of good works.

36. (Verse 38.) Learn now how he turns the eyes of the one whom the Lord has mercy upon away from vanity. We can understand this from what follows, for he adds: “Establish your word for your servant in your fear” (Psalm CX, 10).

The Prophet says that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. What, however, is the beginning of wisdom except renouncing the world? For to have worldly understanding is folly. Indeed, the Apostle says that the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God (1 Corinthians I, 20).

But the fear of the Lord itself, unless it is according to knowledge, is of no benefit; rather, it is exceedingly harmful. The Jews have zeal for God, but because they do not have it according to knowledge, they incur a greater offense against the deity in that very zeal and fear.

They circumcise their infants and observe the Sabbaths: they have the fear of God. But because they do not know that the Law is spiritual, they circumcise the body and not their heart. They fear lighting a fire on the Sabbath, even though the Law of sanctification forbids the fire of lust to be kindled.

37. And why should I speak of the Jews? There are also among us those who have the fear of God, but not according to knowledge, establishing harsher precepts that the human condition cannot bear. There is fear in this, because they seem to themselves to be providing for discipline and demanding an act of virtue; but there is ignorance in it, because they do not show consideration for nature and do not take account of what is possible.

Let fear not be irrational. True wisdom indeed begins with the fear of God, and there is no spiritual wisdom without the fear of God; likewise, fear ought not to exist without wisdom.

Holy fear is a kind of foundation of the Word. Just as an image is set upon a base and then has greater grace when the statue has been placed upon its base and has received firmness for standing, so the Word of God, or the rational principle of God, is better established and more firmly rooted in holy fear—that is, in the breast of one who fears the Lord—lest the Word slip from the heart of a person, lest the birds come and take it away from the careless and indifferent disposition.

[Note: [Col. 1263D] *Rationabile*, that is, “reason” or “rational principle.” For λόγιον (*logion*) and λόγος (*logos*) signify both “word” and “reason.” This is a Greek construction in which a neuter adjective is used in place of a substantive.]

But fear itself also seems to be fitted to the Word of God for usefulness and made firm by it, so that it is not alien to knowledge, just as a statue placed upon a base is not alien to grace. Fear, therefore, is the place of the Word, just as its place is in peace.

[Note: [Col. 1264D] Some written manuscripts read: “Fear is a certain devotion to the Word,” and so forth.]

Fear is a kind of station of the Word; the word of fear is discipline. For fear full of discipline does not waver toward falling.

[Col. 1264D] **38.** And since we have said that fear is the foundation of the word, let no one think that we have introduced anything foreign to the Scriptures. Let him hear what is read from the word of God in the *Song of Songs*: “His legs are marble columns, founded upon golden bases” (Song 5:15). This signifies that the apostles are the columns of the Church, founded upon holy fear. For just as Peter, James, John, and Barnabas appeared to be columns of the Church—and whoever conquers this age becomes a column of God, as the one who says, “I have strengthened its columns” (Ps. 74:4), confirms—so also the golden base is fear full of discipline, because it is the beginning of wisdom. Therefore, in the fear of the wise, apostolic preaching is established like a column upon a golden base. Thus, for the utterance of Christ and the apostolic sermon, the tribunal is the fear of the righteous, and the golden base is full of prudence; while the good image, as the likeness of truth, is the speech of the saints.

And see that the fear of the saints is, as it were, a golden base. Read Isaiah: observe how many things he has placed beneath fear, so as to fashion fear into something blameless and good: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding,” he says, “the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of holy fear” (Isa. 11:2). How many things he has placed beneath fear, so that it might have something to follow! It is shaped by wisdom, instructed by understanding, directed by counsel, strengthened by power, governed by knowledge, and adorned by piety. Remove these things from the fear of the Lord, and it becomes an irrational and foolish fear, one of those of which it is said: “Outside were conflicts, inside fears” (2 Cor. 7:5), by which Paul too would have been afflicted unless he had had the Lord as his comforter.

**39.** Nor is what is said in Proverbs without purpose: “Then you will understand the fear of the Lord” (Prov. 2:5). What does “then” mean? That is: when you have called upon wisdom and given your voice to prudence; and when you have sought it as money and searched it out as treasures, “then you will understand the fear of the Lord” (ibid., 3–4). Therefore he says, as though upon a good foundation: “Establish your word for your servant in your fear.” It is a prayer full of discipline, by which we are taught how we ought to pray: every sentence is instruction in prayer. And because he has taught us to pray, the seventh verse shows what the effect of this prayer is.

**40. (Verse 39.)** “Take away from me my reproach, which I have suspected.” This seems to be expressed somewhat obscurely, but the Apostle explained what appeared obscure here when he said: “I am conscious of nothing against myself; but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:4). For he knew that he was a human being, and therefore guarded himself as best he could, lest after receiving the sacraments of baptism he should sin; and for that reason he was not conscious of guilt against himself. Yet because he was human, he confessed himself to be a sinner, knowing that Jesus alone is the true light, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found; that he alone is justified who is truly free from falling.

So too the Prophet, although he desired to avoid sin, nevertheless desired, as it were, that God should be the remover of his sin. He wanted the reproach that he had suspected to be taken away—either because he had thought of it in his heart but had not committed it, and although it had been erased by repentance, he was nevertheless anxious lest his reproach might still somehow remain. Therefore he beseeches God to take it away, since God alone knows what even the person who committed it may not know. Indeed, the Prophet himself says elsewhere: “You know my reproach” (Ps. 68:20).

Although this reproach belongs to Christ, it is not truly reproach but the glory of God; for the cross of Christ is a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks.

**41.** To them, therefore, it is reproach; to me it is strength, by which I drive back the adversary and conquer the world. To me it is wisdom, by which I escape the snares of folly. Moses preferred this reproach to the treasures of Egypt. “Considering,” he says, “the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt” (Heb. 11:26).

If your reproach is glory, Lord Jesus, how great is your glory? What, then, shall we be through participation in your glory, we who are made glorious by your reproach?

“I gave my back to scourges, my cheeks to blows, but I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting.” Behold your reproach, Lord, in which is the salvation of all, in which is the redemption of the world: through this reproach we have begun not to be ashamed, though we were ashamed, and not to be confounded, though we were confounded. For it is written: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. 33:6).

We do not wish this reproach to be taken away from us—the reproach of the cross of the Lord Jesus, by which our reproaches are taken away. For just as he was made a curse so that he might erase our curses, and was made human so that he might lift the weaknesses of humanity, so he was made reproach so that he might remove the reproaches of all.

**42.** He did not take away reproaches at one time only, nor once for all: he removes them daily. We fall into sin—not one sin, but many—and are covered with reproach and shame. We come to baptism; every sin is erased, and with the sin, the reproach. The Lord Jesus took away my reproach by his reproach, because he was crucified for me; because “all of us who were baptized into Christ were baptized into his death” (Rom. 6:3). I have nothing that I need ask to be taken away.

But after baptism I fell into reproach, and I must do penance, so that I may say: “Take away from me my reproach.” If I do not do penance, how shall I say, “Take away from me my reproach,” when the very fact that I do not do penance is itself the reproach of sin? But if I do penance as I ought, I rightly say: “Take away from me my reproach, which I have suspected”; for your judgments are sweet.

[Col. 1265D] *To the word “sweet,” an old edition and certain Paris editions added: “How one ought to confess.” But these words are found neither in the Vatican manuscripts nor in ours.*

**43.** Why should I fear to confess? Why should I fear to declare my sins? Why should I hesitate to mention my reproach before him whose judgments are sweet? What is severe in others is sweet in Christ, pleasant in Christ, because he himself is sweet. Therefore: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9).

His judgments are sweet to the one who confesses, because he himself said: “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities . . . and I will remember them no more. But you, remember, and let us enter into judgment; declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:25–26). His judgments are sweet to the one who does penance, because he himself said: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance” (Luke 15:7). If, then, the judgments of the Lord are sweet, let us strive to receive the fruit of his sweetness.

**44.** Do you wish to know how sweet the judgments of the Lord are? “The impious do not rise again in the judgment” (Ps. 1:5). But those who rise again in the judgment have hope of pardon, because they have believed.

[Col. 1266D] *Ambrose regularly distinguishes between the impious and sinners in this way: he defines the impious as those who have never believed in Christ, but sinners as those who have embraced faith in him yet, overcome by the allurements of desire, have committed serious sins. Compare this passage with what the holy Doctor teaches in his exposition of Psalm 1, on verse 5, section 56; and see also what we noted there.*

They are not impious, though they may be sinners; they have faith, and although they have not avoided guilt, they believe through faith. “He who believes in him is not judged” (John 3:18). Sweet, therefore, are the judgments to those who believe.

Those who do not believe, however, have not been condemned by Christ’s judgment—he came not to judge the world but to save and redeem it. Rather, they have undergone the judgment of their own impiety, because they refused to believe in the forgiveness of sins. For they cannot share in the benefit of one whom they refused to acknowledge. Therefore those who did not believe in him seem unworthy of his judgment. Recognize what his judgment is from his own words: “This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world” (ibid., 19). Sweet, therefore, is what is light; sweet is the judgment that is preceded by mercy. For it is written: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Ps. 100:1).

**45. (Verse 40.)** And because he has recognized the sweetness of the judgments, he says: “Behold, I have desired your commandments; in your righteousness give me life.” He calls the judgments good by their authority. Behold how he loves the freedom of faith, he who gave freedom. He rejoices to be loved, he who came into this world because he loved this world. He demands to be loved, he who loves all, because he is love.

He desired the commandments of God like a good servant, like a diligent worshiper. He desired them not as a lover desires an adulterous union, nor as a greedy man desires money, nor as a sensual man desires wantonness. Of such things the Law says: “You shall not desire.” But it commanded that the Lord God be loved, and loved with a tender and inward affection of desire.

And because the one who loves is a friend, while the one who fears is a servant, he is like a friend who has done everything that the Lord commanded him: “You are my friends,” he says, “if you do what I command you” (John 15:14).

[Col. 1267D] *An old edition has: “and loved with tenderness,” that is, loved with a certain tenacious and inward affection, etc.; another has: “and loved with a maternal affection.” The manuscripts, finally, have the reading we have printed.*

**46.** “In your righteousness give me life.” He dares to say this because the true life is the life that lives according to the righteousness of God, in which the apostles lived—or rather, in which they live. For there are people who, while living, are dead; and there are those who, though dead, live. Some descend alive into hell; others, though dead in body, live through their merits. For there are those who “will not taste death until they see the Son of Man returning on the day of judgment,” when the saints will rise with glory.

**1033 — SIXTH SERMON. Vau**

**1.** The sixth letter is *Vau*, whose interpretation is “He is, and there is no other.” Or its interpretation is: “And he.”

[Col. 1267D] *Here the manuscripts and editions vary remarkably. In some places it is rendered: “whose interpretation sounds either thus: ‘Not he’;” another interpreter says: “‘And he is not,’ he says.” Elsewhere: “‘. . . not like him’;” another interpreter, and so forth. In some copies its interpretation is: “‘And he’;” in the old edition, “‘like him’”; another interpreter says: “‘And he is not,’ he says.” In some copies also it reads: “‘He also is’;” another interpreter says: “‘There is no other.’” Finally, several manuscripts have the reading printed in the text. We have followed this reading because Ambrose himself confirms it below, in section 4.*

**[Col. 1267D] 2. (Verse 41.)** “And let your mercy come upon me, Lord, your salvation according to your word.”

Since the interpretation of the letter is somewhat obscure, I have thought that its meaning should be gathered from the sequence of the psalm. For when the Prophet asks, “Let your mercy come upon me, Lord; let your salvation come,” there is no doubt whom he asks to see—that is, the one in whom both the fruit of mercy and salvation may come.

Indeed, in an earlier passage he asked the same thing in Psalm 84, in which he prophesied the coming of the Lord Jesus more clearly. It is well known what land he asks to be blessed: namely, that land which contracted sin in Adam, to which it was said, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). God had cursed not the element of the nature of flesh, but the flesh of the transgressors.

[Col. 1268D] *So the old edition and the manuscripts read, except that in some manuscripts the word “of flesh” is omitted; and in those same manuscripts the word is “above,” where the editions read “having overcome.” The Roman edition, however, reads: “not the element of earth, nor the substance or nature of flesh, but, in the element, the transgressing flesh.” Therefore the earth—that is, the flesh—is blessed in Christ, etc.*

The flesh, therefore, is blessed in Christ, so that the flesh formerly under the curse may be freed. The flesh is blessed which the blessed Son of God assumed when he took upon himself the condition of humanity.

**3.** And therefore he added: “God, you will turn and give us life, and your people will rejoice in you. Show us, Lord, your mercy, and give us your salvation. I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me, for he will speak peace to his people and to his saints, and to those who turn their hearts toward him. Nevertheless, his salvation is near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land” (Ps. 84:7 and following).

The whole of this passage proclaims the Lord Jesus, who gave life to the dead: Lazarus before his passion, and many at the time of his own passion. He is mercy itself, since he is the forgiveness of sins. Therefore he says, “Show,” so that he may be seen in the body. For no one could see God in his majesty, since “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

The eager Prophet desires to see the one whom he hopes to hold; if he sees him, he desires to grasp him with his own hands. Therefore he says: “And give us your salvation.” God’s salvation is power; God’s salvation is Christ. Therefore this salvation is near those who fear him.

Christ was far from us; he was far from the nations. He descended to earth and became near, and we began not to fear. For the one who fears Christ is not subject to fear but to devotion. This fear is one of piety, not of weakness. Therefore, nothing is lacking to those who fear him.

But how did he become near? Hear: “So that glory may dwell in our land.” Who is glory except the Lord Jesus? Hence the Apostle Paul also says: “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory” (2 Cor. 1:3). The Father rightly delights in him, because he is the Father’s glory. Whoever separates him from the Father inflicts the greater injury upon the Father, whom he wishes to be without glory. Whoever does not consider him equal to the Father also judges the Father to be inferior, although no other word could praise the Father more greatly, since Christ is his highest praise and glory.

**4.** He is therefore asked to come as God’s salvation. It is he who is asked for—that is, the Lord Jesus—and there is no other, as the interpretation of the letter has it.

Or even in this way the Father alone is not asked: “He also is,” that is, the Son too is asked, and when asked, he comes and gives salvation to the world. Therefore *sōtēr* (σωτήρ), that is, “savior”; therefore Jesus, as the angel said: “He will save his people” (Matt. 1:21).

When the Prophet called, he was present, to confirm what is said: even while we are still speaking, he says to us, “Here I am” (Isa. 58:9).

**5.** He is present because he was raised up by the daughters of Judea, as though raised up by the daughters of Jerusalem. The Church hears the sound of his voice and says: “The voice of my kinsman. Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills” (Song 2:8).

The book is like a company, containing many noble characters, like a triumphal troop, and signifying many actions which we can understand more readily than retain in their fully expressed form. For when the Bride heard the Bridegroom coming and speaking with certain companions traveling together, she says: “The voice of my kinsman.”

While he is speaking with the daughters of Jerusalem and asking them to awaken and raise up the Bridegroom, suddenly, as though hearing from far away the sound of a voice sent forth, she says: “The voice of my kinsman,” announcing the one whom she had previously sought to have announced to her, whom she desired to be raised up by others. Now, believing that he had been raised by the Father and was coming at her request, she joyfully says: “The voice of my kinsman.” He rightly added “my cousin,” so that not others, but his cousin alone, might claim his coming for herself.

[Col. 1269D] *The editions and not a few manuscripts read “as though triumphal companies”; eight of these, however, read “as though a triumphal company.” This is the better reading. A “triumphal company” was called a troop of senators and other illustrious men with whom the emperor proceeded when celebrating a triumph. See Josephus Laurentius, *Polymathia*, book 3, section 11; also John Prusinus, *Roman Antiquities*, book 10, chapter 29, and others.*

**6.** “Behold,” she says, “this one comes.” I am still seeking him, and he has already come; I am still gathering support so that he may come, and he is already near. I desire love to be raised up for me; I consider myself wounded by love; and love itself hastens all the more toward me.

I said, “Come”; he leaps and bounds. I ask him to come with grace; he produces an increase of graces. As he comes, he brings increases of grace with him, and by coming he gains, because he too is eager to please his beloved.

He leaps over the heights in order to ascend to the Bride; for the bridal chamber of the Bride is the tribunal of Christ.

[Col. 1269D] *Thus twelve manuscripts read. The edition, however, together with others, has: “He leaps over the Church.” We think this alteration was introduced so that the Church might be set in opposition to the Synagogue, which is named in the following clause. But Adam is mentioned here for the reason that it may be shown that the state of what is called innocence, and the law of nature, were not alien to Christ.*

He leaps over Adam; he bounds over the Synagogue. He leaps over the nations; he bounds over the Jews.

Let us watch him leaping. He leaps from heaven into the Virgin, from the womb into the manger, from the manger into the Jordan, from the Jordan to the cross, from the cross into the tomb, and from the tomb into heaven.

Prove to me, David, that he leaps; prove to me that he runs—for you said: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course: his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to its summit; and there is no one who can hide himself from his heat” (Ps. 18:6–7).

Therefore even now he leaps, and even now he runs from the heart of the Father over his saints, from east to west, from north to south. He is the one who ascended over the setting sun; he is the one who ascended over the heavens of heavens toward the east. He ascends over the mountains; he ascends over the hills.

**7.** Would that I, wretched as I am, might say—and that my soul might say: “Behold, this one comes,” and that he might come not over earthly places, not over valleys, but leaping over the mountains. For God is the God of mountains, “and not of valleys.”

[Col. 1270D] *The Roman edition omitted the words “and not of valleys,” although all the manuscripts and the old editions contain them.*

Where, then, does he leap? He leaps over the mountains. If you are a mountain, he leaps over you. He leaps over Isaiah, he leaps over Jeremiah, he leaps over Peter, John, and James. “The mountains are around him” (Ps. 124:2). If you cannot be a mountain and do not prevail, at least be a hill, so that Christ may ascend over you; and if he bounds over you, let him bound in such a way that the shadow of his passage may protect you.

[Col. 1270D] *In almost all the manuscripts the words “so that he may bound” had been omitted.*

**8.** We have spoken of Christ and the Church; let us speak of the soul and the Word. The soul of the righteous is the Bride of the Word.

If it desires, longs for, and prays—and prays continually, prays without any hesitation, and directs its whole attention toward the Word—suddenly it seems to hear the voice of the one whom it does not see, and inwardly it recognizes the fragrance of his divinity. This is what usually happens to those who believe well.

Suddenly the nostrils of the soul are filled with spiritual grace, and it senses the breath of his presence breathing upon it, the one whom it seeks. And it says: “Behold, this is the very one whom I seek, the very one whom I desire.”

**9.** Do we not, whenever we think about something in the Scriptures and cannot find its explanation, while we are doubting and searching, suddenly seem to see lofty teachings ascend over the mountains? Then, appearing to us as though upon the hills, the Word illuminates the mind, so that it pours into our understanding what had seemed difficult to discover.

Thus the Word, as though absent, becomes present in our hearts. And again, when something is somewhat obscure to us, the Word seems to withdraw, and we desire the coming of one who is absent. Then, appearing to us once more, it shows itself to us as though it were present in the things we seek to understand.

The Word therefore frequently leaps in each person’s heart: it bounds away and departs, and returns if you follow, seek, and ask—through the grace of the faithful and the discussion of teachers—for the Word that had gone out and passed away to be raised again. So did she who sought and found him say: “My brother passed by; my soul went out at his word” (Song 5:6).

**10.** Therefore, if he leaps over the mountains, follow him; and if he leaps over the hills, follow him. For hunters of the Lord are found in the mountains and hills, investigating those who are captured for life. Thus God said through Jeremiah: “Behold, I am sending many fishermen . . . and many hunters, and they shall hunt them upon every mountain and upon every hill” (Jer. 16:16).

Let the people of God therefore be sought and found there, in the teaching, grace, and discipline of Peter and Paul; let them not be in the valley, where there is weeping, but on the mountains, from which Christ enlightens each person.

When we read Peter, Christ enlightens us. When we read Paul, Christ enlightens us. Paul healed, but Christ enlightened, because when the name of the Lord Jesus was invoked, the one who had been healed by his gift rose. Peter raised a dead woman, but Christ enlightened. Therefore it says: “You enlighten wonderfully from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. 75:5).

**11.** We, then, who cannot be mountains, should stand upon the mountains or hills. Thus, when the Lord sends his fishermen and hunters to hunt those who are upon every mountain or every hill—that is, those who conduct their whole life according to the precepts of the Law and the Prophets and according to knowledge of the New and Old Testament—they may find us ready and gather us like good ears of grain, the reapers having been sent at the proper time.

For if anyone is found outside the mountain or hill, he cannot be gathered as good grain by those who will be sent—as we may mention another comparison—to separate the wheat from the chaff.

The Lord therefore has ministers skilled in many operations. They are fishermen, hunters, and reapers all at once.

**12.** If, at the time of harvest, when they are sent forth, you wait ripe in merit, you will be able to behold him leaping over the mountains, and you will see the Lord Jesus like a young roe or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel (Song 2:9).

For he leaps over the Church, which is the house of bread, because he strengthens the hearts of the faithful. Rightly is he like a young doe, because the doe feeds in high places.

She is called *Dorcas* from seeing. For the *dorcadion* has keener sight.

[Col. 1271D] *All the editions read: “For the sight of the dorcadion is keener.” Three manuscripts have *dioraticon*, three *diorcation*, five *diorcaticon*, and one *dorcaticon*—not badly, if “animal” or “creature” is understood. For all of them have: “It has keener sight.” Nevertheless, no one who examines the sequence carefully should doubt that *dorkadion* (δορκάδιον), that is, “young roe,” ought to be read. Again, where the editions and some manuscripts have: “What is more fitting than Christ?” or, as some have it, “What is more acute than Christ?” the greater number of copies read: “What is keener than Christ?”*

What is keener than Christ, who sees the Father whom no one sees? Or if anyone has seen him in Christ, the Son himself has revealed him.

Rightly is he like a fawn of the deer: a fawn, as a son, in whom the power of his father’s nature has grown, so that hidden things do not escape him, serpents flee from him, and poisons do not harm him. Therefore, when the serpent that had been produced from humanity was brought out from its hiding places, it said: “Why have you come before the time to torture us?” (Matt. 8:29).

**13. (Verse 42.)** Let us therefore watch this fawn leaping, so that we may be unable to fear the serpent.

David did not fear it. Indeed, he spoke of such serpents: “And I shall answer those who reproach me with a word, because I have hoped in your words.” Like a good deer that had drunk from springs of water, he did not fear the breath of human serpents or the poisons of slanderers.

The serpent was not harmful to him but his prey. The venom of serpentine speech was food to him, and so was the food of praise, of which he said: “God, do not keep silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of deceit have opened against me” (Ps. 108:2). He was fattened by the words of poisoners.

[Col. 1272D] *Ambrose seems here to allude to that verse from Book 3 of the* Georgics *about the serpent:*

> “Raising threats and swelling its hissing neck.”

*But below he more clearly reproduces another passage from the same book:*

> “Erect toward the sun, its mouth flashes with three-forked tongues.”

*To flash or dart has the same sense as extending and drawing back, a metaphor taken from a kind of game played with extended and contracted fingers. On this see Erasmus,* Adages, *chiliad 1, centuria 8, adage 27: “Worthy to play finger-games with in the dark.”*

They raised mouths hissing with slanders and surrounded the innocent man with words of hatred. A good deer placed among many serpents did not fear: a deer of friendship and a young creature of grace.

They pretended love but poured out slander. “But I,” he says, “was praying” (ibid.). A good deer grazed unharmed among vipers. They flashed with three-forked tongues, but holy prayer nourished him—or rather, he offered food to those who slandered him.

He answered his slanderers with a word; for the word is food. Therefore, “man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4:4).

“They saw me,” he says, “and shook their heads” (Ps. 108:25). They cursed, but I blessed. They cursed who slandered; I blessed because I preached the word of the Lord.

**[Col. 1272C] 14.** How good it is to endure insult and not return insult! Whoever does not know how to become angry with the one who insults him gains God as his protector. What a grace of patience there is in the words: “They themselves will curse, but you will bless” (ibid., 2)!

Blessed is the one who does not feel curses. Blessed is the one whom curses do not disturb. The one who excludes human curses through the gift of divine blessing cannot be moved by a curse. The one who has the word cannot feel the curse; and the one who always has the word in his mouth cannot return a curse.

**15.** But there is also a good serpent, one whom this deer does not injure. “Be wise,” he says, “as serpents” (Matt. 10:16). And: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14).

My serpent was prefigured in the bronze serpent. My serpent was lifted up upon that wood. A good serpent—a truly good serpent—which poured remedies, not poisons, from its mouth. The one who knows how to worship this serpent need not fear serpents.

Of this serpent she who loves him says: “Behold, he is behind our wall, looking through the windows, appearing above the nets. My kinsman answers and says to me: Arise, come, my neighbor, my beautiful one, my dove; for behold, winter has passed, the rain has gone away and departed, and flowers have appeared on the earth” (Song 2:9, 12).

He is plainly a serpent who, when winter has passed, wished to shed the garment of his body, so that he might bloom in beautiful splendor.

The deer and the serpent are therefore the same. The deer has the horns of the Law and of grace—for its two horns are the two Testaments—is swift in step and tireless in movement, and can easily traverse the whole world in a single moment, celebrated everywhere.

He is also the good serpent, whose front parts do not bite with the tooth of the Law, and whose rear parts do not wound with the gentleness of the Gospel. He protects his head from injury, for he came not to abolish the Law but to guard it from the interpretations of the faithless. He spreads his tail freely for scourging, wishing rather to chastise adversaries than to destroy them.

The good serpent readily slips into the lap of the beloved and into the innermost bosom of the mind; without any perceptible touch, he entwines fire in the bones and feeds upon the very inward parts.

[Col. 1273D] *Since the words “of Gervasius and Protasius” are written above this passage like a title in several manuscripts, and since what follows—“For we celebrate”—clearly indicates that this sermon was delivered on the sacred day of the revelation of those holy martyrs, it should be noted that the words above, “without entangling himself through any touch,” undoubtedly imitate Virgil, Aeneid 7, concerning the serpent slipping into the bosom of Amata, wife of King Latinus:*

> “He slipped between her garments and tender breast,  
> coiled without touching, and deceived the frenzied woman.”

*There, “without touching” has the same sense as “gradually, imperceptibly.” Nor does the following passage, four verses later, express the idea less clearly:*

> “He probes her senses and entwines fire about her bones.”*

**16.** It was fittingly read today: “Behold, I am sending you like lambs among wolves” (Matt. 10:16). For we are celebrating the day of the saints on which the bodies of the holy martyrs were revealed to the people. Like good serpents, having laid aside the coverings of their flesh, having overcome the chill of winter temptations, and renewed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they shone upon the world with the light of summer, truly sent like lambs into the midst of wolves.

For persecutors are wolves, and all heretics are wolves: they do not know how to teach; they are accustomed to howl.

**1038 — 17.** But let no one be disturbed if he is sent into the midst of wolves. Through Christ’s benefit, the wolf itself has been changed. Benjamin, a ravenous wolf, became the apostle Paul—not now a plotter against Christ’s sheepfold, but its defender and guardian.

It is pleasant to live with this wolf. Through this wolf it came about that we are safe in the midst of wolves. No one now fears wolves when we feed with them, as it is written: “Then wolves and lambs will feed together” (Isa. 65:25).

**18. (Verse 42.)** But let us now consider what the Prophet means when he says: “And do not take the word of truth utterly from my mouth, because I have hoped greatly in your judgments.”

The Church, or the soul of the righteous, had seen him leaping like a fawn over the mountains. Suddenly, seeing him near, behind the wall of his house, looking through the windows and appearing above the nets, she exults and rejoices, because she too is loved by the Bridegroom.

He, as though himself wounded by the beauty of love, was present when the beloved, while he was absent, first asked him for kisses—for he is asked when she says, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). Then he did not reject the prayers and caresses of the Bride, who proclaimed the breasts beloved by him, but graciously led her into the inner rooms of the house.

Finally, as though playfully sporting in love, because he wished to test the feelings of the one who loved him, he often went out so that the Bride might seek him, and often returned so that he might be invited to kisses. He stood behind the wall, looked through the windows, and appeared above the nets, so that he would not be wholly absent, nor seem wholly to enter; and he himself called the Bride to him, so that their exchanges in coming to one another might become more pleasing and the force of their love might be kindled by mutual words.

“Arise,” he says, “come, my neighbor, my beautiful one, my dove” (Song 2:10).

[Col. 1274D] *“Might kindle” means “might inflame more,” or “might increase.”*

**19.** And you, if you have a well-founded wall—not the partition that separates the members of a single house, but one built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, so that its joined structure may grow into a temple and not divide its inner parts but fortify them—if, then, you have within you God’s building, and your windows always open toward the east, the Word comes and stands behind your wall.

“For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33:16). He looks through your windows.

**20.** What are these windows? We read of windows concerning which Jeremiah says: “Death entered through the windows” (Jer. 9:21). Through them greed entered; through them lust entered. Your eye is a window: death entered through your eye.

If you look upon a woman in order to desire her, death entered through your eye. If you see the property of a widow or a minor and desire to seize it, thinking that her age or sex leaves her without defense—for those whom the Lord wishes to defend are not without defense—death entered through the window.

If you see the beauty of a woman or the treasures of a minor and arouse your desires, death entered through the window.

But just as death enters through these things, so does life. If, when you look upon the beauty of a consecrated maiden, you revere the Lord Jesus because, in tender years, the maturity of old age and an unstained life have appeared; and if you offer your daughter so that she may be consecrated with a devout veil; if you do not look upon a minor’s property as an eager usurper but, like a diligent parent, protect it with a religious affection—through these windows Christ looks, so that he may call the Bride, appearing above the nets.

[Col. 1274D] *He calls a girl “sacred” when she professed chastity by a publicly pronounced vow. Such a girl was customarily offered by her parents so that she might receive from the bishop the sacred veil of the head as the badge of her profession. Sometimes, however, she made that solemn vow of chastity even against the wishes of her parents. But another occasion will provide the place for discussing this manner of life, which our Ambrose introduced with such care and diligence into the regions of Italy and Mauretania.*
### 21

He is rightly said to be “standing above,” because he alone is the one whom the nets of sins have not entangled. All were within the nets—or rather, we are still within the nets, because no one is without sin except Jesus alone, whom the Father made sin for us though He knew no sin. For He handed Him over to snares; He handed Him over to nets, sending Him [Col. 1275A] not in the sin in which all human beings were, but in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that, in the flesh, He might condemn sin through sin. The flesh was sin in that respect, because it stood condemned by an inherited curse. It was the enticement and handmaid of sin. The Lord Jesus came, [Note: [Col. 1275D] Catharinus cites this passage in his *Opusculum de Conceptione Beatae Mariae*, but reports it in this form: “And in flesh which had been subject to sin in the mother,” and so forth. Yet learned men have already observed that the words “in the mother” are nowhere found in Ambrose. Certainly, the holy Doctor signifies here only that Christ’s flesh was of the same nature as ours, which is subject to sin; he by no means denies the blessed Virgin’s freedom from every sin, since he expressly asserts it near the end of this very psalm in these words: “Receive me, not in the flesh which fell in Adam. Receive me, not from Sarah, but from Mary; so that she may be an incorrupt Virgin, yet a Virgin by grace, wholly free from every stain of sin.”] and in flesh subject to sin carried out the campaign of virtue.

Our members have now become not weapons of lust, but weapons of virtue. For where there had been incitements to lust, there are now dwelling places of chastity. Thus He came to the snares, but willingly; He came to the nets, but secure.

### 22

Everything was full of snares and crowded with nets. Hear him say: “Along this path on which I walked, they hid a snare for me” (Ps. 141:4). And in the Book of the Wisdom of Sirach you are warned to recognize that “you walk in the midst of snares” (Sir. 9:20). As many vices, so many nets; as many sins, so many snares. The bonds of inheritance already held you captive.

Jesus came to the snares in order to set Adam free; He came to liberate what had perished. We were all held by nets, and no one could rescue another, since no one could strip himself free. Therefore one such as this was necessary: one whom the bonds of human generation, subject to sins, could not hold; whom greed could not capture; whom deceit could not bind. Jesus alone was such that, although He had surrounded Himself with the bonds of this flesh, He was not captured and was not bound. Rather, breaking and dissolving them, He called the Church more fully to Himself, looking through the snares, standing above the nets, so that she too might learn not to be held by bonds.

In the end, He was not so far from the bonds that He did not undergo death for us; yet He did not become death’s slave, but was free among the dead. For He was free who possessed the power to undo death. Let Him teach you this Himself, who said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

### 23

Let us therefore hear what He says: “Arise, come, my near one” (Song 2:10)—that is, rise from the dead; arise from the bonds with which you were surrounded. Arise, because I have risen for you; loosen the bond of iniquity, because I have already loosened it for you. Come, because the nets have already been broken.

A virgin has borne a child; a child has been born from a Virgin. He owes nothing to the inheritance of woman; as the son of a woman, He is not held captive by it. Behold the dividing wall of the enclosure has now been broken, the wall that separated the harmony of the inner affections and stirred up divisions among bodily passions.

Come, then, securely. I desire to see your face and hear your voice. Come, so that you may no longer see me through nets, but, as one beloved, may enjoy face to face the countenance of your lover. Let these matters have been treated in their ethical sense. But let us, if we can, gaze upon those mystical meanings from the farthest line.

[Note: [Col. 1276D] “The farthest line” (*extrema linea*) means “from a distance” or “from a more remote point.” For whatever is last in any matter is called *extremum*. The expression is proverbial and is transferred from the circus, where the various tiers and spaces were marked off by lines. See Erasmus, *Adagia*, chiliad 4, century 5, proverb 46, and elsewhere.]

### 24

The Bride was sitting within the house, devoted to the Lord, within the wall of the Law and the prophets, founded upon the construction of spiritual stones. This wall enclosed and fortified the royal house, full of delight and joy. She was admiring the royal treasures and gazing at them attentively, desiring to acquire the wisdom that would reveal these riches to her.

She was in secret, but she was seeking an interpreter of that secret. The Lord Jesus came, leaping over the mountains. To us He seemed slow to come, but He was hastening. Indeed, He leapt and sprang across in order to overleap the corporeal and stony doctrines of the Jews.

He stood beside the wall of the house that existed in the Old Testament, looking through the window of the Law and through the clefts of the prophets. The vestibules of that house had not yet been opened; the keys of knowledge had not yet opened the bolts of the gates by which the inner meanings of the Law were closed.

Yet, looking out from above—that is, from its spiritual part—He calls the Church, so that, rising through the Law and the prophets to the lofty summit of the Gospel, she may trample with fearless step the nets of Jewish interpretation and its knots.

Therefore she is called “near,” so that she may cling to Christ and not seek worldly things; “beautiful,” so that she may bring forth the beautiful feet of those who proclaim the Gospel; “a dove,” so that she may seek spiritual things and leave earthly things behind.

### 25

“Behold,” he says, “the winter has passed; the rain has gone away and departed; the flowers have appeared on the earth” (Song 2:11–12). Before Christ’s coming there was winter; Christ came and made summer. At that time everything lacked flowers and lay naked of virtues. Christ suffered, and everything began to be made fertile with the shoots of new grace.

The rain of overflowing dissipation has gone away, and the clouds that had arisen from foul crimes are now dispersed by the summer brightness of a pure conscience. Therefore those whose flight takes place in winter do not escape, because they do not follow the Lord’s Passion, do not take up their cross, and follow Christ.

Rain hinders the flowers; but now flowers are seen on the earth. The apostles are good flowers, for they poured forth the fragrance of their various writings and works.

### 26

“The time for cutting has come” (ibid. 2:12), because ripe grain is stored in the granaries, and the one who reaps receives a reward. “The voice of the turtledove has been heard” (ibid.), because it has found a nest for itself; for the Church is a house of chastity.

The fig tree that, because of its barrenness, was ordered to be cut down has now begun to bear fruit. The vineyard brought out of Egypt is no longer, with its walls broken down and removed, attacked by beasts; nor is it shapeless with thorns, but is now fragrant with flowers. It has become bowed beneath the fruit of grapes, though formerly it used to produce thorns (ibid. 2:13).

[Col. 1277A]

### 27

Rightly, therefore, holy David, celebrating the Lord’s Passover and entering the summer seasons with fervent spirit, gathering various fruits from the word of God, turns away from winter’s adversity and says: “And do not take the word of truth altogether from my mouth, because I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments.”

What labor it is to receive the word! What danger, again, if you lose it! Therefore it is said to you: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you” (1 Tim. 4:14). Cultivate your field diligently, like a good farmer, so that your lambs may be fed and your crops may flower (Prov. 27:16).

Let the word not be taken from your mouth, lest your words fail to correspond to your deeds and the works of iniquity deform the teaching of discipline. The word is taken from the mouth when it is said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds?” (Ps. 49:16). Eloquence itself falls silent if the conscience is sick.

The birds of heaven come; they too take the Word from your mouth, [Note: [Col. 1277D] All editions read “from your mouth.” There are seasons of temptation that take the seed of the word from the rock, lest, having roots, it bear fruit. The old edition reads “that they may bear fruit”; the Roman edition, “nor even bear fruit.” But the words we have removed from the text are found in none of the Gallican manuscripts. Certainly, anyone who examines the passage more deeply will recognize it as a paraphrase by some superficial reader. For, I ask, what does “lest, having roots” mean? As for the manuscripts that read *afferant* (“may bear”), this can indeed refer to *semen* (“seed”), which is a collective noun.] which take the seed of the word from the rock, lest it bear fruit.

### 28

Now let us consider whether the word of truth can also be taken from the heart. For a word that has taken root, sunk deeply, and been implanted in our minds is difficult to remove.

In the end, the Lord said: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds?” (ibid.). He did not say, “Why did you think about my righteous deeds?” And: “You take up my covenant through your mouth.” He did not say, “Through your heart.”

Speech is restrained because of an unworthy mind, but repentance is not obstructed. He forbids insolence; He does not exclude correction. Yet care must be taken lest the hearts themselves be disturbed inwardly, and wickedness cast darkness over them, so that the heart, blinded by empty thoughts, loses the light of truth and cannot receive the radiance of the word.

If David therefore prays that the word may not be taken from his mouth—and if it is taken, not altogether, that is, not completely—who is so great that he can claim the grace of discourse to be in his own power, especially when his life contradicts what his teaching presumes and he commits acts that must be condemned by God’s judgment?

For the one who hopes in God’s judgments can preserve the word of truth, because, while he fears punishment, he guards grace.

### 29

Therefore he says: “And I will keep your law always, forever and ever” (v. 44). He said two things when one would have been enough, if he had wished to signify only one. But because the promise is to keep the Law not only in the present time of this life, but also in the future after the course of this life has ended, I think that he promises himself a life according both to those who serve the pattern and shadow of heavenly things and to those who, situated in the heavens, render worship to God according to the true Law, so that he may keep the Law both here and there.

Here, in the pattern, in the mirror, in the riddle; there, in the very face of truth.

### 30

We can also understand the passage in this way: *διὰ παντός* (“throughout,” “in all things”) signifies not only what is expressed by “always,” but also what is expressed by “through everything.” For the one who keeps the Law in all things is the one who, although educated in the Law and born under the Law, advances beyond the Law in the degree of his devotion and is set free from the Law, [Note: [Col. 1278D] All editions read “from the Law.” For Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, and therefore “not without the Law,” and so forth. But, apart from the fact that “and therefore” is absent from all the manuscripts, the sequence of the sentence coheres less well; consequently the manuscript reading seemed preferable.] for Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law—not without the law of God, but nourished in the law of Christ.

Or certainly, if we keep the Law in all things, let the practice of our life never exceed the discipline prescribed for childhood and adolescence, the conduct proper to youth, the maturity of old age, and the path assigned to each period of life.

Likewise, our soul also seems to have certain ages through which it runs and passes, so that it may say: “I have finished the course” (2 Tim. 4:7). In the end, there is that age of the soul of which it is said: “And the age of old age is an unblemished life” (Wis. 4:9).

Therefore, he keeps the Law in all things who, both in the ages of our body and in the stages of our soul, does not deviate from the Law.

### 31

“And I walked in spaciousness, because I sought your testimonies” (v. 45). He who walks according to the commandments along the narrow and constricted way walks in spaciousness. Hence we read: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4:2). And elsewhere: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and He answered me in spaciousness” (Ps. 117:5).

The wise person walks in the innocence of his heart, and waters overflow from its fountain upon his streets. He does not confine his mind within bodily and earthly things, but directs it toward heavenly things, so that his way of life may be in heaven.

Hear one who feels no constriction: “We suffer pressure,” he says, “but are not hemmed in” (2 Cor. 4:9). And how could he be constricted whose mouth was always open (2 Cor. 6:11), so that believers would not be confined? Let him explain what it means to walk in spaciousness. He says: “Even though the body is constricted, our heart has been enlarged. You are not constricted in us, but you are constricted in your own inward parts” (ibid. 6:11–12).

### 32

They could not be constricted in Paul, in whom there was the height of wisdom and the breadth of faith. How could they be constricted in him who was a vessel of eternal election?

But a person is constricted within himself, because the wicked person is hemmed in within himself, strangled by the snares of his own wickedness. Consider the miser who daily extends the boundaries of his estates and excludes his neighbors. Does he seem to you to be enlarged rather than constricted, when the earth itself cannot contain him?

However far he may extend the spaces of his house, he is enclosed within the narrow limits of his own opinion—the man for whom what he has is not enough. But such is not the one who can say: “And I walked in spaciousness.” He added the reason: “Because I sought your testimonies.”

### 33

“And I spoke of your testimonies in the presence of kings, and I was not put to shame” (v. 46). This voice fittingly belongs to a martyr who, when summoned to sacrilege, did not blush when kings reproached him for the crucified Jesus. Rather, he gloried in the cross of Christ and established by heavenly testimonies that it was the salvation of the world.

Christ calls such people “the Bride,” saying in the *Song of Songs*: “Come, my dove, in the shelter of the rock, beside the fortification” (Song 2:14)—that is, come according to the Gospel.

The deeds of Christ have become the strongholds of your faith; the words of the Lord are the supports of your walls; the Passion of the Lord’s body is your strength. “Show me your face and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful” (ibid.).

The voice is sweet because confession is made with the mouth for salvation; the face is beautiful because it does not blush at its Author and is not ashamed of its Redeemer.

She therefore shows her face, bearing the sign of the cross; and she makes her voice known, assuming the authority of preaching. In the shelter of Christ’s body, by which she was redeemed from sin, she finds the protection of spiritual grace, so that she may both perceive and speak what brings her salvation.

Sweet, therefore, is the voice that spoke in the divine testimonies; beautiful the face that was not put to shame in the presence of kings.

### 34

We can also understand by “kings” those to whom Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for adoption” (1 Pet. 2:9).

There are kings who offer in Jerusalem the gifts of their wisdom—those who have been given the grace to speak the word, to bend peoples with a certain royal authority, and to soothe the souls of the holy. They do not blush in Him, because they would say nothing alien to honesty; no one could rebuke or reject them on the grounds that they were unworthy, since Christ had made them suitable ministers of the New Testament. They are not ashamed in it because they do not fear being put to shame by the opposing assertion of disputants and overcome in debate.

A king, then, is one who is not ashamed, lest he be censured in conduct or reproved in speech, since his life also ought to be established in the word. Thus, although the Prophet was so perfect that he was not ashamed in the presence of kings, nevertheless he meditated on God’s commandments throughout his life and raised his works upward, doing nothing that clung to earthly desires.

### 35

Therefore he says: “And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved exceedingly. And I lifted up my hands toward your commandments, which I loved exceedingly; and I exercised myself in your justifications” (vv. 47–48).

This is a most beautiful order: first to meditate, so that the commandments we love may become the object of habitual meditation. Through meditation on the heavenly commandments, practice in good works grows strong.

For just as the end of meditation upon words is memory, so that we retain the words we meditate upon, so the aim or end of meditation upon the heavenly commandments is action: a conduct directed toward fulfilling the divine commandments. No one can fulfill them unless he loves them—not merely loves them, but loves them exceedingly.

### 36

Therefore he first said: “And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved exceedingly.” Then he added: “And I lifted up my hands toward your commandments, which I loved exceedingly.”

After meditation, it is good to lift up our actions toward God’s commandments and to do this with charity and joy, so that our goodness may not be compelled or accompanied by grief and sadness, but voluntary. A slave acts unwillingly; a friend acts willingly.

Let us strive so that it may be said to us: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15), because, like friends, you have done God’s commandment willingly.

But whoever meditates, loves, and lifts up his actions in order to do what pleases God must neither neglect nor pass over the divine commandments. He must exercise himself in them, dwell upon them at length, and repeatedly turn over God’s justifications with the attentive affection of his mind.

## SERMON SEVEN. Zain

### 1

Among the Hebrews, the letter Zain signifies in Latin “lead yourself”; elsewhere it signifies “hither.” The meaning of this interpretation is not sufficiently clear, unless perhaps it means that each person should govern himself and be his own leader. Or “hither”—that is, he should direct his journey toward the place to which the verses of this letter call him.

And rightly, at once in the first verse, he asks for his rest, because the number seven belongs to the letter and is the number of rest. What greater rest is there than to rest in the word of God and to be soothed by its grace and consolation?

### 2

“Remember,” he says, “your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope” (v. 49). The Word of God has summoned us, cast down and humbled as we are, to heavenly grace, so that we may desire eternity, despise the present things, disregard temporal matters, and seek future and invisible things.

The Word of God therefore calls us to Himself, as it is written: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). Therefore let us follow the Lord Jesus who calls us, so that we may pass from worldly things to everlasting things and learn to govern ourselves.

### 3

[Note: [Col. 1279D] All editions read: “Therefore David [was summoned by the word of God and had hope in it], because,” and so forth. But the words enclosed in brackets are found neither in the Vatican nor in the Gallican codices. They seem to have been added by someone who, understanding the words “Therefore David” as referring to the lower passage beginning “Having received this response,” thought the sense too incomplete. To remedy this defect, he added the words we have removed.]

Therefore David, since he had often been summoned by heavenly responses in which he might hope that the reward of his faith and merits would come, says—as you have it written—when God spoke through the prophet Nathan: “I took you from the sheepfold, from one flock, to make you prince over my people Israel; and I was with you in all the places where you walked, and I destroyed all your enemies from before your face” (2 Sam. 7:8–9). And below: “And I will give you rest from all your enemies” (ibid. 7:11).

After receiving this response, David said: “Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you have loved me in these things, and that the least things have been remembered in your sight, Lord, and that you have spoken concerning the house of your servant for a distant future?” (ibid. 7:18–19).

And below he says: “And now, my Lord, Lord, you are God. Your words are true, and you have spoken these good things concerning your servant. And now begin to bless the house of your servant, so that I may be forever in your sight; for you, my Lord, Lord, have spoken, and by your blessing the house of your servant will be blessed forever.”

Thus, summoned by this and by other responses, David does not cease to hope, and with the authority of prophetic faith he appeals to the Lord to remember His promises, since He is not accustomed to forget them. Whatever He has promised to the saints, He habitually fulfills, forgetful of our iniquities but not forgetful of His promises.

In the end, it is written: “I am, I am the one who blots out your iniquities … and I will remember them no more. But you remember, and let us be judged” (Isa. 43:25–26).

He wishes to forget whatever threats He has made to sinners, if they should at some point turn from their ways. He also wishes to be summoned to account, so that if someone, pursuing the rewards proposed for virtues, has fought the good fight, he may expect the fruit of his reward—and even claim it—as you have it written: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Tim. 4:7).

This is not an arrogant usurpation, but an act of faith, because he confesses that the true God cannot deceive. Therefore David also admonishes us, saying that the Lord should remember His word, by which He urges us to hope, so that we may renounce earthly things and cling to heavenly things.

[Col. 1281C]

### 4

David therefore says: “I have fought the battle; I seek the prize of your word, which you promised me. Remember your promises, which you pledged to your servant.”

I have not presumptuously hoped for what you yourself made me hope for. I am a servant; I await nourishment from the Lord. I am a soldier; I demand pay from my commander. I have been summoned; I ask for the promise from the one who invited me.

Yet he modestly tempered the authority of his faith by calling himself a servant, because “the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters” (Ps. 122:2). These words, spoken in David’s own person, are well and readily understood.

### 5

But if someone considers the instruction applicable to every person, he can weigh the promises common to the Levites, as you have it: “Give to Levi his men; give to Levi his manifest ones” (Deut. 33:8).

[Note: [Col. 1281D] The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, reads: “It can also be applied to believing peoples, to chosen peoples.” The ancient edition, with other manuscripts, has: “The people of believers, the chosen.” The words that follow in all editions—“It can also suitably be applied to the Church that is about to rise”—are absent from the manuscripts and seem superfluous.]

This address can also be applied to the chosen people of believers. Through Joseph, by a figure first in his name and then through the tribe, the divine promise was transferred to the heirs of the first election, as Moses says: “The firstborn of the bull is his glory; his horns are the horns of the unicorn. With them he will toss the nations together to the ends of the earth” (ibid. 33:17).

For this oracle prophesies the one Word of God, which was to be spread throughout the whole world among the nations. David, therefore, seems modestly to demand this promise made to the Church that was to rise, while impatient for the common progress that was being delayed.

### 6

And he added: “This has comforted me in my humiliation, because your word has given me life” (v. 50).

This is the hope, this is what came to me through your word; it comforted me so that I could endure the bitter things of the present. While Paul acts against the Name, he has no consolation of hope; while he suffers for the Name, [Note: [Col. 1281D] Thus the old edition. The Roman edition, however, had corrected the words by reversing them: “he draws consolation from hope.” But the manuscripts present the whole passage in these words: “While he acts and [makes] future believers” (some have “for future things” or “future”), “receive how he consoles us.” This reading should not be wholly rejected if one reads “future believers” and refers the verb “acts” to hope. Nevertheless, the editions seem preferable here.] he draws hope from consolation.

And how he consoles us once he has become faithful, hear: “Who will separate us,” he says, “from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: For your sake we are handed over to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. 8:35–36).

And, to show how these things can be endured patiently, he added: “But in all these things we conquer through Him who loved us” (ibid. 8:37).

Therefore, if someone wishes to overcome adversities—whether persecution, danger, death, serious illness, attacks by robbers, confiscation of possessions, or whatever else is considered adverse in this world—they are easily overcome if there is hope to console him.

For even if such things occur, they cannot be grievous to one who says: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory” (ibid. 8:18). Whoever hopes for better things is never broken by lesser ones.

### 7

In the time of our humiliation, therefore, hope is our consolation, and it does not put us to shame. I think that the time of temptation is the time of humiliation for our soul.

Our soul is humbled when it is handed over to the tempter to be tested by difficult labors, so that it may wrestle and fight, experiencing an encounter with an opposing power. But in these temptations it is given life by the address of God.

For this is the vital substance of our soul, by which it is nourished, fed, and governed. Nothing else gives life to the rational soul except the address of God.

Just as the word of God increases in our soul when it is received, understood, and grasped, so its life also increases. Conversely, just as the address of God diminishes in our soul, so its life also suffers decline.

Therefore, just as the connection of our soul and body is animated, nourished, and sustained by the vital spirit, so our soul is given life by the word of God and by spiritual grace.

Hence we must strive with every kind of effort, setting aside all other things, to gather God’s addresses for ourselves and heap them up in our ruling faculty, in our senses, our concerns, our reflections, and our actions. Thus our deeds may correspond to the addresses of Scripture, and our actions may not appear to disagree with the sequence of the heavenly commandments, so that we too may say: “Because your utterance has given us life.”

[Note: [Col. 1282D] That is, the soul and our spiritual part, of which he had just spoken above. The holy Bishop often uses this word in the same sense.]

[Col. 1283A]

### 8

The third verse is: “The proud acted wickedly exceedingly; but I did not decline from your law” (v. 51).

The greatest sin in a human being is pride, since the origin of our sin proceeded from it. With this weapon the devil first wounded and struck us. For if the human being, deceived by the serpent’s persuasion, had not wished to be like God and to know good and evil—things which human frailty could not fully discern—although he had received what he was to follow, lest through reckless usurpation he fall from the happiness of paradise; if, I say, he had not, dissatisfied with his own bounds, rashly violated what was forbidden, the inheritance of deadly guilt would never have passed to us.

And why should I speak of the human being? The devil himself lost the grace of his nature through pride. In the end, when he said, “I will set my throne above the clouds … and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14), he fell from the fellowship of the angels. Condemned with the fitting punishment for this crime, he sought a human being to share in it, into whom he might transfer the fellowship of his offense.

### 9

What, then, can be worse than this sin, which began with an insult against God? Therefore Scripture says: “The Lord resists the proud” (Prov. 3:34).

As the defender of His own dishonor, He has undertaken a special contest against pride, as though He were saying: “This is my adversary, the one who provokes me; this encounter belongs to me.”

Hence the Apostle also declared pride to be the source of many kinds of guilt, saying of the heretic: “He does not consent to the teaching that accords with piety; he is proud, knowing nothing, but sick with questions and disputes about words, from which arise envy, contention, sacrilege, evil suspicions, conflicts among people corrupted in mind and alienated from the truth, who think that piety is a means of gain” (1 Tim. 6:3–5).

Of how many sins, then, did he show pride to be the cause? Therefore, wishing to commend his devotion as untouched by any iniquity of the proud, David says: “The proud acted wickedly exceedingly.”

He declared not only that they acted wickedly, but also that they acted with excessive wickedness, as was fitting for the proud. To ensure that he would not be touched by any contagion from them, hear him say elsewhere: “The proud of eye and the insatiable of heart—I did not eat with such a one” (Ps. 100:5).

[Col. 1283D]

### 10

Since he had expressed how great the force of evil in pride was, he ought to teach us how it could be conquered. Rightly, therefore, like a good teacher, he demonstrates the remedy after magnifying the poison.

Hear, then, how you may exclude the venom of pride: “I did not decline,” he says, “from your Law.”

The Law of God alone can blunt the venom of pride. It instructed the man devoted to piety how he ought to govern himself with caution.

For many—not only those who are strangers to the faith, but even those who seem to have tasted no small portion of the precepts of Scripture—are accustomed to be tempted by the prosperous progress of the proud. They see those who violate the Law, arbiters of impiety, arrogant, contemptuous of the faithful, exalting themselves against those who humble their hearts according to the fear of God and the heavenly commandments, abounding in this world in riches, fame, honors, and power.

The graver the offenses they commit, the more abundant are the successes that favor their worldly advantages. Meanwhile, just men often struggle with poverty, the loss of children, and the barrenness of spouses. Agitated and disturbed by these things, they incline the judgment of their mind to think that God’s judgment is somehow mistaken in this matter, because they do not hold fast to the head of truth, by which it is most clearly understood that the reward of our merits is stored up not in this world, but in the future.

### 11

Yet few notice this. In the beginning, David himself was tempted by it, as you have it written: “Behold, these are sinners, and those who abound in the world have acquired riches. And I said: Have I justified my heart without cause, and washed my hands among the innocent, and been scourged all day long?” (Ps. 72:12–14).

Thus each one of us who is not perfect, seeing these things, says: Where is the providence of God? Where is justice? This proud man abounds; this arrogant man grows rich; this impious man is blessed and powerful. But that just man—see how he lies cast down and exhausted; see how he lacks even the food he needs. He is subjected to insults by this impious man, trampled underfoot by this insolent man, and driven away. [Note: [Col. 1283D] All editions read: “cast down and despised.”]

This is certainly no small temptation unless you look ahead to the things that are to come, unless you are more fully instructed in the heavenly commandments.

### 12

In the end, David thought that he already understood these things, but he did not know them; and therefore he labored anxiously with a wavering mind. Hence he says: “And I thought that I knew; this is labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand in the last things” (ibid. 72:16–17).

There, by the fact that the proud had exalted themselves, he saw through the prophetic spirit that they would become more completely cast down, and he said: “How have they become desolate! Suddenly they have failed and have been destroyed because of their iniquity, like the dream of one awakening” (ibid. 72:19–20).

He therefore recognized that the successes of the impious in this world resemble a dream, not reality. Their gains seem to last only while they are asleep.
