When they have slept through their dream, [Note: [Col. 1283D] All editions read “when they have slept their sleep,” and so forth. This is indeed supported by the allusion to Psalm 75:6, “they slept their sleep” (*ὔπνωσαν ὔπνων αὐτῶν*). Yet the manuscripts almost unanimously oppose it; and their meaning is unquestionably more suitable to this passage.] those who seemed to themselves to drink now thirst; those who feasted hunger. They bring back nothing solid or complete from this dream.

And worldly people rightly “sleep” a dream. Although they are awake to the world, they sleep toward God. Holy Job rightly speaks of them: though he had previously marveled at their abundance, he says: “For as straw is tossed by the wind and as dust is scattered by a whirlwind … they die in bitterness of soul, eating nothing and possessing nothing good” (Job 21:18, 25).

But the just person, possessing the confidence of a good conscience, rejoices more in his final things. He understands that, at the end of this life, he is being freed from labors, and he seeks the reward of good work and deeds, saying: “The crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love His coming” (2 Tim. 4:8).

13. But he says this who could say: “I have not turned aside from your law”; in him there shines not only the grace of good works, but also the purity of his innermost conscience. For the Law not only directs the duty of action; it also cleanses the secret inclination of the mind. For we serve the Lord according to the Law not only in our deeds, but also in the very things that are hidden, because the Law says: “Let no hidden word of injustice be in your heart” (Deut. 15:9).

[Note: [Col. 1285D] Not a few manuscripts read: “the word of hidden justice.”]

Thus you should not only commit no offense in deed or action, when you see the proud glorying, nor stumble in speech; you should not even, in the innermost heart, while disputing about God’s judgment, incur the offense of iniquity. The more hidden it is thought to be, the more frequently it ordinarily occurs; for each person safely supposes that such disputes, as though enclosed within his own entrails, are entrusted to his conscience, although he himself will be his own accuser on the day of judgment, because the hidden things of the heart are revealed, with conscience bearing witness to our accusations.

[Note: [Col. 1285D] The Roman edition, from one Vatican manuscript, reads: “because I think this to be the holy man’s purpose, whereby he thinks,” etc. The old edition and all the Gallican manuscripts, however, read as we do in the body of the text, except that the old edition, with one or two manuscripts, reads “in a dispute of this kind,” where we have restored from other copies “disputes.” Anyone who examines the passage somewhat more carefully will not deny that this agrees better with the sense.]

14. What, then, is the purpose of the holy man is set forth more clearly in this passage. First, he must remember the heavenly promises; second, the reward appointed for those who live. Then there is another purpose of the holy man: even if he is placed amid dangers and adversities, he should nevertheless console himself with the hope he has drawn from the sequence of the Scriptures. A third purpose is that, even if he sees the impious and sacrilegious, and the proud who act unjustly flourishing in wealth in this world, he should not, as though unbelieving, turn away from the Law, but persevere in its paths and flee the contagion of the proud. For every unclean person contaminates; and the proud man is unclean, concerning whom it is written: “Everyone of a haughty heart is unclean before God” (Prov. 16:5).

15. A fourth purpose of the holy man is that he remember the heavenly judgments, as David asserts when he says: “I remembered your judgments, which are from of old, and I was consoled.” For unless one who has been instructed by the Law and formed by its examples believes that God’s judgments are always true, he quickly turns aside from the Law. But whoever recalls the past and gathers from himself the sequence of ancient events recognizes that neither does the sinner escape the punishment of his wickedness, nor is the righteous deprived of the rewards of his justice.

For he retraces in his mind that from the beginning Adam, because of his transgression of the heavenly commandment, was expelled from his dwelling in paradise; and that Cain paid the price of his murderous crime, condemned by the authority of the divine sentence; that Enoch, because of his devotion, was taken up to heaven and escaped the poison of earthly wickedness; that Noah, victorious over the Flood because of his righteousness, became the survivor of the human race; that Abraham, because of his faith, spread the seedbed of his posterity throughout the whole world; that Israel, because of its endurance of labors, consecrated the people of believers with the seal of its own name; that David himself, because of his gentleness, was endowed with royal honor and preferred to his elder brothers; that Elijah, because of his zeal for God, was lifted by a chariot into the air and acquired, by his dwelling there, a heavenly lodging of a new kind.

16. Whoever knows how to retrace these things has the means by which to acquire the grace of consolation for himself.

[Note: [Col. 1286D] The editions read: “On the other hand, whoever does not know has no means of being consoled. Therefore let us keep the judgments of God, because the judgments of God are true.” But the manuscripts, with broad agreement, read: “And conversely, because the judgments of God,” etc., as above in the text. Ambrose seems to have intended to supply something which he left for his reader to consider.]

And conversely, because the judgments of God are true, as you have it: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; indeed, your servant keeps them” (Ps. 18:10–11). Divine judgments are therefore sweet to the one who keeps them; but there is no doubt that they are bitter to the one who neglects them, because he perceives that, in the disgraceful shame of his sins, the outcome of the divine sentence has been set before him.

[Note: [Col. 1286D] Thus the manuscripts; the edition, however, reads: “because he did not notice.” The sense is plainly overturned by that negation.]

But the one who is conscious of being upright before God is not disturbed, saying: “We are heirs of God, and fellow heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified together” (Rom. 8:17).

17. But who among us is such that he can console himself with the sequence of the divine judgments? Human judgments are terrifying even to sinners; how much more fearful are divine judgments! Finally, to gather by an example those things which are truly eternal, we see in this world the innocent gladly hastening to judgment, hating delays and desiring the judgment’s speed; but the guilty shrink back and tremble, postpone and avoid it, and finally become sorrowful when they hear that the day of judgment has been appointed. Blessed, therefore, is the one who awaits that heavenly judgment with joy. For he knows that the kingdom of heaven, fellowship with the angels, and also a crown stored up for good merits await him.

18. *(Verse 53.)* Let us now consider what another purpose of the holy man may be, and let us judge it from what follows. “Timidity,” he says, “held me back because of sinners who abandon your law.” This is not shared by many; for most people are grieved if they suffer some injury from another, if they have been harmed, attacked, or disfigured. It concerns ourselves: being weaker, we grieve that some have been harmful to us. But the one who is stronger does not grieve over his own insult, but over another’s sins; in his own injury he laments another’s fall, and he deplores having been the occasion of the error of the one who injured him.

Take an apostolic example. Paul wept over another’s sin, as he himself says: “For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears” (2 Cor. 2:4). And although he himself was distressed, he did not want those very people whom he rebuked to be distressed. Finally he added: “Not that you might be grieved, but that you might know the abundant love that I have for you” (ibid.). He wanted those who had fallen to be grieved unto repentance, not plunged into deeper sorrow; only so that the sorrow of those who were rebuked might become joy for the one who rebuked them. Hence he says: “For if I grieve you, who is there to make me glad except the one who is grieved by me?” (ibid. 2:2). He rebukes, therefore, in order to relieve the duration of sorrow, so that repentance may lead to salvation; he condemns in order to absolve; he excludes in order to receive; he does not pardon in order to set free. Such was Paul because, being well instructed in the Law, he had understood the command of the one who says: “Timidity held me back because of sinners who abandon your law.”

19. David grieved not because he was despised, nor because he himself was attacked, but because God’s law was abandoned; and he grieved over the loss of those who did this, because they were perishing for God.

Just as a good father, when his son is in a frenzy and is cursed, beaten, and subjected to injuries by him, laments not his own but the sick man’s misery, and grieves over the insult not because it has been directed against himself, but because the sick man does not know, in his madness, what he is doing: so the good man, when he sees a sinner failing to show reverence, failing even to honor an elder’s gray hairs, and, in his presence, doing something unworthy, not recognizing, in a kind of madness of sinning, how disgraceful and dishonorable are the things he commits, grieves for him as though he were dying and laments over him as one abandoned by physicians.

And like a good physician, he first gives warning; then, even if he suffers serious things, he nevertheless endures the sick man as one who, though beaten, does not abandon him, and though cursed, does not leave him. He withholds none of the medicine he can apply; nor does he abandon him as obstinate, but strives with every effort to heal him as one who has deserved well of him, exercising not only the skill of his art but also the kindness of his mind.

20. So, too, the righteous man, even when he is despised by a sinner, does not turn away; and when he is injured, he considers it the result of madness, not wickedness. He desires all the more to bring medicine to the other’s wound, sympathizes with him, and grieves not for himself but for the one who is suffering from a desperate illness. He says: “This is one of the brothers suffering and afflicted in such a way that he does me an injury; if he recognized me, he would certainly honor me and surely would not injure me. For what has he been injured by anything I did, that he should have the disposition to injure me?”

Therefore, when there is no cause for doing harm, the fault cannot lie in the intention. Thus, if I am righteous, I am afflicted because of charity, because of love, because of the loss of the Church, because of the injury to the body. I can also grieve over the fact that, even if I have not injured the one who injures me, and am not conscious of having provoked him against me by any injury, I have nevertheless become the occasion of his fall: by injuring an innocent person he commits a sin, and I have become for him the material of sin.

21. This, then, is what David grieves, and he grieves for this reason: that when one member suffers, the other members suffer with it. Perhaps this is why it is also written: “The righteous man is an accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17).

[Note: [Col. 1287D] The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, reads: “even if he can have nothing in himself to accuse, and not be righteous.” Perhaps this was thought to allude to Paul’s statement: “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” etc. Nevertheless, the old edition and the remaining manuscripts read as in the text. What is signified here is that the righteous, even if they do not see in themselves grave sins by which righteousness is lost, at least see those things sufficient to enable them truly to accuse themselves, as the passage cited from Proverbs clearly shows.]

For even if the righteous person can have something in himself to accuse, and can nevertheless be righteous—since no one is without sin except the one God—and even if a sinner can be righteous precisely because he is his own accuser, according to the saying: “Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified”; nevertheless, it may perhaps not seem absurd to some that this too was said of him: that the one who accuses himself on behalf of another is righteous, even if he has nothing in himself to accuse.

22. Let us therefore consider how well the first-person words of the righteous man suit holy David in all these matters. He accused himself when no one accused him; he confessed his own sin when his heart was struck because he had numbered the people. He also said to the Lord: “I have sinned, Lord, in doing this thing; and now, Lord, take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have sinned exceedingly” (2 Sam. 24:10).

Although Scripture says that the anger of God was kindled against Israel, so that the king’s fall might seem excusable, nevertheless, when he saw the angel causing the slaughter of the people, he exposed himself to the blow of the one who was striking and said: “Behold, I have sinned, and I, the shepherd, have acted wickedly; but what has this flock done? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house” (ibid. 17).

Thus, as a righteous man, he was his own accuser at the very beginning of his speech; he acknowledged his sin, and by confessing his own iniquity he was justified in himself. Elsewhere, too, when reproved by the prophet concerning Uriah’s death, he said: “I have sinned against the Lord” (2 Sam. 12:13); and he received the answer that, because of his repentance, the Lord had taken away his sin.

23. Likewise, in another passage, when Shimei cursed him and pelted him with stones, although he was surrounded by warriors through whom he could have avenged himself, he bore it patiently and did not return the insult even in a word. Indeed, when his commander Abishai wanted to take off the head of the man who was cursing him, the king said: “What have I to do with you, son of Zeruiah? Because he curses me, the Lord has told him to curse David” (2 Sam. 16:10).

First, therefore, he excused Shimei’s fault and referred the cause to the Lord’s will. Second, he turned it back upon his own merit, implying that Shimei had not erred but that he himself had deserved it. Third, he declared that the man’s curse not only did him no harm but even benefited him, as it is written: “David said to Abishai and to all his servants: Behold, my son, who came forth from my body, seeks my life; how much more, then, this son of Benjamin?” (ibid. 11). He greatly blunted the attack of the avenger. For how could he avenge the curse of a stranger as an injury to the king, when the parricide of his own son still remained unpunished? The curse of a stranger and the parricide of a son could not reasonably be weighed in an equal balance.

And he added: “Let him alone, let him curse, for the Lord has told him; perhaps the Lord will look upon my humiliation and repay me good for his curse” (ibid. 12).

There is also another purpose of the righteous, far more perfect and powerful than all these: to intercede for persecutors and excuse sinners. We read this in the Gospel, when the Lord Jesus, while being crucified by the faithless, said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

24. It is therefore clear from these teachings of heavenly doctrine that the righteous person prefers to accuse himself rather than disgrace another. Thus, concerning Joseph, to whom Mary, the mother of the Lord, was betrothed, it is written that, when he saw that she was pregnant, “because he was righteous, he did not wish to expose her” (Matt. 1:19); and certainly he had not yet heard any oracle.

The character of the righteous is therefore alien not only to the cruelty of vengeance but also to the severity of accusation; and he prefers to have his own forgiveness blamed because he did not bring a charge than to press another’s crime.

[Note: [Col. 1289D] The old edition, with the greater part of the manuscripts, reads: “because he did not judge.” The Roman edition, with several manuscripts, reads: “because he did not avenge.” The Remigius manuscript reads: “because he did not indicate,” that is, “accuse” or “bring forward the charge,” in which sense this verb is used more than once by Cicero. Here this reading is certainly the best, as the sequence of the discourse shows.]

But you will say: How then did David himself say: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees the vengeance upon the impious” (Ps. 57:11)? It seems to me that he rejoices because he himself has escaped, not because the impious are punished. Let us seek another purpose of the righteous from what follows.

25. *(Verse 54.)* Therefore he says: “Your statutes were songs for me in the place of my pilgrimage.” With good reason he was not broken by his pilgrimages; he avoided the proud and was not moved by their prosperous successes. He consoled himself in the heavenly judgments and was distressed by the sins of others, because he regarded God’s statutes as songs.

For what we retain well we are accustomed to sing, and what is sung adheres more firmly to our minds. Let us not pass superficially over what we read, so that we seem to return to its memory only when we are reading it; rather, even when the book is absent from our hands, let us, like the animals that are approved and considered clean in the Law, which are accustomed to chew the cud even when they are not feeding, bringing forth from within themselves food stored up for them, draw forth from the treasury of our memory and from our inner being spiritual nourishment for rumination.

Let the Lord’s statutes be hymns for us, a song for us, psalms for us. Let us sing with the spirit and sing also with the mind, lest, if we forget them, it be said to each one of us in the time of necessity: “You have cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49:17).

26. And so, to drive forgetfulness away and expel it from his holy house, the true Solomon made singers for himself who devoted themselves with their whole spirit to seeking knowledge of divinity, so that singers would not be lacking in his Church, by whose song the evil spirit might be driven away (2 Chron. 5:12). We are taught this by the example of holy David: when he played, that evil spirit which troubled King Saul’s heart was driven out (1 Sam. 16:23).

The prophets, too, when they were about to prophesy, ordered a skilled player to play, so that spiritual grace might be poured forth, invited by the sweetness of the music (2 Kings 3:14). And in the Gospel we read that, in the house of the father who had recovered his son, music had already sounded, by which the faithful at the banquet were delighted, but which the faithless man heard impatiently (Luke 15:28).

Sweet, therefore, is the song that does not weaken the body but strengthens the mind and spirit. Thus the song is called the Lord’s Testament, because in the Scriptures of the Gospel we sing together, with the mind’s sweet exultation, the forgiveness of all sins and the Lord’s righteous acts. The Lord himself did not disdain to say: “We played music for you, and you did not dance” (Luke 7:32). In the Gospel he sang to us of the forgiveness of sins; the Jews ought to have lifted up their minds, not with the bodily movement of an actor, but with the Holy Spirit. They did not do so, and therefore they are reproved.

27. But even bodily dancing is considered praiseworthy in honor of God.

[Note: [Col. 1289D] Dancing was regarded as an act of worship not only among the Hebrews but also among the Gentiles. Hence, at Rome, the Salii, priests of Mars and Hercules. Hence the various kinds of dances established in honor of the gods, concerning which Lucian writes in his work *On Dancing* (περὶ ὀρχήσεως); and likewise Meursius discusses them at length in his work *On the Orchestra*.]

Finally, David danced before the ark of the Lord. Michal, the daughter of Saul, saw him dancing and playing on harmonized instruments in the presence of the Lord, and, after he had returned home, she said to him: “How glorious the king of Israel made himself today, since he was uncovered in the eyes of the maidservants of his servants, as one of the dancers!”

And David said to Michal in the presence of the Lord: “Blessed is the Lord, who chose me instead of your father and instead of all his house, appointing me prince over his people Israel and Judah. I will dance before the Lord, and I will uncover myself still more in this way; I will be foolish in your sight, and with the maidservants concerning whom you said that I was uncovered, I will be honored.”

And, it says, Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no child until the day of her death (2 Sam. 6:20ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1290D] The Erasmian and later editions place in the margin: “on harmonized instruments,” ἡρμοσμένοις. Amerbach and Gill place in the body of the text: “on armazated instruments.” A large number of manuscripts read *armizatis*. The Remigius manuscript reads best of all: *harmonizatis*.]

[Note: [Col. 1290D] The Roman edition reads: “to Michal: I will dance before the Lord. And: Blessed,” etc. The Septuagint does indeed have the verb ὀρχήσομαι (“I will dance”); but since it is found neither in Ambrose’s manuscripts nor in the old editions, it is likely that it was absent from the copy used by the holy man.]

There is therefore a clear example: the Prophet who played on instruments and danced before the ark of the Lord was justified, while the woman who reproved him was condemned to barrenness.

28. But it is not enough for someone to regard God’s statutes as songs unless he strips himself of enslavement to earthly concerns. Therefore he added: “In the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 38:13). This agrees with what he says elsewhere: “I am a sojourner in this land” (Eph. 2:19).

Hence the Apostle does not want us to be strangers and pilgrims in the house of God and in the calling of faith, but “fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.” Whoever is a member of God’s household is an exile from the world; whoever dwells in heavenly things is a pilgrim on earth.

The Hebrews were pilgrims in this world, not feeling the nature of the fire; they regarded God’s statutes as songs when they sang a hymn to God in praise of the creatures.

29. Moreover, the one who sings is free of burdens: he banishes the cares of diverse thoughts, sets avarice aside, and refreshes himself not only with the voice of his body but also with the liveliness of his mind. The same Prophet did not sing as one sorrowful from anxiety over poverty, but as one free from all bodily passions: “I will sing to you, O God, on the lyre, Holy One of Israel. My lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed” (Ps. 70:22–23).

He sang these things joyfully, as though he were being nourished by better banquets. His spirit feasted on the nourishment of devout worship. Thus not only hymns and psalms, but also the commandments of the Law are songs to the saints.

Finally, Moses, who received the Law, sang when he had crossed the sea on foot and, as leader of the rescued people, proclaimed the Lord’s statutes.

30. *(Verse 55.)* One excellent purpose of the righteous man still remains: he must be intent upon the praises of God at all times, not only by day but also by night. Therefore he added: “I remembered your name by night, O Lord, and I kept your law.”

Let us see whether that person is also mindful who calls upon the Lord in word but does not keep the divine commandments. It has been sufficiently said of him that not everyone who says “Lord, Lord” is acceptable to Christ, but the one who can prove his faithful devotion by good works (Matt. 7:21).

Faith, uprightness, and innocence therefore prove a person mindful. But when he says, “I remembered your name,” this is complete devotion, because no one can say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit. Let this name be invoked by day and by night; let holy devotion allow no time to pass empty of prayer.

31. If, then, those who pursue secular studies allow themselves very little sleep, how much more should those who desire to know God not be hindered by bodily sleep beyond what nature requires? David washed his bed with tears every night; he even rose in the middle of the night to give thanks to the Lord. And you think the whole night should be devoted to sleep?

At that time you should pray to the Lord more earnestly; then you should ask for protection and guard against sin, when secrecy seems to be available. Especially then, when darkness surrounds me and walls enclose me, you should consider that the Lord sees all hidden things.

Do not say, then: “I am surrounded by darkness; who sees me? Whom should I fear, enclosed by walls and shut in?” For “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 33:17).

Moreover, if you do not see the judge, do you not see yourself? Do you not fear the testimony of your conscience? Do you not know that the darkness of night is not a covering but an incentive to sin?

When bodies are heated by sleep and food, the vigor of the mind is also relaxed by drowsiness and loosened by sleep. Then the desire for impure intercourse creeps in.

[Note: [Col. 1291D] The old edition and several manuscripts read: “then the heart is disturbed; it does not fear the filth of uncleanness.” Others read: “then the heart is disturbed by the filth of uncleanness; chastity is not seen.” The Roman edition reads: “the filth does not fear uncleanness; [the glory] of chastity,” etc. But the Remigius manuscript and several others read best of all, and for that reason we have chosen to follow them here.]

Then the heart is disturbed; the filth of uncleanness is not perceived, the purity of chastity is not considered, and the glory of modesty is not recalled. It was night when Judas betrayed the Lord and when Peter denied him.

32. It is therefore especially at that time that God’s statutes should be retraced in the mind and the exhorting commandments reread. Let those precepts concerning chastity not be absent; when the mind is occupied with them, let it extinguish the burning of desire and the heat of the flesh.

Keep this in mind: “Every night I will wash my bed” (Ps. 6:7). For who, devoted to adultery and entangled in wickedness, washes his bed every night? The one who commits things deserving of tears does not know how to weep; and although he himself is worthy of tears, he does not have tears for his punishment.

[Note: [Col. 1292D] The Roman edition reads: “he does not have tears for his guilt.”]

But the one who chastises his body, who is a careful governor of himself, and who, groaning and grieving over the fall of his former offense, seeks how to wash it away with the tears of repentance—this is the one who washes his bed every night.

Let us therefore not sleep through the whole night; let us devote most of it to reading and prayers.

33. Hear the voice of the Church seeking Christ even in the night. “In my bed,” she says, “by night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:1).

Take this according to the literal sense. She sought him at night by praying, entreating, and even lamenting in tears. She sought him at night because he made darkness his hiding place, so that we might learn to seek him more earnestly.

The Church gathered from the Gentiles therefore sought him in the prophets, and for this reason believed. Finally, the evangelists and Paul set forth testimonies of the Lord’s coming from the prophets.

[Note: [Col. 1292D] All the editions read: “the evangelist and the Psalms placed them.”]

Hence it is written: “Night to night declares knowledge” (Ps. 18:3). She sought him at night—in persecutions and adversities, in tribulations and harsh labors.

It is night for all who do not possess perfect security. Hence the Lord says: “Night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9:4); “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” Let us therefore not work in darkness. For if our works shine, we do not work in darkness but in the light. It is day for those with whom Christ is present; it is night for those from whom he withdraws himself.

34. It is no great thing to give thanks to the Lord when you are prosperous and fortunate; but do so when you cling to Christ while a persecutor harasses you, when some storm disturbs you.

Have you lost a son? In that grief, in that night, in that desolation, remember the Lord your God, lest, as though you had not been heard, you become ungrateful and transgress in your misery.

Have you been driven into exile? Remember the Lord your God, lest, because your homeland has been forbidden to you, you place affection for it above God.

Have you lost your possessions because you were oppressed by the power of some rich man, and do you lack the means of support? Remember the Lord your God, lest the night of poverty lead you away from the devotion of your heart.

For this is the commandment of the Law: that you seek him especially in the night, when you are more likely to be heard by the Lord, and can say: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me in a spacious place” (Ps. 117:5).

35. But it is not enough to seek superficially for the attainment of grace; you must persist and devote yourself to the gift. Thus the Church or soul that sought him in her bed and sought him at night did not find him at first, perhaps because she sought him in bed (Song 3:2–4). But after she rose and went into the city—see whether this is the city to which the Lord, intending to celebrate the Passover, sent his disciples, saying: “Go into the city to a certain man” (Matt. 26:18)—afterward, as I said, she sought him in the marketplace and found him whom her soul loved.

She found him where oil is sold, which those awaiting the Bridegroom are accustomed to buy (Matt. 25:9), where there is law and judgment. If the law is spiritual, then the marketplace too is spiritual, where those skilled in the eternal law dispute. This marketplace is not tumultuous with lawsuits but glorious with the tribunals of Christ.

Where did she seek him, I ask? In the marketplace. Then she sought him in the streets, where those who were to gather for the Gospel master’s banquet were assembled, those who, when invited, did not consider themselves obliged to excuse themselves from such a feast (Luke 14:21).

After she had sought him in the marketplace and in the streets, she came upon those who go about the city (Song 3:3). Then at last she was able to find what she sought, perhaps because one placed in tribulation and fear finds grace more readily.

Finally, later she says: “Those who go about the city found me . . . they took my mantle from me” (Song 5:7). She therefore endured a struggle. But I cannot discover why they did not take her mantle earlier, unless perhaps it is because there she said she had asked: “Have you seen the one whom my soul loves?” (Song 3:3). She was speaking of Christ, and she was not stripped of her mantle; and she found the one whom she sought.

36. Learn how Christ is to be sought. He is sought by those who do not seek superficially but hold him fast with force, as she says: “I held him and did not let him go” (ibid. 4). She found him by faith and bound him by meditation.

If we understand the good guardians to be angels, then the one who passes beyond the angels finds the Word. Therefore there was not much distance between passing beyond them and finding Jesus.

How, then, did they later take her mantle, unless it was because, as the Church is oppressed by the advance of her faith—

[Note: [Col. 1293D] The Roman edition reads: “as though by the progress of the work, or of faith.” The old edition reads: “because by the progress of the work of her faith.” The manuscripts variously read: “because by progress”; “of works”; “of laborious faith”; many: “of oppressed faith”; and not a few: “of demonstrated faith.” In the same passage the old edition, with part of the manuscripts, reads: “the Lord is loved more”; the Roman edition, with another part, reads: “is loved more by the Lord.”]

—when she is stripped, she is loved more by the Lord, stripping off the old man in order to put on the new, whom garments do not cover but whose inward thoughts shine forth; or because, as she was about to come to Christ, she laid aside the mantle of secular wisdom? Noah, too, took off his mantle after he began to become more perfect.

37. *(Verse 56.)* Let us therefore remember the heavenly statutes, so that while we sing them with the secret voice of the mind, we may remember the name of the Lord in the night and say, as it is written: “This has happened to me because I sought your statutes.” That is, this remembrance has come to me so that I might remember your name even in the night—not sunk into sleep through drunkenness, not relaxed into slumber by banquets, not occupied by worldly cares, so that forgetfulness of your worship might creep upon me; but chastising my limbs by daily meditation and exercising the mind’s attention, so that through constant practice this solemn course may become habitual for us, and so that even in the night we may venerate the Lord Jesus with our whole devotion. To him belong glory, praise, and perpetuity from age to age, and now and always, for ever and ever. Amen.

## EIGHTH SERMON. Heth

1. The eighth letter, Heth, is called in Latin *pavor*, “dread”; dread is customary among the saints. Thus dread fell upon Abraham (Gen. 15:12) when he was offering a sacrifice full of spiritual mystery. David himself also says: “I said in my dread: Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:2).

For it signifies the reverence of religion more than the weakness of fear, although fear itself according to God is also holy: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). Therefore those who fear God are wise; and those who are wise are blessed: “Blessed is the one whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. 93:12).

Those who fear God are also blessed, as the authority of the example makes clear: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord” (Ps. 127:1). Thus it follows that those who fear God are both wise and blessed. The fear of the Lord is therefore holy, because dread truly belongs to the saints.

2. *(Verse 57.)* After this letter has been introduced, the person of the righteous immediately follows, saying: “The Lord is my portion; I said that I would keep your law.”

[Note: [Col. 1293D] From the entire structure of this work, and especially from this passage, it is evident that in Ambrose’s time the division of this psalm in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin copies was the same as that which we now find in them. It should also be observed in passing that for Ambrose a “verse” means the same as a sentence or a complete unit of meaning; for frequently, when sacred pages are under discussion, “verse” signifies nothing other than a sequence of words, what we French call a line. This consisted entirely of six words and had been devised for the purpose of preventing anything from being either removed from or added to Scripture. See *Criticism of the Old Testament*, chapter 26.]

Most codices place this verse, which is the first of the eighth letter, as the final verse of the seventh letter. But the book of the Psalms, corrected according to the Hebrews among the Greeks, taught us to connect this verse with the eighth letter. Moreover, the order itself and the number of verses agree in such a way that the eighth letter begins with it.

3. “The Lord,” he says, “is my portion.” How rare on earth is the person who can say: “The Lord is my portion”! How far removed from vices, how separated from every stain of sin, is the one who has nothing in common with the world and claims nothing of this world for himself, who is not a possessor of bodily desires,

[Note: [Col. 1294D] Three manuscripts read: “in whom there is no desire for bodily possessions.” Ten manuscripts, together with the old edition, read: “in whom there is no possession of bodily desires.” The Roman edition does not differ from them, except that from one Vatican manuscript it has: “To whom there is,” etc. But since the relative pronoun is found neither in the old edition nor in any Gallican manuscript, we have judged the reading of the Remigius and Vienne manuscripts preferable.]

who is not inflamed by lust, not goaded by avarice, not enervated by wantonness, not disfigured by luxury, not laid low by ambition, not worn down by envy, and not troubled by any care of worldly affairs: a true minister of the altar, born for God and not for himself.

4. For Levi, as the interpretation has it, means “he himself has been taken for me”; it also means “he himself is mine”; it means “taken exclusively”; and it means “taken for me.” The same person is Levi both for me and for God, just as he is both priest for me and priest for God; both my advocate and the Lord’s intercessor; offering sacrifice for me and also offering himself to the Lord.

Finally, elsewhere Levi is also said by interpretation to mean “for me.” For if Levi is named by me, he is “for me”; if he offers for me, he is “for me”; if he intervenes for me, he is “for me.” But if he is called by the Lord, he is said to be “for me,” that is, not tributary to another, not a payer of tithes, not generous from a possession; he is “for me,” that is, as though he abounded in place of all these things.

I do not seek tithes, produce, gifts, or offerings from him; he himself is my gift, he himself is my tribute. He is not generous to me from his own possession; rather, he himself is my possession, he himself is my fruit, he himself is my revenue, taken for me or taken by me.

This cannot exist without divine grace. For just as a possession cannot be mine unless I purchase it, so Levi cannot exist unless he has been taken by the Lord; and when he has been taken, he is rightly called mine.

Thus, when Moses was commanded to divide the dwelling places among the Jewish people by their individual tribes and to distribute a portion to each tribe, God excepted the tribe of Levi, saying: “The sons of Levi shall have no portion or inheritance among their brothers, because the Lord God himself is their portion” (Deut. 10:9). And elsewhere: “I am the Lord, their portion” (Num. 18:20).

## 5

An earthly division is denied to these men, so that, while they claim no worldly portion for themselves, they may become a heavenly possession—or may know that they possess only this: the service of faith and devotion—far richer than those who spread out the extensive territories of their possessions. However far they extend their boundaries, the land fails them, the sea encloses their mad desires, and they pay taxes greater than their revenues. But this man, possessing nothing for himself, serves no one except God; his portion is above the earth. The earth does not fail him, nor is he enclosed by the sea. Whoever has God as his portion is possessor of the whole of nature. Instead of fields, therefore, he is himself sufficient for himself, possessing good fruit that can never perish; instead of houses, it is enough for him to be the dwelling and temple of the Lord, than which nothing can be more precious. For what is more precious to God? Or what can be lacking to the man who can say: “Let it not happen that I should glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:4)? The prince of this world cannot claim fellowship with this man, in whom he finds nothing belonging to him.

## 6

Therefore the Lord, who came to teach us that God should become our portion, says: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14:30). And wishing us to be his imitators, he says: “Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money” (Matthew 10:9). Hence Peter, showing that his portion was in God and not in the world, says: “I have neither silver nor gold, but what I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). This is my portion; this is my lot; Christ is my portion. Rise, therefore, and walk in the name of Christ Jesus—that is, I am rich in my portion, powerful in my portion. Rightly do I anticipate such fruits from this portion that salvation and life may be granted, because this is the inheritance of the portion that I have chosen for myself. He said this to the lame man, and the man who had been lame from his mother’s womb rose. How, then, could Peter feel the loss of his portion, when he was restoring the losses of nature?

## 7

Why do you not have silver and gold, Peter? Tell us; tell us also what this is that you say you have, when you declared that you had left everything you possessed. For this is how you spoke to the Lord: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matthew 19:27)—that is, we did not seek what belongs to the world; we did not seek a share in possessions; but we chose you as our portion. You left, therefore, everything you had, Peter; whence do you have what you say you possess? The lame man rises, and is lifted up by the sound of your words. You give health to others, although you yourself needed the help of your own salvation. You left what you had, therefore, and received what you did not have. Christ is your portion; Christ is your possession.

[Note: The Remian and Fiscian manuscripts and two Sorbonne manuscripts read: “generous to you. And we followed you,” that is, “we sought Jesus. His name to you,” and so forth.]

His name is generous to you, his name is fruitful for you; his name pays your taxes for you—and good taxes, not of money but of grace. Your portion is not dried up by drought, not dissolved by rain, not scorched by cold, and not shaken by storms.

[Note: “To scorch” (*urere*) does not merely signify everywhere the harmful force of heat and cold, but also that of any other thing. Thus Horace, *Epistle* 1.10:

> As once a shoe,  
> if it is larger than the foot, overturns it;  
> if smaller, it scorches it.

That is, it injures it. We find Blessed Jerome and others using the word in this sense as well.]

“By day the sun shall not scorch you, nor the moon by night.” Preserve the portion that you have chosen; for it is a portion that earthly shares cannot equal. What, indeed, could be compared with those of whom God says: “And I shall dwell in them” (Leviticus 26:12)?

What is more magnificent than a heavenly lodging? What is more blessed than divine possession? “And I shall walk among them,” he says (2 Corinthians 6:16). Others complain about the narrowness of their farms; in you God has a spacious possession, in whom he says that he will walk—that is, finding broad spaces for habitation—he who encloses the earth in his hand. For it is written: “Who measured the waters in his hand, and the heavens with a span, and enclosed the whole earth in his closed hand?” (Isaiah 40:12). To him for whom the world is narrow, you are a spacious house.

“The Lord is my portion,” he says. A martyr says this. Let us therefore live for him, for whom to die is glorious. In other words, how well Paul said this, showing that he had no portion in this world! For it is written: “To this very hour we hunger and thirst, and are naked and beaten with blows, and are unsettled, and labor, working with our own hands. We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and endure; we are blasphemed, and we entreat. We have become like the refuse of this world, the scum of all things, even until now” (1 Corinthians 4:11–13).

## 8

Perhaps it may trouble someone that he called himself refuse. For he is not. But this is how it appears to worldly people, who think that the highest glory or beauty lies in riches. Do they not consider all those who serve them because of their wealth to be refuse—those whom they admire on account of their riches, fear because of their power, and praise because of their nobility? Yet Paul considered all these things to be losses rather than advantages. Therefore he says: “The things that were gain to me, these I considered losses for the sake of Christ, because of the surpassing knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of everything and consider them refuse, that I may gain Christ” (Philippians 3:7–8). “I am considered,” he says—not by my own judgment, but by the judgment of others. Frequently that poor man is considered laughable and accursed because of the filth of his clothing or the scars of his wounds, since he has no portion on earth; yet his portion is in heaven. His soul has established its inheritance there, because it heard Jesus saying: “Do not store up treasure for yourselves on earth . . . but store up treasure for yourselves in heaven” (Matthew 6:19–20).

## 9

But the rich cannot hear this. Their ears are closed and dulled by the sound of bronze; money resounds more loudly for them than divine words. Finally, a certain rich man who did not have the Lord as his portion approached the Lord. He had many possessions, but the Lord is not counted among many things, for he does not deign to share fellowship with the world. “For what portion does justice have with iniquity?”

This rich man therefore says: “What must I do to possess eternal life?” (Luke 18:18). The Lord answered him: “You know the commandments: You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not bear false witness” (ibid., 20–21), showing that eternal life consists in these commandments. But he, wishing to justify himself, says: “I have done all these things; what remains for me?”

Then the Lord, wishing to become his portion—not money, not possessions, but the true God—says to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (ibid., 22). But the man whose portion was gold and silver, without which he could not exist, and with which the Lord could not be his portion, became sad. Hence the Lord declared that it was impossible for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, but that what is impossible through human desires can become possible through divine grace alone.

## 10

Elsewhere also he says: “Whoever has left father or mother, house, brothers, or sisters . . . will receive a hundredfold in this age and will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29). Perhaps you will say: Whoever, by leaving his house—by “house” understand his entire estate—and by leaving his relatives, has followed God, has the Lord as his portion and God as his portion; he also has eternal life. And because, by receiving a hundredfold, he becomes rich in this world, you will say that the rich man enters the kingdom of heaven. Furthermore, if the Lord gives a hundredfold of those things which, even in single measure, usually obstruct the receiving of the eternal inheritance, then he returns a hundred possessions for one possession and a hundred pounds of gold for one pound.

## 11

We have indeed known many in this world who, after giving their possessions to the poor, became rich with a more abundant treasure. This is a most beautiful example, intended also to provoke people to mercy. Yet they ought not demand from the Lord a worldly reward of this kind, nor hope for worldly things, but rather recognize that for those who have left everything, God is their portion. He himself is the perfect reward of virtues, measured not by counting a hundredfold but by the estimate of perfect fullness.

“I am your God,” he says (Genesis 17:1). He did not say, “I will be,” but “I already am; I already dwell; I already possess.” He removes delay wherever he finds the confession of the righteous. Certainly elsewhere he says: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). He promises something future, but he does not allow what is future to be postponed for even the space of a single day. Finally, he could have said, “You will be with me in paradise,” but he added “today,” so that grace might not be diminished by delay.

## 12

But the Lord Jesus says not only to that man, “Today you will be with me in paradise”; he says also to you: “You will be with me in paradise,” if you confess the Lord Jesus, if you ask his protection for yourself, and if you say: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (ibid., 42). But he does not say to you, “Today you will be with me”; he says to the martyr: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” He does not say this to you because you are still situated in this fevered body, in this body subject to desire, in this body still longing for earthly things. But when you are able to say: “You have broken my bonds” (Psalm 115:16)—that is, you have brought the course of this life to an end and freed me from this body of death—then he says to you: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

## 13

You have, therefore, human being, among the many portions set before you, a portion of this kind as well. The Lord has set before you, as portions, possessions, gold, silver, honors, and nobility; he has also set himself before you as a portion. You have very many portions; choose the one you think best. Let the number not disturb you, but let grace stir you; let labor not turn you away, but let the fruit invite you.

In the divine portion there are groanings and labors. Hence the holy Apostle, whose portion was God, says: “We are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him” (Romans 8:17). You see that where Christ’s inheritance is, there compassion must also be. Whoever suffers with another does not do so superficially, but so that he may fill up in his body the sufferings of Christ, just as Paul did, and Jeremiah, who says in this very letter:

“The mercies of the Lord are the reason we have not perished, because his compassions have not come to an end; he will renew them like the morning light” (Colossians 1:24). “My groanings are many, and my heart faints. ‘The Lord is my portion,’ I said; therefore I will wait for him” (Lamentations 3:22 and following).

Whoever, therefore, waits for the Lord is the Lord’s portion. Hence David also, who says, “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he inclined toward me” (Psalm 39:2), declares in this passage that God is his portion.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “because his compassions have not been consumed.” Other editions and manuscripts read as in the text. Either reading could have arisen from the Septuagint, which has: “because his compassions have not come to an end” (*hoti ou synetelesthēsan hoi oiktirmoi autou*). This can be explained in either way. Moreover, anyone who wishes to compare the words of this passage, as they stand here, with those expressed in the sacred manuscripts will find no small discrepancy between them.]

## 14

How rare is the person who claims this for himself! It is not claimed through nobility or riches. That rich king says:

“I too am a mortal human being, like everyone else, and descended from the earthly one who was made first; in my mother’s womb I was formed as flesh. For ten months I was coagulated in blood, from the seed of a man and the pleasure of sleep united; and when I was born I drew in the common air, and likewise fell upon the earth, uttering my first cry like everyone else. I was nurtured in swaddling clothes and in great cares.” And he added: “No king has had a different beginning of birth. For all alike have one entrance into life and a similar departure” (Wisdom 7:1 and following).

Because he saw that the beginning of birth was common to all, he labored to be God’s portion; he called upon him, and the spirit of wisdom came into him (ibid., 7). But the pleasure-seekers choose another portion, saying: “Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes, and let no flower of the season pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither” (Wisdom 2:7–8). And below: “For this is our portion, and this our lot” (ibid., 9).

## 15

How great a thing it is to despise riches—and yet how rare this very thing is! Moses, certainly, could have become the successor of the king, having been brought up by the king’s daughter.

[Note: All the manuscripts read, “not merely like Pharaoh, but even Pharaoh; and Pharaoh could have been like Moses.” The editions read instead, “indeed, as though Pharaoh, but he himself could have been Pharaoh. Either . . .” It is clear that the manuscript reading is superior.]

He could therefore have been not merely like Pharaoh, but Pharaoh himself; and Pharaoh could have been like Moses, for both were human beings. But all human power lies in the will.

Moses did not wish to be king, although he could have been. He considered the reproach of Christ preferable to the treasures of Egypt; but by fleeing power he became more powerful. For he became a god to King Pharaoh. Pharaoh was king, but he was not a god; Moses became a god to him—that is, he became terrifying to the king himself, so that the king would fear and dread him. This, however, was the power of holiness.

Among such a gathering of gods, God stands and makes distinctions.

[Note: The Ambrosian and Erasmian editions, together with most manuscripts, read: “And you, if you wish to be a terror as a god to sinners, reverence to kings, and so forth.” The Gillian and Roman editions read: “And you, if you wish, as God, to be a terror to sinners,” followed by “and reverence to kings” in the Roman edition. Since the former reading lacks manuscript support, while the latter does not offer a sufficiently complete sense, the words of the manuscripts, together with those of the Laetian and the second Navarrese edition, seemed preferable; we have therefore transferred them into the text. Nor is the reading of the Regius manuscript displeasing: “. . . a terror and reverence to kings.”]

“And you, if you wish to be a god to sinners, a terror to kings, and reverence to others, so that they may seem subject to you as to God because you act in God’s name, despise the things of the world and strive to place the reproach of the Lord’s passion above all riches.”

I speak of the reproach that appears to them to be reproach: to the Jews, a stumbling block; to the Gentiles, foolishness; but to us, the power and wisdom of God. Yet Pharaoh, considering this reproach—that is, poverty, lowliness, and insults—preferred to belong to the devil rather than to be God’s portion. And therefore, because he did not wish to be subject to God, he subjected himself to the intercession of a human being.

Since the holy prophet David was God’s portion, he rightly says: “I said that I would keep your law.” He certainly speaks of the spiritual law, as Paul also shows. For those who have interpreted the Law bodily do not keep the Law, but transgress it.

## 16. (Verse 58)

Let us come to the second verse, which is as follows:

“I will entreat your face, Lord, with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your word.”

We read in the Old Testament that Moses entreated to see the face of God, and that he received the answer: “No one shall see my face and live” (Exodus 33:20).

Let us first understand this mystically. Moses received the figure of the Law. Through hidden mysteries the Law announces Christ, but it does not display him face to face, as the Gospel displayed him. In him he spoke face to face, although in the Gospel he appeared as a man born from a Virgin, while the Word manifested himself through his works.

Perhaps this was made clear to Moses: that the Jewish people would die, and that they would see Christ face to face and yet would not believe. If you refer this to the Law, Christ is also the end of the Law, according to the apostolic statement:

“For Christ is the end according to the Law for everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” This reading is supported by all surviving copies of Paul’s letters, indeed by Ambrose himself above, in Sermon 5, section 22, and elsewhere. Nevertheless, we have chosen not to abandon the reading of all the manuscripts and old editions. Again, two verses later, seven manuscripts read, “who believe in Christ.” Perhaps the scribes thought that the other manuscripts and all the editions ought to be corrected in this way, since they did not consider the earlier statement that Christ is shown face to face in the Gospel. Thus, after the words “who have seen Christ,” understand “in the Gospel.” The reading of the Regius manuscript, “who live for Christ,” is not without merit.]

The bodily interpretation of the Law died when the Lord Christ Jesus revealed its spiritual grace. Or rather, because all of us who have seen Christ and have been baptized into Christ have died to sin—for while alive we were held by the bonds of the Law—when we died in Christ, we were certainly put to death to the Law through the body of Christ, so that we might belong to another, who rose from the dead. But this is mystical.

## 17

Morally, however, this makes us remember the history of old, concerning holy Moses, who asked God to reveal himself to him and to let him see him face to face. The holy prophet of the Lord certainly knew that he could not see the invisible God face to face; but holy devotion surpasses measure, and he thought that even this was possible for God: that he could cause what is incorporeal to be grasped by bodily eyes.

This error is not blameworthy, but rather a pleasing and insatiable desire: he wished to hold his Lord, as it were, in his hand and see him with the gaze of his eyes. He knew that human beings had been made in the image and likeness of God. When he was chosen by the Lord God to deliver the people, he was filled with the spirit of wisdom. He had seen that angel and his face in glory. Finally, when its light shone, he was terrified; he saw the bush burning without being consumed.

He began to see and admire the radiance; drawn by desire and grace, he approached so that he might consider that radiance in the bush more attentively. Therefore, if he received such ardor and felt such desire when he saw the angel in the flame of fire from the bush—so that, although seized by fear, he did not dare to examine it, yet still wished to do so—how much more did he desire to see the Lord’s face bodily, saying within himself that the face would be full of light, full of glory, full of power, full of divinity.

[Note: All the editions added at this point: “What shall I call him?” The addition is elegant, but nothing of the kind is found in the manuscripts.]

I can neither say nor think more about God. “When a person has finished, then he begins; and when he has ended, then he will be perplexed,” as it is written (Ecclesiastes 18:6), because the eternal majesty of God is incomprehensible.

[Note: The manuscripts read as above, except for two, which have: “He grasped the radiance by sight, which he approached to admire.” The editions do not differ from these except that they prefer: “which he approached after admiring.”]

## 18

The result of his request was indeed unattainable, but the servant’s affection was commendable. Advancing beyond his nature through devotion, he estimated, from the Lord’s angels, how much more he ought to desire the Lord’s face, by which he might satisfy his longing.

He knew that within the human being there would be another glory after death, another brightness. For just as star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead: although the body is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it will rise in glory; it will rise in power; it will rise as a spiritual body.

Whoever could know these things rightly presumed that he might desire to see the face of God, whom he would see after the death of his body. Certainly he had received such a form, and the Lord already approved him as such, so that he did not differ from the angels, being a heavenly minister and executor of the oracle.

Therefore, since he knew that the angels of the little ones daily see the face of the Father who is in heaven, he thought that he ought already to see it, as though he had forgotten his body and laid aside his flesh—like the man who, while still in the body, was caught up into paradise and said that he did not know whether he had been caught up in the body or outside the body to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:3).

For even when the saints bear a body, they are not in the flesh but in the spirit, because those who live in carnal desire and conduct cannot please God. The conduct of the saints, however, was not in the flesh but in heaven, as Paul shows (Philippians 3:20).

[Note: The edition reads: “But the saints are not in the flesh in their conduct.” Two manuscripts omit the phrase. All the others read as above, “in the body.” We think that the word “saints” should be understood of Moses, whose conduct our author proves to have been in heaven by teaching, through the Apostle, that such is the conduct of the saints.]

## 19

And what shall we say about this commendable desire to see the divine face? Even human beings, when they hear that someone is noble, strong, or wise, desire to see him, considering him almost superhuman. The emperor comes forth, to whose royal power a portion of the globe has been entrusted; everyone gathers, and in so great a crowd they eagerly gaze upon him alone, thinking that there is something more than ordinary in the emperor’s face because of the splendor of his purple.

Do you wonder, then, whether the face of God is desirable, when every human affection admires a human being resembling itself?

From this we may also understand why everyone eagerly wishes to meet the emperor without being guilty of any crime. Even if conscience has a crime, the hidden places of the heart conceal it, provided that the person is not publicly implicated in guilt and no crime of his has been openly established. Finally, when certain accused persons have confessed themselves and are forbidden to present themselves before the emperor and the judges—just as the shameful persons of pimps and prostitutes are kept away from the sight of either judge or emperor, lest the appearance of the most disgraceful people offend the brightness of the royal face—the man who is conscious of having no crime, like an innocent person, comes forward into the midst.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “to whom a portion of royal power has been entrusted, to whom . . . has been committed,” and so forth.]

[Note: The same Roman edition reads “having been registered.” This word is used in law, especially in two ways: first, for those whom a governor, after they had been accused in their absence, recorded in the official acts as persons to be sought; second, for those whom a governor recorded as being subject to deportation, or concerning whose deportation he wrote to the emperor, as Brissonius explains under this word. Since neither interpretation fits the sequence of the discourse very well, and since all manuscripts and old editions reject this word, we should say that those are meant here who openly acknowledge their crime. For *advocare* is sometimes used in the sense of acknowledging a deed as having been committed, from which the French word *avouer* is thought to have arisen; this is recorded in the learned Du Cange’s Glossary under the same word. Moreover, in Book 15 of the Theodosian Code, title 7, “On Stage Performers,” law 12, it is decreed that paintings of disreputable persons may not be displayed in places where images consecrated to the emperors are located. This somewhat illuminates Ambrose’s passage.]

## 20

From these examples, then, let us understand the affection of holy Moses. Like an innocent man, he desired to see the face of God, as though with the face of his conscience; he longed to open to him the inner face of his mind and to be more fully known. Moses desired this, and so did holy David, who says elsewhere: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Psalm 25:2). He would not wish to be tested if he recognized crime in himself, nor to be tried if he knew himself subject to grave passions. Free, therefore, from sin, he eagerly offered himself to God.

But perhaps, because he was not yet cleansed from vice by more frequent visitations of God, he was not perfect at the beginning, since shortly before he had been told: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exodus 3:5)—that sandal, certainly, which he had brought from Egypt, that is, the covering of bodily conduct. Therefore the Lord says to him: “No human being shall see my face and live.”

[Note: The manuscripts read as above. The edition instead has: “. . . like an innocent man, he wished, as though with a certain . . . of an attentive mind. To be known,” and so forth. Whoever examines the passage more carefully will not deny that our reading, supported by the manuscripts, is preferable.]

## 21

Consider when this was said. He had not yet been told: “I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:1).

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “He was still a man; it was reserved for him to advance until he became a god, and therefore he was told: ‘Remove the sandal.’ He spoke of the man,” and so forth. Again, a little later, that edition alone has: “so that you may offer yourself before the Lord a third time.” The sense of both readings is the same.]

He was still a man, and therefore he says this to him. Advancement was required for him to become a god; and therefore he was told: “I spoke of a human being: cease to have human sins, and you will see my face.” For whoever sees my face must be without sin. But because a human being cannot be without sin, he is admonished so that he may rise into the designation of god.

And what shall I say about the designation of god? Be an angel—that is, a minister of divine power—and obey the Lord’s commands. When you have become an angel, you will see the face of the Lord.

It is a great thing to see the face of God. The Law tells you to present yourself in Jerusalem three times. The Lord Jesus himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Do you perceive what is required of you, for whom the privilege of seeing God has been set forth?

Cleanse your heart, therefore, so that, with your spirit renewed, you may be created as a new person. Cast every polluted thought from your heart; let there be nothing by which your affection may be defiled. Let your mind be simple and your sincerity pure. To such people the Lord deigns to reveal himself when they have laid aside the covering of the body.

## 22

Now let us speak about the remaining part of the verse itself. “Have mercy on me,” he says, “according to your word.”

Mercy is indeed a portion of justice. If you wish to give to the poor, this mercy is justice, according to the saying: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (Psalm 112:9).

Moreover, since it is unjust that one like yourself should not be helped by his fellow, especially when the Lord our God wished this earth to be a common possession of all human beings and to provide fruits for everyone, greed has distributed the rights of possession. It is just, therefore, that if you claim as private something that was bestowed in common upon the human race—or rather upon all living creatures—you should at least sprinkle some of it among the poor, so that you do not deny sustenance to those with whom you owe a share in your legal rights.

## 23

It is also an act of mercy to pardon sin; it is both mercy and justice. Finally, divine Scripture attributes the forgiveness of sins to justice, according to what was read today: “Blessed is the wood by which justice is brought about, but accursed is the wood which is made by human hands” (Wisdom 14:7–8).

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “by which justice is done,” following the Septuagint, δι᾽ οὗ γίνεται δικαιοσύνη, “through which justice comes about.” But we are reluctant to depart from the unanimous reading of all the manuscripts and early editions.]

The former he referred to the Lord’s cross, the latter to the error of the Gentiles, who venerate pieces of wood. But what is the justice of the cross except that, when the Lord Jesus Christ ascended that gallows, he nailed the record of our sins to the cross and cleansed the sin of the whole world with his blood?

In what respect, then, is God just, except in this: he knew that he had formed the human being from the clay of the earth, and that this earth is subject to corruption and slippery through the vice of passion? Therefore the Lord, who made you according to your soul in his image and likeness—that is, rational, just, and chaste—for you are in the image of God if you are just, so that you may be an image of justice; if you are chaste, so that the figure of the immaculate may shine forth in you—knowing that, according to the frailty of the body, the human being is exposed to corruption, as a just judge he granted pardon to the sins of a frail and slippery nature.

## 24

And lest someone perhaps say: Why, then, was Adam subjected to the curse and the sentence? Was God unjust? Certainly not. But because, as with someone fragile and weak, he had prescribed beforehand what he should guard against—for the weak person ought not to seize what is forbidden, but to obey commands—he therefore held him more accountable for transgression than he condemned him merely for his fall.

[Note: All the editions, and some manuscripts, read: “therefore he held him guilty of transgression, whom he . . .” The other reading, which is supported by the larger number of manuscripts, is better; it is the one we have printed in the text.]

A just sentence of severity therefore proceeded against him, because he wished to know what it did not profit him to know. But toward us, who are bound by the chain of inheritance, who are in this flesh—which, worn down and habituated to sins by the precedent of our ancestors, could not rise above them—he acted as a just man and granted indulgence. For he justly forgave the heir who was afflicted by the precedent of his ancestor.

## 25

There is therefore a just mercy, but there is also an unjust mercy (23, Question 4, chapter “Est injusta”). Thus it is written in the Law concerning a certain man:

[Note: Namely, the man who has killed his neighbor by ambush.]

“You shall not pity him” (Deuteronomy 19:13).

And in the books of Kings you read that Saul incurred offense because he pitied Agag, king of the enemies, whom the divine sentence had commanded to be put to death (1 Samuel 15:9).

Suppose someone, moved by the pleas of a robber’s sons and softened by his wife’s tears, thinks that the robber ought to be released, although he still has the desire to continue robbing. Will he not hand over the innocent to destruction if he frees someone who is planning the destruction of many?

Certainly, if he restrains the sword and loosens the bonds, why does he release him into exile? Why does he not, by whatever more merciful means he can, remove the opportunity for robbery from one whose will he could not extort?

Furthermore, when judgment is being made between two people—the accuser and the defendant—with equal danger to their lives, so that the one is liable if he does not prove his charge and the other if he is convicted by the accuser, would the judge not follow what justice requires, but, while pitying the defendant, condemn the accuser who proved the charge; or, while favoring an accuser unable to prove his case, condemn the innocent? Such mercy cannot therefore be called just.

[Note: “Concerning their lives,” that is, concerning capital punishment, or the penalty of death. For at times the danger of the defendant and the accuser was made equal, so that not only were both kept in custody, but the same punishment that was owed to one, if convicted, was imposed upon the other if he failed to prove the charge, according to the law of retaliation. See the Theodosian Code, Book 9, title “On Accusers,” law 19, and Gratian in the cited passage.]

[Note: The Roman edition, following the old edition of Gratian, reads: “he loosens the exile.” All the others, with the manuscript copies, read: “he releases into exile.” The Fiscian manuscript alone reads: “he releases to destruction.” “He releases into exile” means the same as “he frees from exile,” or “he does not condemn to exile.”]

## 26

Even in the Church, where it is especially fitting to show mercy, the rule of justice must be observed with the greatest care, lest someone who has been excluded from communion obtain, through a brief and prepared tear—or even through more abundant weeping—the communion that he ought to seek for a very long time, by the priest’s easy compliance.

Does he not, when he indulges one who is unworthy, provoke many others to the contagion of falling? For an easy pardon gives an incentive to sin.

This has been said so that we may know that mercy must be administered to offenders according to the word of God and according to reason. If a physician discovers an internal scar from a serpent’s wound, and although he ought to cut away the disease of the ulcer so that it does not spread more widely, nevertheless, softened by the sick man’s tears, abandons his resolve to cut and cauterize and covers with medicines what should have been opened with the knife—would this not be useless mercy, if, because of the brief pain of the incision or cauterization, the whole body should waste away and the use of life perish?

Rightly, therefore, a priest too, like a good physician, must cut away a severe wound from the whole body of the Church, lest it spread more widely, and expose the poison of the crime that lay hidden rather than nourish it. Otherwise, while he does not think that one person should be excluded, he may make many worthy of exclusion from the Church.

## 27

Rightly, therefore, the Apostle exhorts us by the divine example, saying: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness” (Romans 11:22). He shows that the Jewish people were rightly separated from the body of the Church, lest the poison of their faithlessness contaminate the Church; but that the people of the Gentiles were received through the Lord’s goodness and glory in the gift of obedience.

Rightly, therefore, divine goodness supports this people, so long as they remain in divine goodness. But if they too should depart, they will be condemned according to the character of their crime.

Hence the Lord is described as both light and fire: to the one walking in darkness he shines as a lamp, so that he who seeks the brightness of light may not be able to wander any longer; but to the one who has done many things that ought not to remain but to be burned, the Lord is fire, so that he may consume the hay and stubble of our works and save us through a beneficial loss, like gold which, while being refined, is proved more fully.

28. Perhaps someone may ask why the Prophet wrote: “Have mercy on me according to your word” [Psalm 118:58]. For the word of God is justice. If, then, he relied upon justice, why did he put mercy first? Or if he was seeking mercy, why did he consider it necessary to request it according to the measure of justice? For one who acts well and lives well has no need of mercy, since mercy frees from sin. Indeed, we do not ordinarily extend mercy to the rich, the strong, or those supported by good fortune, but to the needy, the weak, or those who have fallen from wealth into poverty, captivity, or some other need. Therefore, whoever needs mercy is a sinner; but whoever is not a sinner is certainly just and has no need of the mercy of God.

29. Accordingly, one must consider in what respect each person needs mercy—or, that is, according to what condition he needs it—or possesses justice. An angel, after all, needs the justice of God in one way, and a human being in another. An archangel needs mercy in one way, and a human being in another. The nature of angels is not, of course, exposed to corruption in the same way as the nature of the human race; and therefore the angel needs the mercy of God so that he may not be able to go astray and, with God’s grace turned away from him, fall into vice. A human being, however, even if already established in a firmer purpose, nevertheless seeks the mercy of God because of the succession of sins he has contracted. Thus, although both need the mercy of God, mercy is owed to the angel in one way and to the human being in another; for a slight fault in an angel is judged by a more severe tribunal. The sin of youth in a human being is also restrained by a milder sentence than the sin of old age, and is more quickly released.

30. The Prophet, therefore, in this verse distinguishes the causes, so that as a human being he may ask for mercy—for no one is without the stain of sin—and as a Prophet he may plead for justice. Or certainly, although he has sinned as a human being and as a sinner needs mercy, nevertheless he has corrected his error, undertaken repentance, abstained from the drunkenness of wrongdoing through the sobriety of virtue. Therefore he asks for justice according to the word of God, because it is the judgment of God’s word that pardon be granted to those who have turned back, provided that their conversion has been made legitimately [Ezekiel 18:21; 33:12].

31. (Verse 59.) “I considered my ways, and turned my feet toward your testimonies.” The meaning is twofold. Either: I considered my former ways, full of falling and sin, and therefore, so that I might deserve the remission of sins, I turned through a change of conduct and devotion to virtue. “I turned my feet toward your testimonies,” so that I might no longer walk by the steps by which I had previously fallen, but by the paths of your testimonies, so that the tracks of your commandments might not allow me to go astray, nor turn my footprint into byways and winding paths. Often, those who do not know the road, if they follow the paved highways, arrive where they wish to go and avoid the winding paths of error. But if they presume to know what they do not know and think that certain shortcuts should be followed, departing from the public road, they frequently encounter labyrinths of error, so that they regret having turned aside from the route; and therefore, after many wasted labors, they hasten to return to the road they had abandoned.

32.
