One meaning, then, is this; but another is as follows: “I considered my ways”—not those behind me, but those before me—so that I might anticipate my actions with reflection, lest, advancing without deliberation, I should fall into some offense in the very process of thinking [Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read, “in the very constraints.” The Roman edition, from the margin of one Vatican manuscript, reads, “in the very actions.” Certain manuscripts read, “in the very discourses.” The great majority agree with us.]. Thus, if I wish to do something, I should first consider whether what I desire ought to be done, and in what manner it ought to be done. Likewise, if someone is to be addressed, I should consider whether I ought to address him, and then whether I should speak publicly or privately, in the presence of some people or of none; as in the case where, if you wish to rebuke a brother, you should first rebuke him alone, secondly in the presence of two or three witnesses, and thirdly, if he has not listened, before the Church. Therefore, if, having set aside the proper order, you wish to rebuke a brother before the Church whom you ought first to have warned, you yourself recognize that you have gone wrong. Do everything, then, with deliberation, so that you may not regret your action.

Or again, if you have entered upon a road and, when you have come to some crossroads—for this is what a place where many roads converge is called—do not know which route you ought to take, nevertheless you stand and consider within yourself whether you should choose the first, second, third, or fourth road, or perhaps the fifth, if there is one, and follow it. You do not think that you should begin the journey before you have determined it in your mind and decided with fuller concentration. You stand, then, considering which road leads to the city to which you think you ought to travel. How much more ought you to pause in spirit and mind, when you are striving toward the heavenly kingdom, and consider within yourself that not every road leads there, and not every road directs one to that Jerusalem which is in heaven [Proverbs 14:12]!

33. There are roads that have evil outcomes, roads worn down by the temptations of the devil; and therefore their ends are the ends of death. These are the roads of which you have read in Proverbs: “There are ways that seem straight to a man, but their ends look toward the depths of hell” [Proverbs 14:12]. There is, however, that narrower road which leads to the kingdom of God. Therefore, if you wish to enter the road that leads to God, do not look around, do not deliberate within yourself, do not weigh the matter—lest you be easily seized by desire, if, enticed by the breadth of the road, you enter upon a path that leads down to hell [Matthew 7:13–14]. Consider beforehand, then, and weigh carefully what you are doing.

34. “Whoever,” he says, “looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” [Matthew 5:28]. Such a person, of course, deliberately thought that he should look at a woman, that he should look in order to desire her; but let this evil thought abandon its ways. Another person did not deliberate beforehand, but suddenly looked, was captured, saw, desired, and therefore fell. If he had considered the weakness of his own desire and feared beforehand lest, when he saw a woman, he should be captured in mind and spirit, he certainly would not have looked at the woman, lest he desire her. By looking at the woman, therefore, he did not direct his foot toward the testimonies of the Lord; but if he had been able to think before his fall, perhaps he would have directed it [Note: One manuscript, the Regius, alone reads: “Perhaps each person would have said: ‘I considered my ways, and turned my feet toward your testimonies.’ Therefore, first …”].

Let each person, then, first consider how he should look at a woman, so that he may not look at her in order to desire her, or may not fix his attention upon her. But if, upon seeing her suddenly—or having been grounded in a good thought—he directs his foot toward the testimonies of the Lord, so that he does not remain in captivity, then reflection has certainly benefited him. Finally, if one loves, cherishes, and desires a woman, let him consider Christ, his judgment, and his testimonies concerning the rewards of chastity; let him abandon the ways of desire and follow the ways of Christ. He will receive praise from them if, contemplating the Lord Jesus, he despises the heat of the flesh, extinguishes the flame of lust as though from some spring, and dashes his tender and feeble desires against the rock of Christ.

35. Let him consider first, then—to repeat what was said—how he should look and how he should speak. He considered well who said: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth” [Psalm 140:3], lest, when the mind inflames desire, the tongue slip in speech, or, through the ease of speaking, even unguarded verbosity incur what the mind had not considered. Let him consider how he directs his foot and brings forward his hand, lest, driven by a sudden impulse of indignation, when he ought to repel an injury, he himself inflict a blow of conspicuous slaughter [Note: The Roman edition reads, “a blow of notable killing.”]. We must therefore consider what we are doing; for where reflection comes first, maturity is brought to the action. Thus this foot is the trace of faith: after careful meditation, it turned away from bodily movements toward the divine testimonies.

36. (Verse 60.) The verse that follows teaches what benefit it brings to consider beforehand what one will later do: “I am prepared, and I am not disturbed, that I may keep your commandments.” When a person anticipates by reflection what he is going to do, he is always ready for action, always firm and strong, so that he cannot be disturbed by some sudden misfortune. No gusts of excessively rocky ambition shake him; no storm or tempest of unjust aggression harasses him; the eye of an impudent prostitute does not ensnare him—for the eye of a prostitute is the lover’s snare. The wretched man is captured in another’s possession who, seized unexpectedly by fire, has lost possession of his own mind.

If persecution presses in, it finds him already prepared, so that where there might be disturbance because salvation is uncertain, the anticipated crown of the sacred contest may soothe him through prudent meditation on what is to come. If he is frequently gnawed at by slanderers who speak evil, let him consider that “the disciple is not above his master, nor the servant above his lord.” If unspeakable insults from those who reproached fell upon the Son of God, how can a servant hope to be exempt from them? Therefore he must prepare his mind, so that, when these things occur, they may not be able to disturb him.

Let him prepare and compose his spirit through meditation, so that he may say, if indeed he is able: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or famine?” and so forth [Romans 8:35]. He added why he would not be separated: “But in all these things we overcome and conquer because of him who loved us” [Romans 8:37]. And, rightly strengthened, he said: “For I am confident that neither death nor life, nor angels … nor powers, nor things present nor things to come … will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” [Romans 8:38–39].

37. The Apostle said many things against which we must struggle; but some are easy, or at any rate do not belong to this time or place, so that we ought to examine everything that might separate us from the love of God unless we resist more diligently. We do not now pass over what seems more obscure, because he says: “Neither height nor depth” [Romans 8:39]—these are serious temptations.

Indeed, you have it written in Isaiah to King Ahaz: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord, in the depth or in the height.” He replied: “I will not ask, nor will I tempt the Lord” [Isaiah 7:11–12]. A mystical meaning had been proposed to him, but he did not understand it; and he feared that he would seem to tempt the Lord if he asked for a sign in the height or in the depth. But the Lord, wishing to overthrow serious temptations by a divine remedy, said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb” [Isaiah 7:14]. This is the great sign that destroyed the temptations of height and depth.

For the Lord Jesus did not consider it robbery to be equal with God; nor did he seek what was his own, but took the form of a servant and humbled himself even to death. Thus he was neither lifted up by power nor disturbed by a kind of abasement through death. This sign, therefore, is proposed to the king, so that he may ask for a remedy by which he would neither be raised up by the arrogance of royal power nor disturbed by the occurrence of some affliction—as he was troubled at heart when he saw war being brought against him by the Assyrians. By the example, therefore, of the divine oracle, we wish to show how serious were those temptations for which Christ alone could provide a remedy.

38. Nevertheless, it is easy also to demonstrate from prophetic speech that these temptations carry a certain burden. The holy Solomon himself declared the two greatest temptations in his own prayer and asked that he might exclude them, saying: “Do not give me riches or poverty; but assign me what is necessary and what is sufficient, lest, when filled, I become a liar and say, ‘Who sees me?’ or, when poor, I steal and perjure the name of God” [Proverbs 30:8–9].

Can you, then, despise these temptations, which Solomon feared, although he requested and obtained wisdom? He was rich and feared being lifted up; he feared becoming poor, lest, through the necessity of poverty, he should not preserve the grace of abstinence [Note: “Abstinence,” that is, from theft, so that it refers back to the preceding words, “or, when poor, I steal.”]. How many who seemed to be holy have fallen from the height of their hearts? How many, cast down by some necessity, were unable to endure the injury, although they had been strengthened by the practice of virtues?

Rare is the Job found on earth who, although he lost his wealth and his children and was marked with stripes upon his body while worms flowed over his entire body, nevertheless could not be separated from the love of Christ [Note: Thus read several manuscripts and all editions, except that Erasmus, Gillot, and the Roman edition prefer “was scarred.” Other manuscripts read, “and with ulcers”; some, “and marked with blows.” But “with stripes” is more characteristic of Ambrose’s diction, as could already be observed in more than one passage.].

Let us therefore prepare our disposition, lest sudden force disturb us when we are unprepared. Knowing, finally, how quickly we are accustomed to be broken, the Lord also said to the apostles: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid” [John 14:27].

If desire and craving tempt you, read the Gospel, and let Jesus Christ say to you: “Let not your heart be troubled.” If some terror presses in, let Christ say to you: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.” If a persecutor inflicts some punishment, read the Gospel, and let Jesus say to you: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.” Read the Apostle saying: “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come” [Romans 8:18]. If, while you are sailing on the sea, a heavy wave rises and a dark storm rages, let Jesus say to you: “It is I; do not be troubled” [Mark 6:50]. Therefore, when you come into some great and serious contest, say beforehand: “I am prepared, and I am not disturbed, that I may keep your commandments.”

39. And what shall I say about secular matters? Be prepared not only against what you see, but also against what you do not see. “Outside,” he says, “there are battles; within, fears” [2 Corinthians 7:5]. You have war within yourself. It is good for your spirit to be at peace and in a kind of serenity; but the better helmsman is the one who steers the ship in a storm.

Rule yourself, then, when your spirit is troubled and your mind fluctuates. Would I praise the skill of a helmsman who has experienced no storms and has directed the course of his ship without being tossed by any tempest? I would praise much more the one who struggles against the winds, rises against the waves, and does not fear whether the ship is lifted upon the waves or lowered into the depths below.

So, too, that person is to be praised as the helmsman of himself who conquers adversity through patience, overcomes it by virtue, is not lifted up by prosperity, and is not broken by adversity. You also have a battle against spiritual wickedness. Do you perceive how great a struggle you face? Therefore meditate and establish it in your mind, so that, going forth into battle, you may say: “I am prepared, and I am not disturbed, that I may keep your commandments.”

40. (Verse 61.) The fifth verse follows: “Sinners have surrounded me with ropes, and I have not forgotten your law.” That is: sinners have encircled me with ropes so that they might entangle my steps and prevent me from avoiding their attacks by foreseeing them quickly.

These are not the ropes of which it is written: “The ropes have fallen to me in splendid places” [Psalm 15:6]. Those are the ropes used by men who measure fields and mark boundaries, distinguishing the extent of possessions. Those ropes are stretched as far as each person’s possession extends. Thus Israel became the rope of his inheritance.

Those, then, are good ropes. But these are the ropes by which sins are dragged along, as by a long rope, and as by the strap of a stubborn heifer of iniquity. An untamed heifer struggles and shakes itself more violently when it is held; it does not submit to authority or remain restrained by the bond, but becomes more exasperated when it is pulled back by the strap. Thus, although compelled, it does not submit, yet it is not free from its bonds.

Just as a heifer drags the strap of the yoke—although it is not held close, it is nevertheless held, and does not free or release itself—so each sinner drags his iniquities through untamed conduct while thinking himself free, because he is not subjected to the yoke or placed under judgment. He does not know that he has not been stripped of his bonds, but, like that heifer, he entangles himself in the bonds of his own sins.

These, then, are the ropes of our offenses, by which we are wrapped and bound, just as they are also the chains of our offenses. Therefore the Savior, who has the power to forgive sin, says to those who are in chains: “Come out.” Would that he might also say to me: “Come out of your chains; come out of the bonds of your sins; loosen the ropes of your error, with which you are surrounded and bound.”

For although I may be the most wicked of all and the most detestable of sinners [Note: All editions, together with a few manuscripts, read, “and detestable through the practice of sins.” The remaining manuscripts agree with us.], nevertheless, at his command I shall be free—the one who in a single moment rescued a condemned criminal from punishment and established him in his kingdom.

41. There are therefore chains by which we are bound, although we may seem free to ourselves. Blessed is the person who loosens these chains for himself. Therefore David says: “Let us break their chains and cast their yoke from us” [Psalm 2:3]. He does not, of course, mean that visible chains are to be broken by the hand, but that the invisible bonds of crimes are to be loosened by a change of conduct and a profession of faith [Note: The Roman edition, from the margin of one Vatican manuscript, reads: “Or, if by the hand, then distribute the works of your hands to the poor,” and so forth. The old edition and three manuscripts read: “Or by the hand, that is, by the works of your hands,” and so forth. All the others read with us, “… by the work,” and so forth.].

Or else, “by the hand”—that is, by the work of your hands. Give to the poor, raise up the weak, ransom captives, and you have loosened your chains. Almsgiving frees from sin. Rescue the one who is being led to death; that is, rescue him by intercession, rescue him by favor—you, the priest. Or you, the emperor, rescue him by signing a grant of clemency; and you have loosed your sins and stripped yourself of your chains [Note: Among the privileges of bishops there was formerly no small one: that on certain days they could visit those held in custody and, after hearing their case, intercede for them before the judges. This is clear from Book IX of the Theodosian Code, title 3, law 11, and from the commentary of Godefroy on that law. But you may understand it even more clearly from law 13 of the Appendix to the Theodosian Code, where the emperors Honorius and Theodosius order that free access to the prison be open to a visiting bishop, so that, they say, “he may heal the sick, feed the poor, comfort the innocent”; and, when he has learned the cases of each, “may regulate his interventions before the competent judge by his own right,” and so forth.].

42. Each person is bound by the chains of his own sins, as you yourself have read: “The enticement of the flesh binds us with chains” [James 1:15]. Avarice is our chain; drunkenness is our chain; desire is our chain; pride is our chain.

There are also chains of the devil. It is written, finally: “This daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound for eighteen years” [Luke 13:16]. The devil also binds us in the bond of crimes: he binds us with the chain of fornication, with the chain of adultery, with the chain of unbelief by which Christ is denied, with the chain of envy by which even a brother is often attacked, with the chain of cruelty by which at times a companion and fellow human being is killed.

These are the chains by which each person, once bound, is bent down, so that he cannot lift his soul or raise the eyes of his mind toward heaven, unless the Lord says to him: “You are released from your infirmity,” and raises him up by the gift of his blessing [Luke 13:12].

These are the chains of the wicked, by which sinners are harshly bound—that is, the devil and his ministers [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “with which the devil harshly binds sinners,” and so forth]. Or certainly, Nimrod—that is, bitterness—or Esau—that is, the earthly and crafty one. These were hunters who were accustomed to capture wild beasts with snares and bind mute animals with chains.

Worthless hunters, who capture beasts to provide pomp for popular spectacles and material for cruelty. Indeed, in the entire sequence of the divine Scriptures we find no just person among hunters.

43. But there are other chains, as I have said, the chains of the Lord Jesus, of whom it is written: “They shall follow him, bound with chains” [Hosea 11:4]—that is, bound with the chains of charity and love, tied with the chains of faith.

This may also be understood in the following way: “Bound with chains, they follow Christ”—that is, the forgiver of sins and crimes, the fountain of forgiveness, the author of redemption.

Let us therefore follow the chains of Christ and flee the chains of hunters, lest, while we walk and are unaware, the foot of our mind encounter their snares, and we insert the neck of our soul into their bonds. For they lie in wait like the worst hunters. Whenever we relax our spirit through an outcome of prosperity, let ourselves go amid favorable circumstances, and do not keep the watches of caution alert, then they cast their snares more vigorously or hide them along the road on which we walk, so that, when our footsteps have become entangled in their snares, they may drag us where they can overthrow the unsuspecting traveler, or strangle those passing by with their necks caught fast.

44. Do not therefore walk with an uplifted neck like the daughters of Judah; for a snare is quickly tied around high necks. Do not fix your mind and spirit upon worldly things, but look carefully around with the eyes of your soul, because the Lord rains snares upon sinners, lest they fall upon you and bind you. You will be able to avoid them if you do not forget the law of the Lord.

Indeed, even one who is bound, if he is conscious of his freedom, does not cease to remember his freedom; and sometimes he pleads his case from his chains, defending it by the prescription of the laws and frequently securing acquittal by judgment [Note: Six manuscripts read: “And by what has been prescribed for him by law, he is released.” The others, together with the editions, agree with us. Here, however, “the prescription of the laws” means the definition or enactment of the laws.].

Therefore, if you have sinned, remember the law. If you have sinned, remember Christ, who frees you, saying: “I am, I am he who blots out iniquities … and I will not remember them” [Isaiah 43:25]. Hold fast to him by day and by night; confess your sins to him.

45. (Verse 62.) The Prophet teaches you how to hold fast to the Lord Jesus: “At midnight,” he says, “I rose to confess to you, because of the judgments of your justice.” The day is not sufficient for entreaty; one must rise at night, and at midnight. The Lord himself spent the night in prayer, so that by his own example he might invite you to entreaty; and certainly he was seeking indulgence for your sins. He asked it from the Father and accomplished it by his own will [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “he acted by his own power.”].

The Prophet does not tell you to rise only at midnight, but to rise at night, and especially at midnight. He had already mentioned rising at night when he said: “I remembered your name in the night, O Lord” [Psalm 118:55]. Anyone may remember and not rise; anyone may rise and, when he has risen, ask for whatever has occurred to his own will. He added, “At midnight I rose,” teaching that one must rise at midnight.

Nor is it without purpose that he added, “to confess to you”—that is, so that at that particular time we should especially entreat God and mourn our own sins; and not only ask pardon for past sins, but also avoid present ones and guard against future ones, for many temptations emerge at that time.

46. Then the enticement of the flesh burns; then the tempter mocks; food is being cooked and drink is being digested; the stomach is sick, the mind sleepy, and the spirit occupied. Thus, whether one is resting, the heat of sleep is increased, or, if one is awake, the fuller vigor has not yet returned, by which one could guard against the incursions of error.

Then the tempter stands by; then he casts nets with which he may disturb the unwary mind. Then spiritual wickedness spreads darkness; then they strive to persuade every kind of evil, when there is no judge of guilt, no one conscious of the crime, no witness to the error. Then they pour various arguments into the sleeping sinner, so that first they may cast down the one who resists from the position of his mind. The example of certain people who are regarded as holy is then presented: they once sinned, but afterward obtained pardon and covered over their former offenses.

Although our enemy hates every amendment of our lives, nevertheless, for a time, so that he may overthrow a man of sober mind, he pretends that pardon will come in the future, in order to persuade him to commit present sins. And when he has driven someone to consent to error, if he sees that the person is now restrained from sin not by love of virtue but by fear of punishment, he introduces various arguments, so that the person says to himself: “Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me, and the walls … whom should I fear?” [Sirach 23:25–26]. The Most High does not see; our sins do not reach him; he does not deign to look upon what is shameful.

We know these things from experience and example; for no one can be free from temptation.

47. Therefore, just as this time is suitable for temptations, so it is also a time of punishment, as we can learn from divine reading. For although the Lord our God could have destroyed the firstborn of the Egyptians at any moment, he nevertheless judged this time more suitable for the grief and mourning of the sinner. Thus it is written that at midnight the firstborn children of the Egyptians were killed by the destroyer [Exodus 12:29].

Therefore the holy prophet Moses, anticipating this time so that it might pass without harm to the Hebrews, sacrificed the lamb beforehand—that is, in the evening—so that, while eating it and celebrating the Lord’s Passover, they would not be caught by the destroyer’s ambushes, lest the nocturnal arrows of the dark enemy overwhelm them unarmed and empty of spiritual nourishment.

48. Pay close attention to these things, understand them wisely, and seek them diligently. These words are not spoken superficially; divine mysteries are being revealed to you. You too should anticipate the tempter’s ambushes and restore the heavenly banquet beforehand [Note: Much can be extracted from this passage that would illuminate knowledge of the discipline of the ancient Church. First, it shows that when a fast had been proclaimed, it was required to keep it until the end of the day. It also shows the custom of receiving the sacrament of the Eucharist only with an empty mouth, while suggesting the practice of the Church of Milan of not fasting on Saturdays and Sundays; for this seems to be inferred from the words, “indeed, many days are of this kind,” and the like, which are better explained in this sense than if they are understood of the fasts of the stations, especially since it is highly probable that the Lenten fast is being described here. Later, mention is made of the offering; we have observed in the preface to this work that this offering means nothing other than the sacrifice of the body of Christ. From the same passage it may also be understood that in the Latin Church it was customary to offer the sacrifice and receive the Eucharist even on days of fasting, contrary to the practice that prevailed in the East. Later there is also mention of the evening sacrifice—that is, of the Mass customarily celebrated in the evening hours on fast days; we find it discussed in the Council of Vasio, canon 3; the Third Council of Orléans, canon 29; and the Council of Mâcon, canon 9. Finally, the marvelous effects of this sacrament are recounted: protection against the temptations of the devil, remission of sins, and so forth.].

A fast has been proclaimed; take care not to neglect it. And if hunger compels you to eat your daily meal, or excess turns you away from fasting, nevertheless preserve yourself rather for the heavenly banquet. Do not let prepared food force you to be empty of the heavenly sacrament. Delay a little; the end of the day is not far away. Indeed, most days are of this kind, so that one must come to the Church immediately at midday, sing hymns, and celebrate the offering.

Then stand ready, so that you may receive a safeguard for yourself: so that you may eat the body of the Lord Jesus, in which there is remission of sins, a plea for divine reconciliation, and eternal protection. Receive the Lord Jesus first as a guest in the lodging of your mind; where his body is, there Christ is.

When the adversary sees that your lodging has been occupied by the splendor of the heavenly presence, understanding that the place has been closed against his temptations through Christ, he will flee and withdraw; and you will pass through midnight without any offense.

The evening sacrifice also admonishes you never to forget Christ. You cannot forget that Lord when you go to bed, to whom you poured out a prayer at the setting of the day, who filled you, when hungry, with the banquets of his body. For what you have considered in the evening you will quickly review when you awaken. The Lord Jesus himself will awaken you; he will admonish you to rise and take up the weapons of prayer at the time when the tempter is accustomed to attack.

49. Therefore the Apostle Paul and Silas, thrown into prison with their feet fastened in the stocks, nevertheless rose at midnight in the movement of their spirit, entreated the Lord, and offered a sacrifice of praise [Acts 16:25–26]. And so, where the duty of devotion was not lacking, the remedy of release was also present.

For suddenly, at midnight, there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken, the doors were opened, and everyone’s chains were loosed. Do you hear how, if you have been bound, you may release yourself—by what hands and by what works—and how you may no longer fear the guards?

Rise, then, to pray. It is the hour at which the tempter is accustomed to do harm and wickedness is accustomed to rush in. It is the hour at which heavenly help ordinarily comes against grave temptations. You must keep watch, lest you be conquered by some deception; you must take care that, at the time when you can conquer, you do not in any way lose the time for conquering.

50. Since we have said that prayer must be undertaken at midnight, it seems necessary to speak no less about the corresponding hour of the day; for night is contrary to day. What has light in common with darkness? And therefore night and day are opposed to one another in the same way. Just as the tempter killed the firstborn of the Egyptians at midnight [Note: Thus all manuscripts and editions read, except one Roman edition, which has: “the destroyer killed.”], and from this it is understood that the adversary works especially at that hour, so, conversely, the power of divine light works at midday.

Hence Abraham, around midday, kept sober watch and awaited favorable events, raising his eyes and surveying the neighboring places, because at that time he was seeking the grace that was coming to him [Genesis 18:1–2]. At that time the divine guest came to him with two holy angels; at that time he received Christ as a guest; at that time the mysteries that you read and understand were celebrated.

For when should divine presence have illuminated a faithful man more than when the fuller light of day was shining? And rightly, too, holy Joseph, after receiving his brothers and calling for the younger brother whom he loved most, prepared a banquet at midday [Genesis 43:16]. It was midday in the heart of holy Joseph when, with shining grace, he served joyful food to his brothers and distributed the sweet nourishment of his conversation, so that, although they feared punishment because of the brother whom they had attacked and sold into slavery, he would tell them by divine judgment that provision had been made for them: he had been brought into Egypt so that he might not deny sustenance to those suffering from hunger [Genesis 45:5–7].

51. We therefore have midday within us. It is midday for the person upon whom the sun of justice shines, and upon whose good works, harmless thoughts, pure and sincere mind, Christ feeds. Learn, then, how to make midday for yourself. “Reveal your way to the Lord,” he says, “and hope in him; and he himself will act. He will bring forth your justice like light, and your judgment like midday” [Psalm 36:5–6].

Where true faith is, there is the grace of true light. Where there is a prolonged guardianship of innocence, progress through long meditation upon the virtues, and the brightness of a good conscience enduring for a long time, there is intelligible midday. There you will offer the banquets of your mind to Christ, and you yourself will be nourished by his riches, so that the setting of the true light does not follow too early and too swiftly, nor does some dark evening quickly descend upon your endeavors and interrupt your good works.

But if the night of temptations arrives, it is not without reason that one must rise at midnight, pray for a long time, and prolong the hours with psalms until day comes and Christ dawns upon you.

[Col. 1316B] **52.** See, therefore, that daylight does not also become midnight for you, when the dark and filthy ruler of this world pours the fullness of temptation upon you. Rise, then, and rouse your mind. He who guards you will not sleep if he does not find you sleeping; but he will rise if he himself has been awakened by the watchfulness of your soul. He will command the wind, and calm will come to your breast, which had been tossed by the whirlwind of various storms.

We must therefore rise. The Bridegroom is accustomed to come at midnight. Beware lest he find you sleeping; beware lest, drowsy, you be unable to light your lamp. We must rise, I say, and confess to the Lord, so that you may give thanks. His eternal judgments must also be confessed, so that whatever good happens to us we may ascribe to his justice. Whether, therefore, we are rich or enjoy sound health, let us attribute this to the Lord’s justice, because he is just: he protects and preserves his work, and, although he has cast those whom nature’s seemingly unendowed lot threw naked into this weakness of the body, he deigns to clothe the poor with strength of spirit and the garment of his mercy. That this must indeed be done at all times is clear, so that neither by day nor by night, nor at any time, ought we to be free from giving thanks.

**53. (Verse 63.)** The seventh verse follows: “I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments.” Christ too has companions and sharers in himself. Thus David proves it when he says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8).

He has companions in the flesh, because he assumed flesh; he has companions in prophecy, because he says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you from among your brothers a prophet like me; you shall listen to him in all things whatever he speaks to you. But every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from among the people” (Deut. XVIII, 18–19). He is the true prophet who knows beforehand what is to come without receiving it from another, who spoke through the prophets the things that were going to happen. Is he not a prophet who makes others prophesy? He is the one who is heard as the Law, because the Law also belongs to him. Thus he says: “If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone should go to them from the dead” (Luke XVI, 31). Therefore, because the Jewish people did not listen to this prophet, it was destroyed from among the people, so that it ceased to be the people of God, although previously it was called the people of God.

He has companions in baptism, because he was baptized for us; he has companions in righteousness, because he himself is righteousness, and from what is his own he gave us a share in himself; he has companions in truth, because he himself is truth, and he willed us to hold the truth; he has companions in resurrection, because he himself is the resurrection; he has companions in an immaculate life, because he himself is immaculate. And whoever walks in newness of life, whoever follows the path of righteousness, is a companion of Christ.

He also has companions in his suffering. Therefore the one who desired to be his companion said: “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ, for his body, which is the Church” (Col. I, 24). We are also companions in his burial, for whoever has been buried with him through baptism into death is his companion. Therefore the Apostle himself, affirming what grace the Lord Jesus has given us, says: “For we have become companions of Jesus Christ” (Heb. III, 14).

**54.** But that person too is a companion of Christ who consoles one who is mourning with compassionate affection; who does not fail to perform his proper duty toward one confined in prison; who sits beside the bed of the sick, not in order to lie in wait for an inheritance, but to mitigate the force of the illness through an attentive ministry and to soothe the weary person with diligent conversation; who clothes the naked and refreshes the hungry. For Christ is frequently present in these people, as he himself says:

[Note: [Col. 1317D] All the manuscripts have this reading. The editions, contrary to the threefold negation in this passage, remove it so that the text may be understood of the righteous. However it is formulated, it has equal force for proving the intended point.]

“I was in prison, and you did not come to me; I was naked, and you did not clothe me . . . . For whatever you did not do for one of these, you did not do for me” (Matt. XXV, 42 and following).

If I hate falsehood, I am a companion of Christ, because Christ is truth. If I flee iniquity, I am a companion of Christ, because Christ is righteousness. Blessed is the person who can say this.

For just as we say that a limb shares in the whole body, so the person joined to all who fear God—one who does not say to another, “You are not part of my body,” that is, the rich person does not say this to the poor, the noble to the lowly, the healthy to the sick, the strong to the weak, nor the wise to the uneducated, “You are not necessary to me”—is a companion of the body of Christ, which is the Church.

But the person who knows that those who appear in the Church to be weak, poor, unintelligent, and even sinners require more abundant honour and must be supported by greater assistance—whoever knows this can say: “I am a companion of all who fear you.” Let such a person have compassion on these people rather than despise them; let him have compassion on the weak, so that he may know that we are all one body, and that the limbs are joined to one another, so that one cannot exist without the other. When one suffers, let him have compassion on the other. Such a person, therefore, can rightly claim the authority of this saying.

[Col. 1318A] **55.** Consider, moreover, how modestly the Prophet said: “I am a companion of those who fear you.” He did not say “of those who imitate you,” but “of those who fear you,” for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Eccl. I, 16). In humility he placed himself among the inexperienced, although in devotion he surpassed the veterans. Yet even fearing is a virtue, because it is written: “Fear the Lord, all his saints” (Ps. XXXIII, 10).

**56.** But lest this fear seem to some people not to be holy—for there are those who are terrified by cowardly dread and tremble with dull fear—he added: “And who keep your commandments.” He showed that he shares in holy fear.

Or understand it in this way. A person may indeed fear with a devout heart but be lazy in action, so that he is religious in feeling but idle in conduct. Yet one who keeps the Lord’s commandments cannot be lazy. Therefore the one who fears keeps them; and keeping belongs to the one who fears.

Thus the saint says: “I cannot claim this for myself. For how many are there who fear God, and yet I do not have compassion on them?” [Note: [Col. 1318D] The edition, with two manuscripts, reads: “They seek help, and I refuse to show mercy; they need money, and I do not assist them.” I have retained the other reading, as above.] “They seek help, and I am unwilling to provide it; they need mercy, and I do not help them with money.” Whoever does these things can himself say that he is a companion of those who fear Christ.

**57. (Verse 46.)** “The earth is full of your mercies, O Lord; teach me your justifications.” How is the earth full of the Lord’s mercies, unless through the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the Prophet, foreseeing it as future, celebrates as though it had been promised? For when prophets foresee things that are to come, they commonly speak of things belonging to a later age as though they had already run their course.

The earth, therefore, is full of the Lord’s mercy because forgiveness of sins has been given to all. The sun is commanded to rise over everyone. And this visible sun does indeed rise over everyone each day. But that mystical sun of righteousness has risen for everyone, has come for everyone, has suffered for everyone, and has risen again for everyone. He suffered in order to take away the sin of the world.

If someone does not believe in Christ, he himself deprives himself of a benefit offered to all. It is like someone shutting his windows and excluding the sun’s rays: the sun has not therefore failed to rise for everyone because that person has deprived himself of its warmth. What belongs to the sun preserves its prerogative; what belongs to the foolish person is that he excludes from himself the common grace of light.

Rain is also over everyone, and this too is attributed to divine mercy, because it rains upon the just and the unjust.

Or the passage may certainly be interpreted in this way: the earth is full of divine mercy because “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness . . . . he founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (Ps. XXIII, 1–2). Indeed, through the Church the Lord’s mercy has been spread among all nations; among all nations faith has been spread.

**58.** Perhaps you will say: Why was it not said, “Heaven is full of the Lord’s mercy”? Because there are also spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. But they do not belong to the common provision of God’s indulgence and forgiveness of sins; eternal fire is reserved for them. And although those beings belonging to the heavenly powers or ministries are supported by the Lord’s help, they do not need his mercy as greatly as those things that are lower and earthly. For they are not clothed in the covering of flesh, in which lies the enticement of frequent error.

Therefore the same Prophet says above: “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord, but the earth he has given to the children of men” (Ps. CXIII, 16). Hence heaven is purer and more cleansed from every stain of sin, and much farther removed from that region of which it is written: “The birds of heaven” (Matt. VI, 26). This heaven is called a kind of aerial region midway between heaven and earth, in which there are also spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

For in that heaven—not merely so called, but the true heaven—even if we read that the devil was not absent from the council in the presence of God’s angels, I nevertheless think that no attempts of wickedness are at work there. Thus it is written that “the angels loved the daughters of men” (Gen. VI, 2), because the ruler of this world and his ministers were captivated and held fast by earthly enticements; in them spiritual wickedness, steeped in the poisons of this flesh, has been infected with human crimes.

Therefore the Lord says in his Gospel: “Let your will be done as in heaven and on earth” (Matt. VI, 10). It is not the same kind of iniquity there to drive a neighbor from a field bordering one’s own property, to defraud a widow of the benefits of her inheritance, to thrust lesser persons out by right of association, or, finally, to enclose within wood—or within any metal of silver, gold, or bronze—something resembling a heavenly power as an image. Although these things are full of the greatest sacrilege, they are absent in heaven and common on earth.

For “by the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII, 6); the earth was not established.

[Note: [Col. 1319D] In the Theodosian Code, *consortium* sometimes means a neighborhood and adjoining buildings; indeed, in Cicero, *Oration against Verres*, *consortes* refers to people whose boundaries are contiguous. Ambrose uses *consortium* here in this sense.]

**59.** And therefore he wishes to be taught God’s justifications by the Lord himself, because it is difficult to find on earth a teacher of such things who has not himself seen them. With inward longing the Prophet therefore hastens to that teacher who alone is the true teacher.

How can a human being teach as true something he does not know, when he himself is a liar? Rightly, therefore, the Lord says that no one should call anyone on earth his teacher, because there is one teacher of all (Matt. XXIII, 8). And how could David seek another teacher, when he himself said of God: “He teaches human beings knowledge” (Ps. XCIII, 10)?

God teaches, illuminates the minds of individuals, and pours into them the brightness of knowledge, if you open the doors of your heart and receive the brightness of heavenly grace. When you are in doubt, inquire diligently; for the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it is opened.

There is much obscurity in the prophetic Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 1319D] Ambrose frequently urged his hearers in his sermons to devote themselves diligently to reading even the more difficult Scriptures. And so that they might not be deterred from so useful a purpose by the obscurity of the prophets—as we learn happened to Augustine from *Confessions* IX, chapter 13—he teaches that prayer must never be separated from reading and diligence. If Augustine himself, while still a catechumen, had used this method, he would not so easily have abandoned his reading of Isaiah, which he had begun at the urging of our Bishop.] But if, with the hand of your mind, you knock at the door of the Scriptures and carefully examine what is hidden, little by little you will begin to gather the meaning of the statements. It will be opened to you not by another but by the Word of God, of whom you read in the Apocalypse (Rev. V, 5) that the Lamb opened the sealed book, which no one previously could open. For the Lord Jesus alone revealed in his Gospel the riddles of the prophets and the mysteries of the Law; he alone brought and gave us the key of knowledge, so that we might open them.

**60.** The Jews say that they possess the key of knowledge, but they do not possess it. For if they had it, they themselves would enter; they themselves would recognize the inner chambers of the Scriptures. But now: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke XI, 52).

For how can you possess the key of knowledge, when you have denied the author of knowledge? Therefore David, turning to him, says: “You teach me your justifications,” because you are true righteousness. You teach what has been spoken wisely, because you are wisdom. You open my heart, because you have opened the book. You open that door which is in heaven, because you are the door. Through you, if anyone enters, he will possess that eternal kingdom. Through you, if anyone enters, he will not be deceived, because whoever has entered the dwelling of truth cannot be deceived.

## NINTH SERMON. *Theth*

[Col. 1320C]

**1.** The ninth letter is *Theth*, whose interpretation is “exclusion.” What is exclusion? Is it perhaps as when someone is excluded from a house and cast out from hospitality? In the same way, is the person who is excluded from the kingdom of God deprived of its good things, like those virgins who were excluded because they did not take oil with them? When the Bridegroom came, their lamps had gone out; while they were occupied with buying oil and lighting their lamps, they delayed, and when the Bridegroom had already entered, they are said to have been excluded even though they wished to enter (Matt. XXV, 2–3 and following)?

I do not think so. For how could he say, “You have made gladness with your servant,” if the holy Prophet had been cast away from the good and excluded from the kingdom of God? [Note: [Col. 1320D] The Reg., Corb., and one Nav. manuscript, together with Laet. and Fisc., read: “How could he say it, if the good and holy Prophet had been cast out?” The Roman edition . . . reads: “How could the holy Prophet say it to the good, if he were . . .,” etc.] Neither does the Prophet’s merit seem to permit such an interpretation, nor does the sequence of what follows.

You hear him saying: “You are sweet, O Lord, and in your gladness teach me your justifications” (below, verse 68). You hear him saying: “The law of your mouth is good for me, above thousands of gold and silver” (ibid., 72). And can you say that one is excluded from the kingdom who is not excluded from the Law? What, then, shall we understand? The interpretation is caught fast, and the language seems to cast obscurity over its own meaning.

**2.** The Prophet’s merits summon us; his grace summons us; the sequence of what follows summons us, so that we must draw out some deeper meaning. [Note: [Col. 1321D] Some manuscripts read: “And the interpretation presents itself.” The edition reads, “in the interpretation.” But nine manuscripts read, “at the right time,” that is, opportunely, while my mind was anxious to discover the meaning of this very matter.] And the thought occurs at the right time that sometimes we are excluded for our good.

For it is written: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John IV, 18). In general, love casts out fear. A soldier who loves his commander does not fear the wars undertaken for his commander. A servant who loves his master, even when sent through trackless and precipitous places, despises every danger for love of his master; and if someone attacks his master, he does not hesitate to offer himself. A person who desires to see children living across the sea does not fear shipwreck; out of love for his children he enters the waves of the sea and undertakes the uncertainties of sailing. The children’s longing lifts the fear of danger.

How beautifully this is also said of the martyrs, who truly fight for Christ: they did not fear persecutions, claws, swords, or fires, but offered themselves to hostile kings. By love of martyrdom they cast out the fear of punishment that they could have felt.

**3.** We can also establish that this is the meaning of this interpretation from the Lamentations of Jeremiah. For there too, under this letter, it is written:

“The Lord is good to those who await him, to the soul that seeks him. It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of God. It is good for a man, when he has borne the heavy yoke from his youth, to sit alone and be silent, because he has borne the heavy yoke” (Lam. III, 25–27).

What else do these words establish except that this interpretation appears to concern a good exclusion? For who awaits the Lord except through the zeal of love? Who hopes except the person who desires and loves what he hopes for? For what we hope for, we await with patience. Therefore the one who hopes waits; and the one who waits certainly casts out the feeling of impatience.

Who bears the heavy yoke from his youth except one who renounces pleasures and flees luxury? Who sits alone except one who, having rejected worldly pleasures, excludes the tumult of all troubles? Such a person, therefore, will be able to fear nothing, because the grace of love has swallowed up the force of fear.

**4.** There is also another person who is excluded for his good: the man who, by apostolic authority, was removed from the midst of the people. Because he had committed an evil deed, he was handed over for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved (1 Cor. V, 5). From this we understand that the person who is commanded to do penance is excluded for his good, so that he may be humbled and pierced in heart. [Note: [Col. 1321D] Here and in several other places Ambrose indicates the ancient custom of the Church, by which bishops were accustomed to lessen the public penances they had imposed on penitents and to shorten the period of excommunication, taking into account their contrition and humiliation. These are consequently said to assist reconciliation.] These things are customarily aids toward reconciliation.

[Col. 1322A] **5.** Finally, the things written under this letter in Jeremiah also seem to signify this. Thus we read concerning that earthly Jerusalem:

“Her uncleanness is before her feet. She did not remember her end, and she fell disastrously; there is no one to comfort her. See, O Lord, her humiliation, because the enemy has been magnified” (Lam. I, 9).

And because Jerusalem was thus humbled, it is rightly said to her afterward: “Your iniquity has ended, daughter of Zion” (Lam. IV, 22). And to everyone who has done penance and mourned his sins with his own tears it is rightly said: “Your iniquity has ended.”

Elsewhere, under this letter, Jeremiah says: “It was better for those wounded by the sword than for those wounded by famine. They went away pierced from the produce of the fields” (ibid., 9). [Note: [Col. 1322D] The Roman edition reads, “from the barrenness of the fields.” The other editions, together with all the manuscripts, read, “from the birth of the fields.” This is better; so too the Septuagint: “They went away pierced from the produce of the fields” (*ἐπορεύθησαν ἐκκεκεντημένοι ἀπὸ γεννημάτων ἀγρῶν*).]

We are therefore pierced when we do penance for our sins; we are also pierced by the recollection of our sins. [Note: [Col. 1322D] All the editions read, “by the recollection of sins.” Most manuscripts more aptly read, “by the recollection of words,” as the immediately cited Psalm IV, verse 5, sufficiently shows.] Hence the prophet David says: “What you say in your hearts, and be pierced upon your beds” (Ps. IV, 5).

But the person who is pierced certainly casts out the pleasure of error; and the person who does penance casts out shame. He sets aside the embarrassment of confessing his crime, so that he may find hope of recovering salvation. Therefore David himself, when he recognized his error, said: “I have sinned against the Lord” (2 Sam. XII, 13). So great a king, so great a prophet, was not ashamed to confess his own sin; and therefore it was said to him: “The Lord has taken away your sin” (ibid.).

**6. (Verse 65.)** After sin had been taken away, he says: “You have made gladness with your servant, O Lord, according to your word.”

Many things in this world appear to be pleasant although they are not; many things are sweet, and very many seem good. Luxury appears pleasant, but once the patrimony has been exhausted it becomes bitter. Lust is sweet while it burns, but the same lust is horrible and detestable when it is exposed. Banquets are pleasant while they are being consumed, but foul when they are digested. Many things in this world are judged good while we live, because they are useful to us—money, gold, silver, possessions—but they can benefit the dead nothing; everything is left here. Indeed, a person dies with greater grief when he laments that he is being deprived of these resources.

There is therefore no true gladness except that which accords with the word of God, so that a person may rejoice that he is fortified by the resources of good merits and virtues.

[1081] **7.** David rejoices in this gladness, or goodness, of God, because he bore the heavy yoke from his youth, endured it, and awaited the Lord’s grace toward himself. He did not seize it prematurely. Although he was often given the opportunity to kill King Saul, he preferred to await from the Lord the proper time to receive the kingdom rather than seize it by killing the king.

God is always good. Therefore Paul also says: “See, then, the goodness and severity of God” (Rom. XI, 22). Goodness is toward all; severity toward a few. The same Apostle added: “Toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness” (ibid.). For if they had not fallen, they too would certainly be enjoying God’s goodness. He is good to you because you remain; but if you do not remain in goodness, you too will be cut off.

God does not therefore cease to be good because you have fallen and need severity. [Note: [Col. 1323D] The edition and four manuscripts read: “Certainly the severity of God returns to goodness, so that each person may turn back,” etc. Twelve manuscripts read: “returns to goodness, so that each person . . .,” although in some of them *recurrat* is found, and the conjunction *ut* is absent.] Indeed, God’s severity also leads back to goodness, so that each person, once chastened, may withdraw his foot from sins and return to the path of virtues and to a good manner of life.

The Apostle teaches this concerning those who fell: “If they do not remain in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again” (ibid., 23). [Note: [Col. 1324D] The Roman edition reads, “just as grafted shoots.” The other editions and all the manuscripts read, “deserted shoots.” This is not a bad reading, provided that one understands them to have been grafted onto good stocks.] Thus, just as deserted shoots, human beings too, grafted as it were onto certain stocks of virtue, may bear the fruits of good merits.

Must you accuse a physician of cruelty because he thinks that the rotting fibers of wounds must be cut out with iron, or because he burns infected and spreading ulcers with fire so that the poison may not extend farther? Or must you accuse a teacher of cruelty because he beats a negligent student so that, through fear of the blows, he may acquire diligence? To chastise is the action of one who loves, not of one who hates; and therefore it belongs to goodness, not cruelty.

Rightly, then, the Lord is good everywhere, both when he forgives sins and when he chastises them: “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves” (Heb. XII, 6).

**8.** David too was chastised. Thus he says: “And I was scourged all day long” (Ps. LXXII, 14). But the wise man who understood that the Lord’s chastisement had benefited him says: “You have shown goodness to your servant, O Lord, according to your word.” That is: Although that chastisement seemed bitter to me for a time—bitter to me according to the flesh, bitter to me according to the sorrow of the body—nevertheless, according to your word, that chastisement brought forth the fruit of goodness.

I understand that chastisement to have benefited me; through that chastisement I was recalled from vices; through that chastisement sins were not long permitted to have power over me; through that chastisement of the Lord the adversary had no power over me, nor did death.

Thus the same Prophet recalls: “The Lord chastising has chastised me, but he has not handed me over to death” (Ps. CXVII, 18). The person who is received is chastised; those who are not received are not scourged. “For they are not in the troubles of men, and they will not be scourged with men” (Ps. LXXII, 5).

Therefore he says above: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!” (ibid., 1). He is therefore good to all, because he wishes all to be upright in heart. But the person whose heart turns aside turns away from himself the grace of divine goodness.

**9. (Verse 66.)** The following verse says: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed in your commandments.”

According to the Apostle, we understand *χρηστόν* (*chrēston*) as “good,” because he says: “See, then, the goodness of the Lord” (Rom. XI, 22). According to the Gospel, we understand *χρηστόν* as “sweet” or “pleasant.” For he says: “Take my yoke . . . for it is easy, and my burden, because it is pleasant” (Matt. XI, 29–30). For he says: “My burden is *χρηστόν*” (*τὸ φορτίον μου χρηστόν*).

Rightly, therefore, he asks to be taught God’s goodness by God himself, lest someone, understanding superficially that God is good, persist in errors because, through God’s mercy, he knows that impunity can be granted for his sins. For even if the Lord forgives, it is nevertheless shameful always to remain attached to crimes. This goodness, therefore, is not ordinary goodness, but goodness that always looks for progress in discipline.

**10.** Therefore the person who understands that God’s goodness is profound desires also to be taught discipline. Many turn away from the pursuit of discipline because they regard it as severe and sad. But the person whose understanding is more perceptive realizes that although discipline may be sad for a time, it later becomes pleasant.

There is a discipline, or correction, that is more severe; there is also one that is more moderate. The more moderate is the one of which the Lord says: “I will correct them in the hearing of their tribulation” (Hos. VII, 12). There is also the more severe correction that occurs in anger and fury. Avoiding that correction, David says: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Ps. VI, 2). And Jeremiah says: “Correct us, O Lord, in judgment, and not in fury” (Jer. X, 24).

Every discipline, therefore, even if it has bitterness and disturbance for a time, nevertheless customarily produces peaceful fruits afterward.

**11.** But the person who asks to be taught goodness and discipline ought also to ask to be taught knowledge. For unless he has knowledge, discipline and correction are burdensome.

Let Solomon teach you what knowledge is, when he says of the Lord our God: “For he himself gave me true knowledge of the things that exist” (Wis. VII, 17). And elsewhere the same Prophet says: “He teaches human beings knowledge” (Ps. XCIII, 10). The person who asks for knowledge believes in God’s commandments.

**12.** It is one thing to believe in God’s commandments, and another to believe the commandments. For the person who believes God’s commandments quickly makes himself live within God’s commandments and conduct himself in them.

Through faith, therefore, knowledge is assumed; through knowledge, discipline. For our very manner of life delights us in what we know can please God. Thus it is written: “But our manner of life is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). Knowledge came first; conduct followed.

We have spoken of believing God’s commandments. To believe in God’s commandments means to be in them, and to believe that the commandments are true. For unless you believe God’s commandments, you cannot have their knowledge—the knowledge that we are taught through God’s commandments.

**13. (Verse 67.)** The third verse follows: “Before I was humbled, I sinned; therefore I kept your word.” [Note: [Col. 1325D] Most manuscripts read: “Another edition has.”]

Another edition reads: “Before I was humbled, I did not know.” Hence some think that the human soul says: “Before I was humbled, when I entered this clay of the body, I did not know your commandments, which I had not read.” [Note: [Col. 1325D] There is no doubt that Ambrose is covertly alluding here to the Origenists, who held that souls existed and sinned before they were sent into bodies. This can confirm what we have already said more than once: that he sometimes presents only those opinions of Origen which he understood to have been accepted by certain other Fathers and not rejected by the Church.]

But because the Church follows the opinion of the Seventy more closely, and because this interpretation is clearer and admits nothing offensive that could trouble anyone’s conscience, let us understand “I was humbled” in the sense that he appears to have been humbled by sin. For temptations often arise because of sin. Thus Adam and Eve were certainly cast down after their fault (Gen. III, 24).

Sin, therefore, is the cause of our humility or humiliation; I do not avoid saying this. Humility can often be understood of adversities, as in the words: “It is good for me that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your justifications.” And: “If your law had not been my meditation, then perhaps I would have perished in my humiliation” (below, verses 71 and 92). And: “I have been humbled exceedingly” (Ps. CXLI, 7).

Here, therefore, he shows that humility arose from fault. And because fault came first, he shows himself humbled—that is, worn down by temptations and adversities and handed over to anxieties. In the same way, the man who was handed over by Paul for the destruction of the flesh was certainly humbled, so that afterward he might merit reconciliation (1 Cor. V, 5).

**14.** Although this humility—that is, a kind of downfall—is a matter of disturbance rather than virtue, it nevertheless often produces virtue and becomes not a punishment but a remedy for the one who has sinned.

For if you attribute your humiliation to your sins, whatever happens you turn back upon yourself, and you begin to be righteous from being guilty, since you condemn yourself. “The righteous is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. XVIII, 17). Nor can you judge yourself unworthy of humility when you recognize your own errors, in which, by feeling shame, you are certainly not exalted but humbled.

You see, then, that you were humbled because you sinned and did not keep the words of God. Therefore keep them more diligently, so that you may not sin; and do not allow yourself, because you have been cast down, to be swallowed up again by sadness. Let your downfall not become an increase of iniquity, when it ought to be an opportunity for correction.

For in temptations a human being is tested like gold in a furnace. See what the Prophet says: “Before I was humbled,” he says, “I sinned.” He was therefore rightly handed over to temptations, because he was sinning. He was sinning because he was not holding fast to the word of God.

But from the place where his fault had arisen he found the order of correction. He began to be subject to the divine word, and the fault came to an end.

**15. (Verse 68.)** The fourth verse follows: “You are good, O Lord, and in your goodness teach me your justifications.”

Even secular judicial practice has adopted the custom that each person praises his judge. Thus the Apostle, following the order of the divine Scriptures, when he had stated the case, began in this way: “Concerning all the things of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to be able to give my defense before you” (Acts XXVI, 2). And below: “Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe” (ibid., 27).

Therefore, if human beings are praised—although in them what is praised is often something belonging to another—how much more ought each person to win God’s grace for himself by saying: “You are good, O Lord.”

For if someone says this to a human being, so that the person may be reminded to be what perhaps he is not, and so that through praise of goodness he may himself become gentler and lay aside the feeling of harshness, how much more must praise be offered to God, who, unless he were good, could anyone stand upon the earth?

It is proper to God to be good. Thus in the Gospel you read: “A good tree produces good fruits” (Matt. VII, 17). Its fruits are the angels; its fruits are human beings—that is, rational and holy people, if they keep the Lord’s commandments. Its fruits are those who are born on earth; its fruits are the virtues of human beings.

Rightly, therefore, a good tree produces good fruits. First, then, let the root be praised, so that the fruit may be approved. Elsewhere the same Lord Jesus also says: “And your Father, who is good, will give good things to those who ask him” (ibid., 11).

**16.** Although God is good, and even his bitter things are more beneficial—for they are not inflicted to harm but to correct—he is nevertheless asked to teach us his justifications in his goodness.

Consider a physician applying useful medicines to wounds, medicines that sting the infection of an ulcer, or cutting out with iron what has become putrid. The physician is good precisely in this, because he acts for the patient’s benefit and does what he knows to be helpful. Yet because the sick person either does not wish or is unable to bear the pain on account of the weakness of his condition, he asks that the physician cure him with a certain goodness and gentleness of his own: that he not apply harsh medicines, that he not cut the fibers of the wounds with iron, or, if this cannot be otherwise, that he act with moderation and soften the force of the pain with a certain delicacy.

Therefore God’s justifications are taught better in the goodness of the Gospel than in the severity of the Law. The work of righteousness, however, is justification.

Hence it is written that the Pharisees “did not wish to justify themselves,” because they were not baptized with the baptism of John (Luke VII, 30). [Note: [Col. 1326D] The old edition reads, “because the Pharisees wished to justify themselves.” The Roman edition, together with the manuscripts, reads more correctly, “did not wish,” as is shown by what is said after the next verse: “because they did not wish to do penance.”]

For in this they did not achieve justification, because they did not wish to do penance for their sins—a penance which the Prophet wishes to be undertaken in goodness, so that forgiveness of sins may be granted to him without the harshness of condemnation, together with the grace of remission.

17. (Verse 69.) It follows: “The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me; but I will search out your commandments with my whole heart.” The more eagerly someone desires to serve God, the more he stirs up adversaries against himself; and, like a strong athlete desiring to carry away the crown of righteousness, he provokes and challenges many who envy our progress. He shows this clearly also later. [Note: [Column 1327D] Seven manuscripts . . . . . . show this, saying: “With those who hated peace,” etc.] He says: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” (Psalm 119:7). Yet his tranquility accomplished nothing toward calming those who hated peace by his own peacefulness and restraining their zeal. “When I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (ibid.); that is, although they had no reasons for attacking, they nevertheless did not abandon their eagerness to attack.

Thus either spiritual wickedness or human beings are multiplied, and their iniquity is multiplied against the righteous. For example, if a righteous man loses his son—as often happens in the course of this world—or loses his inheritance, or is afflicted by various misfortunes of property or by bodily illnesses, then the proud say: “Where is his righteousness? Where is his mercy? Look how he has been punished; look how his innocence benefits him nothing.” Therefore, in order to draw out a specimen of this life, those three men who were outwardly holy Job’s friends but in their slander his enemies, envious of his uprightness and righteousness, heaped grave reproaches upon him; and those who had come to console him began to mock him.

18. But the righteous man is not moved by these things, and therefore Job was not broken. Indeed, when he lost his children or his inheritance, he said: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away . . . blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). Therefore, even when placed amid adversities, let us say: “You have dealt well with your servant” (above, verse 65). 1085 For the Lord can change what has happened for the better, as we have the example of holy Job (Job 42:10 and following), and can restore what has been lost. Even one who has lost children can beget better ones. Is anything difficult for God to give better things?

Even if he gives nothing, a righteous person may nevertheless have been cared for by this very fact, if perhaps those who were going to become wicked were taken away, lest wickedness change their hearts. The same may be said of inheritance: surely we see many brought into danger of salvation because of the wealth of their inheritance, and many for whom the abundance of riches has become a cause of sinning. For one who does not have anything to give cannot be charged with the fault of not having given; but one who has something to give and does not give it certainly begins to be liable to sin.

19. (Verse 70.) It follows: “Their heart has congealed like milk; but I meditated on your law.” The heart of the saints is subtle; the heart of the proud, however, has congealed. For just as milk by its nature is pure, beautiful, and sincere, but curdles through corruption, so the nature of the human mind and heart is pure, sincere, and transparent before it curdles through the admixture of vices. When milk has curdled, a kind of solid mass is formed; it possesses neither the same sweetness nor the same grace.

So also people who formerly, through diligence and the grace and sweetness of their words, presented the appearance of milk, without their nature having been corrupted by envy: if they begin to be envious, their heart congeals into vice, and the sweetness of friendship becomes the bitterness of ill will, together with a certain unpleasant horror of envy. Thus the heart has congealed through pride and envy—vices that have corrupted by the solidification of malice the gentleness of nature flowing with goodwill.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The edition, however, reads: “which have corrupted the goodwill flowing from the gentleness of nature,” and so forth. But the blessed Doctor means that those who embrace someone with goodwill are accustomed to show gentleness toward him.]

The heart of the wicked, therefore, congeals; but the righteous person is humbled by meditating on the precepts of the Law, possessing the instruction of humility.

20. Therefore he adds: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your ordinances.” The Apostle followed this, saying: “I am pleased with weaknesses, insults, necessities, persecutions, and distresses” (2 Corinthians 1:12, 10). Since he is pleased amid weaknesses and is not broken in spirit or overcome by insult, he both deserved to learn God’s ordinances and fulfilled them (2 Corinthians 12:10).

Here, then, “you humbled me” means: “You exercised me through various temptations and hardships.” Symmachus made this clear when he wrote: “It benefited me that I was afflicted, so that I might learn your righteous acts.” Therefore, one who is humbled should not lose heart or be broken; rather, through being humbled, he should advance: by his humility he should soften the proud, by the strictness of his conduct confound the insolent, by his patience break the abusive, and sometimes by his equanimity amid loss draw the greedy away from a quarrelsome disposition.

For thus you have read: “Wisdom has been justified by her children” (Luke 7:35), while Christ offers himself to punishment, submits to insults, does not withdraw from reproaches, and does not turn his face away from the shame of spitting. Therefore he instructed everyone by his patience and healed them by his bruising.

[Note: All editions read: “he instructed them by his wisdom.” All manuscripts read: “he instructed them by his patience.” The latter is better, since it follows from the preceding words—“Christ offers himself to punishment,” and so forth.]

21. (Verse 72.) It follows: “The law of your mouth is good for me, above thousands of gold and silver.” Not everyone says this; indeed, very few say it—that is, those who prefer God’s law to gold and silver, who can leave everything for the sake of God’s law. Yet Christ did not find such a person except among those whom he himself deigned to teach. 1086 Peter said this and proved it by his action, because he valued the Law more highly than gold. Therefore he said: “I have neither gold nor silver” (Acts 3:6).

The greedy man who lies upon buried gold does not say this. Nor does the wealthy man say it—the one who anxiously searches out his daily profits, piles up wealth day after day, hunts for inheritances, and keeps tireless watch around the bed of the sick.

22. Some understand “the law of the mouth of God” here as the law of the Word of God, as when one says “the law of the right hand of God.” Thus this also aptly corresponds to Peter’s saying: “You have the words of eternal life, and shall we leave you?” (John 6:69). That is: “The law of your mouth is above thousands of gold and silver.” Can we abandon such a great good and pursue the profits of this world?

Moses too may be called the law of the mouth of God, through whom the Lord spoke and gave the Law.

# TENTH SERMON. Yod

[Column 1329A]

1. Among the Hebrews the tenth letter begins here, Yod, which in Latin signifies “confession,” or certainly “desolation.” The interpretations do not seem discordant or incompatible. For those who are desolate confess more quickly; the mind is usually lifted up by prosperity, but when it is pressed by adversity, then it implores divine help.

Even in human affairs we recognize this to be the practice: when things go well for someone, his spirit is more elevated; but for one against whom the hostility of this world and the power of another are directed, then he takes refuge and seeks aid—either by entreaty softening the power of his superior, or by arming himself with added strength, lest, like an inferior, he be crushed by stronger forces.

2. Accordingly, Jeremiah says under this letter: “The afflicted stretches out his hands toward all his desirable things. For he has seen nations entering his sanctuary, concerning whom you commanded that they should not enter his assembly” (Lamentations 1:10). The Prophet is speaking of Jerusalem, of course, whose misery he laments, whose desolation and abandonment came first, so that confession might follow afterward.

For the Lord chastises every son whom he receives. Therefore, intending to receive Jerusalem, he first scourged her with the hardships of captivity. She had become excessively insolent and had boasted with an inflated heart, so that she could not hold the Lord Jesus as her head—that is, she could not hold humility, grace, righteousness, and wisdom, the instruction of true faith.

Therefore the Lord chastised her, for he who governs all things knows how to chastise each person. Just as a physician customarily treats more serious wounds with harsher medicines and lighter wounds with milder ones, so also our God chastises more serious sins with greater severity. Yet that chastisement itself contributes to salvation. For the Lord said: “I strike, and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

3. Accordingly, the prophet Jeremiah began to promise hope for Jerusalem. For later, under this letter, he says: “He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him, and he will be filled with reproaches. He will put his mouth in the grave, if nevertheless there is hope of patience” (Lamentations 3:30 and 29).

In the Gospel, the Lord Jesus, teaching the virtue and distinction of patience, 1087 says: “Whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5:39). He wants his disciples to be patient even with insults and not readily strike back—indeed, not even to strike. For patience is a sign of humility.

And therefore, because Jerusalem was desolate and abandoned, he says: “He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him,” so that he may not withdraw from insult or avoid the pain of a blow, but offer his cheek to the one striking him.

This can be understood in either way: whether of the one who is beginning to strike, or of the one who has already struck, so that the Gospel saying may be fulfilled: “Whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also.”

This was also set down prophetically in order to teach Jerusalem—that is, the Church of the Jewish people—that she could be preserved in no other way than through the discipline of the Gospel. When she began to observe the precepts of the Gospel and fulfill in deeds the commandment of the Lord Jesus, then she would remove the yoke of captivity from the neck of her soul, once she had submitted herself to the yoke of Christ.
