4. “And he will be filled,” he says, “with reproaches.” He did not say: “He will undergo reproach.” It is easy to endure one or two insults. But he added: “He will be filled with reproaches,” so that the Lord might more readily arouse mercy, since the multitude of reproaches makes him pitiable.

This you can understand from the Book of Kings. When Shimei son of Gera reviled holy David, calling him a bloodthirsty man and cursing him while he was fleeing from his son Absalom and for a time avoiding a parricidal war, the king remained silent and displayed the highest mark of patience.

For when he understood that the time of his testing had come, when a parricidal battle was being brought against him, he preferred to appear more humble, so as to soften the Lord’s anger, rather than to aggravate the judgment that he believed was being directed against him in his trial, if he were to seek vengeance for his own injuries.

Therefore he said to Abishai, the leader of the people, who wished to take revenge: “What have I to do with you, son of Zeruiah? Let him curse, because the Lord has told him to curse . . . . Behold, my son, who came forth from my body, seeks my life. If now this outsider curses me, leave him, let him curse; because the Lord has told him to do so, to see my humility; and the Lord will repay me good for this cursing” (2 Samuel 16:10 and following).

He spoke this by a prophetic spirit and proved it by the outcome. When humility has been filled to the measure, sin is loosed. Accordingly, in the Book of Isaiah you also find that the Lord said: “Priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her, because her humiliation has been filled, her sin has been loosed, because she has received double for her sins from the hand of the Lord” (Isaiah 40:2).

You see, therefore, that where there is desolation, there is humility. Desolation is followed in due order by humility, humility by patience, patience by testing, and testing by consolation. You have the same sequence written in the Apostle: “Tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 3:3–5), who is certainly the consoler of our affections.

1088 5. When he says, “He will put his mouth in the grave” (Lamentations 3:29), he shows a certain extraordinary silence of patience: as though he buried his own mouth so that it might not speak, and as though he blocked it with a kind of mound of virtues, so that it might not utter a voice of pain.

He asserts such a weight of patience as hope nourishes, so that he buries and encloses his very voice as though in some tomb or burial mound—a voice which no insult can extort and no injury awaken.

We have explained, as best we could, the interpretation of this letter. Let us come to the psalm.

6. (Verse 73.) The first verse is therefore: “Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments.”

He used a grand opening of commendation, saying that he was God’s work, so that favor might more readily incline the author toward the grace of his own work. For even in human affairs it is a great privilege for someone to favor his own works and benefits, without considering another’s merit, but attending to the gift of his own grace, lest he seem to revoke what he himself gave.

Thus, although the substance of our body is from clay, although we are clothed in flesh and the body is covered with bones and sinews, no one would doubt that we are God’s most precious work. For if anyone wishes to consider the structure of the human body itself, he will be able to judge that nothing on earth is more precious.

Man is lofty in stature, beautiful in face, attractive in hair; he is not bent toward the belly like the other animals, but by the very law of nature he is elevated, able to gaze freely toward heaven. He is not pressed down toward the earth by the captive servitude of his neck, but, as though conscious of his own liberty and a rich witness to his own creator, he bears testimony to his creator.

7. Nevertheless, in the other animals the form of their limbs may be praised, since apart from bodily grace there is nothing else required of them. Man is more beautiful in what is not seen than in the body that is seen: he possesses within himself the grace of eternity as well as the beauty of the present.

“For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). In this earthly lodging he is clothed with a heavenly dwelling; he is suited both to be seen on earth and to be joined to God.

It is truly a great gift if he knows himself, and a certain form of righteousness: to be born more for the world than for himself.

[Note: You will find this thought most elegantly expounded by the Roman orator in Book 1 of *On Duties*, in these words: “But since, as Plato has splendidly written, we are not born for ourselves alone, and our country claims a share of our birth, our parents a share, and our friends a share; and, as the Stoics hold, all things that are produced on earth are created for human use, while human beings are born for the sake of human beings, so that each might be able to benefit another—we must follow nature as our guide in this, and bring common interests into the midst,” and so forth.

Lucan also praises Cato of Utica because it was his conviction:

“to believe himself born not for himself, but for the whole world.”

It is therefore remarkable that a Christian was found who dared to attack this noble maxim. You will find his principal arguments refuted in volume 3 of *Ancient and Modern Philosophy*, treatise 3, disputation 1, question 3, article 2.]

Therefore Solomon also says: “A great thing is man, and a precious work is a merciful man; but a faithful man is hard to find” (Proverbs 20:6). Truly great is the one who is both an interpreter of God’s work and an imitator of God.

For he is the man who was able to say: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). He cultivates the earth, uses the sea as his possession, and, as an appreciative observer, marvels at the adornments of heaven.

[Note: All editions read: “a great admirer and defender.” The manuscripts read: “a grateful admirer,” and so forth.]

Nature would have vanished unless divine providence had added one who would use it.

[Column 1331D]

8. Accordingly, after God made heaven and earth and the seas, after he made all creeping things, flying things, and living creatures, he afterward made man, whom he placed above living creatures. Concerning this, the heavenly utterance not unjustly resounded: “Let us make 1089 man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

He merely spoke of the others, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created (Psalm 148:5). But for man to be made, a special exhortation from God was added, so that the operation of God, as though laboring in this work of creation, might be signified.

God is certainly free from labor; yet what else do the words of Scripture show than his painstaking activity on your behalf?

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “unless they show the care of his activity on your behalf.” The older edition reads: “unless they show his diligent activity on your behalf,” and so forth. But “on your behalf” is found neither in the manuscripts nor is it necessary to the sense.]

Therefore, if God created you with a kind of greater diligence, why do you yourself abandon concern for yourself? If God labored over you, though he does not know how to labor, why are you yourself a fugitive from labor?

[Column 1332B]

9. “Your hands,” he says, “made me and fashioned me” (Psalm 137:8). The Prophet cries out to God: “Your work, Lord, do not abandon; do not forsake.” I appeal to you as author; I hold to you as creator; I seek no outside defenses. Gird yourself to help, you who girded yourself to create.

David himself, tell us what you felt and why you said: “Your hands made me.” But later you said: “Lord, you will repay on my behalf; Lord, your mercy is forever; do not abandon the works of your hands” (ibid.). This is what he means: “Your hands did not make the beasts.” Rather, you said: “Let the waters bring forth reptiles with living souls” (Genesis 1:20), and the earth brought forth quadrupeds according to their kinds, reptiles, and beasts of the earth.

“But me,” he says, “you made; with your own hands you fashioned me.” That is: you did not fashion the beasts with your hands, nor the reptiles, nor the flying creatures; but “your hands made me and fashioned me.”

10. It is no ordinary work that has been prepared, since each thing is arranged and prepared with wisdom. Accordingly, Wisdom says: “When he prepared the heavens, I was with him” (Proverbs 8:27).

The same Prophet says concerning human beings: “The voice of the Lord preparing the deer” (Psalm 28:9). What is this voice of the Lord God except: “Let us make man” (Genesis 1:26)? Who are these deer except enemies of serpents, who walk upon vipers and feel no poison?

What God prepared, therefore, I do not consider worthless or merely bodily. Know yourself, man. It is said to your soul in the Song of Songs: “Unless you know yourself, beautiful among women” (Song of Songs 1:7).

Know yourself, soul, because you are not from earth or clay, since God breathed into you and made you a living soul (Genesis 2:6).

[Note: All editions read: “because God breathed into you.” Almost all manuscripts do not recognize the preposition. The older edition again reads: “Man is a magnificent work, inspired by God’s generation.” The Roman edition: “Man is a magnificent work, formed by God’s inspiration.” All the manuscripts read as in the text, except that three reverse the final words: “generated by inspiration.”]

You are a magnificent work, inspired by God’s begetting. “Take heed to yourself,” as the Law says (Deuteronomy 4:9)—that is, take heed to yourself, to your soul. Let secular and worldly things not hold you; let earthly things not delay you. Hasten with your whole attention toward him from whose inspiration you exist.

“A great thing,” he says, “is man, and a precious work is a merciful man; but a faithful man is hard to find” (Proverbs 20:6). Learn, man, where you are great and where you are precious. Earth shows you to be lowly; virtue makes you glorious, faith rare, and the image precious.

Is anything as precious as the image of God? It ought first to infuse faith into you, so that some likeness of the creator may shine in your heart, lest the one who questions your mind fail to recognize the creator.

Is anything as precious as humility, by which, perceiving the nature of body and soul, you submit yourself to the one and 1090 recognize that you govern the other? The inclination of the flesh toward vice urges mercy, because whatever you confer upon another, you repay to yourself; whatever proceeds from you returns to you; and whatever benefit you provide benefits you.

11. Let the vigor of the living soul, capable of sensation, reason, understanding, and judgment, so that it may seem a dwelling worthy of so great an inhabitant, not lose the privilege of its nature, lest it lose the name of “man.” For Scripture calls him a man who is made according to the image and likeness of God. But the sinner it is accustomed to call not a man, but either a serpent, or a horse neighing after females, or a little fox, or a beast of burden.

“Do not become like the horse or mule, which have no understanding. With bit and bridle constrain their jaws, those who do not approach you” (Psalm 31:9).

And concerning Herod he says: “Tell that fox” (Luke 13:32). John calls the people of men “a brood of vipers” (Luke 3:7).

You are therefore a great work of God, man; great is what God has given you. Take care lest you lose what God has bestowed—the great gift of being made according to the image of God—and lest this be punished more severely in you.

For God does not punish his own likeness; he punishes the one who, having been made according to the likeness of God, was unable to preserve what he received.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “was unwilling to preserve.” But here, as we have already said concerning the same verb, the word may be understood in a freer sense: “was unable.”]

What is punished, therefore, is that which ceases to be according to the likeness of God—that is, your sin. For God does not condemn his own image, nor does he cast it into eternal fire; rather, he avenges his own image upon the one who has injured that image, so that through wickedness you cease to be what you were as a man and become a mule out of a man.

The image is therefore avenged, not condemned. It is avenged as though expelled; it is not condemned as though guilty. For after you sinned, you began to be something else; you ceased to be what you were.

How, then, is that punished in you which is not found in you? For if the image and likeness of God is found in you, you do not begin to be worthy of punishment but of reward.

Thus that image by which you were made according to the image and likeness of God is not condemned but crowned. You are condemned in that by which you yourself have been changed, so that you became from a man a serpent, a mule, a horse, or a little fox. Scripture has already condemned us by these names, because, stripped of the adornment of the heavenly image, we also lose the name of man when we do not retain the grace of man.

12. In some manuscripts, however, we find: “Your hands made me and molded me.” This too is not foreign to the sense, since Job also said: “Your hands molded me and made me” (Job 10:8).

Therefore it is declared here also that God should remember that we are dust, so that he may pour in the gift of more abundant grace and not abandon a weak work.

A helmsman expends more labor when the ship is tossing than when the oar glides over a favorable wave, or when he outruns the gust of the winds by his own surpassing exertion.

[Note: The older edition reads: “when it glides over a favorable wave with a second rowing, and advances with the breath of the winds overcoming its sail,” with “hastening” in Gill’s margin. The Roman edition reads: “when it moves over a favorable wave, or when the wind’s breath advances with a favorable sail,” and so forth. The manuscripts all read: “when the second oar moves over the wave”; but they are divided here. Some have “or advances with a favorable breath,” while the more numerous and better manuscripts read as in the text.]

13. “Your hands,” he says, “molded me.” He says “hands” in the plural, not “hand.” Yet elsewhere he says: “I, with my hand, established heaven” (Isaiah 45:12), and: “My hand made these things” (Isaiah 66:2).

In the creation of man, it seems that what had abounded for the making of the whole world did not suffice. One hand established heaven, as it is written; but both hands of God fashioned man, as we read.

Heaven was not made according to the likeness; man was made according to the likeness. Angels were made for service; man for the image.

[Page 1091]

14. Let us suppose that angels too were made according to the image. Nevertheless, Scripture spoke of man as being according to the image.

For we possess something that perhaps angels do not possess: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.” Christ was born for us from a Virgin. For we read: “A child is born for us, and a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6).

For us he assumed flesh; indeed, rather, he assumed us in that flesh, since he established the Son of Man in the seat of God.

I do not read that angels are in the seat of God except standing there and rendering service (Hebrews 1:14; Revelation 8:2; Daniel 7:10). I do not read of angels, but of human beings, buried with Christ and raised in Christ (Romans 6:4–5).

Accordingly, the Apostle says: “He made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved; and he raised us together and made us sit together in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:5–6).

Therefore the Son of Man is at the right hand of God—not an angel, not an archangel, nor a cherub or seraph. Those beings praise him; the Son of Man sits. The Son of Man is praised by the mouths of angels because he conquered the evil angels and triumphed over the spiritual wickedness that is in the heavenly places; because he made human beings like angels, in whom previously there had been the pollution of the dead.

15. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6). Man too received the perfection of life and the completion of virtue through the Spirit of the Lord.

God breathed into him the breath of life, and man became a living soul (Genesis 2:7). Our life therefore began from divine inspiration; but this life is dissolved by the separation of soul and body, whereas divine inspiration is not dissolved.

Therefore understand that one thing is what was formed, and another what was made or prepared. Accordingly, you have two statements written about man.

First it is written: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26–27). And: “They shall rule,” he says, or “they shall have dominion.” And: “God made man according to the image of God.”

In the second passage it is written: “God took dust from the earth and molded man” (Genesis 2:7). Where there is dust, there is molding; but where there is not dust, there is neither earth nor matter, but what is incorporeal and marvelous. There is not matter, but immateriality.

For what is according to the image of God is not in the body or in matter, but in the rational soul. There man operates and is shown to be according to the likeness and image of God—where righteousness, wisdom, and every form of virtue are assumed.

16. If you understand “image,” you will see “according to the image.” Man is not the image of God; he was made according to the likeness.

Another is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, through whom all things were made. He is not “according to the image,” but the image. You are not the image, but “according to the image.”

Therefore, in your substance you possess 1092 something of the image and likeness of God, something resembling the divine image. For this reason the Image came to the one who is according to the image, and the Image seeks the one who is according to its likeness, so that it may mark him again and confirm him again, because you had lost what you received.

God had breathed into you so that, by the gift of his inspiration, you might possess the grace that your own fault had taken from you. You had been made a living soul. Hear what he says: not “into flesh,” but “into a living soul.”

But because the sinner could not retain the seal and, placed in guilt, possessed not the things of God but the things of men, therefore our Lord Jesus Christ came. As you have read in the Gospel, when he rose from the dead and found the disciples shut in, he entered while the doors remained closed and said: “Peace be with you. As the Father sent me, I also send you.” And when he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:21–22).

[Column 1336A]

17. Do you see, then, which hands made man, or what kind of man they made? The man whom we put on according to Christ: “Stripping off the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him; where there is not . . . slave and free, but Christ is all and in all” (Colossians 3:9–11).

Therefore we put on Christ, as it is also said elsewhere: “You have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

We received the Holy Spirit, who not only forgives our sins but also makes us his priests, able to forgive the sins of others.

[Note: Observe that priests or the bishop are here expressly taught to receive in their ordination both the remission of their own sins and the power to forgive the sins of others.]

Therefore the Prophet says: “You fashioned me and placed your hand upon me” (Psalm 138:5). He fashioned him through clay; he placed his hand upon him through spiritual grace, although many understand this psalm as spoken in the person of the Savior.

Hear that the hand of the Lord is also called the Spirit. Job cries out: “The divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33:4). These, then, are the hands that prepared man: Christ and the Spirit.

Therefore the Lord Jesus is also the author of our body. First he made man according to the image; afterward he fashioned him from clay; and he wished to preserve what he had made and save what he had molded, so that he might save the whole man, as he himself said in the Gospel: “Are you angry with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath?” (John 7:23).

[Note: Many manuscripts, including some of no inferior quality, read: “which teaches the Church.”]

The Church teaches this in particular: that not only the soul but also our flesh is saved—the soul through knowledge of God, the flesh through resurrection. The one truth he taught by the authority of divine speech; the other by the example of his own resurrection.

[Column 1336C]

18. This, then, is man of a twofold substance. One is the substance of what was made, another of what was fashioned: the former from the Spirit of God, the latter from clay.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “another of what was breathed into him.” But, with the other editions and all the manuscripts, “another of what was fashioned” must be retained. Here he indicates what has been taught more than once above: that the divine image was impressed upon man not in the body but in the soul.]

Therefore Job says: “He will raise up my skin” (Job 19:26), because what is from clay is raised up; for earth returns to earth. But what was made to have dominion over the other living creatures—you understand that to be the more excellent part.

Clay is common to us and to the beasts, and therefore a special privilege was granted to the soul.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “It was granted so that man might rule the other living creatures, but so that he might be able,” and so forth.]

Yet precisely because he rules the other living creatures, he must be subject to God in order to rule. He is taught to serve so that he may deserve to attain the kingdom.

For one who serves Christ pleases God. One who serves Christ certainly 1093 pleases the truth and must know nothing of falsehood. One who serves righteousness must repel iniquity. One who serves the undefiled must maintain the discipline of chastity. One who serves the light must hate the darkness of sins.

Therefore, because the body is weak, let us ask for the visitation of the Lord. Hence the Prophet says: “What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” (Psalm 8:5).

19. And now, in the remaining part of the verse, he says: “Give me understanding, and I will learn your commandments.”

The Prophet, therefore, knowing himself to be spiritual, asks for the grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Thirteen written codices read this way. Other manuscripts and editions read: “The Prophet recognizes this through the grace of the Holy Spirit.” In the Roman edition, the order of what follows—from “you have learned” up to “understanding”—is inverted as follows: “But the Prophet first places the gift of wisdom, and afterward that of understanding, among the gifts of grace. And because the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for the common good, therefore the Prophet asks for God’s gift: ‘Give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments.’ Observe the order: understanding is placed first,” and so forth.]

For you have learned from the apostolic reading that understanding is given by the Lord and is placed first among the gifts of grace, because “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for the common good” (2 Timothy 2:7); and in the Prophet the grace of spiritual wisdom and understanding is requested first (Isaiah 11:2).

God’s gift is therefore requested. Then observe the order: “Give me,” he says, “understanding, so that I may learn your commandments.” Understanding comes first, so that knowledge may follow.

For unless someone has understood, he cannot be learned. Understanding produces instruction, not memory. It is of no benefit to have read much unless you yourself understand what you have read.

And in the Apostle, after the manifestation of the Spirit, you later read that the word of knowledge is placed, so that you may know that understanding must be preferred to memory and that the one in whom understanding has first shone can possess knowledge (1 Corinthians 12:7).

### 20

Consider humility as well. If the Prophet asks that understanding be given to him, who could be so arrogant as to claim that intelligence lies within his own power? He asks for understanding so that he may know himself and be able to understand the nature of his own being. Yet those who discuss the nature of things and scrutinize the regions of heaven, while unable to know themselves, think that understanding can be granted without God’s gift. Therefore we too ought to assume humility, lest we become elated if perhaps we have understood some one parable from the Scriptures, or because at times we read passages that are plain according to the letter; if perhaps we have understood something according to the letter, let us not claim for ourselves the knowledge of doctrine.

That Prophet who received the Holy Spirit, after he was anointed for kingship and anointed as a prophet, when writing the one-hundred-and-eighteenth Psalm, asks that understanding be given to him, so that he may understand God’s commandments; and he knows that, unless he receives grace from the Lord, he cannot understand his commandments. In the Gospel also I read that, when the Lord Jesus proposed parables, the apostles did not understand them (Matt. XIII, 36). Indeed, they asked for an explanation of the parable that had been proposed.

### 21

The Lord Jesus himself, when he said—as you have read written in the Gospel according to Matthew—“Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V, 3), added later:

[Note: The Roman edition adds after these words, “but whoever does and teaches, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” And in another passage, “Everyone who hears these words of mine,” etc.]

“Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man” (Matt. VII, 24). Therefore it is not merely the one who hears who will be like him, but the one who does what he has heard. 1094 Thus neither action without hearing, nor hearing without action, can belong to a wise person; rather, it belongs to the one who hears and does. Let us therefore hear, so that we may understand; let us act, so that we may prove that we have understood what we heard.

### 22  
*(Verse 74)*

The second verse follows:

“Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped exceedingly in your words.”

Perhaps this may seem contrary to some people, because the righteous man says, “Those who fear you will see me and rejoice”; for to many people the righteous man is burdensome when he is seen. Indeed, in the Gospel many were unable to see the Lord Jesus. Thus the Gerasenes asked him to depart from their region (Luke VIII, 37), and others refused him passage when he did not wish to pass through them (Luke IX, 52–53).

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts and the old edition read. The Roman edition, however, has, “when he merely wished to pass through them.” The sense is clear, unless it is deprived of every other support.]

Hence I think that, just as the form of Jewish impiety is expressed there, so here the grace of the Church is revealed. For he prophesies that the whole world is to be filled with the fear of God; and therefore he says that those who fear God, as it were, rejoice at the knowledge of the saints. Whoever sees a righteous person and rejoices also wishes to be righteous himself. For it is beautiful to take delight in others in what one wishes to preserve in oneself, if one has taken it up.

[Note: The Roman edition has, “if he is able.” The other editions, together with all the manuscripts, have, “if he has taken it up.” The sense seems to be that a righteous man delights in others in that good which he has chosen and taken upon himself to preserve.]

It is implanted in the good that a wise person should love the chaste and modest with devoted affection, a merciful person should love the generous, and that each should love his own virtues in others. To many people the sight of the righteous is a summons to correction, but to the more perfect it is a source of joy. How beautiful, then, that you should be seen and be of benefit! The righteous man is therefore a good thing.

### 23

For this reason the apostle Paul finally went up to Jerusalem in order to see the righteous; and he remained with Peter for fifteen days, so that he might profit in some way from living with him (Gal. I, 18). For this reason Paul himself and Barnabas, when they entered Jerusalem, were magnificently received by the Church, by the apostles, and by the elders (Acts XV, 4). When they wished to depart, they were asked not to leave; and, as we later read concerning Paul, they escorted him with tears (Acts XX, 38).

For if there is such power in natural things that a living creature, when seen, benefits those suffering from jaundice, so that even the horn of a dead animal is said to be beneficial if it is shown to those who have fallen into such an illness—

[Note: The same Roman edition has, “the body of that living creature.” Since Pliny, Natural History, book XXX, chapter 11, attributes the power of curing jaundice to a little bird, the word “horn” did not seem to offer the proper sense. But since the same word is consistently read in all the manuscripts and old editions, it should perhaps be said that this passage refers to some four-footed animal, unless one prefers to understand by “its horn” the claws and beak of that same bird.]

—can we doubt that the sight of the righteous heals? Does a worthless irrational animal possess such power that it can heal a person in the brief moment in which it is seen, while a righteous man—provided that he is looked upon with faith by one who desires to receive benefit from him—contributes nothing? Do not even the rays of the eyes themselves seem to infuse some power into those who desire to look upon him faithfully?

### 24

But just as the righteous man gladdens the hearts of the innocent when he is seen, so the wicked are tormented by knowledge of the righteous, because they are convicted even by the silent conduct of the saints. Chastity torments self-indulgence; generosity, greed; faith, impiety.

Let us take an analogous example from a worthless animal as well. For just as we said that a mute animal is beneficial when it is seen, so we perceive that a wolf is harmful if it has seen someone first; for it is said that those whom a wolf has seen first lose their voice. The basilisk also—that is, a harmful serpent—is said to kill whatever animal it sees first; and it is immediately reported that anyone who has been seen first by such a serpent is killed. The serpent itself is also said to die if it is seen first by a human being.

Therefore, if there is such power either in the eyes of a serpent or in human eyes that, if one sees the other first, he can kill him, is there no power in the eyes of the righteous man, who is filled with the grace of virtue—especially when faith accomplishes so much that the woman who touched the Lord’s fringe was healed (Matt. IX, 22), and the man upon whom the Lord Jesus looked immediately drew the grace of healing from his eyes (Luke IX, 38 and 43)?

### 25

But whoever sees a righteous man must know what he is seeing. He does not see him in his body, in his clothing, in his wealth, or in his face; rather, he sees him inwardly. I say, he does not see him unless he has seen his mind, unless he has attended to his speech, unless he has been able to comprehend his thoughts and draw wisdom from his discourse. Then he will rejoice, when he has discerned and understood these things.

Thus let us too, wherever we hear that a righteous man is present, hasten to see him, like the woman who heard that the Lord Jesus was reclining in the house of the Pharisee, entered, and bathed his feet with ointment (Luke VII, 37–38). Let us imitate her; for who would doubt that the Church was prefigured in that woman? Wherever, then, a righteous man sits or reclines, let us hasten to see him. It is precious to see a righteous man, so that you may see him according to the image of God. What is outward contributes nothing; what is inward heals.

Indeed, even in the one who is outward we frequently behold the one who is inward: when we see a poor person, we honor in the poor person the one in whose likeness he was made. Concerning him Christ says, “You gave me food . . . for whatever you gave to one of these, you gave to me” (Matt. XXV, 35 and 40).

[Note: Nine manuscripts read, “For whoever honors . . . has honored the image.” Other manuscripts and all the editions read, “whoever crowns . . . has crowned it.” The latter is better; for images of emperors were customarily crowned with flowers, as Joseph Laurentius observes in his Polyhistor, book V, p. 391. Nor is it surprising that such honor was also paid to statues of Christian emperors, since it is established that, when these statues were brought into towns, they were received by magistrates and peoples with incense, candles, and adoration. This worship was eventually prohibited by Theodosius the Younger, Code, title 4, single law; consult that law, as well as the commentary of Gothofredus upon it.

It is worth adding here what Hilary, Bishop of Rome, reports from St. Chrysostom, inserted in the second letter of the Nicene Synod; for it is very similar to what our Ambrose says here. He says: “Do you not know that whoever insults the image made of wood and colors is judged not as having dared to act against a lifeless object, but against the emperor” [Greek: Οὐκ οἶδας ὅτι ὄστις τὴν εἰκόνα τὴν ἐκ ξύλου καὶ χρωμάτων λοιδορεῖ, οὐχ ὡς πρὸς ἄψυχον τολμήσας κρίνεται, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τοῦ βασιλέως]?

It is also worth noting that, four verses later, Ambrose locates the idolatry of the pagans not in their believing that idols were gods, but in their worshiping them because they thought that the image of God dwelled in them—even though God, being incorporeal, cannot in any way be likened to a material likeness. From this, however, the opposite conclusion follows: that he did not at all disapprove of the sacred images of Christ the Lord, the Blessed Virgin, the martyrs, and other saints, or of the honors shown to them. Certainly the entire teaching of the Seventh Ecumenical Council, mentioned above, turns almost entirely on this point. For it repeatedly asserts that God’s nature, being spiritual, cannot be painted; in this Gregory II had preceded it, writing to Leo the Isaurian: “It is impossible to represent and paint the nature of God” [Greek: Θεοῦ φύσιν ἀδύνατον ἱστορῆσαι καὶ ζωγραφῆσαι]. But with regard to images of Christ and the saints, the same Fathers plainly infer and decree the opposite. Indeed, since they also support images of angels, chiefly on the ground that they “appeared in human form” [Greek: ὡς ἄνθρωποι ἐνεφανίσθησαν], the same argument proves that it is not unlawful to set before the people for veneration symbolic images of the divine Persons, under which forms Scripture records that they manifested themselves. But these matters belong to the controversialists.]

Whoever crowns the image of the emperor certainly honors the one whose image he has crowned; and whoever despises the statue of the emperor seems to have done an injury to the emperor whose statue he has spat upon. The pagans worship wood because they think it to be the image of God. But the image of the invisible God is not in what is seen, but certainly in what is not seen.

### 26

You see, therefore, that we walk among many images of Christ. Let us beware lest we seem to remove the crown from the image that Christ has placed upon each person. Let us beware lest we take anything away from those to whom we ought to add something.

But what is worse, we not only fail to honor the poor; we also dishonor, destroy, and persecute them. And we do not realize that we heap these injuries upon the image of God when we think that those made in the image of God ought to be harmed. Whoever mocks the poor provokes the one who made him.

But he will come who says: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink . . . I was sick . . . and you did not visit me” (Matt. XXV, 42–43). And how much less serious these things are than if he should say: “You injured me, stripped me naked, and beat me.” If someone asks him, “When did we injure you? When did we strip you? When did we even beat you?” he will say: “As long as you did it to one of these least ones, you did it to me” (ibid., 45).

Therefore let us take the greatest care not to inflict an insult upon anyone, however insignificant, lest we seem to have insulted the Lord himself in those least ones.

### 27

He himself explained why he said, “Those who fear you will see me and rejoice,” when he added, “because I have hoped exceedingly in your words.” This means: They saw me inwardly, touched me inwardly, looked upon me inwardly—where I took hope from your words, where I received your words.

Blessed, therefore, are those who see the righteous and rejoice, because they hope in the words of God. But how many there are who hate righteous people—those who scrutinize the words of God and are righteous; whenever the wicked hear learned people, they customarily avoid them because of their teaching.

### 28  
*(Verse 75)*

The third verse follows:

“I have acknowledged, Lord, that your judgments are just, and in your truth you have humbled me.”

Whoever is able to understand the matters of divine providence uses the language employed by the holy prophet David, because everything happens by God’s judgment: that someone should have a sick body or a healthy one, be rich or poor, die young or old. If someone attends to the divine Scriptures, he understands that these things happen by God’s judgment; for nothing is outside God’s knowledge.

Do we seek an example? It is not hidden. Job would never have lost his possessions unless he had been handed over to the power of the adversary. For the Lord gave the devil power over his possessions, so that Job might be tested to see what his disposition would be after losing his inheritance (Job I, 12). He gave him power over his children and over his body (Job II, 6), so that it might be proved whether he would depart from constancy of mind and spirit because of grief over his dead children or bodily torment.

The Lord knew that he was strong; but in Job he wished to teach and test us, to see whether we could be his imitators. Finally, he also tested Abraham, when he asked that his only son, born to him in his old age, be sacrificed (Gen. XXII, 2). Certainly he knew Abraham’s mind; but the Lord tests even while knowing, as you have read in the Gospel. When the Lord Jesus asked the disciples how many loaves they had, and they answered that they had only five, he said:

[Note: The Roman edition has, “What are these among so many people?” The Evangelist then adds, “But he said this to test them; for he himself knew what he was going to do,” etc.]

“What shall we do among so many people?” But he said this to test them; for he knew what he was going to do (John VI, 5–6).

Therefore, whoever is righteous believes, in the testing of his righteousness, that God’s judgments are just; or, according to the Greek, that God’s judgments are themselves righteousness.

### 29

But the preceding prayer was made so that he might recognize this, since he asked that understanding be given to him in order to learn God’s commandments. He therefore received the grace of understanding and knowledge and recognized that God’s judgments are just. To recognize is the mark of perfection. For it is one thing to believe and another to recognize. Faith belongs to the one who fears; recognition belongs to the wise. The one who fears does not seek an explanation, but the wise person investigates the knowledge of whatever he desires to understand.

“I believed,” he says, “and therefore I spoke” (Ps. CXV, 1); but the one who understands recognized what he spoke.

### 30

In what respect, then, are God’s judgments just? Because through labors, tribulations, and afflictions one reaches the heavenly reward. Just as a crown is awarded to athletes who compete according to the just judgment of human beings, so by divine judgment the palm is granted to Christians who compete lawfully. “To the one who conquers,” he says, “I will grant to sit with me on my throne” (Rev. III, 21).

Our life is therefore tested by fire, like the brilliance of silver, so that virtue may be approved through struggles. “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. LXV, 11). Through these things, therefore, I recognized that your judgments are true.

For I was humbled so that I might see these things, because those who are exalted in heart cannot open their eyes to the truth. But when we are humbled, we recognize our sins, and by that very humility we cleanse our offenses. “I was humbled,” he says, “and he saved me” (Ps. CXIV, 6). He who has been humbled for salvation has therefore been humbled in truth; nor has he endured suffering in vain who has followed the salvation of truth.

### 31

There is therefore a distinction between recognizing and fearing; let us return to this point. The reading of the Gospel ought to teach us. For the Lord says to those among the Jews who believed in him: “If you remain in my word . . . you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John VIII, 31–32).

“If you remain,” he says, “you will know.” You see that whoever fears God and hears his word cannot recognize it from the beginning. Not only are fear and knowledge not the same; faith and knowledge are not the same either. The Apostle also taught that the gifts of grace are different:

“To one,” he says, “is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 8–9).

If faith is therefore given to one person and knowledge to another, you see that where there is faith there is not immediately knowledge; but where there is knowledge, there are also faith and prudence, nor can we separate diligence from it.

### 32

The holy David therefore possessed knowledge, being a perfect prophet, since he recognized so perfectly that he was humbled in the very truth. Whether, then, placed amid adversity, he recognized the grace of testing and understood that laborious and adverse circumstances had to be endured, while God’s judgment was just—and therefore that those who compete well are never abandoned or forsaken, and that a crown can be granted them after their labors—or whether, placed amid favorable and prosperous circumstances, he recognized that the wealth of kings and their various successes commonly provide occasions for temptation, so that the person who uses them is tested by prosperity—

[Note: All the editions, and several manuscripts, read, “the wealth of possessions and various successes commonly provide occasions for temptation” (some have “an occasion”). Others agree with us, except that the Vindobonensis reads, “wealth, kingship,” etc.]

—in this the prophet David is to be praised: that, while recognizing these things, he humbled himself, so that by his humility he might either shut out the temptations of prosperity or undergo with steadfast equanimity the endurance of adversity.

### 33

The Prophet would therefore not be especially praiseworthy if, while enjoying an abundance of prosperity, he praised God’s judgments. For what great thing do we do when we praise God while we are prosperous, while we are wealthy, while we suffer no injuries? It is magnificent to praise God’s judgment when one is subjected to injuries and insults; to proclaim God’s judgments when one is afflicted by illness; if poverty does not deter one from praising God’s justice.

God’s judgments must therefore always be praised, as it is written: “The daughters of Judah rejoiced because of your judgments” (Ps. XLVII, 12). Who are the daughters of Judah except religious souls, the souls of the Church that confess Jesus Christ the Lord, which, seeing the reason of your judgments, always rejoice? For whoever does not draw joy from some outcome of prosperity but receives joy from understanding the reason is established in perpetual rejoicing.

### 34  
*(Verse 76)*

The fourth verse follows:

“Let your mercy now come, that it may encourage me, according to your word to your servant.”

Some have in this place, “that it may comfort me.” But in the Apostle also we read that encouragement is used for consolation, and consolation for encouragement (II Cor. I, 4 and 6).

Great, therefore, is the mercy of God, which not only grants remission of sins but also applies the spurs of encouragement to those who are engaged in the contest, lest they abandon the sufferings of the struggle they have undertaken through cowardly fear.

He does not therefore implore mercy as one who yields after being defeated or as a petitioner for pardon,

[Note: Six manuscripts read, “or as a sinner imploring pardon.”]

but so that, girded by God’s compassion and strengthened by so great a gift beyond his own powers, he may accomplish greater things.

Observe the Prophet’s outstanding and singular virtue. Another person, humbled by hardships, would ask that temptations cease around him and that the Lord deign to calm his adversities, lest the storm of tribulations rage against him. But this man, like a strong and patient athlete who knew that his soul was to be exercised and anointed by tribulations,

[Note: The old edition, together with the greater number of manuscripts, reads, “who knew that his soul was to be exercised and girded.” The Roman edition, with the rest, has, “as in the body.” Both readings arose from the arena, a usage familiar to Ambrose.]

does not desire to remove sad things, to avoid things that attack him, or to ask that everything which brings fatigue and labor cease. Rather, at the time of his labor he asks that a word of consolation be given to him against the storms of temptations, so that he may endure bravely whatever is brought upon him and not be wearied by any disturbance of sadness.

In this way he beseeches God’s mercy, lest, deprived of assistance for completing his task, he abandon the military service he has begun.

### 35

Clear testimony teaches that encouragement comes from divine mercy. For God says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion. Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 15–16).

Perhaps you will say: “Then we ought neither to will nor to run.” Yet God is accustomed to abandon the negligent. He does not say this, then; rather, let us consider what he does say. Perseverance does not belong to the willing or running of a human being; for it is not in human power, but in the mercy of God, that you are able to complete what you have begun.

Again he says to Moses: “For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show my power in you” (ibid., 17). 1099 It follows, therefore, that encouragement must be attributed to divine mercy. Hence it follows: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (ibid., 18). He encourages the one upon whom he has had mercy; the other, whom he has condemned, he does not call back.

And truly the mercy of God is the warfare of our sufferings, through which our sins are diminished. Thus poor Lazarus, because he endured many evils in this life, found repose in the bosom of Abraham, the consolation of rest. But the rich man, who had consolation in this world, lost the fruit of rest after the course of this life. If God had had mercy on him, he would have chastised him in this world, so that he would not afterward be scourged.

Thus Job, although severely scourged—and indeed by many scourges: poverty, the loss of his children, bodily pains, and the reproaches of his friends—nevertheless enjoys eternal consolation.

### 36

Therefore, the greater the tribulations, the more abundant the consolation that is reserved. Yet, lest you fall and succumb, the greater the temptations you see, the more earnestly ask the Word of God to bring you encouragement.

Paul also asked in this way when he said:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who encourages us in every affliction, so that we too may be able to console those who are in every tribulation, through the encouragement by which we ourselves are encouraged by God; for just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ consolation also abounds” (II Cor. I, 3–5).

With such force does he make his apostolic petition that he may receive consolation from the Lord in every tribulation, so that he may not only himself assume endurance but also console others, enabling them to bear the distress of their own minds.

If, therefore, you have been proved capable in every tribulation, only then will you be worthy to receive consolation in every tribulation. Yet not every suffering is worthy of consolation; the suffering that is through Christ deserves the consolation of Christ.

[Note: The old editions and not a few manuscripts read, “not every suffering is divine consolation.” Several others read, “not every consolation is divine consolation.” But best of all are the remaining manuscripts, though fewer in number, which we have followed here together with the Roman edition.]

### 37

He beautifully added: “According to your word to your servant.” For the Lord himself promises assistance to those who fight for his name, saying:

“When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak; for what you are to speak will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but my Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 19–20).

Therefore, lest we be unequal to the contest, let us always pray for divine assistance, so that he may grant us encouragement. For if we have one who encourages us, we do not easily yield.

### 38

Most have, “who will console us,” and this is not contrary to the truth. For encouragement that spurs someone on is a kind of gentle exhortation, which inflames the contestant with zeal for glory and, as though with a certain consolation, caresses him, lest he be called back by the harshness of his labors.

### 39  
*(Verse 77)*

The fifth verse follows:

“Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, because your law is my meditation.”

For the one whose meditation is the law of God, mercies are present, so that he may live forever. For how can anyone be blessed without divine mercy?

“Blessed . . . is the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. I, 1–2). But the one who meditates on the Law is instructed in the Law; and the one whom the Law has instructed has been instructed by the Lord who spoke the Law.

Therefore it is written: “Blessed is the one whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. XCIII, 12).

Let us therefore learn to meditate on the Law as well; let us not be distracted by worldly allurements or occupied by impediments, but let us always be attentive to the law of God. For it is written: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate on wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment” (Ps. XXXVI, 30).

This is in the Old Testament. Hear him saying the same in the New: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. X, 8).

He especially shows that this meditation is necessary for priests when he writes to Titus, saying that a bishop must embrace “the faithful word that is according to the doctrine, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it” (Tit. I, 9). This certainly belongs to attentive and earnest meditation, not to superficial reading.

Writing to Timothy, he also says: “Attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine” (I Tim. IV, 13). Frequent reading, interrupted by no cessation, performs the office of doctrine.

### 40

By asking that he may live, as we have often shown, he indicates that the life of this body does not possess the grace of true life; rather, true life will be that whose goods each of the saints believes he will see in the land of the living. What we believe we shall see is certainly not present but future.

### 41  
*(Verse 78)*

The sixth verse follows:

“Let the proud be put to shame, because they have acted wickedly against me unjustly; but I shall be exercised in your commandments.”

Above the same Prophet said: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Ps. VII, 5). Does he here curse those who acted wickedly against him? Certainly not. For he saw that love was to be shown even to the bitterest enemies, since the preacher of the Gospel had come.

Hence I think that, like a physician, he wishes to heal those very people who have harmed him, so that, confronted with the contemplation of their iniquity, they may blush at their own crimes. In this way they not only begin to recognize the Prophet’s patience but also to correct their own insolence.

Shame is often a corrector of us; and when we begin to be ashamed of what we have done, we are warned to abandon what ought to cause shame, lest we be ashamed for a longer time.

The Prophet does not therefore curse them, but like a good physician wishes them to recognize and understand what they have done, so that, when they withdraw into their own consciences, they may begin to blush at the great mass of their offenses; and, once ashamed, may be able to renounce their former sins.

Consider now certain people who fornicate, ride roughshod over widows and girls, and seize what belongs to others; and who not only do not blush at these things but are even accustomed to glory in them, as though displaying titles to their beauty or power. Concerning them the Apostle rightly said that “their glory is in their shame” (Phil. III, 19). They are more detestable than their crimes themselves because, while committing such deeds, they are not ashamed.

But if one of them later comes into the Church, believes in the Lord Jesus, hears the Gospel, and is pierced in heart, then at last he will begin to recognize how atrocious and grave are the offenses he has committed, and to blush at the things he has recognized.

### 42

What it means to be exercised in the commandments of our Lord, since he said, “I shall be exercised in your commandments,” you learned in the Law (Exod. XXIII, 5):

[Note: The old edition reads, “in the commandments of the Lord—how could I think otherwise, unless because he said . . .” The Roman edition has, “unless because he said what he said.” The manuscripts agree with us, except that in some “unless” is replaced by “in,” while in others both words are missing; hence the interpolation arose.]

“If your adversary’s ox or beast of burden has fallen, do not consider it to be abandoned, but rather lift it up.”

As for the words, “They have acted wickedly unjustly,” consider against whom this is said—unless it is against one who might act wickedly justly. That is, if someone who has been injured begins to avenge himself by the Law, according to the commandments of Moses, he appears to act wickedly justly, but not according to the commandments of the Gospel. And therefore he says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX, 13), because the Jews use the authority of the Law to avenge themselves.

### 43

You have the same teaching in the Apostle: “Be sober righteously” (I Cor. XV, 34). He clearly taught that we must be not only sober but also justly sober.

Someone can be sober and yet not justly sober: he may abstain from wine but not be sober in fairness and justice; for there is a drunkenness of iniquity. Someone who is always indulging in drunkenness and luxury may nevertheless, while attempting to seize what belongs to others, be occupied with that pursuit, sober from wine but not sober from plunder. He too is not justly sober.

Therefore the Apostle admonishes us to possess a just sobriety. He finally adds: “And do not sin” (ibid.). For whoever sins, even if he is sober, cannot be proclaimed justly sober.

“Do not be deceived,” he says (ibid., 33)—that is, do not let the drunkenness of another’s error make you drunk. Evil conversations corrupt good morals, because a kind of drunkenness is poured into the morals of the hearer through the mouth and lips of unbelievers.

He rightly adds: “Be sober justly, and do not sin.” Some possess ignorance of God; the sober person is the one who does not possess ignorance of God and does not stagger in the drunkenness of unbelief. But he is justly sober in whom the grace of works shines together with the sobriety of faith.

### 44  
*(Verse 79)*

The seventh verse follows:

“Let those who fear you turn toward me, and those who know your testimonies.”

Another reading, especially according to the Greek, is: “Let them turn to me” (*convertantur mihi*).

If we read “toward me” (*ad me*), let those who fear God blush at their own offenses, or at least undergo the punishments for their sins; but let them turn toward God’s servant and prophetic teaching, so that they may unlearn shameful deeds and, corrected by so great a teacher, strip off their former ways; and, once cleansed of the stain of sins, put on the discipline of virtues.

But if we read, “Let them turn to me” (*mihi*), this means: Since I shall be exercised in your commandments, let them turn to me—now no longer sinning, now no longer erring.

“Let those who fear you,” he says, “who have renounced their own sins, turn to me,” so that the Prophet may be advanced to greater abundance through the fellowship of the righteous, and may himself contribute greatly to his hearers from the grace that is in him.

Let the righteous, therefore, turn to me, who no longer sin; let them turn to the righteous. Concerning the testimonies, I think there is no need to repeat what has already been said.

### 45  
*(Verse 80)*

The eighth verse follows:

“Let my heart be made blameless in your justifications, so that I may not be put to shame.”

The higher the Prophet is, whether through the gift of prophecy or the grace of kingship, the more he follows humility and teaches what we ought to imitate, since the Prophet asks that so blameless a heart be made for him.

Above he asked: “Create a clean heart in me, O God” (Ps. L, 12). He did not say, “Make” but “Create,” so that his heart might be restored and cleansed anew.

1102 There is indeed a greater scope in this expression. Great is the heart created by the Lord, capable of receiving the Word concerning the heavenly virtues and powers. Great is the heart that receives the Lord himself saying: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (II Cor. VI, 16).

To receive these things, he does not ask that an angel become the creator of his heart, but that the Lord himself—who created heaven and earth—be its creator.

### 46

And he rightly says, “blameless,” because the human heart is stained by a kind of filth of unseemly thoughts. If thought itself pollutes, how much more do deeds themselves defile?

Do not contaminate the inner sanctuaries with thoughts contrary to nature, lest you pollute with a grave defilement what you think you possess as clean. You wash your hands as though you could wash away crimes, although you cannot wash your mind when it has been defiled by unclean thoughts.

[Note: All the editions, together with part of the manuscripts, read, “defiled by bare thoughts.” The remaining manuscripts have, “by unclean thoughts,” etc.]

Pilate also washed his hands, but he could not wash his heart. He remained polluted by his crime, although he had washed his hands by pouring water over them.

Hear that thought also defiles: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth. For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things that defile a person” (Matt. XV, 17 ff.).

If, then, you are defiled inwardly, first cleanse what is inward. If you have cleansed what is inward, you have also cleansed what is outward. Thus, if water flows turbidly—

[Note: All the editions read, “if turbid water flows in.” The manuscripts, however, read, “if water flows turbidly,” with the adverb used as in Horace, book II, ode 19: “The mind . . . rejoices turbulently.”]

—you would think in vain that the basin needed to be cleansed if the spring pours forth muddy water; for it will do nothing to clean the receptacles when the fault lies in the spring.

You must first be cleansed yourself, so that everything that flows forth may be pure. Your heart is the spring of your thoughts. From that spring either turbid water of impurity is vomited forth, or a sincere stream of piety bursts forth.

47. You have learned that the heart must be cleansed; learn how you may cleanse it. This fountain is cleansed by legitimate justification, that is, by the confession of sins. In the end, that publican who confessed his own sins went away from the temple more justified than the Pharisee, because the Pharisee placed his fasts and offerings, as well as his innocence, first. Cleanse, therefore, your water—that water of which it is said: “Deep water is counsel in a man’s heart” (Prov. 20:5). Nature has given you good water, unless you pollute it with your own mud: it washes you itself if it is pure, simple, and also natural, if it contains nothing filthy or earthly. What evil is there if the water that ought to cleanse should itself pollute? But it is not your water that pollutes you. This water is foreign. Thus it has been said to you: “Keep away from foreign water” (Prov. 5:15). Foreign water lies and deceives, and flows contrary to nature. Therefore he says: “The sons of strangers have lied to me” (Ps. 17:46); for if they had not been strangers, surely they would not have deceived me. Let no one, then, boast that he has a pure heart, as Solomon said (Prov. 20:9); but “let him who boasts, boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17), who has deigned to create a pure heart for his saints and to make it immaculate through his justifications. What those justifications are, you have heard when he says: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26). Therefore the one who declares his iniquities is justified; and the one who is justified is not put to shame, because by a timely confession he has forestalled the shame of his sins.

## 1103 — ELEVENTH SERMON. Kaph

### 1

The eleventh letter, Kaph, begins here; in Latin interpretation it signifies “They have been bent down.” The sound of the interpretation itself teaches us what it means to be bent: whoever inclines toward the earth appears to be bent down. Hence, under this letter the Prophet says: “They very nearly finished me on the earth” (below, v. 87). A person who does penance is bent down, because he bends his neck while he humbles himself before the Lord—and, even more, his inward neck, that is, the neck of his mind and heart. For concerning this neck it was said: “Nor, if you bend your neck like a circle” (Isa. 58:5). Whoever does not bend his heart has bent his neck in vain.

### 2

The prophet Jeremiah also teaches that humility is signified by this interpretation. Under this letter, in the Lamentations, he says: “For the Lord will not reject forever; for although he has humbled, he will have mercy according to the multitude of his mercies; for he has not humbled from his whole heart, nor rejected the children of men” (Lam. 3:31–33). It is good, therefore, to be bent down, so that we may humble ourselves before the Lord and the Lord may have mercy. Indeed, earlier also, under this same letter, the prophet Jeremiah, showing the groans and humility of the people, says: “All her people groaning, seeking bread, gave their precious things for food, to revive their soul. See, O Lord, and look, for she has become dishonored” (Lam. 1:11). Therefore whoever seeks refreshment for his soul should bend himself in humility, so that he may reach the Lord’s mercy more quickly.

### 3. (Verse 81)

Therefore David, as one bent down much more in soul and mind than in body, begins by saying: “My soul has failed for your salvation, and I have hoped in your word.” Let us not be captured by the ordinary meaning of the expression, so as to judge this to be a kind of bodily weariness. For he did not merely say, “My soul has failed,” but “My soul has failed for your salvation.” Thus, to take an example from ordinary usage, if we were to say, “He failed for her,” this expression would seem to indicate that he had passed wholly into desire for the woman. And whatever it is that we ardently seek, unless we obtain its fulfillment quickly, seems to weary us through a kind of prolonged intensity. Impatient love, knocking day and night at a prostitute’s door, if the desire for enjoyment is postponed for too long, itself fails through waiting while it hopes; yet in this there is not an end of love but an increase. And whatever is desirable, if it does not come to the one who desires it, he fails for it, and the one who desires seems almost to lay down his very soul. If, however, nearer hope rises up, immediate hope gives strength; but if the beloved is absent, by the very fact that the one who has desired longs for the absent beloved, he suffers the failure of his soul. Therefore, the farther away the desired object is, the more the one who desires fails. This, then, is to fail: for each person to migrate with all his efforts into that which he loves. He thinks of it, clings to it, resounds with it; he pours himself, by a kind of failure of the soul, into that which he has received as worthy of love. Thus a mother may await the presence of her son, as Tobias’s wife awaited her son while he was traveling abroad, failing from longing, placed in distress, and as though weakened in her powers (Tob. 10:3ff.). For what else do her words signify but a kind of failure? Yet the more the affection is wearied, the more love grows; and the longer the desired one is absent, the more fiercely the longing of the one who waits burns with love. The flesh fails, but desire is nourished and increased.

### 4

From this, then, we can gather what is meant by “My soul has failed for your salvation.” For the soul, clinging to the Spirit, fails with respect to what it is as soul and becomes one spirit, since “the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Thus the holy person who fears God knows how to desire nothing else except the salvation of God, which is Christ Jesus. He longs for him, desires him, directs all his strength toward him, cherishes him in the bosom of his mind, opens himself and pours himself out to him; and he fears only that he might lose him. Therefore, the greater the desire with which the soul has been exercised in longing to cling to its salvation, the more it fails. This failure, then, produces a diminution of weakness but an assumption of strength.

Thus elsewhere he himself says: “My soul thirsted for you” (Ps. 62:2), and adds below: “My soul clung after you; your right hand received me” (ibid., 9). For the one who thirsts always desires to cling to the fountain and seems to seek and touch nothing but water, so that he may be nourished by the very act of desiring.

[Note: All printed editions read: “Therefore, with the right hand of God receiving me, my soul yearning for him, and his imparting to me from his own strength.” The manuscripts agree with our text, except that some have the final words as in the editions: “imparting to me from his own strength.”]

“Therefore, the right hand, receiving my soul and imparting its own strength, makes it what it was not,” so that it may say: “Yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). Learn also from this example that such failure is the result of an excessive desire. “My soul,” he says, “desires and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3). First desiring, he says, and as though pouring itself wholly into desire, it is dissolved, suspended by a long cord of failure. Finally, Jeremiah teaches how the soul fails for the salvation of God: “And it came to pass,” he says, “in my heart as a burning fire, flaming in my bones; and I was dissolved on every side, and I cannot endure it.” Thus, inflamed by desire, David says: “My soul has failed for your salvation, and I have hoped in your word” (Jer. 20:9).

### 5

He rightly said, “I have hoped in the word,” for hope comes first, and therefore failure follows. He hoped in the word that was preached as destined to come, which may be understood of God the Word. Or certainly he hoped in the word because he believed the heavenly word by which the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ is announced, or by which his glory is declared.

Thus the Prophet, considering what he had read and seeing that, while he was present in the body—as though bound by certain chains of this life—he was absent from the salvation of God, longed, desired, failed, and was wholly dissolved in affection, so that he might become entirely what he desired, as he himself also says later: “I pour out my prayer before him; I declare my affliction before him, when my spirit fails within me” (Ps. 141:3–4). His spirit failed; indeed, his spirit fails away from him when he denies himself in order to cling to Christ. Hence his paths are known by the Lord, because they are not paths of the flesh but paths of Christ.

### 6

For Christ is the way of those who seek God. Let us, therefore, desire that which is eternal, that salvation of God. Let us not desire money, which the avaricious desire; let us not desire the beauty of another man’s wife; let us not be driven by the desire for ambition; let us not devote ourselves to worldly glory; let us not be occupied with the pursuits of deceitful trickery; let us not desire to circumvent our neighbor by injustice; finally, let us not be parts of foxes, plunged into the inner recesses of earthly pleasure, like exiles from eternal things and cast down from that confidence in heavenly hope.

Let our failing soul, then, lift itself up from its own powers, so that it may cling to the salvation of God, who is Christ the Lord Jesus, which by interpretation is called “the Lord’s salvation.” For he is salvation, truth, strength, and wisdom. Whoever, then, fails with respect to himself in order to cling to strength loses what belongs to him and receives what is eternal.

### 7. (Verse 82)

The text continues: “My eyes have failed for your word, saying: When will you comfort me?”

[Note: All printed editions read: “Above, *praktikon* (πρακτικόν), here *theoretikon* (θεωρητικόν).” By contrast, nearly all the manuscripts agree with our emendation.]

Above we have *praktikon* (πρακτικόν), here *theoretikon* (θεωρητικόν): there the soul fails for salvation because it desires him by whose Passion it has been saved; here the Prophet’s eyes fail for the word of the Lord. Let us consider whether, just as the soul that clings to Christ there fails into one spirit and becomes one spirit, so the eyes may also fail in order that one mind may be formed. For these are the eyes of the mind, namely, of the inner person, not the eyes that perform the service of sight.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “For there is an eye both of the mind and of the flesh.” This is a good sense if considered by itself and separately. But that it does not suit this passage is shown not only by the agreement of the other editions and manuscripts but also by the words that follow: “who has been vainly puffed up with a fleshly mind.” Understand, therefore, that the fleshly mind can also be called an eye, but that eye is blind and proud.]

For there is an eye and a mind of the flesh; but that eye is blind which does not see the things that are divine, which has been vainly puffed up with a fleshly mind. There is also another eye, the mind of Christ, by which the Church sees Christ, just as he himself says to the Bride: “You have captured us with one heart, with one of your eyes” (Song 4:9). Christ is rightly seen with one eye, because he is not seen with a bodily eye; or because the Church, possessing two eyes—the moral and the mystical—sees Christ more fully with the eye of faith. For the mystical eye is sharper, while the moral eye is sweeter.

### 8

And perhaps these are the eyes with which Paul saw eternal things, when he began not to see bodily things. Indeed, he who did not see Christ before he lost his eyes saw him after he had lost his physical sight. He saw him who said: “Who are you, Lord?” (Acts 9:5). Certainly he saw Christ, whom he also acknowledged as Lord. And below: “Lord,” he said, “what do you wish me to do?” (ibid., 6). Did he not, then, see the one whose command he awaited?

With what eyes, then, did Paul begin to see more clearly, unless with those that he himself showed us when he said: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15)? Finally, so that you may know that he saw while praying, he says: “And it happened, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, that I fell into a trance and saw him saying to me: ‘Hurry and leave Jerusalem quickly, for they will not receive your testimony about me’” (Acts 22:17–18).

These eyes, then, fail for the word of God and say: “When will you comfort me?” The prophets were called “Seers” because with these eyes, through revelation, they perceived in their minds the things that were hidden.

### 9

What does it mean for the eyes to fail? Let us speak of bodily things, so that we may understand spiritual ones. When we desire someone and hope that he is about to arrive, do we not direct our eyes toward the place from which we hope he will come? Thus, after being occupied for a long time with daily expectation, we fail. So Anna, looking along the road, watched anxiously for the arrival of her son (Tob. 10:7).

So the prophet David, with watchmen stationed in the tower, eagerly longed, as an attentive father, to ask about the safety of his son from one running from the battle (2 Sam. 18:24).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “with watchmen placed in the tower, one running from the battle after another to announce it, etc.” Anyone who compares the following comparison with the ending of Ovid’s epistle of Phyllis will readily acknowledge that our Ambrose had it in mind.]

So a young wife, from a coastal lookout, awaits her husband’s arrival with tireless expectation. Whenever she sees a ship, she thinks that her husband is sailing in it; she fears that someone else may anticipate her in seeing her beloved, so that she herself may not be the first to say, “I see you, my husband,” just as Anna said to her son: “I see you, my son; now I shall die more gladly” (Tob. 11:8), no longer feeling the pain of death because of the sweetness of the longed-for sight.

Therefore, just as the woman who longs to present herself to her arriving husband, having dismissed all household occupations, traces the traveler’s paths or the marks of his feet, so the Prophet, stripped of worldly cares, kept vigilant watch with the eyes of his inner self upon the word of God until his own exhaustion. He brought his body into subjection and trained his soul in patient humility, wasting away like a spider. For he desired like a deer for springs of water and thirsted for the Lord his God, longing to see his presence and appear before the face of God. Failing through excessive desire and vehement longing, he then confidently anticipated, by prophetic grace, that he would be more capable of obtaining the things he had asked of the Lord.

Let us, too, direct our heart, so that we may understand the sequences of Scripture, and ask that the word come to us from the Lord and that understanding be given. If someone looks from afar upon the Word of God with the gaze of the mind, not yet clearly and distinctly, he sees, as it were, with certain inner eyes the ship of the Word approaching his soul. But the more distinctly he begins to see, the more eagerly he hastens to approach the harbor of truth, so that he may be near when it is brought in.

### 10

The Prophet’s eyes, therefore, failed for the word of God, saying: “When will you comfort me?” If these eyes signify those with which we discern and see, they ought to have said, “When will you comfort us?”—that is, not in the singular but in the plural. But because the eye of the mind and the eye of the flesh become one eye, and a person is supported by consolation when flesh and mind do not desire different things but desire and seek one thing, therefore these eyes, intent upon him who says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), also confess themselves to be one, because they perform one and the same function with one and the same desire.

### 11

The Prophet, then, was failing for the word. But we consider ourselves idle if we seem to devote ourselves only to the word, and we value more highly those who act than those who practice the pursuit of knowing divinity.

[Note: The editions read, “the pursuit of knowing the truth”; the manuscripts read, “the pursuit of knowing divinity.”]

For many say: “Behold the man and his works.” As though the one who devotes himself to the word were not acting, when this is a greater work than the others. For if justice is a work, if temperance is a work, if courage is a work, then wisdom is certainly also a work; these four are held to be the principal virtues. For if Christ works insofar as he is justice, he certainly works insofar as he is the Word. And he was working when he was in the beginning with the Father. Indeed, through him all things were made (John 1:3), so that you may know that he is the maker of all things and that Christ Jesus is our work.

For insofar as he is the Word, the word is a great work for those who seek the word. Thus, when Martha was hurrying about her service while Mary was listening to the word of the Lord, she who was listening deserved to be preferred to her who was serving. For when Martha said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me alone to serve? Tell her, then, to help me,” the Lord answered: “Martha, Martha . . . Mary has chosen the good portion, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:40–42). Thus, by the authority of the divine judgment, it is established that knowing the word is a greater work than serving.

### 12

But perhaps someone may say that the Apostle declared: “The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power” (1 Cor. 4:20). I do not deny that it is written, but understand what kind of speech he means: the speech poured forth by one who is puffed up, speech unable to benefit those who hear it, devoid of the manifestation of spirit and power. Paul does not acknowledge such speech; rather, he wishes to recognize the power of speech.
