[Note: Several manuscripts read “to acknowledge.” Thus he wanted such speech. Other manuscripts and the editions read “to acknowledge” (the Roman edition alone has “to commend”). Thus he did not want such speech. Shortly afterward all the editions read, “to save others and make them stronger,” but all the manuscripts more suitably read, “to make others stronger.”]

Finally, the Apostle did not want his speech to be of this kind: it came in weakness in order to make others stronger—“in fear and trembling,” so that those who feared might fear nothing except the Lord Jesus, and those who trembled might preserve his peace and tranquility. Hear, then, what kind of speech the Apostle had: “My speech and my preaching,” he says, “were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Cor. 2:4), because faith is established not by forensic speech of wisdom but by the power of God.

[Note: After “of wisdom,” the editions read: “but in the demonstration of the Spirit,” a reading found in none of the manuscripts.]

Therefore, in the speech of the saints there is power; but in this forensic and philosophical speech there is the vanity of the world. That there is power in the speech of the saints, this same Prophet teaches you when he says: “The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power” (Ps. 67:12), that is, so that they may preach the Gospel with great power. It has therefore been proved that there is power in the preaching of the Gospel. The preaching of the Gospel is the speech of the saints; thus no doubt remains that there is power in holy speech.

### 13. (Verse 83)

The third verse follows: “For I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your justifications.”

This is the voice of the righteous person who has mortified his body. The righteous person is rightly called a wineskin, because, having been stripped, he is found not naked: a wineskin is made from the hide of a dead animal. Therefore let us also die to sin, so that we may live for God. Filled with spiritual joy and the sweetness of gladness, we shall be spiritual hides, free from bodily weakness, preserving in the intact bosom of the mind the grace of divine mysteries poured into us.

It is concerning these wineskins that it is said that they put new wine into new wineskins (Matt. 9:17), when they wish to preserve both body and grace. Therefore let your wineskin not leak, let it not be full of cracks, let it not grow old with earthly grime, lest the new wine burst the old wineskins, so that the wineskins are torn and grace poured out.

Let it not again be dried by the sun of iniquity and the excessive force of heat; rather, let the various desires of the burning entrails be tempered by a kind of snowy cold. Let the heat of lust grow cold, and, quenched by a frost of continence and fasts, let it be breathed upon by morning prayer.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Let it be breathed upon by the morning dew.”]

Then, like dew, the words of God descend upon our earth, like rain upon the grass and like snow upon the hay. This snow does not harm a good wineskin—the snow that shines with the splendor of divine eloquence. This snow cools; it does not scorch. It makes the crops fruitful; it does not destroy them. This snow is the precept of continence, which causes bodily heat to grow cold and extinguishes all the inner ardor of nature.

And perhaps for this reason, when he displayed the glory of his resurrection, his garments were white as snow: so that not only might he himself be judged free from the contagion of sin, but also that whoever is raised might appear to rise cold, with the desires of marriage frozen. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be like the angels of God in heaven. Good, therefore, are the cold wineskins—that is, those contracted by frost, not loosened by the heat of lust.

### 14

That this body is called a wineskin, you may understand from several passages, but also from this: when Adam and Eve laid aside the image of heaven that they had previously borne, and put on the image of the earthly man, they are said to have been clothed in tunics of skin; for the sin they had committed had made them bodily instead of spiritual (Gen. 3:21).

Nor is it absurd to understand David as saying that he had become like a wineskin in frost because, although placed in icy harshness, he had nevertheless mortified his body, so that he would not feel the harshness of that winter which the Savior says will be severe for those who flee (Matt. 24:20). Just as a wineskin does not feel the ice because it is the hide of a dead animal, so the Prophet, dead to sin, could not feel the cold of sin.

Or certainly it means that he is not broken by necessities and that the flesh does not resist the mind, but, more pliable in its movement, bends itself to the commands of the soul and does not dry out in this frost of the world. Or it means that we are a body of affliction and must always carry the death of the Lord Jesus in our body.

This is the wineskin that chastises its body, unlike that fattened and corpulent people who sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play (Exod. 32:6). This is the wineskin that intoxicates not with wine but with the Spirit. In it there is neither a cluster of bitterness, nor the fury of dragons, nor the rage of asps, but how splendid is the intoxicating cup!

In this, then, David glories: that he has become like a wineskin in frost, feeling none of the activity of sin.

### 15

Sin is rightly compared with frost. For just as frost is useful for no purpose and for no activity, so guilt benefits no purpose and no activity. Therefore it must be avoided like frost, lest it harm and scorch.

It is good for me, then, to become like a wineskin in frost, so that I may not forget the Lord’s justifications and, drenched by their liquid, may cool every heat of inward desire. This wineskin must therefore be not empty but full—full of the Spirit, full of justifications—so that I may confess my sins myself and restrain the luxury of my flesh. We must die to the world in order to live for God.

But if we live according to the flesh, the wisdom of the flesh is certainly death; we cannot live for God, because this carnal wisdom and worldly life are hostile to God.

### 16. (Verse 84)

The fourth verse follows: “How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment for me upon those who persecute me?”

This may be understood as follows: “How many are the days of your servant?”—as though he were saying: How few are human days, how little the time, how brief the span? Why is such a short life begrudged, so that we may not enjoy the tranquil course of this age? Why, within such a brief span, are so many snares of those who persecute us stretched out?

Let judgment now be present—the judgment in which there is punishment for the faithless and in which fitting recompense for their impiety is returned to persecutors.

Or it may be understood in this way: How long will those who seek to afflict us in various ways be able to insult and trouble us? The end will not be late. For, as though measuring the speed with which this life must pass—not by years but by days—the Prophet reckons it when he says: “How many are the days of your servant?”

He rightly said “days,” so that by prophetic vision he might pass not only over the delays of years but also illuminate for himself the splendid course of this life with the light of virtues. And rightly, in confidence, he says: “When will you execute judgment for me upon those who persecute me?” “For me,” he says, “you will execute judgment concerning those who persecute me; you will not give judgment against me to those who persecute me,” because the impious do not rise in judgment.

“But for me,” he says, “give judgment, so that, when you reward innocence, advance faith, and crown mercy, the impious persecutors may be judged by the rewards of prophetic merits.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “by the punishments of their merits.” But, together with the other editions and all the manuscripts, one must read “by the rewards of their merits”; for these are the recompense of innocence, the advancement of faith, and the crowning of mercy.]

### 17

It is not unreasonable also to understand the passage in this way: because the days of this life are short and few, the Lord should not delay his grace toward his Prophet for long, but should himself execute judgment upon those who persecute him.

Here too there is judgment upon persecutors, since whoever does not believe in Christ has already been judged. This judgment is what the Lord Jesus gave to his servants when he said: “You will have power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon every power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). It is a true judgment, in which the enemy is tormented, as he himself confessed when he said: “Why have you come to torment us before the time?” (Matt. 8:29).

### 18

Thus the Prophet, founded upon the stability of the virtues, asks that not a human being but the one who claimed a place for himself in the human being be subjected to him. Hence the Apostle thought that this one, rather, should be condemned in human sin and subjected, concerning whom he says: “God will crush Satan under your feet shortly” (Rom. 16:20).

Therefore he eagerly desires judgment to be made for him concerning this persecutor, so that the adversary may be crushed beneath the footsteps of prophetic faith and the Prophet may crush him beneath his feet like dust.

[Note: In the Roman edition alone, after “dust,” the words “before the face of the wind” are added.]

Established in this warfare of his body, although the days of his life are short, he nevertheless obtains a triumph over the adversary, so that the adversary may groan at the liberty and perceive the power of the human being restored to its former grace—whom he had previously held bound by the chains of sins and wearied with the heat of burning lust.

The adversary, therefore, has been subjected according to the Lord’s sentence. For the Lord Jesus, coming into this world through birth from a Virgin, subjected all opposing powers to our soul, so that they might be crushed by your faith, your word, your way of life, and your works. If, then, you do not crush the adversary, the fault is yours, because you do not use the power that has been granted.

It is therefore in our power either for the adversary to be subjected or for him to resist. If our conduct is displeasing, the adversary begins to grow proud; but if we cling to good works, practice the disciplines of chastity, justice, and continence, we tread upon the serpent and the scorpion. We tread upon him with the feet of chastity; we crush the scorpion with the steps of continence, modesty, and justice, so that he cannot shake us off.

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts and the old editions, except that the Regius manuscript reads *exsurgere* (“to rise up”) instead of *excutere* (“to shake off”). The Roman edition reverses the words as follows: “We crush the scorpion with the footsteps of continence and the steps of modesty and justice, lest he be able to shake us off.”]

We can therefore have an enduring triumph over our adversaries even in this brief life.

### 19. (Verse 85)

The fifth verse follows: “The unjust have told me tales, but not like your law, O Lord.”

He rightly desires judgment to be made for him concerning those who persecute him, since they have tried not only to hinder the works of the righteous but also to subvert faith through superfluous narration. For he says that they have told him, as though they were the senseless tales of some story, *adoleschiai* (ἀδολεχίαι), that is, superfluous loquacities.

For superfluous speakers, like swallows, corrupt the sweetness of discussion by the continuity of their inborn talkativeness, as Aristotle says.

### 20

The heretic, therefore, speaks superfluously, because he does not speak the truth and does not speak according to the law. But the one who is founded upon the law knows how to distinguish false things from true and, through the spiritual training of doctrine, to separate heretical teachings from evangelical doctrines.

Therefore, lest many be deceived, the sinner is commanded by the Lord to be silent: “To the sinner God said: Why do you recite my justices?” (Ps. 49:17). Let faithlessness, then, be silent, for it does not know how to keep to the path of truth and does not observe God’s commandments.

Why do sinners take the Gospel of truth upon their lips when truth is not in their mouths? All God’s commandments are truth, and Christ is truth. Christ, therefore, is not in the disputations of the faithless—the Christ who says to the faithless: “Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit” (ibid., 20). For the tongue that wishes to establish a lie certainly weaves deceit into its assertions.

But such a person is a thief, running together with a thief. For there are many thieves who steal and seize the word of God not for their own benefit but for fraud. They twist the patrimony of the heavenly Scriptures into their own thefts, gathering adulterous profits for themselves, acquired by deceit rather than truth.

These are the people who mix water with wine, like the worst tavern keepers, adulterating the word of God and bringing forth as insincere whatever they have uttered with a faithless and drunken mouth. Therefore they speak things foreign to the law. Hence the Prophet rightly flees from them and rebukes them, knowing what he has received from the prescription of the law.

### 21. (Verse 86)

Rightly, therefore, he says in the following verse: “All your commandments are truth; they have persecuted me unjustly; help me.”

Like a good soldier, he does not flee from wars, nor does a warrior accustomed to battle fear conflicts, however grave the struggles may be. But, faithful and prudent, he prays that divine aid may be breathed upon him and asks for the faithful assistance of holy devotion.

Therefore he does not ask that persecutions cease; rather, he asks to be helped amid persecutions. For he knew that “all who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecutions.” He prefers, then, to suffer persecutions so that he may be able to live devoutly in Christ.

He rightly spoke not of one persecution but of many persecutions, and he did not specify the names of the persecutors, because there are many persecutors—not only those whom we see but also those whom we do not see. Spiritual wickednesses persecute; the heretic persecutes; the Jew persecutes; the gentile persecutes. All who wish to live devoutly are therefore under persecutors, because where there are many persecutors, no time is free from persecutors for one who desires to live devoutly.

And perhaps, when we do not suffer persecutions, we are regarded as condemned, because we do not truly wish to live devoutly in Christ. For since the sentence has been established that “all who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecutions” (2 Tim. 3:12), the one who does not suffer persecutions seems rejected, as though he were not of devout purpose in Christ; for the battles of faith pursue devotion.

If struggles are absent, I fear that the one who desires to struggle may also appear to be absent. “All your commandments,” he says, “are truth” (John 15:20). What commandments, unless those that say: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you”?

David was already hearing these commandments in the Spirit, although he preceded the mystery of the Incarnation. Like a disciple of Christ, he did not withdraw from sufferings but offered himself to struggles. He knew that this was fruitful for his glory and safe for the preservation of salvation: that through frequent exercises the devotion of the righteous might be strengthened.

For faith that is not exercised quickly grows weak, and when idle it is tested by repeated troubles. When the watch is relaxed, the crafty ambusher breaks in; but external fraud trains the man accustomed to war and advances him to the palm of glorious victory. Peace, therefore, is an occasion for the corruption of faith.

### 22

How beautifully the seasons of persecution have proceeded for us! His inner affection toward God was intent, like that of a beggar; it clung to him, and the mind at prayer felt no intrusive thoughts interrupting it. Prayer was poured out with all the inward parts, and a kind of conversation with the Lord was mingled with it. Daily meditation had already acquired contempt for danger and had learned to tread upon death.

The leisure that peace has brought attempts to take away the discipline that battles had not broken. The leisure of peace, therefore, is dangerous. In peace, more persecutions began to arise.

During the time of persecution there was no flatterer to test the mind with cunning flattery. The mind had no leisure to be dissolved by bodily pleasure or to admit passions of the kind that prosperity usually arouses.

Therefore, when the Apostles were beaten and imprisoned, they rejoiced because through those injuries they were gaining the reward of eternal glory, having been found worthy to suffer injuries for Christ’s name (Acts 5:41).

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “the merit of eternal grace,” and so forth.]

They had no concern for property, no desire for powers and honors, no concern for precedence—which is accustomed to trouble even the righteous. Rather, that man considered himself preferred who had been beaten with the greatest number of lashes.

[Note: To the word “beaten,” the Audian manuscript and one Navarre manuscript add: “Therefore fear, you who always wish to be first.” Anyone can easily judge this to be a gloss.]

23. David therefore rightly seeks opportunities for triumph and does not fear the chance to contend, in the discipline of devotion, since he knew that the persecutions of the wicked contribute to the increase of virtue. 1112 For he did not say, “Because I suffer persecutions, help me,” but: “They have persecuted me unjustly; help me.” A person may indeed suffer persecutions, but not unjustly; for there is also a just persecution, if we hate the immoral, if we oppose the unjust, if we wish to suppress the wicked so that they may harm fewer people, if we strip the greedy of the profits of their fraud, if we abhor the insolence of the proud. But whoever suffers persecution for faith, for justice, or for chastity rightly says: “They have persecuted me unjustly; help me.”

24. (Verse 87.) The seventh verse follows: “They all but finished me off upon the earth; but I did not forsake your commandments.” He did not seek divine help without reason, knowing that he was engaged in combat against the strong and that many battles lay ready for him as he fought, now against the spiritual wickednesses that are in the heavenly places, now against the heat of the blood and the countless enticements of this body. Worn out by their varied entanglement and prolonged struggle, he would have fallen into a shameful defeat, unless he had held fast by the root of faith. Let us learn to guard the enemy whom we carry within us: here is our domestic foe, here is the grave enemy arising from the very use of our body. It is inflamed by wine, burns with lust, is kindled by the beauty of a woman who appears before it, nourished by hope, consumed by despair, scorched by enticements; it does not evaporate in its effect, is troubled by fear, broken by dread, softened by luxury, dissolved by wantonness, afflicted by labor, wearied by anxiety, and crushed by passion. Do you wonder that amid so many hostile alternations of passions even the just person can scarcely hold his ground, when we are unequal to the combat even with one passion at a time? Whom does lust alone not avenge itself upon? Whom does greed not subjugate? Whom does fear not shake? Whom does luxury not weaken? Whom does wantonness not soften? Whom does drunkenness not trip up?

25. As one conscious, therefore, of carnal weakness and as an observer of hostile persecution, he says: “They all but finished me off upon the earth.” On this earth, certainly, on which the first Adam fell and, cast down by his shameful collapse, bent the step of all future posterity (Gen. III, 17). On this earth Cain, grieving that his brother’s offerings had been preferred to his own, was laid low as the ruin of envy. Indeed, the voice of his brother’s blood cried out from the earth (Gen. IV, 10). On this earth the holy Noah—whom the floods of the whole world, amid such storms and waves, proved vigilant—nevertheless, when he relaxed his cares in an idle body, fell into the offense of drunken sleep and incurred an insult to his fatherly devotion (Gen. IX, 21–22), teaching that carefree idleness is dangerous even to secure virtue. On this earth Lot, an imitator of his revered parent, whom neither the impurity of the luxurious people of Sodom discolored nor the flame of burning Sodom engulfed, nevertheless did not escape the incest of a shameful union, though it arose from pardonable ignorance (Gen. XIX, 32 ff.). This man is burned by the flames of women, whom the sulfurous flame did not burn.

[Note: All editions read *offendit* (“he incurred an offense”)—“when the middle son was delirious”—and so forth. But the words enclosed in brackets are found in absolutely no manuscript.]

26. On this earth David too said that he had almost been finished off. For he almost felt his feet moved and his steps nearly poured out, because he judged the abundance of worldly riches and the success of bodily prosperity to be the place of blessedness in which sinners abound. For this reason he was also scourged; but scourges are remedies of salvation for the just. 1113 For “the Lord chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6). Therefore David, turning toward the love of the Lord and instructed in his commandments, did not ignore that transient things are bestowed upon the transient by a certain chance occurrence, nor that the merits of a worthy life are weighed not by an abundance of riches but by the grace of virtues. He loved God’s commandments rather than forsaking them; by them alone he could overcome the spiritual wickednesses that assailed him and the desires of this body that rose up against him amid the weakness of such fragile nature. Great, therefore, is the virtue which, established under such persecutions and almost overwhelmed, nevertheless did not forget its defense and did not forsake the Lord’s commandments.

27. (Verse 88.) Since he recognized that God alone had benefited him, he directs his prayers to the Lord and says in the following verse: “According to your mercy, give me life, and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth” (above, verse 17). We have already explained what kind of giving of life he seeks, for he did not pray for what he possessed but for what he desired—that is, that he might live forever—understanding that the blessedness of life cannot exist in this wavering and faithless body of ours, whose weakness abandons the soul’s purpose. God’s mercy is therefore needed so that the giving of life may be continuous and perpetual in this body, so that the just person may live for God each day and die to sin. For if guilt dies within us, there will be a life living for God, together with perseverance in keeping the heavenly commandments; and the person who is given life by the Lord certainly keeps them.

28. Finally, he first asks the Lord to give him life, and afterward promises to keep the heavenly testimonies. For it is not ordinary life that keeps the heavenly commandment, but that life which is supported by an eternal gift through the working of spiritual grace. We may also understand it in this way: since the Prophet had already recognized the things belonging to the Law, he desires the mercy of the Lord’s coming, so that he may receive the commandments by which the Law is fulfilled—not merely to know that adultery must be avoided, but also to shun the desire for adultery. For Jesus the Lord, the Mouth of the Father, spoke in the Gospel that whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has committed adultery in his heart (Matt. V, 28). How much progress the Gospel has brought to the practice of chastity, since it removes the reproach not only of a more shameful deed but also of a debased intention!

29. But who are those of whom he says that they almost finished him off upon the earth, if not persecutors? Of one of them the Lord Jesus says: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke XIII, 32)—that is, Herod. And elsewhere, noticing that he was being questioned deceitfully, he said: “Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests in which to rest” (Matt. VIII, 20), because they linger deceitfully in certain hiding places of earthly passions. Hence Samson also tied two foxes together, fastened torches to their tails, and released them among the fields of the Philistines (Judg. XV, 4–5). By this figure he signified that wicked and deceitful people, and especially heretics, have a free tongue for barking but impeded outcomes: they have contentious beginnings, but the end of their deceit is assigned to fire.

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts read. The editions, however, have “or religious principles.” This is less suitable. Although heretics commonly put forward the appearance of religion as a pretext for their separation, their religious principles should not be stated without qualification, especially in a sermon addressed to the people.]

Therefore he also released three hundred foxes, because the faithless desire to commend themselves by preaching the cross but cannot hold its mystery. By means of this contrived, false, and feigned preaching they strive rather to burn up the fruits of others, whereas the true cross of the Lord does not burn up the merits of others but makes them fruitful. Accordingly it is written in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, so that our vineyards may flower” (Song II, 15).

[Note: Several manuscripts have “because they are already mature in strength.”]

This shows that either the Lord Jesus or the Church commands that the deceptions of the deceitful be driven out of his vineyards, lest they harm the little vineyards, since they cannot harm already mature vines. For a heretic can test the imperfect but cannot trip up the perfect.

## THE TWELFTH SERMON. Lamed

1. The twelfth letter, Lamed, now begins. Its interpretation is “heart,” or, according to another interpretation, “I serve” (*servo*). Hence it seems to admonish us either that these things are to be understood prudently or that the commandments are to be guarded diligently. For the very first verse immediately gives this admonition. In the preceding passage this Prophet asked that a clean heart be created for him, as we read: “Create in me a clean heart” (Ps. L, 12). The son of Solomon prayed to the Lord that a prudent heart be given him. Whoever, therefore, has a clean heart, whoever has a prudent heart, understands the sequence of the following verses and their power (III Kings IX, 9). Thus elsewhere also we find “a solitary heart”—that is, either a unique heart or one that no enticement of this world hinders and no wisdom of the flesh can disturb.

[Note: The Roman edition alone has “one heart, or another heart, which no…” and so forth. This was evidently intended to bring Ambrose’s words closer to Ezekiel XXI, 19: “And I will give them another heart” (Καὶ δώσω αὐτοῖς καρδίαν ἑτέραν). But it is not entirely clear whether the holy man had this passage in mind.]

Whoever has a heart keeps God’s commandments, just as you have read about Mary, who kept all the words and deeds of the Lord and Savior in her heart (Luke II, 51).

2. Let us therefore circumcise our heart. Let us seek nothing bodily, nothing base; and everything earthly is base. Let us therefore establish nothing earthly, nothing worldly, nothing bodily, nothing trivial or changeable in the heavenly utterances. For “the utterances of the Lord are pure utterances” (Ps. XI, 7), so that through spiritual interpretation the immaculate and chaste sincerity of the heavenly mysteries may shine forth in them. Let us not mingle earthly things with divine through some adulterous opinion, nor violate the inviolable sacrament of prophetic vision or of the eternal oracle by an estimate formed according to our nature. For this reason he added: “Silver tested by fire, purified of earth, proved sevenfold” (ibid.), so that, like good money-changers, we may test the silver of prophetic speech in the Spirit, separating the Lord’s money and cleansing it from every earthly stain by the infusion of the saving fountain. Thus we may seem to think thoughts worthy of Christ, who says: “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy . . . but lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matt. VI, 19–20).

3. Your treasure is faith, devotion, and mercy; your treasure is Christ. Do not regard him as coming from the earth—that is, from created things—for the Lord is Lord of all creation. “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jer. XVII, 5); yet salvation came to me through a man. Consider, however, what the ancient Scripture says: “And he is a man, and who will know him?” (ibid., 9). That man therefore forgave all sins for me not by human but by divine power: God in the body, the Lord Jesus, reconciling the world to himself, which he was redeeming from guilt.

4. Our precious treasure is understanding. If the understanding is earthly, if it is fragile, the moth of heresy and the rust of impiety will consume it. Let us therefore raise and lift up our thoughts, and let us not judge it impossible for this weakness of the human body to be advanced to knowledge of the heavenly mysteries, since the Lord Jesus, in whom the treasures of knowledge and wisdom were hidden, has already descended to us through his divine compassion, to unlock what was closed, open what was concealed, and reveal what was hidden. Come, therefore, Lord Jesus, open to us the door of this prophetic utterance also; for it is closed to many, even though it may appear open at first sight.

5. (Verse 89.) “Forever, O Lord,” he says, “your word remains in heaven.” You see that what remains and perseveres in heaven must also remain in you. Therefore keep the word of God, and keep it in your heart; keep it in such a way that you do not forget it. Keep the law of the Lord and meditate upon it, lest the Lord’s ordinances slip from your heart. The interpretation of the letter teaches you to keep it diligently. The Prophet teaches you in the following verses, saying: “Unless your law had been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation. I will never forget your ordinances” (below, verses 92–93). Meditation on the Law therefore enables us to withstand and endure times of tribulation, times in which we are humbled by various adversities, so that we are not broken either by an affect too deeply humbled or by one cast down. Finally, the Lord does not wish us to be broken by humiliation to the point of despair, but to the point of correction.

6. Hence the prophet Jeremiah says under this letter in the Lamentations: “To humble beneath his feet all the prisoners of the earth, to turn aside the judgment of a man before the face of the Most High, to condemn a man when he is judged—the Lord did not say this” (Lam. III, 34 ff.). And below: “From the mouth of the Most High evils will not go forth” (ibid., 38).

[Note: The Lord did not say this, as all the editions have; it is omitted in some manuscripts. In the greater number, however, it reads: “when the Lord is judged.” For he says below as well, and so forth. Nevertheless, the integrity of the meaning and of the prophetic testimony agrees with the other witnesses and with the editions.]

The humility that comes from the Lord is full of justice and full of equity, because evils do not go forth from the mouth of the Lord. Thus the one who was humbled by the Lord said: “I was humbled, and he saved me” (Ps. CXIV, 6).

7. Therefore, just as we must prudently consider when humility comes from the Lord as a cause of testing, and when it is the imposition of humility by a human being—though even that is usually endured with patience and magnanimity—so too we must wisely consider what it means that the Lord’s word remains forever in heaven. Some manuscripts read “unto the age,” because the Greek has εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα (“unto the age”), which translators have rendered in different ways: some as “forever,” others as “unto the age.”

“Unto the age, therefore, your word remains in heaven, O Lord.” And how did you yourself say: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV, 35)? The word remains unto the age, not beyond the age and the ages; for the ages belong to time. Heaven and earth—that is, the works of this world—will therefore pass away, and the times will remain.

Another person, who is spiritual and discerns the words of the Law, says: “Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven.” For the eternity of the abiding word excludes the notion of a passing word. But how does the word remain in heaven if heaven itself passes away? And how can the summits stand if the foundations give way? Or how can the inhabitant remain in his dwelling unless the dwelling also endures?

Perhaps someone will object that it is written: “There will be a new heaven” (Isa. LXV, 17). But even this does not resolve the matter; for what passes away cannot remain in this form, nor can that be said to have remained which will have begun to exist. The moth will tear apart your understanding if you suppose that the word, like heaven, either begins or passes away.

8. Therefore, if we wish to recognize the force of the prophetic meaning, let us first consider in these visible and perceptible things the ethical sense, so that from it we may disclose the intelligible things.

[Note: The old edition reads, “And here let us consider that passage.” The Roman edition has, “let us consider that passage.” Some manuscripts read, “and here let us consider with the passage.” Others, more numerous, read as in the text. The genuineness of this reading is confirmed by the fact that the discourse immediately turns to the moral sense, from which it then proceeds to the intelligible, or mystical, sense. This variation seems to have arisen from nothing other than the ignorance of copyists, who improperly divided the single word *ethicum* into two or three.]

If the word of God remains in heaven, let us imitate the heaven in which the word remains. There the solemn order of heavenly ordinances remains, and the frequent changes of the Lord’s benefits persevere in their appointed gifts. For the earth is watered and nourished by generous abundance from above, whether through rains, heat, or the fostering influence of the air. In heaven the year passes through days and months, through the seasons of autumn and winter, and through spring and the clear arrangement of summer.

Take from heaven an image of your life. Even when you do not produce fruit, nevertheless sow seed for fruit. There are seeds that come from heaven and are sown upon the earth. There is also a heavenly vintage; hence the Prophet says: “Sow for yourselves for righteousness; reap for fruit” (Hos. X, 12). And when your works do not flower, nevertheless foster your seeds, lest through wanton growth they become luxuriant. What grows luxuriantly in the flower of speech becomes thin and dull in its fruit. Cook the fruits themselves until they reach maturity.

9. Let us also be imitators of the heavenly element itself. It is not always heated by a blazing sun; frequently it is covered with clouds, bristles with heavy rains, and covers the earth with falling snow. Therefore let there not be perpetual wantonness in you either. Let periods of sorrowful, mature concerns succeed, and let the hoary maturity of old age, as it were, restrain this field of your body. Often sadness is more useful, since it usually has seriousness as its companion.

Is there any transgression in the sun itself? Does it not maintain its daily courses? Does the moon not know continuous wanings and abandon the duty of the ministry entrusted to it?

[Note: All editions read, “it does not know continuous…” But the negation is better placed first in the manuscripts.]

The year returns through the same cycles; the seasons are restored in the same condition; they are renewed by the same services. The sun illuminates the day, preserving the appointed times. The moon shines with nocturnal splendor, and its light sparkles in the darkness. The globe of shining stars glows, and they fulfill their appointed station, revolution, and change. There is one law for all: to preserve the cycles of their courses once established, and not to cross their prescribed limits. The change itself remains unaltered, and revolution does not know how to overturn its order. There is one obedience among all: with distinct functions, to maintain the harmonious unity of the constitution prescribed for them.

1117 10. The Word remains in heaven because Satan fell from heaven: he had no place in heaven, and therefore he fell. Where did he fall, if not to the earth? Hence adulteries, murders, and drunkenness began to abound here. Excluded from there, he came to us more fiercely and, as though enraged, exercises temptations harsher than usual. The Word therefore remains in heaven because the devil was cast out from there; it does not remain on earth because he came here in his entirety. Consider whether the Word can remain in us here, where the devil has scattered so many snares—he who, while he was in heaven, could not allow the Word to remain even there. Finally, because he himself did not hold fast to the Word, he fell from heaven.

11. The Word therefore remains in heaven, and that heaven is governed and ruled according to the ordering of the Word. But because heaven itself also passes away, he did not say that it remains “unto the ages,” but “unto the age,” although it passes away so that there may be a new heaven and a new earth, a new testament, and so that we may be able to see the glory of the Lord face to face.

12. Nevertheless, because there was also a place for vices in heaven—for the adversary certainly would not have fallen from there unless he had been detected in crimes, and even “the foolish one is changed like the moon,” while heaven itself is covered with darkness—it seems that the passage was not spoken of the element but of the heavenly Virtues and Powers.

There are holy Virtues in heaven, in which there is nothing slippery or earthly. There are also heavens upon earth that declare the glory of God. What heavens are these? Hear him say: “As we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one” (I Cor. XV, 49). These, then, are the heavens which, although placed upon earth, dare to say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

These are the heavens in which there are faith, seriousness, self-restraint, teaching, and a heavenly life. For just as the one who fell from that disobedience to heavenly grace and was cast down into these earthly vices, binding himself with the chains of his disobedience, was called “earth,” so, conversely, the one who practices the life of angels by guarding his integrity is called “heaven.” He restrains his body with disciplined sobriety, composes his mind in gentle tranquility, and distributes his money to the poor with merciful generosity.

There is therefore also a heaven upon earth in which heavenly virtues can exist. “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI, 1): I understand this more as the disposition of the just person than as the element. I consider that person heaven to whose soul Christ comes and at whose door he knocks; and if that person opens, Christ enters. He does not enter alone, but also with the Father, as he himself says: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

13. You see, therefore, that the Word, God, both calls the idle and awakens the sleeping. For he who comes and knocks at the door always wishes to enter. But it lies with us that he does not always enter and does not always remain.

Let your door be open to the one who comes; open your soul, expand the bosom of your mind, so that he may see the riches of simplicity, the treasures of peace, and the sweetness of grace. Enlarge your heart; go out to meet the sun of eternal light, which enlightens every human being. That true light shines upon all, but if someone closes his windows, he deprives himself of the eternal light. Christ too is shut out if you close the door of your mind; and although he is able to enter, he does not wish to burst in uninvited or compel the unwilling.

Born of a virgin, he came forth from the womb, illuminating the whole world so that he might shine upon all. 1118 Those who desire the brightness of perpetual radiance receive it—a brightness interrupted by no night. Only the sun that we see each day is followed by dark night; but the sun of righteousness never sets, because evil does not follow wisdom.

14. Blessed, therefore, is the one at whose door Christ knocks. Our door is faith, which, if it is strong, fortifies the entire house. Through this door Christ enters. Hence the Church says in the Song of Songs: “The voice of my brother is knocking at the door” (Song V, 2). Hear him knocking; hear him wishing to enter: “Open to me, my sister, my bride, my dove, my perfect one, because my head is filled with dew and my locks with drops of the night” (ibid.).

Consider when God the Word knocks most insistently at your door: when his head is filled with the dew of night. For he deigns to visit those placed in tribulation and temptations, lest someone perhaps succumb, overcome by hardships. His head is filled with dew, or with drops, when his body suffers.

Then, therefore, we must keep watch, lest when the Bridegroom comes he withdraw, shut out. If you sleep and your heart does not keep watch, he departs before he knocks. If your heart keeps watch, he knocks and asks that the door be opened to him.

We therefore have a door of our soul, and we also have gates of which it is said: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXIII, 7). There is therefore also a heaven in those who have eternal gates. If you wish to lift up these gates of your faith, the King of glory will enter you, bearing the triumph of his own passion.

Justice too has gates. For we also read that the Lord Jesus says through his Prophet: “Open to me the gates of justice” (Ps. CXVII, 19). And below the prophet David says: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, because he has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. CXLVII, 12–13).

15. There is therefore a soul that has a door, and one that has gates. Christ comes to this door and knocks; he knocks also at the gates. Open to him, then. He wishes to enter; he wishes to find the Bride awake. Do not delay a good lover; he quickly departs. By the sleep of your body you seem to have shut out the one who was knocking.

You shut him out when you are sluggish, lazy, or sleepy; by these barriers Christ is excluded. Even if you are chaste and sober, beware lest you be negligent. The person who repels Christ when he comes does him the greater injury.

16. Sometimes, if you delay, he sends his hand through the window, as the Bride says: “My brother sent his hand through the opening, and my belly was troubled because of him. I arose to open to my brother. My hands dripped with myrrh; my fingers were full of myrrh” (Song V, 4–5).

First, then, he sends his hand, as it were, through the opening, when God is judged to exist by his works. Hence he says: “If you do not believe me, believe at least the works” (John X, 38). Then love increases, and what has been conceived takes root in the innermost bowels.

From there our soul desires to draw from the intelligible womb—the receptacle of the Word, infused with his seeds—the fullness of him who dwells bodily. For a woman’s womb is not troubled except when she is heavy with child.

17. The soul therefore rises to open to the Word of God. But while it expands and opens itself so that through receiving the Word it may put to death the works of this world, as the one who says, “We always carry in our body the death of the Lord Jesus” (II Cor. IV, 10), the Bridegroom passes by. 1119 For he always wishes to be sought and found more frequently; and if he finds the door closed, he knocks, but if he is shut out by delay, he departs. Yet he quickly returns and knocks again, so that afterward he may find the bride prepared.

This may also be understood as follows: “My brother has passed by” (Song V, 6), as we read that he penetrated the beloved’s innermost marrow, and as it was said to Mary: “And a sword will pierce your own soul also, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke II, 35). Finally, the Bride added that her soul had gone out at his word. This happens when the soul is a pilgrim away from the body and is present with God (Song V, 6).

18. We have therefore explained, as best we could, what is meant by: “Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven.” We may nevertheless understand it also in this way: the Word remains forever more truly in heaven, where there are angels and archangels, cherubim and seraphim. For although human beings are holy, their emotions often change. Now we rejoice, then immediately grieve; we become angry and groan. Even in repentance the Apostle does not wish us to be excessively sorrowful, lest we be swallowed up by grief (II Cor. II, 7). Where there is anger or serious grief, the Word does not remain there.

Finally, it was said of the Lord Jesus alone by John that he “saw . . . . . . . . the Holy Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and remaining upon him” (Mark I, 10). For the prophets did not prophesy continually, but only when the grace of the Spirit of prophecy was poured into them. Thus David did not know beforehand what Nathan, sent by the Lord, would announce; and Nathan, certainly inferior as a prophet, recognized what David, the greater, did not know (II Sam. XXII, 5 ff.). Another prophet said: “The Lord concealed it from me” (IV Kings IV, 27).

Hence many understand “the Word of God remains in heaven” to refer to the heavenly Powers, in whom there are no variations of emotion. Others understand it of the Trinity itself, which alone is unchangeable. Therefore the Word remains in heaven—that is, in the Father—because the Word said: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10).

19. (Verse 90.) “Your truth is from generation to generation.” There are many who are called gods but are not gods. Therefore among the nations there is falsehood; in the Church there is truth. Yet the synagogue first possessed this truth, since it had the utterances of God. There is truth also in the Old Testament, which previously existed among the Jewish people. “God is known in Judah” (Ps. LXXV, 1). But God is truth; therefore there was truth in Judah.

Truth existed, then, in the patriarchs, in Moses and Joshua, in Samuel, in David, in Elijah and Elisha, and in those seven thousand men who did not bend the knee to Baal. But because a later generation of Jews departed from the customs of their fathers, truth withdrew from them and came to the Church. It withdrew from them when they said of the Lord Jesus: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him” (John XIX, 15). For they handed over the truth and chose iniquity.

All other generations, therefore, deprived of truth, and all the generations of heretics, do not possess the truth. The Church alone possesses the truth with devoted affection, because the generation of the Jews, which possessed it before the Church, lost it.

The Jewish people were the first generation of faith, and therefore more infantile and weaker; they could not stand firm amid the instability of adolescence. The Christian people are the second generation of faith, and therefore stronger and more venerable with the maturity of old age. That generation belonged to the Law; this belongs to grace. Hence elsewhere he says: “From generation to generation they will proclaim your truth” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 2).

20. The third verse follows: “You founded the earth, and it remains. By your ordinance the day remains.” How God founded the earth Scripture has taught us, when the Prophet says: “God founded the earth by wisdom, and prepared the heavens by understanding” (Prov. III, 19).

The earth is therefore like a foundation, upon which we stand, although it is in the hemisphere of heaven, and the external discourse may celebrate this, and Scripture may seem to signify it when Job says: “He hangs the earth upon nothing” (Job XXVI, 7). It is enclosed, therefore, by the heavenly sphere. For this reason the sun is not seen at night, because, revolving below, it is found in the lower part of the heavenly sphere.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “although it is itself in the middle of heaven,” while the old edition and the manuscripts read *in hemicyclo* (“in the hemisphere”); some have *in hemicyclio*. Our holy author means nothing other than the earth upon which we stand—that is, that our hemisphere corresponds only to the middle part of the heavenly sphere, and therefore we cannot see the sun when it has passed to the other side. From the words that follow, and from the discourse that is external to them, it may be observed that Ambrose is once again indicating philosophical reasoning.]

But it is not the concern of the saints to describe, in philosophical fashion, the axis of heaven, the spaces of the elements, and their numbers—for what benefit does this bring to salvation? The saints always devote themselves to spiritual things and are eager either to know or to teach what will profit eternal life.

21. Finally, Ecclesiastes beautifully opened this passage for us as spiritual rather than material, saying: “What abundance does a man have in all his labor with which he labors under the sun? A generation goes, and a generation comes, and the earth remains forever” (Eccl. I, 3–4). That is: what spiritual abundance belongs to a person laboring under the sun of righteousness?

And he added: “A generation goes, and a generation comes.” A generation goes because “the rich have become poor and hungry” (Ps. XXXIII, 11). Those who previously abounded in grace nevertheless later began to be in need because of their faithlessness. But the peoples of the nations, who were poor, are now filled and abound through faith in Christ, as it is written: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. XXI, 27).

For they heard him say: “You are enriched . . . in every word” (I Cor. I, 5).

[Note: Almost all manuscripts have “in every good thing,” not “in money,” of course.]

Not in money, nor in gold and silver, but, he says, “in every word and knowledge” (ibid.). And elsewhere he says: “In the riches of simplicity” (II Cor. VIII, 2). These are health-giving riches; for worldly wealth cannot bring salvation.

Whoever possesses spiritual abundance has a fruitful earth that remains forever, firmly founded upon the root of virtues; or an upright soul that produces good fruits; or flesh that is not moved toward collapse by any desires.

22. The sun of saving righteousness makes its circuit around this earth. Of it it is written: “And the sun rises and sets, and draws toward its place. The rising sun goes there toward the south and turns around toward the north; turning, the Spirit turns, and the Spirit returns in its circuits” (Eccl. I, 5–6).

[Note: Thus all the editions read, and they are supported by quite a few manuscripts. Eight reliable manuscripts, however, read: “turning, Christ turns, and into his circuits . . . .”]

The sun rises for the just but sets for the unjust; it rises for the tranquility of a devout mind but sets for anger. Hence he says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV, 26). From this it may be inferred that it rises and sets upon the same people—burying their vices and illuminating grace. For he died to sin so that he might live for God; that is, in him we died to sin so that we might live forever for God.

Observe the mystery that was foretold. “The sun rises,” he says, “and sets, and draws toward its place.” This is what the Lord says: “When I have been lifted up . . . I will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32). He drew to himself the desires of all, so that he might either crucify our sins or call a good nature toward righteousness.

Notice how he draws all things to himself: “Father . . . I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24). And to the thief he says: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43). Observe how he draws all things. He was lifted up upon the cross, and the whole world believed.

23. “The sun itself,” he says, “goes toward the south and circles toward the north.” This is that rising one who says: “The Rising One is my name” (Zech. VI, 12), who always rises for the devout and never sets. That Rising One went toward the south for the Hebrew people, toward a softer people, made more ardent by the wantonness of the body than hardened by the savagery of impiety; or certainly toward the nobler people, who were the chosen race and claimed for themselves the lineage of the patriarchs. But because they persisted in their vices and did not correct their error, the Sun of justice therefore turned toward the nations, who previously, deprived of the heavenly utterances, [Note: [Col. 1368D] A considerable number of manuscripts read “empty and ignoble.”] were regarded as savage and ignoble. For the north is a harsh wind, just as the people of the nations were. But those who formerly were weighed down by unbelief have now become lighter than eagles through faith and devotion, after the one came who said: [Note: [Col. 1368D] The Roman edition alone reads: “From the east I shall bring your offspring, and from the west I shall gather you; I shall say to the north, ‘Bring them,’ and to the south, ‘Do not hinder.’” Although it is most probable that Ambrose had this passage in mind, he nevertheless seems not so much to have wished to quote the prophet’s very words as to indicate the passage, as it were, with the tip of his finger.] “Bring them from the north” (Isa. XLIII, 6). And in the Gospel: “They will come from the east and the west, and from the north and the south, and will recline with Abraham in the kingdom of God” (Luke XIII, 29). “And behold, the last will be first, and the first will be last” (Matt. XX, 16). Finally, the Psalmist himself says: “Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Ps. XLVII, 3)—that is, the people who were the side of the north have become the people of the eternal King, who alone is the great Lord.

24. But perhaps you will say: How is it that in the Song of Songs we read: “Rise up, O north wind, and come, O south wind” (Song IV, 16)? For many understand it as though the north wind were being cast out and the south wind invited. If they understand it in this way, the icy harshness of unbelief is driven out from the Church: “Let not our flight be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. XXIV, 20), and the springlike mildness of the south is invited. Or certainly: “Rise up, O north wind”—that is, “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead” (Eph. V, 14). People of the nations, who long ago slept on, awake at last, and Christ will shine upon you.

Finally, everyone is invited to the Church, both the people of the Synagogue and those of the nations—but the people of the Synagogue first, because the apostles who believed were first from the Jews, and afterward through them the peoples of the nations were gathered.

25. See, then, our Sun coming toward the south and afterward circling toward the north. “Jerusalem, Jerusalem”—he came, certainly, to her whom he also deigned to call; but this is the earthly Jerusalem, which killed the prophets, that is, the Synagogue of the Jews—“how often,” he says, “I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house will be left to you deserted” (Matt. XXIII, 37–38).

He therefore turned toward the nations; and, circling, the Spirit of God circled, and turned in his own circuit, so that God might become all things in all. For this reason heaven is called holy, because the radiance of the sun, being nearer to it, continually illumines it. It possesses its own domestic splendor, so that it does not feel the darkness of night.

For this reason the Church is called both heaven and the world: it possesses saints comparable to angels and archangels, and also many who are earthly. It is also called the world, which is founded upon the seas and prepared upon the rivers. Finally, as though it were the world, the Church says: “Do not look at me, because I am dark, because the sun has not looked upon me” (Song I, 5), since the Sun of justice had long judged the gathering of the nations, bound as though by wintry frosts and ice, unworthy of being illumined by the serene light of his countenance because of the error of the nations. Did not the severity of wintertime seem to you to have existed when God was known only in Judea? But now the fullness of summer light shines forth, when Christ is all things and in all.

Is not the earth the Lord’s, and its fullness? Truly, the world is in the Church, in which there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither barbarian nor Scythian, neither slave nor free, but we are all one in Christ. The Sun shines upon all; the day gives light to all.

26. (Verse 91.) Therefore he says: “By your ordinance the day endures.” For unless you understand it in this way, how does the day endure, when after a brief interval sunset follows the day [Col. 1370A] and the succession of night occurs? Yet there are those for whom it is always day—those, namely, who have Christ present, who says: “Walk while you have the light” (John XII, 35).

This is the day that Abraham saw, the day of the remission of sins (John VIII, 56), of which you read: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII, 24). There are therefore saints for whom the sun never sets, because the Lord is their light, as it is written: “And the Lord will be their everlasting light” (Isa. LX, 19).

27. He also expressed the reason for the permanence of the day and added: “By your ordinance the day endures, because all things serve you.” He therefore seems to signify that future time when “there will no longer be night,” and there will be no need of the light of a lamp or of the sun, “because the Lord will illumine them” (Rev. XXII, 5). Who they are he said above, when he stated: “And his servants will serve him” (ibid., 3)—that is, they will do the Lord’s will.

For now we do not all serve. “But when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father . . . then all things will be subject to him” (I Cor. XV, 24, 28), who subjected all things to himself, acquiring the faith of all through the passion of the Only-Begotten. The submission of minds therefore produces diligent service.

When all have believed in the Lord Jesus, then all things will serve God, so that God may be all things and in all. But now not all are servants of God, because many are servants of sin. “For whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34). The Lord, however, does not wish to share his dominion with others.

The day therefore remains unchanging. He could have said, “The day will remain”; but to prophets future things seem, in the Spirit, to be present.

28. (Verse 92.) The fourth verse follows: “Had not your law been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my affliction.” The Prophet shone like the day, because the Law was his meditation; indeed, from the Law he received the oil of light. Finally, lest the light of day should be extinguished by the body of death, he walked in the Law, and therefore walked in the light.

Otherwise, he says, “I might have perished in my affliction.” Humility is not always a virtue; it can also be affliction—that is, it is not always voluntary, but may also be accepted out of necessity when we are tested by some affliction. Otherwise no one perishes in humility, which ordinarily serves rather to preserve. Therefore, when we are in a time of affliction and are shaken by adversity, let meditation on the Law be ours, lest the storm of temptation overwhelm us unprepared.

Unless an athlete has first been accustomed to the exercise of the wrestling ground, he does not dare enter the contest. Let us therefore anoint the muscles of our minds with the oil of our reading. Let us spend the whole day and night in the practice of a kind of gymnasium of the heavenly Scriptures, and let the nourishment of spiritual provisions strengthen the limbs of our souls, so that when the adversary begins to stand against us and sprinkles us with the dust of his temptation, [Note: [Col. 1369] A metaphor transferred from the arena; see the note at the foot of col. 560.] we may stand fearless and strive not as though uncertain, nor “beating the air.”

We strike more effectively after being struck if we offer the other cheek to the one who strikes us, if we do not seek revenge, but reserve the cause of vengeance intact for him who said: “Vengeance is mine, I will repay” (Rom. XII, 19).

We strike the airy powers if we know how to chastise ourselves. Paul chastised his flesh in order to strike his adversaries, and brought his body into subjection so that he might rule over his enemies (I Cor. IX, 27).

Let us therefore train ourselves through unremitting meditation; let us train before the contest, so that we may always be ready for battle. When the adversary’s repeated blows press upon us—now through poverty, now through robbery, now through bereavement, now through bodily illness, now through sorrow of mind, now through the terror of death and the bitterness of punishments—let each of us who is able to endure and bear it say:

“Had not your law been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my affliction.”

29. How many things were heaped together at once, so that holy Job might perish in that affliction? But because he had been formed according to the conduct of the patriarchs and according to the heavenly oracles, and had been instructed in the natural law, [Note: [Col. 1371D] The Roman edition reads “strengthened by instruction.”] he could not perish amid such great temptations.

Finally, when he had suddenly lost such extensive possessions and his beloved children, like one whose daily meditation was on the divine Law, he said: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21).

When his entire body had also been covered with ulcers, and he was tested by his wife’s words, remembering that Adam had been cast down when he trusted his own wife, he replied: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks” (Job II, 10). Had he wished to listen to her as to a wise woman, he himself would not have been wise.

Tested also by the various speeches of his friends (Job XIX, 3), when he had earned from the Lord the rewards of steadfast faith and immovable patience, did he not say: “Had not your Law been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my affliction”?

30. How gratefully he says this today who endured many scourges in martyrdom, who was proved by the rack and hooks, by lead, by burning plates, and by the sword! For he could have perished unless, meditating on the Law, he had believed that future punishments would be more severe than those of the present.

31. How much holy Joseph endured—how bitter and how harsh! First, the hatred of his brothers (Gen. XXXVII, 28); the hardships of degrading slavery; deprived of his parents; sent into exile; the household slave of merchants and the vile chattel of an ignoble Egyptian. What temptation could be more grievous for a boy of noble lineage than, cast down from such family splendor, to serve among the Egyptians?

It is a consoling form of slavery to serve even the just. The injustice of slavery is lightened by the fairness of the master. Therefore, cast down from so noble a station, he considered it sufficiently gratifying if his service should be approved by the royal minister. [Note: [Col. 1371D] Several manuscripts read: “if he served the royal minister.” And shortly afterward, where all editions read “all his strength,” all manuscripts read “his well-known strength.”]

Even this was not enough to intensify the bitterness of the temptation. The adversary returned to his customary arts and deployed all his familiar powers through every kind of deceit, so that through a woman he might weave snares for an innocent conscience. He aroused his master’s wife against him with the goads of lust (Gen. XXXIX, 12). She demanded adulterous intercourse from the young slave; if he consented, he would commit the crime; if he refused, he would incur her displeasure and would not escape the snare of false accusation. [Note: [Col. 1371D] All manuscripts and the old edition read this way; the Roman edition instead substituted “the guilt of slander.”]

Finally, thrust into prison (ibid., 20) and considered innocent among the guilty, he began to be pressed still more by the one to whom he had rendered faithful service at the cost of danger. But because insults could not break the man, the temptation changed, becoming far harsher under the appearance of prosperity. [Note: [Col. 1371D] Six manuscripts of respectable quality read: “far harsher in the array of prosperity.” This is not unreasonable. For the devil ordinarily arrays adversity first, then prosperity, as though in two different battle lines, against the elect.]

For prosperity has overthrown many whom harsh punishments had not broken. By royal command he is brought out of prison, interprets a dream, and is chosen to be greater in honor than all the Egyptians, second to the king, distributing food to peoples suffering hunger (Gen. XLI, 14, 8 ff.).

His brothers are brought before him—brothers who had sold him into the injustice of slavery, not out of fraternal love—so that, tested either by the pain of the insult or by the distress of the salvation they sought, he might cast off the affection of kinship (Gen. XLII, 6 ff.). But the just man forgot the insult and heaped up kindness; and he wished to show himself all the more a brother precisely because he himself had not experienced brotherly treatment (Gen. XLIV, 2 ff.).

Finally, by this kindness [Note: [Col. 1371D] All editions and some manuscripts read this way. More numerous manuscripts, and none inferior: “And he received his father, and by a pious stratagem sought his brother.”] he received back his brothers and by a pious stratagem sought his father.

What better, then, could holy Joseph say to the Lord than this: “Had not your Law been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my affliction”?

32. It is related of a certain prophet—and many relate that it happened to Isaiah when he had been imprisoned [Note: [Col. 1372D] Ambrose clearly indicates here that it was a common opinion among writers of his time that Isaiah perished after being cut in two at the command of King Manasseh. Some, however, together with Tostatus, oppose this view; consequently, they believe that the devil’s words reported by Ambrose must be understood of another prophet.]—that, when he was being pressed by the weight of an impending death, the devil said to him:

“Say that you did not speak what you said from the Lord, and I will change the minds and affections of all toward you, so that those who are indignant at the injury will grant you release.”

But he judged punishment for the sake of truth more welcome than favor for the sake of flattery. He certainly would not have done this unless he had been trained by meditation on the Law.

33. Let daily reading therefore be our exercise, so that we may meditate on imitating what we read. Let us toil in this gymnasium of virtues, so that when temptations arise, the time of testing may not find us untrained, nor deprived of spiritual food, nor weakened by fasting from reading. [Note: [Col. 1372D] All editions read “not as inexperienced”; all manuscripts read better, “not as deprived”—that is, “not as lacking.”]

If it can find our soul nourished by athletic feasts; if the Gospel’s vitality is in us; if the maturity of our mind has strengthened the sinews of our soul through apostolic food; if, through frequent meditation, a tenacious memory brings forth at the proper time examples of the heavenly commandments, no encounter with temptations will be able to disturb us.

[Note: [Col. 1373D] We discussed athletic nourishment at Ps. XLIII, no. 1, col. 885.]

34. (Verse 93.) The fifth verse follows: “I will never forget your judgments, because through them you have given me life.”

According to the Apostle, the Law is the tutor of children, until we reach a more mature age of perfect faith (Gal. III, 24). In the Law there are commandments, judgments, testimonies, acts of justice, and precepts. We are therefore given life in the Law; hence the Apostle also says: “The Law is not from faith, but the one who does it will live by it” (ibid., 12).

But because he also said above: “No one is justified by the Law” (ibid., 11), you understand that the justification of the Law is a form and image, not the truth. According to the truth, therefore, no one is justified in the Law unto perfection; according to the form, he is justified.

Thus the holy Prophet, who was still living by the justifications of the Law, [Note: [Col. 1373D] A certain Paris edition reads: “but was living by the radiance of the Gospel.” Other editions and all manuscripts read “was seeing,” and so forth. Again, all editions read “of the law of the old discipline, as though”; but all manuscripts in both places read as we have printed it, “to preserve honor.”] was nevertheless seeing the radiance of the Gospel. As though mindful of the old discipline, he reserved gratitude for the Law as a useful tutor.

Consider someone advancing beyond adolescence and established in wealth and honors, yet preserving honor for his tutor, whose instruction he recognizes as having formed him, so that he might govern a more mature age.

35. The Law itself also admonishes us that we must never be ungrateful to those who have at some time benefited us (Exod. XII, 28). For, as we have it in the Old Testament, the Passover was celebrated in the territory of Egypt while our fathers, still under King Pharaoh, lamented the oppression of miserable slavery; and afterward, having been freed, they celebrated the Passover again in the land of promise (Josh. V, 10). The first celebration was for admonition, the later one for remembrance. [Note: [Col. 1374D] Codex Aud., Vind., one Colb. manuscript, and likewise one Nav. manuscript read “in the land of resurrection.” We have already noted that this expression was not foreign to Ambrose.]

If someone therefore asks a Hebrew why the Passover was celebrated in Egypt, he will answer:

“Because we were still held under King Pharaoh by the bond of slavery. That lamb freed the people of our fathers; that lamb called them to liberty; that lamb made firm the depths of the sea, so that we could cross Egypt.”

Whenever, therefore, we celebrate the Passover, we must remember the old slavery and the new liberty—what we were and what we have received. For no one can fully understand what he has received unless he remembers first what he was.

36. Let us therefore not forget that the Lord Jesus, the Lamb of God, the sacrifice for the world, freed us from the chains of grave sins by which that most dreadful Pharaoh—not the ruler of one Egypt, but the prince of this present age—held us tightly bound under the heavy yoke of slavery.

Let us never forget, so that when we come into that true land of promise, where the region of the living is, we may remember how many things the dreadful Pharaoh inflicted upon us here, how many sufferings we endured in this world, and from what evils we were finally rescued. Let us give thanks to the Lord Jesus who rescued us and made the disturber of all things a captive.

37. (Verse 94.) The sixth verse follows: “I am yours; save me, O Lord, because I have sought your judgments.”

The expression seems easy and common, but it belongs to few. It is very rare for someone to be able to say to God: “I am yours.” He says this who clings to God with all his faculties, who knows how to think of nothing else. He uses this expression who can say: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV, 8).

Does the person greedy for money, honor, or power use this expression? For many—and indeed for very many—it is not enough to know God. So many peoples and so many nations, so many rich men, consider serving the Lord poverty; and he who is above all seems to them small and narrow. The Son of God, in whom all things exist, is not enough for them.

Finally, that rich man in the Gospel to whom it was said, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX, 21), judged that God was not sufficient for him. He was saddened (ibid., 22), as though he had been ordered to abandon something greater and choose something lesser.

He therefore says, “I am yours,” who can say: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (ibid., 27).

38. This, then, is the voice of the apostles, although not of all the apostles. Judas too was an apostle, and reclined among the apostles at Christ’s banquet. He also said, “I am yours,” but with his voice, not with his heart.

Satan came and entered into him (John XIII, 27), and began to say: “He is not yours, Jesus; he is mine.” For he thinks about the things that are mine; he turns over the things that are mine in his heart. He feasts with you and feeds with me; from you he receives bread, from me money; with you he drinks, and to me he sells your blood. He is your apostle, and my hired servant.

39. A worldly person cannot say, “I am yours,” for he has many masters. Lust comes and says, “You are mine,” because you desire the things of the body: “You sold yourself to me in love for that young woman; in intercourse with that prostitute I counted out the price for you.”

Avarice comes and says: “The silver and gold you possess are the price of your slavery; the possession you hold is the purchase of your rights, the sale of your liberty.”

Luxury comes and says: “You are mine. A banquet lasting one day is the price of your life; that expense on food is the auction price of your head, the total of your contract; and, what is worse, you were bought dearly; you are cheaper than your food. Your table for one day is more valuable than your life for all time. Among cups I redeemed you; among feasts I acquired you.” [Note: [Col. 1374D] The American and Erasmian editions, together with many manuscripts, read “the sacrifice-price of your head”; some read “the auction of your head.” Shortly afterward, seven manuscripts read “you were bought with flesh, cheaper than food,” and so forth. Other manuscripts and editions, as printed above, are better; supply implicitly “at a price.”]

Ambition comes and says to you: “You are plainly mine. Do you not know that I made you command others so that you yourself might serve me? Do you not know that I bestowed power upon you in order to subject you to my power? Or do you not know that the prince of this world said to the Lord and Savior himself, when he had shown him all the kingdoms of the world: ‘I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me’” (Matt. IV, 9)?

The one who wishes to have others subject is therefore himself subjected first. All the vices come, and each says, “You are mine.” What a multitude of claimants—and how vile a slave is he who belongs to so many!

40. How, then, can you, being such a person, say to Christ: “I am yours”? He will answer you: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21). Not everyone who says to me, “I am yours,” is mine.

You are truly mine if your conscience does not contradict your voice, if your mind or your works do not reject your words. I do not deny that one is mine who does not deny himself to be mine—or, rather, who denies himself to himself for my sake.

I do not want to have a little servant who serves several masters. For how is he mine if he says to me in words, “I am yours,” but denies it in his works and by his deeds assigns and binds himself to the devil?

He is not mine whom lust inflames, because chastity is mine. He is not mine whom concern to strip the weaker drives on, because integrity is mine. [Note: [Col. 1375D] All manuscripts read this way. The edition instead reads “because generosity is mine.” The rest of the note concerns a divergent continuation found only in the Regius manuscript.]

He is not mine whom unstable anger disturbs, because tranquility is mine. He is not mine who is drunk with wine into the daylight, drunk with ambition for worldly glory, and unable in danger to preserve the trace of sober moderation.

“I am peace; I do not know how to quarrel.” What have I to do with one concerning whom the devil may come and say, “He is mine”? For he has bowed his neck to me, and I find more of myself in him. He claims your name for himself, but my gift.

41. No one is Christ’s except one who is free from crime; no one is Christ’s except one who can always prove himself Christ’s little servant.

For if someone is changeable—if, like me, he is changed either by grief or by indignation—anger comes and says, “He is mine. An hour ago he was mine; I hope he will become mine again.” Sorrow comes and says, “He is mine. An hour ago he was in my possession, under my control. He could not lift his spirit because of grief or raise his eyes; and if something sad occurs, he will immediately return to me.” [Note: [Col. 1375D] All editions read: “as I, who am changed either by grief . . . is not Christ’s. Anger comes,” and so forth. Manuscripts written by hand read as in the main text.]

Who, then, belongs to God except one who can say: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (I Cor. IV, 4)? Therefore the Apostle Paul said this as a servant of Jesus Christ, because he was held subject to no one else.

But I am now my God’s, now sorrow’s, now anger’s, now an idle word’s; and therefore one who has many masters cannot say to one: “Lord Jesus, I am yours.”

Hence I think Paul also spoke of such masters when he said: “Even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth . . . yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (I Cor. VIII, 5–6).

The Apostle Paul therefore belonged wholly to the Word. That is why he said: “Since you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me” (II Cor. XIII, 3). He said, “I am Christ’s,” and the Lord answered him, “You are mine.”

Whoever truly says, “I am yours,” hears from the Lord, “You are mine.” Finally, concerning him the Lord said to Ananias, when he sent him to heal Paul: “Go, for he is a chosen vessel for me” (Acts IX, 15).
