And because he persevered in belonging to Christ, as though the contest had been completed, he deserved to find the crown of righteousness.

42. Rightly, then, the prophet David said, “I am yours,” since he always remained in the Lord. And to explain why he had said, “I am yours,” he added: “I have sought your judgments”—that is, I sought nothing belonging to others, but desired only what is yours.

Others seek costly necklaces; I seek only your judgments, like garlands of righteousness. Others join house to house and farm to farm, as though they alone could dwell upon this earth and wished to occupy the common element. Others claim possession of the very air; for me, all inheritance is in your judgments.

I do not know how to possess anything except what belongs to your jurisdiction. In your utterances the spiritual concern of silver has shone for me. God is my portion. I am yours, because my share of inheritance is not in gold or silver, but in Christ Jesus.

43. (Verse 95.) The seventh verse follows: “Sinners waited for me to destroy me; I understood your testimonies.”

This voice can suit martyrdom, in which the saint, having passed out from the judgment of the persecutor, may say: “Sinners waited for me to destroy me”—that is, they employed every kind of punishment and every method of persuasion, but they could not draw me away from my purpose. Faith conquered the allurements of this life and the torture of the body.

“Sinners waited to triumph over me,” but thanks be to Christ, who gave me triumph over my persecutors. Return defeated, you who hoped to be victors; return cast down, you who came in pride. “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (I Cor. XV, 53). It has begun to be not your victory but ours, because in you we conquer, though formerly we were conquered in you. [Note: [Col. 1376D] Eight manuscripts read: “because you began to be victory.” One reads: “because you began to be, is victory.” Three words later, instead of “in which formerly,” two manuscripts read “who formerly,” and so forth.]

The martyr therefore rightly says: “Sinners waited for me to destroy me.” After a moment—or rather, while he is still in the body—he sees the choirs of those who are leading him away and the joys of the angels. If they rejoice over the conversion of one sinner, how much more over the passion of the righteous! He sees glory and says: “The righteous waited for me to lead me away.” He sees the Lord Jesus and says: “Christ waited for me to crown me.”

44. Another person who wishes to understand it differently may say: “Many tried to persuade me to sin and to wrest faith from my heart”—one to adultery, another to murder, another to oppressing a widow or an orphan, another to some other crime—and they thought that I could be caught in their nets. They waited for me in order to destroy me through the contagion of sin.

But I did not turn my mind away from the pursuit of divine knowledge through the allurements of sinners, nor did I turn my purpose, O Lord, away from the order of your commandments; rather, I understood your testimonies. For if I had not understood them, those sinners would certainly have destroyed me.

What I understood in my mind I also followed in my works; for it is not a bare understanding, but one that deeds also testify to. Thus it is written: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the poor and needy” (Ps. XL, 1). The one who gives to the poor is the one who understands concerning the poor. For what good is it to pity the needy unless you give him food?

[Col. 1377B] 45. (Verse 96.) The eighth verse follows: “I have seen the end of every completion; your commandment is exceedingly broad.”

We cannot express in every respect the force of the Greek expression; in Greek there is often greater force and magnificence of language. In Greek, τέλος (*telos*) is used, which in Latin we render both as “end” and as “completion.” But τέλος is also the end of completion itself, just as “the end of the Law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4).

You have it written: “Behold, I am with you . . . until the completion of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). The completion of the age is therefore the end of the age; but the end of all things is Christ.

There are many completions. There is a completion when resurrection occurs unto salvation. A completed work is also called a perfect work. Completed wickedness means full wickedness, lacking nothing in the purpose and art of doing harm. There is a completion of a human being, and there are many completions, until he arrives at perfection.

46. We therefore read both of the completion of the age and of the end. We gave an example above of the completion of the age, which resurrection follows: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 22).

After resurrection comes completion: “Each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, afterward those who belong to Christ, who have believed in his coming; then the end, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality and power” (ibid., 23–24).

According to the Apostle, therefore, the end follows the completion of the age. From this it is gathered that the end follows every completion.

47. “The world lies in the evil one,” as John said (I John V, 19); therefore the age too is in the evil one, a world full of sin. The world had completed its wickedness, just as Saul had completed his, when Jonathan his son, seeing Saul’s wickedness completed against David the prophet, told David to turn aside and flee (I Sam. XX, 38).

There is therefore a completion of wickedness, a completion of sins. The Lamb of God came, who took away the sin of the world; he is Christ Jesus, the end of the Law, the beginning and the end, and the remission of sins.

The Prophet saw this end of completion in the Spirit: the one who would abolish the completed error of the age; he saw his blood cleansing the diverse sins of all. Rightly therefore he said: “I have seen the end of every completion”—that is, I saw the one who forgives completed adultery; I saw the one who, through his cross, bestows forgiveness for completed luxury and wantonness, completed cruelty and savagery, and finally every kind of wrongdoing.

48. There is also completed virtue, completed wisdom, and completed justice, but each has an end. The end of all virtues is Christ, who is “the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4). Do you see that he is the end of faith? Rightly therefore he says: “I have seen the end of every completion.”

49. Now that we have recognized the end of completion, let us recognize what it is: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Matt. VII, 14).

We read that the gate is narrow through which those enter who obtain the fruit of eternal life. For virtue is rare, and endurance of sufferings is difficult. There are many who pursue the broad spaces of this age and say: “The road that leads to the Lord is narrow and confined for us; we are crushed on it; let us leave it.”

How then does the Prophet call God’s commandment broad, and exceedingly broad? Because a broad commandment is necessary for the narrow way. Thus this same Prophet says: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. IV, 2). And again: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he answered me in a spacious place” (Ps. CXVII, 5).

50. This breadth of the heavenly commandments enlarged the heart of the Prophet and of the Apostle. The Apostle himself said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged” (II Cor. VI, 11). By dispensing the heavenly commandments, he had enlarged his heart; and what the unbelief of persecution had previously contracted, the grace of Christ enlarged.

Why, then, is the commandment broad? So that we may not be confined by the narrowness of the commandments. Hence he says: “You are not confined in us” (ibid., 12). If this was true of Paul, how much more of Christ, who opened what was closed?

He therefore says: “I do not want my people to be confined within me.” On the narrow path of virtues, the breadth of my commandment must be a comfort to those who travel, so that no one may be able to fail or be crushed.

1130 51. Let us therefore walk in God’s commandment, because it is sufficiently broad. The commandment of wisdom is broad; it is sung at the place of departure and acts boldly in the streets. For πλατεῖα (*plateia*) is the Greek word that is called *latitudo*—“breadth”—in Latin.

Let us therefore enlarge our heart, so that we may receive the force of the Apostle’s statement, which says: “Receive us” (II Cor. VII, 2). Let us therefore receive his words into our heart; let us put on compassion, kindness, humility, and patience.

O human being, how broad you are if you expand the bosom of your mind to the breadth of the heavenly commandments! How broad is the commandment of love! “Love your enemies,” he says (Matt. V, 44). He included all people in the affection of love, since he excluded not even enemies. For who appears to have been left out when the enemy is received?

Hence the Apostle says: “If it is possible . . . while living in peace with all people” (Rom. XII, 18). [Note: [Col. 1377] But the words “to wrest faith from my heart” are omitted in the manuscript copies and do not appear necessary to the context.] This cannot be said to the Jews or to the nations, that they should live in peace with all. They scarcely love their own; but a Christian is not permitted not to love even his enemies.

When I say “Christian,” I mean one who is perfect; for in Christ is the fullness of divinity, whose name you appropriate. Since you bear the name, why do you shrink from fulfilling and perfecting its meaning?

Hear the broad commandment: “Bless those who persecute you . . . and do not curse” (ibid., 14). This very person who says that the commandment is broad proved it above when he said: “They were slandering, but I was praying” (Ps. CVIII, 4).

What were you praying, David? Tell us yourself. But you did tell us; I read you saying: “They will curse, but you will bless” (ibid., 28).

THIRTEENTH SERMON. Mem.

[Col. 1379B]

1. **[Note: [Col. 1379D]]** Thus all the manuscripts read, with only a few exceptions, in which one finds, in the manner of a title: “Here begins the thirteenth letter, which is called Mem, which sounds in Latin as *from the innermost parts*;” or, according to others, “fire from the extremities.” Jerome, too, has “from the very parts,” and it is not obscure that this was added. The editions, however, preferred: “The letter Mem (the thirteenth letter in the Roman edition, the thirteenth Hebrew letter) sounds in Latin as *from the innermost parts*; or, according to others, *fire from the extremities*.” And both interpretations, etc. The thirteenth letter, Mem, signifies “entrails” according to one interpreter, and “from the very parts” according to another; and neither interpretation disagrees with the text. For immediately the first verse expresses the love of the inner parts, which certainly proceeds from the innermost marrow and is bound together by a kind of bond of heat in the bones.

2. Finally, in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, the text of this letter contains the following: “From his height he sent fire into my bones” (Lam. I, 12). Good, therefore, is God, who sends us that by which, when we love him, we may find merit in his sight. Let him himself teach us what fire he sends: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire [Col. 1379C] except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII, 49). Good is the fire whose kindling the Savior of all desires—especially since we read that God himself is fire (Deut. IV, 24), consuming our sins, pouring into our inmost hearts the desire for knowledge of himself, and making our heart burn within us when we read the sequence of the divine Scriptures, if perhaps by spiritual understanding we grasp something by which the hidden things of prophetic reading are opened. Cleopas said that his heart burned with this fire when Christ opened the Scriptures to him and to his companion (Luke XXIV, 32). Concerning this fire the Lord said in the book of Ezekiel:

   **[Note: [Col. 1380D]]** The Roman edition has: “Ezekiel: I will receive you in the midst of Jerusalem, as silver, bronze, iron, and lead are received in the midst of it,” etc. And: “I will blow upon you with the fire of my wrath, and you shall be melted in its midst, as silver is melted in the midst of a furnace.”

“Behold, I will go into Jerusalem, and I will blow upon you the fire of my wrath, so that you may melt away from the lead, iron, and the other materials” (Ezek. XXII, 19–20). We see profound mysteries in familiar words. All this is spiritual. By what prayers may we deserve that the Word of God should come, enter the Church, and become a consuming fire; that it may burn up hay and stubble and consume whatever is worldly; that the heavy lead of iniquity, which exists in many, may be liquefied by divine fire, and the iron hardness of sin softened by heavenly burning; that the golden and silver vessels may be improved; so that every thought of the wise and every word of the prudent, refined by the heat of burning passions, may begin to be more precious? Good is the fire of charity, by which the whole body of the Church grows into mutual grace. Good is the fire of love, by which every saint is kindled to reverence his author. But whoever loves God does not love him superficially: he loves his law, keeps his commandments, and justifies his heart—not by the sonorous proclamation of words, but by diligent imitation in deeds. Let God, therefore, teach us how he is loved by his saints.

3. **(Verse 97.)** Thus the Prophet continues, saying: “How I have loved your commandment, O Lord; it is my meditation all the day.” This is the voice of one devoted to the study of knowing the Law, which teaches the perfection [Col. 1380B] of humanity, the perfection that this entire psalm shapes. And because he recognized that the greatest commandment in the Law is that we love the Lord our God with all our heart and with all our soul, he also wishes us, whom he strives to educate by his own imitation, to be perfect, saying: “How I have loved your commandment, O Lord.” By this very affection love increases, because he summons as witness the one to whom the service of love is offered; and by such an appeal he testifies not to the appearance but to the fullness of love. Peter used this appeal: “You know, Lord,” he said, “that I love you” (John XXI, 15). But whoever loves the Lord loves his law, just as Mary, loving her Son, kept all his words in her heart and pondered them with a mother’s affection (Luke II, 51). “Loving you, I have done your will,” it is written (Isa. XLVIII, 14). Therefore Christ also entrusted Peter with feeding his flock (John XXI, 18) and doing the Lord’s will, because he recognized his love. For whoever loves does what is commanded him willingly; whoever fears does it from necessity. Thus the Lord approves the voluntary actions of his servants rather than their compelled ones. Therefore he makes them free from being servants, so that we may offer the gifts of our wills rather than the services of necessity.

4. A Marcionite cannot say, “How I have loved your Law,” since he does not accept the Law. Nor can the Jew say it, because he is ignorant of the spiritual Law and meditates upon the bare letter of the Law, not upon its meaning and understanding. Therefore only the Christian says it—one who has already advanced far in knowledge of the Law, who does not fear the punishment of the Law with an apprehensive heart, but with fearless affection examines the divine mysteries of the true Hebrew, the true Sabbath, and the true remission.

   **[Note: [Col. 1380D]]** Most manuscripts, and with them all the editions, read: “marvels with fearless affection.” Others read better, “examines with fearless affection,” etc.

He truly loves who preserves the commandments without sadness or fear, by voluntary zeal rather than under compulsion.

5. **(Verse 98.)** Another verse: “You have made me understand your commandments above my enemies; because you are.”

   **[Note: [Col. 1381D]]** The old edition in the margin has: “You have made me prudent through your commandment, because it is eternal for me.” Several manuscripts agree with this. Others read: “You have taught me your commandment, because it is eternal.” Finally, others agree with our text.

He quickly demonstrated the effect of prolonged meditation when he understood the Lord’s commandment above his enemies. But whom does the Prophet have as enemies, when he ought either to embrace the men of his own people with lawful love or to invite foreigners to God’s grace by evangelical preaching? Even wild beasts love creatures of their own nature. How could the Prophet reject love of one like himself? There must therefore be some just reason why those whom he signifies should rightly be regarded as enemies. We can investigate what that reason is if we remember that elsewhere this same man said: “I wasted away because of your enemies, and I hated them with a righteous hatred” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 21–22). Therefore, by evangelical authority, he calls those his enemies who are enemies of God. For if one who does not leave parents for the sake of God’s name is not worthy of God, how much less can one who loves his enemies be acceptable to God? Whom, then, does he have as enemies? If Gentiles:

   **[Note: [Col. 1381D]]** The edition reads: “How did he understand above his enemies, whom,” etc. This is not bad. The manuscript reading, however, is better: “How, whom,” etc.

   **[Col. 1382D]** Here “he has as enemies” must be understood after the word “foresaw.”

how could he have as enemies those whom he foresaw would believe through the prophetic Spirit? Indeed, in the preceding passage he exhorted them also to bless the Lord (Ps. LXVI, 4). And what great praise is it to understand above those who, by venerating metals and stones, have drawn to themselves a similar rigidity of stupor?

6. Whom, then, does he have as enemies except heretics? They are the assailants of faith, the enemies of truth. Whom else, except Jews? They are the more serious enemies, who from being friends have become enemies. He understands above them because he understands that the Law is spiritual. What benefit, then, is the Law if you do not know the end of the Law, if you do not know its mystery, if you do not understand its sacraments? For the Jews a lamb is slain from the sheep for the celebration of Passover; for us, the only-begotten Son of God, born of a Virgin, is sacrificed for the redemption of the world. What benefit do the Jews gain from smearing the blood of a lamb on their houses and doorposts? None whatever, since wood and stones cannot profit them. The whole mystery benefits us, who believe it abhorrent to spiritual grace to stain our dwellings with the blood of an animal and tint our mouths with blood. Rather, we consecrate our bodies by the sacrament of the Lord’s cross, and sanctify the words of our mouths by confessing the death of our Lord Jesus Christ. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10).

What benefit is it that the Hebrews pierce the ear of a servant with an awl and circumcise the foreskins of their own [Col. 1381D] bodies? They do not understand at all what the divine Law distinguishes. These are signs, not the truth. But he understands who purifies his heart by spiritual circumcision, so that he may cleanse away every filth of bodily defilement. He understands who rises above the awl and the ear by the strength of his mind, and raises to the reward of perpetual freedom that soul through which the sword passed to reveal the hidden things of the heart; or, serving attentively in examining words, sanctifies spiritually, by a sacred mystery, whatever he has received through the ear of his virtue.

The Jew is accustomed to make unleavened bread for himself each year, and does not know that he is the leaven of malice. But he who understands what it means to purge out the old leaven, lest it corrupt the whole mass, purges the old person with his deeds, so that he may become a new lump of truth.

These things were spoken to the Jew, and the Christian heard them. For while the Jew pierces his ear with an awl, he could not hear; carrying a wounded ear, he bloodied it with the awl not of the Law but of his own foolishness. The other, by hearing what is revealed spiritually, pierced his ear with iron; for he preferred to believe in iron rather than in the Word. Therefore he is a slave; therefore he was not worthy to be free; therefore [Col. 1382B] not even the grace of the completion of the time assists him, because he did not receive the fullness of time in which the Son of God was sent for salvation and came for redemption, made under the Law and born of a Virgin, victor over death and giver of resurrection. The wound therefore remains in him for whom Christ has not risen.

O wound that cannot be healed—unless perhaps he abandons the awl and takes up for himself the sword that he will not reject for the name of Christ, or by which he may distinguish bodily things from spiritual things and shadow from truth.

   **[Note: [Col. 1382D]]** Thus the manuscripts read. The editions have: “the sword by which he may not reject the name of Christ.”

Let him take up the Word of God, the two-edged sword, and be taught by that divine mouth to recognize the Lord’s commandment, the prescription of the Law—not one whose observance belongs to a temporary celebration, but one that pours salutary and eternal remedies through the substance of spiritual grace.

7. Meditate, therefore, upon the Law all day; your passage through it must not be superficial. If you wished to buy a field or purchase a house, you would employ a more prudent person and examine carefully what the law required; and, lest you should perhaps be deceived in anything, you would not trust yourself alone. But now you yourself must be bought for yourself. Your price is under discussion. Consider what you are, what name you bear, and what you are acquiring—not a field, not money, not necklaces of gems, but Christ Jesus, to whom no prices and no ornaments can be compared. Take as your counselors Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Peter, Paul, John, and Jesus himself, the great Counselor, the Son of God, so that you may acquire the Father. You must deliberate with these, confer everything with these, meditate upon everything throughout the day, just as David meditated; this was his sole meditation. His mind was not led away by worldly allurements; it did not burn with the desire to amass a monetary inheritance. The anxious heat of extending his boundaries and excluding his neighbor did not turn aside the affection intent upon meditation; whatever time the day could contain, all of it was claimed for him by meditation upon the Law alone.

8. But even this is too little for one who is diligent and wishes to attain the grace of blessedness. For the blessed person meditates upon the Law day and night. The day is too narrow for meditation upon teaching. The day in time is not as great as the one who meditates upon the Law.

   **[Note: [Col. 1383D]]** All editions and some manuscripts read: “as great as he who meditated upon the Law.” And below: “he meditates upon the Law and is a preacher of the Gospel.” But the more numerous and better manuscripts in both places read “meditator.”

Hence see whether this may rather signify that for the one who meditates upon the Law it is always day, and there is light without interruption, which no darkness of night breaks. Otherwise, how would he have declared him less diligent in the progress of his work whom, at the very beginning of his work, the Prophet wished to be more diligent? Therefore, by day he meditates upon the Law and preaches the Gospel.

9. And perhaps those who do not accept the New Testament read it at night and therefore neither knew nor understood it.

   **[Note: [Col. 1383D]]** Namely, the Jews, whom the holy man repeatedly attacks here.

Therefore the Savior warns us, lest we too should read in darkness, saying that we must walk in the day, because the one who walks in the day does not stumble (John XI, 9–10); [Col. 1383B] 1134 for he sees the grace of light. But whoever walks in darkness encounters a stumbling-block.

10. **(Verse 99.)** It follows: “I have understood more than all my teachers, because your testimonies are my meditation.” The scribes of the Jews profess teaching, since they were the first to merit possessing the Law and the prophets. But they profess to teach without teaching. It belongs to the people who believed from the Gentiles to say: “I have understood more than all my teachers,” because they did not understand.

The Jew replies: “From where did you obtain understanding? It is written: ‘Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; the elders, and they will tell you’” (Deut. XXXII, 7). “I am your father; ask me.” But even if I ask, you will not answer me, Jesus said (Luke XXII, 68).

   **[Note: [Col. 1383D]]** All the editions, with some manuscripts, read: “and from that I learned to answer, and from that I understand above them what they did not understand.” A greater number have the reading in our text, where after the word “that” the time when Christ spoke these words to the Jews seems to be understood. Again, the Roman edition has: “what they did not know.” Others, with the manuscripts, have: “what he did not know,” which should be referred to the preceding words: “The Jew replies,” etc.

And [Col. 1383C] from that time they cannot answer, and from that time I understand above them—I who did not understand, because I learned the testimonies that he does not know. I learned: “Whoever follows me … let him take up his cross” (Matt. XVI, 24). I learned: “Love your enemies” (Matt. V, 44). And therefore Paul wishes to be accursed for the sake of his brothers by race, though enemies in faith (Rom. IX, 3).

11. This sort of claim might seem inconsistent with prophetic modesty, since he presumed to say that he had understood more than all his teachers, when Moses received the Law from the Lord and handed its institutions on to the people (Exod. XIX, 7), Aaron taught priestly discipline after carrying out the entire rite of sacrifices (Exod. XXVIII, 1–2 and following), Joshua son of Nun showed how circumcision could be repeated (Josh. V, 2–3 and following), and Samuel displayed alike the mysteries of prophetic and royal anointing (1 Sam. XVI, 13). I say, it would seem an incongruous presumption, unless he had first stated what precedes, by which he could rightly prove that he had understood more than his teachers.

[Col. 1384A] He ought to have assumed this confidence because he was taught by the Lord; and the commandment by which he was taught belonged to the Lord, and the Lord himself was the one who taught (above, v. 2). Rightly did he understand more than all, since Wisdom herself was teaching him. Hence elsewhere he says: “Blessed is the one whom you instruct, O Lord, and whom you teach from your law” (Ps. XCIII, 12).

12. He therefore demonstrates that what is divine cannot be taught by human beings; and so those who presume to teach do not know, whereas the disciple who is taught recognizes it.

   **[Note: [Col. 1384D]]** Earlier editions have: “In what respect? Because of the gift of knowledge which he had received … and attained. A moral point,” etc. The manuscripts, however, agree overwhelmingly with the text as given, except that a few read *praeest* instead of the preposition *praeter*; this is not bad if the punctuation is moved to after the word “attained.”

In addition to the gift of knowledge that he had received from the Holy Spirit, there is also a pleasing moral point: there are many teachers who say that they teach what they do not understand, and very many disciples who by their own zeal and diligence attain what they did not learn from their teachers. Indeed, before us someone distinguished between *docentes* (“those who teach”) and *doctores* (“teachers”), perhaps judging that teachers are those selected for this office by the judgment of others, whereas those who teach have assumed the office for themselves by their own usurpation. But even teachers must yield to the one whom the teaching of God, the teacher, has imbued through meditation upon the heavenly testimonies.

13. **(Verse 100.)** It follows: “I have understood more than the elders, because I sought your commandments.” Nor is it difficult for one whom the Lord has taught to understand more than the elders, since the grace of God, bestowed for instruction, may advance beyond the maturity of old age.

For when the age of old age is an immaculate life, the teaching of an immaculate life certainly surpasses senile age (Wis. IV, 19). Hence, when Jeremiah excused himself on the ground that he was young, he received the answer: “Do not say, ‘I am young’” (Jer. I, 7), because one who possessed gray-haired wisdom, in which the grace of heavenly sanctification shone forth, was not to be judged young by the divine definition.

14. Nevertheless, the Prophet does not seem to me to praise himself or to set himself above the elders, since he had read: “Do not neglect the account of the elders; for they too learned from their fathers” (Sir. VIII, 11). Sirach the Wise also said elsewhere: “Where there are elders, do not speak much” (Sir. XXXII, 13). But he knows which elders he places himself above: those, namely, who are made old in sin and in the senility of impiety, and who rave in the old age of faithlessness.

These are the elders of the people of whom it was said that they handed the Lord Jesus over to Pilate the governor: “For the priests, the scribes, and the elders assembled,” as Mark says (Mark XIV, 53). And again: “The priests held council with the elders, in order to hand him over” (Mark XV, 1). In the Acts of the Apostles, the holy Peter and the Evangelist Luke likewise testify that the elders of Israel assembled against the apostles (Acts IV, 1 and following).

He therefore did not disparage the age of old men; rather, by the expression “elder people” he prophesied that the ancient Jewish people, old in days, would be an unteachable people, who had not acquired in their youth what they could not find in their old age. For from the beginning they repeatedly provoked the Lord by their offenses. Since, when young, they had been unable to earn his grace, in old age they did not merit to recognize his coming and could not retain his gift.

   **[Note: [Col. 1385D]]** The old edition reads: “But the understanding of gray-haired old age is a beautiful judgment.” The Roman edition has: “the judgment of gray-haired old age, and of the veteran,” etc. Three manuscripts read: *Sponsum*—that is, “promised.” Two have: “But the evident judgment of gray-haired old age is in understanding.” The rest read as in the text, except that some have “the judgment of old age.”

But understanding in gray hair is the sign of old age in understanding; and the knowledge of experienced counsel is preferred through maturity of understanding, not through length of life.

15. Let us therefore seek the commandments of God, so that we may understand more than the elders. Let us flee the slippery path of sins, so that we may be able to keep the heavenly commandments. This is made clear by what follows.

The younger brother Jacob understood more than the elder, because when his elder brother Esau claimed for himself the privilege of the blessing by right of age, he left the gentler foods while seeking those of the field (Gen. XXV, 32). When he had gone hunting, the younger brother took his garments, and Rebecca, following a mother’s counsel, gave them to me among the peoples of the nations (Gen. XXVII, 15 and following). Rebecca therefore clothed me in that robe of wisdom which the Jewish people had previously possessed. Its good robe is the Law and the prophets. That people was stripped of this robe; we have been clothed in it. That mother, Jerusalem above, clothed us.

We therefore approach the Father and offer him gentler foods: the nourishment of patience, the mildness of mercy, the sweetness of understanding. I receive the blessing; I seize from my elder brother the spiritual grace. He comes and becomes angry; he finds nothing to receive. The mother comes forward and instructs us with devout exhortation. That robe, woven with good commandments, remains with me.

16. “From every evil way,” he says, “I have restrained my feet, so that I might keep your words” [Col. 1385B] 1136. Truly he was worthy to understand more than the elders, since he was honored with the divine Spirit so that he might teach the elders not only the truth of understanding but also the flight from sin and caution against guilt.

Since human frailty is inclined to fall headlong through its affections into the depths of vice, and with swift steps to be carried into wrongdoing, he teaches how the slipperiness of this road and the winding paths of this journey cannot entangle the traveler.

   **[Note: [Col. 1385D]]** The earlier edition reads: “since it is inclined to slip, not toward one evil alone through its affections, and all sins rush upon what is running headlong, and it is carried wholly into vice from the very first step. He teaches how, avoiding the slippery path of this life, [the traveler may avoid] the road,” etc. The Roman edition, after the words “through its affections toward evil,” rearranged the passage as follows: “but the whole is carried into vice from the very first step, and all sins rush upon what is running headlong. He teaches,” etc. All the manuscripts, however, converge toward restoring the passage to its proper form [Col. 1386D], except that two read: “with affections inclined toward the depths, and with swift steps he is carried into vice; he teaches,” etc. This is not bad if the little word *ut* is removed. Some others also have *unum* (“one”) instead of *imum* (“the depths”); from this error the corruption of the whole passage followed. Moreover, what is added concerning “malignant light” is undoubtedly drawn from Virgil, *Aeneid* VI: “Such is the path in the woods beneath the baleful light of an uncertain moon.”

“I have restrained my feet from the evil way”—that is, from the vanity of this age, because the age is placed in the evil one. Whatever is doubtful and has an uncertain effect is evil; just as uncertain light is called “malignant” light, so whatever mingles the darkness of wickedness with truth is evil.

Therefore draw back the feet of your soul and the steps of your mind from the slipperiness of this world. Restrain them, I say; resist desires, oppose the impulses that seem to rush upon you like beasts and cattle, so that they may not devour the tender fruits and the new plantings of this field of ours.

17. “I have restrained my feet,” he says. Certainly it is not the feet of the body that he restrains, for they usually obey the judgment of a devout mind. They should not be restrained when they go forth to the temple of God, hasten to aid a widow, forestall a godless person, or overthrow some fraudulent person. There is therefore another foot that is rightly restrained. What foot is it? Let the Prophet himself teach us: “Let not the foot of pride come to me” (Ps. XXXV, 12).

There is also a foot of iniquity, which quickly slips and cannot stand, just as the foot of the faithless is described, concerning whom it is written: “There all who work iniquity have fallen; they have been driven out and could not stand” (ibid., 13). Therefore restrain your feet, lest you fall; for there are feet not only of crimes but also of weakness. And you must watch lest you fall. Perhaps you may seem to yourself to stand well, but Paul says to you: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. X, 12).

Attend carefully to your way, so that you may hear: “But stand here with me.” Standing with God, you will not be able to fear falling. Standing with God, you will be able to say: “He has rescued … my feet from falling” (Deut. V, 31). But the Lord rescues your feet from every fall only if he knows that you restrain your feet from falling.

Therefore David merited that God should rescue his feet from falling, because he himself restrained his feet, lest they slip into the precipitous and heedless track of sins. Hence he was also able to keep the divine words. For no one can keep them unless he has first been able to stand. But when he has kept them, the Word of God itself begins to guard him.

He rightly says that he restrained his feet from the evil way, since he knows that Christ is the Way.

18. **(Verse 102.)** “I have not turned aside from your judgments, because you established your law for me.” He explained what it means to restrain one’s foot from the evil way: namely, not to turn aside from the divine judgments, to maintain the firm and immovable step of persevering innocence, not to bend one’s stride or turn away from the course of discipline, but to walk in the paths not only of the old Law on Sinai but also of the new Law, according to the clarity of the Gospel.

19. There is also a law of the Gospel, concerning which this prophet said above: “Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are human beings” (Ps. IX, 21). We understand this to prophesy the coming of the Lord [Col. 1386D] and the calling of the nations, which previously seemed to be fixed in a kind of mud of this body, clinging like dregs to the pleasure of their corruption and to lust, because they did not know the Lord.

   **[Note: [Col. 1386D]]** Several manuscripts read: “the calling of the nations is prophesied.” Again, where all the editions, together with the Regius manuscript, have “as dregs and to lust,” many other manuscripts have “which they had made” (three have “which they made”) “and to lust.”

And therefore, in anger, he says: “Let sinners be turned into hell” (Ps. IX, 18), so that they might not see the soul of the Lord Jesus descending and ascending, and might not turn to the Lord, to whom they refused to turn while they were alive. But he speaks of those nations that forget the Lord (ibid.).

20. They therefore knew and forgot; nevertheless, with prophetic kindness he prays that the Lord may arise and that man may not prevail, so that earthly thoughts and all the heated impulses of this body may come to rest.

“Let the nations be judged,” because the Lord is known when the affection of those who fear him is converted, weighed down by terror of judgment: “And let the nations learn that they are human beings”—resolvable through the corruption of clay and formed from hardened mud—which those who had not received the Law previously did not know (ibid., 20).

Hence the Prophet, as though himself disturbed by contemplating earthly frailty, says: “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away?” (ibid., 22). He rightly fears who recognizes that he is human. But because he fears more for us, who are sinners from the Gentiles, he prays that he may not be far from his Gentiles, so that we who were far away may begin to draw near and know that we are human beings—made, of course, in the image and likeness of God, and to whom Christ also was made like through birth from a Virgin.

Thus the statement is rightly understood both with reference to weakness and with reference to grace: “Let the nations know that they are human beings.” In the one sense, through a common and bodily association, humanity shares the condition of beasts; in the other, through the image of God and the sacrament of the Lord’s flesh, the dignity that seemed ignoble has begun to exist.

21. Rightly, therefore, the people of the nations did not turn aside from the judgments of God, who can say: “Because you established your law for me.” Not through Moses, not through the prophets, but you yourself, Jesus, established the law for me—that is, the Gospel. Therefore I did not turn aside from the way, because I looked upon you, I came to know you, and by following your paths I came to know the true Way.

22. **(Verse 103.)** Hearing, therefore, the preaching of the Gospel that the prophetic Spirit had proclaimed beforehand, he says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” And rightly they are sweet, since they proclaim the forgiveness of sins, everlasting life, and even the resurrection of the dead, which have tempered the bitterness of perpetual and grievous death [Col. 1387D]. Through these things we have begun not to fear death, since we have begun to say: “Where, O death, is your victory?” (1 Cor. XV, 55). They are rightly sweet to the throat, because spiritual grace has been poured into the innermost parts.

23. “Sweeter than honey and the honeycomb,” he says, “to my mouth.” And therefore, because your words have begun to be sweet to us, you say to the Church: “Your lips distill the honeycomb, O Bride” (Song IV, 11). What is the honeycomb? Teach us, Solomon. For you said: “Good words are a honeycomb” [Col. 1388A] (Prov. XVI, 24). And truly good is the honeycomb that the Church eats, fragrant with honey gathered through the spiritual abundance of many prophets, like bees.

This is the honey of which he says: “I ate my bread with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk” (Song V, 1). The mystical discourse of the heavenly Scriptures is like bread, which strengthens the human heart, like the stronger nourishment of the Word. But moral discourse is persuasive, sweet, and gentler, because by moral preaching the inner mind is soothed.

   **[Note: [Col. 1388D]]** Thus all the manuscripts and the old editions. The Roman edition, however, reads: “Just as the bitterness of the mouth caused by fevers or other illnesses is made sweet by honey, so the sad things of repentance for sins,” etc.

Hearts made bitter by fevers—that is, by repentance for sins—are sweetened by gentle speech. The lips of the preacher distill honey when the limbs of souls fallen through harsh misfortunes or ruin are restored.

24. There is also a more fervent force of the Word, like wine. There is also, in the form of milk, a clearer kind of discourse. “Eat,” he says, “my companions, and drink, and become intoxicated” (ibid.). Good is the intoxication that produces a certain mental exaltation toward better and more joyful things, so that our mind, forgetful of anxieties, may be cheered by the wine of gladness.

Good is the intoxication of the spiritual table. Hence: “How splendid is the intoxicating cup!” (Ps. XXII, 5). And elsewhere you have: “Make its streams drunk; multiply its offspring” (Ps. LXIV, 11), because when the intoxication of the earth has been infused by heavenly rain, it customarily brings forth seeds and multiplies fruits.

Thus the Word of God, which descends from heaven like rain, when it has watered the veins of our earth—or of our soul and mind—with divine preaching, awakens the pursuits of various virtues and causes the fruits of faith and chaste devotion to grow. Rightly, therefore, it is said to him: “You visited the earth and made it drunk” [Col. 1388C] (ibid., 10). For he visited it by assuming a body, in order to heal the sick; he made it drunk with spiritual grace, in order to soothe the anxious with joy.

25. Rightly, therefore, it is said to the Bride: “Your lips distill the honeycomb, O Bride; honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song IV, 11). For the mouth of the righteous distills wisdom; from the mouth of the righteous flow the honeys of sweetness and mercy. In the mouth of the righteous there is no deceit, no fraud, and no bitterness of sin.

The Church hears the words of the righteous; the people of God hear the commandments of the wise. It delights in the sweetness of his address and is soothed by the joy of moral discourse, saying: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” For the honey of bees delights for a time, but its flavor quickly vanishes, and often diseased innards are harmed; the honeys of moral words, however, even if they sting, do not injure.

Nevertheless, learn to whom such words are entrusted, for it is written: “Say nothing in the ear of a fool, lest he mock your prudent words” (Prov. XXIII, 9). The fool, unable to perceive their sweetness, will vomit out and reject your word.

26. **(Verse 104.)** It follows: “From your commandments I gained understanding; therefore I hated every way of iniquity.” This verse corresponds to: “Desiring wisdom, keep the commandments” (Sir. I, 33). But no one can keep them unless he understands. Every day certain elders of the Jews recite all the words of the Law, yet none of them can keep the commandment.

I would not say that a tree preserves the fruitfulness of its nature when it luxuriates in leaves but withers in fruit. Nor would I say that the earth preserves its fruits when it produces the hated fern for farmers and is not accustomed to yield grain. Nor does the shepherd seem to guard the flock if he does not know how to choose beneficial pastures, avoid wolves, surround his sheepfolds with dogs, or provide water when necessary.

For merely bringing forth a dumb animal without any care is equivalent to the Jewish people merely reading the Scriptures. Where the spiritual pastures of the mystery are, where the letter kills, where intelligible wolves attack, where the rest of refreshment is, where the hope of resurrection lies, and which dogs can bark in defense of the flock, the people—more mute even than the flock itself—does not know.

27. Therefore, if he says, “I keep the commandments,” the reply is made to him: “But you hated discipline and cast my words behind you. When you saw a thief, you ran along with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion. Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit. Sitting, you slandered your brother” (Ps. XLIX, 17–20).

This is not keeping the commandments but transgressing them. To do what is contrary to established commands is not to understand but to be ignorant. How can the words of God be sweet in your throat when the bitterness of wickedness is there? How can honey and milk be under your tongue when your tongue composes deceit, so that you conceive one thing in your heart but present another in public speech in order to deceive the unwary?

Peter the apostle tells you to put away all malice and reject the disguise of hypocrisy, saying: “Like newborn infants, desire rational and guileless milk” (1 Pet. II, 2). He shows us what it means to have honey and milk under the tongue: not to curse those who curse us, but to know how to return a blessing; to know how to hate nothing except the way of iniquity, so that we may beware, with a resisting affection, of doing what we detest.

Therefore Paul guarded against evil in his flesh because he hated it (Rom. VII, 15). Therefore John warns in his epistle that we should not love the world: “For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the boastfulness of life” (1 John II, 16).

[Col. 1389D] **28.** Thus it is within us both to hate something rightly and to love something rightly. For just as we can rightly love the servants of God [Note: Five manuscripts: “we can love the saints of God.”], and can rightly love our enemies according to the Word of the Lord (Matt. 5:44), so we can rightly hate the enemies of God, hate wickedness, hate faithlessness, hate shameful things, hate the vanities of this world. Therefore the things of the world ought to be hateful, lest, when our affections are careless and idle, the seductive enticement of pleasure creep in upon us, ingratiating itself with us. The wanton beauty of a harlot easily captures the eyes, unless just hatreds restrain them and an indignant affection turns them away from impurity.

The boastfulness of nobility and the abundance of worldly possessions often inflate people and throw them backward in swollen arrogance [Note: The old edition: “then, with haughty mouth, the boastfulness of nobility bends the summit backward,” etc. The Roman edition and two manuscripts: “the boastfulness of nobility throws backward with swollen arrogance,” etc. Many others: “with haughty mouth the boastfulness throws backward,” etc. Only four, but in our judgment preferable, read as in the text.].—unless you are ashamed that what belongs to another is praised in you more than what is your own. Although Christ was rich, he became poor: he redeemed you in the poor man, not in the rich. He commanded those confessing that he was the Son of God to be silent, so that God might be recognized more by works than by words; and you call yourself noble, though you were made from earth? King David says: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Ps. 102:14); and yet you glory in this frail and muddy stock, and think yourself rich, though tomorrow you may be a beggar [Col. 1390B], when your life rests not on your abundance but on the mercy of God? To him be honor, glory, praise, and everlastingness, from age to age, now and always, for ever and ever. Amen.

# FOURTEENTH SERMON. NUN.

**1.** Nun is the fourteenth Hebrew letter, whose interpretation is “Unique One,” or, in another interpretation, “Their pastures.” Behold, the letters of the Hebrews themselves testify that the Lord Jesus is the unique Son of the Father, the Word of God. Accordingly, in the very first verse David speaks of the unique Son of God: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” Hence we understand that this psalm has been arranged according to the letters of the Hebrews [Col. 1390C] so that our human nature, like a little child formed from infancy through the elements of letters, to which childhood becomes accustomed, may grow up to the maturity of virtue. Each individual letter is like a title for the verses written under it, declaring their sequence and content. Thus here the letter signifies “unique,” and this portion of the psalm prophesies concerning the only-begotten Son of God and the splendor of his eternal light.

**2.** Nor indeed is the interpretation of this letter found in another manuscript—“Their pastures”—in conflict with this [Note: All editions have “the interpretation, which is ‘their pastures,’ that is, of the faithful.” What are the pastures except Christ? The manuscripts unanimously read as in the text.]. For what are our pastures, that is, the pastures of the faithful, except Christ? The Prophet rejoiced that he had been placed in his pastures, saying: “He has placed me there in a place of pasture” (Ps. 22:2). For he himself feeds and refreshes us. The good pastures are the divine mysteries [Col. 1390D]. There you pluck a new flower that has given forth the good fragrance of the resurrection. You pluck the lily, that is, the splendor of eternity. You pluck the rose, that is, the blood of the Lord’s body [Note: He perhaps calls it a rose because the Lord’s blood was more often consecrated from red-colored wine, especially because of the resemblance. Consult Book 4 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4, and Book 1 of *On the Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 5, no. 9, p. 40.]. The good pastures are also the books of the heavenly Scriptures, in which we feed through daily reading, in which we are restored and refreshed when we taste what has been written or repeatedly ruminate upon it after barely sampling it with our lips. The Lord’s flock is fattened in these pastures.

**3.** [Note: Thus six manuscripts of better quality; in the others and in the early editions, “For in these also . . . are the mountains of the valleys” is omitted. The Roman edition had reversed the words as follows: “The good pastures of Christ are also the mountains of the valleys—for Christ too feeds in them, like a fawn or a young stag—that is, in the splendors of the saints,” etc.]. The pastures of Christ are also good: he feeds among the lilies, in the splendor of the saints; the mountains of the valleys are also good pastures. For Christ too feeds in them, like a fawn or a young stag. The mountains of the valleys are like the luminaries of this world, shining with constant humility; they excel at the summit of their various virtues and rise above the world by their merits. These are the ones of whom it is said: “They are not of this world, just as I am not of this world” (John 17:14), because those who follow Christ are above the world.

The valley, however, is the world; therefore he appointed “a valley of weeping,” because in this world there are weeping and tears. And the Lord, taking thought for us, appointed his Testament in this world, so that here we might weep over our sins rather than preserve them for weeping.

**4.** Our pastures are also these verses, which we are about to discuss today, in which David says: “I was pasturing my father’s sheep,” displaying the true lamp and teaching humility (1 Sam. 17:34) [Note: Seven manuscripts: “in which David was pasturing his father’s sheep.”]. In such pastures the true David—the truly humble and strong-handed one, who did not consider it robbery to be equal to God but emptied himself, and, born as a man through the Virgin’s childbirth, humbled himself even to death—was feeding his Father’s sheep through divine preaching, proving his coming according to the Scriptures (Luke 4:21), when with five loaves and two fish he satisfied many thousands of people (John 6:9 ff.).

**5. (Verse 105.)** These, then, are our pastures; these belong to those who can say: “How sweet are your words to my palate!” (above, v. 103). These are the pastures of those who say: “Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet.” Our mouth is fed by the word when we speak the commandments of the Word of God. Our inward eye is also fed by the light of the spiritual lamp, which shines before us in this night of the world, lest, walking as in darkness, we stumble with uncertain steps and be unable to find the true way.

The movement of the feet is therefore intelligible, and the lamp is intelligible, because the Word of God is a lamp. Was it not “in the beginning the Word,” with God? How, then, is it a lamp? Was it not the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world? How, then, is it called a lamp? Isaiah cries out: “The people sitting in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa. 9:2). How, then, is it called a lamp here?

**6.** But let us see whether perhaps the same Word of God is a great light to some and a lamp to others. To me he is a lamp; to angels he is light. He was light to Peter when an angel stood beside him in prison and a light shone around him (Acts 12:7). He was light to Paul when, as he went to persecute the Christian people, a light from heaven shone around him [Col. 1392A] and he heard him say: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). It was indeed a great light. Accordingly, the light of Paul’s lamp vanished when the splendor of the divine light appeared.

**7.** And truly Christ is a lamp to me when he is recited by this mouth of ours. In the mud he shines; in an earthen vessel that treasure shines which we possess in earthen vessels [Note: All editions and not a few manuscripts: “in earthen vessels.” “The lamp’s light is oil; put in oil lest the lamp’s light fail you. And the oil is not earthly olive oil,” etc. Seven other manuscripts of better quality read as in the text.]. Put in oil, lest it fail you, because oil is the light of the lamp—not earthly oil, but that oil of heavenly mercy and grace with which the prophets were anointed.

Your oil is humility, by which the hardness of our necks is softened; your oil is your mercy, by which even bodies battered against the rocks of sins are comforted. This oil the Samaritan of the Gospel poured into the wounds of the man attacked by robbers as he descended from Jerusalem; when he saw him, he was moved with compassion, bound up his wounds, and poured in oil and wine (Luke 10:33–34). This oil heals the sick, for mercy frees from sin. This oil shines in darkness if our works shine before human beings. This oil shines in the solemnities of the Church.

Accordingly, those whose oil did not fail did not lack the light of faith either; they deserved to enter the wedding place with their lamps. But those who did not carry oil in their vessels—that is, who had neither faith, nor prudence, nor mercy—were excluded on account of their unbelief while their souls remained in these bodies (Matt. 25:10–12) [1142]. Therefore you too should always have a burning lamp, or a shining torch. For if neither your lamp nor your torch shines, you will be called a foolish virgin [Col. 1392C] and will not enter the chamber of your exalted Bridegroom; rather, you will remain in the darkness of blindness, like one who hates the light, lest your shameful deeds be exposed. “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20).

Have faith; have prudence, so that you may always have in your vessels the oil of mercy and the grace of devotion, because the prudent took oil in their vessels along with their lamps. Anoint your lamps, human beings; when you fast, anoint your head. Let us pour oil into our minds, so that our body may be luminous. Let the Word of God always shine as a lamp for you; and let your eye also be the lamp of your body. Your shining conscience is rightly the light of a lamp in this body, because it is your eye. Let your eye be pure. If your conscience is clean, your flesh is clean; but if your conscience is dark, your body too is darkened by the night of your conscience. We too, then, are lamps, covered throughout our bodies and scarcely possessing anything small by which we can shine.

**8.** John too, finally, was a lamp, as the Lord said of him: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35). A good lamp, which received light from Christ so that it could shine in this world; rightly burning, rightly shining, because he was Christ’s messenger, illuminating the hearts of individuals by the preaching of faith. But he also granted these lamps to be the light of the world, saying to the apostles: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). Therefore, if the glory of the saints shone in this world sometimes as a lamp and sometimes as the light of the world, what shall we say of the Word of God, which is also “a lamp to my feet”?

**9.** And perhaps where there is no darkness, the Word of God is not a lamp but something above a lamp, because it is light. There is no darkness for those who see the light. Accordingly, “then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43).

And perhaps according to the Law the Word of God is a lamp, while according to the Gospel it is a great light. To the Jews it is a lamp, and a lamp under a bushel [Col. 1393B]. The Law shines but is not seen, because their teaching is covered by [Note: Most manuscripts read as in the text. Several others, and all the editions, have “by the contamination of vices.” This is not wrong, but there nevertheless seems to be an allusion here to the opinion of the priests of the Jewish people, who did not condemn thoughts and desires contrary to the Law.] the thoughts of vices and by the blindness of faithlessness. But to the people drawn from the nations it is light. Accordingly, “for the people sitting in the region and shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. 9:2).

Open your windows, then, so that the splendor of the great light may enter you. Prepare your lampstand, so that your light may not be covered by the covering of your body and by the measure of this earthly frailty, but that you may shine above the measure of bodily weakness through the virtue of your soul. [Note: The Roman edition: “Or, if you keep to the measure, see that the measures themselves do not fail or overflow,” etc. The old edition, with all the manuscripts: “Or, if you are held to the measure.” In the remainder the manuscripts are divided: some immediately add to *teneris*, “let the measure itself overflow, let it overflow, but let it be filled with good seeds”; others, with the old edition, prefer the reading we have followed.]. Or, if you are held to the measure, see that the measures themselves do not exceed it or overflow; but let them be filled with good seeds. Let your speech not be idle; let your word not be struck down and left empty, lest it become a lamp under a bushel.

God is able to set your lamp upon a lampstand [Col. 1393C], so that it may shine for everyone in the house [1143], so that those who enter may see the light. Our principal faculty is our chief lampstand. Place the word in your chief faculty, and let it shine for everyone who enters the Church.

Take another lampstand as well. Consider your mouth; consider your speech. Is not your mouth a lampstand and your word a lamp when it comes forth from your mouth? Let this lamp always shine for you—that is, let your word shine and never be extinguished.

**10.** Do you ask me to teach you how it cannot be extinguished? It is written: “The light of the righteous is always unquenchable, but the light of the wicked will be extinguished” (Job 18:5). This was the light of the lamp that shone in the tabernacle of Testimony, and today it is the light that shines in the Church: the wise man [Col. 1393D]. He is the eye of the Church, who does not say to the hands—that is, to those who work but are not sharp in understanding—: “You are not necessary to me.” [Note: All editions have “to those who work (though he is covered with narrowness, he is not narrow in understanding): You are not,” etc. Most manuscripts have “to those who work for understanding: You are not,” etc. Best of all, one manuscript each of Navarre, Vindobona, Augsburg, Erfurt, and Fisch read as in the text.].

He shone upon the lampstand who said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). For David too was already dwelling in heaven with his whole mind, and yet he said: “Your word is a lamp to my feet.” Or perhaps, like a good teacher, he wanted to go before me so that I might learn to follow the light and walk in his footsteps. He therefore showed me this lamp, teaching me to follow it while I am placed in the darkness of this ignorance and of this bodily covering [Note: The old edition and several manuscripts: “I shall follow this lamp in the covering of this ignorance, placed in the darkness of this body.” The Roman edition: “in the darkness of this ignorance, placed in the covering of this bodily frailty.” Four other manuscripts: “this lamp.” One: “this lamp, so that I might learn to follow it,” etc. Six, finally, read as in the text. It is admittedly a rather harsh expression, and presumably those who introduced so many variations wished to avoid it. Nevertheless, the preceding words support it: “so that I might learn to follow the light.”].

Peter was wandering in the darkness of ignorance, denying that Christ would die, because he did not yet see that he would die and rise for us. Turning to him, the Lord said: “Get behind me” (Matt. 16:23). He showed him the lamp he ought to follow by saying, “behind me.” Having followed the Word of God, he was strengthened; afterward he began to cling to Christ, fearing that he might again slip into some error.

Was it not he himself who said, “Your word is a lamp to my feet,” who hastened toward this lamp when he said at sea: “Lord . . . command me to come to you upon the water” (Matt. 14:28)? But because he was not following the lamp, he was shaken and stumbled, disturbed by the mass of the violent force of nature [Note: “Of nature,” that is, of the element—namely, the sea.].

**11.** Let us therefore follow this lamp and, as in the night, walk toward the light. Many pits and many rocks are not seen in the darkness of this world. Carry before you the lamp that the Prophet showed; see where you ought to place your step; watch where you should set the foot of your inner mind [Col. 1394C]. Take care with every step. Trust no movement of yours unless the light of this lamp goes before you. For where you think there is light, there is a whirlpool: it seems to shine, but it pollutes; and where you think the ground is solid or dry, there it is slippery. But even if you have a lamp [Note: After the word “for you,” supply the substantive verb “is.”], the journey is long.

Let faith, then, be the guide before your journey; let divine Scripture be your road. The heavenly guidance of eloquence is good. From this lamp kindle a lamp for yourself also, so that your inward eye may shine, which is the lamp of your body.

You have many lamps; light them all, because it has been said to you: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). Since there are many darknesses, many lamps are necessary, so that the light of our merits may shine amid such great darkness.

The Law signified that these lamps should always shine in the tabernacle of Testimony [Col. 1394D], not those which the Jews light every day (Exod. 27:26). Those lamps shine beneath a shadow and are extinguished every day, because they do not understand what they do; they do not know what they read, receiving according to the letter what is commanded according to the spirit.

For the tabernacle of Testimony is this body of ours, in which Christ came, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, as it is written (Heb. 9:11–12), so that through his blood he might enter the holy places and cleanse our conscience from every work of death and defilement. Thus, in our bodies—which testify through the evidence and character of their deeds to the hidden and concealed thoughts of our minds—the clear light of our virtues may shine like a set of lamps.

These are the burning lamps that shine day and night in the temple of God. If you preserve the temple of God in your body, if your members are members of Christ, your virtues shine; no one extinguishes them unless your crime has extinguished them. By this light of a chaste mind and pious devotion, let the festivals of our solemnity shine forth.

**12.** Let your lamp therefore always shine. Christ also rebukes those who use a lamp if they do not use it continually, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). Let us not rejoice in the light only for an hour. The one who hears the word in the Church and rejoices, but on leaving forgets and neglects what he heard, rejoices only for an hour.

This is the one who walks without a lamp in his house; therefore he walks in darkness, doing the works of darkness—in feasting and drunkenness, in beds and indecencies, in quarrels and jealousies—wearing the garments of the devil, not of Christ [Col. 1395C]. These things happen when the lamp of the word does not shine.

Therefore let us never neglect the word of the Lord, from which comes for us the origin of every virtue and a certain progression of all our works. If the members of our body cannot work correctly without light—for feet stumble without light and hands go astray—how much more must the steps of our souls and the movements of our minds be directed by the light of the word!

There are also hands of the soul that touch rightly, as Thomas touched the signs of the Lord’s resurrection (John 20:27), if the light of the present word shines for us. Let this lamp be lit in every word and in every work. By this lamp let our outward and inward steps be directed.

**13.** But now let us proceed to the rest: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” A lamp for the feet is enough for walking; for illuminating paths it is not enough. Yet the same Word is both a lamp for the feet and a light for the paths, because the same only-begotten Son of God is both advocate for those who have sinned and rewarder of the strong, forgiver of sins and giver of rewards.

**14. (Verse 106.)** Therefore, for the one to whom the Word of God is a lamp, the paths shine wherever he goes, as they shone for holy David. Thus, walking as if in the light, he says: “I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your justice” [Col. 1396A]. “I have been humbled utterly” [1145].

It is the voice of one walking in the light to say with authority: “I have sworn and determined.” For the one who has determined is not moved and does not fear falling, because to determine is more than merely to stand. David therefore stands, established by the steadfastness of his mind, and does not fear that he could go astray in the darkness of this world. For if he had feared, he would not have sworn; if he had trembled over whether he could keep the divine judgments, he would not have determined this with the oath’s solemn bond.

No one swears well except one who can know what he is swearing. To swear, then, is an indication of knowledge and a testimony of conscience. And he swears well who directs his feet by the lamp of the word and sees the light upon his paths. Let light go before you if you intend to swear—that is, let knowledge of the truth precede you—so that the bond of the oath cannot harm you. Where reverence is more holy, there faith in the truth is fuller.

Accordingly, the Lord, who came to teach little ones, instruct beginners, and strengthen the perfect, says in the Gospel: “Do not swear at all” (Matt. 5:34) [Note: Nine manuscripts: “to strengthen the imperfect.” The rest and all the editions: “to strengthen the perfect.” What if we should read “to form the imperfect”?]. For he was speaking to the weak. Indeed, he was not speaking only to the apostles but to the crowds; for he wanted you not to swear, lest you perjure yourself. And he added that you should not swear at all, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by Jerusalem, nor by your head (ibid., 34–36)—namely, by things that are not subject to your power.

“The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent” (Ps. 110:4). Let the one swear whom it will not be possible to regret having sworn. And what did the Lord swear? That Christ is a priest forever (ibid.). Was what the Lord swore uncertain? Was it impossible? Could it be changeable? Do not therefore presume to imitate the oath when you do not possess the power to fulfill what you swear.

**15.** What, then, did David swear? To keep the judgments of the Lord’s justice. Nothing at all moved one already perfected and already instructed by the judgments of divine justice.

How many are moved when they see a just person deprived of children and, through repeated losses, reduced to the necessity of utter poverty, so that he cannot even possess the means of daily nourishment; broken by severe illness and afflicted by continual weakness, so that he cannot perform the common duties of nature! But the person who is firm is not moved, and he understands more fully that the justice of God is to be proclaimed, because the Lord chastises the one whom he loves.

Is a son not chastised more often than a servant? Is the father’s compassion therefore unjust, more than the master’s severity? A father exercises his son with harsher measures than a master exercises his household servant. But the father’s harsh blows are not judged to have been inflicted without reason, because he wants the son to be better than the servant [Col. 1396D]. Education, then, is full of justice [Note: Here *eruditio* has the same meaning as correction by words.].

**16.** The holy Job was deprived of his children, over whom the Lord had given the devil power. Was God unjust? Far be it from us. Rather, he was just: in order to test his just man, he made him more worthy of being tested through these trials, in which his patience was proved [Col. 1397A] [Note: Many manuscripts and the old editions: “in which his wisdom was proved.” Other manuscripts and the Roman edition more correctly: “in which his patience was proved.”]. For the clearer the merit of the one crowned, the more abundant the justice of the one who crowns.

He was stripped of his possessions, although he had been rich, and he endured these losses with God’s permission. These were no longer merely losses of money but of life, since all means of sustenance had been taken away. Who would accuse the justice of God, when Job, if he had not lost all his money, would not have found such abundant grace?

God wanted to anoint his naked athlete with the oil of repentance [Note: The Roman edition: “with the oil of patience.” But the other editions and all the manuscripts disagree.], so that by entering the hard contest he might make him stronger and, by earning the prize, more worthy of it. His whole body drenched with a grievous wound, he sat upon dung, scraping away the discharge flowing from the savage red marks of his sores. The devil had inflicted this upon the just man with the Lord’s permission.

The devil would have seemed to have conquered, had he not himself been overcome after receiving the power he had requested. What, then, was that temptation, that loss of possessions, that deprivation of children, that endurance of wounds, except an exercise of faith, a distinguished display of patience, a glorious training in virtue, and a confession filled with victory—so that he who previously had the devil contradicting him would afterward have him no longer?

Let no one therefore think harsh whatever is just. They did not seem harsh to the one who could say: “Naked I was born, and naked I shall depart. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away . . . blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). The righteous blesses the Lord when he suffers; the sinner when he luxuriates [Note: Another manuscript of Navarre has “when he luxuriates,” that is, “abounds.” Are not the commands of justice therefore seen as harsh because of our weakness?]. The force of justice must not therefore be judged from our weakness.

**17.** Do we think anything harsh simply because, through weakness of spirit, we cannot endure it? Take away persecutions, and there are no martyrs. But God also allowed persecutors—that is, the powers of this world—to rise up, lest there be none who might conquer for Christ.

Who at that time did not say in weakness: “Lord, why have you given your people into the power of their persecutors?” But who today would deny that those who suffered were more blessed than those whom no punishment from persecutors afflicted?

**18.** The righteous therefore desires to be proved and does not fear being tested; for the one who has determined to keep the judgments of God does not fear temptations. Where did he determine this, if not in his heart? There we must be rooted and founded, not wavering or shifting with every wind of doctrine.

Let us therefore determine this inwardly, in our heart, in our breast, in our mind, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled for us: “The thoughts of the righteous are paths” (Prov. 12:5). The righteous walks well upon these paths; therefore he says: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Ps. 26:2).

Accordingly, here too, responding to the authority of his own words—he who had sworn and determined to keep the judgments of the Lord’s justice—he says that he wished to be proved, since he believed that humility must be undertaken for Christ.

**19. (Verse 107.)** Therefore he says: “I have been humbled exceedingly.” He rejoices not merely that he has been humbled, but that he has been humbled exceedingly. Blessed is the one who glories more in humility than in power. Power deceives; humility does not abandon.

Good is the humility that even in Christ found praise as a virtue. In him I venerate this more than creation, because we were created for labor but redeemed for rest. Accordingly, he himself, calling peoples to his mercy, glories in his own humility, saying: “I have been revealed to those who did not seek me; I appeared to those who did not ask about me” (Isa. 65:1). And elsewhere: “I gave my back to blows, my cheeks to slaps; I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isa. 50:6).

David therefore rightly wished to humble himself, so that he might fulfill in himself what was lacking of the sufferings of Christ.

**20.** He himself too may have spoken this through the mouth of David in his own person: “I have been humbled exceedingly”—he who said in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29).

Let us therefore learn from him who wished to teach us what would advance our salvation, and who says to us: “Learn from me.” It is no small matter that he says “Learn”; and he added: “Learn from me.” No one who is puffed up can easily teach humility, even if he is endowed with human wisdom; nevertheless, the mind is inflated, and the pride of the flesh exalts it [Note: Thus the edition and a few manuscripts. Others read in part, “to teach humility: human wisdom inflates anyone, the mind of the flesh exalts,” etc.; in part, “to teach humility, being inflated, although the human mind is exalted by the wisdom of the flesh.”].

The one who is content with poverty is not content with insult; the one who can endure the punishments of blows is agitated by verbal abuse; and the one who can disdain offices grieves that someone has been preferred to him in honor. It is a great thing to maintain the proper measure of humility in all circumstances.

Pride first cast the human being down. While we desire more, we are accustomed to lose even what is less. Good is humility, which, desiring nothing, obtains everything it despises.

The Lord Jesus humbled himself so that he might raise us up; and he humbled himself even to the cross. “Therefore,” he says, “God exalted him . . . so that at his name every knee should bend” (Phil. 2:9–10). How many things the Lord did—I dare to say it—and yet I did not bend my knee to him? But I bent it to him after he humbled himself. For in this way, that is, through humility and through the cross, he gathered the Church to himself.

**21.** David was a king and testifies that the uncertain and hidden things of wisdom had been revealed to him; but for that very reason he humbled himself more (Ps. 51:8).

But Hezekiah fell from the height of his heart. That praiseworthy king, the one who had been delivered from siege and illness through the Lord’s benefits and wonders, fell through pride and diminished the grace of his former merit.

What would Joseph have been if he had not been humble? He knew that he had been harmed by being preferred to his brothers; even pious love had found the misery of preeminence. Preeminence armed his brothers; humility reconciled strangers. Preeminence provoked his kinsmen; humility made the king subject. Thus we may truly think that what is said here was spoken as if in Joseph’s person: “I was humbled, and he saved me” (Ps. 116:6), although, if we consider what this man endured, we shall find that he spoke it in his own person [Col. 1399A].

**22.** After Goliath had been defeated, young women came singing: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Sam. 18:7). The king’s bile was stirred, and he sought to kill him. David humbled himself before Jonathan, the king’s son, and turned his affection, so that he preserved against his father’s plans the one whom he could have regarded with suspicion as his successor to the royal kingdom. Jonathan said to his father: “Why do you sin against the blood of the innocent?” (1 Sam. 19:5), and forced from him, against his will, the declaration that David did not deserve to be killed.

David therefore rightly says: “I was humbled, and he saved me” (Ps. 116:6).
