Again, when the prophet came to him and announced the Lord’s indignation in the matter of Bathsheba, the woman, David humbled himself and said: “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan said to him: “Because you have repented, the Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Sam. 12:13) [1148].

Good, therefore, is humility. Accordingly, he was humbled and was saved.

Elsewhere, when the Lord was offended because the people had been counted and had sent the prophet Gad to tell King David, “Choose for yourself what you wish to happen: either three years of famine upon the land, or three months of fleeing from the face of your enemies who pursue you, or three days of death in the land” (2 Sam. 24:13), David replied: “These three things press upon me; but I would rather fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercy is very great, than fall into the hands of human beings” (ibid., 14).

When the Lord sent death upon Israel from morning until the hour of the midday meal, and seventy thousand men had died, David looked toward the Lord. When he saw the Angel striking the people, he said: “Behold, I have sinned; I, the shepherd, have acted wickedly. What have these done, this flock? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house” (ibid., 17).

The Lord was appeased when a sacrifice of reconciliation had been offered to him. Good, therefore, is humility, which saved both king and people. Thus, when the Lord had been reconciled, David said: “It is good for me that I have been humbled” (above, v. 71).

**23.** Good, therefore, is humility, especially when voluntary devotion is joined to it. Therefore he asks to be made alive according to the word, so that he may live according to the word and do everything rationally, not according to the will of the flesh.

Hence that mystical statement can also be understood morally: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3) [Note: Here “mystical” is in no way opposed to “literal,” since Ambrose consistently defends the literal sense of this Gospel text everywhere. Indeed, he argues that the punctuation introduced by the Alexandrians, Egyptians, and Photinians should be rejected, lest it provide even the slightest occasion for the Arian heresy, as may be seen in *Exposition on Psalm 36*, no. 35, and *Commentary on Luke*, chapter 1. This testimony is therefore called mystical because it expounds a reality that is not bodily but far removed from the senses, indeed from the human intellect itself—namely, the eternal generation of the divine Word. Its moral meaning lies in the fact that the Greek word λόγος (*logos*) signifies “word” and “reason” in Latin. Since the new heretics are compelled to admit with us that the literal sense is by no means excluded by the moral sense derived from the words just mentioned, why will they not also admit that, wherever they see the sacred declaration “This is my body” expounded mystically and spiritually by the Fathers, the natural and literal interpretation is not thereby excluded?].

And you too should be an imitator of God. How can you imitate him? Can you make heaven, or earth, or the sea? Certainly not. But you can do everything through the word, nothing without the word; everything with reason, nothing without reason. For you are not irrational, human being, but rational.

### 24. (Verse 108)

The fourth verse follows: “Approve the freewill offerings of my mouth, O Lord, and teach me your judgments.” Whoever humbles himself is given life according to the Lord’s promise; whoever is given life by the Spirit of God is a willing minister. For it makes a great difference whether one does something willingly or under compulsion, if it is to please God. Thus a willing minister receives a reward, whereas one compelled merely administers a service, as we have learned from the Apostle’s teaching. For he wrote: “Woe to me [Col. 1400B] if I do not preach the Gospel! For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (1 Cor. 9:16–17).

See the willing executor of the heavenly decree. He was free from all, [Note: [Col. 1400D] Five manuscripts: “And he became a servant in all things.”] and became the servant of all—by his will, certainly, not by compulsion—“that he might win the more” (ibid., 19–22). To those also who were held under the bond of the Law he presented himself as though he were under the Law, although he was not under the Law, in order to save those who lived under the Law. He became weak to the weak, so that by assuming his own weakness he might support the weak. He became all things to all, not through a lawful necessity, [Note: [Col. 1400D] “Lawful necessity is that which the law imposes.”] but through the obedience of his will.

He disclosed to me the depth of this purpose in the letter written to Philemon, because he wished another to be what he himself was, so that it might appear that he had presented him to the Lord by willingness rather than [Col. 1400C] necessity. Thus, intervening on behalf of Onesimus, he says: “But receive him as my own heart, whom I wished to keep with me, so that he might serve me on your behalf in the bonds of the Gospel; but without your advice I wished to do nothing, lest your good should be as though compelled, but voluntary” (Philem. 12–14).

What a diligent persuader he was! Although he was a chosen vessel of God, he did not disdain to seek another’s agreement in counsel, lest he deprive another of the fruit of his own willingness. Rightly, therefore, David says prophetically: “Approve the freewill offerings of my mouth, O Lord,” offering to the Lord a voluntary sacrifice; for, like that prophetic bee, he was accustomed to gather good flowers with his mouth, form honeycombs with his mouth, compose honey with his mouth, and gather offspring from sweet herbs with his mouth; although, as it says, “being weak in strength, by the proclamation of wisdom she produces the age of her substance” (Prov. 6:8). Recognize what this voluntary sacrifice of the mouth is: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise,” he says (Ps. 49:14).

[Note: [Col. 1400D] Thus six manuscripts. The others, together with the old edition, read: “to gather flowers with the mouth.” The Roman edition reads: “to gather those born with the mouth.” Evidently the editors had noticed that Ambrose was alluding to Virgil’s words from Book 4 of the Georgics:

“Yet they themselves gather from leaves what is born, and from sweet herbs, with their mouths.”

See also Book 5 of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 21, section 67, on this same subject.]

### 25

The Lord awaits willing ministers. Thus, in the Book of Isaiah, the Lord says: “Whom shall I send?” (Isa. 6:8). Certainly he could have commanded his servant, whom he had found worthy to be sent; but he preferred not to deprive him of the reward of a spontaneous offering, since he waited for him to offer himself. Although he knew his devotion, he nevertheless awaited his voice, so that he might increase his grace.

Therefore Isaiah, offering himself, says: “Here am I; send me” (ibid.); and afterward he was sent to the people. Hence it was said of him: “Because Isaiah is bold and says so” (Rom. 10:20). Indeed, Christ filled him as a willing instrument with the more abundant grace of his Spirit.

[Col. 1401B] ### 26

I do not think this was placed here without purpose, because he desires that the voluntary offering of his mouth should please the Lord. There were many prophets, but in all of them it was the willing offering of the mouth that pleased him.

Jeremiah excused himself, saying: “Who are you, Lord and Master? Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am young”; and the Lord said to him: “Do not say, ‘I am young,’ for you shall go to all to whom I send you, and you shall speak everything that I command you” (Jer. 1:6–7).

The prophet modestly pleaded the age of his body, lest his youth be found unequal to carrying out the heavenly commands. But God, who judged that the age of one’s character rather than one’s years should be considered, and who foresaw in his young servant the maturity of vigorous wisdom, said: “Do not say, ‘I am young.’” That is, he forbade him to measure his strength by contemplating his youthful age, since faith would supply him with the gray hairs of wisdom.

Again, later, when the same prophet had said: “You have deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived” … and “I said: I will not mention him, nor speak any longer in his name,” he added: “And it became in my heart like a burning fire, flaming in my bones; and I was dissolved on every side, and I cannot endure it” (Jer. 20:7, 9).

We therefore observe that, even to those who think they ought either to excuse their office or refuse it for some particular reason, our Lord nevertheless either persuades by reason or inspires them with a longing for prophetic revelation, so that they undertake their office willingly rather than mount it under compulsion, and so that the reward of their complete devotion may come to them in greater fullness.

Caiaphas also prophesied: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John 11:50); but this was not a voluntary ministry of the mouth, because he was speaking unwillingly. Indeed, he did not know what he was saying.

### 27

What, then, is the voluntary offering of his mouth that David desires to please the Lord?

“I have chosen to be despised in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11).

“I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9).

“I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak of things proclaimed from the beginning of the world” (Ps. 77:2).

“I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. 131:17).

He prepared for Christ his body, which had formerly been clay and obstructed with the filth of hereditary mire, so that it could not receive spiritual oil, [Note: [Col. 1401D] The editions read: “so that it might be able to receive spiritual oil.” The manuscripts read: “so that it might not be able.” This is better, since before *ut* in this passage one must understand *ita*, “in such a way”; this form of expression is familiar to good authors.] so that it might shine. He shines for Christ whose works shine in Christ’s light.

Peter shone for Christ when he said: “In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). The man who said, “The Lord Jesus heals you,” shone for Christ (Acts 9:34). The lamp of the martyrs shone for Christ, those who underwent martyrdom for Christ. David shone for Christ, who could say: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 83:3).

He had prepared his mind for Christ when, concerning the one by whom he had often been sought for death, he said: “Far be it from me from the Lord that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord’s anointed, and lay my hand upon him” (1 Sam. 24:7). Although he had the strongest reason for defending his own life by killing his persecutor, and although others urged him not to spare his enemy, whom the Lord, according to his promise, had delivered into his hands, he restrained them from the desire to kill him.

The Prophet shone for Christ when, concerning the man who had stained his father’s house with shameful incest and sought his father’s life through murderous battles, he nevertheless, as a dutiful father, said to those setting out for battle: “Spare my son Absalom” (2 Sam. 18:5). He kept silent about the crime of wickedness and placed before them the degree of affection and the name of kinship, so that those going to battle, thinking not of the king’s adversary but of his son, might restrain the pain of violated filial affection.

After his death [Col. 1402C] he covered his face and cried out in a loud voice, saying: “My son Absalom, my son!” (ibid., 33). The parricide did not deserve this cry; but he was prophesying the grace of Christ. The Prophet had learned from Christ to be a good father, who served his good son.

### 28

Finally, this is why he said: “And teach me your judgments,” because the judgments of God are like a great and unfathomable abyss, as the Apostle says (Rom. 11:33). Therefore he could not know them unless Christ taught him, because Christ is the one teacher of all (Matt. 23:8).

These, then, are Christ’s judgments: that we should know that, toward those who have plotted against us, we must not repay injury in kind, but rather offer grace in return for injury. Thus he did not curse those who cursed him, nor strike back at those who struck him; rather, even while crucified, he offered on behalf of his persecutors the aid of devout intercession with the Father, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Whoever, therefore, does these judgments of the Law will be rewarded by Christ. [Note: [Col. 1401D] All editions read: “whoever understands spiritually and does them.” All manuscripts read as in the text. But in many manuscripts the two following words, “the judgments of the Law,” are absent.]

### 29. (Verse 109)

But who can be taught the judgments of God except one who has always directed his soul toward the Lord? Such a person can say: “My soul is always in your hands, and I have not forgotten your Law.”

Some copies read: “My soul is always in my hands,” [Col. 1402D] that is, in my actions, that is, in my works. [Note: [Col. 1402D] Jerome, in his letter to Sunia, testifies that among the Septuagint and all other interpreters he read “in my hands.” Nevertheless, our editions of the same Septuagint, and indeed the written codices, together with Hilary and Augustine, as well as the most ancient handwritten psalters—such as the German, Carn., and others—prefer “in your hands.”]

Although he is placed amid dangers, the righteous says to the Lord: “For your sake I die daily; daily I am in danger”—in danger from the plotter, in danger from the slanderer, in danger from those whom I rebuke and convict, in danger for the sake of truth and justice. Yet I am not terrified by dangers, nor have I forgotten your Law; therefore my soul is in my hands.

But since most copies read, “My soul is always in your hands,” I think this must be explained more fully.

### 30

The prophet knows; he knows where to place the protection of his soul and from where to hope for help. He wishes to place his soul in the hands of God, because “the heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Prov. 21:1).

Whoever has subdued his own body and has not allowed his soul to be disturbed by its passions, but has governed himself with fitting vitality, is rightly called a king, restraining himself with a certain royal power; for he knows how to govern himself and is the arbiter of his own authority. He is not dragged captive into guilt, nor carried headlong into vice.

Such a soul does not perish forever, nor does anyone snatch it from the hand of the almighty Father or of the Son. For the hands of God, which made the heavens firm, do not lose those whom they hold.

### 31

Let us therefore consider what these hands are. In the *Song of Songs* you read: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:6).

The Bride speaks of Christ, and the soul speaks of the Word of God. Christ, however, is himself the Word of God and Wisdom. Blessed, therefore, is the soul embraced by Wisdom.

Great is the hand of Wisdom; great is the right hand that embraces the whole soul. For the soul betrothed to the Word of God is wholly fortified, since the fullness of wisdom is to fear God. Therefore the soul that fears God protects itself with complete protection: Wisdom places her left hand beneath its neck and her right hand around it.

Both her arms are extended toward what is useful, yet each hand has its own particular properties. Wisdom is in the right hand, together with length of life; in the left are riches and glory. Both hands are endowed with good gifts, but they differ in the function of their ministry because they encompass both the present and the future: the left hand is the giver of present rewards, and the right hand of future ones. [Note: [Col. 1403D] The editions read: “each hand has its own particular gifts.”]

### 32

We can also understand this from the prophecy of the holy patriarch Israel. When he had placed his right hand upon Ephraim and his left upon Manasseh, Joseph wished to reverse them with consideration for their ages, so that his father’s right hand might be placed upon the head of Manasseh, the older son. But Israel refused and said: “I know, my son, I know. He too shall become a people, and he too shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he” (Gen. 48:19).

In what respect greater? Certainly in this: he was preferred in blessing, as their descendants said: “May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh” (ibid., 20). Or because his offspring would be a multitude of nations that chose labor in this world, believing in the Lord Jesus, so that they might have the consolation of future things.

Manasseh, however, is the offspring of the people of forgetfulness: having forgotten its own Creator, it was exalted for a time in this world, destined afterward to suffer severe punishments because it denied its God and Lord.

### 33

We have said this in order to show that future things are more excellent. Thus the left hand of Wisdom is beneath the Bride’s head, while the right hand is above and embraces the whole Bride.

The left hand is therefore like a support for present rest, on which the soul leans and rests. It has somewhere to recline its head, because riches and glory are in the left hand of Wisdom. For a time these soothe and provide some consolation.

And therefore the Son of Man had nowhere to recline his head, because, although he was rich, he became poor (Matt. 8:20; 2 Cor. 8:9). Nor did he seek any glory of this world, because he had come not to help one portion but the whole human race, saying: “Are you angry with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath?” (John 7:23).

That is, he made the whole man well—not in order to enrich him by an allotment of possessions, nor to heap upon him marks of honor, nor to increase his worldly glory. These things do not possess the fullness of blessedness and grace. Rather, the whole of this means that he might embrace the length of eternal life.

The life in the right hand of Wisdom is not like ordinary life; it is length of life, so that whoever receives life from Wisdom may attain not a brief life but perpetuity and the length of eternity.

[Col. 1404C] ### 34

Eternity of life is a good garment. The guardians of the walls wished to strip the Bride of this cloak, of which the first man had been stripped; but the soul devoted to God, holding for a long time to what it had sought and not letting go of the Beloved, clothed itself in the precious covering of divine love.

Blessed, therefore, are those who are clothed in such a cloak and have earned such a garment by observing the Law, because they have not forgotten the Law but have done what belonged to the Law. For whoever acts outside the Law has forgotten the Law.

Therefore this soul ascends white from the earth, because it shines clothed in the garment of Wisdom. And those virtues that guard the gates of heaven say of it: “Who is this that comes up white, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5).

She has placed her head upon the left hand of Wisdom in order to open her hand to the poor and assist the needy; she uses the riches prepared or left to her, not riches seized and plundered, and, desiring glory, she acquired it through good works rather than seeking the empty dignities of worldly boasting. [Note: [Col. 1403D] All editions read: “using what had been distributed or left to her … she did not pursue with empty worldly boasting the dignity she had acquired.” Some manuscripts read: “using what had been distributed and left … she did not pursue the empty boasting of worldly dignity.” Others, more numerous and of greater authority, read as in the text.]

This is to place one’s head, and a certain governing principle of the senses, above the hand of Wisdom.

That soul, I say, ascends in whiteness from this life’s desert, as most copies read, [Note: [Col. 1404D] The words “from the desert” are absent from the Roman and Venetian editions of the Septuagint, but are found in the Complutensian edition.] to that ever-flourishing place of eternal delight.

These are the virtues that also say in the Book of Isaiah: “Who is this who comes from Edom, the redness of his garments from Bosor, so glorious in his robe?” (Isa. 63:1).

These, I say, are the virtues that marvel that from this rough and rocky desert any soul can ascend without the stain of great vices. Therefore they rejoice to find one who has not soiled the garments of natural innocence with the ink of worldly foolishness, but has cleansed them with the radiance of spiritual wisdom and grace.

### 35. (Verse 110)

That soul, now secure and now joyful, therefore says: “Sinners have set a snare for me, but I have not strayed from your commandments.”

This is a fitting voice for one leaving this world, because he has escaped the nets of persecutors and the snares of plotters. It is a fitting voice for martyrs, for whom many punishments were set forth and many rewards were also offered, in order to recall them from their devotion to martyrdom either by fear of punishments and the horror of cruel death or by the allurements of rewards.

The snare of confiscation is severe; it often breaks the saints through the disgrace of poverty, though fear of death had not broken them. Another snare is fire, another prison and prolonged punishment. A great snare is laid when riches, honors, and the friendship of tyrants are promised.

Whoever, therefore, has escaped these things and been able to reach martyrdom rightly says: “Sinners have set a snare for me, but I have not declined from the paths of your commandments.” For one who despises present things and seeks future things, the heavenly kingdom has been opened through the promise of your divinity. [Note: [Col. 1405D] One copy, Laet., and one copy, Nav., read: “the kingdom opened by the divine promise has been granted to one satisfied.” Several others read: “has been reserved by the promise of your divinity.”]

[Col. 1405C] ### 36

Who are these sinners who have set the snares? The Apostle disclosed to you the author of all sinners and pointed him out, saying: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 6:9).

You therefore perceive that riches are the devil’s snare, which he also set for the Savior. But the one who had nothing that the prince of this world, when he came, could claim as his own dissolved the bonds of his snares.

And lest you think this a minor snare, this snare strangled the apostle Judas. Wretched man! When he had been caught in the snare so that he betrayed the Lord, and realized how great a crime had been committed, he hanged himself with a noose.

But that noose too was the devil’s snare, so that he would not repent but would suffocate himself by the noose. For God is merciful even toward betrayers themselves, so that they may be summoned to repentance, turned away from their criminal purpose, and recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to do his will.

It is no longer merely a misfortune to have fallen into them, but a crime: they have not only surrendered themselves to be captured, but are also held bound to the devil’s will, although they can say: “Let us break their bonds” (Ps. 2:3).

Divine Scripture has been given to you so that you may not only beware of the devil’s snare but also, through repentance, break his bonds.

### 37

What have you to do, human being, with luxuries and pleasures? A snare does not catch unless the bait has first taken hold of you. While you seek the prey, you yourself fasten the snare around yourself.

The bait of the snare is greed; the devil’s bait is luxury. By these he wishes to entice us, not nourish us. Therefore the Apostle cried out: “Do not touch, do not taste,” things that all lead to corruption through their use (Col. 2:21–22).

Do not touch luxury, and it will not be able to defile you. Do not taste the corruption of greed, and you will be free from the snare.

Finally, what have you to do with earthly things, since you have risen with Christ? “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is … set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Col. 3:1–2).

We have died to earthly things; we have hidden our life with Christ in our God. It is no longer we who live, but Christ lives in us. Why do we return again to earthly things?

“Behold, I have withdrawn, fleeing,” says the holy man (Ps. 54:8). “See the snares of iniquity and contradiction in the city” (ibid., 10). For snares are found where there is usury and deceit.

He withdrew, fleeing from earthly disgrace; therefore he reached heavenly rewards.

### 38

Why, I ask, do you turn yourself back toward the earth, if you have been carried up to heaven in Enoch, raised in a chariot in Elijah, caught up to paradise in Paul, dwelling in heaven, and heard in David, so that you might take up the wings of a dove and fly?

In Christ you have been exalted and made winged in the Spirit. When he descended like a dove, he gave you those wings so that you might learn to fly away from the earth.

Nor should you think it necessary to hesitate about how you ought to fly or by what oars of wings. David did indeed say: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and rest?” (ibid., 7). He seems to have doubted from whom he could receive wings, although divine grace is customarily revealed in this way, since it cannot be found on earth.

Nevertheless, later he clearly taught what these wings are, saying: “Even if you sleep among the middle lots, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the back of its wings has the appearance of gold” (Ps. 67:14).

Even if you sleep, your wings nevertheless rise. For there are those who keep watch while sleeping, as she kept watch who said: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 2:5). Even if it is night, the spirit keeps watch, concerning which it is written: “From the night my spirit keeps watch for you” (Isa. 26:9). [Note: [Col. 1406D] Many manuscripts read: “the one who said was keeping watch.”]

Then wings will be opened for you from spiritual utterances, and the precious prudence of gold will rise as your flight. Where, then, can you fear snares, when spiritual oars are ready for you?

If sincerity of soul and purity of mind shine forth, you are a dove. Therefore it was said to you: “Be … simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16).

If greater oars are lacking, do not despise the smaller ones. Be at least a sparrow, so that you may foresee snares with vigilant inquiry and, although almost captured by the allurements of sins, may nevertheless at some time be recalled and say: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been set free” (Ps. 123:7).

Since we thought this should be treated elsewhere—Book 3, on Luke, chapter 12—it seems necessary to pass on now to another subject.

### 39

It is enough for you to know that you are a bird, endowed with the nature of flight, since the Lord says through the Prophet: [Col. 1407A] “Free yourselves from the snare of the hunters and from the word of disturbance” (Ps. 90:3). [Note: [Col. 1407D] All manuscripts and the old editions, together with the ancient edition of Blessed Hilary, read as here. The Roman edition, on the authority of the sacred codices and other Fathers, reads: “he will deliver you from the snare of the hunters.”]

For birds are not unjustly caught in nets. You are a bird, O human being, who, like a bird, have been renewed into something like the youth of an eagle.

[Note: [Col. 1407D] The words “And therefore birds are not unjustly caught in nets” are absent from the earlier editions but occur in the manuscripts. Again, all editions, together with the much greater part of the manuscripts, read: “you have ceased to belong to the hunters,” whereas the codices Gem., Fisc., and Ebrulph. read: “cease to belong to the hunters.” Finally, where all editions and four manuscripts read: “Before you, the hunter has a snare, before you as prey,” four manuscripts read: “You have one who frees you from the snare. The hunter is before you, as prey.” All the others establish our reading.]

Therefore birds are not unjustly caught in nets. Why do you cast yourself down to earth, when you were already seeking heaven? For nets are not unjustly spread for one who has been renewed, because you have begun to belong to Christ and have ceased to belong to the hunters.

Pay attention to the hunters’ snares. Formerly the devil used to seize you as his prey, by his own right; now, since you are the possession purchased by the Lord’s cross, why should a stranger attack you?

You can nevertheless avoid these snares also, so that you do not say: “The hunters caught me like a sparrow”—if you escape the snare of the heart, which the devil placed in Judas’s heart and thus armed him for the crime of betrayal.

May God turn these snares away from us, the snares that he rains upon sinners. Therefore the Prophet says: “You will give them, O Lord, the snare of their heart, which you prepared for them” (Ps. 34:8). [Note: [Col. 1408D] Only the Roman edition reads: “which they prepared for us.”]

But give us help, O Lord, so that we may follow after you, bound by your bonds. For there are no bonds stronger or more pleasing than the bonds of love. Whoever is bound to you is set free from the world.

### 40. (Verse 111)

“I have inherited your testimonies forever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart.”

This too is the voice of the martyrs, who say that they have received as an inheritance the testimonies of heavenly things.

The Prophet therefore says: “I am heir of your commandments; I have sought your succession by right of faith and devotion.” No one can say this except one who keeps the commandments, having acquired them with heaven and earth as witnesses.

For the Lord said: “Hear, O heaven, and listen with your ears, O earth” (Isa. 1:2). The Lord calls the elements to testify against those who refuse to keep the divine commands, so that he may close off every refuge of excuse.

He also calls human beings to testify, saying: “You are my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord” (Isa. 43:10).

The Lord’s commandments, therefore, are full of testimonies, and they themselves are testimonies. Their witness is entirely trustworthy, since God does not lie; and before him your conscience is also a sufficiently faithful witness, even in an unfaithful heart, accusing or defending through its thoughts, because nothing committed can remain hidden from the judge of all things.

For if even in an earthly court a person who has been suborned to come and lie nevertheless, when convicted by another’s testimony, usually reveals the truth, how much more must he confess what is true in the heavenly judgment before the Lord Jesus, whom he knows to be aware of what has happened?

### 41

He rightly says: “I have sought your testimonies as an inheritance,” because just as we were formerly heirs of the sinner, so now we are heirs of Christ.

The former was an inheritance of crimes; this is an inheritance of virtue. The former bound us; this sets us free. The former, having loaded us with the interest of offenses, assigned us to the enemy; this, having redeemed us by the title of the Lord’s Passion, acquired us for Christ.

The evil succession of Eve was devouring the whole human being; the glorious inheritance of Christ has liberated the whole human being. Jesus did not write his Testament for one person or for a few, but for all.

We are all written as heirs, not by shares but in our entirety. The Testament is common, the right belongs to all, the inheritance belongs to everyone, and each possesses it in full. Each person approaches the New Testament, and all possess it; whatever is claimed by coheirs is not diminished for the heir.

The benefit remains complete, and it increases all the more for each individual the more widely it has been acquired.

The condition of human inheritance is different. If the benefits are divided, they grow smaller; and the coheir’s apportionment is a loss to the heir. Christ’s kingdom is undivided, and his inheritance is undivided.

How could the inheritance have been divided, when the fruit of the inheritance is undivided—that is, the kingdom of heaven? Gold, silver, or an estate left by a human being to several persons is distributed and cut up; Christ’s gifts reach each person whole. All possess them, and no one is defrauded.

### 42

Let us therefore hear of the benefits of this inheritance.

The forgiveness of sins is Christ’s inheritance. Certainly it is complete in each person and beneficial to all together; for to whomever it is granted, it is diminished for no one and increases for everyone. Whatever is released to one person is acquired for the body.

For if the angels rejoice over one sinner who repents, because they consider the redemption of a human being their own gain, how much more is the gain of the race, which is the gain of nature?

The resurrection is Christ’s inheritance. Could anyone call this his loss, when in one person it finds the name of a common grace? For when Christ rose, he rose for all, since “through a man is the resurrection of the dead.” How, then, can that be the loss of individuals which is the restoration of the whole body and of the human race?

Let the Testament therefore be read, and let us consider its provisions. The Holy Spirit is also our witness. For when he says: “But this is the testament that I will testify to them, says the Lord: I will give my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds, and I will remember their sins and iniquities no more” (Heb. 10:15 ff.).

O truly eternal testator, who affixes his laws to our hearts and writes them in our minds, so that we may be able to think of nothing else but the divine commands and ought to perceive nothing else but the oracles of God!

He gave grace, restored nature, and, although he is accustomed to forget nothing, removed from himself the memory of my sins; [Col. 1408D] he gave me the memory of his commandments. [Note: [Col. 1409D] Only the Roman edition reads: “and gave me the law of his commandments.” But you will find the word “law” neither in any manuscript nor in the old editions. Here, therefore, understand “memory,” which is expressed in the preceding clause.]

[Note: [Col. 1410D] Again, all manuscripts and the old editions read: “he presented it as a likeness of future blessedness.” Only the Roman edition reads: “he presented joy.” This is pointless, since the meaning in the first reading is sufficiently clear, because the word “likeness” signifies an example or image.]

### 43

Do not therefore remove the Law of God from your heart and fasten there the law of sin. Do not write the devil’s allurements in your minds and erase God’s commandments.

“Behold,” he says, “I have painted your walls,” says the Lord to Jerusalem (Isa. 49:16)—that is, to the soul devoted to tranquility and peace, which he made in his own image.

Do not, I say, remove the heavenly image and impose the image of death. You have rejected the inheritance of the world; preserve Christ’s testimonies, because in them there are rejoicing and gladness, since every weeping will be wiped away, and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor clamor.

The Passion of Christ was an image of the heavenly kingdom. No one heard his voice in the streets, because by the silence of his Passion he was abolishing all impious speech for the future.

He did not wish to be mourned, he who said to the daughters of Jerusalem: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves” (Luke 23:28). For, about to remove all tears by the benefit of his cross, in his own Passion he displayed the likeness of future blessedness, so that no one would weep except one who did not retain Christ’s benefits.

### 44

Rightly, therefore, the Gospel man says: “I have sought your testimonies as an inheritance forever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart.”

Who would not rejoice who has sought heaven and earth as an inheritance—those two elements that God himself also called to witness when he gave the Law? For he has sought God, concerning whom the holy man says: “The Lord is my portion.” He has sought the Lord Jesus; he has sought the Holy Spirit; and after these he has sought the angels, and lives with them not only today and tomorrow but forever. Nor is he saddened by any injuries suffered for the name of the Lord.

Thus the apostles rejoiced when they were beaten and when they were thrown into prison.

### 45. (Verse 112)

Rejoicing, therefore, in the Lord’s testimonies, he rightly said: “I have inclined my heart to perform your righteous acts forever, because of the reward.”

Whoever hopes for the reward of good works from God and hastens toward him inclines his heart to perform Christ’s righteous acts.

What is Christ’s righteousness? “Allow us,” he says, “to fulfill all righteousness,” through which sin is diminished and guilt is loosened (Matt. 3:15).

He rightly says, “I have inclined,” so that it may not be difficult or burdensome for you, when you turn your mind as though toward low and level places.

Or certainly, because the wisdom of the flesh is not subject to the Law of God, the one who makes his heart subject to the Law seems to incline it, bending the bodily sense that exalts itself through the contemplation of religion.

The one who earlier exalted himself vainly and was puffed up in the mind of his flesh inclines himself when he humbles himself.

But Christ himself humbled himself in order to establish the New Testament. When I read the Gospel and hear that the Son of God took flesh from Mary, I seem to descend with Christ himself (Matt. 1:16).

For I read that, although he was in the form of God, he emptied himself (Phil. 2:6–7). He emptied himself in order to take the form of a servant; and, being found in appearance as a human being, he humbled himself even to death.

For I read him saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:28–29).

He did not say: “Learn from me because I am powerful.” He did not say: “Learn from me because I am glorious.” Rather, he said: “Learn from me because I am humble,” something you can imitate.

“Do not exalt yourselves; do not raise up your heart.” [Note: [Col. 1410D] All manuscripts read as here. The editions read: “Do not exalt your horn.”]

He therefore taught me to humble myself and incline my heart to perform righteous acts—not to iniquity but to equity—because of the reward.

[Col. 1410B] The reward is the kingdom of heaven and dwelling in paradise.

## THE FIFTEENTH SERMON. Samech.

## The Fifteenth Letter: Samech

1. Here begins the fifteenth letter, Samech, whose interpretation is “Hear.” It has another interpretation as well, namely “Firmament.” What does “Hear” mean? It is not said without purpose, since hearing is common to all and available to everyone by the very law of nature. Therefore it is not pointless that you are admonished to hear, since even unwillingly and while engaged in other activities we are accustomed nevertheless to hear a sound or a voice. But it is not enough merely to hear what is supplied by the function of nature; there is also the higher thing: that you hear not so much with the bodily sense as with the understanding of the mind [Col. 1410C]. Therefore consider more carefully the interpretation of this letter and the sequence of the verses that follow.

2. That “hearing” is mystical—that you are to hear and understand mysteries—you may learn from what is written concerning the Jews: “You shall hear with the ear” (Isa. VI, 9), because they heard the mysteries of the Law but did not understand them. Hence the Lord says: “Hear, O my people, and I will speak” (Ps. XLIX, 7). The Law is certainly spiritual; hear, therefore, spiritually. Finally, the one who knew how to hear said: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me” (Ps. LXXXIV, 9), that is, “I will recognize what God will have spoken within me.” Therefore elsewhere he says: “How many things we have heard and known” (Ps. LXXVII, 3), so that he might show that he had not merely heard but also understood. For no one knows anything unless he has first understood it.

Hear, then, lest, if he sees you negligent, Peter come, seize the sword, and cut off your ear: for you possess the bodily ear to no purpose if you do not know how to hear and examine. And perhaps those who cannot hear at the depth at which Scripture is written have had cut off that power of the soul by which whatever is heard is examined.

3. And rightly have others interpreted this letter as “firmament,” since that agrees with the former interpretation [Col. 1411A]. Unless each person hears what he ought to follow, no one is made firm. In the duty of hearing, therefore, lies the firmament of all.

4. Thus the prophet Jeremiah, in the Lamentations, speaks this letter to you: “Hear.” And so that you may know that what you are to hear is mystical, he added the following sequence to this letter:

> “The Lord has taken away all my mighty men from my midst. He summoned a time against me, to crush my chosen men within me. The Lord has trodden the winepress of the virgin daughter of Judah” (Lam. I, 15).

The Lord did not then take away all the mighty men of Judah when the Jewish people were led captive into the region of Babylon, but when Christ came and the captive soul did not see its freedom. It did not know how to raise the neck of its mind, bent beneath grievous sins, or to lift certain necks of faith to the light of knowledge [Col. 1411B]. Therefore the passion of the Savior became a pit for the Jews, which showed the nations [Note: Most manuscripts read, “showed the gate of salvation.”] the harbor of salvation: for the Lord’s cross is a precipice for those who do not believe, but life for those who believe. For this reason he first said, “Hear,” so that he might recognize what was to come.

5. In another passage he likewise added the following to this letter [Note: So all manuscripts and the old Roman edition. The Roman edition, however, reads, “They sounded their hands over you,” a reading that can be defended by the support of all the textual witnesses and versions of Scripture. But perhaps, instead of ἐκρότησαν ἐπὶ σὲ χεῖρας, as it appears in the Septuagint, Ambrose read ἐκράτησαν, etc.; unless one prefers to suppose that our author wrote, “They thundered their hands over you,” etc.]:

> “All who pass along the way have clapped their hands over you; they hissed and shook their heads over the daughter of Jerusalem. Is this the city, they say, which was called the crown of glory and the joy of the whole earth?” (Lam. II, 15).

It is clear that the passion of the Savior was prophesied, and that the destruction of the Jews was lamented by Jeremiah [Note: All editions read, “not the destruction of the Jews.” But the negation is absent from all manuscripts and is not especially necessary, since Ambrose seems to have intended to say that Jeremiah both foretold and lamented Christ’s passion and also the destruction of the Jews that followed from that same passion. The arguments made below, through no. 11, appear to support this reading.], as may be understood from other passages and especially from this one, since later it says:

> “The breath of our nostrils, Christ the Lord, was seized in our destruction; under his shadow, we said, we shall live among the nations” (Lam. IV, 20).

What could be clearer, when the name itself is expressed, the seizure among the hands of the persecuting faithless is declared, and both the life-giving shadow and the grace to be bestowed upon the nations are described?

6. The very words also signify what we read in the Gospel concerning the Lord’s passion, since in this passage the Prophet announced his death. For Matthew wrote:

> “Those who passed by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: ‘You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself, if you are the Son of God!’” (Matt. XXVII, 39–40).

When the mass of the people insults someone, it is accustomed to hiss. At the same time, since those who denied the Word had no voice, they hissed like irrational animals. And therefore they passed along the way, although they ought to have stood in the way. They did not stand as steadfast men, but passed by as unstable men. The feet of the righteous, however, stood in the courts of Jerusalem, in which the faithless could not stand; and therefore they passed by, as Mark indicated (Mark XV, 29).

The shadow passes by, not the truth. “His day passes like a shadow” [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read, “who forgets what he does wrong,” or “who sins.” Nine manuscripts read, “who forgets, who abandons.” One or two have: “which abandons,” where Christ or Jerusalem is to be understood.]—he who forgets, who abandons.

We also read that the faithless pass by, as in the passage:

> “All who pass along the way strip it bare” (Ps. LXXIX, 13).

For who but the faithless strips the vineyard of Christ? Elsewhere too it is written:

> “And those who pass along the way did not say: ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Ps. CXXVIII, 8).

For it is said to those who stand:

> “Behold, now bless the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIII, 1).

Yet we also read of passing by in a good sense, as in Moses’ words:

> “Passing by, I will see this great vision” (Exod. III, 3).

And when he saw the wicked exalted above the cedars of Lebanon, he said:

> “I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Ps. XXXVI, 36).

And no one says to a servant:

> “Pass over and recline” (Luke XVII, 7).

7. Let us therefore consider what the distinction is—unless perhaps it is this: when “passing by” is understood in a good sense, it is read absolutely. He did not say, “passing by this” or “that,” but simply “passing by.” When it is understood in a bad sense, he says, “those who pass along the way” (Ps. LXXIX, 13).

For the good way is frequented by travelers and is not easily attacked by robbers, who are accustomed to lie in wait in the byways. The royal road is fortified. Moses, however, did not pass along the way but stood in the way, to whom it was said:

> “But stand here with me” (Deut. V, 31).

He stood with the one who said:

> “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

Whoever passes across this way falls. Moses, however, did not fall; rather, he passed over from worldly things to spiritual things, from temporal things to eternal things. The one who saw the wicked did not remain but passed over and escaped (Ps. XXXVI, 36), because he did not cling to the wicked man, lest he become one body with him, but separated himself from him.

And he to whom it is said, “Pass over and recline” (Luke XVII, 7), certainly escapes the laborious servitude of present things, so that he may possess the glorious rest of future things. And it is said to the Bride:

> “Come here from Lebanon, Bride; come here from Lebanon. You shall pass over and pass beyond from the beginning of faith” (Song IV, 8).

She passes over and passes beyond because she hastens to the Bridegroom. She passes beyond the world and hastens to Christ.

8. Now let us examine what it means to shake the head. Who is the head of the people if not Christ? For “the head of a woman is the man, and the head of a man is Christ” (I Cor. XI, 3). But the Law too is the intelligible woman’s head. Finally, the woman was under the Law as under a husband. When the Jewish rite, which was according to the letter of the Law, had been put to death, the woman married him who had risen from the dead.

Hence certain interpreters, explaining the matter mystically, wished to understand that, when the Jewish rite had been put to death, the intelligible woman from the Law married the Gospel as the brother of the deceased ancient rite [Note: The edition reads, “as though the rite of the deceased brother, the ancient rite, to the Gospel” (Ambrose: “to the Gospel”), and says that this woman should marry, etc. The better reading is found in the written codices, which we have followed.], because the Law preceded the Gospel by a kind of fraternal proclamation.

Therefore the head of the synagogue is dead; that is, its head, the observance of the Law, is dead. The letter of the Law has been annulled, while its spiritual meaning is affirmed [Col. 1413A]. David remembers this shaking in the forty-third Psalm, saying:

> “You have made us a proverb among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples” (Ps. XLIII, 15),

because a shaking, as it were a transition, has taken place from the Law to the Gospel.

In the twenty-first Psalm, in which the entire sequence of the passion is prophesied, it says:

> “All who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their head. He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him. Let him save him, because he desires him” (Ps. XXI, 8–9).

They therefore shook the Law, which had seemed immovable; and for this reason Christ, the end of the Law, entered.

9. The Pharisees were the ones who shook their heads—that is, they were separated from the truth—and therefore they did not believe in the truth [Col. 1413B].

But it may also be understood in this way: they shook their head, Christ, who had come among his own; but they shook him because his own did not receive him. They shook him when they said:

> “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!” (John XIX, 15).

And they shook their own head although they did not wish to move their own works, when they bound up heavy burdens and laid them upon others:

> “But they themselves,” he says, “do not wish to move them with a finger” (Matt. XXIII, 4).

This is mystical, because they never wished to change the observance of the bodily rite and introduce a spiritual understanding. For we read “finger” as referring to the spirit, since the Law was written by the finger of God (Deut. IX, 10), and therefore the Law is spiritual.

They did not wish, then, to move their burdens, which are heavy, and to receive Christ’s yoke, which is light, and his burden, which is easy.

10. But because the Savior’s passion redeemed all, it is not absurd to understand that they shook their heads in the same way as that leader of the synagogue prophesied:

> “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John XI, 50).

He wanted to say one thing but signified another. They too shook their heads in one way, as though insulting him, but announced something else, because he was the one who came to shake that sluggish and earthly ruling principle of human beings, so that, once the observance of the letter had been annulled, we might seek the mystery in the words.

Hence he says:

> “You have made us a proverb among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples” (Ps. XLIII, 15).

This is certainly understood in a good sense, because he had first said:

> “And you have scattered us among the nations” (ibid., 12).

The Jews were scattered so that their remnant might be saved according to the election of grace; they were placed as a proverb so that we might learn from their end that the things spoken by way of a proverb had been revealed, or so that by their example we might be warned to avoid faithlessness.

Then Jeremiah understood more clearly that Judah was to be lamented, and therefore he prophesied that Jerusalem would be captured at the time when it did not receive its own Redeemer. It is of that city, therefore, that the insult is spoken, when they say:

> “This is the city … of the whole earth” (Lam. II, 15),

because where formerly there was the joy of faith, there is now the bitterness of faithlessness. Or certainly, by shaking its head and passing from bodily things to spiritual things, it may deserve to hear, when it has believed in Christ, that it is the crown of glory.

11. And what is the crown of glory if not the Church, which crowns Christ, its head? What is the joy of the whole earth if not the house of the Christian people, the court of the saints, of whom it is written:

> “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5)?

Therefore, because the Church is the crown of glory, it is said in the Song of Songs:

> “Go forth … and see King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousals and on the day of the joy of his heart” (Song III, 11).

This is said to souls, that they should go forth from bodily huts and enclosures, go outside the thoughts of the body, depart from desires, cares, and the other inclinations and slippery passions of this flesh; that they should rise above the world, come out of this world, meet Christ, and be present, prepared with shining, burning lamps.

As though the angels of Christ were speaking these words, they say: “You cannot see his brightness and his glory unless you go forth from the cares of human frailty, daughters of Jerusalem.” As though they were saying: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” Christ is not sought within this world, for he wished his disciples to be above the world.

And what is the crown with which Christ is crowned if not the crown of glory? Joseph had the crown of chastity, Paul the crown of righteousness, Peter the crown of faith. There are crowns belonging to individual virtues. Christ alone possesses the crown of glory with which the Church crowned him. In this crown all crowns are present, because glory is not the portion of one crown but the reward of all crowns.

12. In a third interpretation, they shook their head—that is, Christ, who is the head of his people.

> “His head is gold, cephas” (Song V, 11).

Hence Aquila rendered it “a golden rock,” while Symmachus rendered it “a golden stone,” signifying a wisdom that is firm and exalted [Col. 1414C].

The body of Christ is the Church. Its head is gold—that is, the precious wisdom of the saints, namely, just and prudent men. “His locks are black fir trees, like a raven” (ibid.); and elsewhere he says:

> “Your hair is like a flock of shorn sheep” (Song VI, 4).

It is called hair because the power of all the senses is in the head:

> “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccles. II, 14).

There is therefore the profound prudence of teachers, which can reveal obscure things and disclose the heights of meanings. Such interpreters are the hair of the Church, like the young of ravens, for which the Lord provides food, as he provided for holy Jacob from his youth and nourished him. The Lord feeds these lofty and profound souls with the abundance of doctrine and with heavenly mysteries.

13. “His eyes are like doves” (Song V, 12). The eyes are men adorned with spiritual perceptions, sharp for seeing mysteries and ready to penetrate the divine secrets of Scripture, shining with rational milk. In them there is no stained confusion of deceit, but the pure and spotless sincerity of a simple affection.

Therefore he mentioned these doves as washed in an abundance of waters and in milk (ibid.).

14. Now certainly we understand the teeth, the cheeks, and “the lips of the bride like a scarlet thread” (Song VI, 5) to be the virtues of the soul and the various kinds of teachers: either those who supply spiritual nourishment to the mind through diligent administration; or those who, by preaching the Lord’s cross, bind the listener with a kind of line of speech; or those who are modest and bashful and most pleasing in the bloom of youth [Note: The Roman edition reads, “even though they are restrained from touching by modesty.” Other editions and manuscripts have the better reading, “even though they are restrained from discourse,” etc. For the ancient Fathers used tractare to mean explaining sacred Scripture to the people.].

Even though they are restrained from discourse by modesty, the fragrance of Christ nevertheless rises from them; and just as ointment descends upon the cheeks, as though from the priestly head, so the beauty of their doctrine shines forth.

The synagogue shook this head also. Therefore the Lord took away “the wonderful counselor, the prudent architect, and the wise hearer” [Isa. IX, 14: “the head and the tail”], because those who did not hold fast to the head cannot possess the last things. But let us now consider what follows.

15. **Verse 113.** “I have hated the wicked, and I have loved your law.” [Note: All editions read, “How much our holy Lord weighs the affection,” etc. Several manuscripts read, “How much, therefore, our holy Lord weighs the affection” (one has “weighs us”), while ten others have the reading followed in the text.]

The holy prophet David declared in this verse how greatly his affection was directed toward the Lord. Although he had by no means persecuted his enemies—for he did not consider even the life of King Saul, whose plots he could scarcely avoid as a danger to his own safety, something to be sought, nor did he regard Saul’s death as something to be avenged; he grieved over the death of his parricidal son; and he forgave the crimes of many who persecuted and attacked him, as he himself says (Ps. VII, 5), because he did not repay those who injured him in kind—nevertheless he shudders with hatred at the transgressors of the divine Law.

In this he reveals both the clemency and gentle piety of his character, as well as the intensity of his devotion, in harmony with the discipline of the evangelical commandment, which he foresaw by the prophetic Spirit.

For the Lord Jesus commanded us to desire the love even of our enemies (Matt. V, 44), but to pursue the enemies of God with hatred, even if they are joined to us by the relationship of parents, children, marriage, or kinship. For it is written:

> “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26).

16. If anyone hears this carelessly, he may perhaps say: “You, Lord Jesus, gave the Law, saying, ‘Love the Lord your God; love your neighbor’ (Deut. VI, 5), and you came to fulfill this Law. Through the Law you said, ‘Honor your father and mother’ (Lev. XIX, 18), yet in the Gospel you command us to hate our parents (Matt. XV, 4). How are these commandments consistent with one another? Did you come as one who is gentle and humble of heart?

“I cannot, without violating the law of piety, hate my father, to whom I owe my creation; nor my mother, who bore the burden of a dutiful fetus for ten months of long discomfort [Note: Some manuscripts read “nine months.” This is incorrect. It is clear that the allusion is to Virgil, Eclogue 4:

> “For the mother had endured the long burdens of ten months.”

Although some wish the poet’s verse to be understood of lunar months, Hippocrates teaches, in his work on seven- and eight-month births, and many others after him, that the period of a legitimate birth is not only the ninth month but also the tenth and eleventh. Indeed, Pliny, Book VII, chapter 5, and Aulus Gellius, Book III, chapter 16, report that a child is sometimes born in the thirteenth month. See also Ulysses Aldrovandi, *On Monsters*, p. 50.], for whom delivery brings greater danger and delay greater weariness.

“What have the dearest children deserved, that they should be excluded from a father’s love, when it is impious to refuse to die for one’s children? What of a most beloved wife, a kind of co-heir of life and partner in our common nature? What of brothers, formed from the same inward parts and fashioned in the same natural dwelling, sent forth into the light for this purpose? Shall I therefore hate pledges of affection?

“Do you bend the harsh rigor of the Law through the gentleness of the Gospel in such a way that, while the Law condemns the injuries committed against them, you condemn their grace through your Gospel?”

17. I see that I cannot answer such an argument. But you, Lord, answer; for you did not need to speak in order to excuse yourself [Note: All editions, along with one or two manuscripts, read, “who did not need [them] in order to conquer”; the remaining codices read, “in order to speak.”].

He will therefore answer:

> “Do I condemn piety, I who hate iniquity? Do I command that parents not be loved, I who urge that enemies be loved?

“But have you not read: ‘There is a time for loving and a time for hating, a time for war and a time for peace’ (Eccles. III, 8)? What does Ecclesiastes mean by this? Is it not that things are to be done according to the proper time, so that we may both love and hate some people dutifully; that it may be appropriate to hate those whom you have loved, and to love those whom you have hated?

“I did not therefore pour hatred of relatives into the breasts of children, nor did I urge husbands to despise their wives. Ask nature what I have required; it testifies by the affection belonging to each relationship to the will of its Creator.

“It is the law of nature that fathers love their children; it is the divine law that husbands love their wives, a law that turns marital affection into nature, so that they become one flesh and one spirit. It is the privilege of nature that brothers love brothers; nature, which accustoms those long nourished in the same dwelling to the grace of affection.”

18. I did not therefore command internal wars among relatives, but I regarded the enticement with suspicion. And was it not rightly regarded with suspicion, when that cunning and crafty serpent, in devising the arts of his wickedness and seeking to weaken the affection of the firstborn Adam, founded upon the gift of an uncorrupted and untutored nature, entrusted himself more to feminine enticements than to his own poisons?

Thus the woman bent the man whom the serpent had not dared to tempt, through the food taken by his mouth and the power of love, leading him astray by a certain gentle and conciliatory affection of wifely attentiveness.

And at that time Eve did not yet have children, whose sake—although it makes one sweetly inclined to love, it also makes one easily liable to fall—has often recalled many from completing martyrdom. Indeed, we have often learned that a man whom the fearful spectacle of executioners did not terrify, whom the furrow of a torn side did not break, and whom glowing plates could not draw away from the firmness of triumphant courage, once already established amid the sacred rewards, was deceived by a wife through the presentation of her tender offspring and pity for a single piteous tear.

Samson was captured through his wife—are you stronger? Solomon was captured in his wife—are you wiser? He whose wisdom is celebrated throughout all the ages became foolish because he loved his wife too greatly.

19. What shall I say about brothers? The house of the Prophet itself experienced in its children [Note: All editions read, “kisses more detestable than the hatred of an enemy … therefore fratricide.” The manuscripts read, “kisses more detestable than hatred … therefore parricide.” This is excellent, since the abominable kisses of the incestuous Ammon are designated here. A little later, nine manuscripts read, “Finally he mourns the parricide, yet recalls the perpetrator of incest.” Other manuscripts and the editions have the better reading, “Finally, although he was a parricide, he nevertheless recalled the perpetrator of incest.” The meaning is that although Absalom had killed his brother as a parricide, he was nevertheless recalled to the court because he had killed an incestuous man.] kisses more detestable than fraternal hatred. Therefore the father indeed wept over the parricide, but he was more indignant at the incest. Finally, although he was a parricide, he nevertheless recalled the perpetrator of incest.

20. There is therefore a time for loving and a time for hating—that is, a time for martyrdom, when things divine must be preferred to every affection belonging to our relationships. There is a time for war, when we must wage war even against faithless pledges in the name of Christ. There is a time for peace, because “his place is in peace” (Ps. LXXV, 3).

Finally, he himself clearly explained in the Gospel the reason why we ought to hate our own relatives, saying:

> “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 37).

He did not say that those who love their parents are unworthy, but he declared unworthy those who love their parents more than Christ. If we show love to our parents because they are the authors of our generation, how much more ought we to love Christ, who is the author of those very parents? They gave what belongs not to their power but to their ministry; Christ gives salvation, while preserving the benefits bestowed by parents.

21. He aptly said, “I have hated the wicked, but I have loved your law,” because if we love the Law, we ought to hate the adversaries of the Law, who attack the commandments of the Law by their deeds [Col. 1417C].

The Greek named them more accurately and precisely when he said παρανόμους (*paranomous*). A *paranomos* is called an *exlex*, “outside the law,” because he is beyond the Law. The one who is in Christ’s Law therefore hates them, because they do not keep the commandments of the Law.

For not only is the one who does not know the Law without the Law; the one who does not act according to the Law is also outside the Law, because:

> “It is not the hearers of the Law … but the doers of the Law who will be justified” (Rom. II, 13).

David himself refutes me if I understand this otherwise. How could he have hated wicked men, when he commended his parricidal son to the soldiers so that no one would kill him? When he even avenged the death of King Saul upon the man who announced that he had killed him?

22. Therefore he did not hate wicked men but wicked words. For he said, “I have hated the wicked,” and did not add “men.”

Moreover, since Jesus says in the Gospel, “Love your enemies” (Matt. V, 44), and the Apostle says, “Bless those who persecute you, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14), how could this man, living under evangelical discipline, be excused if he hated wicked men? Unless you understand that he hated iniquity, not those who, although they practiced iniquity, could nevertheless be converted by evangelical preaching [Col. 1418A].

Or certainly we may understand it in this way: just as the one who does not honor his father is wicked, yet according to the statement, “Whoever does not hate his father or mother … or brothers or sisters, or his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26), the same person may nevertheless be regarded as praiseworthy; so this man too hated the wicked. He hated them in the same way as the transgressing father or his own life is to be hated: namely, by preferring the grace of Christ to the sweetness of this life.

23. **Verse 114.** It follows: “You are my helper and my protector, and I have hoped in your word.”

A helper through the Law, a protector through the Gospel. Those whom he helped through the Law, he received in the flesh, because it is written:

> “He himself bears our sins.”

And therefore I hope in his word (Isa. LIII, 4). Yet the Greek has ἐπήλπισα, which means “I have hoped beyond,” or “I have hoped again.” This is said of one who continually adds to his hope: when he has hoped for something, he hopes again and advances in hope, always stretching himself toward higher things and forgetting what lies behind [Note: Some manuscripts read, “and forgetting the things that pass away.”].

24. He aptly says, “I have hoped in your word,” that is, “I have not hoped in the prophets, nor in the Law, but I have hoped in your word”—that is, in your coming, that you may come and receive sinners, forgive their offenses, and, as the good shepherd, place the weary sheep upon your shoulders on the cross.

If anyone hopes in Christ, he must separate himself from the fellowship of the faithless.

25. **Verse 115.** Therefore he says:

> “Depart from me, evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God.”

The testimony of this verse signifies that where wickedness is, there the keeping of the heavenly commandments cannot exist:

> “For wisdom does not enter into a malicious soul” (Wis. I, 4).

And elsewhere:

> “The wicked will seek me and will not find me” (Prov. I, 28).

Christ loves a simple mind and a pure, cleansed spirit; immaculate virtue cannot have fellowship with stained crimes [Note: The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and Roman editions, together with only two manuscripts, read, “there can be no association”; the Gillian edition, with the others, has the reading followed in the text.]. He hates and avoids contamination and rejects it, he who says:

> “Learn from me, because I am gentle” (Matt. XI, 29).

He drives away the wicked and calls those who labor. Jesus says to the former:

> “Depart from me, all you who practice iniquity” (Matt. VII, 23).

To the latter he says:

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. XI, 28),

not burdened with wickedness of mind, but burdened by the weakness of the flesh; burdened, I say, with the inheritance of another’s sin.

I come to the aid of those who labor; I ought not to benefit the fraudulent, lest they harm many others. Let punishment restrain the latter; let grace correct the former. Malice is the source of sin; the fall is the fault of weakness. I ought to help the one who labors, but also to hate the one who deceives.

He therefore rejects evil deeds. For unless you understand it in this way, he seems to say, “Depart from me, because I am clean, because I am pure.” The Pharisee said this, but he was reproved by Christ. The Prophet therefore does not say, “I am clean,” but:

> “Create a clean heart in me, O God” (Ps. L, 12).

26. **Verse 116.** Therefore, having rejected the fellowship of the wicked—as though one who had previously been mixed with them could not be received by the Lord—he says:

> “Receive me according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.”

If the poor Lazarus lives who is in the bosom of the patriarch Abraham, how much more does the one who is received by Christ live? For how can the one whom eternal life has received fail to live forever? Christ has taken him wholly to himself; he is wholly of the Word, and his life is hidden in Christ Jesus.

But even the one who sits in Abraham’s bosom has been received by Christ. It would seem intolerably presumptuous to say to God, “Receive me,” unless he added God’s promise, namely: “You yourself made it possible for us to dare this. We appeal to you by your own written bond, since you took away our bond. We made a bond of death; you wrote a bond of life.”

27. “Therefore do not put your servant to shame in his expectation,” because I hope in you; for hope does not put to shame.

And if we are afflicted, you supply patience so that we may endure; so that, because I await you, I may not be overwhelmed by weaknesses, yield to temptations, or be distressed by storms in which patience must be tested, so that testing may follow—testing that confirms and strengthens hope and does not put it to shame.

This means: We are often broken by labors and wearied. If hope is absent, we are put to shame and disturbed in our whole mind. But suppose that some are hard against labors and firm in enduring injuries: if you take away hope, their patience cannot be lasting.

Patience itself is not tested if faith is absent, and hope is the root of faith. For what testing can there be unless you endure every hardship and danger for Christ’s name? Therefore hope alone is what does not put our affection to shame. Where hope exists, the apostolic saying, “Outside are conflicts, within are fears” (II Cor. VII, 5), cannot harm us.

28. [Note: Almost all manuscripts have: “Another interpretation: He will not be put to shame who hopes in Christ.”]

Another interpretation has: “Do not cause him to be ashamed.” “He will not be put to shame who hopes in Christ.” Therefore the one who hopes rightly says:

> “In you I trust; I shall not be put to shame” (Ps. XXIV, 2).

And he aptly says, “I trust,” for confidence is the strength of our hope and a certain authority belonging to the one who hopes.

Hope, therefore, always, and no one will put you to shame in your expectation. Our expectation is eternal life. Our expectation is the kingdom of God, fellowship with the angels, and spiritual blessings [1166]. Hope every day. This matter has no end; it knows no postponement.

Hope even when placed amid adversity. If someone says to you, struck perhaps by the loss of a relative, “What benefit does your righteousness bring you?”—still hope, and let your faith not fail.

If someone says to you, “What good did your daily fasts do you? What good did bodily chastity or modesty of mind do you? Behold, you have been wounded like the unjust and the ungodly”—let your faith not fail.

For even if you are weak, Christ, who is faithful, is concerned for you. He says to his disciples:

> “Give them something to eat yourselves” (Matt. XIV, 16),

so that they may not fail on the way.

[Note: Ambrose calls the readings of sacred Scripture “apostolic food,” and he urges that they precede reception of the Eucharist. From the words that follow—“you are weak … let him lay aside the fear of death and his anxieties … the body does not stumble but rises again”—we may reasonably suspect that the holy Doctor is speaking of the Eucharist as a viaticum. Perhaps, in confirmation of this suspicion, one may cite the Gospel passage that he praises, which other Fathers are also known to have interpreted as referring to viaticum. Thus Jerome, commenting on Matthew, chapter XV, says: “Jesus does not wish to dismiss them fasting, lest they fail on the way. The one who hastens to reach the desired dwelling without heavenly bread is therefore in danger,” etc.]

You have apostolic food: eat it, and you will not fail. Eat that first, so that afterward you may come to the food of Christ, to the food of the Lord’s body, to the banquet of the Sacrament, to that cup by which the affection of the faithful is made drunk; so that it may put on joy over the remission of sins and lay aside the cares of this world, the fear of death, and its anxieties.

By this intoxication, therefore, the body does not stagger but rises again; the soul is not put to shame but is consecrated.

29. **Verse 117.** It follows: “Help me,” he says, “and I shall be saved; and I shall meditate upon your justifications always.”

The one who hopes presumes that he will be helped; and where there is God’s assistance, there is certain aid for salvation. Above he said:

> “You are my helper and my protector” (above, v. 112).

Here again he asks to be helped, as though saying: “Help me without ceasing.” It is not enough for me that I have asked once; again I ask that I may be saved.

Here salvation is neither great nor true. I shall be saved then, when I am in paradise, when I begin to live among your chosen angels, when I have escaped the snares of this earth.

30. But lest, after being helped in our necessities, we later neglect when placed in prosperity, he teaches us that we must by no means be forgetful of heavenly benefits, but must meditate on the Lord’s ordinances, so that even when we have done something good, we may nevertheless always confess our sins to him; for this is the Lord’s justification. Indeed, the Pharisees did not justify God, since they refused to be baptized with the baptism of repentance (Luke 7:30).  

[Note: All editions: “Therefore he is justified.” All manuscripts: “Therefore he justifies.” This is suitable if one mentally supplies the word “God,” which is expressed in the preceding sentence.]

Therefore he justifies the one who repents of his sins. For the one who repents confesses, as in the passage: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words” (Psalm 50:6). Hence the Publican went away from the temple more justified (Luke 18:14), because the Pharisee justified himself by proclaiming his own righteousness, whereas the Publican justified God by confessing his own iniquities. Therefore whoever meditates on the Lord’s ordinances is always humbled.  

[Col. 1420D] He is not humbled today and exalted tomorrow; rather, he is always humble in heart and gentle in disposition. “Always” is more than “by day and by night,” or “all day long”; for it transcends time. Therefore, even if you are counted among the angels, you must always declare God’s ordinances, and you must not arrogate to your own merits the glory you have attained, but must always ascribe it to divine mercy, lest it be said to you: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). For every creature, whatever good it possesses, received it from Christ, who is the author of the whole creation.

1167 31. (Verse 118.) “You have despised,” he says, “all who depart from your ordinances, because their thought is unjust.” Every proud person is unclean in the sight of the Lord, because the one who heaps up error with an arrogant spirit cannot cleanse his sins through pride. Therefore he is scorned and despised, because he treats the divine commandments with contempt. Yet the heavenly prerogative of clemency is rightly preserved, because it rejects no one; rather, whoever is unwilling to confess his own sins is himself the one who departs from the Lord our God. Indeed, the one who departed was he who went away to a distant country and squandered everything he had received from his father—the inheritance of faith and grace. And because he repented of having departed, he later returned to the father whom he had abandoned, once he was unwilling to confess his own sin. God is not therefore abandoned by an interval of space, but by depraved conduct and distorted deeds. The one who distances himself from the Lord departs from him, just as Adam, after hearing of God’s presence, desired to hide. But by departing from the Lord he could not possess salvation, for it is written: “Behold, those who distance themselves from you shall perish” (Psalm 72:27). Each person, therefore, by his own pursuits either joins himself or separates himself. Indeed, that for many people distances between places do not separate them, while neighboring and nearby places join others together, is shown by the fact that many are situated in the body who are pilgrims away from the body and present with God—like the one who, when God said, “Whom shall I send?” replied: “Here am I; send me” (Isaiah 6:8). Paul too dares to be present with God, because he saw nothing bodily in himself except the substance of flesh. Cain also went out from the presence of God after committing fratricide and deciding that he need not undertake repentance for his sins.

32. [Note: Roman edition alone: “Rightly he says: ‘You have despised all who depart from their ordinances,’ or, as others have it, ‘You have brought to nothing,’ etc.”]
