Rightly, then, he says: “You have brought transgressors to nothing.” He did not say “sinners,” but “transgressors.” For what hope would there be for us, since we are all under sin? He also says beautifully: “You have brought all the transgressors of the earth to nothing.” Whether a man is rich, his riches profit him nothing; whether honored, his rank profits him nothing; whether powerful, his power profits him nothing. But it is one thing to be a transgressor who departs from God’s ordinances, and another to be a transgressor of the earth. The former is more serious; the latter is lighter.

33. (Verse 119.) Therefore, lest what follows disturb you, observe this: he added to these words, “I have considered all the sinners of the earth transgressors; therefore I have loved your testimonies always.”

[Note: The same Roman edition reads: “lest the preceding words disturb you, see what,” etc. But the old edition and the manuscripts read as in the text, except that “you” is omitted in the edition and several manuscripts, and “what” is also given in place of “for.”]

A transgressor is rightly called one who departs from the Lord. Indeed, in Greek he is called an apostate, from departing. Hence that saying: “Wine and women make one apostatize” (Sirach 19:2). We must therefore beware of the incentives and allurements of sins, lest they turn into crime.

In Latin, a transgressor is also called a transgressor, because he passes from the Lord’s law into error and transgresses the heavenly commandments—he to whom it was said that he should cling to the Lord his God (Deuteronomy 10:20). Cling, therefore, to him always with undivided devotion, lest any force be able to tear you away from him. If the adversary sees anything rare or interrupted in you, he immediately thrusts himself into your breast and heart, so that he may hold you in the snare of his deceit and, bound by the chain of hostile power, draw you back from devotion.

But he alone is not a transgressor who, having set the Church aside, crosses over to the worship of idols; rather, anyone who does not keep the commandments of the Law is also a transgressor. Every sinner, therefore, is a transgressor. Hence the saying: “Every transgression receives a just retribution” (Hebrews 2:2). The name is common, but the merits of the offenses differ; and therefore the penalties of the faults also differ.

34. What does he mean by saying, “the sinners of the earth”? Are there, then, also sinners of heaven, like the one who says, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15:21)? Some say that the person who does not preserve the heavenly oracles is a transgressor against heaven.

[Note: All editions: “But whether this or that is meant, we designate one as a sinner and the other as a transgressor, because …” The portion we have cut away is lacking in all manuscripts.]

But whether this is the meaning, or whether it is because he diminishes the grace that he received from heaven, which the Holy Spirit infused; or whether, having become a bird of heaven, he ought not to return from heaven to earth: you sin against heaven if, being an inhabitant of heaven, you abandon heaven. There is therefore a distinction between them. Some are sinners of heaven, others sinners of earth.

35. “In the mornings,” he says, “I was killing all the sinners of the earth” (Psalm 100:8). How could one person kill all the sinners of the earth? But if you consider the righteous person for whom the night has passed and the day has drawn near, you can see how, when the sun of righteousness rises upon you, you may, keeping watch in the light, kill all the impulses of sin. Would that this grace might breathe upon me, so that with the spiritual sword, which is the word of God, I might be able to destroy from the Lord’s Church every incentive to vice and remove earthly sins, by which we are hurled into a kind of pit of slippery error, so that the worker of iniquity may be expelled from the city of God.

The city of God is the Church; the Church is the body of Christ. He sins against heaven who defiles the rights of the heavenly city and violates the holiness of the immaculate body by the filth of his vices.

36. And see whether perhaps there are those who are sinners both of heaven and of earth. For certainly Adam, while he was in paradise, was heavenly; but after his fall he became earthly and was expelled and cast out of paradise. Hence the Apostle also says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:47). Therefore let the image of the earthly be cast away from us, and let us receive the image of the heavenly—not one represented by cosmetics, wax, or colors, but by conduct, in which Christ may recognize himself.

[Col. 1423A] 37. (Verse 120.) “Nail my flesh with nails because of your fear, for I have feared your judgments.” Whoever loves the Lord’s testimonies nails his flesh with nails, knowing that his old self, crucified with Christ, destroys the wantonness of the flesh, lest its desires run wild with uncontrolled ardor, lest the root of avarice spread itself through serpentine roots.

[Note: Eight manuscripts: “spread itself through serpentine roots.” As many others, and all editions, read as in our text.]

Therefore nail it with nails and destroy the incitements of sin. Let every enticement to wrongdoing die in your flesh; let the desire for pleasures, fastened to the cross, have no freedom to wander. There is a certain spiritual nail that fastens this flesh to the gibbet of the Lord’s cross. And perhaps the soul also has certain flesh, just as the body is the soul’s flesh. The flesh of the soul is carnal thought. Let the fear of the Lord and of his judgments fasten this flesh and bring it into servitude.

But if this flesh rejects the nails of divine fear, then without doubt it is said: “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3). Unless, therefore, this flesh is fastened to the cross and nailed because of the fear of our God, the Spirit of God will not remain in it.

1169 38. Just as there are goads of fear by which we are pricked, so there are nails of fear by which we are fastened. The one who is pricked is awakened; the one who is fastened is put to death, so that he may cease from sin and live for God. To show that the nails are spiritual, there are also spiritual goads, concerning which it is written: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5). Stirred by this goad, Paul rose from the earth and lifted himself up to live in heaven.

The apostle Thomas was fastened with nails so that he might say: “Unless I see in his hands the marks of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails …” (John 20:25). They were nails of good desire; they were nails of one whose faith was not yet perfect, but who was seeking an increase of faith.

39. The one who dies with Christ is fastened with these nails, so that he may rise with Christ. The one who carries the death of the Lord Jesus in his body is fastened with these nails. The one who deserves to hear Jesus say, “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as the grave” (Song of Songs 8:6), is fastened with these nails.

Fasten, then, this seal of the crucified one to your breast and your heart; fasten it also to your arm, so that your works may be dead to sin. Let no crime revive in them; let no error rise again. Perhaps this image is fastened by nails not only of fear but also of love, because “love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as the grave.” Do not, therefore, be offended by the hardness of the nails, because it is the hardness of love; nor by the powerful rigidity of the nails, because love too is strong as death.

For love puts guilt and all sins to death; love kills as the stroke of death. Indeed, we die to vice and sin while we love the Lord’s commandments. Love is God; the word of God is love, and it is powerful, sharper than every very sharp sword, penetrating even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow. The jealousy of love is therefore hard, for it does not yield even to the grave, when, for zeal for God, each person spares not even his own.

With these nails of love let our soul and our flesh be fastened, so that they too may say: “For I am wounded with love” (Song of Songs 5:8). Love therefore has its own nail; it has its own sword by which the soul is wounded. Blessed is the one who has deserved to be wounded by this sword. These are the wounds that are preferred to kisses: “Better are the wounds of a friend than the deceitful kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6).

40. Let us offer ourselves to these wounds; whoever has died by them will not be able to taste death. Such is the death of those who followed the Lord, of whom it was said: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matthew 16:28).

[Note: Namely Peter, James, and John, who were present at Christ’s Transfiguration, as is explained more fully below in the exposition of Luke 9:27.]

With good reason Peter did not fear this death; for he did not fear who said that, even if it were necessary for him to die for Christ, he would not leave or deny him (Matthew 26:35). Let us therefore take up the Lord’s cross, which may fasten our flesh and destroy sin. There is a fear that fastens the flesh: “Unless someone takes up his cross and follows me, he is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:38). For the one who possesses the fear of Christ is worthy, so that he may crucify carnal sin. Love follows this fear; buried with Christ, it is not separated from Christ, dies in Christ, is entombed with Christ, and rises with Christ.

SERMON SIXTEEN. Ain.

[Col. 1424C]

1. The sixteenth letter, Ain, begins; its interpretation is “eye,” or “spring.”  

[Note: Thus all manuscripts. But the editions read, “We use the eye for the function of seeing.”]

The eye makes use of the function of seeing; but often we see things that please us, and often things that displease us. The eye itself is neither at fault nor virtuous according to the quality of what it sees; its duty is to report what it has seen. Yet there is either offense or grace when it is delighted by pleasant things or offended by adverse ones. Therefore it is frequently called the eye of punishments, the eye of temptation, the eye of the kid, the eye of the heifer, the eye of generation, or the spring of generation.

2. We read in the Gospel that John was baptizing at Ennon (John 3:23). They have interpreted Ennon as “the eye of punishments.” Therefore no one comes to baptism except one who desires his own sins to be forgiven and, with a watchful heart, dreads their punishments. Thus, although it is called the eye of punishments, it is nevertheless the eye of one who foresees punishments, not of one who undergoes them—even though the baptism of repentance includes some endurance of receiving punishments. It is the eye’s function to perform the duty of looking; it is your responsibility to beware of what you see.

[Col. 1425A] 3. Hence it is also called the eye of temptation, because we are often tempted through the eye. The eye of a prostitute is the lover’s snare. But the eye commits no sin; therefore the Savior’s judgment is filled with justice when he says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). He did not say, “Whoever looks at a woman,” but “whoever looks in order to desire her.” He acquitted the eye and bound the mind. Nor did he say, “He committed adultery with her in the eye,” but “in the heart.” In the eye there was sight; in the heart, sin.

4. The eye of the kid is the one on the left, because a sinner cannot see the things that are on the right. But the holy man says: “I kept the Lord always before my eyes, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken” (Psalm 15:8). And when the holy apostle Peter had caught nothing all night, as we read in the Gospel, the Savior said to him: “Cast the nets on the right side of the boat” (John 21:6). Trusting in the heavenly command, he cast the nets and gathered a very great number of fish. On the left there was night; on the right the daylight-brightness of the divine word shone.

[Note: The manuscripts read, “lasting brightness,” a reading that can be defended if “lasting” is used for “constant and perpetual.” Here, however, the editions seem preferable, since they create an antithesis with the preceding member.]

5. There is also the eye of the heifer, which likewise refers to sinners, because just as heifers draw iniquities with a continuous rope—not breaking or cutting off what is their own [the reading is uncertain], but dragging sin along with a long cord—so do they. For an untamed heifer is tamed only late, and it drags the reins rather than accepting them, because it cannot bear to be held; and the longer it drags them, the more it is impeded.

6. It is also called the eye of generation, or the spring of generation, because from the sight of the eyes either good things or adverse things are generated. You saw the beauty of a woman and praised the work of the craftsman, the loveliness of nature: this was the generation of faith, the offspring of devotion. You were content with the beauty of her form, did not count wealth as the object of ambition, and took her as your wife; she bore children of more generous grace. Your eye was the generation of prosperity.

You contemplated a holy girl, and the reverence of august chastity restrained your eyes. You praised the Lord Jesus, who had given the gravity of old age to a young girl and infused an immaculate life among human affections, amid the weak enticements of this slippery flesh: this is the spring of good things.

You saw the possessions of orphans, not in order to seize them but to protect them, and with a father’s compassion you grieved if you noticed that anything belonging to the child’s interests had been neglected. You drove away the man who wished to invade his boundaries; you judged in favor of the orphan. Your eye became for you a spring and origin of justice.

You judged in favor of a widow—for just as a bad drachma is no drachma, so a bad judgment is not truly a judgment. You judged, therefore, as a just and good judge. You saw the wicked usurper who considered as his prey the woman deprived of her husband’s protection. You did not tolerate injustice; you gave aid to the defenseless woman. With the protection thus supplied, she practiced chastity without hindrance and was not compelled to seek the assistance of a husband. The Lord says to you: “Come, let us reason together” (Isaiah 1:18). Because you judged in favor of the widow, your eye became for you a spring of grace.

You saw the naked body of a poor dead man lying there; you did not pass by, like the priest and Levite in the Gospel who are mentioned (Luke 10:31–32), but, immediately taking pity, you committed him to the consolations of burial. Your eye generated for you the material of redemption.

7. But if, on the contrary, when looking upon an orphan’s field planted with vines, rich in crops, shady groves, flowing streams, bubbling springs, or grassy couches along the banks, you were inflamed by the torches of avarice, moved the boundaries of your fathers, and wickedly invaded the defenseless possession, your eye generated for you the bitter fruit of perpetual death.

You violated the rights of a neighboring widow and compelled her—although she ought to have nursed either her grief or her modesty enclosed behind private walls—to burst into public view and litigate with greater shamelessness than injustice. Your eye became the offspring of iniquity.

You looked upon the poor man with a proud eye and an insatiable heart; you despised the poor man’s prayer, and passed by with disdain the one whom you ought to have pitied. Your eye became for you a spring and origin of sin.

8. Therefore let your eyes not be the eyes of a wolf, lying in wait for prey, but let them be as is said of the Bride: “Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, by the gates of the daughter of multitudes; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon” (Song of Songs 7:4).

[Note: A large part of the manuscripts reads, “as is said of the Bridegroom.”]

What are the pools in Heshbon except an abundance of rational thoughts, which is found at the gates of the Church, to which a multitude of teaching is rightly entrusted? For she is the daughter of multitudes, brought forth as the offspring of many teachings, whose nose is the fragrance of sacrifices surpassing all flowers.

For what is higher than the fragrance of Christ, which abolished the burning fragrance of incense? Let this eye therefore foresee the things that are to come; and if it foresees adversities approaching, let it not cease to soften and mitigate them by weeping and tears.

9. Therefore Jeremiah, placed in the captivity of the Jewish nation and foreseeing the future hardship of perpetual captivity, which the Jewish people had to pay as the price of their faithlessness, said in the Lamentations under this same letter: “For this I weep; my eyes have grown dim from weeping, because the one who consoled me has gone far from me” (Lamentations 1:15–16).

He was not therefore grieving that he had been led away from his lands, but that the people would be abandoned by Christ; and he perceived that the consolation of the future life had been lost. This is truly the captivity to be lamented, which seemed deprived of freedom and of the hope of eternity.

In another passage, under this same letter, he repeated in the Lamentations: “The Lord has fulfilled what he planned; he has accomplished his word, which he commanded from ancient days. He destroyed and did not spare; he made the enemy rejoice over you and exalted the horn of the one who afflicted you” (Lamentations 2:17). Is not the future judgment of Christ clearly announced, just as it is certainly made evident in the psalm under discussion as well? Let the eye therefore foresee the things that are to come, and let it turn them aside either by an outpouring of tears or by correcting error. Indeed, Jeremiah wept because he had taken up the evil cause of the impious people, who in the stubbornness of their faithlessness denied their own author.

10. (Verse 121.) But David, foreseeing by the prophetic spirit the judgment of Christ, in which no innocent person will be endangered and no criminal will escape, says with a good conscience: “I have practiced judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who harm me.”

He does not praise himself as though he were boastful and insolent, since, being learned in the Law, he certainly knew that everyone should be praised by another’s mouth rather than by his own.

[Note: All editions: “there is here no boasting of a preacher’s virtues.” Quite a few manuscripts: “boasting of the aforesaid virtues,” etc. Yet five others are preferable, as in the text.]

There is not, I say, here any boastful display of the virtues proclaimed, but a rightly presumed assertion of an innocent life, lest he be considered worthy to be abandoned by the Lord on account of grave sins and handed over to the power of the guilty.

It is therefore a defense, not arrogance, when no exceptional honor is claimed, but a fearful calamity is driven away. Indeed, Peter uses this kind of defense when he says: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?” (Matthew 19:27). If there had been in this statement some disfiguring mark of arrogance, he would not have received so much grace from the judgment of the Lord and Savior (ibid. 28), so that he would be announced not only as one who should by no means be subjected to judgment, but also as one who would judge the merits of others.

For if someone, in order to defend his innocence, revealed what he had done, it would not be judged to have been said for boasting rather than for the defense of his case. It is one thing to say that one is worthy of a reward, another to say that one is unworthy of punishment.

11. And yet that very man who was, as they say, the supreme teacher of philosophy, when he was accused and asked what punishment he thought himself worthy of, is reported to have replied that he should be received daily at a public banquet in the Prytaneum.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “as at a public dinner”; others, and the editions, “in the Prytaneum.” The latter is preferable. The Prytaneum was a place at Athens where, at public expense, those who had rendered distinguished service to the state and the victors in public contests were fed. Plato records this response in the Apology of Socrates as follows: “If, then, I must be honored according to justice for what I deserve, I am honored with a meal in the Prytaneum.” See also Cicero, On the Orator, book 1.]

That man claimed honor; this one averted calamity.

[Note: The Ambrosian edition reads, “he prayed for calamity.” Erasmus and others corrected it to “he averted calamity.” This is not unreasonable, if even one manuscript supported it. Likewise below, in Sermon 17, section 22, the editions read, “which he rightly prayed for,” where the manuscripts have, “which he rightly averted.” Anyone can see that the latter reading makes good sense in both places.]

The former arrogated glory to himself; the latter preserved humility. For what greater humility could there be than for one conscious of judgment and of the justice reserved for him to fear being handed over to the devil’s power? He recognized that he was a human being, unequal to himself in the struggle against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. He knew that Enoch had been taken away lest wickedness change his heart; that Noah became drunk; that Lot was involved in incest; that Aaron himself, the first priest, was tested together with his sister Miriam; that Miriam was first covered with the spots of leprosy and afterward cleansed; and that Moses was nearly put to death, unless Zipporah, his wife, had driven every danger away from him by the circumcision of their son and the shedding of that blood.

Warned, therefore, by these examples, he by no means trusts in his own strength. Rather, cautious humility obtains divine help for itself by prayer, asking not to be handed over to those who harm him.

12. For he knows that the prince of the world is the author of all sins. He himself tears apart the inseparable affections of neighbors, stirred up by the goads of anger; he himself kindles the flame of lust; he himself fans the desires of avarice, so that the more we seize, the more we may seek; he himself suggests and supplies the incentives of wantonness; he himself intensifies hatred and inflames the pursuit of immoderate ambition.

This vice, gentle at its beginning and savage as it advances, could not be recalled even by consideration of brotherly kinship. While he grieved that his brother had been preferred to him by the heavenly favor he coveted, he proceeded from sacrifice to fratricide.

The Apostle teaches that the devil is the author of incontinence: “Do not tempt one another because of your lack of self-control” (1 Corinthians 7:5). We also read that he is the instigator of avarice, as Paul says: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil” (1 Timothy 6:9). And elsewhere: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5).

In these things we do the devil’s will and carry out his power; through the desires of this flesh he works the incentive of his deceit.

13. Therefore, whoever he finds in possession of his own vices, he claims as subject to his jurisdiction. Whoever commits adultery, practices wantonness, or seizes what belongs to another is the devil’s portion; but the chaste, self-controlled, and merciful person is Christ’s portion.

He cannot claim Christ’s servant for himself unless he happens to discover that the servant has fallen into vices; and even then he does not claim him as his own, but asks that he be handed over to him as his own. Therefore David says: “I have practiced judgment and justice,” not to boast, but to excuse himself, lest, as a sinner, he be abandoned by Christ.

Let the apostolic reading show us why someone is handed over. Concerning the man who had his father’s wife, the Apostle says: “I handed him over to Satan” (1 Corinthians 5:4–5), because he had acted in this way.

[Note: All editions: “The Apostle handed him over to Satan.” Quite a few manuscripts read, “as the Apostle says.” Others have partly, “the Apostle says that he should be handed over to Satan,” and partly, “I handed him over.” We believe the latter reading should be preferred here.]

He would not therefore have been handed over unless he had done the devil’s works. Hence the prophet is not without reason unwilling to be handed over to those who harm him, since he declares that he has done not the devil’s works but Christ’s. For Christ says: “Judge for the orphan; justify the widow” (Isaiah 1:17). This, then, is the meaning: “I have practiced judgment and justice”: in judgment I did not despise the poor, I did not oppress the widow, I did not show favoritism to the rich; in all my works I preserved justice.

14. The end of judgment is justice. In one there is the preservation of truth; in the other, the fruit of equity. Yet neither is a private virtue, but a public one.

To preserve an immaculate body from sexual intercourse, and to carry the palm of chastity through a body of clay to the fellowship of the angels by guarding one’s integrity, is a private benefit but a public praise. To be thrifty and modest and to maintain the measure of sober restraint is approved by many, but benefits only the individual.

Courage shines in battles and grows cold in leisure; its work is necessary in due season, but contrary to one’s wishes, for people prefer not to fight rather than to win. Justice alone is born for others more than for itself at all times; through daily practice and public benefit, at its own cost it guards the interests of others. It has no utility for itself, but possesses abundant praise.

The Prophet therefore brings this forward to commend his own merit, saying: “I have practiced judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who harm me.” Where there is justice, there is mercy. Mercy frees from sin. How, then, am I handed over to sinners?

There is a similar passage in the Song of Songs: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song of Songs 5:3–4). I have taken off the sinner’s tunic, the covering of the earthly person; why am I judged as though I were a sinner and an earthly man? I have washed my feet, lest any share of sin cling to my footsteps; why do you give those who sin power over me?

15. (Verse 122.) It follows: “Receive your servant in goodness; let not the proud slander me.” As one conscious of judgment and justice, he proceeds with prophetic authority, so that he does not shrink from calling himself the Lord’s servant. For the Lord’s servant owes nothing to outsiders. Precious is this servitude, which is established at the expense of the virtues.

But he clearly explains why he fears being handed over to those who harm him: they are slanderers who hate the truth and attack innocence because they are proud. For what kind of pride can be directed against the servants of God by one who exalts himself against God and says: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will sit upon the high mountain, above the lofty mountains that are toward the north; I will ascend above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13–14)?

What wonder, then, if he can oppress human beings, when in his obstinate spirit he does not yield even to God? How will he preserve the measure of truth and faithfulness toward a human being, when with sacrilegious and shameless falsehood he promises that he will be equal to the omnipotent Lord?

[Note: All editions: “How does he not slander individuals?” All manuscripts: “How does he slander individuals?” The latter is not unsuitable if understood as spoken ironically.]

How does he slander individuals, he who stirred up the whole earth, shook kings, made the entire world desolate, and destroyed cities? Did he not release those who were in captivity?

16. Let us therefore beware lest he destroy the walls of our soul, overthrow the fortifications of our mind, or set his throne above the stars. He sets it above the stars when he deceives the chosen, when he ensnares the righteous, whose works shine like the stars in heaven.

Did not Judas the betrayer hear, together with the others: “You are the light of this world” (Matthew 5:14)? Did not the devil extinguish his light? Indeed, those whom he could not ensnare, he slanders, envying the glory of the heavenly kingdom, so that he may attempt to defraud of the fruit of their deserved honor those whom he could not separate from Christ by his enticements.

Let us therefore flee evil slanderers, who work sin in us and then prepare slanders against us with the fiercest accusation, blaming us for what they themselves have done. Behold, the hand of the Lord is ready to guard and protect you as you flee from your adversaries.

Proud and pitiless Pharaoh held you among your fathers; you fled from him, and the hand of the Lord received you and freed you from dangers. Pharaoh would not have let you go unless you had fled to the Lord. Pharaoh said: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exodus 5:2). Do you see how proud he was? Rightly, then, the one who flees evil is received in goodness.

God therefore does not permit us to remain in evil; he receives us in goodness, nor does he allow his own people to be subjected to slanders.

17. (Verse 123.) “My eyes have failed in your salvation and in the word of your justice.” Consider what eyes these are that fail in Christ while awaiting his coming: the eyes of the soul, not of the body, fixed with the full concentration of faith. For in the one whom we love we are wholly occupied with our eyes, and we take no pleasure in seeing anything else.

No one can say this except one who has turned all the attention of his mind away from worldly concerns and secular pleasures. For how can one say this who is occupied with the mockeries of the theater? But he says it who earlier said: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity” (Sermon 5, verse 37).

And what are the eyes that fail in the word of God except the eyes of the inner person and the gaze of the soul, which are stretched out to see the word of God and fail through excessive concentration and expectation in God’s salvation, enduring their own exhaustion so that they may take up what belongs to the word?

18. And because the word of God can move many people, he therefore added, “the word of justice,” so that it ought not to cause disturbance. It could indeed cause disturbance, because it is written: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). For unless you understand it as a mystery, it is an injury to nature.

And: “I gave you commandments that were not good” (Ezekiel 20:25). Therefore God gives bad commandments. And: “I am the Lord, creating evil” (Isaiah 45:7).

But the matter of the commandments is resolved in this way: he ought not to have given the weak perfect commandments, which they could not endure. When would a Jew have heard: “Give up all that you have … and follow me” (Matthew 19:21)? When would a Jew have heard: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:38)? But these more perfect commandments were reserved for the Gospel.

Nor did God create evil; rather, he created those things that seem harsh to us—beatings, death, and other such things—which have been prescribed for the correction of the guilty. For the law was not made for the righteous, but for the unrighteous. If the guilty feared nothing, the innocent would always be afraid.

19. Who, then, are these eyes that fail in the salvation of God? We have said that the eye of punishments is the eye which, foreseeing the future punishments of sinners, announces that repentance must be undertaken. John the Baptist demonstrated this eye when he said: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3:7–8). For the one who possessed the eye of punishments came to the baptism of John; but the one who sees grace came to the baptism of Christ. This is the eye protected and sheltered by the shadow of the Lord’s passion.

Thus Ennon is one thing, and Ain another. In Ennon the one conscious of grave offenses is baptized; but whoever has a pure eye receives spiritual grace. Perhaps the eye of punishments belongs to the imperfect soul, while the eye of graces belongs to the perfect soul—purer and more sincere. This is signified by the present letter, toward which the righteous person’s pattern is directed; for the imperfect person merely desires to avoid the judgment of sin, whereas the perfect person seeks to acquire the merit of the heavenly kingdom.

Nevertheless, we presume that one soul possesses both eyes: the eye of punishments and the eye of grace—the left eye of punishments, the right eye of grace—for human beings cannot become perfect from the beginning but ascend through the progress of virtue. Thus every soul first comes, as it were, to the baptism of John, so that it may precede it with repentance for its offenses; and, as it gradually progresses, once it has wept over its sins, it is washed with spiritual baptism and receives the sacrament of Christ. Hence the Church also appears to be praised in the Song of Songs, where it is said: “You have captured our heart, my sister, Bride; you have captured our heart with one of your eyes” (Song 4:9). May this eye, then, be the eye of grace, which has acquired for itself the fuller love of Christ.

20. Nevertheless, many understand this passage as referring to the two eyes of the Church: one that sees mystical things, the other moral things; for the holy Church not only maintains the discipline of morals but also teaches the secrets of the heavenly mystery. Hence it is said of her: “Your eyes are like doves, apart from your silence” (ibid., 1)—that is, she sees spiritually and knows that there is a time for keeping silence and a time for speaking, so that she may bring forth her word at the proper time and not incur sin through untimely speech.

21. She therefore has the eyes of a dove, in the likeness of Christ; for it is also written of him: “Your eyes are like doves over an abundance of waters, bathed in milk, sitting upon fullness” (Song 5:12). The Lord baptizes in milk, that is, in sincerity. Those, then, are truly baptized in milk who believe without deceit and bring pure faith, so that they may put on undefiled grace.

Therefore the Bride ascends to Christ in white, because she has been baptized in milk. Therefore the Virtues and Powers marvel at her, saying: “Who is this who ascends made white?” (Song 8:7). A little earlier she was saying, “I am black” (Song 1:4); now she is seen made white and ascends to heaven, and, leaning upon the Word of God, already penetrates the heights.

Nor is it without reason that there is an abundance of waters where Christ is, so that the human mind may desire to be filled. The stag thirsts for these waters; once it has drunk them, it can thirst no more. The Prophet thirsted for these waters when he said: “My soul thirsted for you” (Ps. 41:3). Christ therefore sits upon an abundance of waters and upon fullness.

[Note: Fourteen manuscripts have this reading. The Roman edition alone has: “And therefore he who baptizes in water.” Other editions and two manuscripts, both omitting that reading, append to the word “fullness”: “Hence we have all received from his fullness” (John 1:16).]

And therefore the one who is baptized in milk says: “And we have all received from his fullness” (John 1:16). Hence the eye of punishments is not foreign to the Church; for although John baptized in Ennon, he baptized near Salim, where there was an abundance of water, twelve springs, and seventy palm trees (John 3:25).

22. The Church possesses these springs: in the Old Testament, the twelve patriarchs; in the New, the twelve apostles. Therefore it is said: “In the assembly let us bless the Lord God from the springs of Israel” (Ps. 67:27). Whoever receives the holy mysteries of Christ is first drenched by these springs; for these springs, flowing from the eternal fountain, have spread throughout the whole world.

Where these springs are, there is the ascent of souls. Indeed, they interpreted Salim as “the One ascending.” For the one who truly ascends is the person who lays aside his own sins. This expression therefore conveys the work of purifying sanctification.

Hence Christ also appropriately says to the Church in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and none among them is barren” (Song 4:2). What is said literally of goats is understood mystically of the flock of the Church.

23. Do not therefore regard these animals as worthless. Indeed, hear what the Holy Spirit says about them: “Your hair is like a flock of shorn sheep that have been revealed from Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (Song 6:4, 7). You see that this flock grazes in high places and is bold upon the mountain.

Thus, where there are precipices for others, there is no danger for the goats; where there is danger for others, there is the nourishment of this flock, sweeter food, and choicer fruit. They are seen by their shepherds hanging from the thickets of the crag; there the attacks of wolves cannot occur, and there fruitful trees supply sound fruit. One may see them swollen with abundant milk and tenderly concerned, with maternal devotion, for their young offspring. Therefore the Holy Spirit chose them as the likeness of the assembly of the venerable Church.

24. And, if you would hear it mystically: the hair of the Word is the height and a certain loftiness of righteous souls, since “the understanding of the wise is in his head.” It is certain that wisdom exists in the height of human thought.

And just as goats are shorn so that they may lay aside what is superfluous, so holy Church possesses a flock of shorn souls—that is, the virtues of many souls—in which you can find nothing senseless [Note: “Senseless,” that is, alien to the understanding of the wise, as the whole sequence of the discourse makes clear], nothing superfluous; for faith has made them wise, while spiritual grace has cleansed them from every stain of superfluity.

25. Rightly, then, the souls of the righteous have been revealed, and revealed from Mount Gilead—that is, from the “migration of testimony”—because the heavenly testimony migrated from the Synagogue to the Church.

Thus on this mountain frankincense, resin, and the other spices are produced, which those Ishmaelite merchants, as you find in the first book of the Old Testament, were carrying (Gen. 37:25). The Church possesses these spices, which merchants gathered from the nations and brought with faith and devotion.

Thus, just as goats, refreshed with good food and flourishing in the warmth of the sun, wash themselves in the river and rise joyfully, clean, from the river, so the souls of the righteous ascend from the spiritual washing.

26. These are truly the ones that bear twins, in whom there is no barrenness of virtues or sterility of merits. They bear twins well because they make their understandings twin. Hence you have it written in Proverbs: “And write these things for yourself threefold, in counsel and knowledge” (Prov. 22:20). He first mentioned a threefold writing, and then added two things, counsel and knowledge; but knowledge is twofold: one knowledge of incorporeal things, the other of corporeal things.

27. We have spoken of their fruitfulness; let us speak of their teeth. For many people, whether sailing or hurrying along a land journey, when they have seen some beautiful place, linger there for pleasure, feast their eyes, and lift up their spirits; and the delay is not considered an interruption of the journey but a pleasure. So it is also a delight for us to contemplate the most beautiful teeth of righteous souls.

Scripture taught that the teeth of the righteous are most beautiful when it said, literally of the patriarch Judah but spiritually of Christ: “His eyes are cheerful with wine, and his teeth are like milk” (Gen. 49:12). In this passage it certainly praised not the functions of human flesh but the gifts of divine grace. The example therefore teaches that teeth should not be passed over when we have spoken of eyes.

28. What, then, are the teeth of righteous souls except those which, receiving food that is shapeless and hard—often cold or excessively hot—now crush it, now warm it, now temper it, according to the quality of the nourishment?

They crush what is hard, lest the harshness of the letter in the Old Testament and the rigor of secular understanding, unless dissolved by a spiritual tooth, should block the very vital passages of nourishing food and, through the soul’s heedless greed, suffocate its throat. Therefore it is right first to divide the food, if what is being received seems solid to you; then distinguish it and, once softened, distribute it without harm to the soul throughout all its members by a natural division, so that its whole body may feed upon the vital sap.

Take nothing cadaverous, nothing dead, into your mouth, lest it be said: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Ps. 13:3). Rather, draw in the living word, so that it may work within the innermost parts of your mind.

29. These teeth are whiter than milk, because they are the teeth of the righteous. Indeed, although all our fathers were baptized in Moses, in the cloud and in the sea, it was not without purpose that it was written: “All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10:3–4). This was so that a greater brightness might be added to these teeth of the saints.

After the crossing of the Red Sea, we know that they were cleansed by the bitterness of the spring of myrrh, tempered through the grace of the wood (Exod. 15:25, 27), then by the drink of the twelve springs, and finally by the irrigation of the spiritual rock that poured forth water—for the rock was Christ. Therefore they also ate manna (Num. 20:11), so that, washed so many times, they might eat the bread that is written to be “the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25).

Even now, in the mysteries of the Gospel, you recognize that, although baptized in the whole body, you are afterward cleansed by spiritual food and drink.

[Note: The editions, and not a few manuscripts, read: “You recognize that, although baptized … to be cleansed.” But the manuscripts agree with us, except for a few, where instead of “throughout the whole body” one reads “with the body dipped.” Either reading can be admitted in this final clause; the former nevertheless seems preferable. For it signifies not only that baptism was customarily administered by immersion, but also opposes the absurdity of certain heretics who claimed that all parts of the body were to be defiled, as Theodoret states in Book IV of his Heretical Fables. Consult Ambrose, Book II of On the Mysteries, chapter 3, and the author of the treatise On the Sacraments, Book II, chapter 7, for a fuller discussion of immersion.]

30. Rightly, therefore, David, with his inner eyes purified and his teeth as though illuminated by the whiteness of spiritual teeth, utters these words: “I have practiced judgment and righteousness” (above, v. 121). That is the true radiance of the teeth, where the harmonious confession of a mind conscious of its own goodness resounds.

That is the clean eye which no beam of grave sins has weighed down and no speck of slight impurities has disturbed. This eye failed in the word of righteousness. For “whoever adheres to Christ is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

Balaam, too, asked that his soul might fail among the souls of the righteous (Num. 23:10)—that is, that he might forget his own error, lay aside what belonged to him, and take up what belonged to righteousness and equity. But let us proceed to the rest.

31. (Verse 124.) It follows: “Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your righteous judgments.” He has paved the way and anticipated the increase of his commendation. Above, he asked not to be handed over to the harmful (above, vv. 121–122); again he asked to be received for good, lest the proud should calumniate him. That is: “I do not avoid judgment, but the calumny of the faithless; for they do not know how to judge, but they do know how to calumniate.”

“To you I flee, who know how to present judgment” [Note: “To present judgment” means the same as “to exhibit judgment,” or to render judgment in the present. Codex Theodosianus VIII, title 18, law 42]. And rightly he does not wish to be handed over to calumniators; for righteous Job suffered many things after he was handed over to the evil one. Yet that was a difficult and great contest (Job 2:6), which scarcely anyone except Job, with his extraordinary patience, could have overcome. Nevertheless, he was not handed over entirely, but was received in the better portion.

The one who says, “Do not hand me over” (above, v. 121), comprehends what is greater. We are more in the soul than in the flesh; for it is said to the righteous: “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit” (Rom. 8:9). He therefore refuses to have his soul handed over who was wasting away in body like a spider (Ps. 38:12).

32. At this point, therefore, presuming upon a greater familiarity, he says: “Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your righteous judgments.” He asks that mercy be shown him, and that he be taught righteousness.

Elsewhere also, that is, in the later passages, you find this meaning: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant” (Ps. 142:2). For, conscious of our sins, we ought to ask our God for mercy rather than implore judgment.

[Note: The edition reads: “To some he grants pardon, to others he assigns examination.” Several manuscripts have “To some … to others,” and so forth. The great majority, as in the text, read as follows.]

“To some he grants pardon; to others he assigns examination.” What hope is there for human beings of contending before one whom hidden things do not deceive, from whom sins cannot be concealed? Therefore, knowing his power, he who would not fear a human being said: “Against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. 50:6).

The righteous cannot deny this, because no one is without sin. Nor can a king deny it; for although he has the power of the laws, so that he may sin with impunity, he is nevertheless subject to God [Note: Thus the manuscripts read. The editions add after “who owes nothing to anyone”: “Yet he is subject to God,” and so forth]. Indeed, he himself owes more, since more has been entrusted to him.

33. This, then, is what he says: “Deal with your servant according to your mercy”; for even if I have done something good, as a servant I owe more. A servant is not acquitted by one deed; for no one who has a servant plowing or tending sheep says to him, “Go away and recline,” but says: “Prepare what I am to eat, gird yourself, and serve me. . . .”

[Note: The edition and a few manuscripts read: “Does he thank the servant?” The Greek text and the Latin versions support this reading. Other manuscripts have: “The servant …” This is not unreasonable if one observes that “thanks” here has the same meaning as “merit.” The Persian and Ethiopic translations also render the Evangelist’s passage in this way; they may be consulted in the English Polyglot.]

“Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded him?” (Luke 17:7–8). Therefore, even when we have done what was commanded us, we must not immediately exalt ourselves but rather humble ourselves; for, simply because we have done something, we have not immediately fulfilled every duty of servitude.

Who could equal with worthy service the great gifts of nature, and the divine benefits of life and preserved health? Who can repay what he has received? Therefore, knowing all things, he asks for mercy rather than a hearing [Note: Several manuscripts read “rather than wisdom.” The Roman edition has “rather than an excuse.” Other manuscripts and the ancient edition more correctly have “rather than a hearing”—that is, rather than being granted an opportunity to defend his case]: “For,” he says, “no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2).

34. (Verse 125.) The fifth verse follows: “I am your servant; give me understanding, and I shall know your testimonies.” Understanding is a spiritual gift, and therefore what belongs to God is requested from the Lord. He does not ask as a stranger, since he confesses himself to be a servant. Well does he say: “I am your servant.” For a servant does his master’s will.

A servant seeks the wages of servitude; a servant hopes for a reward [Note: Earlier editions read: “He does not hope for a reward.” The manuscript reading, “He hopes for a reward,” is better. For, besides daily provisions, a personal allowance, and other wages of servitude, a servant also aspires to manumission. Below, where the manuscripts read “but not so as to be superfluous,” the editions had removed the negation. That is less suitable, as will be clear to anyone who considers the passage more carefully].

The servant of the Lord cannot at the same time be a servant of sin. Therefore he asks that understanding be given him, so that he may know how to avoid sin. He did possess understanding, but not in such a way that he considered it sufficient for himself; he seeks a fuller understanding.

35. There is, however, an understanding belonging to nature, and there is an understanding that is not good. Therefore Solomon also says: “Good understanding gives grace” (Prov. 13:15). For if every understanding were good, the qualification would not have been necessary.

Rightly he seeks the grace of his Lord, for he cannot otherwise know the Lord’s secrets unless he receives the gift of spiritual understanding. You have this in Jeremiah: “Make it known to me, Lord, and I shall know” (Jer. 11:18); for unless God makes his mystery known to human beings, we cannot know it.

36. (Verse 126.) The sixth verse follows: “It is time to act, Lord; the wicked have destroyed your law.” He rightly says that it is time to act. “For there is a time for silence and a time for speaking” (Eccl. 3:7). But the time for speaking has arrived, and thus he declares that the time of the Lord’s coming is already present.

Since there has been transgression of the Law, let the end of the Law come, its completion and fullness: the Lord Jesus, who grants human beings forgiveness for all offenses; and, having abolished the record of debts, releases and frees all sinners.

It is time to act, just as, when someone’s illness is growing more severe, you run to the physician so that he may come more quickly, lest afterward he be unable to help. The physician is desired all the more when a serious illness has settled upon the sick person.

Thus, when the holy Prophet sees in the Spirit the transgressions of the people—their luxury, pleasures, deceit, fraud, greed, and drunkenness—he intervenes, as it were, on our behalf and runs to Christ, whom he knew alone could help with such great sins. He presses him to come and does not permit delay.

“It is time to act, Lord”—that is, for you to ascend the cross on our behalf and undergo death. The whole world is being driven toward the final danger: come, that you may take away the sin of the world. Let life come to those who are dying; let resurrection come to those who are already buried. Let your deed come to our aid, since even your commandments could not help.

In the Law there was a command; in the Gospel, a ministry [Note: All editions and not a few manuscripts read “in the Gospel, a mystery.” The Codex Remensis, Corbeiensis, Vindobonensis, and one Navarrus manuscript more correctly have “a ministry.” The meaning is that what had been commanded in the Law was presented or fulfilled by Christ in the Gospel].

37. The whole people was blind and did not see its own author. The world was lame and, with its step faltering, wavered in faith. There was no salve to apply, no oil, no bandage.

That Gospel woman had spent all her resources on physicians (Luke 8:43), representing the gathering of the human race that was assembled from the nations; yet the physicians of this age could not restrain her flowing blood, the deadly discharge of a long-standing disease.

The offspring of the ruler of the people had perished, and all his inheritance had died. Seeing these things, the Prophet says to Christ: “It is time to act, Lord”—not, he says, to command, but to act; for it was not an ambassador or messenger but the Lord who was to save his people.

He knew the time and did not delay; but we did not know at what better time he might come to our aid [Note: The editions added after “he might come to our aid”: “And now he has come, and departed, and again wishes to come, and not to know the time.” This is a foolish gloss, found in no manuscripts].

38. Or perhaps he wishes to be admonished by us; he wishes to be asked. Indeed, if he is asked, he comes before the time.

He came to the fig tree, and he came before the hour, as he says to his mother. She was asking on our behalf; she was hastening, saying: “They have no wine, son.” Jesus replied: “What is that to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John 2:3–4).

And the mother, who knew his affection, says to the servants: “Whatever he tells you, do it” (ibid., 5). Jesus too, who had denied that his hour had come, did what he had earlier deferred; for God did everything in its own time. Whatever he does is not outside its time, but everything he does is opportune.

And it comes to me in its own time; for every time is opportune for salvation, and nothing is premature when it concerns the salvation of those in danger. But he wished to await further correction of the Synagogue.

Therefore he came to the fig tree before the time (Mark 11:13): that is, he came quickly to the Jews, opportunely to the Gentiles; he came quickly to those who were perishing, suitably to those who would believe.

39. (Verse 127.) The seventh verse follows: “Therefore I loved your commandments more than gold and topaz.” The Law is the herald of Christ. Therefore the precepts of the Law convey the hope of future blessings.

For the commandment of the Lord is: “Take heed to yourself; do not forsake the Levite throughout all the days that you live upon the earth” (Deut. 12:19). Who is this Levite? You understand if you consider who it is that came to minister, who is priest forever.

Another commandment says: “Observe the month of new produce, and you shall keep the Passover to the Lord your God” (Deut. 16:1). And below: “In the place which the Lord your God will choose for his name to be invoked, there you shall slaughter the Passover in the evening, at sunset, at the time when you came out of Egypt” (ibid., 6).

Therefore the commandments of God contain signs of the future redemption and emblems of the resurrection. Hence he declares that they are dearer to him than gold and topaz. For what is sweeter than salvation, or more precious than resurrection?

40. Or because Christ chose what is foolish in the world, so that, since the world did not know God through wisdom, he might bring salvation to believers through the foolishness of preaching, therefore he says: “Above the wisdom of heavenly operation, and of the world’s constitution, and above the precious ornaments of the sun and moon and the costly necklaces of the stars, I loved obedience to the Lord’s passion.”

For in redeeming me he contributed more than in creating me; then I was born without understanding, but now I have been saved with my will.

Yet it is not just anyone who says: “I loved your commandments more than gold and topaz.” The avaricious person does not say it—the one who clings to gold, longs for riches, and desires ornaments. Rather, the one who can say it is the person who can say: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6), because I do not seek them, because gold benefits me nothing; but the heavenly precept and commandment has redeemed me.

41. We have spoken of restraint of the senses; now let us set forth the account of the topaz stone. We find it written in the history of Xenocrates, who wrote [Note: Several manuscripts have “as a lithognomon.” This reading is not to be dismissed. Who this Xenocrates was is not entirely clear, since several persons bore that name. Nevertheless, it seems more likely that the reference is to the disciple of Plato whom Diogenes Laertius records as having written six books On Nature; Ambrose could have designated these by the title “history.” But since Pliny, in Book XXXVII of Natural History, chapter 8, attributes this opinion to more recent authorities, we think that the history should be attributed to Xenocrates the physician, who flourished around that time. What follows about the Troglodytes is also taken from the cited passage of Pliny, although there it is not Philo but Philemon who is said to have purchased the same stone. From Pliny, Book V, chapter 8, we learn that the Troglodytes were peoples of Ethiopia, extremely barbarous, who lived in caves not far from the Red Sea]:

—as though he were a lithognomon—that it is born or found near the city of Thebes, either as alabaster or as topaz, as some think; hence it was named from the place in which it was generated.

There are also those who have thought that the island was called Topazion. The Troglodytes were driven there, and, when a sudden disturbance of the sea arose, were unable to return because they had no knowledge of navigation. After remaining there for a very long time, they found the stone on the island. Delighted by its color, they returned home and sold it to Arab merchants.

Philo purchased it from them and brought it to the mother of Ptolemy II, whose name was Berenice. Although she abounded in royal ornaments, she was nevertheless extraordinarily astonished by its color and worked to ensure that the appearance of so precious a stone would not remain hidden for long. Through her efforts the stone was sought out and came into more frequent use.

42. We have explained how the topaz stone became known; now let us speak more precisely about its quality.

[Note: Six manuscripts read: “There is a likeness of two colors in this stone, a κρᾶσις,” and so forth. Whereas all the manuscripts and the ancient edition have “and chrysopa,” the Roman edition emended this from Pliny to “chrysocteron.” But in place of “similar to chrysoprasus,” as found in the edition and most manuscripts, “similar to chrysopastus” should be restored from the same source. We strongly suspect this to be the genuine reading, since in some manuscripts we find “similar to chrysopassus”; for the present, however, we do not depart from the others and the editions. Further below, where the editions have “parychrus,” we write, with the manuscripts, “parichrus,” so that the color may be called Parian—that is, white—from the marbles of the island of Paros.]

There is in this stone a blending of two colors, κρᾶσις (krasis), that is, a certain tempered mixture. It is πρασοειδής (prasoides)—“greenish”—and chrysopa, similar to chrysoprasus, displaying, in both ways, as it were, certain extended patterns of colors; and, according to experts, it is said to display them more fully.

It is also parichrus and sufficiently pure; it is chrysochrus, rich, and similar to something resplendent, especially when struck by the brilliance of the sun. It is also most beautiful and remarkable among all chrysoprasuses in size and, as I said, fuller in appearance.

Its nature is such that, if you wish to polish and smooth it, it becomes rougher, and its quality diminishes through use. By a certain generative work of nature it is euglyphus—that is, well marked and marvelous [Note: The Roman edition alone has “well formable.” Along with other editions and several manuscripts it has “worthy of the greatest effort.” It is difficult to find. But the better-hand manuscripts have the reading given in the text. What all the editions have, “and when found it is distinguished,” is found in no manuscript; no manuscript recognizes the word “distinguished”]. It is difficult to find, as though it were worthy of the greatest effort; and, when found, it is nevertheless rarely used by human beings, like something that a rich queen has admired.

43. But now, just as those Troglodytes, as though they had found the price of their stay, returned home, so let us, having received the benefit of this delay, return to the point from which we turned aside.

It is not fitting for us to continue to bring the arms of our discourse near royal ornaments, since we have in our hands the cross of Christ, which the Prophet reminds us should be preferred above gold and topaz; it turns us back from and corrects every error and fault.

For what righteous person would not desire the consolation of Christ in death and fellowship with him in resurrection? Who would not turn back when he hears that all his former sins are forgiven?

For this reason many were accustomed to be recalled from the pursuit of conversion [Note: The American and Gill editions usually read “to recall to the pursuit of conversion” [Gill: “to be recalled”]. The Roman edition reads, more appropriately, “did not wish to be recalled.” The best reading of all is that of Erasmus, which we have followed together with the majority of the manuscripts. Other manuscripts support partly one group of editions and partly the other. Here the Novatians are touched upon in passing; the holy Bishop attacks them deliberately in his book On Repentance, where we shall discuss the matter more fully], because, conscious of their sins, they presumed no hope of pardon; and the holier the precepts in the Church, the more they thought their sins to be without pardon.

44. (Verse 128.) Therefore he says in the eighth verse: “For this reason I was corrected with respect to all your commandments; I hated every way of iniquity.” He was rightly corrected because he loved; “for love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

See how much it covers and how much it corrects. “Love is patient, love is kind. Love does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails” (2 Cor. 13:4ff.).

In the later passage he placed three things as perfect: hope, faith, and love; but he called love the greater, and rightly so: “For love hopes all things, believes all things” (ibid., 13). Since hope and faith are contained in love, there is no doubt that love is the greater.

The Prophet also answered himself well. Above he said: “The law of the Lord is blameless, converting the soul” (Ps. 18:8). If the Law converts the soul, then surely the one who loves is a lover of the Law.

Then, in this same hundred-and-eighteenth psalm, he placed first: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (above, v. 1). If the one who walks in the law of God is undefiled, then the one who loves the law of God is converted.

Therefore, if the Law makes a person undefiled, love rightly covers a multitude of sins, because love is the fullness of the Law.

45. “I hated,” he says, “every way of iniquity.” If the one who loves the precepts of righteousness does what he loves, then surely the one who hates iniquity does not do what he hates.

And not without reason is the one who hates every way of iniquity corrected with respect to all the Lord’s commandments. For unless you hate every way of iniquity, you cannot be corrected in all the commandments of God.

It can happen that someone restrains himself from the horror of cruelty but, deceived by the slippery attraction of a prostitute and entering the paths of youthful incontinence, cannot withdraw the step once impressed upon them. Many are deceived by more seductive vices, while gloomy and excessively severe cruelty turns very many away from itself.

But youth is freer in love, more careless in falling, more fragile in weakness, and more stubborn in correction. Another restrains himself from luxury but is carried away by greed for money. Often sins are such that, if you avoid one, you fall into another; and the customary tendencies of nature assist weakness.

You hated luxury as a frugal person, but the desire to possess frequently slips in under the pretext of frugality. Robbery itself is subject to greed. And how much more tolerable it is to squander one’s own possessions than to seize those of another!

There are people who, fearing to diminish anything from their own property, refuse even an expense for the needy and consider mercy a loss. There are those who, avoiding the disgrace of low birth, are driven by the bellows of worldly ambition and, like shaken reeds, are carried uncertainly now here, now there.

There are also those who, while following the status of their ancestors and contenting themselves with what seems a respectable way of life, do not even think that their ancestral errors should be avoided; they do not consider that faithlessness must be changed into faith. Yet to change one’s purpose for the better is not fickleness but virtue, and not guilt but grace.

Another, occupied by the pleasures of circus games, theatrical entertainments, or other vanities, does not attend the Church; another is delighted by the quiet of the countryside, and for that reason comes rarely to the Church. Thus, through different habits, both converge upon the same error of irreligiousness.

But the one who hates every way of iniquity is corrected and reformed in every respect. And he rightly says “the way of iniquity,” for the person who has not entered its paths avoids iniquity more easily.

SEVENTEENTH SERMON. Phe.

1. Phe is the seventeenth letter, which in Latin means, “I have erred,” or, “I opened my mouth.” Rightly, therefore, this tearful section of the psalm is placed under this letter: “Look upon me and have mercy on me . . . . . and let no iniquity have dominion over me. Make your face shine upon your servant” (below, vv. 132, 133, and 135), so that upon the people who were in the shadow of death the light of heavenly mercy might rise: Christ, the forgiveness of sins, the redemption of captives, and help for those who labor. But because he seemed to those who longed for him to come too slowly, he says: “Streams of waters my eyes poured down” (below, v. 136).

2. In Jeremiah’s Lamentations too, a more tearful section occurs under this letter: “Zion spread out her hands; there is none to comfort her” (Lam. 1:17). She received a fitting recompense: she who had neglected to heed him stretching out his hands and to take refuge beneath his wings, afterwards herself spread out her hands and could find no one to console her. For although Jeremiah, before the Lord’s coming, seems to bewail the captivity inflicted on the Jews by the Babylonians, yet, foreseeing rather in the prophetic Spirit that captivity by which the intelligible Babylonian subjected them to the bonds of perpetual error, and, banishing them from their native virtue and from the condition of their ancestral devotion, afflicted them with the exile of a distant pilgrimage, he laments with piteous grief. For there is no homeland truer than faith, which made those who were far off to be near, and joined strangers and sojourners to the rights of the heavenly city, as it is written: “Therefore you are now no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. 2:19).

3. Elsewhere too Jeremiah says under this letter: “All your enemies opened their mouths against you; they hissed and gnashed their teeth, and said: ‘We have swallowed her up. This is indeed the day for which we hoped; we have found it, we have seen it’” (Lam. II, 6). Here too, just as the people of the Jews opened their mouths against Christ—as you read in the twenty-first Psalm concerning his Passion, that “they opened their mouths” in cursing (Ps. XXI, 14)—you recognize the fitting lot of recompense: [Note: Four manuscripts read: “you recognize the lot of cursing.”] they themselves were to endure such things at the hands of their enemies, and that intelligible sinner, the devil, was to gnash his teeth at them like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour. Therefore they did not say, “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth” (Ps. CXXIII, 6), because they did not think that they should hope in the Lord. Thus the devil found the destruction he had presumed upon. He swallowed them, because the offended shepherd was lacking who might draw from the lion’s mouth the sheep’s legs,

[Note: The Roman edition has “or the cartilage of the ear”; and certainly the word “ear” is understood in other editions and manuscripts, since there is an explicit allusion to Amos III, 12: “As the shepherd shall draw two legs or a piece of an ear from the lion’s mouth” (Ἐκσπάσῃ ὁ ποιμὴν ἐκ στόματος τοῦ λέοντος δύο σκέλη ἢ λόβον ὠτίου). And below, where the other editions and all the manuscripts have “the face of the saints,” the same sacred codex restored “the face of the priests”; but for the same reason the whole passage ought to have been altered, since its final part reads in those same sacred codices, “and they showed no mercy to prophets” (elsewhere, “elders”).]

or the cartilage of the ear.

4. They refused to follow; they refused to listen. Therefore, when the shepherd departed, he seized their tracks and their ears in his jaws, because they did not accept the face of the saints and showed no mercy to the noble (Lam. IV, 16), as Jeremiah says for the third time under this letter in the Lamentations. Who were the noble, unless those who lived not according to this obscure life but in the light of holiness? Mercy is indeed rightly owed to all the needy; but when hardship casts some from wealth and nobility into the lowest condition and the necessity of poverty, it strikes more forcefully upon the feelings of compassion.

5. Jeremiah, then, grieves with sufficiently mournful sorrow, as one who lamented those lost to the perpetual goad of death; David, however, does so moderately, as one grieving over the intrusion of error and not despairing of the remedy of correction, so that he was saddened but not overwhelmed.

6. (Verse 129.) Finally, strengthened by the sobriety of repentance and prompted by hope of pardon, he began thus: “Wonderful are your testimonies; therefore my soul has searched them out.” This is a moral utterance: although he was ashamed of his error, he nevertheless appealed to God by the testimonies of his own mercy. It is as though he were saying: “At the beginning of my speech, when I confess my sins, I do not dare to lift my eyes to you, the living God; but you, Lord, have prompted me to hope for pardon by the titles of so many acts of forgiveness.”

“Wonderful are your testimonies”: when you were not offended with Abraham by a lapse of youthful negligence,

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “When, in Abraham’s collapse through negligence …” Others, with the editions, read: “When, in Abraham’s lapse … you summoned him so that he might abandon the errors of the Chaldeans and his ancestral kinship,” and so forth.]

when you commanded him to leave the errors of the Chaldeans, his homeland, and his kindred, and, having called him forth, trained him through exercises of virtue. When the Hebrew people had turned away from devotion to their ancestral nobility and preferred the worthless foods of Egypt to divine gifts, you not only freed them when the waves of the Red Sea had been made solid, but also raised them to glory through very many triumphs and granted them rest in possession of a fertile land. He abandoned you when he was nurtured in security; oppressed by the severity of wars, he invoked you and earned your forgetfulness of his offenses. Jesus son of Nun recognized that you had come to him as commander of the heavenly army. The triumphant people had offended you so that Midian might rule over it; it prayed to you so that Midian might be defeated. It did not obey you in King Saul, so that foreigners might triumph over him; under David’s leadership it served you, so that it might carry away victory over foreigners. For I, a shepherd, did evil and obtained pardon by confessing my sin.

Thus this is a most beautiful verse for the encouragement of martyrs. Finally, the prophetic soul advances toward improvement when it believes God’s testimony to be wonderful; and because it believed, it sought it with diligent inquiry. If you seek its progress, recognize it in the verses that follow.

7. (Verse 130.) “The disclosure of your words gives light and grants understanding to the simple.” In the Gospel, when John sent his disciples to the Lord Jesus, he said: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Matt. XI, 3). Jesus replied that the blind see, the lame walk, and the deaf hear; for through the prophet Isaiah he had indicated that this would be the testimony of his coming (Isa. LXI, 1). Therefore the things he announced through the prophets he made manifest in the Gospel, and what he himself spoke through the prophets, he himself fulfilled in the Gospel. His word, therefore, was the prophetic word, as it is written: “Hear, O heaven, and listen with your ears, O earth; for the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I, 2).

8. Understanding, therefore, was also given to those who did not possess perfect wisdom, when the mute spoke and the dead were raised. Through these signs those who were uneducated and still stood, as it were, in the cradle of faith—the people of the nations, for example—understood that the one who was awaited had come. Thus he gives light through the brightness of faith, the glory of his resurrection, and the power of divine works: “And he grants understanding to the simple.” To whom else, surely, than those concerning whom he gives thanks to the Father in the Gospel for what the Son himself was accomplishing—namely, that God had hidden his mysteries from the wise and revealed them to the simple (Matt. XI, 25)? He was showing that the people from the nations, or men of lower station, would believe sooner than the scribes, the leaders of the Jews, and the rich of this age. Therefore, “The rich have become needy and hungry” (Ps. XXXIII, 11); but “the poor man cried out, and was heard.”

9. (Verse 131.) The third verse follows: “I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I longed for your commandments.” We have in the Gospel that the Lord Jesus opened his mouth when he pronounced the blessings (Matt. V, 2). But he opened his mouth in order to give the Spirit to others; David opened his in order to receive it. Finally, Jesus says: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22);

[Note: Only the Roman edition has: “David says: ‘Open wide …,’” and this is erroneous; the sequence shows that this verse belongs not to David but to Christ.]

Jesus says: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX, 11). He says this to a human being; for Christ is fullness. He who fills all things fills your mouth. Therefore write what he says on the breadth of your heart—that is, let your mouth cry out to the Lord.

Your mouth cries out even when it is silent, just as Moses, though silent with his voice, cried out in spirit (Exod. XIV, 15). He was not heard by human beings but resounded before God; for there is an inward cry of feeling that is heard from heaven. Hannah too, when she prayed, cried out silently (I Sam. I, 13): she did not move her lips, but with the inward voice of a devout mind she stirred Jesus. Finally, she who prayed in silence returned with the result she desired, because the Spirit of God cried out within her; and even when we are silent, he cries out: “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII, 6).

10. Understand, then, what the mouth is: whether the heart or the disposition of the inner person. The soul has a mouth, just as it has limbs. Open this mouth not only to Christ but also to Christ’s disciple, who offered his mouth to Christ to be filled; and therefore he says: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (II Cor. VI, 11). For this reason he admonishes us to be his imitators (Phil. III, 17), just as he himself is Christ’s imitator. The holier person opens his mouth to Christ; the one of lower rank, to the Apostle.

First the prophet is read, then the apostle, and so the Gospel, in which the words are luminous but the commandments stronger. The Law says: “You shall love your neighbor” (Lev. XIX, 18); the Gospel says to you: “You shall love your enemy” (Matt. V, 44).

11. David, therefore, as a perfect prophet, opened his mouth to Christ; and for this reason he opened his mouth in parables (Ps. LXXVII, 2). He opened his mouth and drew in breath. Rightly, then, he says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (above, v. 113)! The Bride of Christ opened her mouth to the Bridegroom and received commandments sweeter than every honey. Therefore she testified, saying: “His throat is sweetness, and he is altogether desirable” (Song V, 16). Delighted, she held him and did not release him. “I brought him,” she says, “into the house of my mother and into the chamber of her who conceived me” (Song III, 4). Perhaps the house is where the discipline of moral matters shines forth; the chamber, however, is where the higher mysteries are found.

Rightly, then, he longed for the Lord’s commandments, in which the honeys of divine grace gave off their fragrance. Is not the forgiveness of sins sweeter than every honey? Is not the resurrection of the dead more delightful than every flower?

12. (Verse 132.) The fourth verse: “Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name” (Exod. XIV, 24–25). Beautifully he added: “Look upon me and have mercy on me” (Gen. XIX, 21), because God also looks upon people in anger, as he looked upon the camp of the Egyptians and, binding the axles of their chariots, cast them all into the waves. He looked upon Sodom and Gomorrah, both of which, about to suffer punishment for their sins, paid the price of divine displeasure. It is also written: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. CIII, 32). Conversely, “He looked upon Abel’s offerings, but he did not look upon Cain’s offerings” (Gen. IV, 4–5). Enraged by this, Cain shed his brother’s blood in the crime of fratricide.

13. What it means for God to look upon someone is most clearly explained by that testimony: “For he looked upon the children of the poor and did not despise their prayers” (Ps. CI, 18); for the eye of the Lord does not disdain the offerings of the righteous.
