Finally, when we are moved against someone, we turn our eyes away, as though we judged unworthy of our sight the person whom we hate in our feelings.

14. (Verse 133.) The fifth verse follows: “Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me.”

[Note: Several manuscripts read “for the affections of the soul.” Others, together with the editions, read “for the progress of the soul.” The latter is more suitable, as is clear from what follows. See also the discussion of the soul’s various progresses in *Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 6.]

We are reminded by frequent testimonies of Scripture that “steps” should be understood as the soul’s progress. For who is so dull-witted as to suppose that David was concerned about the bodily movement of his feet and sought divine assistance to direct them? Rather, as a holy man, he desired the course of his life to be directed, as Scripture also testifies elsewhere: “A man’s steps are directed by the Lord” (Prov. XX, 24).

Finally, let us use his own testimony. Earlier he says: “My steps almost slipped, because I envied the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII, 2–3). Thus he shows that the step of his mind had limped, since he thought the peace of sinners worthy of admiration. They seem to have tranquility; they seem to enjoy rest. But there is no rest where the mind is disturbed; there is no tranquility of spirit where the mind is agitated by the goads of a guilty conscience. How can there be security where there is conflict among diverse passions, where there is a struggle of grave thoughts?

Therefore the Lord, defining what it means to have peace, says: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you. Not as the world gives do I give you” (John XIV, 27), showing that the peace given by the world does not possess the grace of true peace. And wishing to teach that peace does not reside in human beings, he added: “My peace I leave you.” And again: “My peace I give you.” Finally, the Prophet said: “Peace, peace—and where is peace?” (Jer. VI, 14). It is therefore clear that he was speaking of the stumbling of his judgment, in which the step of his mind, not of his body, had stumbled.

14. Moses too says: “I will pass over and see this great vision” (Exod. III, 3). In order to see God, he advanced by a certain progression of virtue toward what lay farther on. He was a shepherd of sheep and became a leader of citizens.

And in the Song it is said to the Bride: “Your steps have become beautiful in sandals, daughter of Aminadab; the curves of your thighs are like necklaces, the work of an artist” (Song VII, 1). There is no doubt that here too the steps of the Church, or the progress of the soul, are signified: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Isa. LII, 7)! He plainly calls beautiful the advances of evangelical preaching and discussion, as it is said elsewhere: “Cross the rivers” (Isa. XLVII, 2)—that is, pass through the flowing and slippery things of this world with a firm step of mind.

[Note: The old edition reads: “What he says here about the steps of the soul, David himself says later,” and so forth. The Roman edition reads: “What David himself says later about the steps of the soul that he mentions here,” and so forth. The only reason for this inversion is that they wrongly thought Ambrose was referring by the word “here,” used adverbially, to our Psalm CXVIII, whereas Psalm CXXIII is noted in the margin of that same edition farther on. The manuscripts, as printed in the body of the text, are therefore preferable.]

David himself clearly shows later that this is said of the soul’s step, asserting that his soul had passed through a torrent of iniquities (Ps. CXXIII, 5).

15. But let us return to the steps of the Bride. What does it mean that he added that the steps of the Church are beautiful in sandals? We read that Moses was told: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exod. III, 5), by which he seems to have been warned not to remain bound by bodily ties. Therefore in the Song he signifies the beauty of the soul, which uses the flesh as a sandal and suffers no impediment in that sandal but surpasses it in the beauty of its gait.

[Note: The edition reads: “Thus the ecclesial grace clothes the soul with flesh.” Several manuscripts have nothing sound at this point. Many others read: “Thus the soul clothes itself with ecclesial grace.” This is not wrong, but the reading of the Regius and Corbeiensis manuscripts, which we follow here, is better.]

Let the soul, then, clothe itself with the flesh, or the Church with grace, so that it may pass honorably through the course and passage of this life. This happens if it does not soil its sandal with bodily mud or sink it into the abyss of vices; if it chastises its flesh, so that it does not delay its course and is not weighed down by the burden of fatty indulgence. Chastity is a good sandal for the soul. A good step is one made in the path of purity.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “But wisdom is a friend of the soul.”]

Wisdom, however, is the soul’s garment; hence it is written: “Honor her, and she will embrace you” (Prov. IV, 8).

Let us therefore use the body as a sandal for works of lower virtue: for service, not for command;

[Note: All the editions and a few manuscripts read “not for precipitous action”; many others, more suitably, read “not for a command,” that is, “not for domination.”]

for attendance, not for pleasure; for obedience, not for disagreement. Let us place our footprint on the way of wisdom, lest some force of the torrent obstruct our steps.

16. Therefore Moses was told: “Remove the sandal” (Josh. V, 16). Jesus son of Nun was told this also. But it was not said to Christ; rather, the Baptist wrote of him: “After me comes a man … whose sandals I am not worthy to carry” (Matt. III, 11). Those who could not be without sin are rightly admonished to remove their sandal. But he not only did not remove his sandal; he also removed the sandals of others,

[Note: Twelve manuscripts read: “But he did not remove not only his sandal but also his sandals, because …” The reading of the others and of the editions, however, agrees better with the structure of the sentence. Below, instead of “he gave to all,” some manuscripts have “he gave to everyone.” This is not unsuitable.]

because he not only kept his own body free from sin but also granted forgiveness of the sins of all. Therefore the Church, in imitation of Christ, is beautiful and, in sandals, cleansed of every fault.

17. Perhaps, when he speaks wisdom among the perfect, he is beautiful in his higher members; but when people of lower rank or of lesser instruction follow the word, do not forget the order of faith, and keep the priest’s commandments, he is beautiful in sandals.

Often the clergy went astray;

[Note: The old edition reads: “The priests changed their judgment”; the Roman edition: “The priest changed his judgment.” The manuscripts, in broad agreement, support our reading.]

the priest changed his judgment; the rich sided with the earthly ruler of this age; the people preserved their own faith. Hence we may also rightly say of the Lord Jesus that the Word has beautiful steps even in what is bodily, when moral matters are discussed.

And perhaps for this reason the apostles are sent barefoot (Matt. X, 10), so that their discussion might not be overshadowed but might shine forth. Thus the Church is the daughter of Aminadab—that is, of the willing or well-pleasing one—because he gathered her willingly and favorably, and she is beautiful in sandals.

18. Rightly, then, it is added in the Song: “The curves of your thighs are like necklaces, the work of the hands of an artist” (Song VII, 1), so that the ornaments of the Church’s posterity might be sung. For in the thigh we recognize the emblem of generation, according to the words: “Gird your sword around your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. XLIV, 4). This signifies that, when the Son of God had emptied himself, girded with the divinity of the Word and shod with human generation, he came forth from the Virgin to give salvation to all.

The word *moduli* refers to precious ornaments customarily hung around the necks of married women. Thus the Church’s entire progress is signified as comparable to the most precious ornaments and to the necklaces of triumphant men, for these are the ornaments of warriors. Hence Symmachus also says ἐπιτραχήλια, that is, “things around the neck.”

Whether, then, it is Christ’s generation from the Virgin or the Church’s propagation, he crowned the necks of the faithful, in appearance as with necklaces adorned by an artist’s hand, but in reality with the spiritual insignia of true virtue.

19. Finally, this entire description of the Church’s members is full of beauty and praise. Her navel too is proclaimed to be like a turned bowl that does not lack mixed wine (Song VII, 2), because, turned in every doctrine, she does not fail in fullness of knowledge or in spiritual drink. Her belly is not only filled with a heap of wheat—that is, with the stronger foods of the heavenly mystery—but is also filled, as it were, with lilies, with the sweetness of moral teaching.

20. Hence she herself, like a queen who has merited well, is crowned with the blood of Christ, as it is written: “And the adornment of your head is like purple” (ibid., v. 5). The blood of Christ is purple; it stains the souls of the saints, shining not only in color but also in power, because it makes them kings—and better kings—to whom it grants an eternal kingdom.

21. And rightly, at the sight of such beauty of the Church, upon which Christ’s blood shines, the Holy Spirit exclaims: “How beautiful and how sweet you have become, O love, in your delights!” (ibid., v. 6). Beautiful with the beauty of virtue, sweet with the delight of grace and the forgiveness of faults, which no bitterness of sin disturbs; and she is now herself love, because by loving God she has received his name, since “God is love” (John IV, 16).

22. David therefore rightly asks that his steps be directed according to God’s word, so that they too may become beautiful and iniquity may not rule over him,

[Note: The old edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads: “which he rightly prayed against.”]

which he rightly guarded against. For he knew that Abraham had directed his steps according to the Lord’s commandments and, when tempted by the desire for a beautiful wife, had been tested but not put to shame;

[Note: So the manuscripts read; the edition, however, has: “and in the sacrifice of his only son, after the affection of ancestral feeling had been set aside, had struggled.”]

and that, when the sacrifice of his only son was demanded, he had struggled through the devotion of ancestral affection but had been crowned. He knew also that he himself had been assailed by the savage temptations of wicked iniquity—in Saul’s fury, Ammon’s incest, and Absalom’s parricide—and that he had escaped this only because, directing his steps according to devotion to the Lord, he had not departed from paternal affection: inwardly groaning over the crime of incest and banishing hatred of the parricide from himself.

“My son Absalom, my son,” he says, “Absalom, who will grant me death in your place?” (II Sam. XVIII, 33), mindful of natural affection and forgetful of the offense. Of him he had earlier asked: “Is the boy alive?” (ibid., v. 29).

23. Perhaps one should ask why earlier he called him a boy and afterward called him a son; why he did not call him either a boy in both places or a son in both. If he were alive, he was a boy, because he was seeking his father’s death through parricide. He therefore ought not to receive the name of affection but of weakness. Thus the just man was silent about what belonged to religion and sprinkled in what belonged to weakness. Once he was dead, however, before his affectionate father the guilt of the person disappeared, while the name of nature remained.

24. (Verse 134.) It follows: “Deliver me from the slander of men, so that I may keep your commandments.” Our affliction is not of one kind: there is temptation, and there is slander. Temptation is lighter; slander is heavier. Indeed, temptation can become slander, while slander contains temptation in itself.

There is also human temptation, which we can endure; but slander is grievous. Therefore the Lord took upon himself the things that are more grievous, and, assailed by slanders, offered a triumphant silence (Matt. XXVI, 63).

Slander is more grievous because it not only fabricates falsehoods but also discolors deeds that were piously performed. Thus Joseph was not only tempted by the offer of adultery and by the invitation of his mistress’s enticement (Gen. XXXIX, 10 ff.),

[Note: The earlier edition reads: “He was tempted by the accusation of adultery.”]

but was also assailed by slanders, through the fabrication that he had tried to commit adultery with his mistress; and, when he was seized, he left his garment,

[Note: The earlier edition reads: “and invited to the crime by his mistress’s allure.” The Roman edition reads: “by his mistress’s allure.” Some manuscripts read: “and by the incitement of a boy’s allure.” Many others read as in the text. In certain editions the word “charge” was added to “fabrication”; this was unnecessary, since “falsehood” or “crime,” that is, “accusation,” is understood.]

so that he would not be held with the evidence of deceit and the mark of the crime;

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “lest he himself, as an indication of fraud and a mark of the crime, should be held; and therefore, having put it on …” We make no change in the reading of the manuscripts and old editions. But for the meaning to be clear, after “lest it be an indication of fraud,” understand: “in the one who had been seized and had not escaped.”]

for he had left the garment behind while fleeing precisely so that he might escape the snares and bonds of the one attempting violence through seductive craft.

David himself had experienced what he feared. What slanders of King Saul had he endured! When everyone else was terrified, he frustrated the attack of the Philistines, received upon himself alone the decisive struggle and the whole burden of the battle, refuted by his own courage the common accusation, and turned back upon the enemy the reproach directed against the entire people. Yet when the young women said, “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (I Sam. XVIII, 7), glory was turned into envy, and he began to be driven by hatred.

And, to speak of later events, Susanna was well aware of her own innocence, but she could not make it prevail among human beings. Two old presbyters brought false testimony against her; the number and age of the priests took away the girl’s voice. Only her conscience was free before God. Finally, condemned by human judgment, she was acquitted by a divine sign (Dan. XIII, 34 ff.).

25. Therefore the Prophet says: “Deliver me from the slander of men, so that I may keep your commandments.” For one who is oppressed by slander cannot easily keep the divine commandments. Such a person must often yield either to sadness or to fear, and is afflicted either by dread of slander or by grief.

26. (Verse 135.) The seventh verse follows: “Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your ordinances.” The Lord illuminates his saints and shines in the hearts of the righteous. Therefore, when you see a wise person, understand that the glory of God has descended upon him and illuminated his mind with the brightness of knowledge and divine understanding.

He also illuminated Moses’ face bodily, and the glory of his face was transformed. When the Jews saw it, they trembled; therefore Moses placed a veil over his face, lest the children of Israel gaze upon it and be disturbed (Exod. XXXIV, 29 ff.). At the same time, a mystery was being disclosed: the veil that was placed bodily upon Moses’ face was mystically placed in the hearts of the Jews, because they could not see the true radiance of the Law.

The face of Moses is the radiance of the Law; but the radiance of the Law is not in the letter—it is in spiritual understanding. Therefore, as long as Moses lived and addressed the people of the Jews, he had a veil over his face. After Moses died, Jesus son of Nun addressed both the elders and the people not through a veil but with an unveiled face, and no one trembled (Josh. I, 10). Yet God had told him that he would be with him as he had been with Moses and would likewise illuminate him—not with the glory of his face but with the glory of his deeds (ibid., v. 5). The Holy Spirit signified by this that the true Jesus would come, and that if anyone turned to him and wished to hear him, he would remove the veil from his heart and see the true Savior with unveiled face.

27. Therefore God almighty the Father blinded the people of the Jews in Moses’ face, not through harshness but through foreknowledge, not through malice but through equity and justice. They themselves placed the veil upon themselves because they did not wish to understand the Law; for the Law is spiritual, as the Hebrew said (Rom. VII, 4).

He, in accordance with what he gives to each of us—in which the fault lies not with the giver

[Note: The old edition, together with part of the manuscripts, reads: “but with the one who is diligent.” The Roman edition, more suitably, with the others, reads: “but with the one who is not diligent,” and so forth.]

but with the one who is not diligent—he, I say, illuminated the heart of the people of the nations in the face of Christ Jesus through his coming. This is clearly declared by the Apostle’s example, as we read: “For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus” (II Cor. IV, 6).

28. Therefore David says to the Lord Jesus: “Make your face shine upon your servant.” He desired to see Christ’s face so that his mind might be illuminated. This may also be understood according to the Incarnation. Many prophets and righteous people desired to see it, as the Lord himself declared (Luke X, 24).

He was not seeking what had been denied to Moses (Exod. XXXIII, 20): to see bodily the face of the incorporeal God—if indeed Moses, so wise and learned, could have asked this in a merely literal sense rather than as a mystery. Yet it is human to extend one’s desires beyond oneself.

Nor was it without reason that he sought to see the face of him who was coming from the Virgin, so that he might be illuminated in his heart, just as those were illuminated who said: “Was not our heart burning within us … when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV, 32).

If someone wishes this to be understood as spoken to God the Father, it may be taken to mean that the Son is the Father’s face; for whoever sees the Son sees the Father also.

29. Nevertheless, God’s face illuminates according to the sense in which his eyes are understood to be upon the righteous. Although this must be established spiritually, the history of Moses’ illuminated face has arisen; therefore, lest anyone suppose that it could not have happened bodily, let him understand.

Through exposure to the sun, even in many whose entire body has been weakened by pallor, the body’s appearance is changed; and when people are warmed by the vapor of fire, the appearance of a glowing face becomes visible. At daybreak, the lands redden when suffused with a saffron color,

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Having borrowed the likeness of God’s benefit.” Others, more suitably, together with the editions, read: “from the benefit,” with “of the rising day” or “of the light” understood.]

borrowing an image from the beneficence of the rising day; and shining necklaces of gems likewise cast upon nearby objects the radiance they themselves have received. Do you marvel, then, if Moses’ face was tinged with the brightness of the divine presence? Do you marvel if the mind of the righteous grows warm when God’s grace shines upon it?

The Prophet did not hesitate to ask first to be illuminated, so that he might be able to learn the Lord’s ordinances.

30. (Verse 136.) The eighth verse follows: “The streams of waters descended from my eyes, because I did not keep your law.” He expressed with great force the feeling of one doing penance, saying that streams of waters had descended from his eyes: either because, as through channels of surging streams, a kind of conduit of overflowing tears had poured forth through them, producing a continuous and unceasing flood of weeping; or because the eyes themselves had descended.

For this is the force of the greatest grief: that, together with tears, the eyes themselves seem somehow to descend, since the force of the tears is so great that the eyes seem to dissolve into weeping and pour themselves out into tears.

31. The eyes themselves therefore descended as though into streams of waters. By this expression the violent force of those who lament is more vividly revealed, according to what is written in the Song: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living water, and a stream descending from Lebanon” (Song IV, 15).

The Church brought these streams down from Lebanon. By this stream sins are washed away. By this stream of the pure fountain and the Holy Spirit, the Bride flows from Lebanon; from the beginning of faith she passed through the world and crossed over into the kingdom.

For some, spiritual grace is a fountain; for others, a well, according to our capacity; for others, a closed garden and a sealed fountain; for others, a fountain of gardens, which is counted among the Church’s possessions; for others, a stream descending from Lebanon, a great stream that never fails.

For the breasts do not fail from the rock, nor the snow from Lebanon, nor the water that is carried by a mighty wind from the virgin Jerusalem (Jer. XVIII, 14). The stream descended from Lebanon when, with the apostles and many believers gathered together, there suddenly came from heaven a sound as though the Spirit were being carried by a great force, and all were filled with the Holy Spirit, who granted the diversity of tongues (Acts II, 1–3). It is a good stream, incapable of harming and knowing how to fill.

32. If anyone therefore wishes to merit this stream of grace descending from heaven, let him also descend with his eyes into streams of waters. Whoever first pours forth this stream will merit it. She descended with her eyes into these channels of water—the eyes with which, in the Gospel, she watered the Lord’s feet with tears (Luke VII, 38)—and thus, by the price of her faith, purchased health for soul and body, no longer flowing with blood but with spiritual grace (Luke VIII, 44).

33. The Prophet David therefore descended, and for this reason brought back grace from his sin. He descended into channels of waters—that is, he filled them and heaped up the currents of flowing waters with the tears of his own eyes; or he filled empty and vacant channels with tears alone; or, as a certain moral sense of the expression indicates, he descended into channels of waters and crossed them.

We could say: “He transcended them and rose above them.” But this diminishes the force of the expression, by which the greater force of descending abundance, rather than of ascending, is conveyed. Consider, I ask, what power the words possess through usage, so that prophetic speech does not lose its force, although usage itself customarily serves the meaning of writers with greater elegance.

He expressed this in different ways and often, and almost always took on an increase. First he said: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI, 7). Again he said: “My tears have been my bread” (Ps. XLI, 4). He also said: “And I mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI, 10). Here he added: “The streams of waters descended from my eyes.”

34. Following this example, Jeremiah in the Lamentations expressed the feeling of grief by imitating the force of the descending eye; for you read: “My eyes failed in tears;

[Note: Ten manuscripts read: “My eyes grew dim.” Others, together with all the editions and the sacred codices, read: “My heart was troubled.”]

my heart was troubled” (Lam. II, 11). The eyes that fail in tears are as though they descend.

And elsewhere: “My eye was swallowed up” (Lam. III, 49). But it is more to conquer waters with tears than to have the eyes swallowed up by weeping.

And elsewhere the same Jeremiah says: “Their heart cried out to the Lord: Let the walls of the daughter of Zion pour down torrents; let tears flow day and night. Do not grant yourself rest; let the pupil of your eye not be silent” (Lam. II, 18).

Therefore the eyes that pour down torrents through their tears themselves descend as channels of waters—that is, they are heaped up—so that, increasing the channels with their own weeping, they may make them overflow with the force of torrents.

35. Nevertheless, there are manuscripts that read: διεξόδοις ὑδάτων κατεβίβασαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοί μου—that is, “The channels of waters directed my eyes.” [Col. 1451D] But in my Greek manuscript 1194 I read κατέβησαν, that is, “they descended”: in this matter it may be that the scribe erred in either direction by adding or omitting two letters.

[Note: The Aldine and Complutensian editions have κατέδυσαν, with a meaning not greatly different.] [Col. 1452D]

36. He certainly had many things to weep over, whether his daughter’s incest or the death of his sons; [Col. 1452A] but here he says that he did not weep for these things, but because he had not kept the law of the Lord. In a holy man, guilt is mourned more than misfortune.

He wept, therefore, when Nathan announced to him the Lord’s indignation over Uriah’s death, and he acknowledged his sin in transgressing the law. Accordingly, when his son was lying ill, he neither took food nor mounted the royal throne or bed; but, lying on the ground, he washed his fasting face with tears, desiring to relieve in him not so much the death of his son as the punishment of his own sin (II Kings XII, 16 ff.). He wept when, after numbering the people, he was suddenly struck in his heart. Accordingly, he says: “I have sinned greatly; I have acted very foolishly” (II Kings XXIV, 10). He wept, then, first because, elated by royal power, he had exceeded the measure of human condition in seeking to number the people; [Col. 1452B] then because the price of his error was exacted from the people.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “the price of his error was exacted from the people,” which is perhaps the genuine reading.] [Col. 1452D]

But this punishment had been proposed by the Lord; it had not been requested by the king. Nevertheless, by committing himself to the Lord’s mercy, he demonstrated the reason for his choice; and at the same time, because the people were suffering on his account, by offering himself on behalf of the people he made satisfaction for the offense of his pride and proved the disposition of his piety.

# THE EIGHTEENTH SERMON. Sade.

## 1.

The eighteenth letter, Sade, follows; in Latin interpretation it is called “consolation.” After tears flowing like torrents and the heavy weeping of grief, consolation ought to follow. For those who are in pain need consolation; those who have paid the penalties of their crimes through grievous afflictions hope for pardon; and those who have washed away their sins with weeping and tears deserve rest. [Col. 1452C]

## 2.

Whoever seeks all these things in the divine Scriptures finds them. First, concerning the duty of consoling those who are placed in sorrow, that passage teaches us which cries out mournfully in the Book of Jeremiah to the captives and exiles of the Jews:

“Go, depart, children; for I have been left desolate. I have removed from myself the robe of peace; but I have put on the robe of my prayer, and I shall cry out to the Most High in my days. Be of good courage, children; cry out to the Lord, and he will draw you out of the hand of your enemies’ rulers. For I have hoped in him for your eternal salvation” (Baruch IV, 19 ff.). [Col. 1452D]

For those who believe in the Lord, then, there is consolation in the Lord’s mercy.

There is also another kind of consolation for those who have paid severe penalties, as it is written in the Book of Isaiah:

“Be comforted, be comforted, my people, says the Lord. Priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her, because her humiliation has been filled up, her sin has been released, because she has received double punishment from the hand of the Lord” (Isaiah XL, 1 and 2). [Col. 1453A]

Even if faith was lacking, punishment had made satisfaction. Those who are absolved through the commendation of their merits are relieved by the discharge of their penalties. The third case is when crime is washed away with tears, as in the passage:

“Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, because the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.”

This too is easily found here and in many passages of the Book of Psalms. 1195

## 3.

The first consolation, therefore, in order is that God does not forget to show mercy and does not cast off forever those whom he has judged deserving of correction (*On Repentance*, distinction 3, chapter “Prima consolatio”). The second is that, when the punishments we have endured on account of our sins have run their course, we attain forgiveness.

Hence certain philosophers have argued that acquittal harms the wicked, while death benefits them: acquittal contains an incentive to wrongdoing, whereas death is the end of wrongdoing. Who could doubt that this was taken from our writings, since we read in Solomon’s Proverbs: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Proverbs XIII, 24); and, “The Lord chastises him whom he loves” (Proverbs III, 12); and below: “A whip for the horse, a goad for the ass, and a rod for a foolish nation” (Proverbs XXVI, 3). Punishment corrects and reforms the one who errs.

If someone is such that he cannot be reformed, he is removed from the midst of the living, lest he commit worse offenses; for once dead, he no longer knows how to err. Therefore Ecclesiastes says: “And I praised the dead more than the living; and better than both is the one who has not yet been born, who has not seen this evil work” (Ecclesiastes IV, 2 and 3). The dead person is preferred to the living because he has ceased to sin. The one who has not been born is preferred to the dead because he has not known how to sin. [Col. 1453B]

[Note: Plato discusses this matter at length in the *Gorgias*, where, arguing against Polus, he writes among other things: “And indeed it appeared that paying the penalty was release from this evil . . . but not paying it was persistence in evil.” Ambrose evidently had these words in mind.] [Col. 1453D]

## 4.

Let us now speak also of those who have paid the penalties for their crimes. Have they not paid the price of their guilt, so that no complete penalty is now owed them? The Lord cries out through Isaiah:

“Comfort my people . . . because she has received double punishment from the hand of the Lord” (Isaiah XL, 1 and 35). [Col. 1453C]

Learn from where Plato took this. He went to Egypt for the sake of learning, so that he might become acquainted with the deeds of Moses, the oracles of the Law, and the sayings of the prophets. There he heard of the consolation of a people who seemed to have been punished beyond the measure of its sin; and, clothing this passage in a certain embellishment of words, he transferred it into the *Dialogue* he wrote on Virtue.

The Lord, however, grasped and explained the passage more fully and clearly in the Gospel, saying through Abraham’s person to that rich man of this age:

“Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is being comforted here, while you are in torment. And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to here” (Luke XVI, 25 and 26). [Col. 1453D]

[Note: Concerning Plato’s journey to Egypt, besides Diogenes Laertius, Book III, Justin in his *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, Jerome in his letter to Paulinus, Augustine in Book VIII of *The City of God*, and others speak of it. Strabo, in Book XVII, asserts that he spent thirteen years there among the Egyptian priests. What Ambrose says was transferred by that philosopher from the *Dialogue on Virtue* may most conveniently be referred to these words:

“For those to whom Persephone receives recompense for ancient grief, in the ninth year beneath the sun she sends their souls back again; from them arise illustrious kings, swift in strength, and men greatest in wisdom increase.”

The foundation of Platonic recollection rests upon these words.] [Col. 1454D]

But now let us hear what the righteous man says in consoling himself.

## 5. (Verse 137)

“You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right. You have commanded righteousness: your testimonies, and your truth, exceedingly.” [Col. 1454A]

Truly he is a righteous man who, pouring forth tears and wrapped in afflictions, paying his debts for his sins through severe punishment, is not overcome by weariness, broken by fear, or exhausted by labor; he is neither ungrateful nor sorrowful.

For the common crowd of human beings, generally failing to reckon its sins, unjustly considers itself to be enduring what it suffers. But the righteous man, who accuses himself at the very beginning of his speech, proclaims the Lord’s justice, acknowledging that he suffers what is worthy of his merits.

By calling God righteous, he first pronounces judgment concerning his own unrighteousness; but he hopes for pardon through the Lord’s justice. For the righteous man is not always angry: just as he is the avenger of guilt, so he is the moderator of punishment; just as he is the avenger of sins, so he is the rewarder of virtues and of the best merits. [Col. 1454B]

Whoever wishes to give a prize must observe the contest, because no one is crowned without a contest. Therefore he often permits us to be tempted, wishing to give just rewards to one who struggles, not to one who sleeps. A crown does not suit those decked with flowers, but those covered in dust; victory does not adorn the soft and luxurious, but the strong through the labor of training.

## 6.

The righteous man, therefore, praises God’s justice in his adversities. But a parent who has lost tender children does not feel this; nor does one deprived of a spouse by untimely widowhood, nor the sick man in pain, nor the shipwrecked man in danger, nor the accused man at trial, nor the captive in a snare.

Yet Jeremiah cried out when, announcing to the peoples the future misery of captivity, he was plunged into a pit of mud and threatened with death in foul filth:

“You are righteous, O Lord” (Jeremiah XII, 1).

He cried out again when he was distressed by the pitiable servitude of a conquered people:

“The Lord is righteous, because she provoked his mouth . . . . Outside he has made her childless, and within there is death” (Lamentations I, 18 and 20). [Col. 1454C]

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts; but many editions have inserted the following: “Because I provoked his mouth to anger.” Under another heading they add: “Thus he made her childless outside, so that there was death within; that is, just as he acted in paradise, so also he raged against the misery of this age. Through the devil’s envy death entered the world. You are righteous, O Lord. They cried out,” and so forth.] [Col. 1454D]

The Hebrews cried out when, on account of the virtue of their devotion and the grace of their faith, they were surrounded by the flames of the burning furnace:

“You are righteous, O Lord, in all the things that you have done” (Daniel III, 27).

Therefore they deserved, unharmed by the fire, to proclaim the Lord’s righteousness.

The prophet Daniel too, after being thrown a second time into the lions’ den and surrounded by the savagery and horror of monstrous beasts, asserted with fearless voice that all things were right in the sight of the Lord (Daniel VI, 22).

Jonah, enclosed in a beast’s belly and scarcely having room to draw breath, condemned by the lot of the unrighteous though himself righteous, cried from the whale’s belly in the sea:

“With a voice of praise and confession I supplicate you” (Jonah II, 10).

David, when he fled from Absalom’s face, driven from his lands and kingdom by parricidal arms, and when he offered himself for the destruction of the whole people, said:

“You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right. What has this innocent flock done? I, the shepherd, have done evil; let punishment be taken from the author of the guilt before the righteous God.” [Col. 1454D]

Abraham himself, the father of faith, when his only son was demanded from the old man for sacrifice, tempered his paternal affection with a confession of divine justice, saying:

“You are righteous, O Lord; for you do not demand what belongs to another, but reclaim what is yours. I return to you the one whom you gave.” [Col. 1455A]

Imitating him, Job, after his children had been killed and he had been stripped of his possessions, tearing the garment from his body, said:

“Naked I was born, naked, he says, shall I die. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away . . . . Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21 and 22).

## 7.

Let us all, then, proclaim that the Lord is righteous. Let the one who lays his dying limbs in the grave, and the one who is struck by loss or by the funeral of his children, say:

“You are righteous, O Lord.” [Col. 1455B]

For what of our own do we lose? The Apostle cries out:

“What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Corinthians IV, 7).

Whatever we have, therefore, we received; whatever we lose, we return—we do not lose it. The Lord is righteous in dangers, righteous in losses, righteous in punishments, not only because each person justly pays the price of his guilt, but also because, while one is punished, many are corrected.

Ananias in the Acts of the Apostles committed a crime by withholding part of the price he had received from the sale of his field (Acts V, 1 ff.), although he could have offered nothing and escaped the crime. But lest anyone suppose that the apostles could be deceived with impunity, or contaminate the gift of mercy with the fraud of faithlessness, he was handed over to eternal death and by a just terror brought everyone to zeal for the faith.

[Note: The old editions read, “the faithless, handed over to eternal death”; the Roman edition, “the faithless, handed over to eternal death.” It is sufficiently clear, however, that this was composed by those who wished, after the name of Ananias, to insert Sapphira as well—although there is no mention of her in the manuscripts—by whatever right or wrong. We reproduce the passage according to the testimony of all the manuscripts. As for Ambrose’s assertion that eternal death was inflicted upon the same married couple whose crime, but nowhere their repentance, is declared, in this he differs from Origen and certain other Fathers, who maintain that the punishment was temporal only. Certainly Augustine and some others speak of the matter with hesitation. More may be seen in Baronius under the year 34, no. 269, and in the commentators on this passage.] [Col. 1455D]

Pharaoh, drowned in the waters together with his people, is an example of worldly conduct, so that no one may persecute the people of God. In the end, God could have made him obedient to his will, but through his punishment he wished everyone to be corrected. Therefore the Lord says to him:

“For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth” (Exodus IX, 16). [Col. 1455C]

The Lord was seeking not the increase of his own praise, but the increase of our correction.

## 8.

All the wise, then, say:

“You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right.”

For we are not handed over to our adversaries without his judgment, nor do we enter into tribulations without his judgment. This is the consolation of the righteous; this is the Lord’s judgment.

Accordingly, above also you find:

“I remembered your judgments, which are from eternity, and I was comforted” (above, verse 52). [Col. 1455D]

You perceive, then, that the Lord’s judgments are consolations. [Col. 1456A]

## 9. (Verse 138)

“You have commanded righteousness: your testimonies, and your truth, exceedingly.”

Is it “you have commanded exceedingly,” or “your truth is exceedingly great”? But an exceedingly great truth is full of praise, and commanding exceedingly belongs to providence and care. For he knew that they were weak; therefore he admonished them more frequently, so that they would not forget.

## 10. (Verse 139)

The third verse follows: [Col. 1455D]

“Your zeal has sought me out, because my enemies have forgotten your words.”

[Note: Thus read all the manuscripts and editions with great agreement. Nevertheless, not only do the various texts and versions of Scripture contradict this reading, but so do the Greek and Latin Fathers who cite the same verse. It is quite probable that in Ambrose’s manuscript, through a copyist’s error, ἐξεζήτησέ με (“has sought me out”) was written instead of ἐξέτηξέ με ὁ ζῆλος (“zeal has consumed me”).] [Col. 1456D]

There is a zeal leading to life, and there is a zeal leading to death. Zeal leading to life consists in keeping the divine precepts and guarding the commandments through love of the Lord, as Phinehas did. Concerning him we read in Numbers, where the Lord says to Moses:

“Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned away my wrath from the children of Israel, because he was zealous with my zeal among them; and I did not consume the children of Israel in my zeal, as I said. Behold, I give him my covenant of peace, and it shall be for him and for his offspring after him a covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was zealous for his God, and he did not make atonement for the children of Israel” (Numbers XXV, 11 ff.).

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “and he made atonement,” a reading supported by the Hebrew and Syriac text and by all the versions of Scripture. Since, however, the manuscripts and the ancient editions read “and he did not make atonement,” or, in certain manuscripts, “and he did not intercede,” it is quite probable that καὶ οὐχ ἱλάσατο (“and he did not make atonement”) was written in Ambrose’s manuscript instead of καὶ ἐξιλάσατο (“and he made atonement”). The alteration would have been very easy.] [Col. 1456D]

Twenty-four thousand of the people lay slain; the punishment extended to all, and there was no end to the destruction. Phinehas seized a spear, killed the two who had joined themselves in a forbidden union, redeemed everyone, mitigated the Lord’s indignation, and gave victory to those to whom he denied salvation. How salutary, then, is the zeal of God!

1198

## 11.

That vice was not confined to one period of time: even now a Midianite is joined to a Jew. A Midianite is a woman joined to no lawful marriage and united to no fellowship of faith. The faithlessness of heretics is a Midianite when it tempts the people of God. [Col. 1456C]

Into how many peoples has this savage harlot crept, burying the whole people in a common death through a public funeral! Come now, Phinehas; seize the sword of the word, kill faithlessness, slaughter heresy, lest the whole people perish on its account.

The heavenly anger presses upon us. Strike the very womb of impiety and the generative organ of faithlessness, lest an unhappy offspring be formed, lest adulterous conception spread a seedbed of transgression and crime; so that the Lord may establish with you a covenant of peace, a covenant of grace, and a covenant of heavenly promises.

A priest ought to possess zeal when he strives to preserve the chastity of the Church undefiled. Therefore the High Priest said:

“The zeal of your house has devoured me” (John II, 17). [Col. 1456D]

[Note: The Vindobonensis and Colbertinus manuscripts read, “has crowned me,” and so also below.] [Col. 1457A]

Phinehas too was a priest, the grandson of a priest and the son of a priest. Zeal is good and useful in a priest, especially so that he may not be negligent or lax. It is better that many be delivered through the condemnation of one or two than that more should perish through the acquittal of two.

## 12.

“Your zeal,” he says, “has sought me out.”

You see that the zeal of God is grace: it seeks, it comes upon, it pours itself into the breast of the righteous. The zeal of God is life.

Accordingly, the Lord says:

“The zeal of your house has devoured me.”

For just as previously prevailing death had devoured the human being in Adam, so zeal devoured the one whom it made alive in Christ.

Elijah possessed zeal, and therefore he was taken up into heaven. “With zeal I have been zealous for the Lord,” he says (III Kings XIX, 10).

Mathathias Butanus possessed zeal; he stirred up the people of God against the sacrileges of Antiochus. [Col. 1457D]

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “Mathathias son of John.” But besides the fact that it is contrary to Ambrose’s practice to construct such names from the Hebrew and Syriac, all the manuscripts and ancient editions disagree. We have therefore restored the ancient reading, although we remain somewhat uncertain whether it too is genuine.] [Col. 1458D]

Those who possess zeal consider all their enemies to be their own enemies who are enemies of God, even if they are father, brothers, or sisters. David says of them all:

“They have become enemies to me” (Psalm CXXXVIII, 22). [Col. 1457B]

What more need be said? The Apostle of the Lord too was designated by this name, so that Judas was called “the Zealot,” as we read in the Gospel (Luke VI, 15).

## 13.

Through the zeal of faith, the people of the Gentiles acquired eternal life for themselves, which the people of the Jews lost through negligence and indolence. Therefore it is written:

“Zeal has seized an unlearned people” (Isaiah XXVI, 11),

because the people who had been instructed in the Law possessed no ardor of faith.

Zeal turned to the Gentiles, and its grace was so great that it surpassed the privilege of election and the diligence of instruction. Indeed, by seizing an unlearned people, it made that people better.

Thus grace worked in the people of the nations, so that it might deserve the inheritance of the Lord; and through it the Lord worked to join a Church to himself from the nations. Zeal, therefore, is love. [Col. 1457C]

Accordingly:

“Love is strong as death; zeal is hard as hell” (Song of Songs VIII, 6). 1199

Zeal is hard when no enticement of this life can conquer it; hard as hell, through which we die to sin so that we may live to God.

## 14.

The angels too are nothing without zeal, and they lose the privilege of their nature unless they support it with the ardor of zeal. Accordingly, in the Apocalypse of John the Lord says to the angel of Laodicea:

“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth; because you say, ‘I am rich, and have grown wealthy, and lack nothing,’ and you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. I advise you to buy from me gold tested by fire” (Revelation III, 15–18). [Col. 1457D]

This is the zeal of God; this is the vapor of faith and the fervor of devotion, which softens and forms us like a pleasant food in Christ. How great is the Lord’s grace, that he places us in his mouth and feasts upon certain dishes of our merits; and, if we deserve it, devours us, taking pleasure in the sweetness of our food.

Blessed is the one whom wisdom devours, whom virtue absorbs, whom justice receives. Guilt cannot possess any portion in the one whom remission of sins has swallowed up; for where will error find a place in one whom immaculate integrity has received?

[Col. 1458A]

## 15.

Why should we wonder if the angels possess it? God the Father himself says:

“Zealously I will be zealous for Jerusalem with great zeal” (Zechariah VIII, 2).

Because God is great, his zeal is therefore great; and according to the measure of each person’s capacity, zeal is either moderate or great.

By zeal Jerusalem is avenged; by zeal the Church is gathered; by zeal faith is acquired; by zeal chastity is possessed.

The Lord Jesus also says:

“The zeal of your house has consumed me” (John II, 17),

rebuking the Jews because they had made the house of prayer a den of thieves and had made it a house of commerce.

## 16.

But we must be zealous not only for the place of the Church, but also for this inner house of God within us, lest it become a house of commerce or a den of thieves.

For if we pursue profits, gain, and financial advantage, we have made it a house of commerce. If we seize the possessions of others—the boundaries of widows or minors—we have made it a den of thieves. [Col. 1458B]

Let the Word of God therefore come and drive thieves, robbers, and merchants from this house, so that your heart and your breast may be clean.

## 17.

But there is a zeal leading to guilt, and there is also a zeal leading to grace. David himself says:

“I was envious of the peace of sinners” (Psalm LXXII, 2).

And it is written in Ecclesiasticus:

“Do not be jealous of the wife of your bosom, lest she display against you the wickedness of an evil teaching” (Ecclesiasticus IX, 1).

A jealous woman is rightly rebuked for jealousy toward a faithful woman. We therefore perceive that zeal has a certain measure and discipline, just as virtue has a discipline.

Blessed, therefore, is the one who knows the discipline of zeal and hates those who, abandoning the Lord’s grace, desert their own salvation and take upon themselves the errors of deceit. [Col. 1458C]

## 18.

Therefore he says:

“Because my enemies have forgotten your words.”

Who are these enemies? If they are the people of the Jews, how were they enemies while subject to his rule? David governed all the Jews under his own kingdom. If they are the Gentiles, how could they have forgotten the words of God when they did not know the Lord’s law? No one can forget anything except what he has received.

Those, then, are my enemies who are your enemies—those who would not receive the Lord when he came among his own. The Prophet testifies that these were grave adversaries and his enemies, not because they were enemies of him personally, but because they were rebels against Christ.

Accordingly, elsewhere he says:

“I wasted away because of your enemies, and I hated them with a perfect hatred” (Psalm CXXXVIII, 21 and 22),

considering the weapons of faithlessness more grievous than those of battle. No one is a more grievous enemy of all than the one who harms the author of all. [Col. 1458D]

Therefore the people of the nations were acquired through great zeal, because God was denied by his own people. For those who did not retain the memory of the heavenly commandments could retain neither the devotion of faith nor the discipline of virtue.

Thus Adam was expelled from paradise, and thus the people of the Jews were excluded from the privilege of election.

## 19. (Verse 140)

The following verse says:

“Your word is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it.”

The Lord indeed sent fire upon the earth—not so that it might again burn in a conflagration like that of Sodom, as it is written, nor so that it might be stripped of the gift of its fruitfulness or of the use and beauty of its verdure (Genesis XIX, 24). [Col. 1459A]

For the Lord is accustomed rather to approve and increase his work than to diminish or condemn it. Nor was it fitting that innocent elements should pay the penalty for our crime. What had nature done wrong if its grown offspring had gone astray? The offspring was not at fault in its birth if it fell through deviant error; the fault lay in its use.

[Note: After the word “offspring,” the editions add: “nature is not here.” This is omitted from all the written manuscripts.] [Col. 1459D]

What fire, then, did the Lord scatter in the New Testament? A fire that would inflame the hidden affections of minds with the ardor of divine knowledge, kindle the vapor of faith and devotion, and set the desire for virtue ablaze.

Warmed by this fire, Jeremiah says:

“And there was a flaming fire in my bones” (Jeremiah XX, 9).

Cleopas and the other man who had traveled with the Lord from Jerusalem as far as the village were heated by this fire of heavenly words, and they said:

“Was not our heart burning within us . . . when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV, 32). [Col. 1459B]

## 20.

This fire, then, is the word of Christ. It is a good fire, which knows how to warm and does not know how to burn, except for sins alone.

By this fire the apostolic gold placed upon a good foundation is tested; by this fire the pure silver of works is examined; by this fire those precious stones are illumined, while hay and straw are consumed (I Corinthians III, 12 and 13). [Col. 1459D]

This fire therefore cleanses the soul and consumes error. Hence the Lord says:

“Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John XV, 3).

This is the fire that burns before the Lord; for unless someone takes on the flame of devotion, he cannot possess the Lord’s presence (Leviticus VI, 12). First kindle this fire in your minds, so that the light of Christ may shine upon you.

By this fire the bush burned and was not consumed (Exodus III, 2). The divine word burns in order to correct the sinner’s conscience; it does not consume in order to destroy. [Col. 1459C]

[Note: The old editions and some more recent ones read, “This fire makes Christ dwell through faith.” The Roman edition, together with all the manuscripts, reads as we do. Certainly the former reading arose only from someone who did not know that *hebetare* here means “to blunt” or “to diminish.”] [Col. 1459D]

This fire is accustomed to blunt and extinguish the savage fires of material flames. Accordingly, the Hebrews, kindled by this fire, were unable either to fear or to feel the vapor of the burning furnace (Daniel III, 50). 1201

Rightly, then, the good servant loves the Lord’s word refined by fire, with which charity is clothed—a charity that casts out fear.

## 21.

He aptly added “exceedingly,” because every teacher inflames the affection of the hearer, but above all others is the word of God, penetrating the divisions of the joints and the innermost marrow. [Col. 1459D]

Describe the word of God refined by fire to yourself in three ways: as that which cleanses, that which kindles, and that which illumines its hearers. [Col. 1460A]

Therefore the Lord says:

“I searched Jerusalem with a lamp” (Zephaniah I, 12).

But he found no one in it who could be cleansed, kindled, or illumined; therefore he left it in darkness.

## 22.

Nor should you wonder if the servant loves the Lord’s word of fire, since the Bride too loved it. She says:

“Your lips are like a scarlet cord.”

For in scarlet there is the appearance of fire, and the blood of the Lord’s cross gleams. The Lord’s lips were scarlet because they spoke of his own passion.

Accordingly, in Exodus, scarlet was set in place of fire.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “scarlet was compared with fire,” or, “scarlet was set in place.” The others, together with the editions, read as in the text. Ambrose seems to be referring to a passage of Flavius Josephus in Book III, chapter 8, of the *Jewish Antiquities*, where the mystical significance of the colors with which the curtains of the Tabernacle were woven is explained as follows:

“The fabrics woven from four materials signify the nature of the elements. The linen seems to indicate the earth, because flax grows from it; the purple, the sea, through its being dyed with the blood of the shellfish; the hyacinth indicates the air; and the scarlet may be a sign of fire.”

Origen was the first to follow this interpretation, in Homily 13 on Exodus XXX, and others followed him.] [Col. 1460D]

The world was not made from scarlet, but from the four elements; nevertheless, the figure of fire was expressed in scarlet. Unless its vapor penetrated heaven, air, seas, and lands, all things would dissolve as though their powers had been exhausted. [Col. 1460B]

By the scarlet cord, therefore, we recognize the bond of persuasion; by scarlet, either the ardor of desire that sparkles in the minds of hearers, or the sign of passion.

Hence the Bride says elsewhere:

“His lips are lilies, dripping with flowing myrrh” (Song of Songs V, 13).

Through myrrh the ointment of passion and the grace of resurrection are revealed; this pours the revived fragrance of life into the resurrected limbs of the dead.

Rightly, then, receiving the sweetness of his address, the Bride exclaims:

“His throat is sweetness, and he is altogether desirable” (ibid., 16).

## 23. (Verse 141)

The fifth verse follows:

“I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your righteous ordinances.” [Col. 1460C]

This verse can apply to many of the saints who were trained from their earliest youth through hard labors.

Joseph too, when he was sold into Egypt by his brothers as the younger one, was young and despised; he was sold into the humiliation of slavery. Later, when he was brought out of prison and placed in charge of Egypt, distributing grain to the peoples, he did not repay his brothers’ injury, but, returning their payment, gave them food and rescued his father’s old age from hunger and fasting. He went to meet him with his chariot lowered, while the others served him with the insignia of his great power, and he worshiped him. Rightly he said:

“I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your righteous ordinances.”

## 24.

David himself, younger than his brothers, was tending his father’s sheep as though assigned to a lowly duty. He was not presented to the priest, as though unworthy to be anointed king; but, sought out by the priest and summoned from the pastures, he received the privilege of royal anointing. [Col. 1460D]

Later, when he went forth to war and Goliath, despising the whole Jewish people because of the bulk of his body, challenged them to single combat, while the others were afraid, he asked the king to permit him to engage him. [Col. 1461A]

He was not yet considered fit for so great a contest, when the king said:

“You cannot go against the Philistine and fight with him, because you are a boy, while he is a warrior from his youth” (I Samuel XVII, 33). 1202

Nor would he have been admitted unless he had proved that in his youth he had strangled a lion with his own hands and killed it after drawing out the legs of the sheep it had seized.

Despised also by the Philistine because he advanced against an armed warrior with a staff and stones, he declared that he did not go forth to battle relying on strength or weapons, but trusting in the name of the Lord, so that he might remove the reproach brought upon the insulted people.

This young and despised man therefore struck down the Philistine, and, having gained the victory, triumphed to the testimony of ten thousand young women singing. [Col. 1461B]

## 25.

For he bore the type of the one who was to come upon the earth as one despised, who, without an ambassador, helper, or messenger, would free the whole people of this world through the battle of his cross. The souls of the saints, renewed through the sacrament of baptism, would applaud him because he had revealed to us the true Goliath and struck him down with the sword of his word.

The true Goliath, then, lies prostrate, overthrown by the humility of the Son of God. He has lost the head that turned itself toward many devices and deceits.

The souls that once mourned the torments of their sins now sing in security. They sing with timbrels—that is, with their bodies, dead to sin, resounding:

“Saul has triumphed over thousands, David over ten thousands” (I Samuel XVIII, 7). [Col. 1461C]

That harsh king is indignant, and the devil grows angry, because the young women sang that the son of harshness had deceived a few, whereas Christ redeemed the whole world.

Therefore Christ, born of a Virgin, says:

“I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your righteous ordinances.”

## 26.

The people of the nations also speak—once despised in the first election, still inexperienced in faith, growing in the zeal of its first devotion, or certainly renewed with the youth of the eagle through the sacrament of baptism:

“I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your righteous ordinances.”

I, who was formerly despised, am now preferred and placed before the elect. I, the people formerly despised because of sins, now possess the venerable fellowship of heavenly mysteries.

Now I am received with the honor of the heavenly table. My feasts are supplied neither by rain, nor by the labor of the earth’s offspring, nor by the fruits of trees. [Col. 1461D] For my drink I need seek neither rivers nor springs. Christ is my food; Christ is my drink. The flesh of God is food for me, and the blood of God is drink for me.

I no longer await annual harvests for my nourishment; Christ is served to me every day. I shall not fear that any inclemency of heaven or barrenness of the countryside will diminish him for me, if the diligence of reverent worship endures.

I no longer wish for rains of quail to descend upon me, which I once admired, nor for manna, which I once preferred to every food; for the fathers who ate manna became hungry. My food is the one who, if anyone eats him, will not hunger. My food is the one who does not fatten the body, but strengthens the human heart. [Col. 1462A]

## 27.

Previously, bread from heaven had been wondrous to me; for it is written:

“He gave them bread from heaven to eat” (John VI, 31).

But that was not the true bread; it was the shadow of what was to come. 1203 The Father reserved the true bread from heaven for me.

For me that bread of God descended from heaven which gives life to this world. It did not descend for the Jews; it did not descend for the Synagogue; it descended for the Church, for the younger people of God. [Col. 1462B]

For how did the bread that gives life descend for the Jews, when all who ate that bread—that is, the manna which the Jews thought was the true bread—died in the desert?

How did it descend for the Synagogue, when the whole Synagogue perished and, weakened by the eternal fast of faith, failed?

Accordingly, if they had received the true bread, they would not have said:

“Lord, give us this bread always” (ibid., 34).

### 28

What are you asking, Jew—that he should give you the bread which he gives to everyone, gives [Note: [Col. 1461D] The ancient practice of the faithful at Milan still continued: they used to participate daily in the sacred Communion. Hence, in *On the Sacraments*, book V, chapter 4: “Receive daily what benefits you daily,” and so forth. Yet the same author remarks that the Greeks were then content with receiving the Eucharist only once a year. In most of the Churches of the West, however, the custom of daily Communion had fallen into disuse, to such an extent that bishops and other more learned men neither censured nor commended it. See Jerome, Letter 50 to Pammachius, and Augustine, Letter to Januarius.] daily, gives always? It lies within you yourself to receive this bread: approach this bread, and you will receive it. Of this bread it is said: “All who distance themselves from you shall perish” (Ps. 72:27). If you distance yourself from him, you will perish; if you draw near to him, you will live.

This is the bread of life; therefore whoever eats life cannot die. For how will one die whose food is life? How will one fail who possesses a life-giving substance? Draw near to him and be filled, because he is bread; draw near to him and drink, because he is a fountain; draw near to him and be enlightened, because he is light; draw near to him and be freed, because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17); draw near to him and be absolved, because he is the forgiveness of sins.

“Who is this?” you ask. Hear him himself saying: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). You have heard him and seen him, yet you did not believe in him; therefore you are dead. Believe now at least, so that you may be able to live.

### 29

But you marvel at Moses, because he led your fathers through the sea by a path over dry ground. Moses did not command; he obtained the favor: he did not order the sea, but served him who ordered the waves. You praise Moses because he drowned King Pharaoh with his army. Moses prayed, and another commanded. Moses pleaded; Christ acted. Moses fled; Christ pursued. Moses followed the pillar in order to avoid the darkness of night; Christ gave light.

You acknowledge Moses because he tempered the bitterness of the water. You acknowledge Moses because he brought water forth from the rock; yet you do not acknowledge Christ, who overthrew the army of that true Egyptian king and plunged it into the depths of the abyss; who daily delivers us from the waves of this world, lest the storm of this age drown us.

What benefit was it for the fathers to cross the Red Sea, when they were not permitted to reach the land of promise? For all who came out of Egypt perished in the desert. Aaron died, Miriam died, and Moses himself also died; only Joshua son of Nun was preserved by the likeness of his sacred name.

Let the Jew applaud because, when he was thirsty, the rocks spewed out water for him. For me, an eternal fountain flowed from the body of God. Christ drank my bitterness in order to bestow upon me the sweetness of his grace.

### 30

Therefore the Christian people say: “I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your justifications.” He says this rightly who has justified God through the sacraments of baptism. For whoever is baptized justifies God, because he confesses his own sins and awaits from the Lord the forgiveness of his sins [Note: [Col. 1463D] One manuscript, the Laetian and Navarrese manuscript, reads: “forgiveness of sins is granted.” The others, together with the printed editions, read as in the text, except that in place of the verb *praestolatur* (“awaits”), several manuscripts have *sperat* (“hopes”), which does not differ in meaning.].

David justified him when he said: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words” (Ps. 50:6). The Pharisees did not justify him, for they refused to be baptized with John’s baptism, as you read in the Gospel (Luke 7:30).

Nor is it enough merely to justify God; one must also not forget God’s justifications—that is, one must preserve inviolate the gifts of spiritual grace and keep the blessings of sacred forgiveness undefiled and unharmed.

### 31

These things are general; but each individual Christian also possesses the particular privilege of saying: “I am young and despised,” if he is humble of heart, meek, and gentle. Let him therefore say: “I am young and despised.” Let him first state the general boast of youth, so that he may commend the grace of his humility all the more.

Humility in old age is not remarkable: old age, exhausted in strength, broken by infirmities, saddened by pain, breathless with sighs, baked by the heat of anxieties, and wearied by the very disgust of living, has forgotten the liveliness of boasting. Humility in the young, however, is rare and therefore astonishing.

While youth is vigorous, while strength is sound, while the blood is boiling, while anxiety is unknown, while weakness is not recognized, while joy is frequent—then boasting burns; then the proud impulse of youth lifts itself up; then humility, as though worthless, is scorned in its lowliness; then submission is judged to be the weakness of a base mind. Great, therefore, must be the maturity into which one’s character is trained—a maturity that conquers nature.

### 32

Indeed, if we consider the matter, humility failed in paradise; and therefore it came from heaven. Disobedience arose in paradise; and therefore obedience descended with the Savior. The flesh was puffed up, and thus submission born of gentleness could not be found on earth. The whole inheritance of the transgressor had swollen with pride.

When the Lord Jesus came, he first “emptied himself” (Phil. 2:6–8), not considering it robbery to be equal with God, taking the form of a servant, and being found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.

Do not be troubled because it is written “as a man.” He did not assume the likeness of a man, but the reality. For the Apostle himself says elsewhere: “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

And, to offer an example from the Gospel, John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Surely, because he said “as of the only-begotten,” did he intend that he be regarded as more a likeness of the only-begotten than the reality?

### 33

Christ therefore did not come without purpose. Now a human being may say, “I am young and despised”—the one who previously, among the former people, was an arrogant old man. He says, “I am young and despised,” just as the Church says: “I am black and beautiful” (Song 1:4). It placed “black” first in order to increase the beauty.

So here too he placed “young” first in order to increase the humility. He did not say, “I am black, beautiful,” lest what is black be judged beautiful. Nor did he say, “I am young, despised,” lest youth be thought contemptible; rather, he says, “Young—and, what you may wonder at, humble”: closer to one cast down than to one swollen with pride.

So also there: “I am black because of my former sin, but beautiful through confession of sin, devotion to amendment, and love of virtue.”

Although the word *and*, as grammarians call it, is a conjunction, it nevertheless creates a distinction by which confusion is separated and divided. Thus, if you say, “Ambrose Bassus is inside,” one person is understood; but if you assert, “Ambrose and Bassus are inside,” two people are clearly meant.

### 34

Let him therefore say: “I am young and despised,” because Christ redeemed the world in the poor and despised person, because Christ conquered the devil through humility.

Let him say, “I am despised,” because God does not scorn a humbled heart; because that despised Lazarus now rests in Abraham’s bosom, while that boastful rich man is tormented in hell.

Moses was despised and did not regard himself as capable when he was sent to liberate the Hebrew people. Jeremiah was despised, saying: “Sovereign Lord, behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am young” (Jer. 1:6). Yet this despised man is chosen more readily. For it is said to him: “Do not say, ‘I am young,’ because you shall go to all those to whom I send you, and you shall speak everything that I command you. Do not fear their presence, because I am with you, says the Lord, to deliver you” (ibid., 7–8).

Despised was that tax collector who did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven; and for this reason he was heard more readily than the Pharisee: “For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

### 35

(Verse 142.) It continues: “Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and your law is truth.”

Individuals can indeed perform works of righteousness, but not works that endure forever. That rich man whose wealth abounded in this world may perhaps have performed some works of righteousness and received their reward in the present life [Note: [Col. 1465D] All the printed editions connect the words “and received” with what follows, namely, “which did not pertain to eternal life.” These words, however, are absent from all the manuscripts.], though those works were neither great nor worthy of an everlasting reward.

Moreover, even when we perform some works of righteousness, we do not perform them continually, but only occasionally. Many do not seize what belongs to others, yet do not know how to give generously from what is their own. Others, while appropriating possessions to which they have no right, commonly bestow something on the poor in order to acquire for themselves the appearance of righteousness. This is not righteousness forever.

Many who are generally just have often committed serious offenses, possessing no fruit of eternal righteousness. Only God possesses righteousness perpetually and in all things: he feeds both the just and the unjust. Righteousness is not to be attributed only to benefactors [Note: [Col. 1465D] All the printed editions and many manuscripts read *beneficiis solis* (“only by benefits”). The more elegant reading in the Regius, Sorbonic, Remigius, and one Navarrese manuscript is *beneficis solis* (“only to benefactors”), so that benefactors are set in opposition to enemies, and both terms refer to the just and unjust mentioned above.]; rather, that is true righteousness which is extended even to enemies.

Accordingly he rightly says, “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5:44).

### 36

Therefore, just as the righteousness of God alone is eternal, so the law of God is truth. But how are we to understand this? Is it because the law of God is truth—that is, true—and everything God establishes is true, as he says below: “All your commandments are truth”? Or is it because truth itself is the law of God, since God does not lie?

With him, therefore, truth is law, while falsehood is transgression. This too can be understood in the following way: the law of God is truth; therefore, among the Jews there is no law of God, because they do not receive the truth.

The law of God is spiritual (Rom. 7:14), as the Apostle says. Those who have not received it spiritually, therefore, do not possess the true law. Whatever is not true is false, and whatever lies kills. The letter, therefore, which kills, lies; the Spirit, who gives life, is true.

### 37

Let us understand it in this way as well: the law of God is not a type, not a shadow, not a copy of heavenly things, but the heavenly things themselves. Hence it is also written that “the end of the Law is Christ” (Rom. 10:4).

In Christ there is not the abolition but the fullness of the Law, because he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. For just as the Old Testament exists, but all truth is in the New Testament, so the law given through Moses is a figure of the law.

[Note: [Col. 1465D; 1466D] All the manuscripts read as above, except that a few at the end have: “Therefore that is the true Law.” All the printed editions instead read: “The Old Testament came not to abolish but to fulfill, and likewise to confirm the New. But just as all truth is in the New Testament, so also the law . . . is of the true law. Therefore that Law,” etc. Those who patched the passage together in that fashion do not seem at all to have grasped Ambrose’s meaning. We judge his meaning to be as follows: just as, although the Old Testament existed, its truth—that is, the fulfillment of its figures—is in the New, so, although the law was given through Moses, it was nowhere fulfilled except in the new law.]

Therefore that Law is truly an image of the truth: in the image, the blood of a lamb is poured out; in the truth, Christ is sacrificed.

And rightly, after mentioning the sacrifice of calves according to the Law, the Apostle adds: “It was therefore necessary for the copies of heavenly things to be cleansed by these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices. For Christ did not enter into a sanctuary made by human hands, a copy of the true one, but into heaven itself, and now appears before the face of God on our behalf” (Heb. 9:23–24).

To recognize that the Lord Jesus gave a new law, you have the Holy Spirit saying: “This is the covenant which I shall make with them, says the Lord: I shall put my laws in their hearts, and I shall write them on their minds, and I shall remember their sins and their iniquities no more” (Heb. 10:16–17). Where there is forgiveness, there is no longer an offering for sins.

This clearly shows that all truth is contained in the Gospel, because the law of God is written in human minds and hearts, not on stone tablets. Those who do not have God’s commandments in their hearts do not have the law—either because it grows old among the Jews and is renewed among us.

### 38

It is a shadow, not the truth: when an offering is made for sins according to the Law, forgiveness of sins does not take place. For “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to cleanse sins” (Heb. 10:4). That forgiveness, therefore, was false until the truth of forgiveness arrived.

What could be clearer than the statement of the evangelist John, who says: “The Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17)? He introduced truth “in contrast to the Law” (*πρὸς ἀντιδιαστολὴν*—“for the sake of distinction from it”). Since *but* indicates separation, we must understand that the separation was inserted for this reason: if truth had been in the Law, [Note: [Col. 1466D] All the printed editions read, “there would not have been grace made through Christ.” The manuscripts, however, omit the word “grace,” and more coherently so; for the word “made” must refer to the preceding “truth,” which is the chief subject here.] it would not have been made through Christ.

### 39

We can understand it in this way as well: Christ is the truth; therefore the truth is the law. And if the commandment of the Lord is law, then much more is the living and effective Word of God the law.

### 40

(Verse 143.) The seventh verse follows: “Tribulation and necessity found me; your commandments are my meditation.”

Tribulations and necessities seek the just person; sometimes they find him, sometimes they do not. He is found to whom a crown is owed; he is not found who is not proved fit for the contest.

Tribulation, therefore, is like a kind of grace. For it is written: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50:19). Is that not grace which produces endurance? Therefore, since he knew that tribulation brings progress, he was found when tribulation sought him, and he did not flee from it.

### 41

Wisdom says: “The wicked shall seek me and shall not find me” (Prov. 1:28)—not because the Lord did not wish to be found by human beings, since he offered himself even to those who did not seek him, but because they sought him through deeds that made them unworthy to find what they sought.

Simeon, however, who was waiting for him, found him (Luke 2:25 ff.). Andrew found him. Indeed, he says to Simon: “We have found the Messiah,” which means “Christ” (John 1:41).

Philip also says to Nathanael: “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, the one whom Moses wrote about in the Law and the prophets, from Nazareth” (John 1:45). And to show how Christ would be found, he says: “Come and see” (ibid., 46).

Whoever therefore seeks Christ should come—not by bodily movement, but by the footsteps of the mind; he should see him not with outward eyes, but with inward ones.
