The eternal cannot be seen by bodily sight, because [Note: [Col. 1467D] Most manuscripts read: “the things that are seen are bodily.”] “the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18).

Christ, therefore, is not temporal, but existed with the Father before time, as God, the true Son of God; as everlasting power above time, whom no end of time can contain; as life above time, whom no day of death can ever find. For “the one who died, died to sin once for all; but the one who lives, lives to God” (Rom. 6:10).

### 42

Do you hear what the Apostle said today? “He died to sin,” he says, “once for all.” Christ died once for you, a sinner; do not sin again after baptism. He died once for all collectively, and he dies once for each individual, not repeatedly.

You are sin, O human being; therefore the almighty Father made Christ sin for you. He made him human, so that he might bear our sins. Therefore the Lord Jesus died for me, a sinner, “so that we might be the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:21). He died for me so that he might rise again for me. He died once; he rose once.

And you, having died with him, been buried with him, and been raised with him in baptism, beware lest, after having died once, you die again. You will no longer die to sin, but to forgiveness. Do not, after rising, die a second time; for “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him” (Rom. 6:9).

Therefore, did death rule over him? Certainly: by saying “it shall no longer rule,” he shows that it did rule. Only do not lose this benefit, O human being. For your sake Christ submitted himself to the dominion of death, so that he might strip you of the yoke of that dominion. He accepted the servitude of death in order to grant you the freedom of eternal life.

### 43

Whoever therefore seeks Christ also seeks his tribulation and does not flee from his passion. David, who was worthy to be sought by tribulation, himself sought tribulation. If he had not sought it, he would not have found it.

He himself testifies to what he found, saying: “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 114:3–4). And elsewhere: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he answered me in a broad place” (Ps. 117:5).

Tribulation, then, is good: it makes us worthy to be heard by the Lord in a broad place. To be heard by the Lord our God is a grace.

### 44

Whoever therefore seeks tribulation does not flee from it; whoever does not flee from it is found. He does not flee who meditates upon God’s commandments in understanding and in deeds [Note: [Col. 1467D] One Navarrese manuscript reads, “he does not flee from God’s commandments,” but with the sense “he does not flee from tribulation.” The other manuscripts and the printed editions agree with the text; after the verb “flees,” “tribulation” is to be understood.].

Contests certainly find the athlete who has been trained through continual exercise; but whoever has abandoned his training will unquestionably not be found, since he is unworthy to be sought.

David therefore, like a good athlete, says: “Tribulation and necessity found me,” because they always found him ready—not fleeing from the battles of necessity and tribulation, but seeking them.

### 45

(Verse 144.) It continues: “Your testimonies are righteous forever; give me understanding of them, and give me life.”

Who is so great that he can understand the testimonies of the Lord? Therefore understanding must be requested from the Lord, whose power is so great that its beginning is the fullness of virtue.

For it is written: “Piety toward God is the beginning of understanding” (Prov. 1:7). It is the foundation of all virtues according to the discipline of human and heavenly things.

Piety is dear to God, pleasing to parents, and reconciles one to the Lord. It nourishes relationships; it is the worship of God, the reward owed to parents, and the service of children. Piety, I say, is the tribunal of the just, the harbor of the needy, the refuge of the wretched, and the forgiveness of sinners.

### 46

Whoever has understanding is truly pious, for he understands the slippery weakness of human nature and quickly forgives the one who errs. He understands that the use and fellowship of nature have been given to us in common; therefore he pays what is due to the poor, rather than denying it as though it were not owed.

He understands that calamities have their turns; therefore, amid the shipwrecks of this world, he comes to meet them as though with some harbor of his humanity.

This is perfect virtue in human beings; in God, it is complete praise.

### 47

For this reason Solomon too, following his father’s instruction, asked the Lord for understanding, saying: “I am a humble child, and I do not know my entrance or my departure; and your servant is in the midst of your people, whom you have chosen, a numerous people like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted because of its multitude. And you shall give your servant an understanding heart, to hear and judge your people with justice, and to understand between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:7–9).

This pleased the Lord, because he did not ask for length of life or an abundance of royal riches, but for wisdom to understand the Lord’s judgments and justifications. Therefore he governed so great a people in peaceful rule: he did not usurp, as Adam did, the knowledge of the distinction between good and evil, but prayed to Christ for the grace of understanding it [Note: [Col. 1467D] The Roman edition reads, “he prayed to the Lord.” But it is not unusual for Ambrose to attribute to Christ the things that properly belong to the Word, because of the unity of person. Thus, in Sermon 15, no. 30, Christ is called “the author of all creation.” The same occurs frequently elsewhere.].

Whatever is divine knowledge must be sought from the Lord your God, so that you may be able to understand it. If Adam had asked, as David asked [Note: [Col. 1468D] All the printed editions read, “as Solomon asked.” All the manuscripts read, “as David asked.” This is not inappropriate, since David himself asks the Lord for understanding in this very verse.], he would certainly not have fallen into those inextricable snares of error by which all his descendants are strangled.

Therefore he died—and, what is more serious, the death of sin—because he first presumed to know before receiving the understanding by which he might be made alive.

### 48

Understanding therefore gives life, as the Spirit does, because understanding itself is a spiritual grace. Therefore the Holy Spirit brings about understanding through his gift.

“Good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Ps. 110:10). By this we are taught that we must not merely grasp what we understand intellectually, but also carry out in deeds what we understand.

## NINETEENTH SERMON. Koph

### 1

The nineteenth letter, Koph, begins. Its interpretation is “Conclusion”; elsewhere we find it rendered “Look.” The letter differs, but the meaning agrees. For whoever is enclosed must look around himself and not conceal the cause of the danger, especially when the peril is deadly.

A person is enclosed by swelling in the viscera or in the inner passages when, with the passage of breath obstructed, the processes of inhalation and exhalation are constricted. A woman is enclosed when there is a prolapse of the womb, by which the vital region of her chest is compressed; hence severe distress arises, and unless that chamber for receiving seed is restored to its proper place, it commonly excludes life.

Likewise, one who is distressed in spirit and pressed by certain impending adversities is said to be enclosed by mental anguish no less than by bodily anguish. For the heats and fevers of the soul are greater than those of the body [Note: [Col. 1469D] The printed edition reads “fevers of the soul”; the manuscripts read “heats” or “fervors of the soul,” and so forth.].

### 2

When enclosed, therefore, by swelling of the viscera, a person seeks a physician, so that he may drive away the danger and loosen what has been constricted. When the physician comes, he tries everything and examines the inner parts.

And you, enclosed by the heat of your spirit, look at yourself with the inner eye. The force of disease presses you; a harmful conscience burns; the burden of sins weighs upon you; anguish obstructs the mind’s perception. Know yourself and seek the medicine of prayer. Ask that the physician may come—the one who descended from heaven, who especially seeks out the gravely ill, as he himself says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12).

Do you have wounds? Do not delay: with him there is no postponement of healing. Do you have ulcers? Do not be afraid: he is accustomed to heal by his word, not by the knife.

Look, therefore, with those eyes with which David sought and obtained help: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains,” he says; “I sought from where my help would come” (Ps. 120:1–2). He found it only from the Lord, for the one who created the world protects the inhabitants of the world.

Look, therefore, and look always, because the eyes of the just are always toward the Lord.

### 3

Jeremiah also teaches you this in the Lamentations under this same letter, saying to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1469D] The Roman edition reads, “Rise to meditate in the night,” perhaps so as to conform more closely to the Vulgate, where it reads, “Rise up, praise in the night.” All the manuscripts and the old editions agree with us. Certainly our reading agrees better with the Septuagint, where one reads: “Ἄναστα, ἀγαλλίασαι ἐν νυκτὶ” (“Rise, rejoice in the night”), and so forth.]: “Rise and awaken in the night; at the beginning of your watch pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord; lift your hands to the Lord for the lives of your little ones, who faint from hunger in the streets of all the roads” (Lam. 2:19).

Does he not plainly reveal the anguish of enclosure and urge you to provide yourself with saving medicine through the attention of the heart, in which the sight of the better eye resides?

Indeed, further on, again under this letter, he says: “For our time has drawn near; our days have been filled; our end has come. Those who pursued us have become swifter than the eagles of heaven. They set ambushes for us in the mountains; they lay in wait for us in the wilderness” (Lam. 4:18–19).

### 4

He has shown the extremity of enclosure and that there is no remedy except in the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone can bring medicine to the despairing.

And, as though showing him to us, he says: “The breath before our face, Christ the Lord, has been seized in our destruction . . . . . In his shadow we shall live among the nations” (ibid., 20).

And further on: “You shall drink,” he says, “and become drunk” (ibid., 21). Again: “He shall visit your iniquities; he shall reveal them upon your sins” (ibid., 22).

How briefly he has expressed Christ’s coming and passion, and the forgiveness of all sins! How plainly he has declared the future gathering of the nations! Hence the Apostle’s statement: “A partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel may be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

### 5

Come, Lord Jesus—but now not in shadow, but in the sun of righteousness. If the shadow was beneficial; if the shadow of your passion protected us; if the shadow of your body saved us—how much will the open brightness of your power accomplish?

Through a shadow leprosy was healed (Matt. 8:3); through a shadow, too, the bleeding of that woman who touched the fringe of the Lord’s garment stopped (Luke 8:44). Through a shadow we saw you when you had “neither form nor beauty.”

Your shadow was the flesh, which cooled the heat of our desires [Note: [Col. 1470D] The manuscripts agree overwhelmingly on this reading; all the printed editions, after the word “desires,” add the phrase “which restrained the insolence of vices.”], restrained the fires of lust, and tempered the conflagrations of greed and the various passions.

And what shall I say about the Lord’s shadow, when even the shadow of the apostles healed (Acts 5:15)? For when Peter came, each person brought out his sick, whom the shadow of the passing apostle restored to health.

### 6

Hear that the Lord’s flesh was a shadow: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud, and he shall come into Egypt” (Isa. 19:1). David also says: “Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16:8).

He was made an emptied shadow for us, whom the sun of iniquity had scorched. We therefore saw him in shadow when faith was still beginning to emerge. But now he illuminates the whole world; nevertheless, we still see him through the shadow of his body, which is the Church, not yet face to face. For bodily eyes cannot receive the radiance of divinity.

This shadow too protects the whole world every day. Enclosure was therefore beneficial: “For God enclosed all things in unbelief, so that he might have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32).

But now let us consider what must be said in connection with enclosure and from where we must begin.

### 7

(Verse 145.) “I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, Lord; I shall seek your justifications.”

When we suffer bodily assaults, we commonly cry out so that we may call others to our aid. The holy Prophet was under pressure, as persecutors drew near him. First Saul, hostile and armed, pursued him with an army; afterward his parricidal son threatened him. Not content with the exile of the fugitive, he sought to take his father’s life.

But he could suffer less from those whom he saw in the present than from those whom he did not see. For the saints have a struggle not only against flesh and blood, but also against “principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this world,” who, like bandits, lie in wait for human affections in the night of this age.

When holy David saw their violent attacks being made against him, he cried out with his whole heart. For against the devil one must use not loudness of voice, but greatness of heart.

### 8

There is nevertheless also a voice of the heart, just as there is a voice of blood that reaches God. Indeed, God says: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. 4:10).

Our heart therefore cries out not with bodily sound, but with the loftiness of its thoughts and the harmony of its virtues. Great is the cry of faith. In the Spirit of adoption we cry, “Abba, Father,” and the Spirit of God himself cries out in us.

Great is the voice of righteousness; great is that of chastity, through which even the dead speak. They not only speak, but also cry out, like Abel.

The soul of the unjust, however, does not cry out even while alive, because it is dead to God. There is nothing sublime, nothing magnificent in it—nothing like those “whose sound has gone out into all the earth, and whose words to the ends of the world.”

Moses spoke in a feeble voice, yet he was heard more than everyone else. He is heard daily in the Church, but he is not heard by those alone—namely, the Jews—who hear with their ears but do not heed [Note: [Col. 1471D] The Roman edition alone reads, “Moses had a feeble voice and did not speak; yet he was heard more than everyone.” Shortly afterward, where that edition has “and they do not understand with the heart,” the old manuscripts read “they do not hear.” The manuscripts omit the word “with the heart”; of these, only two give, instead of “but they do not hear,” “but they are not heard.” This is not inappropriate, since it means the same as “they do not consent.”].

To another the Prophet says: “Raise your voice with strength” (Isa. 58:1).

### 9

Hannah, however, did not cry out in her heart (1 Sam. 1:13), as Moses did, but spoke. Perhaps this was because she was asking for children—that is, something good but private, not public—and therefore she did not cry out.

But because she was asking from the Lord, because she offered to the Lord whoever she might receive, she spoke to God. Moses, however, cried out because he prayed not for himself but for the whole people.

Hence the Lord said to him: “Why do you cry out?” (Exod. 14:15). He cried out with devoted affection, profound understanding, and a voice that resounded in heaven, asking through miracles for things worthy of heaven, so that he might change the elements of the world.

### 10

Finally, to review the sequence of the passage itself: Pharaoh was pressing forward, accompanied by countless Egyptian chariots, and was driving the Hebrews onward. On one side the enemy surrounded them; on the other, the intervening sea enclosed the people of God. There was no confidence in arms, no hope in strength.

Only a pitiable complaint was heard: that it would be better for them to bear the harsh burdens of slavery in Egypt than to be consumed by a bitter death in the wilderness—a complaint offering no help and bringing great offense.

Moses therefore stood sorrowful, anxious, and troubled by both the dangers and the complaints of the people, awaiting faith in the heavenly promises. Silently within himself he pondered by what means the Lord, mindful of grace though forgetful of the offense, might come to their aid.

The Lord says to him: “Why do you cry out to me?”—“I do not hear its sound; I recognize its voice. I read its silence; I detect its cry in its deeds.”

The people cried out, and were not heard; Moses was silent, and was heard.

The Lord did not say to the people, “Why do you cry out to me?” For the people were not crying out to God when they uttered complaints that were unjust and unworthy of men. But he said to Moses, “Why do you cry out to me?” That is: “You alone cry out to me, because you hope in me; you alone cry out to me, because you stir up my power; you alone cry out to me, because you expect my name to be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.”

### 11

Moses therefore cried out in his heart, and every wise person cries out in his heart. Thus Wisdom, with the loftiest proclamation, calls people to the mixing bowl, saying: “Abandon foolishness . . . and seek wisdom” (Prov. 9:6).

This proclamation, which promises wisdom to the foolish, is one of great sublimity and a great voice. The Lord Jesus also cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

And truly he cried out with a great voice, for he called human beings to the kingdom of heaven, to that venerable drink into which the flood of eternal life is poured [Note: [Col. 1472D] All the printed editions read, “And with a truly great voice he cried out.” But since “voice” is found in none of the manuscripts, “great” here seems to be in the same case as in the expression below, “great mouths,” and so forth. Again, the Roman edition, together with some manuscripts, reads “the fruit is poured in”; the other editions, together with the remaining manuscripts, read “the flood is poured in.” The latter is better, since it appears to allude to the scriptural phrase, “You shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight.”].

And when you pray, pray greatly—that is, pray for things that are eternal, not things that perish. Pray for things that are divine and heavenly, so that you may be like the angels in heaven.

Do not pray for money, because it is rust; do not pray for gold, because it is metal; do not pray for property, because it is earth. Such prayer does not reach the Lord.

God does not hear anything unless he considers it worthy of his gifts. But he hears a devout voice, full of dedication and grace.

### 12

Therefore one must not merely cry out in the heart; one must cry out with the whole heart. Just as one cries out bodily only when one cries out with the whole mouth, so spiritually one must cry out with the whole heart if we wish to accomplish great things and obtain from the Lord what we ask.

The Lord demanded this voice from the people, but the people did not know it. Therefore the Lord said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

Whoever draws near with the heart is heard by the Lord. Let the heart therefore cry out first, so that the spoken word may be heard.

### 13

But it is not enough to cry out to the Lord; one must also seek out his ordinances. He seeks out the ordinances who ascribes to divine providence whatever is just in all creatures, and especially in rational creatures, or even in irrational ones. [Col. 1473A]

[Note: All manuscripts and the old edition have *in corpore* in the text. Fra. and Gill., however, have *insitum est* in the margin, which the Roman edition transferred into the text. Our reading is correct, since here we are being taught how God’s justice is to be investigated in all living creatures: this is declared to occur when whatever justice we discover in them is referred back to him. Compare, if convenient, what follows immediately with Book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapters 18, 19, and 22. [Col. 1473D–1474D]]

Whence comes the turtle-dove’s devotion to chastity, which, after losing its mate, does not know how to indulge in intercourse—something human beings cannot preserve? Whence comes the restrained care with which most living creatures preserve their offspring, so that once they have recognized the gift of conception, they do not think intercourse should be repeated there, lest the seeds already received be adulterously mingled?

The phoenix knows nothing of bodily intercourse and does not know the allurements of lust; rather, it rises again from its own funeral pyre. It is the surviving bird for itself, itself the heir of its own body, and the offspring of its own ashes.

The eagle carefully weighs its offspring in a diligent examination, lest it nourish degenerate young. It even suspends the still-tender fledglings with its loving talon and exposes them to the rays of the sun, so that, if they should turn their eyes away under the force of the brightness, it may release its grip and let them fall headlong as degenerates. But if they are able to prove the vigor of their nature by steadfastly enduring the sun’s rays, it carries back, with grateful burden, offspring worthy of their lineage. [Col. 1473B]

### 14

All the birds of heaven neither sow nor reap, and God feeds them, because they keep the ordinances of the Lord, claiming nothing as their own, but content to relieve their hunger from the fruit-bearing tree which, by the Lord’s judgment, has been given as common food.

From these creatures, then, we learn how the supports of divine providence would not be lacking to human beings if we were willing to preserve God’s ordinances. He who feeds the birds—would he not feed human beings, whom he made in his own image and likeness? Are we not worth more than they? By the privilege of nature we are worth more, but by reason of devotion we are inferior, because of the injustice of transgression. [Note: All editions and two manuscripts have “by reason of the diminution of grace.” One manuscript has “because of the diminution”; the remainder have “by reason of devotion,” that is, obedience, which is plainly greater in brute creatures than in human beings. [Col. 1474D]]

### 15. (Verse 146)

The second verse follows: “I cried out to you; save me, and I shall keep your commandments.”

He repeats that he cried out to the Lord, and promises that he will be a keeper of the heavenly statutes which the Lord God established, with heaven and earth as witnesses, so that transgressors may be convicted by the testimony of the elements. How will they look upon heaven, which knows of their transgression? How will they expect fruits from the earth, which knows the ungrateful?

See, therefore, how substantial a promise the Prophet makes. In crying out, a faithful and ready disposition is expressed; in keeping the testimonies, the virtue of self-restraint and the diligence of obedience are made evident.

### 16. (Verse 147)

The third verse follows: “I anticipated the dawn and cried out; I hoped in your words.”

The Greek says *ἐν ἀωρίᾳ* (*en aōria*), which means “before the hour,” “before the appointed time.” Therefore, the person who entreats the Lord should not wait as though special times had been prescribed, unaware that there is some particular time for supplications to the Lord; rather, he should be continually engaged in them.

Whether we eat or drink, let us proclaim Christ, ask Christ, think of Christ, and speak of Christ. Let Christ always be in our heart; always, in our mouth.

### 17

But perhaps you will say: How is it written, “There is a time for everything, and a time for every matter under heaven” (Eccles. III, 1)?

But the Lord Jesus is above heaven and is circumscribed by no time. Let Arian impiety close its mouth. “A time for every matter,” he says, “under heaven”: how much more is time under God, and not above God? The generation from the Father has no time; for a work does not precede its maker, but the maker is above the beginning of the work.

Perhaps they may object that he said, “My time has not yet come” (John VII, 6), and again, “Father, the hour has come” (John XVII, 1). But this is the hour of his Passion. There is also the time of the virginal conception: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isa. VII, 14), because the Virgin conceived within time, and therefore conceived at the appointed age.

### 18

Therefore, let the one who asks always ask; and if he does not pray continually, let him always keep ready the disposition of one who prays.

The Lord Jesus spent the night in prayer (Luke VI, 12), not because he needed the help of prayer, but to establish for you an example of imitation. He spent the night praying for you, so that you might learn how to pray for yourself. Therefore, repay him what he offered on your behalf.

Hear the Prophet saying above: “At midnight I rose to confess you” (Sermon 8, verse 63). You too should rise even at midnight, if you cannot keep watch throughout the entire night, so that, while you pray at night, the splendor of the true Sun may shine into your breast. For every soul that thinks upon Christ is always in the light: the day shines, and Christ continually breathes light upon you. [Note: The Roman edition has “is always”; for it adds, “For Christ breathes the light of day upon you.” Two manuscripts have “is always of day.” “The light for you,” and so forth. The old edition and the remaining manuscripts have the reading printed in the text. [Col. 1474D]]

But since the following verse clearly expresses the time for praying, I think that in this verse the time of actions and works, rather than the time of prayer, is intended. [Col. 1474C]

### 19

Whoever, while still in adolescence, assumes the gravity of old age, and governs youthful years by a certain veteran self-restraint, bringing the ardor of a vigorous body into harmony with the gray maturity of conduct, anticipates the maturity of age.

For what praise can there be if someone turns a body exhausted by pleasures and already chilled by the frost of old age toward the late duties of devotion, after its vigor has been diminished by sluggishness? There is no crown unless there has been a struggle in a difficult contest; and few can reach it. Not all who enter the stadium arrive at the finish.

That person is praiseworthy who has the contest within himself before the contest: who restrains his rebellious flesh by the command of the mind, chastises it with frugal moderation, and brings it into servitude, lest it revel in unbridled freedom and, burning with untamed desire, break the reins of the ruling soul.

The old man is therefore “in the hour” if he performs the duties of sober maturity. The young person anticipates the hour if, before the hour, he suppresses the incentives of pleasure with the weight of old age and extinguishes the allurements of burning desire.

“For the Lord is good to those who endure,” says Jeremiah (Lam. III, 25). And, “It is good for a man who has borne the yoke from his youth: he will sit alone and be silent, because he has borne the yoke of the word” (ibid., 27).

For whoever has borne the yoke from his youth and, willingly, has placed his tender neck beneath the reins of mature discipline will sit alone, removed from the tumult of passions that clamor for attention, and will remain quietly silent. He will no longer need to quarrel with his body or contend with various desires, because the soul that seeks God has borne the yoke of the word and has made all the delights of youth its captives.

Hence perhaps we may also understand the Lord’s saying, “He will not cry out, nor contend, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets” (Matt. XII, 19; from Isa. XLII, 2), not only as referring to silence in defense, contempt of acquittal, and endurance of suffering, but also as referring to the repression of all bodily pleasures.

Thus it is written elsewhere: “Because he committed no sin” (1 Pet. II, 22). Rightly, then, he was silent when placed in danger of death, because he did not fear the sting of death. [Col. 1475B]

### 20

“I hoped in your words,” he says. The Greek uses *ἑπήλπισα* (*epēlpisa*), which means continually growing in hope and adding hope to hope.

The righteous person always hopes. Even when placed amid adversities and afflicted by repeated troubles, he does not know how to despair. Rather, the graver the things he endures, the more he hopes, and he gains progress in hoping, according to the oracle:

“Comfort, comfort my people, says the Lord. Priests, speak justice to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her, because her humiliation has been filled up and her sin has been released, because she has received from the hand of the Lord double for her sins” (Isa. LX, 1–2).

How quickly he said that the fullness of humiliation is the release of sin, and repeated the reason for consolation: the mark of reconciliation is greater in proportion as the punishment has been greater than the offense. [Col. 1475C]

### 21

Job, weighed down by so many bitter afflictions, accumulated hope through a devout disposition, asserting that the cause of the impious was distinct from that of the devout, since “their light will be extinguished” (Job XVIII, 5). But, according to Solomon, “the light is always for the righteous” (Prov. XIII, 9).

From this it follows that the righteous person always hopes in the words of God and adds hope to hope. Isaiah expressed this more clearly, saying: “Expect tribulation upon tribulation, hope upon hope” (Isa. XXVIII, 10). [Note: No edition recognizes the reading *exspecta*, “expect,” although all the manuscripts contain it, except for a few in which *exspectat*, “he expects,” is read. This is incorrect; for the Septuagint consistently reads, “θλῖψιν ἐπὶ θλῖψιν προσδέχου” and so forth. In the Hebrew text and in the other versions, however, there is considerable variation at this point, which may be seen in the Polyglot Bibles. [Col. 1475D]]

He was speaking to those who had been weaned and taken from the breasts—that is, to those who had passed beyond the first nourishment of infancy and were now capable of stronger food.

Let Isaac the patriarch serve as an example: after being weaned, he grew to such greatness that, while still at the beginning of his early life, he nevertheless did not shrink from the sword of his father, who was about to strike him (Gen. XXII, 10). Abraham had several sons, but he weaned no other one; only in Isaac is it written that he made a great feast (Gen. XXI, 8).

And Scripture rightly called it a great feast, because it was a type of the one whose feast the hearts of the saints continually celebrate. [Col. 1476A]

### 22. (Verse 148)

The fourth verse follows: “My eyes anticipated the morning, to meditate on your words.”

Above (verse 147) he said, “I anticipated *ἐν ἀωρίᾳ*,” that is, before the hours, before the appointed time. Here he says, “in the morning,” signifying a different time for praying and singing psalms to the Lord.

The former, then, is in accordance with the saying, “At midnight I rose” (Sermon 8, verse 63); the latter with, “I anticipated the rising sun.” For it is shameful if the ray of the rising sun finds you idle in your bed, confronting you with shameless reproach, and the clear light strikes eyes still weighed down by sleepy torpor.

It reproves us for having let such an interval of time pass in a night devoid of any service of devotion or offering of spiritual sacrifice. Do you not know, human being, that every day you owe God the first fruits of your heart and voice? Your harvest is daily; your fruit is daily.

Therefore, hasten to meet the rising sun, so that it may find you already prepared when it rises, lest the first brightness of day disturb your eyes as they are still submerged in wet sleep.

### 23

“In my bed, during the nights, I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song III, 1), says the Church. For this reason she deserved to find him and to obtain his favor: because she sought him even in her bed; she sought him during the nights.

Therefore, having obtained his presence, she later speaks to the Bridegroom:

“Come, my brother; let us go out into the field; let us lodge in the villages; let us rise early for the vineyards” (Song VII, 11).

Do you perceive how the Bride invites the Word of God to come upon the earth and take away the sins of the world?

This field had previously been deserted, made foul by the thorns of our sins and bristling with prickles. It was a village in which Adam, confined in exile, held the heirs of his entire posterity in perpetual banishment.

The Church therefore leads Christ there, so that he may free Adam. Then, once the exiles had been released, the field of this world began to have suitable cultivators; and what had previously been barren became fruitful through the planting of the eternal vine.

Yet even so, she does not wander joyfully among spiritual branches; rather, she calls Christ to these vineyards, where there may be singing and prayer, and where harmless fruit may endure through nights and days.

### 24

“There,” he says, “I will give you my breasts; the mandrakes have given forth their fragrance” (ibid., 13). [Note: Here our saint follows chiefly the opinion of Dioscorides, Book IV, chapter 7, though he does not reject the opinions of others. These may be consulted in Matthiolus’s discussion of the same book and chapter; the Sacred Critics also offer some material on mandrakes in Genesis XXX, verse 14. Consult them. [Col. 1476D]]

Many distinguish a certain sex among mandrakes, believing that there are both males and females, but that the females have the stronger odor.

He therefore signifies the nations which previously stank, when they were weaker through a certain emasculated feebleness of unbelief, but began to bear the fruit of a good fragrance after they believed in the coming of the Lord.

We also read that the holy Rachel received mandrakes from her sister Leah, so that Leah might allow her to sleep with the holy Jacob that night (Gen. XXX, 14 and following).

Reuben, the firstborn, had brought the mandrakes to his mother Leah, who, with dim eyes, represented the Synagogue, because she could not see the grace of Christ, her weak mental vision having grown dull. [Col. 1477A]

This makes clear that the fruits which the Synagogue had previously received from the firstborn Son of God it ceded to the Church. But because Leah, having obtained the intercourse of that night, gave birth to the heir of her posterity, she fulfilled the mystery: when the apostles believed, the remnant of the Jews was saved through the election of grace. [Note: After the word “received,” certain Paris editions inserted “because she received the grace of Christ.” We have rejected this as spurious. [Col. 1477D]]

### 25

Hence the Church says: “New things and old, my brother, I have kept for you” (Song VII, 13). “Who will grant that you were a nursing brother, at the breasts of my mother? Finding you outside, I will kiss you, and indeed they will not despise me. I will take you and lead you into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her who conceived me; there you will teach me” (Song VIII, 1–2).

Thus, possessing an understanding of the new and ancient Scriptures and not considering herself contemptible, she not only holds the Word in the secrecy of her heart through prayers, but also kisses him with the kisses of grace, as it were, through the singing voices of choirs. [Col. 1477B]

### 26

Accordingly, rich in pomegranates—that is, in diverse and innumerable fruits—and especially in the fragrances of faith, grace, wisdom, and glory, supported by the riches of eternal life which are found around the Bridegroom’s left and right sides, she rouses Christ through the applause of holy souls gathered in praise, saying:

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken or stir up love until it wishes” (ibid., 4). [Note: This is the reading of the editions and many manuscripts. Others, though not few, have “pleasing through the fragrances of faith, of wisdom,” and so forth. [Col. 1477D]]

### 27

Therefore, the daughters of Jerusalem—holy souls of the patriarchs, prophets, and righteous people of ancient times, or the heavenly powers—marvel at her, saying:

“Who is this who ascends, made white, leaning upon her brother?” (ibid., 5)

That is, the Church shines with such solemn celebrations; she who formerly was dark by day now shines in the nights and gleams. [Col. 1477C]

### 28

The Lord himself, delighted by such a gift of those singing psalms, says:

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as hell. Its wings are wings of fire and flame. Much water will not be able to extinguish or exclude love, and rivers will not inundate it” (ibid., 6–7).

Because he saw such devotion in the Church, he considers the peoples now worthy to be able to bear his seal upon our heart and arm.

For God the Father sealed him; and whoever has received his testimony has set his seal that God is truthful. Therefore, those who work for food that endures unto eternal life have been sealed according to the image and likeness of Christ, who is the image of the invisible God.

Therefore, just as God is truthful, so also mark truth in your understanding and in your works, so that your mouth may not speak falsehood and your hand may not perform the works of human beings, which belong to this deceitful world, but those which belong to God: so that you may give generously to the poor, raise up the weak, and honor the dead with burial in a tomb.

Through such works love is sought, so that no one may be separated from Christ even by the danger of death. Hence he says: “Who will separate us from Christ? Tribulation, or distress . . . or persecution?” (Rom. VIII, 35). And below: “For I am confident that neither death nor life nor angels” (ibid., 38). [Col. 1478A]

### 29

Jealousy is likewise hard in the form of love, and its wings are wings of fire. It has wings like a dove, for “the feathers of the dove are silvered”; with these the one who loves flies away, saying: “Behold, I have gone far off, fleeing, and I remained in the wilderness” (Ps. LIV, 8).

But the wings of love are wings of fire, with which it kindles the ardor of affection. With this vapor the Lord made his angels spirits and his ministers burning fire—burning, but not consuming.

We also read of the wing of the temple, upon which the devil, tempting him, made the Savior ascend; it was situated at the summit of the temple (Matt. IV, 5).

Thus there are the pinnacles of the wing, there are the heights of love, which habitually kindle the vapor of grace in human breasts, so that much water cannot extinguish or exclude love, and rivers of worldly storms cannot shut it in. [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts have “the pinnacles of piety.” Others, somewhat more numerous, have “the pious pinnacles.” Finally, the remaining manuscripts have “the pinnacles of the wing.” The best reading is the last, since it refers to the previously mentioned “wing of the temple,” the pinnacle of which the Vulgate calls *pinnaculum*. [Col. 1478D]]

### 30

Since, then, such great grace of the Church and such great rewards of devotion invite us, let us anticipate the rising sun; let us hasten to meet its rising before it says, “Behold, I am here” (Isa. LVIII, 9).

The Sun of justice wishes to be anticipated, and he waits to be anticipated. Hear how he waits and desires to be anticipated.

He says to the angel of the church of Pergamum: “Repent; otherwise I will come to you quickly” (Rev. II, 12 and 16).

He says to the angel of Laodicea: “Be zealous, therefore, and repent. Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter to him” (Rev. III, 14, 19, and 20).

He could enter; indeed, when he rose again with his body, no barrier of closed doors could hold him back, and suddenly, unannounced, he entered the apostles’ inner room (John XX, 19). But he desires to test the devotion of your efforts; he already had apostles whose faith had been proved.

Or perhaps he anticipates in persecution; where there is tranquility, he desires to be anticipated. Certainly anticipate this sun whom you see. “Rise, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (Eph. V, 14). If you anticipate this sun before it rises, you will behold Christ illuminating you.

He first shines in the secret place of your heart. When you say to him, “My spirit watches for you from the night” (Isa. XXVI, 9), he will cause morning light to shine during the night, if you meditate on the words of God.

For while you meditate, there is light; and when you see a light not of time but of grace, you will say, “Your commandments are light” (ibid.).

When day finds you meditating on the divine words, and the pleasing work of praying and singing psalms delights your mind, you will again say to the Lord Jesus: “You will delight the goings forth of morning and evening” (Ps. LXIV, 9). [Col. 1479A]

### 31

Or does the Jewish people, having Moses as its teacher, use its elders—who have been chosen for this duty—to recite the divine Scriptures every day, through nights and days without any cessation? And if you ask an elder anything else, he knows nothing except to recite the sequence of the divine Scripture (Exod. XVIII, 14 and following). [Note: All manuscripts have this reading. The editions, however, have “the Jewish people used Moses daily in its discourses, performing the judgment of God from morning until evening.” His kinsman, seeing that this was intolerable, gave counsel for completing the task by dividing the burden among others who had been chosen for this duty. This is a mere gloss. [Col. 1479D]]

There is no discourse there about the world; only Scripture is woven together. The mouths of individuals succeed one another in turn, lest that sacred sound of the heavenly commandments ever be silenced.

And you, Christian, are asleep, although Christ is your teacher; and you do not fear that it may be said of you, “This people honors me with its lips”? The Jew honors him at least with his lips, but you do not even honor him with your lips. If the heart of the one who honors him merely with his lips is far from God, how can your heart be near, when you do not honor him even with your lips?

How long will sleep hold you? How long will worldly affairs hold you? How long will the cares of this life hold you? How long will earthly things hold you? [Col. 1479B]

### 32

At least divide your time between God and the world. Or, when you cannot carry out in public the affairs of this world and the darkness of night prevents you, devote yourself to God and give yourself to prayers. And so that you do not fall asleep, sing psalms; cheat your sleep by a good deception.

Hasten in the morning and bring to the Church the first fruits of your devout vow. Afterwards, if worldly necessity calls you, you will not be prevented from saying, “My eyes anticipated the morning, to meditate on your words”; you will proceed confidently to your activities.

How delightful it is to begin with hymns and songs, with the Beatitudes which you read in the Gospel (Matt. V)! [Note: Ambrose calls “beatitudes,” or “blessings,” especially the first part of the discourse which Christ delivered to his disciples on the mountain; indeed, he sometimes applies the term to the whole of that most divine sermon, as may be observed from his preface to the Gospel according to Luke. It seems not unreasonable to infer from this passage that the Beatitudes were accustomed to be recited at the first gathering of the Church even on those days when Christians were occupied with secular business, so that they might thereby be stimulated to works of mercy. Perhaps this was a particular custom of the Church of Milan; for in many other places we read of this morning gathering of Christians, but nowhere have we found any indication that the evangelical Beatitudes were so often recited there. As for Ambrose’s addition, “so that Christ’s discourse may bless you,” this is said in the sense in which, in Luke VI, when Christ begins that discourse, he is described as drawing a blessing from the treasury of divinity, and so forth. [Col. 1479D–1480D]]

How beneficial it is that Christ’s discourse should bless you, and that, while you recite the Lord’s blessings, you should undertake the pursuit of some virtue, so that you may also recognize in yourself the merit of divine blessing. [Col. 1479C]

### 33. (Verse 149)

The fifth verse follows: “Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord, and according to your judgment give me life.”

Every human being, even if holy and righteous, ought to pray that the Lord hear him according to his mercy, not according to the merits of any virtue, because virtue is rare and sins are many; and according to his judgment, so that he may bring aid to the weak.

We ought especially to pray this when we are pressed by some adversities. Hence the holy David did not ask idly for divine mercy in advance.

### 34. (Verse 150)

For the next verse says: “Those who persecute me unjustly have drawn near; but they have gone far from your law.”

The Greek has it thus: “Those who persecute me with iniquity have drawn near,” that is, those who were persecuting me with iniquity. The closer they came to me, the farther they separated themselves from your law, because whoever persecutes his brother is separated from the law.

For the law says: “You shall love the Lord your God . . . you shall love your neighbor” (Deut. VI, 5). Therefore, let me not hate my brother, lest it be said to me: “If you do not love your brother, whom you see, how can you love God, whom you do not see?” (1 John IV, 20).

Do you not know that your brother is the price of Christ’s blood? You therefore do not love Christ’s price if you do not love your brother. [Col. 1480A]

### 35

Therefore, the persecutor approaches me in order to harm me; but he separates himself from the law. For what partnership is there between justice and iniquity?

Whoever separates himself from the law of God separates himself from eternal life, for the law is life. Thus, while displaying the law of God, the Prophet says: “Behold, this is life: whoever does the things that belong to the law will live by them” (Lev. XVIII, 5)—which certainly applies to the spiritual law.

And perhaps the one who approaches me in order to harm me, while separating himself from the law, separates himself from Christ, because Christ is life.

But if I cling to Christ, he does not approach me; for even if he has power over my body, he will nevertheless be unable to harm my soul. Indeed, how far removed from the merits of the martyrs are the persecutors of the martyrs! [Col. 1480B]

### 36. (Verse 151)

But perhaps you will say: How do the saints cling to God? Therefore the verse continues:

“You are near, O Lord, and all your commandments are truth.”

The Lord is near to everyone, since he is present everywhere. We cannot flee from him if we offend him, deceive him if we sin, or lose him if we worship him.

God observes everything, sees everything, and stands beside each person, saying: “Am I not a God who is near?” (Jer. XXIII, 23).

And how can God be absent anywhere, when you read concerning the Spirit of God: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. I, 7)? For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is the Lord God.

“I fill heaven and earth,” says the Lord (Jer. XXIII, 24). Where, then, can the one who fills all things be absent? Or how have we all received from his fullness, unless he is near to all? [Col. 1480C]

### 37

David, therefore, knowing that God is everywhere and fills heaven, earth, and the seas, says:

“Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings before the light and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 7–10).

How plainly he signified that God is everywhere, that where God is, there his Spirit is present, and that wherever the Spirit of God is, there God is. Here the undivided union of the Trinity has been expressed. [Note: All editions have, “and where the Spirit of God is, there God is, and where God is, there the Spirit of God is present.” Several manuscripts have this no less awkwardly; but the more numerous and better manuscripts have the reading printed in the text. [Col. 1481D]]

For the Son of God spoke these words through the mouth of the Prophet, speaking in the person of a human being: through the incarnation he descended to earth, through the resurrection he ascended into heaven, and through the death of his body he entered hell in order to release those who were bound.

Or, if you refer the passage to the Prophet, you perceive that it expresses how the hand and right hand of God, Christ, are present everywhere—where God the Father and the Holy Spirit of God are.

### 38

Can we doubt concerning the sun, since, as the day advances, it spreads its rays throughout the whole world and pours light upon everyone—even those who cannot see, but nevertheless perceive through the warmth of the air itself that it is present? For where is its heat absent? To what place do its rays not reach, when, dispersing the darkness of night or clouds, it illuminates the earth?

It shines in heaven, glows upon the sea, and burns upon the earth. You do not doubt concerning the sun, that it shines everywhere; yet do you doubt concerning God, that everywhere the splendor of his glory and the image of his substance shine?

What place can the Word of God, eternal splendor, fail to penetrate? It even illuminates the hidden places of the mind, which this sun cannot penetrate. For the Word of God is a spiritual sword, reaching to the division of soul and limbs, and of joints and marrow.

Concerning this, the righteous Simeon says to Mary: “And a sword will pierce your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke II, 35). [Col. 1481B]

### 39

The Word therefore penetrates the soul and illuminates it like the radiance of eternal light.

Although he is spread through all, in all, and above all powers, since he has risen from the Virgin for everyone, both good and evil—as he also commands his sun to rise upon the good and the evil—he nevertheless cherishes the one who approaches him.

For just as the one who closes the windows of his house and chooses a dark place in which to stay shuts out the sun’s radiance from himself, so the one who turns away from the Sun of justice cannot behold its splendor. He walks in darkness and, amid universal light, is himself the cause of his blindness.

Open your windows to him, therefore, so that your entire house may shine with the brightness of the true Sun. Open your eyes, so that you may see the Sun of justice rising for you.

But beware lest some splinter of straw disturb them. If there is any dirt in the eye of your mind, you will not be able to look; if there is any sickness, it will weigh more heavily. Light strikes an unfocused eye and arouses greater pain.

Therefore, let your eye be single, lest your whole body begin to be dark and you stagger in the light like the steps of blind people. [Col. 1481D]

### 40

If someone closes the doors of his house, is it the sun’s fault that it does not illuminate his house?

Therefore, if some sinner decides that his own mind should be barred by the barriers of his sins, and foolishly turns away from himself the splendor of the Word and brings upon himself the blindness of folly, can he complain that the Sun of justice was unwilling to enter, or accuse the weakness of the heavenly light?

The Word of God knocks at your door. “If anyone opens to me,” he says, “I will enter” (Rev. III, 20). If someone does not open, is the fault that of the one who does not enter, or rather of the one who does not open?

Nothing is barred from God; nothing is closed to eternal light. But he disdains to open the doors of wickedness and does not wish to enter the chambers of iniquity. [Col. 1482A]

### 41

When the vigor of our soul recoils from the decaying portion of the body, so that corrupted limbs cannot feel its grace, would God deign to dwell in certain members of a corrupted soul?

Yet the soul’s vigor is spread throughout the entire body, whether hand, foot, or finger participates in sensation. Can the wisdom of God be absent anywhere, or his majesty be absent anywhere?

Certainly, he does not hold back those who flee, nor compel the unwilling; but neither does he disdain those who approach him. His power, his Word, God, is near to all:

“For in him all things consist, and he is the head of the body, the Church” (Col. I, 17–18), “in whom all fullness dwells” (Col. II, 9). [Note: All editions have “the fullness of divinity.” But the word “divinity” is absent from all the manuscripts and does not seem particularly necessary to Ambrose’s meaning. [Col. 1482D]]

Yet sins separate many from him, concerning whom it is said: “Behold, those who remove themselves far from you will perish” (Ps. LXXII, 27). Hence the holy Prophet says: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (ibid., 28).

And the Apostle, showing that God is not far from each one of us, says: “In him we live and move and exist” (Acts XVII, 27–28).

For, supplying vital grace to all, he is present to all through the gift of his goodness; but he is nearer to those who are contrite in heart. [Col. 1482C]

### 42

The ancient history also teaches this through enigmas. Moses was upon the brow of Mount Sinai and was alone; the people were in the valley, at the foot of the mountain; the elders were on the side of the mountain, above the merits of the people, but separated by a very great distance from the merits of Moses (Exod. XIX, 20 and following).

Not all were at the summit, nor were all at the bottom; rather, the people were below, while Moses alone was at the summit of Mount Sinai, which in Latin interpretation means “temptation.”

And you, if you ascend above temptations and offer prayer with a contrite heart, will be near to God. If you are pure in heart, you too will see God; for “blessed are the pure in heart, because they will see God” (Matt. V, 8).

### 43

The one who is therefore near to God says: “You are near, O Lord, and all your commandments are truth.”

A Jew cannot say this, because he does not receive the Lord Jesus. He has separated himself and believes not in the truth but in the shadow.

How can he say, “Your commandments are truth,” when grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, since he does not acknowledge him who, through the truth and fullness of his circumcision, redeemed the whole world?

### 44. (Verse 152)

The eighth verse is: “From the beginning I learned from your testimonies, because you founded them forever.”

“From your testimonies,” he says, “I received knowledge and faith from the beginning, because they were founded forever.” For the testimony is faithful and gives wisdom to the simple.

If Adam and Eve had known that, as for children, more cautious commandments had been given to them, so that they should not usurp for themselves the knowledge of good and evil, which they could not define with sound judgment, they could have claimed the habitation of paradise forever.

If human beings consider that the blood of a human being cries out to God, they will keep their own hands from killing another human being.

If they keep the commandments which the Lord gave in the presence of heaven and earth as witnesses, saying, “Hear, heaven, and listen with your ears, earth” (Isa. I, 2), [Note: The Roman edition alone has “as witnesses,” evidently because the Prophet says, “Hear, heaven . . . earth.” But it is not sufficiently clear why that alteration was introduced, since anyone can understand that God is speaking through the Prophet. [Col. 1483D]] then, knowing that whatever crime they commit is committed against the law of the Lord and that they will be convicted by the testimony of angels, Powers, and holy human beings, they will establish their foundation upon these testimonies, because they are eternal and everlasting.

Let us, then, build our work upon the foundation of the heavenly testimonies, so that it may not burn like wood or straw, but be tested like gold, remaining forever supported upon an eternal foundation. [Col. 1483B]

## TWENTIETH SERMON. Resch.

1. The twentieth letter, Resch, begins. In Latin interpretation this word is called “head” or “primacy.” It is the head, if we consider the form of the human race, which nourishes all the members and directs and fills them with the senses: “The sense of the wise is in his head” (Eccles. II, 14). From it the course of the veins and the passages of the breath, together with the strength of the blood, are distributed through all parts of the body. It surveys everything and adorns everything. Once the head has been removed, the body is nameless, unrecognizable, and no usefulness of life remains. Therefore those who are condemned for some crime, because the head is the ornament of the whole body, are deprived of their heads; and because they have been discovered to have committed, through a shameful or criminal offense, the filth of brutish degradation or the horror of bestial savagery, as people who have departed from the purpose of human restraint, they are ordered also to strip off the form of their human condition. For when the head has been cut off, the remaining trunk of the body is compared with the body of beasts and is deprived of the citadel of wisdom, because it was unable to maintain the rule of wisdom. The body is therefore buried without its proper dignity; for in the head is the vigor of life, and in the head is the grace of beauty.

[Note: Besides the punishment of decapitation, there were indeed other ultimate penalties, such as cutting the veins, poison, beasts, and the noose. But, omitting the rest, the holy man mentions only this one, either because it served his purpose better, or perhaps because at that time it was more common than the others, or finally because not only the punishment of death but also that of exile and slavery was classified under the name “capital.” See Brisson, *De verborum significatione*, book III, under “Capitalia crimina.”]

2. It is said that when a serpent is pressed by danger, it always hides its head; and, gathering itself into a coil, it protects only this by exposing the remaining part of its body, so that, although its other members may be struck, it can restore them while the strength of its head remains intact.

[Note: Some manuscripts and the old edition read: “so that, if it is uninjured, it may be carried away . . . restore.” The Roman edition alone reads: “so that, if they have been injured, they may be carried away . . . restored.” Other manuscripts, more numerous and of better authority, have the reading found in the text. Compare this passage with *Enarrationes in Psalmum* XXXVII, no. 19.]

Do you likewise preserve this head morally, and preserve it mystically. Christ is the mystical head, because “all things consist in him,” and “he is the head of the body, the Church” (Coloss. I, 17–18). Whoever has lost this head cannot possess the use of life. By this alone we are distinguished from beasts, formed according to the image of God and by the vigor of the virtues. Faith separates us from comparison with irrational cattle. Preserve this head, O human serpents; even if all the members are cut off, the whole body burned in fires, plunged into the deep, or disemboweled by beasts, if this head is guarded, life remains whole and salvation secure. No one can perish whose Christ has not been taken away.

3. The head is also the summit of our study and work, the summit of our business, our hope, and our virtues. The whole summit of our study is that we should be humble and follow the truth—something the person who exalts himself does not see, being vainly puffed up in the mind of his flesh and “not holding fast to the head” (Coloss. II, 18–19). What this head is he clearly expressed when he said: “From whom the whole body, supplied and knit together through its joints and bonds, grows with the increase of God” (ibid., 19). And in the Book of Isaiah the Lord says through the Prophet: “I will take away from Judah the head and the tail, the beginning and the end” (Isa. IX, 14).

Judah lost this head, which it had possessed, because it did not receive Jesus the Lord. Where there is faith, we have both beginning and end. Where there is faithlessness, there is neither beginning nor end. The Church has a beginning because it has Christ; for Christ is the beginning of the Church, the firstborn from the dead. It also has an end, because he is himself the first and the last. He is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The synagogue has neither beginning nor end, because at the beginning it found nothing to follow, and at the end nothing to hope for. Therefore the person who is puffed up does not hold the head—that is, the humility of Christ, by which he descended even to the cross and descended even to the underworld. The Jew therefore did not believe, because he despised the one who said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29). This humility is the head of all the virtues; it nourishes the entire body, as it were, of our actions.

4. Even if someone is weak, poor, and of low birth, if he does not exalt or put himself forward, he commends himself by that very humility. Suppose someone is exceedingly rich and noble; if he boasts of the nobility of his birth and of his wealth, his own insolence makes him base. Suppose someone is eloquent and strong, and, lifted up by the swelling of his eloquence and virtue, claims much for himself. Is not someone generally foolish and weak preferred to him because of his modesty?

Finally, the Pharisee in the Gospel, although he was abstinent and sparing with what belonged to others, generous with what belonged to himself, and not reluctant to fast, as he himself said, nevertheless lost even those things that he could have possessed because of his boastfulness (Luke XVIII, 10 ff.). None of the many kinds of virtue, discolored by one vice, could benefit him. The publican, who could enumerate nothing that might be approved, nevertheless, because of his humility, went down from the temple more justified than that Pharisee, according to what is written in the Prophet: “He will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. XXXIII, 19).

[Note: Erasmus and subsequent editions read *cum abstinens*, “being abstinent.” The Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts read *cum abstemius*, “being abstemious.” This is not improper; for *abstemius* often simply means “abstinent,” as is clear from Horace:

“If perhaps, abstinent amid things set before you, you live on herbs and nettles.”

Hence we are very suspicious of Varro’s derivation, according to which *abstemius* is formed from abstaining from *temetum*, that is, wine—especially since reputable authors use *abstemius* of someone abstemious from wine.]

5. That this is the head expressed by this letter is also clearly taught to us in the Lamentations of Jeremiah. For, after placing this letter first, the Prophet says: “The Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord . . . under his shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. IV, 20). This, then, is truly the head, which is the head of all.

6. We have spoken of “head”; let us also speak of “primacy,” although the word and the letter differ, for in meaning they converge upon the same understanding. We read of the birthright in the Old Testament (Gen. XXV, 33), which Esau yielded to his brother in exchange for the lentils; and therefore his name was called Edom, that is, “earthly” and “crafty.”

These are the brothers concerning whom the Lord was asked by their father Isaac to give him heirs of his posterity by his wife Rebekah, who for twenty years had given no sign of offspring. He heard him, and Rebekah conceived; and when the little ones seemed to be tossing about in her womb, she asked the Lord and received this answer: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be separated from your womb; and one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (ibid., 23).

Is it not clear that the mystery signifies two peoples: the older Jewish people and the younger Christian people, who, by the cooking of the lentils, received the birthright of their elder brother? This plainly indicates that the older, earthly people, because of its intemperance of appetite, lost the birthright it had possessed; while the people of the Church, through sobriety and self-restraint, seized the birthright which it did not possess by order of age, but obtained by fraternal concession and by the pious theft of the father’s blessing.

What, then, did the Christian people steal, if not the Lord Jesus? “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it,” as the Lord himself declared (Matt. XI, 12). A good fraud, which steals eternal life.

But since we think enough has been said about the interpretations of this letter, let us consider what the Prophet added to this letter.

[Col. 1485D] 7. (Verse 153.) The first verse is therefore: “See my humility, and deliver me; for I have not forgotten your law.” Perhaps someone may say: “The Prophet is boasting about himself.” And if he boasts, he boasts in his weaknesses, in which the Apostle also boasts, saying: “I will boast in my weaknesses” (II Cor. XII, 5). One boasts in riches, another in the titles of his nobility and ancestry, another in offices and honors; the righteous person boasts in humility. For it is a good glory to be subject to Christ.

But so that you may know that he does not wish to boast of himself, but to summon the Lord’s grace upon himself, the same Prophet says elsewhere: “See my humility and my labor.” Thus, as one who has humbled his heart, as one who has labored greatly, he desires his sins to be forgiven there, while here he prays to be delivered.

8. Imagine a priest concerned for the salvation of his minister, whom he recognizes as approved by God; or a father deeply distressed over a son afflicted by serious illness; or a woman sorrowful either for her son or for her husband, devoting herself to prayers, pouring out abundant tears by night and by day, humbling and prostrating herself upon the ground, multiplying her fasts, and—what is more grievous than these things—worn out by the sorrow of mind and spirit, benumbed by the delay of the illness and danger, saying to the Lord: “See my humility, and deliver me.”

9. Consider also that Holy Scripture daily anoints and exercises us with a certain spiritual oil of heavenly commandments; and our Lord, eager to summon many to undertake their contests, has set forth various rewards of crowns. Consider, I say, the athlete of Christ, wearied by countless struggles and now resisting with nearly exhausted strength, disturbed by the weight of danger, seeing that his contest is not only against flesh and blood but also against the spiritual powers of wickedness in the heavenly places. Let him say: “See my humility, and deliver me; for I have not forgotten your law.” For he could not have forgotten it who fought according to its commandments.

10. Consider also someone standing in martyrdom, afflicted by repeated tortures, thrust into darkness, broken by the heavy weight of chains, his legs stretched upon the rack, his entrails torn out by the torture horse, his flesh scored by claws, burned with glowing plates—an unwavering man in faith, but whose spirit is already weary because the crown of sacred death is delayed too long—saying: “See my humility, and deliver me; for I have not forgotten your law.”

The testimonies of Scripture teach us that humility can be spoken of not only in studies and purposes but also in trials. For it is written: “Acceptable men are in the furnace of humility” (Ecclus. II, 5). The Greek has *ταπεινώσεως* (*tapeinōseōs*), which means “of humility.”

I have mentioned this because many Latin manuscripts read “in the furnace of affliction.” Latin makes a distinction; Greek does not. *Ταπείνωσις* (*tapeinōsis*) can mean both the humility of virtue and the humility of affliction. It makes no difference if Latin distinguishes them; for Greek did not translate from Latin, but Latin from Greek.

11. Finally, the Hebrews, as long as they were in Egypt, were in an iron furnace—that is, in the furnace of trial and in the furnace of affliction—when they were oppressed by harsh commands. Hence it is also written: “God brought them out of the iron furnace, from Egypt” (Jerem. XI, 4).

It was an iron furnace because no one’s work of virtue yet shone fully in Egypt; no one’s gold had there been tested, and no one’s lead of iniquity had been burned away. A harsh furnace, the furnace of everlasting death: no one could escape that furnace, which consumed everyone, in which there would be only pain and mourning.

But the furnace in which Ananias, Azarias, and Misael sang a hymn to the Lord (Dan. III, 51) was a golden furnace, not an iron one. Through it the wisdom of faith and devotion shone throughout the whole world. This furnace too was in Babylonia, where there was no spiritual gold, except perhaps what was captive; for “he led captivity captive” (Eph. IV, 8).

This was the gold in God’s saints, who were captives in body among the Babylonians but free in spirit before God, released from the bonds of human captivity and bound to the yoke of spiritual grace. And perhaps the same furnace is iron for the weak, but golden for those who persevere.

12. Everyone who desires to return to paradise must be tested by fire. For it was not written without purpose that, after Adam and Eve had been expelled from the seat of paradise, God placed at the entrance of paradise a flaming sword that turned in every direction (Gen. III, 24).

Everyone must pass through the flames—whether it is John the Evangelist, whom the Lord loved so much that he said of him to Peter: “I will that he remain thus . . . what is that to you? You follow me” (John XXI, 22). Some have doubted his death, but we cannot doubt his passage through the fire, because he is in paradise and is not separated from Christ.

Or whether it is Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and walked upon the sea, he must say: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Ps. LXV, 12).

But the fiery sword will quickly turn for John, because no iniquity is found in him whom equity loved. If there was in him any human fault, divine charity has burned it away: “For its wings are wings of fire” (Cant. VIII, 6).

13. Whoever has here the fire of charity will not be able there to fear the fire of the sword. To Peter himself, who so often offered his death for Christ, the Lord will say: “Pass over, recline” (Luke XVII, 7).

But Peter will say: “He tested us by fire, as silver is tested by fire.” For in one in whom much water could not extinguish charity, how will fire extinguish it?

Yet he will be tested as silver, while I shall be tested as lead. Until the lead melts, I shall burn. If no silver is found in me, woe to me! I shall be thrust into the deepest hell, or I shall be burned entirely like straw. If some gold or silver is found in me—not because of my own deeds, but through the mercy and grace of Christ, through the ministry of the priesthood—perhaps I shall say: “Indeed, those who hope in you shall not be put to shame” (Ps. XXIV, 3).

14. By that fiery sword, therefore, the iniquity which sits upon the leaden talent will be burned away. For that reason the one who is the justice of God, Christ, could not feel that fire: he had committed no sin, and the fire found nothing in him that it could burn.

Finally, the eternal gates were raised only for him to enter as the King of glory, not as one accused in a legal case. His flesh did indeed taste death; for otherwise it could not have risen again.

What I have read, I venture to affirm; what I have not read, I reverently leave to those who know. I confess only this: whatever that flesh underwent, it underwent so that by his footsteps he might show the way to the others, either to triumph through the suffering of martyrdom or to pass into paradise.

Let no one therefore claim anything for himself; let no one boast of his merits or his power. Rather, let us all hope to find mercy through the Lord Jesus, for we shall all stand before his tribunal. From him I shall ask pardon; from him I shall ask forgiveness. For what other hope is there for sinners?

15. He who here thinks himself gold has lead; and he who thinks himself a grain of wheat has straw that can be burned. Yet here many seem to themselves to be gold. I do not envy them; nevertheless, gold will be tested and burned so that it may be proved. For it is written: “As gold in the furnace I will test them” (Zech. XIII, 9).

Let them therefore understand that all will be tested. Many, then, who think themselves gold should also follow humility, so that they may burn away their vices. But here there is empty boasting. Therefore to many who think themselves masses of gold, a wiser mass of gold says: “The furnace will test us all.”

Since we are to be tested, let us conduct ourselves in such a way that we may deserve to be approved by the divine judgment. While we are placed here, let us hold fast to humility, so that when each of us comes to God’s judgment, to those fires through which we must pass, he may say: “See my humility, and deliver me.” For if he has been proud, arrogant, or defiant, he will not be able to say this. No one will say: “See my pride”; but rather: “See my humility,” so that by its grace he may deserve to be delivered from that fire.

16. There is therefore the humility of labor and weariness; and there is also the humility of virtue and purpose, which the righteous person maintains amid favorable and prosperous circumstances and while at rest. Though broken by no labor and uncertain of the outcome of no contest, he displays a humble disposition toward all and does not seek to exalt his own achievements; rather, he strives to lessen the value of his work and the credit of his merit.

Hear the righteous person humbling himself: “I am,” he says, “the least of the apostles” (I Cor. XV, 9). That vessel of divine election, that teacher of the nations, calls himself the least, unworthy of the name of the office which he valued above his own works; he claims nothing for himself but attributes everything to the grace of God. This is indeed fitting for the righteous person.

17. By this humility Abraham was called the father of faith. When he was admitted to converse with God, he said that he was earth and mud (Gen. XVIII, 27).

The Lord himself also says: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. XXI, 7), when he was speaking of the suffering of his body—he who sought not what was his own but what belonged to others.

The Apostle wants us to imitate him and exhorts us, saying: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 5–7).

Let us not, therefore, seek nobility of birth or riches if we wish to follow Christ. Although he was in the form of God, he emptied himself; although he was rich, he became poor. Do not you despise the commoner because you are noble; do not look down on the slave because you are powerful; do not disdain the poor because you are rich. Are you nobler, more powerful, or richer than Christ? For your sake he assumed what you despise.

For your sake he humbled himself even to death, and death on a cross, to erase the fall of your pride; so that what we had lost through the disobedience of one Adam, we might recover through the obedience of the one Lord Jesus: “Therefore,” he says, “God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow . . . because the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 9–11).

[Col. 1489B] 1227 18. Consider, O man, what you are reading. The Apostle did not labor to prove Christ’s power, but to proclaim his obedience and to demonstrate how great is the grace of humility and how great its fruit.

If you take the words with simple ears, you may understand that God also exalted Christ. But Christ, by that humility, sought not what was his but what was yours.

[Note: Earlier editions prefixed the words “Receive this”: “I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” But these words are absent from all the manuscripts. Nor are they especially necessary, since the discussion is still concerned with Paul’s words.]

Receive this, then, with discerning ears: morally, it benefited you; mystically, it wrought your salvation. Understand it as you wish: it is your salvation. If you think that Christ’s humility benefited Christ, whom would it not benefit? If it exalted him, whom would it not increase?

The Lord of all became the servant of all; the author of all was beaten, washed feet, was crucified, and died. Yet in all these things I see no diminution of his divinity; I recognize an advancement in his work. He who had nothing to add to his power had something to add to the worship of his majesty.

I dare to say that he would have lost the work of his own ministry if humility had not recovered it. Thus he redeemed us, but he also acquired us for himself. Humility therefore brings no loss. He who emptied himself is full. He who did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but took the form of a servant, is in the glory of God the Father.

I received the one whom I did not know; I recognized the one whom I had not known; I confess the one whom I had denied. To him I bend the knee of the body; to him I bend the knee of the mind; I adore the one from whom I formerly fled.

19. We give you thanks, Lord Jesus, because you created us, yet, once created, you set us above beasts, wild animals, and dumb creatures. Greater are the gifts of your visitation.
