Having visited us, you honored us with participation in your majesty, saying: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI, 23). For, having assumed a body, you became our brother, yet did not cease to be Lord.

[Note: The old edition reads: “You bestowed a greater grace of redemption, because those who were perishing . . .” The Roman edition and the manuscripts agree among themselves, except that the Roman edition has “because those who were perishing,” while some manuscripts have “those who were perishing through a greater grace of redemption.” The latter reading is not bad.]

A greater grace of redemption: you redeemed those who were perishing by your own death, as it is written: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John XVIII, 14).

You raised the dead, saying: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19). For in that temple of the Lord’s body the right of resurrection accrued to all.

You made those who rise equal to the angels, as you said: “Those who do not marry, and those who do not take wives, will be like the angels in heaven” (Matt. XXII, 30).

Finally, you placed us at the right hand of God, in that throne of the Son of Man, as you yourself deigned to say: “From now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God” (Luke XXII, 69).

20. Therefore the Apostle, marveling at the gifts of divine mercy and at the same time showing that the Father and the Son possess one liberality, says: “But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us” (Eph. II, 4).

You hear, O man, in what you ought to be rich and what virtues you ought to possess: to love in God, to prove them in yourself, and to undertake the gifts of heavenly mercy and charity.

[Note: Earlier editions read *virtutes. Amorem Dei te probato imitari*, “virtues. Prove that you imitate the love of God.” The Roman edition reads *virtutes. Amorem Dei te habere probato, imitare coelestis charitatis dulcedinem*, “virtues. Prove that you have the love of God; imitate the sweetness of heavenly charity.” The manuscripts have the reading found in the text, except that many prefer *imitari*; it is nevertheless better to read *imitare* with the others, so that it serves as a conclusion to the preceding words.]

And he added: “And when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved; and he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus” (ibid., 5–6).

In Christ, therefore, the flesh too is honored. He who sits at the right hand of God was humbled for our sake. Therefore he says to us: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29).

He did not say: “Learn from me, because I am powerful,” but “because I am humble of heart,” so that you might imitate him and say to him: “Lord, I heard your voice; I fulfilled your command. You said that we should learn humility from you. We have learned it not only from your words but also from your deed; I have done what you commanded: See my humility.”

[Col. 1490C] 21. A good athlete displays his limbs, to demonstrate the discipline of his way of life. He also displays his limbs when, after certain more severe contests, he is compelled to compete again, so that the judge, seeing his exhausted body, may not compel him to compete.

You too should show the humility of your heart, so that you may display the titles of your virtue. Display also the contests of your body, so that you may say: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the race” (II Tim. IV, 7). Then may the spiritual judge, seeing your contest, decree the crown of righteousness, because you have fulfilled the law of the arena.

[Note: After the word *certaminis*, the editions add *agonem*, “the contest.” This word is absent from all the manuscripts and is not particularly necessary, since the participle *videns*, “seeing,” can refer to the preceding words: “Display also the contests of your body.”]

22. (Verse 154.) The second verse follows: “Judge my judgment, and deliver me; because of your word, give me life.”

The innocent hasten to judgment and desire to be proved more quickly by arbiters of their own innocence. This is also customary in the world, which it shares with the saints. But the person who is righteous before God has another reason for not fearing judgment: before the merciful Judge he has his cause; before his Redeemer he wishes and hopes to be acquitted quickly.

Early acquittal belongs to the saints. Therefore the Lord also says through Ezekiel to the angels who are ministers of vengeance: “Begin with my saints” (Ezek. IX, 6). The Lord does not wish the saints to share the common judgment with the companions of the devil; for the devil and his ministers will not be scourged together with human beings. The punishment is separate where the guilt is also different.

Therefore Scripture says elsewhere: “It is time for judgment to begin from the household of God” (I Pet. IV, 17). Those whom he pities he chastises quickly, so that they may not be afflicted for a longer time by awaiting the future judgment, nor be tormented longer by the miserable lot of their guilt; so that each may repay even double for his sins and at last be able to be acquitted. For the punishment of the guilty is a kind of acquittal from their offenses.

23. In this world we see guilty persons inserted into the bonds of chains and led in the appearance of a pitiful spectacle; and sometimes innocent people suffer this, so that death is more tolerable than undergoing such punishments. Those who know themselves to be good wish to be heard; those too who are weighed down by grave crimes wish to get through the punishment by the speed of death, so that they may gain some shortening of their penalties. There is also hope in the judge’s mercy.

Prison confinement is harsher than exile itself, and return is not forever barred to all who are banished. If human judgment produces such results, how much more desirable is Christ’s judgment for everyone!

The devil’s judgment is deferred, so that he may always remain guilty in punishments, always bound by the chains of his wickedness, and himself endure forever the judgment of his conscience.

[Note: If anyone argues that this refers to the rich banqueter in the Gospel, about whom the parable is given in Luke VIII, let him understand the statement in the sense of those matters on which we made some observations in *Enarrationes in Psalmum* I, at no. 54. But the assertion that the devil has not yet undergone judgment, or is not at all in punishment, was the opinion of all the ancient Fathers; Maldonado gives their sequence in *De angelis*, question 7, “On the punishments of demons.”]

Thus that rich man in the Gospel, although a sinner, is oppressed by penal sufferings so that he may escape more quickly (Luke XII, 20); but the devil is shown not yet to have reached judgment and not yet to be subject to punishments—except those which he, conscious of such great crimes, pays through perpetual fear, lest he ever be secure.

24. Rather, to speak more truly, the holy person comes to judgment, while the impious does not come: “For the impious do not rise in judgment” (Ps. I, 5). One asks to be acquitted; the other, having been restrained, is sent away.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “But whoever does not believe is not judged.” This is not unsuitable, except that it departs from the agreement of the other editions and the manuscripts.]

The person who is not judged did not believe; he is punished by the judgment of his own impiety. Among earthly emperors, barbarian criminals are not punished for crimes committed among their own people, because they are not subject to those emperors; rather, they are regarded under the more serious designation of enemies and are punished without an examination of their private crimes.

So too Christ chastises his own, whom he loves, while he consigns outsiders, bound by the general condemnation of impiety, to eternal punishment: “The last enemy . . . death shall be destroyed” (I Cor. XV, 26). Yet the Prophet teaches this modestly by his own example, so that even the person who distrusts his own works may nevertheless hope for a more merciful sentence because of God’s word.

25. One wishes to live because of riches, another because of children; this man asks to be given life because of God’s word, just as Simeon awaited the Lord’s coming. For he saw the Lord in the temple and said: “Now you dismiss your servant . . . in peace; because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II, 29–30), declaring that he had no other desire to live than to see Christ. Finally, he saw him and asked to be released from the bonds of the body.

[Note: All editions read: “Therefore, receiving the Lord in the temple, he said: ‘Now you dismiss . . .’” The manuscripts have the reading found in the text.]

26. We can also understand “Judge my judgment” as though the case concerning our judgment were more serious than the case concerning our error. For forgiveness is more readily granted to someone who has erred than to one who has wickedly judged another. The form of judgment that you yourself think should be pronounced upon another must necessarily return upon you.

27. (Verse 155.) The third verse follows: “Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your righteousnesses.”

Those whose judgment is delayed have salvation far away; but they themselves are the authors of their danger, because they have not drawn near to the Lord. They have become far away because by their own will they separated themselves from the grace of salvation.

Salvation does not flee from them; they themselves flee from salvation, having distanced themselves. It came to the Jews, but they did not receive salvation. How did they not receive it? Listen: Jesus is salvation; Jesus was called the Son of Man. For “the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Luke XIX, 10). But the Jews asked that the robber be released to them and rejected Jesus (John XVIII, 10).

28. Who, then, is the person who makes himself far from the Lord, except the one who does not seek his righteousnesses? But whoever seeks the righteousnesses of God is near and clings to God. Therefore the Apostle says to those who seek the righteousnesses of God: “You who were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Eph. II, 13). The blood of Christ is righteousness. Finally, he himself says to John: “Allow us . . . to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. III, 15).

29. (Verse 156.) The fourth verse follows: “Your mercies are exceedingly many, O Lord; according to your judgments give me life.”

Even if salvation is far from sinners, let no one despair, because the mercies of the Lord are many. Those who perish through their own sin are delivered by the mercy of the Lord. “I will have mercy,” he says, “on whom I have mercy” (Exod. XXXIII, 19).

He appeared openly to those who were not seeking him; he called those who were fleeing; he gathered the ignorant; he offered himself to suffering for all.

Is he not therefore greatly merciful? “The mercy of man is toward his neighbor; the mercy of the Lord is toward all flesh,” so that all flesh might ascend to the Lord, granted this by the Lord’s mercy.

30. But since he has said that the Lord’s mercies are many, how does he ask to be given life according to his judgments, especially when elsewhere he himself says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant” (Ps. CXLII, 2)?

One judgment is the judgment of Christ’s benefits, to which we cannot respond—for who can repay the debt of nature, the debt of salvation and grace? Another is the judgment by which we are assessed according to an estimation of our weakness. Yet even in this very judgment, judgment is joined with mercy, so that the truth of judgment may be tempered by the Lord’s mercy.

31. Or perhaps, because he had said, “Judge my judgment” (above, verse 154), he therefore added that the Lord’s mercies are exceedingly many. For it is a serious matter to judge another. Hence it is also written: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Luke VI, 37).

Since each person is conscious of his own sins, how can he judge another person’s sin? Let the person judge (3, question 7, chapter “Judicet”) another’s error who has nothing in himself to condemn; let the person judge who does not do the same things that he thinks should be punished in another, lest, when he judges another, he pronounce sentence upon himself. Let the person judge who is led to pronounce judgment by no hatred, offense, or levity.

You have heard today what the true and just Judge said: “I can do nothing of myself” (John V, 30).

32. Some heretics used to raise questions from this passage, as though the Son were weak because he could do nothing of himself, as though he were also subject according to his divinity and subordinate to the Father’s authority. They do not perceive that this too more strongly proves the unity of divine power, precisely where they think there is a difference of power between the Father and the Son.

The Son does nothing of himself because, through the unity of operation, neither does the Son act without the Father nor the Father without the Son. Finally, the Father says to the Son: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26), asserting that the operation is common where the counsel is common.

What does he do without Wisdom, who did all things in Wisdom, as it is written: “You made all things in Wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24)? Finally, Wisdom said: “When he made the heavens, I was with him . . . I was the one in whom he rejoiced” (Prov. VIII, 27, 30).

And the Evangelist says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3), teaching not only that the Son is the maker of all things but also that he shares in the Father’s operation.

33. Nevertheless, I think that this passage should be referred to the pattern of judgment. For the Gospel is not only instruction in faith but also a teacher of morals and a mirror of upright conduct.

I find in the Gospel that the Lord Jesus assumed the feelings and duties of many persons, so that he might teach how we ought to conduct ourselves in these duties. He assumed the role of shepherd and said: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X, 11).

Therefore, for the sake of his rational flock, he did not refuse the suffering of the body; placing the weary sheep upon the shoulders of his cross, he refreshed it by the performance of that loving burden.

34. He assumed the role of advocate: “For we have him as an advocate with the Father” (1 John 2:1). He spent the night in prayer for us (Luke 6:12), so that by his example he might teach us how we ought to plead for forgiveness for our sins. He did not spend the night in prayer because, as though otherwise unable, he could not reconcile us to the Father; rather, he wished to show what an advocate ought to be, what a priest ought to be—namely, that he should stand as intercessor for Christ’s flock not only by day but also by night. Did he need assistance in obtaining what he asked, when he himself could do what he requested, as he himself said: “I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask of him in my name, I will do” (John 14:12–13)? Finally, elsewhere, when he raised Lazarus, he said: “I knew that you always hear me” (John 11:42). As though weak, he spent the night in prayer, though he knew that he was always heard, and he cried out: “Lazarus, come out!” (ibid., 44). The resurrection spoke, and death withdrew.

35. He also assumed the condition of an accused man and stood before the judge as though guilty; nor did the Lord of all disdain the lowliness of the governor. When questioned, he remained silent (John 19:9), showing that the defense of innocence lies not in the shouting of one’s voice or in forensic advocacy, but in the integrity of one’s conscience; and that one should seek not the preservation of the body, but purity of soul. Finally, he who acquitted Susanna when she was silent offered himself to death. In her case he showed that no one should despair; in this case, that he would not refuse the sacrifice by which the whole world was to be redeemed. Finally, when struck, he did not revile or strike back. And the Lord of heaven and earth laid aside his desire for vengeance and uttered a humble appeal, saying: “If I have spoken wrongly, testify to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). As though weak, he lamented the injustice of the blows; though he could have avenged himself, he preferred to complain rather than retaliate.

[Col. 1494C]

36. Therefore here too he assumed the role and purpose of a judge, saying: “I can do nothing of myself” (John 5:30). A good judge does nothing according to his own arbitrary decision or the inclination of his private will, but pronounces according to laws and legal rights; he obeys the established principles of law [Note: [Col. 1493D] The Roman edition reads, “he obeys the statutes of the law.”], does not indulge his own will; he brings nothing prepared and premeditated from home, but judges as he hears and decides according to the nature of the case. He obeys the laws and does not oppose them; he examines the merits of the case and does not alter them.

[Col. 1494D]

37. Learn, judges of this world, what attitude you ought to maintain in judging—what sobriety and sincerity. The Lord of all says: “I can do nothing of myself.” Elsewhere I read: “He cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). He cannot, certainly—not through weakness, but through integrity; not through inability to act, but through conscientiousness in judging. What can he not do who can do all things, except what he does not wish to be able to do? [Note: [Col. 1494D] Most manuscripts read, “unless he is unwilling to do what he can.” This is not bad. [Col. 1495D] Nevertheless, several others, as well as all the printed editions, read, “unless he is unwilling to be able to do it.” This reading seems to be confirmed by the following words, “He does not wish to be able,” and so forth.] He does not wish to be able to condemn; he does not wish to be able to act against the faith; he does not wish to be able to act against the truth. Finally, hear him himself explain why he cannot do anything of himself: “As I hear,” he says, “I judge” (John 5:30)—that is, I do not decide according to my own power whatever pleases me, but according to the religious obligation of judging what is just. Therefore my judgment is true, because I do not indulge my own will, but equity. Hear what the heavenly Judge says: “I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge.”

[Col. 1495A]

38. And Pilate said to the Lord Jesus: “I have authority to release you, and I have authority to crucify you” (John 19:10). You usurp, O man, an authority that you do not possess, while God denies that he possesses it—he who has authority over all things! Hear what Justice says: “I can do nothing of myself.” Hear what the Judge of equity declares: “As I hear, I judge.” [Col. 1495B] Hear what the unjust judge says: “I have authority to release you, and I have authority to crucify you.” You are bound by your own words, Pilate; by your own sentence you are condemned. Thus, claiming authority rather than equity, you handed the Lord over to be crucified: by your authority you released the robber, but you killed the author of life. Yet you did not even possess the authority which you assert that you possessed. For the Lord Jesus says to you: “You would have no authority against me at all unless it had been given you from above” (ibid., 11). Evil is the authority that permits what is not permitted. This authority belongs to the powers of darkness: not to see the truth, but to despise it.

[Note: [Col. 1495D] A considerable number of manuscripts and the old edition read, “to permit what harms.” More numerous manuscripts and the Roman edition, however, have the reading in the text, except that instead of “to permit” the latter has “to be able.”]

39. Hear what the true Judge says: “I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:30). He speaks as a human being; as a judge he teaches, because one who judges ought not to obey his own will, but to uphold what belongs to the laws [3, question 7, chapter *Judicet*, § *Qui*]. Set up a judge from this world: can he act contrary to the form of an imperial rescript [Note: [Col. 1495D] A few manuscripts read, “contrary to the decree.” The others, as well as all the printed editions, read, “contrary to the rescript,” which is better; for a rescript was an imperial constitution, customarily called by various names. In an old glossary it is called Βασιλέως ἀντίγραμμα (*Basileōs antígramma*, “the emperor’s counter-letter”) in legal usage, *sacri affatus* (“sacred utterance”), and here by Ambrose himself, *augusta definitio* (“august decision”). See the Theodosian Code, book 1, title 2, and Godefroy-Brissonius, etc.]? Can he exceed the standard of an august decision? How much more ought we to preserve the form of divine judgment! Christ says: “I do not seek my own will”—that is, the will of a human being, which is directed either by hatred, bent toward ambition, swayed by favor, or corrupted by the falsehood of others; for “every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:2). “But,” he says, “the will of him who sent me”—that is, I came to teach the form of divine knowledge, so that in judging the preservation of truth might be more important than obedience to one’s will [3, question 7, chapter *Judicet*, § *In judicando*]. Therefore here too it is not weakness of power that is expressed, but the form of justice.

[Col. 1495D]

40. The judgment of the Son of God, therefore, is just, because it accords with the will of God, not with human inclination. For God is full of mercies: his mercy is accompanied by judgment, and judgment by mercy. He neither shows mercy without judgment nor judges without mercy. Finally, it is written: “His mercy is upon the scales” (Isaiah 28:17). “But the children of men are deceitful in the scales, so that they may deceive” (Psalm 61:10). God therefore examines and weighs the merits of each person, and just as he grants grace according to measure, so that it may not exceed the measure, so he grants mercy according to measure. Hence he says: “They will give into your lap a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, overflowing. For with the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Luke 6:38). Likewise, the deeds of each person are weighed on the scales, so that if good works outweigh evil ones, the reward of recompense may be bestowed; but if sins outweigh virtues, a harsher punishment may bind the guilty person. You have this expressed in the letter to Timothy, where the apostle Paul says: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, but for others they follow afterward” (1 Timothy 5:24). Likewise, good deeds are manifest, and those that have a different character cannot remain hidden.

[Col. 1496A]

41. Everything, therefore, is done by the Lord our God according to a certain measure and weight. “Who,” he says, “has placed the rocks upon the scales?” (Isaiah 40:12–13). And above: “Who has measured the waters in his hand, and the heavens with a span?” (ibid., 12). He who examines our affairs certainly bestows his own gifts after examination, and decides all things only after a sound assessment. He weighs mercy; he weighs vengeance. In both there is a fixed weight and an appropriate measure. Hence David also says: “You will give them drink with tears, in measure” (Psalm 79:6), lest they be burdened by the mass of punishment without moderation of measure and be unable to endure it. Elsewhere the same prophet says: “The cup in the Lord’s hand is full of unmixed wine with mixture. And he inclined it from this to that; yet its dregs were not emptied” (Psalm 74:9). And Jeremiah says: “Babylon is a golden cup in the Lord’s hand, by which the nations were made drunk” (Jeremiah 51:7)—that is, punishment was exacted from the nations [Note: [Col. 1496D] Several good manuscripts read, “so that they might no longer exult.”], lest they continue to exult because they had afflicted God’s people with the bitterest devastation. The meaning, then, of David’s verse is this: The punishment owed to the impious is prepared and full, and the Lord inclines it toward the faithless; yet in his compassion he does not deign to pour it out as far as the dregs, lest they be unable to bear the full measure of punishment. He inclines the cup, therefore, but does not empty it. Its inclination belongs to judgment; its not being emptied belongs to mercy.

[Col. 1496C]

42. Thus the Lord our God also tempers judgment with mercy [Col. 1496D]. For who among us can endure without divine compassion? What can we do that is worthy of heavenly rewards? Who among us rises so far in this body that he lifts up his soul to cling continually to Christ? To what extent, finally, is any human merit carried, so that this corruptible flesh may put on incorruption and this mortal flesh put on immortality? By what labors, by what injuries, can we wash away our sins? “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come” (Romans 8:18). Therefore the order of heavenly decrees concerning human beings proceeds not according to our merits, but according to the mercy of God.

[Col. 1497A]

43. (Verse 157.) The fifth verse follows: “Many are those who persecute and trouble me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies.” It is no great thing if you do not turn aside from God’s testimonies when no one afflicts you and no one persecutes you. [Note: [Col. 1497D] The Roman edition reads “without offense,” when the success of prosperous events attends favorably.] For who, with the success of prosperous events proceeding safely for him, would become ungrateful? Who, abounding in wealth and strengthened by continual well-being, would not attribute to God’s grace the fact that these things had been granted to him? Finally, when the Lord praised the holy Job, the adversary said: “Does Job worship the Lord for nothing? Have you not enclosed him with a hedge? . . . Stretch out your hand over all that he has; surely he will bless you to your face” (Job 1:9–11). He was therefore proved all the more when, after losing his wealth and children, he did not withdraw from the worship and grace of the Lord. But there is not just one persecutor; he has many agents. Do not, however, let them frighten you: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21). If there are many persecutions, there are many trials; where there are many crowns, there are many contests. Therefore the fact that there are many persecutors benefits you, so that amid many persecutions you may more easily find how you are to be crowned.

[Col. 1497B]

44. Let us use the example of the martyr Sebastian, whose feast is celebrated today. He was born in Milan [Col. 1497C]. Perhaps the persecutor had already departed, or had not yet come into these regions, or was more lenient. He noticed that the contest was either absent or lukewarm. He went to Rome, where, because of his zeal for the faith, the bitter fires of persecution were raging. There he suffered—that is, there he was crowned. Thus, in the place to which he had come as a guest, he established a dwelling of perpetual immortality. If there had been only one persecutor, this martyr would certainly not have been crowned.

[Note: [Col. 1497D] You see that the day on which Ambrose delivered this sermon was dedicated in the church of Milan to the martyr Sebastian. Although the holy bishop seems to speak so distinctly about this martyr’s homeland, historians have drawn his words into different interpretations. For Baronius, under the year 284, number 12, says: “He was born in Narbonne but educated at Milan,” or, as Saint Ambrose and others report, “born at Milan to a father from Narbonne and a mother from Milan” [Col. 1498D]. Saussaius, however, writes that he was born at Narbonne to a Gallic father and a Milanese mother. The others readily assent, some to one opinion and some to the other. Finally, the Acts of this same martyr, most recently published by Bollandus under the name of our Ambrose from ancient manuscripts, have the following according to several manuscripts: “Sebastian was educated in the territories of the Milanese”; but according to certain others, “a citizen of the territories of the Milanese,” which agrees very well with our text.]

45. But what is worse, these are not the only persecutors—the ones who are visible. There are also those who are invisible, and they are far more numerous persecutors. For just as one persecuting king sent commands of persecution to many, and throughout individual cities or provinces there were different persecutors [Col. 1497D], so too the devil directs many of his agents, who carry out persecutions not only outside, but also within the souls of individuals. Of these persecutions it has been said: “All who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12). He said “all”; he excepted no one. For who could be exempt, when the Lord himself endured the trials of persecution? Greed persecutes; ambition persecutes; luxury persecutes; pride persecutes; fornication persecutes. Hence the Apostle also says: “Flee fornication” (1 Corinthians 6:18). For what reason would you flee unless it were pursuing you? There is an evil spirit of fornication, an evil spirit of greed, an evil spirit of pride.

[Col. 1498A]

46. These are serious persecutors, who frequently crush the human mind without the terror of a sword; they conquer the minds of the faithful more through enticements than through threats. These are the enemies you must beware of; these are the more dangerous tyrants, through whom Adam was captured. Many who were crowned in public persecution have fallen in this hidden persecution. “Outside are conflicts, within are fears” (2 Corinthians 7:5). Do you perceive how serious the contest is that takes place within a human being, so that one fights against oneself and battles against one’s own desires? The Apostle himself is tossed about, hesitates, is bound, and declares that he is held captive under the law of sin and defeated in the body of death, and that he could not escape unless he were freed by the grace of the Lord Jesus (Romans 7:23–25).

47. Yet just as there are many persecutions, so there are many martyrdoms. Every day you are a witness of Christ. You were tempted by the spirit of fornication, but, fearing Christ’s future judgment, you did not consider the chastity of mind and body something to be violated: you are Christ’s martyr. You were tempted by the spirit of greed, so that you might seize a poorer person’s property and violate the rights of an undefended widow; yet, considering the heavenly commandments, you judged that help ought rather to be offered than injury inflicted: you are Christ’s witness. Finally, Christ wishes such witnesses to stand forth, according to what is written: “Judge for the orphan, and justify the widow; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:17–18). You were tempted by the spirit of pride, but, seeing a poor and needy person, you felt compassion with a devoted heart and loved humility rather than arrogance: you are Christ’s witness. And, what is more, you have borne witness not merely by speech but also by deed [Note: [Col. 1498D] All the printed editions read, “you have borne witness; you are Christ’s witness.” The manuscripts omit these final words, and anyone who considers the passage a little more carefully will understand that they are superfluous.] For who is a richer witness than one who confesses that the Lord Jesus came in the flesh while keeping the commandments of the Gospel? [Col. 1499A] For whoever hears and does not act denies Christ; even if he confesses him in words, he denies him by his deeds. To how many who say, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons, and perform many mighty works?” (Matthew 7:22) will he reply on that day: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (ibid., 23)! He, therefore, is a witness who, with his deeds testifying alongside him, bears witness to the commandments of the Lord Jesus.

48. How many, then, are Christ’s martyrs every day in secret, confessing Jesus as Lord! The Apostle knows this martyrdom and this faithful testimony to Christ, for he said: “This is our boast: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). How many have confessed outwardly and denied inwardly! For the sake of taking a wife—a woman whom Christian parents refused to give to a pagan man—many are exposed as having denied inwardly what they confessed outwardly [Col. 1499B]. Do we think that our Lord God was moved so severely against the Jewish people merely because of fornication, so that twenty-three thousand of the people were killed (Numbers 25:9), because they engaged in intercourse with women of the Midianite nation? Or was it not rather because, through those unions, they were compelled to depart from the faith and deny the Lord?

[Note: [Col. 1499D] Ambrose, following the ancient Fathers, invariably disapproved of marriages between a believer and an unbeliever. Whether they wished such marriages, once contracted, to be dissolved is disputed among ancient and more recent theologians. The former, following Gratian and the Master of the Sentences, affirm this strongly; later writers have entirely denied it. We discuss these matters more fully in the letter to Vigilius.]

[Note: [Col. 1499D] Certain manuscripts read “twenty-two thousand”; the others, as well as the old edition, read “twenty-three thousand”; only the Roman edition has “twenty-four thousand.”]

49. “Do not believe every spirit” (1 John 4:1), but recognize by their fruits whom you ought to believe. Someone comes into the Church while seeking honor under Christian emperors; pretending to be afraid, he feigns that he is offering a prayer [Note: [Col. 1499D] Observe from this passage that among ancient Christians it was customary during prayer in church not only to incline the head and bend the knees, but also to prostrate the entire body on the ground. For it is clearly not catechumens or penitents who are being discussed here, but the faithful.]: he bows and lies prostrate on the ground, though he has not bent the knee of his mind. A human being sees him and thinks him a Christian; a human being sees him praying submissively and believes him; but God hears him denying. He departs approved by human beings but condemned by the Judge. How much more tolerable it would have been for him to deny before human beings and confess before God! Yet even this is blameworthy, for perfect confession requires both devotion of soul and profession of voice: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

50. Therefore, in interior persecutions, be faithful and strong, so that you may also be approved in these external persecutions. In the innermost persecutions too there are kings and governors, terrifying judges by their authority [Note: [Col. 1500D] All the printed editions read, “terrifying through the power of judgment”; all the manuscripts read, “terrifying judges”; some have, “through the power of the judge.” Accordingly, where Ambrose and the manuscripts read “You will give an example,” the editions of Erasmus and later editors have substituted “You have an example.”]. You will give an example in the temptation endured by the Lord: all the kingdoms were shown to him, and it was said to him: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:9). It is also written elsewhere: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6:12). You see before what kings you are placed, O human being, before what governors of sins, if guilt reigns? As many sins, as many vices—so many kings. We are brought before them and stand before them. These kings too have a tribunal in the minds of many; but if someone confesses Christ, he immediately makes that king captive and casts him down from the throne of his mind. For how can the devil’s tribunal remain in one in whom Christ’s tribunal rises?

[Col. 1500A]

51. “Many are those who persecute and trouble me.” Perhaps Christ says this, and says it in the voices of individuals; for the adversary persecutes him in us. If you turn away from the persecutor, you cast Christ aside, who allows himself to be tempted so that he may conquer. Wherever the devil sees him, there he prepares ambushes; there he brings up the engines of temptation; there he weaves his deceptions, so that, if possible, he may drive him out. But where the devil fights, there Christ stands beside us. Where the devil lays siege, there Christ is enclosed, and there he defends the enclosure of spiritual walls. Therefore whoever flees from the persecutor also rejects the defender. But when you hear, “Many are those who persecute and trouble me,” do not be afraid, for you can say: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). Yet this is said by the one who does not turn aside from the Lord’s testimonies through any winding path of vice.

52. (Verse 158.) The sixth verse follows: “I saw those who do not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, because they did not keep your words.” Blessed is the person who wastes away in the love of God, because he sees those who do not keep the covenant. Another wastes away because of vicious loves: he languishes while delayed in the love of his beloved, and while the fulfillment of his burning desire is postponed, his spirit fails and the strength of his body is diminished by a certain disfigurement of pallor and by the wasting of his exhausted limbs. Another, who covets money, wastes away in miserly desire until he obtains it. Another, impatient to seize excessive honor, if he sighs under prolonged longing, is consumed by no slight wasting of mind. Such is not the one who says: “How my flesh has wasted away in a deserted land, in a pathless and waterless place” (Psalm 62:2–3)! He was disciplining his flesh and making it waste away while, intent upon the unwearied desire for divine contemplation and anticipating the light of day with anxious expectation, he longed to offer the Lord the service of songs and hymns before dawn.

53. The peaceful person therefore wastes away when he sees others breaking their covenants, abolishing the concord of mutual agreements, renewing quarrels out of peace, and returning from grace to turmoil. [Col. 1500D] Certainly the one who keeps the Lord’s commandments does not do this; he does not do this who hears him saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). Therefore the one who keeps the covenant obeys Christ’s commands; but the one who does not keep it despises Christ’s commandments—and what is worse, he disdains and neglects what he has recognized.

[Col. 1501A]

54. (Verse 159.) The seventh verse follows: “See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; in your mercy give me life.” Here too he invites the Lord to look upon the fullness of his love. No one says “See” except one who judges that, if he is seen, he will be pleasing. Beautifully he says “See,” and says it according to the Law, because the Law commanded each person to present himself three times a year in the sight of the Lord (Exodus 23:17). The holy person presents himself daily; daily he appears, and he does not appear empty. For he is not empty who has received from his fullness. David was not empty when he said: “Our mouth was filled with joy” (Psalm 125:2), because joy is the fruit of the Holy Spirit. And just as we have all received from the fullness of the Word, as John said (John 1:16), so too the Holy Spirit from his fullness filled the whole world. Zechariah was not empty, for he was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied the coming of the Lord Jesus (Luke 1:67). Paul was not empty, for he evangelized in abundance; he was filled, receiving from the Ephesians the fragrance of a good savor, a sacrifice pleasing to God (Ephesians 5:2). The Corinthians were not empty, for God’s grace abounded in them, according to the testimony of the same Apostle (1 Corinthians 1:7).

[Col. 1501B]

55. David therefore offered himself to God daily, and he did not offer himself empty; he could say: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (above, verse 131). Therefore he said: “See that I have loved your commandments.” Hear in what way you ought to offer yourself to Christ—not in things that are seen, but in what is hidden and secret, so that your Father, who sees in secret, may repay you and reward your faithful devotion. “I have loved,” he says, “your commandments.” He did not say, “I have observed them”; he did not say, “I have kept them,” for the foolish have not kept the Lord’s commandments. Some manuscripts, indeed, have ἀσυνετοῦντας (*asyne­tountas*), that is, “those acting without understanding, not understanding” [Note: [Col. 1501] All the printed editions have the Septuagint reading εἶδον ἀσυνετοῦντας, καὶ ἐξετηκόμην (*eidon asynetountas, kai exetēkomēn*), “I saw those acting without understanding, and I wasted away,” to which the Arabic version also corresponds. But the Latin Vulgate, from the Hebrew, has “I saw transgressors, and I wasted away.”]. Therefore those who do not understand do not possess wisdom; they do not keep the commandments. But the one who is perfect in understanding, perfect in wisdom, loves them—which is more than keeping them. For keeping is generally a matter of necessity and fear; loving is a matter of charity. The one who evangelizes keeps the commandments; but the one who evangelizes willingly receives a reward. How much more will the one who loves be granted a reward! For we can fail to love what we will; we cannot refuse to will what we love. Yet although he awaits the reward of perfect charity, he asks for the support of divine compassion, so that the Lord may give him life in it. He is therefore not an arrogant exactor of a deserved reward, but a modest supplicant for divine mercy.

[Col. 1501D]

56. (Verse 160.) The eighth verse follows: “The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your justice are forever.” Since the beginning of God’s words is truth, truth is certainly the foundation of faith. First, we must believe that the utterances of the supreme God which we read in the divine Scriptures are true. Second, we must learn their power through fuller understanding. For just as “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110:9), while love is the fullness of wisdom—for the law is wisdom, but the fullness of the law is love—so the fullness of God’s words is wisdom and knowledge of justice. For just as there is a certain progression from fear of the Lord to the grace of charity, so there seems to be a certain progression from truth to the judgment of divine justice.

[Col. 1502A]

57. You have come to the Church; you have heard that there is one God, from which the Law begins, as it is written: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Believe that there is one God, not many gods. But when you begin to read that the Lord Jesus, the Son of God, came in the flesh for the redemption of the whole world, distinguish wisely that there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we are for him, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things and we are through him. Recognize that he came so that our disposition might be formed along the paths of virtue, so that we might learn gentleness of conduct by the example of his way of life, and so that guilt might be abolished through grace. Then you have progressed from confession of the truth to knowledge of justice. Faith is the beginning of the Christian; the fullness of the Christian is justice. Faith is found in the confession of peoples; justice in the passion of martyrs.

[Col. 1502B]

58. Knowing, therefore, that all the judgments of God’s justice will endure forever, let us beware lest our works displease him and we begin to undergo eternal judgment; nor, if we have done something good, should we be released into a complacent attitude. “We must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10). You see that Paul too will stand, as he himself recalls. Beware of wood; beware of straw, lest you bring with you to God’s judgment what the fire will consume. Beware lest, while you have one or two things that can be approved, you bring forward in many works what gives offense. “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; yet he himself may be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15). From this it follows that the same person is partly saved and partly condemned. Since we know, therefore, that there are many judgments, let us examine all our works. In a righteous person, the loss is serious, and the burning of any work is serious; in the impious, the punishment is miserable. May all the judgments instead be full of grace and full of flourishing crowns, lest, when our deeds are weighed, guilt perhaps outweigh the balance.

## THE TWENTY-FIRST SERMON. Schin.

1. The twenty-first letter, *Schin*, begins; in Latin it is called “Upon the wound.” What is “upon the wound” except a medicine by which the wound’s bitterness is eased? Oil is poured upon a wound so that all the wound’s harshness may be softened. A poultice is placed upon a wound; a bandage is placed upon a wound—things by which every wound is tended. Wherever, therefore, there is hope of restoring health, medicines are applied to wounds. But where “the whole head is in pain, and the whole heart in sorrow,” where there is “no wound, nor bruise, nor a burning sore” (Isaiah 1:5–6)—that is, where not a part but the whole is in danger [Note: [Col. 1503D] The Roman edition reads, “and is consumed by a certain wasting of the whole body.” This is not a bad reading, unless it departs from all the other editions and manuscripts, whose reading, although less usual, can nevertheless be defended, since a certain corruption of the whole body means exactly the same thing as a body corrupted in some way. Again, where all the manuscripts and the old edition read, “let interior death spread,” the Roman edition has, “let interior disease spread.” But there is no need for this alteration.] and a certain corruption of the whole body is consumed by wasting—there it is not possible to apply a poultice, oil, or bandage. It is therefore much better that there be a wound for you to tend and bind than for interior death to spread without a wound.

[Col. 1503A]

2. But there is not only a wound of the body; there is also a wound of the mind, which is softened by the oil of gentler speech and by the sweetness of peaceful discourse. There are soothing applications of words; there are medicines of heavenly commandments by which every poison of wickedness is removed. There are bonds of the Law that do not burn but rather free those who are bound; there is a spiritual poultice by which certain shattered members of the soul are strengthened.

[Col. 1503B]

3. Let us therefore consider what the wound is and what is upon the wound. “Princes persecuted me without cause”—that is the wound. “I exult in your words, like one who finds great spoils”—that is what is upon the wound, because the harsh injuries of the wound are healed by the Lord’s words.

4. In the Lamentations of Jeremiah too, you find written under this letter: “You have heard their reproach, O Lord, all their plans against me, the lips of those rising up against me, and their thoughts against me all day long, their sitting down and their rising up” (Lamentations 3:61–63)—that is the wound. But he added: “Look upon their eyes; repay them, O Lord, according to the works of their hands” (ibid., 64)—that is what is upon the wound, because vengeance often tends to ease the pain of a wound. And within the same Jeremiah it says: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, you who dwell in Geth; indeed, the cup will pass to you also: you will drink and become drunk” (Lamentations 4:21)—that is what is upon the wound. For the Lord’s cup is the remission of sins; it is the cup in which the blood is poured out that redeemed the sins of the whole world. This cup intoxicated the nations, so that they would not remember their own pain but would forget their former error. Good, therefore, is the spiritual drunkenness that does not know how to disorder the body’s movement [Note: [Col. 1504D] The Roman edition, with part of the manuscripts, reads, “does not know how to lift the step of the mind.” The other manuscripts rightly omit the negation.], but knows how to lift the step of the mind. Good is the drunkenness of the saving cup, which removes sorrow from the sinful conscience and pours in the joy of eternal life. Therefore Scripture says: “And how excellent is your cup that intoxicates!” (Psalm 22:5).

[Col. 1503D]

5. A medicine, therefore, is placed upon the wound, because the Lord Jesus himself is the physician who healed our wounds, pouring in wine and oil and binding the wounds of that Adam who, descending from Jerusalem, was wounded by robbers. Let each person beware lest he descend from Jerusalem; for each person descends through his sins and ascends through his merits. Or, because we are fragile, let the one who has descended run to that Samaritan, the guardian of his work [Note: [Col. 1504D] All the printed editions read, “of his body.” All the manuscripts read, “of his work,” except two in which both expressions have been omitted.], the guardian of the Law and of grace, so that he may find medicine for his wound. Let him place the bandage of heavenly words upon his wound, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2). Good is the bandage that may bind together the bones of your soul when they have been pulled apart, restore them with renewed solidity, reform them to their former strength, and return the severed limbs to one another without any scar disfiguring them.

[Col. 1504A]

6. (Verse 161.) We think that enough has been said, as far as our ability permits, about the interpretation of the letter. Let us now undertake to consider the verses of the holy Prophet which, after revelation by the Holy Spirit, he added: “Princes persecuted me without cause, and my heart trembled at your words.” If we recall the ancient history, Saul, Absalom, and many foreign princes persecuted the holy David; but no one could triumph over him. There are also princes of the world and rulers of darkness who attempt to crush you in your own breast and carry out savage persecutions within, promising kingdoms, honors, and riches if you yield with a fragile mind and think that their commands must be obeyed. These princes sometimes persecute without cause, sometimes not without cause. They persecute without cause the one in whom they find nothing belonging to themselves and whom they strive to subjugate; but they do not persecute without cause the one who has handed himself over to their power and entered wholly into the possession of the world. For over what belongs to them they rightly claim dominion for themselves, and from such people they demand the wages of iniquity.

7. The martyr rightly says that he endures the torments of persecution unjustly—he who has stolen nothing, violently oppressed no one, shed no one’s blood, [Note: [Col. 1504D] Many manuscripts read *nullum justorum* (“none of the righteous”). But this variation arose because in some manuscripts the word *nullius* was divided in such a way that its final letters were attached to the following word; hence in some copies we still read *nulli justorum*. Since this is plainly corrupt, others emended it on their own initiative to *nullum justorum*.] deemed no one’s marriage-bed inviolable; who owes nothing to the laws, yet is compelled to endure punishments more severe than those of robbers; who speaks what is just, yet is not heard; who speaks words full of salvation, yet is attacked, so that he can say: “When I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Psalm 119:7). He therefore suffers persecution without cause who is attacked without guilt; he is attacked as though guilty, although in such a confession he is worthy of praise; he is attacked as though a sorcerer because he glories in the name of the Lord, although piety is the foundation of all virtues. Truly he is attacked in vain who among the impious [Col. 1505A] and faithless is accused of impiety, although he is a teacher of faith.

8. Yet he who is attacked without cause ought to be strong and steadfast. Why, then, did he add: “And my heart trembled at your words”? To tremble is a sign of weakness, fear, and dread; but there is also a weakness that leads to salvation, and there is also the fear of the saints: “Fear the Lord, you his saints” (Psalm 33:10); and: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Psalm 111:1). Why is he blessed? “Because he will greatly delight in his commandments.” Imagine, then, a martyr placed amid dangers: on one side the ferocity of beasts roars to instill terror; elsewhere the hissing of glowing metal plates and the heat of a blazing furnace surge up; on another side the dragging of heavy chains resounds; here a bloodstained executioner stands nearby. Imagine him, I say, looking around at all these instruments of punishment, then thinking of the divine commandments, of that everlasting fire, that endless conflagration of the faithless, that misery of punishment continually renewed; let him tremble in his heart lest, while yielding to present sufferings, he give himself over to everlasting destruction; let his mind be disturbed while he beholds with the terrible sharpness of his gaze that dread sword of the coming judgment. [Note: [Col. 1505D] Thus read several manuscripts; others, and all printed editions, have: “they behold it with a certain appearance of its being seen.” Both readings are acceptable. But since the same editions subsequently read: “Does not the confidence of the steadfast man correspond to this trembling and produce the same effect…” no clear sense, or at least a very confused one, could be extracted. Therefore we have restored the passage from the manuscripts.] Will you not equate this trembling with the confidence of the steadfast man? The confidence of one desiring eternal things and the trembling of one fearing divine things converge upon the same result. Nevertheless, let the one who hopes be stronger; let the one who trusts be stronger.

9. Would that I might deserve to be such a man, so that, if a persecutor should arise, I would not consider the harshness of my punishments; would not measure the torments or penalties; would not think of any particular cruelty of pain; [Col. 1505C] 1241 but would regard all these things as light. Let me tremble, however, lest Christ deny me, lest Christ exclude me, lest he repel me from the council of priests if he judges me unworthy of that company. Let him see me, perhaps, shaken by fear of bodily punishments, yet trembling far more at the future judgments. And if he says to me, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:31), nevertheless he will extend his right hand and, with a steadfastness of faithful mind, strengthen me when I am disturbed by the swelling waves of this world.

10. (Verse 162.) The second verse follows: “I rejoice in your words, like one who finds much spoil.” Thus trembling at God’s words is good if it generates rejoicing; for whoever trembles at God’s words afterward rejoices in God’s words. Therefore whoever has God’s words in his palace—that is, in his heart—excludes the words of princes from his heart; fear excludes fear. If someone enters a bath and merely lays aside the heat, with one heat excluding another, how much more does the terror of divine judgment exclude human terror, and the fervor of eternal grace the fervor of worldly favor!

[Col. 1506A] 11. He who possesses the word of God therefore rejoices, for he possesses much spoil which he took from the Jews; he possesses the spoils of the fallen enemy (1 Kings 17:51). Just as David took Goliath’s sword and cut off his head with that same sword, so the true David, the humble and gentle Lord Jesus, cut off the head of the intelligible Goliath with his own weapons. For the weapons of the devil were the nations; but when he was wounded by the faith of the nations, he lost the head he had possessed. The spoils were stripped from the fallen man, and his vessels were plundered, because the strong man was bound. The devil’s vessel was the flesh of sinful humanity; but after we believed in Christ, our flesh began to be a vessel of election, as you have it concerning the apostle Paul, who was sent to the nations. The Lord Jesus said to Ananias: “Go, for he is a vessel of election for me” (Acts 9:15). Rightly, therefore, Christ’s name was called: “Swiftly seize the spoil, divide it quickly.” [Note: [Col. 1505D] Some manuscripts, together with the Hebrew text and most versions, read *cito praedare* (“quickly plunder”). But many others, and all printed editions, divide the words as *cito: divide* (“quickly: divide”). The Septuagint agrees with them, where one reads: “ὀξέως προνόμησον” (*oxeōs pronomēson*, “quickly plunder”).] For before the child knows how to call his father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians (Isaiah 8:3–4). Thus the king of the Assyrians—that is, of those whom their faithlessness had made vain—lost the spoil he had held. And so that you may again recognize that Christ reclaimed from the devil the spoils which that enemy had seized in Adam, the Sabeans, men of high stature, passed over to the Lord Jesus in chains and began to worship him, because he led captivity captive. Therefore he took off the devil’s head, so that he himself might be the head of the body that had been slain. Rightly now the nations throughout the whole world carry the royal head, because they are members of Christ.

12. You have learned this concerning the nations; learn it also concerning the Jews, from whom the Lord Jesus took the spoil. That is, he took away the kingdom of heaven and gave it to a nation producing its fruits. He took away the power of bread and the power of water, the prophet, the wonderful counselor, the skillful architect, and the wise hearer (Isaiah 1 and following). He took these from them and gave them to us. Rightly I rejoice . . . “like one who finds much spoil.” Without any labor of mine I found spoil that I did not possess. I found [Note: [Col. 1506D] By the *Heptateuch* understand the first seven books of the Old Testament, with Judges and Ruth counted as a single book. Josephus, *Against Apion* 2, Origen in the *Philocalia*, chapter 3, and others after them teach that the Hebrews customarily appended Ruth to Judges as a part or appendix.] the Heptateuch; I found the books of the Kingdoms; I found the writings of the prophets; I found Ezra; I found the Psalms; I found Proverbs; I found Ecclesiastes; I found the Song of Songs; I found Christ, the wonderful counselor; I found Paul, the skillful architect; I found the Christian people, the wise hearer, who knows how to hear what is read—for he hears who understands what he hears.

The Law is spiritual. The Jew does not hear it who hears it bodily; rather, he hears it who hears in the Spirit. They have the books, but they do not possess the meaning of the books. They have the prophets, but they do not possess the one whom those prophets foretold. For how can they possess the one whom they did not receive? Therefore he appeared to me with Moses and Elijah, because he had departed from them. He possesses much spoil who possesses the Word of God. He possesses resurrection, justice, power, and wisdom; he possesses everything, because everything subsists in him. The Hebrews despoiled the Egyptians and carried off their vessels (Exodus 12:36); the Christian people possess the spoil of the Jews, and we possess everything that they did not know themselves to possess. They carried away material gold and silver; we have received the gold of the mind, we have acquired the silver of heavenly speech.

13. (Verse 163.) The third verse follows: “I have hated and abhorred injustice; but I have loved your law.” Rightly does he hate injustice who possesses the weapons of justice. When the Hebrew possessed these weapons—that is, the Law and the prophets—he abhorred a dead mouse, because the Law says: “Everyone who touches a dead body . . . shall be unclean” (Numbers 19:11), and he denied the dead the final offices of humanity. But according to the Law, no one is dead except the unjust. This is the uncleanness of the just person: iniquity. For what is more unclean than to defile with shameful crimes and savage imaginings the mind, than which nothing more precious has been given to humanity? What does it profit them that they fear to look upon a dead man? [Note: [Col. 1507D] Thus read all manuscripts and the Roman edition, a reading that also agrees well with what follows. The older editions, however, read: “Would that their vices did not pollute.”] Would that the life of those whose death can contaminate no one did not pollute the one who approaches them! Death harms no one; would that life did not harm anyone! For the contagion of defilement is participation in iniquity. How, then, can one who can no longer be unjust contaminate anyone, since even if he once was unjust, he has ceased to be so? Flee, therefore, iniquity, lest it seize you. Flee injustice, which makes the living dead while they still live.

14. But no one flees iniquity except one who loves righteousness; therefore he says: “But I have loved your law.” In the Law there is righteousness, if you receive the spiritual law, if you rise with Christ and there behold that most holy heavenly altar, not the earthly altar that was destroyed by hostile devastation; if you look upon that Jerusalem which is in heaven, not the one that was frequented by the Jewish people on earth and which, because of the faithlessness of its inhabitants, was conquered by the Roman army and consumed in the fire that was set to it; if you look upon that chief priest of whom it is written: “Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our faithful confession” [Col. 1507D] (Hebrews 4:14)—he who is our advocate before the Father every day, so that for those toward whom he showed compassionate mercy in the days of his flesh, he may work the remission of sins every day. For what other hope is there for the human race except that the offenses of all the living be forgiven? He alone, therefore, is the chief of priests, attended by pious priests who have rightly entered that highest heavenly sanctuary by the merit of their own blood. That law, then, is to be loved in which the true Hebrew is free from every slavery to vices; in which there is the great Sabbath and the unhindered rest of the dead; in which the seed of the dead people is raised again, not through physical mingling but through fraternal redemption. According to this law, therefore, the holy man hates injustice, not the unjust person, who can often be converted; he curses and rejects not the remains of the dead but dead iniquity.

15. (Verse 164.) The fourth verse follows: “Seven times a day I have praised you, because of the judgments of your righteousness.” The number certainly expresses devotion’s zeal for holy worship. But I think it more particularly declares an affection that is pure, peaceful, and free from every burden of sins, so that prayer may be offered without any fire of angry cursing or shameful desire; so that we may ask nothing that harms another, nothing that disfigures us through worldly petitions. Let us praise in hymns and songs, always confessing as true and just the things we sing in praise of divine matters. Let the judgment not be hesitant or uncertain; let the mind’s intention not be divided or diverted from carrying out its spiritual purpose by material concerns. Let God’s justice always be justified with a tranquil mind, not with idle leisure.

16. (Verse 165.) The fifth verse follows: “Great peace belongs to those who love your name, and there is no stumbling-block for them.” Above (verse 162) we said that love excludes fear; now we say that it excludes every disturbance. Indeed, profound is the tranquility of a mind established in the person who loves God. “Many waters,” he says, “will not be able to extinguish love, and rivers will not overwhelm it” (Song of Songs 8:7). The many waters are the various passions, and the rivers are worldly desires stirred up by bodily impulses, [Note: [Col. 1507D] Six manuscripts read: “yet they cannot overturn love of morals.”] yet they cannot overturn the wall of love. Therefore the person founded upon love says: “Our soul has passed through the torrent” (Psalm 123:5). Could the water of the sea exclude Moses’ love? And, to support you according to the literal sequence of the Psalms, surely the one who loved God believed that his passage through the seas was safe. But those who did not love God were submerged by the waves and met an end worthy of their sacrilege. Elijah and Elisha crossed the Jordan on foot (2 Kings 2:8), and this was the reward and grace of extraordinary love. Thus, in order to cross the waters of the Jordan River, they first crossed the streams of our passions by the footprint of the mind. Of this water the Lord says: “If you pass through water, I am with you, and the rivers will not overwhelm you” (Isaiah 43:2). He is always present with his righteous when they are worn down by adversities, provided that they pass through them with a steadfast, undoubting mind and are not shaken by uncertainty of faith. [Note: [Col. 1508D] Thus the old edition and all manuscripts read: “when they are worn down by adversities.” The Roman edition alone reads: “when they are terrified by adversities.” This is less suitable. Below, however, the old edition and certain Paris editions read: “even if much love is in your heart.” The Roman edition, together with all manuscripts, reads: “even if much peace is in your heart,” and so forth.]

17. You, too, therefore, cross over with the direction of a faithful mind, if you want the divine presence to be with you; if not merely peace but great peace is in your heart; if no battles of conflicting desire attack you, if anger does not spur you, if lust does not. And if there is a battle, let it be outside, not within. Fight against your persecutors, although you must often yield to them in silence, because they are victorious for you. Their power is your victory. They are finally triumphed over when they believe that they have won. Let greed not attack you; let desire not harass you; let sadness not cast you down; let lust not inflame you; let pride not overturn you; let ambition not bend you; let fear not terrify you. Let great peace abound in you, that peace which surpasses every mind, according to the Apostle’s judgment (Philippians 4:7)—nothing more beautiful could be said. For it is the highest end of wisdom that we should be tranquil in mind, that our affection should not be disturbed by the slippery fables invented by poets. It is the highest end of justice that iniquity should not be able to move the mind of the just. This is the end of every virtue, [Note: [Col. 1509D] The old edition and certain Paris editions read: “so that he may make the soldier’s bodily strength itself wage wars.” The Roman edition agrees with the manuscripts in our reading, except that it transfers the word *miles* (“soldier”) to the following clause, producing: “so that the soldier may restore peace.” This alteration is not necessary for the sense.] and of bodily strength itself: that, when the war has been completed, it may restore peace. Therefore even the strength that wages war often serves peace; let no one, then, disturb a peaceful affection.

18. Many things arise to disturb a person. A wife, often deceived by the serpent’s snares, attempts to agitate her husband’s mind; a father frequently mocks his son’s faith; a husband tests his wife’s mind with insults. But in all these things the just person prevails and says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress . . . or persecution?” (Romans 8:35). How often are good deeds themselves counted as crimes? How often is virtue regarded as a reproach? How often is grace itself met with ingratitude? The just man sold his possessions and distributed them to the poor; he kept nothing for himself. Yet he is often despised within the very Church because he has ceased to be rich, as it is written: “If a man gives all his possessions for love, he will be utterly despised” [Col. 1509C] (Song of Songs 8:7). Let him not therefore be disturbed; for he did not seek the reward or favor of this age, but of eternal life. Let him not be indignant because people honor money more than good works. For if he is honored in this world because of a good work and receives here the fruit of this devotion, it is said of him: “He has received his reward” (Matthew 6:2). He does indeed have a good work and favor here, but this is only a small portion of the salvation that must be won. Preserve your reward for the future, and judge the reproaches of this age to be increases of your reward. Always remember that apostolic saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come” (Romans 8:18). Let the just person therefore be broken by no insults, moved by no dangers, tested by no storms—whether death should threaten, or life, or the angels of heaven. Let him neither be cast down by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity. Let his affection be weak nowhere. Both death tests, and life tests; beware of stumbling.

19. He who possesses the peace that surpasses every mind is great; he is not one of those little ones. Therefore he ought not to suffer scandal, because it belongs to the little ones to be agitated by scandal. Hence the Lord also says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones, the least of all, to stumble” (Matthew 18:6). He called them not merely little ones but the very least, those whom scandals disturb; and therefore, as you have read, whoever unsettles the infancy of a weak mind is liable to a severe punishment. Just as one is worthy of a more severe penalty [Col. 1510A] who persuades a child to commit a crime and precipitates an unwary age, so is one who ensnares a weak, ignorant, and imprudent person through persuasive error or agitation of the heart’s affection. Do you wish to know how weak the one who is scandalized is? “I will not eat meat,” he says, “lest I scandalize my brother” (1 Corinthians 8:13). What weakness, and a kind of infancy of mind, that even a brother’s food should disturb him! How, then, can anything be a precipice for a person, when even this presents a danger?

20. And what is worse, this kind of weakness spreads among many. You see a just person in poverty—you are tested; you see a wicked person rich—you are tested; you see a holy person without children—you are tested; you see an unjust person abounding in children, honors, and worldly praises—you are tested. How many pits, how many snares—and, what is more grievous, snares that strangle very many! In the city of Sodom scarcely one Lot was found who was not tested, and even his wife could not escape the snares of temptation. The Hebrew people crossed the seas, but could not cross the trials. All were tested except Jesus and Caleb, who therefore deserved, from among the elders, to enter the promised land because they were free from temptation. Aaron did not enter, nor Miriam, because they too were tested. Moses did not enter, because he was the leader of the people who were being tested: he was a type of the Law, which could neither exclude temptations nor lead them into the land of resurrection, because this grace was owed to the Gospel. The Law could not give peace; therefore Moses fought continually as long as he lived, and the people of the Law were always in the uncertainty of battles. But Jesus son of Nun settled the minds of the people in profound peace, because the one who is under the Law is shaken by uncertainties, whereas the one who is under the Gospel hears him saying: “I leave you peace; my peace I give you” (John 14:27). Therefore those who love have no stumbling-block.

21. Understand it in another way: the Lord’s cross is a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks. It is a stumbling-block to the faithless, because the Jew says: “So this is God, who appeared as a man? This is God, who fasted? This is God, who was beaten? This is God, who was crucified? This is God, who could not descend from the cross and free himself?” Indeed, they said this at the time of the Lord’s Passion: “Let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him” (Matthew 27:42–43). Let such thoughts not test you; let them not disturb you; let such ideas not force their way into your mind. Where there is peace, and great peace, Christ’s cross is not a reproach but salvation. Christ’s cross was not a reproach to Peter; it gave him such glory that he honored Christ with his footsteps reversed, fearing that if he were crucified in the same manner as the Lord, he might appear to have sought the Lord’s glory. The cross is therefore a reproach to the faithless; but to the faithful it is grace, redemption, and resurrection, because the Lord suffered for us; because by that blood he redeemed us; because by that resurrection he recalled us to paradise. How can one who believes these things be disturbed, when the hope of the heavenly kingdom rises before him?

[Col. 1511A] 22. (Verse 166.) The sixth verse follows: “I waited for your salvation, O Lord, and I fulfilled your commandments.” Whoever waits hopes. Hope therefore precedes love; salvation follows; hope, then, runs ahead of the fulfillment. Therefore the one who awaited salvation from the Lord fulfilled the Lord’s commandments. Hence in the Gospel the Lord calls those who have fulfilled his commandments friends, not servants (John 15:14–15). For the one who loves acts, and the one who acts is rightly granted the reward of love.

23. (Verse 167.) The seventh verse follows: “My soul has kept your testimonies, and loved them exceedingly.” To love is more than to keep; and above we said (verse 159, no. 55) that keeping is sometimes a matter of necessity or fear, whereas loving is a matter of charity. Therefore, after saying here, “I have kept,” he added, “I have loved,” so that his keeping might be that of one who loves, not one who fears. Whoever loves exceedingly keeps exceedingly.

24. (Verse 168.) The eighth verse follows: “I have kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you, O Lord.” Blessed is the one who can say: “All my ways are before you”; who does not wish to conceal all his thoughts and all his actions. Adam concealed his way; Eve concealed hers after the offense; Cain concealed the murder of his brother. We have the desire to conceal, though not the ability to do so. Full of treachery is the one who conceals, even though there is no hiding place from God. Therefore the Church showed him her secrets in the Song of Songs, saying: “I will take you and bring you into the house of my mother, and into the secret place of her who conceived me” (Song of Songs 8:2). Although God sees all the hidden things of the heart, it is nevertheless good for each person to open and spread out his soul before him, and to come before him as before light or warmth. Not without reason does the Church glory, saying: “I was in his eyes as one who finds peace” (ibid., 10), because she was not afraid to reveal her ways. This, then, is the voice of the just: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Psalm 33:16). Thus this is rightly said to the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the way and the truth, by those who desire to conform to that true way in faith, conduct, and action: “All my ways are before you, O Lord.” For no way can be good except the one that you have judged worthy of being illumined by the visitation of your light. To him be honor, glory, praise, and eternity from age to age, now and always, forever and ever. Amen.

## THE TWENTY-SECOND SERMON. Tau.

[Col. 1511D]

1. The letter Tau begins here; in Latin interpretation it means “He went astray”; another interpretation has “He completed.” What does “he went astray” mean? It is the twenty-second letter, which is the last among the Hebrews. In this Psalm—that is, the one hundred eighteenth—we have said that the progress of a person is signified (above, in the prologue to this Psalm): one who has been instructed by the teachings of moral doctrine lays aside all the childishness of an untrained mind and assumes the knowledge of mature counsel and the age of old-man wisdom. But where there is error, guilt is indicated. Thus this is the end of progress: that there may also be an end to guilt. But observe what the word means. It says “he went astray,” not “he is going astray.” “To have gone astray” belongs to past time; “to go astray,” to the present. He who went astray has ceased to go astray and condemns his former error. For the one of whom it is said “he went astray” is no longer in error; the one who still remains in error is not said to have gone astray but to be going astray. To be going astray belongs to one who persists in vice; to have gone astray belongs to one who corrects his fall.

2. Thus the reformer of morals says: “For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, going astray in desires and pleasures” (Titus 3:3). He would certainly not have said, “We were once foolish,” unless he had afterward acquired the discipline of wisdom. Nor would he have said, “We were going astray,” unless he had laid aside his former error. Finally, to show that the fall had been abolished and that no trace of offense remained, he says: “But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, not from works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 4–5). Having therefore laid aside his former error and been renewed by the Holy Spirit and by every correction of conduct, he says: “For we were once going astray.” You see, then, that to renounce error is not a vice but progress.

3. Finally, let the Lord Jesus himself teach you this, if you do not think that human counsels or opinions should be trusted. For in his Gospel he himself affirmed that the shepherd left the ninety-nine sheep and sought the one that had gone astray (Luke 15:4). It is the hundredth sheep that he says went astray; let the perfection and completeness of the number itself instruct and shape you. It is not without reason preferred to the others, because it is more to have recalled oneself from vice than never to have known vices at all. To strip minds imbued with vices of the reins of desires and to reform them belongs not only to perfect virtue but also to heavenly grace.
