To reform what lies ahead belongs to human attentiveness; [Note: [Col. 1511D] The old edition reads “to forgive past things”; the Roman edition, “to condemn past things.” Again, below, the old edition reads “the fallen condition is restored,” while the Roman edition reads “the weary condition is restored.” The manuscripts in both places are divided, some agreeing with one reading and some with the other.] to condemn the past belongs to divine power. Thus, after finding the sheep, the shepherd placed it on his shoulders (ibid., 5). You recognize the mystery: how the weary sheep is restored, for the weary human condition cannot otherwise be restored [Note: [Col. 1512D] The old edition, together with some manuscripts, reads: “the fallen condition is restored.”] except through the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion and the blood of Jesus Christ, “whose rule is upon his shoulders” (Isaiah 9:6). On that cross he bore our weaknesses, so that there he might empty away the sins of all. [Col. 1512D] Rightly the angels rejoice, because the one who went astray now goes astray no longer; he has now forgotten his error.

4. It is therefore not “error” but “completion,” as the other interpretation teaches. Completion is the perfection of discipline. Hence Jeremiah also says in his Lamentations under this letter: “Your iniquity is ended, daughter of Zion; he will not continue to exile you. He has visited your iniquities, daughter of Edom; he has revealed your sins” (Lamentations 4:21). Do you perceive that iniquity could not end without God’s visitation, nor correction be complete except through the grace of the Lord Savior? But how does iniquity end? Hear the Church saying: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song of Songs 5:3). Having therefore laid aside in the washing of regeneration the garment of the old man, woven with the vices of error, she does not know how she could put it on again; for through the zeal of correction the forgetting of sins had grown within her. So great is the power of completed reform that the person returns to a kind of spiritual childhood, one that does not know the ways of error and, even if it wished, could not commit a crime, because it has lost the habit of sinning. I think enough has now been said about the interpretation of this letter. Let us now learn from what follows [Note: [Col. 1513D] Seven manuscripts read: “what the confidence of the perfected man is.” This reading is supported by the fact that shortly afterward all manuscripts and editions have: “This, then, is the confidence of the perfected man.”] what the perfected man’s declaration is.

5. (Verse 169.) Thus he says: “Let my prayer draw near before you, O Lord; according to your word grant me understanding.” A good life makes prayer fly and gives spiritual wings to supplications, by which the prayer of the saints is lifted up to God. But the Spirit by whom we pray also raises the prayer of the just, especially when a compassionate affection commends it from a contrite heart. This, then, is the confidence of the perfected man. Thus David himself earlier in this Psalm sought a lamp for his feet (above, verse 105), lest he should go astray while walking on this earthly journey. But now, as though already placed at the end and in the course’s completion, having finished the task of traveling, he rises up entirely. He directs his prayer toward heavenly things; he sends it into the presence of the Lord Savior, giving it the breath of justice, the wind of wisdom, the oars of devotion and faith, and the supports of innocence and purity. For sin makes prayer heavy, and it goes far from God. The more blameworthy the life of the one who prays, [Note: [Col. 1514D] All editions read “the more wicked”; all manuscripts read “the more blameworthy.” Again, where the old edition and the manuscripts read “they decline from doing earthly things,” the Roman edition alone has “they decline from earthly works.”] the more heavily it is burdened. But the prayer of the innocent rises, as does the groaning of a compassionate affection, if they hate the mud of Egypt and decline from doing earthly things. Thus you read (Exodus 2:23) that the groaning and cry of the Hebrews, who could not endure the harsh commands of the Egyptians and who, because the tasks were burdensome as well as muddy, rejected them as unworthy of the nobility of their race, rose up to the Lord our God. Their prayer rose because, although they performed the work, they performed it unwillingly. God’s mercy therefore descended to them, because their devotion ascended to God.

6. Their prayer rose, then, not bodily—for such a great prophet was not asking that his prayer should bodily approach God. Whoever thinks this confines God to some definite place or seat, as though he supposed a more spacious place in which God exists, although the invisible, ineffable, incomprehensible one fills all things and the fullness of divinity dwells in him. I have read that Moses approached God (Exodus 24:18) when he received the Law. But David, with his customary modesty, asks not that he himself but that his prayer approach God, so that a certain distinction of order may appear: those who are more perfect themselves approach God, while it is enough for righteous men of the next order that their prayer approach him.

7. Let us consider from the usage of our speech what it means to approach. Set before yourself a teacher and a student. If the student has either absorbed the teacher’s talent more diligently or devoted himself to his instruction, so that he seems to come very near the likeness of the teacher’s work and doctrine, do we not customarily say that he has approached his teacher? So too, if you show yourself an imitator of Christ, like the one who says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4:16); if you know no deceit, hate falsehood, follow truth, do not shun justice, and love chastity, you have approached Christ, and through Christ, God. For he is the way by which one reaches the Father, and he is always with the Father.

8. We have learned what it means for prayer to approach: namely, that it should be raised by our actions. If you raise your actions, you have raised your prayer. Whoever knows how to raise his hands directs his prayer before God, as you read below: “Let my prayer be directed like incense before you; the lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140:2). This prayer leads to life; another prayer leads into sin: “Let his prayer become sin” (Psalm 108:7). If you ask for worldly things, if you demand shameful things, your prayer is not directed toward God but into sin. Therefore understand what you ask.

9. “According to your word,” he says, “grant me understanding.” Observe what he requests. He did not say understanding in general, but understanding according to the word of God. For there is an understanding that leads to death, just as there is a prudence that leads to destruction: “The children of this age are more prudent than the children of light in their generation” (Luke 16:8). But this prudence, which belongs to the world, does not assist eternal life. It concerns honors and small profits; it is intent on amassing earnings rather than acquiring merits. Finally, it is a wisdom concerned with the elements of the world, more showy than true, as is all philosophy, which seeks what belongs to others while not knowing what belongs to itself. It investigates the regions of heaven and examines the spaces of the world, things that can benefit it in no way; it does not know God, whom alone it ought to seek.

10. Therefore the true wise man says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise; for the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God” [Col. 1514D] (1 Corinthians 3:18–19). We must therefore strive to be foolish in this age, having nothing to do with philosophy, lest anyone lead our faith away from the truth through the elements of this world, lest anyone plunder our confession through philosophy. For we know that the Arians fell into faithlessness in this way, when they thought that Christ’s generation could be inferred from the ways of this world. They abandoned the Apostle and followed Aristotle. They abandoned the wisdom that is with God and chose the snares of disputation and the trapping of words according to dialectical discipline, although the Apostle cries out: “Let no one plunder you through philosophy and empty deception, according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ” (Colossians 2:8).

11. Would that I could imitate that folly by which I might be wise: that man who has extensive possessions but is careless of their fruits, intent upon God; that man who rejects even honors conferred upon him, does not seek philosophical doctrine; even if he formerly knew it, he pretends not to know it, learning by not seeking; he does not seek what is his own, but bestows his possessions upon others and acquires eternal things for himself. He can say: “Give me understanding according to your word,” that is, not according to philosophers, not according to lawyers, [Col. 1515B] not according to the merchants of this age, not according to the architects of houses, but according to your word, which is the foundation of true wisdom and good works; so that upon it the prophet may establish the gold of his heart, the silver of his speech, and the precious stones of his deeds, so that his work may neither collapse nor perish.

12. (Verse 170.) The second verse follows: “Let my petition enter before you; according to your word, deliver me.” Observe the order. First he said: “Let my prayer draw near”; afterward he asked for understanding, “according to the word”; thirdly he says, “Let my petition enter before you.” Does the Lord not invite us by a certain practice and graciously deign to receive us? When you desire to meet one of the chief men, do you not first draw near to his house; afterward do you seek to be informed and instructed, so that you may know the mind of the head of the household; then, in order to enter his house, do you not implore him lest someone reject and exclude you? Knock, then, you too, at that royal heavenly door—not with the hand of the body, [Note: [Col. 1515D] All editions: “but with a certain right hand of your reason.” All manuscripts read better: “with the right hand of your prayer.”] but with a certain right hand of your prayer. It is not only the bodily hand that knocks: the voice also knocks; for it is written: “The voice of my brother knocks at the door” (Song of Songs V, 2). We knock also with a finger. Indeed, Thomas deserved to open the door of the resurrection with his finger. And Jesus says to you: “Put your finger here . . . . .” [Note: [Col. 1515D] Several manuscripts: “and put it into my hands and my side.”] “and put your hands into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing” (John XX, 27). Knock, then, with a finger, if you cannot with your whole hand. Knock at the door. Christ is the door, who says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X, 9).

[Col. 1515D] 13. When, therefore, you have knocked at this door, observe how you enter, lest perhaps, even after entering, you remain outside the king’s sight. Many enter palaces and do not immediately see this earthly king; rather, they keep watch frequently, so that they may at some time deserve to see him. They do not presume upon the opportunity of seeing him; instead, when ordered, they are brought before him, and they pour out their prayers so that they may be received with goodwill. His first concern is the beginning of his speech, lest anything stumble or give offense. How much more must God be entreated that our prayer may enter the door of his mercy! Indeed, Paul also asks that “a door of the word” be opened to him for speaking the mystery of Christ (Colossians IV, 3).

14. But since the Greek has Εἰσελθέτω ἀξίωμά μοῦ—that is, “Let my dignity enter”—although the writer may have been mistaken and may have written ἀξίωσις, that is, “petition,” nevertheless let us explain this reading also as best we can. [Note: [Col. 1515D] All editions: “Clearly, when you ask a man, you call yourself a king.” The meaning is absurd. We have therefore restored the reading found in all the manuscripts. The corruption arose only because a few manuscripts transposed the word “king” after the verb “you ask,” which gave some half-learned person an opportunity to insert the little word “yourself.”] For when you ask a man who is a king, you ask him to take account of your honor, to let the awareness of your dignity touch him, so that either he may show mercy if pardon is being sought, or show the deference due to the rank of your dignity. [Col. 1516B] [Note: [Col. 1515D] Several manuscripts: “And what shall I say? Everyone who asks enters in this way,” and so forth. This is not a bad reading.] And what shall I say about asking? Everyone enters in such a way that respect is shown to dignities. Rightly, therefore, the one devoted to God also says: “Let my dignity enter before you.” The Christian too possesses his dignity, for he serves so great an emperor.

15. There are dignities of the greatest and truest faith, and different ranks of honors before Christ: “God has appointed in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers” (I Corinthians XII, 28). But these are the dignities of those who administer. There are also dignities belonging to private persons, such as devotion, justice, sobriety, chastity, and discipline. There are also dignities of prayer: if you pray for a widow, if you pray for an orphan, if you pray for one deserving mercy, if you pray for someone exceedingly devoted and faithful; if you pray in tribulation, if you pray with grief, if you yourself share with sorrow in the distress of the one for whom you pray, your prayer enters the grace of God. It enters his house if the Church entreats together with you, if the whole people implore, so that the Lord may incline his favor.

16. But what does he ask? That he be rescued, that he be delivered, because for a long time now he has been fighting against spiritual wickedness and against the temptations of this age; because it is sufficiently burdensome, over the prolonged course of this life, to endure an unbroken campaign. [Note: [Col. 1516D] Thus five manuscripts. Others, together with the old edition, omit the word “life”; if that reading is preferred, the relative “of this” must be referred to the previously placed word “age.” But the Roman edition corrected the passage on its own authority as follows: “it is sufficiently burdensome for one of great age to endure the prolonged course of this life,” and so forth.] Indeed, below he also says: “Alas for me, that my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Psalm CXIX, 5). He groans because he stretches out unceasing watches in unremitting labor; and therefore he asks to be delivered from so many adversaries, nor does he wish to associate with earthly human beings.

17. (Verse 171.) The third verse follows: “My lips shall pour forth a hymn, when you teach me your ordinances.” He has poured forth a hymn who can say: “For we are the good odor of Christ to God” (II Corinthians II, 15). And he pours forth well who has tasted the Lord’s many sweet commandments. He pours forth a hymn who has poured forth the word. Indeed, David first poured forth “a good word” (Psalm XLIV, 2), and this man pours forth a hymn. [Col. 1517A] For he has tasted the good bread that descended from heaven—the good bread which, if anyone eats it, he will not die forever. The word of God has its banquets: some are stronger, such as the Law and the Gospel; others are sweeter, such as the Psalms and the Song of Songs. The Church, or the devout soul, poured forth a hymn, to whom God the Word said: “Let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet” (Song of Songs II, 14). She poured forth a hymn to whom he said: “Your lips drip honey, O bride; honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song of Songs IV, 11).

18. But no one can pour forth a hymn beforehand unless he has learned the ordinances of God, and learned them from the Lord God himself. Therefore David expressly asks God to teach him; for he had heard and had recognized in the Spirit that “one is the teacher” (Matthew XXIII, 10), and for this reason everywhere he asked that God himself become his teacher, so that he might learn his ordinances from him. For how can anyone sing while placed in fear and dread of punishments? How can one sing who is conscious of serious offenses, unless he first becomes secure of pardon? Indeed, later you find: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm CXXXVI, 4)—in a land where he is attacked, where he is held captive under the law of sin, where he laments and bewails the misery of his captivity?

19. Therefore, you too, eat the food of the heavenly Scriptures, and eat it so that it may remain with you for eternal life; eat daily, so that you may not hunger; eat so that you may be filled; eat so that you may pour forth the richness of heavenly words. Spiritual banquets ordinarily do not harm but benefit those who are satisfied by them. Therefore the Prophet wished to be filled, saying: “Let my mouth be filled with praise, so that I may sing your glory” (Psalm LXXVIII, 8). Whoever sings the glory of God pours forth a hymn to the Lord from his heart.

20. (Verse 172.) The fourth verse follows: “My tongue shall speak your word, for all your commandments are justice.” Whoever has learned the ordinances of God speaks the word of God; and whoever speaks the word of God does not speak an idle word. It is an idle word to speak of human works. Therefore the Holy One says (Psalm XVI, 4) that the Lord grants him the grace not to speak with his mouth of the works of human beings, because it is an idle word—indeed, not only idle but dangerous, for which we shall have to render an account. “For every idle word that we shall have spoken, we shall render an account for it” (Matthew XII, 36). For it is no slight danger, when you possess so many words of God and the works of God—what he did in Genesis, what he did in Exodus, what he did [1252] in Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, the Book of Judges, the Books of Kings and Ezra, what he did in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles—to set these aside and speak of the things of the age, to listen to the things of the age. [Note: [Col. 1517D] Several manuscripts: “Hedge your ears with thorns.” This is not a bad reading. Others, however, as well as all the editions, have “Hedge,” and so forth. All the editions add after the word “hedge,” “so that you may not speak of the things of the age or hear the things of the age”; these words are found in no manuscripts and are certainly a mere repetition of what precedes.] “Hedge your ears with thorns” (Ecclesiasticus XXVIII, 28). Would that you also hedge your tongue! But what is worse, your tongue is surrounded by thorns that prick and wound the one speaking the things of the world. Therefore the adversary also frequently pours worldly thoughts upon those who are praying. If, then, we ought not to hear what is alien or superfluous, how much more ought we not to speak it, since venerable Scripture says to each one of us: “Bind your silver and gold, and place a yoke and a weight upon your mouth” (ibid., 29). [Note: [Col. 1517D] The editions: “Bind your understanding with faith and silence”; the manuscripts: “with faithful silence.”] Bind your understanding with faithful silence; bind your words; place a yoke upon your mouth, lest, with an unrestrained neck, it boast itself in words. Place a weight upon it, so that we may weigh everything we say with careful examination. But with what thorns does Scripture tell you to hedge your ears, except with a contrite heart and fear of judgment? These things prick us for our healing: they stimulate but do not wound; although even wounds inflicted by a friend are useful.

[Col. 1518B] 21. “All,” he says, “the commandments of God are justice,” because they are commandments of justice and therefore cannot be without justice. The commandment of God is that you love your God (Deuteronomy VI, 5). Hence Paul says: “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law; for it is written: ‘You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet,’ and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word” (Romans XIII, 8–9). If every commandment is summed up in that word, and that word is justice—for what is as just as loving your God and loving your brother?—then certainly all God’s commandments are justice. For just as [Note: [Col. 1518D] The Corbie manuscript: “who wishes to kill his brother.” One Sorbonne manuscript: “who seeks to kill his brother.” But this alteration arose only from the ignorance of scribes. They did not see that “can kill” here has the same force as “actually kills,” as in Virgil’s line: “Could you have left her alone?”—which is equivalent to “How did you abandon her?”] whoever can kill his brother certainly does not love him; whoever commits adultery with his brother’s wife certainly does not love his brother; whoever steals or covets what belongs to another certainly does not love the one whom he desires to defraud; so whoever contemptuously despises his brother, tries to disgrace him, and feeds upon his injuries is estranged from the fellowship of charity.

22. (Verse 173.) The fifth verse follows: “Let your hand be there to save me, for I have chosen your commandments.” He seems to be praying for the Lord’s coming, because the hand of God is Christ. We read that he is the right hand of God, concerning whom he said above: “The right hand of the Lord has acted with power; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Psalm CXVII, 16). Why, then, did he say “hand” here, unless perhaps it was said not only because of the difference of grace, which writers ordinarily do not neglect, but also because of a certain propriety concerning hands: so that “right hand” is said where it is written that he exalted him by power, while “hand” is said here where it ought to be understood that he saved him through humility? The hand of the Lord can also be understood in the ordinary sense in which one says: “Great is that king’s hand,” meaning, “His army is great”; or, “That man’s hand is inferior.” Thus here too we may understand: “Let your aid and support be made available, so that you may send your angels, your help, and the resources of your power to deliver your people.” This is the hand of God concerning which it is written: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to be heirs of salvation?” (Hebrews I, 14). Whoever, therefore, has chosen God’s commandments makes use of confidence, so that with authority he may request divine assistance for himself.

23. (Verse 174.) The sixth verse follows: “I have desired your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation.” One person delights in the length of this life and desires to prolong the life of this body until the end of an advanced old age. Others are broken by the weakness of illness; of them no one can say: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (II Corinthians XII, 10). They consider themselves blessed if they enjoy uninterrupted bodily health; for them illness is not directed toward salvation. No one of these can say: “I have desired your salvation, O Lord,” for they seek their own health rather than God’s salvation, obeying physicians rather than the Scriptures. The prescriptions of those devoted to divine knowledge, however, are contrary to such remedies (Decree, Distinction 5, “Contraria”). They call one back from fasting, do not permit one to keep vigil, and draw one away from every intense meditation. Therefore whoever gives himself over to physicians denies himself. But whoever seeks God’s salvation follows Christ, who is called [Note: [Col. 1519D] The Roman edition has “God’s salvation” here and shortly afterward. Below, after the word “seeking,” the earlier editions add “while he dwells in this body,” although this entire clause—“for it is salvation that is sought”—had been removed by the same Roman edition. It would have been enough to remove “for it is salvation that is sought,” since these words are not found in the manuscripts.] “the salvation of God”: seeking not what belongs to the body but what is eternal, while he dwells in this body. Whoever seeks God’s salvation meditates on the law day and night. Constant meditation on divine decrees belongs to him, and no concern for this body diverts him from his devotion to discipline.

[Col. 1519C] 24. (Verse 175.) The seventh verse follows: “My soul shall live, and it shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.” He is surely consoling himself with the reward of the future life, not the present one; for how can this life be called life, concerning which it is written: “You have brought me down to the dust of death” (Psalm XXI, 16)? How many living people are in hell! Paul himself desired to be freed from this body of death, the one who truly desired God’s salvation, saying: “For I desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is much better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary” (Philippians I, 23), rather than voluntary. How, then, does the soul live when covered by a shroud of death, or what kind of life is it that exists in shadow? We are in the region of the shadow of death. Our life is hidden, not free; for it will be free in the region of the living, where the righteous take confidence in pleasing the Lord: “that he may please the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm CXIV, 9). There, then, our soul lives, where it is clothed with nothing mortal, nothing weak, nothing liable to punishment.

25. There it will praise the Lord, when, having laid aside the body of weakness, it has begun to be conformed to the glory of Christ’s body. For while we are in sin, how can we praise him fully? To the sinner God said: “Why do you recount my ordinances?” (Psalm XLIX, 16). Here we are placed in shadow; in shadow we live; in shadow we praise; in shadow we cannot praise perfectly. We are in a foreign land. Indeed, later you heard them saying: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm CXXXVI, 4).

26. The judgments of God help the saints when the reward of eternal life is bestowed for good works. Blessed is the one who says: “Your judgments shall help me.” I am weak; I am a sinner; I fear God’s judgments because of the consciousness of my offenses. They bring terror to me and drive me on; they help the saints. Yet they will also help the sinner, though in a different way. The saint will be helped when he is tested; the sinner will be helped when he is humbled and chastised, so that he may pay double for his sins, while his work is burned up so that he himself may be saved, yet as through fire. Perhaps the meaning also fits in this way: “If I am worthy of judgment, I shall be worthy to be stripped of the fellowship of the ungodly, for ‘the ungodly shall not rise in judgment’” (Psalm I, 5). And the judgments will help me, because whoever believes in the Lord is not judged. Faith will benefit him and plead for pardon, even if there is some offense in his works.

27. (Verse 176.) The final verse follows: “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; revive your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments.” The Greek has: “Seek your servant,” that is, ζῆτησον; and the scribe could have made a mistake and written ζήσον, which means “revive.” Both meanings are coherent, but “Seek your servant” is more suitable to this passage: the sheep that has gone astray must be sought by the shepherd, lest it perish. Therefore he says, “I have gone astray.” You too, declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified (Isaiah XLIII, 26). In confessing that you have fallen, you acknowledge a fellowship common to you with everyone, because no one is without sin. To deny this is sacrilege, for God alone is without sin. To confess this to God is a remedy for impunity. “I have gone astray,” he says; but one who has gone astray can return to the way and can be recalled to the way. Beautifully he adds: “Like a sheep that was lost”; for the one who recognizes his error is not lost.

28. “Seek,” he says, “your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments.” Come, then, Lord Jesus; seek your servant, seek your weary sheep; come, shepherd, seek as you sought the sheep of Joseph. Leave your ninety-nine sheep and come to seek the one that has gone astray. Come without dogs; come without evil workers; come without the hireling who did not know how to enter through the door. Come without a helper, without a messenger; for I have long awaited your coming. I know that you will come, “for I have not forgotten your commandments.” Come not with the rod but with charity [Note: [Col. 1520D] The Roman edition: “and with a spirit of gentleness.”] and with a spirit of gentleness.

29. Do not hesitate to leave your ninety-nine sheep in the mountains, because wolves of prey cannot attack those established in the mountains. In paradise the serpent once did harm; there it lost its food after Adam was driven out from there; it will no longer be able to do harm there. Come to me, whom the attack of savage wolves torments. Come to me, whom, cast out of paradise, [Note: [Col. 1521D] Thus most manuscripts; the editions differ only in that the old edition reads “of the serpent-like long-standing wound,” while the Roman edition reads “of the serpent’s long-standing wound.” Another group of manuscripts does not include the words “long-standing” or “of the savage wound.”] the poisons of the dreadful serpent’s long-standing wound afflict, because I went astray from those higher flocks of yours. For you had also placed me there, but the nocturnal wolf turned me away from your sheepfolds. Seek me, because I seek you. Seek me, find me, receive me, carry me. You can find the one whom you seek. [Note: [Col. 1521D] The editions: “deign to receive the one whom you have found; place upon your shoulders,” and so forth. But almost all the manuscripts support our reading.] You deign to receive the one whom you have found; place upon your shoulders the one whom you have received. The burden is not distasteful to you in your devotion; the conveyance of righteousness is not a burden to you. Come, then, Lord; for although I have gone astray, I have not forgotten your commandments—I retain hope of healing. Come, Lord; for you alone can recall the wandering sheep, and you will not sadden those whom you have left behind; they too will rejoice at the sinner’s return. Come, so that you may bring salvation on earth and joy in heaven.

30. Come, then, and seek your sheep, no longer through little servants or hirelings, but through yourself. Receive me [Note: [Col. 1521D] The Paris edition: “not in the flesh which fell in Adam.” But all the other editions and all the manuscripts reject the negation. Quite rightly so; the meaning here is simply that Christ’s flesh was of the same nature as Adam’s flesh, from which it was propagated through the succession of generation, although it was in no way stained by Adam’s sin.] in the flesh that fell in Adam. Receive me not from Sarah but from Mary, so that she may be an incorrupt virgin, yet a virgin wholly untouched by every stain of sin through grace. Carry me on the cross, which is saving for those who go astray, on which alone there is rest for the weary, on which alone all who die will live.

31. It can also beautifully be said “revive,” because the one whom power has carried on its shoulders cannot die.

32. Therefore the soul says, and the Church says: “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost.” But she says: “I sought him whom my soul has loved” (Song of Songs III, 1). For this is what it means to say: “Revive your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments.” I sought you, but I cannot find you unless you wish to be found. And you do indeed wish to be found, but you wish to be sought for a long time; you wish to be investigated more diligently. Your Church knows this, for you do not wish her to seek you while sleeping; you do not wish her to investigate you while lying down. Indeed, you knock at the door to awaken the sleeper; you test whether the heart is awake while the flesh sleeps. You wish to raise up the one lying down, saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead” (Ephesians V, 14). You put your hand through the opening so that she may rise; and if she rises too slowly, you withdraw it. You wish her to seek again and to seek from many, and not to forget to seek, not to forget your words; and if she holds fast to them, you offer yourself to be seen and do not shrink from being held.

33. When she has deserved to embrace you, she will display her fruits; she will show that she has not forgotten your commandments, and she will say to you: “Come, my brother; let us go out into the field . . . . . and at our doors is every fruit, new and old; my brother, I have kept them for you” (Song of Songs VII, 11 and 13). This means: “I hold fast to all your commandments of the New and Old Testament.” The Church alone can say this. No other assembly says it; neither does the Synagogue, which possesses neither the New according to the letter nor the Old according to the spirit. The Manichaean heresy does not say it: “I have kept the old things for you,” because it does not accept the Prophets. [Note: [Col. 1522D] Understand “through the Prophets” as referring here to the whole Old Testament, which the Manichaeans rejected in its entirety. Epiphanius, Heresy 68; Augustine, On Heresies, chapter 46.] Rightly she is seen as whitened, she who shines with the grace of both Testaments.

34. The Bridegroom answered her: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song of Songs VIII, 6), you who have kept the new and the old things for me. You are my seal; you are made according to my image and likeness. The image of justice, the image of wisdom, the image of virtue shines in you. And because the image of God is in your heart, let it also be in your works. Let the likeness of the Gospel be in your deeds, so that you may keep my commandments in your conduct. The likeness of the Gospel will be in you if, when struck on one cheek, you offer the other; if you love your enemy; if you take up your cross and follow me. Therefore I carried the cross [Note: [Col. 1522D] Thus a large number of manuscripts. Some, however, together with all the editions, have: “I carried it for you, so that you would not hesitate to carry it for my sake.” This is not a bad reading.] for you all, so that you would not hesitate to carry it for yourself.

35. The daughters of Jerusalem heard this, that the Lord Jesus was already joining the Church to himself. And because, considering the greatness of the Word, [Note: [Col. 1522D] Erasmus and the later editions: “they could not bear themselves unequal to so great a marriage,” and so forth. Amerbach, together with the manuscripts, more elegantly has “unequal to so great a marriage,” for this refers to the Church, not to the daughters of Jerusalem.] they thought her unequal to so great a marriage, lest perhaps she should be unable to bear the weight of so great a union, they make excuses, saying: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts” (ibid., 8). For those who wish to postpone a marriage customarily make excuses in this way, alleging the weakness of immature age and asserting that she has no breasts, which signify the age suitable for marriage. This symbol is commonly applied to all virgins who are about to marry: when their breasts begin to project, they are then judged capable of union.

36. Since they were therefore troubled that the Bridegroom was pressing the marriage out of the zeal of love, they say: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is spoken of?” (ibid.); or, as Symmachus has it, “on the day when he speaks to her.” That is, conversation and confirmation of the marriage ordinarily take place with the celebration of the betrothal. “What shall we do?” they say, troubled because the spiritual union is being pressed forward. They cannot excuse her from so great a marriage, for no one fails to consider the union either of soul and Spirit or of Christ and the Church blessed. But because the fullness of the Word or of the Holy Spirit flashes and shines, and there is nothing that can be compared with it, they desire to delay, so that through that delay either the soul or the Church may become more perfect.

[Col. 1522D] 37. They say, therefore: “If she is a wall, let us build defenses upon her; and if she is a door, let us carve cedar panels upon her” (ibid., 9). The soul of the saint is a wall. The Church also has her walls, and, now more perfect, she says: “I am a fortified city” (Isaiah XXVII, 3). This is the wall that has twelve apostolic gates, through which entry into the Church lies open to the people of the nations. But although a wall encloses the circuit of the entire city, it is more strongly fortified when it has defenses prepared, in which the city’s defenders can have secure support for watching and protecting it. But since this city is rational and all its hope is in the word of God, it requires not iron but silver defenses, accustomed to repel hostile attacks more by heavenly utterances than by bodily pleasures. Supported by this protection and shining with this splendor, it is judged more fit for union with Christ.

38. And because Christ is the door, who says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X, 9), the Church too is called a door, because through her access to salvation lies open to the peoples. Lest she be corrupted by the moths or worms of heretics, the daughters of Jerusalem—or the angels, or the souls of the righteous—say: “Let us build cedar panels upon her,” that is, the good odor of sublime faith. For this material has a sweet odor, which neither worm nor moth can corrupt. Therefore this material is chosen for raising the ridges of roofs and for forming the elements of letters, by which childhood is instructed in the pursuit of liberal learning. This material is therefore sublime in grace, light as a burden, sweet in odor, useful as an instrument of knowledge, and suited to the service of eternal understanding.

39. But just as Christ, loving his Bride, pressed her toward the solemnity of spiritual union, [Col. 1523C] so the Church, already captivated by the beauty of the Word, hastened toward the marriage. Therefore, impatient of the delays that the daughters of Jerusalem eagerly sought to impose, she says: “I am a wall, and my breasts are towers” (Song of Songs VIII, 10). This means: “Do not doubt whether I am a wall”—for they had said, “If she is a wall.” “I am,” she says, “a wall, and I do not have small breasts; my breasts are like towers. How can you say that I have no breasts?” I have, as it were, towers of understanding, in which there is abundance, as it is written: “And abundance in your towers” (Psalm CXXI, 7). With these breasts, that is, with these understandings, she considered herself fit for so great a marriage; but the daughters of Jerusalem still could not judge her so, because they did not see the abundance of her understanding.

40. And she added: “I was in his eyes as one who finds peace” (Song of Songs VIII, 10). This means: “Having reflected upon my understanding, when I found the peace of God, which surpasses every mind [Note: [Col. 1523D] Several manuscripts: “and guards bodies and understanding.”] and guards hearts and understanding in Christ Jesus, I was in the Bridegroom’s eyes such as one who possesses peace.” For it is written: “Those who rightly seek peace shall have it as their testimony” (Proverbs XII, 20). [Note: [Col. 1523D] The Roman edition: “Those who seek peace will rejoice.” In the margin it noted Proverbs XII, 20, where that passage is consistently read in the Hebrew and in all versions. [Col. 1524D] Nevertheless, we do not dare depart here from all the manuscripts and the old edition.] Therefore, while the beloved and the beloved were hastening, the spiritual union was celebrated by mutual consent.

41. Therefore, as though singing a nuptial song, [Col. 1524A] the Spirit exulted in the Prophet, saying: “Solomon had a vineyard in Beelamon; he gave his vineyard to those who guard it” (Song of Songs VIII, 11). The Spirit therefore cries out: “The assembly of the peoples has been planted, and the vine has been founded on an eternal root; with a meek heart it has bowed spiritual necks beneath the yoke of the Word.” It was planted among the multitude of the nations; for Symmachus, Aquila, [Note: [Col. 1524D] Nearly all written codices and other traditions.] and other translations taught in Greek that this is what Beelamon is to be understood to mean. The former union, which could not produce fruit, was rejected; the vineyard was given to new and faithful cultivators who could not only produce fruit but also guard it. One sheep therefore went astray; but when recalled, it filled the whole expanse of the world. Error led away one sheep; but the grace of the Lord gathered a multitude of peoples. A human being went astray; but the Church is now a wall, and a strong wall. Adam went astray; but David is a wall, for he did not forget God’s commandments.

42. This vineyard, therefore, guarded and enclosed with spiritual protection, gives a thousand fruits to Christ and two hundred fruits to its guardians. Therefore the Church says: “My vine is before me; a thousand for Solomon, and two hundred for those who guard the fruit” (ibid., 12). The perfection and fullness of Christ is the portion of the servants. You have this mystery in Genesis, where Joseph assigns five portions to Benjamin, his younger brother, and one portion to each of the remaining brothers (Genesis XLIII, 34). To the Lord, therefore, the portion and prerogative of the five senses is offered—something that he himself grants to the one whom he loves, just as he loved Paul and gave him the primacy of wisdom for calling the nations (Acts XX, 21).

[Col. 1524C] 43. Delighted, therefore, by these fruits, the Church says to Christ: “You who sit in the gardens, the friends attend to your voice; let me hear your voice” (Song of Songs VIII, 13). She delighted that Christ sat in the gardens and that his friends, placed in the gardens, attended to his voice. But because those friends were from the heavenly realm—Archangels, or Dominations and Thrones—for human beings had been expelled from paradise on account of disobedience to the heavenly commandments and therefore the Church still could not hear the voice she desired, she says: “Let me hear your voice.” Thus, if we too wish him to sit within us, let us be enclosed and fortified gardens; let us bear the flowers of virtues and the sweetness of grace, so that we may be able to hear the Lord Jesus conversing with the angels.

44. But because it was destined that, when the Church had reached fullness, she would be tested by various persecutions, therefore, while she was delighting in the grace of the Word, she suddenly perceived the plots of her persecutors. And because she feared more for the Bridegroom than for herself—or because Christ is more sought by persecutors in us—she says: “Flee, my brother, and be like a young gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of spices” (ibid., 14). He flees on account of the weak, who could not endure more severe temptations. Therefore it is written that we should flee from city to city (Matthew X, 23); and if they persecute us in this city, let us flee to another. For the sake of the weak, therefore, as we have said, let him flee from those who persecute; [Note: [Col. 1525A] Thus most manuscripts. Several others, together with all the editions, have “or let him flee from the lowly,” so that the lowly may be opposed antithetically to the mountains. But “the weak” is better opposed to “the martyrs.”] or let him flee from the weak and pass to the mountains of spices, which can bring forth, in place of martyrdom, the fragrance of the blessed resurrection. The saints are mountains of spices. Christ takes refuge with them, because “his foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm LXXXVI, 1). He therefore takes refuge with those who are his firm foundations. He flees among us; among them he remains in a secure station. Paul is therefore a mountain of spices, who can say: “For we are the good odor of Christ to God” (II [Col. 1526A] Corinthians II, 15). David is a mountain of spices, whose prayer rose like fragrance to the Lord; therefore he said: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm CXL, 2).

45. Symmachus and Aquila, however, translated the passage as Christ addressing the Church: “You who sit in the gardens,” that is, “You now sit in the gardens, worthy of the heavenly paradise”; and therefore, “Let me hear your voice, which the friends attend.” “I too desire to hear it.” The Church began to be in the gardens after Christ suffered in the gardens. [Note: [Col. 1526A] The Roman edition alone has: “Christ was captured in the gardens.” Apart from the fact that this can be understood of Christ’s agony, gardens were also customarily planted outside the city walls, where Mount Calvary was situated.]

[EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE.]

[Col. 1525B]

ADMONITION TO THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE.

[Col. 1525]

This work consists, beyond dispute, of the sermons in which Ambrose expounded the Gospel of Luke to the people. For this is understood not only from the form of the discourse and from the places where Scripture was recited in church before the holy man began to speak (Book VII, on chapters X and XIV, and elsewhere), but much more clearly from the fact that we find him preaching on Sundays (Book VIII, on chapter XIX) and on other more solemn occasions (Book IV, on chapter V). Indeed, we can readily observe that the Gospel text which he intended to expound had been publicly read, since he explains several passages of that same Gospel without quoting the text (Book II, on chapter III) in such a way that what was being discussed (Book V, on chapter VII; Book VII, on chapter IX, and elsewhere) could scarcely have been understood by the hearers unless the subject of the discourse had first been read aloud. To prevent the reader from suffering the same inconvenience, the Roman editors took care to present the entire Gospel text, including passages on which Ambrose had said nothing. But since they could not do this without frequently interrupting Ambrose’s discourse and also partly rearranging and partly adding a good deal to it, it seemed preferable, wherever the verse being expounded is missing from the manuscripts, to indicate it in the margin of the edition.

Although Ambrose had proposed to himself the exposition of Luke’s Gospel alone, he occasionally explains passages from the other Gospels as well (Book V, on chapter VII; Book VI, on chapter IX), whenever those passages seem either to contain some particular difficulty (Book II, on chapters II and III) or to have been omitted by blessed Luke, while he otherwise judges that knowledge of them will be useful to the people. He labors especially to reconcile what appears contradictory in the evangelists (Book III, beginning; Book V, on chapters V and VI; Book VII, on chapter VII, and elsewhere very often), and whenever he encounters a harder knot in the literal sense, he has recourse to spiritual interpretation (Book V, on chapter VII; Book X, on chapter XXIII), in which he demonstrates that these passages agree remarkably well. He is abundant in explaining the natural and historical sense, yet he frequently turns the discourse toward the mystical; and from this he repeatedly draws excellent moral precepts with which he illuminates his commentary throughout. He also attacks the principal heresies of his own time, by which the divinity of Christ was assailed—namely, the Manichaeans, Photinians, and Arians, and especially the latter, since they were at that time the most bitter enemies of Catholics. Hence it may rightly be affirmed that this was his chief reason for deciding to interpret the Gospel of Luke.

He gathered all these sermons into a single work and wished it to bear the title *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*. This is how it is cited once and again by Augustine (Book I, *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 44; Book II, *On Original Sin*, chapter 41; Book I, *Against Julian*, chapter 3, and Book II, chapter 5), and not a few manuscripts also support this title. But Sixtus of Siena is mistaken when he asserts that this commentary was not divided by its author into books, on the grounds that Augustine nowhere cites the number of a book (Bibliotheca, Book IV). Clearly he had not read the first book of that Father’s *On the Grace of Christ*: for in chapters 44 and 45, the numbers of most of the books of the work under discussion are given, up to the tenth. Possevinus errs still more seriously (*Apparatus*), for, following Sixtus’s judgment against Augustine’s authority, he denies the division just mentioned. There can be no doubt that considerable trust must be placed in the copies which Augustine himself read, not only because they were close to his time, but much more because of that Doctor’s close association with Ambrose. We do indeed admit that Augustine once calls Book VI Book VII; but unless one thinks that this slip should be attributed to the later copyists of Augustine’s works, perhaps it must be said that the error was made by those who copied Ambrose’s exposition, placing there the beginning of Book VII where the limits of Book VI ought to have been extended.

Baronius maintains that these books were written in the year 376 (*Annals*, under the year 376), persuaded, evidently, by a single passage in which the holy man mentions the wars of the Alans and other barbarians, as well as a certain famine and pestilence raging against all animals (Book X, on chapter XXI). But the great Cardinal is not sufficiently consistent with himself when he states that the *Apology of David* [Col. 1527] was composed only after the year 383; for it is certain that it is cited in this very exposition (Book III, on chapter III), and therefore this work must be said to be later than it. Accordingly, in order to establish something more certain, it should be observed that before writing on Luke’s Gospel, Saint Ambrose had published many books which he mentions there—for example, *On Widows* (Book II, on chapter II; Book IV, on chapter IV), after the year 377; *On the Faith* (Book III, on chapter III), after 379; *On the Holy Spirit* (Book VI, on chapter VI), in the year 381; and finally the *Apology of David* (Book II, on chapter II, and elsewhere), composed after 383. He does not even omit mention of his commentary on the prophecy of Isaiah (Book III, on chapter III). Since this is so, if Baronius had weighed the many books that preceded this exposition, he would readily have observed that so many works could not have been composed within two years by one who had been transferred from the prefecture to the episcopate only in the year 374. But what our Saint writes concerning Justina’s persecution of him (Book VII, on chapter IX) bears such close resemblance to what is read in the treatise *On the Basilicas Not To Be Handed Over* that it is clear that the commentary of which we are speaking was completed only after those very difficult times had passed—that is, not before the year 386. For elsewhere (Book IX, on chapter XX) he plainly mentions the peace which the Church afterward enjoyed. As for Baronius’s argument, anyone may reasonably answer that Ambrose was speaking of those barbarian incursions and other calamities as events already past.

A great deal of time was spent while he was engaged in this exposition. For when, near the end of Book IV, he indicates that the feast of Epiphany had been celebrated a few days earlier (Book IV, on chapter V), it follows that the preceding books must have been delivered to the people over several months of the immediately preceding year. Since, moreover, in Book VIII (on chapter XVIII) he says that he preached at the annual anniversary of his consecration, which in both the Greek and Latin Churches is always announced on the seventh day before the Ides of December (Baronius, *Martyrology*, etc.), it is evident that this material was treated over approximately two years. Yet there is nothing here for us to wonder at, since from Augustine (*Confessions*, Book VI, chapter 3) we learn that Ambrose was accustomed to preach only on Sundays. Nor are we unaware that he was sometimes called away from his subject by greater solemnities, as happened during Holy Easter, when he personally instructed the catechumens. Perhaps, too, it happened that the work, interrupted because of Justina’s persecution, was completed only after tranquility had finally been restored.

In the earlier books he borrowed some material from Origen (*Homilies on Luke*). Whether he also continued at times to imitate him in the later books cannot be determined with certainty, since not all the works of that most learned Father have come down to us. Yet from Ambrose’s discourse you can understand well enough that he was attached privately to no single man, but presented the opinions of various authors (Book VII, on chapters XIV and XVI, and elsewhere very often) as they seemed useful to his purpose; he also said many things appropriate to his own Church and to those times, which were by no means compatible with Origen’s teaching. Moreover, if he drew anything from that writer’s works after the manner of the other Fathers, later authors likewise did not hesitate to glean much from this most beautiful commentary. Saint Maximus was among the first to thrust his sickle into this harvest, so much so that Lanfranc, in the eleventh century, cited under Maximus’s name certain passages taken from this Ambrosian treatise (*Booklet on Concealing Confession*).

Furthermore, if we believe Rufinus (*Book II of the Invectives*), this very work was one of two commentaries, of which Jerome reports—on the authority of Paula and Eustochium—that the one was dull both in sense and in language, while the other played with words and dozed over its meanings (*Letter to Paula and Eustochium*). Even if it were established that Jerome spoke very variously about the literary works of Saint Ambrose, and that he sometimes descended from the highest praise to a contempt that was scarcely fair, the fact remains acknowledged. We have explained the reason for this inconsistency elsewhere (*Preface*). In the meantime, the usefulness and excellence of Ambrose’s exposition are amply vindicated both by the fact that it is so often mentioned with praise by Augustine (the places cited), Cassiodorus (*On the Institutions of Divine Literature*, chapter 7), and others, and by the fact that we find the Second Synod of Seville, held in 619, and the Sixth Ecumenical Council, held in 680 (Act 10), making use of its authority. Nor did Jerome himself consider this exposition so utterly worthless that he did not occasionally send his readers back to it (*Letter* 151, question 6).

[Col. 1527D]

# THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE BY SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, CONTAINED IN TEN BOOKS. (C, S)

[Col. 1527]

# PROLOGUE

[Col. 1527] 1261

## 1. On the Gospel according to Luke

As we are about to write on the Book of the Gospel which holy Luke arranged in a somewhat fuller and more discriminating account of the Lord’s deeds, we think that its very style should first be explained; for it is historical. Although divine Scripture empties out the discipline of worldly wisdom, since the latter is supported more by an elaborate embellishment of words than by the substance of things, nevertheless, if anyone seeks in the divine Scriptures even those matters which worldly people consider marvelous, he will find them there.

## 2. The three kinds of wisdom

For there are three things which the philosophers of this world have considered most excellent: namely, that wisdom is either natural, moral, or rational.

[Note: This division of philosophy is commonly attributed to Plato. Concerning it, Saint Augustine writes as follows in Book VIII of *The City of God*, chapter 4: “Plato is praised for having perfected philosophy, which he divided into three parts: one moral, chiefly concerned with action; another natural, assigned to contemplation; and a third rational, by which truth is distinguished from falsehood.” Cicero gives the same account in Book I of the *Academic Questions*; Laertius in his *Life of Plato*; Eusebius in Book XI, chapter 2, of the *Preparation for the Gospel*; Plutarch, and others. Some, however, divide philosophy into only two branches, natural and moral; this does not conflict with Augustine’s view, since in the passage cited he adds that the rational part of philosophy is necessary for both—that is, for action and contemplation.]

We can already discern these three in the Old Testament. For what else do those three wells signify, one called Vision, another Abundance, and the third Oath, except that the patriarchs possessed this threefold virtue?

The well of rational wisdom is Vision, because reason sharpens the mind’s sight and purifies the vision of the spirit.

The ethical well is Abundance, because, when the Philistines—whose outward appearance represents the vices of the body—withdraw, Isaac discovers the living water of the mind. Good morals flow forth pure, and goodness itself abounds for others, though it is more restrained toward itself.

The third well is the well of Oath—that is, of natural wisdom—which comprehends things above nature as well as things belonging to nature. For what is affirmed and, as it were, sworn with God as witness also embraces divine things, when the Lord of nature is called upon as witness to the faith.

What else do Solomon’s three books signify—the first on Proverbs, the second Ecclesiastes, and the third the Song of Songs—except that they show us holy Solomon to have been skilled in this threefold wisdom? In Proverbs he wrote of rational and ethical matters; of natural matters in Ecclesiastes, because “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2), namely, the things established in this world; for “the creation was subjected to vanity” (Romans 8:20). In the Song of Songs he wrote of moral and rational matters, because when the love of the heavenly Word is poured into our soul and the holy mind is joined in a rational fellowship, marvelous mysteries are revealed.

[Note: The manuscripts of Carthusian and Turin read “of moral matters,” that is, ethical matters. But apart from the fact that here something obscure would be explained by something more obscure, these two codices are too recent to be preferred to the agreement of the other manuscripts and editions. The common reading can also be confirmed by these words from number 3 of the *Prologue to the Exposition of Psalm 118*: “And in Proverbs you will find many mystical things.” Further below, where all editions and most manuscripts read “but of moral and rational matters,” or, as most manuscripts have it, “and rational matters,” the Corbie manuscript and seven others read “marvelous matters” instead of “moral matters.” Although the latter manuscripts might seem to be supported by what we read at the end of the sentence, “marvelous mysteries are revealed,” the received reading is defended by the passage from the same exposition already mentioned: “And in the Song this shines forth, both as mystical and as moral.”]

## 3. The wisdom of the evangelists

What wisdom, then, do you suppose was lacking in the evangelists? Although they are all filled with various kinds of material, each excels in a different kind. There is truly natural wisdom in the book of the evangelist John. I dare to say that no one has seen the majesty of God with such a lofty wisdom and disclosed it to us in his own words. He rose above the clouds, above the heavenly Powers, above the angels, and found the Word “in the beginning”; he saw the Word with God.

Who, however, pursued each matter more morally according to the human condition than holy Matthew, who gave us rules for living?

What is more rationally joined together than that which holy Mark thought should be placed immediately at the beginning? “Behold,” he says, “I send my angel” (Mark 1:2–3), “and the voice of one crying in the wilderness,” so that he might both arouse wonder and teach that a person must please God through humility, abstinence, and faith, just as that holy John the Baptist ascended by these steps toward immortality—in clothing, food, and proclamation.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “in a marvelous conjunction.” More and better manuscripts have “conjoined.” Certainly there is nothing preventing us from saying “conjoined” in the masculine and “conjoined” in the neuter, just as one says “an act” and “something acted upon.” Again, the Roman edition reads “whom Saint Mark”; the older edition and the manuscripts read “which Saint Mark.” These words yield a not inappropriate sense, provided that one interprets the passage as meaning that Mark is rationally conjoined, but that what immediately led him to place this at the beginning is still more rational.]

## 4. Luke’s historical order

But holy Luke maintained something like a historical order and revealed to us more of the Lord’s miracles and deeds, yet in such a way that the history of this Gospel embraced all the virtues of wisdom. For what is more excellent for natural wisdom than that he revealed that the Holy Spirit was also the creator of the Lord’s incarnation (Luke 1:35)?

[Note: The Roman edition had placed this material after the words “and they shall be created,” contrary to the testimony of the older edition and all the manuscripts. Nor was there any necessity for doing so, since the words “that he revealed that the Holy Spirit was the creator” conclude the preceding sentence, and the following words, “Hence also David,” confirm it. Three more recent manuscripts, moreover, read “the secrets of the Spirit” instead of “if the Spirit creates.”]

Thus he teaches natural matters, if the Spirit creates. Hence David too, teaching natural wisdom, says: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created” (Psalm 103:20).

He teaches moral matters in the same book, when he teaches me conduct in those beatitudes: how I ought to love my enemy (Luke 6:27ff.); how I ought not to strike back or return blows to one who strikes me; how I should do good and lend, while abandoning hope of recovering the loan, or of reward and payment. For reward follows more readily when it is not expected.

He also taught rational matters when I read: “Whoever is faithful in what is least is faithful also in what is greater” (Luke 16:10).

What more shall I say about natural matters, since he taught that the powers of heaven would be shaken (Luke 21:26), that the Lord alone is the only-begotten Son of God, at whose passion darkness covered the day, the earth was obscured, and the sun withdrew (Luke 23:44)?

## 5. Spiritual wisdom and the Trinity

Therefore spiritual wisdom truly possesses the sovereignty which worldly prudence falsely claims for itself. This is especially so when, to venture to claim something more boldly, our very faith and the very mystery of the Trinity cannot exist without this threefold wisdom—unless we believe that the Father is natural, who begot the Redeemer for us; that the Son is ethical, who, obeying the Father as man unto death, redeemed us; and that the Spirit is rational, who infused into human hearts the reason by which divinity is to be worshiped and life governed.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “and that natural Father . . . and that moral Father.”]

Let no one suppose that we have made a distinction in power or virtue, since this accusation could also be brought against Paul. For he made no distinction when he said: “There are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4–6). The Son also works all things and in all, as you find elsewhere: “Christ is all, and in all” (Colossians 3:11). The Holy Spirit also works, because “one and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). Therefore there is no difference or distinction of operations where, whether in the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, no one possesses a lesser fullness of power.

## 6. Diligence in seeking truth

When we read these things, therefore, let us consider them carefully, so that they may shine more clearly for us in the very passages where they occur. For whoever seeks will find, and to whoever knocks it will be opened (Matthew 7:8). Diligence opens for itself the door of truth; therefore let us obey the heavenly commandments.

For it was not said idly to man—something said to none of the other living creatures: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Genesis 3:19). To those animals which by nature are irrational, God commanded the earth to provide food; but for man alone, so that he might exercise the rational faculty he had received, the course of life was prescribed in labor.

For whoever is not content with the food of the other animals, for whom the fruit-bearing tree given in common to all as food is not enough, but seeks for himself the delicacies of various banquets, imports delicacies from lands across the sea, and gathers delicacies from the waves, ought not to refuse—if he seeks nourishment through labor—to undergo a brief labor for the sake of eternal life.

Therefore, if anyone comes to these contests of sacred disputation and strips himself of the anxiety of this life, which is exposed to error, and, naked of malice, like an athlete anointed with the spiritual oil of piety—as though the limbs of his soul had been coated with it—undertakes the contests of truth, he will undoubtedly earn the everlasting prizes of sacred crowns. For the noble fruit of good labors is great, and the more numerous the contests, the more excellent is the crown of virtues.

[Note: “The more excellent the crown of virtues.” The Roman edition had omitted the words “of virtues.”]

## 7. Luke’s historical style

But let us return to our subject. We have said that this Gospel book is arranged in a historical style. Indeed, we see that greater effort has been devoted to describing events than to expressing precepts, in comparison with the other evangelists. The evangelist himself also began, in historical fashion, with a narrative: “There was,” he says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah” (Luke 1:5), and he pursues that history in a complete and orderly fashion.

Hence those who have judged that the four books of the Gospel are to be understood through the four forms of the four living creatures revealed in the Apocalypse (Revelation 4:7) wish this book to be represented by the form of a calf; for the calf is a priestly victim.

This Gospel book appropriately corresponds to the calf, because it began with priests and ended with the calf which, taking upon itself the sins of all, was sacrificed for the life of the whole world; for that calf is priestly. The same being is both calf and priest: priest, because he is our propitiator—for we have him as our advocate with the Father; calf, because by his blood he washes us clean and redeems us.

And it was fitting that, since we have said that Matthew’s Gospel is moral, this opinion should not be passed over; for morals properly concern human beings.

## 8. The four forms of Christ

Nevertheless, many think that our Lord himself is represented in the four books of the Gospel by four forms of animals, since he is shown to be the same man, the same lion, the same calf, and the same eagle.

He is man because he was born of Mary; lion because he is strong; calf because he is a sacrificial victim; eagle because he is resurrection.

The form of the animals is thus represented in the individual books, so that the sequence of each book may seem to correspond to the nature, power, grace, or miracle of the animal assigned to it. Although all these things are present in all the books, there is nevertheless in each one a certain fullness of its particular virtues.

One evangelist, Matthew, described the origin of the man more fully and instructed human conduct with fuller precepts. Another, Mark, began with the expression of divine power: the King from the King, the strong from the strong, the true from the true, who in living power despised death.

The third, Luke, placed the priestly sacrifice first and spread abroad the sacrifice of the calf itself in a somewhat fuller style.

The fourth expressed more abundantly than the others the miracles of the divine resurrection.

Thus there is one who is all things, and one in all, as it is written (Colossians 3:11): not unlike in the individual books, but true in all of them.

But now let us approach the Gospel discourse itself.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 1533]

[Col. 1533A] 1265

## Chapter I — Verse 1

“Forasmuch as many,” he says, “have taken in hand to set forth an orderly account of the events.”

### 1. Many attempted writings of the Gospel

Most things among us, just as among the ancient Jews, are formed from similar kinds and causes, agree through a similar use and outcome of examples, and correspond in both their beginnings and their endings.

For just as many among that divine people, filled with the Spirit, prophesied, while others claimed to prophesy but abandoned their profession to falsehood (Jeremiah 28:1)—for they were false prophets rather than prophets, such as Hananiah son of Azur—so there was given to the people the grace of discerning spirits, so that it might recognize whom it ought to count among the prophets and whom, like a good money-changer, it ought to reject, since in them the material appeared more corrupted and stained than the radiance of the true light shone forth.

[Note: Do not suppose that this was Ambrose’s intention: that he attributed this grace to every individual among the Jewish people, since the sacred books so often report that the vast majority of them were deceived by false prophets. It is more credible that he attributed this prerogative to the college of priests, which they called the Sanhedrin, since the people are commanded to have recourse to their judgment in serious controversies (Deuteronomy 17:9ff.). Perhaps he meant only this: that divine benevolence had provided that the entire people would never be led astray by false prophets, as we read happened in the time of Ahab (1 Kings 19).]

So now also in the New Testament many have attempted to write Gospels which good money-changers did not approve. But they judged that only one Gospel, arranged in four books from among them all, should be understood.

### 2. Spurious Gospels

There is also reported another Gospel, said to have been written by the twelve. Basilides too dared to write a Gospel, called the Gospel according to Basilides. Another Gospel is also reported, written according to Thomas. I know of another written according to Matthias.

We read certain things—not so that they may be read; we read them so that we may not be ignorant; we read them not to retain them, but to reject them, and to know the kinds of things in which those magnificent people exalt their hearts.

[Note: The Roman edition adds “which the twelve apostles wrote”; Jerome also calls this spurious Gospel by the name “of the apostles” in his *Prologue to Matthew*. The word “apostles,” suppressed in the older edition and manuscripts, is sufficiently understood by the reader. Below, where all editions and most manuscripts read “according to Basilides,” five manuscripts of better quality read “according to its proper name.” Jerome discusses this Gospel of Basilides in the passage cited and in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 64, where he lists several other apocryphal Gospels of this kind. Jerome also mentions the Gospels of Thomas and Matthias in the same *Prologue to Matthew*, as well as the Gospel according to Bartholomew. Finally, the heretics expanded the number of pseudo-gospels so far that one was even attributed to Judas the betrayer, as may be learned from Epiphanius, heresy 38, and Theodoret, Book I of the *Heretical Fables*. Origen, *Homily 1 on Luke*, Athanasius in the *Synopsis*, and others mention certain products of these mad evangelists’ inventions; all of them are condemned by the decree of Gelasius and by Innocent I, Letter 3, to Exuperius. It should further be noted that what is said here—“We read certain things, so that they may not be read”—indicates by these words that it is the duty of good bishops themselves to examine bad books, expose their poison, refute them, and forbid their people this pestilential reading.]

But the Church, possessing the four books of the Gospel, abounds in evangelists throughout the whole world.

[Note: The Roman edition reads “abounds in Gospels.”]

Heresies, though they have many books, do not have one Gospel. For many attempted, but, deprived of God’s grace, failed.

Many also have combined material from the four books of the Gospel into one, inserting into it those things which they thought suited their poisonous assertions.

[Note: Tertullian, in his books against Marcion, and Epiphanius, heresy 4, attest that Marcion used this audacity to corrupt the sacred pages in the Gospel of blessed Luke. Ambrose our author, like Pope Leo in Sermon 4 on the Epiphany, openly complains here of the audacity of the Manichaeans in defiling the divine books. Finally, in the decree cited, Gelasius declares the Gospels of Lucian and Heraclius apocryphal. In passing, it may be mentioned that this decree concerning apocryphal books, which some later writers attribute to Pope Hormisdas, is cited by us under the customary title of Gelasius because I found it prefaced with the same inscription in manuscripts written more than a thousand years ago. See our Mabillon, *Dissertation on the Gallican Chant*, section 1, number 9.]

Thus the Church, which has one Gospel, teaches one God; whereas those who assert that there is one God of the Old Testament and another of the New have made from their many Gospels not one God but several.

### 3. Those who attempted but did not complete their work

“Forasmuch as many,” he says, “have taken in hand.”

They certainly attempted it, those who could not complete it. Thus holy Luke himself, by a more authoritative testimony, confirms that many began but did not finish, when he says that many attempted it.

Whoever attempted to arrange an account attempted it by his own labor and did not complete it. For God’s gifts and grace exist without striving; when grace has poured itself in, it habitually waters the writer’s talent, so that his ability does not lack but overflows.

Matthew did not attempt it; Mark did not attempt it; John did not attempt it; Luke did not attempt it. Rather, with the divine Spirit supplying an abundance of words and of all events, they completed what they began without any laborious exertion.

And therefore he says:

“Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth an orderly account of the events which have been fulfilled among us, or which abound among us.”

[Note: In Greek, πεπληροφορημένων ἐν ἡμῖν, which some also translate, “which have been fully confirmed among us.” See Corderius’s note in the Greek *Catena of the Fathers* on this verse.]

### 4. The fullness of the Gospel

For what overflows is lacking to no one; and no one doubts what has been completed, since its effect establishes its credibility and its outcome reveals it.

Therefore the Gospel has been completed and overflows for all the faithful throughout the whole world; it waters the minds of all and strengthens the spirit.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript and not a few others read: “It rules the minds of all.”]

Thus the person founded upon the rock, who has received the whole fullness of faith and the support of steadfastness, rightly says: “Which have been fulfilled among us.”

For those who describe the Lord’s saving deeds—or who direct their minds toward his wonders—distinguish true things from false not by signs and wonders, but by true word and reason.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “but by word and true reason,” and so forth.]

For what is more rational than to believe, when you read of deeds that surpass human ability, that they belong to a higher nature? Yet when you read of moral matters, you should believe that they are passions of the body he assumed.

Thus our faith is founded on word and reason, not on signs.

## Verse 2

“Just as they delivered them to us,” he says, “who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word.”

### 5. Seeing and hearing the Word

This expression is not compatible with believing that the ministry of the Word was seen rather than heard.

[Note: Thus all editions and some manuscripts. Nevertheless, nine manuscripts of no inferior quality read “more than the ministry of the word,” rather than “more than hearing.” Four of these have “the greater ministry of the word than hearing.” From this group, some perhaps through a scribal error read “than the hearing.” But in all of them the word “seen” is absent.]

But because the reference is not to a spoken word, but to that substantial Word which became flesh and dwelt among us, let us understand it not as an ordinary word but as that heavenly Word whom the apostles served.

And yet it is written in Exodus that “the people saw the voice of the Lord” (Exodus 20:18). Certainly a voice is not seen but heard. For what is a voice except a sound which is not perceived by the eyes but received by the ear?

Nevertheless, Moses, with the deepest insight, wished to declare that God’s voice is seen: it is seen by the vision of the inward mind. In the Gospel, however, it is not the voice but that which is superior to the voice—the Word—that is seen.

Hence holy John the Evangelist also says:

“That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen, which we have looked upon with our eyes, and which our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested, and we have seen it, and bear witness, and proclaim to you the life which was with the Father and was manifested to us” (1 John 1:1–2).

You see, therefore, that the Word of God was both seen and heard by the apostles. For they saw the Lord not only according to the body but also according to the Word. They saw the Word when, together with Moses and Elijah, they saw the glory of the Word (cf. Augustine, Letter 148, formerly 111).

Those, then, saw Jesus who saw him in his glory; the others did not see him, who were able to see only his body. For Jesus is seen not with bodily but with spiritual eyes.

### 6. Those who did not see Christ

Finally, the Jews did not see him because they did not see in the spirit.

Abraham did see him, for it is written: “Abraham saw my day, and rejoiced” (John 8:56). Abraham therefore saw him, although he certainly did not see the Lord in the body.
