But whoever saw him in the spirit saw him also in the body; whoever saw him in the body but did not see him in the spirit did not see what he was seeing even in the body.

Isaiah saw him, and because he saw him in the spirit, he also saw him in the body. Finally, he says: “He had neither appearance nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2).

The Jews did not see him, for their foolish heart had been blinded. He himself also testifies that he could not be seen by the Jews, saying: “Blind guides, who strain out a gnat but swallow a camel” (Matthew 23:24).

Pilate did not see him. Those who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him!” (John 19:6) did not see him. For if they had seen him, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty.

Whoever, therefore, saw God saw Emmanuel—that is, saw “God with us.” Whoever did not see God with us could not see the one whom the Virgin bore.

Finally, those who did not believe that he was the Son of God did not believe that he was the Son of the Virgin.

7. What, then, does it mean to see God? I do not want you to ask me; ask the Gospel, ask the Lord himself—or rather, listen to him as he teaches: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father who sent me. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:9–10).  

[Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read: “rather, hear him saying.”]

Certainly, a body is not seen in a body, nor a spirit in a spirit; but the Father alone is seen in the Son, or this Son is seen in the Father. For unlike things are not seen in unlike things; rather, wherever there is unity of operation and power, the Son is seen in the Father and the Father in the Son. “The works that I do,” he says, “he also does” (John 5:19). Jesus is seen in the works of the Father, and the Father is discerned in the works of the Son.

He saw Jesus who saw that Galilean mystery (John 2:9)—that is, wine made from water.

[Note: That is, wine made from water. These words, which are found only in three manuscripts and in the Roman edition, may quite plausibly have entered the text from a gloss.]

No one but the Lord of the world could transform the elements. I see Jesus when I read that he smeared clay on the blind man’s eyes and restored his sight. For I recognize the same one who fashioned a human being from clay and breathed into him the spirit of life and the light of sight (Gen. 2:7). I see Jesus when he forgives sins; for no one can forgive sins except God alone (Mark 2:6–7). I see Jesus when he raises Lazarus—and those who saw did not see (John 11:44). I see Jesus, and I also see the Father, when I raise my eyes to heaven, turn them toward the seas, and direct them back to the earth: “For his invisible attributes are perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20).

8. “As they handed them down to us, who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word.” In the perfect human being there is a twofold virtue: intention and action. Thus the holy Evangelist attributes both virtues to the apostles; for he says not only that they saw, but also that they were ministers of the Word. The intention of vision is the ministry of action; the end of intention is action, and the beginning of action is intention.

To use the apostles’ own example, intention is shown when Peter and Andrew, after hearing the Lord’s voice say, “I will make you become fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19), immediately left the boat and followed the Word.

[Note: Corb. and several others read: “I will make you fishers of men.”]

But action does not immediately accompany intention. Even there, when Peter says, “Lord, why cannot I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37), there is not yet action, but intention. It was an intention toward martyrdom, though action was already present in fasting, in vigils, and in contempt for bodily pleasures; for this is the Christian’s action.

For intention and action are not simultaneously present in every matter. When there is action concerning one thing, there may still be intention concerning another. Peter himself, after he had endured many things with apostolic courage, nevertheless, when the Lord later said to him, “Follow me” (John 21:22), took up his cross, followed the Word, and entered upon the action of suffering.

[Note: The Roman edition and a few manuscripts read: “when he had preferred to endure many things with apostolic courage”; two manuscripts read: “had greatly preferred.” Other editions and written codices read: “when he had accomplished many things with apostolic courage” (some have *perpete*, while others omit one or both words). Yet the sense shows that this last reading is the best and should be retained. For *apostolica* is not to be taken in the sixth case but in the fourth, nor is *perpeti* to be understood as a verb, but as an adjective.]

Thus there had been an equality of intention and action in Peter, Andrew, John, and the other apostles.

[Col. 1537B]

9. Sometimes, however, there is more in intention than in action, or more in action than in intention, as we see in the difference between holy Mary and Martha in the Gospel. One was listening to the Word; the other was hastening about her service. She stood and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, therefore, to help me.” And the Lord said to her, “Martha, Martha … Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:40–42).

Thus in one there overflowed the devotion of intention, and in the other the ministry of action; yet both possessed the devotion to each virtue. Indeed, unless Martha had heard the Word, she would not have undertaken the ministry, whose action is an indication of intention. And Mary received such grace from the perfection of both virtues that she anointed Jesus’ feet, wiped them with her hair, and filled the whole house with the fragrance of her faith (John 12:3).

Sometimes, too, there is the greatest intention but empty action: for example, if someone devotes his mind to medicine and, after learning all the rules of healing, does not carry out the duties of treatment. Thus, because the action is empty, the intention too becomes empty.

At other times there is an action that is more abundant, but a weaker intention: for example, if someone receives the sacrament of saving baptism but refuses to devote his mind to learning the precepts of the various virtues. It often happens that through negligence of intention he loses the fruit of action.

Therefore, the fullness of both virtues must be sought. The apostles were able to attain it, those “who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word”: by the fact that they saw, the intention of divine knowledge is understood; by the fact that they were ministers, their action is revealed.

[Col. 1537D] (Verse 3.) “It seemed good,” he says, “to me also.”

10. It may also be that what he declares to have seemed good to him did not seem good to him alone. For it did not seem good merely by human volition, but as it pleased him in whom, he says, Christ speaks; and he works so that what is good may also seem good to us—he “whom he has mercy upon and calls” (2 Cor. 13:3).

Therefore, one who follows Christ, if asked why he wished to be a Christian, can answer: “It seemed good to me.” When he says this, he does not deny that it seemed good to God; for the will of human beings is prepared by God. That God is honored by the holy person is itself the grace of God. In fact, many wished to write a Gospel, but only four, who had merited divine grace, were accepted.

[Col. 1538B] “It seemed good,” he says, “to me also, having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, to write it in order.”

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts read. The old edition adds: “to write to you.” The Roman edition shortened the passage as follows: “everything carefully.” And so, etc.]

11. No one will doubt that this book of the Gospel is longer than the others. This does not mean that it claims for itself things that are false, but things that are true. Indeed, it also earned testimony to its diligence from the holy apostle Paul. For he praises Luke in these words: “His praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches” (2 Cor. 8:18). And truly praiseworthy is the one who deserved praise from so great a teacher of the nations.

Thus he says that he investigated not a few things but everything; and having investigated everything, he thought it good to write not everything, but something from everything. For he did not write everything, but he investigated everything, because, as Jesus says, “if everything that Jesus did were written down, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books” (John 21:25).

You see that he deliberately passed over even those things written by others, so that a different grace might shine forth in the Gospel and that each book might stand out through certain distinctive mysteries and miracles of events. For the soldiers of Christ divided among themselves the Lord’s garments; this will be explained more fully in its proper place (below, Book 10, on chapter 23, §34).

[Col. 1538D]

12. The Gospel was written to Theophilus—that is, to him whom God loves.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “who loves God.” This seems to agree better with the following words, “if you love God”; but all the old editions and manuscripts oppose this reading. Moreover, Ambrose seems here to understand by *Theophilus* not the name of some particular person, but a designation applicable to all Christians. The more common opinion, however, maintains that a definite and particular person is meant. It relies especially on the fact that he is greeted as “most excellent,” a title customarily bestowed only on illustrious men. See Baronius, under the year 58, no. 35, and the commentators on this passage, as well as on Acts 1:1, 23:26, and elsewhere.]

If you love God, this has been written to you. If it has been written to you, receive the Evangelist’s gift; carefully preserve in the inner chambers of your soul the pledge of a friend. “Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (2 Tim. 1:14); look into it frequently and examine it often.

Faith is owed first to the pledge; diligence follows faith, lest either moth or rust consume the pledges entrusted to you.

[Note: What has been entrusted to you can be consumed; the Gospel cannot be consumed. These words had disappeared from the Roman edition, evidently because Ambrose might otherwise seem to speak with insufficient coherence when he warns us not to allow the Gospel to be corrupted in our minds. But there is no contradiction here, since the whole truth remains incorruptible in itself, even though it may be adulterated in the minds of many people by an admixture of falsehood.]

For what has been entrusted to you can be consumed; the Gospel cannot be consumed. The Gospel is a good pledge; but see to it that neither moth nor rust consume it in your soul. Moth consumes it if you believe wrongly what you have read correctly.

13. The moth is the heretic; the moth is Photinus; your moth is Arius. He tears the garment who separates the Word from God. Photinus tears the garment when he reads, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was” (John 1:1).

The garment is whole if you read, “And the Word was God” (ibid.). He tears the garment who separates Christ from God. He tears the garment who reads, “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God” (John 17:3), unless he also knows Christ.

For eternal life is not to know the Father alone as truly God, but also to know Christ as true God, true from true, God from God.

[Note: Thus the old editions read, and the written codices agree. The Roman edition interpolated the passage as follows: “To know Christ, God from God, true from true, is eternal life.”]

The moth is to know Christ without faith in his divinity or without the sacrament of his body. Arius is a moth; Sabellius is a moth. The spirit of the wavering suffers these moths; the spirit that does not believe that the Father and the Son are one in divinity suffers them. He tears what is written, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), who divides the one by separating the substances.

The spirit that does not believe that Jesus Christ came in the flesh suffers this moth—and he himself is the moth, for he is the antichrist. But those who are from God hold the faith, and therefore cannot suffer the moth that tears the garment. For everything that is divided against itself, like Satan’s kingdom, cannot endure.

[Col. 1539C]

14. There is also rust of the soul, when the keen edge of religious intention is covered over with the filth of worldly desires, or when the purity of faith is discolored by the cloud of faithlessness.

The rust of the mind is the desire for possessions and household wealth; the rust of the mind is negligence; the rust of the mind is ambition for honors, if one places the highest hope of the present life in these things.

Therefore, turning ourselves toward divine things, let us sharpen our understanding and exercise our affections, so that we may be able to keep that sword—which the Lord commands us to purchase after selling our garment (Luke 22:36)—always ready and bright, stored as though in the sheath of the mind.

For spiritual weapons, powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, must always be at hand for Christ’s soldiers, lest, when the commander of the heavenly host comes, offended by the rust of our weapons, he separate us from the fellowship of his legions.

[Col. 1539D] (Verses 5–6.) “There was,” he says, “in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly.”

15. Divine Scripture teaches us that not only the character of those who are worthy of praise but also their parents ought to be commended, so that, as it were, an inheritance of unstained purity transmitted to those whom we wish to praise may shine forth in them.

For what other purpose does the holy Evangelist have here than to ennoble Saint John the Baptist by his parents, miracles, character, office, and suffering? In the same way the mother of holy Samuel, Hannah, is praised; in the same way Isaac received from his parents a nobility of piety, which he handed down to his descendants.

Thus Zechariah was a priest—and not merely a priest, but of the division of Abijah, that is, noble among the higher families.

16. “And his wife,” he says, “was of the daughters of Aaron.” Therefore the nobility of holy John is derived not only from his parents but also from his ancestors—not exalted by worldly power, but venerable through a succession of religious observance.

For the forerunner of Christ ought to have ancestors such as these, so that he might seem to proclaim the faith in the Lord’s coming not as something suddenly conceived, but as something received from his ancestors and infused by the very law of nature.

17. “They were both righteous,” he says, “walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly.”

What answer do those give to this who, preferring consolation for their sins, think that a human being cannot exist without frequent sins, and use the verse written in Job: “No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life on earth were only one day; his months are numerous” (Job 14:4–5)?

They must first be asked to define what it means for a human being to be without sin: does it mean never to have sinned at all, or to have ceased sinning? If they think that being without sin means having ceased to sin, I agree with them: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23).

But if they deny that a person who has corrected an old error and transformed himself into such a way of life that he abstains from sin can refrain from offenses, I cannot agree with their opinion, since we read: “Christ loved the Church … so that he might present it to himself glorious, without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but holy and without blemish” (Eph. 5:25, 27).

For since the Church has been gathered from the nations—that is, from sinners—how can it be without blemish if it comes from those who were blemished, unless first by the grace of God it has been cleansed from sin, and then, through a disposition not to sin, it abstains from offenses?

Thus it was not without blemish from the beginning, for that is impossible for human nature; but through the grace of God and through its own disposition, because it no longer sins, it comes to be seen as without blemish.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “never to have sinned at all.” The other editions and all the manuscripts read: “to have ceased sinning.” To remove the ambiguity, understand the passage in this sense: if they say that the person without sin is one who has ceased to sin, I agree with them in this definition, since no other can apply to human beings. But if they further maintain that one who has turned away from former sins cannot thereafter abstain from the same or other sins, I emphatically reject that claim.

It is certain that the sins intended here are not the light and daily sins, but grave sins—such as exclude sanctifying grace—since Ambrose himself frequently acknowledges the wretched necessity of sinning until we are freed from this body of death. And certainly, how beautifully he agrees with Augustine on this point has already been observed by us.]

18. Nor did he idly call them righteous before God, walking in the commandments and ordinances of the Lord; for in this he includes the almighty Father and the Son. That the Son is the one who gave the law and prescribed the commandments is also declared by the holy evangelist Luke (Luke 6:47).

And he rightly says “righteous before God,” for not everyone who is righteous before human beings is righteous before God. Human beings see one way, God another: human beings look at the face, God at the heart.

Therefore it can happen that someone, through an affected desire for popular approval, seems righteous to me but is not righteous before God, if his righteousness is formed not from simplicity of mind but simulated through flattery; for a human being cannot detect what is hidden within it.

Perfect praise, therefore, is to be righteous before God. Hence the Apostle says: “Whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (Rom. 2:29).

Truly blessed is the one who is righteous in God’s sight. Blessed is the one of whom the Lord deigns to say, “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47). For the true Israelite is the one who sees God, knows that he is seen by God, and presents to God the secrets of his heart.

Only the one approved by him who cannot be deceived is truly perfect: “The judgments of the Lord are true” (Ps. 18:10). Human judgments, however, are often mistaken: they frequently ascribe the grace of righteousness to the unrighteous, and either persecute the righteous out of hatred or disfigure them by falsehood.

But the Lord knows the ways of the blameless (Ps. 36:18). He neither calls the sinner praiseworthy nor the praiseworthy a sinner; rather, he judges each according to the measure of his proper merits, for he is the judge both of the mind and of the deed.

Divine judgments measure the merit of the righteous by the disposition of the mind, not by the outcome of particular deeds. Often either a good mind is disfigured by the blameworthy outcome of an action, or an evil thought is concealed beneath the beauty of some deed.

But even if you have done what is good, if you have thought what is evil, it cannot be approved by divine judgment. For it is written: “You shall pursue what is just justly” (Deut. 16:20). If it were not possible to do what is just unjustly, it would never have been said, “You shall pursue what is just justly.”

And the Savior himself taught us that what is just can be done unjustly when he says, “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you,” and, “When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites” (Matt. 6:2, 5).

Mercy is good; prayer is good. But they can be done unjustly if someone gives to the poor for the sake of boasting, so that he may be seen by human beings.

[Col. 1541D]

19. Therefore the holy Evangelist says not only that they were righteous before God and walked in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord, but also that they walked blamelessly.

This wonderfully agrees with the prophetic saying used by holy Solomon in Proverbs: “Provide good things always before God and before human beings” (Prov. 3:4).

There is no complaint, therefore, wherever goodness of mind and deed are in harmony. And frequently a stricter righteousness provokes human complaint.

20. Carefully observe how appropriate the very distinction and order of the words are. “Walking,” he says, “in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.” The commandment comes first; the ordinance follows.

Therefore, when we obey the heavenly commandments, we walk in the Lord’s commandments; when we judge and judge appropriately, we seem to hold the Lord’s ordinances.

[Col. 1542B]

21. Full praise, then, is that which embraces lineage, character, office, deed, and judgment. Lineage is found in one’s ancestors; character in justice; office in the priesthood; deed in obedience to the commandment; judgment in the ordinance.

(Verses 8–10.) “It came to pass, while he was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, according to the custom of the priesthood, that he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense.”

22. Here holy Zechariah appears to be designated as the high priest, because, as it is written, in the first tabernacle the priests were always entering to complete their ministries—not entering the temple only once a year; but in the second, the high priest alone entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins of the people (Heb. 10:6–7).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “In the first tabernacle the priests always entered, completing their ministries; but in the second …” The old editions and manuscripts add: “… completing their ministries, they entered the temple only once a year,” etc. Some manuscripts read: “… he entered the temple.” Finally, the single Claromontanus manuscript has a negation after “completing,” and although it is more recent, it seemed preferable to follow it, since it presents the clearer sense.

Those who read “he entered,” however, are not entirely unacceptable, if the reference is to the high priest; but even then the negation seems to need to be inserted. Finally, if you understand the passage of the lesser priests and remove the negation, it must be said that Ambrose held the view that the turn of each family to minister in the temple came only once a year, although it returned after 168 days, as Grotius observes on this passage from J. Scaliger.]

This is that high priest who is still being sought by lot, because the true one is still unknown; for the one chosen by lot cannot be apprehended by human judgment. He was therefore being sought, while another was being represented.

The true priest was being sought—the priest forever, to whom it is said, “You are a priest forever” (Ps. 109:4)—who would reconcile God the Father to the human race not by the blood of victims but by his own blood.

At that time blood was poured out symbolically, and the priest was appointed symbolically; now that the truth has come, let us leave the symbol and follow the truth. Then there were successive turns; now there is permanence.

[Note: The Roman edition had cut out the following words from the text: “There was, therefore—and certainly there was—one whose turns were also being performed.” We restored them to their place on the authority of the old editions and all the manuscripts.]

There was, therefore—and certainly there was—one whose turns were also being performed.

23. The priest was chosen by lot, therefore, so that he might enter the temple. If, then, in the figure no witness could be admitted, what else was signified except that a priest was to come whose sacrifice would not be shared with the others—one who would sacrifice for us not in temples made with hands, but in the temple of his own body would do away with our sins?

The priest was therefore sought by lot. Perhaps this is also why the soldiers cast lots for the Lord’s garments (John 19:24): because, as the Lord was preparing to offer sacrifice for us in his own temple, he was also fulfilling the commandment of the Law concerning the casting of lots.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Perhaps, concerning the very casting of the lot, the precept of the Law was also fulfilled. Therefore he says …”]

For this reason he says, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17). Certainly, this was so that he himself might be seen as the one both awaited in the Old Testament and chosen by God’s command.

Finally, the lot also fell upon the apostle Matthias (Acts 1:26), so that the election of the apostle would not seem to differ from the command of the ancient Law.

[Note: No one is unaware that the use of lots was frequent in the Old Testament. Nor was this practice entirely rejected in the New Testament by Augustine (Letter 180, now 228); it was also approved in the Council of Barcelona in 599, canon 3.

Someone may perhaps be surprised that Ambrose wrote that the lot was used there so that the apostles’ election would not seem to differ from the command of the ancient Law. The difficulty arises because such legal observances are generally thought already to have fallen into disuse at that time.

But the Venerable Bede, when reporting this very passage in his commentary on Acts, addresses the objection in this way: “Matthias was chosen by lot before Pentecost, because the fullness of the Holy Spirit had not yet been poured out.” Hence he concludes: “Until the truth was fulfilled, the figure could be practiced.” This is why Matthias, who was appointed before Pentecost, was chosen by lot.

He confirms this later by noting that afterward, in the election of the deacons, no lot is mentioned. It may also be added that this may have been done so as not to give offense to Jews who had recently come to the faith; for the same reason Acts 16 relates that the Apostle circumcised Timothy, who was born of a Gentile father. See also Thomassinus, *Discipline of the Church*, Book 2, chapter 14.]

(Verses 11.) “An angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense.”

[Col. 1543B]

24. The angel appropriately appears in the temple, because the coming of the true Priest was already being announced and a heavenly sacrifice was being prepared, in which the angels would minister (compare Augustine, Letter 148, formerly 111, and elsewhere).

And he is rightly said to have appeared to the man who suddenly caught sight of him. Scripture is accustomed to use this expression especially of angels or of God: what cannot be foreseen is said to appear. Thus we read: “God appeared to Abraham by the oak of Mamre” (Gen. 18:1).

[Note: The same reading is found in Corb. and several others: “who previously does not present himself.”]

For one who was not previously perceived but is seen suddenly is said to appear.

For sensible things are not seen in the same way as the one whose being seen depends on his will and whose nature is not to be seen, but whose will determines that he be seen. If he does not wish it, he is not seen; if he wishes it, he is seen.

God appeared to Abraham because he wished to; to others, because he did not wish to, he did not appear. It also seemed to Stephen, when he was being stoned by the people, that heaven was opened; Jesus was also seen standing at the right hand of God, yet he was not seen by the people (Acts 7:55).

Isaiah saw the Lord Sabaoth, but another could not see him, because he appeared to the one to whom he was pleased to appear (Isa. 6:1).

25. And why should we speak of human beings, when we read even of the heavenly powers and authorities that “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18)?

[Note: Since no Catholic can doubt that the blessed angels always see the face of the Father, this passage must be understood as referring to what is called comprehensive vision. The Doctor himself makes this sufficiently clear when he adds below that no one has perceived or comprehended with mind or eyes the fullness of divinity.

Nor should Chrysostom’s statement be understood otherwise: “Since God himself, as he is, was seen not only by the prophets, but neither did angels see him nor archangels.” For in what follows he explains himself in unmistakable words, where he says, “but no one knows in this way as the Son.” And below he attributes to the Son alone “the precise apprehension of the Father.”]

And he added something beyond the heavenly powers: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (ibid.).

Therefore, one of two conclusions must be accepted: if no one has ever seen God the Father, then the Son was seen in the Old Testament—and let heretics cease to give him his beginning from the Virgin, since he was seen before he was born of the Virgin—or else it cannot be denied that either the Father, or the Son, or certainly the Holy Spirit—if indeed there is a vision of the Holy Spirit—was seen in whatever form the will chose, not one formed by nature.

[Note: Only the Roman edition reads: “if the Holy Spirit too was seen.” This must be understood in the sense in which St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, question 43, article 7, reply to objection 6, denies that there was a visible mission of the Holy Spirit in the Old Testament. Otherwise, in his books on the patriarch Abraham and elsewhere, Ambrose clearly teaches that the three persons of the Holy Trinity appeared to Abraham.]

For we have also received the Spirit as seen in the form of a dove. Therefore no one has ever seen God, because no one has perceived or comprehended with mind or eyes the fullness of divinity that dwells in God.

The statement “he saw” must be referred to both. Finally, when it is added, “The only-begotten Son himself has declared him,” the vision of minds rather than of eyes is indicated. A form is seen, but power is declared; the former is comprehended by the eyes, the latter by the mind.

26. But what shall I say about the Trinity? The seraph appeared when it wished, and Isaiah alone heard its voice (Isa. 6:6). An angel appeared and is now present, but is not seen. Nor is it in our power to see him; it is in his power to appear.

Nevertheless, although the power to see is not ours, there is a grace by which we may merit the ability to see. Therefore, the one who has received grace has merited the opportunity; we do not merit the opportunity because we do not possess the grace of seeing God.

27. And what wonder is it if, in the present age, the Lord is not seen unless he wishes it? Even in the resurrection itself it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart. Therefore he says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

He had already counted so many as blessed, yet he had not promised them the ability to see God. If, then, those who are pure in heart will see God, clearly others will not see him. Neither will the unworthy see God, nor can one who does not wish to see God see him.

God is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart. God is not sought with bodily eyes; he is not bounded by sight, held by touch, heard through speech, or sensed by movement.

When he is thought absent, he is seen; when he is present, he is not seen. Finally, not all the apostles saw Christ. Therefore he said, “I have been with you for so long, and still you have not known me” (John 14:9)!

The one who has known what the breadth, length, height, and depth are, and the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, has seen both Christ and the Father.

For we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face; may he deign by his mercy to fill us with the entire fullness of God, so that he may be seen by us.

Thus the angel appeared to Zechariah at the right side of the altar of incense because he appeared when he wished and did not appear for as long as he did not wish to.

[Col. 1545B]

28. He appeared at the right side of the altar of incense because he was bearing the sign of divine mercy: “The Lord is at my right hand; I shall not be moved” (Ps. 15:8). And elsewhere: “The Lord is your protection over the hand of your right side” (Ps. 120:5).

[Note: Cardinal Bona uses the testimony of this passage, *On Liturgical Matters*, Book 1, chapter 25, no. 9, to prove the antiquity of incensation. Yet it can no less demonstrate that the ancient Fathers admitted a true sacrifice in the Church, on which subject numerous passages of Ambrose remain, as we have elsewhere observed.]

Would that, when we too burn incense at the altars and offer sacrifice, the angel might stand beside us—or rather, might make himself visible to us. For do not doubt that the angel is present when Christ is present, when Christ is sacrificed. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7).

Nor should you fear that your heart will be disturbed by the angel’s appearance—for we are disturbed and estranged from our ordinary disposition when we are struck by the encounter with some higher power. The same angel who will come to us will be able to strengthen us, just as he strengthened Zechariah’s troubled spirit earlier, saying:

[Col. 1545C] (Verses 13–14.) “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for behold, your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth shall bear a son, and you shall call his name John. And he shall be joy to you, and many shall rejoice at his birth.”

29. Divine benefits are always full and overflowing. They are not confined within a small number, but are heaped together in an abundant accumulation of blessings: here first comes the fruit of prayer, then the birth of a son from a barren wife, then the joy of many, and finally greatness of virtue.

The prophet of the Most High is also promised; indeed, so that there might be no doubt, even the name of the one to come is designated.

Since such things were flowing beyond his hopes, silence is rightly imposed as the penalty for disbelief; we shall explain this later.

Solemn joy accompanies the birth and generation of the saints; for a saint is not only a grace to his parents but also the salvation of many. Hence we are admonished in this passage to rejoice at the birth of the saints.

[Col. 1546A]

30. Parents are also admonished to give thanks no less for the birth of their children than for their virtues. For it is no small gift of God to grant children who propagate the race and inherit the succession.

Read how Jacob rejoiced in the generation of twelve sons (Gen. 49:28). A son was given to Abraham (Gen. 21:2). Zechariah’s prayer was heard.

Fecundity, then, is a divine gift to the parent. Let fathers therefore give thanks because they have begotten children; children, because they have been begotten; mothers, because they are honored with the rewards of marriage—for children are the wages of their service.

Let the earth blossom in praise of God because it is cultivated; the world because it is known; the Church because it is increased by the number of a devoted people.

Nor was it without purpose that at the beginning Genesis immediately joined husband and wife in marriage at God’s command (Gen. 2:24), unless it was in order to destroy heresy.

For God so approved marriage that he joined them together; and he rewarded it in such a way that divine goodness granted children to those whom barrenness had denied them.

(Verses 15.) “And he shall be great before the Lord.”

31. Here he has declared not the greatness of the body but that of the soul. Before the Lord there is greatness of soul, greatness of virtue; there is also smallness of soul and childishness of virtue. For we reckon the ages of soul and body alike, not according to the measure of time but according to the quality of virtue: that man is called perfect who is free from the error of childhood and does not experience the instability of adolescence in his mature mind; but he is little who appears not yet to have made any progress in virtue. Hence that passage in Jeremiah, when the Lord had mercy on Ephraim lamenting and pleading for his own sins:

[Note: [Col. 1546D] Thus the Amerbach edition reads in the text. Erasmus and Gillot read in the margin, with nearly all the manuscripts. But the editions of Erasmus, Gillot, and Rome read in the text, with very few manuscripts: “lamenting his own sins.”]

> “Ephraim is a beloved son to me from my youth, a child in delights” (Jer. XXXI, 20).

For if he had not been “a child in delights,” he would never have sinned. And he rightly said both things: “in delights” and “a child”; for there is also a child who does not sin: “Behold my child, whom I have chosen” (Isa. XLIII, 10). Therefore he sinned through delights, because he had been formed by the Lord in such a way that he was ignorant of error.

[Note: All editions read, “who had not been so instructed by the Lord.” Nearly all manuscripts read, “who had been so instructed,” or “because he had been so instructed,” and so forth. The negation here seems plainly superfluous, as the conclusion that follows sufficiently indicates: “Therefore, even if he had not been a child in delights,” and so forth.]

Therefore, even if he had not been a child in delights, and if with advancing age he had progressed into a perfect man of virtue, he would never have fallen, so that he would have needed to seek pardon for his sins, when rather he ought to have hoped for the rewards of his merits. What else, moreover, does our Lord seem to express in the Gospel when he says, “Do not despise one of these little ones” (Matt. XVIII, 10)? But let more be reserved for its proper place. Therefore the little one is contrary to the great. And if, according to the Apostle, the little one is under the elements—“For when we were little ones, we were under the elements of this world” (Gal. IV, 10)—then the great one is above the elements of the world.

[Col. 1547A]

32. John, therefore, will be great, not in bodily strength but in greatness of soul. Indeed, he did not extend the boundaries of any empire, nor did he prefer the triumphs of any military contest; but—something greater—in his preaching in the desert he subdued the delights of men and the wantonness of the body by great strength of soul. Thus he was little in the world but great in spirit. Indeed, as a great man, not captivated by the enticements of life, he did not exchange constancy of judgment for the desire to live.

*(Verse 15.)* “And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit,” he says, “even from his mother’s womb.”

33. There is no doubt that this was truly the angel’s promise; for holy John, before he was born, while still in his mother’s womb, manifested the grace of the Spirit he had received. For although neither his father nor his mother had previously performed any wonders, he leaped in his parent’s womb and proclaimed to the parent of the Lord that he was coming. Thus you have it: when the mother of the Lord had come to Elizabeth, she said:

> “Behold, as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped in my womb” (Luke I, 44, below).

For he did not yet possess the spirit of life, but the Spirit of grace.

[Note: Here “spirit of life” is not to be understood as the rational soul, but only as the breathing of air, as the Angelic Doctor sharply explained in Part III, question 27, article 2. It is also necessary to understand in this sense what he says: that the grace of sanctification precedes the substance of life; for Ambrose clearly indicates that the substance of life designates this same breathing when, contrasting the spirit of grace with it, he says of the former, “he receives its beginning at birth,” but of the latter, “he is not excluded from the mother’s womb.” This may also be confirmed by the fact that the words, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you,” from which the passage in Jeremiah begins in all editions and in some manuscripts, are omitted in the oldest manuscripts. Compare also, if you wish, this passage with what the same holy Ambrose teaches in *Apology of David*, chapter II, no. 56.]

Moreover, elsewhere also we can observe that the grace of sanctification precedes the substance of life, when the Lord says:

> “Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jer. I, 3).

For one is the spirit of this life, and another is the Spirit of grace: the former begins at birth and fails at death; the latter is not confined by times or ages, is not extinguished by death, and is not excluded from the mother’s womb. Indeed, holy Mary also prophesied, full of the Holy Spirit (Luke I, 46, below); and Elisha, though dead, raised a dead man’s corpse by the touch of his body (IV Kings XIII, 21); and Samuel, after death, according to the testimony of Scripture, did not remain silent about things to come (I Kings XXVIII, 17 ff.).

34. “And he will be filled,” he says, “with the Holy Spirit.” For whoever possesses the Spirit of grace lacks nothing. And whoever is infused with the Holy Spirit possesses the fullness of great virtues. Indeed—

*(Verse 16.)* “Many of the children of Israel,” he says, “he will turn to the Lord their God.”

35. We do not need testimony that holy John turned the hearts of very many, since both the prophetic and evangelical Scriptures support us in this. There is “the voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight” (Isa. XL, 3; Matt. III, 6); and the baptisms administered in great numbers to the peoples declare that the converted people made no small progress, because when John is believed, Christ is believed. For the herald of Christ preached not about himself but about the Lord. And therefore—

[Col. 1548A]

*(Verse 17.)* “He will go before him in the sight of the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah.”

36. These words are rightly joined together; for the power of the spirit never exists without the spirit, nor the spirit without power. And therefore perhaps he is said to come “in the spirit and power of Elijah,” because holy Elijah possessed both great power and grace: power to turn the minds of the peoples from faithlessness back to faith; the power of abstinence and patience; and the spirit of prophecy.

Elijah was in the desert, and John in the desert. The former was fed by ravens, the latter by wild plants; and, having trampled underfoot every enticement of pleasure, he preferred frugality and despised luxury. The former did not seek the favor of King Ahab; the latter rejected Herod’s. The former divided the Jordan; the latter converted it into a bath of salvation. The latter dwells with the Lord on earth; the former appears with the Lord in glory. The latter was the precursor of the Lord’s earlier coming; the former of the later one. The former, after three years, watered the earth, withered by the lack of rain; the latter, after three years, drenched the soil of our body with the rain of faith.

Do you ask what the three years signify? “Behold,” he says, “for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I do not find any” (Luke XIII, 7). For a mystical number was required, so that salvation might be restored to the peoples. One year was in the patriarchs; indeed, the yield of humanity at that time was of a kind that never afterward existed upon the earth. Another was in Moses and the other prophets. The third was in the coming of the Lord and Savior: “Behold,” he says, “the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution” (Luke IV, 19). And the master of the household who planted the vineyard sent not once but repeatedly for those who were to collect its fruits: first he sent servants, then other servants, and finally he sent his Son (Matt. XXI, 33 ff.).

37. John therefore came in the spirit and power of Elijah; for one cannot exist without the other, as is also found later, when it is said:

> “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 35, below).

But perhaps this example may seem to surpass us and even the apostles.

[Note: [Col. 1548D] The Roman edition reads, “may seem fulfilled.” But without doubt the reading of the other editions and of all the manuscripts is to be preferred.]

For when, under Elijah, the river’s waters were divided and their current flowed backward toward the source of the stream, as Scripture says, “The Jordan was turned back” (Ps. CXIII, 5), this signifies the future mysteries of the saving bath, through which those who have been baptized—especially little children—are restored from wickedness to the beginnings of their nature (cf. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book I, chapter 2).

And what of the fact that the Lord himself promised that the power of the Spirit would also be given to his apostles, saying:

[Note: More numerous and older manuscripts read, “You will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you.” Two manuscripts read, “the Holy Spirit.” Nevertheless, some manuscripts, and all the editions, read with us. This reading agrees better with the sacred text, which consistently has: ἀλλὰ λήψεσθε δύναμιν ἐπελθόντος τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος ἐφ᾽ ὑμᾶς—“but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.”]

> “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you” (Acts I, 8).

Then, later:

> “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as though a mighty wind were carrying the Spirit” (Acts II, 2).

“Mighty” is rightly said, because “by the breath of his mouth is all their power” (Ps. XXXII, 6). And this is the power that the apostles received from the Holy Spirit.

1280 38. Holy John also rightly goes before the face of the Lord, since he was born as a herald and died as a herald. And perhaps this mystery is celebrated even today in this life of ours. For a certain power of John runs ahead of our soul when we prepare to believe in Christ, so that it may prepare the ways of our soul for faith and make straight paths for our journey from the winding track of this life, lest we slip through the twisting turns of error. Thus every valley of our soul may be filled with the fruits of virtue, and every height of worldly merits may humble itself before the Lord in greater fear, knowing that nothing fragile can be sublime.

*(Verses 18, 19, 20.)* “And Zachariah said to the angel: How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days. And the angel answered him, saying: I am Gabriel, the angel who stands before God, and I have been sent to announce these things to you. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things come to pass, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their own time.”

39. The priest’s unbelief is condemned to silence, and the faith of the prophets is proved by an oracle. “Cry out,” he says. And I said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is grass” (Isa. XL, 6). You see the authority of the one who commands, the obedience of the one who complies, the disposition of the one who asks, and the oracle of the one who obeys. For he believed who asked what he should cry; and because he believed, he prophesied.

But Zachariah, who did not believe, could not speak. Rather—

[Col. 1549C]

*(Verse 22.)* “He was making signs to them, and he remained mute.”

40. The mystery is not that of one person alone, nor is the silence that of one person alone. The priest is silent; the prophet is silent. Unless I am mistaken, in one person the voice of the entire people was silenced, because in one person the whole people had spoken to the Lord through Moses.

[Note: “To the Lord through Moses.” The Roman edition reads, “He had taken away the voices through Moses.”]

The cessation of sacred rites and the silence of the prophets are the silence of the prophet and the silence of the priest. “I will take away,” he says, “the mighty man, the prophet, and the counselor” (Isa. III, 1–2). And truly he took away the prophets, from whom he took away the word that used to speak through the prophets. And truly he took away their power, from whom the power of God had departed. He took away from them the counselor whom he had declared to be the Angel of the great counsel.

[Note: Thus read the more numerous and better manuscripts. Nevertheless, some manuscripts and all the editions prefer “whom,” or “from whom the Angel of the great counsel withdrew.”]

He took away the voice, because the voice belongs to the Word, not the Word to the voice. For unless that Word works in us, there is no sound of the voice. John is the voice, for “he is the voice of one crying in the desert” (Luke III, 4); Christ is the Word, and this Word works. Therefore, when it ceased to work, the mute tongue, deprived of spirit as though of a soul, suddenly fell silent.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “deprived of spirit, as though of a certain soul,” and so forth.]

For the Word of God has passed over to us, and in us it is not silent. Indeed, the Jew can no longer say what the Christian can say:

> “You seek proof of Christ speaking in me” (II Cor. XIII, 3).

41. “And he was making signs to them.” Zachariah therefore remained mute and was making signs to them.

[Note: The old editions, with some manuscripts, read, “What is a mute?” The Roman edition, with several more numerous and better manuscripts, more suitably reads, “What is a sign?” But below the old editions and all the manuscripts read, “placed in the death of vital hope”; the Roman edition alone has, “of the vital spirit,” and so forth.]

What is a sign but a certain bodily action without words, attempting to indicate but not expressing the will—a sort of speech of the dying, when, at the approach of final death, the voice is suppressed? Does not the Jewish people seem to you to resemble this, so irrational that it cannot give an account of its actions? Established at the final death of its living hope, it lost the voice it had possessed; by the gestures of a faltering body it seeks to explain the sign of the word, not the word itself. Thus the people is mute, without reason and without the Word.

For why should the one who does not know the mystery seem more mute to you than the one who does not know sound? And indeed there is a voice of works and a cry of faith, as it is written:

> “The blood of your brother cries out to me” (Gen. IV, 10).

And he cries out who cries out in his heart throughout the day. Therefore, whoever has lost the cry of the heart has also lost that of the tongue. For whoever does not preserve the distinction of faith, how can he preserve that of words?

Moses had earlier said that he could not speak (Exod. IV, 10); but after he spoke, he received the Word and displayed the splendor of good works. Therefore, just as Moses was a type of the people and a type of the Law, so also Zachariah was silent.

42. Each point must therefore be considered so that the parts may converge. The Word is in the womb; the Law is in silence; John is called, and Zachariah speaks. The Word is brought forth; the Law is fulfilled, but the fulfillment of the Law is the exposition of the Word. Therefore whoever has spoken the Word speaks, even if previously he had not spoken.

The angel commands Zachariah to be silent; through the angel the voice of the Jews is suppressed. For this command belongs not to human but to divine authority: the one who did not believe Christ is not to speak to God. Therefore let us believe, so that we may speak. Let the Jew believe, so that he may be able to speak.

Let us speak spiritual mysteries; let us understand the meaning of the ancient sacrifices and the enigmas of the prophets. He is mute who does not understand the Law; he is mute who does not understand the sequence of the divine Scriptures. For our voice is faith; and therefore I would rather speak five words with my mind in the Church, so as to instruct others, than ten thousand in a tongue . . . . For tongues are “for a sign not to believers but to unbelievers” (I Cor. XIV, 19, 22), whereas prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers.

*(Verses 24, 25.)* “After these days Elizabeth his wife conceived and hid herself for five months, saying: Thus has the Lord dealt with me in the days when he looked upon me to take away my reproach among men.”

43. The saints have great concern for modesty, so that often even their desires are accompanied by shame.

[Note: Some manuscripts, and all the editions, read, “so that modesty itself is in the vows.” A greater number of manuscripts, and those of greater authority, read, “so that modesty is in the desires”—that is, in the things they have sought with the greatest eagerness.]

Thus in this passage we observe holy Elizabeth, who certainly desired to have children, hiding herself for five months. What was the reason for her concealment except modesty? For every duty has an age prescribed for it; what is fitting at one time is unfitting at another; and a change of age often changes the nature of the same act.

There are also prescribed times for marriage, when it is seemly to devote oneself to children: while the years are vigorous, while there is hope of receiving children, while the practice of begetting is exemplary, there is also eagerness for marital union. But when mature old age has arrived, and a person’s age is more suited to governing children than to producing them, it is shameful, even in a lawful union, to bear the signs of intercourse, to be burdened with the weight of another age, and to have the womb swell with a fruit that does not belong to its proper time.

For the aged are restrained by age itself and, with a proper shame regarding intemperance, are recalled from performing the acts of marriage.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “are recalled from the work of marriage.” This is excellent, unless the remaining editions and all the manuscripts disagreed. Understand “are recalled from doing” as a Greek construction used here for “are recalled from performing.” As for the fact that the same edition, after two verses, inserted “the heat of age, the desire for generation,” this not only conflicts with all the other editions and manuscripts, but also with the meaning of our author, as the sequence makes clear.]

Young men themselves often put forward the desire for children and consider the heat of age excusable on account of the desire for generation. How much more shameful is it for the aged to do what young men are ashamed to confess? Indeed, young men themselves, when they restrain hearts made sober by fear of God, often, after offspring has been received, renounce the works of youth.

44. And what is surprising about human beings, if even brute animals by a certain mute action express their concern to generate offspring rather than a desire to copulate? For once they have felt their womb heavy and seed received in the generative field,

[Note: The words “having felt their womb heavy” are omitted in the Roman edition.]

they neither indulge in intercourse nor assume the wantonness of a lover, but the care of a parent. Human beings, however, spare neither what has been conceived nor God: they defile the former and provoke the latter.

“Before I formed you in the womb,” he says, “I knew you; and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you” (Jer. I, 5). To restrain your wantonness, you perceive in the womb the hands of your Creator forming the human being. He is at work, and you defile the sanctuary of the womb with lust? Either imitate the animal or fear God.

And why do I speak of animals? The earth itself often rests from the work of generation; and if, through the impatient zeal of human beings, it is frequently occupied by seeds cast upon it, the farmer’s impudence is punished, and fertility is changed into sterility. Thus, in certain elements and animals alike, nature’s modesty regards it as shameful not to cease from the use of generation.

45. Holy Elizabeth therefore rightly blushed even at the gift, although she recognized no fault. For although she had conceived from a man—for it is not lawful to believe otherwise concerning the origin of a human being—

[Note: In the same edition, the words “concerning the origin of a human being” have been deleted.]

she nevertheless blushed at the age of her childbirth. And again she rejoiced that she had been freed from reproach; for it is a shame to women not to possess the rewards of marriage, for whom this alone is the reason for marrying.

[Note: “For whom this alone is the reason for marrying.” As the Gloss on the Decree says, “alone” means “chiefly.” Nor should one believe that Ambrose intended to exclude the other two reasons which theologians, after Augustine, add to offspring, namely faith and sacrament—especially since below he defends the existence of a true marriage between Mary and Joseph, which was also Augustine’s opinion (*On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book II, chapter 1; *Against Faustus*, book XXIII, chapter 8; and *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 11). See also Blessed Thomas, Part III, question 29, article 2, and others. Perhaps the expression may be explained more simply by supplying “for the most part”: that is, the most ordinary reason.]

This reproach, therefore, consoles her by having been removed, with that shame, as I have said, which made her ashamed on account of her age (32, q. 2, canon *Pudor*). Hence it can be understood that they no longer came together in marital intercourse; for she who would not have been ashamed of intercourse with an old man would not have been ashamed of childbirth.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “although she was an old woman, she would not have been ashamed of intercourse, while she was ashamed of childbirth.”]

And yet she is ashamed of the burden of parenthood so long as she does not know the mystery of religion.

[Note: The Roman edition adds to the word “religion” the words, “But when she understood this.” And a little later it replaced, on its own authority, the words “because she was generating a prophet” with “because she was carrying a prophet.”]

46. She who had hidden herself because she had conceived a son began to boast because she was giving birth to a prophet. She who had previously blushed now blesses; she who had previously doubted is now strengthened.

“For behold,” she says, “as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb” (Luke I, 44, below).

Thus she cried out with a loud voice when she sensed the Lord’s coming, because she believed the birth to be holy. For there was no reason for shame where she accepted as genuine the birth of a prophet, granted not by human desire but by faith.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1551]

[Col. 1551D] 1281 *(Verses 26, 27.)* “At that time the angel Gabriel was sent by the Lord to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.”

1. Divine mysteries are indeed hidden, and, according to the prophetic saying, no human being can easily know the counsel of God; nevertheless, from the other deeds and commands of the Lord and Savior we can understand that this too was the result of a carefully considered plan: the woman chosen above all to bear the Lord was one who was betrothed to a man.

Why was she not made pregnant before she was betrothed? Perhaps so that it might not be said that she had conceived through adultery. And Scripture rightly included both facts, that she was betrothed and that she was a virgin: a virgin, so that she might be seen to be free from intercourse with a man; betrothed, so that she might not be branded with the disgrace of violated virginity, and so that a pregnant womb might not seem to bear the mark of corruption.

The Lord preferred that some should doubt the origin of his birth rather than the modesty of his mother. For he knew that a virgin’s modesty is tender and the reputation of chastity unstable; nor did he think that the credibility of his birth should be established by injury to his mother.

Thus the virginity of holy Mary is preserved: intact in modesty and inviolable in reputation. For the saints ought also to have testimony from those who are outside; nor was it fitting to leave a veil of excuse for virgins living under a sinister suspicion, as though even the mother of the Lord appeared to have been disgraced.

2. What accusation could have been brought against the Jews or Herod if they appeared to have persecuted one born of adultery? How could he himself have said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 18), if he seemed to have begun with an injury to the Law, since the Law condemns the offspring of an unmarried woman (Deut. XXIII, 17)?

Moreover, a husband, the more credible witness of her modesty, is brought forward—one who could both grieve over the injury and avenge the disgrace if he did not recognize the mystery.

What is more, greater credibility is also granted to Mary’s words, and the possibility of a lie is removed. For an unmarried pregnant woman might seem to wish to conceal her fault by a lie. But an unmarried woman had a reason for lying; a betrothed woman did not, since childbirth is the reward of marriage and the grace of the wedding for women.

3. There is also no small reason why Mary’s virginity should deceive the prince of this world: when he saw her betrothed to a man, he could not suspect the birth. That the plan was to deceive the prince of this world is declared by the Lord’s own words: the apostles are commanded to remain silent about Christ (Matt. XVI, 20), those who were healed are forbidden to boast of their remedy (Matt. VIII, 4), and the demons are ordered to be silent about the Son of God (Luke IV, 35).

[Note: The Roman edition, with several words cut out, reads: “about the Son of God, as the Apostle also declared,” and so forth.]

As I have said, the Apostle also declared that the plan was to deceive the prince of this world, saying:

> “We speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, hidden . . . which none of the princes of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 7–8),

that is, they would never have brought about my redemption through the Lord’s death.

He therefore deceived for our sake; he deceived in order to conquer; he deceived the devil when he was tempted, when he was entreated, and when he was called the Son of God, so that he nowhere confessed his own divinity. Yet he deceived the prince of the age still more. For although the devil sometimes doubted, when he said, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matt. IV, 6), nevertheless, even if late, he recognized him and departed from him.

The demons also recognized him, saying:

[Note: All the editions read, “We know you, that you are Jesus, the Son of God.” The manuscripts instead read, “We know who you are, Jesus, Son of God,” with a few exceptions, some of which have “who Jesus is,” and others “that you are,” and so forth.]

> “We know who you are, Jesus, Son of God. Why have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. VIII, 29).

And they recognized that he had come because they knew beforehand that he was to come. But that the princes of this age did not know this—what better proof can we offer than the Apostle’s statement: “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory”?

The malice of demons easily detects even hidden things; but those occupied with worldly vanities cannot know divine things.

[Col. 1554B]

4. The Evangelists wisely divided the matter between them: holy Matthew presents Joseph as being warned by an angel to take Mary as his wife (Matt. I, 20), while Luke the Evangelist there bears witness that they had not come together; here Mary herself confesses this when she says to the angel, “How shall this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke I, 34).

[Note: Thus read the old editions and most manuscripts, except that the editions omit “there,” while the manuscripts read “to receive.” Some others read, “he would induce him not to dismiss Mary,” and so forth. One manuscript reads simply, “he would induce him.” “There” Matthew would bear witness to Joseph; Luke would bear witness here to Mary. What Matthew and Luke had not known, Mary herself would confess. We strongly suspect this reading to be genuine, especially because in some manuscripts, instead of “they had not come together,” the words “here she herself” are also read as “they had not known this, she herself.” The Roman edition, however, attempted to correct the entire passage in this way: “he would induce him not to be afraid to receive Mary as his wife, so that he might bear witness that they had not come together; here she herself,” and so forth.]

The same holy Luke also declared her to be a virgin when he said, “And the virgin’s name was Mary.” And the prophet taught this when he said, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isa. VII, 14). And Joseph indicated it, since, seeing that she was pregnant whom he had not known, he desired to dismiss her (Matt. I, 19). And the Lord himself made it clear while hanging on the cross, when he said to his mother, “Woman, behold your son,” and then to the disciple, “Behold your mother” (John XIX, 26–27).

Both the disciple and the mother also bore witness, because “from that hour the disciple took her into his own.”

[Note: Some manuscripts and the latest Paris edition read, “into his own home.” The remaining manuscripts and editions, together with the sacred codices, read “into his own,” following the Greek εἰς τὰ ἴδια—that is, “into his own possessions,” or “among his own affairs,” or, as others wish, “into his dwelling.” On this matter see William Estius on these words. As for our Doctor’s assertion that Joseph was still alive at the time of the Passion, in this he agrees with St. Cyprian, *Treatise on the Passion of the Lord*, but disagrees with Epiphanius, *Heresy* 78, no. 10, whom more recent writers have thought should be followed. Consult Cardinal Baronius, on the year 12 of Christ, no. 9; Estius, at the cited passage; and others.]

Certainly, if they had come together, she would never have left her own husband, nor would the just man have permitted her to depart from him. But how could the Lord have commanded divorce, when it is his own judgment that no one ought to dismiss his wife except on account of fornication (Matt. V, 32)?

5. Holy Matthew beautifully taught what the just man ought to do when he discovers his wife’s disgrace: he ought to show himself free from bloodshed and murder, and chaste rather than adulterous. “He who is joined to a prostitute is one body” (I Cor. VI, 16).

Thus everywhere the grace and character of Joseph the just are preserved, so that he may be honored as a witness; for the mouth of the just man knows no falsehood, and his tongue speaks judgment—his judgment speaks the truth.

Nor should it trouble you that Scripture frequently calls her his wife; for it declares not the loss of virginity but the testimony of marriage and the celebration of the wedding. Indeed, no one dismisses a woman whom he has not taken; and therefore the one who wished to dismiss her confessed that he had taken her.

6. Nor should it cause concern that the Evangelist says, “He did not know her until she had borne a son” (Matt. I, 25). For this is either a biblical idiom, as you have elsewhere: “Until you grow old, I am he” (Isa. XLVI, 4). Did God cease to exist after their old age? And in the Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1). Will he therefore not sit afterward?

Or it is because the one who is making a case considers it sufficient to say what belongs to the case and does not require what is superfluous. It is enough for him to establish the case he has undertaken and defer what arises incidentally.

Therefore, having undertaken to prove the incorruptible mystery of the Incarnation, he did not think that Mary’s virginity needed a fuller exposition, lest he be thought more a defender of the Virgin than an advocate of the mystery. Certainly, when he taught what was just in Joseph, he made it sufficiently clear that he could not violate the temple of the Holy Spirit, the womb of the mystery, the mother of the Lord.

7. We have learned the sequence of the truth; we have learned the plan. Let us also learn the mystery. She was rightly betrothed, but a virgin, because she is a type of the Church, which is immaculate yet married. As a virgin she conceived us from the Spirit; as a virgin she gives birth to us without a groan.

And therefore perhaps holy Mary was married to one and filled by another, because the individual churches too are filled with the Spirit and with grace, yet they are joined to a priest in the appearance of one who is temporal.

[Note: Thus read the ancient edition and the more authoritative manuscripts. The Roman and Vatican codices instead read, “Yet they are joined, in the appearance of time, to a priest.” The others read, “in the appearance of the time to a priest,” or “of a priest.” Our reading is to be interpreted in this sense: they are joined outwardly to a priest who appears in the temporal order.]

*(Verses 28, 29.)* “And the angel entered to her and said: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women. But when she saw him, she was troubled at his entrance.”

8. Learn the virgin from her conduct; learn the virgin from her modesty; learn the virgin from her oracle; learn the virgin from her mystery. It is characteristic of virgins to tremble and to be fearful at every entrance of a man, to be wary of every address from a man. Let women learn to imitate the purpose of modesty.

Alone in her inner chamber, where no man would see her, but where the angel alone would find her; alone without a companion, alone without a witness—lest some corrupting address should debase her—she is greeted by an angel. Learn, virgin, to avoid wantonness in speech: Mary herself was wary even of an angel’s greeting.

“Yet she was thinking,” he says, “what kind of greeting this might be.”

9. And therefore she was modest, because she was afraid; prudent, because she wondered at the new form of blessing, which had nowhere been read and nowhere previously discovered. This greeting was reserved for Mary alone. For she alone is rightly called “full of grace,” since she alone received the grace that no other woman had merited, so that she might be filled by the author of grace.

[Note: Some manuscripts, though not the oldest, place the following text of the Gospel here.]

Thus Mary blushed, and Elizabeth also blushed; and therefore let us recognize the difference between the modesty of a woman and that of a virgin. The former blushed because of the circumstance; the latter through modesty. In a woman the measure of shame is applied; in a virgin the grace of modesty is increased.

*(Verses 30, 31, 32.)* “And the angel said to her: Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great.”

10. It was also said of John by the angel that he would be great (Luke I, 15); but John is great as a man, whereas Christ is great as God: “For the Lord is great and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no end” (Ps. CXLIV, 3).

And indeed John is great, because “among those born of women no prophet is greater than John the Baptist” (Luke VII, 28). Yet he has one greater, because “the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he” (ibid.).

John is great, but great before the Lord.

[Note: The Roman edition reads here, “This one is great, but the Lord,” which produces an excellent sense, but is confirmed by no other edition or manuscript.]

John did not drink wine or strong drink; Christ eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners. John gathers merit through abstinence, though he possesses no power over nature; but Christ, who naturally possessed the power to forgive sins, why would he avoid those whom he could make better than the abstinent?

[Note: “Naturally,” that is, to indicate the distinction between him and the ministers.]

11. In a mystical sense also, he does not disdain the table of those to whom he is going to give the sacrament. Thus he eats, while John fasts; the type of both peoples fasts in the latter and is nourished in the former.

[Note: Some manuscripts of no mean authority read, “the spirit of both peoples.”]

But Christ also fasted, so that you would not evade the commandment; he ate with sinners, so that you might perceive grace and recognize power.

[Note: Observe that the commandment of fasting and its obligation are by no means a new invention in the Church.]

John, therefore, is also great, but his greatness has a beginning and an end. The Lord Jesus, however, is both the end and the beginning, both the first and the last (I Tim. VI, 16). Nothing comes before the first; nothing extends beyond the last.

### 12

Nor let the customary human understanding of generation lead you into error, so that you think he is not first because he is a son. Follow the Scriptures, so that you cannot go astray. The Son is called First. It is also written that the Father alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, as you have read: “To the immortal alone … God” (1 Tim. 1:17); yet he is neither first before the Father nor alone without the Son. If you deny one, you establish the other; follow both, and you confirm both.

[Note: [Col. 1556D] The Amerbach and Erasmus editions read, “You destroy the other.” Gillot and the Roman edition, with the greater part of the manuscripts, read, “You establish the other.” The rest read, “You do not establish the other.” Again, some have, “and confirm both.” But the entire passage is not free from obscurity.]

He did not say, “I am earlier, and I am later,” but, “I am the first, and I am the last” (Rev. 1:17 and 22:13). The Son is first, and therefore coeternal; for he has the Father, with whom he is eternal.

I dare to say it: the Son is first, but he is not alone; and I say this rightly and reverently. Why do you raise your ears toward impiety, heretics? You have fallen into the snares you yourselves set. The Son is first, and he is not alone: first, because he is always with the Father; he is not alone, because he is never without the Father.

I do not say this myself; he himself said it: “And I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32). The Father alone, because there is one God; the Father alone, because there is one divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and what is one is alone.

The Father alone, the Only-Begotten alone, and the Holy Spirit alone; for he who is Son is not Father, nor he who is Father Son, nor he who is Holy Spirit Son. The Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another; for we read: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16).

The Father alone, because he is the one God from whom all things are; the Son alone, because he is the one Lord through whom all things are. Only divinity makes this so; generation testifies both to the Father and to the Son, so that nowhere may the Son be seen to exist without the Father, or the Father without the Son.

Therefore he is not alone, because he is not the only immortal one; nor does he alone dwell in inaccessible light, because “no one has ever seen God, except the Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18), who sits at the right hand of the Father.

And from this some dare to say that the inaccessible light is the light in which the Father dwells. Is the light, then, better than the Father? What light is inaccessible to him for whom the Father is not inaccessible?

He himself is also the true light and the begetter of the eternal light, of which it was said: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). See to it that the inaccessible light in which the Father dwells is not also the light in which the Son dwells, since the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father.

### 13

He is rightly called great, therefore, for the power of God is spread far and wide, and the greatness of the heavenly substance extends everywhere. The Trinity has nothing prescribed, nothing circumscribed, nothing measured out, nothing delimited. It is not confined by place, comprehended by opinion, enclosed by estimation, or altered by age.

The Lord Jesus did indeed give greatness to human beings: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5); yet not to the ends of the world, nor to the ends of heaven, nor beyond the heavens.

But in the Lord Jesus all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible … “and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. 1:16–17).

Look upon heaven: Jesus is there. Gaze upon the earth: Jesus is present. Ascend by thought to heaven; descend by thought to hell: Jesus is present.

[Note: [Col. 1557D] *By the word*, that is, by reasoning and thought; so below, “If by thought you penetrate the abysses,” and frequently elsewhere.]

For if you ascend into heaven, Jesus is there; if you descend into hell, he is present. Today, while I am speaking, he is with me, within this instant, within this moment. And if a Christian is speaking now in Armenia, Jesus is present; for “no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3).

If by thought you penetrate the abyss, there too you will see Jesus at work; for it is written: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’—that is, to bring Christ down—or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead” (Rom. 10:6–7).

Where, then, is he not, who has filled heavenly, infernal, and earthly things? He is rightly called great, therefore: his power has filled the world; he is everywhere, and he will always be, because his kingdom will have no end.

*(Verse 34.)* “Then Mary said to the angel, ‘How will this happen, since I have not known a man?’”

### 14

She may seem here not to have believed, unless you pay careful attention; for it is not right that she who was chosen to give birth to the Only-Begotten Son of God should be thought unbelieving.

[Note: [Col. 1557D] The Roman edition: “be considered unbelieving.” How, then, could it have happened ([Col. 1558D] with the mother’s prerogative preserved, to whom certainly greater deference was due; and, as the prerogative was greater, greater faith also ought to have been reserved) that Zechariah, etc.?]
