How could it have happened—for, while preserving the prerogative of the mother, to whom greater honor was certainly due, greater faith ought also to have been reserved—that Zechariah, who had not believed, should be condemned to silence, while Mary, if she had not believed, should be exalted through the infusion of the Holy Spirit?

Yet Mary could neither disbelieve nor presume so rashly: not to believe the angel would have been unbelief; to presume would have been to usurp the divine prerogative. For it was not easy to know the mystery hidden from the ages in God, which even the higher Powers could not know.

And yet she neither rejected faith nor refused her duty; rather, she offered her willingness and promised obedience. For when she says, “How will this happen?” she does not doubt that it will occur, but asks about the manner of its occurrence.

### 15

How much more measured is this reply than the priest’s words! She says, “How will this happen?” He replies, “How shall I know this?” (above, v. 18). She is now dealing with the matter itself; he is still doubting the messenger.

He denies that he believes who denies that he knows, and, as though still seeking another guarantor of his faith, he asks for one. She professes that she will do what is required and does not doubt that what she asks how to be done must indeed be done. Thus you have: “How will this happen, since I have not known a man?”

An incredible and unheard-of generation had first to be announced before it could be believed. That a virgin should give birth is a sign of divine mystery, not of human nature.

Finally, he says: “Receive a sign for yourself: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14). Mary had read this, and therefore believed that it would happen; but she had not previously read how it would happen. For even to so great a prophet had the manner of its happening not been revealed.

The mystery of so great a commission was not to be proclaimed by a human mouth but by the mouth of an angel. Today it is heard for the first time: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you.” It is both heard and believed.

Finally:

*(Verse 36.)* “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word.”

### 16

Observe her humility; observe her devotion. She calls herself the Lord’s handmaid, though she is chosen to be his mother, and she is not suddenly exalted by the promise.

At the same time, by calling herself a handmaid, she claimed no prerogative for herself on account of such great grace, but showed herself ready to do what was commanded. Since she was to give birth to one who was meek and humble, she too ought to display humility above all.

“Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word.” You have her obedience; you see her vow. “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” is the preparation for service; “let it happen to me according to your word” is the conception of her vow.

### 17

How quickly, then, did Mary believe even in an unequal conception!

[Note: [Col. 1559D] Thus all manuscripts and old editions in the text. Erasmus and Gillot in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text, read “of unequal condition”; this also seems confirmed by the fact that below the manuscripts and editions read, “Zechariah, however, did not disbelieve because of unequal condition,” except for one manuscript, where *conception* stands in place of *condition*.]

For what is more unequal than the Holy Spirit and a body? What is more unheard-of than a pregnant virgin, contrary to law, contrary to custom, contrary to modesty, whose preservation is especially precious to a virgin?

Zechariah, however, did not believe because of an unequal condition, but because of old age; for the condition itself was fitting. Birth from a man and a woman is customary, and what accords with nature ought not to seem incredible.

Since age belongs to nature, not nature to age, it often happens that age hinders nature. Yet it is not unreasonable that the lesser cause should yield to the greater, and that the stronger prerogative of nature should exclude the ordinary use of age.

Moreover, Abraham and Sarah had received a son in old age, and Joseph is the son of old age. If Sarah is reproved because she laughed (Gen. 18:13), then he is more justly condemned who believed neither the oracle nor the example.

But when Mary says, “How will this happen, since I have not known a man?” (above, v. 34), she does not seem to have doubted the fact, but to have asked about the manner of the fact. It is clear that she believed it had to happen, since she asked how it would happen.

Hence she deserved to hear: “Blessed is she who believed” (below, v. 45). And truly blessed: she was superior to the priest. When the priest denied, the virgin corrected the error.

Nor is it surprising that the Lord, intending to redeem the world, began his work with Mary, so that through the woman by whom salvation was prepared for all, the first to receive the fruit of salvation might be the same woman.

[Note: [Col. 1559D] This passage makes clear that Christ is no less Redeemer when, by the protection of grace, he prevents sins from being committed than when he forgives sins already committed. For he is said to have begun redemption with his mother, because he himself prevented her from being unbelieving toward the angel’s words. By this wedge the most knotty argument, as they suppose it, of those who attack the immaculate conception of the Mother of God is easily broken and scattered.]

### 18

And she rightly asked how it would happen; for she had read that a virgin would give birth, but she had not read how she would give birth.

[Note: [Col. 1560D] All editions read, “because a virgin would conceive”; all manuscripts, “because a virgin would give birth.”]

As I said, she had read: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isa. 7:14). But how she would conceive, the angel was the first to declare in the Gospel.

*(Verses 39–40.)* “Then Mary arose in those days and went with haste into the hill country, to a city of Judah, and entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth.”

### 19

It is a moral lesson for everyone that those who demand faith should themselves provide grounds for faith.

And therefore, when the angel was announcing hidden things, so that faith might be established by an example, he announced to the virgin Mary the conception of an elderly and barren woman, in order to assert that everything God wills is possible for God.

When Mary heard this, she went into the hill country—not as an unbeliever concerning the oracle, nor as one uncertain about the message, nor as one doubting the example, but joyful because of the promise, devout because of her duty, and hurrying because of her joy.

For where else would she go, already filled with God, except to hasten upward with all speed? The grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow delays.

### 20

Learn also, holy women, what diligence you owe in attending to pregnant relatives. Mary, who had previously remained alone in her innermost retreat, was delayed neither by the modesty of virginity that avoids public exposure, nor by the ruggedness of the mountains, nor by the length of the journey required by duty.

A virgin in the hill country, she hastened; a virgin mindful of her duty, unmindful of the affront, with affection vigorous, not her sex, she left her home and went.

[Note: [Col. 1560D] The affront is that suffered by a virgin’s modesty when she is compelled to go out in public. Subsequently the Roman edition reads, “with affection urging”; the other editions and all manuscripts, “with affection vigorous.” This is more fitting, since the vigor of charity is opposed to girlish weakness. Below, all editions with the greater part of the manuscripts read, “Mary, late in the house”; from the Vatican and Corbie manuscripts and several others we have restored, “Mary, serious in the house.” Corbie, indeed, indicates in a gloss that *late* should be read, that is, “slow,” a correction perhaps followed by others. Yet *serious*, that is, grave, is preferable; for haste is generally considered contrary to gravity.]

### 21

Learn, virgins, not to run about through other people’s houses, not to linger in the streets, and not to engage in conversations with people in public.

Mary was serious and reserved at home, hurrying in public, and remained with her relative for three months. For she who had come because of duty clung to her duty.

She remained for three months, not because another person’s house delighted her, but because she disliked being seen in public too frequently.

### 22

You have learned Mary’s modesty; learn her humility as well. A relative comes to a relative, a younger woman to an older woman. She not only comes but greets her first; for the more chaste the virgin, the more humble she ought to be.

Let her know how to show honor to her elders. Let her be a teacher of humility, in whom chastity is professed. She is also an example of devotion and a rule of instruction.

We must observe that the superior comes to the inferior so that the inferior may be helped: Mary to Elizabeth, Christ to John. Finally, later also, to sanctify John’s baptism, the Lord came to John’s baptism.

The benefits of Mary’s speedy arrival and of the Lord’s presence are soon made clear.

*(Verse 41.)* “For as soon as Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant leaped in her womb. And she was filled with the Holy Spirit.”

### 23

Observe the distinction and the proper force of each word. Elizabeth heard the voice first, but John felt the grace first. She heard according to the order of nature; he leaped because of the mystery. She perceived Mary’s arrival; he perceived the Lord’s. The woman perceived the woman, and the child perceived the child.

These women speak of grace; those children work inwardly. They undertake the mystery of devotion through maternal advances, and in a double miracle the mothers prophesy through the spirits of their infants.

The infant leaped; the mother was filled. The mother was not filled before the son, but when the son was filled with the Holy Spirit, he filled his mother also.

John leaped, and Mary’s spirit leaped as well. When John leaped, Elizabeth was filled. Yet we recognize that Mary was not filled with the Spirit, but that her spirit leaped; for the incomprehensible one was working incomprehensibly in his mother.

One is filled after conception; the other before conception.

*(Verses 42–43.)* “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And from where is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

### 24

The Holy Spirit knows his own speech and never forgets it. Prophecy is fulfilled not only through the miracles of events but also through the precision of its words.

What is this fruit of the womb except the one of whom it was said: “Behold, the heritage of the Lord is sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb” (Ps. 126:3)?

That is, the sons are the Lord’s heritage; they are the reward of the fruit that came forth from Mary’s womb. He himself is the fruit of the womb, the flower of the root, of whom Isaiah prophesied well, saying: “A branch shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1).

The root is the family of the Jews, the branch is Mary, and the flower is Christ. Like the fruit of a good tree, he now flowers and bears fruit in us according to the progress of our virtue, and now is restored through the renewed resurrection of the body.

“And from where is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

### 25

She does not speak as though ignorant; for she knows that it is the grace and work of the Holy Spirit that the mother of the prophet should be greeted by the mother of the Lord, for the advancement of her child.

But recognizing that this is not a gift earned by human merit but by divine grace, she says: “From where is this granted to me?”

[Note: [Col. 1561D] The Roman edition alone reads, “that so great a good should happen to me,” etc.] That is: “What great good has happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? I do not recognize any merit of my own. From where is this granted to me—by what justice, by what deeds, for what merits?”

Such services are not customary among women: “that the mother of my Lord should come to me.” I perceive a miracle; I recognize a mystery. The mother of the Lord is pregnant with the Word and full of God.

*(Verses 44–45.)* “For behold, as soon as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb; and blessed is she who believed.”

### 26

You see that Mary did not doubt but believed, and therefore obtained the fruit of faith. “Blessed,” she says, “is she who believed.”

But you also are blessed, who have heard and believed; for every soul that believes both conceives and gives birth to the Word of God, and recognizes his works.

Let Mary’s soul be in each person, so that it magnifies the Lord; let Mary’s spirit be in each person, so that it rejoices in God. If according to the flesh one alone is the mother of Christ, according to faith Christ is nevertheless the fruit of all.

For every soul receives the Word of God, provided that, immaculate and free from vices, it guards chastity with undefiled modesty.

### 27

Therefore, whatever soul is able to be such, magnifies the Lord, just as Mary’s soul magnified the Lord, and her spirit rejoiced in God her Savior.

The Lord is magnified, as you also read elsewhere: “Magnify the Lord with me” (Ps. 33:4). This does not mean that anything can be added to the Lord by a human voice, but that he is magnified in us.

For Christ is the image of God. Therefore, if the soul does anything just or devout, it magnifies that image of God according to whose likeness it was created.

And so, while it magnifies him, it is exalted by a certain participation in his greatness, so that it may appear to express in itself that image through the splendid color of good works and through a certain emulation of virtue.

Mary’s soul magnifies the Lord, and her spirit rejoices in God, because, devoted both in soul and in spirit to the Father and the Son, she worships with pious affection the one God from whom all things are and the one Lord through whom all things are.

### 28

The sequence is that the more excellent the person, the fuller the prophecy.

[Note: [Col. 1561D] All editions read, “But as for Mary, why …” Some manuscripts read, “For it follows that, as for Mary, why …” Others, and those of better age, read, “It follows, as for Mary, why …,” as in our text.] Nor does it seem without significance that Elizabeth prophesies before John and Mary before the Lord’s birth; for the first beginnings of human salvation are already spreading.

Just as sin began with women, so good things also begin with women, so that women too, laying aside womanly works, may renounce weakness, and that the soul, which has no sex, may imitate in devout zeal the chastity of Mary, who knows no error.

*(Verse 56.)* “And Mary remained with her for about three months, and returned to her own house.”

### 29

Holy Mary is rightly presented both as having fulfilled her duty and as having preserved the mystical number.

[Note: [Col. 1562D] The Albinus manuscript: “and fulfilled the mystery,” so that she might neither abandon the woman giving birth [perhaps “about to give birth” or “in labor”] nor fail to preserve the mystical number.]

Her long stay was not due merely to family affection, but also to the advancement of so great a prophet. For if such progress appeared at her first entrance, so that at Mary’s greeting the infant leaped in the womb and the infant’s mother was filled with the Holy Spirit, how much do we think the presence of holy Mary added through the use of so much time?

“And Mary remained with her for about three months.” Thus the prophet was anointed and, as a good athlete, trained in his mother’s womb; for his virtue was being prepared for the greatest contest.

Finally, Mary remained as long as Elizabeth’s time for giving birth was fulfilled. If you pay close attention, you will find this stated nowhere except in the generation of the righteous.

The days were fulfilled, and Mary gave birth; the time was fulfilled, and Elizabeth gave birth; the time of life was fulfilled when holy men departed from the course of this life. The righteous possess the fullness of life; the days of the wicked are empty.

### 30

Elizabeth therefore gave birth to a son, and the neighbors rejoiced with her.

[Note: [Col. 1563D] The Victor manuscript reads, “neighbors.” At that time Elizabeth’s time for giving birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son. The account of the saints has, etc.]

The account of the saints has the joy of many, because the good is common; for justice is a common virtue. And therefore, at the birth of the righteous, a sign of the future life is sent beforehand, and the grace of the virtue that will follow is marked out by the neighbors’ rejoicing, which prefigures it.

The period during which the prophet was in the womb is beautifully described, so that Mary’s presence may not be passed over; but the period of infancy is left unmentioned, because the presence of the Lord strengthened him in his mother’s womb, and he knew none of the impediments of infancy.

Therefore in the Gospel we read nothing concerning him except his birth, the oracle, his leaping in the womb, and his voice in the wilderness. For he experienced no period of infancy who, placed in his mother’s womb above nature and above his age, began with the fullness of the measure of Christ’s perfect age.

[Note: [Col. 1563D] The Roman edition reads, “the period of infancy is silent,” because he knew none of the impediments of infancy. Yet there is no reason why the intervening words should be cut away. One Colbert manuscript reads, “of Christ.” Note that the neighbors hesitated concerning John’s name. Hence we know without doubt that the name of him which Zechariah had learned from the angel’s announcement in the temple was revealed by the spirit of prophecy to Elizabeth his mother. Thus, objecting, they say, “There is no one in your family called by this name.” And she answered, etc. But these words are not so much the author’s as a paraphrase.]

*(Verses 60, 64.)* “And his mother answered and said, ‘No, but he shall be called John.’ And they said to her, ‘There is no one among your relatives who is called by this name.’ Then they made signs to his father, asking what he wanted him to be called. And he asked for writing tablets and wrote, saying, ‘John is his name.’ And they all marveled. Immediately his tongue was released, his mouth was opened, and he spoke, blessing God.”

### 31

The holy Evangelist wonderfully thought it necessary to mention beforehand that many supposed the infant should be called by his father’s name, Zechariah, so that you might understand that his mother was not displeased with the name of some unworthy ancestor, but that what had been infused into her by the Holy Spirit was the name previously announced by the angel to Zechariah.

Indeed, since he was mute, he could not communicate his son’s name to his wife; but through prophecy Elizabeth learned what she had not learned from her husband: “John is his name,” she says. That is, “We do not give him a name; he has already received a name from God.”

He has his own name, which we have recognized, not one that we have chosen. The saints have this privilege, that they receive their name from God.

Thus Jacob is called Israel (Gen. 32:28), because he saw God. Thus our Lord Jesus was named before he was born; and it was not an angel but the Father who gave him his name.

“For my son Jesus will be revealed,” it says, “with those who rejoice with him, those who remain for four hundred years. And after these years my Son Christ Jesus will die … and the age will be changed” (4 Esdras 7:28–30).

You see that angels announce what they have heard, not what they have arrogated to themselves. Nor should you be surprised if a woman asserted a name that she had not heard, since the Holy Spirit, who had entrusted it to the angel, revealed it to her.

She who had prophesied Christ could not be ignorant of the Lord’s herald.

### 32

And it is rightly added that no one in his family was called by this name, so that you may understand that the name belonged not to the family but to the prophet.

Zechariah is also questioned by a sign; but because unbelief had deprived him of speech and hearing, he spoke by hand and writing what he could not speak with his voice. For he wrote, saying: “John is his name.”

This name is not imposed but affirmed; and therefore his tongue was immediately released, because faith freed what unbelief had bound.

Let us too believe, then, so that we may speak, so that our tongue, which is bound by the chains of unbelief, may be released by the voice of reason.

Let us write the mysteries in the spirit, if we wish to speak. Let us write the herald of Christ not on stone tablets but on tablets of fleshly hearts. For whoever speaks John prophesies Christ.

Let us speak of John; let us speak also of Christ, so that our mouth too may be opened—our mouth which, in that great priest, the reins of an unreasonable, nodding faith had restrained like those of a beast.

*(Verse 67.)* “And Zechariah, his father, was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying.”

### 33

See how good God is and how ready to forgive sins. He not only restores what has been taken away but also grants what was not expected.

The man who had recently been mute prophesies. For this is the greatest grace of God: that those who had denied him confess him.

[Note: [Col. 1564D] The Erasmus edition and those following it, with a few manuscripts, read, “that he whom [they] had denied, [they] confess.” Many others read, “that those who had denied, confess.” The Amerbach edition and the Corbie manuscript, with other more reliable witnesses, read, “that those who had denied, confess.” This is rightly said not so much of Zechariah as inferred generally on the occasion of his case.]

Let no one, then, lose faith; let no one who is conscious of former sins despair of divine rewards. The Lord knows how to change his judgment, if you know how to amend your sin (*On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter “The Lord Knows”).

*(Verse 76.)* “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High.”

### 34

When he was prophesying about the Lord, he rightly turned his words toward the prophet, so that he might also designate this as the Lord’s benefit. Otherwise, when he publicly enumerated his own blessings, he might have seemed ungrateful by remaining silent about the benefits he had received, which he recognized in his son.

But perhaps some may think it an irrational excess of mind that he addresses an eight-day-old infant. Yet if we hold fast to this, we understand clearly

[Note: [Col. 1564D] After “hold fast,” not a few add “the foregoing”; one adds, “what we read.”] that the newborn could hear the voice of his father, just as he had heard Mary’s greeting before he was born.

The prophet knew that a prophet has other ears, which are opened by the Spirit of God, not by the age of the body. He had the capacity for understanding, since he had the disposition for rejoicing.

### 35

At the same time, observe how briefly Elizabeth prophesies and how extensively Zechariah does; both spoke when filled with the Holy Spirit. Yet the discipline is preserved: a woman should strive more to learn what is divine than to teach it.

We do not easily find anyone who prophesied more abundantly than the mother of the Lord. The prophetess Mary, the sister of Aaron, how quickly she brought the words of her song to an end (Exod. 15:20–21)! And when she spoke at greater length with her brother, she did not escape the punishment for her speech (Num. 12:1 ff.).

## Chapter II

*(Verse 1.)* “And it happened in those days that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled.”

### 36

Since we are going to speak of the Savior’s birth, we do not think it irrelevant to inquire at what time he was born.

For what would a secular enrollment have to do with the Lord’s generation unless we should recognize that this too is a divine mystery? While a secular enrollment is being proclaimed, a spiritual one is fulfilled—not an enrollment to be declared to an earthly king, but to the king of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1565C] After “This enrollment,” the Roman edition had moved the word “of faith,” which is nevertheless defended by the authority of all the old editions and manuscripts. Again, that edition substituted “which would not exact tributes” for “which would not exact tortures.” Incorrectly: the allusion to the Roman censorial system is plainly not obscure, and it is known to have been extremely severe. Ambrose himself sufficiently indicates this below, when, contrasting Christ’s census with it, he says: “Fear nothing terrible, nothing harsh, nothing sad in this census; faith alone marks each person.” These last words allude to the ancient custom of the censors of entering certain persons on the tablets of Caere as a mark of disgrace; Horace, *Epistles* I.6, refers to this: “Forgetful of what is fitting and what is not, worthy of the Caeretan wax,” etc. On this matter see Erasmus, *Chiliads* I, cent. 10, adage 81.]

This enrollment is an enrollment of faith, a census of souls. For the ancient census of the synagogue had been abolished, and a new census of the Church was being prepared, one that would not inflict punishments but remove them. And spiritually, in the figure, his people were already registering their names with Christ.

Here it is not the spaces of the earth that are counted, but minds and souls; boundaries are not recorded but extended; no age is distinguished, but everyone is enrolled.

No one is exempt from this census, because every age is generous toward Christ: children, though crying, confess him by martyrdom; those placed within the womb testify to him by their rejoicing.

[Note: [Col. 1565D] Males before their fourteenth year and females before their twelfth were not compelled to make declaration before the censors, since before that age tribute was not exacted from them. On this, consult Justus Lipsius, *De Magnitudine Romana* II.3.]

You need fear nothing terrible, nothing harsh, nothing sad in this census; faith alone marks each person.

Do you wish to hear Christ’s census officials? They are commanded to enroll without rods;

[Note: [Col. 1566C] Thus all manuscripts. All editions, on the contrary, read, “They are commanded to enroll, but without rods.” This is less good, since there is a manifest allusion to Luke 9:3, where the apostles, setting out to sow the Gospel, are forbidden to carry a staff.] to seek the people not by terror but by grace; to put away the sword and not possess gold (Matt. 10:9–10). Through such census officials the world was acquired.

### 37

Finally, so that you may know that the census belongs not to Augustus but to Christ, the whole world is ordered to enroll.

When Christ is born, everyone enrolls; when the world is brought to its close, everyone is put in danger. Who, then, could demand an enrollment of the whole world except the one who possessed dominion over the whole world?

For “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. 23:1), not Augustus’s.

Augustus did not rule the Goths; he did not rule the Armenians. Christ ruled them. They certainly received Christ’s census official, since they produced Christ’s martyrs.

And perhaps that is why, as present events show, they surpass us: the one whom they confessed by the offering of their blood is the one against whom the Arians raised the question of his lineage.

*(Verse 2.)* “This enrollment,” he says, “was the first one made.”

### 38

Yet histories say that many parts of the earth had already often been registered. This, therefore, is the first enrollment—but of minds.

[Note: [Col. 1566C] All editions read, “the first enrollment, not of lands but [Col. 1566D] of minds.” The sense is clear. But because “not of lands” is absent from all the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts, and the sentence can stand without it, we preferred to follow the consensus of the manuscripts. “The first enrollment” is said not absolutely, but as the first under Quirinius, in contrast with the second carried out under him, as Baronius teaches in the *Apparatus to the Ecclesiastical Annals*, p. 29, along with Jansenius of Ghent and other interpreters of this passage. Since little profit could accrue to his readers from the literal sense, blessed Ambrose does not examine it here. The following words, “not at the summons of a herald,” sufficiently show that the censors had their own heralds, although some deny this. Whoever wishes to know more about the census and its office should consult *Codex Theodosianus* XIII, titles 10, *On the Census*, and 11, *On Those Registered*; Rosinus, *Roman Antiquities* VII.10; Laurentius Polymathes, III, Synopsis 4, §4; and elsewhere.] Everyone enrolls in it, because no one is excluded, not at the summons of a herald but at that of the prophet, who long beforehand proclaimed:

“All nations, clap your hands; shout to God with a voice of rejoicing, for God is the Most High, terrible, the great king over all the earth” (Ps. 46:2–3).

Finally, so that you may know that this is an enrollment of justice, Joseph and Mary come to it: that is, a righteous man and a virgin. He is the one who would preserve the Word; she is the one who would give birth to him.

Where do the righteous man and the virgin enroll, if not where Christ is born? For “every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God” (1 John 4:2).

And where does Christ come to birth according to the higher meaning, if not in your heart and in your breast? “The Word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. 10:8).

### 39

It is beautifully done that he also added the name of the governor, so that he might mark the sequence of time. “When Quirinius was governor of Syria,” he says, “this first enrollment took place.”

It is as though the Evangelist had entered a consul’s name in this book as an indication of the date. For if consuls are recorded on documents of sale, how much more ought the time to be recorded for the redemption of all?

You therefore have everything customarily found in contracts: the name of the person exercising supreme authority, the day, the place, and the cause. Witnesses are also normally called upon; Christ likewise called witnesses to his birth and generation according to the flesh, witnesses who would authenticate the Gospel, saying: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem” (Acts 1:8).

*(Verses 6–7.)* “And it happened that, while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and placed him in a manger, because there was no place in that lodging.”

[Note: [Col. 1566D] All editions and the more recent manuscripts read, “because there was no place for him in the lodging.” The others read, “because there was no place in that lodging,” a reading confirmed by the fact that below the manuscripts and editions with great agreement state, “he had no other place in that lodging.” Understand that Ambrose took the Greek words ἐν τῷ καταλύματι, not as though τῷ were an article, but as a demonstrative, as even approved authors not infrequently use it. Observe further that he differs from the opinion of Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel* VII.5; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 20; Jerome, Letter 28 to Marcella; and others, since all these hold that Christ was born not in a stable belonging to some house but in a rocky cave. Yet defenders of our Doctor are not lacking; they may be consulted among the interpreters.]

40. Saint Luke has briefly explained both how, at what time, and in what place Christ was born according to the flesh. But if you ask about his heavenly generation, read the Gospel of Saint John, who, beginning with heavenly things, descended to earthly ones. There you will find when he was, how he was, what he was, what he had done, what he was doing, where he was, where he came from, how he came, at what time he came, and for what reason he came.

“In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1): here you have when he was. “And the Word was with God”: here you have how he was. You also have what he was: “And the Word was God.” What he had done: “All things were made through him” (ibid., 3). What he was doing: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (ibid., 9). And where he was: “He was in the world” (ibid., 10). Where he came: “He came to his own” (ibid., 11). How he came: “The Word became flesh” (ibid., 14). When he came, John bears witness to him, saying: “This is he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me was made before me, because he was before me’” (ibid., 30). The reason for which he came, John himself attests: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (ibid., 29).

If, then, we have come to know both generations, and have perceived that the gift of each is one and the reason for which he came is one—namely, that, taking upon himself the sins of the perishing world, he might abolish in himself the stain of sin and the death of all, since he could not be overcome—it follows that now also the holy evangelist Luke should teach us and show us the ways of the Lord as he grew according to the flesh.

[Note: Some manuscripts of better quality read, “and the gift of each is one.” Several others omit the word “gift,” which certain more recent editors evidently attempted to correct by replacing it with “and the reason of both is one,” and so on; all the editions have followed that reading.]

41. No one should be disturbed because, by a higher design, we have said that John’s infancy was passed over, whereas we maintain that Christ’s infancy has been described.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “but that Christ’s infancy ought to be described.”]

For it is not given to everyone to say: “I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak; I became all things to all people” (1 Corinthians 9:22). Nor can this be said in the same way of anyone else, because: “He was wounded for our iniquity, and he was weakened for our sins” (Isaiah 53:5).

He, therefore, was a little child, an infant, so that you might be a mature man. He was wrapped in swaddling clothes, so that you might be released from the snares of death. He lay in a manger, so that you might be at the altars.

[Note: “So that you might be at the altars,” namely, in order to receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body. The same point is made in the work *On the Initiation*, chapter 8: “When the people, having been washed, hasten to the altars”; and shortly afterward: “He came, therefore, and saw the most sacred altar prepared.” A more suitable place will occur for saying more about the rite by which that most divine sacrament was administered in the ancient Church.]

He was on earth, so that you might be in heaven. He had no other place in that lodging, so that you might have many dwelling places in the heavenly seats.

“For though he was rich,” he says, “he became poor for your sake, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). That poverty, then, is my inheritance; and the Lord’s weakness is my strength. He preferred to lack for himself, so that he might abound for all. The cries of his infancy wash me; those tears washed away my sins. Therefore, Lord Jesus, I owe more to your insults, by which I have been redeemed, than to your works, by which I was created. It would not have benefited me to be born, unless it had benefited me to be redeemed.

42. But let no one confine the whole form of divinity within the limits of the body’s appearance. The nature of the flesh is one thing; the glory of divinity is another. For your sake there is weakness; in himself, power. For your sake there is poverty; in himself, abundance. Do not judge by what you see, but recognize by what you have been redeemed.

Because he is in swaddling clothes, you see him; because he is in heaven, you do not see him. You hear the cries of an infant; you do not hear the lowing of the ox that recognizes its Lord: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isaiah 1:3). Indeed, I should say “manger,” as the translator wrote; for in my judgment there is no difference in the word when there is no difference in the meaning.

For if that orator of theirs who pursues the embellishments of speech—Demosthenes, in the speech *Against Ctesiphon*—denies that the fortunes of Greece depended on whether this or that word was used, but thinks that the matter itself must be considered; if even their philosophers, who spend whole days in disputation, have used expressions less Latin and less customary in order to employ their own proper terms; how much more ought we to disregard words and contemplate the mysteries, by which the baseness of speech is overcome, because the miracles of divine works, adorned by no rhetorical embellishments, shine forth with the light of their own truth?

Finally, that irrational donkey was fed at the sacred mangers not with the coloring of delicacies but with the nourishment of natural sustenance.

[Note: All editions and many manuscripts read “not with the seasoning of delicacies” (*non succo deliciarum*). A manuscript of better age reads “not with the coloring of delicacies” (*non fuco deliciarum*), that is, with richly and sumptuously prepared foods. For why should it not be permissible to call those delicate dainties a coloring applied to food?]

43. This is the Lord; this is the manger in which the divine mystery was revealed to us: that irrational nations, living among the mangers like cattle, were to be fed with the abundance of sacred nourishment.

Therefore the donkey—the figure, to be sure, and form of the Gentiles—recognized the manger of its Lord. Hence it says: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Psalm 22:2).

Are God’s proofs insignificant—that angels minister, that Magi worship, that martyrs confess? He is poured forth from the womb, but he shines from heaven. He lies in an earthly lodging, but he flourishes with heavenly light.

A married woman gave birth, but a virgin conceived. A married woman conceived, but a virgin gave birth. Saint Matthew taught us a mystery of no small importance, which Saint Luke, because it had already been fully explained, thought should be passed over in silence, believing that he would have sufficient wealth if he claimed for himself from all things the Lord’s manger.

44. This little child, whom you, being unbelieving, regard as contemptible, the Magi coming from the East follow over so great a distance; they fall down and worship him, call him king, and acknowledge that he will rise again, offering from their treasures gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matthew 2:1 ff.).

What are these gifts of true faith? Gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for the dead. One is the insignia of kingship, another the sacrifice of divine power, another the honor of burial—which does not corrupt the dead body but preserves it.

[Note: All editions read, “another is the sacrament of power”; all manuscripts read, “another is the sacrifice of power.” Both readings are suitable. The mystical interpretation of the gifts brought by the Magi has, moreover, been celebrated by so many Fathers that there seems no need to dwell on it in recounting them.]

We also, brothers, who hear and read these things, should bring forth such gifts from our treasures. “For we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7). If, then, in yourself—that is, in what you are—you ought not to judge yourself from yourself but from Christ, how much more, in Christ, ought you to judge not what is yours, but what is Christ’s.

45. Therefore the Magi offer gifts from their treasures. Do you wish to know how great their merit was? A star is seen by them; where Herod is, it is not seen; where Christ is, it is seen again and shows the way.

Therefore this star is the way, and Christ is the way; for according to the mystery of the Incarnation Christ is the star: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Numbers 24:17). Finally, wherever Christ is, there is also the star; for he himself is the bright and morning star. He marks himself out by his own light.

46. Receive another lesson. The Magi came by one road and returned by another; for those who had seen Christ and understood Christ returned better than they had come.

There are, in fact, two roads: one that leads to destruction, the other that leads to the kingdom. The former belongs to sinners and leads to Herod; the latter is Christ, by whom one returns to the homeland. Here is only a temporary dwelling, as it is written: “My soul has dwelt too long” (Psalm 119:6).

Let us therefore beware of Herod, the worldly ruler for a time, so that we may attain the eternal dwelling of our heavenly homeland.

47. These rewards have not been set before the chosen alone, but before everyone, because “Christ is all and in all” (Colossians 3:11).

For you see that it was not without purpose either that Abraham, who came from the Chaldeans, reputed to be more skilled in numbers, believed God, or that the Magi, although versed in magical arts and devoting themselves to winning divinity over to themselves, believed that the Lord had been born on earth. I say, not without purpose, but so that testimony to the holy religion might be taken from hostile nations, and an example of the fear of God might be given.

[Note: All editions and the majority of manuscripts read “although they were versed in magical arts, while they devoted themselves to winning divinity over to themselves.” The Roman edition reads “to the divinity.” The Corbie, Prat, Carnot, and Gembloux manuscripts have the reading retained in the text, which is better, since the former reading is not free from ambiguity.

As for the fact that these Magi are said to have derived their origin from the prophet Balaam, this is taken clearly from Origen, *Homily 13 on Numbers*. That they are represented as instructed in magical arts seems to have been drawn not only from the same passage in Origen but is also plainly found in his Book I *Against Celsus*. Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*; Ignatius, *Letter to the Ephesians*; Jerome, on Isaiah, chapters 19 and 47; and others followed him in this.

As for the knowledge of numbers which the holy Doctor assigns shortly before to the Chaldeans, it must be understood as astrological numbers, from which the genethliaci believed that they could predict the future. Hence Horace, Book I, Ode 11:

“Do not attempt the Babylonian numbers.”

They write that this science was brought from Abraham to the Egyptians. We, however, maintain that what was transmitted by the Patriarch was not that superstitious practice, but merely the sound and honorable study of the stars, which human curiosity afterward distorted and turned toward wicked arts.]

48. But who are these Magi, unless they are those who, as a certain history teaches, derive their lineage from Balaam, through whom it was prophesied: “A star shall rise from Jacob”? They are therefore heirs no less of faith than of succession.

He saw the star in the spirit; they saw it with their eyes and believed. They saw a new star, such as had not been seen since the creation of the world. They saw a new creation, and they sought the grace of the new human being not only on earth but also in heaven, according to what Moses prophetically set down: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel.”

They recognized that this was the star signifying both man and God. They worshiped the child; surely they would not have worshiped him if they had believed him to be merely a child.

[Note: The Remigius manuscript reads: “Therefore the Magus understands through his own arts, but you do not understand,” and so forth.]

Does the Magus, then, understand that his arts have ceased, while you do not understand that your gifts have come? He confesses what is alien, while you do not recognize what was promised. He believes against himself, while you do not think that belief ought to be exercised for your sake.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “You do not recognize what is your own.”]

49. The Magi therefore announce that a king has been born. Herod is troubled, gathers the scribes and chief priests, and asks where Christ is to be born.

The Magi announce only a king; Herod seeks Christ. Therefore he confesses the very king about whom he asks. Then, when inquiry is made as to where he was to be born, he is shown to have been foretold; for one could not seek someone who had not been announced.

O foolish Jews! You do not believe that he has come whom you see. You do not believe that he has come whom you say will come.

“Tell me,” he says, “so that I may come and worship the child” (Matthew 2:8). Herod is indeed plotting, but he does not deny the God whom he mentions as one to be worshiped.

Then he orders the infants to be killed (ibid., 16). To whom but God was such a victim owed? Though infancy lacks understanding, it nevertheless confesses the God for whom it is slain.

We have touched briefly on these matters from Matthew so that it might be clear that the time of infancy was not empty of divine works. And if the age of the flesh was inactive in its works, certainly it was God who exercised the age of the flesh through the works of divinity—God who also caused the shepherds in that region to keep watch, guarding their watches by night over their flock.

50. Behold the beginning of the rising Church. Christ is born, and the shepherds begin to keep watch, so that they might gather into the Lord’s hall the flocks of the nations, which had previously lived like animals, and prevent them from suffering the attacks of spiritual beasts amid the obscurity of the nights.

[Note: A few manuscripts, and those more recent, insert the scriptural text “And there were shepherds,” which the Roman edition presents somewhat earlier, while it is absent from all the ancient editions and other manuscripts.]

The shepherds rightly keep watch, whom the good Shepherd instructs. The flock is therefore the people; the night is the world; the shepherds are the priests.

Or perhaps the shepherd is also the one to whom it is said: “Be watchful, and strengthen” (Revelation 3:2), because the Lord appointed not only bishops to protect the flock but also sent angels.

“Behold, an angel of the Lord stood before them” (Luke 2:9).

51. See how divine care establishes faith: an angel instructs Mary, an angel instructs Joseph, and an angel instructs the shepherds. It is not enough for one person to have been sent once; “every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

52. “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will’” (Luke 2:13–14).

The angels are rightly called an army, since they followed the commander of the host. To whom, then, would the angels give praise except to their Lord, according to what is written: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels” (Psalm 148:1–2)?

The prophecy has therefore been fulfilled. The Lord is praised from heaven and is seen on earth.

Saint Mark says of him: “He was with the beasts, and the angels ministered to him” (Mark 1:13), so that in the one you may recognize a sign of mercy, and in the other an indication of divine power. What he suffers from the beasts is yours; what is proclaimed by the angels is his.

And they say:

53. “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this Word that has come to pass, as the Lord has shown us.” And they came in haste (Luke 2:15–16).

You see the shepherds hastening; no one seeks Christ with sluggishness. You see that the shepherds believed the angel; you too must believe the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, the angels, the prophets, and the apostles.

[Note: All manuscripts read as in the text. In contrast, all the editions read: “Do you not wish to believe?”]

See how precisely Scripture weighs the significance of each word. “They hasten,” it says, “to see the Word.” For when the Lord’s flesh is seen, the Word is seen, who is the Son.

Let this not seem to you an insignificant example of faith, though the persons of the shepherds are lowly. Certainly, the lower one is in worldly prudence, the more precious one is in faith.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “not because the person of the shepherds is insignificant.” Certainly this alteration is unnecessary, as becomes clear when the passage is considered more carefully. After three words, the Corbie and Michel manuscripts read, “the more precious he is in prudence,” while the others and the editions read, “the more precious he is,” and so forth.]

The Lord did not seek gymnasia crowded with wise men, but a simple people who would not embellish or disguise what they had heard. Simplicity is sought; ambition is not desired.

Nor should you regard the words of the prophets as contemptible because they seem humble. Mary also gathers faith from the shepherds; through the shepherds the people are gathered into reverence for God. For they marveled at what the shepherds said to them.

54. “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19).

Let us learn the Virgin’s chastity in all things. She was no less modest in speech than in body, and she brought the proofs of faith together in her heart.

If Mary learns from the shepherds, why do you refuse to learn from priests? If Mary remains silent before the apostolic commandments, why, after the apostolic commandments, do you desire more to teach than to learn?

Learn that the fault belongs to the person, not to the sex; for the sex itself is holy. Finally, Mary did not receive a command; she offered an example.

55. The child is therefore circumcised. Who is that child except the one of whom it was said: “A child is born to us; a Son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6)? For he was made under the Law in order to win those who were under the Law.

56. “He is presented in Jerusalem.”

[Note: The words “he is presented in Jerusalem” occur in the ancient editions but are absent from all the manuscripts. The Roman edition removed them and replaced them with the scriptural text, which is likewise absent from the manuscripts and old editions; but since that edition frequently claims this right for itself, it is enough to have noted it once.

As for the fact that the holy Bishop refers to his commentaries on Isaiah, we have found them cited more than once by Augustine. We regret all the more that they have perished, since we understand that they were valued by so great a Doctor.]

I would explain what it means for the Lord to be presented in Jerusalem, if I had not already said so in the commentaries on Isaiah. For, circumcised from vices, he was judged worthy of the Lord’s gaze, because “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Psalm 33:16).

You see that the entire sequence of the ancient Law was a type of what was to come; for circumcision also signifies the cleansing of sins. But because the weakness of human flesh and mind, driven by a certain ready eagerness to sin, is entangled in inextricable vices, the future cleansing of every fault was prefigured by the eighth day of circumcision, in the age of the resurrection.

For this is what is meant by: “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exodus 13:2). In the words of the Law, the birth of the Virgin was being promised. And truly he is holy, because he is immaculate.

Finally, that he is the one marked by the Law is declared by the words repeated in the same manner by the angel: “For the holy one who shall be born,” he says, “shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

For no male intercourse opened the secrets of the virginal womb; rather, the Holy Spirit poured immaculate seed into the inviolate womb. For the Lord Jesus alone, among all those born of woman, was holy in every respect: he did not experience the contagions of earthly corruption because of the novelty of his immaculate birth, but drove them away by his heavenly majesty.

57. For if we follow the letter, how can every male be holy, when it is clear that many were most wicked? Was Ahab holy? Were the false prophets holy, whom the avenging heavenly fire consumed at Elijah’s prayer?

But he was holy through whom the pious prescriptions of the divine Law marked out a figure of the future mystery, because he alone would open the secret generative passage of the holy virgin Church for the generation of the peoples of God with immaculate fecundity.

[Note: All editions read “the one who, in a figure of the future mystery,” whereas all manuscripts read “the one through whom the figure of the future mystery.” The latter is not unsuitable. The holy Doctor means that Christ, opening the virginal womb of his mother through an immaculate birth, was a figure of himself opening the spiritual womb of the Church for the generation of the faithful.

But was the most chaste Virgin’s womb truly opened physically in giving birth? Theologians who deny this interpretation rely on the dogma of faith, supported by the authority of all the Fathers, the Council of Nicaea, and the subsequent councils, namely, that Mary remained a virgin even in giving birth; they believe this cannot be reconciled with the opening of the womb.

Ambrose himself arranged for the opinion of certain people to be condemned at the Council of Milan: those who did not deny that the Virgin conceived the Lord but denied that she gave birth as a virgin. This may be understood from his letter to Pope Siricius, where, after gathering many examples and figures from the Old Covenant, he establishes the possibility of a virginal birth.

He does the same in *On the Institution of the Virgin*, chapter 8, and in the hymn *On the Nativity of the Lord*, and elsewhere.

Nevertheless, Erasmus, in his annotations on Luke, citing the words that follow—“This is he who opened his mother’s womb, so that he might come forth immaculate”—maintains that our Doctor, together with Origen (*Homily 14 on Luke*), taught that Christ, in being born, opened his mother’s womb.

Certainly this passage is not entirely free of difficulty, but Blessed Thomas resolves it in the *Third Part*, question 28, article 2. After presenting Venerable Bede’s testimony on the subject, he concludes that “the opening” does not signify the ordinary breaking open of the enclosure of virginal modesty, but only the exit of the offspring from the mother’s womb. Erasmus himself does not reject this interpretation.

Others offer another explanation, understanding “opening the womb” as “granting fertility,” just as “closing the womb” is said of making it barren.

Perhaps it may also be added that virginity is not violated by every opening of the womb, but by one effected through a sexual act, or at least resulting from one. Augustine teaches this clearly in *The City of God*, Book I, chapter 18. Indeed, after Saint Thomas, the scholastics must acknowledge this very point in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 152, article 1, in the body and in the response to the third objection, where he says: “If, by some accident, the integrity of a member is corrupted, this is no more prejudicial to virginity than if a hand or foot were corrupted.”]

He alone opened his own womb. Nor is this surprising, for he who had said to the prophet: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5)—he who sanctified another’s womb so that a prophet might be born—is the one who opened his mother’s womb, so that he might come forth immaculate.

58. “And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25).

The Lord’s generation receives testimony not only from angels and prophets, shepherds and parents, but also from the elderly and the righteous. Every age, both sexes, and the miracles of events establish the faith.

A virgin gives birth; a barren woman bears a child; a mute man speaks; Elizabeth prophesies; a Magus worships; the unborn child leaps in the womb; a widow confesses; a righteous man awaits.

And rightly is he called righteous, since he sought not his own grace but that of the people. He himself desired to be released from the bonds of bodily frailty, but waited to see the promise; for he knew that blessed are the eyes that would see him.

59. “Now,” he says, “you may dismiss your servant” (Luke 2:29).

See the righteous man, as though enclosed in the prison of bodily weight, desiring to be released so that he may begin to be with Christ; for to be released and to be with Christ is far better.

But whoever wishes to be dismissed should come to the temple, come to Jerusalem, await Christ the Lord, receive the Word of God in his hands, and embrace it with the arms, as it were, of his faith.

[Note: The old edition reads, “let him embrace it with the works of his faith, as with certain arms.” The Roman edition, reversing the phrase, reads, “let him embrace it with his works, as with the arms of his faith,” and so forth. The manuscripts have the reading retained in the text.]

Then he will be dismissed, so that one who has seen life may not see death.

60. You see the Lord’s abundant grace spread through his generation over all people, and prophecy denied to unbelievers but granted to the righteous.

Behold, Simeon also prophesies that the Lord Jesus Christ has come for the fall and resurrection of many, so that he may distinguish the merits of the righteous and the wicked and, as the true and just judge according to the quality of our deeds, decree either punishments or rewards.

61. “And your own soul,” he says, “a sword shall pierce” (Luke 2:35).

Neither the letter nor the history teaches that Mary departed this life through the suffering of bodily death; for it is not the soul but the body that is pierced by a material sword.

Therefore this saying displays Mary’s understanding, which was not ignorant of the heavenly mystery. For “the living Word of God is powerful and sharper than every very sharp sword, penetrating to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts of the heart and searching the secrets of souls” (Hebrews 4:12), because all things are naked and open to the Son of God, whom the secrets of conscience do not deceive.

[Note: Erasmus and the editions that follow him read, “and sharper than every sword.” Amerbach and the manuscripts read, “and sharp,” and so forth. The latter is not unsuitable, since the preposition *prae* (“exceedingly”) may be understood, as in many other expressions of this kind; see Francisco Sánchez, *Minerva*, on comparatives.]

62. Simeon prophesied; the Virgin had prophesied; the woman joined in marriage had prophesied; the widow also had to prophesy, so that no profession or sex might be lacking.

Therefore Anna is introduced as one of such character both in the years of her widowhood and in her conduct, so that she may rightly be believed worthy to announce that the Redeemer of all had come.

Since we have described her merits elsewhere, when we were exhorting widows (*On Widows*, chapter 1), and since we are hastening here to other matters, we do not think they should be repeated. Yet it was not without purpose that he specified eighty-four years of her widowhood, because seven twelves and two forties seem to designate a sacred number.

63. “And when he was twelve years old” (Luke 2:42).

As we read, the beginning of the Lord’s disputation is taken from his twelfth year; for this was the number appropriate to those who evangelize and preach the faith.

Nor was it without purpose that he, not forgetful of his parents according to the flesh—he who, according to the flesh, was filled with the wisdom and grace of God—was found in the temple after three days. This indicated that, after three days, he would rise from that triumphal passion and present himself to our faith in the heavenly seat and divine honor, though he had been believed dead.

64. “What is this, that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things of my Father?” (Luke 2:49).

There are two generations in Christ: one paternal, the other maternal. The paternal is more divine; the maternal is that by which he descended into our labor and use.

Therefore whatever occurs above nature, above age, or above custom must not be assigned to human powers but referred to divine authority.

Elsewhere his mother urges him toward the mystery; here his mother is corrected (John 2:3), because she still demands what belongs to human things.

[Note: The editions of Erasmus, Gill, and Rome, together with some manuscripts, read “ministry.” The same editions have this reading below as well. The Amerbach edition in the body of the text, and Erasmus and Gill in the margin, have “mystery” in both places, together with the rest of the reading retained here, except that in the manuscripts alone “from the Son” is read instead of “by the Son.”

As for the expression “his mother is corrected” here, do not infer from it, with Calvin, that the holy Bishop intended to indicate that the Mother of God sinned—nothing could be farther from the holy man’s mind, as has already been noted more than once. Understand “is corrected” in a broad sense, meaning “is instructed” or some similar expression, which is not contrary to common usage.]

But since here he is described as twelve years old, while elsewhere he is taught to have disciples, you see that the mother learned something about the Son: in the one passage she demanded a mystery from the stronger one, while in the other she marveled at a miracle in the younger.

65. “And he came to Nazareth and was subject to them” (Luke 2:51).

What else should the teacher of virtue do but fulfill the duty of piety? Do we marvel that he defers to the Father when he is subject to his mother?

This subjection is not weakness but piety. Let the serpent of unbelief, released from its savage hiding places, raise its head and pour forth its venom from its serpentine breast.

When the Son says that he was sent (John 8:29), the heretic calls the Father greater, so that he may declare the Son imperfect, since the Son can have someone greater; and so that he may assert that the one who is sent requires the assistance of another.

But did he also need human assistance in order to obey his mother’s command? He deferred to a human being; he deferred to a handmaid—for she herself says, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1:38); he deferred to his supposed father. Do you marvel if he deferred to God?

Is it piety to defer to a human being, but weakness to defer to God? Or weigh divine things from human ones and recognize what love is owed to a father.

The Father honors the Son (John 8:54 and 49); do you not wish the Son to honor the Father? The Father professes in a heavenly voice that he is well pleased in the Son (Luke 3:22); do you not wish the Son, clothed in the garment of human flesh and speaking with a human voice and human affection, to say that the Father is greater (John 14:28)?

For if “the Lord is great and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no end” (Psalm 145:3), then surely greatness that has no end has no increase either.

But why should I not receive with reverent ears that the Son is obedient to the Father in assuming a body, when I reverently receive that the Father defers to the Son?

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “and what honor we ought to owe the Father.” But nothing should be changed, since love toward parents is always understood to be joined with honor.]

66. Learn rather the commandments of your own advantage and recognize examples of piety.

Learn what you owe your parents when you read that the Son does not differ from the Father in will, work, or time; although they are two in persons, they are one in power.

That heavenly Father experienced none of the labor of generation. You owe your mother the violation of her modesty, the expenditure of her virginity, the danger of childbirth, long vexations, and long perils. For that poor woman, even in the very fruits of her hopes, there is greater danger; and when she has brought forth what she desired, she is released from childbirth, but not from fear.

Why should I speak of anxious fathers laboring for their children’s advancement, of wealth multiplied for the use of others, and of the seeds sown by the farmer for the benefit of generations to come? Ought not at least some services to be repaid for these things?

Why does a wicked person regard his father’s longer life as burdensome and the sharing of the inheritance as restrictive, when Christ does not refuse co-heirs?

67. (Chapter III.—Verse 2.) “The word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness” (Luke 3:2).

The Son of God, about to gather the Church, first works in his servant. Therefore Saint Luke rightly says that the word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness, so that the Church might not have begun from a human being but from the Word.

For the Church itself is the wilderness, because “the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1).

Finally, it is said to her: “Rejoice, barren woman” (ibid.), and “Rejoice, wilderness” (Isaiah 52:9), because as yet she was cultivated by no works of the assembled people, nor did those trees—which could not yet bear fruit—raise up the summit of their merits.

The one who said, “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Psalm 52:10), had not yet come. That heavenly vine had not yet supplied fruit to its branches through a kind of channel of its words.

The Word therefore came to pass, so that the earth that had previously been desolate might produce fruit for us. The Word came to pass, and the voice followed; for the Word first works inwardly, and the office of the voice follows.

Hence David also says: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Psalm 115:1). He first believed, so that he might be able to speak.

68. Now the word came, for Saint John the Baptist to preach repentance. And therefore many impose upon Saint John the type of the Law, because the Law could denounce sin but could not forgive it. For the Law recalls from error anyone who followed the way of the nations and restrains him from crime; it urges repentance so that he may obtain grace. “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16); but John was Christ’s herald.

[Note: Thus the old edition, together with most and the best manuscripts. This reading is correct, for it signifies nothing other than that the Law, whose type John was, prepared the way, as it were, for the Church, and that the repentance which the same John preached opened access to grace. In certain manuscripts, however, the word “repentance” is absent; and in others the passage reads as follows: “Thus the Law announces beforehand the grace of repentance to the Church.” The Roman edition, however, altered it in this way: “And so the Law is the Church’s herald beforehand and a precursor of grace.”]

Thus the Law is the Church’s herald, and repentance is the precursor of grace. Saint Luke therefore wisely used a concise form to make John known as a prophet, saying that the word of the Lord came upon him; he added nothing else, for no one who abounds in the word of God needs an indication of his own identity. He said one thing, therefore, and declared everything.

69. Saint Matthew and Mark, however, wished to identify the Prophet by his clothing, his belt, and his food, because he had a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his loins; and he ate locusts and wild honey (Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6). For Christ’s herald did not permit the cast-off skins of unclean beasts to perish; by this very indication of dress he also signified that Christ would come—he who, taking upon himself the sins of unclean heathendom, woven of beastliness and filth because of the deformity of our merits, would upon that trophy of the cross put off, as it were, the garment of our flesh.

[Note: All editions read: “who, clothed in the hides of beasts, which are woven together with our own …” The manuscripts of the Vatican and Gallican families, however, strongly support our reading, except that in some, through a scribal error, *ingluvie* is written for *illuvie*; in one, “in filth and defilement.”]

70. What, then, does the wearing of a leather belt signify, except that this flesh, which formerly used to weigh down the mind, after the Lord’s coming began to be not an impediment but a belt? Certainly, in accordance with David: “Upon the willows … we hung our instruments” (Psalm 136:2); and in accordance with the Apostle (Philippians 3:3), we do not place our confidence in the flesh, yet we do place our confidence in the body: we do not place it in pleasures, but we do place it in sufferings. For thus the affection, fervent in spirit, grows strong, and we gird ourselves for every service of the heavenly commandments, intent through the devotion of the mind and unencumbered by the equipment of the body.

[Col. 1578A] 71. The prophetic food also is an indication of his office and a herald of the mystery. For what is so useless for a human task as searching for locusts, and what is so full of meaning for a prophet’s mystery? For the more locusts are useless for fruit, inert for labor, elusive to the touch, wandering in their leaps, and shrill in their mouths, the more suitably the figure of the gentile peoples is applied to them: a people useless for every labor, producing no fruit from its work, without dignity, uttering only the sound of complaint without a voice, and ignorant of the word of life.

[Note: Many manuscripts, and not inferior ones, read “inert for use,” omitting the word “labor.” Here our Doctor differs from those who think that *akrídes* (ἀκρίδες) are not locusts but a kind of shrub or herb—or, if one may say so, even delicate fish. The overwhelming majority of the Fathers and interpreters agree with Ambrose. Nor does the contrary opinion seem to have been introduced for any other reason than that people did not believe that locusts could be eaten, although historians report that certain peoples both formerly lived on them and still do so. On this matter Erasmus and Drusius may be consulted in their commentaries on this passage.]

This people, therefore, is food for the prophets; for the greater the number of the people gathered together, the more abundantly the service of the prophetic mouth increases. The grace of the Church also is prefigured in wild honey, found not within the honeycomb of the Law, in the offspring of the Jewish people, but spread through the fields and leaves of the forest by the error of the gentiles, according to what is written: “We found it in the fields of the forest” (Psalm 131:6).

72. He ate this wild honey, announcing that the peoples would be filled with the honey of the rock, as it is written: “He filled them with honey from the rock” (Psalm 80:17). Thus also ravens fed Elijah in the wilderness with food brought from elsewhere and with drink freely supplied (1 Kings 17:6).

[Note: All editions and many manuscripts read “with food brought from elsewhere … brought from himself.” The remaining manuscripts, including the oldest, read “with food carried in,” and so forth. As for what the Roman edition had cut out—“and with drink freely supplied”—all the manuscripts and ancient editions contradict it.]

This was to signify that the peoples of the nations, foul and filthy in the color of their merits, who had previously sought food in stinking corpses, would now provide the prophets with nourishment brought from themselves. For the food of the prophets is the accomplishment of the divine will, as the Lord himself declared, saying: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).

**(Verse 4.) “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.”**

[Col. 1578C] 73. John, the herald of the Word, is rightly called a voice. For when John himself was asked, “What do you say about yourself?” he answered: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:22–23). And therefore he said: “He who comes after me was made before me” (ibid., 30), because the voice, which is lower, goes before, while the Word, which surpasses it, follows. For this reason also he wished to be baptized by John, because among human beings the Word is consecrated through the teacher’s voice. Perhaps this is why Zechariah received his voice: because he spoke of the Voice.

**(Verses 7–8.) “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance. And do not begin to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”**

74. The wickedness of the Jews does indeed seem to be reproved, because, through the varied venom of a guilty mind, they bring forth the serpent’s falls and earthly lairs rather than producing any recognition of the divine mystery. Yet when it is said, “Who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” the prudence infused into them by God’s mercy is revealed, so that they may repent of their sins and fear the terror of the future judgment with watchful devotion.

The comparison with vipers, therefore, must be referred to their generation, not to their succession. Or perhaps, in accordance with what is written, “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16), they are shown to possess natural prudence: they see what will benefit them and ask for it willingly, but they have not yet abandoned what harms them.

75. And therefore they are admonished to claim for themselves the distinction of their deeds rather than the nobility of their ancestry, since succession provides no privilege unless an inheritance of faith supports it. God’s will had revealed through prophetic speech that this inheritance would be transferred to the peoples of the nations, saying: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”

Although God can convert and change different natures, the mystery benefits me more than the miracle. Therefore, in the herald of Christ, I ought to recognize nothing so much as the building up of the rising Church. She was built not from rocky stones but from living stones, and through the conversion of our minds she rose as God’s dwelling and the summit of his temple.

For God was preparing to soften the hardness of our minds and to raise worshipers from stones of stumbling. What else were those people considered but stones, who served stones and were plainly like the things they made? The prophecy therefore promises that faith will be infused into the stony hearts of the gentiles, and that through faith they will become children of Abraham—those in whom, through the hardness of their minds, a certain stony, insensible, and irrational disposition had taken root.

For if the apostolic judgment compared men strengthened by the power of faith to living stones, according to what is written, “You also, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices” (1 Peter 2:5), then here, in a much deeper sense, men seem to be compared by the prophetic voice to stones. They had so lost the sense of the human mind that, while they thought some divine reason existed in stones, they themselves were changed into the nature of stones—not through the use of the body but through the disposition of the mind.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “formed men through the strength of faith.” This is less suitable, as the context of the sentence itself makes clear.]

Finally, although they descended from Abraham’s succession according to the flesh, they are called “rulers of Sodom” (Isaiah 1:10) and “whitewashed walls” (Matthew 23:27). Thus similarity of character claims for itself the privilege of ancestry more than the order of forefathers (Acts 23:3).

And so that you may know that men are compared to stones, the Prophet also compared men to trees, adding:

**(Verse 9.) “For the axe has already been laid to the roots of the trees.”**

[Col. 1580A] 76. The example is changed for this reason: so that, as the comparison proceeds, a certain more merciful progress of the human being may be understood. Previously deformed for usefulness, naked of adornment, barren of fruit, and irrational for advancement, they are now represented in the likeness of trees. Trees rise to their tops, spread out their branches, fill themselves with fruits, and clothe themselves with leaves; they are beautiful for use through a rational gift of nature, lovely to behold, and rich in fruit.

Would that we could imitate the usefulness of fruitful trees and, growing in merits, founded upon the root of enduring humility, raise from the ground the lofty tops of fruitful works, mature and beautiful to behold, lest the Gospel’s axe, wielded by the farmer, cut away the root of the wild trunk.

“For woe is me if I do not preach the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:16). But that is an apostolic saying. Woe is me if I do not weep over my sins; woe is me if I do not rise in the middle of the night to confess to you; woe is me if I have practiced deceit toward my neighbor; woe if I have not spoken the truth.

The axe has been laid to the root. Let him produce fruit who can produce the fruit of grace and who ought to produce the fruit of repentance. The Lord is present, seeking fruit, giving life to the fruitful, and reproving the barren. It is three years since he came, and he could not find fruit among the Jews; would that he find it in us. He is about to command that the unfruitful be cut down, lest they occupy the land. But whoever still has no fruit should strive to produce it in the future. That good cultivator of the field will intervene for us, the unproductive and fruitless, so that time may be granted and patience extended—lest perhaps we too should be able to bear some fruit for God.

77. Saint John the Baptist also gave an appropriate answer to each class of people, one answer for all (Distinction 86, chapter “In singulis”): to tax collectors, that they should exact nothing beyond what was prescribed; to soldiers, that they should not commit extortion or seek plunder. He taught that military pay had been established for this very reason: lest, while expenses were being sought, the plunderer should run rampant.

But these and the other instructions concerning the duties proper to individuals are distinct; mercy is a common practice. Therefore it is a common commandment, necessary for every duty and every age, and to be practiced by everyone.

[Note: Many manuscripts, and not inferior ones, read: “the practice of common mercy … necessary for the ages,” while some read “necessary,” but all agree that it must be extended to everyone. Others read: “Mercy … is necessary and must be extended by all.” The remaining manuscripts, as well as the editions, read as in the text.]
