No tax collector, no soldier is exempt; neither farmer nor townsman, rich nor poor—everyone alike is admonished to contribute to one who has nothing. For mercy is the fullness of the virtues.

[Col. 1580D] And therefore the perfect form of virtue is set before everyone: they must not spare their clothing or their food. Yet the measure of mercy itself is observed according to the capacity of human circumstances, so that no one deprives himself of everything but shares what he has with the poor.

**(Verses 15–16.) “While the people were considering and reflecting in their hearts about John, whether perhaps he himself were the Christ, he answered, saying: ‘I indeed baptize you with water, in repentance.’”**

78. John therefore saw the hidden things of the heart. But let us consider whose gift this was. Paul shows how the hidden things of the heart are made known to prophets when he says: “The secrets of his heart will also become manifest; and falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you” (1 Corinthians 14:25). It is therefore God’s gift that reveals these things, not a human power; the person is aided more by divine favor than he perceives them through any natural faculty.

But what does this thought of the Jews accomplish except to prove, in accordance with the Scriptures, that Christ had come? The one who was expected had come; and surely the one who was expected arrived, not one who was not expected.

What, however, is more foolish than that the one thought to be the Christ in another is not believed to be the Christ in himself? They thought that he would come through a woman, yet they do not believe that he came through a virgin. What birth, according to the flesh, was more worthy of God than that the spotless Son of God should preserve the purity of an immaculate generation even in assuming a body? Indeed, the sign of the divine advent was established in the virgin’s childbirth, not in that of a woman.

[Note: Clearly this refers to Isaiah 7:14: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son,” and so forth. Ambrose rightly rebukes the Jews, who, believing that Christ would come from a woman, stubbornly insisted that Isaiah’s Hebrew word should be understood as referring to any woman rather than to a virgin who would preserve her virginity in conception and childbirth. See Huet, *Demonstratio Evangelica*, chapter 9.]

79. “I,” he says, “baptize you with water.” He quickly proved that he was not the Christ, since he performed a visible office.

[Note: Thus all the editions and almost all the manuscripts. The Corbie manuscript, however, and a few others read: “For since man consists of two natures …” Again, in the same passage all the editions, together with the manuscripts, read “the visible through the visible, the invisible through the invisible,” and so forth. Eight manuscripts read “the visible through the invisible, the invisible through the visible,” and so forth. Others, closer to the editions, read “the visible through invisibles,” and this is sufficiently appropriate to the argument.]

For since man subsists from two natures—that is, from soul and body—the visible mystery is consecrated through visible things and the invisible through the invisible. With water the body is washed; by the Spirit the sins of the soul are cleansed.

We do one thing and invoke another, although even in the font itself the sanctification of divinity breathes upon us. For not every cleansing is effected by water, but these things cannot be separated from one another. Therefore one baptism was the baptism of repentance, while the other is that of grace. The former proceeds from one element, the latter from both; for since sins are common to mind and body, purification also ought to be common.

Saint John rightly indicated that he understood what they were thinking in their hearts and, as though he did not understand, avoided the envy directed toward majesty. He declared by his action, not by his words, that he was not the Christ. To practice repentance for sins is a human work; to fulfill the mystery with grace is God’s gift.

**“But one mightier than I is coming.”**

80. He did not make a comparison by saying that Christ was merely stronger than he—indeed, there could be no comparison between the Son of God and a human being—but because there are many strong ones. The devil too is strong: “No one can plunder the vessels of the strong man … unless he first binds the strong man” (Mark 3:27). There are therefore many strong ones, but no one stronger except Christ.

Finally, he did not make a comparison to such an extent that he added: “Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry,” showing that the grace of evangelical preaching had been granted to the apostles, who are shod for the Gospel.

81. Yet he seems to say this also because John often assumed the person of the Jewish people. Hence they refer to this saying: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30), meaning that the Jewish people must become smaller and the Christian people, in Christ, increase.

Moses, too, assumed the person of the people; but he did not carry the Lord’s sandal, but the sandal of his own feet. These men were perhaps shod with a sandal that was not their own; but Moses was commanded to loosen the sandal of his own feet (Exodus 3:5), so that the steps of his spirit and mind, freed from the bonds of bodily attachment, might walk the spiritual path.

The apostles had put aside their bodily sandals when they were sent without sandals, without a staff, without a bag, and without a belt; but they did not immediately carry the Lord’s sandals. Perhaps they began to carry them after the resurrection. Before then, they were warned not to tell anyone what the Lord had done. Later, however, it was said to them: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel” (Mark 16:15), so that, bringing forth the imprint of evangelical preaching, they might carry throughout the whole world the complete sequence of the Lord’s deeds.

The sandal, therefore, is evangelical preaching. But we shall explain something about this more appropriately elsewhere (below, chapter 10).

**(Verse 17.) “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and with fire. He has his winnowing fan in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor and gather the wheat into his barn; but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.”**

82. “He has his winnowing fan in his hand.” By the image of the winnowing fan, the Lord is declared to possess the right of distinguishing merits. When the grain is winnowed on the threshing floor, full grains are separated from empty ones, and fruitful from barren, as though by an examination of the breath of air.

Through this comparison, therefore, it is shown that on the day of judgment the Lord will distinguish solid merits and the fruits of virtue from empty boasting and the unfruitful frivolity of vain deeds; and that he will place those of more perfect merit in a heavenly dwelling.

The more perfect fruit is the one that has deserved to be conformed to him who, like a grain of wheat, fell in order to bear abundant fruit in us—hated by the chaff and not a friend to empty merits. Therefore fire will burn before him, not harmful by its nature, since it consumes the evils of wickedness and increases the splendor of righteousness.

**(Verses 21–22.) “Now it came to pass, when all the people had been baptized and Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, that heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove upon him; and a voice came from heaven: ‘You are my Son; in you I am well pleased.’”**

[Col. 1583A] 83. The Lord was baptized, therefore, not because he wished to be cleansed, but to cleanse the waters, so that, having been washed through the flesh of Christ, which knew no sin, they might possess the authority of baptism. And therefore whoever comes to Christ’s bath lays aside his sins.

Saint Luke the evangelist aptly condensed what the others had said, leaving it more to be understood than explicitly stated that the Lord was baptized by John. The Lord himself declares the reason for his baptism when he says: “Allow it for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15).

84. Since God, by such great divine favor for the building up of his Church, granted that after the patriarchs, prophets, and angels the only-begotten Son of God should descend and come to the bath, have we not truly and divinely understood the saying about the Church: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126:1)?

Nor is it surprising that a human being cannot build if he cannot guard: “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (ibid.). These words come from a certain psalm. Yet I also dare to say that a human being cannot set out upon the way unless he has the Lord going before him. Hence it is written: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 13:4), and, “The paths of a man are directed by the Lord” (Proverbs 20:24).

Finally, the more perfect person is the one who understands that he cannot walk without the Lord: “Teach me your ways,” he says (Psalm 24:4). And, to come to the historical account—for we ought not merely to draw a simple account of what happened, but also to relate our actions for imitation to what has been written—the people came out of Egypt but did not know the way that led to the holy land. God sent a pillar of fire by night so that the people might learn the way through the pillar. He also sent a pillar of cloud by day so that they would not turn aside either to the left or to the right (Exodus 13:21).

But you, human being, are not such that you deserve a pillar of fire as well. You do not have Moses; you do not receive a sign. Now, after the Lord’s coming, faith is required and signs are concealed. Fear God and place your confidence in the Lord, for “the Lord sends his angels around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 33:8).

You see, therefore, that everywhere the Lord’s power cooperates with human efforts, so that no one can build without the Lord, no one can guard without the Lord, and no one can begin anything without the Lord (cf. Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, book 1, chapter 44).

And therefore, in accordance with the Apostle: “Whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31); and elsewhere, “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Colossians 3:17). In two epistles he commands you in one place to act “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and in another to act “for the glory of God,” so that you may know that the glory of the Father and the Son is the same, and their power likewise the same; nor do the Father and the Son differ in any respect concerning their divinity, since they do not differ in their assistance to us.

David therefore taught me that no one builds a house or guards a city without the Lord (Psalm 126:1).

85. Moses also taught me that no one but God made the world: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). He also taught that God made the human being by his work. He did not idly write: “God fashioned man from the clay of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7), so that through a kind of bodily action you might perceive God’s activity in building the human being.

He also taught that God made the woman: “God cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he slept, and he took one of his ribs from his side, and filled his flesh in its place; and the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman” (ibid., 21–22).

[Note: Thus eleven manuscripts of excellent quality. Others read in part “he filled it with flesh,” and in part, together with the editions, “he filled its place with flesh.” These words do not badly render the Greek of the Septuagint elders, καὶ ἀνεπλήρωσε σάρκα ἀντ’ αὐτῆς (“and he filled it with flesh in its place”), although it is credible that the preposition ἀντί was absent from the Ambrosian manuscript.]

As I have said, Moses does not without reason introduce God as working upon Adam and Eve with something like bodily hands. God commanded the world to come into being, and it came to be; Scripture indicates that the work of the world was completed by a single word. But when it comes to the human being, God’s prophet has taken pains to show you, as it were, the very hands of the laboring God (Psalm 140:5).

86. The elaborate works of God compel me to understand something more in these things than I read. The Apostle came to the aid of my struggling mind and, by the divine Spirit, revealed to me what I did not understand in the words, “Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” and, “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man” (ibid., 23), saying: “This is a great mystery” (Ephesians 5:32).

What mystery? “The two shall be one flesh”; and, “A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife” (ibid., 31); and, “We are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones” (ibid., 30).

Who is this husband for whose sake the woman leaves her parents? The Church, which has been gathered from the gentile peoples, leaves her parents. To her it is prophetically said: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44:11).

For what husband, unless perhaps that one of whom John says, “After me comes a man who was made before me” (John 1:27)? From his side, while he slept, God took a rib. For he is the one who slept, rested, and rose again, because the Lord received him.

What is this rib except power?

[Note: The Roman edition reads “except life”; the remaining editions and all the manuscripts read “except power.” This reading is confirmed by the citation below: “I perceive that power has gone out from me.”]

For when the soldier opened his side, immediately water and blood came out, which was poured out for the life of the world (John 19:34). This life of the world is Christ’s rib; this rib belongs to the second Adam.

For the first Adam became a living soul, while the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. The last Adam is Christ; Christ’s rib is the life of the Church. We therefore are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones.

And perhaps this is the rib of which he said: “I perceive that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:46). This is the rib that came forth from Christ without diminishing his body. For it is not a bodily rib but a spiritual one; the Spirit himself is not divided, but he divides to each one as he wills.

This is Eve, the mother of all the living. For if you understand that the living one is sought among the dead, you understand that those who are without Christ are dead, because they do not share in life. Not to share in Christ means this: that Christ is life.

The mother of the living, therefore, is the Church, which God built upon Christ Jesus himself, the supreme cornerstone, and in whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a temple of God.

87. Let God therefore come and build the woman—there the helper of Adam, here the helper of Christ. Not because Christ needs assistance, but because we seek and desire to reach Christ’s grace through the Church.

Even now she is being built; even now she is being formed; even now the woman is being shaped; even now she is being created. And therefore Scripture has used a new expression: “We are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Ephesians 2:20). Even now the spiritual house rises into a holy priesthood.

Come, Lord God; build this woman, build this city. Let your servant also come, for I believe you when you say: “He himself will build the city for me” (Isaiah 45:13).

88. Behold the mother of all; behold the spiritual house; behold the city that will live forever, because it does not know how to die. For she is the city of Jerusalem, which now appears on earth but will be snatched above Elijah—for Elijah was one.

She will be transferred above Enoch, whose death is not found. He was snatched away lest wickedness change his heart; but she is loved by Christ as a glorious bride, holy, immaculate, and without wrinkle.

And how much better it is for the whole body to be taken up than for one individual to be taken up! For this is the hope of the Church. She will certainly be snatched away, taken up, and transferred to heaven. Behold, Elijah was snatched away in a fiery chariot; the Church too will be snatched away.

Do you not believe me? Believe Paul, in whom Christ spoke: “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

89. Many are sent to build her: patriarchs are sent, prophets are sent, the archangel Gabriel is sent, countless angels are dispatched, and the multitude of the heavenly host praises God, because the building of this city is drawing near.

[Col. 1585D] Many are sent to her, but Christ alone builds her—and yet he is not alone, because the Father is present. And if he alone builds her, he does not alone claim the grace of so great a building.

It is written concerning the temple that Solomon built, in which there was a type of the Church, that seventy thousand carried burdens on their shoulders, eighty thousand cut stones, and three thousand six hundred were appointed over the work (2 Chronicles 2:2).

[Note: The old editions and seven manuscripts read: “because there were three thousand six hundred who carried on their shoulders, and seventy thousand stonecutters or cutters of stone, or even stonecutters, and eighty thousand who carried burdens. Let them come …” Others, together with the Roman edition, read as we do in the text, except that in most of them the words “and three thousand six hundred overseers of the work” are missing. Still others, with the order slightly inverted, preserve the same meaning as the text.]

Let those angels come; let the stonecutters come; let the excess be cut away from our stones, and let the rough places be smoothed. Let those who carry on their shoulders also come, for it is written: “They shall be carried upon the shoulders” (Isaiah 49:22).

90. He came, then, to John, since you have learned the rest. He came to John’s baptism; but John’s baptism involved repentance for sins (Matthew 3:13). And therefore John tried to prevent him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (ibid., 14).

Why do you come to me, who have no sin? The one who has sin ought to be baptized by me. But why should the one who committed no sin seek a bath of repentance?

“Allow it for now”—that is, while the Church is being built—“for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (ibid., 15).

What is righteousness except mercy? “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains forever” (Psalm 111:9). He gave grace to me, the poor man; he gave it to me, the needy, when I had not previously possessed it. His righteousness therefore remains forever.

What is righteousness except that, whatever you wish another to do, you should first begin yourself and urge others by your example? What is righteousness except that the one who assumed flesh should not, as God, exclude the experience or service of flesh, but, as a human being, conquer the flesh in order to teach me to conquer it?

He taught me by what means I could bury the filth of a flesh weighed down and burdened by earthly vices beneath my crimes and renew it through virtues.

91. O truly divine providence displayed in the Lord’s very humility! The more abject the humility, the more divine the providence. God is revealed through the bitterness of his injuries; and through the use of remedies, he is proved to be God who needed no remedies.

For what is more divine for drawing peoples to himself than that no one should avoid the bath of grace, when Christ did not avoid the bath of repentance? Let no one say that he is excluded from sin when Christ came as the remedy for sins.

If Christ washed for us—indeed, if he washed us in his own body—how much more ought we to wash away our own sins? By what work, then, and by what mystery is God more clearly proved, although he is God in all things, than by this: that throughout the whole world, wherever the condition of the human race extends, across the divisions and expanses of separate regions, in one moment, in one body, God abolished the deceit of the ancient error and poured out the grace of the heavenly kingdom?

One went under [the water], but he raised all; one descended so that we all might ascend; one took upon himself the sins of all, so that in him the sins of all might die.

[Note: The editions Era., Gill., and Rom. read “but washed”; all Am. editions read “but raised.” The manuscripts unanimously read “but raised”; but Ful. and two Colb. manuscripts read “many” for “all.”]

Purify yourselves, therefore, as the Apostle says (James 4:8), because he purified himself for us, although he had no need of purification.

This is what concerns us.

92. Now let us consider the mystery of the Trinity. We speak of one God, but we confess the Father, and we confess the Son as God. For although it is written, “You shall love the Lord your God, and you shall serve him alone” (Deuteronomy 10:20), the Son denied that he was alone when he said: “Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32).

Nor is he alone now, for the Father testifies that he is present. The Holy Spirit is also present; for the Trinity can never be separated from itself.

Finally, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove. How, then, do heretics say that he alone is in heaven who is not alone on earth?

Let us attend to the mystery: why in the form of a dove? Grace requires the simplicity of the bath, so that we may be simple like doves. Grace requires the peace of the bath, which in the ancient type a dove once carried to the ark, the only place preserved from the flood (Genesis 8:11).

He taught me whose type that dove was—he who has now deigned to descend in the form of a dove. Through that branch and that ark he taught that there was a type of the peace of the Church, because amid the very floods of the world the Holy Spirit brings fruitful peace to his Church.

David also taught this when, seeing through the prophetic Spirit the sacrament of baptism, he said: “Who will give me wings like a dove?” (Psalm 54:7).

[Note: The Roman edition reads “which in the ancient type [the dove] brought as a symbol of the olive.” It is indeed certain that the words “in the ancient type” designate the olive, as is clear from what follows; but that is no reason for forcing the word into the text. Moreover, among secular authors as well, the olive as a symbol of peace is too well known to be unknown even to one only lightly educated. They explain the reason for this symbolism by saying that olive oil is useful in the arts that flourish most in peacetime.]

93. The Holy Spirit therefore came, but attend to the mystery. He came to Christ. For all things were made through him . . . . . and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17). But observe the benevolent Lord, who alone submitted himself to insults, who alone did not seek grace. And where did he build the Church? “I will ask the Father,” he says, “and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor recognizes him” (John 14:16–17). It was therefore fitting that he displayed himself in bodily form, since the substance of divinity is not visible.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “because in the substance of divinity,” etc.]

94. We have seen the Spirit, but in bodily form; let us also see the Father. But because we cannot see him, let us listen. For the benevolent God is present and will not abandon his temple. He wishes every soul to be built up completely; he wishes to shape it for salvation; he wishes to transfer living stones from earth to heaven. He loves his temple; let us also love him. If we love God, let us keep his commandments. If we love him, let us know him. For whoever says that he knows him but does not keep his commandments is a liar (1 John 2:4). How can one love God who does not love truth, when God is truth?

Let us therefore listen to the Father. For the Father is invisible; but the Son also, according to his divinity, is invisible, since “no one has ever seen God.” Since, therefore, the Son of God—insofar as he is God the Son—is not visible, he wished to manifest himself in bodily form. And because the Father did not bear a body, the Father therefore wished to prove to us that he was present in the Son, saying: “You are my Son; in you I am well pleased.” If you wish to learn that the Son is always present with the Father, read the Son’s utterance: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psalm 138:8). If you seek the Father’s testimony, you have heard it from John. Believe, therefore, the one to whom Christ entrusted himself to be baptized, to whom the Father entrusted the Son with a heavenly voice, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “Although the Son of God, insofar as he is God, is not seen, he wished to manifest,” etc. The old edition reads, “Although the Son of God . . . . . is God, he is not seen, but he wished to manifest himself.” The written codices we follow depart less from these readings.]

95. Where are the Arians, who do not approve of the Son in whom the Father was well pleased? This is not something I say, nor did any human being say it. For God did not speak through a human being, nor through angels or archangels; rather, the voice sent from heaven by the Father himself confirmed it. Elsewhere the same Father repeats this, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5)—that is, plainly, “listen to him”: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Therefore, whoever does not believe in the Son does not believe in the Father. He is the Father’s witness concerning the Son; if the Son is doubted, the Father’s testimony is not believed.

Moreover, when he says, “In whom I am well pleased,” he praises not something alien to the Son, but what is his own. For what does “In whom I am well pleased” mean except that everything the Son has, the Father also has, just as everything belonging to the Father belongs to the Son? The Son said: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). For the power of an undivided divinity does not distinguish between the Father and the Son, but shares one power between the Father and the Son.

Let us believe the Father, whose voice the elements echoed; let us believe the Father, to whose voice the elements rendered obedience. The world believed in the elements; let it believe in human beings. It believed in lifeless things; let it believe in the living. It believed in mute things; let it believe in those who speak. It believed in things that lack understanding; let it believe in those who have received understanding so that they might know God.

[Note: The words “It believed in those things that have no sense” are absent in seven manuscripts, including some of no low quality. Since these words are not absolutely necessary to the meaning, they may have entered later codices. Since, however, they occur in many manuscripts and all the printed editions, it seemed best not to remove them.]

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1589]

[Col. 1589A] 1313 (Verse 23.) “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being thought to be the son of Joseph.”

1. Since we are going to speak about the genealogies, and since we see that there is some divergence between the Gospel according to Matthew and this Gospel whose interpretation we have in hand, let us demonstrate, with as much diligence as we can, that the holy men did not say contradictory things. For it is not credible that they could have disagreed, especially concerning the deeds of the Lord and Savior.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “especially concerning the genealogies,” etc.]

2. First of all, no one should be troubled by what is written: “Being thought to be the son of Joseph.” He was rightly thought to be so, because he was not so by nature; but he was thought to be so because Mary, who was betrothed to Joseph her husband, had given birth to him. Thus you have: “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter?” (Matthew 13:55).

We have explained above why he was born through a virgin; we have also explained why through a betrothed woman, and why the Lord and Savior wished to be born at the time of the census. It does not seem out of place also to explain why he had a carpenter for a father. For by this typology he demonstrates that the one who fashioned all things and created the world was his father, in accordance with what is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1).

For although human things are not to be compared with divine things, the type remains complete: the Father of Christ works with fire and Spirit and, like a good craftsman of the soul, rounds away our faults. He quickly applies the axe to unfruitful trees; he knows how to cut away what is small and preserve what is lofty in the heights; by the fire of the Spirit he softens hardened minds; and he forms the entire human race for various uses through the differing quality of its ministries.

[Note: What kind of craftsman Saint Joseph was is disputed. Some maintain that he was a blacksmith, some a stonemason, and more commonly a carpenter. Hence the saying of the churchman addressed to Julian the Apostate: “But this son of the carpenter prepares for himself a wooden coffin for his death.” Ambrose seems to indicate that Joseph practiced both the crafts of blacksmithing and carpentry, as the following clearly shows.]

Why, however, is Joseph’s genealogy described rather than Mary’s, since Mary gave birth to Christ through the Holy Spirit, while Joseph seems to have had no part in the Lord’s generation? We might wonder about this if the custom of Scripture did not instruct us; Scripture always seeks the origin through the man. Thus you have: “Perez was the son of Judah, prince of the tribe. He fathered Hezron, and Hezron fathered Aram, and Aram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, and Nahshon fathered Salmon, and Salmon fathered Boaz, and Boaz fathered Obed, and Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David” (Matthew 1:3ff.).

For the person of the man is sought; he also asserts the dignity of lineage in the senate and in the other civic curiae.

[Note: Among the Romans there were thirty curiae into which Romulus divided the entire people; other cities also imitated this custom. Our Doctor therefore indicates that men, not women, were customarily entered and registered in the records of their respective curiae. The word also has other meanings, which may be gathered from the Theodosian Code, Book 16, Title 2, Books 2, 3, and 21, and elsewhere. Rosinus, Book 6 of Roman Antiquities, chapter 2, and others also report some of them.]

How disgraceful it would be, then, if, leaving aside the origin of the man, the origin of the woman were sought, so that he who was to be proclaimed to all the peoples of the world might appear to have had no father!

4. But elsewhere also let us show that the genealogy proceeded in a different order, lest here too the Evangelists seem to disagree, since they followed the ancient order. Thus you have: “There was a man from Arath, and his name was Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Eli, son of Tohu, from Mount Ephraim” (1 Samuel 1:1).

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “from Ramathaim Zophim . . . . . son of Jeroham, son of Eli, son of Zophai.” The manuscripts of Car, Gem, and Prat read, “from Ramath,” etc. Again, Gem and Prat have “son of Jeremel”; Car has “Jeromel, son of Eli, son of Zoi.” Corb agrees with these, except that it reads “from Arath” and writes “Jeremel.” The remaining manuscripts, together with the old editions, give our reading.]

You see that the description of lineage from fathers to sons and from sons to fathers has been arranged according to ancient custom. Everywhere you see the family traced through the generations of men.

[Note: “Do not be surprised if Saint Matthew . . . . . traverses the order”; these words were omitted in the Roman edition.]

Do not be surprised that Matthew traces the order of the generations from Abraham to Joseph, while Luke traces it from Joseph to Adam and to God. Do not be surprised that Joseph’s origin is described. For since he was born according to the flesh, he ought to follow the usage of the flesh; and since he came into the world, he ought to be described according to the custom of the world—especially since Mary’s origin is also contained in Joseph’s origin.

For since Joseph was a just man, he certainly took a wife from his own tribe and homeland; nor could a just man act against what was prescribed by the Law. Thus you have: “The sons of Israel shall each remain attached to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers, and they shall not pass from one tribe to another; and every daughter who possesses an inheritance among the tribes of the sons of Israel shall be the wife of one of the people and of the tribe of her father” (Numbers 36:6–8).

Therefore, at the time of the census Joseph also went up from the house and homeland of David (Luke 2:4–5), to register with Mary his wife. Since she, from the same house and the same homeland, brought forward a registration, she plainly indicates that she belonged to the same tribe and the same homeland.

5. Elizabeth is also introduced as Mary’s kinswoman (Luke 1:36). First, because all Jews are kinsmen, as the Apostle taught you when he said: “For I could wish that I myself were accursed . . . . . for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Romans 9:3–4). They were therefore kinswomen because both were Israelites; and they were likewise kinswomen because both were from the tribe of Judah.

You have learned that Mary was from the tribe of Judah; learn the same of Elizabeth. For: “Mary arose in those days and went into the hill country with haste, to a city of Judah,” he says, “and entered the house of Zechariah” (Luke 1:39–40). Since Moses prescribed that each person should dwell within his own tribe (Numbers 2:2), she was certainly also in the tribe of Judah when she remained in a city of Judah—especially since priests belonged to Elizabeth’s family, and God is their portion.

How beautiful it is, moreover, that while one woman bore Christ’s herald and the other bore Christ, while one conceived through the Holy Spirit and the other, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied, they should also according to the flesh have been kinswomen—women who according to God were not without the fellowship of spiritual kinship.

And if the man is the head of every woman according to the holy Apostle (Ephesians 5:23), and “the two shall be one flesh” according to divine law (Genesis 2:24), surely those who were one flesh and one spirit could not have appeared to possess different homelands and tribes. In addition, the angel Gabriel had foretold concerning the Lord: “God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1:32). It is therefore certain that Mary too sprang from the line of David. At the same time we learn that it makes no difference in what order the sequence of the genealogy is expressed, since the route is open in either direction.

6. Why Saint Matthew began to enumerate Christ’s genealogy from Abraham, whereas Saint Luke carried it from Christ all the way to God, must now be explained. But first, why, although Saint Matthew began the genealogical order from Abraham, did he not write, “The book of the genealogy of Abraham,” but rather, “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1)? And why did he name these two above all others? I think this should by no means be passed over.

For the most faithful authors of the lineage are not chosen without purpose, so that we may understand that in the very generation according to the flesh, spiritual succession is chiefly required. These are the two men into whom the divine promises flowed.

7. The first is Abraham, who, before the Law of Moses and before the Jewish people, left his own things behind, came to know God, and earned the testimony of faith: “He believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). From God he also received the oracle spoken to him: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you; and I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you will be blessed. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you, and in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:1–3).

You see, therefore, that the gathering of the nations and the most sacred assembly of the Church were first promised to this man by the divine oracle. For this reason he had to be designated as the author of the lineage, since he was the first to merit the promise of restoring the Church.

8. David too is rightly declared an author of the lineage, because he received under oath the response that Christ would arise from him according to the flesh. Thus it is written: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not retract it: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne’” (Psalm 131:11). And elsewhere: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: if I should lie to David, his seed will remain forever, and his throne like the sun before me” (Psalm 88:36–38).

[Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read, “And in Chronicles.” Several others read, “And in the book of Chronicles.” Corb and some others have the better reading, “in Chronicles,” from the Greek ἐν Παραλειπομένοις, “in the Paralipomena,” that is, Chronicles.]

And in Chronicles: “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, one who shall come from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He himself shall build me a house, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me, and I will not withdraw my mercy from him, as I withdrew it from those who were before you” (1 Chronicles 17:11–13).

Through Isaiah also the same Lord God revealed the Lord’s generation, saying: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isaiah 11:1–2). And below: “There shall be a root of Jesse, and the one who rises up to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (ibid., 10).

And elsewhere: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, whose beginning is upon his shoulders, and his name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel. For I will bring peace upon the rulers and salvation; his power shall be great, and of his peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David and in his kingdom” (Isaiah 9:6).

In this passage, according also to Aquila’s translation, we see that the promise was made not as concerning a human being, but concerning one who would be beyond a human being. For Aquila translated it: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his measure has been made upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Powerful One, Father of the Age, Prince of Peace. His discipline has been fulfilled, and of his peace there is no end, upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom.”

9. All these things correspond to Christ, as is clearly marked by the oracles; nor can the fruit of divine power be attributed to Solomon, who was David’s son and whose end is unquestionably known. For the end of Solomon’s reign and peace is shown in the books of Kings. There is one Christ, whose kingdom has no end.

Furthermore, Solomon ruled over no nations, whereas Christ gathered the Church from all the nations. Finally, while David was still alive, Solomon was born and attained the kingdom. But the one who is promised is shown to arise after David’s death, as you have it: “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up from your seed one who shall come from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He himself shall build me a house, and I will establish his throne forever” (1 Chronicles 17:11–12).

Did Solomon reign forever, when he reigned only forty years? “I will be a father to him,” it says, “and he shall be a son to me” (ibid., 13). Who is this true Son of God, except the one to whom it was said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7)? And: “I will not withdraw my mercy from him . . . . . and I will preserve him faithfully in my house and in his kingdom forever” (1 Chronicles 17:13–14)?

But we learn from the sequence of the divine readings that Solomon perhaps went so far astray for this reason: so that human beings would not go astray and believe that the promise had passed to him. For he built a temple to the idol Astarte because of his love for a woman, and the Lord was angry with Solomon (1 Kings 11:4ff.).

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “because of his love for women.”]

If, therefore, he began to reign while David was alive—for you have it that when David was informed that Solomon was reigning, King David worshiped on his bed and said: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who has given me today one of my seed sitting upon my throne, and my eyes see it” (1 Kings 1:48)—if he went astray, if he offended, you see that the sequence of the promise pledged Christ.

10. For this reason the Evangelist selected these two authors of the lineage: one who received the promise concerning the gathering of the peoples, and the other who received the oracle concerning the generation of Christ. Therefore, although David is later in the order of succession, he is described before Abraham in the genealogy of the Lord, because it is greater to have received the promise concerning Christ than concerning the Church, since the Church itself exists through Christ.

Thus one is the prince of the lineage according to the flesh, [Note: Nine manuscripts in an older hand read, “the other prince of the lineage.”] and the other is the prince of the lineage according to the spirit; one according to the grace of the seed, the other according to the faith of the peoples. For the one who saves is greater than the one who is saved.

Therefore he is called the son of David: “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matthew 1:1). He had to be called the son, in the first place, of the one to whom the giving of a son had been promised, although the Apostle also says that Christ was promised to Abraham: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say, “and to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as referring to one: “And to your seed,” who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Thus the particularity of the generation is assigned to one, while primacy is assigned to the other.

To David it was granted that Jesus should be called his son; to Abraham, as the prince, was reserved the prerogative of the family and of the nations, so that the beginning of the Lord’s generation might flow from Abraham. For since he is the author of faith, Scripture also had to assert him as the author of the divine generation.

11. Hence Luke also thought that Christ’s origin should be referred to God, since God is the true begetter of Christ—either the Father according to true generation, or the author of the regeneration of the mystical gift according to baptism. Therefore he did not begin to describe Christ’s genealogy from the beginning; rather, after explaining his baptism, wishing to demonstrate through baptism that God is the author of all things, he asserted that Christ also proceeded from God in the order of succession.

He wove everything together, so as to demonstrate that Christ is the Son of God both according to nature, according to grace, and according to the flesh. What could be a clearer indication of divine generation than that, when he was about to speak of the genealogy, he first presented the Father himself speaking: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22 above)?

12. Here too some are accustomed to raise questions: Matthew enumerates forty-two generations from Abraham to Christ, whereas Luke gives fifty; and Matthew describes the genealogy as proceeding through different persons from those through whom Luke describes it. In this you can now establish what we said: although Matthew wove the ancestors of the Lord’s lineage through some persons and Luke through others in the order of generation, both nevertheless signified Abraham and David as the remaining authors of the lineage.

13. The fact that Matthew thought the genealogy should proceed through Solomon, whereas Luke proceeded through Nathan, seems to indicate, respectively, Christ’s royal and priestly family. We should not understand this as though one were more truthful than the other; rather, each agrees with the other in equal faith and truth.

For he truly belonged according to the flesh both to a royal family and to a priestly family: king from kings, priest from priests, although the oracle is expressed not concerning carnal things but concerning heavenly things. For he is both a king who rejoices in God’s power, to whom judgment is entrusted by the Father, the King, and a priest forever, according to what is written: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4).

Both therefore rightly preserved the faith: Matthew demonstrated the origin traced through kings, while Luke, by tracing to Christ the series of the lineage transmitted by God through priests, declared that origin itself to be holier. At the same time, in this the figure of the calf is also signified, since everywhere it considers the priestly mystery something to be preserved.

14. Nor should you be surprised that according to Luke there are more successions from Abraham to Christ and fewer according to Matthew, since you acknowledge that the genealogy proceeded through different persons. It can happen that some people lived to an advanced age, while men of another generation died prematurely, since we see many old men living with their grandchildren, while other men die immediately after their sons are born.

15. We also observe that Saint Matthew remembered Jacob, who was Joseph’s father, as the son of Matthan (Matthew 1:15), whereas Luke described Joseph, to whom Mary was betrothed, as the son of Heli, and Heli as the son of Melchi (Luke 3:24).

How could one person have two fathers, namely Heli and Jacob? How could there also be two paternal grandfathers, Matthan and Melchi? But if you inquire carefully, you will find that, according to the prescription of the ancient Law, two brothers could father different sons by the same wife.

[Note: The Roman edition removed the word “uterine.”]

[Note: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, chapter 7.]

It is related that Matthan, who traced his descent from Solomon, fathered Jacob and died while his wife was still alive. Melchi then took her as his wife, and Heli was born from her. Again, when Heli died without children, Jacob was joined to his brother’s wife and fathered Joseph. Joseph is called Jacob’s son according to the Law, because, according to the ancient Law, a brother was to raise up the seed of his deceased brother.

Thus Joseph was called the son of two men, not because he was begotten by both, but because he became the son of one according to generation and of the other according to the Law. In this prescription of the Law, the Jewish people did not understand that the enduring continuation of the seed of the dead was being promised to us; instead, by receiving the oracle according to the letter, it corrupted its grace.

For there was another brother who would raise up the seed of deceased brothers—not a brother according to physical kinship, but a brother according to the purity of grace. And therefore perhaps: “A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem” (Psalm 48:8). For that brother was not a biological brother, but the Lord and mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, propagated the grace of the resurrection.

Although this verse also has another interpretation, we shall discuss it in its proper place (Commentary on Psalm 48).

16. Nor does it seem unreasonable that Saint Matthew, by doubling the mystical number, thought that the generations should be divided into four tens: from Abraham to David, from David to the Babylonian captivity, and from the Babylonian captivity to Christ. In this he likewise signified the stages of the changes.

For from Abraham to David the Jewish people lived without kings; the just kingdom began with David. Then the entire lineage of the Jews proceeded through kings, and their kingdoms remained inviolate until their captivity. After the captivity, the circumcised nobility of a people declining toward ruin began to wane.

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read, “But concerning the fifty generations”; several more numerous and better manuscripts read, “. . . . . successors.”]

Concerning the fifty successions that Luke thought should be woven together from Abraham, the preservation of the mystical significance of the number is sufficiently clear. For both the number ten and the number seven are mystical, and when each is repeated three times, it signifies a mystery. Luke’s fifty and Matthew’s forty also revealed the mystical number abundantly and unmistakably.

17. Many also wonder why Matthew thought that the memory of Tamar, a notorious woman as they regard her, should be woven into the Lord’s genealogy. Why also Ruth? Why also that woman who was Uriah’s wife and, after her husband was killed, entered into marriage with David? This is especially puzzling since he nowhere mentions Sarah, Rebecca, or Rachel, those holy women.

Thus you have: “Abraham fathered Isaac, Isaac fathered Jacob, Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers; Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar” (Matthew 1:2–3). The Evangelist therefore did not insert this woman’s name without purpose; her case must meanwhile be treated separately.

18. First, if you apply your mind to the truth, this woman was not so much notorious as just. For she did not seek the use of temporal lust, but desired the grace of succession. It was shameful not to have children; this too was punished by the authority of civil laws.

[Note: How shameful it was before the virgin birth for married people to remain childless is shown by Rachel in Genesis 30:1, where she says to her husband Jacob, “Give me children, or else I shall die.” We learn the same from the grief of Hannah, Samuel’s mother (1 Samuel 1), and from the words of Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist (Luke 1:25). Civil laws were also enacted among the Romans against the unmarried and the childless, namely the Papian and Julian Laws. Augustus increased their penalties, as Suetonius and Tacitus report. Christian emperors eventually abolished them, although Constantine the Great and Theodosius the Younger had already reduced them substantially, as may be understood from the Theodosian Code, Book 8, Title 16, single law, “On the weakening of the penalties against celibacy,” etc., and Title “On the right of children,” etc., Laws 2 and 3. On these matters, as also on the Papian and Julian Laws, consult Gothofredus. Furthermore, the statement that “before Christ’s coming the grace of virginity and widowhood had not yet flourished” should be interpreted so that it does not absolutely deny that there were people who practiced these virtues before the Lord’s coming—the contrary is demonstrated by Elijah and Elisha concerning virginity, and by Judith and Anna the prophetess concerning widowhood—but indicates that these virtues were neither very common nor highly esteemed before Christ’s time.]

Judah had promised her to his son and had long postponed the marriage pact. During the delay her betrothed died. Before Christ’s coming the grace of virginity and widowhood had not yet flourished.

[Note: The words “before Christ’s coming” are omitted in the Roman edition.]

Grieving that she had remained without children, she devised a stratagem out of her desire for offspring and forestalled Judah’s plan: she offered herself to him in an adornment after she learned that his wife had died. You see that the woman’s life is approved. She did not seize another’s marriage bed; she was not adorned like a prostitute out of a prostitute’s motive. She did not seek wandering lust, but, after being defrauded for a long time of the promise made by her father-in-law, she wished, through a reversal of the deception, to obtain the fruit of succession from the family she had chosen.

Who, then, was more chaste: she who waited so long for the promise, or he who could not endure the love offered to him? She who did not shun her betrothed’s family, or he who thought her a prostitute? She who did not permit her body to those willing for intercourse, or he who completed by the woman’s chastity, for the grace of succession, what he had begun through an erring intention? She who had no children and feared that the delay of marriage would exclude her from the proper time of conception, who chose the gravity of the more mature man, or he who loved the age of the younger woman?

Finally, he himself confessed, saying: “Tamar has been justified more than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah” (Genesis 38:26). Thus she wished to put the very one who exacted it to the test of her chastity. In the end she never afterward sought a man; she assumed the dress of widowhood and abstained from intercourse. But he, unable to endure even one hour, though he had demanded years of chastity from the girl, drove away his mourning, changed his clothing, cut his hair, left the funeral pyre, and as a lover climbed into the bed.

[Note: He changed his clothing, namely the clothing of mourning or widowhood. The statement that he also “cut his hair” alludes to the ancient custom, especially among eastern peoples, of growing the hair and beard during mourning. What follows, that he “left the funeral pyre,” uses “pyre” broadly for a tomb. For the Hebrews, like the Egyptians, did not burn the dead.]

19. But we do not defend her in such a way as to accuse him; rather, the mystery expressed by the fruit of their union excuses both. For the woman gave birth to Perez and Zerah, sons; she gave birth to twins.

Therefore Matthew did not mention both without purpose, although the argument required only the mention of Perez: “Perez fathered Hezron, and Hezron fathered Aram” (Matthew 1:3), and thereafter each in sequence. Why, when Isaac fathered two sons and Jacob several, did the sequence of Scripture mention only those individual sons whom the purpose of the Lord’s succession required, whereas here it mentioned both, unless there is a mystery in both?

20. We have treated the moral aspect, because she did not practice the works of a prostitute but chose the gifts of fertility. Let us treat the historical aspect and examine the mystical one. For it cannot be without mystery that she received a ring, a necklace, and a staff. The person who deserves to receive an ornament, a seal, and authority is not insignificant: the seal of deeds, the adornment of the breast, and the emblem of royal liberty.

To begin with the history: when Tamar was giving birth, you read that one of the children extended a hand from her womb. The midwife seized it and tied a scarlet thread around it, saying: “This one shall come out first” (Genesis 38:28). But when the child drew his hand back into his mother’s womb, his brother immediately came out. The midwife said: “Why has the hedge been cut through by you?” and she called his name Perez. After him his brother came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread, and she called his name Zerah (ibid., 29–30).

You see how many enigmas the mystery reveals: the hand extended first, the scarlet thread tied, the hand withdrawn, the midwife’s twofold utterance—that one should come out first and the other should cut through the hedge.

[Col. 1597C] 21. Why did one extend his hand from the womb, while the other came first in his actual birth, unless the mystery of the twins describes the twofold life of peoples: one according to the Law, the other according to faith; one according to the letter, the other according to grace? Grace came first, before the Law; faith came first, before the letter.

Therefore the type of grace extended its hand first, because the action of grace came first. This occurred in Job, Melchizedek, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who lived by faith without the Law: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Melchizedek also displayed the grace of the holy sacrifice as a preceding figure (Genesis 14:18). For the holy patriarchs, preceding the Law, released from the bonds of prescriptions, shone forth with the free and similar grace of the Gospel that we possess.

[Note: “The life of the peoples.” The final word was omitted by the Roman edition.]

[Col. 1597D] 22. Their younger brother represents the second order of piety. For the first order is found among the patriarchs, and the second among kings and priests. Both lives are according to God, because those who served in a religious and pious warfare according to the law of Moses are not excluded from grace and honor. But the fruit of piety is earlier in its founders than in its heirs.

Zerah comes first; his name means “rising” or “east.” For the light of piety is the true splendor of the East—of the one who said: “The Rising One is my name,” whose ray of light first shone among the patriarchs (Zechariah 6:12). These men first sent forth the course of their life in this world; in their hand the pattern of our own actions also went before, as though we were still held in the womb of nature, which was in the process of giving birth to a fuller body.

But the observance of the Law was set in the middle like a hedge placed across the way, and in a certain sense the life of our ancestors appears to have been cut through. Concerning this, the midwife in the type—perhaps Justice—who received us when we were brought forth from the womb of mother Nature, is reported to have said: “This one shall come out first.”

And truly that order of piety was marvelous: it was impressed not by Moses, nor by any human being, nor through a human being, but by a certain gift of wisdom freely pouring itself forth.

### 23

The first discipline of piety, then, is according to the Gospel; for through the cross and the blood we believe in Christ, whose day Abraham saw and rejoiced (John 8:56); whose grace Noah, in the type of the Church, perceived beforehand through spiritual understanding; whose place in the sacrifice Isaac did not refuse (Genesis 22:10); whom Jacob, when he had overcome, worshiped (Genesis 32:25); whose garments Isaiah saw reddened—for according to the Gospel, the life even of the prophets is [the Gospel’s life] (Isaiah 63:2). In whose blood that Rahab, the prostitute, by a type indicated the future public emblem of salvation amid the world’s destruction (Joshua 2:1), in mystery indicated the Church as the future public emblem of salvation amid the world's destruction: she does not refuse the union of many strangers, and the more closely joined to many she is, the more chaste she is: an immaculate virgin, without wrinkle, sound in modesty, popular in love, a chaste prostitute, a barren widow, a fruitful virgin.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “and through the blood we believe in Christ . . . prefigured in the type of the ark,” etc.]

[Note: One manuscript of the Codex Mich. and the Codex Colb. reads “undefiled mother.” After three words where the editions read “filled with love,” a few manuscripts read “chaste with popular love,” while by far the majority read “popular in love, chaste.” This is better; it means the same as “beloved by the people,” which is not unsuitably applied to the Church.]

A prostitute, because she is frequented by many lovers with the enticement of affection, yet without the defilement of sin: “He who joins himself to a prostitute is one body” (1 Corinthians 6:16). A barren widow, who does not know how to bear children to her husband while he is absent: the husband came, and generated this people and populace. A fruitful virgin, who gave birth to this multitude with the fruit of love, without the practice of lust.

### 24

But, to return to the history: what do the words of the midwife mean when she says, “This one will come out first,” except that he bore the type of the one who, later in bodily birth, was first in power and truth, and claimed for himself primacy over all? Hence John also says: “After me comes a man who was made before me” (John 1:17).

What does it mean that she tied the scarlet thread on his hand, except that he was a type of the one who, by the sign of his cross and the shedding of his blood, made the act of humankind illustrious?

[Note: Some manuscripts read “by the incision of his own cross.”]

Therefore, after he withdrew his hand, as though an opening had been made in the hedge, his brother came out—the one whom the Apostle called the middle wall of the hedge or enclosure (Ephesians 2:14)—and he himself received his name from the incision; for *Phares* means “division.” Hence the Pharisees were so called because they separated themselves from the associations of many.

Yet it would have been happier and far better if the hedge had not been cut, but had remained one and undivided. This could have happened if the life that first put forth its hand—that is, displayed its conduct—had been followed by the practice of the life that came afterward.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “It would have followed that the life which came afterward…”]

For it would have been much better if the circumcised people had wished to imitate the life of their ancestors. Thus there would have been one hedge, one enclosure, one building of those who came before and those who followed. But because the weakness of the later generation could not fulfill that first course of life, an incision was undoubtedly made in the hedge or enclosure that had been built according to God, and a middle wall was inserted, so that the hedge—that is, the perpetual and continuous building of good conduct—might be broken.

A hedge is what surrounds a fruitful field, keeps out the attacks of thieves, encloses cultivated land, and separates the deserted. An enclosure also closes off a house: if it remains, the house is safe. Therefore he says: “I will take away its enclosure, and it shall become a spoil” (Isaiah 5:5).

### 25

Let us desire that this enclosure of our house, the spiritual house that is within us, remain intact. For it cannot be built up by man, but by the living God, who says: “And I surrounded it with an enclosure” (Isaiah 5:2). Those who lost the enclosure therefore lost salvation. Let the enclosure remain, then; let this hedge remain.

Do you wish to know how useful a hedge is? “Hedge your ears with thorns and briars, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Sirach 28:28). For this hedge defends you from guilt.

### 26

Therefore the Lord Jesus, who afterward came into the light according to the flesh, restoring that ancient fortification of the hedge, reformed us according to the conduct of our ancestors and the ancient simplicity of faith. Hence the prophet also said of him: “You shall be called the builder of the hedge” (Isaiah 58:12).

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “And the prophecy said.”]

For he removed that obstacle which divided the unity of mind and body and the continuity of a simple life; and he himself became our peace, who made both one and dissolved the middle wall of the hedge.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “He dissolved the middle wall of the enclosure.”]

The Apostle explains that wall as “the hostility in the flesh” (Ephesians 2:14). The Lord therefore removed this hostility and restored peace; he nullified the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in one new man. In this he signifies not only the outward and the inward, but also the Jew and the Greek, so that Christ might be all and in all.

The Lord of the Sabbath removed the superstition of the bodily Sabbath and, as it were, dissolved the middle wall of the Law, which by the difficulty of its decrees prevented us from that piety which is according to God. For according to the Law of Moses it was neither easy nor practicable for the nations to serve God, since the empty superstition of the Jews held the pure devotion of the nations back from undertaking its observance.

[Note: The Roman edition, contrary to the authority of the other editions and manuscripts, reads “had removed, and possible.” But we have already observed that *possible* is often used for “difficult.”]

What then? Is the Law useless? Far from it. It is useful for unbelievers, necessary for the weak; it restrained the unstable and erring by the severity of a saving commandment and enclosed them through careful observance.

The Law is good, however, because it is spiritual. It is therefore not good to the one who does not think it spiritual: the one who, made small and lowly in mind, could not see the majesty that is above the Law, namely Christ. But Isaiah, lofty in mind, looking as though above that wall, saw the glory of God (Isaiah 6:1), which is seen upon mountains, not upon hills.

### 27

The Church therefore taught us in the Song of Songs that this wall could not obstruct our Lord Jesus Christ, nor the one who followed Christ, saying:

“The voice of my brother: behold, here he comes, leaping over the mountains and bounding over the hills. My brother is like a goat or a fawn of deer upon the mountains of Bethel. Behold, here he is behind our wall, looking through the windows, looking through the lattice. My brother answered and said to me: Rise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove; for behold, the winter has passed, the rain has gone away and departed; flowers have appeared on the earth, the time for pruning has come, the voice of the turtledove has been heard” (Song of Songs 2:8–12).

The flowers are the apostles; the time of harvest is the fruit of Christ.

[Note: The edition and some manuscripts read: “The fruit is Christ.”]

The voice of the turtledove is the voice of the Church.

Rightly, therefore, after the Son of God saw earthly human beings neither walking toward heavenly things nor able to move because they were hemmed in by bodily constraints—for “there was no one who did good, there was not even one” (Psalm 13:3)—he himself deigned to descend to the earth, so that he might remove that wall of the Law, that is, a certain mass and superstition of bodily understanding, which oppressed and overshadowed the hearts of the peoples.

An enclosure, therefore, is better than a wall. Hence a whitewashed wall is not good. This was not said without purpose to the high priest, because he preserved the obstacles of the middle wall (Acts 23:3), which the Lord Jesus removed as a harsh service, so that he might infuse a clearer observance of religion. Thus not merely one nation of Jews, enclosed as it were by a bodily prescription of the Law, but all nations would be called through the Gospel to the worship of God.

### 28

There are therefore two twin persons and two twin lives; they are two twin forms of service, so that the earlier is better than the later. And therefore what is better has been restored.

Who, however, would deny that the Gospel surpasses the Law? The Law is nevertheless good, if you raise the mind above the letter; for “the letter kills” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

But what would this history possess of grace if we did not see the light of so great a mystery? The holy Apostle taught us to seek the secret of truth in the simplicity of history and to refer the meaning to certain discussions unintelligible according to the letter, when he wrote:

“Tell me, you who read the Law, have you not heard the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the one from the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one from the free woman was born according to the promise. These things,” he says, “are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants” (Galatians 4:21–24).

And below: “But the Jerusalem above is free” (ibid., 26).

[Note: All manuscripts read as above. The edition, however, reads: “Tell me, you who wish to be under the Law, have you not heard the Law?” This is supported by the Apostle’s text and by all versions except the Ethiopic, where, according to its translator, it reads: “You say to me: We are under the commandment of the Law, and you have not heard the Law.”]

### 29

Let us therefore reach, with loftiness of mind, toward that wall which the middle wall could not cut and divide. That wall of the Old Testament has been dissolved according to bodily understanding; the slave woman has been cast out, and the free woman is held fast.

From the free woman we are free; for the Church is free, and the Synagogue has been cast out. The Jewish people were serving as slaves; the yoke of slavery has been removed, a yoke that pressed down certain necks of our soul, preventing us from looking beyond the wall of the former life.

We have a good and light yoke, which, through the reins of peace and the bonds of grace, raises rather than weighs down those who are joined to it. This is the Lord whose type was previously represented in Zara, because the Lord Jesus, according to the flesh, was generated from the tribe and seed of that Zara—not only from a woman, but also under the Law—in order to redeem those who were under the Law by the price of his blood.

The reason his figure preceded in the hand of that Zara was that he might promise us that the one was coming who would restore the practice of the former life and reform, in the last Adam, the freedom he had granted to the first Adam, so that now the human race would be without the slavery of the Law.

### 30

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Thus, then, … described: ‘who was Obed, who was Boaz,’ and so forth. Why did Matthew also mention Ruth?”]

If, then, we have understood that Tamar was included among the Lord’s generations because of the mystery, we must certainly judge that Ruth too was not omitted for an equal reason. The holy Apostle seems to have had her in mind when, foreseeing in the Spirit that the calling of the nations of foreigners would be celebrated through the Gospel, he said that “the Law was not established for the righteous, but for the unrighteous” (1 Timothy 1:9).

How did Ruth, being a foreigner, marry a Jew? And for what reason did the evangelist think that mention of her union ought to be made in Christ’s genealogy, when it was forbidden by the order of the Law?

[Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read: “Therefore it does not appear that the Savior flowed from a legitimate generation,” etc. Gill, with a few manuscripts, reads: “Therefore it does not appear that the Savior, who was not from a legitimate generation, flowed,” etc.—a reading without sense. The Roman edition reads: “Therefore it appears that the Savior did not flow from an illegitimate generation,” etc. This is no better, although one Vatican manuscript supports it, except that the word “not” is absent before “legitimate.” The genuine reading is the one we restored from ten manuscripts of excellent authority.]

“Therefore, did the Savior not come from a legitimate generation” (Deuteronomy 23:3)? This seems offensive unless you return to the Apostle’s judgment, because the Law was not established for the righteous, but for the unrighteous.

For although she was a foreigner and a Moabite—especially since the Law of Moses prohibited these marriages and excluded Moabites from the Church, for it is written: “The Moabites shall not enter into the assembly of the Lord until the third and fourth generation, and forever”—how did she enter the Church, unless because in her conduct she became holy and immaculate, above the Law?

If the Law was established for the ungodly and sinners, then Ruth, who exceeded the definition of the Law, entered the Church, became one of the Israelites, and deserved to be counted among the ancestors of the Lord’s lineage. Chosen because of kinship of mind, not of body, she is a great example for us, because in her a figure preceded of the entrance into the Church of all of us who have been gathered from the nations.

Let us therefore imitate her, so that, because she deserved by her conduct this privilege of being admitted into her fellowship, as the history teaches, we too may, on account of our choice of conduct and with merits assisting us, be counted into the Church of the Lord.

### 31

For when famine pressed the Israelites in the earlier days of the Judges, a man went from Bethlehem, a city of Judea in which Christ was born, to dwell in the land of Moab with his wife and two sons. The man’s name was Elimelech, and the woman’s was Naomi.

His sons took Moabite wives for themselves: the name of one was Orpah, and the name of the second was Ruth. They lived there for about ten years, and then died. But the woman, left destitute of her two sons and her husband, learning that God had visited Israel and preparing to return home, began to urge her sons’ wives to return to their own home.

One consented; Ruth, however, remained with her mother-in-law. When her mother-in-law said to her, “Behold, your sister-in-law has returned to her people and to her gods; you too return with your sister-in-law,” Ruth replied:

“May it not happen to me that I should leave you and return to my gods; for wherever you go, I will go with you, and wherever you dwell, I will dwell. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. And wherever you die, I will die, and wherever you are buried, I will be buried” (Ruth 1:15, 17).

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “and return to my God.” Others, together with the editions, read: “and return to my gods.” But neither expression is found in the sacred copies, so it is likely that the mere repetition of Naomi’s words was introduced into the Ambrosian text by some copyist.]

And so the two came to Bethlehem. When Boaz, David’s great-grandfather (Ruth 4:13), learned of these qualities—of her holiness toward her mother-in-law, her devotion toward the dead, and her reverence toward God—he chose her as his wife according to the Law of Moses, in order to raise up the offspring of the deceased kinsman.

### 32

It is also worth observing that, when she was found in a field full of harvest, gathering the sheaves, as it is written (Ruth 2:17), and reserving fruit for her mother-in-law, she did not follow a young man but followed a mature man. Hence she deserved to hear: “You are a woman of virtue,” or, “You have shown your final mercy better than your first” (Ruth 3:10).

The final mercy of the gathered Church surpasses the earlier one.

[Note: Six highly esteemed manuscripts read as above, and the editions do not depart from them except that they read “to comprehend” in place of “we say,” as do many manuscripts. Some others read “surpasses the former,” in which there is no insignificant mystery; some: “surpasses the former. And there is no insignificant mystery,” etc. Some also omit “no.” Certainly, however, the words “in which there is no insignificant mystery” seem to have been displaced or added through the carelessness of copyists, since the same words are repeated shortly afterward.]

What we say here more briefly, because we have set it forth more fully in the books I wrote on the Faith (Book 3, *On the Faith to Gratian*, chapter 5), is that the one who was far away drew near, because the one who was near withdrew; and he acquired the sandal of the kinsman by accepting the woman.

For it was customary that, if the nearest kinsman did not wish to take his relative in marriage, he would remove his sandal and yield her to another (Ruth 4:7). In this there is no insignificant mystery, because the one who, in the type, took a foreign woman received the opportunity to evangelize.

### 33

Finally, the blessing of the elders testifies that this marriage occurred in a type. They said:

“May the Lord grant you the woman who enters your house, like Rachel and Leah, who built up the house of Israel; and may you act virtuously in Ephrathah, and may your name be renowned in Bethlehem. May your house become like the house of Phares, whom Tamar bore to Judah. May the Lord grant you offspring from this young woman.”

And Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife (ibid., 11–13), and she bore Obed, the father of Jesse and grandfather of David.

Rightly, therefore, the holy Matthew, intending through the Gospel to call the nations to the Church, recalled that the Lord himself, the founder of the gathering of the nations, assumed the generation of foreigners according to the flesh.

[Note: The editions of Erasmus and those following him read: “the Lord of the Gentile gathering.”]

Thus it was already then an indication that this generation would produce the one who would call the nations, whom all of us gathered from foreigners would follow, leaving our ancestral ties and saying to him who called us to the worship of God—for example, to Paul or to any bishop:

“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16).

Thus Ruth, like Leah and Rachel, forgetting her people and her father’s house, loosening the bond of the Law, entered the Church.

### 34

The one who did not accept the Church removed his sandal. And Moses is told: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exodus 3:5), so that he himself would not be believed to be the bridegroom of the Church.

Only the one who is the true bridegroom did not remove his sandal. Therefore John says: “Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen.”

Thus this too is a type, and he built up the house of Israel.

### 35

That her mention ought to have been inserted into the Lord’s genealogy is made clear by the expression of a deeper mystery, in which it was prophesied that Christ would be born from her stock in Ephrathah, when it is said:

“May the Lord grant you … to act virtuously in Ephrathah, and may your name be renowned in Bethlehem” (Ruth 4:11).

For what is the virtue except that which, through Christ, gathered together the peoples of the nations? And what is the name except that by which Bethlehem became the birthplace of the Lord according to the flesh?

Hence it was said through the prophet:

“And you, Bethlehem of Judah, are not the least among the princes of Judah; for from you shall come forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel” (Micah 5:2).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are not the least among the thousands of Judah,” evidently following the Septuagint, where it reads: καὶ σὺ Βηθλεὲμ οἶκος Ἐφραθὰ, ὀλιγοστὸς εἶ τοῦ εἶναι ἐν χιλιάσιν Ἰούδα —“And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are small to be among the thousands of Judah.” Yet you see that the negation is absent there, as it is acknowledged by no Bibles in other languages either.
