The older edition reads: “Bethlehem of Judah … among the princes of Judah.” Manuscripts support this reading, except that the best have “Bethlehem of Judea”; and some others read, “you are by no means the least,” as it is also found at Matthew 2:6.]

We therefore see that history, conduct, and mystery correspond to the mention of these women.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “that the commemoration of the history corresponds, and the mystery to the conduct.” The old edition, with a few manuscripts, reads: “to the commemoration, history; to the conduct, mystery,” while many manuscripts of great number and authority read as in the text.]

### 36

Nor do I deny, when I defend Tamar and Ruth, that sinners too were counted among the ancestors of the Lord’s lineage. The holy Luke, wishing to avoid mentioning them, followed another order of succession: he thought that neither Ahab, nor Jechoniah, nor finally the wife of Uriah should be named, so as to display an unstained succession of priestly lineage.

But just as the reasoning of Matthew’s purpose remains sound, so too Matthew’s purpose does not depart from the justice of reason.

[Note: All editions and manuscripts except three read: “Thus the reasoning of his purpose remains.” On the other hand, fourteen manuscripts of excellent quality have at the end of the passage: “which is contrary to the justice of reason,” whereas the edition and only four manuscripts read: “which is contrary to the reason of justice,” etc. Finally, where the editions read “to have been generated from Zara,” the fourteen manuscripts mentioned do not contain “from Zara.” This appears absurdly added, since Ambrose himself observes above, in section 19, not that Christ descended from Zara but from Phares. For what he says in section 29—that the Lord was generated from the tribe and seed of Zara—we interpret as though it had been written: “Christ was descended from the same tribe and seed from which Zara was born.”]

For when he was proclaiming that the Lord was generated according to the flesh, the one who would take upon himself the sins of all, subjected to insults and submitted to suffering, he did not think that the Lord should be declared exempt even from this aspect of piety: he did not refuse the disgrace of a defiled origin.

At the same time, he wished to prevent the Church from being ashamed of being gathered from sinners, since the Lord himself was born from sinners. Finally, he wished the benefit of redemption to begin even with his own ancestors, so that no one would think that the stain of origin could impede virtue; nor would anyone, insolently, boast of the nobility of his own lineage, or blush with excessive shame at the crimes of his parents, when the opportunity was given to overshadow the stain of origin with the flower of virtue.

### 37

Was not holy David, although many things concerning him are represented in mystery, all the more exalted because he recognized that he was a human being and thought that the sin committed in seizing Uriah’s wife had to be washed away by the tears of repentance, showing us that no one ought to rely on his own virtue?

For we have a great adversary, who cannot be overcome by us without God’s favor. And often you will find grave sins in illustrious and blessed men, so that you may recognize that, as human beings, they were subject to temptation, and that they were not to be considered more than human on account of their outstanding virtues.

For when David, lifted up by presumptuous confidence in his virtue, had said, “If I have repaid those who did evil to me” (Psalm 7:5), and elsewhere, “But I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved” (Psalm 29:7), he immediately recalled that he had suffered the punishment of this insolence, saying: “You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (ibid., 8).

If he himself, the founder of the Lord’s lineage, incurred offense through insolence, how much more ought we other sinners, for whom no privilege of merits comes to our aid, fear the rock of insolence, on which the good suffer shipwreck? Especially since so great a man is for us both an authority of teaching and an example. He thought that a kind of recantation should be sung in the later part of his work to propitiate the Lord, saying:

“Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up on high” (Psalm 130:1);

and:

“The Lord is at my right hand; I shall not be moved” (Psalm 15:8).

For he knew that when he trusted in himself, he had fallen.

Finally, he indicated that there is nothing else in man except that he knows God. Thus you have:

“What is man, that you have made yourself known to him, or the son of man, that you reckon with him?” (Psalm 143:3).

If David, therefore, condemned insolence and put on humility, rightly in the history of Uriah’s wife he assumes this instruction in the pursuit of humility.

### 38

And yet, if the peaceful Solomon was born from her, let us see whether there may perhaps be a mystery in the fact that, after the one who previously claimed the people of the nations for his marriage was removed from their midst, the Church married another man, the true David.

David is the name by which Christ is called, having taken upon himself the name of his ancestor, according to what is written: “I have found David my servant” (Psalm 88:21). The Church married him; filled with the seed of the Word and the Spirit of God, she brought forth the body of Christ, namely the Christian people.

There is therefore a woman who, while her husband lives, is bound to the Law; and for this reason her husband died, so that she would not be an adulteress if she were with another man.

The mystery, therefore, is in the type, but the sin is in the history; guilt comes through the human being, sacraments through the Word.

Since we have spoken more fully of this history elsewhere, it seems that we should pass over it here briefly. And rightly did holy David write the mystical fiftieth Psalm because of his marriage to Bathsheba, saying:

“Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm 50:4).

If God’s friend acknowledges his iniquity and that his sin obstructs his merits; if, finally, he confesses to God that he has sinned, why should you blush at confessing your crime, when the invention of a crime, not its confession, is shameful?

### 39

Since David did not omit the history of Bathsheba from his Psalms, so that through it he might teach us either a mystery or the practice of complete repentance, we rightly see that it was not omitted from the Lord’s genealogies either, because David himself, who took her as his wife, is asserted to have preceded the Lord’s generation according to the flesh.

His particular merit, as we have said, is that in this mystery he saw the Church arise and received the oracle that Christ would be born from his lineage.

One part pertains to the Church, where he said:

“Behold, we heard of her in Ephrathah; we found her in the fields of the forest” (Psalm 131:6).

The other pertains specifically to the promise concerning the Lord’s body, which is revealed by a most evident oracle when it says:

“From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne” (ibid., 11).

[Note: All editions read “with reference to the reception of the Lord’s body”; all manuscripts read “with reference to the promise of the Lord’s body.”]

Do not, however, be so negligent concerning so great a promise; for it was not given without a condition.

[Note: The Roman edition reads “without condition.” The other editions and all manuscripts read “without definition.” Here, however, the meaning of both is plainly the same.]

But if you keep the covenant and preserve the testimonies of the Lord, which he promises in the Gospel to declare, the opportunity of an eternal throne will also be opened to you.

This much concerning Uriah’s wife.

### 40

As for Ahab, the matter is sufficiently clear: his wife was Jezebel (1 Kings 16:31). As for Jechoniah, Jeremiah is a sufficiently trustworthy witness that he was guilty of the greatest crime; Jeremiah even took away the name he had borne.

Therefore the one who is called Joachim in the Books of Kings (2 Kings 24:1) is called Jechoniah by Jeremiah, who says:

“Jechoniah is rejected like a vessel that is not useful; therefore he himself and his offspring have been cast out. Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord; write this man down as disowned, because none of his offspring shall rise to sit upon the throne of David, ruling any longer in Judah” (Jeremiah 22:28–30).

[Note: The Roman edition, together with only two or three manuscripts, reads “whose use is not in him”; one or two others read “which has no use in him.” Shortly afterward the Codex Corb. alone reads “and his seed from the earth. Hear,” while Ful. reads “and his seed in the earth. Earth, hear.” Finally, the larger and better part of the manuscripts reads “ruler.” Since he was still reigning, three manuscripts read “while he was reigning in Judea,” etc.]

[Note: Some manuscripts read “and his seed from the earth. Hear,” etc.]

While he was reigning, the Babylonians devastated Judea, and afterward no one from his offspring was ever able to obtain the kingdom in Judea. For afterward the people, released from captivity, were under priests and tetrarchs. Hence tetrarchs remained all the way to Christ’s generation, not even preserving, as far as history shows, the dignity of royal descent.

### 41

For it is related by those who have handed this down to us—whether they reasoned it out, taught it simply, or truly established it—that Idumean brigands entered the Palestinian city of Ascalon and carried away captive, among others, Antipater, the son of a certain Herod’s temple-servant, from the temple of Apollo, which was near the walls.

[Note: *Hierodulus*, that is, the servant or minister of a sacred building, perhaps its keeper, as one Colbertine manuscript and Ful. interpret it.]

His father was unable to ransom him because of his poverty. Having therefore been instructed in the disciplines and mysteries of the Jews, he was joined in friendship to Hyrcanus, king of Judea. Hyrcanus sent him as his representative to Pompey; and because he obtained the reward of his embassy, he aspired, through that favor, to a share in the kingdom.

After Antipater was killed through envy of his success, his son Herod was later ordered by a decree of the Senate, under Antony, to rule the Jews. Herod, Antipater’s son, and the other tetrarchs followed.

[Note: These matters are related in almost the same words by Eusebius, Book 1 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 7; he testifies that he took them from Africanus. But the account is rejected as wholly fabulous and fictitious, and Ambrose does not altogether approve it. The reason why such care is taken here in discussing Christ’s genealogy seems to be that the Jews and Gentiles who, together with Julian, continually objected to Christians to the evangelists’ disagreement—so Cyril relates in Book 8 and elsewhere—might be refuted.]

We thought it necessary to transfer this account from the Greek histories so that it might be clear that Herod was related to no Jewish family and had sought the kingdom by adulterous fraud.

Finally, conscious of his ignoble origin, lest some question concerning his descendants be raised from the ancient record, he burned their Scriptures, supposing that if he removed the public evidence, it could not be established by any other testimonies that he descended from the line of patriarchs or ancient proselytes.

But since most things are subject to human care, this could not prejudice knowledge or the investigation of truth.

### 42

Let us see, then, lest he be able to prejudice us, since we call Christ of true and royal lineage and trace the Lord’s descent through true and noble kings.

But when an adulterous offspring aspired to kingship, the order of succession preserved the continuity of its nobility—not of its power, but of its generation.

Nevertheless, we do not accept Christ as a king according to the honor of this world.

How, then, does the Psalm say: “From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne” (Psalm 131:11)? How does the angel also say of him: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob” (Luke 1:32)? How is he promised that he will reign, when this is not shown? Or how can the prophet say that no one from the seed of Jechoniah will reign?

For if Christ reigned, and Christ is from the seed of Jechoniah, then the prophet lied, and the oracles lied as well.

But the prophet does not deny that future descendants would come from the seed of Jechoniah; and therefore Christ is from his seed. And the fact that Christ reigned is not contrary to the prophecy: he did not reign with secular honor, nor did he sit upon Jechoniah’s seats, but he reigned upon the throne of David.

### 43

But since Jechoniah himself sat upon David’s throne, how is the statement resolved that the descendants of Jechoniah would not sit upon David’s throne, when the same throne seems to have belonged to both?

We too cannot deny that it was David’s throne; nevertheless, Christ did not sit upon the same throne of King David upon which Jechoniah sat. Indeed, no one else from David’s lineage could sit upon his throne except Christ, because his seed is eternal in no one else but in Christ, just as God himself swore, saying:

“Once I have sworn by my holy one: if I should lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne as the sun before me” (Psalm 88:36–38).

[Note: The edition reads “in my Christ”; the manuscripts read “in my holy one.”]

Whom, then, does he name here? Certainly not Solomon, not Rehoboam, not Nathan, but the one of whom alone he can say:

“I will place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers. He will call upon me: You are my Father” (ibid., 26–27);

and:

“I will establish his seed forever and his throne like the days of heaven” (ibid., 30).

Certainly Solomon did not sit upon this throne, nor Rehoboam, nor Jechoniah.

Do you wish to know who sat upon it? He is the one of whom the angel says to Mary:

“Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:31–32).

If you do not believe the angel, at least believe the Lord himself, who says:

“You say that I am a king” (John 18:37).

Did he then also lie, because he said that he would reign although he did not reign on earth? How is the Scripture to be resolved, which says that he will reign, yet does not assert that he reigns?

### 44

We have come to a precipice in our discussion; we are stuck in shallow water and tossed about in a kind of shipwreck of truth.

Let us therefore awaken Christ; let us question him himself, and let him answer. Let us question the Scriptures.

We find that the Lord’s kingdom is not of this world, for he himself said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (ibid., 36). The one who says that his kingdom is not of this world shows that it is above the world.

Thus his kingdom both was and was not: it was not in the age, but it was above the age.

There was therefore another kingdom of the true David, which Christ alone received; and there was another seed of David, which remains forever, from which Christ alone was generated—he alone the true Son of David, whose name alone he also received, according to what is written:

“I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him” (Psalm 88:21).

The preceding words make clear that this is said not of the prophet David but of the Lord. For it is written:

“I have placed help upon the mighty one and exalted the chosen one from my people” (ibid., 20).

For Christ alone is mighty; Christ alone is chosen.

The seed of the saints is greater in faith than in generation. Therefore the Apostle says: “For those who are of faith are the sons of Abraham” (Galatians 3:7).

45. We think that this too ought not to be passed over: from the time of David up to Jechoniah—that is, up to the Captivity—although there were seventeen kings of Judea, Saint Matthew set down fourteen generations; and again, from Jechoniah to Joseph, twelve generations are counted individually, while afterward he recalls that fourteen generations were described.

[Note: Not a few manuscripts vary here. Others, together with all the editions, read more correctly: “individually.”] For thus you have it:

> All the generations, from Abraham to David, are fourteen generations; and from David to the Babylonian Deportation, fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian Deportation to Christ, fourteen generations (Matt. I, 17).

First, we must recognize what we have already said: there can be more successions and fewer generations. Some may live longer and beget children later, or may be entirely without offspring. Thus the periods of kingship and of generations are not identical. Hence Matthew passed over those whom he did not consider relevant to the genealogy. For if his purpose had been to describe successions, we would reasonably be troubled about why, although he agrees with the Books of Kings and Chronicles that after Joram Ahaziah, then Joash and Amaziah, reigned, and that Uzziah succeeded Amaziah, Saint Matthew passed over those three kings—Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah—and placed Jehoshaphat after Joram.

[Note: All the editions, “and after Joram he placed Uzziah.” The manuscripts, on the contrary, “and after Joram he placed Jehoshaphat.” This is indeed the true reading, since below this very name is found everywhere in all the manuscripts and editions. Therefore we think that the person who affirmed that Uzziah had three names would say nothing absurd: he was called not only Uzziah and Azariah, the names by which he is designated in the sacred pages, but also Jehoshaphat, after the name of his grandfather. Nor are examples lacking of Hebrews who were similarly called by three names, as may be seen in Cornelius Jansenius, *Commentary on the Harmony of the Gospels*, part I, chapter 6.]

(IV Kings VIII and following; II Chronicles XXII and following). But he placed him not in the succession of kings, but in the genealogy. Finally, he declared himself to be a recorder of generations. It could, however, have happened that Joram begot children later, and that Jehoshaphat received the kingdom later; and thus Joram succeeded his father in generation, although he did not succeed him in authority.

46. But as for the fact that the Evangelist appears to have counted twelve generations after Jechoniah, if you pay careful attention, here too you will be able to find the reason for fourteen generations. Twelve generations are counted up to Joseph, not up to Christ.

[Note: Several manuscripts: Christ is the thirteenth, proceeding from Joseph.]

Christ is the thirteenth. But it makes no difference whether the error lies in two generations or in one.

[Note: Here the manuscripts are divided into three groups. Corbeiensis, Mediolanensis, and six other manuscripts of excellent quality prefer: “Yet even here you will not find him encountering some reef, or finding”—some have “find”—“a shipwreck of the truth.” The others read partly, with the old edition: “Yet even here, although you cannot encounter some reef or shipwreck, you will find the truth”; and partly, with the Roman edition, as above in the text. Although this manuscript is less numerous, it nevertheless seems to us preferable here, since it offers a clearer sense and a more elegant phrase.]

Yet here too you will not find some hidden reef or shipwreck of the truth. History indicates that there were two Joachims—that is, two Jechonias: one begotten before the Deportation, the other during the Deportation itself; that is, father and son. Therefore the father is counted among the earlier generations, the one who succeeded Josiah; the son among the later generations, the one who succeeded his father, that is, Josiah’s grandson.

The Books of Kings indicate that there were two of them. For thus it is written:

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and the old edition agree with great unanimity. Nevertheless, we do not deny that this passage differs considerably from sacred history as it appears in all the Bibles. Therefore the Roman edition attempted to correct it in the following form: “And Pharaoh appointed Eliakim, son of Josiah, king over Judah and Jerusalem in place of Josiah his father, and changed his name to Jehoiakim . . . in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah . . . . When Jehoiakim reigned, and for three months . . . his mother was Nehushta.” And again, after a short interval: “that son whose name Pharaoh changed”—this grandson to whom Jeremiah, and so forth. Moreover, the agreement of the old edition and the Ambrosian manuscripts confirms what we noted elsewhere: the ancient Greek Testament codex used by our Bishop differed in many respects from those we now possess.]

“And Pharaoh ruled over Israel, while Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah, reigned in Judah in place of Josiah his father; and he changed the name of Jehoiakim when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem” (IV Kings XXIII, 34 and 36). To this he added:

“And the rest of the words of Jehoiakim, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the words, and in the days of those who reigned in Judah? And Jehoiakim slept with his fathers; and Jehoiakim his son reigned in his place . . . . Jehoiakim was eighteen years old, and when he reigned, he reigned three months in Jerusalem; the name of his mother was Mesholah . . . . and all that his father had done in the sight of the Lord, he also did; and in his days Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up against Jerusalem” (IV Kings XXIV, 5 and following).

You see, therefore, that one was Josiah’s son and the other his grandson: that son whom Jeremiah named, and this grandson who was called by his father’s name. Saint Matthew rightly did not wish to disagree with the Prophet, and therefore named him not Joachim but Jechoniah. At the same time, as we said above, he increased the fruitfulness of the Lord’s mercy, since the Lord did not seek nobility of descent in every case, but willed to be born suitably from captives and sinners—the one who came to proclaim remission to captives. The Evangelist therefore did not suppress one of them, but identified both, since both were called Jechoniah. Thus, with the younger Jechoniah added, fourteen generations are counted. Such, then, is Matthew’s account.

47. Luke, however, because he could not include all the sons of Jacob without seeming to wander beyond the generations in a superfluous sequence, although he judged that in other cases—that is, among those much later—he ought by no means to omit the names of the patriarchs, nevertheless chose Joseph, Judah, Simeon, and Levi above the others (Luke III, 30).

For in these men, whose descendants they are, we recognize four kinds of virtue. In Judah—that is, in the earlier Judah—the mystery of the Lord’s Passion was prophetically announced through a figure (Gen. XLIX, 11); in Joseph, an example of chastity had gone before (Gen. XXXIX, 7); in Simeon, vengeance for violated modesty (Gen. XXXIV, 25); in Levi, the priestly office (Num. III, 6). Through Nathan also we perceive the expressed dignity of prophecy (II Kings XII, 1), so that, because Christ Jesus is one and contains all things, different kinds of virtue might also precede in each of His forefathers.

48. Nor ought the remembrance of Noah the righteous to have been omitted among the Lord’s ancestors, so that, since the Builder of the Church was being born, He might appear to have placed before Him as the author of His lineage the one who had earlier founded it in a figure (Gen. VI, 14).

[Note: At what time Methuselah died is a very famous question—as Jerome says in his *Book on Hebrew Questions*—and one debated throughout all the Churches. Many, among whom Ambrose here concurs, relying too much on certain corrupted copies of the Septuagint, believed that he lived fourteen years after the Flood. To prevent the Scriptural accounts concerning the Flood from being brought against them, they said that at that time he had been translated from the earth together with his father Enoch and had continued to live. But Augustine, *City of God* XV, chapter 11, and *Questions on Genesis* 2, together with Jerome in the place cited, having detected the falsity of those copies from other Hebrew sources, demonstrated that Methuselah died either, as one contends, six years before the Flood, or, as the other maintains, in the very year of the Flood. Finally, many later chroniclers and interpreters wholeheartedly adopted this latter opinion.]

For what shall I say about Methuselah, whose years are counted beyond the Flood (Gen. V, 27)? Thus, since Christ alone is the one whose life experienced no age, He might appear, even in His ancestors, not to have experienced the Floods.

And Enoch—is he not clearly an indication both of the Lord’s piety and of His divinity, in that the Lord neither experienced death but returned to heaven, and the author of whose lineage was taken up into heaven?

Hence it is clear that Christ could have avoided death, but chose to die, so that His death might benefit us.

[Note: All the editions, together with some of the manuscripts, read “but wished to,” evidently referring to what follows, “so that that death might benefit us.” The Corbeiensis manuscript and ten other manuscripts of better quality, however, read “but did not wish to.” This is the best reading. “Not to die,” which precedes, is understood.]

Enoch was taken away lest wickedness change his heart; but the Lord, whom the wickedness of the world could not change, returned by the majesty of His nature to the place from which He had come.

Certainly the fratricide is passed over in silence; for it was not reasonable to number among the Lord’s ancestors the man who struck down his brother (Gen. IV, 8), while this one preserved his servants so as to grant them the honor of a brother’s name:

[Note: In all the editions and in several manuscripts, the following words were missing: “this one did not preserve him, nor spare his brother.” We have restored them from ten manuscripts of more ancient date; otherwise, to make the contrast fuller, the words would not be entirely superfluous.]

“This one did not preserve him, nor spare his brother.”

Nor is it without significance that Seth was not passed over (Gen. V, 3), whom the later Adam received in his generation, so that, since there are two generations of the people, it might be indicated in a figure that the Lord Jesus Christ was to be reckoned in the later rather than in the earlier generation.

49. And concerning Adam himself, who according to the Apostle received the figure of Christ (Rom. V, 14), what could have corresponded more beautifully than that the most holy genealogy should begin from the Son of God and be brought down to the Son of God; that the one who was created should precede in a figure, so that the one who was born might follow in truth; that the one made according to the image of God (Gen. I, 27) should go before, because of whom the Image of God would descend?

And if we examine the mystery of the first error, Adam tasted the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, when the devil deceived him and Eve persuaded him (Gen. III, 6), so that Christ might choose the good for us before He knew evil, and, with the Church persuading, might nullify the snares of the dreadful serpent, according to what is written:

> For before the child knows good or evil, he will not believe wickedness, so as to choose what is good (Isa. VII, 16).

And:

> Before he knows how to call father or mother, he shall receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria (Isa. VIII, 4).

For this is the child whose swaddling clothes the Magi filled with eastern spoils (Matt. II, 11), because the nation that had been unbelieving before Christ, now changed in faith, offered the Lord, from the spoils of idols, the triumphal plunder.

50. I have thought, brother, that these matters concerning Christ’s genealogy—though not unknown to you—ought to be pursued at greater length, lest anyone, reviewing them in the Gospel with insufficient attention, should waver in some degree. The holy Evangelists, hastening toward greater miracles and the more divine deeds of the Lord, thought these things better touched upon briefly than unfolded at length.

Therefore, following the practice of those who think it sufficient to point out to travelers ignorant of the roads certain landmarks and paths of a journey, and gathering together the paths of the spiritual way, let us see whether, with the truth’s outcome assisting us—or at least under the devout guidance of faith—we have pressed forward into the secrets of the mysteries. We fear that anyone who reads these things may, as the proverb says, handle a sword like a child, not knowing in childishness how to wield powerful weapons, and may feel a wound through lack of judgment rather than salvation through reading.

Weapons wound the weak who wield them, and no one can use weapons well who does not know how to carry them. Therefore, in matters of faith, a mature man is required: one in whom childhood does not creep along the ground of knowledge; in whom an enfeebled or senseless age does not stumble in mystical understanding; one who, having lost the strength of youth, does not seek the crown of glorious combat; and not like an aging eagle which, once accustomed to seize a hare or a goose with its talons, now, weary with age, seeks the featherless young of smaller birds, unable to bring more substantial food.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1611]

1. I think that we have completed a work on the Lord’s genealogy that is not absurd; certainly it was not fruitless to linger longer over the Lord’s ancestors. For if those who prepare to cross the great sea by a coastal voyage, avoiding—as we do—the shorter route across the open sea through weakness of confidence, frequently visit the fields and cities drawn along the shore, captivated by the beauty of the places, how much more ought we, in so vast a deep—not of the elements but of heavenly deeds—to read the nearer ports and love the frequent excursions, lest anyone, wearied by the tedium of a long voyage, be unable to hold back the vomit of disgust?

[Note: The Roman edition had excised this passage, as we have done. Yet these words are omitted neither in any other edition nor in the manuscripts, nor do they produce an inept meaning.]

Certainly, if someone has perceived the defects of an unsafe and untrustworthy vessel, when a frequent harbor of books is offered, he may lower the sails of his ears and cast the anchor of reading.

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts and the old edition. The Roman edition, however: “Certainly, if anyone has perceived the defects of an untrustworthy boat . . . when a harbor lies before him, let him lower the sails of his ears.”]

He does not seem to have abandoned the ship but to have completed his course who has descended into the harbor.

2. In many places, perhaps, the pleasantness of the locations themselves may invite the passerby to linger. For if, as the tales relate—and even the Prophet said, “The daughters of the Sirens shall dwell in it” (Isa. XIII, 21)—even if the Prophet had not said this, no one could justly object, since Scripture also includes giants (II Kings V, 22, and XXIII, 13) and the Valley of the Titans—

[Note: If the passage begins, “If, then, that Ulysses,” these words had been omitted in the Roman edition. Yet the very frequent practice of writers plainly shows that the opening words of the first period are aptly repeated after the lengthy parenthesis.]

if, then, that Ulysses, hastening toward his homeland after the ten years of exile during which the war was waged at Ilium, and after ten years of wandering, could be detained by the Lotophagi through the sweetness of their berries; if the gardens of Alcinous delayed him; if, finally, the Sirens, enticing him with the song of their voices, had almost led him to that famous shipwreck of pleasure, unless the wax inserted against the sounds of their seductive song had closed the ears of his companions—how much more should religious men allow themselves to be soothed by admiration for heavenly deeds!

Here, however, it is not the sweetness of berries that must be drunk, but that bread which came down from heaven; it is not the vegetables of Alcinous that must be viewed, but the mysteries of Christ. For:

> Let the one who is weak eat vegetables (Rom. XIV, 2).

Therefore the ears must not be closed but opened, so that the voice of Christ may be heard. Whoever receives it will not fear shipwreck.

[Note: “To the mast”—that is, to the ship’s tree, or mast. See Homer, *Odyssey* XII, where the whole sequence of this tale is described at length.]

One must not, like Ulysses, be bound with bodily bonds to the mast, but the mind must be bound by spiritual ties to the wood of the cross, lest it be moved by the allurements of lust and turn the course of nature toward the danger of pleasure.

3. For the tale is colored by poetic inventions, so that certain maidens are said to have lived upon a rocky seashore. If, by their sweet voices, they had induced any to turn their ship aside for the delight of the ears, they would lead them into blind shoals and, deceiving them with an unsafe anchorage, destroy them in the miserable fate of shipwreck.

This has been composed in outward form and embellished with an elaborate comparison, so that sea, voice, women, and shallow shores may be imagined. But what sea is more abrupt than the world—so untrustworthy, so changeable, so deep, so storm-tossed by the blasts of unclean spirits? What does the figure of the maidens signify except the allure of emasculated pleasure, which weakens the steadfastness of the captivated mind?

And what are those shoals except the rocks of our salvation? For nothing is so blind as the peril of worldly sweetness: while it soothes the mind, it overwhelms life and dashes the mind’s understanding against certain bodily rocks.

4. Rightly, therefore, our Lord Jesus Christ, through His fasting and the desert, trains us against the allurements of pleasures; and the Lord of all permits Himself to be tempted by the devil, so that in Him we might learn to conquer all things.

Let us observe, then, that the Evangelist did not idly describe three things as principally ordained by the Lord. For there are three things that contribute to the practice of human salvation: sacrament, desert, and fasting. For:

> No one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully (II Tim. II, 5).

But no one is admitted to the contest of virtue unless, first washed from every stain of sin, he has been consecrated by the gift of heavenly grace.

5. The Lord therefore came to the washing, so that the grace of the mystery might be proved to us both by sight and by perception.

[Note: The Roman edition alone gives a reading supported both by usage and by meaning. Below, however, the same words occur in reverse order, but “the voice of God” performs the office of a witness when it is conveyed from heaven.]

And since the Law is promulgated with heaven and earth as witnesses, so that you might believe that the mystery of the divinity hidden from the ages in God is something greater than the Law, heaven is no longer summoned to give testimony but performs the office of a witness, while the voice of God is conveyed from heaven.

At the same time, lest you stumble against the mystery of faith through doubt of mind, invisible things are visibly declared to be at work for you.

6. The Lord came to the washing, for He became everything for your sake. To those who were under the Law, He was circumcised as though He were under the Law, although He Himself was not under the Law, so that He might win those who were under the Law. To those who were without the Law, He joined Himself through participation in their meals, so that He might win those who lived without the Law.

He became weak to the weak through the suffering of the body, so that He might win the weak. Finally, He became all things to all: poor to the poor, rich to the rich, weeping to those who weep, hungry to the hungry, thirsty to the thirsty, overflowing to those who abound.

He is in prison with the poor; with Mary He weeps; with the apostles He feasts; with the Samaritan woman He thirsts. In the desert He hungers, so that by the Lord’s fasting the food of the first man, which he had tasted through transgression, might be undone. To our peril Adam satisfied the hunger for the knowledge of good and evil; for our benefit this man accepted hunger.

[Cap. IV—Verse 1.]

[Note: This text agrees with Matthew’s wording, in place of which the Roman edition substituted Luke’s wording. Nevertheless, we have decided to follow the authority of the other editions and manuscripts, especially since there is no difference in meaning.]

> Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert, to be tempted by the devil.

7. It is appropriate to recall how the first Adam was expelled from paradise into the desert (Gen. III, 24), so that you may perceive how the second Adam returned from the desert to paradise.

For see how the prejudices are undone by their own bonds, and how divine benefits are restored by their own traces. Adam was from virgin earth (Gen. II, 7); Christ was from a virgin. Adam was made in the image of God (Gen. I, 27); Christ is the Image of God. Adam was placed before all irrational animals (Ibid., 28); Christ was placed before all living things.

Through a woman came folly (Gen. III, 6–7); through a virgin, wisdom. Death came through a tree; life through the cross. The former, naked of spiritual things, clothed himself with the spoils of trees; the latter, naked of worldly things, did not desire the coverings of the body.

Adam was in the desert; Christ was in the desert. For He knew where He could find the condemned man whom He would restore to paradise once his error had been undone.

But since Adam could not return clothed in worldly spoils, and no one can be an inhabitant of paradise unless naked of guilt, Christ stripped off the old man and put on the new, so that, since divine decrees cannot be dissolved, the person rather than the sentence might be changed.

8. But the one who lost the path he had received in paradise without a guide—how could he recover the lost path from the desert without a guide, where temptations are many, the effort toward virtue difficult, and the fall into error easy?

The nature of virtue is like that of trees. If small shoots still rise from earthly things toward heavenly things, while youth grows with tender leaves, exposed to the venom of the savage tooth, it can easily be cut down or burned. But if it has established itself with a deep root and lifted itself up through the height of its branches, then a sturdy tree is assailed in vain either by the bites of wild beasts, the arms of country people, or the storms of various winds.

9. Whom, then, would He set up as guide against so many allurements of the world and so many deceits of the devil, knowing that we must first wrestle against flesh and blood, then against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places?

Would He set up an angel? He too had fallen, and legions of angels scarcely benefited individuals. Would He send a seraph? That one too descended into the midst of a people with unclean lips and cleansed the lips of only one prophet by applying a burning coal (Isa. VI, 6–7).

Another guide had to be sought, one whom we could all follow. Who could be such a guide as to benefit everyone, except the one who is above all? Who could establish me above the world except the one who is greater than the world? Who could be such a guide as to govern male and female, Jew and Greek, Barbarian and Scythian, slave and free, under one direction, except the one who is all things and in all things—Christ?

10. For there are many snares wherever we advance. Snares are laid in the body, snares in the Law,

[Note: There appears to be a clear allusion here to Ecclesiasticus IX, 20: “Know that you are passing through the midst of snares, and walking upon the battlements of cities.”]

snares on the pinnacles of temples and on the ledges of walls by the devil. Snares are in philosophers, snares in desires. For the eye of a prostitute is the sinner’s snare. There is a snare in money, a snare in religion, a snare in the pursuit of chastity.

For the human mind is inclined by very small impulses and is frequently driven here and there through the deceits of the persuader.

[Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read “through the cunning of the persuader.”]

[Note: Here a threefold error is especially indicated, into which not a few people disastrously plunge under the appearance of piety. The first and second pertain to the error of the Manichaeans; the third, to that of the Sabellians.]

The devil sees a religious man reverently honoring God and esteeming what is sacred as incapable of injury; he trips him up precisely in his religion, so that he makes him refuse to believe that the Son of God truly assumed this flesh of ours, this body of ours, this weakness of our members, although the suffering belonged to the body and the divinity remained untouched by injury.

Thus religion becomes guilt; for:

> Everyone who denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God (II John 7).

He sees a man upright and undefiled in chastity and persuades him to condemn marriage, so that he may be cast out of the Church and, through his zeal for chastity, separated from a chaste body.

Another has heard that:

> There is one God, from whom are all things, and he worships and venerates Him (I Cor. VIII, 6).

The devil lies in wait for him and closes his ears so that he may not hear:

> There is one God through whom are all things (Ibid.).

Thus, through excessive piety, he compels him to be impious: while separating the Father from the Son, he confounds the Father and the Son and thinks there is one person, not one power.

Therefore, while he does not know the measure of faith, he falls into the misery of faithlessness.

11. How, then, shall we avoid these snares, so that we too may say:

> Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare was broken, and we were set free (Ps. CXXIII, 7)?

He does not say, “I broke the snare.” David did not dare to say this, but:

> Our help is in the name of the Lord (Ibid., 8),

so that he might show from where the snare would be undone and prophesy that the one who was to come into this life would break the snare prepared by the devil’s deceit.

12. But the snare could not have been broken more effectively unless it had displayed some prey to the devil, so that, while he hastened toward the prey, he might be bound by his own snares, and I might be able to say:

> They prepared snares for my feet, and they themselves fell into them (Ps. LVI, 7).

What prey could there have been except a body?

It was therefore necessary that this deception be practiced upon the devil: that the Lord Jesus should assume a body, and a corruptible body, a weak body, so that He might be crucified in weakness.

For if it had been a spiritual body, He would not have said:

> The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak (Matt. XXVI, 41).

Hear, then, both voices: that of the willing spirit and that of the weak flesh:

> Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me (Ibid., 39).

This is the voice of the flesh.

> Yet not what I will, but what You will.

[Note: The Amerbach edition, together with three manuscripts of more recent hand, reads: “You have here how we teach devotion to the spirit.” The manuscripts read: “of the spirit,” and so forth.]

Here you have the devotion and strength of the spirit.

Why do you reject the Lord’s condescension? It is an act of condescension that He assumed my body; it is an act of condescension that He assumed my injuries; He assumed my weaknesses, which the nature of God could not experience, although even human nature has learned to disregard, endure, and bear them.

And therefore let us follow Christ, according to what is written:

> You shall walk after the Lord your God, and cling to Him alone (Deut. X, 20; XIII, 4).

To whom shall I cling except to Christ, as Paul said:

> Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit (I Cor. VI, 17).

Let us therefore follow His footsteps, so that from the desert we may be able to return to paradise.

13. And see by what roads we are led back. Now Christ is in the desert: He acts as man, instructs, trains, disciplines, and anoints with spiritual oil. When He sees someone stronger, He leads him through sown and fruitful fields, when the Jews complained (Matt. XII, 2) that His disciples were plucking ears of grain from the field on the Sabbath—for He had already placed His apostles in a cultivated field and in fruitful labor.

Afterward, at the time of His Passion, He placed him in paradise. For thus you have it:

> When Jesus had said these things, He went out with His disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which He entered, He and His disciples (John XVIII, 1).

The Prophet teaches in the *Song of Songs* that a garden is superior to a fertile field, saying:

> A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain; your shoots are a paradise (Song IV, 12–13).

For this is the pure and undefiled virginity of the soul, which is moved neither by terror of punishments, nor by the allurements of worldly pleasure away from the faith, nor by love of life.

Finally, this Evangelist above all testifies that man was recalled by the Lord’s power, since he alone introduces the Lord saying to the thief:

> Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke XXIII, 43).

14. Jesus, therefore, full of the Holy Spirit, was led into the desert: by counsel, so that He might challenge the devil—for unless He had fought, this man would not have conquered for me; by mystery, so that He might free that Adam from exile; by example, so that He might show us that the devil envies those who strive toward better things, and that we must then be especially on guard lest weakness of mind abandon the grace of the mystery.

## (Verse 2.) Now for forty days.

15. You recognize the mystical number. For you remember that the waters of the abyss were poured out for that many days (Gen. VII, 12), and that, after the prophet had been sanctified by that many days of fasting, the clemency of a clearer sky was restored (III Kings XIX, 8). By that many days of fasting holy Moses merited receiving the Law (Exod. XXXIV, 28).

For that many years the fathers who remained in the wilderness obtained the bread of angels and the grace of heavenly nourishment (Num. XIV, 32); nor did they merit entering the promised land before they had completed the period of the mystical number.

By that many days of the Lord’s fasting His entrance into the Gospel is revealed to us. Therefore, if anyone desires to attain the glory of the Gospel and the fruit of the resurrection, he must not violate the mystical fast, which Moses in the Law and Christ in His Gospel prescribed, by the authority of both Testaments, as the faithful contest of virtue.

16. But what does it mean that the Evangelist indicated that the Lord was hungry, when we see nothing of this sort expressly stated concerning the fasts of Moses and Elijah? Is human endurance stronger than God?

Rather, the one who was unable to be hungry for forty days showed that He was not hungry for bodily food but for salvation. At the same time, He provoked the adversary, who was already afraid, having been wounded by a forty-day fast.

Therefore the Lord’s hunger is a pious deception: the devil, fearing greater things in the one whom he was already avoiding, was lured by the appearance of hunger into tempting Him as a man, so that the triumph might not be hindered.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “carried away by the appearance of hunger.” Some others, more correctly, “rejoicing.” The rest, best of all with the editions, “delighted.” Shortly afterward, the editions of Erasmus and those following him, together with two manuscripts, read: “the work of the Spirit, that is, divine,” and so forth. The Amerbach edition, together with other written codices, reads as in the text.]

At the same time, learn this mystery: this divine judgment was the work of the Holy Spirit, so that Christ might offer Himself to be tempted by the devil.

## (Verse 3.) Then the devil said to Him: If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.

17. We are taught chiefly that there are three weapons of the devil with which he is accustomed to arm himself for wounding the human mind: one directed toward gluttony, another toward vainglory, and a third toward ambition.

He began from the point at which he had already conquered. Therefore I begin to conquer in Christ from the point at which I was conquered in Adam—provided that Christ is for me the image of the Father and an example of virtue.

Let us learn, then, to beware of gluttony and to beware of luxury, because they are weapons of the devil. A snare is set when a royal banquet is prepared, which often weakens the firmness of the mind. For we must avoid the snare not only when we hear the devil’s words but also when we see his forces.

You have learned, then, the devil’s weapon; take up the shield of faith and the breastplate of self-restraint.

18. But what does the opening of such a speech mean—“If You are the Son of God”—unless he knew that the Son of God was to come, but did not think that He had come in this weakness of the body?

One thing belongs to investigation and another to temptation: he professes to believe in God, and attempts to mock the man.

19. But observe the weapons of Christ, with which He conquered for you, not for Himself. For He who showed, by the majesty of His power, that stones could be changed into bread through the transformation of one nature into another teaches you to do nothing at the devil’s command, nor for the sake of displaying virtue.

At the same time, in the very temptation, learn the devil’s skillful cunning. He tempts in order to investigate; he investigates in order to tempt. The Lord, on the contrary, deceives in order to conquer; He still conquers in order to deceive.

For if He had changed the nature, He would have betrayed the Creator.

[Note: Some Paris editions: “Therefore He answered deservedly.” The other editions and all the manuscripts more suitably read: “He moderated,” that is, He so tempered His response that He might conquer the devil without revealing His divinity.]

Therefore He answered in a measured way, saying:

## (Verse 4.) It is written: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.

20. Do you see what kind of weapons He uses, by which He defends man from the assault of spiritual wickedness and encloses and fortifies him against the provocations of gluttony?

For He does not use power as God—for what benefit would that have been to me?—but, as man, He claims a common aid for Himself, so that, intent upon the nourishment of divine reading, He may disregard bodily hunger and acquire the food of the heavenly word.

Intent upon this, Moses did not desire bread; intent upon this, Elijah did not feel the hunger of his prolonged fast. For one who follows the word cannot desire earthly bread, since he receives the substance of heavenly bread. There can be no doubt that divine things surpass human things, and spiritual things bodily things.

Therefore, whoever desires true life should seek that bread which strengthens human hearts through an imperceptible substance.

[Note: Many manuscripts correctly read, “he awaits that bread”; some read, “let him await it.” Others, together with the editions, “let him seek it.”]

At the same time, when He says, “Man shall not live by bread alone,” He shows that the one tempted was man—that is, our assumed nature—not His divinity.

21. The weapon of vainglory follows, through which one readily falls into sin; for while people desire to boast of their virtue, they withdraw from the place of their merits and from their proper station.

[Note: The Roman edition: “This certainly belongs to vainglory, so that while . . .”]

## (Verse 9.) And he led Him, it says, to Jerusalem, and set Him upon the pinnacle of the temple.

22. Such indeed is vainglory: while each person thinks that he is ascending to higher things, through the usurpation of exalted deeds he is thrust down to lower things.

23. And he said to Him: If You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down.

Truly this is a diabolical voice, which strives to hurl the human mind down from the higher step of its merits. For what is more characteristic of the devil than to persuade each person to cast himself downward?

24. Learn, then, to conquer the devil yourself. The Spirit moves you: follow the Spirit. Let not the enticement of the flesh turn you back; filled with the Spirit, learn to despise pleasures. Fast, if you wish to conquer. It follows that the devil supposes he must test you through a human being: Christ, as the stronger, is tested face to face; you, through a human being. [Col. 1619A] And this too is a word of the devil, [Note: [Col. 1619D] All editions and some manuscripts have: “when he says, ‘Man, be strong and remain steadfast,’” while the latest Paris edition has: “and if you wish, remain.” But the manuscripts of better quality and greater number have: “when he says, ‘Man, you are strong,’” etc. This is preferable, for it refers back to the preceding statement: “It follows that the devil supposes that you must be tested through a human being.”] when he says: “Man, you are strong; eat and drink, and remain as you are.” Do not trust yourself; do not be ashamed to need the safeguards that Christ did not need—and yet he did not neglect them, so as to teach you, saying: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with wine and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). Paul was not ashamed when he said: “Thus I run with certainty, not as beating the air” (1 Cor. 9:26). The Apostle was indeed not beating the air, but he was striking the powers of the air. “But I chastise my body,” he says, “and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (ibid., 27).

25. At the same time, the devil reveals his own weakness and malice; [Note: [Col. 1619D] The Roman edition alone has: “because the devil can harm no one unless he has cast himself down.”] for the devil can harm no one unless that person has cast himself down. For whoever, abandoning heavenly things, chooses earthly ones incurs a voluntary plunge into a declining life. At the same time, when the devil saw that his weapon was blunted—for he had subjected all human beings to his own power—he began to judge more than a human being. But the Lord again did not think that even those things which had been prophesied about him were to be done at the devil’s discretion. Rather, preserving the authority of his own divinity, he confronted the devil’s cunning, so that, because the devil had produced an example from Scripture, he might be defeated by examples from Scripture. For God has the power to conquer; [Note: [Col. 1619D] All editions and not a few manuscripts have: “Scripture conquers for me.” But the manuscripts of better quality have: “who conquers for me.” This reading is preferable.] he conquers for me.

26. Learn here also that Satan disguises himself as an angel of light and often prepares a snare for the faithful from the divine Scriptures themselves. Thus he creates heretics, thus he tears faith apart, thus he attacks the laws of piety. Therefore, let no heretic ensnare you merely because he can produce some examples from Scripture, nor let him arrogate to himself the learning he appears to possess. The devil too uses testimonies from Scripture, not to teach, but to ensnare and deceive. He recognized someone attentive to religion, distinguished for his virtues, powerful in signs and works; he stretches out the snare of vainglory, so as to inflate such a man with swelling pride, [Col. 1619C] so that he would not entrust himself to piety but would trust in vainglory; so that he would not ascribe it to God but claim it for himself. Therefore the apostles commanded demons not in their own name but in the name of Christ, lest they appear to arrogate anything to themselves. Thus Peter [Note: [Col. 1619D] So read all manuscripts and the old editions; the Roman edition has, “he heals a lame man.” But what if our Ambrose thought that he limped as a result of paralysis, or relaxation of the sinews?] heals a paralytic, saying: “In the name of Jesus the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). Learn also from Paul to flee vainglory. “I know,” he says, “a man, whether in the body or outside the body I do not know, God knows, who was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak. On behalf of such a one I will glory, but on my own behalf I will not glory, except in my weaknesses” (2 Cor. 12:3–5).

27. Therefore here too, because the devil perceived that he was strong, he displayed vainglory, which deceives even the strong. [Col. 1620A] But the Lord answered him: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” In this you recognize Christ as both Lord and God, and the Father and the Son as possessing one power, according to what is written: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Therefore, if the devil holds up the word “one,” confront him, because it is written: “I and the Father are one.” And distinguish “one,” [Note: [Col. 1620D] The Roman edition has: “not so that you distinguish the power, but so that you separate the Father and the Son.” The meaning is clear if it were supported by any manuscripts or other editions. We therefore interpret the earlier reading in this way: Receive the word “one” as placed there so that you do not distinguish the power of the Father and the Son or separate one person from the other; for, as Hilary says in *On the Trinity* VII: “In the divine persons there is nothing different … nothing separable,” since the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father by unity of nature. Ambrose himself explains this more fully in *On the Faith* I, chapter 2.] not so that you distinguish the power; distinguish “one,” so that you do not separate the Father and the Son.

*(Verse 5.)* “And the devil led him again onto a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time.”

28. It is appropriate that worldly and earthly things are shown “in a moment of time.” For this indicates not so much the speed of the sight as it expresses the frailty of perishable power: in a moment all those things pass away, [Col. 1620B] and often the honor of the world departs before it has even arrived. For what can belong to the world that is lasting, when the ages themselves are not lasting? Here we are taught to despise the gusts of empty ambition, because every worldly dignity lies subject to the devil’s power: fragile in use, and empty in its outcome.

29. But how does the devil give power here, when elsewhere it is written: “All power is from God” (Rom. 13:1)? Can anyone serve two masters, or receive power from two? Is there, then, a contradiction? Certainly not. But see that all things are from God. The world is not without God, for “the world was made through him” (John 1:10). Yet although it was made by God, its works are evil, because “the world is placed in the Evil One”; the ordering of the world is from God, but the works of the world are from evil (John 5:19). So too, the ordering of powers is from God; the ambition for power is from evil. Finally, Scripture says: “There is no power except from God, and those that exist have been ordered by God” (Rom. 13:1)—not “given,” but “ordered.” And: “Whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God” (ibid., 2). Here too, although the devil says that he gives power, he does not deny that all those things have been permitted to him for a time. Therefore, the one who permitted it ordered it. The power is not evil, but the person who uses the power evilly. Finally: “Do you wish not to fear the power? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (ibid., 3). Therefore the power is not evil, but ambition. Finally, God’s ordering of power extends so far that the one who uses power well is God’s minister: “He is God’s minister for your good” (ibid., [Col. 1620D] 4). Therefore the fault is not in the office, but in the minister; nor can God’s ordinance be displeasing, but only the action of the administrator. For, to transfer the example from heavenly things to earthly ones, the emperor gives honor, and he has praise. But if someone uses honor badly, the fault is not the emperor’s, [Note: [Col. 1621D] The Roman edition alone has: “but the user’s fault.” That the matter here concerns judicial power is clearly proved by what precedes.] but the judge’s. Crimes have their own accused, not because power entangles each person, but because his own malice does.

30. What then? Is it good to use power, to strive for honor? It is good if honor is conferred, not seized. Yet distinguish this very good carefully. One kind of good exists in the world; another is the use of perfect virtue. For it is good to devote oneself to knowing divinity, without being hindered by any occupations. Although there are many good things, there is nevertheless one eternal life: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). Therefore the greatest fruit of eternal life—and God alone is the one who rewards eternal life—is this. Let us adore God alone and our Lord, and serve him alone, so that he alone may reward us with the greatest fruit. Let us flee everything subject to the devil’s power, lest, like an evil tyrant, he exercise the savage power he has received against those whom he finds within his kingdom.

31. Power, therefore, is not from the devil, although it is exposed to the devil’s snares. Nor is the ordering of powers therefore evil because powers are exposed to evil. It is good to seek God, but a certain winding and error of that very search creeps in. For if the seeker is turned toward sacrilege by a savage interpretation, the offense of the seeker is turned toward something worse than if he had not sought at all; [Note: [Col. 1621D] The Roman edition had omitted these words, “than if he had not sought,” as well as the later words “is exposed to evil.” But since they are found in all the old editions and manuscripts, it would have been wrong not to restore them in full.] yet the fault is not the search but the seeker’s; nor is the search itself exposed to evil, but the seeker’s disposition. If the one who seeks God is often tested because of the weakness of the flesh and the narrowness of the mind, how much more is the one who seeks the world exposed! Ambition is all the more pernicious because it is a kind of flattering mediator of dignities; and often those whom no vices delight, whom no luxury could move, and whom no greed could overthrow, ambition makes criminals. [Note: [Col. 1621D] The same Roman edition alone has: “no vices deflect them”; and shortly afterward, with the other editions and a few manuscripts, “domestic danger.” But the more numerous and better manuscripts have “domestic crime.” This fits the preceding discussion better, since ambition makes people criminal.] For it has a public charm but a domestic crime; and, in order to rule others, it first becomes a servant. It bends in servility so that it may be granted honor. [Note: [Col. 1622D] All editions and several manuscripts have: “And while he wishes to be higher, he becomes more lax.” But the words inserted here have been restored from nine excellent manuscripts.] And while it wishes to be higher through simulated humility, it becomes more contemptible and more lax, since within power itself what excels is something belonging to another; it rules the laws but serves itself.

32. Someone may perhaps say that only the person who has done evil is afraid; yet the person who sails the sea is more afraid. Conversely, one standing securely on immovable land is not accustomed to fear shipwreck; but if he boards the moving element, he becomes exposed to more frequent dangers. Flee, then, the sea of the world, and you will not fear shipwreck. Even if the gusts of winds repeatedly beat the tops of breathing trees, yet when their roots are firmly established there is no falling. [Col. 1622A] But in the sea, when the winds rage, even if not everyone suffers shipwreck, everyone is nevertheless in danger. Thus, amid the adverse blasts of spiritual wickedness, no one is safe on sand or sea, and the ships of Tarshish are often shattered by a violent wind. This is the moral interpretation.

33. But as regards the mystical order, you see the bonds of the ancient error loosed along their own sequence, so that first the snare of gluttony, second that of frivolity, [Note: [Col. 1622D] “Second, of frivolity.” That *facilitas* denotes vainglory and vanity is evident from what precedes, and rightly so, since this vice arises from a certain readiness and lightness of soul.] and third that of ambition might be undone. For Adam was ensnared by food; [Note: [Col. 1622D] Thus the manuscripts and the ancient edition agree almost unanimously in the main text. The Roman edition, however, has: “and in the eating of the forbidden tree,” etc.; this it transferred from the margin of the editions of Erasmus and Gill into the text.] and, by the frivolity with which he transgressed the sentence concerning the forbidden tree, he also incurred the crime of reckless ambition, while he desired the likeness of divinity. Therefore the Lord first undid the ancient bond of injury, so that, having shaken off the yoke of captivity, we might learn to conquer crimes with the support of the Scriptures.

34. But if the Lord Jesus did not desire what was his own, why do you seek what belongs to another? If the Creator of all things despised the glory of the world through the virtue of embracing poverty, why do you disdain what you were born as and desire what is not owed to you? Why do you demand for punishment those things which cannot be lasting for your use? Beware of snares; beware of frauds. And precisely because the cunning devil shakes the whole world by fraud in order to overthrow humanity and fights with all the enticements of the world, you must be especially on guard against his flattering words. Food had not bent Eve; forgetfulness of the commandments had not abandoned her. Rather, the seductive ambition of promised honor deceived her. If she had wished to adore the Lord alone, she would not have sought what was not owed to her. Therefore the remedy is given by which you may blunt the weapon of ambition: let us serve the Lord alone; [Col. 1622C] for religious devotion is free from ambition.

*(Verse 13.)* “And when every temptation had been completed, the devil departed from him until an opportune time.”

35. These three kinds of vice are shown to be the sources of almost all crimes. For Scripture would not have said that every temptation had been completed unless in these three lay the material of all sins, whose seeds must be guarded against at their very origin. The end of temptations, therefore, is the end of desires, because the causes of temptations are the causes of desires. The causes of desires are the delight of the flesh, the appearance of glory, and the thirst for power. How religious it may seem not to refuse continued association with a Christian woman! [Note: [Col. 1622D] Some manuscripts, together with the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Paris, have “association with a Christian woman”; [Col. 1623D] the other printed and written copies have “association,” that is, more frequent and longer conversations and excessive familiarity. This is more appropriate.] But from this comes frequent temptation. If the devil sees people attentive to God, he suggests something by which to deceive them. But although you may rely on your purpose, beware of temptation, knowing human nature. If you remember these three things, Paul too prescribes that they be avoided, indicating three kinds of sin, from which the free person awaits the crown of righteousness. “For,” he says, “we did not come with a word of flattery, nor with an occasion for greed, God is witness, nor seeking glory from human beings” (1 Thess. 2:5–6). And thus he conquered the devil and sought the crown.

36. You see, then, that the devil himself is not persistent in striving, but is accustomed to yield before true virtue. And although he does not cease to be envious, he nevertheless fears to persist, because he more often retreats rather than be defeated. Therefore, having heard the name of God, “he departed,” it says, “until an opportune time”; for afterward he came not to tempt again but to fight openly.

37. Divine Scripture therefore teaches you that your struggle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual snares (Eph. 6:12). You see the magnificence of the Christian man, who fights with the rulers of the world and, although established on earth, contends by the strength of his soul against the spiritual forces of wickedness that are in the heavenly places. We do not contend over earthly things so as to fight on earth; but since spiritual rewards have been set before us, spiritual obstacles must first be overcome in the struggle for the kingdom of God and the inheritance of Christ. A crown has been set before us; struggles must be undertaken. No one can be crowned unless he has conquered; no one can conquer unless he has first fought. The fruit of the crown itself is greater where the labor is greater: “For narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life … but broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (Matt. 7:14, 13). Therefore we must by no means fear temptation; for it is the cause of victory and the material of triumphs.

38. That rich man who experienced no temptation in the world is in punishment in the underworld. But that poor Lazarus, so afflicted and worn down by poverty and illness that the dogs licked his sores, sought the crown of eternal glory through the miserable labor of this life (Luke 16:22). For “many are the tribulations,” not of just anyone, but “of the righteous” (Ps. 33:20). Finally, those whom the Lord loves he often chastises (Heb. 12:6). Peter was tested so that he might deny; he denied so that he might weep (Luke 22:57ff.). And what should I say about the others? Job, certainly, had been approved by God; but although he had been approved, he was not yet victorious (Job 1:12; 2:6). His devotion had been tested, but he did not yet possess the reward of virtue. Therefore he is offered for testing, so that he might be made more glorious.

39. It is also important that you observe the stages of that contest. The devil does not have only one weapon; he repeatedly uses missiles, so as to conquer either through reward or through weariness. First he wounds through desire, second through devotion, third through health; [Col. 1624A] for he fights with wounds of both mind and body. The diversity of temptations also corresponds to the diversity of those who fight. The rich man is pressed by the loss of wealth, the father by the loss of his children, the human being by pains, the body by sores. What weapons these are! Therefore the Lord did not wish to have anything that he could lose; and so he came poor, lest the devil have something to take away. Do you wish to know how true this is? Hear the Lord himself saying: “The prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14:30). He also did not wish to be the father of only a few, so that he might be the father of all. It would have been futile to test him with bodily sores, since he would despise all bodily sufferings; at the same time, he wished to show us that, once the enemy of the body had been driven away, victory was owed to him who was without blemish. But Job is tested as a private individual, whereas Christ is tested for the whole world; Job’s patrimony is taken away, [Col. 1624B] while Christ is offered the kingdom of the world. Nor is the devil entirely without cunning: he would have feared to exasperate the Son of God, so he tests Job with injuries and Christ with rewards. Job, like a little servant, says: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away” (Job 1:21); but Christ, conscious of his own nature and disposition, laughs at what is offered to him. And, to return to that matter, messenger follows upon messenger (ibid., 14ff.); the wounds are doubled, yet the strong athlete is not disturbed in mind. The woman, the enticement of the first fraud, is brought in (Job 2:9); but Christ, born through a virgin, had no woman subject to error. Friends are brought in to crush the one who resists with evil counsel. Yet in all that happened to him, Job nowhere sinned with his lips in the sight of God (ibid., 10).

40. As for his cursing the day when he says: “May that day perish in which I was born” (Job 3:3), and later: “Let him curse it who cursed that day, who has a great sea-monster to oppress” (ibid., 8), this pertains to prophecy: for our Lord Jesus Christ crushed the devil as the Leviathan of this stormy age, and he desires the day of his carnal generation to perish, so that his day may be counted in regeneration. “Let the worldly day perish,” he says, “so that the spiritual day may arise.” Thus holy Job was speaking mysteries in his temptation; for the one who conquered the world saw Christ.

41. Therefore let us not fear temptations, but rather glory in temptations, saying: “When we are weak, then we are strong”; then the crown of righteousness is woven (2 Cor. 12:10). But perhaps that saying applies to Paul; as for us, since there are many crowns, we ought to hope for whichever one we may. In the world, laurel is a crown; [Note: [Col. 1623D] Certain interpreters, commenting on Psalm 5:13, relate that after the time of Saint Thomas it was customary among the ancients for victors in a chariot to be crowned with a shield placed upon the head, before the use of crowns had become established. But since there are few traces of this practice, it is difficult for many to understand how a shield can be called a crown. Certainly Jerome, commenting explicitly on the same passage, says: “In the world, a shield is one thing and a crown another.” Hence he and others, following Origen, have recourse to the spiritual sense. Ambrose, however, not only here but also in *Hexaemeron* III, chapter 14, section 60, counts the shield among crowns, that is, among the rewards of victory. There, after describing the leaf of the vine in the likeness of a shield, he adds: “For it seems to fashion the form of a prize … the appearance and distinction of victory are born within it. Thus it carries its prize with it, by which it also provides itself protection,” etc. This is also supported by Cassiodorus, who says of the same verse of the cited Psalm: “A shield placed upon the head is a crown, fitted to the heart as a defense.” Nor perhaps is there another reason why shields can be seen adorned with crowns on Trajan’s Column, although Lipsius gives a somewhat different explanation of this matter in his notes on *The Greatness of Rome*.] but for you a crown of delights has been set forth: “For a crown of delights will overshadow you” (Prov. 4:9). And elsewhere: “With the shield of his good will he will surround you” (Ps. 5:13). [Note: [Col. 1625D] The Roman edition has, “You have crowned us with the shield of your good will”; the reading here is, “He will surround you with a shield.”] “With glory and honor he crowned him whom he loved” (Ps. 8:6). Therefore the one who wishes to give a crown suggests temptations. And whenever you are tempted, recognize that a crown is being prepared. Take away the contests of the martyrs, and you have taken away the crowns; take away the torments, and you have taken away the blessedness.

42. Was not Joseph’s temptation the consecration of his virtue? [Note: [Col. 1625D] The same Roman edition has: “the celebration of virtue.”] Was not the injury of imprisonment a crown of chastity? How could he have attained a share in the kingdom of Egypt unless he had been sold by his brothers? That this happened by God’s decree, so that the righteous man might be tested, he himself showed by saying: “How could it have happened today that a great people might be fed?” (Gen. 50:20). Therefore we must not fear the temptations of the world as evils, since good rewards are gained through them; rather, in view of the human condition, we should ask to undergo temptations that we are able to bear.

*(Verse 14.)* “And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee.”

43. At this point the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, where he says: “The region of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and the others inhabiting the coastal region, [Note: [Col. 1625D] The words “and those along the coast,” which had been deleted in the Roman edition, are not entirely inappropriate, since they are included in the preceding phrase “inhabiting the coastal region.” Nevertheless, they are found in all the manuscripts and old editions. Ambrose could have immediately explained in Latin what he had designated by the Greek expression.] and those along the coast, and across the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in the shadow of death have seen a great light” (Isa. 9:1–2). For what is the great light except Christ, who enlightens every human being coming into this world?

44. *(Verse 17.)* Then he received the book, to show that he himself was the one who had spoken in the Prophets [Col. 1625C] and to remove the sacrileges of the faithless, who say that the God of the Old Testament is one God and the God of the New Testament another, or who say that Christ began from the virgin. For how could he have begun from the virgin, when he was speaking before the virgin existed?

*(Verse 18.)* “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.”

45. You see the coeternal and perfect Trinity. Scripture itself speaks of Jesus as God and human being, perfect in both respects; it speaks of God the Father and of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is shown to be a co-worker when he descended upon Christ in bodily form like a dove, while the Son of God was being baptized in the river and the Father was speaking from heaven. What greater testimony, then, do we seek than the fact that he indicated in his own voice that he was the one who had spoken in the Prophets? He is anointed with spiritual oil and heavenly power, so that he might water the poverty of the human condition with the eternal treasure of resurrection, turn away captivity of mind, illumine the blindness of souls, and proclaim the Lord’s year spread throughout perpetual ages—a year that does not know how to return to the cycle of labor and that grants human beings the continuance of fruitfulness and rest. And he bent himself to every service so completely that he did not even disdain the office of reader.
