Yet we were impious, denying, through contemplation of the body, the faith in his divinity that ought to be gathered from the miracles of his works.

*(Verse 24.)* “Amen I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his own country.”

46. Envy is revealed here in no small degree: having forgotten civic affection, it turns the causes of love into bitter hatreds. At the same time, this example and oracle alike declare that you wait in vain for the aid of heavenly mercy if you envy the fruits of another’s virtue. For the Lord rejects the envious, and from those who persecute divine benefits in others he turns away the miracles of his power. The actions of the Lord’s flesh are, of course, an example of divinity, and his invisible realities are demonstrated to us through those things that are visible.

47. Therefore the Savior does not without reason excuse the fact that he worked no miracles of power in his own country, lest perhaps someone should think that affection for one’s homeland ought to be held in lesser regard by us. For he could not fail to love his fellow citizens, since he loved everyone. But those who envy have themselves cut themselves off from love of their homeland: “Love does not envy … it is not puffed up” (1 Cor. 13:4). Yet his homeland is not deprived of divine benefits. For what greater miracle is there than that Christ was born in it? [Note: [Col. 1626D] Ambrose extends what Christ says about the country in which he was raised also to the country that received him at his birth. And rightly so, since we read that no miracle was performed by Christ there either.] See, then, what evil envy brings. Because of envy, the homeland is judged unworthy in which the citizen might work, although it was worthy to be the place in which the Son of God would be born. [Note: [Col. 1626D] The Roman edition has: “that the Son of God might be conceived”; all the other editions and manuscripts have: “that he might be born.” Conception is indeed the beginning of birth.]

*(Verse 25.)* “In truth I say to you: There were many widows in the days of Elijah.”

48. This does not mean that Elijah’s days existed as such, but that they were the days in which Elijah worked; or because he made days for those who saw the light of spiritual grace in his works and were converted to the Lord. And therefore heaven was opened to those who saw eternal and divine mysteries; it was closed when there was famine, because there was no abundance of knowledge of divinity. But we have written more fully about this when writing on widows (*On Widows*).

*(Verse 27.)* “And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.”

49. This saving word of the Lord clearly instructs us and exhorts us to pursue the reverence of divinity: no one is shown to have been healed and freed from the stain of bodily disease except the one who devoted himself to health through religious duty. For divine benefits are bestowed not upon those who sleep, but upon those who keep watch. And fittingly, by this comparison, the arrogance of envious citizens is blunted, while the Lord’s deed is shown to agree with the ancient Scriptures. In the books of Kings too we read that the foreigner Naaman was freed from the spots of leprosy by a prophetic oracle, while very many Jews were being consumed by leprosy of both body and mind (2 Kings 5:14). Indeed, the history relates that the four men who, compelled by hunger, first went toward the camp of the king of Syria were lepers (2 Kings 7:3). Why, then, did the prophet not cure his brothers, not cure his fellow citizens, not heal those associated with him, while he healed foreigners—those who had no observance of the Law or fellowship in religion? It was because healing depends on will, not nationality; the divine gift is chosen by petitions, not bestowed by right of nature. Learn, Christian, to ask for what you desire to obtain; those who disdain the gifts of heaven do not follow spiritual progress.

50. But although a simple explanation shapes the moral disposition, the grace of the mystery is not hidden. For just as what follows is derived from what precedes, so what precedes is also confirmed by what follows (*On Widows*). We said in another book that in the widow to whom Elijah was sent the type of the Church was prefigured. [Note: [Col. 1627D] All editions, together with four very late manuscripts, have: “The people gathered the Church.” A large number of others have: “The people agrees with the Church.” The latter is better. For it cannot properly be said that the people gathered the Church, since the Church was gathered from the people. But “the people agrees with the Church” should be followed; the sense becomes clear if the words are transposed and explained in this way.] It is fitting that the people follow the Church. That people, gathered from the nations; that people, formerly leprous; that people, formerly stained before it was mystically baptized in the river—after the sacrament of baptism it was cleansed of the stains of body and mind, and, no longer leprous, began to be an immaculate virgin without wrinkle. Therefore Naaman is rightly described as great in the sight of his Lord and admirable in appearance, because in his type the future salvation of the nations is declared. By the counsel of an unmarried girl, [Col. 1627C] who, having been carried captive into enemy power after the strength of her fellow citizens had been broken, he was urged to hope for salvation from the prophet (2 Kings 5:2); and he was healed not by the command of an earthly king but by the generosity of divine mercy. [Note: [Col. 1627D] The Roman edition alone has: “who, by the counsel of the holy girl.” The old edition and eleven manuscripts have: “who, by the counsel of the consecrated girl,” etc. But the excellent Corbie and Michael manuscripts and six other more reliable copies have: “who, by the counsel of the unmarried girl,” that is, one bound by no bonds of marriage—or, if you prefer, free from the yoke of ancestral ceremonies. In either sense she can present a figure and likeness of the Church.]

51. Why is he commanded to immerse himself in a mystical number? Why is the river Jordan chosen? “Are not,” he says, “Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than the Jordan?” (ibid., 12). But, though angry, he preferred those rivers; after reflection, he chose the Jordan. Anger does not know the mystery; faith knows it. Learn the grace of saving baptism: the one who entered the water a leper emerged faithful. Learn that spiritual sacraments are signified: the remedy of the body is requested, but that of the mind is acquired. The flesh is washed, and the disposition is washed. For I do not see that the leprosy of the body was cleansed more than that of the mind, when, after the filth of the ancient error had been washed away, he declares that he will not sacrifice to foreign gods the sacrifices he had promised to offer to the Lord (ibid., 17).

52. Learn also the commands of fitting virtue: the one who refused rewards proved his faith. Learn from both the teaching of words and the example of deeds what you should follow. You have the Lord’s command and the prophet’s example: to receive freely and to give freely, not to sell ministry but to offer it (Matt. 10:8). For God’s grace is not assessed by a price, nor is profit sought in the sacraments, but the priest’s service.

53. Yet it is not enough if you yourself do not seek profit; the hands of your household must also be restrained. Nor do we ask only that you preserve yourself alone as chaste and immaculate. For the Apostle did not say “yourself alone,” but: “Keep yourself chaste” (1 Tim. 5:22). What is sought, then, is not only your own purity from such markets but also that of your household: “It is necessary for the bishop to be blameless … presiding well over his own household, having children subject to him with all chastity. But if anyone does not know how to preside over his own household, how will he care for the Church of God?” (1 Tim. 3:2–5). Therefore instruct your household, exhort it, guard it. And if a servant deceives you—for I do not exclude human weakness—once discovered, let him be rejected according to the prophetic example. [I, q. 1, chapter “Cito.”] Leprosy quickly follows shameful payment, and ill-gotten money stains body and soul. “You have received money,” he says, “and you shall possess from it a field, a vineyard, olive groves, and flocks; and Naaman’s leprosy shall attach itself to you and to your seed forever” (2 Kings 5:26–27). [Note: [Col. 1628D] The handwritten manuscripts agree overwhelmingly in this reading. All the printed editions, however, read: “And Naaman’s leprosy shall cling to you,” etc.] You see that the succession of the heir is condemned because of the deed of the originator. For the guilt of selling the mystery is inexpiable, and the vengeance of heavenly grace passes to descendants. Finally, “the Moabites and the others shall not enter the Church of God until the third and fourth generation” (Deut. 23:3)—that is, to interpret it more simply, until the succession of many generations has erased the guilt of the originators.

54. But if those who sinned against God through the error of idolatry appear to have been punished to the fourth generation, the sentence certainly seems harsher by which the seed of Gehazi is condemned forever for his desire to possess, and this especially since our Lord Jesus Christ granted forgiveness of sins to everyone through the bath of regeneration—unless you understand this as referring to the seed of vices rather than of race. For just as those who are sons of promise are reckoned as good seed, so those who are sons of error are reckoned as evil seed. The Jews too are from their father the devil, not through succession of flesh but of crime. Therefore all the greedy and all the avaricious possess Gehazi’s leprosy together with their riches; and, through ill-gotten payment, they have gathered not so much a patrimony of possessions as a treasury of crimes, with eternal punishment and a brief profit. For although riches are transient, punishment is everlasting, because neither the avaricious, nor the drunkard, nor the one who serves idols shall possess the kingdom of God.

[Col. 1629A] *(Verses 28–29.)* “And all in the synagogue were filled with anger when they heard these things; and they rose up and drove him outside the city.”

55. The sacrileges of the Jews, which the Lord had foretold long before through the prophet and declared in a verse of the Psalm what he would suffer when established in the body, saying: “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. 34:12), he teaches in the Gospel to have been fulfilled. For while he himself poured out benefits among the peoples, they inflicted injuries upon him. It is no wonder that they lost salvation, since they drove the Savior from their borders. For the Lord is considerate; and he who had taught his apostles by his own example to become all things to all people neither rejects those who wish for him nor binds those who do not wish for him, neither resists those who drive him out nor is absent from those who ask. Thus elsewhere, when the Gerasenes could not endure his powers, he left them as weak and ungrateful people (Luke 8:37).

56. Understand at the same time that this was not compelled but a voluntary suffering of the body: he was not seized by the Jews, but offered himself. For when he wishes, he is seized; when he wishes, he slips away; when he wishes, he is hung; when he wishes, he is not held. And here he had ascended so that he might be thrown headlong from the brow of the mountain; and behold, passing through their midst, when the minds of those raging had suddenly changed or been struck senseless, he descended—for the hour of his passion had not yet come. Indeed, he preferred to heal the Jews rather than destroy them, so that, when their fury had ended ineffectually, they would cease wishing for what they could not accomplish. You see, therefore, that here too it was an act of divinity, and that there it was an act of will that he was seized.

[Note: All editions read: “that he was not seized.” All manuscripts read: “that he performed,” namely, the change in the minds of those who were raging.]

For how could he have been held by a few, who was not held by the people? But he did not wish the sacrilege to belong to the many, so that he might turn the odium of the cross back upon those responsible for the crime; and so that he might indeed be fastened to the cross by a few, but might die for the whole world.

*(Verses 33, 38.) And in the synagogue there was a man who had an unclean spirit. And later: Rising from the synagogue, he entered the house of Simon and Andrew. Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a severe fever.*

57. Observe the mercy of the Lord and Savior: neither provoked to anger, nor offended by crime, nor injured by insult, he does not abandon Judea. Indeed, forgetful of the injury and mindful of mercy, now by teaching, now by delivering, now by healing, he soothes the hearts of the faithless people. And rightly does Saint Luke first place the man freed from the spirit of wickedness and then introduce the woman’s healing. For the Lord had come to heal both sexes; and the one who was created first ought to be healed first. Nor was she to be passed over who had sinned more through fickleness of spirit than through depravity.

58. *(Verse 31.)* The fact that the Lord’s work of healing began on the Sabbath signifies that the new creation began where the old had previously ceased; and it indicates from the very beginning that the Son of God is not under the Law, but above the Law; and that the Law is not abolished but fulfilled. For the world was not made through the Law, but through the Word, as we read: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII, 6). The Law, therefore, is not abolished, but fulfilled, so that the renewal of humanity, already falling, may take place. Hence the Apostle also says: “Stripping off the old man from you . . . put on the new man, who was created according to Christ” (Eph. IV, 22 and 24; Col. III, 9 and 10).

And rightly did he begin on the Sabbath, so that he might show himself to be the Creator, who interwove works with works and carried forward the work that he himself had already begun. It is as if a craftsman, intending to renovate a house, begins to remove its oldness not from the foundations but from the roof. Thus he first lays his hand there where he had previously stopped.

59. Then he begins with lesser things, so as to arrive at greater ones. Human beings can indeed be freed from a demon through the word of God, but to command the dead to rise belongs to divine power alone.

60. *(Verse 34.)* No one ought to be troubled by the fact that in this book the devil is first introduced as having spoken the name “Jesus of Nazareth.” For Christ did not receive his name from him—the name that the angel brought from heaven to the Virgin (Luke I, 31). It is characteristic of his shamelessness to be the first among human beings to appropriate something and to bring it to human beings as though it were new, in order to inspire terror of his power.

Finally, in Genesis too he was the first to name God to the human being. Thus you have: “And the serpent said to the woman: Why indeed did God say, ‘You shall not eat from every tree’?” (Gen. III, 1). Both, therefore, were deceived by the devil and healed by Christ.

61. Follow what comes next, learn the mysteries of the Gospel reading, and recognize in the healing of the two the sacrament of universal salvation. For “as all die in Adam, so also shall all be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. XV, 22).

Who is the one who had an unclean demonic spirit in the synagogue, if not the Jewish people, which, as though bound and knotted by serpent-like coils and the snares of the devil, polluted its simulated bodily purity with the filth of its inner mind? And rightly was there a man in the synagogue who had an unclean spirit, because it had lost the Holy Spirit. The devil had entered where Christ had departed.

At the same time it is shown that the nature of the devil is not evil, but his works are wicked. For by his superior nature he confesses the Lord, but by his work he denies him.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “the nature of the devil is not disapproved”; others: “does not disapprove,” with “wicked works.” But it is clear from what follows that the reading of the other manuscripts and editions is preferable.]

And in this his wickedness appears, as does the wickedness of the Jews: he had so poured the blindness of madness over the people that the people denied the one whom the demons confessed. O inheritance of disciples worse than their teacher! He tests the Lord by word; they attack him in deed. He says, “Throw yourself down” (Luke IV, 9 above); they assault him in order to throw him down.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “his wickedness and depravity, because he thus . . . upon the Jewish people.” The old edition, together with three manuscripts, has the reading given in the text. Other manuscripts read: “his wickedness, the depravity of the Jews.” This is not entirely unsuitable if *nequitia* is taken in the ablative, meaning “through wickedness.”]

62. If we consider these things according to a deeper plan, we must understand both the health of the soul and that of the body, so that first the soul, which had suffered from the serpent’s snares, might be set free. For the soul would never be overcome by the body unless it had first been tempted by the devil. Since the soul moves, gives life to, and governs the body, how could it be dragged captive into the body’s enticements unless it too had been bound by the chains of some higher power?

Indeed, Eve did not first become hungry before the serpent’s cunning had tempted her. Therefore the remedy of salvation ought first to work against the very author of sin.

63. Perhaps also, in the figure of that woman, Simon’s and Andrew’s mother-in-law, our flesh languished under various fevers of sin and burned with the excessive allurements of different desires. I would not say that the fever of love is less than that of bodily heat. Thus the former fever inflames the soul, while the latter inflames the body.

Our fever is greed; our fever is lust, because our desires are fiery. Hence the Apostle says: “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn” (I Cor. VII, 9). Our fever is extravagance; our fever is ambition; our fever is anger. Although these are vices of the body, they nevertheless wrap fire around the bones and assail the mind, soul, and senses.

These things are first stirred up by the devil’s art. For a fertile field, a garment, and a necklace are the serpent’s persuasion. The desire for honors, the loftiness of positions of power, the sweetness of banquets, and the beauty of a prostitute are the devil’s snare—something like a seductive utterance of spiritual wickedness—which, through the allure of the flesh, quickly softened by a certain feminine fickleness, also casts the soul down from its station.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “by which he may quickly soften the woman’s heart through the allurements of the flesh.”]

For the soul does not desire a woman’s appearance before the eye of the body does. In the end, what you have not seen you will not love; but once the flesh has desired, the steadfastness of the soul that shares its condition also grows weary, and the mind is bent by participation in love—for “the two are one flesh”—and thus death creeps in through the accomplishment of the crime, while the devil tempts and the flesh persuades.

64. Yet the fever of the soul is more violent than that of the body. Therefore bodily health is often disregarded for the sake of the soul’s pleasure, and people do not abstain from dangers. Hence it does not seem irrelevant to recall how Theotimus, when suffering from a serious disorder of the eyes and in love with his wife, was forbidden by the physician to have intercourse with her. Unable to bear his desire and carried away by the impulse of lust, he could not restrain himself.

Knowing full well that he would lose his eyes, before approaching his wife, in the very heat of burning desire and preparation for intercourse, he said: “Farewell, friendly light.” Thus lust burns more fiercely than fever and drives and inflames more severely.

65. But when someone recovers from his frenzy, then the sight of his inner conscience is opened; repentance for what has been done follows, and each person blushes at the consciousness of his shameful crime. Then God is feared, and the sinner wishes to hide himself but cannot. Then the flesh is accused, and the devil is blamed: the former as the procuress of vices, the latter as the author of error.

Deformity is exposed; for every secret is naked before God. Nor are the hidden secrets of crimes concealed by the leaves of that fig tree—that is, by bodily covering or worldly boasting. And each person, conscious of sin in his divine-minded soul, fears judgment, saying: “When the mountains fall upon me, in what clefts of the rocks shall I hide myself when he comes to shatter the earth?”

Then the flesh generates thistles and thorns in the soul—that is, the bites of cares and anxieties—and the burning torments that the soul itself has surrounded itself with through the desire of the flesh. For the soul is fastened, as if by certain nails, to bodily pleasures; and once it has sunk into and clung to earthly desires, it can scarcely fly back upward, from where it descended, without God’s favor. Bound by the snares of its actions and already enslaved to the allurements of worldly pleasures, it is held captive.

66. The Lord therefore came to free this Adam and this Eve. One of them was made in the image of God; the other, receiving the power of her husband, so long as she remained subject to the stronger, possessed with him, in one spirit, a single will pleasing to God. Placed in God’s paradise, they worked for the nourishment of heavenly life.

But after the flesh began to persuade them otherwise and ceased to keep its proper law, they were made exiles from paradise and, by the merit of sin, fell into this lower and sunken place.

[Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, together with three manuscripts, read: “it began not to fear its own law.” Gill, with two manuscripts, reads: “it began not to fear the first law.” The Roman edition alone has: “not to fear the first.” Finally, eleven manuscripts, including Corbie and others of better quality, have the reading found in the text.]

No one should think it incongruous if Adam and Eve are understood as figures of the soul and body, since they are also understood as figures of the Church and Christ. For when the Apostle said that the two are one flesh, he added: “This is a great mystery; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 32). If this is a mystery of the heavenly God, it can much more be a mystery of our soul.

67. But the soul remains fixed and fastened, captured and inflamed by bodily fevers; it grows sick through compassion with the flesh. A physician must be sought. But who is so great that he can heal the ulcers of the wounded mind? What human being is so great that he can help others when he cannot help himself? Who could restore life to others when he cannot escape death himself?

For all died in Adam, because “through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death; and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (I Cor. XV, 12). Therefore the death of all comes from that man’s guilt (cf. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book I, chapter 3).

Finally, holy men were sent, and prophets were also sent, to speak divine oracles; yet they could accomplish nothing. Let us therefore seek a physician from among the angels or archangels. But how can they bring me assistance so that I do not sin, when the archangel himself could not abstain from sin? How can an angel restore me to paradise, when Satan himself and his angels could not preserve the position they had received?

### Chapter V

*(Verse 3.)* “And when he had entered one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he asked them to put out a little from the shore.”

68. When the Lord had bestowed various kinds of healing on many people, the crowd did not begin to be restrained from seeking healing either by time or by place. Evening came, and they followed him; the lake intervened, and they pressed on. Therefore he entered Peter’s boat.

This is that boat which, according to Matthew, is still tossed by the waves (Matt. VIII, 24), but according to Luke is filled with fish, so that you may recognize both the beginnings of the Church while it is tossed about and its later abundance. For the fish are those who sail through this life.

There Christ still sleeps among the disciples; here he commands. He sleeps for those who are fearful, but he keeps watch for the perfect. Yet how Christ sleeps you have heard him say through the prophet: “I slept, and my heart is awake” (Song V, 2).

69. And Saint Matthew rightly thought that the indication of eternal power should not be omitted, where Christ commands the winds (Matt. VIII, 26). For this is not human teaching, as you heard the Jews say: “He commands the spirits with a word” (Luke IV, 36), but a sign of heavenly majesty.

When the troubled sea is calmed, when the elements obey the command of the divine voice, and insensible things receive the sense to obey, the mystery of divine grace is revealed. When the waves of the world grow calm and the unclean spirit rests at the word, one thing does not invalidate the other; both are celebrated. You have a miracle in the elements and a lesson in the mysteries.

70. Therefore, because Saint Matthew had already given a preliminary account of those things, Saint Luke chose for himself the boat in which Peter was fishing. The boat that has Peter is not troubled; the one that has Judas is troubled. Although many merits of the disciples were sailing there, the faithlessness of the traitor still drove it.

Peter is in both boats; yet he who is steadfast through his own merits is troubled by those of another. Let us therefore beware of the faithless person; let us beware of the traitor, lest through one person many of us be tossed about.

This boat, therefore, in which prudence sails, is not troubled; faithlessness is absent, and faith breathes within it. For how could the boat be troubled when it was governed by him in whom the Church’s foundation rests? There, then, is disturbance where faith is slight; here, security where love is perfect.

71. *(Verse 4.)* Finally, although the others are commanded to let down their nets, Peter alone is told: “Put out into the deep”—that is, into the depth of disputation.

For what is so deep as to see the depth of riches, to know the Son of God, and to embrace the confession of his divine generation? Although the human mind cannot grasp this by a complete investigation of reason, the fullness of faith embraces it. For even if I am not permitted to know how he was born, I am nevertheless not permitted not to know that he was born.

I do not know the sequence of his generation, but I acknowledge the authority of his generation.

[Note: Thus the old edition and several manuscripts. The Roman edition, together with some manuscripts, reads: “but I acknowledge the author of the generation.”]

We were not present when the Son of God was born from the Father; but we were present when the Son of God was declared by the Father. If we do not believe God, whom shall we believe? For everything that we believe, we believe either by sight or by hearing. Sight is often deceived; hearing belongs to faith.

Is the person who makes the assertion to be examined? If good men were speaking, we would consider it wicked not to believe them. God asserts it; the Son proves it; the fleeing sun confesses it; the trembling earth bears witness.

In this deep place of disputation the Church is led out by Peter, so that she may see the Son of God rising on one side and the Holy Spirit flowing forth on the other.

72. What are the apostles’ nets that they are commanded to let down, if not the interweavings of words, as it were certain folds of speech, and the recesses of disputation that do not release those whom they have caught?

And rightly are apostolic instruments nets for fishing: they do not kill those who have been caught, but preserve them, and draw them from the depths into the light. They lead those tossed about from the lowest places to the heights.

73. There is also another apostolic kind of fishing (24, q. 1, c. “There is another”), by which the Lord commands Peter alone to fish, saying: “Cast a hook, and take the fish that first comes up” (Matt. XVII, 26).

This is indeed a great and spiritual lesson (11, q. 1, c. “A great and spiritual lesson”): Christian men are taught that they ought to be subject to higher powers, lest anyone think that the constitution of an earthly king may be disregarded.

If the Son of God paid the tax, who are you, so great a person, that you do not think it should be paid? He paid the tax who possessed nothing; but you, who pursue the gain of the world, why do you not acknowledge the world’s obligation? Why do you exalt yourself above the world with a certain arrogance of soul, when through wretched desire you are subject to the world?

74. The didrachma is therefore paid. It was the price of our redemption and of the body, promised in the Law and paid in the Gospel; and it was not accidentally found in the mouth of a fish: “For by your mouth you will be justified” (Matt. XII, 37).

For our confession is the price of immortality for us, because, as it is written: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “the price of the redemption of our soul and body.” But in all the others, and in the manuscripts, *soul* is absent. That word does not seem at all necessary, since our redemption is the same as the redemption of our soul.]

75. Perhaps this first fish is the first martyr, having the didrachma in its mouth—that is, the price of the tax. Our didrachma is Christ.

That first martyr, then—namely Stephen—had a treasure in his mouth when he spoke of Christ in his passion.

But let us return to the passage before us and learn apostolic humility.

*(Verse 5.)* “Teacher,” he says, “having labored throughout the whole night, we have caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the nets.”

76. And I too, Lord, know that it is night for me when you do not command. No one has yet given his name; I still have night. I cast the javelin of my voice during the Epiphany, and still I have caught nothing. I cast it during the day; I wait for you to command. At your word I will let down the nets.

[Note: The same edition alone reads: “I am still laboring through the night.” The fact that Saint Ambrose adds that he himself had sent out a *javelin*—the name of a kind of net, derived from throwing—during the Epiphany celebrations indicates that he had urged the unbaptized to ask that their names be entered on the register of catechumens. From this one may reasonably infer that they gave their names twice: first when they became catechumens, and second, more solemnly, when they were enrolled among the *competentes*, as we have noted elsewhere. From this it may also be gathered that this sermon was delivered around the beginning of the sacred Lenten season.]

O empty presumption! O fruitful humility! Those who had previously caught nothing enclose a great multitude of fish at the word of the Lord. This is not the work of human eloquence, but the gift of a heavenly calling. Human arguments yield; the people believe by their faith.

77. *(Verses 6, 7.)* The nets break, but the fish do not slip away. Companions who were in another boat are called to help. What is that other boat, unless perhaps Judea, from which John and James are chosen? “For Judea became his sanctuary” (Ps. CXIII, 2).

These men therefore came from the synagogue to Peter’s boat—that is, to the Church—so that they might fill both little boats. For everyone bends the knee in the name of Jesus, whether Jew or Greek: “Christ is all and in all” (Col. III, 11).

But I am suspicious of this great catch, lest the boats nearly sink under its fullness; for heresies must also exist, so that the good may be proved.

78. Yet we may also understand another Church, the boat of the other. For from one Church many Churches are derived.

Behold Peter’s other concern: he already suspects his own catch. But the perfect man knows how he can preserve those stored away, because he knows how he can catch those scattered abroad. Those whom he catches by the word, he entrusts to the Word.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “He restores by the Word.” The meaning is not absurd. Nevertheless, the reading of the other editions and manuscripts is also suitable: “He entrusts to the Word”; some manuscripts read: “He entrusted.” For it means the same thing as committing them to the Word and to his protection.]

He denies that the catch is his; he denies that the gift is his.

*(Verse 8.)* “Depart from me, Lord,” he says, “for I am a sinful man.”

79. For he marveled at the divine gifts; and the more he had merited, the less he presumed. Say this too: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man,” so that the Lord may answer you: “Do not be afraid.”

[Note: Thus the edition of Amerbach, together with nearly all the manuscripts. In some of them, however, it is written: “Do not be afraid to confess your sin to the Lord who forgives.” This occasioned Erasmus and the later editions to alter the punctuation as follows: “Do not be afraid to confess your sin to the forgiving Lord.” This fits less well with what precedes.]

Confess your sin to the Lord who forgives. Do not be afraid to bring even what is yours before the Lord, because he has granted us what is his. He does not know how to envy, he does not know how to rob, he does not know how to take away. You see how good the Lord is, who grants human beings so much that they have the power to give life.

# Book Five

*[Col. 1635]*

*(Verses 12, 13.)* “And it happened, when he was in one of the cities, that behold, a man full of leprosy, falling on his face, begged him, saying: ‘Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.’ And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying: ‘I will; be cleansed.’”

1. It is fitting that when the leper is cleansed, the precise place is not stated, so that it may be shown that not one people belonging to some particular city, but the peoples of all cities, were healed.

It is also fitting that, according to Luke, this man is healed as the fourth sign after the Lord came from Capernaum. For if on the fourth day he illuminated the world by the sun (Gen. I, 14) and made that day brighter than the others when the elements of the world began to shine, we ought to judge this work to be brighter still.

And according to Matthew, this is presented as the first person healed by the Lord after the blessings (Matt. VIII, 3), so that, since the Lord had said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17), the one who was excluded by the Law (Lev. XIII, 3), presuming that he could be cleansed by the Lord’s power, might judge that grace—which could wash away the leper’s stain—was not from the Law but above the Law.

2. Yet just as the authority of power is revealed in the Lord, so the constancy of faith is revealed in the leper. He fell on his face, which is an act of humility and shame, so that each person might blush at the stains of his life; but shame did not suppress his confession.

He showed his wound and asked for a remedy; and this itself is a confession full of devotion and faith. “If you will,” he says, “you can cleanse me.” He attributed the power to the Lord’s will. In speaking of the Lord’s will, he did not doubt as one distrustful of his mercy, but, conscious of his own pollution, he did not presume.

To him the Lord answered with a certain moral holiness: “I will; be cleansed.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “He answered with mercy.” But it is not unusual for our Author to use *holiness* in place of *mercy*.]

*(Verse 13.)* “And immediately his leprosy departed from him.”

3. For there is no interval between God’s work and his command, because the work is contained in the command. Finally, he said, “and they were made” (Ps. XXXII, 9).

You see, therefore, what cannot be doubted: God’s will is power. If, then, his will is power, those who assert the Trinity of one will necessarily assert the unity of power.

Thus the leprosy departed immediately, so that you might understand the affection of the healer, who added truth to the work.

4. Finally, according to Mark, the Lord had pity on him (Mark I, 41); and this is beautifully placed. The evangelists included many such details because they wished to ground us in both respects: describing signs of power for faith and expressing works of power for imitation.

Thus he touches him without disdain and commands without hesitation. This is an indication of power, because, as one possessing the power to heal and the authority to command, he does not shrink from giving testimony through his work.

[Note: “I will” is said because of Photinus. Although Photinus was a disciple of Marcellus of Ancyra and attached to the Arian party, in many matters he agreed with Sabellius. It is known that he denied that the same power was found in the Father and the Son, as Ambrose indicated above, Book IV, no. 10. Since in God will and power are one, it follows appropriately that Christ, by showing his will to have the same efficacy as the Father’s, also showed that the power of both must be regarded as the same, and consequently that their substance and complete likeness are the same—something Photinus denied.

“Commands” is said because of Arius, who, by denying Christ’s divinity, also deprived him of the authority to command. “Touches” is said because of Manichaeus, who denied Christ the capacity to touch when he rejected the true and natural flesh assumed by Christ.]

“I will,” therefore, he says because of Photinus; he commands because of Arius; he touches because of Manichaeus.

5. Nor is the leprosy of only one person healed, but that of all to whom it is said: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John XV, 3).

If, then, the remedy for leprosy is the word, contempt of the word is certainly leprosy of the mind. But lest leprosy be able to pass into the physician, let each person avoid boasting by the example of the Lord’s humility.

For why is he commanded to tell no one, unless to teach that our benefits are not to be publicized but kept concealed, so that we may abstain not only from monetary reward but also from the recompense of favor?

Or perhaps there is also this reason for the command to keep silent: he considered those better who believed with more spontaneous faith than those who believed because they hoped for benefits.

6. He is commanded, according to the Law, to show himself to the priest—not in order to report another person, but to offer himself to God as a spiritual sacrifice. Thus, after the pollution of his former conduct has been wiped away, he may be consecrated as a victim pleasing to God through knowledge of the faith and the discipline of wisdom: “Every sacrifice shall be salted with salt” (Mark IX, 49).

Hence Paul also says: “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God” (Rom. XII, 1).

7. It is also remarkable that he healed him in the manner in which he had been entreated: “If you will, you can cleanse me.” “I will,” he says, “be cleansed.” You have the will, and you also have the effect of mercy.

“And stretching out his hand, he touched him” (Lev. XIII, 3). The Law prohibits touching lepers; but he who is Lord of the Law does not obey the Law—he makes the Law.

He did not touch him because he could not cleanse him without touching him, but to prove that he was not subject to the Law and did not fear contagion as human beings do. For he could not be contaminated, since he was the one who freed others. At the same time, by contrast, the leprosy that used to contaminate the person who touched it was driven away by the Lord’s touch.

8. *(Verse 14.)* He is commanded to show himself to the priest and to offer a sacrifice for his cleansing, so that, when he offered himself to the priest, the priest might understand that he had been healed not according to the order of the Law but by God’s grace above the Law.

And when, once he had been cleansed, he commanded him to offer a sacrifice according to Moses’ precept, the Lord showed that he was not abolishing the Law but fulfilling it. Walking according to the Law, he appeared to heal above the Law those whom the remedies of the Law had not healed.

And rightly did he add, “as Moses commanded.” For “the Law is spiritual” (Rom. VII, 14); therefore he appears to have commanded a spiritual sacrifice.

[Note: The old edition reads: “and while he is cleansed through the sacrifice”; the Roman edition: “while he is cleansed, to offer a sacrifice”; but nearly all the manuscripts have the reading given in the text.]

9. Finally, he added: “That this may be a testimony to you.” That is: if you believe God; if the leprosy of impiety departs; if the priest is a knower of hidden things; if his disposition is the testimony of purity.

From this, who can appear more truly a priest than the one whom hidden things do not escape, to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4)?

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “Finally he adds: ‘As a testimony to you.’”]

*(Verses 18, 19.)* “And behold, men carrying on a bed a man who had been paralyzed, and seeking to bring him in and place him before him; and, not finding by what way they could bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and lowered him through the tiles, together with his bed, into the middle, before Jesus.”

10. The healing of this paralytic is neither trivial nor narrow in scope, since the Lord is first said to have prayed—not for assistance, but for an example. He gave us a model to imitate; he did not seek the importunate solicitation of one seeking to obtain.

[Note: The edition reads: “He did not seek the display of prayer.”]

And when the teachers of the Law had gathered from all Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem, among the remedies of the other afflicted, the healing of this paralytic is described.

First of all, as we said earlier, every sick person ought to enlist intercessors from whom the structure of our life, once loosened, and the halting footsteps of our deeds may be restored by the remedy of the heavenly word.

Let there therefore be certain instructors of the mind who may raise toward higher things the spirit of a human being, even though it is sluggish through the weakness of the external body. Then, with their assistance, let him be easy both to lift up and to humble himself, and let him be placed before Jesus, worthy to be seen by the Lord’s gaze.

For the Lord looks upon humility: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke I, 48).

*(Verse 20.)* “When he saw their faith,” he says.

11. Great is the Lord, who forgives some through the merit of others and, while testing some, releases the offenses of others. Why should a fellow human being have no power with you, when before the Lord a servant has both the merit of intervening and the right of obtaining?

Learn to forgive, you who judge; learn to obtain, you who are sick. If you distrust pardon for grave sins, bring intercessors; bring the Church, which may pray for you. For her sake the Lord may forgive what he might have denied you.

12. *(Verses 21, 22.)* Although we must not abandon faith in the historical account, so that we truly believe that the body of this paralytic was healed, nevertheless recognize the healing of the inner human being, whose sins are forgiven.

When the Jews assert that sins can be forgiven by the Lord alone, they confess him to be God and by their own judgment expose their faithlessness: they affirm the work while denying the person.

Thus from them the Son of God receives testimony to his work, and he does not require the support of their voice. Faithlessness can confess; it cannot believe. Testimony is therefore not lacking to his divinity; faith is lacking for salvation.

Indeed, what unwilling people confess is more powerful for faith; and what those who are refuted by their own assertions deny is more destructive for guilt.

Great, then, is the madness of the faithless people: although they confess that forgiving sins belongs to God alone, they do not believe God when he forgives sins.

But the Lord, wishing to save sinners, demonstrates by his knowledge of hidden things that he is God, and by the wonder of his deeds he adds:

*(Verse 23.)* “Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’?”

13. In this passage he displays the complete form of resurrection: by healing the wounds of the mind and the body, he forgives the sins of souls and removes the weakness of the flesh. For this is what it means for the whole human being to be healed.

Although it is a great thing for human beings to forgive sins—for who can forgive sins except God alone, who also forgives through those to whom he has granted the power of forgiving?—

[Note: Ambrose could not have proclaimed more clearly the power granted by Christ to the ministers of the Church to forgive sins.]

nevertheless, it is much more divine to grant resurrection to bodies, since the Lord himself is the resurrection.

14. *(Verse 24.)* What else is this bed, which he commands to be carried away, than the human body, which is commanded to be raised? It is the bed that David washes every night, as we read: “Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will water my couch” (Ps. VI, 7).

[Note: Everything between the words “washed by David” and “the bed of pain” was absent from all the editions. Yet it is found in all the Gallican manuscripts, except Reginensis and Claromontanus; both are more recent, and this passage is not so much Ambrose’s exposition as its epitome.]

This is the bed of pain on which our soul, sick with the severe torment of conscience, lay. But if someone conducts himself according to Christ’s commands, it is no longer a bed of pain but of rest.

Through the Lord’s mercy, what had been death began to be rest; for he turned the sleep of death for us into the grace of delight.

He is judged worthy not only to carry away his bed but also to return to his own house—that is, to return to paradise. For that is the true home which first received the human being: it was not lost by right, but by fraud. Therefore the house is rightly restored, because the one who would abolish the bond of fraud and restore the right had come.

15. *(Verse 25.)* No delay intervened in the healing; the saying and the remedy were simultaneous. The unbelievers watch him rise and marvel as he departs, but they prefer to fear the miracles of the divine work rather than believe them.

For if they had believed, they certainly would not have feared but would have loved; “perfect love casts out fear” (I John IV, 18).

Therefore, because they did not love, they brought accusations. To those making accusations he says: “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (Luke V, 22).

Who says this? The great Priest. He saw leprosy in the hearts of the Jews and showed that they were worse than the leper. The cleansed man was commanded to offer himself to the priest; the priest rejects these men, lest their leprosy contaminate others as well.

16. (Verse 27.) [Note: [Col. 1639D] The Gill edition inserted into the text: “There follows the mystical account of the tax collector and of the fact that he came not to call the righteous, but sinners. The mystical call, etc.” But it is obvious that these words have the character and form of a heading, not of the text. The Roman edition, omitting the verb, restored it as follows: “This is mystical, etc.”] There follows the mystical calling of the tax collector, whom He commands to follow Him, not with bodily steps but with the disposition of his mind. And so, having first turned the wages earned through the labors and dangers of sailors into harsh gains of avarice, he was called by a word and abandoned what was his own, he who had been taking what belonged to others; and leaving behind that cheap seat, he proceeds with every step of his mind after the Lord. He also prepares a great feast; for whoever receives Christ into the inner dwelling of his heart is nourished by the greatest delights of overflowing pleasures. Thus the Lord gladly enters and reclines in the affection of the one who has believed.

17. But again the envy of the faithless is kindled, and an image of the punishment to come is foreshadowed. For while the faithful feast and recline in that kingdom of heaven, faithlessness will be tortured by hunger. At the same time it is shown how great is the difference between the rivals of the Law and of grace: those who follow the Law suffer the eternal hunger of an unfed mind, whereas those who have received the Word within their souls, refreshed by the abundance of heavenly nourishment and the fountain, cannot hunger or thirst. And therefore those who fasted in spirit were murmuring, saying:

(Verses 30.) “Why does He eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” [Col. 1640C] [Note: [Col. 1640D] The Roman edition here and below has, “eat and drink.” This is supported by the Evangelist’s text and by all its versions, except the Ethiopic; for the latter, together with the ancient edition and all the Ambrosian manuscripts, supports our reading. The sequence of the passage also favors it, if it is examined carefully rather than superficially.]

18. This is a serpentine voice. Indeed, the serpent first uttered this voice, saying to Eve: “Why indeed did God say, ‘Do not eat from every tree’?” (Genesis 3:1). Thus they spread the poisons of their father who say: “Why indeed does He eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” Therefore, by eating with sinners, the Lord also does not forbid us to join in a banquet with Gentiles, saying:

(Verses 31.) “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick.”

19. A new physician has brought a new medicine. This did not sprout from the earth; for every creature is ignorant of this preparation. Come, all of you who have fallen into various sufferings of sin; use this foreign medicine by which the serpent’s poison is driven out—medicine that not only removed the scar of the diseases, but also cut away the source of the dreadful wound. This medicine does not impose hunger but supplies food for the soul. For “the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon’” (Luke 7:34); and therefore our mind is not fasting. Those who lack Christ fast, and are in need of an abundance of good works. [Note: [Col. 1641D] Several manuscripts have this reading: “But to him whose own virtue suffices by his will.” Others, including the ancient edition, read: “But to him to whom virtue is supplied.” The Roman edition rightly restored the latter reading. That same edition, instead of the words “And therefore … the bridegroom is with them,” as found in the others and in all the manuscripts, had substituted, in its usual manner, a long passage from Luke’s Gospel.] But he whose will itself is sufficient for virtue, who receives Christ into his own house, provides a great banquet—that is, a spiritual banquet of good works—at which the rich people are in need, while the poor feast. And therefore, He says, the children of the bridegroom cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them.

(Verses 35.) “But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them.”

[Col. 1641B] 20. What are those days on which Christ is taken away from us, especially since He Himself said, “I am with you until the end of the world” (Matthew 28:20), and said, “I will not leave you orphans” (John 14:18)? For it is certain that if He abandons us, we cannot be saved. No one can take Christ away from you unless you yourself take yourself away from Him. Let neither your boasting nor your arrogance take you away; do not presume upon the Law, for He came not to call the righteous but sinners.

21. How, then, did the Lord love righteous deeds, and did David not see a righteous man abandoned (Psalm 10:8)? Or what sort of justice of God is it if the righteous is abandoned and the sinner is admitted (Psalm 36:25)? You must understand that He calls those “righteous” who presume upon the Law and do not seek the grace of the Gospel. No one is justified by the Law, but is redeemed by grace. There is therefore righteousness in the Law, but righteousness is not through the Law. For the Apostle himself says: “A Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the Law a Pharisee, according to the righteousness that is in the Law, living without blame” (Philippians 3:5–6)—he who boasts on the basis of the Law: “The things that were gains to me,” he says, “I have considered losses because of Christ” (Philippians 3:7); that is, I cast aside the righteousness and glory of the Law. For the righteousness of the Law is empty without Christ, because Christ is the fullness of the Law. And therefore, although there is righteousness in the Law, righteousness is nevertheless not through the Law: “For if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21). Christ died in order to fulfill righteousness. Finally, when John said, “I ought to be baptized by You, and You come to me,” He replied, “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:14–15). Therefore He did not die for nothing, but Christ died for us, so that the righteous might shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. But they are not the Jews who are called righteous, to whom it is said: “When you see the righteous entering the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 13:28). These are the righteous who do not strike back at one who strikes them, who love their enemy.

22. (Verse 32.) If we do not understand it in this way, a contradiction results: “I came not to call the righteous.” But He does not call those who say that they are righteous: “For, being ignorant of God and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3). Therefore, usurpers of righteousness are not called to grace; for if grace comes through repentance, whoever disdains repentance rejects grace. [Note: [Col. 1641D] Not a few manuscripts, together with the ancient edition, read: “These will be wounded”; several others, including the Corbie manuscript, read: “The wounded thirsted.” [Col. 1642D] The latter is the true reading. Here those who fast are not being contrasted with those who do not fast; but since it is written below of the latter, “How does one who does not thirst appear to fast?” we understand that those are said to fast who “thirsted.” Here “wounded” means the same as “not healed by repentance”—or perhaps “ardently thirsting,” since those pierced by wounds commonly suffer the greatest heat of thirst because of the loss of blood.] The wounded thirsted, those who sanctify themselves; the bridegroom will be taken away from them. But from us neither Caiaphas nor Pilate took Christ away, nor can we fast, because we have Christ and feast upon Christ’s flesh and blood. For how can one appear to fast who does not hunger? How can one appear to fast who does not thirst? But how can one thirst who drinks Christ, when He Himself said, “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give will never thirst forever” (John 4:13)? Finally, the following words also make clear that the fasting spoken of is a fasting of the soul.

(Verses 36.) “He also told them a parable: ‘No one puts a patch from a new garment onto an old garment.’”

23. He had said that the children of the bridegroom—that is, the children of the Word, who through the regeneration of the washing have been adopted into the right of divine generation—cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them. Certainly this does not exclude the fast by which the flesh is disciplined and bodily indulgence is chastened; for this fast commends us. For how could the Lord here have forbidden the disciples to fast when the Lord Himself fasted (Luke 4:2), and finally said that the most wicked spirits are accustomed to be overcome only by fasts and prayers (Matthew 17:21)? Indeed, here too He called fasting an old garment, which the Apostle judged must be removed when he said: “Strip off the old man with his deeds, and put on the one who is renewed through the sanctification of baptism” (Colossians 3:9–10). The sequence of the commandments therefore corresponds to the same pattern: we must not mix the deeds of the old and new persons, since the former performs the bodily outward works of the flesh, whereas the latter, the inner person who is reborn, ought not to display a multicolored appearance of old and new deeds, but, in the same color as Christ, imitate Him through the zeal of the mind, since he has been reborn in the washing. Let there therefore be no discolored coverings of the mind, which displease the bridegroom; for he displeases Him who does not have a wedding garment. And what can please the bridegroom except peace of soul, purity of heart, and love of mind?

24. The Lord Jesus is a good bridegroom; through a new birth He initiated nature into a new condition. To Him she is betrothed, freed from the corruptions of the flesh. He does not seek mortal children; He does not delight in Eve’s sorrows; He does not seek a husband burdened by guilt, nor the inheritance of a condemned father. For she saw the wounds of the flesh, which she had previously desired; she perceived that true beauty is not present where there is the deformity of vices. And therefore, woman, what have you to do with such a bridegroom? Examine carefully, and you will find a scar on every body. Know another bridegroom instead, one surrounded with light, whose appearance cannot perish. Take Him into your mind; consecrate Him in your temple; take Him into your body, as it is written: “Take up the Lord in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20). Enter the new chambers of this bridegroom; behold His foreign beauty; put Him on; see Him at the right hand of the Father; and rejoice that you have such a bridegroom. He will clothe you with blessing, so that no rent of sin may harm you.

[Col. 1643B] 25. Let us therefore preserve the garment with which the Lord clothed us as we emerged from the sacred font. The garment is quickly torn if our deeds do not correspond; it is quickly worn away by the moths of the flesh and stained by the error of the old person. Therefore here He joins new things to old things; but in the Apostle we are forbidden even to put old things over new ones. Rather, we must strip off the old and take up the new, so that, having been stripped, we may not be found naked (2 Corinthians 5:2–4). For we strip ourselves in order to put on better things; but we are made naked when the garment is removed from us by another’s fraud, not laid aside by our own will.

(Verses 37.) “And no one puts new wine into old wineskins.”

26. The fragility of human condition is disclosed when our bodies are compared with the skins of dead animals. [Col. 1643C] And if only we could fulfill the use of good wineskins, so that we might preserve the sacrament we have received! Skill alleviates the damage if new wines are entrusted to renewed wineskins. Therefore we must always keep these wineskins full; for empty ones are quickly consumed by moth and rust, while grace preserves them when they are full.

27. These commandments beautifully suit this work: for this is the sixth work, by which Levi is represented in a certain new form (Luke 5:27). On the sixth day the human being was made (Genesis 1:26); therefore, by the sixth work of Christ, it is no longer the old but the new creation that is reformed, and a certain foreign form. And so, as a new creation, he provides a banquet for Christ, since Christ would delight in him and he himself would deserve to share in delight with Christ. To shape him, therefore, the Lord gives commandments; for he was already following Him, joyful, eager, and exultant, saying: “I am no longer a tax collector; I no longer bear the name Levi. I stripped off Levi after I put on Christ. I hate my former kind; I flee my former life. I follow You alone, Lord Jesus, who heal my wounds. For who will separate me from the love of God that is in You? Tribulation, or distress, or hunger? I am bound by certain keys of faith and fastened with the good fetters of love. I will hold every commandment of Yours as though it were a cautery impressed upon me. And if the cautery of the commandment burns, nevertheless it burns away the putrefaction of the flesh, lest the infection spread to the living tissue; and if the medicine bites, nevertheless it removes the disease of the ulcer. Therefore, Lord Jesus, take away with Your powerful sword the putrefactions of my sins. While You hold me bound by the bonds of love, cut away whatever is diseased. Come quickly, cutting into the hidden and concealed, the various passions; open the wound, lest the harmful humor spread. Cleanse everything that is foul with a foreign washing. Hear me, earthly human beings, who carry thoughts made drunken by your sins. I too, Levi, was wounded by such passions. I found a physician who dwells in heaven and scatters medicines upon the earth. He alone can heal my wounds, who knows no wounds of His own; He alone can remove the pain of the heart and the pallor of the soul, who knows what is hidden.”

(Chapter VI. — Verse 1.) “It happened on the second-first Sabbath that, as He passed through the sown fields, His disciples were plucking ears of grain and eating them, rubbing them in their hands.”

28. Not only through the comprehension of His words but also through the actual practice and appearance of His actions, the Lord Jesus begins to strip the human being of the observance of the old Law and clothe him with the new garment of grace. Thus He now leads him on the Sabbath through the sown fields, that is, [Note: [Col. 1643D] All editions have “He brings him near to fruitful journeys.” But the manuscripts do not have “journeys”; the word appears to have been introduced by someone who did not think that “He brings him near to fruitful” could be elegantly understood with “works” or “actions” supplied.] He brings him into contact with fruitful works. What the Sabbath, the field, and the ears of grain signify is no small mystery. For this whole world is a field; the crop of the field, in the sowing of the human race, is the abundant fruitfulness of the saints; the ears of the field are the fruits of the Church, which the apostles, threshing them through their works, fed upon, nourishing themselves on our progress.

29. The crop therefore already stood fruitful in virtues, with ears of grain sprouting, to which the fruits of our merit are compared. For these likewise either wither in rain, are scorched by the sun, are moistened by showers, are battered by storms, or are stored by reapers in the receptacles of blessed granaries. The earth had already received the Word of God, and the fertile field, sown with heavenly seed, had poured forth rich offspring. The disciples hungered for the salvation of human beings and, as though drawing the fruits of minds from bodily husks, brought them out into the light of faith through the splendid miracles of their works. But the Jews thought that this was not lawful on the Sabbath, whereas Christ, by the gift of the new grace, was indicating the Sabbath-rest of the Law and the work of grace.

30. I think that it was not without a mystery that the Evangelist, according to Matthew (Matthew 12:1) and Mark (Mark 2:23), wrote “Sabbaths simply” [Note: [Col. 1643D] The old edition, together with a few manuscripts, seems to have read “the second Sabbath” (the Roman edition has “second-first”), because “the Sabbath is an everlasting festival,” etc. The remaining manuscripts, many in number and written in a better age, have the reading given in the text. Interpret “Sabbaths simply placed” as meaning “placed plainly,” as they say, without addition. By examining the passages in both Evangelists, you can easily discover that this is the genuine reading.] because the Sabbaths are perpetual festivals of eternal resurrection. Therefore, either in this world, when you rest and abstain from the superstitions of the Jews, or in the future, when you yourselves celebrate festivals with perpetual solemnity, we shall eat the good things of the earth, according to what is written: “They shall eat, but you shall hunger” (Isaiah 65:13).

31. Yet Luke wonderfully said “second-first,” not “first-second” Sabbath: for δευτερόπρωτον is what is written. What excels should have precedence. It is “second” because the first had previously come from the Law, in which punishment was prescribed if anyone worked (Exodus 31:14). But it is “first” because that Sabbath which had been the first under the Law was released from the Law, and this became first which had been established second. For when it is lawful to work on the Sabbath, and there is no punishment for the one who works, the force of the Sabbath according to the Law has evidently been dissolved, and even its name did not remain. Nevertheless, the former was first in order, while this is first in gift. Nor is this less because it is second; Adam too was first, yet he cannot be compared with the second Adam: “The first Adam became a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit … The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:45, 47). The second was certainly preferred to the first: the former was the cause of death, the latter of life. Thus this is also called the second-first Sabbath: second according to number, first according to the grace of its operation. For the Sabbath on which impunity is given is better than that on which punishment is prescribed. The first is the Law, the second the Gospel; yet fear is inferior to grace. Or perhaps “first” here refers to the predestination of the plan, and “second” to the enactment of the decree.

32. In this passage too the Lord rightly demonstrates in the Law a type of the future and rebukes the defenders of the Law for not knowing what belongs to the Law, bringing forward the example that David, when he himself and his companions were hungry, entered the house of God, took the bread of the Presence, ate it, and gave it to those who were with him (1 Samuel 21:1 ff.). A great and truly prophetic example, by which we are shown that what must first be followed is not the empty content of the Law, [Note: [Col. 1645D] The old edition and some manuscripts read, “but of utility alone.” The Roman edition has, “but solid truth.” Most manuscripts have, “but solid utility.” Consistently, where all the manuscripts have, “Then, because David …,” the Roman edition altered the text to read: “Then, because in David, fleeing with his companions from the face of King Saul, Christ was prefigured with the apostles, so that he might conceal the ruler,” etc.] but its solid usefulness. Then, because David, fleeing with his companions from the face of King Saul, prefigures Christ here in the Law, Christ concealed Himself with the apostles from the ruler of the world.

33. How could that observer and defender of the Law himself eat the bread and give it to those who were with him—bread which no one was permitted to eat except priests—unless he was demonstrating through that figure that priestly food would pass over for the use of the peoples? Or else, because we must all imitate the priestly life; or because all the children of the Church are priests. For we are anointed for a holy priesthood, offering ourselves to God as spiritual sacrifices.

[Col. 1646A] 34. The doctrine of Christ therefore now overflows beyond the Law, yet it does not abolish the Law but fulfills it, because it does not abolish the Sabbath either. [Note: [Col. 1645D] Only the Roman edition has: “For the Sabbath was made for human beings; but if usefulness …”] For if the Sabbath was made for human beings, and human usefulness required that a hungry person who had long been deprived of the fruits of the earth should avoid the fasts of his former hunger, then the Law is not abolished but fulfilled. How, then, can the Lord be accused of a crime which is not held to be a crime in a servant?

35. What is clearer than this figure, which runs through the whole history? David entered the house of the priest Ahimelech; yet even when the danger of death had been set before him, he did not reject his guest, nor did the holy priest’s spirit refuse an exile (1 Samuel 21:1). Such is the grace of hospitality that we gladly take upon ourselves the dangers of others.

[Col. 1646B] 36. But this was foretold morally in the history and prophetically in the mystery: even though the outcome of a presumed future death had been set before them, the priests did not exclude that true David from the hospitality of their minds in devotion. Christ is taught to be found as a guest not only in the house of every prophet, but also, through the figure, as one who takes up the spoils and weapons of spiritual wickedness. For whoever receives Christ as a guest strips the intelligible Goliath of his weapons.

37. What is clearer than the fact that in the house of Ahimelech David asks for five loaves and receives one (ibid., 3, 6), the type showing that food would now be prepared for the faithful not from the five books [Note: [Col. 1646D] That is, from the five books of Moses, the Pentateuch.] but from the body of Christ, so that Christ might assume a body lest any of the faithful should hunger? Nor is the figure of Doeg without significance. He was keeper of the mules (ibid., 7), since no one else but the keeper of an unfruitful flock would fulfill the type of Judas the betrayer.

38. The fact that Saul persecuted the whole house of Ahimelech because David had been received, except Abiathar, who was then chief among the priests (1 Samuel 22:20), shows us prophetically that no one can harm the true chief of priests, who is Christ alone.

39. (Verse 7.) From here the Lord Jesus proceeds to other matters. For He who had determined to save the whole person moved through each member [Note: [Col. 1646D] All editions and some manuscripts have, “He cared for each member.” Many others have the more elegant reading, “He ran through each member”; this corresponds to the preceding verb, “He proceeds.”] so that He could truly say: “Are you angry with Me because I made the whole person well on the Sabbath?” (John 7:23). Thus in this passage He irrigated with the life-giving sap of good works the hand that Adam stretched out and with which he plucked the fruit of the forbidden tree (Genesis 3:6), so that what had withered through crime might be healed through good works. In this He rebukes the Jews, who violated the commandments of the Law through evil interpretations, supposing that on the Sabbath one must abstain even from good works, although the Law in present realities prefigured the form of future things—in which, certainly, there will be rest from evil works, not from good works. For although worldly works cease, the activity of good work is not idle when it rests in the praise of God.

40. You have therefore heard the words of the Lord saying: “Stretch out your hand.” This is a common and universal medicine. And you who think that your hand is healthy, beware lest avarice contract it, beware lest sacrilege contract it. Stretch it out more often; stretch it out toward the poor person who begs you; stretch it out so that you may help your neighbor, so that you may bring protection to the widow, so that you may rescue from injustice the one whom you see subjected to unjust insult; stretch it out toward God for your sins. This is how the hand is stretched out; this is how it is healed. Thus Jeroboam contracted his hand when he sacrificed to idols, and again stretched it out when he entreated God (1 Kings 13:4, 6).

(Verses 12.) “It happened in those days that He went out onto the mountain to pray, and He spent the night in the prayer of God.” [Note: [Col. 1647D] All editions and two manuscripts have this reading. All the others have, “spending the night in prayer.” The latter is less suitable to what follows.]

41. Not everyone who prays ascends the mountain—for there is a kind of prayer that produces sin—but the one who prays well, advancing from earthly things to higher things, ascends to the summit of the lofty heavenly court. He does not ascend the mountain who is anxious about the riches or honor of the world; he does not ascend the mountain who desires the legal title to another’s estate. The one who seeks God ascends; the one who asks for the Lord’s help in his course ascends. All the great, all the exalted, ascend the mountain. For the Prophet does not say to just anyone: “Ascend a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem” (Isaiah 40:9). You ascend this mountain not by many bodily footsteps but by more exalted deeds. Follow Christ, so that you yourself may be a mountain; “the mountains surround Him” (Psalm 124:2). Seek in the Gospel, and you will find that only the disciples ascended the mountain with the Lord.

42. The Lord therefore prays not to plead for Himself but to obtain something for me. For although the Father has placed all things under the Son’s power, the Son, in order to fulfill the form of a human being, nevertheless considers that the Father must be entreated for us, because He is our advocate. Do not open ears prepared for ambush, so that you may think the Son, as though weak, is asking to obtain what He could not accomplish by the authority of His power. The teacher of obedience instructs us in the commandments of virtue by His own example. “We have an advocate with the Father,” he says (1 John 2:1). If He is an advocate, He ought to intervene for my sins. He therefore pleads not as one who is weak but as one who is compassionate. Do you wish to know that He can do everything He wishes? He is both advocate and judge. In the one role there is the duty of compassion; in the other, the distinction of power.

43. “And He spent the night,” He says, “in the prayer of God.” You are given an example and prescribed a pattern that you must imitate. What ought you to do for your salvation when Christ spends the night in prayer for you? What should you do when you wish to undertake some act of devotion, when Christ, about to send the apostles, first prayed and prayed alone? Nowhere else, if I am not mistaken, is He found to have prayed with the apostles; everywhere He entreats alone. For human prayers cannot grasp the counsel of God, [Note: [Col. 1647D] The latest Paris edition has, “nor can any of those below.” Some manuscripts have, “nor can any of those outside.” Other manuscripts, and the ancient editions, more appropriately have, “nor can any of those within.”] nor can anyone among those within share in Christ. Do you wish to know that He prayed for me, not for Himself?

(Verses 13.) “He called His disciples,” He says, “and chose twelve of them.”

44. He was to send them throughout the world as sowers of faith, to spread the aid of human salvation. At the same time, observe the heavenly plan: He did not choose certain wise men, nor the rich, nor the noble, but fishermen and tax collectors, whom He would send. This was so that He would not appear to have drawn anyone by wisdom, purchased anyone by wealth, or attracted anyone by the authority of power and nobility; [Note: [Col. 1648D] Several manuscripts have, “so that the reasoning of truth might prevail for the sake of the argument.”] rather, the reasoning of truth might prevail, not the charm of argument.

45. (Verse 16.) Judas too is chosen, not through lack of foresight but through providence. How great is the truth, which even an adversary’s ministry does not weaken! How great is the Lord’s moral character, who preferred that His judgment should be put at risk among us rather than His affection! He had assumed human frailty and therefore did not refuse even these aspects of human weakness. He wished to be abandoned; He wished to be betrayed; He wished to be handed over by His own apostle, so that when you are abandoned by a companion and betrayed by a companion, you may bear moderately the fact that your judgment has erred and your benefit has been lost.

(Verses 17.) “And He came down with them,” He says, “and stood on a level place.”

46. Observe everything carefully: how He ascends with the apostles and descends to the crowds. For how could the crowd see Christ except in a lowly place? It does not follow Him to heights; it does not ascend to exalted places. Finally, when He descended, He found the sick; for in the heights there can be no sick people. Matthew likewise teaches that the weak were healed in the lower places (Matthew 8:1); each person must first be healed [Note: [Col. 1648D] The Roman edition and the Claromontanus manuscript read, “must be healed so that he may be able to ascend.” The others, together with the remaining manuscripts, have the reading in the text, except that some of them read “may be able” instead of “might be able.”] so that, as virtues gradually advanced, he might be able to ascend the mountain. And so He heals each person in the lower places: that is, He recalls him from lust and turns him away from the wound of blindness. He descends to our wounds so that, through a certain experience and abundance of Himself, He may make us participants in the nature of heaven. [Col. 1649A] He healed these people, but left them in the lower places.

1367 47. “Seeing the crowds,” as you have read, “He went up onto the mountain. And when He had sat down, His disciples came to Him” (Matthew 5:1). [Note: [Col. 1649C] The latest Paris edition has: “For as He was about to evangelize and bring forth blessing from the treasury of His divinity, He begins with an oracle,” etc. The Claromontanus manuscripts have: “The Lord, about to evangelize and bring forth blessing and oracles, begins,” etc. The other written codices and editions agree with ours.] For as He is about to evangelize and bring forth the oracles of blessings from the treasury of His divinity, He begins to be more exalted. Here, although He stood in a lowly place, He nevertheless raised His eyes upward. Thus also, when He raised Lazarus, He groaned in spirit (John 11:33); thus also He raised His head when He forgave the adulterous woman’s sins (John 8:10). For what is it to raise the eyes except to open the inner light?

48. Finally, Saint Matthew says: “He opened His mouth” (Matthew 5:2)—namely, the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God, [Note: [Col. 1649C] Almost all the manuscripts, like the ancient editions, present this passage in the same words as ours. But since in them the period ended after the word “opened,” with a point placed there, no legitimate sense could be extracted.
