Therefore, to remedy this difficulty, the scribe of one of the Colbertine manuscripts substituted “mouth” for “face”; these words are entirely omitted in the Claromontanus manuscript. The Roman edition agrees with the Claromontanus manuscript, but in addition inserted the word “old” before “temple.” We, in order both to preserve the sense and retain the common reading, judged that the punctuation should be restored as you see it.] with the inner chambers of His temple opened. He opened His mouth; therefore you too open your mouth, but first implore that it may be opened. For if Paul implores help in the opening of his mouth, much more ought you to implore it (Ephesians 6:19). The Prophet also shows you the key of knowledge with which you ought to open your mouth, saying: “Open your mouth with the word of God” (Proverbs 31:9). The Word of God is the key of your mouth; the key of knowledge is the key of your mouth, by which, when the chains of silence have been loosened, the barriers of ignorance are opened.

(Verses 20–22.) “Blessed are you who are poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who hunger and thirst now, for you shall be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. Blessed are you when people hate you.”

49. Saint Luke records only four beatitudes of the Lord, while Saint Matthew records eight (Matthew 5:3 ff.). Yet those four are contained in these eight, and those eight in these four. Here he embraced four virtues, as it were, the cardinal virtues; there he reserved the mystical number eight. [Note: [Col. 1649D] All editions have “opened.” By contrast, almost all the manuscripts have “preserved”—that is, he kept, using a compound word instead of the simple one. Since this passage appears to many to be shrouded in darkness more than Cimmerian, let us illuminate it as best we can. The reader should note that the number eight is called mystical for two reasons. First, many psalms are written “for the octave”; and by the octave the blessed resurrection is understood, as we learn both from the frequent testimony of Greek and Latin Fathers—for example, Gregory of Nyssa, Didymus on Psalm 6, Hilary in the Prologue to the Psalms and on Psalm 118, Jerome, Augustine, and Cassiodorus on Psalm 6, and others—and from Ambrose’s own words above, in Book II on chapter 3, and below, in Book VI on chapter 9: “The resurrection took place on the eighth day”; hence many psalms are written “for the octave.” From this it may be understood that he adds that the octave is the perfection of our hope, that is, its end and crown. He gives a second reason: we are commanded in Ecclesiastes 11:2 to give a portion to eight; and Jerome on Micah, as well as Vatablus, Estius, and others, have observed that the word “eight” signifies universality. Therefore, to give a portion to the eight beatitudes is the same as to devote oneself to all the virtues. Hence it is added that the octave is also the sum of the virtues; “sum” is said allegorically with reference to numbers, from which a sum is formed when they are collected. The adverb “perhaps” is included for no other reason than to indicate that this is not the native interpretation of the passage, which is taken literally as concerning almsgiving; or even that it may be understood mystically of the Old and New Testaments, as he himself often interpreted it elsewhere. The meaning, therefore, is that by the octave both the future resurrection and the totality of the virtues are signified equally.] For many psalms are written “for the octave” (Psalms 6:1; 11:1), and perhaps you receive the command to give a portion to those eight beatitudes (Ecclesiastes 11:2). For just as the octave is the perfection of our hope, so the octave is the sum of the virtues.

50. But first let us consider the matters that are more extensive. “Blessed,” He says, “are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3). Both Evangelists placed this as the first blessing. For it is first in order and a kind of parent and generation of the virtues, because whoever despises worldly things will merit eternal things. No one can obtain the merit of the kingdom of heaven who, possessed by desire for the world, has no ability to rise above it.

51. The second blessing is: “Blessed are the meek.” The third: “Blessed are those who mourn.” The fourth: “Blessed are those who hunger.” The fifth: “Blessed are the merciful.” The sixth: “Blessed are the pure in heart.” The seventh: “Blessed are the peacemakers” (ibid., 4–9). And rightly is this the seventh, because on that day God rested from all the works of the world (Genesis 2:2); for it is the day of rest and peace. The eighth is: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5:10).

52. Come, Lord Jesus, teach us the order of your beatitudes; for you did not speak without order when you first pronounced blessed the poor in spirit, second the meek, and third those who mourn. For although I know something, I know only in part. If Paul knew in part (I Cor. XIII, 9), how much can I know? In life as in speech I am inferior to Paul; for life demands and acquires speech, but speech without life is not the speech of God. How much wiser than I was Paul! He glories in dangers (II Cor. XII, 5 and 7), whereas I glory in successes; he glories because he is not puffed up by revelations, whereas I would glory if any revelations happened to me. Yet God can raise up human beings from stones and bring forth speech from the closed and a voice from the mute. And if he opened the eyes of the she-ass so that it might see the angel (Num. XXII, 27), he is also able to open our eyes, so that we may be able to see the mystery of God.

53. “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor.” Not all poor people are blessed; poverty is morally neutral, for both good and evil people can be poor. Unless perhaps that poor person is to be understood as blessed whom the Prophet described, saying: [Col. 1651A] “For the poor righteous man is better than the rich liar” (Prov. XIX, 1). Blessed is the poor man who cried out, and the Lord heard him: poor in crime, poor in vices, poor in the one in whom the prince of this world found nothing; the poor man who imitates that Poor One who, although he was rich, became poor for our sake. Hence Matthew explained this fully, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V, 3); for the poor in spirit is not puffed up, nor lifted up in the mind of his flesh.

54. This, then, is the first blessing: when I have laid aside all sin, stripped off all wickedness, and been content with simplicity, destitute of evils, it remains that I also discipline my conduct. For what does it profit me to be free of worldly possessions unless I am meek and gentle? For whoever follows the straight way follows, of course, him who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29). Lay aside, therefore, what is wicked; be poor in vices according to the good poverty; calm your passions, so that you do not become angry—or at least, when angry, do not sin—in accordance with what is written: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 5). For it is a splendid thing to regulate an impulse by deliberation; and to restrain anger and curb indignation is considered no lesser a virtue than not becoming angry at all, although the former is generally judged slower and the latter stronger.

[Note: [Col. 1651D] The Roman edition, together with the single Regius manuscript, has “I lack wealth,” which fits the context less well.]

1369 55. When you have done this, remember that you are a sinner; mourn your sins, mourn your transgressions. And rightly is the third blessing that of the one who mourns his sins, because it is the Trinity that forgives sins. Wash yourself, then, with your tears, and cleanse yourself with weeping. If you yourself weep for yourself, another will not weep for you; for if Saul had wept over his sins, Samuel would not have wept over him (I Kings XV, 35). Each person has his own dead for whom he should mourn. We are dead when we sin, when we are filled with the bones of the dead. Dead is the evil word that comes out of the mouth; for it comes out of an evil grave: “Their throat is an open grave” (Ps. V, 11). Therefore the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me” (I Cor. IV, 16). He wishes us to remember our transgressions. Paul had nothing to mourn after he believed in Christ, and yet he wept over his former deeds, saying: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Cor. XV, 9). He was a sinner before faith, whereas we still sin after faith. Whoever is a sinner should weep for himself and accuse himself, so that he may become righteous; for “the righteous man is the accuser of himself” (Prov. XVIII, 17).

[Note: [Col. 1651D] The Roman edition, with the single Regius manuscript, reads “I lack wealth,” which is less appropriate to the context.]

56. Let us therefore pursue the order, because it is written: “Order charity in me” (Song II, 4). I have laid aside sin, disciplined my conduct, and mourned my transgressions; I begin to hunger and thirst for righteousness. For when a sick person is in a serious illness, he does not hunger, because the pain of sickness excludes hunger. But what is this hunger for righteousness? What are these loaves for which the righteous man hungers? Perhaps those loaves of which it is said: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread” (Ps. XXXVI, 25). Whoever hungers is seeking an increase of strength. And what greater increase of virtue is there than the standard of righteousness?

57. After these comes: “Blessed are the merciful” (Matt. V, 7); for mercy follows righteousness. Hence it is said: “He has dispersed, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains forever” (Ps. CXI, 9). Yet even the one who shows mercy loses his reward unless he shows mercy with a pure heart; for if he seeks ostentation, there is no fruit. Cleanse, then, the inner parts of your mind; and if you have carefully purified the secrets of your heart, have compassion on those who are attacked, and understand how many human beings, how many of your brothers, seek your help.

[Col. 1652B] 58. But unless you first empty your inner parts of every stain of sin, so that dissensions and quarrels do not emerge from your passions, you cannot bring healing to others. Begin peace, therefore, with yourself, so that when you yourself are peaceful, you may bring peace to others. For how can you cleanse the hearts of others unless you have first cleansed your own?

59. You have therefore benefited others and brought help to many; hasten and strive toward the end. Although there were many ways by which life might end, one was fitting for the Lord; for what had been born according to the flesh had to die according to the flesh. He chose suffering so that he might die for us; and you too should say concerning all that the Lord has repaid you: “I will receive the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord” [Col. 1652C] (Ps. CXV, 13)—that is, suffering. Hence also he said to those who wished to sit at his right or left: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. XX, 22). He leads you to the end, pursues you even to martyrdom, and establishes the palm of the beatitudes.

1370 60. Observe, then, the order. You must become poor in spirit; for humility of spirit is the wealth of virtues. Unless you become poor, you cannot be meek. Whoever is meek can mourn present things; whoever mourns what is inferior can desire what is better; whoever seeks what is above avoids what is below, so that he himself may also be helped by what is above; whoever shows mercy cleanses his heart. For what is it to cleanse the soul except to remove the filth of death?

[Note: [Col. 1651D] The Regius manuscript alone reads “let him help those below,” so that this may form an antithesis with the following clause; but for that reason the common reading should not be abandoned. A little later, all editions have “unless he washes away the filth of the mind,” as do several manuscripts, except that they read “remove” with the others. The majority of the more authoritative manuscripts have “unless he washes away the filth of death,” that is, corruption. This fits better with the words that follow.]

“For almsgiving delivers from death” (Tob. IV, 11); patience, however, is the perfection of charity. But whoever suffers persecution, placed in the final contest, is tested by adversity, so that when he has fought lawfully he may be crowned. Some wish these to be stages of virtue, by which we can ascend from the lowest to the highest.

61. Finally, just as there are increases of virtues, so there are also increases of rewards; for to possess the earth and to deserve consolation is less than to be the Son of God. But since the first reward is the kingdom of heaven, and the last reward is the kingdom of heaven, is the reward equal for beginners and for the perfect? For to be the Son of God is more than to possess the earth and to deserve consolation. Perhaps we are taught mystically that the first kingdom of heaven is that apostolic state: “To depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23). You have the first kingdom when the saints are caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; for many of those who sleep will rise, some to eternal life, others to reproach. The first kingdom of heaven, then, is prepared for the saints in the release of the body; the second kingdom of heaven is to be with Christ after the resurrection. When you are in the kingdom of heaven, there is then a progression of dwelling places; although there is one kingdom, there are nevertheless different merits within the kingdom of heaven.

After the resurrection you will begin to possess your land, released from death. For the one to whom it is said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19), does not possess his land; for one who does not receive its fruit cannot be its possessor. Released, therefore, through the Lord’s cross—provided that you are found under the Lord’s yoke—you will find consolation in that very possession; consolation is followed by delight, delight by divine mercy. And the one whom the Lord shows mercy to, he also calls; the one who is called sees the one calling him; whoever has seen God is admitted to the right of divine sonship. Then at last, as a son of God, he delights in the riches of the heavenly kingdom. One begins; the other is filled. For even within this world there are many in the Roman empire, but those who are nearer to the emperor obtain a greater share in the dignity of the empire.

[Col. 1653C] 62. Let us now explain how Saint Luke gathered eight beatitudes into four blessings. We know, indeed, that there are four cardinal virtues: temperance, justice, prudence, and fortitude. Whoever is poor in spirit is not greedy. Whoever weeps is not proud, but meek and peaceful. Whoever mourns is humbled. Whoever is righteous does not deny what he knows has been given to all for common use.

[Note: [Col. 1653D] Thus the Amerbach and Erasmus editions, with the majority of the manuscripts. Gill and the Roman edition, with other manuscripts, read: “that it belongs to all,” and so forth.]

Whoever shows mercy gives from his own. Whoever gives what is his does not seek what belongs to another, nor does he lay a snare for his neighbor.

63. The virtues are therefore connected and linked together, so that whoever possesses one seems to possess several; and one virtue belongs to the saints, but the more abundant that virtue is, the more abundant is the reward. What hospitality there was in Abraham! What humility (Gen. XVIII, 2)! [Col. 1653D] What holiness, so that he rescued his brother’s son from the enemy (Gen. XIV, 16)! And what abstinence, so that he sought nothing from the spoils (ibid., 23)! But because he excelled in faith, he deserved the primacy of faith above others (Gen. XV, 6). Thus each person receives several rewards, because there are several incentives to virtue; but whatever is more abundant in a particular merit also overflows more abundantly in the reward.

[Note: [Col. 1653D] The Roman edition has “what charity,” but piety toward relatives is not so improperly designated by the term “holiness” that the reading of the other editions and all the manuscripts should therefore be abandoned.]

[Col. 1654A] 64. “Blessed, then, are the poor in spirit.” Here you have temperance, which abstains from sin, tramples upon the world, and does not seek what is alluring.

65. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst”; for whoever hungers has compassion on the hungry, gives through compassion, and becomes righteous by giving, because “his righteousness remains forever” (Ps. CXI, 9). Hence in Matthew we understand thirst and hunger spiritually: one desires the food or drink of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 1653D] Thus all the manuscripts and the older editions, except that some manuscripts and the editions of Erasmus and Gill read “which” instead of “because.” The Roman edition, suppressing the word “virtue,” transposed the passage as follows: “the food or drink of righteousness is desired, which, as it were,” and so forth.]

For virtue is, as it were, the material of virtues, so that the righteous man may show himself equal to those beneath him, exclude deceit, and seek truth.

66. “Blessed are you who now weep, because you will laugh.” Here you have prudence, whose task it is to weep over things that perish and seek those that are eternal; to mourn worldly things that pierce themselves; to seek the God of peace, who chose the foolish things of the world [Col. 1654B] to confound the wise, and who destroys the things that are not, so that he may attain the things that are.

[Note: [Col. 1654D] Several manuscripts read: “which will pierce themselves.” This is not at all inappropriate.]

67. (Verse 23.) “Blessed will you be when people hate you.” Here you have fortitude, but the kind that does not purchase hatred by crime; rather, it suffers persecution because of faith. For one reaches the crown of suffering in this way, if one disregards human favor and follows divine favor. Finally, to show that suffering is the completion of fortitude, he says: “According to these things their fathers used to do to the prophets”; for the Jews persecuted the prophets even to bodily death.

Fortitude also consists in overcoming anger and restraining indignation; thus fortitude strengthens both soul and body and does not allow them to be disturbed by any fear or pain, by which we are often struck as though by wicked interpreters.

68. Thus temperance has purity of heart and soul, justice has mercy, prudence has peace, and fortitude has gentleness.

[Note: [Col. 1654D] Several manuscripts have “purity of flesh and soul.”]

(Verses 24.) “Woe to you who are rich, because you have your consolation!”

69. Although there are many enticements to sin in material wealth, there are also many incentives to virtue. Although virtue does not require supports, and the gift of a poor person is more commendable than the generosity of a rich person, nevertheless the heavenly judgment condemns not those who possess riches, but those who do not know how to use them. For just as that poor person is more praiseworthy who gives with ready affection and is not restrained by the barriers of impending poverty, and who does not consider himself needy when he has what is sufficient for nature, so that rich person is more criminal who neither ought to have returned thanks to God for what he received nor ought to have hidden without use the wealth given for common use, lying upon treasures buried in the earth.

It is not wealth, then, but one’s disposition that is at fault. And although throughout his life the miserly mind may anxiously keep watch, extending its wretched guards, in order to preserve what is to benefit successors with anxious fear—a punishment than which none is more severe—nevertheless, because the practices of greed and the desire to accumulate are nourished by a certain empty pleasure, those who had the consolation of the present life have lost the everlasting recompense.

[Note: [Col. 1655D] The Roman edition reads: “and which, with no punishment . . . , he preserves for the benefit of successors in anxious fear.” The reading is clear, but has the support neither of the other editions nor of the manuscripts. We therefore think that a Greek construction is present here, and that the verb “to preserve” should be understood as meaning “for preserving,” τοῦ φυλάττειν, with the preposition suppressed.]

70. We can nevertheless understand the rich man here as the Jewish people, or heretics, or certainly the philosophers of the world, who, delighting in an abundance of words and in a certain patrimony of ambitious eloquence, have gone beyond the simplicity of true faith and stored up useless treasures. Does not some heretic seem to you, when you hear him disputing about the generation of the Lord according to worldly custom—rich in words, poor in strength? He thinks that in this present time he possesses abundant riches, but in the future he will recognize the poverty of his faith; and, weakened by the eternal fast of faith, he will understand that the food of unbelief which he belched forth in the present age is the cause of so great a punishment.

[Note: [Col. 1655D] The Gembloux and Prat manuscripts read: “which he will have belched up because of satiety.”]

And there will come a time when those who now laugh at our words will mourn their laughter.

[Note: [Col. 1655D] Not a few manuscripts, including some of inferior authority, read: “who do not believe our words.”]

To them it will rightly be said:

(Verses 26.) “Woe, when all people speak well of you!”

71. Does he not seem to be saying this to those who, formerly authors of treacherous apostasy at the Council of Rimini, lost the grace of God while pursuing the emperor’s favor? While they sought to please the powerful, they subjected themselves to an everlasting curse.

[Note: [Col. 1655D] The celebrated Council of Rimini was held in A.D. 359. Eighty Arian and three hundred fifty Catholic bishops took part in it. Although at first these bishops vigorously defended the Nicene faith, they eventually, whether by force, threats, deceit, or enticement by the greater promises of the emperor Constantius, miserably defected to the Arian party. More about them is found in the letter to Marcellina and in the work On Not Handing Over the Basilicas.]

72. Thus Saint Matthew urged the peoples toward virtue and faith by means of rewards; here he also deterred them from crimes and sins by announcing future punishments. He did not proceed casually through an enumeration of many heavenly deeds, only to come later to the place of the beatitudes; rather, he taught peoples strengthened by divine miracles to advance beyond the path of the Law by the footsteps of the virtues.

[Note: [Col. 1656D] Thus the manuscripts and the editions of Amerbach, except that in this edition and two manuscripts “it was” is read instead of “it will have been.” The editions of Erasmus, Gill, and the Roman edition read: “There the singing had to be done.” Perhaps this was intended to set singing and the blast of the trumpet against each other. But “there” should be retained because it was said above that Matthew invited the peoples to faith by rewards.]

There, caution had to be exercised, where the hearts of the still-weak people were wavering; here, virtue had to be roused by the blast of a trumpet. The discourse of this book makes this clear, both in what is revealed in its opening and in what unfolds in the course of the speech. There, those who are weak are still fed with a certain milk of the Law, and therefore are led through the path of the Law to grace; they hear what belongs to the Law so that, by following the Law, they may advance beyond the Law. Here, the more firmly established Church is not nourished with milk but fed with solid food; for charity is stronger food. Finally, among the three greatest things—faith, hope, and charity—charity is the greatest.

[Col. 1655D] 73. (Verse 27.) Charity is therefore ordered when it is said: “Love your enemies,” so that what was already said concerning the Church may be fulfilled: “Order charity in me” (Song II, 4). Charity is ordered when the precepts of charity are formulated. Observe how he began with higher things and cast the Law behind him, beyond the back of the evangelical beatitude. The Law commands retaliation for injury (Exod. XXI, 24); the Gospel grants love toward enemies, kindness toward hatreds, prayers in place of curses, assistance to persecutors, patience toward the hungry, and the grace of recompense. How much more perfect is the athlete who does not feel an injury!

74. (Verse 31.) And lest the Lord seem to abolish the Law, he preserves reciprocity in benefits, although he rejects it in injuries. Yet when he says, “As you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them,” reciprocity itself is made more complete when conduct is equal to desire. Virtue knows no measure of grace; and, not content merely to return what it has received, it wishes to increase what it has taken up, so that it may not be inferior in beneficence, even if it is equal in service. Benefits are weighed not only by their amount, but also by their order and timing: in an equal benefit, the one who began first has priority; for the one who first grants a favor is beneficent, while the one who returns it is a debtor.

[Note: [Col. 1656D] “Primacy” is used here for “beginning” or “first act,” just as elsewhere “beginning” is found used for “primacy” or “authority.” Saint Ambrose therefore wishes to say that the one who first confers a benefit deserves merit in two ways.]

The primacy of a benefit is therefore itself another benefit. For if someone has returned money, he has not discharged the favor and remains a debtor in gratitude, although he is no longer a debtor in money, why should we think that by returning a favor we can exhaust the gratitude, whose return is more a testimony that it was received than a discharge of it?

75. (Verse 32.) The Christian is therefore instructed by a good example, so that, not content with the law of nature, he may seek its grace. For if loving in return is common to everyone, even sinners, then one whose profession is more exalted ought also to have a richer zeal for virtue, so that he may love even those who do not love him. Although no merits of the beloved exclude the practice of love, they have not therefore excluded virtue. For just as, when someone loves you, you are ashamed not to return the favor, and through the love of returning the favor his love grows in you, though previously you did not love him, so also in the case of one who does not love you, you ought to love virtue, so that while you love virtue you may begin to love the one whom you do not love. The reward of the lover is rare and fleeting; the reward of virtue is eternal.

76. What, moreover, is as astonishing as offering the other cheek to one who strikes you? Is not every burst of indignation broken, and anger calmed? Does it not happen through patience that you rebuke the striker even more sharply by his own repentance?

[Note: [Col. 1656D] Some manuscripts read: “so that by your repentance you may strike back at the striker even more.”]

[Col. 1657A] Thus it will happen that you both repel the injury and seek favor. Often the greatest causes of love arise when patience is returned for insolence and gratitude for injury. Indeed, as I remember hearing, we think that philosophy’s proud brow was humbled by this alone: that it seemed to divide justice into three parts—one toward God, called piety; another toward parents and the rest of the human race; a third toward the dead, so that the proper rites of burial might be paid to them (Diogenes Laertius, Life of Plato). But the Lord Jesus, surpassing both the oracle of the Law and the height of philosophy, extended the duty of piety even toward those who had injured him.

For if an enemy who has contended with you in war and arms, after laying down his weapons, obtains mercy for his life—and this is generally granted either out of regard for nature or by the law of war, so that the defeated may be spared—how much more should it be granted for the nobler consideration of religion! For if a combatant is not moved to kill a defeated enemy by the fact that the enemy had attacked his own life, what ought to move the soldier of peace?

[Note: [Col. 1657D] By “soldier of peace,” understand the Christian. The sense of the whole passage is this: if a combatant is not driven to kill a defeated enemy by the fact that his own life had been attacked by that enemy, there should be nothing that moves a Christian to vengeance.]

77. We therefore see that the apostolic saying—“Charity is patient, is kind, does not envy . . . is not puffed up” (I Cor. XIII, 4)—is fulfilled in these precepts. If it is patient, it must show patience toward the one who strikes; if it is kind, it must not answer curses with curses; if it does not seek what is its own, it must not resist the one who robs; if it does not envy, it must not hate an enemy. And yet the divine precepts of piety go beyond the apostolic ones; for it is more to give than to yield, and more to love enemies than merely not to envy them.

The Lord both said and did all these things. When he was cursed, he did not curse in return; when he was struck, he did not strike back; when he was stripped, he did not resist; when he was crucified, he requested forgiveness for his very persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them their sin, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 3). He excused his accusers from their crime. They were preparing a cross; he was returning salvation and grace.

78. (Verse 35.) Yet because the pursuit of virtues grows sluggish without reward, he both gave us an example and promised a reward from heaven, promising that those who imitate him would become sons of God. Whoever hastens toward a reward ought not to disdain the example; for the more excellent the reward, the more devoted the duty. What a reward of mercy it is, that one is admitted to the right of divine adoption! Follow mercy, therefore, so that you may deserve grace.

79. (Verse 36.) The kindness of God extends widely: he rains upon the ungrateful, and the fruitful earth does not refuse its produce to the wicked. The same sun of the world illuminates sacrilegious and devout alike. Or, if we weigh these things mystically, the Lord watered the Jewish people with prophetic rains and shone upon them with the rays of the eternal sun, even though they did not deserve it. But because they were moistened only with worldly dew, the Church of God is raised to heavenly light, although even for them the privilege of mercy is preserved if they believe.

80. He added that one should not judge rashly, lest, being yourself conscious of your own offense, you be compelled to pass sentence upon another.

[Note: [Col. 1658D] The Roman edition reads: “of your offense, while judging another, you are compelled to pass sentence upon yourself.” This is excellent if one considers the sense. But all the manuscripts and the old editions disagree with it. They agree with our reading, except that in place of “you are compelled” the manuscripts prefer “you will have considered.”]

81. (Verse 44.) There is also a great lesson: do not seek fruit from what is fruitless, nor expect a harvest of fertility from what is uncultivated. Each person’s cultivation produces its own fruits. That fig cannot be found among the thorns of this world; because it is the better kind, rich in fruit, the image of the resurrection is fittingly applied to it: either because, as you have read, “the fig trees have put forth their green figs” (Song II, 13)—the immature, useless, and perishable fruit that first appeared in the Synagogue—or because our life is immature in the body and mature in the resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 1654D] Some manuscripts read: “which will prick themselves.” This is not entirely inappropriate.]

Therefore we must cast far from us worldly anxieties that bite the soul and burn the mind, so that by diligent cultivation we may obtain mature fruits—something we cannot find in the uncultivated things of this world: “For they do not gather figs from thorns, nor grapes from a bramble bush.” One part refers to the world and resurrection, the other to soul and body; or because no one acquires fruit for his soul through sins, since the soul, like a grape near the ground, is corrupted below and ripens in higher places; or because no one can escape the condemnation of the flesh unless Christ redeems him, he who hung like a grape upon the wood.

[Col. 1658C] Far, then, from that flesh which was commanded, for condemned humanity, to produce thorns (Gen. III, 18), let us raise our spiritual eyes and stretch out our hands, so that we may be able to harvest Christ.

82. (Verse 46.) He teaches, moreover, that the foundation of all virtues is obedience to the heavenly precepts. Through this obedience our house cannot be shaken by a flood of pleasures, an assault of spiritual wickedness, a worldly rain, or the cloudy disputations of heretics.

83. (Chapter VII—Verse 1.) Beautifully, after completing the precepts, he teaches us to carry out the form of his precepts; for immediately the servant of a gentile centurion is brought to the Lord to be healed. In him the people of the nations are represented, held in the bonds of worldly servitude and sick with deadly afflictions, yet to be healed by the Lord’s favor. When the Evangelist said that he was about to die, he did not err; for he would have died unless he had been healed by Christ. He therefore fulfilled the precept through heavenly charity: he loved his enemies so greatly that he rescued the servant from death and admitted him to the hope of eternal salvation.

84. (Verse 6.) What an outstanding example of divine humility: that the Lord of heaven did not disdain to visit the centurion’s servant! Faith shines forth in deeds, but humanity works more powerfully in the affections. He did not do this because he was unable to heal while absent, but to give you an example of the humility to be imitated, by which he taught that regard should be shown both to those beneath us and to those above us.

Finally, elsewhere he says to the royal official: “Go, your son lives” (John IV, 50), so that you may know both the power of divinity and the grace of humility. There he did not wish to go, lest he seem to have shown greater regard for the royal official’s wealth; here he himself went, lest he seem to have despised the servile condition of the centurion’s servant. For all of us—slave and free—are one in Christ.

85. But observe that faith is the privilege of healing. Notice also that even in this gentile people there was a perception of the mystery. The Lord proceeds; the centurion excuses himself, lays aside military arrogance, assumes reverence, and is both ready for faith and prompt in showing honor. And Luke rightly says that the centurion sent friends to meet him, lest his own presence seem burdensome to the Lord’s modesty, and lest one duty appear to challenge another. This is the moral interpretation.

86. Mystically, however, the people of the nations desired that the one whom the Jewish people had crucified should remain unharmed by injury. As far as faith is concerned, the centurion believed the word—that is, he inferred that healing was given to human beings by Christ’s power, not by the power of a human being. As far as the mystery is concerned, he saw that Christ had not yet penetrated the hearts of the gentiles. And because he had not yet washed away the stains of his former thoughts, he considered himself more burdened by the Lord’s gracious condescension than helped by it. Thus the widow of Zarephath judged herself unworthy of prophetic hospitality (III Kings XVII, 18). Therefore the Lord preferred the faith of the gentiles in this one instance.

87. (Verse 9.) If you read it this way—“I have found no such faith in Israel”—the straightforward and easy meaning is clear. But if, in accordance with the Greek, you read, “Nor in Israel have I found such faith,” then the faith of this man is placed above that even of the elect and of those who had previously seen God.

88. (Verse 10.) Observe the arrangement: the master’s faith is proved, and the servant’s health is strengthened. The merit of the master can therefore benefit servants, not only through the merit of faith but also through the devotion of discipline. Observe also another arrangement of the Lord’s humility:

[Note: [Col. 1659D] The Roman edition alone reads: “another arrangement: the Lord accomplishes what he does not promise,” and so forth.]

what he does not promise, he accomplishes; for although he had not yet commanded the healing, the servants who had been sent found the servant well.

(Verses 12–14.) “When he drew near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow; and a large crowd from the city was with her. When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her: ‘Do not weep.’ And he drew near and touched the bier.”

89. This passage abounds in both kinds of grace, so that we may believe that divine mercy is quickly moved by the lamentation of a widowed mother, especially one who is broken by the labor or death of her only son; yet the merit of the widow’s dignity is enhanced by the crowd accompanying the funeral. And this widow, surrounded by a crowd of peoples, may be understood as more than a woman: she represents the holy Church, which by contemplation of its tears recalls its younger people from the pomp of burial and the final rites of the grave to life through the resurrection of its only young son. She is forbidden to weep, since resurrection is owed to her.

[Note: [Col. 1659D] All editions and many manuscripts read: “which is forbidden to weep for him to whom resurrection was owed.” Several others, however, including the more authoritative manuscripts, agree with us. The meaning there is that the resurrection of her children is owed to the Church herself; this corresponds more neatly to what precedes.]

[Col. 1660B] 90. The dead man in the bier was carried to the grave by the four material elements, but he had the hope of rising because he was carried upon wood. Although this had not previously benefited us, after Jesus touched it, it began to contribute to life, so that it might signify that salvation would be poured out upon the people through the gallows of the cross.

When the word of God was heard, the bearers of that bitter funeral stopped—those who were pressing the human body with the deadly flow of material nature. For what else are we doing but lying lifeless in a kind of bier, that is, an instrument of final burial, when either the fire of immoderate desire boils over, or cold moisture floods out, or the vigor of our souls is weakened by a certain sluggish condition of the body, or our spirit, congealed by defilement, nourishes the mind while deprived of pure light? These are the bearers of our funeral.

91. But although the final powers of death have destroyed every hope of life, and the bodies of the dead lie near the tomb, nevertheless, by the word of God the corpses that are already about to die rise again; the voice returns, the son is restored to his mother, he is recalled from the tomb and snatched from the grave.

[Note: [Col. 1659D] The Roman edition reads: “the already dead rise again,” which is quite suitable. Since, however, the other editions and all the manuscripts prefer “already about to die,” and since the bodies of the dead have been named in the preceding clause, the third sense of the passage seems to be this: that bodies, whether dead or already about to die, are said to rise again by the word of God. Unless one prefers to call sinners “corpses already about to die,” because they are not yet truly dead.]

What is this tomb of yours except evil conduct? Your tomb is unbelief; your grave is your throat: “Their throat is an open grave” (Ps. V, 11), from which dead words are brought forth. Christ frees you from this grave; from this tomb you will rise if you hear the word of God.

92. And if your sin is so grave that you cannot wash it away yourself with the tears of your repentance, let Mother Church weep for you; she intervenes for each individual as a widowed mother for her only sons. For she shares, with a kind of spiritual pain, the condition of nature when she sees her children being driven toward death by deadly vices.

[Note: [Col. 1660D] Compare this, if you wish, with what is found in Book II, chapter 2, On Repentance, where you will find many things, similar and nearly identical, to what various authors commonly explain about canonical sins and their public penance.]

We are the inward parts of her inward parts; for there are also spiritual inward parts, as Paul says: “Yes, brother, may I enjoy you in the Lord; refresh my inward parts in Christ” (Philem. 20).

[Note: [Col. 1660D] Thus the editions and a few manuscripts. Others read partly, “We are the inward parts of God, the inward parts of the Church,” and partly, “We are the inward parts of that Church.”]

We, then, are the inward parts of the Church, because we are members of her body, of her flesh and of her bones. Let the pious mother grieve, and let the crowd stand by; not merely the crowd, but a great crowd, should share the suffering of the good mother. You will already rise from the funeral; you will already be freed from the grave. Your funeral attendants will stand still; you will begin to speak words of life; all will be afraid, for many will be corrected by the example of one. They will also praise God, who has granted us such great remedies for avoiding death.

(Verses 19.) “And John summoned two of his disciples and sent them to him, saying: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’”

### 93

The meaning is not simple in simple words; otherwise the statements immediately at hand would conflict with what precedes. For how could John, whom earlier he recognized when God the Father revealed him, now not know him? How could he there recognize one whom he had not previously known, and here be ignorant of one whom he had already known? “I did not know him,” he says; “but the one who sent me to baptize told me: ‘Upon whoever you see the Holy Spirit descending’” (John 1:33). He believed the saying, recognized him when he was pointed out, worshiped him when he was baptized, and prophesied of him when he was to come. Finally he says: “I myself saw, and I bore witness that this is God’s chosen one” (ibid., 34).

[Note: The Roman edition, with a few and those more recent manuscripts, reads, “This is the Son of God,” a reading also favored by the sacred text. The other editions, with the remaining manuscripts, read, “this is God’s chosen one.”]

How, then, could so great a prophet have erred in such a way as not to believe that the one of whom he had said, “Behold, the one who takes away the sins of the world” (ibid., 29), was still the Son of God? For either it is presumptuous to attribute divine things to one whom you do not know, or it is unbelief to have doubted concerning the Son of God. Suspicion of so great an error therefore cannot fall upon such a prophet.

### 94

Accordingly, if the form of the literal meaning conflicts with itself, let us seek a spiritual figure. Since we have already said above (in *Luke*, book 3) that John represents the Law, which was Christ’s herald, it is fitting that the Law—which was physically enclosed in the breasts of the faithless, as though in eternal prisons deprived of light, and which the fruitful entrails of punishments and the doors of madness held back—cannot convey the full expression of its testimony concerning the Lord’s dispensation without the Gospel’s confirmation.

[Note: The editions read *astipulatione* (“with confirmation”); some manuscripts read *praeferre* (“to present”), others *perferre* (“to convey”).]

The Law indeed prophesied the grace of baptism in Exodus through the cloud and the sea; it foretold spiritual food in the lamb (Exodus 12:3); it indicated an everlasting fountain in the rock (Exodus 17:6); it revealed the remission of sins in Leviticus (Leviticus 25:10); it announced the kingdom of heaven in the Psalms; and it most clearly declared the promised land in Joshua.

### 95

All these things also agree with John’s testimony. Nevertheless, the Law is confined and restrained by the tyrannical powers of this world, so that it cannot pour forth the light of the Lord’s resurrection. John therefore sends his disciples to Christ, so that they may receive the completion of knowledge, because Christ is the fullness of the Law. Since words often waver without deeds, and faith is displayed more fully by the testimony of actions than by promises of words, what was then wavering in the hearts of the Jews, as though the Law had been sealed shut, would be opened by the very spectacle of the Lord’s cross and by the full testimony of the resurrection.

### 96

Perhaps these two disciples are the two peoples: one believed from among the Jews, the other from among the Gentiles.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “who believed in God,” and so forth.]

The latter believed because he heard. These therefore wished to see, in accordance with the saying: “But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear” (Matthew 13:16). Yet we too have seen in John; with our own eyes we have perceived him in the apostles; and with our hands we have examined him in Thomas’s fingers. “What was from the beginning, what we heard, and what we saw with our eyes, what we looked upon, and what our hands examined, concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested” (1 John 1:1–2).

When was it manifested? When we saw it. It was not manifested in this way before it was seen. Let us therefore give thanks to the Lord, who was crucified for our faith and crucified for our desires. My mind has been crucified in him.

### 97

Accordingly, even now those who read the Old Testament before they know the Gospel, and who read in it, as it were, certain traces of the Lord’s body, think that he is to come and ask whether he is himself the Christ, the Son of God, who is to come. When they read of the time when he spoke with Abraham (Genesis 18:20 and following, and 22:1), or when he revealed himself as the commander of the heavenly army (Joshua 5:14), they say: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect another?”

But when they come to the Gospel and learn that the blind are illuminated, the lame walk, the deaf hear, lepers are cleansed, and the dead rise, then they say: “We have seen him, and with our eyes we have perceived him, and we have inserted our fingers into the marks of his nails.” We seem to ourselves to have seen the one whom we read about, to have gazed upon him hanging, and, while the spirit of the Church examined them, to have touched his wounds. For if demons are cast out by the finger of God, faith too is discovered by the finger of the Church.

Or perhaps, in some operative part of our body, we all seem to have examined the sequence of the Lord’s passion; for faith passes from the few to the many. The Law therefore announces that Christ is to come; the writing of the Gospel confirms that he has come.

### 98

Some also understand this passage concerning John himself in the following way: he was indeed a great prophet, so great that he recognized Christ and announced that the remission of sins would come; nevertheless, not as one in doubt, but as a devout seer, he did not believe that the one whom he had believed would come would die. He therefore doubted not in faith but in devotion.

Peter too doubted when he said: “Be favorable to yourself, Lord; this shall certainly not happen” (Matthew 16:22).

[Note: The editions read, “Be favorable to yourself, Lord”; but the word “to yourself” is not found in the manuscripts.]

He was the leader of the faith—Christ had not yet called himself the Son of God, and yet Peter had believed that he was the Christ (ibid., 16)—but he did not believe Christ concerning his death. His lapse arose from an affection of piety, not from irreligion. Elsewhere, finally, he refuses to have his feet washed because he does not understand the mystery, while he is burdened by his devotion to the Lord (John 13:8).

Therefore even the saints did not believe that Christ would die: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—these things God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

[Note: All the editions and some manuscripts read, “Therefore the religious man.” Many others read, “Therefore the religious men.” Two manuscripts, both more recent, add “men.”]

Thus a lapse arising from devout love does not impede the faith of the devout.

### 99

Finally, the Lord knew that no one could believe fully without the Gospel, because just as faith begins from the Old Testament, so it is completed in the New. When questioned about himself, he indicated that he was the one not by some word but by his deeds.

### (Verse 22)

“Go,” he says, “and report to John what you have heard and seen. The blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear, lepers are cleansed, the dead rise, and the poor are evangelized.”

### 100

This is surely a complete testimony by which the Prophet might recognize the Lord; for it had been prophesied concerning him, not another: “The Lord gives food to the hungry; the Lord raises up those who are bowed down; the Lord releases those who are bound; the Lord gives sight to the blind; the Lord loves the righteous; the Lord protects the resident alien; he will receive the orphan and the widow, and he will destroy the way of sinners” (Psalm 145:8–9). “The one who does these things,” he says, “will reign forever” (ibid., 10).

Therefore these are not insignia of human but of divine power: to open to the blind the darkness of perpetual night; to heal, by pouring in light, the wounds of eyes buried in darkness; to introduce hearing into the ears of the deaf; to restore loosened limbs by releasing their joints; and to call the dead back to the light by restoring the vigor of life.

### 101

Before the Gospel, such things were either rare or nonexistent. Tobias received his eyes again (Tobit 11:12), but this is a single example; and that healing belonged to an angel, not to a human being. Elijah raised a dead man, but he pleaded and wept (1 Kings 17:20); Christ commanded. Elisha caused a leper to be cleansed (2 Kings 5:14), but there the authority of a command did not operate; rather, it was a figure of the mystery.

The flour of the hungry widow did not fail, being multiplied by prophetic commands (1 Kings 17:16); nevertheless, that flour preserved one widow—or rather, the prefigured form of the sacrament preserved the same woman.

Yet these are still small examples of the Lord’s testimony. The fullness of faith is the Lord’s cross, death, and burial.

[Note: Many manuscripts read, “death and burial.” Hence, and so forth.]

Therefore, after he had said the preceding things, he added:

### (Verse 23)

“Blessed,” he says, “is the one who is not scandalized by me.”

### 102

The cross could indeed bring scandal even to the elect. Yet nothing is a greater testimony to the divine person: nothing appears more beyond human capacity than that one should have offered himself wholly for the world. By this alone the Lord is fully revealed.

Finally, John designated him in this way: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

This answer, however, is addressed not to those two men, John’s disciples, but to all of us: we are to believe in Christ when the deeds correspond. For one will come who will claim this name for himself; although you may not be able to distinguish him by the designation of a human being, you will nevertheless discern him by considering his deeds.

### (Verse 24)

“What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind?”

### 103

After he had warned John’s disciples that the Lord’s cross was to be believed in, and after they had departed, he turned to the crowds and began to summon the poor to courage, so that those who were proud in heart, unstable in mind, and weak in judgment would not prefer appearances to usefulness or perishable things to eternal ones. Rather, with humble spirit they should take up the cross instead of displaying the finery of this world; and, like the blessed poor, who possess nothing in this age that they might lose, they should willingly exchange bodily life for immortal glory.

It is therefore not without purpose that the person of holy John is praised here: having set aside his love of life, he did not alter the pattern of righteousness even through fear of death.

### 104

“What,” he says, “did you go out into the desert to see?”

This world seems comparable to a desert: still uncultivated, still barren, still unfruitful. The Lord denies that we should go forth into it in such a way that we regard as an example and image for imitation men puffed up in their carnal minds and empty of inward virtue, boasting of themselves in the fragile elevation of secular glory. Their unstable life is troubled by the storms of this world; they are rightly compared to a reed. In them there is no fruit of solid righteousness. With worldly finery in their hair, covered with knots, noisy with the empty clatter of their mouths, they pursue things inwardly hollow but outwardly attractive, without any benefit to themselves and often with much offense to others.

We are reeds, founded upon no root of stronger nature. If the light breeze of more favorable success blows upon us, we strike those nearby with our wandering movement: poor in supporting others, quick to do harm. Reeds love rivers, and we delight in the world’s flowing and perishable things.

### 105

Yet if someone pulls this reed from the plantations of the earth and strips it of what is superfluous—stripping off the old human being with his deeds—and shapes it with the hand of a swift-writing scribe, it begins to be not a reed but a pen. Such a pen impresses the commands of the heavenly Scriptures upon the inner chambers of the mind and writes them upon the tablets of the heart.

Concerning this pen it is said: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Psalm 45:2); others wish to refer this to Christ. Thus, in one place, the Word, the pen, and the scribe are all mentioned.

He is the Word because he proceeded from the hidden generative mystery of the Father: “My heart has uttered a good word” (ibid.). He is the pen because Christ’s flesh expressed the course of the Father’s will and fulfilled the commands of the divine tongue through the sacred outpouring of blood. He is the scribe because, by means of his pen, with an indivisible distinction between the New and Old Testaments, or between divinity and flesh, he revealed to us the mysteries of the Father’s dispensation.

### 106

Imitate this pen by disciplining your flesh. Dip your pen—that is, your flesh—not in ink but in the Spirit of the living God, so that what you write may be eternal.

With such a pen Paul wrote that letter of which he says: “You are our letter . . . written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God” (2 Corinthians 3:2–3).

Dip your flesh in Christ’s blood, as it is written: “So that your foot may be dipped in blood” (Psalm 68:24). Therefore dip the imprint of your soul and the course of your mind in an unwavering confession of the Lord’s cross.

You dip your flesh in Christ’s blood if you wash away vices, wipe away sins, and carry the death of Christ in your flesh, as the Apostle says: “Always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:10).

Do not bend toward earthly things, lest you break your reed. Therefore it was prophesied concerning Christ, because he was not to be bent toward earthly things: “He will not break the bruised reed” (Isaiah 42:3), because by the power of the resurrection he strengthened the flesh that sins had bruised.

Good is the reed that is Christ’s flesh: by the gallows of the cross it fastened the serpent’s head—the devil—and the enticements of worldly desire.

### (Verses 24–25)

“But what did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing?”

### 107

The Lord’s saying here is not about clothing, although concern for softer garments makes many effeminate. As though they could not bear the weight of wool, they drag silk garments along the ground with their hems and, through use, make their clothing a burden.

Yet here he seems to signify another kind of clothing; and, unless I am mistaken, human bodies are meant, in which our soul is clothed. Finally, Joseph’s tunic was stained with blood as a likeness of the Lord’s body (Genesis 37:31). The Apostle also says:

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “Stripping off principalities.” The Apostle’s text, and all the versions except the Syriac, support it.]

“Stripping off the flesh, he led all principalities and powers in triumph” (Colossians 2:15).

What else does this show except that the body was like a garment, which the Lord stripped from himself in his passion, so that his divinity might remain free and untouched by injury?

This entire passage therefore exhorts us by a prophetic example to undertake the virtue of suffering. Finally, he added:

### (Verse 25)

“Behold, those who are in splendid clothing are in the houses of kings.”

### 108

Soft garments also signify luxurious actions and habits. For this reason the Apostle exhorts us (Colossians 3:9–10), that, stripping off the old human being with his deeds, we should put on the new, in which there is not sweet enticement and the sport of wantonness, but the practice of labor and its fruit. For the heavenly court does not receive those softened by tender care of the body, luxury, and desire for wantonness. One ascends to it by the hard steps of laborious virtue.

Those whose limbs are relaxed by indulgence, excluded from the kingdom of heaven, grow old within the dwellings of this world. There is no doubt that they are inhabitants of the rulers of this world and of darkness.

[Note: Seven manuscripts of better quality read, “and of darkness they began.” Several others read, “and of darkness he calls them. These are the kings.” The rest, and the editions, read, “and of darkness, the Apostle calls them. For these are kings.” The Roman edition removed “for these are.”]

These are kings—for they rule with a certain secular power—and they have received imitators of their own works.

### (Verse 26)

“But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Indeed, I tell you, and more than a prophet.”

### 109

[Note: The Roman edition excised, “How, then . . . shut up in prison?” That these words are not entirely superfluous here is clear from the fact that what follows concerns the foretelling of the passion.]

How, then, did they wish to see John in the desert, when he was shut up in prison? The Lord presents him to us for imitation: he prepared the way for the Lord not only by the order of his birth according to the flesh and by the announcement of faith, but also by a kind of foretelling of his glorious passion.

He was truly a greater prophet, in whom the prophets came to an end. He was a greater prophet because many desired to see the one whom he prophesied, whom he saw, and whom he baptized.

### 110

Yet was he also greater than the one of whom Moses said: “The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you” (Deuteronomy 18:15)? And of whom he said: “Every soul that does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from among the people” (ibid., 19)?

If Christ is a prophet, how is John greater than all? Do we deny that Christ is a prophet?

[Note: Amelote and Erasmus, with the more reliable manuscripts, read: “Indeed, I confess both the Lord of the prophets” (the manuscripts read “prophet”), “and I assert that this one is greater than all.” This reading is not displeasing to Gill. However, the Roman edition and other manuscripts read as in our text.]

On the contrary, we confess him to be the Lord of the prophets. I assert that John is a prophet and say that he is greater than all, but only among those born of women, not among those born of a virgin. For he was greater than those with whom he could be equal by the condition of birth (Luke 7:28).

That other nature is different and cannot be compared with human generations. There can be no comparison between a human being and God; each is preferred among those of his own kind. Finally, no comparison between John and the Son of God could exist to such an extent that John is even reckoned below the angels.

### (Verse 28)

“For the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is greater than he.”

### 111

Since he had called him an angel, he was rightly placed above human beings. And because he had declared him superior among those born of women (verse 27), he therefore added: “For the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he,” so that you might know that John must yield to the angels.

John is rightly preferred to those equal to him, since from his days the kingdom of heaven suffers compulsion (Matthew 11:12). This expression seems somewhat obscure, and for that reason we thought it had been derived from another book of the Gospel. For if we follow the letter, what is inferior is surely compelled by what is superior; yet the kingdom of heaven is superior to human things. But since some things are said to become compact through pressure, it is not absurd that the kingdom is compelled when it is thronged by many.

### 112

“And those who compel it seize it” (ibid.).

If we recall that saying of the Lord written elsewhere, when the Son of God says, “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21), we understand that the heavenly kingdom is consolidated within us when Christ, having shattered the kingdom of the world’s prince and driven out secular pleasures, reigns within the secret places of our souls.

Force is therefore brought to bear upon the human mind, which, softened by various enticements, flees labor and seeks pleasure, while, either restrained by fear of punishment or summoned by a reward, it strives to conquer itself. Like one who has endured exhausting labors, it strives to seize the palm that was being snatched away from it by many adversaries.

We seize the palm of salvation from this world, and, as though fruits were beset by watchful serpents, we pluck them through sleepless labor. Yet this is not a theft performed secretly, but a triumphant seizure.

There is another kind of seizure, when we seize what has been taken from others. We do not have difficulty understanding who those raiders are, since we know that we derive from Benjamin, the tribe of the ravenous wolf (Genesis 49:27).

John had gone before in order to justify the Jewish people. The Lord himself had come to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. He had sent the apostles so that they might establish the faith of the Jewish people either by argument or by signs and miracles. But when the Jews avoided the gifts offered to them, tax collectors and sinners began to believe in God and to gather into the faith.

Thus, through apostolic preaching, the kingdom of heaven is compelled among them and consolidated by the aspiration of the faithful people.

### 113

The woman who had suffered from a flow of blood seized the kingdom (Luke 8:44). When the Lord was going toward the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, she secretly tasted the remedy of healing by touching him.

[Note: In the Fulda manuscript and two Colbert manuscripts, the following words are inserted after *praelibavit*: “Cast out demons,” he says, “and learn who among them is worthy, and remain there.” Thus there does not seem to be a command here that they should proclaim Christ as the Son of God. The order of the discussion is therefore the order of the treatise; and hence, “if she seizes the kingdom here,” and so forth. It is clear, however, that all these words were transferred into the text from elsewhere.]

The Canaanite woman seized the kingdom when, having left her own borders, she cried out: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon” (Matthew 15:22).

Truly she compelled the kingdom: persistent in prayers, wise in her answers, faithful in her words. She recalls him as he passes by; she begs him when he is silent; she worships him when he makes excuses; she bends him when he refuses.

Does she not seem to seize it when she draws out what is denied and takes in advance what is reserved for others? For the Lord had denied that the children’s bread ought to be given to dogs. But she agreed, and by agreeing seized it, saying: “Yes, Lord; for even the puppies eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table” (ibid., 27).

### 114

You have learned how the kingdom of heaven is seized. Let us therefore compel it and seize it ourselves, for no one eats the Passover except in haste (Exodus 12:11).

But what is it that seizes the kingdom? Not shamelessness, not wantonness, not pleasure, but the faith of which it is said: “Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (Matthew 15:28).

Behold, she seized it: she obtained what she wished and wrested away what she asked for. The widow too seized it: by praying repeatedly, she wrings out a hearing, if not because of her innocence, at least because of her persistence (Luke 18:3).

### 115

The Church therefore seized the kingdom from the Synagogue. Christ is my kingdom. I seize him who was sent to the Jews under the Law, born under the Law, and raised according to the Law, so that he might preserve me, who was without the Law.

Christ is seized when he is promised to some and predestined for others; Christ is seized when he is born for some and supports others; Christ is seized when he is killed by some but buried by us; he is seized from those lying in wait and from those who sleep.

You have the proof where they themselves confessed that we had seized him and that they had slept, saying: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping” (Matthew 28:13).

Rise, therefore, you who sleep, lest while you sleep you also lose Christ. Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead (Ephesians 5:14). Do you see that those who sleep are dead? Therefore we do not envy others but provide for ourselves; the dead could not preserve the living.

### 116

Let those who have slept rise, even if late—those also who have lost Christ. Christ is not lost in such a way that he does not return, provided that he is sought.

[Note: All the manuscripts read thus. Conversely, all the editions read, “so that he is not found.”] He returns to those who keep watch and is present to those who rise. Indeed, he is present to all, for he is everywhere and always, because he fills all things.

He fails no one; we fail. He fails no one, I say; he abounds for all. For sin abounded so that grace might abound.

Grace is Christ; life is Christ; Christ is the resurrection. Whoever therefore rises finds that he is present.

### 117

The kingdom of heaven is therefore seized when Christ is denied by his household but worshiped by the Gentiles; it is seized when he is rejected by them but honored by us; it is seized when he is not acknowledged through inheritance but acquired through adoption.

# Book Six

[Col. 1667]

### (Verses 29–30)

“And all the people who heard, and the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with John’s baptism; but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected God’s purpose for themselves, not having been baptized.”

### 1

Saint Luke opened up, by adding specific details, what Saint Matthew had left somewhat obscure by speaking in general terms. For Matthew says: “And wisdom was justified by her children” (Matthew 11:19).

Here we first see expressed what that wisdom is, for Luke says: “They justified God.” God, therefore, is wisdom, because the Son of God is Wisdom: wisdom by nature, not by advancement.

The wisdom that is the power of God the Father is one thing; the wisdom that is the power of the soul is another. The former is born; the latter is created. The wisdom that is the author of works is one thing; the work itself is another—for it is the work of the mind to understand prudently and to perceive keenly.

These are gifts of nature. The one who produces them, however, is not a creature but the Creator: that is, he is not the gift of nature but the giver of nature.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “that one was begotten.” But why this alteration, since Christ is commonly called not only begotten but also born from the Father in the writings of the Fathers and in various Creeds that the Church accepts and daily sings?]

### 2

God himself is therefore justified through baptism, when people justify themselves by confessing their own sins, as it is written: “Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26).

He is justified in this respect: he is not rejected through defiance, but the gift of God’s justice is acknowledged: “For the Lord is righteous, and he has loved righteousness” (Psalm 11:8).

The justification of God therefore consists in this: he is seen to have transferred his gifts not to the unworthy and guilty, but to those made innocent and righteous through cleansing.

Let us therefore justify the Lord, so that we may be justified by the Lord.

### 3

Let us inquire more earnestly what it means to justify God. The Apostle says: “Let God be true, and every human being a liar, as it is written: ‘So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged’” (Romans 3:4).

David also says: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done what is evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm 51:6).

Therefore the one who sins and confesses his sin to God justifies God by yielding to him as the victor and hoping for grace from him.

Thus God is justified in baptism, in which there is confession and forgiveness of sins.

[Note: It is established that in the earliest times of the Church this custom prevailed: those who were to be washed in holy baptism prepared themselves for the sacrament of regeneration not only through fasts and prayers but also through confession of sins. Witnesses to this custom include Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 1; Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration 40, On the Holy Washing*; Chrysostom, *Homily 10 on Matthew 13*; and Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 17; Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 19; and others. Menardus, our own scholar, wisely observed that this confession was not itself a sacrament but only a preparation for receiving baptism with greater reverence. See him in *On Gregory’s Sacramentary*, page 138.]

### 4

Let us therefore not despise God’s purpose, as the Pharisees did. God’s purpose is present in John’s baptism; who, then, would doubt that God’s purpose is present in Christ’s washing?

This is the purpose that the Angel of the Great Counsel discovered, which no one knew: “For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11:34).

No one despises a human being’s purpose; who would reject God’s purpose? Therefore, as children, let us justify our mother and follow our mother. We know that a mother offers herself to danger for her children.

[Note: Many manuscripts read, “By the wise counsel of the mother.” One has, “By the wisdom of the mother, by the counsel of the mother.” Others, and the editions, more suitably read, “By the counsel of the Wisdom of the Mother,” so that it refers to the preceding statement: “And wisdom was justified by her children.”]

Let us obey the command of Mother Wisdom.

### (Verse 32)

“We sang to you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not weep.”

### 5

Although these words seem to fit the character of children, who in their immaturity still exercise a light movement of the body without mature judgment, I nevertheless presume that they can be referred to a deeper meaning. For the Jews seem to have believed neither the psalms at first nor the prophetic lamentations afterward: they were summoned to rewards by the psalms and called back from error by the lamentations.

David sang so that we might hang our instruments upon the willows (Psalm 137:2). He himself sang and danced before the ark of the Lord, not for wantonness but for religious devotion (2 Samuel 6:14).

Thus what is signified is not the leaping of a body bent in theatrical movements, but the energetic movement of the mind and the religious agility of the body.

Yet correction did not follow either the triumphs or the destruction of the Jews. Although provoked by the gifts of divine indulgence, they ought to have lifted their minds, raised their bodies, abandoned earthly things, and sought heavenly things. Worn down by the injuries of captivity, they ought to have mourned the sin that had been the cause of the injury.

### 6

### (Verse 35)

“Therefore wisdom was justified by all her children.”

Well does he say “by all,” because justice is preserved toward everyone, so that the faithful are received and the faithless rejected.

Hence many Greek manuscripts have: “Wisdom was justified by all her works,” since it is the work of justice to preserve measure according to each person’s merit.

### 7

Well, then, he says: “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Exodus 15:1).

Moses sang when, in the Red Sea, the waves became rigid for the passage of the Jews, the waters stood around them, and then, flowing back, engulfed the horses of the Egyptians and their riders.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “Isaiah sang to the beloved of the beloved vineyard,” and so forth.]

Isaiah sang a song for his beloved vineyard (Isaiah 5:1), signifying that the people, formerly fruitful in the fruits of virtue, would become harsh through their crimes.

The Hebrews sang when their footprints were moistened by the touch of dew-bearing flame, and although everything within and without was burning, the harmless fire alone licked them and did not scorch them (Daniel 3:24).

Habakkuk too, taught by his song to soothe the public sorrow, prophesied that the Lord’s passion would be sweet to the faithful (Habakkuk 3:2).

The prophets therefore sang with spiritual melodies, resounding the oracles of public salvation. The prophets wept with mournful lamentations, soothing the hardened hearts of the Jews.

### 8

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “He also taught us to sing psalms wisely.”]

Scripture taught us to sing gravely and to chant spiritually (Psalm 47:8). It also taught us to dance wisely, when the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Clap your hands and strike your foot” (Ezekiel 6:11).

For God, the judge of morals, would not demand theatrical movements of a flowing body, nor command indecent clatter for men and feminine clapping, in order to lead so great a prophet into the mockery of stage performers and the softness of women.

[Note: The old edition reads, “the theatrical movements of a body flowing.” The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, reads, “the bending of the body,” which is not unsuitable. Yet the larger number and better manuscripts read, “the flowing movements,” that is, soft and effeminate movements.]

The revealed mysteries of the resurrection do not accord with the reproaches exacted against dancing. There is, however, a certain proper applause of good actions and deeds, whose sound goes out into the world and whose glory resounds from things well done.

There is also an honorable dance in which the soul rejoices and the body is raised up by good works, when we hang our instruments upon the willows.

[Note: The editions and some manuscripts read, “indecent clatter for men.” More and better manuscripts read, “. . . clatter for men.” This is preferable, since clatter was customarily produced during dancing by the fingers and by small instruments.]

### 9

The prophet is therefore commanded to clap his hands and strike his foot; he is commanded to sing psalms because he already saw the bridegroom’s wedding, at which the Church is betrothed and Christ is loved.

And it is a good wedding when the soul is married to the Word and the flesh to the spirit.

At this wedding the prophet David wished us to celebrate; he invited us to it, since he was joining his descendants together. Therefore, as though placed in the very act of the wedding and happier than the others, he exhorts us to celebrate the joyful festival, saying: “Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob. Take up the psalm and give the tambourine, the pleasant psalter with the lyre” (Psalm 81:2–3).

Do you not recognize a kind of dancing prophet? Elsewhere he says: “I will sing to you on the lyre, Holy One of Israel. My lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed” (Psalm 71:22–23).

You hear the voices of those playing the lyre; you hear the clatter of those who dance. Believe that it is a wedding.

### 10

You too should take up the lyre, so that, when the inner string of your veins is struck by the plectrum of the spirit, it may produce the sound of a good work.

Take up the psalter, so that the harmony of your words and deeds may sing together.

Take up the tambourine, so that the inner spirit may modulate the instrument of your body, and the sweetness of your character may be expressed through your active deeds.

Thus the prophet sang when he said: “Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon” (Song of Songs 4:8).

### 11

The children sang this song, but they were not heard. Which children? Those of whom he says: “Behold, I and the children whom you have given me” (Isaiah 8:18).

But this song was not sung in the forum or in the streets, but in Jerusalem. For Jerusalem itself is the Lord’s forum, in which the laws of the heavenly commandments are established.

### (Verse 37)

“And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city.”

### 12

At this point many seem to feel a difficulty and raise the question whether the two Evangelists appear to have disagreed concerning the fact, or whether they intended to indicate some difference of mystery in the diversity of their statements.

For in the Gospel according to Matthew you have the account that, when Jesus had come to Bethany, to the house of Simon the leper, a woman approached him carrying an alabaster jar of costly ointment; and while he reclined, she poured it over his head (Matthew 26:6–7).

Then, in the present passage, the Pharisee says to himself that, if Jesus were a prophet, he would know that she was a sinner and would have to avoid her ointment (ibid., 8).

There, the disciples complain about the ointment being poured out. Both accounts must therefore be explained, but the account that stands earlier in the order of the writings should also receive the earlier order of interpretation.

13. The Lord Jesus therefore came into the house of Simon the leper. The divine arrangement becomes apparent: he does not shrink from the leper, he does not avoid the unclean, so that he might be able to erase the stains of the human body.
