The house of the leper was in Bethany, which by interpretation is called “house of obedience.” Bethany, then, is the whole place, while Simon’s house is a portion of the whole place. Does it not seem to you that Bethany is this world, in which we ought to offer the service of obedient submission, while the house of Simon the leper is the earth, which is a portion of the world? The prince of this world is, in a certain sense, the leper Simon. Thus the Lord Jesus Christ came from those higher regions into this world and descended to earth. He was not in this world, but in obedient piety he was sent into this world. He himself says: “As you sent me into this world” (John VI, 57). This woman therefore heard that Christ had come and entered Simon’s house; for this woman could not have been healed unless Christ had come to earth. And perhaps she too enters Simon’s house for this reason: because she represents a certain higher soul—or the Church—which descends to earth in order to gather a people to herself through a good fragrance.

14. (Verse 38.) Saint Matthew therefore introduces this woman pouring perfume over Christ’s head (Matthew XXVI, 7); and for that reason perhaps he did not wish to call her a sinner, for according to Luke the sinful woman poured perfume over Christ’s feet. It is possible, then, that they were not the same woman, so that the evangelists would not appear to have said contradictory things.

[Note: Whether the sinful woman, Mary the sister of Lazarus, and Mary Magdalene were several persons or only one has long been disputed and remains disputed today. Most of the Greek Fathers seem to defend the first opinion, while many Latin Fathers support the other. The Sorbonne proposed that its students follow these latter; nevertheless, there are also those who cast their vote for the opposite view. Indeed, most recently a booklet has appeared publicly in which it is argued, with many proofs, that there were several women. What, then, are we to do amid so great a controversy? We believe that we should imitate the example of our Ambrose, who defined nothing in a matter that was by no means clear.]

The question can also be resolved by a difference in merit and time, so that the former is still a sinner while this latter is already more perfect. For even if the Church, or the soul, does not change its identity, it does change in progress. Therefore, if you understand the soul as approaching God faithfully—not through shameful and obscene sins, but serving the Word of God devoutly, possessing the confidence of unblemished chastity—you perceive that it ascends to Christ’s very head (and “the head of Christ” is God [I Corinthians XI, 3]) and scatters the fragrance of its merits. “For we are the good fragrance of Christ before God” (II Corinthians II, 15). The good-smelling life of the righteous honors God.

[Note: A number of manuscripts, and not of the lowest quality, read: “but piously preserving the words of God.” Nevertheless, the reading of the others and of the editions seems preferable.]

15. If you understand these things, you will see that this woman is exceedingly blessed: wherever this Gospel is preached, she is named, and her memory will never fade (Matthew XXVI, 13), because she poured out upon Christ’s head perfumes fragrant with good conduct and righteous deeds. Whoever approaches the head does not know how to become exalted, like that man who was vainly puffed up by the mind of his flesh and did not hold fast to the head. But whoever does not hold fast to Christ the head should at least hold fast to his feet, because “the whole body, joined and supplied together, grows into the increase of God” (Colossians II, 19).

16. There is another woman, whether another person or another stage of progress, who is close to us. For we have not yet renounced our sins. Where are our tears, where our groans, where our weeping? “Come, let us worship and fall down, and let us weep before the Lord our maker” (Psalm XCIV, 6), so that at least we may be able to come to Jesus’ feet. We cannot yet come to the head, because the sinner [comes] to the feet, the righteous to the head [the source has a lacuna].

[Note: Several manuscripts of better age read: “the righteous has perfume for the head: Bring forth,” and so on. This is less satisfactory; for there seems to be a lacuna here, which perhaps was taken over from the exemplar from which those manuscripts were copied.]

17. Yet even the woman who has sinned possesses perfume. Bring me, you too, repentance after your sins. Wherever you hear that the righteous man has entered either the house of an unworthy person or the house of a Pharisee, contend: seize the host’s grace, seize the kingdom of heaven. “From the days of John the Baptist ... the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matthew XI, 12). Wherever you hear the name of Christ, hurry there; when you learn that Jesus has entered the inner house of anyone, hurry there yourself. When you find wisdom, when you find justice reclining in someone’s innermost chambers, hurry to the feet—that is, seek even the outermost part of wisdom. Do not despise the feet: “She touched his fringe and was healed” (Luke VIII, 44). Confess your sins with tears; let that heavenly righteousness say of you also:

(Verse 44.) “She has washed my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.”

18. And perhaps Christ did not wash his own feet for this reason: so that we might wash them with our tears. Good are the tears that can not only wash away our sin, but also water the footprint of the heavenly Word, so that his steps may abound in us. Good are the tears in which there is not only redemption from sins but also refreshment for the righteous; for the voice of the righteous says: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm XLI, 4).

19. And if you cannot approach Christ’s head, let Christ touch your head with his feet. His fringe heals, and his feet heal. Let down your hair; spread before him all the dignities of your body. These are no ordinary hairs that can wipe Christ’s feet. He testifies to this—that is, the one who, as long as he had his hair, could not be conquered (Judges XVI, 5 and following). Finally, a woman with shorn hair ought not to pray (I Corinthians XI, 5). Let her plainly have hair with which to wrap Christ’s footprints, with which, through the locks of her beauty and dignity, to wipe the feet of Wisdom, so that they may at least be moistened by the last dew of divine power; let her fasten her kisses upon the feet of righteousness. This is no ordinary merit, of which Wisdom can say:

[Col. 1673D] (Verse 45.) “From the time I entered, she has not ceased kissing my feet.”

20. Let her know how to speak of nothing but wisdom, how to love nothing but justice, how to taste nothing but chastity, how to kiss nothing but purity. For a kiss is a sign of mutual love; a kiss is a pledge of charity.

[Col. 1674A] 21. (Verse 46.) Blessed is the one who can also anoint Christ’s feet with oil; for Simon had not yet anointed them. But more blessed is she who anointed them with perfume, for the grace of many flowers gathered into one spreads abroad various sweetnesses of fragrance. And perhaps no one but the Church can bring this perfume, since she possesses countless flowers of diverse fragrance. She rightly assumes the appearance of a sinner, because Christ too assumed the form of a sinner.

22. (Verse 47.) And therefore no one can love as much as she who loves in greater measure. Not even Peter himself, who said: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John XXI, 17). Not even Peter himself, who was grieved because he was asked, “Do you love me?” (ibid.). For what was obvious, he did not want to be questioned about as though it were unknown. Therefore not even Peter himself, because the Church loved in Peter.

[Note: All the editions read: “because he loved the Church in Peter.” Against this, nearly all the written manuscripts read: “because the Church loved in Peter”; the sense and reasoning plainly require this reading.]

Nor Paul himself, because Paul too is a part of her. And you also should love greatly, so that much may be forgiven you. Paul sinned greatly, for he was even a persecutor; but he loved greatly, for he persevered even to martyrdom. Many sins were forgiven him because he too loved greatly, since he did not spare his own blood for the name of God.

23. (Verse 39.) Observe the divine arrangement: in the house of the Pharisee the sinful woman is glorified; in the house of the Law and the prophet, not the Pharisee but the Church is justified. The Pharisee did not believe; she did believe. For he said: “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him.” The house of the Law is Judea, where the Law is written not on stones but on the tablets of the heart. In this house the Church, already greater than the Law, is justified; for the Law knows no remission of sins, nor does it contain the mystery by which hidden things are cleansed. Therefore what is deficient in the Law is perfected in the Gospel.

[Note: After the word “Law,” the Roman edition alone omitted the word “Judea,” although it is clearly necessary to the sense.]

(Verses 41.) “There were,” he said, “two debtors to a certain moneylender: one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.”

24. Who are these two debtors, if not the two peoples—one from the Jews and the other from the Gentiles—indebted to that moneylender of the heavenly treasure? “One,” he says, “owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.” This denarius is no insignificant thing: in it the image of the king is formed, and it bears the impress of the emperor’s triumph. We do not owe this moneylender material money, but assessments of merits and bronze coins of virtues, whose worth is weighed by the weight of seriousness, the appearance of justice, and the sound of confession. Woe to me if I do not possess what I received; or, because scarcely anyone can repay this moneylender his debt in full, woe to me if I do not ask: “Forgive me my debt” (Matthew VI, 12)! For the Lord would not have taught us to pray in such a way that we asked for our debts to be forgiven unless he knew that some would scarcely be capable debtors.

25. But who is this people that owes more, if not we, to whom more has been entrusted? To them the utterances of God were entrusted; to us the Virgin’s childbirth is entrusted. You possess the Virgin’s childbirth as a talent; you possess the hundredfold fruit of faith. Emmanuel—God with us—was entrusted to us; the Lord’s cross, death, and resurrection were entrusted to us. And although Christ suffered for all, he nevertheless suffered especially for us, because he suffered for the Church. Therefore there is no doubt that the one who has received more owes more. And according to human judgment, perhaps the one who owes more has offended more; but through the Lord’s mercy the situation is changed, so that the one who owed more loves more—provided that he obtains grace. For both the one who repays possesses grace, and the one who possesses it repays in the very fact that he possesses it;

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “for it is possessed through believing and returned through possessing”; others: “redeemed.”]

for it is possessed by returning it, and it is returned by possessing it (compare Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, Book I, chapter 44).

26. And therefore, since there is nothing that we can worthily give back to God—for what shall we give in return for the injury of the flesh he assumed? What for the blows? What for the cross, death, and burial?—woe to me if I do not love! I dare to say: Peter did not repay, and therefore he loved more. Did Paul not repay? He did indeed repay death with death, but he repaid nothing else, because he owed much. Hear him saying that he did not repay: “Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Romans XI, 35). Let us repay a cross with a cross, a funeral with a funeral—but do we repay what we have from him, through him, and in him, all things?

Let us therefore repay love for the debt, charity for the gift,

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “grace for blood, money for the price.” Several others read: “grace for money.”]

grace for the price of blood; for the one to whom more is forgiven loves more.

27. But let us return to that earlier woman, whose meaning even the apostles still do not understand, which was hidden from the ages in God. “For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (ibid.). The disciples therefore complained because the woman had poured perfume upon his head, and they asked: “Why was this wasted in this way? For it could have been sold for a price and given to the poor” (Matthew XXVI, 8). You cannot discover what precisely displeased Christ in their words unless you understand the mystery; for it is the behavior of a luxurious person—or rather, not of a person—to smell of perfume. Certainly even those who smell of perfume customarily anoint themselves, not drench themselves. What, then, displeased him in the statement: “It could have been sold for a price and given to the poor” (Matthew XXV, 40)? Certainly he himself had said above: “Whatever you did for one of these least ones, you did for me.” But he himself was offering his death for the poor.

28. The figure is therefore not a simple one; and for that reason the Word of God answered them: “Why do you trouble this woman? ... You always have the poor with you, but me you do not always have” (Matthew XXVI, 10 and 11). You always have the poor with you, therefore do good. Should you then put off helping the poor because they are always with you, when the Prophet says to you: “Do not say to the poor ... ‘Tomorrow I will give’” (Proverbs III, 28)? But he spoke only of mercy; here, however, he placed faith before mercy, which has merit when it is bestowed with faith preceding it. “By pouring this perfume upon my body, she has done it for my burial” (Matthew XXVI, 12). The Lord therefore loved not the perfume but charity; he accepted faith and approved humility.

29. And if you desire grace, increase your charity. Pour into the body of Jesus faith in the resurrection, the fragrance of the Church, and the perfume of common charity; and then, as you advance, you will give to the poor. That money will benefit you more if you give it not as one who possesses abundance, but as one who bestows it in Christ’s name for the benefit of others; if you give it to the poor in such a way that you offer it to Christ. Do not therefore understand only according to the letter that perfume was poured over the head; “for the letter kills” (II Corinthians III, 6), but understand it according to the spirit, because the spirit is life.

30. What, then, is the perfume of this woman? Who can hear this? Who has ears such that, when Jesus speaks the word he received from the Father—indeed, since he himself is the Word—he can grasp so great a depth of mystery? The disciples understand it in part, although they do not understand it wholly. Hence some think that the disciples said that the faith of the Gentiles ought to have been purchased for the price of the perfume, since it was owed only at the price of the Lord’s blood; this seems plausible. Finally, the Evangelist John introduces Judas Iscariot as estimating that perfume at three hundred denarii, as you have it: “For it could have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor” (John XII, 5). The three hundred bronze coins declare the sign of the cross; but the Lord seeks not a superficial foreknowledge of the mystery, but prefers that the faith of believers be buried with him.

31. Yet we understand this from the words of the other apostles. Judas, however, is condemned for his greed: he preferred money to the Lord’s burial, and even if he perceived something concerning the Passion, he erred through so costly a valuation. Christ wishes to be valued cheaply, so that he may be purchased by all and no poor person be deterred. “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew X, 8). The height of wealth does not seek money but grace. He himself redeemed us with precious blood; he did not sell us. We would say more about this, unless we remembered that we have treated it elsewhere ourselves (*On the Holy Spirit*, Book III, chapter 18).

32. Therefore, in accordance with the words of the Lord, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians II, 3)—treasures that no one could foresee—I must work for his burial, so that it may be believed that his flesh rested and did not see corruption; and so that the death of his body may fill our house with its fragrance, so that we may believe that he commended his spirit into the Father’s hands, and that, separated from death, the divinity did not undergo participation in bodily sufferings.

[Col. 1677A] 33. Understand how the body of the Son gives off the fragrance of perfume. It is the body that was stripped, not the body that was lost. His body is the transmission of the Scriptures. His body is the Church. We are the fragrance of his body; and therefore it is fitting that we adorn the death of his body. Although it does not need our adornments, the poor do need them. I shall adorn his body if I become a preacher of his words and can open the mystery of the cross to the nations. He adorned it who said: “We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; yet to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Corinthians I, 23 and 24). The cross is adorned when what through ignorance is thought foolish is judged wiser through the Gospel, so that we may teach how the opposing power is destroyed through the Lord’s cross. I have poured perfume upon the Lord’s body; what was thought dead begins to breathe forth fragrance.

34. Therefore let each person undertake to purchase, through his labor and the exertion of his virtues, an alabaster of perfume—not some cheap and common perfume, but precious alabaster perfume, and “pistic” perfume. For if someone gathers the flowers of faith and preaches Jesus Christ crucified, he pours the perfume of his faith into the whole Church, which is Christ’s body, dead to the world and resting in God. The whole house of the Lord begins to give off the fragrance of the Passion; it begins to give off the fragrance of death; it begins to give off the fragrance of the resurrection, so that each person from the number of the holy people may say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians VI, 14). The fragrance breathes forth, the perfume is fragrant in the body, if someone can—and would that I could—speak confidently: “But the world has been crucified to me” (ibid.). The world has been crucified to the one who does not love riches, who does not love worldly honors, who does not love what belongs to himself but what belongs to Jesus Christ; who does not love visible things but invisible things; who does not cling to life but hastens to depart and be with Christ. For this is to take up the cross and follow Christ: that we too may die with him and be buried with him, so that we may be able to give off the fragrance of the perfume that this woman poured out for his burial. This is no ordinary perfume by which Christ’s name is spread far and wide. Hence it is also said prophetically: “Your name is perfume poured out” (Song of Songs I, 2). It was poured out so that faith might breathe forth a greater fragrance.

35. From this woman, then, we understand what the apostolic saying means: “Sin abounded, so that grace might abound all the more” (Romans V, 20). For if sin had not abounded in this woman, grace would not have abounded; she acknowledged her sin and brought forth grace. And for that reason the Law is necessary: “Through the Law I came to know sin.” If the Law had not existed, sin would have remained hidden. By acknowledging sin, I ask forgiveness. Through the Law, then, I recognize the kinds of sins, and also acknowledge the crime of transgression; I run to repentance and obtain grace. The Law, therefore, is the author of good, since it sends us to grace.

## Chapter VIII

(Verses 21.) “My mother and my brothers are these: those who hear the word of God and do it.”

36. He is a moral teacher who offers himself as an example to others: he is himself the teacher, and himself also the executor of his own instructions. For when he is about to prescribe to others that whoever does not leave his father and mother is not worthy of the Son of God, he himself first submits to this sentence—not because he rejects the duties of filial affection (for his own commandment is: “Whoever does not honor father or mother, let him die the death” [Exodus XX]), but because he recognizes that he owes himself more to the mysteries of the Father than to maternal affections.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “he devotes himself to the Father’s ministries.”]

Yet parents are not rejected insultingly; rather, unions of minds are taught to be more religious than unions of bodies.

37. Therefore those who sought to see Christ ought not to have stood outside. “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Romans X, 8). The Word, then, is within; the light is within. Hence he also says: “Draw near to the Lord, and be enlightened” (Psalm XXXIII, 6). For if parents themselves are not recognized when they stand outside—and perhaps are not recognized for our example—how shall we be recognized if we stand outside?

38. Let no one suppose that piety is offended where the commandment of the Law is fulfilled. For if “a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,” this sacrament is rightly preserved in Christ and the Church (Ephesians V, 31 and 32). Therefore he could not place his parents before his own body. Here, then, the mother is not denied—as certain heretics seek to insinuate—for she is recognized even from the cross (John XIX, 26); rather, the pattern of heavenly commands is placed before bodily kinship.

[Note: Who those heretics were, and why they so shamelessly asserted that Christ denied his mother, Jerome clearly explains in his commentary on Matthew XII. “He did not deny his mother,” he says, “according to Marcion and Manichaeus, so that he might be thought to have been born from a phantom; rather, he preferred the apostles to kinship,” and so forth. You will find similar remarks in Epiphanius, *Heresies* 42, and Chrysostom on Matthew XII, and elsewhere.]

It is also not unreasonable to understand that, through the figure of parents, he indicates to the Jews—from whom Christ is according to the flesh—that the Church which believed is to be preferred.

39. Therefore, recognizing that he had come into the world because of the divine mystery and the gathering of the Church, he left his parents and boarded the ship. For no one could sail across this world without Christ, since even those with whom the Lord is present are often disturbed by the storm of worldly temptations. The divine arrangement is also preserved in the apostles, so that you may understand that no one can depart from the course of this life without temptation, because temptation is the exercise of faith.

40. We are therefore subjected to the storms of spiritual wickedness; but, like watchful sailors, let us awaken the helmsman. Yet even the sailors themselves are accustomed to be in danger. What helmsman, then, shall we seek? Surely the one who does not serve the winds but commands them, of whom it is written:

[Col. 1679A] (Verse 24.) “But he rose and rebuked the wind.”

41. What does “he rose” mean? He had been at rest; but he was at rest in the sleep of his body while he was intent upon the mystery of his divinity. For where there is wisdom, where there is the Word, nothing happens without the Word, nothing without prudence.

42. Above you have it that “he spent the night in prayer” (Luke VI, 12). How, then, could he sleep here in the storm? The security of his power is being expressed: while everyone was afraid, he alone rested without fear. He is therefore not a partner of our nature if he is not a partner of our danger. And if his body sleeps, his divinity works; faith works. Finally, he says: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew VIII, 26). And rightly are those rebuked who were afraid while Christ was present, since whoever clings to him cannot perish.

43. He therefore strengthened faith and restored tranquility. He commanded the wind to cease—not the north wind, not the south wind, but that wind to which the angel Michael said in the Letter of Jude: “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude IX).

[Note: After Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapters 23 and 24, and Book III, chapter 25, and Jerome in the *Catalogue*, he relates that although this letter had already gained authority through antiquity and use, it was nevertheless rejected by many because in it the author had cited testimony from the Apocrypha. Yet, setting this objection aside, it was received by the Fathers of the Church and by councils among the canonical Scriptures—for example, by Tertullian, *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 3; Cyprian, *Against Novatian*; Origen, Homilies 13 on Genesis, on Joshua, on Matthew, and elsewhere; Athanasius in the *Synopsis*; Clement of Alexandria in Book I of the *Hypotyposes*; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 50; the Council of Laodicea, canon 59; the Third Council of Carthage, canon 47; and so forth. Nevertheless, the authority of so many distinguished men and the prescription of so many centuries could not prevent our Reformers from erasing this same letter once again from the list of canonical books, relying on no other arguments. But what prevents an apocryphal work from being cited in a canonical letter, when the Apostle himself praised the songs of pagans, and Ambrose, Jerome, and others frequently teach that we ought to enrich ourselves with such spoils?]

Hence Saint Matthew also says: “He rebuked the wind and the sea” (Matthew VIII, 26). Would that he might deign to restrain his harsh blasts within us, so that tranquility poured back into our tossing life might remove the fear of shipwreck! And even if he no longer sleeps in the sleep of his own body, let us nevertheless beware lest, through the sleep of our body, he sleep and rest for us.

44. Since it is enough to have briefly touched upon what we discussed above, let us now consider this matter. We know from the book according to Matthew that two men possessed by demons came to meet Christ in the region of the Gerasenes (ibid., 28); here, however, Saint Luke introduces one, and the same man naked—for everyone is naked who has lost the covering of his nature and virtue. Since the evangelists therefore appear to differ in number, I think this should not be passed over carelessly but should be investigated.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “exposed in his vices.” The others, together with all the manuscripts, read: “covered with vices.” Neither reading should be rejected.]

Although the number differs, the mystery nevertheless agrees. For this man who had a demon is a figure of the Gentile people, covered with vices, naked in error, exposed to guilt. Those two men likewise receive the figure of the Gentile people, since Noah fathered three sons—Shem, Ham, and Japheth (Genesis IX, 18)—but only the family of Shem was adopted into the possession of God. From those other two sprang peoples of different nations. One was cursed because he had not covered his naked father; the other was blessed because, although he had turned away lest he behold the shame of his naked parent, he nevertheless, led by filial piety, covered his father and washed away the curse of his brother’s seed.

[Note: The manuscripts and the old Roman edition read thus. The Roman edition, however, reads: “covered him through piety ... avoided the seed”; the others read as in the text.]

(Verses 27.) “He was driven,” he says, “for many years.”

45. Naturally, since he had been tormented from the Flood until the coming of the Lord, breaking the bonds of nature in mad fury. And not without reason Saint Matthew also indicated that they lived among the tombs (Matthew VIII, 28), since the souls of such people seem to dwell in certain mounds of sepulchers.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “in the burial mounds of sinners.” But the word “sepulchers” is inserted for the sake of distinction; for *tumulus* in itself and properly means any elevated place.]

For what else are the bodies of the faithless than certain tombs of the dead, in which the words of God do not dwell? He was therefore driven into desolate places—that is, barren of spiritual virtues—fugitive from the Law, separated from the prophets, removed from grace.

46. (Verses 30–33.) For he was not afflicted by one demon but by the attack of an entire legion. When it saw the Lord and, with foreknowledge of the Lord’s coming, recognized that it would be thrust into the abyss at the appointed time, it began to ask permission to enter the pigs. First, we must note the Lord’s clemency: he condemns no one beforehand, but each person is the author of his own punishment. The demons are not sent into the pigs; they themselves ask to go there, because they could not endure the brightness of the heavenly light—just as diseased eyes cannot bear the sun’s ray. They choose darkness and abandon what shines. Let demons therefore flee the splendor of eternal light and fear the torments due to them before the appointed time—not foreknowing what will happen, but remembering what has been prophesied. For Zechariah said: “And on that day the Lord will destroy the names of idols from the earth, and their memory shall no longer exist ... and I will burn the unclean spirit from the earth” (Zechariah XIII, 2).

[Note: The same Roman edition reads: “I will remove [the unclean spirit] from the earth.”]

We are therefore taught that they will not remain forever, lest their wickedness be perpetual among human beings. Fearing that punishment, they now say: “You have come ... to destroy us” (Matthew VIII, 29). But because they still desire to exist, and are now withdrawing from the human beings for whose sake they know they must undergo punishment, they ask to be sent into the pigs.

47. Who are these pigs, if not perhaps those of whom it was said: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them under their feet” (Matthew VII, 6)? These are the people who, through the use of unclean animals, deprived of speech and reason, have polluted the ornaments of natural virtues through the muddy acts of their lives. They are driven headlong into the abyss, because they are not restrained by consideration of any merit. As though thrust down from higher things to lower through the slope of wickedness, they are suffocated in the waters; amid the waves of this world they perish like strangled people, the passage of their spirit being blocked. For among those who are carried here and there, uncertain amid the fluid surging of pleasures, there can be no life-giving communion of the spirit.

48. We see, then, that a person himself is the author of his own misery. For unless someone had lived like a pig, the devil would never have received power over him; or, if he had received it, it would have been not to destroy but to test him. Or perhaps, because after the Lord’s coming he could no longer corrupt the good, he now seeks the destruction not of all people but of the frivolous—the way a robber does not lie in wait for the armed but for the defenseless, and attacks the weak when he knows that he will either be crushed by the strong or condemned by the powerful.

[Note: The manuscripts, numerous and authoritative, read thus. Some, together with the editions, read: “or be despised by the strong.”]

49. But someone may say: Why is this permitted to the devil by God? I reply: so that the good may be tested and the wicked punished; for this is the punishment of sin. Read, finally, that the Lord sends fever, trembling, evil spirits, blindness, and every scourge according to the merits of sinners (Deuteronomy XXVIII, 59 and following). But let us return to the text.

[Col. 1681C] (Verse 34.) “When the herdsmen,” he says, “saw this, they fled.”

50. For neither the teachers of any philosophy nor the rulers of the Synagogue can bring medicine to peoples who are perishing. Christ alone takes away the sins of peoples—provided that they do not refuse the patience required for healing. Otherwise he does not deign to heal the unwilling, and he quickly abandons the sick when he sees that his presence is a burden to them, as happened with the people of the Gerasenes. They came out of the city in which the figure of the Synagogue seems to exist and asked him to depart:

(Verses 37.) “For they were seized with great fear.”

51. A weak mind cannot contain the Word of God, nor can it bear the weight of wisdom; it grows exhausted and collapses.

[Col. 1681D] 52. And therefore he did not remain troublesome to them any longer: “He went up and returned.” He went up, certainly, from lower things to higher things—from the Synagogue, that is, to the Church. He returned across the lake, as Luke says here, or, as Matthew says, across the strait (Matthew IX, 1); for there is a great strait between us and them. Therefore no one passes from the Church to the Synagogue without danger to his salvation. But the one who desires to pass from the Synagogue to the Church must take up his cross in order to escape the danger.

[Col. 1682A] 53. Why, however, is the man who had been delivered not received, but told to return home? Is it not so that the cause for boasting may be avoided and that he may be an example to unbelievers, since that house is his natural dwelling place? Therefore the man who had obtained the remedy of health is commanded to return from the mounds and tombs to that spiritual house, so that he may become a temple of God, in whom there had been a tomb of the mind.

1396 (Verses 41, 42.) “And behold, there came a man whose name was Jairus, and he was the ruler of the Synagogue. He fell at Jesus’ feet, asking him to enter his house, because he had an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying.”

54. Christ had left the Synagogue among the Gerasenes, as we have said; and the one whom his own people had not received, we foreigners received—we received the one whom we were awaiting. Nor was he long absent from us, who had been awaiting him; nor, if asked, does he disdain to return to them. For this man was the ruler of the Synagogue, and he pleaded for the remedy of the dying Synagogue, which was being driven toward death because it was being abandoned by Christ. Who should we think the ruler of the Synagogue is, if not the Law? On account of the Law, the Lord did not wholly abandon the Synagogue but reserved the medicine of salvation for believers. While the Word of God was hurrying toward this ruler’s daughter in order to save the children of Israel, the holy Church gathered from the Gentiles—she who was perishing through the fall into lower sins—by faith seized the healing prepared for others.

55. We thought this passage should be sufficiently expressed in its moral sense; therefore we did not review what has already been said,

[Note: All the editions and a few manuscripts read: “we review.” The more numerous and better manuscripts read: “we reconsider”; one or two read: “we retract.” Here “reconsider” means to treat again and with renewed attention, not to sing a recantation.]

but wished briefly to touch upon the mystical meaning. Was it not in fact the case that, when the Word of God came to the Jews, he was received by the Gentiles, and that those who had not believed in the Law were the first to believe in grace?

56. (Verse 43.) For just as that woman who had spent all her substance on physicians, so too the congregation of the Gentiles had lost all the gifts of nature and squandered its life-giving inheritance [Note: The Roman edition reads, “which had lost everything … had squandered … and became modest … more steadfast in shame.” Several others, together with all the manuscripts, agree with our reading, which itself is not to be despised]: holy, modest, devout, more prompt in faith, more restrained through shame. For this is the mark of shame and faith: to acknowledge weakness, yet not despair of pardon. Modest, therefore, she touched the fringe; faithful, she approached; devout, she believed; wise, she recognized that she had been healed. Thus the holy Gentile people who believed in God was ashamed of sin so as to abandon it; it brought faith, so that it might believe; it displayed devotion, so that it might ask; it assumed wisdom, so that it too might perceive its healing; it took confidence, so that it might confess that it had seized what belonged to another.

(Verse 44.) She came up behind him.

57. But why is Christ touched from behind? Is it because it is written: “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Deut. XIII, 4)? What else does it mean that the ruler’s daughter was dying at twelve years of age, while this woman had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, except that, as long as the Synagogue flourished, the Church suffered? The decline of the one is the strength of the other, because “through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles” (Rom. XI, 11); and the completion of the one is the beginning of the other—not the beginning of nature, but of salvation: “For blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (ibid., 25).

The Synagogue, therefore, is older than the Church not in time but in the appearance of healing; for as long as the one believed, the other did not believe, and through various afflictions of body and soul it languished with a remedy incapable of healing [Note: The Roman edition reads, “with a remedy incapable of healing.” This is not a bad reading, except that the other editions and all the manuscripts omit the phrase here. Accordingly, *immediabili* should be understood as meaning ineffective and unsuitable for healing].

The Church heard that the Jewish people were sick and began to hope for the remedy of her salvation. She recognized that the time had come when the physician would be present from heaven. She rose to meet the Word and saw that he was being pressed by the crowds; for those who press do not believe, whereas those who touch do believe. Christ is touched by faith, Christ is seen by faith. He is not touched bodily, nor grasped by the eyes; for one does not see who, though seeing, does not perceive, nor does one hear who does not understand what one hears [Note: So the old edition, together with most manuscripts. The Roman edition, with others, reads: “nor does he understand who does not touch faithfully”]. Nor does one touch who does not touch faithfully. Finally, to express the faith of the woman who touched him, he said:

(Verse 46.) “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me.”

58. This is a clear indication that Wisdom and divinity were not confined within the limits of human condition or enclosed within the prison of the body [Note: All editions read, “the wisdom of divinity has been confined.” All the manuscripts read, “wisdom, divinity,” and so forth]. They are not restricted by bodily narrowness or held within it; rather, eternal power overflows beyond the limits of our mediocrity.

For the Gentile people are not liberated by human assistance; the congregation of the nations is God’s gift. Even through a brief act of faith it inclines eternal mercy. Now, if we consider how great our faith is and understand how great the Son of God is, we see that, in comparison with him, we merely touch the fringe, while we cannot reach the upper parts of his garment. If, therefore, we too wish to be healed, let us touch the fringe of Christ by faith.

59. He is not unaware of anyone who touches the fringe, even one who touches him from behind; for God does not need eyes in order to see, nor does he perceive bodily, but possesses knowledge of all things within himself. Blessed, therefore, is the one who has touched even the outermost part of the Word; for who can comprehend him in his entirety?

But, to return to the one who is still sick, let her not be thought dead because we delay too long while delaying Christ’s entrance [Note: Several manuscripts read, “lest through us rather than through her own delay she be believed to have died”]:

(Verse 49.) “They came,” he says, “and said to the ruler: ‘Do not trouble him; your daughter is dead.’”

60. First, let us consider that, when he was about to raise the dead girl, he first healed the woman with the issue of blood, in order to establish faith. And so that you may know that the flow of blood stopped, while the girl is being sought, the woman is healed [Note: All editions read, “while she is being sought, lest she be asked.” Some manuscripts read, “while she suffers.” Many others, and of better quality, read, “while she is being sought.” This is excellent, for it means the same as “while she is being approached,” or “while one goes to her”].

Thus the temporal resurrection is celebrated in the Lord’s passion, so that the eternal resurrection may also be believed. Thus the barren woman who was to give birth is made known to Mary (Luke I, 36), so that the virgin who was to conceive might be believed. Finally, Mary heard that Elizabeth was to give birth and did not doubt concerning her own conception.

61. “They came,” he says, “and said to the ruler: ‘Do not trouble him.’” These people too were still unbelieving concerning the resurrection, which Jesus had foretold in the Law and fulfilled in the Gospel. Therefore, when he had entered the house, he chose a few witnesses of the future resurrection; for the resurrection was not immediately believed by many. Finally, when the Lord said:

1398

62. (Verses 52–53.) “The girl is not dead, but sleeping.” And, he says, “they laughed at him.”

For whoever does not believe ridicules. Let those, then, who think their dead are truly dead, weep over them. Where there is faith in the resurrection, there is not the appearance of death but of rest.

Nor does this conflict with Matthew, who says that flute players were in the ruler’s house and that the crowd was making a tumult (Matt. IX, 23): either because, according to an ancient custom, flute players appeared to be employed to kindle and stir up mourning [Note: Some say that the Greeks were the first originators of this custom, which Ovid touches upon in Book IV of the *Fasti* and in *Tristia* V, elegy 1, where he indicates fairly clearly that it was common both at the funerals of adults and of children. Lactantius, however, testifies that flutes were customarily used at the funerals of children, and trumpets at those of adults. Nevertheless, some maintain that flutes also had a place at the funerals of adults who were not of noble rank]; or because, through the chant of the Law and the letter, the Synagogue could not receive spiritual rejoicing.

63. (Verses 54–56.) Jesus therefore took the girl’s hand, healed her, and commanded that food be given to her. This is testimony to life, so that she might be believed to be not a phantom but a reality.

Blessed is the one whose hand Wisdom holds. Would that he might also hold my actions, that righteousness might hold my hand, that the Word of God might hold me, lead me into his inner chambers, turn away the spirit of error, convert me to salvation, and command that food be given me! For the heavenly bread is the Word of God. Hence also that Wisdom which has filled the holy altars of the divine body and blood with nourishment says: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Prov. IX, 5).

64. What, then, is the reason for so great a difference? Above, the son of a widow is raised publicly (Luke VII, 12); here, several witnesses are removed. But I think that the Lord’s compassion is also revealed in this: the widowed mother could not endure delay concerning her only son, and therefore, lest she be afflicted any longer, speed is added.

There is also a figure of wisdom here: the Church would believe quickly in the widow’s son, whereas the Jews would indeed believe in the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, but fewer of them.

### Chapter IX — Verse 5

“And whoever does not receive you, when you leave that city, shake even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.”

65. What sort of person the one who proclaims the kingdom of God ought to be is indicated by the evangelical commands: without a staff, without a bag, without shoes, without bread, without money (verse 3)—that is, not seeking the supports of worldly assistance [Note: So read most manuscripts, including those of the best quality. Several others, and all the editions, read: “and secure in faith, let him think that, since he requires less of these things, more may be available to him”]—but devoted to faith. The less he desires temporal things, the more he should hope that they can be supplied to him.

Those who wish may apply these matters to the preceding treatment, so that this passage may seem to shape only a spiritual disposition: one that appears to have stripped away the body as though it were a garment—not merely by rejecting power and scorning riches, but also by renouncing the enticements of the flesh.

66. First of all, a general command of peace and steadfastness is given to them (verse 4): they are to bring peace, preserve steadfastness, and keep the obligations of hospitality. The text declares it alien to a preacher of the heavenly kingdom to run from house to house and change the inviolable rights of hospitality.

But just as the grace of hospitality is to be offered, so also, if they are not received, they are commanded to shake off the dust and leave the city. By this, the reward of hospitality is shown to be no small thing: we are not only to grant peace to our guests, but also, if earthly sins of frivolity overshadow them, these are to be removed when the traces of apostolic preaching have been received.

Nor is it without purpose that, according to Matthew, the house into which the apostles enter is to be selected (Matt. X, 12), so that there may be no opportunity to change one’s lodging and violate the obligations of relationship. Yet the same precaution is not imposed upon the one who receives them, lest, while a host is being chosen, hospitality itself be diminished.

67. As this is a venerable form of command concerning the observance of hospitality according to the letter, so also its spiritual meaning is pleasing. For when a house is chosen, a worthy host is sought. Let us therefore see whether perhaps the Church and Christ are being designated as preferable.

What house is more worthy of the entrance of apostolic preaching than the holy Church (24, question 1, chapter “Quae dignior”)? Or who appears more worthy to be preferred above all than Christ, who is accustomed to wash the feet of his guests, and who does not allow those whom he receives into his house to remain with polluted footsteps, but, although they bear the stains of their former life, deigns nevertheless to cleanse their future walk?

He alone, therefore, is the one whom no one ought to abandon and no one ought to change. To him the words are fitting: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe” (John VI, 69–70). You see the executor of the heavenly commands: because he did not change his lodging, he earned a share in the heavenly fellowship of consecration.

68. First, therefore, faith in the Church is to be sought; if Christ dwells in it, it is certainly to be chosen. But if an unbelieving people or a heretical teacher deforms the dwelling, communion with heretics is to be avoided, and the Synagogue is to be shunned.

The dust of the feet must be shaken off, lest, when the barren dryness of unbelief is crumbling away, the imprint of your mind be polluted as though by dry and sandy ground. For just as the preacher of the Gospel ought to take upon himself the bodily weaknesses of the faithful people and, comparing empty deeds to dust as though they were his own, lift them up and wipe them away with his footsteps, according to what is written: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Cor. XI, 29), so, if there is a Church that rejects the faith and does not possess the foundations of apostolic preaching, it must be abandoned, lest it be able to sprinkle any stain of unbelief. The Apostle also clearly asserted this when he said: “Avoid a heretical person after one … admonition” (Tit. III, 10).

[Col. 1686B] (Verse 13.) “He said to them: ‘Give them something to eat yourselves.’ But they said: ‘We have no more than five loaves.’”

69. (Verse 8.) What is the reason that, although John’s passion is described later, he is already shown here as dead in Herod’s words? Perhaps it is because, after the decline of the Law, the evangelical food begins to nourish the hungry hearts of peoples.

Indeed, after the woman who received the figure of the Church had been healed of the flow of blood, and after the apostles had been appointed to proclaim the kingdom of God, nourishment from heavenly grace is imparted.

But observe to whom it is imparted. Not to the idle, nor to those sitting in a city—as in the Synagogue—or in worldly dignity, but to those seeking Christ in deserted places. For those who do not disdain him are received by Christ, and with them the Word of God speaks not of worldly matters but of the kingdom of God. And if some bear bodily wounds of suffering, he willingly grants them his medicine.

70. It followed, therefore, that those whom he had healed from the pain of their wounds should be freed from fasting by spiritual nourishment. Thus no one receives Christ’s food unless he has first been healed. Those who are called to the supper are first healed by being called. If someone was lame, he received the ability to walk so that he might come. If he had been deprived of the light of his eyes, he could not have entered the Lord’s house unless his sight had first been restored.

71. Everywhere, therefore, the order of the mystery is preserved: first, through the remission of sins, medicine is applied to wounds; afterward, the nourishment of the heavenly table overflows. Yet this crowd is not nourished with more substantial food, nor are hearts of firmer faith, fasting, fed with Christ’s body and blood.

“I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, and even now you are not able” (I Cor. III, 2). The five loaves are like milk. More substantial food is the body of Christ; stronger drink is the blood of the Lord.

We do not immediately feast upon everything from the beginning, nor drink everything. “Drink this first,” he says (Isa. IX, 1). There is therefore a first thing that you drink, and also a second. There is a first thing that you eat, and also a second, and a third. The first is the five loaves; the second, the seven; the third is Christ’s own body.

72. Let us by no means, then, abandon such a Lord, who deigns to distribute nourishment to us according to each person’s strength, lest stronger food crush the weak, or scanty nourishment fail to satisfy the strong: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (Rom. XIV, 2).

And let the one who already appears to be escaping the snares of weakness eat from these five loaves and two fish. Certainly, if he is afraid to ask for stronger food, let him himself leave all that is his and hasten to the Word of God. As soon as he begins to hear, he begins to hunger. The apostles begin to see that he is hungry. And if they still do not understand what he hungers for, Christ understood it. He knows that he hungers not for worldly food but for Christ’s food.

Let him say: “I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way” (Matt. XV, 32). The good Lord demands zeal and supplies strength.

73. Would that you, Lord Jesus, might not send these hungry people away with me, but refresh them with the feasts you have brought, so that, strengthened by your nourishment, they may not fear the weakness of fasting. Would that you might also say of us: “I do not want to send them away hungry!” And tell me the reason why you do not wish to send them away hungry. Indeed, you have already said it: because if you send someone away hungry, he faints on the way—that is, he either faints during the course of this life or before reaching the end of the way, before he comes to the Father and understands that Christ is from the Father, understands that Christ is from heaven, and understands that Christ who descended is himself also the one who ascended.

Otherwise, when he has accepted that Christ was born of a Virgin, he may begin to regard him not as the power of God but as a human being. “Therefore,” he says, “lest they faint.”

1401

(Verse 13.) “Give them something to eat yourselves.” But they said: “We have no more than five loaves and two fish, unless we go and buy food for all this crowd.”

74. The apostles did not yet understand that the food of the believing people is not for sale. Christ knew it; he knew that we ourselves, rather, had to be redeemed, while he gives his feasts freely.

The disciples therefore did not yet possess food that could redeem us. Yet they already had food that could satisfy us, food that could strengthen us: “Bread strengthens the human heart” (Ps. CIII, 16).

The Lord therefore has compassion, lest anyone faint on the way. If someone does faint, then, he does not faint because of the Lord Jesus but because of himself. You have no grounds for assigning blame to the Lord, who conquers when he is judged. What could you say to him who placed within you every support of strength? Did he not himself beget you? Did he not himself nourish you? His food is strength; his food is power.

But if through your negligence you lost the strength you had received, then it was not the support of heavenly nourishment but of your own mind that failed you. Finally, just as the Lord rains upon the just and the unjust, so also he feeds the unjust and the just.

75. Did not holy Elijah, when he was already fainting on the way, walk for forty days by the power of the food that the angel gave him (III Kings XIX, 8)? If Jesus nourishes you and you preserve the food you have received, you will walk not forty days and forty nights but—I dare say, relying on the examples of Scripture—forty years. You will go out from the borders of Egypt until you reach a broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, which the Lord swore to give to our fathers.

The strength of this land is what you must seek, the land possessed by the meek. I do not mean the land that is dry, but that land which is strengthened by Christ’s nourishment, which, established under the rule of the eternal King, is filled with the dwelling places of the saints.

76. The Lord Jesus therefore divides the food. He wishes to give to everyone and refuses no one, for he is the steward of all. But when he breaks the loaves and gives them to the disciples, if you do not stretch out your hands to receive food for yourself, you will faint on the way. You cannot lay your fault upon him who has compassion and divides the food, for he divides it among those who remain with him even in the desert, who do not depart on the first, second, or third day.

Thus you read elsewhere: “I have compassion on this crowd, because they have now continued with me for three days” (Matt. XV, 32). What condescension, what humanity he inspires in human beings! He does not want to send them away hungry; he does not want them to faint on the way.

77. Do not therefore fall away from the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him. Do not grow weary now, lest you grow weary later. What will you answer him, or how will you excuse yourself, if you have lost the strength of the food he supplies?

You cannot say that he did not give food, for he gives it to everyone. You cannot say that he did not wish to make you good, since he placed good and evil before you, so that your good would not be imposed by necessity but voluntary.

There is a great difference between one who does something unwillingly under compulsion and one who chooses what is good voluntarily: “If I do this unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship; if willingly, I receive a reward” (I Cor. IX, 17).

Let us therefore consider that we shall stand before the tribunal of Christ, and, if our work is burned, we shall have no excuse to offer. For he will say what he has already spoken through the prophet: “My people, what have I done to you … or in what have I wearied you? Answer me” (Mic. VI, 3).

He will also say to the one who has fainted on the way: “How did you faint on the way? Did I not break the loaves? Did I not bless them? Did I not command that they be given?” [Note: By far the majority of manuscripts read, “Did I not make loaves?” The Corbie manuscript, through correction, and several others, together with the editions, read, “Did I not break loaves?”] “But why did you refuse to receive them?”

78. How many even among those present will faint on the way, and, after these sermons—which, although they are ours, must nevertheless be regarded as loaves, since no one says “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit (I Cor. XII, 3) [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “They are to be regarded as the Lord’s.” This is less suitable. Ambrose plainly means that his own sermons too are loaves through the grace of the Holy Spirit]—how many, I say, will faint and depart, committing fornication on the roads of the nations by crooked paths!

Would that there were only one, and not many! But Jesus is not the author of their falling away, even if someone does fall away; for he distributes to all who follow him, whether there are five thousand or four thousand.

79. Neither the number, nor the order, nor the leftovers of those who ate are without significance. Why are more people—that is, five thousand—satisfied with five loaves, which is a smaller number, while fewer people—four thousand—are fed with seven loaves, which is a larger number?

If we merely follow the miracle as an event, what came from the smaller quantity and abounded for the greater number appears to be more divine. Why, then, was what is less added as though it were superior to what is greater? [Note: So read all the editions together with several manuscripts. Others, after removing many passages that are neither inferior in number nor in age, contract the text as follows: “First, the five thousand, as though the five bodily senses still close to bodily foods …” This produces a perfectly reasonable sense if one supplies here the verb “are referred to,” expressed in the following clause.]

First, we read that five thousand were satisfied with five loaves (Matt. XIV, 19); afterward, four thousand with seven loaves (Matt. XV, 36). Let us therefore seek the mystery that surpasses the miracle.

80. It appears, then, that those five thousand received from Christ five loaves as though they were the five bodily senses, foods still close to bodily things. The four thousand, although they are still in the body and in this world, which consists of four elements, are nevertheless not without reason said to have received the mystical food of rest; for they are already being made equal to the world, destined to be above the world.

For although they are in this world, they are not within the world, since they receive the nourishment of mystical rest. The world was made in six days, rest was taken on the seventh day, and the Lord sanctified it. Rest, therefore, is beyond the world, and beyond the world is also the fruit of rest.

Finally: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God” (Matt. V, 9). Since God is above the world, no one can see God unless he first transcends the world through spiritual perception.

The seventh blessing, therefore, belongs to the peacemakers; and seven baskets of fragments also remain for those four thousand (Matt. XV, 37). This is no ordinary bread: it is the bread of the Sabbaths, sanctified bread, the bread of rest.

Perhaps, if you have eaten the first five loaves in a literal manner, I shall dare also to say that, after the five loaves and the seven, you will no longer eat bread on earth for a third time; rather, above the earth you will eat eight loaves, like those who are in the heavens. For just as seven loaves are loaves of rest, so eight loaves are loaves of resurrection.

Thus those who are nourished by seven loaves remained for three days (ibid., 32), and perhaps attained the complete faith and steadfastness of the future resurrection. Finally, it is the voice of the saints: “We shall walk for three days, so that we may feast for the Lord our God” (Exod. V, 3) [Note: Some manuscripts read, “so that we may feast for the Lord,” and so forth]. But that belongs in its proper place.

81. Concerning the five loaves, holy John taught me what I did not know and what holy Matthew had not taught, nor holy Luke—for grace was distributed differently to each of them. John taught me, I say, that these five loaves were barley loaves (John VI, 9), and therefore we rightly said that this food was suitable for bodily beings [Note: Gill, in the margin, reads “for bodies or cattle.” Two manuscripts also read “for cattle.” The reading of the others and of the editions, “for bodily beings,” is nevertheless better; it refers to the preceding phrase, “foods still close to bodily things,” which appears in this form in all manuscripts and editions].

Why barley first? Because the one who approaches the faith must first be nourished with milk and afterward with food; for we were not yet able, and perhaps most of us still are not able. For since there are contentions and dissensions among us, are we not carnal and walking according to human standards?

Each kind of nourishment is suited to its own degree of strength. Thus barley is first given to us for nourishment and afterward wheat (III Kings XVII, 13). To the stronger person, as to Elijah, a flour-bread from the inner grain is supplied [Note: Some manuscripts read, “a hearth-baked loaf is supplied”], bread which sinners cannot consume [Note: The editions, with not a few manuscripts, read: “whom (the Roman edition: because) the prophet (some manuscripts: but) sinners cannot defile, but can feed.” But what sense can be drawn from this except an inept one? We have restored the passage from five manuscripts of better quality.].

82. There is a difference not only in the bread and the numbers but also in the manner of reclining. The former recline upon grass; the latter lie upon the ground: five thousand upon grass, four thousand upon the ground.

It is more to press upon the earth than to lie upon grass. Those who still possess bodily senses delight in softer things and therefore recline upon grass: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. XL, 6). The others, upon the earth that produces wheat, wine, and olives, receive the food of grace.

The former recline at table; the latter lie back. For the rest of one lying back is in some way greater. There are two fish in the first account; here they are without number. Hence many have thought that the grace of the sevenfold Spirit is signified in the loaves, while in the fish the figure of the two Testaments is also to be understood.

83. We are therefore not reluctant to judge that the four thousand, gathered from the four regions of the world in which the Church is figured, receive food of greater grace, according to what is written: “They will come from the east and the west and the north and the south, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII, 11).

Therefore here Christ gives thanks to the Father for grace. It is not without reason that in the one account there is only blessing, while here there is also thanksgiving. For the Lord is accustomed to give thanks to the Father on behalf of his Church, because he has revealed to little ones the things he hid from the wise.

Blessing, therefore, is given over us, who are inferior; thanksgiving over those who have triumphed over the weaknesses of their bodies through consecrated sufferings.

We touched briefly upon this earlier: when they were ordered to recline in groups of fifty, although this was defined by a sacred number, nevertheless the people of the more firmly established Church appears here, reclining without a numerical definition.

1404

84. It is also mystical that the people both eat and are satisfied, while the apostles minister. In their being satisfied, an indication is given that hunger has been banished forever, because whoever has received Christ’s food will not hunger. In the ministry of the apostles, the future distribution of the Lord’s body and blood is foreshadowed.

And it is divine how the five loaves overflowed for five thousand people. It is clear that the people were satisfied not by scant food but by food multiplied.

85. You might see, by some incomprehensible outpouring, particles bearing fruit between the hands of those distributing them—hands that had not broken them—and fragments slipping forth of their own accord beneath the fingers of those breaking them, untouched.

Whoever reads this may marvel at the continuous courses of waters and wonder at the unbroken succession flowing from liquid springs. How much more, then, when bread itself overflows and the outpouring of a more solid nature abounds?

These things were done so that we might also see those things we do not see. By them he clearly showed that he is also the author of those things and the creator of all material nature—nature which, contrary to what the philosophers maintain, was not discovered but made, and which supplies a flowing succession for the generation of all things.

86. This is indeed wondrous: whatever you draw from rivers is not marked by any sign of loss; whatever you take from springs is restored by a sort of usurious flow. Yet although nothing seems to be taken away from rivers, nothing also appears to be added. And although springs are seen with their waters heaped up, when the waters diminish, the loss is revealed.

But this bread that Jesus breaks is mystically the Word of God and the discourse concerning Christ, which, while divided, increases. From a few sayings he supplied overflowing nourishment to all peoples. He gave us sayings like loaves, which, when tasted in our mouth, are multiplied.

Visibly too, this bread, in an incredible manner, while it is broken, divided, and eaten, increases without any discernible loss.

87. Do not doubt that it grows either in the hands of those who minister or in the mouths of those who eat, since everywhere the testimony of our work is added to strengthen belief.

Thus at the wedding, water from the springs is changed into wine through the activity of the ministers, and those who had filled the jars with water drew out wine that they had not brought (John II, 5 ff.).

Understand, if you can, the greatness of these miracles. Here, as the people eat, their fragments increase through their own expenditure, and from five loaves larger leftovers are collected than the original quantity. There, the elements are changed into another form, and nature neither permits its usual losses nor recognizes its usual origins, though in use it recognizes what it has become.

Indeed, the nature of the changed wine is better than that of wine produced naturally, because it lies within the Creator’s discretion both what uses to assign to natures and what natures to impart to things being generated.

See how many works he uses to establish his work: while the servant pours in the water, fragrance is infused, the changed color gives it form, and the taste one drinks also increases faith.

88. Let the Gentiles, if they wish, compare with Christ’s benefits the things attributed to their gods—not things done, but things invented. Their stories certainly tell of a certain king who turned whatever he touched into gold [Note: Understand this as Midas, king of Phrygia. The poets invented him as a figure to place before the eyes of men how foolish are the desires of the avaricious. They say that Bacchus granted him the power by which whatever he touched was turned into gold. See Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book XI, fable 3].

But even his banquets were deadly. The napkins themselves, grasped by his fingers, became rigid; the food crackled in his mouth, bringing not nourishment but wounds; and the drink stuck in his throat, unable either to pass easily inward or to return.

Worthy benefits for such prayers, worthy gifts for so great a suppliant, worthy generosity from such a giver! Such are the benefits of idols: when they appear to help, they do greater harm. Christ’s gifts, however, appear small, yet they are great.

Finally, they were not bestowed upon one person but upon peoples. The food of those eating increased in their mouths and appeared to be bodily nourishment, but it was received as eternal salvation.

89. Why, however, does more overflow for the five thousand than for the four thousand? Because these four thousand remained with Christ for three days, and therefore received more heavenly nourishment.

90. Nor is it without purpose that the things remaining from the crowd are collected by the disciples. Divine things can more easily be found among the elect than among the masses.

Would that it might happen to me to hear: “Gather up what remains!” If I hear and obey, I shall have many things that the crowd—and many things that the children and women—could not eat. Blessed is the one who can gather what remains even for the learned.

91. Let us see how he gathers. The Law said: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX, 14). Christ broke this bread and divided this word, adding nothing from elsewhere but distributing from what was his own: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her” (Matt. V, 28). You have a fragment from what is his own.

He added: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out” (ibid., 29). You have another fragment. And: “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off” (ibid., 30); and: “Whoever marries a woman divorced by her husband commits adultery” (Luke XVI, 19). You see how many fragments come from one loaf.

Moses says that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman (Gal. IV, 22). Paul said: “These are the two Testaments” (ibid., 24). He divided this word and found its mystery.

Blessed, therefore, is the one who gathers what Christ divides.

92. Why did Christ fill twelve baskets, unless in order to resolve that saying concerning the Jewish people: “His hands served in the basket” (Ps. LXXX, 7)? That is, the people who formerly gathered clay in baskets now, through the cross of Christ, work for the nourishment of heavenly life; and there it heaps up the food of faith where previously there was the mire of Gentile unbelief.

Nor is this gift limited to a few; it belongs to everyone. For through the twelve baskets the support of the faith of the individual tribes overflows, as it were: “Bread strengthens the human heart” (Ps. CIII, 16).

[Col. 1693A] (Verse 20.) He said to them: “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered: “The Christ of God.”

### 93

Nor indeed is the crowd’s opinion unfounded: some thought him Elijah, whom they expected to come; others John, whom they knew had been beheaded; or they believed that one of the earlier prophets had risen again. But to inquire into this is beyond us.

[Note: [Col. 1693D] The Amerbach edition, with by far the greater part of the manuscripts, reads, “of another opinion.” Nevertheless, the other reading is preferable.]

It belongs to another kind of knowledge and prudence. For if it is enough for the Apostle Paul to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (II Cor. II, 2), what more should I desire to know than Christ? In this one name there is expressed both the divinity and the incarnation, and there is faith in his passion. And therefore, although the other apostles knew him, Peter answered before the others: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16). He therefore embraced everything who expressed both the nature and the name in which the sum of virtues resides.

[Col. 1693B] Shall we too introduce questions concerning the generation of God, when Paul judged that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified, and Peter thought that nothing more than the confession of the Son of God was required? We investigate when and how he was born, and how great he is, by contemplating with human weakness. Paul knew that in these matters there was more occasion for the stumbling-block of disputation than for progress in edification; and therefore he judged that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ. Peter knew that everything is contained in the Son: “For the Father gave all things to the Son” (John XIII, 3). If he gave him all things, he transferred to him the eternity and majesty that he possesses. But why should I go on farther? Christ is the limit of my faith; the Son of God is the limit of my faith. I may not know the sequence of his generation; yet I may not fail to know the faith concerning his generation.

### 94

Believe, then, as Peter believed, so that you too may be blessed and may deserve to hear: “For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 17). Flesh and blood can reveal only earthly things; but one who speaks mysteries by the Spirit is grounded not in the teaching of flesh and blood, but in divine inspiration. Do not, therefore, yield to flesh and blood, lest you imbibe the precepts of flesh and blood and yourself become flesh and blood. For whoever clings to flesh is flesh; “and whoever clings to God is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17). “My spirit,” he says, “shall not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI, 3).

### 95

But would that those who hear were not flesh and blood, but, removed from the desires of flesh and blood, each of them could say: “I will not fear what flesh can do to me” (Ps. LV, 5)! Whoever has conquered the flesh is a foundation of the Church. If he cannot equal Peter, he can imitate him. Great are the gifts of God, who not only restored to us what had belonged to us, but also granted us what properly belongs to him.

### 96

It nevertheless matters why the crowds thought of no one else but either Elijah, Jeremiah, or John the Baptist. Perhaps they thought of Elijah because he was taken up into heaven. But Christ is not Elijah: the former is taken up, the latter returns. The former, I say, is taken up; the latter did not regard equality with God as something to be seized. The former is avenged by the fires he requested; the latter preferred to heal his persecutors rather than destroy them.

Why did they think of Jeremiah? Perhaps because he was sanctified in the womb. But this man is not Jeremiah: the former is sanctified, the latter sanctifies; the sanctification of the former began from the body, whereas the latter is holy from the Holy One.

Why did the people also think of John, unless perhaps because, placed in his mother’s womb, he perceived the presence of the Lord? But this man is not John: the former worshiped in the womb, the latter was worshiped; the former baptized in water, Christ in the Spirit; the former urged repentance, the latter forgave sins.

### 97

And therefore Peter did not wait for the opinion of the people, but declared his own, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John VIII, 12).

[Note: All editions, together with a few manuscripts, read, “who always is.” The rest agree with the remaining manuscripts, except that the Roman edition continues, “neither did he begin, nor does he cease to be.”]

He is and always is; he did not begin to exist, nor does he cease to exist. Great, however, is Christ’s grace: he granted nearly all his own titles to his disciples. “I am,” he says, “the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14); yet he bestowed upon his disciples the name in which he himself glories, saying: “You are the light of the world.” “I am the living bread” (John VI, 1); and, “We are all one bread” (I Cor. X, 17). “I am the true vine” (John XV, 1). And to you he says: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true” (Jer. II, 21).

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “every true seed”; many others and all the editions read, “every true vine.” Thus the Septuagint translates it: πᾶσαν ἀληθινήν (“every true one”).]

Christ is the rock: “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). He did not deny his disciple the grace of this name either (Matt. XVI, 18), so that he too might be Peter, possessing from the rock the solidity of constancy and the firmness of faith.

### 98

Strive, then, so that you too may be a rock. Do not seek your rock outside yourself, but within yourself. Your rock is your conduct; your rock is your mind. Upon this rock your house is built, so that it cannot be battered by any storms of spiritual wickedness. Your rock is faith; the foundation of the Church is faith. If you are a rock, you will be in the Church, because the Church is founded upon the rock. If you are in the Church, the gates of hell will not prevail against you. The gates of hell are the gates of death; but the gates of death cannot be the gates of the Church.

### 99

What, then, are the gates of death—that is, the gates of hell—if not the individual sins? If you have committed fornication, you have entered the gates of death. If you have injured the faith, you have penetrated the gates of hell. If you have committed a mortal sin, you have entered the gates of death. But God is powerful: he can raise you from the gates of death, so that you may proclaim all his praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.

[Note: Nearly all the manuscripts read simply, “in the gates.” All the editions, however, read, “of the daughter of Zion.” For there are gates of chastity and gates of righteousness.]

The gates of the Church are gates of chastity and gates of righteousness, which the righteous habitually enter, saying: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, and I shall enter them and confess to the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 19). But just as the gate of death is the gate of hell, so the gate of righteousness is the gate of God. “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (ibid., 20).

Therefore flee the persistence of sins, lest the gates of hell prevail against you; for if sin has dominion over you, the gate of death will prevail. Flee, then, quarrels, dissensions, clamor, and the disturbances of discord, lest you enter and fall into the gates of death. For the Lord Jesus Christ first refused to have himself preached, lest any clamor arise.

[Note: Only the Roman edition reads: “For thus the Evangelist writes: But he rebuked them and commanded them to tell no one.” Such alterations are frequent in that edition.]

He rebukes his disciples, commanding them not to tell anyone this, namely:

> **(Verse 22.) “The Son of Man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day rise again.”**

### 100
