And perhaps the Lord added this because he knew that even the disciples would find it difficult to believe in his passion and resurrection. Therefore he preferred to be the guarantor of his own passion and resurrection, so that faith might arise from the event and discord not arise from hearsay. Christ therefore did not wish to glory, but preferred to appear of no account in order to undergo his passion. And you, who were born of no account, do you glory? You must walk by the same road on which Christ walked. This is his acknowledgment; this is his imitation: through lowliness and a good reputation, so that you may glory in the cross of the Lord as he himself gloried. Paul walked in this way, and therefore he glories, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI, 14).

### 101

But let us see why, according to Matthew, we find that the disciples were warned not to tell anyone that he was the Christ, whereas here it is written that they were rebuked lest they tell anyone that he would suffer many things and rise again (Matt. XVI, 20). You see that everything is contained in the one name of Christ. For he is the Christ who was born of the Virgin; he is the one who performed wonders among the people; he is the one who died for our sins and rose from the dead. If you remove any one of these things, you have removed your salvation.

For even heretics seem to have Christ for themselves; no one denies the name of Christ. But he denies Christ who does not confess everything that belongs to Christ. For many reasons, then, he commands the disciples to be silent: to deceive the ruler of this world, to avoid boasting, to teach humility, and at the same time lest disciples still inexperienced and imperfect be crushed beneath the burdens of the greatest proclamation.

### 102

Now let us consider why he also commands unclean spirits to be silent. Scripture has disclosed this to us as well, since God said to the sinner: “Why do you recite my ordinances?” (Ps. XLIX, 16). This was so that no one, while hearing a preacher, might follow one who was in error. For the devil is a wicked teacher, who often mixes falsehoods with truths so that, under the appearance of truth, he may conceal the testimony of fraud.

### 103

Let us also consider whether here he first commanded the disciples not to tell anyone that he was the Christ, or whether he had given the command earlier, when he appointed the twelve apostles and charged them: “Do not go on the roads of the Gentiles, and do not enter the towns of the Samaritans; but go rather to the sheep that have perished, the house of Israel . . . heal the sick . . . cleanse lepers, cast out demons . . . and into whatever town . . . you enter, learn who in it is worthy, and remain there” (Mark X, 5–11). Thus even here he does not appear to have commanded them to preach Christ as the Son of God.

### 104

The order of the discussion, therefore, is the order of the exposition.

[Note: That is, just as philosophers customarily proceed in their discussions from easier and simpler matters to those that are more difficult and complicated, so also one must proceed in treating the Gospel.]

And therefore, when some from the Gentiles are called to the Church, we too must arrange the sequence of instruction in such a way that first we teach that there is one God, the creator of the world and of all things, in whom we live, move, and exist, and whose offspring we are. Thus he should be loved by us not only because of the gifts of light and life, but also because of a certain kinship of origin.

Next, we should destroy that opinion which concerns idols, so that no material of gold, silver, or wood can possess divine power within itself. When you have persuaded someone that there is one God,

[Note: The Amerbach edition, together with several manuscripts, reads, “then you will establish by his judgment.” This is less satisfactory.]

then, by this evidence, you should establish that salvation has been given to us through Christ. Begin with the things he did in the body, and describe them as divine, so that he may appear to have been more than a human being: death conquered by the power of the One, and the dead man raised from the underworld. For faith gradually grows, so that he who first appears to have been above human beings may be believed to be God. For unless you prove that he could not have done those things without divine power, how can you prove that divine power was in him?

### 105

But perhaps too little authority and faith will be accorded to us. Read the speech that the Apostle delivered at Athens. If he had wished to destroy the rites of idols from the outset, the ears of the Gentiles would have rejected his speech. He therefore begins with the one God, the maker of the world, saying: “The God who made the world and everything in it” (Acts XVII, 24). It could not be denied that there was one maker of the world, one God, and one creator of all things.

He added that, as Lord of heaven and earth, he does not deign to dwell in things made by human hands.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “not in idols made by human hands.” Other manuscripts, together with the editions, more correctly omit the word “idols,” which is understood as “temples,” so that the phrase corresponds to the Apostle’s words: οὐκ ἐν χειροποιήτοις ναοῖς κατοικεῖ (“he does not dwell in temples made by human hands”).]

Next he taught that it was wholly unbelievable that the power of divinity could be enclosed by human craft within lifeless material of gold or silver, and he showed that the remedy for error is the pursuit of repentance.

Then he came to Christ, yet he preferred to name him not God but man, saying: “In the man whom he appointed, giving faith to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts XVII, 31).

[Note: Four manuscripts read, “yet he did not remain silent about God when he called him man.” Below, where all the manuscripts and ancient editions read, “he established faith for all,” the Roman edition has, “he established, giving faith to all,” for which the Apostle’s text provides support.]

Whoever teaches must take account of the persons among his hearers, lest he be mocked before he is heard. For how could the Athenians believe that the Word became flesh and that a Virgin conceived from the Holy Spirit, when they mocked at hearing of the resurrection of the dead (ibid., 32)? Nevertheless Dionysius the Areopagite believed, and others believed in the man so that they might believe in God (ibid., 34). What difference does it make in what order each person believes? Perfect things are not sought at the beginning; rather, one proceeds from beginnings to what is perfect. Thus he instructed the Athenians by such a method; such an order must be observed by us among the Gentiles.

### 106

But when the apostles addressed the Jews, they said that it was Christ himself who had been promised to us through the prophetic oracles. They did not first call him the Son of God on their own authority; rather, they called him a man who had been approved, a just man, a man raised from the dead, that man of whom it was said in the prophets: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Acts II, 22; III, 14; XIII, 33, from Ps. II, 7).

Thus you too should bring the authority of the divine word to bear upon things that are difficult to believe, and point out his promised coming by the voice of the prophets. Teach also that the resurrection was known long beforehand through the testimonies of Scripture—not an ordinary and common resurrection like that of others—so that in asserting the raising of his body you may obtain testimony to eternal divinity.

For when you have proved that the bodies of others underwent corruption after death, you prove that this one, of whom it is said, “You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10), was free from human frailty, had surpassed the bounds of the human condition, and is to be ranked with God rather than with human beings.

### 107

But if a catechumen, advancing toward the mysteries of the faithful, is to be instructed, it must be said that there is one God from whom all things come, and one Jesus Christ through whom all things come (I Cor. VIII, 6). We must not say that there are two lords. The Father is perfect, and the Son is perfect; yet the Father and the Son are of one substance. He is the eternal Word of the eternal God—not a word that is uttered, but one that acts; begotten from the Father, not brought forth by speech.

The apostles are therefore forbidden to evangelize him as the Son of God, so that afterward they may evangelize him as crucified.

[Col. 1698A] This is the glory of faith, if you truly understand the cross of Christ. Other crosses do me no good; only the cross of Christ is useful to me, and truly useful. Through it the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world (Gal. VI, 14). If the world has been crucified to me, I know that it is dead and do not love it; I know that it is passing away and do not desire it; I know that corruption consumes this world, and I avoid it as something foul, guard against it as against a plague, and abandon it as something harmful.

### 108

But some cannot immediately believe that salvation has been restored to the world through the cross. Establish, therefore, through the histories of the Greeks, that such a thing was possible, as the Apostle himself sometimes urges upon unbelievers (Acts XVII, 28). Nor does he avoid poetic verses in order to destroy the tales of poets.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “prophetic verses.” This is less appropriate, unless one wishes to allude to the fact that the Apostle calls the poet Epimenides a prophet of the Cretans in Titus I, 12; his poems were also inscribed under the title χρησμοί (“oracles”). On this matter, see Grotius on that passage.]

For if it is recalled that histories of the Greeks assert that legions and great peoples were often delivered when the lives of certain persons were offered; if it is remembered that the daughter of a commander was summoned to sacrifice so that the armies of the Greeks might be transported; if we consider our own text, because “the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh,” as it is written to the Hebrews (Heb. IX, 13);

[Note: When plague was devastating the whole of Boeotia and an oracle replied that it would cease only if two maidens devoted themselves to death, the daughters of a certain Orion of Boeotia are said to have voluntarily inflicted violent death upon themselves and ended the plague. See Antoninus Liberalis, from Nicander, Book IV of the *Metamorphoses*, and Corinna, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*. But perhaps Ambrose had in mind here the Theban plague that occurred under Oedipus and is said to have ceased when he went into exile and his mother Jocasta was killed. On this matter consult Diodorus, Book I, Statius, Seneca, and others.]

if a plague affecting regions because of certain human sins is said to have been brought to an end by the death of one person;

[Note: Only the Roman edition reads, “which prevailed either by reason or by providential arrangement.”]

then it will be easy to believe in the cross of the Lord. Those who cannot deny what belongs to their own traditions will readily confirm what belongs to ours.

### 109

But since no human being could have been so great as to remove the sins of the whole world—not Enoch, nor Abraham, nor Isaac, who, although he offered himself to death, was nevertheless preserved (Gen. XXII, 9)—because he could not abolish all sins—for what human being could be so great that all sins would die in him?—therefore it was not someone from the common people, not one from the ordinary number of human beings, but the Son of God, chosen by God the Father, who, being above all, could offer himself for all.

He had to die so that, being stronger than death, he might free others: “Free among the dead, without help” (Ps. LXXXVII, 6)—without the assistance, that is, of a human being or of any creature, free from death. And rightly free, since he rejected the slavery of desires and knew nothing of the bonds of death.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1699]

> **(Verse 27.) “But I tell you truly: there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.”**

### 1

The Lord always both raises the future rewards of virtues before us and teaches that contempt for worldly things is useful; yet he also supports the weakness of the human mind by rewarding it in the present. For it is difficult to take up the cross and offer one’s soul to dangers and one’s body to death; to deny what one is in order to wish to be what one is not. Even the loftiest virtue rarely exchanges present things for future ones.

It seems difficult to human beings to purchase hope at the price of dangers and to purchase the gain of the future age at the loss of present things. Therefore the good and moral teacher, lest anyone be broken by despair or weariness—for the sweet allure of life soothes even a steadfast affection—promises the faithful continual success in living. Consolations grow cold under fear of death, and the great love of life reluctantly balances the blandishments of hope against the terror of the salvation desired.

You have no reason, then, to complain; you have no excuse to make. The judge of all has given both a reward to virtue and a remedy to weakness, so that weakness may be sustained by present things and virtue by future things. If you are strong, despise death; if you are weak, flee it. But no one can flee death unless he follows life. Christ is your life—the life that cannot die.

### 2

Therefore, if we do not wish to fear death, let us stand where Christ is, so that he may say of us also: “There are some standing here who will not taste death.” It is not enough to stand unless one stands where Christ is; for only those who can stand with Christ cannot taste death. This may be discerned from the very character of the word: those who seem to have deserved fellowship with Christ will not even have a slight experience of death. Certainly, let the death of the body be tasted in passing, while the life of the soul is held in possession.

### 3

But what does it mean to taste death? Perhaps, just as bread is life, bread may also be death; for there are those who eat the bread of sorrow (Ps. CXXVI, 2), and there are also peoples of Ethiopia who received a dragon as food (Ps. LXXIII, 14). Far be it from us to devour the dragon’s poison. We have the true bread, that bread which came down from heaven. Whoever observes the things that are written eats that bread.

There are therefore some who do not taste death until they see the kingdom of God. There are also some who do not see death, as it is written: “What human being is there who shall live and shall not see death?” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 49).

### 4

But who is the human being who does not die, since there can be no resurrection except of one who has died? Although we have not learned that Enoch and Elijah underwent bodily death, and although the Lord said concerning the evangelist John: “So I wish him to remain until I come” (John XXI, 22), nevertheless we do not think that this was expressed concerning John alone; rather, we understand it as a general saying concerning many. Here it is not bodily death that is denied, but death of the soul.

For there are people who, though dead, live; just as there are people who, though alive, are dead, like that widow who is dead while she lives (I Tim. V, 6), and as it is written: “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into the underworld” (Ps. LIV, 16). If, then, someone alive descends into the underworld—for one dead in sin descends into the dwelling-place of hell—

[Note: All the editions read: “For he descends into hell because of the sin of death; there are, and so forth.” The manuscripts instead read as in the text, except that a few have *mortis* (“of death”) for *mortuus* (“dead”), and *the dwelling of hell* for *the dwelling-place of hell*. Ambrose could have called “the sin of death” what above, in Book VI, no. 99, he called “mortal sin.”]

there are certainly people whose order of life has not been interrupted even by bodily death, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whom we know by the authority of the divine judgment to be alive. Since God is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, he is certainly not the God of the dead but of the living (Matt. XXII, 32).

### 5

He therefore speaks not of one person but of many. For Peter did not die, since, according to the Lord’s decree, the gates of hell could not prevail against him (Matt. XVI, 18). Nor did James and John, the sons of thunder, die (Mark III, 17); when they were taken up for the use of heavenly glory, earthly things do not prevail over them but lie beneath them.

Be Peter, then: devoted, faithful, peaceful, so that you may open the gates of the Church and escape the gates of death. Be a son of thunder. You say: “How can I be a son of thunder?” You can be one if you recline not upon the earth but upon the breast of Christ. You can be a son of thunder if earthly things do not move you, but you yourself rather shake the things that are earthly by the power of your mind. Let the earth tremble before you; let it not contain you. Let the flesh fear the power of your soul, and, shaken, submit to it.

You will be a son of thunder if you are a son of the Church. From the cross’s gallows Christ will say to you also: “Behold, your mother” (John XIX, 27). And to the Church he will say: “Behold, your son” (ibid., 26). For you begin to be a son of the Church when you see Christ victorious upon the cross. Whoever thinks the cross a scandal is a Jew; he is not a son of the Church. Whoever thinks the cross foolishness is a Greek. But he is a son of the Church who thinks the cross a triumph and recognizes the cross of the triumphing Christ.

[Note: This is how all the editions and a few manuscripts read. Others, both more numerous and more ancient, instead read: “who recognizes the voice of the triumphing Christ,” and so forth.]

### 6

> **(Verse 28.)** Therefore, so that you may know that Peter, James, and John did not taste death, they deserved to see the glory of the resurrection. For after nearly these words he took only these three and led them up the mountain after eight days.

What does it mean when he says, “after eight days,” after these words? Perhaps it is because whoever hears and believes the words of Christ will see the glory of Christ at the time of the resurrection; for the resurrection took place on the eighth day. Hence many psalms are entitled “For the eighth” (Ps. VI and XI).

Or perhaps he wished to show us that he had said that whoever lost his soul for the sake of the word of God would save it, because he restores his promises in the resurrection.

### 7

Matthew and Mark, however, say that these men were taken up after six days (Matt. XVII, 1; Mark IX, 1). We could say that this means after six thousand years, for “a thousand years in the sight of God are like one day” (Ps. LXXXIX, 4). But more than six thousand years are reckoned.

[Note: Sixtus Senensis states that this calculation was peculiar to Ambrose, *Bibliotheca*, Book V, annotation 190. “For,” he says, “according to the calculation of the Hebrew truth, in Ambrose’s time four thousand four hundred years had not yet passed.” Nevertheless, this opinion of the holy bishop is defended by great authorities—Theophilus, Cyprian, Clement of Alexandria, and others. The reason for the difference is that those who followed the seventy elders assign a much greater number of years to the ages of the world, especially to the first age, than do those who adhered to Hebrew and Latin manuscripts. On these matters, if you have the leisure, consult Genebrard, Torniel, and Baronius in the *Apparatus Historiae*, § 119; Scaliger, *De Emendatione Temporum*; Calvisius, *Chronologia*; Petavius, *De Doctrina Temporum*; and others.]

We prefer to understand the six days symbolically, since the works of the world were created in six days,

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “so that we may understand the world through the ages.”]

so that through time we may understand the works, and through the works the world. Thus, when the ages of the world have been completed, the future resurrection is shown. Or it is because the one who has ascended above the world and passed beyond the moments of this age, placed as it were on high, will await the eternal fruit of the future resurrection.

### 8

Let us therefore transcend the works of the world, so that we may see God face to face. Ascend the mountain, you who evangelize Zion (Isa. XL, 9). If the one who evangelizes Zion ascended the mountain, how much more the one who evangelizes Christ, and Christ rising in glory?

Perhaps many see him in the body, for “we knew Christ according to the flesh”; but now we no longer know him in that way.

### 9

Many knew him because many saw him. “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty” (Isa. LIII, 3). But only three, and three chosen men, are led up the mountain.

I would have thought that the human race was mystically included in the number three, because the whole human race descended from the three sons of Noah, unless I saw that these were chosen. Or perhaps it is because only those from among all people who confess Christ will deserve to attain the grace of the resurrection, since the impious do not rise for judgment but are punished as though judgment had already taken place (Ps. I, 5).

Three, then, are chosen to ascend the mountain, just as two are chosen to be seen with the Lord. In both cases the number is sacred. And perhaps this is because no one can see the glory of the resurrection unless he has preserved the complete mystery of the Trinity with the uncorrupted sincerity of faith.

Peter ascended, the one who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVI, 19); John also, to whom the Lord’s mother was entrusted (John XIX, 2); and James as well, who first ascended the priestly throne.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “who first endured martyrdom,” with “of the apostles” understood. This is a sound correction, for James is nowhere recorded as having held the episcopal see of Jerusalem. Eusebius, after Clement of Alexandria, and others report this of James the son of Alphaeus and brother of the Lord, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 1. Nevertheless, with Maldonado on Matthew XVII, we prefer to recognize in our Ambrose a lapse of memory, which Maldonado likewise attributes to Augustine, rather than depart from all the manuscripts and ancient editions. It should incidentally be observed that some do not identify James the son of Alphaeus with James the brother of the Lord, and argue that the former was the first apostle, not the second, while the latter was bishop of Jerusalem, not the former. See the continuation of the Bollandists under 1 May.]

### 10

> **(Verse 10.)** Moses and Elijah then appear—that is, the Law and prophecy with the Word. For the Law cannot exist without the Word, nor can anyone be a prophet unless he has prophesied concerning the Son of God.

Those sons of thunder, in bodily glory, indeed contemplated Moses and Elijah as well. But we too see Moses every day with the Son of God; for we see the Law in the Gospel when we read: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. VI, 5). We see Elijah with the Word of God when we read: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isa. VII, 14).

[Note: The same Roman edition reads, “we see Moses and Elijah with the Son of God.” For we see Moses in the Gospel. The other editions and all the manuscripts more correctly read as in the text. First he proves only concerning Moses that we see him, because we read in the Gospel the words of the Law that Moses represented on the mountain; afterward he asserts that Elijah also is seen by us, since a prophecy appears in the Gospel of which Elijah on the same mountain offered a certain foreshadowing.]

Therefore Luke rightly added that:

> **(Verse 31.)** “They were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem.”

### 11

The mysteries teach you about his departure. Moses teaches today, and Elijah speaks today, and today we can see Moses in greater glory. For who cannot, when even the Jewish people could see him—indeed, did see him? They saw the face of Moses in glory (Exod. XXXIV, 30 and following), but they received a veil and did not ascend the mountain. And therefore they went astray, because they saw Moses alone and could not see the Word of God at the same time.

### 12

Let us therefore unveil our face, so that, contemplating the glory of God with unveiled face, we may be transformed into the same image. Let us ascend the mountain and entreat the Word of God, so that he may appear to us in his form and beauty, be strengthened, prosper, and reign.

These too are mysteries, and they are understood at a higher level. For according to your capacity the Word is either diminished or increased for you. Unless you ascend to the summit of a higher understanding, wisdom does not appear to you; the knowledge of mysteries does not appear to you; the greatness of the glory and beauty of the Word of God does not appear to you.

Instead, the Word of God appears as though embodied in some form, without his own appearance or beauty. He appears like a man in a wound, able to bear our weaknesses; he appears to you like a certain utterance born from a human being, covered by the wrappings of letters and not shining with the power of the Spirit.

But if, while considering the human being, you believe that he was begotten from the Virgin, and if faith gradually begins to breathe within you that he was born from the Spirit of God, you begin to ascend the mountain.

If you see him placed upon the cross triumphing over death, not destroyed; if you see that the earth shook, the sun withdrew, darkness obscured the eyes of the faithless, tombs were opened, and the dead rose—so that it might be a sign that the Gentile people, who had been dead to God, rose again as though the tombs of their bodies had been opened and the light of the cross poured into them—if you see this mystery, you have ascended the lofty mountain and behold another glory of the Word.

### 13

His garments are some below and some above. Perhaps the garments of the Word are the sayings of Scripture, and certain garments of divine understanding. For just as he appeared in another form to Peter, John, and James, and his clothing shone white (verse 29), so the meaning of divine readings already grows white before the eyes of your mind.

The divine words therefore become like snow; the garments of the Word become exceedingly white, such as no fuller on earth can make.

### 14

Let us seek this fuller; let us seek this snow. We read that Isaiah went up to the fuller’s field (Isa. VII, 3). Who is this fuller, unless perhaps the one who is accustomed to wash away our sins? Indeed, he himself said: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white as snow” (Isa. I, 18).

Who is this fuller, unless the one who washes the garments of our understanding and clothes us in the garments of virtues, and, after washing away bodily stains, offers us to the divine Sun?

### 15

I have also heard—and let us take this example in order to refute those who hold contrary views—that two wise men’s eloquence was compared with snow and bees.

[Note: Understand Ulysses and Nestor, concerning whom Homer writes in *Iliad* I and III, and after him Cicero, *On Old Age*, and Quintilian, Book XII, chapter 10.]

I have also found David saying: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 103). And below: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths” (ibid., 105).

The word of God is light; the word of God is snow. The word of God is also above honey and the honeycomb. The utterance that flowed from the divine mouth was sweeter than honey, and, clear like snow, its words fall in gentler sentences.

Truly, this is the only speech that can be compared with snow: sent from heaven to earth, it made fertile the barren fields of our hearts. This is not presumptuously claimed, but is drawn from the sequence of the reading, as God himself testifies, saying:

> “Let my speech be expected like rain, and let my words descend like dew, like a shower upon the grass, and like snow upon the hay” (Deut. XXXII, 2).

16. Would that, Lord Jesus, my mind might grow green with the moisture of your rain [Col. 1703D]! Would that you might sprinkle my earth with the whiteness of this snow, so that the fields of my flourishing body might not luxuriate in premature heat, but rather that the compressed seeds of the heavenly word might be made fruitful by the nurturing warmth of snow! When snow falls, the birds of the sky have no place in which to dwell, and the grain harvest flourishes more abundantly than usual.

17. (Verse 32.) [Note: [Col. 1703D] Some Paris editions and certain manuscripts, though more recent ones, read “this glory.”] Peter saw this grace, and those who were with him saw it too, although they had been weighed down by sleep; for the incomprehensible splendor of the Godhead overpowers the senses of our bodily nature. If the bodily eye cannot endure even a sunbeam when it looks directly at it, how could the corruption of human limbs bear the glory of God? For this reason the body’s condition is fashioned purer and more refined in the resurrection, once the aggregation of vices has been exhausted. Perhaps they were therefore weighed down by sleep so that, after rest, they might see the likeness of the resurrection. Thus, when they awoke, they saw his majesty; for no one sees the glory of Christ unless he is awake. Peter was delighted, and he whom the seductive attractions of this world could not capture was enticed by the grace of the resurrection.

18. (Verse 33.) “It is good,” he says, “for us to be here”—and for this reason Saint Paul also says (Phil. I, 23), “For to depart and to be with Christ is much better.” Nor was he content merely to praise it: superior not only in feeling but also in the devotion of his actions, he eagerly offers the service of a common obedience as an industrious laborer, to build three tabernacles [Col. 1704B]. And although he did not know what he was saying, he nevertheless promised his service; thus, not reckless presumption but premature devotion accumulates the fruits of piety. The fact that he did not know belonged to his condition; what he promised belonged to his devotion. Yet the human condition cannot, in this corruptible and mortal body, make a tabernacle for God. Whether in soul, in body, or in any other place, avoid seeking what it is not permitted to know. If Peter did not know, how can you know? If he did not know—the one who made the promise, and who in the greatness of his spirit did not know the limits of the body—how can we know, shut up by a certain sluggishness of mind within the enclosure of the flesh? In the end, such great devotion pleased God.

[Col. 1704C] (Verse 34.) “And while he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them.”

19. This overshadowing is the work of the divine Spirit, which does not darken human affections but reveals hidden things. It was also manifested elsewhere, when the angel said: “And the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 35). Its effect is shown by the voice of God that was heard saying:

(Verses 35.) “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.”

20. That is: not Elijah the son, nor Moses the son, but “this is the Son,” whom alone you see. For they had withdrawn when the Lord began to be identified. You see that this is the perfect faith not only of the foolish but also of the perfected—indeed, even of the heavenly beings: to know the Son of God. But since we have already said these things above, understand that this cloud was not formed from the vaporous moisture of smoking mountains [Col. 1704D], nor a black darkness of condensed air spreading beneath the heavens with the horror of gloom; rather, it was a luminous cloud, which does not drench us with rainwater or the inundation of a wet downpour, but from which the dew of faith, issuing from the voice of almighty God, watered human minds.

(Verses 36.) “And when the voice came, Jesus was found alone.”

21. Thus, although there had been three, one came to be. Three are seen at the beginning, one at the end; “for at the end they are one in perfection” [Col. 1705A]. Indeed, the Lord also prays this to the Father: “that we all may be one” (John XVII, 21). And not only are Moses and Elijah one in Christ, but we too are one body of Christ. Therefore they too are received, as it were, into Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 1705D] All printed editions read “as though into one body.” But no manuscript attests the words “into one body.”], because we also shall be one in Christ Jesus. Or perhaps because the Law and the prophet are from the Word, and what began from the Word ends in the Word: “For Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4).

[Note: Six manuscripts have “for they are one in perfection.” Five have “for they are one in perfect faith.” Several others, as well as all the printed editions, have “for they are one in perfect faith.” But best of all is one manuscript from Colbert, “for at the end they are one,” since this explains the preceding phrase, “one at the end.”]

(Verses 58.) “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the sky have nests where they may rest; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”

[Note: From these words through section 30, everything was transposed in the Roman edition so as to conform to the order of the scriptural verses. But, besides the fact that all manuscripts and old editions oppose this arrangement, the sequence of Ambrose’s discourse is plainly corrupted, as will be evident to anyone who examines it carefully. We have not reproduced the changes made by the Roman edition here, lest the margins be burdened excessively. If desired, compare that edition with the old one.]

22. It does not seem consistent with reason to regard as simple and faithful this man who is rejected by the Lord’s condescension, although he had promised the service of tireless devotion. But the Lord seeks not the appearance of service, but the purity of the affection. Accordingly, above he says:

(Verses 48.) “Whoever receives this child in my name…”

23. In this passage the Lord teaches that simplicity must exist without arrogance, charity without envy, and devotion without anger. For the child’s mind is commended as something to be received with a more mature affection: since the child claims nothing for himself, he enacts the form of virtue; and if he does not know the reason, he is ignorant of guilt. Yet because simplicity without reason seems to many to be not virtue but weakness, you are urged to receive true simplicity—that is, to perform the task of nature with diligence [Note: Several manuscripts have “the diligence of one nature”]. And therefore he says:

(Ibid.) “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me. And whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”

24. For whoever receives an imitator of Christ receives Christ; and whoever has received the image of God receives God. But because we could not see the image of God, the presence of the Word was made available to us through the Incarnation, so that the divinity above us might be reconciled to us.

25. As for the fact that John, moved by an especially ardent zeal of charity and therefore especially beloved in return, thought that the man who did not use the service should be excluded from the benefit: he is rightly not rebuked but instructed. He is not rebuked because he acted out of love, but he is instructed so that he may recognize the difference between the weak and the strong. Therefore, although the Lord rewards the stronger, he does not exclude the weak.

(Verses 50.) “Allow them, and do not forbid them; for whoever is not against you is for you.”

[Col. 1705D] 26. Well said, Lord; for Joseph and Nicodemus too, secret disciples because of fear, nevertheless did not refuse you their service at the proper time. Yet elsewhere you said: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.” Open this to us, lest it seem contradictory. And I think that if anyone considers the one who searches the minds, he ought not to doubt that each person’s deed is discerned according to his mind. Thus to one he says, “Follow me”; to another, “Foxes have dens.” One is compelled, the other removed, so that you may know that the devoted person is admitted and the undevoted excluded.

27. (Verses 53–59.) As for the fact that he rebuked the disciples because they wanted fire to descend upon those who had not received Christ, this shows us that vengeance is not always to be taken upon those who have sinned, because clemency sometimes benefits you by teaching patience and the fallen person by leading him to correction (23, q. 4, ch. “Quod Christus”). In the end, the Samaritans believed more quickly, although fire is kept away from them in this passage. Learn at the same time that he did not wish to be received by those whom he knew had not turned to him with a sincere mind [Note: Amerbach, with most manuscripts, has “he did not wish to receive those who had not turned with a sincere mind.” The Roman edition reads “he did not wish to receive,” etc. Erasmus and Gill, with fewer but better manuscripts, have the reading adopted here]. For if he had wished, he would have made the devoted out of the undevoted.

But why they did not receive him, the evangelist himself records, saying: “Because his face was turned toward Jerusalem.” The disciples, however (cf. Augustine, book I, On the Grace of Christ, ch. 46), eagerly wanted him to be received in Samaria. But God calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wills. Nor do the disciples sin when they follow the Law: they knew that Phinehas too had been counted righteous because he had killed sacrilegious men, and that at Elijah’s prayer fire had descended from heaven, so that the prophet’s injury might be avenged [Note: Some manuscripts have “injury.” “He who fears does not seek vengeance; he who does not fear displays retribution.” This is less suitable]. Let the one who fears be avenged; the one who does not fear does not seek vengeance. At the same time it is shown that the apostles possessed the merits of prophets, since they presume, by right of petition, to obtain the same power that the great prophet had earned. And they presume rightly, because fire would descend from heaven at their word, since they are sons of thunder.

28. The Lord, however, does everything wonderfully: he neither received the man who rashly offered himself, nor was he moved against those who rejected the Lord in an undevoted manner. He thereby showed that perfect virtue has no zeal for vengeance, that there is no anger where the fullness of charity exists, and that weakness is not to be excluded but helped. Indignation is far from the religious; the desire for vengeance is far from the magnanimous; and rash association and incautious simplicity are far from the prudent [Note: Several manuscripts have “inconsiderate agitation.” Others, more suitably, along with the printed editions, have “inconsiderate association,” so that it refers to what follows]. So too it is said to him: “Foxes have dens.” Nor is the service of one whose devotion is not approved accepted. Hospitality in faith must be circumspect, lest, while we open the inner chambers of our houses to the faithless, we fall through heedless credulity into the traps of another’s perfidy.

29. But lest we seem to have passed over that matter carelessly—why here he denies that those who can command unclean spirits in the name of Jesus by laying on hands should be forbidden, whereas according to Matthew he says to such people: “I never knew you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matt. VII, 23)—we must recognize that there is no difference of meaning or disagreement of statements. Rather, the point is that in clerics works are required not only of office but also of virtue; and that the name of Christ is so great that it helps even those who are only slightly holy as a defense, though it does not help them toward grace. Therefore no one ought to boast or claim for himself the grace of a purified person when the power of the eternal name, not any human capacity born of weakness, has acted in him. For it is not by your merit that the devil is overcome, but by hatred of himself.

30. Whatever a person can do, let him display sincere faith and observe the commandments with a religious mind, lest it be said to him: “Foxes have dens.” For the deceitful animal, always intent upon ambushes, practices plunder through fraud. It allows nothing safe, nothing at leisure, nothing secure when it seeks prey even among human dwellings.

31. He compares heretics to foxes. Indeed, while he calls the nations, he excludes the heretics. The fox is an animal full of deceit, preparing a den and always desiring to hide in it. So are heretics: they do not know how to build a house for themselves, but attempt to deceive others by their evasions [Col. 1707C]. Jacob inhabits a house; the heretic is in a den, like a deceitful fox always directing a trick against that evangelical hen of whom it is written: “How often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling? Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 37–38). Therefore they rightly have dens, because they have lost the house they once possessed.

This animal is never tamed; hence the Apostle also says: “Avoid a heretical person after one … correction” (Titus III, 10). Nor is it useful for any purpose or fit for food; for Christ does not say of it: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John IV, 34). Indeed, he excludes them from their fruits: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song II, 15)—that is, those that destroy the lesser vineyard, not the greater. And therefore Samson tied torches to their tails and sent them into the crops of the foreigners (Judg. XV, 4), because heretics try to burn up the fruits of others, being more sonorous in their barking than polished in their speech [Note: Some manuscripts have “more burdensome than polished in their utterances.” The Roman edition, with other editions and manuscripts, reads “more sonorous,” but removed the word “polished.” The meaning is that they are loud rather than refined in speech; for whoever denies the Word has no true voice]. With mouths free for the present but with their end already bound in the future by torches at the tails, they signify the conflagration of their own end [Note: All editions have “free in mouth but already bound for the future end, the tails with torches,” etc. All manuscripts, however, differ from this and read as in the text, except that one has “by a rope” for “by the end,” and another has “bound” plural for singular. We prefer the common manuscript reading, in which the burning of the heretics’ end is signified by torches tied to the extremity of the fox’s tail].

32. The birds of the sky, which are often taken as an image of spiritual wickedness, also construct certain nests in the breasts of the wicked. Therefore the Son of Man, because iniquity has abounded, has nowhere to lay his head. For when cunning dominates and there is no place for simplicity, there can be no possession of divinity in the affections of individuals: “The head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI, 3). When he has found the mind innocent, he reclines, as it were, upon it with the power of his majesty. This seems to be indicated by the fact that a more abundant grace is implanted in good hearts.

33. (Verse 59.) Thus, understand that God does not disdain religious observance but fraud. He who rejected the fraudulent chose the innocent, saying: “Follow me.” But he said this to one whose father he already knew to be dead—the father, that is, of whom it was said to him: “Forget … your father’s house” (Ps. XLIV, 11). See, then, that the Lord calls even the thoughtless whom he pities, and to the one asking permission for his father’s burial he replied:

(Verses 60.) “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you go and announce the kingdom of God.”

34. Since we have received the religious duty of burial, why is even the burial of a father’s corpse here forbidden, unless it is so that you may understand that human concerns must be placed after divine ones? A good devotion, but a greater impediment; for whoever divides his devotion diverts his affection (Acts VI, 2 ff.), and whoever divides his care delays his progress (Luke X, 4). Therefore the greatest duties must be undertaken first. The apostles too appointed ministers for the poor so that they would not occupy themselves with the task of distribution [Note: The Gill and Roman editions, with a few recent manuscripts, have “so that they would not be occupied with the task of distributing.” Amerbach and Erasmus, with the remaining manuscripts, have “so that they would not occupy the task,” that is, take it upon themselves and carry it out]. And when they were sent by the Lord, they were instructed to greet no one on the way—not because the duty of benevolence was displeasing, but because the intention of pursuing devotion was more pleasing.

35. How, then, can the dead bury the dead [Note: Thus the Corbie manuscript, with six other manuscripts of better quality, except that the same Corbie manuscript, by correction, reads “body” instead of “heart.” This is less appropriate, since the heart is mentioned here, because many philosophers taught that the soul principally resides there. The others, together with the printed editions, have a more compressed reading, unless one understands here a double death: one of nature, the other of guilt], unless when, among unbelievers, a corpse is buried whose heart has lost its soul in such a way that their souls have lost God? Or is a double death to be understood here, one of nature and the other of guilt? There is also a third death, in which we die to sin and live to God, as Christ did, who died to sin: “For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. VI, 10).

36. There is therefore one death by which the bond between body and soul is separated. It is not dreadful or to be feared, since it seems to be a kind of departure from ourselves, not a punishment. It is not to be feared by the brave, but desired by the wise and sought by the miserable—the death of which it is said: “People will seek death and will not find it” (Rev. IX, 6).

37. There is another death that brings about the destruction of worldly pleasures, in which not nature but sins die. We undergo this death when buried with Christ in baptism and dead with Christ to the elements of this world, as we suffer the forgetting of our former deeds. Balaam desired this death when he prophesied so that he might live to God, and therefore said: “Let my soul die among the souls of the righteous, and let my offspring be like their offspring” (Num. XXIII, 10).

38. There is also a third death, when Christ, who is our life, is not known. To know Christ is eternal life, which is now present to the righteous in shadow, but in the future will be face to face; for “Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face” (Lam. IV, 20), of whom he said: “In his shadow we live among the nations” (Ps. LVI, 2). David hoped in the shadow of his wings; he desired in his shadow, and the Church sat there (Song II, 3).

39. If your shadow, Lord Jesus, grants so much, what will the truth certainly bring? How shall we live when we are no longer in the shadow but in life itself? For now our life is hidden with Christ in God. But, he says, “when Christ, our life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. III, 3–4). That life is sweet which has no death. But this bodily life has death through the violation of nature [Note: All editions and most manuscripts have “by the lot of nature.” The Corbie manuscript, with several others, more suitably has “through the violation of nature”]. The soul itself also often has death through the stain of sin: “The soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4). But when, strengthened by the firmness of blessedness, it begins to be no longer subject to sin, it will no longer be mortal but will attain eternal life.

40. Let us hasten toward this life, brothers, sorrowful in this world because we are away from the Lord (II Cor. V, 6); for whoever is not away from the body is away from the Lord. It is much better, however, to depart from the body and cling to God, so that we too may be one with almighty God and see the only-begotten Son of God, having been taken up through the glory of the resurrection into the brightness of our nature, and imitating the unity of enduring peace through the eternal bond of unbreakable harmony of souls. Thus may be fulfilled what the Son of God promised concerning us when he prayed to the Father: “That they themselves may be one, just as we are one” (John XVII, 23).

41. Therefore the burial of a father’s corpse is not forbidden [Col. 1710A], but the piety of divine religion is placed before the obligation of kinship. The former is left to relatives; the latter is commanded to the elect. Or because “their throat is an open grave” (Ps. V, 11), the memory of the wicked is prescribed to be abolished, since their merit perishes together with their body. The son is not recalled from his father’s duty, but the faithful person is separated from fellowship with the faithless.

42. There is a particular burial of the righteous, like that of which it was said: “For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she has done it for my burial” (Matt. XXVI, 12). Therefore whoever buries Christ within himself in good faith, so that he may rise with him, ought not to bury within himself the perfidy of the devil.

43. There is also that prophetic burial, so that, as we said above, we may set out certain graves of our ancestors (Tob. IV, 18), which you, reader, recognize but which an unbeliever ought not to understand [Note: The old edition, in the body of the text, has “the burial of the wicked.” The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, has “the burial of the righteous.” Erasmus and Gill in the margin, and fourteen manuscripts, have the reading printed here. A few manuscripts inserted between these, where the edition and part of the manuscripts have “so that food may be commanded,” have “so that it may be obtained”; two others have “so that it may be filled with food or drink”]. This does not mean that food or drink is commanded, but that the revered communion of the sacred offering is disclosed. Therefore it is not the gift that is forbidden, but the mystery of religion: communion with the dead among the nations will not be ours. For since the sacraments belong to the living, those who have life are not considered dead.

(Cap. X.—Verse 3.) “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves.”

44. He says this to the seventy disciples, whom he designated and sent two by two before his face. Why did he send them two by two? Because animals were sent into the ark in pairs—that is, male with female [Note: They are called “unclean in number” because mixture and composition are signified by the number two, and this is opposed to simplicity, whose figure is unity. Hence Philo Judaeus, On the Unchangeableness of God: “For what is unmixed is a monad, and the monad is unmixed; but the dyad resembles what is mixed (supply ἔοικε), for neither is simple, since each admits both combination and separation.” Greek: Καὶ γὰρ τὸ ἄκρατον μονὰς, καὶ ἡ μονὰς ἄκρατον· τὸ δὲ δὶς τῷ κεκραμένῳ (ἔοικε), ἑκάτερον γὰρ οὐχ ἁπλοῦν, ἅτε καὶ σύγκρισιν καὶ διάκρισιν ἐπιδεχόμενον]. They were unclean by number, but were cleansed by the sacrament of the Church. This was fulfilled by the oracle received by Saint Peter, when the Holy Spirit said to him: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts X, 15). He understood that this was spoken of the nations, which followed more the succession of bodily generation than that of spiritual grace. The Lord cleansed them and made them heirs of his Passion.

45. Sending his disciples, therefore, into his harvest—which, although planted by the word of God, nevertheless required the labor of cultivation and the diligent service of a worker—he said, lest the birds of the sky scatter the seeds that had been sown: “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves” (Isa. LXV, 25).

46. These animals are contrary to one another, so that one kind is devoured by the other. But the good shepherd does not know how to fear wolves for his flock. Therefore these disciples are sent not as prey but for grace; for the care of the good shepherd ensures that the wolves can attempt nothing against the lambs. He sends lambs among wolves so that this might be fulfilled: “Then wolves and lambs will feed together.”

47. And since our recent treatment of the fox was not unwelcome, if I have tested your faithful judgment in the figure of a tiny animal (On Luke, chapter IX), I presume that, with the support of your zeal, I may disclose the profound mysteries veiled under the appearance of wolves. Above we explicitly stated that heretics are signified by the form of foxes: they claim by name to follow Christ, but renounce him through the zeal of fraud. The Lord does not receive them, but keeps and bars them from his nest. We must now consider what the wolves appear to signify.

48. They are beasts that lie in wait for sheepfolds and linger around shepherds’ huts [Note: A few manuscripts have “dare to enter the dwellings of shepherds,” etc.]. They do not dare to enter the homes, but watch for the dogs’ sleep, or for the shepherd’s absence or negligence; they attack the throats of sheep so as quickly to strangle them. They are wild and rapacious, and also stiffer by the nature of their bodies, so that they cannot easily bend themselves; they are carried forward by a kind of momentum of their own and are therefore often mocked [Note: Several manuscripts have “often injured.” Others, more suitably, have “often mocked,” so that the meaning below is clear: “Christ, the true interpreter of Scripture, mocks them”]. Moreover, if they see a human being first, they are said, by a certain force of nature, to snatch away his voice; but if a human being sees them first, they are said to be disturbed. Therefore I must beware lest, if the grace of spiritual mysteries cannot shine forth in today’s discourse, the wolves be thought to have seen me first and to have wrested from me the customary support of speech.

49. Are not heretics to be compared with these wolves? They lie in wait for Christ’s sheepfolds and growl around the enclosures more at night than by day. For it is always night for the faithless, who strive to cover Christ’s light with the savage fogs of interpretation and, as far as they can, to darken it. Thus they linger around the enclosures, but do not dare to enter Christ’s stalls. And therefore they are not healed, because Christ does not wish to bring them into his stall, in which the man who descended from Jerusalem and fell among thieves was healed. The Samaritan bound his wounds, poured in oil and wine, placed him on his own beast, took him to the stall, and left him with the innkeeper to be healed (Luke X, 30 ff.). They do not receive medicine because they do not seek the physician; for if they sought him, they would not disparage him.

50. They watch for the shepherd’s absence, and therefore strive either to kill the shepherds of the churches or drive them into exile, because they cannot attack Christ’s sheep while the shepherds are present. Thus robbers attempt to strip the Lord’s flock; being hard and rigid in a bodily kind of intention of mind, they are wholly unaccustomed to turn aside from their error. Therefore the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after one … correction” (Titus III, 10), knowing that such a person is perverted. Christ, the true interpreter of Scripture, mocks them, so that they may expend their empty assaults in vain and be unable to do harm.

51. If they happen to get ahead of someone through the cunning entanglement of their disputation, they make him fall silent. For the person who does not confess the Word with the glory that belongs to it is mute. Beware, therefore, lest a heretic take away your voice if you do not first detect him yourself. His perfidy creeps along while it remains hidden; but once you have recognized his impious inventions, you will not have to fear the loss of your pious voice. Beware, then, of the poisons of crafty argument: they seek the soul, attack the throat, and inflict a wound upon the vital organs. The bites of heretics are grievous; they are more grievous and rapacious than the beasts themselves, and they know no limit either to greed or to impiety.

[Col. 1712B] 52. Nor should it disturb you that they seem to assume a human form. Even if a human being is seen outwardly, a beast growls within. Therefore there is no doubt that they are wolves, according to the divine judgment of the Lord Jesus, who says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves; you will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII, 15–16). If anyone is influenced by appearances, let him inquire about the fruit.

You hear someone called a priest; you recognize his plunder. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts have “you do not recognize his plunder.” Several others, more numerous and more authoritative, reject the negation, which seems wholly inadmissible. Here one may understand that the Arian Auxentius is being indicated, since he is described in nearly the same words in Basil, On Not Handing over the Faith, where we read, “Auxentius himself, who calls himself bishop,” etc. There too the statement “he did lesser things in Scythia” clearly corresponds to the words below, “his limbs hardened by Scythian frost,” etc.] He has a sheep’s clothing, but the deeds of a robber. Outwardly he is a sheep; inwardly he is a wolf. He has no limit to his plunder; as though his limbs were hardened by Scythian frost in the night, his mouth bloodstained, he flies about seeking someone to devour. Does he not seem to you a wolf, who desires to satisfy his madness with the death of faithful peoples, through an insatiable cruelty toward human slaughter?

53. He howls; he does not expound [Note: “He does not expound,” that is, he does not interpret Scripture. This is the sense in which the word is especially familiar among the Fathers]. He denies the author of the voice and, with sacrilegious speech, interrupts it with a bestial murmur; he does not confess the Lord Jesus as ruler of eternal life. We heard his howls when a sword was sent throughout the world [Note: Not “into the city,” namely Milan rather than Rome, as elsewhere in authors; a number of manuscripts of no inferior quality have that reading. “Throughout the world” is better. By the word “sword,” Ambrose alludes to that cruel law written by Auxentius’s own hand and promulgated on January 21. Basil, On Not Handing over the Faith, also writes of it: “Auxentius sent a flying sword through all the cities.” Compare the two passages, for they remarkably explain and confirm one another]. He displayed harsh teeth and swollen jaws, and thought that he had taken everyone’s voice away, when in fact he alone had lost it.

And therefore, so that we may escape these wolves, the Lord teaches us what we should follow, saying:

(Verses 4.) “Do not carry a purse, or a bag, or sandals.”

54. What it means not to carry a purse he expressed clearly elsewhere. Matthew wrote that the Lord said to the disciples: “Do not possess gold or silver” (Matt. X, 9). If we are forbidden to possess gold, what are we to seize or take away? If you have been commanded to give away what you possess, how do you accumulate what you did not have? You preach that one must not steal, yet do you steal? You say that one must not commit adultery, yet do you commit adultery? You curse idols, yet do you commit sacrilege? You glory in the Law, yet through transgressing the Law do you dishonor God? “For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you” (Rom. II, 21–24).

55. Not so the apostle Peter, who was the first to carry out the Lord’s sentence. To show that the Lord’s commands had not been poured out in vain, when a poor man asked him to give him some money, he said: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts III, 6). He boasts that he does not have silver or gold. Is it a shame for you to have even less than you desire? There is therefore also a glorious poverty, because it is blessed as well, as it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V, 3).

Yet Peter does not boast so much that he lacks silver and gold as that he keeps the Lord’s commandment, who ordered: “Do not possess gold.” This is as if to say: “You see that I am a disciple of Christ, and yet you seek gold from me?” He gave us something far more precious than gold, so that we might act in his name. Therefore I have what he gave, not what he did not give: “In the name of the Lord Jesus, rise and walk” (Acts III, 6).

56. Therefore, just as the person who wishes to build storehouses for gathering grain is rebuked by the authority of the Lord’s judgment (Luke XII, 26), so the person who wishes to prepare a purse for storing gold incurs the blemish of rebuke.

[Col. 1713C] 57. “Neither a bag nor sandals.” Both are customarily made from the hide of a dead animal. But the Lord Jesus wants nothing mortal to exist in us. Accordingly, he says to Moses: “Remove the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III, 5). Thus he is commanded to remove a mortal and earthly sandal when he is sent to free the people; for the minister of this task must fear nothing and must not be held back from the duty he has undertaken by the danger of death.

Moses himself, when he had voluntarily undertaken the defense of his brothers—that is, the Jews—was recalled from his undertaking by fear of accusation and fled from Egypt (Exod. II, 15). Therefore, when the Lord had approved his devotion but had seen the weakness of his condition, he judged that the trace of his spirit and mind should be stripped of mortal bonds [Col. 1713D].

[Col. 1714A] 58. If anyone is troubled by the question of why, while in Egypt, people are commanded to eat the lamb with sandals on (Exod. XII, 11), whereas the apostles are sent to preach the Gospel without sandals, he should consider that one who is still situated in Egypt must continue to guard against the serpent’s bite. For there are many poisons in Egypt, and the person who celebrates Passover in the form or symbol may be exposed to a wound. But the minister of truth blunts the poisons [Note: All editions and some manuscripts have “avoids the poisons.” Others, more numerous and more ancient, have “blunts,” that is, dulls, overcomes them], and is not afraid.

Accordingly, a viper bit Paul on the island of Malta, and when the inhabitants saw the viper hanging from his hand, they thought that he would die. But when they saw him remain unharmed, they said that he was a god whom poison could not harm (Acts XXVIII, 3 ff.). And so that you may know this to be true, the Lord himself says: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy; and nothing shall harm you” (Luke X, 19).

59. The apostles are not commanded to take up staffs in their hands; for Matthew thought that this was how it should be written (Matt. 10:10). But what is a staff except an emblem of authority to be displayed, and an instrument of punishment and pain? [Note: The Roman edition: “except as an emblem of authority to be displayed.” Less suitably; for bundles of rods were customarily borne before ancient magistrates not to bring forward—that is, enlarge—authority, but to bear it before them—that is, to signify and display it.] Therefore the disciples carry out the command of the humble Lord—for “in his humiliation” (Isa. 53:8) [Note: All editions and almost all manuscripts read, “His judgment was taken away.” Corb. nevertheless has, “was exalted.” This is better, since the same passage is reported in the letter to Vercellae as, “His judgment was exalted”; the Arabic version, according to the Latin translator, supports this reading, for it too has, “His judgment is high.” The difference arose because the verb ᾔρθη, which we see used by the Septuagint, can equally be rendered “exalted” or “taken away.” The Hebrew, Syriac, and Latin Vulgate, however, prefer: “He was taken away [or carried off] from judgment.”]—the humble Lord, I say, through acts of humility. For he sent those to sow the faith who would not compel but teach: [Note: Quite a few manuscripts, as well as all editions, read, “nor exercise the force of authority”; the Roman edition has, “nor exert it.” Other manuscripts, however, more numerous, read, “nor exercise authorities”; the older ones have, “nor exert them.”] they were not to exercise authority, but to raise up the teaching of humility. In this passage he thought that patience too should be joined to humility, because he himself also, according to Peter’s testimony, “when he was reviled, did not revile in return; when he was struck, he did not strike back” (1 Pet. 2:23). This, then, is what he means: “Be imitators of me; lay aside the desire for vengeance. Do not answer the insolence of those who strike you by returning the injury,” [Note: All editions read, “but bear it patiently.” All manuscripts, on the contrary, read, “but strike back with patience.” The latter is more elegant, since what is meant here is expressed more clearly in Book V, §76, as follows: “Is it not accomplished through patience, so that . . . you strike back at the one who strikes?”] “but strike it with the greatness of patient endurance.” No one ought to imitate in himself what he condemns in another: gentleness inflicts more grievous wounds upon the obstinate. With this blow the Lord struck back at the one who struck him, saying: “To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also” (Matt. 5:39). For it comes about that a person condemns himself by his own judgment and is pierced, as it were, by the goad of his own feeling, when he recognizes the attentiveness shown toward him as a return for the injury he committed.

60. Nevertheless, he sent some with a staff, as Paul testifies when he says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a staff, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” [Col. 1714D] (1 Cor. 4:21). The Apostle also gave this staff to Timothy, saying: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke” (2 Tim. 4:2). Or perhaps before the Lord’s passion—which strengthened the wavering hearts of the peoples—gentleness alone was necessary, whereas after the passion correction was necessary. Certainly, let the Lord soothe and Paul rebuke; let the one who can soften even hardened hearts persuade; let the one who cannot persuade everyone reprove. Paul therefore took up the staff from the teaching of the Law. For he had read: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. 13:24). He had also read that those eating the lamb were commanded by prophetic ordinance to hold a staff in their hands (Exod. 12:11). And therefore the Lord says in the Old Testament: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. 88:33). But in the New Testament he offered himself in order to forgive all, saying: “If you seek me, let these go away” (John 18:8). Elsewhere, too, you have the account that when the apostles wished to call down fire from heaven to consume the Samaritans who had refused to receive the Lord Jesus into their city, “he turned and rebuked them, and said: You do not know of what spirit you are. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy human lives, but to save them” (Luke 9:55–56).

61. The more perfect, then, are sent without a staff; the weaker eat with a staff. Paul too threatens with a staff, but he visits those who offend in a spirit of gentleness. Finally, to show that he is a mild teacher, he consults the wishes of the very people whom he rebukes: “What do you want,” he says, “shall I come to you with a staff, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4:21). He mentioned the staff once, but twice added milder things, joining gentleness to love. Yet he first threatened with a staff and then displayed gentleness; for in the second letter to the same Corinthians he writes: “I call God as witness against my soul, that to spare you I did not come again to Corinth” (2 Cor. 1:23). Hear for what reason he thought they should be spared: “I did not want,” he says, “to come to you again in sorrow” (2 Cor. 2:1). He cast aside the staff and took up the affection of love.

(Vers. 4.) “And greet no one on the way.”

62. To some this may seem harsh and arrogant, and inconsistent with the command of the gentle and humble Lord: the one who even commanded that the lower place at table should be yielded now commands his disciples, “Greet no one on the way” (Luke 10:4), although greeting is a common expression of goodwill. Thus inferiors have usually sought to win the favor of their superiors. Gentiles too exchange such courtesies with Christians. How, then, does the Lord remove this customary expression of human kindness?

63. But consider that the command is not simply, “Greet no one”; rather, “on the way” has been added for a reason. Thus Elisha too (2 Kings 4:29), when he sent his servant to place his staff upon the body of the dead child, commanded him not to greet anyone on the way. For he ordered him to proceed hastily, so that he might carry out the service of accomplishing the resurrection and not be turned aside from his commission by conversation with anyone he met. Here, therefore, it is not diligent greeting that is taken away, but the obstacle that might impede devotion is removed, so that when divine commands are given, human concerns may for a while be set aside. Greeting is beautiful, [Note: The edition of Amerbach, together with quite a few manuscripts, reads, “but more beautiful, the more promptly divine things are carried out.” Erasmus, Gill, and the Roman edition read, “but all the more beautiful because the more promptly divine commands are carried out.” Other manuscripts, and those of better authority, have the reading printed in the text.] but the timely execution of divine things is more beautiful, since delay has often brought offense. Honorable things are therefore prohibited as well, lest the solemnity of the courtesy creep into the service and impede the ministry, delay in which would be blameworthy.

64. (Vers. 8.) Now this is another virtue: that no one should wander with careless ease from house to house, so that we may preserve constancy even in our love of hospitality and not lightly dissolve a bond of friendship once formed; that we may put forward the message of peace, so that the very first entrance may be celebrated with the blessing of peace; that, once food and drink have been offered, we should be content; that the standards of faith should not be suppressed; that the Gospel of the heavenly kingdom should be preached; and that the dust should be shaken from our feet if anyone does not think us worthy to be received as guests by the city.

[Note: All editions read, “those moral virtues.” All manuscripts read, “that other virtue” (one has “that virtue, another”). The meaning is the same as if it were read: “That which we are now about to discuss refers to another virtue.”]

65. (Vers. 13–21.) He also teaches that those who refuse to follow the Gospel will be liable to a heavier punishment than those who judged that the Law ought to be dissolved, because if Tyre and Sidon had seen such great miracles of heavenly works, they would not have despised the remedy of repentance. He teaches also that worldly wealth or arrogance is neither to be compared with the heavenly gift nor, on the other hand, abandoned without a remedy, since everyone has the resource of repentance. Finally, he discloses the heavenly mystery: that it pleased God to reveal his grace more to little ones than to the wise of this world. The apostle Paul set this out at greater length when he said: “Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish? For since the world did not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1:20–21).

66. Let us therefore understand by “little one” the person who does not know how to exalt himself or to boast of his wisdom through ornate speeches, as most philosophers do. He was a little one who said: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; neither have I walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me” (Ps. 130:1). And so that you might know that this little one was such not in age or understanding but in his humility and in a certain avoidance of boasting, he added: “But I have exalted my soul” (ibid., 2). You see how exalted this little one was, how sublime in the summit of his virtues. The Apostle wants us to be little ones of this kind when he says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise; for the wisdom of this age is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:18–19).

67. (Vers. 22.) A most beautiful passage concerning faith is connected here, when he says that all things have been delivered to him by his Father. When you read “all things,” you acknowledge the omnipotent one, not unlike or degenerate from the Father. When you read “delivered,” you confess the Son, to whom all things properly belong by nature as being of one substance, not bestowed by grace as a gift. He added:

(Ibid.) “No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and who the Father is except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.”

68. I remember that I did not pass over this passage in the little books I wrote on the Faith (Book IV, ch. 6). But so that you may know that just as the Son reveals the Father to whom he wills, so too the Father reveals the Son to whom he wills, hear the Lord Jesus himself speaking when he praised Peter because he had confessed him to be the Son of God: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17).

69. (Vers. 25.) Closely connected with these words is the passage [Note: Only the Roman edition has, “in which those who,” etc.] in which those who seem to themselves to be experts in the Law are exposed: they hold the words of the Law but do not understand its force. From the very first chapter of the Law he teaches that they are ignorant of the Law, proving that at the beginning the Law immediately proclaimed both the Father and the Son and also announced the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God . . . And you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. 6:5).

70. (Vers. 28.) Therefore the Lord says to the expert in the Law: “Do this, and you will live.” But because he did not know his neighbor—for he did not believe in Christ—he replied: “Who is my neighbor?” Thus the one who does not know Christ does not know the Law either. For how can he know the Law when he is ignorant of the truth, when the Law announces the truth?

(Vers. 30.) “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers.”

71. So that we may explain more clearly the passage set before us, let us recall the ancient history of the city of Jericho. We remember, then, that Jericho, as we read in the book entitled Joshua, was a great city surrounded by walls, which could not be penetrated by iron or breached by a battering ram (Josh. 6:1). In it lived Rahab the prostitute, who received the spies sent by Joshua as guests, instructed them by her advice, answered the citizens who asked that they had departed, and hid them on the roof. And so that she might rescue herself and her family from the destruction of the city, she tied a scarlet cord in the window (Josh. 2:4ff.). The city’s otherwise impregnable walls collapsed at the sound of the seven priestly trumpets and the united shouting of the jubilant people (Josh. 6:20).

72. See how each person preserves his own office: the spies their watchfulness, the prostitute the mystery, the victor faith, and the priest religion. The spies do not fear danger for the sake of praise; the prostitute does not betray those she has received even in danger; the victor, concerned to preserve faith more than to conquer, first commands the prostitute’s salvation and only afterward the city’s destruction; the emblems of religion are the priest’s weapons. Who would not consider it a complete miracle that from the whole city no one was saved except the one whom a prostitute delivered?

73. This is the simple truth of the historical account; but if it is considered more deeply, it signifies astonishing mysteries. Jericho is a figure of this world, into which Adam descended from paradise—that is, from the heavenly Jerusalem—through the fall of transgression; that is, he migrated from things belonging to life to things lowly. [Note: All editions and several manuscripts read, “descending to the underworld.” Other, more numerous and better manuscripts read, “to lowly things.” This is better, since “lowly things,” or “weaknesses,” is set in opposition to “things belonging to life.”] It was not a change of place but a change of conduct that made him an exile from his nature. For having been greatly changed from that Adam who enjoyed untroubled blessedness, when he flowed down into worldly sins he fell among robbers. He would not have fallen among them had he not made himself liable to them by deviating from the heavenly command. Who are these robbers except the angels of night and darkness, who sometimes transform themselves into angels of light but cannot persevere in that disguise? First they strip away the garments of spiritual grace that we have received, and thus they are accustomed to inflict wounds; for if we preserve undefiled the garments we have put on, we cannot feel the robbers’ blows. Beware, therefore, lest you be stripped first, as Adam was stripped first when, deprived of the protection of the heavenly command and divested of the garment of faith, he received a mortal wound. In that wound the whole human race would have perished unless that Samaritan, coming down, had healed its grievous injuries.

74. This Samaritan is no ordinary one: the person whom the priest and the Levite had despised, he did not himself despise. Do not despise him because of the name of his sect; rather, marvel at him through the interpretation of the word, for the name “Samaritan” signifies “guardian.” This is what the interpretation means. And who is the guardian except the one of whom it is said: “The Lord guards the little ones” (Ps. 114:6)? Thus, just as one Jew is found in the letter and another in the spirit, so too one Samaritan is outward and another hidden within.
