Who, then, is this Samaritan who came down? Surely the one of whom it is said: “He who descended from heaven and who ascended into heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13)? Seeing the half-dead man, whom no one had previously been able to heal, as he had seen the woman suffering from a flow of blood, who had spent all her property on physicians, he came beside him (Luke 8:43–44); that is, by taking on our compassion he made himself our neighbor, and by bestowing mercy drew near.

(Vers. 34.) “And he bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.”

75. This physician has many medicines with which he is accustomed to heal. His word is a medicine. One of his words binds wounds; another soothes them with oil; another pours in wine. He binds wounds with a sterner command; he soothes them by the remission of sin; and, like wine, he causes them to smart through the announcement of judgment.

(Ibid.) “And he placed him,” he says, “on his own beast.”

76. Hear how he places you upon it: “He himself bears our sins and suffers for us” (Isa. 53:4); and the shepherd placed the weary sheep upon his shoulders (Luke 15:5). Human beings were made like a beast; therefore he placed us upon his own beast, so that we would not be like horse and mule, and so that by assuming our body he might abolish the weaknesses of our flesh.

77. Finally, he led us, who had become beasts, into an inn. An inn is a place where those wearied by a long journey usually take shelter. The Lord therefore led us into the inn—he who “raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap” (Ps. 112:7).

78. “And he took care of him” (ibid.), lest the sick man fail to keep the commands he had received. [Note: Some manuscripts add after “keep” the words, “in which the she-ass recognized the manger of her Lord.” One Colbertine manuscript further adds: “and where the needy are raised from the earth, and the poor are lifted from the dung heap; certainly where flocks of lambs are enclosed, lest, while ravenous wolves roar at the folds, entry into the sheepfolds be easy.” We understand from what follows shortly afterward that these words have been torn from their proper place and interpolated with several spurious expressions.] But this Samaritan could not remain long on earth; he had to return to the place from which he had descended. Therefore:

(Vers. 35.) “On the next day.”

79. What is this “next day,” unless perhaps that of the Lord’s resurrection, of which it is said: “This is the day which the Lord has made” (Ps. 117:24)?

(Ibid.) “He brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, and said: Take care of him.”

80. What are these two denarii except perhaps the two Testaments, which bear within themselves the image of the eternal King, and by whose price our wounds are healed? For we were redeemed by precious blood, so that we might avoid the wounds of the final death.

81. The innkeeper receives these two denarii—although it is not unreasonable to understand these books as having four forms as well. Who is he? Perhaps the one who says: “I consider them as dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3:8), so that he might care for the wounded man. The innkeeper, then, is the one who said: “Christ sent me to evangelize” (1 Cor. 1:17). The innkeepers are those to whom it is said: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature; whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:15–16)—saved, certainly, from death and from the wound inflicted by the robbers. Blessed is that innkeeper who can heal another’s wounds. Blessed is the one to whom Jesus says:

(Vers. 35.) “Whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you.”

82. He is a good steward who even spends more than he has received. Paul is a good steward, whose words and letters overflow beyond the account entrusted to him. He carried out the Lord’s moderate command with almost immoderate labor of mind and body, so that he might raise many from grievous illness through the ministry of spiritual instruction. A good innkeeper, then, is the keeper of the inn in which the she-ass recognized the manger of her Lord and in which the flock of lambs is enclosed, lest, while ravenous wolves roar at the folds, entry into the sheepfolds be easy.

83. [Note: Only the Roman edition has, “Therefore he promises that he will return. When will you return, Lord?”] He therefore promises that he will repay the reward. [Col. 1720A] When will you return, Lord, except on the day of judgment? For although you are everywhere always, and stand in our midst without being seen by us, there will nevertheless be a time when all flesh will look upon you returning. You will therefore repay what you owe. Blessed are those to whom you are debtor! Would that we might be worthy debtors; would that we might be able to repay what we have received, and that neither the office of priesthood nor of ministry might exalt us! How will you repay, Lord Jesus? You have indeed promised that a plentiful reward awaits the good in heaven (Matt. 5:12). Yet you will also repay when you say: “Well done, good servant, because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

84. Therefore, since no one is more our neighbor than the one who healed our wounds, let us love him as Lord; let us love him as neighbor, for nothing is so near as the head is to the members. Let us also love the one who imitates Christ; let us love the one who, through the unity of the other’s body, suffers with another’s poverty. Kinship does not make a neighbor, but mercy does, because mercy is according to nature; for nothing is so according to nature as to help one who shares our nature.

85. (Vers. 38–42.) Thus the discussion has been about mercy, but virtue does not have only one form. The example of Martha and Mary is added: the active devotion of one in works, the religious attention of the other in mind to the word of God. If this attention is joined with faith, it is even placed before works themselves, in accordance with what is written: “Mary chose the best portion for herself, and it will not be taken away from her.” Let us therefore strive to possess what no one can take from us, [Col. 1720C] so that not cursory but diligent hearing may be given to it. For even the seeds of the heavenly word itself are often taken away if they are sown beside the road (Luke 8:12). [Note: Five manuscripts read, “Therefore the desire for wisdom is praised in Mary.” One has, “May desire for wisdom sharpen you as it did Mary,” etc.] May the desire for wisdom, as in Mary, move you; for this is the greater and more perfect work. Let not the care of ministry turn you away from knowledge of the heavenly word, nor rebuke or judge as idle those whom you see devoted to the pursuit of wisdom; for that peaceful Solomon took wisdom to dwell with him.

86. Yet Martha is not censured for her good ministry; Mary is preferred because she chose the better portion. Jesus abounds in many things and bestows many things, and therefore she is judged wiser because she noticed and chose what was primary. Finally, the apostles did not think it right to abandon the word of God and serve tables (Acts 6:2). Yet both ministries belong to wisdom, for Stephen too was chosen as a minister full of wisdom (ibid., 5). Therefore, let the one who ministers show respect to the teacher, and let the teacher invite and encourage the one who ministers. The Church is one body, even though its members are diverse; one needs the other. The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of your work,” nor can the head say this to the feet, nor can the ear deny that it belongs to the body. For although some members are primary, others are necessary. Wisdom is in the head, action in the hands: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccles. 2:14), because the truly wise person is the one whose mind is in Christ and whose inner eye is lifted toward heavenly things. Therefore: “The eyes of the wise are in his head, but the eyes of the fool are in his heel.”

(Chap. 11—Vers. 5.) “Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him: Friend, lend me three loaves.”

87. Another point of the teaching is that prayer should be offered at every moment—not only during the day but also at night. You see that the man who went at midnight, asking his friend for three loaves and persisting in the very intention of his request, is not deprived of what he asks. [Col. 1721B] What are these three loaves except the nourishment of the heavenly mystery? If you love the Lord your God, you will be able to obtain it not only for yourself but also for others. Who is a greater friend to us than the one who handed over his body for us? David asked loaves from him at midnight and received them; for he asked when he said: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Ps. 118:62). Therefore he deserved these loaves, which he set before us to eat. He asked when he said: “Every night I will wash my bed” (Ps. 6:7); for he did not fear waking the one whom he knew to be always watchful.

88. Therefore, mindful of the Scriptures, let us devote ourselves to prayer night and day and ask forgiveness for our sins. For if that man was so holy, and was occupied with the necessities of the kingdom, yet praised the Lord seven times a day, always intent upon the morning and evening sacrifices (Ps. 118:164), what ought we to do? We ought to pray all the more because we sin more frequently through the weakness of flesh and mind, so that for those wearied on the road and heavily exhausted by the course of this age and the winding path of this life, the bread of refreshment may not be lacking—the bread that strengthens human hearts.

89. The Lord teaches that we must keep watch not only at midnight but at almost every moment. For he comes during the evening watch, the second watch, and the third watch, and he is accustomed to knock: “Blessed, therefore, are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke 12:37). If you desire the power of God to gird itself and minister to you, you must always keep watch. There are many snares for the good, and the body’s sleep is heavy; for if the mind begins to sleep, it loses the vigor of its virtue. Awaken your sleep, therefore, so that you may knock at Christ’s door. Paul too asks that it be opened to him, entreating not only his own prayers but also those of the people to help him, “so that a door may be opened to him for speaking the mystery of Christ” (Col. 4:3). Perhaps this is the door that John saw opened. For he saw and said: “After these things I saw, and behold, a door was opened in heaven; and the first voice that I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me and saying: Come up here, and I will show you what must take place” (Rev. 4:1). The door was therefore opened to John; the door was opened to Paul, so that they might receive for us the loaves that we were to eat. He persevered in knocking at the proper and improper time, so that he might refresh the Gentiles, wearied by the labor of the world’s path, with the abundance of heavenly nourishment.

90. Therefore this passage first presents the command to pray frequently, the hope of obtaining what is requested, and the reason for persuasion in the command; afterward it presents the same things by example. For the one who promises something ought to inspire hope in the promise, so that obedience may be offered to admonitions and faith to promises. Through the contemplation of human piety, this faith gains greater hope of eternal piety—provided that the things requested are just, lest prayer turn into sin. He was not ashamed to ask repeatedly, lest he appear either to distrust the Lord’s mercy or arrogantly to grieve that he had not obtained something at his first prayer. “For this reason,” he says, “I besought the Lord three times” (2 Cor. 12:8). And he shows that God often does not grant what is requested because he judges useless the things we believe will benefit us.

(Vers. 17.) “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house.”

91. [Note: Only the Roman edition has, “The reason for this saying, since Jesus was said to cast out demons by Beelzebul . . . is to show,” etc.] The reason for this saying is that Jesus was accused of casting out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, and wished to show that his kingdom was undivided and everlasting. And rightly he also answered Pilate: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Therefore those who place their hope not in Christ but think that demons are cast out by the prince of demons—he declares that they do not belong to an everlasting kingdom. This applies to the Jewish people, [Note: The same Roman edition had deleted the words “by passions of this kind.” Below, in place of “was generated from the Law, and is not not from the Law,” it had put, by its own authority, “under the Law,” etc.] who summon the aid of a demon to cast out a demon through passions of this kind. For how can the kingdom remain undivided when faith itself is split? Since the Jewish people are in the Law, and Christ too, according to the flesh, was generated from the Law, how can the kingdom of the Jews be everlasting when it is from the Law, while the people themselves divide the Law by denying Christ—the one who, as coming from the Law, is owed by the Law? Thus the faith of the Jewish people attacks itself in part; by attacking itself it is divided, and by being divided it is dissolved. The kingdom of the Church, however, will remain forever, because undivided faith is one body: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in all” (Eph. 4:5–6).

92. [Col. 1722D] What madness of sacrilegious fury this is: when the Son of God took flesh to crush unclean spirits and seize the spoils of the world’s ruler, and gave human beings power as well to destroy spiritual wickedness, dividing up its spoils—which is the mark of a triumphant victor—some nevertheless claim for themselves the aid and defenses of diabolical power, although demons are cast out by the finger of God, or, according to Matthew, by the Spirit of God (Matt. 12:28). From this it is understood that divinity and the kingdom are, as it were, one undivided body. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “as if the kingdom of divinity were the body.”] For Christ is the right hand of God. The Spirit appears to express the likeness of a finger, as though it were one member in the sequence of the divine body. Does the kingdom not appear to be undivided when it is, as it were, an undivided body? For, as you have read, “the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ” (Col. 2:9). You cannot deny this of the Father, nor ought you deny it of the Spirit. Nor should you imagine, by comparing it with our bodily members, that some portion of power is being assigned; for an undivided reality cannot be divided. Therefore the designation “finger” must be referred to the form of unity, not to a distinction of power, since the right hand of God also says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Yet although the divinity is undivided, the person is distinct.

93. Nevertheless, when the Spirit is called a finger, operative power is signified: just as the Father and the Son, so too the Holy Spirit is the agent of divine works. David says: “For I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8:4). And in the thirty-second Psalm: “By the Spirit of his mouth is all their power” (Ps. 32:6). Paul also says: “All these things the one and same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). And when he says:

(Vers. 20.) “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has surely come upon you,”

94. he simultaneously shows that the Holy Spirit possesses a kind of imperial power, in whom the kingdom of God exists. We too, in whom the Spirit dwells, possess a royal dwelling. Hence he also said later: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). Therefore we must regard the Holy Spirit as sharing in divinity, dominion, and imperial majesty, because “the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

(Vers. 24.) “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, he travels through waterless places, seeking rest, and not finding it.”

95. There can be no doubt that this was said about the Jewish people, whom the Lord separated from his kingdom above. Hence understand all heretics and schismatics as likewise separated from that kingdom and from the Church. It is therefore plainly evident that the assemblies of all schismatics and heretics belong not to God but to the unclean spirit.

Thus the whole Jewish people are compared in one person, from whom the unclean spirit had gone out through the Law. But because he could not find rest among the nations and Gentiles through faith in Christ—for Christ is a fire to unclean spirits, and when the breasts of the Gentiles, previously dry, were afterward moistened by the dew of the Holy Spirit through baptism, he had restrained the flaming darts of the adversary—therefore he returned to the Jewish people, which, though adorned outwardly with a superficial and merely external appearance, remains inwardly more polluted in mind. It neither washed nor quenched its burning through the irrigation of the sacred font. Therefore the unclean spirit rightly returned to it, bringing with him seven spirits more wicked than himself, because with a sacrilegious mind it committed the mystery of the week of the Law and of the eighth day. Thus, just as the grace of the sevenfold Spirit is multiplied for us, so every injury of unclean spirits is heaped upon them; for the totality is often comprehended by this number, since on the seventh day, when the works of the world had been completed, God rested (Gen. 2:2). Hence also “the barren woman bore seven, while she who had many children languished” (1 Sam. 2:5). Finally, to show that the people of the Synagogue are disfigured wherever the blessedness of the Church is praised, he added:

(Vers. 29–30.) “This generation is an evil generation; it seeks a sign, and a sign will not be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so also will the Son of Man be.”

96. In this condemnation of the Jewish people as well, the mystery of the Church is clearly expressed. The Church is gathered from the ends of the whole world: in the Ninevites through repentance, and in the queen of the South through the pursuit of wisdom, so that she may know the words of the peaceful Solomon—a true queen whose kingdom is undivided, rising from diverse and distant peoples into one body. Therefore, “this is a great mystery . . . concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32). Yet this is greater still: the former preceded in figure, whereas now the mystery is complete in truth. There, Solomon was a type; here, Christ is present in his own body. The Church therefore consists of these two things: that you either do not know how to sin or cease from sinning; for repentance removes wrongdoing, and wisdom guards against it. This is the mystery.

97. The sign of Jonah, as it is a type of the Lord’s passion, is also a testimony to the grave sins committed by the Jews. At the same time one may perceive both a prophetic oracle of majesty and an indication of mercy; for through the example of the Ninevites, punishment is announced and a remedy is shown. Therefore the Jews too ought not to despair of pardon if they are willing to repent.

(Vers. 33.) “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, or under a bushel, but on a lampstand.”

98. Since in the preceding discussion he preferred the Church to the Synagogue, he now urges us to transfer our faith rather to the Church. For the lamp is faith, in accordance with what is written: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet” (Ps. 118:105). The word of God is our faith; the word of God is light; faith is a lamp. “There was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9). But a lamp cannot shine unless it has received light from elsewhere. This is the lamp that is lit: namely, the power of our mind and understanding, so that that [word uncertain] which had been lost may be found (Luke 15:8). Therefore let no one place faith under the Law. The Law is within measure; grace is beyond measure. The Law casts a shadow; grace gives light. Therefore no one should confine his faith within the measure of the Law, but should transfer it to the Church, in which the grace of the sevenfold Spirit shines forth—a grace that the chief priest illuminates with the radiance of heavenly divinity, lest the shadow of the Law extinguish it.

99. Finally, that lamp of the Law, which the high priest used to light at morning and evening according to the ancient Jewish rite (Exod. XXVII, 21), has vanished, as though placed beneath a bushel; and that earthly city, Jerusalem, which killed the prophets, lies concealed as though situated in the Valley of Tears. But that Jerusalem which is in heaven, in which our faith is engaged, placed upon that highest of all mountains—that is, in Christ—the Church cannot be hidden by the darkness and ruins of this world. Rather, shining with the radiance of the eternal sun, it illuminates us with the light of spiritual grace.

**(Verse 39.)** “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and the dish first.”

100. You see that our bodies are signified by the representation of earthly and fragile objects, which are shattered when they fall after a brief descent; and that what the mind has willed within is easily betrayed through the body’s senses and actions, just as what the cup contains within shines forth outside. Hence, in what follows also (Luke XXII, 42), there can be no doubt that the passion of the body is indicated by the word “cup,” when the Lord says: “The cup which the Father has given me, do you not wish me to drink it?” (John XVIII, 11). For he drinks his own body who absorbs bodily frailty through a spiritual disposition and, as it were, pours it into the mind and soul, so that the weakness of external things is imbibed by what is within. You see, therefore, that it is not the exterior but the interior of this cup or dish that defiles us. And so, like a good teacher, he taught how we ought to cleanse ourselves from the contamination of the body, saying:

**(Verse 41.)** “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.”

101. [Note: [Col. 1725D] Several manuscripts read: “You see by what great remedy he cleanses us.”]

You see how many remedies there are! Mercy cleanses us; God’s word cleanses us, according to what is written: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John XV, 3). Nor is this the only place where you find expressed how great this grace is; elsewhere also: “Almsgiving delivers from death” (Tob. XII, 9); and, “Enclose almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will plead for you on the evil day” (Ecclus. XXIX, 15).

102. Thus, from this point onward, the whole of this most beautiful passage is directed toward the following end: since it invites us to pursue simplicity, it condemns the Jews’ superfluous and earthly practices. Because they understand the things of the Law according to the body, they are not unjustly compared to glass and a dish on account of their fragility; they observe things from which we derive no benefit, but neglect those in which the fruit of our hope lies, and therefore commit a great sin while despising better things. Yet even they are promised the abolition of sin, if they obtain mercy.

[Note: [Col. 1725D] Some manuscripts read: “if they receive mercy.” Inappropriately; the meaning is that the Pharisees are promised the abolition of sins if they acquire and merit it through mercy, that is, through almsgiving distributed to the poor.]

1435. **103. (Verse 42.)** He briefly touches upon their many vices: they devote all their zeal to paying tithes of the least valuable produce, yet possess neither fear of the future judgment nor any love of God, since works without faith are empty. For they pass over judgment and the love of God: judgment, because they do not bring everything they do into judgment; love, because they do not love God from the heart.

104. But lest he should once again make us zealous for faith while neglecting works, he sums up the perfection of the faithful person in a brief statement, so that one may be approved both by faith and by works, saying: “These things you ought to have done, and not to omit those others.”

105. **(Verses 43, 44.)** He also rebukes the arrogance and ostentation of the Jews, since they seek the places of honor at banquets. Against the experts in the Law as well the sentence of condemnation is pronounced: they are like graves that are not visible, deceiving by their appearance and misleading by what is seen, so that although they promise beauty outwardly, within they contain bones full of stench. This is what many teachers do: they demand from others what they themselves are unable to imitate. And therefore they themselves are tombs, as it is also said elsewhere: “Their throat is an open grave” (Ps. V, 11).

106. **(Verse 47.)** This is also a good passage against the Jews’ most empty superstition. By building tombs for the prophets, they condemned the deeds of their fathers; but by imitating their ancestral crimes, they turned the sentence back upon themselves. For by building the prophets’ tombs they accused those who had killed them of crime; and by imitating similar deeds they showed themselves also to be heirs of their fathers’ wickedness. Therefore it is not the building but the imitation that is counted as the crime. For those who crucified the Son of God—and thereby added what was more grievous to their fathers’ crimes—cannot be absolved from inherited wickedness. Hence he rightly added elsewhere: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matt. XXIII, 32), because they can commit no sin more grievous than an injury against God.

107. **(Verse 49.)** Therefore Wisdom sends apostles and prophets to them. Who is Wisdom except Christ? Indeed, in Matthew you have: “Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men” (Matt. XXIII, 34).

108. **(Verse 52.)** They are still reproved under the name of Jews and declared liable to future punishment, because, while they claim for themselves the knowledge of divine teaching, they hinder others and do not themselves recognize what they profess.

**(Chapter XII.—Verses 6, 7.)** “Are not five sparrows sold for two asses, and not one of them is forgotten before the Lord? But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows.”

109. The Savior has woven into his discourse a most beautiful passage concerning the preservation of simplicity and the imitation of faith, so that, following the pattern of Jewish faithlessness, we may not suppress one thing in our affections while pretending another in our speech. At the final time, the secret of our minds will be disclosed, together with the hidden thoughts that accuse or even defend us, so that they may be seen. For what is a greater inducement to simplicity than that each person should recognize that there can be no hiding place for deceit?

[Col. 1727A] 110. But since faithlessness has a twofold cause—arising either from ingrained malice or from an accompanying fear—1436 lest anyone, terrified by fear of power, should attempt to deny the God whom he knows in his heart, he beautifully added that only punishment of the soul is to be feared, while punishment of the body is not to be feared. Death is the end of nature, not a punishment; therefore death is the cessation of bodily punishment, whereas the punishment of the soul is perpetual. God alone, then, is to be feared, since his authority is not limited by nature, but nature itself is subject to him. Death, however, is not terrible, since immortality will redeem it with richer interest.

111. The Lord had inspired a disposition toward simplicity and raised up the power of the mind; only faith was wavering. He rightly strengthened it by means of things of lesser value: if God does not forget the sparrows, who can imagine that he forgets human beings? And if God’s majesty is so great and so eternal that not one of the sparrows, nor the number of our hairs, is outside God’s knowledge, how unworthy it is to suppose that the Lord either does not know or despises the hearts of the faithful, when he knows things of less value!

112. Someone may perhaps say: How did the Apostle say, “Does God care for oxen?” (I Cor. IX, 9), when surely an ox is more valuable than a sparrow? But care is one thing, and knowledge another. Indeed, the number of the hairs is understood not as an actual process of counting but as the ease of knowledge. God does not keep a watchful, anxious vigil like one who counts; rather, for him who knows all things, all things are as though numbered. Yet they are rightly said to be numbered, because we count the things that we wish to preserve.

113. We can also investigate here a hidden spiritual meaning, especially since it might seem absurd that human beings should be compared not to other human beings but to sparrows. These five sparrows appear to be the five bodily senses: touch, smell, taste, sight, and hearing. If, however, in the manner of sparrows, they sift through the filth of earthly mire and seek food in uncultivated and foul places, then, caught in the snares of their sins, they cannot fly back to the fruits of higher works on which souls feast. There is a certain snare of pleasure that plays the seducer, attaching certain bonds to the footsteps of our souls,

[Note: [Col. 1727D] Some manuscripts read: “which attaches certain bonds to the oars of our souls.”]

so that, if the fiery vigor and purity of nature have been dulled by the senses’ contact with earthly matter, it may place a person, enslaved at the price of luxury, under a kind of auction of vices.

114. There are also certain markets of our sins. Thus, captured by the allurements of various pleasures, we are either sold under sin or redeemed from sin. Christ redeems us; the adversary sells us. The latter puts us up for sale unto death; the former redeems us unto salvation. Hence Matthew rightly speaks of two sparrows (Matt. X, 29), signifying body and soul. For if the flesh also consents to the law of God and, stripping itself of the law of sin, passes into the nature of the soul through purity of the senses, it is lifted on spiritual wings to heaven. Thus we are taught that nature gave us the grace of flight, but pleasure took it away.

[Note: [Col. 1727D] Some manuscripts read: “the will took it away.” But it is familiar for scribes to write *voluntas* for *voluptas* indiscriminately, and conversely.]

115. And rightly he said that none of them falls without the will of God (ibid.). For what falls inclines toward earth, while what flies is raised to the summit of immortality. But lest anyone doubt what Matthew said, Luke makes it clear, because the will of man is known to God.

[Note: [Col. 1727D] All printed editions, together with some manuscripts, read: “the will of God is the knowledge of God”; but the manuscripts, instead of “the knowledge of God,” have “knowledge is.” Others, and those of better quality, have the reading given in the text. Correspondingly, where the editions prefer “for no one,” the Ambrosian edition has “each person falls by the will of God”; all the manuscripts agree with us, except that in some the first occurrence of “falls” is omitted.]

For not everyone who falls falls by the will of God; but whoever falls beneath the weight of his sins cannot remain hidden from God. For Job also is tested by God’s will (Job I, 12). He gave you an adversary, but he set before you a reward. Do not excuse your frailty: you possess the image and have received protection. This too contributes to salvation, namely, that you recognize that the devil cannot harm you without God’s permission, lest you fear the devil’s power more than you fear offending the divine majesty.

116. It is now beyond doubt that the soul is compared to a sparrow, since you read: “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. CXXIII, 7). And elsewhere: “How do you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. X, 2). We also read that the human being himself is compared to a sparrow, because it is written: “But I am like a solitary sparrow on a building” (Ps. CI, 8)—namely, formed from two sparrows into one sparrow, that is, into the subtlety of spiritual substance, by the joining together of the two concordant wings. Therefore the good sparrow is the one to whom nature supplies the ability to fly. There is also a bad sparrow, one that has destroyed the use of flight through the fault of its earthly stain. Such are these sparrows that are sold for two asses.

117. Elsewhere they are sold for an as, elsewhere for two asses (Matt. X, 29). What great cheapness in sins! For death is cheap, but virtue is precious. The adversary, as though assigning captive slaves, sells us for a price based on a cheaper valuation; but the Lord, as one who made us a noble household of servants in his own image and likeness, a capable assessor of his own work, redeemed us at a great price, as the holy Apostle said: “For you were bought with a great price” (I Cor. VI, 20). And rightly “great,” since it is valued not in bronze but in blood. For Christ died for us, and he freed us with his precious blood, as Saint Peter also recalls in his Epistle, writing to us: “You were not redeemed with perishable things, silver or gold, from your empty way of life handed down from your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb” (I Pet. I, 18–19). And rightly “precious,” because it is the blood of an immaculate body, because it is the blood of the Son of God, who redeemed us not only from the curse of the Law but also from the everlasting death of impiety.

118. In summary, then, this is the meaning here: if the Lord has regarded lowly birds and faithless human beings, whether in the rising sun or in earthly fecundity; if he grants to all the gift of his mercy, there can be no doubt that the merits of the faithful will be valued in his sight. Yet he admirably interwove this while sharpening faith, and he laid the foundations of virtues beneath faith itself. For just as faith is an incentive to courage, so courage is the support of faith.

**(Verses 9, 10.)** “But whoever denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.”

119. Certainly we understand the Son of Man to be Christ, who was generated from the Holy Spirit in the Virgin, so that his only parent on earth is the Virgin. Is the Holy Spirit, then, greater than Christ, so that those who sin against Christ receive forgiveness, while those who offend against the Holy Spirit do not deserve to obtain remission? But where there is unity of power, there is no question of comparison and no controversy concerning greatness, since the Lord is great and there can be no end to his greatness. If, then, as we believe, there is unity in the Trinity—undivided greatness, just as there is undivided operation—this is demonstrated in what follows. For while elsewhere it is said, “The Father will give you what you should say,” here he adds: “For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that hour what you ought to say” (Matt. X, 19). Therefore, if the operation is one, the insult is one.

120. But let us return to the matter at hand. Some think that here we should understand Christ as both the Son of Man and the Holy Spirit, while preserving the distinction of persons and the unity of substance, because Christ is one, both God and man, and the Spirit is the same, as it is written: “The Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord” (Lam. IV, 20). He is also the same Holy One; for just as God the Father is God and the Son is God, and the Father is Lord and the Son is Lord, so also the Father is holy, the Son is holy, and the Holy Spirit is holy. Indeed, the Cherubim and Seraphim cry out with tireless voices: “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. VI, 3), so that the Trinity is signified by the thrice-repeated title. If, then, both are Christ, what is the distinction except that we should know that we may not deny Christ’s divinity? Indeed, what is sought in persecution except that Christ the God be denied? Therefore, every spirit that does not confess God in Christ, and Christ as from God and in God, does not merit forgiveness.

[Note: [Col. 1729] The editions and a few manuscripts read: “whoever does not confess”; the larger and more reliable number of other manuscripts read: “every spirit [that does not confess],” and so forth.]

But whoever does not confess that Christ came in the flesh is not from God. For whoever has denied the human being has denied God, because Christ is God in the human being and the human being in God.

121. Nevertheless, many maintain that the blasphemy is unforgivable if someone says that Christ casts out demons by Beelzebub and not by divine power.

**(Verses 13, 14.)** “And someone from the crowd said to him, ‘Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.’ But he said to him, ‘Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?’”

122. The whole of this passage is arranged to prepare us to undergo suffering for confessing the Lord—whether through contempt of death, hope of reward, or the threat of an enduring punishment for which forgiveness will never be granted. And because avarice often tests virtue, a command and example concerning the eradication of this vice are also added, when the Lord says: “Who appointed me judge or divider over you?” He rightly turns away from earthly matters, since he had descended for the sake of divine matters; nor does he consider himself worthy to be judge of disputes and arbiter of possessions, though he possesses judgment over the living and the dead and the authority to assess merits.

Therefore, it is not what you ask but from whom you ask it that must be considered. Nor should you suppose that, when standing before those who are greater, you may with an intent mind obstruct those who are lesser. Hence this brother is rightly rejected: he was eager to occupy the steward of heavenly things with corruptible matters, although among brothers it is not an intermediate judge but affection that ought to divide an inheritance. Yet what human beings ought to seek is the inheritance of immortality, not money. For he gathers wealth in vain who does not know that he will use it, like the man whose barns burst with their new harvests and who prepared storehouses for his overflowing fruits without knowing for whom he was gathering them (verses 27 and following).

All things belonging to the world remain in the world, and whatever is gathered passes to our heirs; for those things are not ours which we cannot take away with us. Virtue alone accompanies the dead; mercy alone follows us. As the guide who goes before us to the heavenly dwelling places, it acquires eternal tabernacles for the dead through the small interest of money, as the Lord’s commands testify when he says to us: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into their eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI, 9).

It is therefore a good and salutary command, suitable even to encourage the avaricious, so that they may strive to exchange corruptible things for everlasting things and earthly things for divine ones. But because devotion to faith is often held back by weakness, and those who are ready to distribute their patrimony are restrained by concern for their livelihood, the Lord added, saying:

[Col. 1730D] **(Verses 22, 23.)** “Do not be anxious about your soul—what you will eat—or about your body—what you will wear. The soul is more than food, and the body more than clothing.”

123. Nothing is more effective for producing faith that God can bestow everything upon believers than the fact that this airy spirit, the vital fellowship joined in partnership with the soul and the body, preserves itself without our labor, and that the salutary use of nourishment does not fail until the final day of death arrives. Since the soul is clothed with the garment of the body and the body is animated by the soul’s vigor, it is absurd for us to think that the provision of food will fail us when we receive the continuous substance of life.

124. “Consider,” he says, “the birds of the air” (Matt. VI, 26). This is a great and fitting example for us to follow in faith. For if divine providence grants unfailing nourishment to the birds of the air, which have no practice of cultivation and no produce from the fertility of harvests, then it is true that our poverty appears to be caused by avarice. Their supply of food, obtained without labor, abounds precisely because they do not know how to claim for themselves, by any special domination, the fruits given in common for food. We have lost what is common while claiming what is private; for nothing is truly private where nothing is permanent, and there is no secure abundance where the outcome is uncertain.

Why do you value your riches, when God has willed even your food to be shared with the other living creatures? The birds of the air claim nothing as specially their own, and therefore do not know want of food, because they do not know how to envy others.

**(Verses 27, 28.)** “Consider how the lilies grow.” And below: “But if God so clothes the grass which is today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith!”

125. This is certainly a good and morally instructive saying. To draw us toward faith in divine mercy, the Lord uses the comparison of the flower and the grass, whether literally, because of the stature of our body (verse 25), or spiritually, because without God’s favor we cannot add anything beyond the measure of our stature. What could be more morally persuasive than seeing that even irrational creatures are so clothed by God’s providence that they need neither practical use nor adornment? How much more should you believe that a rational human being, if he places all his use of himself in God and does not violate faith through a desire for change, can never be in want, since he has rightly presumed upon divine favor?

126. Yet, if we consider these things more deeply—for it does not seem accidental that the flower is either attributed to the human being or, certainly, preferred above human beings in the case of Solomon, who merited so much that, either in outward form, he built a temple for God, or, in mystery, prefigured the Church of Christ—it does not seem inappropriate to understand the glory of the heavenly angels as expressed through the brilliance of their color, since they are truly the flowers of this world. The world is adorned by their splendor, and they breathe forth the good fragrance of sanctification.

Strengthened by their protection, we can say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved” (II Cor. II, 15). Unhindered by anxiety and untried by any laborious use, they preserve in themselves the grace of divine generosity and the gifts of heavenly nature. Hence Solomon is rightly shown here clothed in his glory and elsewhere covered with it (Matt. VI, 29): the glory of his works clothed the weakness of bodily nature as though it were covered by a certain virtue of the mind.

The angels, however, whose more divine nature remains free from bodily injury, are rightly preferred even to the greatest human being, though only in view of our own injury. Therefore, since through the resurrection human beings will be like the angels in heaven, the Lord, who grants glory to the angels, has commanded us also to hope for an increase of heavenly glory after the example of the angels, until “this mortal is swallowed up by life”; for “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (I Cor. XV, 53).

127. Many also think that this comparison is more suitably understood according to the nature of the flower and the use of the plant in question. Lilies require no cultivation for annual use, nor does the labor of farmers return in a yearly cycle for the generation of this flower, as it does for the production of other fruits. However great the droughts of the fields, everything that is nourished into a flower is continually animated by a certain generative power from itself and within itself, through the ever-abiding sap. Thus, when you see the stalk covered with young leaves wither, the nature of the flower nevertheless remains green; its greenness is hidden, not lost. But when it is summoned by the gentle breezes of spring, it resumes the garment of its shoot, the crown of the flower, and the adornment of the lily.

Since we remember that this passage has been treated more fully elsewhere, it is enough to have touched upon it here, lest we return to the same subject again.

[Col. 1732C] 128. It should also be noted that lilies are produced not among the roughness of mountains and uncultivated forests but amid the beauty of gardens. There are indeed certain gardens bearing the fruits of various virtues, according to what is written: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song IV, 12). For where there is integrity, chastity, religion, faithful silence concerning hidden things, and the splendor of the angels, there are the violets of confessors, the lilies of virgins, and the roses of martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 1731D] “Confessors,” who are sometimes taken by the ancients to mean the martyrs themselves, are clearly distinguished from them in this passage. Whether this term refers to those who, after suffering imprisonment or torments for the faith, nevertheless ended their lives by an unbloody death, or to those whom we now commonly designate by this word on account of the prolonged martyrdom of their penitence, is not sufficiently certain. In this latter sense, you will scarcely find this term used among the ancients. For other interpretations of the same word, see our Menard in several passages of the *Sacramentary of St. Gregory*, and Du Cange in his *Glossary* under the same word. The reason violets are assigned to confessors is that bodies livid from severe chastisement, and in some way not very different from corpses, display a violet color. See the *Forest of Allegories* under the word “violet.”]

Let no one think it incongruous that lilies are compared with angels, since Christ himself spoke of himself as a lily when he said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II, 1). And Christ is rightly a lily, because where there is the blood of martyrs, there is Christ, who is the exalted, immaculate, innocent flower, in whom there is no harshness of thorns to wound, but the surrounding grace shines forth. Roses have thorns, because the thorns are the torments of the martyrs. Uninjured divinity has no thorns, since it did not suffer torments.

129. Therefore, if lilies or angels are clothed above the glory of human beings, we too should not despair of God’s mercy, since through the grace of the resurrection the Lord promises us an appearance like that of the angels (Matt. XXII, 30). Here he also seems to touch upon the question that the Apostle did not omit: for the peoples of this world ask how the dead rise and with what kind of body they come (I Cor. XV, 35).

130. **(Verse 31.)** When he says, “Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you,” he shows that grace will not be lacking to the faithful either in the present or hereafter, provided that those who desire divine things do not seek earthly things. For it is unbecoming that people who are engaged in the kingdom should concern themselves with food. The king knows how to feed, nourish, and clothe his household; therefore he said: “Cast your care upon God, and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. LIV, 23).

**(Verses 49, 50.)** “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it already be kindled? I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how distressed I am until it is completed!”

131. In what precedes, he wished us to keep watch, awaiting the coming of the Lord and Savior at every moment, lest anyone, by relaxing and neglecting his duties and postponing his works from day to day, be overtaken by the day of the future judgment or by his own death and lose the merit of his commendation. That general form of the command certainly applies to everyone; but the sequence of the following example seems to be directed toward stewards, that is, priests, so that they may know that they will face a severe punishment in the future if, intent upon worldly pleasures, they neglect to govern the Lord’s household and the people entrusted to them.

132. But because it is a small advance, and the grace of merit is slight, to be recalled from error by fear of punishment, and because the prerogative of charity and love is greater, the Lord sharpens our zeal for earning his favor and inflames us with the desire to acquire divinity, saying: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.” It is certainly not a fire that consumes good things, but the author of good will; this fire refines the golden vessels of the Lord’s house, while consuming hay and stubble. That divine fire burns up all worldly things hardened by the world’s pleasure and the works of perishing flesh. It is the fire that blazed in the bones of the prophets, as Saint Jeremiah says: “It became like a burning fire, flaming in my bones” (Jer. II, 9).

It is the Lord’s fire, of which it is said: “Fire shall burn before him” (Ps. XCVI, 3). The Lord himself is also this fire, as he said: “I am a burning fire, and not consuming” (Exod. III). For the Lord’s fire is eternal light. By this fire those lamps are kindled of which he said above: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning.” And because the night is the day of this life, a lamp is necessary.

[Note: [Col. 1733D] Several manuscripts read: “this life is not of this day.”]

Amaon and Cleophas also testify that this fire was sent into them by the Lord when they say: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV, 32). They clearly taught what the operation of this fire is: it illuminates the secrets of the heart. Perhaps the Lord will therefore come in fire, so that at the time of the resurrection he may consume every vice, fulfill each person’s desires by his presence, and kindle the light of merits and mysteries.

133. So great, then, is the Lord’s condescension that he testifies that the zeal to pour devotion into us, to bring perfection to completion in us, and to hasten his passion for our sake is present in him. Though he possessed nothing in himself that should cause him grief, he was nevertheless distressed by our hardships, and at the time of death he displayed a sadness that he had assumed not from fear of his own death but from the delay of our redemption, according to what is written: “And how distressed I am until it is completed!” Certainly, whoever is distressed until completion is secure concerning completion. And elsewhere he says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38). The Lord is sorrowful not because of death but unto death, because it was the condition of bodily feeling, not fear of death, that afflicted him. For whoever assumed a body had to undergo everything that belongs to the body: to hunger, thirst, be distressed, and be sorrowful. Divinity, however, does not know how to be changed by these emotions. At the same time, he shows that in the struggle of the passion, bodily death is the release of anxiety, not the accumulation of pain.

**(Verses 51–53.)** “Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? I tell you, no, but division. For from now on there will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three. Father will be divided against son and son against father; mother against daughter and daughter against mother; mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.”

134. Although spiritual understanding operates in almost every passage of the Gospels, in the present passage especially the sequence of the meaning must be tempered by spiritual depth, lest anyone be offended by the harshness of a bare exposition. This is particularly so because the holy religion, through moral instruction and gentle examples of piety, kindly invites even those exiled from the faith to reverence for itself. By the discipline of faith that precedes it, it dissolves the harshness of superstition through its gentleness and compels minds subject to error to believe even through faith—minds that it was able to soothe through piety. For when the depths of faith cannot be grasped by weak hearts, the things that are to be revered are assessed through the things that have been commanded, so that righteous things may bear witness to a righteous author, holy things to a holy author—the good author of their good things.

135. Shall we then suppose that the Lord, who embraced both reverence for divinity and the grace of piety when he said, “You shall love the Lord your God . . . and you shall love your neighbor” (Luke X, 27), [Note: [Col. 1733D] All printed editions and some manuscripts read *sua lege complexus* (“having embraced by his own law”); the remaining manuscripts, far more numerous and authoritative, read as in the text.] has now been changed, so that we should believe that he commanded the names of family relationships to be abolished and the affections of love to be thrown into conflict? And how is he himself our peace, who made both one (Eph. II, 14)? How does he say, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27), if he has come to separate parents from children and children from parents by a rupture of their relationship? How is one who does not honor his father “accursed” (Deut. XXVII, 16), while one who abandons him is religious?

136. But if we observe that the first cause is religion and the second is filial duty, we shall also find this question easily resolved.

[Note: [Col. 1733D] The old edition and a few manuscripts read *in eodem*, “in the same,” incorrectly. The Roman edition reads *enodandam*, “to be unraveled,” more correctly. Most manuscripts have *enodem*, that is, “easy and straightforward.”]

For it is necessary to place human things after divine things. If duty must be shown to parents, how much more to the author of your parents, to whom you owe gratitude even for your parents! Or if they do not recognize the parent at all, how will you recognize him? He is therefore not saying that one must renounce one’s loved ones, but that God must be preferred to everyone. Indeed, elsewhere you have: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 37). You are forbidden not to love your parents, but to prefer them to God. For the gifts of nature are the Lord’s benefits, and no one ought to love the benefit he has received more than God, by whom the benefit he received is preserved. Thus, even according to the literal meaning, a pious interpretation is not lacking for those who understand it properly. Yet the passage also contains a deeper meaning, as we may suppose, because he added:

**(Ibid.)** “There will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three.”

137. Who are the five, when a listing appears to have been made concerning six persons—father and son, mother and daughter, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law? Yet the same woman may be understood as both mother and mother-in-law: she who is the mother of the son is the mother-in-law of his wife. Thus, even according to the literal meaning, the reckoning of the number is not absurd, and it becomes plainly clear that faith is not bound by the bonds of nature: although people may be subject to the duty of filial affection, they are free in faith.

138. It also seems not inappropriate to unravel this meaning through a mystical interpretation. The one house is one human being. For each person is either the house of God or of the devil. Thus the spiritual house is the spiritual human being, as we have in Peter’s Epistle: “You yourselves, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood” (I Pet. II, 5).

In this house, therefore, two are divided against three, and three against two. We frequently read that the two are soul and body (Matt. XVIII, 19). And if two should agree on earth, it has made both one. Elsewhere also: “I chastise my body and bring it into bondage” (I Cor. IX, 27). One thing is that which serves; another is that to which it is subjected.

[Col. 1735D] **139.** If we have recognized two, let us also recognize three—a point that is readily understood from those two. For there are three affections of the soul in the body: one rational, another appetitive, [Note: [Col. 1735D] Amerbach has “the third impenetrable.” Other editions have “irascible.” One manuscript has “impassive,” another “not susceptible,” and this is perhaps not inappropriate. The remaining manuscripts, however, agree almost unanimously on *impetibilis*, that is, “which attacks,” or “which is carried forward with force” [Col. 1736D] against obstacles.] the third *impetibilis*—that is, *λογιστικὸν, ὀρεκτικὸν, ὀργιστικόν* [rational, appetitive, irascible]. Thus it is not two into two, but two into three, and three into two, that are divided; for through Christ’s coming the human being who was irrational [Col. 1736A] became rational. Previously we were like beasts that know nothing of reason; we were carnal, we were earthly, in accordance with that saying: “You are earth, and into earth you will go” (Gen. III, 19). The Son of God came and sent his Spirit into our hearts; we became spiritual children.

**140.** We can say that in this house there are another five—that is, smell, touch, taste, sight, and hearing. Therefore, if in accordance with what we hear or read, separating the senses of sight and hearing, we exclude the body’s superfluous pleasures, which arise through taste, touch, and smell, we divide two into three, because the disposition of the mind is not captured by the allurements of vices but withdraws itself from the seductions of pleasure through its emulation of virtue. Thus there is not one common accord of everything, which [Col. 1736B] would plunge it into error, but, by dividing themselves, the desires of the heart and the duties of virtue separate from one another. Or, if we understand the five as the bodily senses, then the vices and sins of the body are separated. And perhaps these are the five whom that rich and luxurious man in the Gospel calls his brothers (Luke XVI, 28)—the man who is described as being tormented in hell and asks that they be warned to renounce pleasures in this world, so that through devotion to virtue they may be able to have rest after this age.

**141.** It may also be understood (cf. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book II, chapter 5) that flesh and soul, separated from luxury through smell, touch, and taste, divide themselves within one house against the vices that assail them: flesh and soul submitting themselves to the law of God and removing themselves from the law of sin. Although their dissension, through the transgression of the first human being, has passed into nature [Col. 1736C], so that they could by no means agree with one another in equal zeal for virtue, nevertheless, through the cross of the Lord and Savior, after both their enmities and the law of commandments had been nullified [Note: [Col. 1736D] The Roman edition has: “they were brought together into the harmony of fellowship.”], they were joined in harmonious fellowship, after Christ, descending from heaven as our peace, had made the two one and had broken down the dividing wall of the barrier, abolishing in his flesh the enmity, the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, so that he might create the two in himself into one new human being, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God (Eph. II, 14–16).

Who are the two, unless one is the inner and the other the outer person? The one refers to the vigor of the soul, the other to the bodily sense; [Note: [Col. 1736D] All editions, together with part of the manuscripts, have “although inseparable.” Others, more aptly, have what appears in the text, except that one manuscript has “although equal in itself,” while another has “the other is equal in itself.” Both readings are faulty.] although their distinct affections agree through a harmony within themselves, when the flesh, subjected to what is better, obeys the soul’s salutary commands—not that it passes over into the nature of the soul through the subtlety of matter, but because, having renounced pleasures and been cleansed of every defilement of vices, it proceeds by an obedient affection along the path of heavenly conduct. It no longer, as before, resists the law of the mind, but, through the law of the mind and the spirit of life, is freed from the law of sin, so that the flesh becomes an appendage of the soul [Col. 1737A], no longer a procurer of vices but a kind of rival and, as it were, attendant of virtue.

**142.** And again, when the soul does not connive at the body’s allurements, nor is overcome by the delight of carnal pleasures, but the pure mind, stripped of service to this world, entices and draws the bodily senses toward its own pleasures, so that by the practice of hearing and reading it may feast on the increase of virtue and, knowing no hunger, be satisfied with the spiritual nourishment of inward sap, [Note: [Col. 1737D] Some manuscripts have “with inner furrows.” A few others have “with the juices of the interior”; but in that case *alimenta* [“nourishment”] would have to be read instead of *alimentis* [“with nourishment”]. Again, where all editions, along with some manuscripts and the Leuven edition of Augustine, prefer *etenim ratio* [“for reason”], the more numerous and better manuscripts read *etenim oratio* [“for prayer”]. Where the Amerbach and Roman editions, the cited passage in Augustine, and most manuscripts agree with us in reading *diversoriumque vitiorum* [“a lodging-place of vices”], Erasmus and Gill, with several manuscripts, preferred *diversorumque vitiorum* [“of various vices”]. If that reading is preferred, the *volutabrum* [“wallowing-place”] expressed above must be understood again.] For prayer (cf. Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book II, chapter 5) is food for the mind, and an excellent nourishment of sweetness, which does not burden the limbs or turn itself toward the shameful parts of nature, but toward adornments; when the wallowing-place of lust is changed into a temple of God, and the lodging-place of vices begins to be a sanctuary of virtues.

[Col. 1737B] It does this, certainly, when the flesh, restored to its proper nature, recognizes the source that nourishes its strength and, laying aside the boldness of defiance, is joined to the judgment of the soul that governs it. Such was the flesh when it first undertook to inhabit the secrets of paradise, before, infected by the poison of the destructive serpent, it learned sacrilegious hunger and, through eagerness for eating, passed beyond the memory of the divine commandments implanted in the soul’s senses.

**143.** From this, sin is said to have arisen, as though from parents consisting of body and soul, while the nature of the body was being tempted and the unhealthy soul shared in it. If it had restrained the body’s appetite, the origin of sin would have been extinguished at its very beginning. But the soul, as though moistened after being impregnated by the masculine movement of the body, its own vigor also corrupted, gave birth to alien, burdensome works. [Note: [Col. 1738D] All editions and a few manuscripts have, incorrectly, “the impregnated soul … for he is stronger.” A large number of manuscripts, as in the text, have the present reading.] For the more violent and stronger sex, carried along by a powerful impulse, as though by a masculine affection, [Col. 1737C] is more forceful; the soul strives to maintain a gentler rather than a more vehement reason. From these, therefore, the movement of differing desires grew strong.

**144.** But when the soul returns to itself, summoned to shame by the deformity of its offspring, it disowns its degenerate heirs, renouncing its impulses and hating sin. The flesh too, having been exhausted by the burdensome lot of its labors and wearied by the miserable interest of injury, when it feels that it has been pierced, as by thorns of the world, by the desires that it itself generated, hastens to strip off the old human being, so that it may remove itself from itself, [Note: [Col. 1738D] Several manuscripts have: “lest envy” (one has “envious and improvident”) “leave the parent without a successor destined to perish”; two have “destroy”; and just as many have “be destroyed.” Other manuscripts, more suitably, and the editions, as in our text, have: “lest a succession destined to perish leave the improvident parent.”] lest a succession destined to perish leave the improvident parent without an heir.

Again, the irrational movement of desires, alluring the soul by the seductions of pleasure, as though by the painted beauty of a certain form, drew it to itself as though for the use of companionship. Thus pleasure, as it were a daughter-in-law of body and soul, is joined in marriage to the movement of depraved desire.

**145.** Therefore, as long as it remained in one house, with the vices conspiring together in an undivided and inseparable agreement, there appeared to be no division. But when Christ sent into the world the fire [Col. 1738A] by which he would burn away the offenses of the flesh, or the sword that signifies the edge of manifest power, by which the secrets of spirit and marrow are penetrated, then flesh and soul, renewed through the mysteries of regeneration, forgot what they had been and began to be what they had not been. Thus they separated themselves from the fellowship of the old vice, although previously beloved by them, and, as it were, expelled the union of a prodigal posterity, so that parents might be divided from children: the uncontrolled movement being rejected by the body’s self-control, and the soul turning away from partnership with guilt, with no place remaining for a foreign pleasure taken from outside.

**146.** The children too are divided from the parents, when the vices of old age avoid the discipline of the renewed human being, and youthful pleasure, as though fleeing from a serious household, rejects the standard of piety. Nor is it inappropriate to think that these too divide themselves for the purpose of becoming better than their parents, especially since he says later: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father or mother, or children, and brothers, and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26). Therefore, according to the simple meaning, the son who follows Christ is preferred to gentile parents; for religion takes precedence over duties of natural affection.

**147.** There is also this point according to a deeper interpretation: since sin is born from the flesh and works, as it were, in the womb of the flesh, the Apostle says of it: “If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. VII, 20). When the Lord’s blood, poured out for the life of this world, has abolished vices, offense is transformed into grace: “For sin abounded, so that grace might abound even more” (Rom. V, 20). Thus repentance, arising from sin, impels one toward a change of purpose and toward desire for spiritual grace. Therefore what was for me unto death will be for me unto salvation. Sin, then, washed away in the irrigating fountain, is separated from the flesh from which it was generated; and while each person desires to redeem his offense, the succession of guilt becomes an eagerness for discipline.

**148.** The desire for evil things, too, and a certain more fervent movement of longing, are transformed by the word of God into an appetite for divine charity and love. Within that same nature a different discipline is formed, and that appetite of body and soul acquires for itself a pleasure in the heavenly mysteries far better than before. [Col. 1738D] For the mind is nourished by knowledge of things, and, made more exalted by discovering the promise of future things, the soul disdains its former works: “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him” (I Cor. II, 14); “but the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one.”

[Col. 1739A] **(Verses 58, 59.)** “When you go with your adversary to the magistrate, make an effort on the way to be released from him, lest perhaps he accuse you before the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer send you to prison. I tell you, you will not come out from there until you have paid even the last *quadrans*.”

**149.** Matthew also included this passage (Matt. V, 25), but he did so specifically, whereas Luke does so generally. Matthew, indeed, is thought to have spoken of restoring peace between brothers who are at odds; here the subject is repentance and every correction of sin. Let us therefore examine who the adversary is, who the magistrate is, who the judge is, who the officer is, and what we should understand by the *quadrans*, which, unless someone pays it, he is sent to prison.

**150.** According to Matthew, the adversary is the person with whom you appear to have been unable to reach agreement in this life, who pursues you before the future judge of the living [Col. 1739B] and the dead with the charge of an enduring hostility. According to Luke, however, our adversary is above all that one who sows the allurements of sins, so that he may have as companions in punishment those whom he had as partners in error. Therefore he seeks associates in guilt, so that he may betray the guilty to punishment. The Apostle Peter warns us to beware of him, saying: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring and devouring lion, seeks someone to devour” (I Pet. V, 8).

**151.** According to Matthew, our adversary is also the practice of every virtue and the apostolic and prophetic word, which binds us to sterner commandments and the lessons of a harsher life. We ought to agree with it, so that we may emulate it in our works and not be exposed by some obstinacy of ours as having deserted it. According to Luke, however, no one is more our adversary than our own fall, which accuses us by the evidence of our life—not because the future judge seeks the office of any accuser, but because our conduct accuses us before the knower of all things, when it is found to be alien to the practice of virtue and to apostolic commandments.

**152.** Thus every practice of vice is our adversary; lust is our adversary; avarice is our adversary; every wickedness is our adversary; every unrighteous thought is our adversary. Finally, an evil conscience is our adversary: it afflicts us here and will accuse and betray us in the future, as the Apostle testifies, saying: “Their conscience bears witness to them, and their thoughts accuse or even defend them in turn” (Rom. II, 15). If conscience betrays each person, how much more is the work of our deeds present before God? It will be reviewed at the end, expressed in our body, and the secret of our thought, written in our hearts, will be read. Let us therefore make every effort, while we are placed in this course of life, to be freed from wicked action just as from an evil adversary [Col. 1740A], lest, while we go with our adversary to the magistrate, our error condemn us on the way.

**153.** Therefore Matthew also says: “Be reconciled to your adversary while you are with him on the way” (Matt. V, 25). The Greek has *εὐνοέων* (*eunoéōn*), that is, “being well-disposed” or “showing goodwill.” For if, while we are in this life, we release ourselves from the devil’s bonds, then neither will he be condemned on our account, nor will we remain subject to his bonds. Hence Psalm LXXV is entitled “For the Assyrian.” You therefore deal well with your adversary, and do well on behalf of that Assyrian—that is, the vain one—if, freed from his snares, you show him this goodwill, so that he may escape both the punishment of your fall and death. But if you cling to his bonds, he will hand you over as guilty to the magistrate, being both accuser and betrayer.

**154.** Who is the magistrate except the one in whose hands all power lies, and who claims for himself the sublime dignity of the fullness and perfection of time? Relying on the conscience of his good works and fearing no adversary, the holy Prophet hastens toward him, saying: “My soul thirsted for the living Lord; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI, 3). This magistrate will hand the guilty person over to the judge, namely, to the one to whom he has granted authority over the living and the dead. He granted it by nature, not by grace; for he did not receive what he had not possessed, but assumed what he had from the substance of the Father when he was begotten.

The one who revealed the accuser shows you this magistrate and judge, and indicates when he is to be revealed: “On the day,” he says, “when God will judge the secrets of human beings according to my Gospel through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. II, 16). [Col. 1740C] This, then, is the judge, Jesus Christ, through whom hidden things are exposed, [Note: [Col. 1739D] Some manuscripts have: “and punishment is imposed as a reproach for the deed.”] and punishment is imposed for wicked action.

**155.** Do you wish to know that Christ is the judge who hands one over to the officer and sends him to prison? Ask him—or rather, read him in the Gospel saying: “Take him and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII, 13). He himself also revealed his officers elsewhere, where he says: “So it will be at the consummation of the age: the angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and they will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XIII, 49–50).

**156.** It remains now for us to understand what the figure of the *quadrans* signifies. It appears to express, under the name of an ordinary object, a hidden spiritual meaning. For just as those who pay money discharge a debt, and the name of the debt is not canceled before the whole principal has been paid down to the last coin, whatever the mode of payment by which the entire amount is discharged, so, through the recompense of charity and other deeds, or through whatever satisfaction is offered, the penalty of sin is dissolved. [Col. 1740D] [Note: [Col. 1739D] The Roman edition alone has “down to the very least.” What is added below concerning the *quadrantaria permutatio*, although it presents some obscurity, signifies nothing other than a certain exchange: when one who pays money receives freedom from prison and from the other bonds or punishments to which he was subject. Cicero, however, uses the expression *quadrantaria permutatio* with a somewhat different meaning in *For Marcus Caelius*: he calls it the transaction by which Clodia, having received a *quadrans*, offered the use of her body to a bath attendant.]

**157.** It is also not without significance that he did not put here “two small coins” (as elsewhere, Luke XXI, 2), nor an *as* (Matt. X, 29), nor a denarius (Matt. XX, 2), but a *quadrans*. For a *quadrantaria permutatio* is a kind of compensation, when one thing is returned and another is signified as paid. Thus here either an injury is redeemed by the price of charity, or punishment is released through an assessment of the injury.

**158.** We remember that a *quadrans* is customarily given at the baths. Just as there each person, by offering it, receives the opportunity to bathe, so here he receives the opportunity to be cleansed; for each person’s sin is washed away by the kind of condition described above, when the guilty person is exercised by punishments for as long as necessary to pay the penalties of the error committed.

**159. (Chapter XIII.—Verse 1.)** Concerning those Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices: this appears to touch upon, in a figurative sense, those who, under compulsion from the devil, do not offer sacrifice purely. Their prayer becomes sin, just as is written concerning Judas (Ps. CVIII, 7), the betrayer who, while placed among the sacrifices, was contemplating the betrayal of the Lord’s blood.

**(Verse 6.)** “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard.”

**160.** What does it mean that in his Gospel the Lord frequently introduces the parable of the fig tree (Matt. XXI, 19; Mark XI, 13)? Elsewhere you have the account that, at the Lord’s command, all the greenness of this leafy tree withered. From this you understand that the Creator of all things can command nature either to wither suddenly or to flourish. Elsewhere he mentions that from the tenderness of this tree and its leaves people customarily infer the arrival of summer (Matt. XXIV, 32), signifying by both images that the empty glory which the Jewish people displayed, like a flower, fell away at the Lord’s coming [Col. 1741C], because it continued fruitless in works; and also that the day of judgment is like the arrival of summer, when the ripe fruits of all the earth are stored away—a day to be inferred from the fullness of the Church, into which the Jews too will come to believe. [Note: [Col. 1741D] Many manuscripts have *metuendum* [“to be feared”], which is not altogether inappropriate.]

**161.** Here, then, let us also seek some secret of the deeper meaning (Isa. V, 5). [Note: [Col. 1741D] So all editions, together with part of the manuscripts. Nevertheless, eight manuscripts of no inferior quality prefer: “A fig tree was found.”] The fig tree is in the vineyard. The vineyard, however, was the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, which he gave over to the nations for plunder. Therefore the one who allowed his vineyard to be plundered also commanded that the fig tree be cut down.

The comparison of this tree with the synagogue is appropriate. Just as this tree, overflowing with flowing leaves, frustrates its owner, depriving him of the expected yield through the empty expectation of anticipated produce, so in the synagogue, while its teachers boast of fruitless works and abound only in words, like leaves, the empty shadow of the Law luxuriates, while the false hope of an expected yield mocks the desires of the believing people.

**162.** There is also something in the nature of the tree that makes you more inclined to believe that the character of the synagogue is expressed through this comparison. For if you investigate carefully, you will find in this tree a natural practice distinct from that of other trees.
