Other trees produce a flower before the fruit and announce their future apples by the flower that precedes them; [Col. 1742A] this one alone, from the beginning, produces fruit in place of flowers. In other trees the flower falls away and fruit is born; in this one the fruit falls away so that fruit may follow.

Therefore those earlier growths [Note: [Col. 1741D] Some manuscripts have: “shaken out in place of the fruit, like a flower,” and so forth.] emerge in place of flowers, devoid of fruit. Thus, through a premature manner of growth, those things that do not know the order of nature cannot preserve nature’s gift. For wherever the bud is accustomed to thrust itself from the bark, the smallest fruits of this kind burst forth. Of these we read in the Song of Songs: “The fig tree produces its early figs” (Song II, 13).

Thus, while all other shrubs grow white in early spring, the fig tree alone does not know how to become white with its own flower—perhaps because none of these fruits is more mature in its use. For when others succeed them, these, as though degenerate, are rejected and burned when their weak root has dried up; the renewed ones have more useful sap. [Col. 1742B] [Note: [Col. 1742D] Many good manuscripts have *exuuntur* [“are stripped off”]. This is by no means inappropriate.]

Some, however, remain, exceedingly rare, and do not fall away—those to which this yield has been favorable. They emerge from the middle of two rods by a short stalk bursting forth, so that, covered by a double protection, as though in the lap of their mother nature, they may grow stronger through the nourishment of fuller sap. Brought forth by the mildness of a gentler breeze and matured over longer periods, once they have cast off the wild character of their earlier sap, they surpass the others in appearance and in the grace of ripeness.

**163.** Now observe the cultivation and dispositions of the Jews, who, as the first fruits of the poorly productive synagogue, fell like the likeness of a falling early fig. [Note: [Col. 1742D] So all editions and not a few manuscripts. Nevertheless, more and better manuscripts have: “so that the fruits of our kind might succeed and remain above it.” This is not inappropriate if the relative is referred to the word *grossi* [“early figs”].] Thus fruits of our kind, destined to remain throughout the ages, might succeed them.

For the first people of the synagogue, weak as though by the root of their dried-up works, could not draw forth the abundance of natural wisdom. Therefore, like useless fruit, they fell, so that, as it were, from the same stalks of the fruitful tree, a new people of the Church might emerge from the richness of the ancient religion.

Thus the one who was ceased to be, so that the one who was not might begin to be. Yet the first men from Israel, whom a branch of stronger nature had raised up, under the shadow of the Law and the cross, colored by a double sap in the bosom of both, surpassed the others, after the example of the ripening early fig, in the beauty of their most excellent fruits. To them it is said: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28).

**164.** Nor is it irrelevant that Adam and Eve, those first parents both of our race and of our error, who covered themselves with the leaves of this tree (Gen. III, 7), deserved to become exiles from paradise when, conscious of their transgression, they avoided the presence of the Lord as he walked. This signified what was to happen in the final times: at the coming of the Lord and Savior, who came to call them, the Jewish people, recognizing that they had been stripped of virtues through the devil’s temptations and fearing the exposed shame of their conscience, would depart from religion, confounded by transgression, and withdraw from the Lord, covering the shamefulness of their deeds with veils of flowing words, as though with leaves.

[Col. 1743A] **165.** Therefore those who plucked leaves from the fig tree rather than fruit were expelled from the kingdom of God; for they were made into a living soul. The second Adam came, and he sought not leaves but fruit; for he was made into a life-giving spirit. In the spirit the fruit of virtue is acquired, and the Lord is worshiped (I Cor. XV, 45).

The Lord sought fruit—not because he did not know that the fig tree lacked fruit, but to show figuratively that the synagogue ought by then to have fruit. Finally, what follows teaches that he had not come before the appointed time, since he came over a period of three years. Thus you have:

**(Verse 7.)** “Behold, these three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I do not find any. Cut it down, therefore; why does it also occupy the ground?”

**166.** He came to Abraham, he came to Moses, he came to Mary—that is, he came in a sign, he came in the Law, he came in the flesh. We recognize his coming through his benefits. In one place there is purification, in another sanctification, in another justification: circumcision purified, the Law sanctified, grace justified. He is one in all things, and all things are in one.

For no one can be cleansed unless he fears the Lord; no one deserves to receive the Law unless purified from guilt; no one approaches grace unless he knows the Law. Therefore the Jewish people could neither be purified, because they possessed circumcision of the body, not of the mind, nor be sanctified, because they did not understand the power of the Law, following carnal rather than spiritual things—for “the Law is spiritual” (Rom. VII, 14)—nor be justified, because they did not practice repentance for their sins and therefore did not know grace.

[Col. 1743C] **167.** Rightly, therefore, no fruit was found in the synagogue, and for this reason it is commanded to be cut down. But the good cultivator—and perhaps the one in whom the foundation of the Church lies—foreseeing that another was to be sent to the Gentiles, but he himself to those of the circumcision, intervened reverently so that it might not be cut down, relying upon his calling and also upon the possibility that the Jewish people might be saved through the Church. [Note: [Col. 1743D] The Roman edition has: “might be saved in the Church.”] And so he says:

**(Verse 8.)** “Let it remain this year also, until I dig around it and put a basket of manure on it.”

**168.** How quickly he recognized the hardness and pride of the Jews as the causes of their sterility! Therefore he knows how to cultivate because he knows how to detect vices. He promises that the hardness of their hearts will be dug up by apostolic mattocks, so that the word, with its two-edged force, may overturn the stagnation covering the mind through its long neglect; and, when the heart has been plowed, may awaken a perception already growing strong through the breath of air. Thus the heap of earth may not bury and conceal the root of wisdom.

He also says that a basket of manure is to be applied. Great indeed is the power of manure, since it is such that it makes the unfruitful fruitful, the dry green, and the sterile productive. In it Job sat when he was being tested, and he could not be overcome (Job II, 8). And Paul considers all things as manure, so that he may gain Christ (Phil. III, 8). Finally, although Job had lost many things beforehand, after he sat in manure the devil had nothing that he could take away from him. Good, therefore, is the earth that is dug; good is the manure that is applied. For the Lord raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the manure (Ps. CXII, 7).

**169.** Thus, through the exercise of understanding and an attitude of spiritual humility, that good cultivator considers even the Jews capable of becoming fruitful for the Gospel of Christ. For he remembered that the Lord spoke through Haggai: “On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day on which the temple of the Lord Almighty was founded, the vine,” he says, “and the fig tree, and the pomegranate, and the olive trees that do not bear fruit—from this day I will bless” (Hag. II, 20).

This reveals that, at the very decline of the year, that is, at the setting of the already aging world, the holy temple of God, which is the Church, was to be founded. Through its grace, by the sanctification of the bath, the Jewish people and the peoples of the nations might be able to possess the fruit of their merits.

**170.** Therefore, through the nature of the tree, the character of the synagogue is indicated: fruitful in later yields, for we come from the seed of the fathers. The Jews are rightly compared to falling early figs, because, with an obese heart and an exceedingly stubborn neck, they cannot reach their own perpetuity. If they die and, as it were, fall away from this world so that they may be reborn into the inner person through the grace of the bath, they will certainly be fruitful. But the faithlessness of obstinate people made the synagogue useless; and for this reason it is commanded to be cut down as though sterile.

**171.** What has been said about the Jews, I think, must be guarded against by everyone, and especially by us, lest we occupy the fruitful place of the Church while empty of merits. Blessed as though we were pomegranates, we ought to bear inward fruits: fruits of modesty, fruits of union, fruits of mutual charity and love, enclosed within the one womb of the mother Church. Let not the breeze harm us, let not hail knock us down, let not the heat of desire burn us, and let not the rain of moisture crush us.

**172.** Some, however, think by allegory that this fig tree represents not the synagogue but malice and wickedness. Yet they differ in nothing except that they choose a species instead of a genus. They say that they avoid this interpretation because the Lord said to the fig tree: “May fruit never be born from you forever” (Matt. XXI, 19), although we know that very many Jews believed and will believe.

But the one who believes is no longer a fruit of the synagogue but of the Church; nor is the one who is reborn in the Church born from the synagogue. For “there are those who went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us” (I John II, 19). So concerning those who believe from among the Jews, we say that if they were of the synagogue, they would remain in the synagogue. But they went out from the synagogue for this reason: so that they might be understood not to have belonged to the synagogue.

Moreover, if the tree represented malice, someone might intervene and say that it ought to be cultivated so that it might bear fruit, whereas the Lord came precisely in order to abolish the seeds of wickedness (I John III, 5).

**(Verses 10, 11.)** “He was teaching in their synagogue on the Sabbaths. And behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, and she was bent over.”

[Col. 1745A] **173.** How quickly he indicated what he was going to say about the synagogue (Matt. XV, 23)! He shows that he had come to the very tree, since he was preaching in it. Finally, in the infirm woman there follows, as it were, a figure of the Church. When she has fulfilled the measure of the Law and of the resurrection, she will be raised upright to a lofty height in that perpetual rest and will no longer be able to feel the bending of our weakness.

Nor could this woman have been healed in any other way except because she fulfilled both the Law and grace: the Law in the commandments, grace in the bath, through which we, dead to the world, rise again with Christ. For in the number ten there is the perfection of the Law; in the number eight there is the fullness of the resurrection.

The work of the Sabbath, therefore, is a sign of what is to come: each person who has completed the course of the Law and grace will, through Christ’s mercy, be stripped of the troubles of bodily weakness. [Col. 1745B] For this reason sanctification was first set forth symbolically through Moses (Exod. XIX, 10), so that it might be an exercise of future sanctification and spiritual observance, by abstaining from secular works.

Finally, God rested from the works of the world [Note: [Col. 1745D] The Roman edition alone has: “he rested from the works of the world, but not from holy works.” Some manuscripts have: “he did not rest from the works of the world, but he rested from the works of the world.” Others, in large numbers and together with the ancient editions, have the reading in the text. This is certainly the correct reading, for Ambrose means nothing other than that God rested from the works of the world, but not simply from all works, since his operation is eternal.] (Gen. II, 2), but not from works, since his operation is everlasting and continual. As the Son says: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V, 17). Thus, in imitation of God, our secular works, but not our religious ones, should cease.

**174. (Verse 14.)** The ruler of the synagogue, however, did not understand this and prohibited anyone from being healed on the Sabbath, although the Sabbath is a type of future rest. Therefore those rests are not rests from good works but from evil ones; and it was prescribed that, bringing no burden of sins and not fasting from good works, we should celebrate the future Sabbaths after death. Hence the Lord appears to respond spiritually when he says:

**(Verse 15.)** “Hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey and lead it away to drink?”

**175.** Why did he indicate no other animal, unless to show that, despite the opposition of the rulers of the synagogue, it would nevertheless come about that the Jewish and Gentile people would lay aside the thirst of the body and the heat of this world through the abundance of the Lord’s fountain? For “the ox knows his owner, and the donkey his master’s manger” (Isa. I, 3).

Therefore that people, which had previously been fed on cheap hay that withers before it is plucked, received the bread that descended from heaven. And for this reason, through the calling of the two peoples, he says that the Church would be saved. When the time of the Law had been fulfilled and the age of the Lord’s resurrection had arrived, it had received the time of its release.

How merciful, then, is the Lord, how gracious toward both, whether he shows mercy or exercises judgment! In the type of the synagogue he commands the tree to be cut down; in the type of the Church he saves the woman. How sweet the parable—and how easy its explanation! He compares bond with bond, [Note: [Col. 1745D] All editions and several manuscripts have: “so that the action of the Jews may be accused of hypocrisy,” and so forth. But more and better manuscripts agree with us, except that in some the phrase *per divisionem* [“through division”] is read instead of *in simulatione* [“in hypocrisy”].] so that, through the accusation of the Jews, their own conduct may be rebuked. For while they themselves untie the bonds of animals on the Sabbath, they criticize the Lord for freeing human beings from the bonds of sins.

**(Verses 18, 19.)** “To what is the kingdom of God similar, and to what shall I compare it? It is similar to a mustard seed, which a man took and put in his garden; and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air rested in its branches.”

**176.** The present reading teaches us that we must consider the nature of comparisons, not their outward appearance. Let us therefore see why the lofty kingdom of heaven is compared with a mustard seed. For I remember that elsewhere too a mustard seed is mentioned, where it is compared with faith, when the Lord says: “If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain: ‘Move and cast yourself into the sea’” (Matt. XVII, 19, 21).

This is not a small faith but a great one, which can command a mountain to move itself; for the Lord does not demand mediocre faith from the apostles, knowing that they must struggle against the height of spiritual wickedness that exalts itself. Do you wish to know that great faith is required? Read in the Apostle: “And if I have all faith, so that I move mountains” (I Cor. XIII, 2).

**177.** Therefore, if the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed and faith is like a mustard seed, then faith is certainly the kingdom of heaven, and the kingdom of heaven is faith. Thus whoever has faith has the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom of God is within us, and faith is within us; for we read: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21). And elsewhere: “Have faith in yourselves” (Matt. XVI, 19). Finally, holy Peter, who possessed complete faith, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven so that he might also open it to others.

178. Let us now assess, from the nature of the mustard seed, what force the comparison possesses. Its seed is certainly a humble and simple thing; but if it begins to be crushed, it pours forth its power. Faith likewise at first appears simple; but if it is crushed by adversities, it pours forth the grace of its power, so that it fills even others—whether they hear or read—with the fragrance of itself. The mustard seed is our martyrs Felix, Nabor, and Victor [Note: So nearly all the manuscripts read. All the printed editions, however, add “Gervasius, Protasius, and Nazarius.” If the authority of those editions were to be accepted, our view concerning the date of this work would be decisively established against Baronius’s opinion assigning it to the year 376, for in that year not even the names of these saints were known. But there is a strong suspicion that the names of these three were added to the first three by someone in a manuscript of a later period, because all of them, having suffered at Milan, were held in particular honor in that city and are found celebrated in Ambrose’s writings.]: they had the fragrance of faith, but it lay hidden. Persecution came; they laid down their weapons, bent their necks, and, crushed by the sword, scattered the grace of their martyrdom throughout the boundaries of the whole world, so that it may rightly be said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” [Col. 1746D] (Psalm 18:5).

179. But faith is crushed in one way, pressed down in another, and sown in another. The Lord himself is the mustard seed. He was whole and untouched by injury; but the people who had not crushed him like a mustard seed did not know him. He chose to be crushed, so that we might say: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15). He chose to be pressed down; hence Peter also said: “The crowds press upon you” (Luke 8:45). He chose to be sown, like the seed that a man took and planted in his garden; for Christ was both seized and buried in a garden. In the garden he grew, where he also rose again, and became a tree, as it is written: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons” (Song of Songs 2:3).

180. Therefore you too should sow Christ in your garden. A garden is, of course, a place full of various flowers and fruits, in which the grace of your work may blossom and the manifold fragrance of diverse virtue may breathe forth. Let Christ therefore be there where the fruit is. Sow the Lord Jesus. He is a seed when he is seized; he is a tree when he rises again—a tree overshadowing the world. He is a seed when he is buried in the earth; he is a tree when he is lifted up to heaven.

181. Press down together with Christ, and sow faith. Faith is pressed down when we believe Christ crucified. Paul pressed down faith when he said: “And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come with superiority of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the mystery of God. For I judged that I should know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:1–2). And because he taught how to press down faith, he also taught how to lift it up, saying: “For now we no longer know Christ as crucified” (2 Corinthians 5:16). We sow faith when, from the Gospel and from the apostolic and prophetic readings, we believe in the Lord’s passion. We therefore sow faith when, as though with soil softened and cultivated, we cover it with the Lord’s flesh, so that, as if through the vapor and pressure of the sacred body, faith may disseminate itself. Whoever believes that the Son of God became human believes that he died for us, believes that he rose again for us, and believes that he ascended for us. I therefore sow faith when I insert the account of his burial.

182. Do you wish to know the seed that is Christ, and Christ who has been sown? “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). We were therefore not mistaken, since we said what he himself had already said. He is also a grain of wheat, because he strengthens the human heart; and a mustard seed, because he sets the human heart on fire. Although both descriptions apply to everything, he appears as a grain of wheat when his resurrection is being discussed: “For he is the bread of God who comes down from heaven” (John 6:33), since the Word of God and the example of the resurrection nourish minds, sharpen hope, and strengthen affection. He is a mustard seed because the word concerning the Lord’s passion is more bitter and more penetrating—more bitter for causing tears, more penetrating for stirring the heart. Thus, when we hear and read that the Lord fasted (Matthew 4:2), that the Lord thirsted (John 4:7), that the Lord wept (John 11:35), and that the Lord was beaten, and when we hear him also say during the time of his passion, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41), then, as though rebuked by the sap of a more bitter word, we temper the bodily sweetness of pleasures that are sweeter than is fitting [Note: Some manuscripts read: “with sweeter wine, the sweetness of pleasures,” and so forth.]. Therefore whoever sows the mustard seed sows the kingdom of heaven.

183. Do not despise this mustard seed: “It is indeed the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown, it becomes greater than all the garden plants” (Matthew 13:32). If the mustard seed is Christ, how is Christ either smallest or growing? Yet once again he grows not according to nature [Note: The old edition adds the words “but according to appearance,” and also “our”; the Roman edition adds “assumed.” The manuscripts recognize neither addition.], but according to appearance. Do you wish to know how small he is? “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2). Learn how great he is: “Beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 45:3). For he who had neither appearance nor beauty was made superior to the angels, beyond all the glory of the prophets, whom infirm Israel had, as it were, eaten like vegetables; for it had rejected the bread by which hearts are strengthened and had not received the other.

184. Christ is also a seed because he is the seed of Abraham: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say, “And to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as referring to one: “And to your seed, which is Christ” (Galatians 3:16). Christ is not only a seed, but also the smallest of all seeds, because he did not come in royal power, nor in riches, nor in the wisdom of this world. Suddenly, however, like a tree, he spread out the lofty summit of his power, so that we might say: “Under his shadow I desired and sat” (Song of Songs 2:3). And often, I think, he appeared simultaneously as both tree and seed. He is a seed when it is said: “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter?” (Matthew 13:55). But amid these words he suddenly grew, as the Jews themselves testified, unable, as it were, to grasp the branches of the broad tree, when they said: “Where did this man get this wisdom?” (Matthew 13:56).

185. The seed, then, is his appearance; the tree is his wisdom. In its leafy branches may that night bird rest in its dwelling, that solitary sparrow in its building (Psalm 102:7–8), and that one who was snatched up into paradise and is to be caught up into the air and the clouds, now resting in a secure seat (2 Corinthians 12:4; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). The powers and angels of heaven also rest there, together with all who by spiritual deeds have deserved to fly upward. Holy John rested when he reclined upon Jesus’ breast; indeed, he himself is extended like a branch by the sap of that tree. Peter is a branch; Paul is a branch, forgetting what lies behind and reaching toward what lies ahead.

186. Into whose bosom and into certain recesses of disputation, we who were far away—that is, we who were gathered from the nations—fly, taking up the oars of virtue, while for a long time the storm and whirlwind of spiritual wickedness had driven us through the emptiness of the world [Note: All the printed editions and some manuscripts read “through the sea of the world.” The more numerous manuscripts read “through the emptiness of the world,” which fits better with what follows. Some, however, read “through the empty storm of the world, a whirlwind,” and so forth.]. Thus the shadow of the saints may defend us from the heat of this world, as we now flourish in the security of a firm anchorage; for our soul, previously bent down by grave sins like that woman, has migrated like a sparrow rescued from the snare of the hunters into the branches and mountains of the Lord. Formerly vain through superfluous observances and fluttering about in empty lightness, we are now released through faith in Christ and freed from the bonds of Sabbaths, and we devote ourselves to good works. Even at the banquets themselves we possess freedom and exclude excess, lest, freed from the Law, we become slaves to desires. The Law bound us to itself in order to release us from desires. Grace, which removed the lesser servitude, imposed commands that are far more serious. “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial” (1 Corinthians 10:23); for it is a grave matter to use one’s power in such a way as to fall under power. Cease to be under the Law, so that by virtue you may be above the Law.

**(Verse 21.)** “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.”

187. This comparison casts so much ambiguity upon the question of the interpretations to be sought that it has produced different opinions among many. Appropriately, therefore, we said above that Christ is a grain of wheat, because spiritual leaven was already present for us; and so many think that the leaven is Christ, since it raises up the power that has been received. And because leaven comes from flour, so that it does not excel its own kind in appearance, Christ likewise, arising from the fathers and equal in body, excelled incomparably in divinity. Therefore let holy Church, represented under the figure of this Gospel woman, whose flour we are, hide the Lord Jesus in the inner parts of our mind, until the warmth of heavenly wisdom covers the secret recesses of our soul.

188. And because in Matthew we read that the leaven was hidden in three measures (Matthew 13:33), it seemed fitting that we should believe the Son of God to be hidden in the Law, covered over in the Prophets, and fulfilled in the preaching of the Gospel, so that he may acquire for us perfect faith from all sources. Formed in us, who are his body, through the comparison of the Scriptures, may he be fulfilled as all things and in all things—he who was the Word of God and the mystery hidden from ages and generations; nothing could be said more tellingly in expression of his eternity (Colossians 1:26). For he was certainly hidden from the sacrilegious, manifested among the saints, and predestined before the ages, to be preserved for glory. This, then, is the glory: that we, brothers, may be able to investigate the mystery hidden from the ages in God. And what is in God is surely also from God; for God cannot contain a nature foreign to himself.

189. Nor am I uncertain that some think this was said of the world, until it is leavened in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel, so that every tongue may confess the Lord. Let us therefore examine everything and seek more diligently. No one finds anything unless he has first sought it. Let us build a tower; let us calculate the cost of the Scriptures and compare the expenditure, lest someone also say of one of us: “This man wanted to build, and was unable to finish” (Luke 14:30). Whoever builds a house ought to lay a good foundation. The good foundation is faith, the good foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20); for our faith rises upon the two Testaments. Nor does he do an injustice who says that the measure of faith is equal and perfect in both, since the Lord himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also” (John 5:46), because the Lord also spoke through Moses. The perfect measure is therefore rightly found in both, because he is perfect in both; and the faith of both is one, because the oracle and response possess one power and one meaning.

190. Nevertheless, I am pleased to follow what the Lord himself taught: that the leaven of the Church is spiritual teaching. For when it is written, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matthew 16:6), and when the Apostle says, “Not in the leaven of wickedness and evil” (1 Corinthians 5:8), it is shown that doctrine is leaven. But one kind of leaven is the leaven of weeds, and another the leaven of wheat. Hence we also assent to good authorities when we say that the Church sanctifies the reborn human being—who consists of body, soul, and spirit—with spiritual leaven. The body and soul are sanctified, and spiritual grace itself receives an increase of sanctification [Note: All the printed editions read, “the body and soul through spiritual grace, and it receives,” and so forth. In contrast, all the manuscripts read, “and spiritual grace itself receives,” and so forth. The latter is better; here spiritual grace and the spirit itself mean the same thing, just as “the grace of virtue,” or “the beauty,” often means nothing other than virtue itself. Otherwise the sanctification of the spirit would be omitted, although above and below it is always numbered together with soul and body.], when, through the Church’s kind of leavening activity and through the teaching of the Scriptures—which grows as though through the comparison of heavenly words and through abundance—the practice infused into and mingled with the whole human being has become established, so that these themselves may also become one leaven [Note: Some manuscripts read, “the same through leaven.”]. This happens, of course, when these three agree with one another in an equal balance of desires, and an equal harmony of pleasures breathes through them [Note: The printed editions read “harmony of wills.” This is not wrong, but most manuscripts nearly unanimously read “harmony of pleasures,” that is, when body, soul, and spirit take delight in the same things.].

191. This, then, is the Church’s work—not hasty or accidental, but brought together through prolonged meditation: that these three may be one, entire and free from the law of sin. We have the Apostle as the defender of this view, saying: “May the Lord himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit, soul, and body may be preserved whole and blameless at the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Yet this does not come about through worldly trials unless that leaven to which the kingdom of heaven is compared is hidden by the Gospel woman in the three measures of flour, until all is leavened (Matthew 13:33). For the three measures are, as I said, flesh, soul, and spirit [Note: The words “but the spirit by which we all live while situated in this body” are more probably genuine. They are not found in ten manuscripts; with them removed, the sense appears to suffer no harm.], but the spirit by which we all live while situated in this body. This is more truly so when the wantonness of the flesh does not overflow, the soul is not bent down by bodily errors, and the measure of life is preserved unharmed in the whole human being. But because equality among the measures can scarcely endure without the aid of the Church and its teaching, the woman who bears the figure of the Church mingles spiritual teaching into them for as long as necessary, until that entire inner human being, hidden within the heart, is leavened and rises into the grace of heavenly bread. Leaven is rightly called the teaching of Christ, because Christ is bread, and the Apostle says: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

192. The leaven therefore becomes one when the flesh does not desire against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh; but when we mortify the deeds of the flesh, and the soul, conscious that it has received the breath of life from God’s breath, avoids the contagions of earthly worldly necessity. Hence the Apostle commands us to walk not in the flesh but in the spirit, so that, sanctified through the washing of regeneration, we may strip off the old human being with his desires and put on the new, who is created according to Christ, walking not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit (Colossians 3:9–10). Thus, even at the time of the resurrection, the communion of body, soul, and spirit may remain incorrupt for us, and then we may obtain everything that we ask (Romans 6:4). The Lord also appears to have signified this to many when he says: “If two of you agree on earth about any matter whatever that you ask, it will be done for you by my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:19).

193. Some therefore understand the two as soul and body; others as soul and spirit: if, on earth—that is, in the body—the soul and spirit agree with one another and do not fight each other through differing desires, then everything prayed for may be seen to be capable of being brought into effect. This happens when the two have become one, when, after hostilities have been removed or dissolved, the two are formed into one new human being—that is, soul and spirit: “Let us pray with the spirit, and let us pray also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14:15). Many, however, understand the two as the two peoples, from Israel and from the nations, who are to be gathered together at the time of the resurrection, so that a perfection lasting forever may come to be and what is partial may be destroyed. Others understand them as husband and wife agreeing with one another in the pursuit of love.

194. Therefore, if in this life the three measures remain in the same leaven until they are leavened and become one, so that there is no difference of equality and we do not appear to be composed from the diversity of three elements, then in the future there will be incorrupt communion for those who love Christ; nor will we remain composite. For we who are now composite will be one and will be transformed into one substance. In the resurrection one thing will not be inferior to another, as now the weakness of the flesh is fragile within us, and the bodily condition of our nature is exposed to wounds, subject to injuries, or weighed down by the mass of its own burden, unable to raise itself higher above the earth and lift its foot upward. Rather, we shall be formed according to the grace of simple creation, when what John said has been fulfilled: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be; but we know that when it is revealed, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). Since God’s nature is simple—for God is spirit—we too shall be formed according to the same image (2 Corinthians 3:18), so that as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of this heavenly one (1 Corinthians 15:48–49), which our mind ought to put on.

195. **(Chapter 14 — Verses 2–14.)** And therefore, at the beginning of what follows, the man suffering from dropsy is healed: in him the excessive flow of the flesh weighed down the functions of the soul and extinguished the fervor of the spirit. Then humility is taught, when at that nuptial banquet the desire for the higher place is restrained [Note: Some manuscripts read, “is kept away from the power of the higher place.” A few lines later, where the old edition and manuscripts read “the kindness of persuasion,” the Roman edition, by reversing the words, has “the persuasion of kindness.” Finally, where all the printed editions and a few manuscripts read “at the nearest threshold,” the others more elegantly offer “at the nearest boundary.”]. Yet this is done mercifully, so that the kindness of persuasion may exclude the harshness of coercion, reason may contribute to the effect of persuasion, and correction may amend the affection. To this, as though at the nearest boundary, kindness is joined; and it is distinguished by the definition of the Lord’s teaching in this respect: that it be bestowed upon the poor and weak. For the intention of those who would make hospitality profitable is an intention of greed.

196. **(Verses 18–21.)** Finally, as though for a man who has completed his military service, a rule for despising possessions is prescribed: the man who, intent upon inferior pursuits, has purchased earthly possessions for himself cannot attain the kingdom of heaven, since the Lord says: “Sell all that you have, and follow me” (Matthew 19:21); nor can the man who has bought oxen, when Elisha killed and distributed among the people those he had (1 Kings 19:21); and the man who takes a wife thinks about the things of the world, not the things of God. This is not because marriage is condemned, but because integrity is called to a greater honor; for “the unmarried woman and the widow think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But she who is married thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:34).

197. But, just as above we returned to the widows’ favor, so now let us also return to that of married people. We do not reject the opinion followed by many, namely, that three classes of people are to be considered excluded from participation in that great supper: Gentiles, Jews, and heretics.

198. Therefore the Apostle says that greed must be avoided, lest, hindered in the Gentile manner by wickedness, malice, immorality, and greed, we be unable to reach the kingdom of Christ (Romans 1:29). For every impure or greedy person—which is the service of idols—does not possess an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God (Ephesians 5:5).

199. The Jews, however, impose upon themselves the yokes of the Law through bodily observance, and therefore, according to the Prophet: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Psalm 2:3); for we have received Christ, who hangs upon our necks the gentle yoke of his piety. The five yokes are, moreover, the ten sayings, or the five books of the old Law, concerning which the Samaritan woman in the Gospel appears to say: “For you have had five husbands” (John 4:18).

200. But heresy, like Eve, tests the firmness of faith with feminine feeling, and, slipping through slippery ease, seeks the allurements of false beauty while neglecting the undefiled beauty of truth. They are therefore excused because the kingdom is closed to no one except the one whom his own profession of speech has excluded. The Lord, however, invites everyone mercifully, but either our negligence or our error turns us away.

201. Therefore the man who bought a country estate is also a stranger to the kingdom; for “those buying and selling were overwhelmed by the flood in the time of Noah, as you have read” (Luke 17:27) [Note: Thus read all the manuscripts and the old edition, except that the latter, together with some of the former, has “swallowed up” instead of “overwhelmed.” The Roman edition reads: “Lot, as you have read, perished by fire at that time.” But it is clear that Ambrose cited the passage from memory. Moreover, everything from the words “excuses himself on account of a wife” to the beginning of the following paragraph had, in the Roman edition, contrary to the evidence of all the other editions and manuscripts, been transposed after the words “he sinned with such stubborn wickedness” in paragraph 206.]. So too is the man who chose the yoke of the Law rather than the gift of grace; and the man who excuses himself on account of taking a wife. For it is written: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, and wife, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26). For if, on your account, the Lord renounces his own mother, saying, “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” (Matthew 12:48), why should you wish to put her before your Lord? Yet the Lord does not command us either to ignore nature or to be enslaved to nature. Rather, he commands us to show such indulgence toward nature that we honor its author and do not, through love of our parents, depart from God.

202. **(Verses 21–23.)** Therefore, after turning away from the proud disdain of the rich, he turned to the nations and commands the good and the bad to enter, so that he may increase the good and change the disposition of the bad for the better, so that what was read today might be fulfilled: “Then wolves and lambs shall feed together” (Isaiah 65:25). He invites the poor, the weak, and the blind. By this it is shown to us that no bodily weakness excludes anyone from the kingdom, and that the one who lacks the enticement to sin is less likely to offend; or else that the weakness of sinners is forgiven through the Lord’s mercy, so that one is redeemed from guilt not by works but by faith, so that “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord.”

203. Therefore he sends them to the exits of the roads, for wisdom is proclaimed at the exit. He sends them to the streets, because he sent them to sinners, so that they might come from the broader roads to the narrow one that leads to life. He sends them to the roads and along the hedges, because those are suited to the kingdom of heaven who, occupied by no present desires, hurry toward the future, established upon a path of good will; and because those who recognize the hedge that separates cultivated ground from uncultivated land and restrains the incursions of beasts should know how to distinguish good from evil and set up the protection of faith against the temptations of spiritual wickedness. Finally, to show that his vineyard had been fortified, the Lord said: “I surrounded it with a hedge and dug around it” (Matthew 21:33). The Apostle says that the middle wall of the hedge, which had broken through the continuity of the fortification, has been removed (Ephesians 2:14). Faith and reason are therefore sought, and they are sought in the streets—that is, in the passages of the inner affection—for it is written: “Let your waters be poured out in your streets” (Proverbs 5:16).

204. Yet this is still not complete: it is not enough for someone who has been invited to come unless he has a wedding garment—that is, unless he possesses faith and love [Note: Quite a few manuscripts, and not of the inferior class, read “unless he possesses firm” or, in some, “faithful” love.]. And therefore whoever has not brought peace and love to the altars of Christ will be taken away with hands and feet bound and cast into the outer darkness. “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 22:13). What is this outer darkness? Are there perhaps prisons and dungeons to be entered there as well? Certainly not. Whoever is outside the promises of the heavenly commandments is in the outer darkness, because God’s commandments are light; and whoever is without Christ is in darkness, because Christ is the light in the darkness [Note: Most manuscripts, and the editions of Erasmus and Gill in the margin, read: “Christ is the inner light.”].

205. Therefore there is neither any bodily gnashing of teeth nor any physical, flaming fire [Note: Coquaeus, in book 21 of *The City of God*, chapter 9, writes that although Ambrose appears to interpret these punishments metaphorically, he nevertheless does not deny a true and proper fire that torments the condemned. Huetius, however, in *Origen*, book 2, question 11, citing this passage of our Doctor, says that Ambrose, like Origen, establishes the fire in the flames and torments of conscience. Ambrose’s words are certainly too explicit to admit Coquaeus’s interpretation. Nor was Ambrose alone in embracing Origen’s opinion on this matter. Gregory of Nyssa holds the same view in *On the Soul and the Resurrection*, as does John of Damascus in book 4 of *The Orthodox Faith*, near the end. Jerome testifies that many others also held this opinion in book 3 of his commentary on Ephesians 5:6. Although Jerome sharply rejects that opinion here and elsewhere, in some places he does not appear to reject it—for example, in book 18 of his commentary on Isaiah. Augustine, after speaking hesitantly and anxiously in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 32–33, and in *The City of God*, book 20, chapters 9, 10, 16, and 26, finally says in book 22, chapter 10: “Why should we not say that, although in wondrous ways, incorporeal spirits too can be afflicted by the punishment of bodily fire?” By this he sufficiently shows that he inclines toward the opinion now prevailing in Catholic schools. Ambrose himself is not entirely foreign to that view in various passages of his commentary on Psalm 118, especially where he discusses the fire by which even the just and holy are said to be burned. No one should therefore be surprised if he presents opposing views, since this is a controversy in which both sides rely upon the authority of great and holy men, while neither has been rejected by the Church—as the theologians admit along with Bellarmine, book 2 of *On Purgatory*, chapter 11.]. Nor is the worm physical. These things are mentioned because, just as both fevers and worms arise from excessive undigested matter, so, if someone does not digest his sins by introducing a kind of sober abstinence, but by mingling sins with sins contracts a sort of undigested mass of old and recent offenses, he will be burned by his own fire and consumed by his own worms. Hence Isaiah also says: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled for yourselves” (Isaiah 50:11). The fire is what the sorrow of offenses produces; the worm is that the sins of the irrational soul [Note: The old editions and not a few manuscripts read “the irrational sins of the soul.” Corbey and several others more suitably read “the irrational part of the soul,” that is, the lower part, which Ambrose often calls simply “the soul,” while above he recognizes three elements in the human being: body, soul, and spirit. In this he appears to imitate the Platonists; for Photinus, according to Numenius, says that the human being consists “of three: body, soul, and mind” (συνιστάναι ἐκ τριῶν, σώματος, καὶ ψυχῆς, καὶ νοῦ).] pierces the mind and the consciousness of the guilty, and gnaws away certain inner parts of the conscience. These worms arise from each person, as it were from the body of the sinner. Finally, the Lord declared this through Isaiah, saying: “They shall see the limbs of the men who transgressed against me; their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isaiah 66:24).

206. The gnashing of teeth likewise reveals an indignant disposition: for each person repents too late, groans too late, and becomes angry with himself too late, because he sinned with such stubborn wickedness.

**(Chapter 15 — Verse 4.)** “Which one of you,” he says, “is a man who has a hundred sheep, and if one of them should go astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that went astray?”

207. In the preceding passages you had learned to drive away negligence, avoid arrogance, assume devotion, not be held captive by worldly occupations, and not prefer things that perish to things eternal. But because human frailty cannot keep a firm foothold amid so great a slippery instability of the world, the good physician has also shown you remedies against error, and the merciful judge has not denied the hope of pardon. Therefore holy Luke, not without purpose, set three parables in sequence (verses 8 and following): the sheep that was lost and found, the drachma that was lost and found, and the son who was dead and came back to life, so that, summoned by this threefold remedy, we might heal our wounds; for “a threefold cord will not be broken.”

208. Who are this father, shepherd, and woman? Are they not God the Father, Christ the shepherd, and the woman the Church? Christ carries you in his body, having taken your sins upon himself; the Church seeks you; the Father receives you. As a shepherd he brings you back, as a mother he searches, as a father he clothes. The first is mercy, the second assistance, the third reconciliation. Each corresponds to each: the Redeemer helps, the Church intercedes, the Author reconciles. It is the same mercy of the divine work, but grace varies according to our merits. The sheep, wearied, is recalled by the shepherd; the drachma that was lost is found; the son returns to the Father by his own footsteps, and returns with repentance fully condemning his error. Hence it is well written: “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord” (Psalm 36:7). What are these beasts? The prophet said: “The seed of Israel as the seed of men, and Judah as the seed of animals” (Jeremiah 31:27). Israel, therefore, is saved as a human being, while Judah is gathered as a sheep. I would rather be a son than a sheep: the sheep is sought again by the shepherd, but the son is honored by the Father.

209. Let us therefore rejoice, because that sheep which was lost in Adam is raised up in Christ. Christ’s shoulders are the arms of the cross. There I laid down my sins; upon that noble neck of the gallows I found rest. That sheep is one in genus, not in species: “For we are all one body, but many members” (1 Corinthians 10:17); and therefore it is written: “You are the body of Christ and, individually, members of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27). The Son of Man therefore came to save what was lost (Luke 19:10)—all, that is; “for as all die in Adam, so also shall all be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

210. The shepherd, then, is rich, and we are all his one-hundredth portion. He possesses innumerable flocks of angels, archangels, dominions, powers, thrones, and others, which he left upon the mountains. Since they are rational beings, they rightly rejoice at the redemption of humanity. This too contributes to incentives toward goodness, if each person believes that his conversion will be welcome to the gatherings of angels, whose protection he should either seek or whose offense he should fear. Therefore be a cause of joy to the angels as well; let them rejoice at your return.

211. It is not without significance that the woman rejoices when the drachma is found. This is no ordinary drachma, since it bears the image of a ruler. Therefore it is the king’s image, the wealth of the Church. We are sheep; let us pray that he may deem us worthy to place us beside the waters of refreshment. We are sheep, I say; let us seek pastures. We are drachmas; let us possess our value. We are sons; let us hasten to the Father.

212. Let us not fear that, having received the spiritual patrimony of dignity, we have squandered it in earthly pleasures, since the Father bestowed the treasure he possessed upon his sons [Note: So all the manuscripts and printed editions read, except the Roman edition, which reverses the whole passage as follows: “Nor should we fear that the Father bestowed the treasure upon the Son whom he possessed. For the meaning of faith … nor should you fear that, having received the spiritual patrimony of dignity, he squandered it on earthly pleasures, lest he not receive you.”]. The wealth of faith is never exhausted: even if he has given everything, he possesses everything, because what he has given he does not lose. Nor should you fear that he will not receive you: “For God does not delight in the destruction of the living” (Wisdom 1:13). Even as he runs to meet you, he will fall upon your neck, for “the Lord raises up those who are bowed down” (Psalm 146:8). He will give you the kiss that is the pledge of compassion and love. He will order the robe, the ring, and the sandals to be brought out. You still fear injury, but he restores dignity; you fear punishment, but he offers a kiss; you fear reproach, but he prepares a feast. But now let us examine the parable itself.

**(Verses 11–12.)** “A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to him: Give me the portion of the substance.”

213. You see that the divine inheritance is given to those who ask for it. Do not think it was the father’s fault that he gave it to the younger son: no age is weak for the kingdom of God, nor is faith burdened by years. He himself certainly judged himself fit, since he asked. And would that he had not withdrawn from his father and had not known the impediment of age! But after leaving his ancestral home and departing abroad, [Note: [Col. 1756D] “He began to be in want” is absent from all the manuscripts. But since it appears in all the editions, and without it the sense remains almost suspended, we have therefore thought it should not be removed. Those, however, to whom the manuscripts here seem preferable may mentally supply “he felt the impediment of age,” or something similar; unless, instead of *derelinquens* (“leaving”), one prefers, with certain more recent manuscripts, to read *dereliquit* (“he left”).] he began to be in want. Rightly, therefore, he squandered his inheritance, since he withdrew from the Church. “After leaving,” he says, “his ancestral home,

**(Verse 13.) He departed into a distant country.**

214. For what is more distant than to depart from oneself—not to be separated by regions, but by ways of life; to be divided by pursuits, not by lands; and, as though the flood of worldly luxury lay between, [Note: [Col. 1757D] The Roman edition alone has “to have the separations of holy people.”] to have one’s deeds divided? Indeed, whoever separates himself from Christ is an exile from his homeland and a citizen of the world. But we are not strangers and foreigners; we are citizens with the saints and members of God’s household (Ephesians 2:19). We who were once far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ (ibid., 13).

Let us not begrudge those who return from a distant country, for we too were in a distant country, as Isaiah teaches when he says: [Col. 1757B] “For those who sat in the land of the shadow of death, light has dawned” (Isaiah 9:2). Thus the distant country is the shadow of death. But we, for whom Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face, live in the shadow of Christ. Therefore the Church says: “Under his shadow I desired and sat” (Song of Songs 2:3).

Thus, by living luxuriously, he consumed all the adornments of nature. Therefore you who have received the image of God and possess his likeness, do not consume it through irrational degradation. You are God’s work; do not say to wood, “You are my father” (Jeremiah 2:27), lest you receive the likeness of wood, for it is written: “Let those who make them become like them” (Psalm 113:8).

**(Verse 14.) A famine arose in that country.**

215. It was not a famine of food, but of good works [Col. 1757C] and virtues—fasts more pitiable than hunger. Indeed, whoever withdraws from the word of God hungers: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matthew 4:4). Whoever withdraws from the spring thirsts; whoever withdraws from the treasury is in want; whoever withdraws from wisdom becomes dull; whoever withdraws from virtue falls apart.

Therefore he rightly began to be in want, because he abandoned the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God and the height of heavenly riches. He began to be in want and to suffer hunger because nothing is sufficient for extravagant pleasure. Whoever does not know how to be filled with lasting nourishment suffers perpetual hunger for what is his own.

**(Verse 15.) So he went and attached himself to one of the citizens.**

216. Whoever clings to someone is in a snare. This citizen appears to be the prince of this world. In the end, the one who excuses himself from the kingdom is sent to his estate, which he has purchased. And he feeds pigs—those, certainly, into which the devil sought to enter, those whom he casts headlong into the sea of this world, living amid filth and stench.

**(Verse 16.) And he desired, he says, to fill his stomach with the pods.**

217. For the luxurious have no other concern than to fill their stomach, since “their god is their belly” (Philippians 3:19). What food, then, is more suited to such people than that which, like a pod, is empty within and soft outside—food by which the body is not restored but merely filled, so that it becomes more a burden than a benefit?

218. [Note: [Col. 1757D] Most manuscripts read: “There are those who take the pods to signify worldly words, the pigs, etc.” Others, and all the editions, read: “There are those who take the pigs, etc.” The latter is better; for the words omitted here plainly suggest interpolation, and could easily have been transferred from the margin into the text by an inexperienced copyist.] There are those who understand the pigs as herds of demons, and the pods as the meager virtue and boastful speech of empty people—things unable to benefit anyone, displaying more pomp than usefulness through a certain empty seduction of philosophy and a kind of sonorous applause of eloquence. But such pleasures cannot last. Therefore,

219. “No one gave him anything”; for he was in the country of the one who possesses no one, because he does not possess those who exist. “All the nations are regarded as nothing” (Isaiah 40:15). God alone gives life to the dead and “calls into existence the things that do not exist as though they did” (Romans 4:17).

**(Verse 17.) But coming to himself, he said: How many hired servants of my father have bread in abundance!**

220. He rightly comes to himself, having departed from himself. For whoever returns to the Lord restores himself to himself; whoever withdraws from Christ renounces himself. Who are the hired servants except those who serve for wages—those from Israel who do not pursue what is good out of zeal for integrity or for the sake of virtue, but are moved by a desire for profit?

But the son who has the pledge of the Holy Spirit in his heart does not seek the small worldly earnings for which he might serve. Hired servants are also heirs, those who are hired to work in the vineyard. Peter, John, and James were good hired servants, to whom it is said: “Come, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19). These have an abundance not of pods but of bread. In the end, they collected twelve baskets of fragments (Matthew 14:20).

O Lord Jesus, if only you would take away the pods from us and give us bread! For you are the steward in the Father’s house. If only you would also deign to hire us as laborers, even though we come late! For you hire even at the eleventh hour (Matthew 20:9) and deign to pay an equal wage—an equal wage of life, not of glory. For the crown of righteousness is not laid up for everyone, but for the one who can say: “I have fought the good fight” (2 Timothy 4:7).

221. I have thought this should not be passed over because I know that some people say they should reserve the grace of the washing, or repentance, for themselves until death. First, how do you know whether your soul will not be demanded from you on the coming night? Then why do you think everything can be deferred for you while you remain idle? Grant that there is one grace and one wage; nevertheless, the prize of victory is different—the prize toward which Paul stretched himself, who, after receiving the wage of grace, still pursued the prize so that he might attain it (Philippians 3:14). He knew that, although the wage of grace might be equal, the palm of victory nevertheless belonged to few.

[Note: [Col. 1758D] This was a frequent and familiar complaint among the holy Fathers. Would that in our own time it did not find a much more justified place in the matter of repentance!]

222. Since we have come into the Lord’s vineyard, let us not depart empty-handed; for it is worthwhile to gather its fruits and to see its laborers. What does it mean that workers are hired at different hours on one day (Matthew 20:1 and following), except that a thousand years are in the Lord’s sight like yesterday, which has passed, and like a watch in the night (Psalm 89:4)? What is the night except that which preceded the approach of day? And rightly is it a watch in the night, because “a thousand years are like one day” (2 Peter 3:8).

He knew the power of this day who said: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8). He also knew that the day is manifold who wrote: [Note: [Col. 1759D] The Roman edition, following the Septuagint, has: “This is the book of the generation of heaven,” and so forth.] “This is the day of the generation of heaven and earth, when they were made; on the day when God made heaven and earth and every green plant of the field” (Genesis 2:4). For after describing seven days above, he later gathered together in one day everything that had been made, showing the whole age of the world in the sight of the Lord as one day, since the form of this world proceeded from what was unformed and dark through the brightness of the divine work.

Therefore, if the day is the whole duration of the world, it certainly has its hours throughout the ages; or the ages themselves are the hours. There are twelve hours of the day. Thus, symbolically, Christ is the day, and his apostles are twelve, shining with heavenly light through the distinct movements of grace within them.

223. The master of the household therefore came and hired workers at the first hour—perhaps those who from the beginning of the world until the Flood were worthy to be righteous. Of them he says: “I spoke to you before dawn, and I sent my servants the prophets to you before dawn” (Jeremiah 7:25).

The third hour begins after the Flood, comprising the times of Noah and the others who, like good workers, are sent into the vineyard. Hence Noah became drunk as though at lunchtime. The sixth hour and those that follow distinguish the merits of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the patriarchs. At the ninth hour, when the age of the world was already declining and the light of virtue was, as it were, growing pale, the Law and the Prophets marked the discolored morals of humanity. The eleventh hour, and what remained of the day, brought forth the sacred Advent. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Walk while you have the light” (John 12:35).

224. But let us now return to the Father. Although I do not fear that, by considering the example of this repentant man, we may seem to have been away for a long time—for we were never away, since we were laboring in the vineyard, and if he too had remained there, he would not have withdrawn from the Father—we must nevertheless take care not to delay his reconciliation, since the Father did not delay it. He is easily reconciled when earnestly entreated. Therefore let us learn with what sort of entreaty the Father is to be approached.

“Father,” he says. How merciful, how loving is he, who, although offended, does not disdain to hear the name of father!

[Col. 1760A] **(Verse 18.) “Father,” he says, “I have sinned against heaven and before you.”**

225. This is the first confession before the author of nature, the overseer of mercy, and the judge of guilt. Although God knows everything, he nevertheless awaits the voice of your confession. For confession is made with the mouth for salvation (Romans 10:10), because whoever burdens himself lightens the weight of his error; and whoever anticipates his accuser by confessing removes the hostility of accusation: “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Proverbs 18:17).

It is useless to wish to conceal from the one whom nothing escapes; and you reveal without danger what you know is already known. Confess, rather, so that Christ may intervene for you—he whom we have as an advocate with the Father; let the Church plead for you, and let the people weep with you.

Do not fear that you will not obtain forgiveness. The advocate guarantees pardon; the patron promises grace; the defender promises you reconciliation through the Father’s mercy. [Note: [Col. 1760D] Many manuscripts, and not ones of the lowest authority, read: “The father’s loving-kindness promises you reconciliation; believe the advocate, because…”] Believe, because it is truth; accept, because it is power. He has reason to intervene for you, lest he have died for you in vain. The Father has reason to forgive, because what the Son wills, the Father also wills.

226. **(Verse 18.) “I have sinned against heaven and before you.”** The element “heaven” is not literally meant; rather, the heavenly gifts of the Spirit are signified as diminished by the sin of the soul. Or it may mean that one ought not to have strayed from the bosom of that mother, Jerusalem, which is in heaven.

**(Verse 19.) “I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”**

227. The one who has been cast down ought not to exalt himself, so that he may be raised up deservedly through his humility.

[Col. 1760C] **(Ibid.) “Make me like one of your hired servants.”**

228. He knows that there is a distinction among sons, friends, hired servants, and slaves: a son comes through the washing, a friend through virtue, a hired servant through labor, and a slave through fear. Yet even from slaves and hired servants friends are made, according to what is written: “You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants” (John 15:14–15).

229. He said these things within himself. But it is not enough to speak unless you come to the Father. Where should you seek him, where find him? Rise first—that is, you who were previously sitting asleep. Therefore the Apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead” (Ephesians 5:14).

Iniquity sits upon a leaden talent. Moses is told: “But you, stand here” (Deuteronomy 5:31). Christ chose those who stand. Rise, therefore, and run to the Church; here is the Father, here is the Son, here is the Holy Spirit.

230. **(Verses 20–21.)** He comes to meet you who hears you speaking within the secrets of your mind. While you are still far away, he sees you and runs to you. He sees into your heart; he runs lest anyone hinder you; he also embraces you. [Note: [Col. 1760D] Eight manuscripts of excellent quality read this way. Others, as well as the editions, have: “In his coming is presence” (Erasmus and Gill in the margin: “foreknowledge”), “in his embrace is mercy.” And, as though moved by a certain affection of fatherly love, he falls upon his neck.] In his coming there is foreknowledge; in his embrace, mercy; and in it there is, as it were, an affection of fatherly love.

He falls upon your neck to raise up the one lying prostrate, and to turn back toward heaven the one weighed down by sins and bent toward earthly things, so that he may seek his Creator there. Christ falls upon your neck to remove the yoke of slavery from your neck and to hang his easy yoke upon it.

Does it not seem to you that he fell upon John’s neck when John was in Jesus’ bosom, reclining with his neck bent back? Therefore he saw the Word who was with God, because he was raised toward heavenly things. He falls upon the neck when he says: “Come to me, all you who labor … and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:28–29). He falls in this way if you turn back.

231. **(Verse 22.)** And he orders the robe, the ring, and the sandals to be brought forth. The robe is the clothing of wisdom, with which the apostles cover the nakedness of the body, since each person wraps himself in it. Therefore they receive the robe so that they may clothe the weakness of the body with the power of spiritual wisdom.

For it is said of Wisdom: “He will wash his robe in wine” (Genesis 49:11). Thus the robe is spiritual clothing and a nuptial garment. What else is the ring except the seal of sincere faith and the expression of truth?

The sandal, however, is the preaching of the Gospel; and therefore he received the first wisdom. [Note: [Col. 1761D] All the editions, together with some manuscripts, read: “For there is also another mystery, unknown except to the one who has received the seal of the sayings … and a certain monument,” and so forth. Other manuscripts, among them the most ancient, more appropriately preserve the reading printed in the text. Although this reading does not convey a sufficiently clear sense, we see no reason for astonishment here; for there is no doubt that the subject is the sacrament of the Eucharist, concerning which no one is unaware that the Fathers often spoke deliberately in obscure and perplexing terms. Consider also the following section.] There is also another mystery known only to the one who has received the seal of his words and deeds and a certain defense of good intention and progress, so that he may not strike his foot against a stone and, being tripped up by the devil, abandon the ministry of the Lord’s preaching.

This is [Note: [Col. 1762D] Several of the better manuscripts and the editions, with Erasmus and Gill in the margin, have this reading. Other manuscripts and all the editions in the body of the text read: “the preaching of the Gospel.”] the preparation of the Gospel, directing those who have been prepared toward the heavenly course, so that we may walk not in the flesh but in the Spirit.

232. **(Verse 23.)** The fattened calf is also killed, so that the one restored through the grace of the sacrament to participation in the mysteries may feast on the Lord’s flesh, rich in spiritual power. No one ought to participate in the heavenly sacraments unless he fears God—which is the beginning of wisdom—unless he has either guarded or received the spiritual seal, and unless he has proclaimed the Lord.

Whoever has the ring also has the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because God has sealed us, whose image is Christ; and he has given us the Spirit as a pledge in our hearts. Thus we know that the ring given on the hand is a seal by which the inner parts of the heart and the ministries of our deeds are marked.

Therefore we have been sealed, as we also read: “Having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13). It is appropriate that the flesh of the calf is mentioned, because it is a priestly victim offered for sins.

233. **(Verse 23.)** [Note: [Col. 1762D] A few manuscripts and Gill in the margin read: “The son introduces the father as feasting.” The same wording appears in the body of the text in the remaining manuscripts and all the editions: “The son introduces the father as one who is feasting,” except that the Roman edition removed the word “son.”] The son introduces the father as feasting, to show that our salvation is the Father’s food, and that the Father’s joy is the redemption of our sins.

If you refer this to the Father, since the Son is the sacrifice for sins, the Father rejoices at the sinner’s return. Above, the Son rejoices when the sheep has been found, so that you may know that the Father and the Son have one joy and one operation in the foundation of the Church.

The father rejoices:

**(Verse 24.) Because this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.**

234. The one who once existed is the one who is lost; for the one who never existed cannot be lost. Thus the nations “do not exist,” whereas the Christian does, according to what was said above: “God chose the things that are not, to destroy the things that are” (1 Corinthians 1:28).

Yet this passage can also be understood as referring, in one person, to the human race. Adam existed, and in him we all existed. Adam was lost, and in him we all were lost (cf. Augustine, *Against Julian*, book 1, chapter 3). Thus humanity is restored in that man who was lost; and he who was made according to the likeness and image of God is repaired through divine patience and greatness of soul.

What, then, does “God chose the things that are not, to destroy the things that are” mean? It means that he chose the people of the Gentiles, who did not exist, in order to destroy the people of the Jews.

235. This can also seem to have been said of the person who performs repentance, because only one who once lived can die. Therefore the Gentiles do not die, but are dead; for whoever has not believed in Christ is always dead. When the Gentiles believe, they are brought to life by grace; whoever has fallen rises again through repentance.

236. The passage follows so that we ought to favor those whose sins are remitted after repentance, lest, while we begrudge another’s forgiveness, we ourselves fail to deserve it from the Lord. Who are you to contradict the Lord and prevent him from releasing someone’s guilt if he wishes, when you forgive whomever you wish? He desires to be asked; he desires to be entreated. If all righteousness belonged to human beings, where would God’s grace be? Who are you to begrudge God?

237. **(Verses 25, 27.)** For this reason the brother is marked out here, to such an extent that he is said to come from the estate—that is, occupied with earthly works and ignorant of the things of God’s Spirit. In the end, he never complains that a young goat has been killed for him; for the Lamb was sacrificed not because of envy, but for the forgiveness of the world.

The envious person seeks a young goat; the innocent desires a lamb to be sacrificed for him. He is also called “the older” because someone can quickly grow old through envy. He stands outside because malevolence excludes him through the discoloration of his embittered spirit.

Therefore he cannot hear the chorus and symphony—that is, not the theatrical incitement to luxury, nor the harmony of courtly sounds, [Note: [Col. 1763D] The Roman edition reads: “that is, not the harmony of the people singing together, which produces the sweet delight of joy over the sinner who has been saved, but that theatrical incitement to luxury, or the harmony of courtly sounds.” This is not sufficiently appropriate. The sense of this passage is the same as if one read: “He cannot hear the chorus and symphony,” where chorus and symphony do not signify fuel and incitements to luxury, but the concord of the people, and so forth. Moreover, by “the sounds of courtly instruments” (*aulicorum sonorum*) he does not seem to mean sounds made in courts, that is, in royal palaces, but rather sounds “from the pipes” (*ἀπὸ τῶν αὐλῶν*), that is, from flutes or pipes.] but the harmony of the people singing together, which resounds with the sweet delight of joy over the sinner who has been saved.

238. Set before me one of those who consider themselves righteous, who do not see the beam in their own eye but cannot tolerate the speck of another’s fault. How indignant he becomes when forgiveness is granted to someone confessing his sin and long lamenting for pardon! How his ears cannot endure the spiritual symphony of the people!

This is the symphony: when different actions and virtues sing together in the Church [Note: [Col. 1763D] Seven manuscripts of more approved quality read this way. Others, as well as the editions, have: “of different ages and virtues.” Neither reading is bad. It should be observed in passing that Ambrose says several things here that seem to criticize the cruelty of the Novatians toward sinners who return to repentance.] like the undivided harmony of various strings, a psalm is sung responsively, and “amen” is said.

This is the symphony Paul also knew; therefore he says: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14:13). We have thought these points should be treated concerning the present parable.

239. Nor do we object if someone wishes to refer these two brothers to two peoples, so that the younger represents the people from the Gentiles, like Israel, while the older brother begrudged the benefit of the Father’s blessing. This is what the Jews did when they complained that Christ feasted with the Gentiles. Therefore they sought a young goat, a sacrifice of evil odor.

The Jew seeks a young goat; the Christian, a lamb. Therefore Barabbas is released for them, while the Lamb is sacrificed for us. Hence among them there is the stench of crimes, but among us the remission of sins, sweet in hope and pleasant in its fruit. Whoever seeks the young goat awaits Antichrist; Christ is the sacrifice of good odor (Ephesians 5:2).

240. [Note: [Col. 1764D] Several manuscripts, together with the editions, Gill in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text, read: “What matter.” The remaining manuscripts and editions read: “To seek,” which can be explained if “Christ” is mentally supplied, since that word appears immediately before. Nevertheless, we think “To complain” is more correctly written, so that it may signify that the older son, when he mentions that no young goat was killed, is symbolically lamenting that the rite of the ancient sacrifice has perished, and so forth.] He also seems to complain about the young goat, because the Jews [Col. 1763C] lost the rite of the ancient sacrifice; or because no blood benefited them, as Christ’s blood benefits the Church. The blood of the prophets could not redeem them.

He is shameless and like that Pharisee who arrogantly justified himself in prayer, thinking that he had never transgressed God’s commandment because he observed the Law in its letter. He is impious, accusing his brother because he had squandered his father’s property with prostitutes, when he ought to have noticed that it was said to him: “Prostitutes and tax collectors go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 21:31).

241. **(Verse 28.)** He stands outside, but he is not excluded; he does not enter because he is ignorant of God’s will concerning the calling of the Gentiles, having now become a slave instead of a son. For “a slave does not know what his master is doing” (John 15:15).

When he learned of it, he became envious and was tormented by the Church’s blessings, and he stood outside. Outside, Israel hears the chorus and symphony, but is angry because here the grace of the people sings together and the united rejoicing of the people resounds.

But the good father also wanted to save him, saying:

**(Verse 31.) My son, you are always with me;**

242. Either as a Jew under the Law, or as a righteous person in communion—and you are so, if you cease to envy.

**(Ibid.) And everything that is mine is yours;**

243. Either, as a Jew, you possess the sacraments of the Old Testament, or, as one baptized, you possess those of the New Testament as well.

**CHAPTER 16**

**(Verse 13.) No servant can serve two masters.**

244. Because there are not two masters, but one. For although there are people who serve Mammon, Mammon itself does not know any rights of mastery; rather, they impose the yoke of slavery upon themselves.
