For it is not [Note: [Col. 1764D] Certain Paris editions read: “not unjust power, but just servitude.” This is out of order.] just authority, but unjust servitude. Therefore he says:

**(Verse 9.) Make friends for yourselves from the unrighteous Mammon.**

245. By giving to the poor, so that we may acquire for ourselves the favor of the angels and of the other saints. Nor is the steward criticized; in him we learn that we are not owners ourselves, but rather stewards of other people’s possessions. Therefore, although he sinned, because he secured future assistance for himself through his master’s indulgence, he is praised.

He aptly called Mammon unrighteous, because through the various enticements of riches [Note: [Col. 1764D] The Roman edition reads: “our disposition toward greed tempts us.”] greed was tempting our affections, so that we might wish to serve riches. Hence he says:

**(Verse 12.) If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?**

246. Riches are alien to us because they are contrary to nature: they are not born with us, nor do they depart with us. But Christ is ours, [Note: [Col. 1764D] Many manuscripts, and ones of no inferior quality, read: “because he is the way.”] because he is life. In the end: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). Therefore no one will give you what is yours, because you did not believe what was yours and did not receive what was yours.

247. The Jews therefore appear to be accused both of fraud and of greed. Since they were not faithful with their possessions, although they knew those possessions were not their own—for the fruits of the earth were given by the Lord God for the common use of all—they ought certainly to have shared them with the poor. Nor did they deserve to receive Christ, whom Zacchaeus offered half of his possessions in order to acquire (Luke 19:8).

248. Therefore let us not serve what is alien, since we ought to acknowledge no master except Christ: “There is one God, the Father, from whom all things come and we exist in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things come” (1 Corinthians 8:6).

What, then? Is the Father not Lord, or is the Son not God? The Father too is Lord, because “by the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm 32:6); and the Son is God, who is “God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5).

How, then, can no one serve two masters? There is one Lord because there is one God. Therefore: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Matthew 4:10). Hence it is clear that the Father and the Son have one dominion.

It is one, however, if it is not divided, but is wholly in the Father and wholly in the Son. Therefore, [Note: [Col. 1765A] Several manuscripts written by approved hands read: “because we assert that the divinity is one.”] because we confess the Trinity as possessing one divinity and one dominion, we confess one God and one Lord.

But those who speak of one power of the Father, another of the Son, and another of the Holy Spirit introduce into the Church, through the error of pagan misunderstanding, many gods and many lords.

**BOOK EIGHT**

[Col. 1765]

[Col. 1765B] **(Verse 16.) The Law and the Prophets lasted until John.**

1. This does not mean that the Law failed, but that the preaching of the Gospel begins. For lesser things seem to be completed when greater things succeed them. Therefore let us do violence to the kingdom of heaven; for everyone who does violence hastens with vigorous zeal and does not grow sluggish through a listless disposition. There is therefore a religious violence of faith, and a criminal sluggishness.

The Law established many things according to nature [Note: [Col. 1765D] Many and excellent manuscripts read: “sons divide the father’s house and substance.” Better, however, other manuscripts with all editions: “fathers divide to sons”; for the LXX consistently has μερίζουσι πατέρες παισί (“fathers divide to children”). The Roman edition’s reading in this very passage, “is prepared,” followed the authority of the LXX, where, as also in the old Ambrosian edition, ἁρμόζεται (“is fitted/prepared”) consistently appears. Nevertheless, the agreement of the ancient editions and all manuscripts here and below, which give “will be prepared,” leads us to believe that Ambrose read ἁρμόσεται (“will be fitted/prepared”). For future middles are not unusually taken in a passive sense. Observe also how our Doctor disapproved a marriage contracted between persons of different worship; on this see the note on Psalm 118, sermon 20, no. 48, and the letter to Vigil.] *Statuit* (“established”) is absent from all the editions and from many manuscripts, but it is found in seven.] in order to call us to the pursuit of righteousness by showing indulgence toward natural desires. Christ cuts into nature, because he also cuts away natural pleasures. Therefore let us do violence to nature, so that it may not sink toward earthly things but raise itself toward heavenly things.

**(Verse 18.) Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery; and whoever marries a woman divorced by her husband commits adultery.**

2. I think I should speak first about the law of marriage, and afterward discuss the prohibition of divorce. Some people think that every marriage is from God, especially because it is written: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Mark 19:6). Therefore, if every marriage is from God, no marriage may be dissolved.

And how did the Apostle say: “If the unbelieving person departs, let that person depart” (1 Corinthians 7:15)? In this, he both remarkably refused to allow the cause of divorce to remain among Christians and showed that not every marriage is from God. For Christians are not joined to pagans according to God’s judgment, since the Law forbids it.

3. But there is the statement of Solomon: “Fathers divide the house and substance among their sons; but a wife is prepared by God for a man” (Proverbs 19:14). Whoever reads this in Greek does not think it contradictory. The Greek rightly says **ἁρμόσεται** (*harmosetai*). For *harmonia* means the joining together of all things in a fitting and appropriate connection.

There is harmony when the pipes of an organ, joined together in order, preserve the proper beauty of the song, and the fitting order of the strings maintains concord. Thus marriage does not possess its harmony when a Gentile woman is unlawfully joined to a Christian man.

Therefore, where there is marriage, there is harmony; where there is harmony, God joins. Where there is no harmony, there is struggle and disagreement, which is not from God, because “God is love” (1 John 4:8).

4. Therefore do not divorce your wife, lest you deny that God is the author of your union. Indeed, if you must tolerate and correct the character of strangers, you must do so all the more with your wife.

Hear what the Lord said: “Whoever divorces a woman makes her commit adultery” (Matthew 5:32). For since she is not permitted to change her marriage while her husband is alive, the desire to sin may creep upon her. Therefore whoever is the cause of the error is also guilty of the fault.

Where will she go when she is dismissed with little children? Where will the aged woman, whose steps are unsteady, be thrust? You are harsh if you exclude the mother but retain the children, adding an injury to affection and also an affront to parental devotion. You are harsh if, because of the mother, you drive away the children as well, when the children ought rather to redeem the mother’s fault from the father.

How dangerous it is if you expose the fragile age of a young girl to error! How impious if you abandon the old age of one whose youth you have stripped away!

[Note: [Col. 1766D] All the editions, together with three manuscripts, read: “the veteran is dismissed without honor for his years of service.” Other manuscripts read: “with dishonored years of service.” This is excellent if by *stipendiis* (“years of service”) you understand years spent in military service and mentally supply “the soldier.” A little later, where all manuscripts and editions have “as though lawfully, without crime,” three manuscripts of Gratian, as their correctors testify, read: “whom you know to live without crime.” As for the statement that human law does not prohibit divorce, it is plausible that the holy Doctor is referring to the law enacted by Constantine the Great, contained in Book 3, Title 16 of the *Theodosian Code*, concerning divorces. Although this law reduced the grounds for divorce, previously numerous and sometimes very trivial, to fewer grounds, it by no means abolished its use. But Ambrose indicates clearly that this was a toleration of a lesser evil in order to avoid a more serious one.]

Therefore, should an emperor dismiss a veteran after years of service, inglorious and without honor, and drive him from possession of his empire? Should a farmer drive from his field the rustic exhausted by his labor? Or is something permissible toward an equal that is a crime toward subordinates? (33rd Question, 2nd canon, “Or is something…”)

[Col. 1767A] 5. You dismiss your wife as though lawfully and without crime, and you think this is permitted because human law does not forbid it; but divine law forbids it. You who obey human beings, fear God. Hear the law of the Lord, which even those who enact laws obey: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6).

6. But not only is a heavenly command dissolved here; a work of God is also destroyed. Do you allow your children, while you are alive, to be under a stepfather, or, while their mother remains unharmed, to live under a stepmother?

Suppose the woman does not remarry after being repudiated. Yet she ought to have displeased you for this very reason: she preserves faith with you, an adulterer. Suppose she does remarry. That marriage is compelled by your crime, and what you think is marriage is adultery.

For what difference is there [Note: [Col. 1767D] Erasmus and Gill in the body of the text read: “whether you admit an open adulterer”; in the margin, together with two manuscripts and the Roman edition, they read: “whether you admit adultery.” The remaining manuscripts read as we have in the text. In two, however, a scribal slip has produced: “whether you dismiss an adulterous woman”; Amerbach likewise has “whether you dismiss an adulterous woman,” through a typographical error. The husband who dismisses a wife who marries another seems to be called an adulterer because his wife’s adultery returns upon him, as was explained immediately beforehand.] whether you admit an adulterer openly confessing his crime, or under the appearance of a husband? [Col. 1767B] Except that it is more serious to make yourself the cause of a crime than to commit theft?

7. But perhaps someone says: “How did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and a wife dismissed” (Deut. XXIV, 1)? Whoever says this is a Jew; whoever says this is not a Christian. And therefore, since he raises the objection that was raised against the Lord, let the Lord answer him: “Because of the hardness of your hearts,” he says, “Moses permitted you to give a bill of divorce and to dismiss your wives; but from the beginning it was not so” (Matt. XIX, 8). “Moses permitted it,” he says; “God did not command it. But from the beginning there is God’s law.” What is God’s law? “A man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24). Therefore, whoever dismisses his wife tears his own flesh and divides his own body.

[Col. 1767C] 1472

8. This passage shows that what was written on account of human frailty was not written by God. Hence the Apostle says: “I charge—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband” (I Cor. VII, 10). And further on: “To the rest,” he says, “I say, not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife and she leaves him” (Ibid., 12). Therefore, where there is an unequal marriage, God’s law is not present. And he added: “But if the unbelieving person departs, let him depart” (Ibid., 15). The same Apostle thus denied that it belongs to the divine law for a marriage of whatever kind to be dissolved; he himself neither commanded it nor gave the deserter authority, but removed blame from the abandoned spouse. These points are to be understood morally.

9. (Verse 17.) Yet because above he had proposed to preach the kingdom of God, and after saying that not even one stroke of the Law could pass away, he added: “Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.” The Apostle rightly admonishes us, saying that “this is a great mystery concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 32). You therefore find here a marriage that no one can doubt was joined by God, since he himself says: “No one comes to me unless my Father, who sent me, draws him” (John VI, 44); for he alone could join this marriage. And therefore Solomon said mystically: “A wife is prepared for a man by God” (Prov. XIX, 14). Christ is the husband; the Church is the wife—wife through love, virgin through integrity. Therefore, let neither persecution separate the one whom God has drawn to the Son, nor lust turn him away, nor Philosophy plunder him, nor Manichaeus defile him, nor the Arian turn him aside, nor the Sabellian infect him. God has joined them; let the Jew not separate them. All who desire to adulterate the truth of faith and wisdom are adulterers.

10. “What is this bill of divorce of your mother,” he says, “with which I dismissed her?” (Isa. L, 1). You have heard of divorce; believe in the marriage. You have heard what the husband himself says to the Jewish people: “Behold, because of your iniquities you were sold, and because of your sins I dismissed your mother” (Ibid.). Therefore remain in your father’s house; remain with your bridegroom; strive to please your husband. Let the mind that has believed in God be a strong woman,

[Col. 1768B] like that ecclesial soul—or the Church—of whom Solomon says: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Prov. XXXI, 10).

[Note: Or “the ecclesial soul”; the final word had been omitted in the Roman edition.]

She is more precious than precious stones: “Her husband trusts in her” (Ibid., 11). Let us see what this woman does for her husband, what her work and service are, and why Christ trusts in her.

11. A good wife clothes her husband. May our faith clothe Jesus with its own body; may it clothe his flesh with the glory of its divinity, just as that woman made two garments for her husband (Ibid., 22 and following), so that she may honor him both in the present age and in the age to come. This is no ordinary woman, whose loom is such as this; her husband will find her not picking soft threads of wool, but handling the tasks of precious virtue. May she raise her hands during the nights, set her work by the balance, examine the weight of her conduct, and know how to preserve the measure of her deeds, weaving in the underthread of glorious labor; anxious for her husband’s return, troubled and sighing, and already longing to be with her husband, saying: “My husband delays in coming; I myself will hurry to him. I will meet him face to face when he begins to come in his glory.”

12. Come, Lord Jesus, that you may find your bride undefiled, unadulterated, one who has not violated your house and has not neglected your commandments. Let her say to you: “I found him whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs III, 4). Let her lead you into the house of wine—for “wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII, 15); let her be intoxicated in the Spirit, recognize the mystery, and speak the oracle.

[Col. 1768D] (Verse 19.) “There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple.”

13. It seems more a narrative than a parable, since even a name is given. The Lord does not idly represent this rich man, indulging in worldly pleasures and established in the misery of perpetual hunger among the dead. It is not without reason that he seems to have had five brothers—that is, the five bodily senses—joined to him by a kind of natural kinship; they burned with immoderate and innumerable desires. Lazarus, however, he placed in Abraham’s bosom, as though in a certain lap of rest and retreat of holiness, lest, enticed by the pleasure of present things, we remain in vices, or, overcome by weariness, flee the hardships of our labors.

Thus Lazarus may be poor in the world but rich in God; or he may be some apostolic man, poor in speech but wealthy in faith—for not all poverty is holy, nor are riches criminal: just as luxury disgraces riches, so holiness commends poverty. Or, then, he may be an apostolic man who holds the true faith and does not seek the tinsel of words, the counterfeit of arguments, or the ambitious veils of sentences. He receives a reward that bears interest, attacking the heretics Manichaeus, Marcion, Sabellius, Arius, and Photinus

[Col. 1769B]—for these are nothing other than brothers of the Jews, bound to them by kinship in unbelief—and also restraining the desires of the flesh, which, as I have said, are inflamed in them through the five senses. He receives, I say, a reward bearing interest: compensation for overflowing resources and the interest of perpetuity.

14. Nor do we think it irrelevant to understand this as also referring to faith, which Lazarus gathered, cast down from the rich man’s table. The fastidious rich man would naturally recoil from his sores in the literal sense, nor would he endure, amid precious foods and perfumed companions, the stench of sores for the dogs to lick—he for whom the scent of the air itself would be offensive, and nature itself would constitute an object of disgust. Yet the arrogance and swelling pride of the rich are expressed through fitting indications: they are so forgetful of the human condition that, as though placed above nature, they derive incentives for their pleasures from the misery of the poor; they laugh at the needy, mock the destitute, and take away from those whom they ought to pity.

[Note: The Roman edition reads “for whom the sharp odor…”; the other editions and manuscripts more correctly read “for whom the odor of the air…” For the point is to censure the proud fastidiousness of the rich man, who would corrupt the natural sweetness of the air with artificial scents.]

15. Whoever wishes may gather both things, like Lazarus. I consider him similar to the man who, repeatedly beaten by the Jews (II Cor. XI, 25), offered the sores of his body to be licked, as it were, by certain dogs, for the endurance of believers and the calling of the Gentiles, because it is written: “They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs” (Ps. LVIII, 15). That Canaanite woman recognized this mystery, to whom it is said: “No one takes the children’s bread and throws it to dogs” (Matt. XV, 26). She recognized that this bread was not the bread that is seen, but the one that is understood; and therefore she answered: “Certainly, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters” (Ibid., 27). These crumbs are from that bread. And because bread is the Word, and faith is faith in the Word, the crumbs are, as it were, certain doctrines of faith. Therefore the Lord answered, showing that she had spoken faithfully: “O woman, great is your faith!” (Ibid., 28).

[Col. 1770A] 16. O blessed sores, which exclude everlasting pain! O abundant crumbs, which drive away eternal hunger, which fill the poor person who gathers them with everlasting nourishment! The ruler of the synagogue was casting you away from his table when he rejected the inner mysteries of the prophetic Scriptures and the Law (Luke XIII, 14); for the crumbs are the sayings of the Scriptures, concerning which it is said: “You cast my words behind you” (Ps. XLIX, 17). The scribe cast you away, but Paul gathered you with the greatest diligence, reading the people in his own sufferings. They licked the sores of the man who, after shaking off the serpent, was seen to be unharmed by its bite and believed (Acts XXVIII, 6). The jailer licked them, the one who washed Paul’s wounds and believed (Acts XVI, 33). Blessed are the dogs upon whom the moisture of such sores drips, so that it may fill their hearts and fatten their throats—those who learn to guard the house, protect the flock, and beware of wolves.

17. Now place before your eyes the Arians, intent upon worldly ambitions, who seek the fellowship of royal power in order to attack the truth of the Church with military weapons. Do they not seem to you to be lying in a certain purple and fine linen, and upon constructed couches, defending what is false in place of what is true? Do they not seem rich in words when they proclaim that at the Lord’s bodily presence the earth trembled, the heavens were covered with darkness, and the seas were roused or calmed by a word—and yet deny the Son of God?

Set before them also that poor man who, knowing that the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power, expressed in a few words what he believed, saying: “You are the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16). Do not those riches seem to you needy, and this poverty overflowing? The rich heresy composed many Gospels; poor faith held only the one Gospel it received. Rich Philosophy made many gods for itself; the poor Church knew one God.

[Col. 1770C]

[Note: Concerning such pseudo-Gospels, consult what the holy Doctor wrote above, Book I, no. 2, and what we noted there.]

18. (Verse 24.) Between this rich man and the poor man there is therefore a great chasm, because after death merits cannot be changed. Thus the rich man is introduced in hell, desiring to draw something from the poor man’s spirit that might refresh him; for water is the refreshment of a soul established in pains, concerning which Isaiah says: “And water shall spring forth with delight from the fountains of salvation” (Isa. XII, 3).

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “desiring to draw some refreshment of spirit from the poor man.” This is less satisfactory; for, as we think, you will not find water named by anyone under the word “spirit.” Therefore refer the word “spirit” (or “by the spirit,” as the Ambrosian edition and two manuscripts prefer) to “poor man,” unless with one or two manuscripts and the editions of Erasmus and Gill you prefer to read “from the poor man’s spirit.”]

Why, however, is he tormented before the judgment? Because for the luxurious person, deprivation of pleasures is itself a punishment. For the Lord also says: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of heaven” (Luke XIII, 28).

19. (Verse 27.) At last this rich man begins to become a teacher, when he has no time left either to learn or to teach. Here the Lord most clearly declares that the Old Testament is the foundation of faith, bluntly rebuking the unbelief of the Jews and excluding the wickedness of heretics, by whom the weaker mind is overthrown; for they themselves are little ones, who still do not know the growth of virtue.

20. It may also be observed that, in the earlier comparison with that steward and in the present comparison with this rich man, there is an incentive to mercy: in the former case, perhaps, toward the saints whom he calls friends and to whom he grants tabernacles; here, however, he teaches that assistance should be given to the poor.

## (CHAPTER XVII.—Verse 3.) “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him.”

21. How appropriately, after the rich man who is tormented in punishments, he added the command to grant forgiveness—to those, of course, who turn away from error—lest despair prevent anyone from being recalled from guilt! How measured he was, so that forgiveness would be neither difficult nor indulgence lax; lest either a harsh rebuke strike someone down or connivance invite him to sin!

Thus also elsewhere: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him” (Matt. XVIII, 15). Friendly correction accomplishes more than turbulent accusation: the former instills shame, while the latter provokes indignation. Let the one who is admonished fear rather that his fault will be exposed. It is good, indeed, that the person being corrected should consider you a friend rather than an enemy; for one more readily yields to advice than submits to an injury. Hence the Apostle also says: “Rebuke him as a brother, so that he may be ashamed; do not regard him as an enemy” (II Thess. III, 15).

[Note: Thus the old edition and all the manuscripts, except two, where it reads: “For fear is a lasting guardian for the weak.” The Roman edition instead reads: “For the weak person is the lasting guardian of lasting goodness,” and so forth.]

Fear is a weak guardian of lasting conduct; shame, however, is a good teacher of duty. The one who fears is restrained, not corrected; but the one who is ashamed to do something makes that shame part of his nature.

[Col. 1771C] 22. He rightly said: “If he sins against you”; for sinning against God and sinning against a human being are not equivalent conditions. Finally, the Apostle, who is the true interpreter of the divine oracle, says: “Avoid a heretic after one admonition” (Titus III, 10).

[Note: Certain Paris editions read “after one or two admonitions.” But Ambrose plainly seems to have read “after one admonition.” For not only here, but also in Book II on Abraham and elsewhere, all the other editions together with the manuscripts agree on this reading. A little later the Roman edition inserted: “If he turns to you seven times in a day, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.” But since our reading is found in the ancient edition and in all the manuscripts, it must be supposed that the passage was abridged by Ambrose himself.]

For unbelief is not, in the same way as guilt, pardonable. And since error often creeps in through ignorance, he commanded that the person be corrected, so that either obstinacy might be avoided or a fall might be corrected. But what does this mean:

“(Verse 4.) If he turns to you seven times, forgive him”?

23. Is a number set for forgiveness, or is the point rather that, since God rested on the seventh day from all his works, after the week of this world a lasting rest is promised to us? Thus, just as the evils of this world will cease in a sabbatical rest, so also the severity of vengeance may come to rest.

The Sabbath is not only of days but also of months; therefore, on the tenth day of the seventh month, there is “a Sabbath of Sabbaths” (Lev. XXV, 9). It is not only of months but also of years; not only of years but also of generations; and finally of the world itself, whose type is the great Sabbath. Thus in the Law there is a seventh week, after which the year of Jubilee is celebrated.

The Lord wished to reveal this mystery to us when he said: “Not only seven times, but also seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII, 22). For in the seventh generation, as you have it according to Luke (Luke III, 37), Enoch was taken away, lest wickedness change his heart (Wis. IV, 11); and in him the sting of pain came to rest.

[Note: The same edition places Enoch in the seventh generation according to Luke; he was taken away.]

But in the seventy-seventh generation the Lord was born from Mary, taking upon himself the sins of the human race and granting remission of all offenses.

24. Therefore, although according to the literal sense you learn to forgive frequently and not to retain anger—for there is nothing by which the one accustomed to forgive can be offended—nevertheless recognize the mystery. For the Lord did not say idly to the woman on the Sabbath: “You are released from your infirmity” (Luke XIII, 12), showing his people—who, like that woman, were called to follow him—that by his coming he had forgiven sins.

Thus Lamech is condemned seventy-seven times (Gen. IV, 24), because he commits a graver offense when, in punishing a crime, he himself commits one. The sacraments of baptism, however, forgive every enormity of crime. Learn, therefore, to forgive the injuries done to you, because Christ forgave his persecutors.

[Note: Ambrose here seems to follow the opinion of certain Hebrews, who asserted that Cain was killed by Lamech, though they nevertheless held that this happened by accidental misfortune. Interpreters have discussed this matter extensively in their comments on this passage.]

25. Nor is the following without significance: Christ suffered on the great Sabbath, signifying that there would be a Sabbath on which death would be destroyed.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “that he was buried on the Sabbath.” But the authority of the other editions and of all the manuscripts, which agree in the word “suffered,” leads us to suppose that Christ is said here to have suffered on the Sabbath either because that day was the παρασκευή (*paraskeuē*, preparation) for the following Sabbath, or because, as is immediately added, the Jews observed the Sabbath in such a way that both a month and a year were regarded as equivalent to a Sabbath. Where all the editions and many manuscripts immediately add “signifying the great…,” we have preferred to read, with other and better manuscripts, “signifying by the great….” For the Jews had three festivals called great Sabbaths—Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles—the first of which that year fell on the lesser Sabbath, as we understand from the sacred histories. As for the statement that fifty days were to be celebrated as Passover, this is to be understood of certain rites, concerning which see *Apology of David*, chapter 8, no. 42.]

And if the Jews celebrate the Sabbath in such a way that they regard a whole month and a whole year as a kind of Sabbath, how much more ought we to celebrate the Lord’s resurrection! Therefore our predecessors handed down to us that all fifty days of Pentecost should be celebrated as Passover, because the beginning of the eighth week produces Pentecost.

Hence the Apostle, as a disciple of Christ who knew that times differ, writes to the Corinthians: “Perhaps I shall remain with you, and spend the winter” (I Cor. XVI, 6). And further on: “I shall remain at Ephesus until Pentecost; for a great door has been opened to me” (Ibid., 8 and 9). Thus he spends the winter among the Corinthians, whose errors distressed him, because their affection toward the worship of God had grown cold; but with the Ephesians he celebrates Pentecost, handing on the mysteries to them and relaxing his spirit, because he saw them burning with the ardor of faith.

Therefore, throughout these fifty days the Church knows no fasting, just as on the Lord’s Day on which the Lord rose, and all the days are like the Lord’s Day.

26. There will also be another Lord’s Day on which the Lord’s body will rise. Paul knows of this, saying: “You are the body of Christ, and members from his members” (I Cor. XII, 27). For this body and these bones of the Lord will be joined to the Head from his bones. “The head of the Church is Christ” (Eph. V, 23).

Then, therefore, fasting will cease, because in everlasting joy weariness, care, and fatigue will cease. Then death will be destroyed: “The last enemy, death, will be destroyed” (I Cor. XV, 26). For although death ceased in Enoch and was not found in him, it was not destroyed; he was taken away so that he might escape it (Gen. V, 24). Christ was sacrificed so that he might destroy it.

And therefore he rightly said: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (I Cor. XV, 55). In this resurrection, therefore, Christ will rise again in the body, as though in his own body. Blessed, then, is the one who will have a share in the first resurrection. For just as Christ is the firstfruits of those who sleep, so then the Church and his saints will be the firstfruits of those who rise (I Cor. XV, 20).

[Note: The old edition reads: “the firstfruits of the Church and its saints who rise”; the manuscripts: “the Church and its saints who rise”; the Roman edition: “his saints who rise.”]

27. Peter could not have known this mystery. Perhaps he knew about Enoch; yet who could comprehend with a human mind the mystery hidden in God? Let the Lord therefore come into my soul and into my mind, and subject it to himself, so that, when my mind has been subjected, I may say: “I will not fear evil, for you are with me” (Ps. XXII, 4).

“(Verse 6.) If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mulberry tree: ‘Be uprooted and thrown into the sea,’ and it will obey you.”

28. We have spoken above about the mustard seed; now we must discuss the mulberry tree. I read “tree,” but I do not believe that it means a tree. For what reason or progress would there be for us if a tree that bears fruit through the labor of farmers were uprooted and thrown into the sea? Even if we judge this possible on account of the power of faith, so that insensible nature obeys sensible commands, what, nevertheless, is the meaning of the particular kind of tree?

I have indeed read: “I was a herdsman of goats, nipping mulberries” (Amos VII, 14), and I think that the prophet signified to us that the sinner himself was converted from the flock of sinners. It is also fitting that the future prophet of the Gentiles should appear to have sought fruit among thorns, to have drawn food from thorns, and to have placed the discolored and foul-smelling flocks of the Gentiles—the peoples of the nations—in the pastures of his writings, so that they might grow fat through spiritual nourishment; while he himself milked spiritual milk from the converted sinner.

[Col. 1774A] 29. But since in another book of the Gospel (Matt. XVII, 19) the saying concerns a mountain whose naked appearance is devoid of plants, barren of olives, unfruitful in harvests, suited to the hiding places of beasts and disturbed by the paths of wild animals, it seems to express the height of spiritual wickedness lifting itself up, just as it is written: “Behold, I am against you, corrupting mountain, which corrupts the whole earth” (Jer. LI, 25). It is therefore fitting that we understand the saying in this passage in the same way, since faith drives out the unclean spirit, especially because the nature of the tree supports this interpretation.

For its fruit is first white in the flower; then, once formed, it shines red; at maturity it becomes black. So too the devil, from the whitish flower of an angelic nature and a radiant power, was cast down through transgression and bristled with the foul odor of sin.

Behold him when he says to the mulberry tree: “Be uprooted and thrown into the sea,” when he cast out the legion from the man and allowed it to enter the swine; and the swine, driven about by the demonic spirit, plunged themselves into the sea.

30. This passage, then, exhorts us to faith, teaching morally that even things which have become solidified can be dissolved by faith. From faith comes love; from love, hope; and these pour back into one another in a kind of holy circle.

31. (Verses 7, 8.) It follows that no one should boast in his works, because we owe service to the Lord as a matter of right. For if you do not say to your servant who is plowing or feeding sheep, “Come over and recline”—which implies that no one reclines unless he has first come over; indeed, Moses also first came over in order to see the great vision—if, then, you do not say to your servant, “Recline,” but demand another service from him and do not thank him, so also the Lord does not permit you to claim that a single work or labor is enough for you; for as long as we live, we must always work.

32. (Verse 17.) Recognize, then, that you are a servant who has incurred a debt through very many services. Do not exalt yourself because you are called a son of God: grace must be acknowledged, but nature must not be ignored. Nor should you boast if you have served well, since you ought to have done so. The sun serves; the moon obeys; the angels are servants.

The chosen vessel of the Gentiles says: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Cor. XV, 9). Then elsewhere, showing himself conscious of no fault, he added: “But I am not thereby justified” (I Cor. IV, 4). Therefore let us not demand praise from ourselves, nor seize God’s judgment, nor anticipate the sentence of the Judge; but let us reserve it for its proper time and for its proper Judge. After this the ungrateful are rebuked, and only then does he come to the discussion of the judgment to come.

“(Verses 31, 32.) In that hour, whoever is on the housetop, with his possessions in the house, must not come down to take them; and whoever is in the field likewise must not turn back. Remember Lot’s wife.”

33.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “When he was questioned by the Pharisees … indeed, through the freedom of grace.” Saint Ambrose may have been mistaken in his memory or in the manuscript he used concerning the word “Pharisees”; moreover, the disciples are mentioned in the following verse. The word “truth,” however, is correct, since, as we have already observed, among reliable authors it sometimes has the same meaning as “equity.” Thus “through the truth of grace” will have the same meaning as “through the equity or justice that arises from grace.”]

When the Lord was asked by his disciples when the kingdom of God would come, he said: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Verse 21)—that is, through the truth of grace, not through the slavery of guilt. Therefore, whoever wishes to be free should be a servant in the Lord; for in the measure in which we share in servitude, we also share in the kingdom.

He said, then: “The kingdom of God is within you.” But when it would come, he did not wish to say; instead, he said that the day of judgment would come, so that he might strike terror into all at the approaching judgment and not provide the security of delay.

34. And lest he seem to distress the disciples by denying them something, he says elsewhere: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son” (Matt. XXIV, 36).

[Note: Thus the old edition and all the manuscripts, except that in some the phrase “in another book” is omitted. The Roman edition altered the passage to read: “If he should conceal something from them, it follows: And he said to his disciples, ‘Days will come.’ And in another book.” A little later, where the Ambrosian edition and a few manuscripts read “He rightly placed the Son in the middle,” Erasmus and Gill, together with the rest, and the Roman edition read “He rightly interposed the Son.” But “in the middle” must certainly be read, that is, without determining whether the Son is of God or of man.]

He rightly placed the Son in the middle, for the Son of man is also the Son of God. We should therefore consider the saying to have been spoken more according to the Son of man, because he knows the end of the times not through the nature of man but through the nature

[Col. 1775B] of God.

Yet it is not contrary to faith if you understand “the Son” as the Son of God. For what is it that the good Father would have concealed from the Son, to whom he gave all things? Or how could he not have given knowledge of the time to him to whom he gave power over the judgment itself?

[Note: Several manuscripts read “above their foundation.”]

How could the Son not know what the Father knows, when the Son is in the Father, and the Spirit searches even the depths of God (John XIV, 11; I Cor. II, 10), since the Son himself is the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God? But why he does not wish to say it, he shows elsewhere: “It is not for you to know the times and years that the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts I, 7).

35. You see where the one who denies that the Trinity possesses one power is heading: toward asserting that there is something the Son does not know. For why would the Father conceal his own Son? Either we refuse to disclose to others what we know out of envy, or lest we be betrayed; but neither envy toward the Father nor the suspicion of betrayal toward the Son can be entertained. They therefore possess one knowledge, because they possess one power.

Moreover, the one who knows the signs of the future judgment surely also knows its end.

36. (Verse 24.) What is there that he does not know, like a flashing of lightning, since the light—the Son of God—illuminates the inner mystery of heaven?

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Matthew spoke concerning the day and hour.” But this alteration was introduced only because, after rejecting the earlier Lucan text, it substituted, after the words given below, other passages omitted by Ambrose, to which this exposition could not refer. The phrase that follows shortly, “he knows for himself, he does not know for me,” must be referred to the preceding words, “but why he does not wish to say it, he shows.” Therefore there is no ambiguity here, but a form of metonymy in which the cause is named from its effect. We find this passage explained in the same way by Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 60. For that great Doctor teaches there that the Son is said not to know in the sense that he causes human beings not to know—that is, he does not disclose to them what it would be useless for them to know.]

He says: “In that hour.” Therefore he knows the hour; but he knows it for himself, he does not know it for me. He rightly asserts that the cause of the flood, the fire, and the judgment proceeded from our sins, because God did not create evil, but our merits discovered it for themselves.

“(Verse 27.) For they were eating and drinking; they were marrying wives, and giving women in marriage.”

37. This is not because marriages are condemned, nor because food is condemned, since in the former there are means of succession and in the latter supports of nature; otherwise one would have to leave this world. But moderation is sought in all things. Whatever is in excess is from evil.

Let there be mutual agreement for a time, so that we may devote ourselves to prayer; let there be, amid the anxieties of the world and the excesses of gluttony, some sobriety of religion and intervals of chastity (I Cor. VII, 5).

38. Since, then, on account of the wicked, the good must necessarily suffer in this age the anguish of heart and soul, so that they may receive a more abundant reward in the future, they are instructed with remedies: those who are in Judaea should flee to the mountains (Matt. XXIV, 16).

What Judaea is this? For I know another Judaea according to the spirit, not according to the letter: “God is known in Judaea” (Ps. LXXV, 1). But what mountains could restrain the fear of the coming judgment, when it is written: “Trembling will seize the mountains” (Isa. LXIV, 3)?

“Heaven and earth will pass away” (Luke XXI, 33). How, then, will any portion of the earth remain unharmed or be able to protect me, when it cannot even preserve itself? Where, then, shall I hide from his wrath, the one who troubles the depths of the sea? “If I ascend into heaven, he is there; if I descend into hell, he is present” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 8). Therefore the one who is everywhere cannot be deceived, but he can be appeased.

39. The day of judgment is therefore present. If you do not wish to be overtaken, fear every day; flee every day. Do you ask how to flee? Ascend the mountain that evangelizes Zion (Isa. XL, 9), so that from the summit of exalted merits you may be able to rise above all. For he is the God of mountains, and not the God of valleys (III Kings XX, 28).

Ascend to where Christ sits at the right hand of God, whose foundations are in the holy mountains (Ps. LXXXVI, 1), and “the mountains are around him” (Ps. CXXIV, 2). Paul is your mountain; Peter is your mountain. Set the footstep of your mind upon their faith. For those established in the Law of God and in the inheritance of faith, the days of judgment do not find punishment but glory.

[Col. 1776D] 1480

40. If someone is also situated on a housetop—that is, if he has already ascended the upper parts of his house and the summit of eminent virtues—let him not fall back into the earthly works of this world.

For I know a roof on which that harlot Rahab, in a type (Josh. II, 1 and following)—the Church, joined to the peoples of the Gentiles through the sacramental fellowship of the mysteries—hid the spies whom Jesus sent. If they had descended to the lower parts of the house, they would have been killed by the pursuers who had been sent to seize them.

The housetop, then, is the lofty work of the mind and the summit of the soul, by which the naked weakness of the body is covered.

Hence it seems to me that the paralytic was healed for this reason (Mark II, 3): he was lowered from the roof by four young men, because by the aid of four virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice—he submitted himself to Christ’s feet through a certain elevated understanding. For nothing is loftier than humility, which, although it is above, does not know how to exalt itself, because no one desires what he judges to be beneath him.

41. But since we are engaged in judgment, let us not depart from the housetop, lest, while we wish to carry away the vessels that are in the house, we ourselves be seized. For not every house contains vessels of gold and silver; in most there are wooden vessels. Nor is every house full; there are also empty houses, which the prophet knew when he said: “What has happened to you now, that you have gone up into empty houses? The city is filled with those who cry out” (Isa. XXII, 1 and following).

And he added: “All your rulers have fled, all who were wounded in you,” and who had fallen from faith into unbelief. Sabellius was wounded; Valentinus was wounded; Arius was wounded. They were found in an empty house.

42. Do you wish to see a house that is full? Follow Peter as he went up to the upper parts of the house when he was hungry (Acts X, 9). There he recognized the mystery of the Church to be gathered, so that he would not judge the Gentile people to be unclean, whom faith could cleanse from every defilement.

[Note: Faith is not to be understood here in such a way as to exclude the necessity of good works; those who are not altogether strangers to Ambrose’s writings know that this is utterly foreign to his teaching. Faith alone is mentioned here because it is the foundation of salvation and of all virtues, as our Saint teaches in Book II *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 9, no. 28, and elsewhere.]

The vessels, however, are made of clay; therefore the vessel is the body. And so take care lest, through desire for the body, you abandon the noble pursuits of the mind.

If Peter did not receive the mystery while situated below, how will you receive it? He received it because he ascended, so that he might preach the Lord and not fear the suffering of the body.

43. Therefore, whoever is on the housetop must not come down, and whoever is in the field must not turn back. How shall I understand what the field is unless Jesus himself teaches me, saying: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke IX, 62)?

The idle man sits in the country house; the laborer sows in the field. The weak man is beside the hearth; the strong man is at the plow. The field has a good fragrance; “the fragrance of Jacob is like the fragrance of a full field” (Gen. XXVII, 27). The field is full of flowers and full of various fruits.

Plow your field, then, if you wish to be directed toward the kingdom of God. Let a fertile harvest of good merits bloom for you. Let there be “a fruitful vine on the sides of your house, and young olive trees around your table” (Ps. CXXVII, 3).

Let your soul, already conscious of its fruitfulness and sown with the word of God, also plowed by spiritual cultivation, say to Christ: “Come, my brother; let us go out into the field” (Song of Songs VII, 11). Let him answer: “I have entered my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh” (Song of Songs V, 1).

For what harvest is better than the harvest of faith, in which the fruit of the resurrection is stored and the fountain of everlasting joy is watered?

[Col. 1778A] **44.** Therefore, since you are forbidden to look back, you are much more forbidden to return and to take up your tunic; for you have learned that, if someone asks you for your tunic, you must also hand over your cloak (Matt. 5:40). Therefore, once directed toward the kingdom of God, do not seek riches or inheritance. Scripture also knows another tunic, concerning which the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “Having stripped off the old man with his deeds and put on the new” (Col. 3:9–10); let us not seek again the tunic of our former error. Hence she also says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” (Song 5:3)—meaning that you must not only renounce sins but also erase every memory of your former conduct. Finally, Paul, “forgetting what lies behind,” stripped off guilt but did not abandon repentance (Phil. 3:13).

[Col. 1778B] **45.** And therefore the Lord says: “Remember Lot’s wife.” Because she looked back, she lost the gift proper to her nature; for behind us is Satan, behind us is Sodom. Therefore flee intemperance and turn away from lust. And so that you may understand that not everyone can flee to the mountain, remember that the man who did not turn back to his former pursuits—for he had previously chosen Sodom—escaped for this reason: he reached the mountain (Gen. 19:30).

[Note: The Roman edition has *qui se ad vetera studia non reflexit* (“who did not turn back to his former pursuits”).]

But she, who was weaker, because she looked back, was unable to reach the mountain even with the aid of her husband’s support, and remained behind.

**(Verse 34.)** “In that night there will be two in one bed: one will be taken and the other will be left.”

**46.** He rightly spoke of night, because the Antichrist is the hour of darkness, since he spreads darkness over human hearts when he says that he is Christ. False prophets will arise, claiming now that Jesus dwells in the deserts, so that they may deceive people with the wandering error of opinion; now that he is in inner chambers, so that those who hear them may be confined by the name of exalted power. But Christ, like lightning flashing, scatters throughout the whole world the spheres of his light (Matt. 24:27). Therefore he neither wanders in the deserts nor is confined to particular places, because the Lord says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). Rather, he shines with the radiance of his brilliance, so that in that night we may be able to see the glory of the resurrection. What, then, does he mean when he says:

**(Verse 35.)** “Two in one bed … two grinding at the mill … two in the field: one will be taken and the other will be left”?

[Col. 1778D] **47.** Is God unjust, that he should distinguish by the reward of merits people equal in their pursuits and fellowship of life, and indistinguishable in the quality of their actions? It is not so; rather, the quality of the reward corresponds to a person’s actions. The union of human beings, therefore, does not make their merits equal: a father may rise up against his son, and a son against his father, in devotion to religion, because not everyone accomplishes what he undertakes. “But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

Moreover, the Lord examines not service rendered in public but the inward disposition; for even if you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, the sacrifice is not acceptable to God (Gen. 4:7). [Col. 1779A] Therefore, from one bed—for the bed is a symbol of human weakness, since it is written: “You have turned his whole bed in his sickness” (Ps. 40:4)—one is left and the other is taken. The one who is taken is snatched up to meet Christ in the air; the one who is left is rejected.

**48.** “Two grinding at the mill.” The meaning seems to be that these signify those who seek nourishment from hidden things and bring forth into the open what comes from within. Yet we must ask what these two women are grinding. Unless perhaps it is what we read in Isaiah: “If you bring fine flour, it is in vain,” so that the fine flour may be what is offered by those who grind (Isa. 1:13).

Let us therefore examine [Col. 1779B] what they grind, what sort of thing they grind, and what the mill is. Perhaps this world is a mill in which, I think, the form of the human body is aptly represented: our soul is enclosed in it as though in a bodily prison, working—if it consults what is good—to produce heavenly bread.

In this mill, then—whether it is the Synagogue or a soul enslaved to sins—the wheat, soaked by grinding and corrupted by heavy moisture, cannot separate what is within from what is without. It is therefore left behind, because its fine flour has been displeasing. But the holy Church, or the soul unstained by any contagion of sins, grinds wheat that has been dried by the heat of the eternal sun, wheat which God clothed as he willed and which the angels cleansed from every stain of refuse. Offering good fine flour from the inner chambers of human beings to God, [Col. 1779C] it commends the offerings of its sacrifice.

[Note: All manuscripts and editions have this reading, except that some of them have *reformatur* (“is restored”) instead of *referatur* (“is represented”). One manuscript has *reseratur* (“is opened”). The Roman edition, however, replaced *in quo aptius reor quia* with *quod aptius reor quod in eo* (“which I think is more aptly [understood], because in it…”).]

[Note: Some manuscripts read *si bonis consulat* (“if it takes thought for good things”); others have *si bene consulat* (“if it takes good thought”). Neither reading is entirely satisfactory.]

**49.** And not only will there be two women grinding, but also two working in one field, of whom one will be taken. The good sower is the one who does not sow upon the wayside but upon soil that has been ploughed and cultivated, so that the earth may multiply fruit pressed down by humility, not scattered by boasting. But the sower of weeds is left behind, from which unacceptable fine flour is produced.

Who these differing farmers are, we can discover if we consider why the Apostle said that there are two νοῦς—that is, two minds—in us. Perhaps it is because one belongs to the outward person, who is being corrupted, and the other to the inward person, who is renewed through the sacraments. The worse one, perhaps, is the person who is lifted up, vainly inflated in the mind of his flesh and not holding fast to the head, [Col. 1779D] because he turns away from observing the saving commands of our Lord Jesus Christ. He himself is the head of all, because he is the author of all.

The other is the superior one: he loves humility, seeks wisdom, and does not neglect mercy—the good sower, for “he scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (Ps. 112:9). The one, therefore, is spiritual; the other is carnal. For just as we understand from the Apostle’s words that the deceiver who exalts himself, inflated with a proud mind, is puffed up by the mind of his flesh (Col. 2:18), so we also show that the holy man is renewed in the spirit of his mind, as the same Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4:23). He thus demonstrates that there are two minds: one which becomes the mind of the flesh, bound by sin; the other joined to the spirit, which renounces the allurements of the flesh.

**50.** There are therefore not only two minds in us but also two laws, both of which the Apostle explained to us, saying: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward person, but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:22–23). There is therefore a law of the inward person, [Col. 1780B] and also one of the outward person: the former prohibits sin, the latter encourages it; the former condemns error, the latter suggests it; the former instructs the mind, the latter tests it.

There are also two other, more powerful laws in us, one of God and the other of sin, according to the same Apostle: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (ibid., 25). It is shown that, if you speak only of the mind, you indicate something opposed to the flesh. When Paul says that with his mind he serves the law of God, he clearly demonstrates that the mind in itself is good unless it is overcome by the flesh, and that by nature it was created to resist error.

Therefore, when it is conquered, the mind becomes the mind of the flesh—not having from its nature what slips, but receiving it from the flesh—and, as though succeeding into the name and possession of the victor, the conquered mind takes the victor’s place. By nature, however, it is opposed to the flesh. Finally, with the mind we serve God, and with the flesh sin. The mind will be better if, cooperating with the Holy Spirit, it does not interrupt its religious service.

**51.** These, then, are the workers in our field. One, through diligence, produces good fruit; the other, through negligence, loses it. The Legislator calls this latter one “blood,” saying: “The life of every flesh is its blood” (Lev. 17:14). Many refer to this also what is written: “You shall not eat flesh with its blood” (Gen. 4:9), lest we regard bodily pleasures stained with the wounds of the soul as nourishment rather than as guilt of blood, when we ought to be nourished by the word of God.

[Note: Gratian, in the passage cited, attributes these words in the margin to St. Leo. But Gratian’s correctors observed that they are found nowhere except in Ambrose. They also did not overlook a similar error in the words “There is also a body,” etc., in section 56; Blessed Anselm likewise did not avoid this error.]

There is therefore food for nourishment, and there is food of blood. For just as the Lord’s flesh is truly food, so his blood is truly our drink (*De Consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter *In quibus*, section “Est cibus”). Let us therefore offer the Lord good food from our works, lest when he comes again and finds no fruit on us, as he found none on that fig tree, he turn away from his purpose of mercy, fasting because of the barrenness of our merits, and say to that soul which he finds naked of fruit and stained with blood: “May no fruit ever come from you again” (Matt. 21:19).

Thus the life of every flesh is its blood. There is also a superior soul, concerning which God said: “All souls are mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine” (Ezek. 18:4).

**52.** Nor should we pass over the interpretation of the two peoples. In this world, which is very often compared with a field, there are two peoples: one of believers and the other of those who do not believe. Each will receive the return corresponding to its merits. Therefore the one who is faithful will be taken, while the one who is faithless will be left.

Those two women grinding are two souls, or certainly the Church and the Synagogue. For Scripture is accustomed to contain not only one figure but many, so that a single passage may encompass several meanings. Thus the mind of the flesh, the soul of the flesh, and the Synagogue gather that wheat and grind the fine flour that is offered in vain. But the mind joined to the soul, and the soul that receives the saving word, or the Church of God, cultivate and grind the spiritual fine flour of the true law. From it the loaves of the Presence are also made, which the priests alone eat, since they are commanded to eat purer bread (Lev. 24:8)—that bread, of course, which came down from heaven (John 6:31). We are all priests of righteousness, if our merits permit it, consecrated to kingship and priesthood by the anointing of joy.

[Note: Several manuscripts read *receptrix est salutis* (“is the receiver of salvation”); others, and all editions, have the reading given in the text, except that several of those manuscripts also read *salutis* (“of salvation”) instead of *salutaris verbi* (“of the saving word”).]

**53.** Let us therefore cultivate and work our field in this way, having been appointed to the service of this cultivation, so that in that higher Jerusalem, where the true observance of the law is celebrated, we may possess fine flour from our sheaves. Blessed are those who are able to gather them: “Coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 126:6).

These, then, are spiritual fruits and the happy yield of true labor, which no useless rain may soak. The fruit of the flesh, however, is subject to corruption; therefore whoever sows carnal things will also reap carnal things (2 Cor. 9:6). What should I say about the field, when it is clear that in the work of the cultivator there is either praise or blame?

**(Verse 36.)** “And answering, they said to him: ‘Where, Lord?’”

**54.** The disciples said this. But the Lord, having already indicated where one should flee, where one should remain, and what should be avoided, summed up the whole matter in a general statement, saying:

**(Verse 37.)** “Where the body is, there the eagles will also be gathered.”

[Col. 1781D] **55.** Let us first determine what the eagles are, so that we may define what the body is. The souls of the righteous are compared with eagles because they seek what is high, leave behind what is low, and are said to lead a long life. Hence David says to his soul: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 103:5).

If we have understood the eagles, we can no longer doubt concerning the body, especially if we remember that Joseph received the body from Pilate (John 19:38). Do Mary of Clopas, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of the Lord, and the gathering of the apostles not seem to you to be eagles around the body at the Lord’s burial? Do the eagles not seem to you to be around the body when the Son of Man comes with intelligible clouds: “Every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” (Rev. 1:7)?

**56.** There is also a body of which it was said: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56). Around this body are eagles, flying about on spiritual wings. There are also eagles around the body who believe that Jesus came in the flesh, because “every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God” (1 John 4:7). Where faith is, therefore, there is the sacrament; there is the dwelling-place of holiness.

There is also the body that is the Church, in which we are renewed in spirit through the grace of baptism, and the fading age of old age is restored to renewed life.

[Note: In a considerable number of manuscripts, a lengthy interpolation concerning the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector is inserted here. It is found neither in the older manuscripts nor, even at first reading, does it display anything Ambrosian; moreover, it is found in exactly the same words in Bede, *Commentary on Luke*, book 5, chapter 71. We have therefore judged that a foreign birth should not be mixed with a legitimate one.]

**(Chapter XVIII.—Verse 16.)** “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them; for of such is the kingdom of God.”

**57.** This age is weak in strength, deficient in understanding, and immature in judgment. Age, therefore, is not preferred to age; otherwise growing older would be harmful. What need would there be for vows in order to attain maturity of age, if what is heavenly were going to deprive me of the merit of the kingdom (Luke 6:13)?

God therefore gave the progression of life for the sake of vices, not for the growth of virtue. Why, then, did he choose apostles not of childish but of more advanced age? Why does he say that children are suited to the kingdom of heaven? Perhaps because they do not know malice, do not know how to defraud, and do not dare to retaliate; they do not know how to investigate wealth, and do not seek honor or ambition.

[Note: The ancient edition and all manuscripts read this way, except that in some manuscripts *honorum* (“of honors”) appears instead of *honorem* (“honor”). Only the Roman edition has *scortari ignorent, opes, honorem, ambitionemque non appetant* (“they do not know prostitution and do not seek wealth, honor, or ambition”).]

But ignorance of these things is not virtue; contempt for them is. Nor is there praise for self-restraint where integrity results from weakness. It is not childhood, then, but goodness that imitates childish simplicity which is being indicated. For it is not virtue to be unable to sin, but to be unwilling to sin, and to maintain such perseverance of will that the will imitates infancy and practice imitates nature.

Finally, the Savior himself expressed this, saying: “Unless you turn and become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:8).

**58.** What child, then, is to be imitated by the apostles of Christ? Is it one of the little children? Is this, then, the virtue of the apostles? What child is it? Perhaps the one of whom Isaiah says: “A child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6). For this child said to you: “Take up your cross and follow me” (Matt. 16:24).

And so that you may recognize the child: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he was struck, he did not strike back” (1 Pet. 2:23). This is perfect virtue. Thus even in childhood there is a kind of venerable old age of character, and in old age an innocent childhood. “Old age is venerable not because of its length, nor is it measured by the number of years; rather, the understanding of a person is gray hair, and an unblemished life is the age of old age” (Wis. 4:8–9).

Hence it is also written: “Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 113:1), because no one praises the Lord unless he is perfect. “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3).

**59.** This seems to have been prophesied concerning the people of the Church, who, though younger, surpassed the older people of the Jews in the pursuit of virtue. Therefore: “Behold, I and the children whom you have given me” (Isa. 8:18).

These are the children who, following the Lord as he rode upon a colt, with prophetic voices declared that the redemption of the nations had come (Matt. 21:15). These are the children, or infants, who drank deeply from those breasts of Christ, full of nourishment like wine. “From the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. 8:3).

**60.** It may therefore seem harsh and unfeeling to some that the disciples prevented the little children from approaching the Lord, unless you understand either the mystery or the motive. They did not do this through the harshness of an envious mind toward children, but offered the Lord the attentions of diligent service, lest he be pressed by the crowds. For elsewhere it is written: “Teacher, the crowds press upon you” (Luke 7:45).

Our own advantage must indeed be rejected where there is an insult to divinity. Let us therefore flee pride and follow childish simplicity, because truth is opposed to pride, while simplicity, allied with truth, is exalted in humility. God does not dwell in a debased heart, but, as the prophets have handed down to us: “The throne of glory has been exalted” (Jer. 17:12)—that is, in the one whose wisdom is raised to the height of truth.

Nor should one, like Cain, conceal the deceit of a murderer beneath the appearance of brotherhood; rather, one must be a brother outwardly and inwardly. This concerns the motive.

In the mystery, however, the disciples were eager that the Jewish people should first be saved, since Christ’s human ancestry came from that people; yet they also pleaded on behalf of the Canaanite woman (Matt. 15:23). They therefore knew the mystery: that the call was owed to both peoples, but perhaps they did not yet know the order.

**61.** Now pay attention to the distinction in the words. When he commands infants to approach him, so that he may bless them either by preaching or by the laying on of hands, he calls them “children.” When he commands that the little ones not be scandalized (Matt. 18:6), he calls them *pusilli*, “little ones.” Those touched by Christ are not scandalized; those who draw near to Christ do not fall. Rather, those fall whom not the smallness of their age but the smallness of their virtue has made little.

At the same time he teaches that the weak must not be tested, lest the sins of those whose prayers are carried up to the Lord by the protection of angels be turned against us, even if they themselves are weak in the merits of virtue. Let no one, therefore, mock the poor, because he provokes the one who made him. Let no one test the weak, lest he injure the angels. Let no one cast down the infirm, lest he dissolve the benefit of the Redeemer (Prov. 12:5).

[Note: The Roman edition reads *vel precatione* (“or by prayer”). We would gladly embrace this reading if it were defended by even a single manuscript.]

**62.** And therefore he said: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7), because many judged the Lord’s cross to be a scandal, whereas the humility of the Lord’s passion is the sacrament of our salvation. We should therefore undertake the service of virtue and adopt the example of humility.

Woe, then, to the one who has not believed in the Lord’s cross, by which the weak are scandalized: “It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the depth of the sea” (Matt. 18:6).

**63.** In the divine Scriptures we must examine not the sequence of words but the weight of realities. For an unheard-of and hideous, almost bestial display of punishment is more effective in restraining sins. Nevertheless, lest this too cause scandal to any weak person, we do not think it was without purpose that the millstone, the human neck, and the depth of the sea were placed together.

Since the Gentile people have received the figure of the donkey, does it not seem to you that they are turning a millstone so long as they remain caught in the error of their ignorance—bound, indeed, by the chains of nature, so that they grind out the word and seek God, but overwhelmed by the blindness of a covered mind, so that they do not know how to raise the face of their soul toward God or open the eyes of their heart?

Therefore, without any liveliness of progress, repeatedly returning upon their own tracks, they labor unwillingly for another’s use. Yet the one who turns the millstone eventually has an end to the work that must be completed and retains hope of casting off his blindness. But the one whose neck bears the millstone carries the stone because he refused to bear the Lord’s yoke.

Thus the donkey belongs to the millstone, the blind person to the stone, and the Gentile to the rock: he worships what he does not see and does not recognize. For God does not dwell in things made by hands (Acts 17:24), nor is he recognized in stone, but in the spirit.

**64.** Both peoples, Gentile and Jew, are therefore set forth through a kind of rhetorical display in this passage, but a more severe punishment is decreed against the Jews. The memory of the Gentiles will be overwhelmed by the waves of this age and obliterated by the mire of this world. They wished to be among those things that do not exist, and, alienated from the knowledge of God, they were plunged as into the depth of the sea.

The Jews, however, who were taken up through the patriarchs, marked by circumcision, and instructed through the Law, will not perish as unknown people but will be punished as sacrilegious. For God was unknown to the Athenians, but known in Judea and not received (Acts 17:23). Therefore the one who does not know will be unknown; the one who transgresses will be condemned. Neither is the one free from guilt who did not know his creator, nor is the one deprived of pardon who did not receive the Lord. Nevertheless, it is more tolerable not to have brought faith to Christ than to have laid hands upon him (Ps. 76:2).

**(Verses 18–19.)** “A certain ruler asked him, saying: ‘Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?’ But Jesus said to him: ‘Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.’”

**65.** A crafty question, and therefore a pointed answer. For this ruler, who was testing him, called him “Good Teacher,” though he ought to have called God good. Although goodness exists in divinity and divinity in goodness—for “no one is good except God alone,” while “every human being is a liar” (Ps. 116:11), and whatever is a liar is certainly not good—nevertheless, by adding “Good Teacher,” he called him good in a partial sense, not in the universal sense. God is good in his entirety; a human being is good in part.

Therefore the Lord says: “Why do you call me good, when you deny that I am God? Why do you call me good, when no one is good except the one God?” He is not denying that he is good, but indicating that he is God. For what is good except that which is full of goodness?

[Col. 1785B] When it is written: “There is no one who does good, not even one” (Ps. 14:3), it was certainly spoken of human beings, not of God. God is one, not one among a number (Deut. 6:4). Thus the Son of God, as the only one, is excepted; he is not one among many. He is the only-begotten, not one among those begotten.

Therefore “no one is good” does not prejudice Christ, because no one judges Christ. “No one” is not spoken of us as a general category, for Christ has nothing in common with us.

**66.** If anyone is troubled because it says, “No one is good except the one God,” let him also be troubled by the statement that no one is good except God. If the Son is not excluded from God, then Christ is certainly not excluded from goodness.

But since in God the Son is another person yet one in power—“one God, from whom are all things, and one Lord, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6)—and since God and Lord are not two gods but one God, because “the Lord your God is one Lord” (Deut. 6:4), then, according to majesty, God is one in both persons, and the one who is good is good in both.

For how can he who is born from the good not be good? “A good tree produces good fruits” (Matt. 7:17). How can he not be good when the substance of goodness, received from the Father, did not degenerate in the Son, any more than it degenerated in the Spirit? Therefore: “Your good Spirit will lead me into the right path” (Ps. 143:11).

If the Spirit who received from the Son is good, then certainly the one who gave is also good. And if the Father is good, then the one who possesses everything that the Father possesses is also good. If you deny that the Son possesses goodness, you also deny it of the Father (John 17:10).

[Col. 1785D] **67.** The argument is clear and needs no examples, but at least follow the authority of the Scriptures. It is written: “The Lord is the good judge of the house of Israel” (Isa. 33:22). Does this refer to the Son or to the Father? But the Father judges no one, because he has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). Therefore the Son is the good Lord.

Take another example: those who come to baptism certainly confess the Trinity, because they are baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore they confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

[Note: A few manuscripts read: “he confesses the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”]

When it is said, therefore, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. 136:1), the Father is good, the Son is good, and the Holy Spirit is good, but God is one, because “the good Lord is patient toward those who wait for him” (Lam. 3:25). Is he not good who grants good things to the soul that seeks him? Is he not good who “satisfies your soul with good things” (Ps. 103:5)? Is he not good who says: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11)?

**68.** But perhaps you think that God is good because he does not possess judgment, in which there is a necessity of vengeance.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “in which there is no necessity of vengeance.”]

Although it has already been stated that he is the good judge of the house of Israel, elsewhere you have: “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart!” (Ps. 73:1). Of whom do you think this was said—of the Father or of the Son? If of the Father, then he is not good to everyone. Why, then, do you detract from the Son? If of the Son, then you confess that the Son is the good God. For he is “the blessed God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people” (Luke 1:68). He is the king and God of Israel, to whom it is said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel” (John 1:49).

Thus he says here: “Since you, who are testing me, cannot perceive me as good, why do you call me good?” I am indeed good, but good to the upright in heart, to whom goodness belongs by nature, not by cunning.

The Son is therefore good: “He is the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wis. 7:26). How, then, can he not be good when he is the image of goodness? Just as the image of God is God, yet God is one, so the image of divine goodness is good, yet goodness is one.

For my part, it is useful to believe that God is good, since he will be the judge of my sins. Let those who do not wish to believe that he is good see to themselves. Since this man was a lawyer who was testing him, as is shown in another Gospel, he rightly said: “No one is good except God” (Mark 10:18), in order to remind him that it is written: “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:16), but rather confess to the Lord: “For he is good” (Ps. 136:1).

**69. (Verse 21.)** Finally, he often rebukes him. When the man boasted that from his youth he had kept everything prescribed by the Law, Jesus exposed his empty boasting and showed him that he still lacked what the Law required. Therefore he is led sadly toward the commandment of mercy, so that a certain natural form of judgment might be given against him.

[Col. 1786D] **(Verse 25.)** “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

[Note: The Roman edition, on its own authority, transposed several passages here across four or five columns. Although we restore them to their former order, we have refrained from reproducing in the margins the material that could scarcely contain so much.]

**70.** Great force, great weight in these words. With what other words could he have expressed more forcefully that a rich person must not boast in his riches than with words that define a rich person as being contrary to the nature of mercy? Take away from me the seductive coloring and embellishment of words, which usually weaken sentences.

[Note: The editions of Erasmus and Gill, in the margin, as well as the Roman edition in the body of the text, together with most manuscript copies, read *lactari non debuit* (“this man should not be flattered”). The older edition in the body of the text, and some of the later Paris editions together with several manuscripts, read *jactari non debuit* (“he should not have been made boastful”). The latter is less suitable.]

This man, who rejected mercy, should not have been flattered but broken.
