Yet if some people are more delighted by verbal ornament than by the manly and natural character and form of meaning—just as good suitors behave when taking a wife, examining her character rather than her beauty, and not being put off by an unattractive appearance when the virtue of her soul attracts them—then let them also seek a mystery in the words, which is a kind of mind and soul of the words; but let them not dissect the words within the mystery.

**71.** The camel, then, is understood typologically as the Gentile people. The lion seeking someone to devour drives into the desert, loaded with prophetic treasure, [Col. 1787D] by means of symbolic forms.

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read *agit affatibus* (“drives by utterances”). Seven manuscripts read *agit aspectibus* (“drives by appearances”), which is not unreasonable. Seven others, however, read *agitat speciebus* (“drives by forms”), that is, by the figures and images through which prophetic vision is expressed. Where, shortly afterward, most manuscripts read *ad aspides* (“to the asps”), some others and all editions omit the preposition, which better agrees with the prophetic text.]

“For in tribulation and distress the lion and the lion’s cub, the asp and the offspring of flying asps, carried their riches upon donkeys and camels” (Isa. 30:6).

The camel is fittingly used as a figure of the Gentile people, because, degenerating through the deformity of superstition, before the people of the nations believed, it displayed the ugliness of a beast, absurd tracks, and shameful mouths.

Therefore this sinner entered more easily by the narrow way—which is the way of Christ, who, penetrating the way of death through the passion of his own body, like a needle restored certain torn garments of our nature—than did the Jewish people, rich in the Law but poor in faith, precipitous in fury, and disgraceful in guilt.

**72.** This may also be understood morally of every sinner and of the arrogant rich person. Does not that tax collector seem to you, burdened by the consciousness of his sins and unable to lift his eyes toward God (Luke 18:13), like a camel entering more easily through the eye of the needle by the remedies of his confession than that Pharisee entered the kingdom of God?

The Pharisee was arrogant in prayer, boastful of his innocence, presumptuous of glory, reproachful toward mercy, a preacher of himself and an accuser of another. He was one who would more readily confront the Lord than entreat him.

If anyone therefore recoils from the camel, let him recoil from the person whose deeds are uglier than the camel.

[Note: In the Roman edition, the words “into the kingdom of God” were excised.]

**(Verse 20.)** “Honor your father and your mother.”

**73.** The beginning of the Law is beautifully read today, since it is the anniversary of my priesthood. For every year the priesthood seems to begin anew, when it is renewed by the passage of time.

It is also good that we read: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:12).

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “For so many years … how great the periods of time,” etc. Here an ancient custom is indicated: the annual celebration of the consecration of bishops. It is by no means unworthy of our observance. On this, see Baronius, *Roman Martyrology*, on 18 January, and others.]

You are my parents, for you conferred the priesthood upon me.

[Note: It is said here that the people conferred the priesthood, meaning that, as Paulinus testifies, they agreed with wondrous and incredible unanimity that Ambrose should be ordained—not that they conferred the rank or jurisdiction upon him. These must in no way be confused, as heretics do in order somehow to defend the deficiency of the mission and authority of their ministers. It is beyond doubt that ordination, through which jurisdiction is conferred, has always been carried out in the Catholic Church only by bishops.]

You, I say, are children—or parents: individually, children; collectively, parents. I gladly call you either my children or my parents, you who hear and do the word of God: children, because it is written, “Come, children, hear me” (Ps. 34:11); parents, because the Lord himself said: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers? My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it” (Luke 8:21).

**74.** The Law, therefore, rightly placed after “You shall love the Lord your God, and you shall love your neighbor” the command: “Honor your father and your mother.” This is the first step of filial devotion, for God wished them to be your originators.

Honor them with services, refraining from insults, because filial devotion must not be wounded even by one’s expression. But it is not enough merely not to injure them, because the Law took care that they should suffer no wrong: “Whoever curses his father or mother shall die” (Exod. 21:17). You, however, honor them, so that you may be good.

One thing is the benefit of the Law, another the duty of filial devotion. Honor your own parents, because the Son of God honored his. For you have read: “He was subject to them” (Luke 2:51). If God was subject to servants, how much more should you be subject to your parents?

Christ therefore honored Joseph and Mary not from a debt imposed by nature but from the duty of filial devotion. He also honored God the Father, as no one could honor him, by becoming obedient unto death. Honor your parents, then.

75. Honor, however, consists not only in showing respect but also in generosity: “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:3). For honor means rendering what is due according to merit. Feed your father; feed your mother. And if you feed your mother, you still have not repaid the pains, nor the sufferings she endured for you; you have not repaid the services by which she carried you; you have not repaid the nourishment she gave with tender affection, putting her breasts to your lips; you have not repaid the hunger she endured for you, lest she eat anything harmful to you or drink anything injurious to her milk. For you she fasted; for you she ate. For you she refused food she wanted and ate food she did not want. For you she kept watch; for you she wept. And you [Note: Three manuscripts read: “do you allow her to lack the food she wanted?”] allow her to suffer hunger? O son, how great a judgment you incur if you do not feed your parent! You owe what you have to the one to whom you owe what you are. How great a judgment, if the Church feeds those whom you do not wish to feed! “If any faithful man or any faithful woman,” he says, “has widows, let them provide for them, so that the Church may not be burdened and may have enough for those who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:16). This concerns outsiders; what, then, of parents?

76. We did not speak idly a little earlier, because a mother’s complaint constrained us; but we preferred to admonish publicly the person who is like this [Note: From this you may understand that bishops formerly possessed not only the right and authority to admonish but also to coerce], rather than correct him privately. And even if he is not exposed by our voice, let him nevertheless be ashamed through his own feeling. Do not allow, my son, your parents to be fed by the hunger of others; do not allow, my son, the fasts of the poor to seek food for your parents. If not for gratitude and salvation, then at least for shame, feed them yourself, whether you are son or daughter. Are you not ashamed if, when you enter the church, your aged mother extends her hands to strangers and, passing over her daughter, asks alms from outsiders, while you pass by with your neck held high, drawing your garment along with the movements of your eyes, wearing earrings, bracelets, rings, and the other things Isaiah mentions (Isa. 3:16 and following)? What if she turns her speech upon you, demanding the debt of nature, the price of your nourishment, and the service your hand owes your mother? What will you answer?

77. Will you give to others? What if they say to you: “Go, feed your mother first.” For even if they are poor, they do not seek an impious contribution. Have you not heard above that the rich man reclining in linen and purple, from whose table Lazarus gathered crumbs, is tormented by eternal punishments because he did not share food with the poor (Luke 16:19 and following)? If it is grievous not to give to outsiders, how much more grievous is it to exclude one’s parents? But you say that you prefer to give to the Church what you were going to give to your parents. God does not seek a gift extracted from the hunger of parents. Hence, when the Jews reproached the Lord’s disciples for not washing their hands, Jesus answered: “Whoever says, ‘Whatever gift comes from me will benefit you,’ will not honor his father or mother” (Matt. 15:5–6).

78. Therefore we have not unwisely clarified the obscurity of the meaning. For while the Jews follow human tradition, they neglect God’s; while the disciples, preferring God’s tradition, neglected human tradition by not washing their hands when they ate bread, because “the one who has been washed is completely clean and does not need to wash his hands” (John 13:10). Jesus had washed them, and they did not seek another washing; for by Christ’s one baptism all baptisms are done away with. Therefore one whom the Church has washed does not need to be washed again. Thus the disciples were intent on the mystery, seeking not the cleanliness of their bodies but that of their souls [Note: Many manuscripts, and manuscripts of no inferior quality, read: “not seeking the cleanliness of their soul, not of their body.” We do not know whether that may not be the true reading. Still, the reading followed in the text, found in the other manuscripts and in all printed editions, is not without merit].

This the Jews reproached them for; but the Lord cleverly refutes them because they observe empty practices and disregard what is beneficial. And therefore he says to them: “Why do you say to your father or mother, whom the Law commands to be honored, ‘Whatever gift comes from me will benefit you’” (Exod. 20:12)? That is, when a needy father or mother asks a son for something to support them [Note: Thus read the majority of the better manuscripts. Others, including the printed editions, do not recognize the word “Jew,” in whose place the Roman edition substitutes “son,” before the words “because he fears the Law”], because the Jew, fearing the Law, seeks an excuse for not giving, he is accustomed to say: “The gift that comes from me will benefit you,” so that the devout father may hesitate to accept money dedicated to God by his children. But this is a human tradition, concealing the excuses of avarice. God’s tradition, on the other hand, is that you feed your parents first (Dist. 86, chapter “Caeterum”). For if, according to the divine oracle, an insult against a parent is punished by death (Exod. 21:17), how much more so is hunger, which is worse than death!

79. In this passage the Lord restrains insolent boasting. For many, in order to be praised by people, give to the Church what they take away from their own household, although mercy ought to begin at home through the duty of filial devotion. Give, therefore, first to your parent; give also to the poor; give to the presbyter what earthly goods you have in abundance, so that you may receive from him the spiritual gift you lack—for whoever honors will be honored [Note: Observe that it is in no way blameworthy if presbyters, imparting to laypeople the spiritual things belonging to their office, in turn receive earthly alms from them, provided that shameful greed and the sordid trafficking of sacred things are absent]. See, then, that when he receives, he gives; and he receives not as one in need, but as one who will repay with a greater measure. Give to the poor for his repose, so that you too, by sharing what you have with the needy, may attain repose. But just as Scripture says that parents are to be fed (Luke 14:26), so, for God’s sake, parents are to be abandoned if they hinder the devotions of a dedicated heart.

(Verse 35.) “And it happened that, when he drew near Jericho, a certain blind man was sitting beside the road.”

80. In the book according to Matthew two blind men are introduced (Matt. 20:30), here one; there, as Jesus was leaving Jericho, here, as he approached it. But there is no discrepancy. For since in this one man there is a type of the Gentile people, who through the Lord’s mystery receive the brightness of lost sight, it makes no difference whether he receives healing in one person or in two. For they trace their origin to Ham and Japheth, the sons of Noah; in the two blind men they were presenting the two ancestors of their race.

81. Luke also appears not to have omitted this meaning when he next introduces Zacchaeus, who was small in stature—that is, not elevated by any innate dignity of nobility [Note: Some manuscripts read: “elevated by the prevailing dignity of nobility”; several others: “elevated by the nobility of his innate freedom”]—and insignificant in merits. Like the people of the nations, having heard of the arrival of the Lord and Savior, whom his own people had not received, he desired to see him. But no one readily sees Jesus; no one can see Jesus who is established on the earth. And because he had neither prophets [Note: The old edition reads: “he had no kingdom elsewhere.” The word “elsewhere” is omitted in the manuscripts; the Roman edition emended the text to read: “he had no law.” This is not an unsuccessful conjecture] nor a kingdom, he climbed the sycamore as though toward the grace of his natural form, trampling underfoot the vanity of the Jews and correcting also the errors of his earlier life. Therefore he received Jesus into the hospitality of his inner house. And he climbed the tree appropriately, so that a good tree might produce good fruits, and, cut off from the natural wild olive and grafted contrary to nature into a good olive, he might be able to bear the fruit of the Law. For the root is holy, and even if the branches are useless [Col. 1790D], the Gentile people transcend their fruitless glory by faith in the resurrection, as though by a certain elevation of the body.

(Chapter 19.—Verse 2.) “And behold, a man named Zacchaeus.”

82. Zacchaeus was in the sycamore; the blind man was on the road. The Lord awaits one of them in order to show mercy, and ennobles the other by the glory of his dwelling. He questions one whom he is about to heal; he invites himself to the other, though he did not intend to invite himself [Note: All printed editions and many manuscripts read: “he invites himself, though he had not been invited”; others, including those of better quality, read: “he invites himself, though he was not going to invite him.” Again, the same printed editions and several manuscripts read: “of his hospitality”; others, more numerous, read: “of his being a guest.” Finally, where the editions mentioned above read “he had already seen his affection,” nearly all the manuscripts instead prefer “he had heard his affection”]. For he knew that his host’s reward would be abundant. Yet although he had not yet heard the voice of the one inviting him, he had heard his affection.

83. But lest we seem to have quickly abandoned this blind man, as though he were a tiresome poor person, and passed on to the rich man, let us wait for him, because the Lord also waited; let us question him, because Christ also questioned him. We question because we do not know; he questioned because he knew. We question in order to learn by what means this man was healed; he questioned so that through one man we might learn by what means we might merit to see the Lord. For he questioned so that we might believe that no one can be healed unless he confesses.

“And immediately he saw, and followed him, glorifying God. . . . And he passed through Jericho” (Chapter 18, verse 43).

84. For he would not otherwise have seen unless he had followed Christ, unless he had proclaimed the Lord, unless he had passed beyond the world. Let us return to good relations with the rich also. We do not wish to offend the rich, because we wish, if possible, to heal all, lest those who have been struck down by the comparison with the camel and abandoned in Zacchaeus sooner than was appropriate should have just cause for resentment.

85. Let them learn that guilt does not cling to possessions but to those who do not know how to use their possessions. For riches are impediments among the wicked, but aids to virtue among the good. Certainly Zacchaeus was rich, yet he was chosen by Christ. By giving half of his possessions to the poor and also restoring fourfold whatever he had taken by fraud—for the other half is not enough, and generosity has no grace if injustice persists, since what is sought is not spoil but gifts—he received a richer reward than he had bestowed.

86. (Verse 2.) Appropriately he is introduced as chief of the tax collectors. For who would despair of himself when even this man attained salvation, whose wealth came from fraud [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “this man, whose understanding came from fraud, attained salvation”]? “And he himself,” it says, “was rich.” Thus you may know that not all rich people are greedy.

87. (Verse 3.) What does it mean that Scripture specifies the stature of no other person except this one: “because he was small in stature”? See whether perhaps he was small in wickedness, or was still small in faith. For he had not yet made his promise when he climbed; he had not yet seen Christ, and therefore was rightly still small [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “he had again promised to repay”]. Finally, John was great because he both saw Christ and saw the Spirit, like a dove, remaining upon Christ, as he himself says: “I saw the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him” (John 1:32).

88. And what is the crowd except the ignorant confusion of the multitude, which cannot see the summit of wisdom? Therefore, as long as Zacchaeus is in the crowd, he does not see Christ. He climbs above the crowd and sees him; that is, having passed beyond the ignorance of the common people, he was found worthy to behold the one he desired. Beautifully, he adds [Note: All editions and many manuscripts read: “having now passed beyond the common people, he was found worthy to behold the knowledge which,” etc.—an inept reading. The manuscripts Corbie, one Colbert manuscript, Victorius, and several others restore the text followed here. After “behold,” the Roman edition inserts “in which one may also observe a mystery,” and continues “for he was small in stature,” etc., as in section 87.]:

(Verse 4.) “Because the Lord was going to pass that way.”

89. Whether where the sycamore stood, or where he was going to believe; so that he might both preserve the mystery and sow grace. For he had come in order to pass through the Jews to the Gentiles [Note: The Roman edition alone, in a passage partly shortened and partly rearranged, restored the text as follows: “For he had come in order to pass through the Jews to the Gentiles, so that he might both preserve the mystery and sow grace”].

90. Zacchaeus therefore saw him above; for already, by the elevation of faith, he stood out among the fruits of new works like the fruitful height of a tree. And since we have turned from the typological meaning to moral matters, on the Lord’s day it is pleasant to relax the mind amid the wishes of so many believers and to mingle in a festival. Zacchaeus was in the sycamore, clearly the new fruit of the new age, so that this saying too might be fulfilled: “The fig tree has put forth its young figs” (Song 2:13). For Christ came so that human beings, not fruits, might be born from trees.

We read elsewhere: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:48) [Note: The Roman edition and manuscript Reg. read: “Therefore Nathanael.” But the other editions and the remaining manuscripts preserve the negation]. Therefore Nathanael was not under the tree—that is, above the root—because he was righteous, for the root is holy. Yet Nathanael was under the tree because he was under the Law; Zacchaeus was above the tree because he was above the Law. The former was Christ’s hidden defender, the latter his public preacher. The former was still seeking Christ from the Law; the latter, now above the Law, was leaving his possessions and following the Lord.

(Verses 16.) “Behold, your mina has earned ten minas.”

91. The order is appropriate: since he was going to call the Gentiles and command the Jews—who did not want Christ to reign over them—to be killed, he first presented this comparison, lest anyone say: “He had given nothing to the Jewish people; how could it have become better? Or what is demanded from one who received nothing?” This mina is not insignificant, since, when the Gospel woman did not find it, she lit a lamp, searched for it with the light, and rejoiced when she found it (Luke 15:8).

92. (Verse 18.) Finally, one person made ten minas from one, another five [Note: The old edition reads: “Perhaps this one has moral meanings . . . the other ten doubled.” The Roman edition differs from it only in having cut off the word “ten.” But no other manuscript tradition provides a basis for the variation, except that in some manuscripts a simple vowel is written in place of the diphthong]. Perhaps the five have a moral meaning, because there are five bodily senses; the ten, being doubled, signify both the mystical meaning of the Law and moral integrity. Hence Matthew also set down five talents and two talents (Matt. 25:15): in the five talents, let there be moral meanings; in the two, both the mystical and the moral. Thus what is lower in number is richer in substance.

Here too we can understand the ten minas as the ten words, that is, the teaching of the Law; and the five minas as the principles of discipline. But I wish the teacher of the Law to be perfect in all things; for the kingdom of God is not in speech but in virtue.

93. Appropriately, since he is speaking of the Jews, only two are said to bring back the money multiplied—not money of bronze, certainly, but the interest of teaching [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “the interest of stewardship.” But the word “discussion” frequently has in Ambrose the same meaning as exposition or evangelical preaching. Again, that same edition, together with the editions of Erasmus and Gill, differs from the others. For there is a different kind of interest on money. The edition of Amerbach and the manuscripts agree with us, except that in two manuscripts one reads: “the interest of money,” or “of profit”]. For one thing is monetary interest, another is the interest of heavenly doctrine.

94. (Verse 23.) Finally, when the Lord says, “Why did you not put my money on the table?” (Matt. 25:18), he seeks interest not on our money but on his own.

95. One man says that he hid it in the earth. He buried the reason that was given to us in the image and likeness of God beneath the pursuit of pleasure, and hid it, as it were, in a pit of flesh. Nothing is said about the others, who, like wasteful debtors, lost what they had received (Luke 20:10). In those two there are the few who were sent twice to the tenants of the vineyard; in the rest are all the Jews (Matt. 24:18). Matthew also wished this comparison to apply to us: just as the rich man who does not share his money with the poor is guilty, so also the person who does not distribute the grace of his teaching to the uninstructed, though he is able to teach, is guilty of no small fault (Book 5 on the Faith, chapter 1). Since we have discussed this in the books on the Faith, it will be better to pass over it briefly.

96. What can the ten cities be (verse 17), unless perhaps they are souls over which, by right, the one who has lent out the Lord’s money—and those pure, tested utterances, like silver—to human minds is placed? For just as Jerusalem is said to have been built “like a city” (Ps. 121:3), so there are peaceful souls. And just as angels preside, so do those who have merited the life of angels.

BOOK NINE

(Verses 29–30.) “And it happened that, when he drew near Bethphage and Bethany, at the mountain called the Mount of Olives, he sent two disciples, saying: ‘Go into the village opposite; as you enter it, you will find a colt of a donkey tied up, on which no one has ever sat.’”

1. Beautifully, having left the Jews, the Lord ascended the temple, intending to dwell in the affections of the Gentiles. For this is the true temple, in which the Lord is worshiped not in the letter but in the spirit. This is God’s temple, founded by the sequence of faith, not by a structure of stones. Those who hated are therefore abandoned; those who were going to love are chosen.

2. And therefore he came to the Mount of Olives, in order to plant young olive trees in the height of virtue, whose mother is the Jerusalem that is above. On this mountain is the heavenly farmer, so that all who have been planted in the house of God may individually say: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord” (Ps. 51:10). And perhaps the mountain itself is Christ. For who else would produce such fruits of olives—not through the swelling abundance of berries, but through the fullness of the Spirit of nations made fruitful? He is the one through whom we ascend and to whom we ascend. He is the door; he is the way, the one who is opened and who opens, who is knocked upon by those entering and worshiped by those who have earned their reward.

3. Therefore the colt was in the village, and it was tied up with the donkey. It could not be released except at the Lord’s command. The apostolic hand released it. Such an act, such a life, such grace. Be such a person yourself, so that you too may be able to release those who are bound.

4. Now let us consider who those were who, after their error had been exposed, were expelled from paradise and are bound in the village [Note: All editions read “are in the village”; Amerbach reads “bound again,” while other editions read “banished.” Nearly all manuscripts, however, agree with the reading followed in the text. Allegory clearly demands it, since sinners bound by the chains of their offenses are represented by the donkey and colt tied up in the village]. And you see how those whom death had expelled were recalled by life (Matt. 21:2). Therefore, according to Matthew, we read of both the donkey and the colt: since both sexes had been expelled in the two human beings, both sexes are recalled in the two animals.

Thus in the mother donkey he represented Eve, as it were, in her error; here, in the colt, he expressed the universality of the Gentile people. And therefore the colt is ridden upon the donkey.

5. And appropriately: “on which no one has sat,” because no one had sat upon it before Christ called the peoples of the nations to the Church. Accordingly, according to Mark, you have: “on which no human being has yet sat” (Mark 11:2). It was held bound by the chains of unbelief, enslaved to an unjust master, serving error [Note: The Roman edition and a few manuscripts read “serving error.” Other editions and by far the majority of manuscripts read “serving through error,” that is, through error serving the demon, to whom the following words refer. In those words, for “one whom he had made guilty,” as the editions and many manuscripts have it, four manuscripts read “not nature but God,” and three read “not nature but the Lord”; the latter may perhaps be the true reading]. But he could not claim dominion over one whom guilt, not nature, had made subject. And therefore, when he is called “Lord,” one is recognized; for there are “many gods and many lords,” but in a general sense [Note: Many manuscripts read: “but one God in general”]. For us, however, there is one God and one Lord. Therefore, even if he is not explicitly named, the Lord is defined not now by the addition of a person [Note: The same Roman edition alone reads: “by the unity of nature.” But Ambrose calls that universality the common nature equally belonging to the three persons. Below, where the old edition and part of the manuscripts read “is outside by sight,” our text, with the others, reads “is outside on the road,” except for one or two manuscripts in which . . . “in the village” appears. The Roman edition retained only “is outside”], but by the universality of nature.

6. Mark, however, introduced him as tied up before the door (Mark 11:4), because whoever is outside Christ is outside on the road, while whoever is in Christ is not outside. “In a thoroughfare,” he added, where there is no fixed possession—neither manger, nor food, nor stable. Miserable is the slavery whose right of possession is wandering; for the one who has no single master has many masters. Outsiders bind him in order to possess him; this one releases him in order to hold him, for he knows that gifts are stronger than bonds [Note: The Roman edition reads “some bind him.” Other editions and all manuscripts more appropriately read “outsiders bind him,” that is, those who are not the legitimate Giver. Again, that edition, together with the old edition and several manuscripts, reads “he knows that he has rights”; Gill in the margin and the larger number of better manuscripts read “he knows that he has gifts.” Both readings may have their own meaning].

7. Nor is it without significance that two disciples are sent: Peter to Cornelius, Paul to the others (Acts 10:23 and 13:3). And therefore he did not designate persons but specified a number. Yet if anyone insists on identifying persons, he can consider Philip, whom the Spirit sent to Gaza (Acts 8:26), when he baptized the eunuch of Queen Candace and sowed the word of the Lord from Azotus to Caesarea through all the cities. Nor should we pass over the fact that he immediately says they are to be sent back, because those who would proclaim the Lord Jesus in the territories of the Gentiles were to be dispatched.

8. (Verse 34.) When those men had been sent and were untying the colt, did they use their own words? Certainly not. They said what Jesus had told them, so that you may recognize that they infused faith into the Gentile peoples not by their own speech but by the word of God, not in their own name but in Christ’s; and that the hostile powers, which claimed the service of the nations for themselves, yielded to the divine command.

9. (Verse 35.) Hence the apostles also spread their own garments beneath Christ, whether so that they might exalt the glory of the work through evangelical preaching [Note: Thus read all manuscripts and editions except the Roman edition, which has: “so that they might exalt the glory of the deed of evangelical preaching.” This has no intelligible sense]. For in the divine Scriptures garments are often virtues, which by their own virtue would somewhat soften the hardness of the nations, so that they might offer the services of a successful ride with diligent devotion [Note: Several manuscripts read: “so that, as happy servants of an unhindered rider, they might offer their services,” and so forth].

For the Lord of the world did not choose to be carried on the back of a donkey in the manner of a public spectacle; rather, through the hidden mystery, he wished to spread out the inner chambers of our mind, and in the secret places of our souls the mystical rider might take his seat in the inner assembly, with divinity infused, as it were, into a certain body, directing the footsteps of the mind and restraining the wantonness of the flesh, so that, by the guidance of devotion, he might tame the accustomed inclination of the Gentile people. Blessed are those who have received such a rider upon the inner reins! Truly blessed are those whose mouths, lest they break out into excessive speech, the bridle of the heavenly word has restrained!

10. What is this bridle, brothers? Who will teach me how it either restrains or releases human mouths? He showed me the bridle who said: “That speech may be granted to me in the opening of my mouth” (Acts 9:5). Speech, then, is a bridle; speech is a goad. Therefore it is hard for you to kick against the goad. He taught us, then, to open the heart, endure the goad, and bear the yoke. Let another teach the restraints of the tongue. For the virtue of silence is rarer than that of speech. Let that person teach us who, like a mute, did not open his mouth against deceit (Ps. 37:14), prepared for lashes and refusing no blows, so that he might be a devout seat for God [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “to open the mouth,” a conjecture that is sufficiently attractive].

11. Learn from God’s household servant to carry Christ, because he first carried you when the shepherd brought back the wandering sheep (Luke 15:6). Learn to spread out the back of your mind with attentive devotion; learn to be beneath Christ so that you may be above the world. Not everyone easily carries Christ, but the one who can say: “I am bowed down and humbled exceedingly; I roared because of the groaning of my heart” (Ps. 37:9). And if you desire not to be moved, fix your foot firmly upon those garments of the saints that have been spread beneath you. Take care not to walk with muddy feet; take care not to leave the paths of the prophets spread out for you by walking across them [Note: The same manuscripts read: “by taking crosswise steps”]. For, so that the journey might be safer for the nations to come, those who went before Jesus had fortified the path with their own garments all the way to the temple of God. So that you might walk without stumbling, the Lord’s disciples stripped off the garments of their own bodies and, amid the opposition of the crowds, spread the road for you through their martyrdom. Yet if anyone wishes to understand it this way, we do not object: the colt had already begun to walk upon the garments of the Jews.

12. As for the fragments of branches (Matt. 21:8), which ordinarily entangle the steps of those walking, I would certainly have hesitated about their meaning, had not the good farmer of the whole world taught me in the preceding passages that the axe has already been placed at the roots of the trees, so that, at the coming of the Lord and Savior, it might cut down the unfruitful and lay low upon the ground the empty glory of the unproductive nations, to be trampled under the feet of the faithful. Thus, by the spirit of a renewed mind, the nations, like shoots of young trees, can sprout from ancient trunks.

13. Do not therefore despise this little donkey. For just as there are ravenous wolves in sheep’s clothing, so, conversely, there is a human being hidden within beneath the appearance of a beast; for beneath the cast-off coverings of the body, which we share with animals, a mind full of God is kept alive. That this pertains to the figure of human beings Saint John made clearer (John 12:13) by adding that “they took for themselves the piths of palm trees” [Note: The Roman edition reads “palm branches.” The other editions and all manuscripts read “the medullas of palms.” We also find the author using this expression in the work Questions on the Old and New Testaments, question 82, in Appendix III of the new edition of the works of Saint Augustine]. For “the righteous flourishes like a palm.” And therefore, as Christ approached, the banners of righteousness and the insignia of triumphs were already being raised above human shoulders. Why does the crowd marvel at what it performs as a mystery? Even if it does not know what it is marveling at, it nevertheless marvels because wisdom sits in that colt, power remains, and righteousness adheres.

14. Do not despise that donkey either, which once saw the angel of God (Num. 22:23), whom a human being could not see. It saw him, carried him, and spoke, so that you might recognize that in later times, at the coming of the great angel of God, those Gentiles who had previously been like donkeys would speak.

15. (Verse 37.) Beautifully, according to Luke, we read that the crowds praising God came to meet him as he descended from the mountain [Col. 1797B], so that they might signify that the worker of the spiritual mystery had come to them from heaven. The crowd therefore recognizes God, calls him king, and repeats the prophecy (Ps. 117:24): “Hosanna to the Son of David.” That is, it declares that the expected redeemer of the house of David had also come in the flesh as David’s son [Note: Erasmus criticizes Ambrose, as though here, together with Hilary of Poitiers, he were teaching with insufficient learning that the word “Hosanna” signifies “the redemption of the house of David.” But the correction is not very clever. Saint Ambrose is not discussing the grammatical meaning of that word; he is indicating only that the people, by auspicious and prophetic acclamations, declared the arrival of the redeemer of David’s house]. And this same crowd, after a brief interval, would crucify him. Truly a memorable sign of divine action: testimony is wrested from unwilling witnesses against themselves, when by their affections they deny the God whom they confess with their voices. Hence also that saying of the Lord:

(Verses 40.) “If these should be silent, the stones will cry out.”

16. Nor is it surprising if stones, contrary to their nature, respond with the praises of the Lord, when those who are harder than rocks proclaim the one they have killed. Or perhaps, because after the Lord’s Passion the Jews became silent, there were living stones, according to Peter, destined to cry out (1 Pet. 2:5). Thus, although their affections were in conflict, the crowd nevertheless escorts God to his temple with praise.

17. But God does not wish his temple to be a merchant’s lodging house, but a dwelling place of holiness; nor does he form the use of priestly ministry through a religion that can be bought, but through free service. Consider, therefore, what the Lord’s deeds prescribe for you as an example of how to live.

18. “And he was casting out all those who were buying and selling in the temple; and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves” (Matt. 21:12) [Note: This text from Matthew is found in all manuscripts and old editions. The Roman edition rejected it and substituted another passage from Luke. Yet in this work Ambrose more than once proposes and explains passages from other evangelists without naming the author].

Thus, in general, he taught above that secular transactions ought to be absent from God’s temple; but specifically he drove out the money changers. Who are the money changers except those who seek profit from the Lord’s money and do not distinguish between good and evil? For the Lord’s money is divine Scripture. He distributed denarii to his servants when he was about to depart, and he divided talents (Matt. 25:14); and for the healing of the wounded man he left two coins with the innkeeper (Luke 10:35), for our wounds are healed by the two Testaments.

But you, as a good money changer, store up the Lord’s utterances—the pure utterances, silver tested by fire and purified by the sevenfold Spirit (Ps. 11:7). Do not accept the counterfeit image of the king—for Satan also disguises himself as an angel of light—through an impious exchange [Note: Several manuscripts read: “and do not counterfeit the image of the King . . . accepting an impious exchange”]. Do not mix with your treasure an adulterated image of your prince, produced by the fraud of Arian unbelief. Do not test the ears of the faithful with the sound of money, lest the ringing of bronze drive out their attention to sacred Scriptures, or the desire to possess become inserted into devout affections. Therefore not all money changers are to be excluded; for there are also good ones. Finally, he says: “You should have given my money to the money changers, and when I came I would have received it with interest” (Matt. 25:27). If the coin is Scripture, then the interest also is Scripture.

19. But why he overturned the seats of those selling doves I do not understand according to the literal meaning. For dealers in birds could not claim for themselves the dignity of an honored seat in the marketplace. What distinction of rank is there in doves? Yet the form of the Lord’s baptism admonishes us, when the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove (Luke 3:22): by the type of those merchants expelled from the temple, it shows that those who trade in the grace of the Holy Spirit cannot have a share in the Church of God. “Freely you have received,” he says; “freely give” (Matt. 10:8).

Finally, to Simon, who thought that the gift of sanctification could be conferred upon him for a price, Peter replied: “May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money. You have no part or share in this faith” (Acts 8:20–21).

20. I also think that the sellers of sheep and oxen (John 2:15) are those who, from the labor or simplicity of others, pursue sordid auctions and set up certain markets; or, because the sheep and oxen are driven out while the doves are ordered to be removed, the Jewish people seem to be excluded. For Ephraim is like a dove, because their Lord hates both their offspring and their labors (Hos. 7:11). Bronze is poured out so that grace may be gathered; the table of the money changers is overturned so that the Lord’s table may take its place; the altar is cast down so that altars may be raised.

21. He did this not with any force at hand or with riches (John 2:15), but struck the crowds with a whip made of cords, and no one dared resist. And now he uses a rod, now a whip—for “your rod is upright” (Ps. 44:7), “the rod of your kingdom.” A rod, to correct; a whip, to persuade. There it was direct; here it is a moral instruction, as though bent, by which the conscience of the sinner is scourged with a slow blow. The terrors of the prophets are one thing, the appeals of the apostles another; yet in both there is the discipline of one word.

And therefore he made a whip from cords, because it says: “The cords have fallen to me in excellent places; indeed, my inheritance is excellent to me” (Ps. 15:6). For cords are what surveyors use to divide the boundaries of measured fields [Note: The edition reads: “the boundaries of lands to be measured”; below, “that he might measure spaces.” The manuscripts read: “of lands to be surveyed . . . that he might survey them”]. Thus, like a good surveyor, he distinguished the boundaries of the Synagogue and the Church and ordered the sacrilegious to leave the temple. For a new measurer of fruitful souls had come, measuring the kinds of fields, not their extent.

22. Yet beautifully, no limit of possession is enclosed by stretched cords, nor are the boundaries of faith confined as though belonging to a defined property. Instead, by the whip freely extending without limit, the boundaries of the Church are extended immeasurably. The Jews are expelled, not by some prescribed exile, but without limit, so that nowhere in the world would a place remain for the Synagogue.

(Chapter 20.—Verse 9.) “A man planted a vineyard.”

23. Most people derive various meanings from the designation “vineyard”; but Isaiah clearly stated that the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isaiah 5:7). Who other than God founded this vineyard? He, therefore, is the one who leased it and went away into a distant country—not because the Lord moved from one place to another, since he is always everywhere, but because he is more present to those who are diligent and absent from those who are negligent. He remained away for a long time, so that the exaction would not seem premature. For the more indulgent the generosity, the less excusable the obstinacy.

24. Accordingly, in Matthew you rightly find: “And he surrounded it with a hedge” (Matthew 21:33)—that is, he enclosed it with the fortification of divine protection, lest it be easily exposed to the attacks of spiritual beasts. “And he dug a winepress in it” (ibid.). How are we to understand what the winepress is, unless perhaps because the psalms are inscribed “for the winepresses” (Psalms 8; 80; 83), inasmuch as in them the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, like holy must fermenting through the Spirit of the prophets, have surged with greater abundance? Indeed, those upon whom the Holy Spirit poured out were thought to be drunk (Acts 2:13). Here, then, he also dug a winepress into which the interior fruit of rational grapes might flow through spiritual infusion. “He built a tower” (Matthew 21:33), raising up, that is, the summit of the Law; and thus he leased this vineyard, fortified, equipped, and adorned, to the Jews.

25. (Verse 10.) “And at the season of the fruits he sent his servants.” He rightly says “the season of the fruits,” not “the yield”; for no fruit appeared among the Jews, no yield from this vineyard, of which the Lord says: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isaiah 5:2). Thus the winepresses overflowed not with the wine of joy, nor with spiritual must, but with the blood of the prophets. Jeremiah, for example, was thrown into a pit (Jeremiah 38:6); these were already the winepresses of the Jews, filled not with wine but with gore. And although the prophets in general seem to be represented, the reading nevertheless permits us to believe that the one who was stoned was Naboth (1 Kings 21:13). Even if we have received no prophetic word from him, we have nevertheless received a prophetic deed, because by his own blood he prophesied that many martyrs would arise for this vineyard. But who is the one wounded in the head? Surely Isaiah, whose bodily frame was more easily divided by the saw than his faith was bent, his constancy worn down, or the strength of his mind cut away.

26. (Verses 11–14.) It therefore came about that, after he had appointed many others whom the Jews dismissed dishonored and empty-handed, since they had been unable to accomplish anything through them, at last he sent even his only-begotten Son. The treacherous, wishing to remove him as though he were the heir, killed him by crucifying him and cast him out by denying him.

27. Let us briefly consider how great and how many the implications are. First, because goodness is natural and often trusts those who are unworthy; then, because Christ came as the final remedy for evils; and finally, because the one who denies the heir despairs of the author. Christ is the heir, and likewise both testator and heir, because he survives his own death and receives, as hereditary benefits, the fruits of the Testaments that he himself established in our spiritual progress.

28. (Verse 15.) He therefore rightly asks the question, so that they may condemn themselves by their own sentence. He says that the lord of the vineyard will come, either because the Father’s majesty is also present in the Son, or because in the final times he comes more fully into contact with human affections. They therefore pronounce sentence against themselves: the wicked will perish, and the vineyard will be transferred to other tenants. Let us consider, then, who the tenants are and what the vineyard is.

29. The vineyard is a type of us: the people of God, planted upon the eternal root of the vine, rises above the earth. Though it presents the appearance of a lowly soil, it now grows young with budding blossom, now is clothed in encircling greenery, and now accepts a gentle yoke, when it has grown through more mature branches, like the shoots of a second vine, as though arms.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “with more mature shoots, as though arms.”]

For the all-powerful Father is the cultivator, and Christ is the vine (John 15:1 and following); we, however, are the branches, and unless we bear fruit in Christ, we are cut off by the pruning hook of the eternal cultivator. The people are therefore rightly called Christ’s vineyard, either because the sign of the cross is displayed upon the forehead, or because its fruit is gathered at the final season of the year, or because in the Church of God there is an equal measure and no distinction among all classes, just as among the rows of a vineyard: among the poor and the rich, the lowly and the powerful, slaves and masters.

As the vine is joined to trees, so the body is joined to the soul, and the soul likewise to the body. As the vineyard is raised when it is tied up, and when it is pruned it is not diminished but increased, so the holy people, when bound, are stripped [of their bonds]; when humbled, they are raised up; when pruned, they are crowned.

[Note: Supply “of bonds,” as is expressed at the end of the following section.]

Moreover, just as a tender shoot, cut from an old tree, is grafted into the growth of another root, so this holy people, with the scars of the old shoot disentangled, is nourished and grows upon that wood of the cross as in the lap of a loving mother. And just as water is sent down into the deep furrows of the earth, so the Holy Spirit, poured into this prison-like body, washes away everything foul with the irrigation of saving water and raises the condition of our limbs into heavenly discipline.

[Note: The Roman edition has, “And the Holy Spirit, poured into this prison-like body, as though sent down into the deep furrows of the earth, [is] water,” and so forth.]

30. The diligent cultivator is accustomed to dig, [Note: All editions read “to irrigate, prune,” while almost all manuscripts read “to yoke”; yet many, together with the editions, read “to prune.” Earlier witnesses, however, have “to stretch out,” which here must be understood as “to extend.” Again, in the following verse, instead of the word “covered,” which all editions and some manuscripts have, several more and older witnesses prefer “cultivated.” If this word is correct, it means the same as “tilled”; but we fear that it may sound somewhat harsh to educated ears.] to yoke, and to stretch out this vineyard. After digging away the mounds of earthly mass, he is accustomed to expose the coverings of our body sometimes to the sun’s heat and sometimes to the rain, and to clear the soil, lest a bud be injured by thorns, lest the shade of leaves grow luxuriant, and lest the fruitless boasting of words, overshadowing the virtues, hinder the maturity of our natural character.

But let us fear no adversity for this vineyard, which the ever-watchful guardian of the Lord our Savior has enclosed against all the allurements of worldly wickedness with the wall of eternal life and has extended its branches as far as the sea (Psalm 79:12). For “the earth is the Lord’s” (Psalm 23:1). Everywhere God the Father is worshiped; everywhere Christ the Lord is adored.

31. This is our vintage. Let us therefore rejoice and be secure. Let one portion load its gentle lap with bunches of grapes upon the cords; let others sip heavenly gifts with their mouths; let many, pressing out the fruit of the divine gift through the steps of good intentions, dip their bare feet, stripped of their boots, into the flowing must. For the place on which we stand is holy ground, and therefore the sandals must be removed (Exodus 3:5), so that, as the spiritual footprint ascends to the tribunal of the most sacred seat, the body may be stripped of the bonds of corporeal attachment. It is fitting that the vintage here should belong to the whole world, since the vineyard belongs to the whole world.

32. Behold the acceptable time, when the year is not chilled by the wintry frosts of darkening treachery, nor does an ugly crust of blasphemy form in the high clouds while the ice endures. [Note: The Erasmian edition and those following it, together with some manuscripts, read “nor by deep snows.” Amerbach’s edition, with several more and better manuscripts, has the reading printed in the text. Nor is this improper, if that shapeless crust formed in the high clouds is understood to signify hail, which is always harmful to crops.]

Rather, freed from the storms of sacrilege, the earth now brings forth new fruits. [Note: All editions read “It passes over the old”; most manuscripts read “It bears the old”; some have “It drives them away”; Corbie and several others have “It truly bears.” The last is more suitable, as is clear from what follows, where Justina’s persecution and the peace that followed it are unmistakably indicated.]

It truly bears fruit; for the storm of all dissensions has died down, and all the fires and heats of worldly desire by which the people of Italy were formerly seethed amid the flames of Jewish savagery and, more recently, of Arian savagery are now tempered by a calm breeze. The storm has subsided, harmony sails on, faith breathes. Eagerly the sailors return to the harbors of faith that they had abandoned, and press sweet kisses upon their native shores, rejoicing that they have been freed from dangers and released from errors.

33. Hail, vineyard worthy of so great a guardian! It was consecrated not by the blood of one Naboth alone, but by the blood of innumerable prophets and, greater still, by the precious blood of the Lord. Although Naboth was not frightened into suppressing his constancy by royal threats, nor induced by lavish rewards to sell his religious devotion, but resisted the king’s desire (1 Kings 21:3), so that no mallow vegetable might be planted in his little gardens after the vine had been cut down, and, since he could do nothing else, extinguished with his own blood the fires prepared for the vines, he nevertheless defended a temporal vineyard. You, however, were planted for us forever by the death of many martyrs. The cross of the apostles, emulating the Lord’s Passion, spread you to the ends of the whole world.

(Verses 24.) “Whose image and inscription does it have?”

34. Here the Lord teaches that we must be prudent in answering heretics or Jews. Elsewhere he said: “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16). Most people understand this passage to mean that, because Christ’s cross was proclaimed through the serpent lifted up, so that it might abolish the serpentine venom of spiritual wickedness, one ought to be wise like Christ and simple like the Spirit. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “may seem to abolish; one ought to be wise as the simple Spirit of Christ.”]

Here, then, is that serpent for you, the one who always guards the head and excludes the deadly wound. [Note: The larger and more valuable number of manuscripts reads thus. Some manuscripts, and all editions, read: “Imitate that serpent too.”] When the Jews asked him whether he had received authority from heaven, he replied: “The baptism of John—was it from heaven or from human beings?” (Luke 20:4). Since they did not dare deny that it was from heaven, he refuted the madness of those who denied that its author was from heaven.

When asked for the two-drachma tax, he asks about the image, for one image is the image of God and another is the image of the world (Matthew 17:23). Hence that apostle also admonishes us: “As we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one” (1 Corinthians 15:49).

35. Christ does not have Caesar’s image, because he is the image of God. Peter does not have Caesar’s image, because he said: “We have left everything and followed you” (Matthew 19:27). Caesar’s image is not found in James or John, because they are “sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17). But it is found in the sea, where those dragons, their heads crushed upon the water, and the great dragon himself, his head shattered, are given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia (Psalm 73:14).

If, therefore, he did not have Caesar’s image, why did he pay the tax? He did not give what was his own; he returned to the world what belonged to the world. And you, if you wish not to be subject to Caesar, do not possess what belongs to the world. But if you possess riches, you are subject to Caesar. If you wish to owe nothing to an earthly ruler, leave all that is yours and follow Christ.

36. (Verse 25.) He rightly decides first that what belongs to Caesar must be returned to Caesar; for no one can belong to the Lord unless he has first renounced the world. Yet we all renounce it in words, but not all renounce it in affection. For when we receive the sacraments, we renounce it. [Note: Understand here the sacrament of baptism, in which even now we renounce the devil and his pomp—that is, the vanities of the world. This custom is explained more fully in *On the Initiation*, chapter 2, and in Book 1 of *On the Sacraments*, also chapter 2.]

How grievous are the bonds incurred when one promises something to God and does not fulfill it! “It is better,” he says, “not to vow than to vow and not to pay” (Ecclesiastes 5:4). The contract of faith is greater than that of money. Pay what you have promised while you are in this body, before the collector comes and sends you to prison. “Amen I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last penny” (Matthew 5:26).

(Verses 28.) “If someone’s brother has died.”

37. The Sadducees—that is, the more detestable portion of the Jews—test the Lord in this passage. Their folly is openly reproved, but mystically the argument is turned back upon them, because they excluded from themselves the example of chastity. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “What an example of chastity they gave from themselves!” The remaining—and better—part reads as printed here.] According to the letter a woman is compelled to marry, even against her will, so that a brother might raise up offspring for his deceased brother (Deuteronomy 25:5). Thus the letter kills, as though it were a procuress of vices; but the spirit is the teacher of chastity (2 Corinthians 3:6).

38. Let us therefore see whether this woman is the Synagogue, which had seven husbands, just as it is said to the Samaritan woman: “You have had five husbands” (John 4:18). For the Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses. [Note: A certain learned and keen critic thinks this is why the Samaritans admitted only the five books of Moses: at the time when the separation between Jews and Samaritans occurred, namely under Rehoboam, none of the other divine books had yet been published. But we fear that this conjecture will not be sufficiently convincing to everyone.]

The Synagogue follows seven principally, and because of its treachery received from none of them the seed of hereditary posterity. Therefore it will not be able to share in the resurrection with its husbands, because it inverted the spiritual command according to the sense of the flesh (Revelation 20:6). For no carnal brother was appointed to raise up the seed of a deceased brother; rather, it was the one who, when the Jewish people had died, would take for himself as wife the wisdom of divine worship and would raise up from her a seed among the apostles. These, like the still-unformed remnants of the deceased Jews, left in the womb of the Synagogue, were deemed worthy, according to the election of grace, to be preserved through the admixture of a new seed.

39. The Synagogue frequently receives a stole, which is the insignia of marriage, as though it were the author of the faithful. [Note: Here “stole” is called the insignia of marriage because, as the holy man teaches above in Book 7, section 231, it is a nuptial garment. These words indicate that it was customary among the ancients for married matrons to receive a stole, without which, Tertullian states in *On the Pallium*, chapter 4, they were thereafter not permitted to go out in public.]

It is also frequently introduced as repudiated, because it is the mother of the faithless. The bodily Law died to it so that the spiritual Law might rise again. Therefore, if the holy people of God have loved the five books of the Law with a certain marital affection and have obeyed them as marital commands, they will have a heavenly fellowship in the resurrection, not confused by the shame of bodily pollution but enriched by the gifts of divine grace. [Note: Most manuscripts and all editions except the Roman one read this way. The Roman edition, together with two more recent manuscripts, has “if it has loved seven books.” This is less appropriate, since Ambrose is dealing with the books of the Law, by which name the five books of Moses are commonly designated.]

# BOOK TEN

1503

(Verses 42.) “The Lord said to my Lord.”

1. As the Lord brings his commandments to completion, he also concludes, at the end of his Testament, the faith and mercy that precede his Passion: faith, namely, that we believe Christ to be our Lord and God and believe him to sit at the right hand of God—not that he sits bodily, since he is everywhere. Indeed, he himself is in the Father, because he is in the substance of God, with one power and one majesty. He is therefore in the Father, and the Father in him, because the Word is in God and God in the Word. He is in the Father because he is the Word; he is at the right hand of the Father because he shares the Father’s nature and is second to none; he was sent by the Father because he descended from heaven to fulfill the Father’s will.

Remove from this the questions of treachery, and religion is complete. He is not placed above the Father because he sits at his right hand, nor does he suffer insult because he is sent. No hierarchy of dignity is sought where there is the fullness of divinity.

2. (Verse 44.) We must also consider that he rebukes those who call Christ the son of David. How, then, did that blind man merit healing by confessing him to be the Son of David (Luke 18:43)? How did the children, saying “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matthew 21:9), offer glory to God through their exalted proclamation?

But they are not rebuked here because they confess him to be David’s son; they are rebuked because they do not believe him to be the Son of God. In true faith, it is not one or the other, but both together. For although at the beginning we judged that we should know nothing except “Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2), now, as though near the judgment, we no longer know Christ as crucified but await him coming upon the clouds. The unbeliever [text corrupt: “is struck by wounds …”]; the faithful, snatched up into the air, goes out to meet Christ.

3. Let us therefore believe that Christ is both God and human: one in both, not one rather than the other. His enemies are subjected to him by the Father, not through any weakness of his power, but through the unity of nature, because one works in the other. For the Son also subjects enemies to the Father, who glorifies the Father upon earth (John 17:4).

And the Father gave the Son the Name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–10); yet the Son also says to the Father: “I have manifested your name to human beings, which you gave me” (John 17:6). In giving the Name that is above every name, he did not give more than the Son possessed, but gave him everything that he possessed. He gave this name so that “every tongue might confess to God that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).

4. Consider each point. The Father subjects things to the Son, and the Son subjects things to the Father. The Father raises the Son, and the Son himself raises himself. Hence he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

The Father is Lord and the Son is Lord: “The Lord said to my Lord.” Yet there are not two Lords, but one Lord, because the Father is God and the Son is God; yet there is one God, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. There is one God because there is one divinity: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of your kingdom is a righteous scepter. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Psalm 44:7–8).

But there is one God, in whom the teaching of the New and Old Testaments agrees. For in the Old Testament it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God,” and “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:5, 13). In the New Testament: “One God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4:6).

Thus the Father is Lord and the Son is Lord, but there is one Lord. Finally, it is written: “Know that the Lord himself is God” (Psalm 99:3). It is written in the New Testament: “Do not serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24); in the Old Testament: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

Therefore the Apostle speaks wondrously, so as neither to say that there are two Gods nor to name two Lords, and so as not to detract from either the Son or the Father: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6). For the one who is God is also Lord, and the one who is Lord is God. Finally, it is written: “Know that the Lord himself is our God” (Psalm 99:3).

5. Everything, therefore, that the Father has, the Son also has. The Father is God according to the principle of generation; the Son is God according to the unity of the image. [Note: “The Son … subjected” is absent from Amerbach. The Erasmian and Gillot editions and our manuscripts have the text as printed, except that Erasmus places it after “is the Son’s root.” In the Roman edition the final words are changed to: “… subjects to himself all that the Father is able.”]

The Son is Lord because, although he could subject everything to himself by his power, he subjected it by reason; the Father is Lord because he is the Son’s root. Thus the Father is distinguished for us from the Son by the definition of the persons and joined to him by the unity of power. Therefore each is in the other, and one in both.

It is the Father’s glory that he has not degenerated in the Son; and the Son’s grace that the Father is seen in the Son. He is therefore not degenerate, in whom is the supreme majesty of unity; nor is he alien, in whom the distinctiveness of generation and the expression of truth are present.

(Cap. 21. Verse 6.) “Not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.”

6. The passage concerning the widow followed (verse 1 and following); since we have already praised her in the book we wrote about widows (*On Widows*), we now set her aside. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Yet, according to what has been proposed, although it is understood of the temple that Solomon built—and that this first was to be overthrown by the enemy of judgment…”]

The statement was made, however, with reference to the temple that Solomon built, and to its destruction at the time of judgment. For nothing made by human work and hand escapes either decay through age, collapse through force, or destruction by fire. Yet there is also another temple constructed of beautiful stones and adorned with gifts, whose overthrow the Lord seems to signify: namely, the Synagogue of the Jews, whose old structure is dissolved when the Church rises.

There is also a temple in each individual person, which collapses when faith fails, especially if someone falsely assumes the name of Christ in order to attack the inner disposition.

7. There can also be an interpretation that benefits me more. For what benefit is it to me to know the day of judgment? What benefit is it to me, conscious of so many sins, if the Lord comes, unless he comes into my soul and returns to my mind, unless Christ lives in me and Christ speaks in me? Christ must therefore come to me; his coming must take place in me. The Lord’s second coming occurs in the world’s decline, when we can say: “But the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

8. But if such a decline of the world finds this person in the upper rooms, so that his way of life is in heaven, then the bodily and visible temple will be destroyed, as will the bodily Law, the bodily and visible Passover, and the bodily and visible unleavened bread. I even dare to say that the temporal Christ will be destroyed, as he was for Paul before he believed, because in the one for whom the world has declined, Christ is eternal.

For this person there is a spiritual temple, a spiritual Law, and also a spiritual Passover, because Christ is killed only once. He feasts on unleavened bread not from earthly grain but from the grain of righteousness. Thus the presence of wisdom, the presence of power and righteousness, and the presence of redemption come to him. For Christ died once for the sins of the people (1 Peter 3:18), but every day he redeems the sins of the people.

(Verses 9.) “When you hear of wars and reports of wars…”

9. When the Lord was asked when the temple’s destruction would occur and what sign would indicate his coming, he teaches about the signs but does not think the time should be disclosed. Matthew added a third question (Matthew 24:3), so that the disciples might ask about the time of the temple’s destruction, the sign of his coming, and the consummation of the world. Luke considered it sufficient for the consummation of the world to be understood if the Lord’s coming were mentioned.

10. No one is more a witness to the heavenly words than we are, whom the end of the world has overtaken. What wars we have experienced, and what reports of wars! The Huns rose against the Alans, the Alans against the Goths, the Goths against the Taifali. [Note: Most manuscripts read “Tatfali”; others, and the editions, more correctly read “Tayfali”; this is how the name is always found in Ammianus, Book 31. But another occasion will arise for discussing this people and the others mentioned here.

As for that plague which devastated not only human beings but cattle as well with such misery, Hermannus, in Book 2, chapter 12 of the *Life of Saint Ambrose*, observes from Baronius that it was very easily driven away by the sign of the cross. The great cardinal relies on the *Eclogue* of Severus Endelechius, the Christian poet, where among other things we find:

**BUCULUS:** Tell me, Tityrus,  
what god snatched you away  
from these calamities,  
so that the plague of cattle,  
which ravaged the neighboring lands,  
did not touch you?

**TITYRUS:** The sign which they say is the cross of God…

This sign, placed upon the middle of the foreheads,  
was the sure salvation  
of all the cattle.

Moreover, what Ambrose said in the preceding book concerning the end of dissensions and the relaxation of the spirit clearly proves that here he is discussing events that had already passed.]

We too, in Illyricum, have been exiles; the exiles of the Goths made us exiles from our homeland, and the end has not yet come. What famine there has been, what plague alike among oxen and human beings, and among other livestock! Thus even those of us who did not endure the war have been made the equals of the conquered by the plague.

Since, therefore, we are at the setting of the world, certain illnesses of the world precede its end. Famine is an illness of the world; pestilence is an illness of the world; persecution is an illness of the world.

11. There are also other wars that the Christian man endures: the battles of different desires and the conflicts of competing pursuits. Domestic enemies are far more serious than external ones. Now greed goads him, now lust inflames him, now fear terrifies him, now anger drives him onward, now ambition moves him, and now the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places attempt to terrify him (Ephesians 6:12).

Thus the wavering disposition of his soul is pressed as though by certain battles and shaken as though by certain earthquakes.

12. But the stronger man says: “Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear; though battle rise against me, in this I will hope” (Psalm 26:3). He stands in the battle line, presenting his breast to the enemy, even if some harsh and towering Goliath should arise (1 Samuel 17:4). While the others are afraid, the lowly man will rise like David, casting aside the weapons of the earthly king, taking up the lighter weapons of faith, and hurling, with a triple cord, the missile of pure confession. [Note: An allegorical confession of the Trinity is described. The words “hurling a missile with a triple cord” do not designate a hurled spear, but a stone thrown from a sling; for whatever we throw may properly be called a missile. “Spartum” denotes the sling itself, since slings are woven from cords that the ancients twisted from that plant.]

He wounds the persecutor’s shamelessness, despising threats, disregarding authorities, and even becoming one in whom Christ may speak. In one place Christ speaks, in another the Father, in another the Spirit of the Father. These do not conflict but agree. What one speaks, three speak, because the Trinity has one voice.

To this victor, who has slain his own Goliath with Goliath’s sword, accepting death for Christ, the young women come after the Philistines have been put to flight—those women who are like eagles—saying: “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7). This indicates that the victors of the world are preferred to its rulers. Finally, when kings have died, the martyrs succeed them forever in the kingdom, honored by heavenly grace; the former become suppliants, the latter patrons.

13. There is also another sword of Goliath (1 Samuel 21:9), another weapon of the devil: namely, the speech of heretics. A man skilled in singing takes it up in order to conquer the adversary, hearing these battles but not suffering them, and not being unsettled or disturbed like one tossed by every wind of doctrine (Ephesians 4:14). He does not suffer from a famine of the word (Amos 8:11), but is filled with the abundance of heavenly Scripture and does not fear challenging the heretic who rings out with empty words.

Then let the weaker man wait, lest he harm the others by entering an unequal contest. Let David come, to whom Christ opens his mouth for speaking the mysteries. Let that Nazarite come (Judges 16:17), whose hair does not fall, either because he has nothing superfluous that could fall, or because he will lose nothing of the virtues above. Let him be whole in sobriety, strong in peace, guarding all his thoughts and words to the end.

14. Let the Gospel be preached, so that the world may be destroyed. For just as the preaching of the Gospel went before throughout the world (Matthew 24:14), to which even the Goths and Armenians have now believed, and therefore we see the end of the world, so the Gospel is preached by the spiritual man when he carries out every advance in wisdom and all the virtues, with mind and spirit singing psalms, destroying the final death. [Note: The editions read “and every form of virtue”; the manuscripts, “and all the virtues.”]

For then comes the end, when Christ in him has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, and he has been subjected to the one who subjected everything to him, so that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:25). “And the Gospel will be preached throughout all the cities”—that is, the cities of Judea: “God is known in Judea” (Psalm 75:1). The cities of Judea are built when the foundations of the virtues are laid.

(Verses 20.) “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army…”

15. Truly Jerusalem was besieged by an army and conquered by a Roman commander. Hence the Jews thought that the abomination of desolation had then occurred, because the Romans threw a pig’s head into the temple, mocking the observance of the Jewish rite. I would not say this even in madness.

The abomination of desolation is the detestable coming of Antichrist, because he contaminates the inner regions of the mind with sacrilegious and accursed things. According to the historical interpretation, he sits in the temple, claiming for himself the throne of divine power. According to the spiritual interpretation, he is beautifully introduced as standing, because he desires to establish the mark of his treachery in the affections of individuals, arguing from the Scriptures that he is Christ.

16. Then desolation will draw near, because many will fall away from true religion and depart through error. Then will be the day of the Lord, as the Apostle also clearly explains when he says (2 Thessalonians 2 and following) that we must not be afraid as though the day of the Lord were imminent, lest anyone deceive us in any way. For unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed—the one who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped as God, so that he sits in the temple of God and presents himself as though he were God—the day will not come.

17. He will therefore sit in the temple, and in the inner temple of the Jews, who will deny Christ. He will sit in a temple that is not inviolable but subject to corruption, one that either collapses under the weight of treachery, is overthrown by the force of anger, or is consumed by the fire of desires.

And rightly the day of the Lord will then come, and the days will be shortened for the sake of the elect (Matthew 24:22). For just as the Lord’s first coming was for the redemption of sins, so his second is for restraining sins, lest more people fall through the error of treachery. [Note: The Amerbach and Roman editions, with a few manuscripts, read “for the redemption of transgressions.” This is less appropriate.]

18. Then there will be false prophets; then famine. Recall the time of Elijah, and you will find then prophets of confusion, then Jezebel, then famine, then the barrenness of the earth. Why? Because “iniquity had abounded, and charity had grown cold” (Matthew 24:12). Finally, the righteous man is in the desert, while the wicked man is in the kingdom.

19. There is another Antichrist, the author of this—namely, the devil—who strives to besiege my Jerusalem, my soul, indeed the soul of God, the peaceful soul, with the army of his legion. [Note: Almost all manuscripts read “with the army of his law.” All the editions, however, more correctly read “with the army of his legion.” The omission of three letters is an easy scribal error.]

For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness (Ephesians 6:12). The apostasy occurs when the soul falls away from itself; and again, when it thinks of the Lord, it trembles and is troubled.

Then, while Antichrist holds the inner regions, until he is removed from the midst, injustice exults and iniquity reigns. Then faith is rare, so that the Lord, as though in doubt, says: “When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8)—whether in our land, certainly, or throughout the world.

Likewise elsewhere: “The Lord looked down upon the children of human beings to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God” (Psalm 13:2). God does not doubt; rather, faith will be so rare among human beings that, according to human judgment, doubt might seem necessary. [Note: Some manuscripts read “will he find peace upon the earth?”]

20. Therefore, when the devil is in the midst of the temple, there is the abomination of desolation, according to the prophet Daniel (Daniel 9:27). But when the spiritual presence of Christ has shone upon each person who is struggling, the wicked one is removed from the midst, and righteousness begins to reign, emptying every dominion from the minds of the faithful.
