21. There is also a third Antichrist: Arius or Sabellius. Indeed, all who deceive us through a distorted interpretation are Antichrists. Therefore, “let the one who reads understand” (Matthew 24:15). Let the one who understands not be deceived into believing false things in place of true things, following the example of the Jews, who denied the true Christ. Consequently, they will believe that the one who is false is true. So too the Arians will not deny to Antichrist what they deny to Christ.

(Verses 23.) “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants in those days!”

22. Is conception, then, criminal? Yet children are the rewards of marriage. And how did the Lord bless Sarah, and she gave birth? How did Hannah pray, and bear a child? How did Rachel, blessed, receive sons? Did the prophets err, since the Lord could not err? But the Lord also spoke through the prophets, and therefore they too could not have erred. [Note: [Col. 1810D] The editions of Erasmus and Gill in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text, together with some manuscripts, read: “What then? Could the disagreement of the letters be mistaken?” The same editions of Erasmus and Gill in the text, together with Amerbach and the greater part of the manuscripts, read: “What could make the disagreement of the letters fit together?” Corbie and certain others, whom we have followed, have the more elegant reading.] Who, then, could make the disagreement of the letters fit together?

23. But since there is war there, let us turn to the spirit of peace. For Peace said: “When a woman is in labor, she has sorrow, because her hour has come; but when she has given birth, she no longer remembers her sorrow.” [Note: [Col. 1810D] The edition and a few manuscripts omit “she does not remember the distress.” And it added; others, with great agreement, read as we do in the text.] You have again what he added: “So you indeed now have sorrow, but I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice” (John 16:21–22)—to show that rejoicing belongs to the perfect, while wavering belongs to the weak, as to those who still fear uncertain things. But above he also said: “They were eating and drinking; they were marrying and giving in marriage” (Luke 17:27), thereby binding themselves to this life and fettering themselves with worldly anxieties. These, then, are the pregnant women to whom woe is spoken: women who extend the bulk of their flesh, whose inward steps of soul grow sluggish, exhausted of virtues and pregnant with vices. [Col. 1810B]

24. Nor are those pregnant women exempt from condemnation who are engaged in the effort of good works but have not yet produced any progress from the work they have undertaken. For there are also those who conceive from fear of God and say: “We have conceived and brought forth from fear of you” (Isaiah 26:18). But not all give birth; not all are perfect; not all can say: “We have brought forth the spirit of salvation upon the earth.” Not all are Marys who conceive Christ from the Holy Spirit and give birth to the Word. For there are those who expel the Word as an abortion before giving birth; there are those who have Christ in the womb but have not yet formed him, to whom it is said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). Those, therefore, who are still in the womb are being brought forth in labor as imperfect; but those are more perfect to whom it is said: “I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15).

25. Many fathers through the Gospel, and many mothers who give birth to Christ. Who, then, will show me Christ’s parents? He himself showed them, saying: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers? . . . Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew 12:48, 50). Do the will of the Father, so that you may be Christ’s mother. Many have conceived Christ and have not given birth. Therefore she who gives birth to righteousness gives birth to Christ; she who gives birth to wisdom gives birth to Christ; she who labors to bring forth the word labors to bring forth Christ. 1510

26. There is also one who labored to bring forth injustice and gave birth to iniquity. Woe to these pregnant women, who, heavy in body, are slower to escape danger! Woe to those upon whom the pain of the coming birth, by which the whole body is shaken, is inflicted. [Note: [Col. 1811D] All the editions and most manuscripts read “the whole pain.” Other manuscripts read in part “the pain enters,” and in part “the pain is inflicted.” The latter is more elegant. Again, where all the editions read “they quickly bring forth an abortion,” the manuscripts, almost unanimously, have “the abortion quickly falls,” with “body,” or rather “pledge,” understood—the latter word being used more than once below.] These pains are the beginnings, the signs, of the future judgment (Matthew 24:8).

27. Moses also taught that there is a pregnant woman who, if two men quarrelling trample upon her, will quickly suffer an abortion (Exodus 21:22). Therefore a good woman should flee litigation and pursue peace, so that she may complete the birth; nor should she wait for the period of nine months, for the birth of the word depends not on time but on the fullness of diligence. “The righteous, though he was perfected quickly, fulfilled many years” (Wisdom 4:13). But, on the contrary, an imperfect soul is quickly trampled, and loses the word it conceived. Yet woe to the one who causes one of these little ones to stumble (Mark 9:41)! Woe to the one who tramples a pregnant woman! For if he casts out a still unformed pledge, there is loss of money; but if it was formed, he shall give soul for soul, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand.

28. But why “eye” or “hand,” when the aborted child that has already been formed has both a hand and an eye, having been violently expelled? Hence it is evident that each person must be condemned according to the manner in which he has caused harm. For if someone, whether heretic or schismatic, has cast out a catechumen as though from the womb of the laboring soul or Church, he is punished more lightly; if he has cast out a believer, more severely. Therefore we must beware lest, by quarrelling with such people, we trample the Church. “Avoid foolish controversies and disputes without discipline,” knowing that they generate quarrels by which the Church, like a woman in labor, is afflicted through the trampling of her whole body (2 Timothy 2:16).

[Col. 1811C] 29. Therefore quickly fill your belly, so that you may give birth more quickly. Hear how and with what you should fill it: “From the fruit of his mouth,” he says, “a man fills his belly, and he shall be satisfied with the fruits of his lips” (Proverbs 18:20).

30. Concerning those who nourish, Solomon’s sublime judgment and the dispute between the two women also taught me this: even though they have already been freed from the pains of childbirth, they nevertheless still waver through fear for the pledges entrusted to them. [Note: [Col. 1812D] More manuscripts, and all the editions except the latest Paris editions, prefer “for confirming the pledges.” The other reading, however, is preferable.] For through the intoxication of the nursing woman, sleep may steal over her, and the mother may crush the little one, deny that it is hers, and seek another’s; but even the woman who did not kill the child is endangered by her own, because she remains attached to an uncertain judgment (1 Kings 3:25).

31. Therefore let us also hasten to wean our little ones, lest either the day of judgment or death find us parents of imperfect works. Weaned Isaac was not exposed to his mother’s sleep; and therefore Abraham held a great feast when he weaned his son (Genesis 21:8). Weaned David hopes for the requital of his soul (Psalm 130:2); for, unlike the Corinthian at the beginning of faith, still weak and unable to bear stronger food, he is not nourished with milk, but, already strengthened by solid bread, had grown into the fullness of mature age (1 Corinthians 3:2). 1511 Therefore concern for begetting is not enough unless the effectiveness of nourishing is also present.

32. Thus, for you also, as for Mary, let the word of God grow, and let it advance in wisdom and age. This happens if you keep all the words of righteousness in your heart and do not wait for old age; but, while still in your first youth, betrothed to another, righteous man, quickly conceive wisdom, quickly give birth, and quickly nourish it without corruption of your body. Consider Paul: yesterday persecuting, today believing, tomorrow preaching (Acts 9:21).

33. “Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew 24:20). Since the Lord will come on the day of judgment, before whom fire will burn—and fire, whether its force is always the same or whether it consumes more quickly in summer—why does he say that we should pray that our flight may not take place in winter, unless perhaps because the one who flees to the mountains must fear the cold and ice, storms and hail of sins, [Note: [Col. 1812D] The old edition, together with most manuscripts, reads “he ought not to fear, but to desire”; the Roman edition, together with others, “he ought to fear and desire.”] and desire the serenity of summer light, lest his weak bodily footsteps slip on treacherous ground?

34. Hence that woman, now secure in her progress and already resting on firm roots, rejoices, saying: “Winter has passed; the time for pruning has come” (Song of Songs 2:11–12). In winter the wind strips trees of their natural adornment, and the harshness of the cold kills the tender leaves into the appearance of death; but in spring the seeds rise again, and, like a new summer, the greenness of nature grows. In spring there is Passover, when I have been preserved; in summer there is Pentecost, when we celebrate the glory of the resurrection as an image of what is to come.

[Col. 1812C] 35. We must also pray that the Lord, when he comes, may not find you on the Sabbath—that is, idle from works. Therefore, according to the Law, perform each day’s work in its day, be fervent in spirit, and labor with constant vigilance. Nor is that saying idle, because it is written: “On the Sabbath you shall humble your soul” (Leviticus 23:32); and because the people endured seventy years in captivity, when religion was violated, liberty crushed, and chastity wounded. Therefore you should depart from this life when the virtues are vigorous and the vices captive—not when the soul is captive, the body’s vigor and virtue are idle, and sins hold dominion.

**(Verse 25.) “And there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars.”**

[Col. 1812D] 36. There is both a true sequence of prophecy and a complete unfolding of the mystery: the captive Jews will again be led captive into Babylon and Assyria; they will be captives throughout the whole world because they denied Christ; and Jerusalem, as it is seen, will be trampled by a hostile army, with the Jews falling by the edge of the sword; and all Judea will be subjected to the nations that will believe, by the edge of the spiritual sword, which is the two-edged word; and different signs will appear in the sun, moon, and stars. [Col. 1813A]

37. These signs are expressed more clearly according to Matthew: “Then,” he says, “the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall” (Matthew 24:29). For when very many depart from religion, clear faith will be darkened by the cloud of faithlessness; since that heavenly sun is either diminished or increased for me according to my faith. Just as, if very many people look upon the rays of the earthly sun, the sun appears paler or brighter according to the capacity of the observer, so spiritual light is poured into each person according to the devotion of the believer. And just as the moon, in its monthly courses, disappears when it is opposite the earth and aligned with the sun, so the holy Church, when the vices of the flesh obstruct the heavenly light, cannot borrow the splendors of divine light from Christ’s rays. For in persecutions, it is usually love of this life alone that shuts out the light of God.

38. “The stars will fall”—those, surely, who already shine with the glory of the resurrection; those men who, like lights in the world, contain the word of life; those men of whom it was said to Abraham that, just as the heavens and the stars shine, so also would his offspring (Genesis 13:16). The patriarchs will therefore be cut off from humankind; the prophets will be cut off, if the harshness of persecution grows strong. These things must happen until the fullness of virtues is increased in every respect throughout the Church and in each individual; for in this way the good are tested, and in this way the weak are exposed. The various agitations of souls will therefore be so grievous that, because those burdened by the multitude of their sins are ill conscious of themselves and fear the future judgment, the sacred dew of the fountain within us will dry up. Faithlessness dries; faith gives dew. [Col. 1813C]

**(Verses 26–27.) “For the powers of heaven will be shaken, and then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds.”**

39. Perhaps, just as the coming of the Lord is awaited so that his presence may be established throughout the whole world of humanity or throughout the world—which certainly takes place in individuals when they receive Christ with all their affections—so also the powers of heaven must obtain an increase of grace at the coming and return of the Lord our Savior (Psalm 13:10), for he is the Lord of powers, and they are shaken when the fullness of divinity pours itself more closely into them.

40. There are also heavenly powers that declare the glory of God (Psalm 18:1), spiritual powers that are shaken by a fuller infusion of Christ and see Christ. David taught us how these powers are shaken, saying: “Come to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm 34:5). Paul also taught how one sees Christ (2 Corinthians 3:16): when you have turned to the Lord, the veil is removed, and you see Christ.

41. You see him in the clouds. I certainly do not think that Christ will come in dark gloom and the horror of rain; for when clouds appear, they cover the sky beneath a dark and fearful appearance. And how has he placed his tabernacle in the sun (Psalm 19:5), if his coming is to be rainy?

42. But there are clouds which, as is fitting, cover the brightness of the heavenly mystery; there are clouds that grow moist with the dew of spiritual grace. Consider the cloud in the Old Testament: “In the pillar of cloud,” he says, “he spoke to them” (Psalm 99:7). He spoke, certainly, through Moses and through Jesus son of Nave, who made the sun stand still (Joshua 10:12), so that he might receive the glory of fuller light. Moses and Jesus, therefore, are clouds. Consider that holy men are clouds, who “fly like a cloud, and like doves with their young.” Isaiah and Ezekiel are clouds over me; through the Cherubim and Seraphim they show me the holiness of the divine Trinity (Isaiah 60:8). All the prophets are clouds; in these clouds Christ comes. He comes in a cloud in the Song of Songs, a serene cloud, radiant with the joy of the Bridegroom (Song of Songs 3:11). He also comes in a light cloud, incarnate from the Virgin; for the prophet saw a cloud coming from the East (Isaiah 19:1). He rightly called it a light cloud, one not weighed down by earthly vices. See the cloud upon which the Holy Spirit came and the power of the Most High overshadowed (Luke 1:35).

43. Therefore, when Christ appears in the clouds (Matthew 24:30), the tribes of the earth will strike themselves; for there is a certain order of crimes and sequence of sins that will be severed by Christ’s coming. 1513

**(Verses 29–30.) “Look at the fig tree and all the trees: when they are already producing fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near.”**

44. The Evangelists’ meaning seems to converge in one sense, though expressed in different ways. Matthew spoke only of the fig tree, when its branch becomes tender (Matthew 24:32); here he speaks of all the trees. But whether, when fruit grows green on all the trees and the fruitful fig tree already blossoms, so that every tongue may confess to God—including the confessing people of the Jews—we ought to hope for the Lord’s coming, when the fruits of the resurrection will be harvested as in the season of summer; or whether, when the man of iniquity puts on a light and fragile boastfulness like the leaves of the branch of the synagogue, we ought to infer that judgment is near: for the Lord hastens to reward faith and bring an end to sin.

45. This fig tree, then, has a double meaning, either when hard things become gentle or when sins luxuriate. Through the faith of believers, what had previously withered will blossom; and through the grace of offenses, sinners will boast. In the former there is the fruit of faith; in the latter, the wantonness of faithlessness. The cultivation of the Gospel’s farmer promises me the fruit of the fig tree (Luke 13:9). We must not despair if sinners have covered themselves with fig leaves as with a garment of deceit, in order to veil their conscience; therefore the leaves are suspect when there is no fruit. Such garments belong to those exiled from paradise (Genesis 3:7).

**(Chapter 22.—Verse 10.) “Behold, when you enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you.”**

46. It is good to consider where the Lord will celebrate Passover. [Note: [Col. 1813D] Some manuscripts read “come to the Passover” (one, “at the Passover”).] According to Matthew you have: “Go into the city to a certain man” (Matthew 26:18). First, observe the majesty of his divinity. He speaks with the disciples and already knows what will happen elsewhere. Then consider his condescension: it is not the person of a rich or powerful man who is chosen; rather, a poor man is sought, and the poor man’s narrow lodging is preferred to the spacious houses of the noble. “Go,” he says, “to a certain man.” You knew, Lord, his name—whose service you knew; you knew the service of the one whose meeting you knew. [Note: [Col. 1815D] Thus ten manuscripts of better quality. Others, and the editions, read: “whose service you knew, whose meeting you knew.”] Yet for that reason he is designated without a name, so that he may be considered insignificant. Nothing here is contrived, where not the person but the reason is expressed. According to Mark, he is “carrying a jar of water” (Mark 14:13). The apostles are therefore commanded to follow him.

47. **(Verses 11–12.)** And why is he called the master of the house? So that you may recognize that the definition of holiness, not wealth, is intended. Why is he said to have “a large furnished room upstairs”? So that you may perceive his great merit, in which the Lord, with his disciples, might rest in delight at his lofty virtues. Would that it might therefore fall to me to carry a jar of water; would that it might fall to me to carry the flask of water carried by the master of the house, who has a large furnished room upstairs. For what is a jar except a more perfect measure? [Note: [Col. 1815D] Almost all manuscripts read “a more perfect measure,” rather than “having no ordinary measure.” The editions nevertheless seem preferable here.] Those are not ordinary people who possess measure. Finally, the Lord says: “They will give you a good measure, pressed down and overflowing” (Luke 6:38). 1514

48. For what shall I say about water? Before the world’s beginnings, the Holy Spirit, as we read, was borne over the water (Genesis 1:2). O water, which, sprinkled with human blood, washed the world, going before as a figure of the present washings! O water, which deserved to be Christ’s sacrament, which washes everything but is not washed! You begin first; you complete the perfect mysteries. From you is the beginning; in you is the end—or rather, you make us unaware of the end. Through you the stench of decaying flesh is removed, and the organs perishing through putrefaction, sprinkled with salt, are preserved for a long time. [Note: [Col. 1815D] From this passage, as well as from testimonies of Origen, Augustine, and others, Joseph Vicecomes demonstrates the antiquity of the rite by which salt is placed in the mouth of catechumens, in *On the Ancient Rites and Ceremonies of Baptism*, book II, chapter 42.] Through you, for bodies parched by heat, a drink sweet for grace, health-giving for life, and pleasant for enjoyment is poured in. You gave your name to the prophets and apostles; you gave your name to the Savior: they are “the clouds of heaven” (Isaiah 60:8), they are “the salt of the world” (Matthew 5:13), and he is “the fountain of life” (John 7:38). [Note: [Col. 1815D] Most manuscripts read “he is the salt” (some, “he is the Savior”) “of the world”; “you are the fountain of life, which …” [Col. 01816D].]

You are not confined when pressed by mountains; you are not broken when dashed against cliffs; you do not fail when poured into the earth. Rather, springing from the innermost veins, you either breathe in the vital spirit enclosed within you, or, poured out, provide fertile sap, or, spread over the ground by irrigation, supply what is useful, lest, when the vital organs have been drained dry, the earth deny its customary produce. [Note: [Col. 1815D] A considerable number of manuscripts and the ancient editions read: “or, spread over the irrigated ground, you supply what is useful, lest, when it has been examined after being dried out …” The Roman edition removed the preposition from this point onward, perhaps because it would more properly have joined it with the adjective, so that it would read *adcommodum* instead of *accommodum*, as we now write it. More and better manuscripts, however, agree with us. The passage should therefore be interpreted as though you read: “or, spread over the ground by irrigation, you supply it for usefulness,” namely, lest …] The substance of all the elements—heaven, air, sea, and earth—returns you. Struck by the prophetic touch so that you might water the hearts of thirsty peoples, the rock vomited you forth (Exodus 17:6). When you burst forth from the Savior’s side, those who struck him saw you and believed (John 19:34). Therefore you are one of the three witnesses of our regeneration; for there are three witnesses: water, blood, and spirit (1 John 5:8). Water for the washing, blood for the price, spirit for the resurrection.

**(Verse 29.) “And I appoint for you, just as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom.”**

49. The kingdom of God is not of this world. Therefore the human being’s striving is not for equality with God but for likeness; for Christ alone is the complete image of God, because the unity of the Father’s splendor is expressed in him. A righteous person, however, is in the image of God if, in order to imitate the likeness of divine conduct, he despises this world through knowledge of God and rejects earthly pleasures through reception of the word of God, by which we are nourished for life. Hence we also eat the body of Christ (On Consecration, distinction 2, chapter *In quibus*, section “The Body”), so that we may become sharers in eternal life. For food and drink are not promised to us as a reward or honor, but the sharing of heavenly grace and life. Nor are the twelve thrones bodily places for sitting (verse 30); rather, just as Christ judges according to divine likeness through knowledge of hearts, not through interrogation concerning deeds, rewarding virtue and condemning impiety, 1515 so also the apostles are formed for spiritual judgment through the rewarding of faith and the abhorrence of faithlessness, reproving error by virtue and pursuing sacrilegious people with hatred.

50. Let us therefore turn back and beware lest any contention over precedence arise among us toward destruction. For if the apostles contended, this is not put forward as an excuse but as a warning. If Peter himself was converted at some point—he who followed the Lord’s first call (Matthew 4:20)—who can say that he has been converted quickly? Beware, therefore, of boasting; beware of the world. For the one who said, “We have left everything and followed you” (Luke 18:28), is commanded to strengthen his brothers.

51. Next, we must observe that humility is not defined by every pursuit of honor. [Note: [Col. 1816D] All the editions read: “not every pursuit of honor is defined as humility” (the Roman edition has “humility”). A large number of written manuscripts read as we do in the text. After the words “not every pursuit of honor,” “to be shown to others” must be understood, as the following makes clear.] For you may show deference to someone because of worldly favor, fear of power, or regard for usefulness. Your own edification is being sought, not another’s honor. Therefore one standard of judgment is given to all: the contention should not be about precedence and boasting, but about humility. In this the Lord presents himself for imitation. We had need of everything; he had need of nothing. Yet he offered himself as the author of humility when he ministered to the disciples. Certainly he did not do this out of a pursuit of usefulness, but as an exercise of virtue.

52. **(Verse 31.)** Peter, although prompt in spirit, is nevertheless declared still weak in bodily affection and destined to deny the Lord; for he could not equal the steadfastness of divine intention. The Lord’s Passion has imitators, but it has no equals. Thus I do not blame him for denying; I praise him for weeping. One thing belongs to the common condition; another is the special quality of virtue. Therefore he is instructed to beware, not compelled to deny.

**(Verse 36.) “Now,” he says, “let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let the one who has none sell his tunic and buy himself a sword.”**

53. O Lord, why do you order me to buy a sword, when you forbid me to strike? Why do you command me to have one, when you prohibit its use? Unless perhaps it is so that defense may be ready, though vengeance is not necessary; so that I may appear to have been able to avenge myself but unwilling to do so. The Law, however, does not forbid striking back, and therefore perhaps, when Peter offers two swords, you say, “It is enough” (verse 38), as though it were permitted up to the Gospel: so that in the Law there may be instruction in equity, and in the Gospel the perfection of goodness.

54. **(Verse 37.)** This seems unjust to many; but the Lord is not unjust, for when he could have avenged himself, he preferred to be sacrificed. There is a spiritual sword, so that you may sell your patrimony and buy the word by which the naked inner chambers of the mind are clothed. There is also the sword of passion, so that you may strip off the body and, through the vesture of sacrificed flesh, purchase for yourself the sacred crown of martyrdom. You can gather this from the Lord’s blessings, since he proclaimed that the supreme crown belongs to anyone who suffers persecution for righteousness. Finally, so that you may know that he was speaking of his Passion, and so that he might not disturb the disciples’ minds, he offered himself as an example, saying: “For this that is written must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was reckoned among the lawless.’”

55. Yet it still raises a question that the disciples brought out two swords: perhaps one of the New Testament and the other of the Old Testament, with which we are armed against the devil’s ambushes? Finally, the Lord says, “It is enough,” as though nothing were lacking to the one whom the teaching of both Testaments had armed.

**(Verses 42–43.) “Father, if it is possible, take this cup away from me.”**

56. Many are perplexed at this point. [Note: [Col. 1817D] These words correct the Apollinarists, who, according to Epiphanius (*Against Heresies* 77.33), obstinately maintained that even Christ’s divinity had suffered; or perhaps, as Blessed Thomas says in his commentary on Matthew, those who asserted that in Christ the Word took the place of the soul, so that everything pertaining to weakness might be attributed to the Word. The entire sequence of the discourse confirms this interpretation. Maldonatus is therefore mistaken if he had this passage in mind when he wrote in chapter 26 of Matthew that, formerly, some people had existed who denied that Christ had experienced true sorrow, on Ambrose’s authority. It is indeed true that below there are certain passages directed against the Manichaeans, who denied that Christ had truly suffered, but this is incidental and treated lightly.] They incline the Savior’s sorrow toward an argument for an innate condition existing from the beginning rather than for a weakness assumed for a time, and they wish to distort the natural meaning of the statement. But I think it should not merely be excused; nowhere do I admire his piety and majesty more. For he would have contributed less to me unless he had assumed my affect. Therefore he grieved for me, who had nothing for which he himself should grieve; and, setting aside the delight of eternal divinity, he was affected by weariness at my weakness. He assumed my sorrow in order to bestow his joy upon me; and he descended along our footsteps even to the anguish of death, so that he might call us back to life along his footsteps. I therefore confidently name sorrow, because I proclaim the cross; for he assumed not the appearance of incarnation but its reality. He had, therefore, to assume pain in order to conquer sorrow, not to exclude it. Nor do those possess the praise of courage who have endured the numbness of wounds rather than pain: “He was a man in suffering and knew how to bear weakness,” he says (Isaiah 53:3).

57. He wishes to instruct us so that, just as we had learned in Joseph not to fear prison, we might learn in Christ to conquer death; and, what is more, how to conquer sorrow at the prospect of future death. For how could we imitate you, Lord Jesus, unless we followed you as a human being, unless we believed you dead, unless we had seen your wounds? How could the disciples believe that he was going to die unless they had experienced the sorrow of one who was about to die? But they still sleep and do not know how to grieve, although Christ grieved for them; for thus we read: “He bears our sins and grieves for us” (ibid. 4). You grieve, therefore, Lord, not for your wounds but for mine; not for your death but for our weakness. And we thought that you were in pain, when you were grieving not for yourself but for me; for you were made weak because of our sins (ibid. 5)—not because that weakness had been assumed by you from the Father, but because it was assumed for me. For it benefited me that the discipline of our peace should be in you, and that by your bruise our wounds should be healed.

58. But what is astonishing if he grieved for all, when he wept for one? And what is astonishing if, about to die for all, he was distressed, when, about to raise Lazarus, he wept (John 11:35)? There also he is moved by the tears of his devout sister, because they touched the human mind; here he acts with profound feeling, so that, because he was destroying our sins in his flesh, the sorrow of his soul might also abolish the sorrow of our soul. And perhaps he is sorrowful because, after Adam’s fall, it was necessary for us to depart from this world by such a passage, so that it was necessary to die; for God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living (Wisdom 1:13). Therefore he is displeased by what he himself did not make.

59. Finally, he says: “Take this cup away from me,” as a human being refusing death, as God preserving his own sentence. For we must die to the world so that we may rise to God; so that, according to the divine sentence, the law of the curse may be dissolved when, at the end of nature, we are resolved into the clay of the earth (Genesis 3:19). As for what he said:

**(Verse 42.) “Not my will, but yours be done.”**

60. He referred his own will to his humanity, and the Father’s will to divinity; for the will of humanity is temporal, while the will of divinity is eternal. The Father’s will is not one and the Son’s another; for where there is one divinity, there is one will. Learn nevertheless to be subject to God, so that you may not choose what you yourself desire, but what you know will be pleasing to God.

61. Next, let us consider the precise meaning of the words themselves: “My soul is sorrowful,” he says (Matthew 26:38). And elsewhere: “Now my soul is greatly troubled” (Psalm 6:4). It is therefore not the one assuming that is troubled, but what has been assumed; the soul is subject to passions, while divinity is free. Finally: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41). It is not he himself who is sorrowful, but the soul. Wisdom is not sorrowful; the divine substance is not sorrowful, but the soul. [Note: [Col. 1819D] All the editions, together with one or two manuscripts, read: “but the soul; for he assumed my soul, he assumed my body.” The remaining manuscripts, and the Second Synod of Seville, where this passage is cited, agree with our reading, except that in quite a few manuscripts and in the margin of the aforementioned synod one reads: “but the soul which he assumed,” and so forth. This is less appropriate.] He assumed my body; he did not deceive me, so that one thing would be and another seem to be. He seemed sorrowful, and he was sorrowful—not for his own suffering, but for our scattering. Finally, he says: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Matthew 26:31). He was sorrowful because he was leaving us, his little ones. But Scripture shows how steadfastly he offered himself to death (John 18:4). When those seeking him came, he went out to meet them; he strengthened the disturbed, challenged the frightened, and received the betrayer with the favor of a kiss. [Note: [Col. 1819D] The old edition reads “the following things make clear”; the Roman edition, “the connected things make clear”; the manuscripts, “Scripture makes clear.”]

62. Nor is it contrary to the truth if he was sorrowful for his persecutors, whom he knew would pay the penalties for monstrous sacrilege. And therefore he said: “Take this cup away from me” (Luke 22:42)—not because the Son of God feared death, but because he did not even wish the wicked to perish. [Note: [Col. 1819D] The Roman edition alone reads: “Therefore he says: Father, forgive them this sin” [Col. 1820D]. The old edition and the manuscripts differ among themselves only in this: most manuscripts, as we do, read “Lord”; a few others and the editions prefer “Father.” But where all the editions have “lest his Passion prove fatal to the people, though it would be salutary for all,” all the manuscripts without exception support our reading.] Finally, he says: “Lord, do not charge this sin against them” (Luke 23:34), so that his Passion might be salutary for all.

**(Verse 48.) “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?”**

63. Great is the manifestation of divine power; great is the discipline of virtue. The plan of betrayal is exposed, and yet patience is not withdrawn. You showed, Lord, whom he was betraying when you revealed hidden things. You also showed whom he was handing over when you said, “the Son of Man,” because flesh, not divinity, is apprehended. Yet what more thoroughly rebukes the ungrateful man is that he handed over the one who, although he was the Son of God, had nevertheless willed to be the Son of Man for our sake. It is as though he said: “For your sake, ungrateful man, I assumed what you betray.” [Note: [Col. 1820D] The editions of Gill and Rome, together with a few manuscripts, read: “whom you betray in hypocrisy. Therefore …,” clearly referring “in hypocrisy” to the detestable pretense of that faithless disciple. Amerbach and Erasmus, together with some manuscripts, read: “whom you betray. Into hypocrisy” (Erasmus: “in hypocrisy”), “therefore …,” where “hypocrisy” signifies nothing other than imitation, or the manner of expressing the feeling with which the Savior’s words were spoken; for ὑπόκρισις (*hypokrisis*) properly denotes the imitation of an action. This also appears to be the sense of the reading in Corbie and certain other manuscripts, which we follow.] Behold the hypocrisy. Therefore I think it should be pronounced as a question, as though he were reproving the betrayer with loving affection: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” That is: Do you inflict a wound by a pledge of love, shed blood through the duty of charity, and bring death by an instrument of peace? A servant betrays his master, a disciple his teacher, the chosen one his author? This is what is meant by: “The wounds of a friend are more useful than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6). This is said to the betrayer; but what is said to the peacemaker? “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:1).

64. “And he kissed him,” it says (Matthew 26:49). This was not to teach us to feign, but so that he would not appear to avoid betrayal, and so that he might affect the betrayer more deeply, since he did not refuse him the offices of love; for it is written: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm 120:7).

65. “And when the sign had been given,” he says, “he was seized by those who had come with clubs” (Matthew 26:50). But the mysteries of the Lord of all, not weapons, held him. Finally, he spoke, and they fell backward (John 18:6). What need have I of legions of angels, what need of a heavenly army? The Lord’s voice alone terrifies more powerfully. The one who reclined on Christ’s breast chose this voice in order to demonstrate a sign of divine majesty. Therefore the crowd lays hands on him who wills it; bonds are fastened. O madmen! O faithless ones! Wisdom is not seized in this way; justice is not held in this way.

### 66. (Verses 49–51)

Nor were the disciples’ efforts lacking. Peter, finally, instructed in the Law and prompt in affection, [Col. 1820C] knowing that Phinehas had been reckoned righteous because he had slain sacrilegious men, struck the servant of the ruler (Ps. 105:31). But the Lord wiped away the bloody wound and disclosed the divine mysteries, so that the servant of the ruler of this world—that is, not by the condition of nature but by guilt, a servant of secular powers—might receive a wound in his ear, because he had not heard the words of Wisdom: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). “You were sold,” he says, “because of your sins” (Isa. 50:1). There is sale because of our sins; but because of God’s goodness there is redemption from sins.

Or, if Peter struck the ear intentionally (24, question 1, chapter “If Peter”), he taught that they ought not to have an ear in outward appearance when they did not possess one in the mystery. But the good Lord restores hearing even to him, demonstrating, according to the prophetic words (Isa. 35:10), that those who were wounded in the Lord’s Passion can themselves be healed if they convert, since every sin is washed away by the mysteries of faith.

### 67.

Peter therefore removes the ear. Why Peter? Because he is the one who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 16:19): for he condemns who also absolves, since he has obtained the power both of binding and of loosing (ibid.). But he removes the ear of one who hears badly; with the spiritual sword he removes the inner ear of one who understands badly.

### 68.

Let us beware lest anyone’s little ear be removed. The Lord’s Passion is being read: if we refer the weakness of bodily suffering to his divinity, the little ear is cut off—and it is cut off by Peter, who did not suffer Christ to be regarded as a prophet, but taught by faithful confession that he was marked out as the Son of God. Therefore, when we read that Jesus was seized, let us beware lest we hear from anyone and suppose that he was seized according to his divinity, seized unwillingly, seized as though weak. He is indeed seized and, as John says (John 18:12), bound according to the reality of his body; but woe to those who bind the Word! They bind him who think Christ merely human [Note: Certain Paris editions read: “who do not think him present”; the Turin codex: “who do not think him perfect”]; they bind him who do not think him foreknowing, who do not confess him omnipotent. Evil are the bonds of the Jews, by which they do not bind Christ but bind themselves.

He is bound, moreover, not in the house of some godly and righteous man, but in the house of Caiaphas (John 11:50)—that is, in an ungodly house—where he was also prophesied as the one who would die for all. How foolish, then, are those who confess the divine benefits [Col. 1821C] and persecute the author of those benefits!

### 69.

That is why they lose the ear: because they have lost the benefit of hearing. Many do not possess hearing although they believe that they do. In the Church all possess it; outside the Church they do not. Or perhaps he removed the ear for this reason: so that those who could not preserve what they had heard might no longer sin by hearing. Thus, too, God once confused the languages of those building the tower, so that they could not hear one another and increase the work of their impiety (Gen. 11:7).

### 70.

Understand, if you can, how pain flees at the touch of the saving right hand, and how wounds are healed not by medicine being applied to them [Note: Thus the old edition and almost all manuscripts read, except that some have *conspersa* (“sprinkled over”) instead of *aspersa* (“sprinkled”), from which the Roman edition seems to have produced *compressa* (“pressed together”).], but by touch itself covering them. The clay recognizes its maker, and flesh follows the Lord’s hand as its maker; for the Creator restores his work as he wills. Thus elsewhere, too, the sight of that blind man was restored, as though he had returned to his original nature, when mud was applied over his eyes (John 9:6). He could have commanded, but he preferred to work, so that we might recognize that he himself is the one who formed from the clay of the earth the members of our body, adapted to various functions, and gave them life by breathing in the power of the mind.

### 71.

So they came and seized him, only to perish more grievously through the fruit of their wicked undertaking. The wretched men understood neither the mystery nor revered so great a movement of merciful love: for he did not even allow his enemies to be wounded. They were inflicting death on the righteous man; he was healing the wounds of his persecutors.

### (Verses 54–55)

But Peter was following at a distance.

### 72.

And rightly was he following at a distance, since he was soon to deny him; for he could not have denied him if he had clung closely to Christ. Yet perhaps even in this he deserves our greatest admiration: he did not abandon the Lord even when he was afraid. Fear belongs to nature; concern belongs to devotion. What he fears is another’s; what he does not flee is his own. What follows is devotion; what he denies is weakness. His stumbling is shared by all; his repentance belongs to faith.

A fire was already burning in the high priest’s house. Peter approached in order to warm himself, because when the Lord had been shut away, the warmth of his mind had also grown cold within him.

### 73. (Verse 56)

What does it mean that a maidservant is the first to betray him, [Col. 1822B] when men could certainly have recognized him more readily, unless it was so that this sex too might seem to have sinned unto the Lord’s death, and so that this sex too might be redeemed through the Lord’s Passion? And therefore a woman is the first to receive the mystery of the Resurrection (John 20:17) and to keep the commandments, so that she might abolish the ancient error of transgression.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “having gone before in the killing,” and so forth.]

### 74. (Verse 57)

Peter, then, being betrayed, denies. Let us suppose that Peter denied, because the Lord said: “You will deny me three times” (Matt. 26:34). And I would rather Peter have denied than that the Lord should have been proved false. What did he deny? What he had rashly promised. He considered his devotion but did not regard his condition. He was punished because he had said that he would lay down his life (John 13:37)—something belonging not to human weakness but to divine power. If he paid so great a penalty for the imprudence of his speech, how great is the punishment of treachery!

### 75.

Where, however, does Peter deny? Not on the mountain, not in the Temple, not in his own house, but in the praetorium of the Jews, in the house of the high priest. There he denies where truth is not; there he denies where Christ has been seized, where Jesus has been bound. What else could one expect but error from the man whom the doorkeeper let in, whom the doorkeeper questioned (John 18:17)—and a Jewish doorkeeper at that?

Eve brought Adam in badly; a woman brought Peter in badly. But Adam stumbled in paradise, where guilt is not pardonable; Peter here stumbles in the praetorium of the Jews, where innocence is difficult. Adam’s fall was forbidden; Peter’s error was foretold. Adam’s transgression prejudged Peter’s; Peter’s undid Adam’s.

[Col. 1822D] ### 76.

Let us also consider the circumstances in which he denies. “It was cold,” he says (ibid. 18). If we consider the season, it could not have been cold; but it was cold where Jesus was not recognized, where there was no one who saw the light, where the consuming fire was denied. It was therefore cold in the mind, not in the body. Finally, Peter stood beside the coals because he was cold in affection (Mark 14:54). Evil is the Jewish flame: it burns but does not warm. Evil is the hearth that spreads a kind of soot of error even over the minds of the saints; beside it Peter’s inward eyes also grew dim. Those were not eyes of flesh and blood, [Col. 1823A] but the eyes of the mind by which he saw Christ.

### 77.

Someone will say: “Are you condemning even the elements of the Jews?” I do not condemn the elements, because they are not the Jews’ but Christ’s; but what I condemn is another thing: the flame of treachery. I condemn this flame of the Jews, following the divine oracles. For the Lord says: “Your silver is rejected” (Jer. 6:30). If the Jews’ silver is rejected, then the Jews’ hearth is rejected as well. Finally, it was from the hearth and gold of the Jews that the head of the calf was fashioned (Exod. 32:24)—that is, the chief manifestation of sacrilege.

[Note: In not a few manuscripts, and not inferior ones, the words “but Christ’s” are absent.]

### 78.

But let us examine the manner of the denial, which I see differs among the evangelists. So extraordinary was it that Peter could sin that his sin could not be fully captured even by the evangelists. Accordingly, when the maidservant betrayed Peter by saying that he was one of those who had been with Jesus the Galilean, Matthew records that he answered at the first utterance: “I do not know what you are saying” (Matt. 26:70). Mark says the same (Mark 14:68); he followed Peter and could therefore have learned it more accurately from him.

[Note: More accurately, according to the customary judgment of men; otherwise all that the evangelists wrote is equally true.]

Peter’s first words are the words of one denying; yet by them he seems not to deny the Lord but to separate himself from the woman’s accusation of betrayal.

### 79.

Consider, however, what he denied: namely, that he was one of those who had been with Jesus the Galilean—or, as Mark says (ibid. 67), with Jesus the Nazarene.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Did he perhaps deny that he was the Son of God?”]

Did he deny that he himself belonged with the Son of God? This is what he means: “I do not know the Galilean; I do not know the Nazarene, whom I know to be the Son of God.” Let men have the names of places; the homeland of the Son of God cannot be named, since no place encloses his majesty.

And so that you may know this to be true, it is also demonstrated by an example. Elsewhere, when the Lord asked the disciples, “Who do men say that the Son of Man is?” they said, “Some, Elijah; others, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets” (Matt. 16:13). But Peter said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid. 16). Did he deny there too because he preferred to confess Christ not as the Son of man but as the Son of God? Surely, what should seem ambiguous here, Christ himself has also confirmed.

### 80.

Receive another interpretation. When Peter was asked, “And are you one of those who were with Jesus the Galilean?” (Matt. 26:69), he rejected the word of eternity. For those who began to exist are not, in the proper sense; that is to say, only he “was” who “was in the beginning” (John 1:1). Finally he says, “I am not”; for being belongs to him who always is. Hence Moses also says: “He who is has sent me” (Exod. 3:14).

### 81.

Again, when he was pressed about whether he was one of them, he denied it according to Mark (Mark 14:70), so that you may know that the evangelist gave greater weight to truth than to favor. Yet he denied that he was one of them; he did not deny Christ. He denied association with men, not the grace of God. He denied that he was one of those who were with the Galilean; he did not deny that he was with the Son of God.

### 82.

Finally, according to Matthew, when he was betrayed as one who had been with Jesus the Nazarene, he said: “I do not know the man” (Matt. 26:72). Both evangelists whom we have cited likewise report this in his third utterance; with an oath, they say, he answered that he did not know the man. And rightly did he deny the man whom he knew to be God.

Finally, where there is an oath, the answer is cautious. For although Peter denied, he did not commit perjury, because the Lord had not foretold that he would swear falsely. But if there is uncertainty even in Peter, how dangerous is an oath!

### 83.

John, however, records it this way: when Peter was questioned by the maidservant whether he was one of that man’s disciples, he answered at the first utterance: “I am not” (John 18:17). For he was not the apostle of a man; he was Christ’s.

Finally, Paul too denied that he was the apostle of a man, saying: “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Gal. 1:1). But lest he seem to introduce any ambiguity concerning the Incarnation, he added: “Who raised him from the dead” (ibid.), so that you might believe him to be man after first believing him to be God. Elsewhere too he maintains the same order when he says: “For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5). He named the mediator of God before naming him the mediator of men; for it is not enough to believe both unless the order of faith is preserved.

### 84.

The answer therefore agrees everywhere. For the one who said, “I do not know the man,” appropriately said, when asked whether he was one of the man’s disciples: “I am not.” Thus he did not deny himself to be Christ’s disciple; he denied that he was the disciple of a man.

Thus both Peter and Paul denied the man whom they confessed to be the Son of God. Peter perceived what Paul expressed; from this, too, Peter made progress. Peter’s error is the teaching of the righteous, and Peter’s hesitation is the rock of all.

Finally, he hesitates upon the waves but stretches out his right hand to Christ; he falls on the mountain but is raised by Christ. Peter certainly hesitated at sea, but he walked (Matt. 14:30).

[Note: All editions read: “but he walked more firmly. Peter’s hesitation is our firmness.” The manuscripts, however, have the wording retained in the text.]

Peter’s hesitation is firmer than our firmness. There he falls where no one ascends; there he wavers where no one walks. And yet, although he hesitates amid the waves, he does not sink; he wavers but does not fall; he floats but is not plunged into the depths. And if he fell, he fell on the mountain; yet he fell more fortunately than others stood, and he fell more fortunately because Christ raised him.

### 85.

Again, when he was asked whether he was one of his disciples, John wrote that he denied it (John 18:25).

[Note: The Roman edition, with three manuscripts, reads: “For when he denied for the third time that he had been with him.”]

And rightly did he deny, since he was said to be one of the disciples of the one whom they had previously called a man. For when he denied a third time that he had been seen with him, this too derives from what came before: “I was not with the one whom you call a man; but I have not departed from the Son of God.”

### 86.

Luke too wrote that, when Peter was asked whether he was one of them, he answered at the first utterance: “I do not know him.” And he spoke rightly. For it would have been rash for him to say that he knew the one whom the human mind cannot comprehend. “No one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11:27).

Again, in his second utterance, according to Luke, the same Peter said: “I am not.” Clearly he preferred to deny himself rather than Christ. Or because he seemed to be denying fellowship with Christ, he certainly denied himself. Indeed, when he denies the man, he sinned against the Son of Man, so that it might be forgiven him, not against the Holy Spirit.

When questioned a third time, he said: “I do not know what you are saying”—that is, “I do not know your sacrileges.”

### 87.

But we excuse him. [Note: All editions read: “The Lord himself did not excuse him.” In the manuscripts, however, “the Lord” is omitted, so that “he himself” refers to Peter, which fits the following context more appropriately. Some criticize Ambrose for having tried too much to lessen Peter’s sin; among them is William Estius, a man distinguished equally for piety and learning. He writes as follows: “Ambrose comments at length on the denial … and speaks as though Peter, in denying Christ, had not sinned, at least mortally. But Ambrose seems truly to err in this respect: he excessively diminishes Peter’s sin, for which Peter wept bitterly. We must certainly beware lest, while we are too anxiously occupied in excusing that sin, we make Christ a liar because he foretold it, and Peter foolish because he wept most bitterly over it. Yet, with due respect to that learned man, whoever reads this entire commentary of Ambrose more attentively will find nothing from which it can rightly be inferred that the holy Doctor regarded Peter’s sin as merely venial. For among mortal crimes one is lighter than another; and Ambrose therefore thought he might, for the sake of honoring so great an apostle, bring forward in an oratorical manner whatever could serve to lessen his sin. Indeed, among the other Fathers there were some who pressed Peter’s defense even more strongly, continuing to call him righteous even after the denial. See the same Estius, *Annotations on the Principal and Most Difficult Places of Sacred Scripture*, on Matthew 26:70.”]

He himself did not excuse him; for it is not enough for one who confesses Jesus to give an evasive answer, but an open confession is required. What does it profit to veil one’s words if one wishes to appear to have denied him? And therefore Peter is not presented as having answered in this way deliberately, because afterward he remembered and nevertheless wept. He preferred to accuse his own sin, so that by confessing he might be justified, rather than be burdened by denying it. “The righteous man is first an accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17); and therefore he wept.

### 88.

Why did he weep? Because guilt had crept upon him. I ordinarily weep if guilt is absent from me—that is, if I do not avenge myself, if I do not obtain what I wrongly desire. Peter grieved and wept because he had erred as a man.

[Note: Those who use this passage to try to diminish the necessity of sacramental penance, which is not at all under discussion here, accomplish nothing. For what follows clearly shows that satisfaction does not mean our confession, or its final part. Just as the words “can be washed” refer to Peter’s tears, so the words “but what cannot be defended” refer to satisfaction, not to confession. It is therefore clear that satisfaction here means nothing other than defense: to satisfy accusations is the same as to wash away or refute the charges brought against one.

Nor do the following words—“Let tears wash the offense, which shame forbids one to confess aloud”—exclude at least a vocal, even secret, confession. The passage shows only that someone who has committed a grave crime ought to begin his conversion with tears; thus Peter kept silent, lest a request for pardon made too quickly should give further offense. “First there must be weeping,” and so forth.

Ambrose therefore alludes to the ecclesiastical discipline of his own time, by which penitents were commanded first to mourn their offenses privately before approaching to seek reconciliation. Yet the holy Doctor explicitly acknowledges oral confession in Peter more than once: above, in the preceding section, he says, “He preferred to accuse his own sin, so that by confessing he might be justified rather than be burdened by denying”; and below, in section 90: “If perhaps you should stumble in some matter … so that you may remember and confess your error. Imitate Peter,” and so forth.

Other explanations of this passage may also be found in Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 17, section “Now according to”; Robert Pullen, *On the Sixth Book of the Sentences*; Hugh of Saint Victor, book II of *On the Sacraments*, page 14, chapter on Confession; Cardinal Bellarmine, *On Penance*, book III; and, to omit others, in Dom Denis de Sainte-Marthe’s treatise written in French, *On Confession*, pages 351, 357, and 567.]

I do not find what he said; I find that he wept. I read his tears; I do not read a defense. But what cannot be defended can be washed away. Let tears wash the offense that shame forbids one to confess aloud. Tears plead both for pardon and for modesty. Tears speak of guilt without horror; tears confess the crime without offending modesty; tears do not ask for pardon, yet they merit it.

I have found why Peter kept silent: lest a request for pardon made too quickly should give further offense. First there must be weeping; then one must pray.

### 89.

Good are the tears that wash away guilt. Finally, those whom Jesus looks upon weep. Peter denied the first time and did not weep, because the Lord had not looked upon him. He denied the second time and did not weep, because the Lord had still not looked upon him. He denied the third time; Jesus looked upon him, and he wept most bitterly.

Look upon us, Lord Jesus, so that we may know how to mourn our sin and wash away our offense. Hence even the falls of the saints are useful. Peter’s denial did me no harm; his correction benefited me. I have learned to beware the conversation of the treacherous. Peter denied among the Jews; Solomon was deceived and went astray through association with foreign women (1 Kings 11:4).

### 90.

Peter therefore wept, and wept most bitterly; he wept so that he might wash away his offense with tears.

[Note: In many manuscripts the words “he wept with tears, even until that very moment” are absent. Since, however, they occur in some manuscripts and in all editions, and since they produce a fuller sense, we have not removed them from the text.]

And you, if you wish to merit pardon, wash away your guilt with tears. At that very moment, at that very time, Christ looks upon you. If perhaps you stumble in some matter—

[Note: Eight manuscripts of no inferior quality read: “perhaps you are struggling.” This is not inappropriate, for *laboro* often means “I am in danger concerning salvation,” as in Horace, book I, ode 27: “How greatly you struggle in Charybdis!”]

—because he who witnesses your secrets stands beside you, he looks upon you so that you may remember and confess your error.

Imitate Peter, who elsewhere says a third time (6, question 1, chapter “Imitate Peter”): “Lord, you know that I love you” (John 21:15). For because he had denied three times, he confesses three times. He denied in the night; he confesses in the day.

### 91.

These things have been written so that we may know that no one ought to boast. For if Peter fell because he said, “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will not be scandalized” (Mark 14:29), who else can rightly presume about himself?

Finally, David too confesses that his boast harmed him, because he had said, “In my prosperity I shall never be moved,” saying: “You hid your face, and I was troubled” (Ps. 29:7–8).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “If he fell, who said …” Other editions and all the manuscripts read: “because he said …” This is better, since many ancient writers acknowledge Peter’s boasting as the cause of his falling into sin.]

### 92.

From where shall I summon you, Peter, so that you may teach me what you thought while weeping? From where, I ask, shall I summon you? From heaven, where you are now joined to the choir of angels? Or even from the tomb, since you do not think it an insult to be there, from which the Lord rose?

Teach us what benefit your tears brought you. Yet you taught us immediately. You who fell before you wept, after you had wept were chosen to rule others, though you had not previously ruled yourself.

[Note: The same Roman edition, together with one Vatican manuscript and the Regius manuscript, reads: “You were raised up so that you might raise up others, whom you had not raised up before.” Other editions and our native manuscripts differ among themselves only in this: where several better manuscripts read “you were chosen,” others, with the editions, read “you were raised up.” Two manuscripts, instead of “so that you might restore others,” have “so that you might govern others.”]

### 93.

Peter therefore had tears, which he poured out in devout affection. The betrayer did not have tears with which to wash away his guilt, but torments of conscience with which to confess his sacrilege, so that, while he was condemned by his own judgment and the crime was expiated by voluntary punishment, the Lord’s mercy might be demonstrated—for the Lord did not wish to avenge himself—and his divinity proved, since by invisible power he questioned the conscience of the mind.

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds “to confess,” when he hanged himself with a noose after throwing down the silver.]

### 94.

“I have sinned,” he says, “because I betrayed innocent blood” (Matt. 27:5). Although the betrayer’s repentance is empty, because he sinned against the Holy Spirit, there is nevertheless some shame in the crime: the acknowledgment of guilt. And although he is not absolved, the shamelessness of the Jews is refuted. Although the seller’s confession convicts them, yet, though criminal, they claim for themselves the rights of the transaction and believe themselves free from guilt when they say: “What is that to us? You see to it” (ibid.).

Utterly foolish are they, thinking that they are released from the author of the crime rather than bound by it. In monetary cases, the obligation is discharged when the price is returned. These men receive the price, pursue the sacrilege, and by stubborn determination claim for themselves the deadly sale of blood, even while the seller returned the payment for the sacrilege.

### 95.

Clearly, therefore, while the price of blood is separated from the treasuries of the Jews, and the potter’s field is purchased with the money for which Christ was sold (ibid. 7); while that place is designated for the burial of the remains of foreigners; while the prophetic oracle is fulfilled (Jer. 32:44), and the mystery of the rising Church is revealed—during all this, the meaning is as follows.

The field, according to the divine commandments, is this whole world (Matt. 13:38). The potter is the one who formed us from clay, of whom you have in the Old Testament: “God formed man from the clay of the earth” (Gen. 2:7). He possesses, according to his own will, the power to form us by nature and reform us by grace. For although we fall through our own vices, nevertheless, through his mercy, when the spirit of our mind has been restored, we are reformed according to the oracles of Jeremiah.

### 96.

The price is also the price of the Lord’s Passion. Therefore, by the price of blood the world is bought by Christ; for he came so that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). In this there is both the work and the right of the author. He came, therefore, to preserve for the grace of eternity those who, through baptism, had been buried with Christ and had died with him.

But not every place is indiscriminately available for burial. For although the world includes everyone, it does not preserve everyone. And although the dwelling is common, legitimate burial belongs to those who are now members of God’s household through faith but were formerly foreigners under the Law.

Who are these except those of whom it is said: “Remember that at one time you Gentiles, who were in the flesh, were alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise” (Eph. 2:11–12)? But now these are no longer strangers and foreigners, since by the right of faith they have merited being citizens of the saints.

[Note: Here the Roman edition, as usual inserting several Gospel verses, adds: “According to Matthew, when he was accused by the chief priests and questioned by Pilate, he answered nothing. Admirable …” In what follows, from section 99 through section 129, that edition contains continuous alterations, additions, and transpositions. Compare it with another edition or with a manuscript and you will acknowledge this; we shall supply only the principal differences.]

### 97.

There follows an admirable passage, by which moral endurance in bearing injuries is infused into human hearts. The Lord is accused and remains silent (Matt. 27:11), and rightly remains silent, since he has no need of defense. Let those who fear defeat seek to be defended. He therefore does not confirm the accusation by fearing it, but despises it by refusing to refute it. For what would he fear who did not seek salvation for himself? The salvation of all gave up his own, so that he might acquire all.

But why should I speak of God? Susanna remained silent and conquered; for the better cause is the one that is not defended yet is proved. Here too Pilate acquitted him: he acquitted him by his judgment but crucified him in accordance with the mystery. Yet the former is peculiar to Christ; the latter is human, so that before unjust judges he might appear to have been unwilling, rather than unable, to defend himself.

[Note: All editions and most manuscripts read “confirms by remaining silent.” The Corbie manuscript, together with several others, reads “confirms by fearing.” This is more harmonious, so that it may be understood from what follows: “For what would he fear who did not seek salvation?” After these words, the Roman edition alone reads: “Salvation itself reveals itself,” instead of “the salvation of all,” and so forth.]

### 98.

But why the Lord remained silent, he himself stated beforehand, saying: “If I tell you, you will not believe me; and if I ask you, you will not answer me” (Luke 22:67–68). Yet this is most excellent: he preferred to prove himself king rather than to say so, so that those who accused him could have no grounds for condemning him, since they themselves confessed what they brought against him.

### 99. (Verse 8)

When Herod desired to see some miracle performed by him, he himself remained silent and did nothing, because neither did Herod’s cruelty deserve to see divine things, nor did the Lord seek display. Perhaps, in a figurative sense, all the ungodly are represented in Herod: if they do not believe the Law and the prophets, they cannot see Christ’s wondrous works even in the Gospel.

### 100. (Verse 11)

He is sent to Herod and sent back to Pilate. Although neither declares him guilty, both nevertheless comply with the purposes of another’s cruelty.

Pilate did wash his hands (Matt. 27:24), but he did not wash away his deed. A judge ought neither to yield to hatred nor to fear, so as to hand over the blood of an innocent man. His wife warned him (ibid. 19); grace shone in the night; divinity stood forth; yet even so he did not restrain himself from a sacrilegious sentence.

[Note: The same Roman edition reads: “Then, according to Matthew, Pilate washed his hands before the people, saying: ‘I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man.’”]

### 101.

Likewise, I think that in this a figure has been set forth beforehand of all judges who would condemn those whom they considered innocent. Yet the fact that the Gentiles are more tolerable than the Jews is demonstrated by Pilate’s person, together with that of his wife; and they are more strongly admonished to faith by divine works.

[Note: The person of Pilate’s wife is joined to the passage.]

But what of those who crucified the Lord of majesty?

### 102. (Verse 18)

Nor is it without reason that they ask for the murderer’s release who demanded the death of the innocent. Such are the laws of iniquity: they hate innocence and love crime.

[Note: The Victor manuscript reads: “so that it may hate what innocence hates and love crime.”]

Yet in this the interpretation of the name gives shape to the figure. For Barabbas is said in Latin to mean “son of the father.” Thus those to whom it is said, “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44), are shown to prefer to the true Son of God the Antichrist, the son of their own father.

### (Verse 11)

And having clothed him in a white garment, he sent him back.

### 103.

It is not without purpose that he is clothed by Herod in a white garment, imparting the signs of an immaculate Passion: the Lamb of God, without blemish, was to receive the sins of the world with glory.

In the figure of Herod and Pilate, who became friends from being enemies through Jesus Christ, a representation is also preserved of the future concord between the people of Israel and the Gentile nation. Yet this is so arranged that the devout people of the nations receive the word of God and, through the devotion of their faith, transmit it to the people of the Jews, so that they too may clothe with the glory of their majesty the body of Christ, whom they had previously despised.

### 104.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Then, according to Matthew, he is clothed by the soldiers in a scarlet cloak; and according to John he is surrounded with a purple garment.”]

He is clothed by the soldiers in a scarlet cloak and a purple tunic (Matt. 27:27): in the one, signifying the palms of the martyrs; in the other, the emblems of royal power. His flesh was to receive for us the blood poured out throughout the whole world, and his Passion was to bring forth a kingdom from us.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript and the Regius manuscript read: “because his flesh was going to pour out blood throughout the whole world.” The Claromontane manuscript reads: “because his flesh was going to undergo the Passion.”]

### 105.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Finally, according to Matthew, a crown of thorns is placed upon his head. Since this is something else …” A little later, where all editions and most manuscripts read “as though with the punishments of the world,” six manuscripts have “as though with the thorns of the world.” This reading seems preferable.]

The crown also fastened from thorns upon his head (ibid. 29) shows nothing other than the gift of a divine work: from the sinners of the world, as from the thorns of the age, a triumphal glory was to be sought for God.

[Note: The same Roman edition reads: “Then, according to John, Pilate scourged Jesus. Nor are the scourges without a mystery.”]

Nor are the scourges without meaning, because he himself was scourged so that we might not be scourged: “A man in suffering, and knowing how to bear infirmities, he grieves for us” (Isa. 53:3–4), turning away the scourges from us, who formerly fled from God. So patient is the Lord that he offered his own hands to the bonds of fugitives and his body to the scourges of fugitives.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “According to Mark, the soldiers then plaited a crown of thorns, placed it upon his head, and saluted him, saying: ‘Hail, King of the Jews.’ And they knelt and worshiped him. Although they did this with a detestable disposition of mind …”]

Thus the Jews reveal, although with a detestable disposition of mind, the honor paid to him at his death. Even if they crown him while piercing him, they worship him while mocking him; even if they do not believe in their hearts in the one whom they kill, they confess him. They lacked the affections of a good work; yet God did not lack the honor due to him: he is saluted as king, crowned as victor, and worshiped as God and Lord.

### 106.

A reed also is taken into his hand according to Matthew (Matt. 27:29), so that human weakness might no longer be shaken like a reed by the wind, but might be strengthened and established by Christ’s works; and so that, when the bond written against us had been affixed to the cross, the ancient sentence might cease.

Or, according to Mark, the reed strikes his head (Mark 15:19), so that our condition, made firm by the touch of divinity, might no longer be able to waver.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Established and strengthened”; or, according to Mark, “the remaining words being omitted.”]

### 107. (Verse 26)

But now let the victor raise up his own trophy. The cross is placed upon his shoulders as a trophy, whether Simon or he himself carried it; and both Christ in man and man in Christ bore it.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “According to John, Christ carries the cross for himself; according to Luke, it is placed upon Simon. But whether Simon or he carried it, the cross is nevertheless placed upon the shoulders, so that both Christ in man and man in Christ might carry the trophy.”]

The statements of the evangelists do not conflict when the mystery agrees. And the order of our progress is good: first he himself raised the trophy of his cross; afterward he gave it to the martyrs to raise.

It is not a Jew who carries the cross, but a foreigner and a stranger; he does not go before but follows, according to what is written: “Take up your cross and follow me.” For Christ did not ascend his own cross but ours.

Nor was that death a death of divinity, but as though of a man; hence he himself says: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46).

### 108.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Finally, according to Mark, the soldiers stripped him of the purple garment, which is not without a mystery. For Christ, about to ascend …”]

Beautifully, when he was about to ascend the cross, he removed his royal garments, so that you might know that he suffered as a man, not as God and king—even though Christ is both—yet that he was fastened to the cross as a man, not as God.

But the soldiers, not the Jews, know at what time and what sort of garments are appropriate for Christ.

[Note: The same Roman edition reads: “For at the judgment he stands in purple as a victor, but for the Passion he comes humbly in his own garments as one accused.”]

At the judgment he stands as a victor; for the Passion he comes humbly, as one accused.

109. Now that we have seen the trophy, let the triumphant victor ascend his chariot; and let him suspend from the triumphal gallows the spoils captured from the world—not the booty won from a mortal enemy, hung upon tree-trunks or four-horse wagons. Here we do not see nations with their arms bound behind their backs; nor do we admire images of cities destroyed, likenesses of captured towns, or the bowed necks of captive kings, such as human triumphs usually display [Col. 1831B]; nor boundaries of victory marked out by the limits of a region. Rather, we see peoples of the nations exulting, summoned not to punishment but to reward; kings worshiping with free affection; cities surrendering themselves through willing devotion and transformed for the better; images of towns which not pigment (*fucus*) [Note: *Fucus* properly denotes a certain kind of red color; here, however, it is used loosely for every color employed by painters, as in Horace, Book III, Ode 5, for any dye with which cloth is stained. In this and the following sections, the author also carefully runs through the elements formerly observed by the Romans in their triumphs. On these matters see Sigonius, Rosinus, Laurentius, and others.] has portrayed, but devotion has colored with the faith; weapons and the rights of victory extending throughout the whole world; the captive prince of the world; and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, dominions subjected to the command of the human voice, and the forms of various virtues, shining forth not in silk garments but in moral conduct.

Chastity gleams, faith shines, and devotion, clothed in the spoils of death, now rises again in strength. The one triumph of God has made nearly all human beings triumph, the cross of the Lord [Note: The editions read “has made all human beings triumphant”; the manuscripts read “has made human beings triumph.” In some manuscripts the two following words, “the cross of the Lord,” are omitted.]

[Col. 1831C] 110. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “It is worth considering what sort of person he is who ascends the cross; for according to Mark, those crucifying him divided his garments.”] It is therefore worth considering what sort of person ascended. I see him naked: let the one who prepares to conquer the world ascend in this manner, so that he may not seek the world’s supports. Adam was defeated when he sought clothing; he conquered who laid aside his coverings.

And he ascended in the condition in which, with God as author, nature formed us: thus the first man lived in paradise [1528]; thus the second man entered paradise. And so that he might conquer not for himself alone but for everyone, he stretched out his hands, drawing all things to himself; so that, released from the knot of death and suspended upon the yoke of faith, he might unite with heavenly things those that previously belonged to earth.

111. (Verse 38.) A title is also written: a procession usually precedes conquerors; but before the Lord’s triumphal chariot [Col. 1831D] there went the noble procession of the dead rising again. A title also usually indicates the number of the nations brought under subjection. Let there be in those triumphs, arranged in a certain order, the pitiable defeat and shameful captivity of conquered and perishing nations; here, however, the grace of redeemed nations blossoms—companions worthy of so great a triumph, so that heaven, earth, the seas, and the regions below may be changed from corruption to grace.

112.
