A title, then, is written [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “The title is also, according to John, placed above the cross, so that, when the bond that stood against us was affixed to the cross, the ancient sentence might come to an end.” And below: “The title, according to John, was: Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, which many of the Jews read. Let us read it also. I read the title of the king,” etc.], and it is placed above the cross, not beneath the cross, because the Beginning is above his shoulders. And what is the Beginning except his eternal power and divinity? Hence, when he was asked who he was, he answered: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you.” Let us read this title:

“Jesus,” it says, “the Nazarene, the king of the Jews.”

[Col. 1832B] 113. The title is rightly above the cross, because the kingdom that Christ possesses belongs not to human flesh but to divine power. The title is rightly above the cross, because although the Lord Jesus was on the cross, he nevertheless shone above the cross with the majesty of a king.

A worm on the cross, a scarab on the cross—and a good worm, which clung to the wood; a good scarab, which cried out from the wood. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “Father, forgive them—that is, do not hold this sin against them.”] What did he cry? “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” He cried out to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” He cried out like a scarab: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” And a good scarab, which used to turn the clay of our body, previously shapeless and sluggish, by the imprint of virtues; a good scarab, which raises the poor from the dung. He raised Paul, who was regarded as refuse; he also raised Job, who sat upon dung. Therefore the title is no ordinary one.

114. As for the place of the cross itself, it was either in the middle, so that it might be visible to all, or above the burial place of Adam, as the Hebrews argue [Note: Ambrose, with his customary modesty, makes no determination here. Of these opinions, Maldonatus, in his commentary on Matthew 27, citing the ancient Fathers who supported it, calls the latter opinion “renowned through the authority of many ancient writers.” Yet it pleased Saint Jerome less, and he embraced the former opinion in his commentary on Ezekiel 5 and likewise on Ephesians 5.]. For it was fitting that the first-fruits of our life should be placed where the beginnings of death had been.

115. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “They divided his garments and cast lots. This too is not without a mystery. For some received one thing and others another,” etc. Below, after four lines, it adds: “who wrote the Gospel.”] The garments are divided, and different portions are assigned to different persons by lot; for the Spirit of God is not grasped by human opinion but slips unexpectedly into us, as though by some chance occurrence. And perhaps these four soldiers represented the four Evangelists, who wrote the title that we should all read.

I read the title “King of the Jews” when I read: “My kingdom is [1529] not of this world” (John 18:36). I read the cause of Christ written above his head when I read: “And the Word was God” (John 1:1); for God is the head of Christ.

116. [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “And according to Matthew, sitting down they kept watch over him, and said: ‘If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross.’ These men, therefore,” etc.] These men, then, kept watch over Jesus—and they still keep watch today—lest anyone should slip, lest anyone should come down from the passion, which the Jewish people demanded. For my part, let Christ die in the passion, so that after the passion he may rise again. [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts read: “He did not wish to come down for himself, so that he might die for me.” By contrast, all the editions and the manuscript of Regensburg read: “He did not wish to come down for himself, but”—Amerbach reads “but so”—“that he might die for me.” This is not sufficiently appropriate to the context.]

He did not wish to come down for himself, so that he might die for me.

Thus Christ is now preserved for us; for our sake his garments are divided. Individuals cannot possess everything, and therefore lots are cast over the tunic, because the distribution of the Holy Spirit does not occur according to human will. For there are distributions of graces, but the Spirit is the one who works, distributing to each as he wills.

117. Look now at Christ’s divided garments. Where shall I seek them? Look in Matthew: there you will find only a scarlet cloak (Matthew 27:28); in John, a purple garment (John 19:2); in Mark, only purple (Mark 15:17); in Luke, a white garment (Luke 23:11). With this alone he was content as his portion. How many, then, did Christ clothe with his garment? I think that he clothed not only four soldiers but all of them, and that it was sufficient for all. [Note: The Roman edition adds: “Take also another point. These four parts,” etc.] But let us return to the Evangelists.

118. Mystically, therefore, these four parts seem to me to be not portions of garments but qualities of virtues. One wrote more sublimely about the kingdom; another more extensively about the formation of the human being; Luke chose for himself the splendor of priestly clothing; but Mark did not seek a woven fabric of words. Finally, John interwove certain sentences, as it were, with which he might clothe our faith.

Does not that woven passage seem to you to be: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God, and all things were made through him” (John 1:1–3)? But Mark, content as though with the radiance of purple, without any interweaving of words, says: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mark 1:1).

119. Thus Christ’s garments are divided, whether as deeds or as grace, because the tunic could not be divided—that is, faith—for it belongs not by individual portions but by common right to everyone; what is not divided remains whole for each person.

120. And rightly it says, “woven from above” (*desuper texta*); for Christ’s faith is woven in such a way that it descends from divine things to human ones: he who was born from God before the ages [Note: All the manuscripts and editions read this, except the Roman edition, which restores “begotten from God.”] assumed the taking on of flesh at a later time. It is therefore signified to us that faith must not be torn apart but remain solid.

(Verses 43.) “Amen, amen, I say to you: Today you will be with me in paradise.”

121. A most beautiful example of the conversion to be desired: pardon is granted so quickly to the thief [1530], and grace is more abundant than prayer; for the Lord always gives more than is requested. The thief was asking that the Lord remember him when he came into his kingdom; but the Lord said to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Today you will be with me in paradise” (Matthew 27:44). For to be with Christ is life; therefore, where Christ is, there are life and the kingdom. The Lord therefore forgives quickly (Mark 15:32), because the thief is quickly converted.

122. (Verse 39.) Hence the apparent discrepancy can also be resolved: some introduce two thieves insulting him, while this evangelist introduces one insulting him and one asking him [Col. 1834B]. Perhaps this one too insulted him at first, but was suddenly converted. Nor is it surprising that he forgave the converted man his guilt, since he granted pardon to those who insulted him.

He could also speak of one in the plural, as in: “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together into one” (Psalm 2:2); for in the Acts of the Apostles, only King Herod and the ruler Pilate are reported, by Peter’s voice, to have conspired against Christ (Acts 4:27). Likewise, in Hebrews you have: “They went about in skins of goats, they were sawn apart, and they stopped the mouths of lions” (Hebrews 11:37), although we are taught that Elijah alone possessed a *melotis* [a sheepskin cloak], Isaiah alone was sawn apart (2 Kings 1:8), and Daniel alone remained unharmed by the lions (Daniel 6:22).

123. (Verse 40.) How execrable was the iniquity of the Jews in their deed, that they should crucify the Redeemer of all as though he were a thief! Yet the thief is good in the mystery, for he lay in wait for the devil in order to carry off his vessels.

Mystically, the two thieves signify two sinful peoples who must be crucified with Christ through baptism; their disagreement likewise signifies the diversity of believers. Finally, one was on the left and the other on the right (John 19:30). The rebuke also reveals that the future scandal of the cross would extend even among believers.

124. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “Then, according to Matthew, one ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, and gave him drink—and he drank it. For according to John it says: ‘When Jesus had received the vinegar.’ But he did not drink wine mixed with gall. For Matthew has: ‘They gave him wine to drink mixed with gall; and when he had tasted it, he would not drink.’”] The Jews also offered vinegar (Matthew 27:48). It is fitting that, to complete everything, the corruption of purity is also drained, so that everything that had been spoiled might be fastened to the cross. Vinegar, therefore, is drunk; wine mixed with gall is not drunk (ibid., 34)—not because of the gall itself, but because the bitterness mixed into the wine is rejected. For he assumed the bitterness of our life according to the condition of the body. Hence he himself says: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68:22).

But bitterness ought not to be mixed with purity, so that it might be shown that the immortality of those who rise again will be without bitterness. Since this immortality had congealed in the human vessel, it is separated in Christ. Therefore vinegar is drunk—that is, the corruption of the immortality corrupted through Adam is abolished in the reed, so that it might be absorbed from the human body. [Note: More and better manuscripts read this. Several others, together with the ancient editions, read: “It is restored in Christ … abolished in the reed” (two manuscripts read “abolished also in the reed,” which is not displeasing), “so that it might be released from the human body” (Erasmus and Gill add in the margin “absorbed”). The Roman edition gives the whole passage as: “It is sweetened in Christ. Therefore the vinegar is drunk, which had been placed upon a reed, that is … it is absorbed in the reed, so that it might be abolished from the human body.”]

Let us also transfer our vices, accumulated through the negligence of mind and body, into Christ; let us transfer them through baptism, so that we may be crucified in Christ; let us transfer them through repentance, so that from him the incorruptible purity of heavenly wine and blood may be poured back into us.

125. Finally, when he had drunk the vinegar, he said: “It is finished” [1531] (John 19:30); for the entire mystery of the mortality he had assumed had been fulfilled, and, with all vices exhausted, only the joy of immortality remained. Therefore he said:

(Verses 46.) “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.”

126. And rightly the spirit is commended—that spirit which is preserved; for what is commended is certainly not lost. The spirit, therefore, is a good pledge, a good deposit. Hence he says there also: “O Timothy, guard the good deposit” (2 Timothy 1:14).

The spirit is commended to the Father; therefore he says: “For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld” (Psalm 15:10). Observe, however, the great mystery. Now he commends his spirit into the Father’s hands; now he sits in the Father’s bosom, because no one else wholly contains Christ. Hence he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

The spirit, therefore, is commended to the Father. But while he is in the regions above, he illuminates even the regions below, so that all things may be redeemed; for Christ is all things, and all things are in Christ, although Christ works in each individual (Colossians 3:11). The flesh dies so that it may rise again; the spirit is commended to the Father so that heavenly things too might be released from the bond of iniquity, and peace might be made in heaven, which earthly things would follow.

(Ibid.) [Note: The Roman edition reads: “And saying this, he gave up his spirit. And rightly he gave up his spirit.”] “And having said this, he gave up his spirit.”

127. And rightly he gave it up, since he released his spirit not unwillingly. Hence Matthew says: “He gave up his spirit” (Matthew 27:50); for what is released is voluntary, while what is lost is necessary.

Therefore he added: “With a loud voice.” In this there is either a glorious confession that, even unto death, he descended on account of our sins—so I too should not be ashamed to confess what Christ was not ashamed to proclaim in a loud voice—or an evident manifestation that God was testifying to the separation of divinity and body. [Note: Did Ambrose suppose that divinity withdrew from Christ’s body or soul, once assumed, contrary to Paul’s clear testimony? Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, Book III, Distinction 21, §1, and Saint Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* III, question 50, article 2, reply to objection 1, answer that divinity withdrew with respect to its effect—that is, that it withdrew its protection. For, as the former says, if he had not restrained his power but exercised it, Christ would not have died.]

For you have: “Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). The man cried out, about to die through the separation of divinity. For since divinity is free from death, death could not exist unless life departed, because divinity is life.

128. (Verses 44–47.) The events that follow show that the end of the world will come because of human impiety. Thus, through the Lord’s passion, the present age is signified as setting, so that future things may arise.

Darkness, therefore, was spread over the eyes of the faithless, so that the light of faith might rise again [Note: All editions read “might shine forth”; all manuscripts read “might rise again.”]. The sun set for the sacrilegious, or withdrew, so that it might overshadow the spectacle of the dreadful crime.

The rocks were split (Matthew 27:51), so that through the broken cliffs of the stones it might be shown that the power of the Word would in the future penetrate the hard places of sinners; thus those hunters whom Jeremiah foretold (Jeremiah 16:16) might more easily hunt for the Lord from the hollows of the rocks.

But what else does the opening of the tombs signify (Matthew 27:52), once the barriers of death have been shattered, except the resurrection of the dead? Their appearance signified faith, their coming forth a type: by going out into the holy city, they manifested in visible form what would be the everlasting dwelling-place of those who rise again in that Jerusalem which is in heaven.

[1532] The veil too is torn, signifying either the division of the two peoples or the profanation of the Synagogue’s mysteries. The old veil is therefore torn, so that the new Church may hang out the sails of her faith. The veil of the Synagogue is removed, so that, once the inner mysteries of religion have been revealed, we may see them with the gaze of the mind.

Finally, even the centurion now confesses the Son of God whom he had crucified. O hearts of the Jews harder than stones! The rocks are split, but their hearts are hardened. The judge condemns, the servant believes, the traitor condemns his own crime by death, the elements flee, the earth is shaken, the tombs are opened; yet the immovable hardness of the Jews remains while the world is shaken.

129. (Verse 49.) The women were also standing there, seeing these things; his mother too was standing, placing her own dangers second to the devotion of her love. And the Lord, hanging on the cross, who had disregarded his own dangers, commended his mother with loving affection.

John has pursued this matter at greater length, and not without reason (John 19:25) [Col. 1836D]. The others described the world shaken, heaven covered with darkness, and the sun withdrawn. Matthew and Mark added, and treated more fully, the human [Note: All editions and many manuscripts read “and mortal things”; but several others, including some of better quality, read “and moral things.” A little later, where Amerbach and nearly all the manuscripts support “clearly asserted,” Erasmus, Gill, and the Roman edition prefer “competently asserted”; we see no reason to prefer that reading.], and moral, aspects:

“My God, my God, look upon me” (Matthew 27:46); “Why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34).

Thus we should believe that the assumption of human condition had reached the cross of Christ. Luke, however, clearly asserted that forgiveness was granted to the thief through priestly intercession, and that indulgence was requested by the same service for the Jews who were persecuting him (Luke 23:45).

130. John, therefore, who penetrated the divine mysteries more fully, rightly labored to declare that she who had borne God remained a virgin. He alone teaches me what the others did not: how, while he was hanging on the cross, he addressed his mother (John 19:26), considering it more important that, as victor over punishments and sufferings and victor over the devil, he should distribute the duties of filial devotion than that he should bestow the heavenly kingdom.

For if it is a religious act that the Lord grants pardon to the thief, it is much more religious that the mother is honored by her Son.

131. Let it not be judged improper that I have written the absolution of the thief before the address to the mother. For he who had come to save sinners did not act absurdly if he first fulfilled in my writings the task he had undertaken in redeeming the sinner’s salvation.

Hence he himself says: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” (Matthew 12:48), because he had not come to call the righteous but sinners. There, this was said according to the setting; here, on the cross, he is not forgetful of his mother, but addresses her, saying: “Behold your son”; and to John: “Behold your mother” (John 19:26–27).

Christ gave testimony from the cross, and John, worthy to be the witness of so great a testator, sealed his testament. It is a good testament—not of money but of life; it is written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Psalm 44:3).

132. Nor was Mary less than was fitting for the mother of Christ: while the apostles fled, she stood before the cross [1533] and watched the wounds of her Son with devoted eyes, because she was awaiting not the death of her child but the salvation of the world.

Or perhaps, because she knew that through the Son’s death the world’s redemption would come, the royal hall thought that she too, by her death, would add something to the public service. But Jesus did not need an assistant for the redemption of all, he who said: “I became like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87:5). He accepted his mother’s affection, but he did not seek human assistance.

We therefore have a teacher of devotion [Note: The Roman edition alone reads “a lesson in devotion”; other editions read “Let the reading teach.” Nearly all manuscripts, however, agree with the text. Below, where all editions and the great majority of manuscripts read “maternal solicitude,” the reading of two Colbertine manuscripts, “maternal solitude,” is by no means displeasing; for *solitudo* frequently means the same as bereavement among good authors. Moreover, nearly everything said here about Mary and John is found almost word for word near the end of the *Letter to the Church of Vercellae*.]: the reading teaches what maternal affection ought to imitate and what children’s reverence ought to follow—so that mothers may offer themselves in their children’s dangers, and maternal concern may cause them more grief than sorrow over their own death.

133. Here a very strong testimony to Mary’s virginity is supplied. For a wife is not taken away from her husband when it is written: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6). Rather, she who had put forward a marriage for the sake of the mystery no longer needed marriage once the mysteries had been fulfilled.

Or, if we follow the moral interpretation, chastity is commanded in mourning. [Note: The reference is to the mourning period. This explains why widowed women who, during the period of mourning for their husbands—which Theodosius, in Book III, title 8 of his Code, concerning second marriages, prescribed as twelve months—hastened to a second marriage, as the jurists put it, were subject to the penalty imposed by the same law. Ambrose probably had this in mind.]

134. Yet there is a mystery in the fact that she is commended to John, the younger among the others; we must not receive this with inattentive ears. The association of a young man with women, and the appearance of youth, is dangerous, lest some woman—curious about the example but careless about the mystery—who desires to live luxuriously in Christ, should put forward Mary’s appearance but not imitate her devotion, as the common rumor now wrongly speaks of women who leave an older husband in order to follow a younger one.

Let her therefore learn that here there is a mystery of the Church. The Church, formerly joined in outward appearance, not in actual use, to an older people, after she had borne the Word and sown him in human bodies and minds through faith in the cross and the burial of the Lord, chose, at God’s command, fellowship with a younger people.

135. I also ask why we do not find him pierced before his death, but do find him pierced after his death (John 19:34) [Note: The Roman edition reads: “Finally, according to John: ‘When they came to Jesus … they opened his side.’ I therefore ask why,” etc.]. Perhaps it was so that it might be shown that his departure was voluntary rather than compelled, and so that we might understand the mystical order: not the sacraments of the altar before baptism, but baptism first, and then the cup.

Next, we should observe that although the nature of his body was mortal, and although its condition was similar to ours, its grace was nevertheless different. For in our bodies blood certainly congeals after death; but from that incorrupt body, though dead, the life of all flowed forth. “Blood and water came out” (ibid.): the water that washes, the blood that redeems. Let us therefore drink our price, so that by drinking we may be redeemed.

136. (Verse 50.) What does it also mean that not the apostles but Joseph and Nicodemus buried Christ? [Note: Again the Roman edition reads: “As John says, they buried Christ. One was just and steadfast, the other was a teacher in Israel. Such is Christ’s burial, possessing both justice and teaching.”]

One was just and steadfast, the other one in whom there was no deceit (John 19:38–39); for Christ’s burial is such that it contains no fraud or iniquity. The opportunity for evasion is [1534] therefore closed, and the Jews are refuted by the testimony of their own people. For if the apostles had buried him, they would certainly have said that he had not been buried—the very one whom they claimed had been taken away after burial.

137. The just man covers Christ’s body with a linen cloth, the innocent man anoints it with ointment (John 19:40); for we find these details distinguished, and not without reason: justice clothes the Church, while innocence supplies grace.

Therefore clothe the Lord’s body also with his glory, so that you too may be just; and although you believe him dead, cover him nevertheless with the fullness of his divinity. Anoint him with myrrh and aloe, so that you may be the good fragrance of Christ.

That just man Joseph brought a fine linen cloth, and perhaps it was the cloth that Peter saw lowered from heaven to him, containing kinds of quadrupeds, wild beasts, and birds, figured in the likeness of the nations (Acts 10:11). Thus the Church is buried with that mystical, genuine (*pistic*) ointment, the Church that has joined the diversity of peoples through the communion of her faith.

138. Of this Joseph I find only in John that he came secretly to Pilate because of fear of the Jews (John 19:38). How did a just man seek concealment because of fear of danger? I think that he asked secretly in order to obtain the body, not to avoid danger.

And yet what wonder if the just man was hidden, when the apostles, the teachers of the just, were also hidden? Come, you too: whether late, or at night, or at whatever hour you come, you will find Jesus ready to receive you, and in his gracious generosity paying no smaller reward to those who come later. For even the one who came at the sixth hour was not deprived of his reward, and the one who came at the eleventh received the fullness of his reward (Matthew 20:4 and following).

Nicodemus too came at night (John 3:2). It was night because there was not yet a resurrection. Finally, Christ rose, and the just man said: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Romans 13:12).

139. Luke called this Joseph just (Luke 23:50), while Matthew called him rich (Matthew 27:57). And rightly he is called rich here, where he received Christ’s body; by receiving the rich man, he did not know the poverty of faith. Therefore the just man is rich.

The Israelite therefore wraps him in a linen cloth (John 19:39), mixes various fragrances of virtues, and adds aloe, as though a hundred pounds—the measure of perfect faith. “And they bound the body of Jesus according to the custom [Note: Thus the ancient edition, together with all the manuscripts. The Roman edition instead reads: “according to the distinctive custom of the Jews.”] of the spiritual Jews,” not with the knots of unbelief but with the bonds of faith.

“And they placed him in a garden” (ibid., 41), to which the Church is frequently compared, since it possesses fruits of diverse merits and flowers of virtues.

[Col. 1839D] 140. Nor is it without significance that one evangelist called it a new tomb and another Joseph’s tomb (ibid.; Matthew 27:60). Christ therefore did not have a tomb of his own; for a tomb is prepared for those who are under the law of death. The victor over death has no tomb of his own. For what fellowship is there between a tomb and God?

Hence Ecclesiastes says concerning the one who meditates on good things: “And he has no burial” (Ecclesiastes 6:3). [Note: The Septuagint reads: “And his soul shall not be filled with goodness” (*Καὶ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ οὐ πληθήσεται ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγαθωσύνης*), “and his soul shall not be filled with goodness.” The Vulgate reads: “And his soul does not make use of the good things of his substance.”]

Christ’s death, therefore, is distinct from the common [1535] death of all, and for this reason he is not buried with others but alone enclosed in a tomb. For the Lord’s incarnation had everything in the likeness of human beings, [Col. 1840A] but the likeness was accompanied by difference. He was born of a Virgin: likeness in generation, difference in conception. He healed the sick, but he commanded them. John baptized with water; he with the Spirit (Luke 3:16). Christ’s death, too, is common according to the nature of the body, but distinct according to its power.

141. (Verse 53.) But who is this Joseph, in whose tomb he is placed? Surely, the just man. Therefore Christ is rightly entrusted to the tomb of the just man [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read “he is placed in the tomb of the just man” (the Roman edition, “in the tomb”); the remaining manuscripts, in large number, read “he is believed in the tomb of the just man” (some corruptly, “he enters”)], so that the Son of Man might have somewhere to rest his head, and might rest in the dwelling of justice.

He is rightly said to be placed in a new tomb—according to the literal sense, so that no other person raised from the dead might be said by the unbelieving to have been raised. But what can we understand mystically, unless perhaps because we read: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Psalm 5:11)?

The human throat, therefore, is an open tomb in which deadly unbelief and dead words are buried; through age and some assault by beasts it becomes cracked and comes apart. By contrast, there is a tomb hidden within human beings, which the just man cuts for himself in the hearts of the Gentiles with a penetrating word, hard as stone, polished by works of faith and teaching, so that the power of Christ might be displayed among the nations.

142. A stone was most fittingly placed against it (Matthew 27:60), so that it might not be open. Whoever has buried Christ well within himself must guard him carefully, lest he lose him, and lest unbelief gain entry.

You see that Peter and John were worthy to enter first. Indeed, John himself did not enter until he believed (John 20:6 and 8).

143. And rightly he is said to have been hewn out in a rock (Matthew 27:60), that is, in the firmament of faith, from which true Israelites have sucked the sweetness of honey and spiritual oil. The just man and the one who saw God buried Christ; for no one buries Christ except those who believe in God. [Note: After the words “believe in God,” the Roman edition inserts several verses from the Gospel and removes many words from Ambrose’s text, altering it to read: “Although the women stood at a distance.” Anyone who examines the passage rather than reading it superficially will understand for himself that there is no need to change the reading found in all the manuscripts and ancient editions.]

144. (Verse 55.) Finally, not everyone can bury Christ. Although devout women stand at a distance, because they are devout they carefully observe the place, so that they may bring ointments and pour them over him.

Yet, though concerned, they withdraw from the tomb later and return to the tomb earlier. Although constancy is lacking, diligence is not lacking. Their sex wavers; their devotion burns.

[Col. 1841A] 145. Finally, at the time of the resurrection they are present, and, while the men flee, they alone are instructed by the angel not to be afraid (John 2:1–2). They summon Peter, earlier in zeal but later in confidence. Finally, he comes without fear, and he who had arrived later enters first with firmness, as one who had received the keys of the kingdom in order to open it for others. [Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “while the men were fleeing.”]

146. The earthquake (Matthew 28:2), however, is resurrection for the faithful and fear for the impious: for the former, because the sluggish body [1536] is moved from the sleep of death; for the latter, because, shaken by bodily trembling and earthly movement, they fall away from faith and belief in the resurrection.

(CHAPTER XXIV — Verses 1–4.) “But very early in the morning on the Sabbath they came to the tomb.”

147. At this point a major doubt arises for many [Col. 1841B]. For although the Evangelists do not seem to have said contradictory things, they nevertheless said different things. This evangelist says: “Very early in the morning”; Mark: “Very early” (Mark 16:1); Matthew: “In the evening of the Sabbath” (Matthew 28:1); John: “On the first day of the week, while it was still dark” (John 20:1)—they said that the women came to the tomb.

Next, this evangelist remembered that two men were seen; Mark, one young man sitting in white (Mark 16:5); Matthew, one angel (Matthew 28:2); John, two angels sitting in white (John 20:12).

Finally, what seems scarcely capable of resolution: John wrote that Mary Magdalene was told: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17). Matthew wrote that the Lord met Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, and described most clearly how they approached, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him (Matthew 28:9).

148. How, then, can this be resolved unless you suppose that the four Evangelists spoke of four different times, so that you may infer that there were different women and different visions? For some come with ointment on the first day of the week; others, without ointment, on the evening of the Sabbath. The names of the former are given explicitly; the latter are identified as those who had followed the Lord from Galilee.

149. Lest anyone be offended at this point by the harshness of a thorny interpretation at the end, where something pleasant may perhaps have been anticipated, consider that we are now lowering the sails in order to complete our discourse, since we have reached the harbor. A ship that has crossed the seas at swift speed, when it begins to approach the shore, brushes against hidden rocks with an unbroken course [Col. 1841D]. Therefore, lest my discourse, like that of an inept helmsman, become stranded on the sands of the shore, I judge that the course should be slowed rather than rushed through hidden shallows [Note: [Col. 1841D] Thus in several manuscripts of better quality. Others, and the printed edition, read: “I shall read *the path should be tested*, ... the discourse may become clear” (Gill. and Rom. have *tentandum*, “should be tested”; the Roman edition adds *prius*, “first,” though *potius*, “rather,” would perhaps be preferable, which is implied by our reading). The editions of Erasmus and those following him have *the discourse may gape open* (*fatiscat oratio*), evidently because that learned man thought there was an allusion to Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> “And they gape open with fissures.”

But *patescat* (“may become clear”) is not absurd, and is found in all the manuscripts. Moreover, *lentandum* here means nothing other than [Col. 1842D] “to be moderated slowly”; for in Virgil it has the same sense as “to be bent.”]—so that our discourse may not gape open with cracks.

[Col. 1842A] 150. First, then, we must consider what is written: “Now in the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath” (Matthew 28:1), the Lord rose. For this is what you have: “In the evening of the Sabbath Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake.” It was not on the Sabbath day—for [Note: [Col. 1842D] *Siluerunt* (“they were silent”) is used, by the usage and convention of Scripture, for *quieverunt* (“they rested”).] “they rested on the Sabbath according to the commandment” (Luke 23:56)—but after the Sabbath day, certainly during the night, that he rose. Finally, those who came in the morning, even though it was very early, nevertheless learned that the Lord had already risen.

151. The matter must therefore be understood in such a way that we believe the resurrection occurred neither in the morning of the Lord’s Day, which is the first day after the Sabbath, nor on the Sabbath itself. For how would the three days then have been completed? He therefore rose not as the day was growing toward evening, but in the evening of the night. 1537 Finally, the Greek says “late,” that is, ὀψέ. “Late” marks an hour at the setting of the day, but it also signifies the lateness of anything whatsoever—as when you say, “It was suggested to me late,” that is, “belatedly.” “He came late” means that he arrived after the appointed time. Even if he came in the morning [Note: [Col. 1842D] The Roman edition inserted the words “on the following day”; for what reason it did so is not sufficiently clear.] of the following day, he is nevertheless late once the time for acting has passed. “Late” also denotes the deep time of night, as when you say, “He rose late to keep vigil,” that is, he rose not at evening but in the depth of night.

152. Hence the women also have the opportunity to approach the tomb, since the guards were by then resting; and the guards themselves are even more terrified, as happens when people are awakened from sleep. Finally, the chief priests too, gathered with the elders, affirm that this took place at night [Col. 1842C], saying to the guards: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping” (Matthew 28:13). For from the time that they learned the matter from the guards, they seize upon an argument for fraud. John indicates that Mary Magdalene came to him and Peter in the morning, while it was still dark, and yet presents her as ignorant of the resurrection that had taken place (John 20:2); for surely, if it had occurred as the day was growing toward evening, it could immediately have become known.

153. It is morning, and Peter does not know; John does not know. Would the Lord have allowed his disciples to remain longer uncertain of his death [Note: [Col. 1842D] The Roman edition reads “uncertain of his resurrection.” The older edition and most manuscripts read “uncertain of his death”; several manuscripts of better quality have simply “uncertain.” The latter is more elegant. Below, where all the editions read “immediately the angel of the Lord,” nearly all the manuscripts instead have “immediately the angel, immediately the Lord,” and so forth. This also agrees well with the Gospel narrative.] when he immediately sent the women to announce the event—first the angel, then the Lord himself? And, so that you may know that it happened at night, some women do not know and others do know: those who kept watch through nights and days know; those who departed do not. According to John, one Mary, Mary Magdalene, does not know (John 20:15); according to Matthew, another Mary Magdalene does know (Matthew 28:9). For the same person could not both know beforehand and afterward not know. Therefore, if there were several Marys, perhaps there were also several Magdalene women, since the former is a personal name, while the latter is a place-name.

154. Finally, recognize that they are two different women. One is permitted to hold the Lord’s feet; the other is forbidden to touch the Lord. One was worthy to see an angel; the other, when she first came, saw no one. One announced to the disciples that the Lord had risen; the other indicates that he had been taken away. One rejoices; the other weeps. To one Christ already appears in his glory; the other still seeks the dead man. One saw the Lord and believed; the other could not recognize him when she saw him. One worshiped in faithful spirit; the other was made sorrowful by a doubtful affection.

155. She is rightly forbidden to touch the Lord. For we touch Christ not by bodily contact but by faith [Col. 1843B]. “For I have not yet ascended,” he says, “to my Father” (John 20:17)—that is, “I have not yet ascended for you,” who seek the living among the dead. And therefore she is sent to those who are stronger, so that she may learn to believe by their example, so that they may preach the resurrection [Note: [Col. 1843D] Corbie and four other manuscripts have “so that she may be compelled by their example.” Here, however, the verb “compelled” would have to be understood in a broad sense, meaning “instructed” or “induced.”]

156. Just as at the beginning the woman was the author of the fault and the man the executor of the error, so now she who had first tasted death before the man first saw the resurrection—first in the order of guilt and first in its remedy. And lest she bear perpetual reproach among men, she who had transmitted guilt to the man also transmitted grace and compensated for the misery of the ancient fall by announcing the resurrection. Through a woman’s mouth death had first advanced; through a woman’s mouth life is restored.

157. But because steadfastness is necessary for preaching, and the weaker sex is less capable of carrying it out, the duty of evangelizing is entrusted to men [Col. 1843C]. For just as through Jesus the guilt of women is not only absolved but grace is also multiplied—so that she who had once deceived one man might persuade many—so too the man who had earlier believed rashly ought to recover his entrusted gift with increase, so that he who had been unreliable in believing for himself might become suitable for preaching to others.

158. But let us consider carefully the words of the command: “Do not touch me; for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). How had you not ascended, Lord Jesus? How were you absent, when you had commended your spirit into the hands of the Father? Or when can you be absent, who are always in the Father and always with the Father? Finally, you yourself said: “If I descend into the underworld, you are there. If I take my wings before the light and dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me” (Psalm 138:8 ff.). Or how do you ascend, who are always everywhere?

159. You descended indeed, Son of Man, yet you were not absent from the Father when you descended; but you descended for us, so that we might see you with our eyes and minds, so that we might believe in you. Therefore you also ascended for us, so that we might follow with our minds the one whom we cannot see with our eyes. [Col. 1844A] You ascended for the apostles, to whom you said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9). Finally, John knew where to seek you. He sought and found you with the Father, and therefore he said: “And the Word was with God” (John 1:1). You also ascended for Paul, who was not content to follow you alone but taught us also how we should follow you and where we can find you, saying: “Therefore, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1). And lest we think that this is more a duty of the eyes than of the soul, he added: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (ibid., 2).

160. Therefore we must not seek you above the earth, nor on the earth, nor according to the flesh, if we wish to find you; for now we no longer know Christ according to the flesh. Finally, Stephen did not seek you above the earth, for he saw you standing at the right hand of God. Mary, however, because she was seeking you on earth, could not touch you (John 20:17). Stephen touched you because he sought you in heaven; Stephen saw you absent among the Jews, while Mary did not see you present among the angels. But the Evangelist himself taught us why she could not touch you, saying that when she saw you she did not know that you were Jesus. Thus it is written: “She turned around and saw Jesus standing there, and she did not know that it was Jesus” (ibid., 1). Rightly she could not touch the one whom she had not been able to see; for whoever sees, touches.

161. Thus Scripture distinguishes what difference there is between that Mary and this one. One came forward to see Jesus; the other turned backward. One was greeted; the other was reproved. Finally, this is what you have: “Jesus said to her: Woman” (John 20:14). She who does not believe is a woman and is still designated by the appellation of bodily sex. But she who believes comes forward as a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age, already lacking the name of the world, bodily sex, the instability of youth, and the loquacity of old age. 1539 Jesus therefore says: “Woman, why are you weeping?” (ibid., 15). It is as though he said: “God does not demand bare tears but faith. Your tears are good if you recognize Christ. Whom are you seeking?” he says (ibid.). For the Lord condemns belated efforts. But he rightly added: “Whom are you seeking?” Not because he is uncertain whom she seeks, but because she does not know whom she is seeking; for she is not seeking Christ, whom she thinks has been taken away. Christ is present—how, then, is he sought? The one who is sought is unknown when he is not recognized while being seen.

[Col. 1844D] 162. Finally, she saw Christ but thought him to be the gardener. Thus it is written: “Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him: Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have put him, and I will take him” (ibid.). Although uncertain in faith, she was not slippery in speech; although she thought him a gardener, she nevertheless designated him as the Son of God; although she still did not believe, she nevertheless desired to believe. For he who raised it had himself taken up the body [Note: [Col. 1844D] Several manuscripts of better age have “who received it,” with the meaning indicated below, where it is said that the body was assumed through the glory of the resurrection.]. Therefore the woman’s error is pardonable: although she ought not to have doubted that Christ’s body had been assumed through the glory of the resurrection, she nevertheless desires to be taught by Christ and devotedly promises him her faith, so that she herself may now take it away from earthly things and seek it at the right hand of God.

163. Finally, after these words she is called not “woman” but “Mary” (John 20:16). For one thing is the common name of the multitude, another the distinctive name of a person who follows Christ. And although she is not yet fully convinced of the faith, she is nevertheless sent as a messenger to the disciples [Note: [Col. 1845D] Erasmus and the editions following him, together with some manuscripts, read: “not yet convinced, yet now a messenger of complete faith.” Amerbach’s reading, with other manuscripts and as in the text, is better, except that Amerbach separated the word “convinced” by a comma from what follows.]. She is forbidden to touch because she had not yet received, as Paul had, “the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in Christ” (Colossians 2:9); she had not yet emptied herself of the world’s instability or of the ambiguity of the flesh; she had not yet lived the life of Christ. [Note: [Col. 1845D] All editions and many manuscripts have: “Finally, she neither worships.” Many others, and manuscripts of good quality, have: “Finally, she stands; she does not worship.”] Finally, she stands and does not worship the Lord, nor does she hold his feet, as that other Mary does. In that other Mary, it is not so much bodily service as the disposition of complete faith that is signified: she believes Christ to be both man and God. For the one who is worshiped is God; the one whose feet are held is man (Matthew 28:9) [Col. 1845B].

164. The Lord therefore does not disdain to be touched by a woman, whose feet Mary also anointed with perfume (Luke 7:38). Nor does he reject the touch; rather, he teaches progress, because not everyone can touch the risen Christ who touched him while he dwelt in this life and in the body. Whoever wishes to touch Christ must mortify his own members, put on, in likeness to the one who will rise, a heart of compassion, and not hesitate to renounce earthly things.

165. What, then, does “Do not touch me” mean (John 20:17)? “Do not lay your hand upon the greater ones” [Note: [Col. 1845D] Corbie alone has: “Do not lay your hand upon the lesser ones.” The following words strongly favor this reading: “But go ... to the more perfect.”], but “go to my brothers,” that is, to the more perfect. For “whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my 1540 brother, and sister, and mother” (Matthew 12:50). Since the resurrection cannot easily be grasped except by the more perfect, the privilege of this faith is reserved for those more firmly grounded: “I do not permit a woman to teach in the Church; let them ask their husbands at home” (1 Corinthians 14:35). She is therefore sent to those who are of the household and receives the prescribed commands (1 Timothy 2:12).

166. Nor has it escaped the notice of some at this point that Christ did not wish to be touched because he had not yet received [Note: [Col. 1845D] Two manuscripts, and the editions of Erasmus and Gillotius in the margin, as well as the Roman edition in the text, have “received the spirit.” Other manuscripts and older editions have “received the type.” Although the latter may seem somewhat obscure, it can nevertheless be explained without difficulty if we say that by “type,” or “form,” is understood the perfect glorification of Christ’s humanity, which he received only when he ascended to the right hand of the Father. Before receiving it, Magdalene could in no way touch him; that is, the Church of the Gentiles, which was signified by that woman, did not yet believe in him. See Augustine, *Tractate 121 on John*, no. 3.] the form he had commended to the Father, as though he still ought not to be touched.

167. “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). He rightly made the distinction, because he was speaking to a woman. For we have no nature in common with Christ except the condition of human nature. He has the Father by proper generation; we, by voluntary adoption. He, by nature; we, by grace. He has God through the unity of the mystery; we, through heavenly power [Col. 1845D].

168. Someone may say: How, then, did Thomas touch Christ when he still did not believe (ibid., 27)? But he seems to have doubted not the Lord’s resurrection but the quality of the resurrection. And by his touch he ought to teach me, just as Paul also taught: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53), so that the unbeliever might believe and the doubter could no longer doubt. For we more readily believe what we see. Thomas had cause for wonder when he saw the body inserted, with its structure unharmed, through all barriers and with every door closed. Hence it is marvelous how corporeal nature infused itself through an impenetrable body, by an invisible entrance but with visible appearance—easy to touch, difficult to comprehend.

169. (Verse 37, 39.) Finally, the disciples, troubled, thought they were seeing a spirit. Therefore, so that he might show us the appearance of the resurrection, the Lord said: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” [Note: [Col. 1846D] Several manuscripts have “so that he might show us the form,” and so forth.]. He therefore penetrated closed spaces—not through an incorporeal nature, but through the quality of a bodily resurrection, which by its nature passes through what is impassable. For what is touched is a body; what is handled is a body; and in a body we shall rise: “It is sown an animal body; it rises a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44). But the one is more subtle, the other denser, being still compacted by the condition of earthly stain [Col. 1846B].

170. For how could it not be a body in which the marks of wounds and the traces of scars remained, which the Lord offered to be touched? In this he not only strengthens faith but also sharpens devotion, because he preferred to carry the wounds received for us into heaven rather than erase them, so that he might display to God the Father the price of our freedom. Such a one the Father seats at his right hand, embracing the trophies of our salvation; he will show us there such martyrs, with the crown of their scars [Col. 1846C].

171. 1541 And since our discourse has extended this far, let us consider with what explanation the apostles believed according to John, since they rejoiced (John 20:20), while according to Luke they are reproved as though unbelieving (verse 25); why there they received the Holy Spirit, whereas here they are commanded to remain in the city until they are clothed with power from on high (verse 49). It seems to me that the one, like an apostle, touched upon greater and higher matters, while the other treated what followed and what was closer to human experience. The latter used a historical circuit; the former a concise account. For there can be no doubt about the one who bears witness to what he himself witnessed (John 19:35), and his testimony is true. It is right, therefore, to remove from this evangelist also any suspicion either of negligence or of falsehood. [Col. 1846D] We therefore consider both accounts true, distinguished neither by diversity of opinions nor by diversity of persons. For although Luke first says that they did not believe, he nevertheless demonstrates that afterward they did believe. If we consider the first statements, they are contradictory; if the later ones, it is certain that they agree. Let us therefore consider the very words of Scripture.

172. (Verses 35–37.) John says: “And the disciples rejoiced when they had seen the Lord. Therefore he said to them again: Peace be with you. As the Father sent me, I also send you. And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:20 ff.). Luke, however, says: “And how they recognized him in the breaking of bread. While they were speaking of these things, he himself stood in their midst and said to them: Peace be with you; it is I, do not be afraid. But they, troubled and terrified, thought they were seeing a spirit.” It might seem that there were more persons here. But since both here, on the evening of the day of the resurrection—for those who had entered the village with the Lord and remained there, when he suddenly withdrew from them, are reported to have returned to the disciples at that same hour as the day was already declining [Note: [Col. 1847D] The Roman edition reads: “who had entered the village with the Lord.”]—and according to John, on the evening of that day, the first day of the week, he is presented as having appeared to the disciples and offered his wounds to be touched (John 20:19), we thought it necessary to investigate the matter more carefully, lest it introduce any ambiguity [Col. 1847B].

173. For he seems to have revealed himself separately to these eleven, just as he had already shown himself separately in the evening to Ammaon and Cleopas [Note: [Col. 1847D] Petavius observes the following in his notes on Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 23: “Ambrose calls this man Ammaon in his commentary on Luke, chapter 24. But I suspect that something is missing in Ambrose. For Ammaon seems to have been the name of the place, through a slight corruption, in place of Emmaus. Moreover, the name of the other disciple should be substituted.” Yet, with due respect to so great a man, that conjecture cannot stand. For not only here but in many other places—such as in this very *Exposition* on chapter 17, in *Apology 2 of David*, chapter 8, in the *Treatise on the Creed*, in the sermon for the sixth Sunday after Epiphany, and elsewhere—the other of those disciples is called Ammaon. Nor should Ambrose therefore be mocked, as though he had taken a village for a disciple of Christ. For since Origen, in the preface to his *Commentary on John*, also calls him Simeon, what prevents us from thinking that Ambrose may have read “Ammaon” there through a scribal error, as some have supposed? It may also be said that this was the opinion of our Doctor—or perhaps of Origen himself—that Ammaon or Emmaon was named from the place, just as above, in no. 153, Magdalene is said to be a place-name. This opinion seems to be strengthened by the fact that the Evangelist describes these same disciples entering and reclining in the village in such a way that one would think they were returning to their own homes rather than lodging with strangers.]. And just as these two, so too those eleven seem to have been able to assemble in order to confirm the others. Finally, they were troubled, as you have it according to Luke; and therefore he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the things that had been written. It is beyond doubt that one writer gave the fuller account and the other the more concise. For how could they say that he appeared to Cephas alone if he had been seen by everyone? But just as among the women he appeared to Mary and the other Mary Magdalene, so among the men he appeared first to Peter in the morning. Paul says: “For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas” (1 Corinthians 15:3 ff.). Therefore Mark specifically has the young man command the women to tell Peter and the disciples that the Lord had risen (Mark 16:5, 7).

1542 174. Peter therefore saw the Lord alone. For his devotion was always prepared and ready to believe, and therefore he sought to gather more frequent signs for his faith. In one place with John, in another place alone, everywhere eager to run, everywhere either alone or first: not content to have seen what he had seen, he returned to look again. Inflamed by love of seeking the Lord, he was not satisfied merely with seeing him. [Col. 1848A] He saw him alone; he saw him with the eleven; he saw him with the seventy; he saw him when Thomas believed; he saw him while he was fishing. But not content with having seen him, impatient in his desire, heedless of the catch, forgetful of danger, though not forgetful of reverence, when he saw the Lord on the shore he covered himself with a garment, judging it too slow to reach him by boat with the others. Thus, when the Lord was walking upon the waters, he ran out over the waves of the sea, forgetting his own nature (Matthew 14:28); thus, when the Lord was being seized by the Jews, he alone drew a sword against the crowd (Matthew 26:51); thus now, when the Lord stood on the dangerous shore, he hastened his reverent service by taking a shortcut (John 21:4).

175. There is therefore no doubt that Peter believed, and believed because he loved, and loved because he believed. Hence he is saddened because he is questioned for the third time: “Do you love me?” (ibid., 17). For the one about whom there is doubt is questioned. But the Lord does not doubt when he asks—not in order to learn, but in order to teach whom, as he was about to be raised into heaven, he was leaving us as a kind of representative of his love. Thus it is written: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” “You know, Lord, that I love you.” Jesus says to him: “Feed my lambs” (ibid., 16). Fully conscious of himself, Peter testifies that his affection had not been assumed for the moment but had long been known to God. For who else could readily make such a profession about himself? And because he alone among them makes the profession, he is placed before them all; for love is greater than all.

176. We must also consider more carefully why, when the Lord said, “Do you love me?” Peter replied, “You know, Lord, that I love you.” It seems to me that “love” (*dilectio*) contains the affection of the mind, while “love” (*amor*) denotes a certain heat conceived through the ardor of body and mind. I think Peter signifies not only the fervor of his mind but also that of his body in the worship of God. Finally, the third time the Lord did not ask, “Do you love me?” but, “Do you have love for me?” (John 21:17). And he is now commanded to feed not lambs, as at first—those nourished by a kind of milk—nor little sheep, as at the second questioning, but sheep: the more perfect, so that the more perfect man might govern them.

177. And therefore, as one perfect in all things, whom the flesh could no longer recall from the glory of martyrdom, he is granted a crown: “When you were younger,” he says, “you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you have grown old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (ibid., 18). A good old age—not weakened for service by the length of life, but prepared for martyrdom by the maturity of virtue [Col. 1849A]—which restrains the wantonness 1543 of bodily pleasures and does not indulge desires; which avoids whatever is sweet and does not seek what is attractive. For “the flesh desires against the spirit,” and finds for itself crosswise paths on which to walk wherever it wishes amid various pleasures (Galatians 5:17). Good, rather, is the old age of the mind, which chooses not what is pleasant to the body but what is useful to the mind; it is not carried away by bodily appetite [Note: [Col. 1849D] Several manuscripts read: “is not seized by appetite, but is drawn back, as though unwilling, by the restraint of resistance,” and so forth.], but is recalled, as though unwilling, by the discipline of resistance.

178. Thus Peter, although he was mentally prepared to undergo martyrdom (Luke 22:33), nevertheless, when danger arrived, bent the steadfastness of his mind. For the enjoyment of a heavenly gift captivates us by its sweetness. Who among us would not choose martyrdom if he could die willingly? [Col. 1849B] Peter therefore seems unwilling, but he prepares himself to conquer. And what is surprising if Peter is unwilling, when the Lord says: “Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Matthew 26:39)? Finally, after the temptation arising from his presumption, Peter no longer dares to promise perseverance in his own will; rather, as though seeking consolation for himself, he seeks the companionship of another.

179. (Verses 37, 45.) With so many examples of virtue brought forward, we believe that Peter could not have doubted. It is also clear that John believed (John 20:8), when he saw the Savior; for he believed then, after he had seen the tomb empty of the body. Why, then, does Luke present several as troubled? First, because the opinion of the few is included within the judgment of the majority; secondly, because although Peter had believed in the resurrection, he could nevertheless have been troubled when he saw the Lord, with his body, suddenly entering through the closed spaces enclosed by vestibules and built walls [Note: [Col. 1849D] The edition reads: “with the walls enclosed and obstructed”; the manuscripts have: “with the walls enclosed and constructed,” and so forth.]. Luke therefore followed the individual events historically; the other writer looked to the conclusion, while Luke looked to the sequence. For by saying, “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the things that were written,” he too plainly professes that the disciples believed.

180. (Verse 49.) Either he breathed the Holy Spirit upon those eleven, as the more perfect, and promised that it would afterward be given to the others (John 20:22), or he breathed upon those same men there and promised it here. There seems to be no contradiction, since there are divisions of graces: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the grace of healings in the one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12:8 ff.). Therefore there he breathed one operation, and here he promises another. For there the grace of forgiving sins was bestowed, which seems the greater; and therefore Christ breathes upon them, 1544 so that you may believe it is the Spirit of Christ, and believe that the Spirit is from God—for God alone forgives sins. Luke, however, describes the grace of tongues being poured out. Thus there you have: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John, passage cited). But in the Acts of the Apostles you have: “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4).

181. The diversity of visions signifies the multitude of ministering angels (Matthew 28:2), in accordance with what the Lord himself had promised, saying: “And you will see angels descending and ascending to the Son of Man” (John 1:51). Would that our discourse too might be brought to a close together with the Gospel!

182. Why, according to Matthew and Mark, does he command the disciples: “I will go before you into Galilee” (Matthew 26:32); “there you will see me” (Mark 16:7), while according to Luke and John he also presented himself to be seen inside a room (verse 36)? We have indeed proved by apostolic testimony that he repeatedly offered himself to be seen (John 20:19), and that he appeared to more than five hundred brothers, to Peter, and to James (1 Corinthians 15:6). Luke also taught in the Acts of the Apostles that he showed the disciples that he was alive after his passion, appearing to them through many proofs and speaking about the kingdom of God (Acts 1:3). Therefore, since he appeared more frequently and in different places, Scripture does not indicate any prescribed or definite time for when he was seen in Galilee. But when he presented himself in Jerusalem, it specified both the day and the hour. The more timid were revisited inside rooms [Col. 1850C]; the stronger gathered on the mountain.

183. Finally, John presents the disciples gathered inside a room, with the doors closed, because of fear of the Jews (John 20:19). Luke writes that these were not eleven but more (verse 33), whereas Matthew does not omit the fact that only eleven gathered with him in Galilee. Thus you have: “The eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. And seeing him, they worshiped him; but some doubted” (Matthew 28:16–17). To them he granted the authority to teach and baptize. Mark too writes that he appeared at the end to the eleven disciples as they reclined (Mark 16:7), when he likewise entrusted to them the duty of preaching throughout the whole world.

184. Hence I consider this the more fitting explanation: the Lord certainly commanded the disciples to see him in Galilee, but while they were remaining inside the room out of fear [Note: [Col. 1850D] The edition reads: “they are visited inside the room ... they gathered”; Amerbach has “they may have gathered”; the manuscripts agree with us by a large majority, except that some read: “they are revisited ... so that the stronger might gather.”], he first presented himself to them. Later, once their minds had been strengthened, those eleven went to Galilee. Or, certainly—and I find that this too has pleased careful writers—there is no obstacle to saying that fewer were inside the room, while more were on the mountain.

[Col. 1851]

COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, COLLECTED FROM THE WRITINGS OF SAINT AMBROSE BY WILLIAM, ONCE ABBOT OF SAINT-THIERRY, LATER A MONK OF SIGNY.

[Col. 1851B]

TO THE READER

Our intention had indeed been to present in this volume no other works than those relating to the exposition of the Old and New Testaments, and those demonstrably written by Ambrose—if one excepts only the second *Apology of David*. But when, on considering the number of spurious treatises that we have decided to publish at the end of the following volume, we feared that the latter might become excessively large, we thought some supplement should be added to this first volume. Since none of our Doctor’s genuine works presented itself that either sufficiently agreed with the subject of the preceding works or was sufficient to establish an appropriate balance between the two volumes, nothing seemed more suitable than to append this commentary.

It occupies a certain middle position between the genuine and spurious works of blessed Ambrose. It is not wholly foreign to him, since it consists of his words and opinions; yet it is not entirely his own, since it was arranged by another. It is certain that Ambrose never deliberately wrote a work on the Song of Songs. But because he plainly took such great delight in that book that he never missed an opportunity to elucidate it in his various writings, this suggested to some students of Ambrosian works that, by gathering together what was scattered and dispersed there, they might stitch it together, in the manner of a patchwork garment, into a single body of commentary.

Hence in 1558 there appeared at Louvain an *Exposition on the Song of Songs* excerpted by Costerius, a Regular Canon. Although Gillotius praises Costerius’s diligence, he testifies that Costerius altered everything, removed much, and added still more of his own. A decade later, Gillotius published at the end of the works of Saint Ambrose, which he had revised under his own care, another *Exposition of the Song of Songs*, said to have been excerpted and collected into a single body by Antonius Monchiacenus Demochare, a doctor of the Sorbonne.

Nevertheless, it seems much more likely that this collection was merely expanded and interpolated by Demochare. For it is contained, though in a shorter form, not only in the manuscript of the College of Navarre, approximately four hundred years old, and in a codex of the monastery of Vendôme written six hundred years ago, but also in a copy at least eight hundred years old. It is cited as well in the still unpublished commentary on the Epistles of Saint Paul by Florus, deacon of Lyons, who lived around the year 855. Peter Francis Chifletius kept these two codices in his possession during his lifetime.

We now offer a third commentary on the same subject, never before committed to the press. Although we find it handwritten in many libraries without the author’s name, it is nevertheless established that it was collected by no one other than William, formerly abbot of Saint-Thierry and later a monk of Signy. This can be understood from William himself, when, in the preface to his treatise *On the Solitary Life*, while reviewing his writings for the brothers of Mont-Dieu, he says: “For I excerpted from the books of Saint Ambrose whatever he discussed in them concerning the Song of Songs—a great and celebrated work.”

This cannot in any way be understood of Chifletius’s commentary, since that William flourished only around the year 1142. But the decisive evidence is that William’s own autograph codex, bearing his name, still exists at Signy. From it the Reverend Father Casimir Oudin, a Canon Regular of Prémontré from the reformed congregation, a man born to deserve well of all, copied a manuscript for us with his own hand.

The title of this collection in the aforesaid codex of Signy is: *Excerpts from the Books of Blessed Ambrose on the Song of Songs.*

[Col. 1851C]

[COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS (G,S)*]

PROLOGUE

[Col. 1851]

[Col. 1851A] 1545 I. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1): here the inducements to indecency are not celebrated, but the mysteries of chastity; here the marriage and union of Christ and the Church, of uncreated spirit and created spirit, of flesh and spirit, are treated spiritually and with a certain affective contemplation. [Note: [Col. 1851D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 12, no. 2.] Let us therefore circumcise our heart: let us seek nothing base, nothing corporeal; everything earthly is base. Let us therefore establish nothing earthly, nothing carnal, nothing worldly, nothing corporeal, nothing frivolous or changeable in these heavenly utterances. For “the utterances of the Lord are pure utterances,” so that in them the immaculate and chaste sincerity of heavenly mysteries may shine forth through spiritual interpretation. Let us not mingle earthly things with divine through some adulterous opinion, nor violate that inviolate sacrament of prophetic vision or everlasting oracle by an estimation based on our nature. Whether the subject is kisses or matters of that kind, everything offered to religion ought to be fitting, so that we may not be ashamed of any service that advances the worship and observance of Christ—as in David’s dancing before the ark. For that dance was not the companion of pleasure and luxury, but signified that each person should raise an active body and not allow his sluggish limbs to lie upon the ground or his feet to grow numb through slow steps. This instruction we have not discovered for ourselves but received; thus heavenly teaching established the order of the mystical song.

1547 2. [Note: [Col. 1852D] On Virgins, book II, chapter 6.] “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth; for your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices. Your name is an ointment poured out” (ibid.). This entire passage of delights sounds like play, arouses applause, and provokes love. “Therefore,” it says, “the maidens loved you and drew you; let us run after the fragrance of your ointments. The king brought me into his chamber” (ibid., 3). She began with kisses in order to reach the chamber; and she, impatient of the Lord’s labor and exercised in virtue, is moved to open the bolts with her hand, go out into the field, and remain in the villages. At the beginning, however, she runs after the fragrance of the ointment; when she has entered the chamber, she will change the ointment for the villages. Finally, observe where she arrives.

3. “If she is a wall,” he says, “let us build upon her towers of silver” (Song 8:9). She who was playing with kisses now raises towers, so that, crowned with the precious pinnacles of the saints, she may not only frustrate hostile attacks but also construct secure defenses of good works. Even in these temporal marriages, the bride is first applauded before she is commanded, lest harsh commands offend her before love, fostered by endearments, has matured. A young cow learns to love the sound of applause, so that she will not refuse the yoke upon her neck; finally, she is accustomed to the word of [1548] playfulness before the blows of discipline. But once she has submitted her neck to the yoke, the reins constrain her, the goad drives her, her companions pull her, and the yoked partner invites her.

Thus our Virgin, too, ought first to have been fashioned by devout love; she ought to admire the golden supports of the heavenly bridal chamber, and at the very vestibule of the wedding to see the doorposts crowned with garlands of foliage, and inwardly to taste the delights of the resounding choir, lest she withdraw in fear from the Lord’s yoke before she bowed when called. For we ought to recognize certain stages of progress and a certain order: what must come first and what afterward. To know what you should do, but not to know the order in which it should be done, is not perfect knowledge; things done out of order generally cause offense.

Therefore, since there are as many opinions as there are people, let everyone read whatever in our speech has been clarified; let the more mature approve whatever has been refined; let whatever is modest cling to their hearts and color their cheeks; let a flourishing age not reject whatever is flowery. We ought to awaken love for the bride; for it is written, “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:5). [Col. 1854B] We ought to adorn the bride’s hair at the wedding with certain curling-irons of prayer; for it is written, “Clap your hand and stamp your foot” (Ezek. 21:14). We ought to scatter roses throughout the everlasting bridal chambers.

## THE TEXT BEGINS

[Col. 1853]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1853B]

1547 1. [Note: [Col. 1853D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 1, no. 2.] Life must be sought before teaching. A good life even without teaching possesses grace, but teaching without life does not possess integrity. For “wisdom does not enter a malicious soul” (Wis. 1:4); and therefore it says, “The wicked will seek me and will not find me” (Prov. 1:28), because the eye of the mind is blinded by depravity, and when iniquity has darkened it, it cannot discover profound mysteries.

First, therefore, the warfare of life must be undertaken and morals corrected. When we have ordered these toward their proper course, so that correction may remove offense and grace may produce purity, then let us proceed in its proper order and way to the studies by which knowledge is acquired. The moral things are therefore first, the mystical second: in the former there is life, in the latter knowledge. Thus, if you seek perfection, there must be neither life without knowledge nor knowledge without life; each must support the other.

Following this instruction, Solomon wrote the book of Proverbs, in which he expressed the moral realm more fully; the natural realm in Ecclesiastes; and the mystical realm in the Song of Songs. Yet, if you examine carefully, you will find many mystical things in Proverbs and the sweetness of moral teaching in the Song of Songs. For this is certainly mystical: “Wisdom built herself a house and set up seven pillars; she slaughtered her sacrifices,” and so forth (Prov. 9:1). Indeed, what is mystical shines in the Song of Songs as moral teaching does—where the sweetness of endearments and the affection of the lover are expressed.

2. (Verses 1–2.) “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth; for your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.” Imagine, then, a betrothed Virgin who has waited a long time and burns with a righteous love; who has learned, through the testimony of trustworthy witnesses, of the beloved’s many splendid works; who, having often been delayed while her desires remained suspended, can no longer endure delay; and who would have done everything in order to see the bridegroom. At last, having obtained what she desired and being disturbed with joy at the bridegroom’s unexpected arrival, she does not seek the beginnings of a greeting or an exchange of words, but immediately demands what she had desired.

So also the holy Church, betrothed at the beginning of the world in paradise, prefigured in the Flood, announced through the Law, and summoned through the prophets—after having long awaited the redemption of humanity, the beauty of the Gospel, and the coming of the beloved—impatient of delay, rushes to his kisses, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” And delighted by the kisses, she adds: “For your breasts are better than wine.”

3. And, to speak in a more moral manner, I understand this as that flesh which had been drenched in the serpent’s poison in Adam, which languished in the stench of crimes, which went forth among the daughters of Zion with an arrogant neck and with glances of the eyes, dragging its garments along with the movement of its feet and playing with its feet, with curled hair, composed faces, and ribbons, and which, through every affected adornment, became more disgraceful. Yet this same flesh, instructed by many oracles [1548] that the one was to come who, driving out the serpent’s seductions, would pour in the grace of the Holy Spirit—so that all flesh might see the salvation of God and all flesh might come to God—languished with desire.

But it feared that, being impatient, wanton, luxurious, or querulous, as it had formerly been, it might displease him, even as it was shaken by expectation of the Lord’s delayed coming—delayed longer than it could now endure. Nevertheless, it did not murmur or transgress; rather, it lifted pure hands in every place, without anger or dispute, adorning itself with modesty and sobriety. It did not adorn itself with braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but with those things that befit the grace of chastity and good conduct. It prayed and said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth; for your breasts are better than wine.”
