Already the flesh wished to cling to Christ; already it hastened to enter into marriage with him, so that it might become one spirit and that the flesh which had formerly been a harlot might become the flesh of Christ. “Let him kiss me,” it says. The Word of God kisses us when the spirit of knowledge illumines our understanding.

4. [Note: [Col. 1855D] On Isaac, chapter 3.] Thus, either it is the Church, long held in suspense by the Lord’s coming promised to her through the prophets over the course of many ages, or it is the soul which, lifting itself above the body, having cast off luxury, delights, and carnal pleasures, and having also stripped itself of concern for worldly vanities, has long desired for itself the infusion of the divine presence and the grace of the saving Word. It is worn away and afflicted because he comes late; therefore, as though wounded by love and unable to endure his delays, it turns to the Father and asks that God send the Word to it, declaring the reason for its impatience by saying: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”

5. It does not seek one kiss but many kisses, so that it may fulfill its desire. For she who loves is not content with the sparing gift of a single kiss; she demands many, claims many, and is accustomed in this way to commend herself more fully to the beloved. Finally, that woman in the Gospel was commended in this way: “She has not ceased,” says the Lord, “to kiss my feet; and therefore her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:46–47).

Therefore this soul, too, desires many kisses of the Word, so that it may be illumined by the light of divine knowledge. For this is the kiss of the Word: the light of sacred knowledge. God the Word kisses us when he illumines our heart and the principal element of the human being itself—the spirit—with divine knowledge. Having received through this gift of love a pledge of marriage, the soul, joyful and exultant, says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118:131).

For the kiss is that by which lovers cling to one another and, as it were, enjoy the sweetness of inward grace. Through this kiss the soul clings to the Word of God, because the spirit of the one who kisses is poured into it. Likewise, those who kiss one another do not seem content with a mere tasting of the lips, but appear to pour their spirit into each other.

1549 6. [Note: [Col. 1855D] On the Sacraments, book V, chapter 2.] “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” Do you wish to apply this to Christ? Nothing is more pleasing. Do you wish to apply it to your soul? Nothing is more delightful.

“Let him kiss me”: he sees that you are clean from every sin, because offenses are earthly; therefore he judges you worthy of the heavenly sacraments and therefore invites you to the heavenly banquet, so that he may kiss you “with the kisses of his mouth.”

Yet, in view of what follows, your soul—or human nature—or the Church saw that it had been cleansed from all sins and was worthy to approach the altar of God. For what is the altar except a representation of the body of Christ? It saw the wondrous sacraments and said: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth”—that is, let Christ impress his kiss upon me. Why? Because:

7. “Your breasts are better than wine”—that is, your senses are better, your sacraments better than wine—better than that wine which, although it has sweetness, joy, and grace, contains worldly joy, whereas in you there is spiritual delight.

Already then Solomon was introducing the marriage either of Christ and the Church or of spirit and flesh and soul. [Note: [Col. 1855D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 1, no. 5.] And, as though scorning all his joys and delights and desiring to cling to heavenly commandments, he says: “For the best precepts of your covenants are better than every appetite of the flesh and the pleasure of the world.” For he remembered that he had previously fallen in Eve in this way, when he preferred bodily pleasure to heavenly commandments.

[Note: [Col. 1855D] On Isaac, chapter 3.] Showing, therefore, that she loves not merely the appearance of the Word or a certain face, but all his inward parts, she adds to the grace of kisses: “For your breasts are good,” she says, “better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.”

She asked for a kiss; God the Word poured himself wholly into her, exposed his breasts to her—that is, his teachings and the disciplines of inward wisdom—and filled her with the sweet fragrance of his ointments. [Col. 1856B] Captivated by these, she says that the delight of divine knowledge is more abundant than the joy of every bodily pleasure.

8. [Note: [Col. 1855D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 1, no. 5.] “Your name is an ointment poured out,” or “an oil poured forth.” That is: this world once stank everywhere with the unclean impurities of various crimes; now the sweetness of chastity breathes everywhere, the ointment of faith, the flower of integrity.

[Note: [Col. 1856D] On Isaac, chapter 3.] In the Word there also breathes the fragrance of grace and the forgiveness of sins. Poured out over the whole world, it filled everything like an ointment poured forth, because the heavy filth of vices has been wiped away throughout the world.

[Note: [Col. 1856D] On Virginity, chapter 11.] This ointment was poured out upon the Jews and gathered by the Gentiles; it was poured out in Judea and gave its fragrance throughout all lands. Mary was anointed with this ointment, and the Virgin conceived; the Virgin gave birth to the Son of God, the good fragrance. This ointment was poured out over the waters and sanctified the waters. The three young men were anointed with this ointment, and the flame sprinkled them with moisture. Daniel was anointed with this ointment, and it softened the mouths of the lions and soothed their ferocity.

This ointment flows every day and never fails. Take your vessel, virgin, and approach, so that you may be filled with this ointment. Take the ointment valued at three hundred denarii, but given freely, not sold, so that all might have it freely. Virgin, anoint yourself. Do not grieve like Judas, because this ointment is poured out; rather, bury Christ within yourself. Close your vessel securely, lest the ointment flow away. Close it with the key of integrity, with modesty in speech, and with abstinence from boasting. She who possesses this ointment receives Christ: “Your name is an ointment poured out.”

[Col. 1856D] 9. (Verse 2.) [Note: [Col. 1856D] On the Sacraments, book V, chapter 2.] “Therefore the maidens loved you.” Who are these maidens except the souls of individuals who have laid aside the old age of this body and have been renewed through the Holy Spirit?

[Note: [Col. 1856D] On the Holy Spirit, book I, chapter 8.] “Your name is an ointment poured out,” whose power in speech can have nothing more excellent. For just as ointment enclosed in some vessel restrains its fragrance—the fragrance which, while confined within the narrowness of that vessel, cannot reach many, yet preserves its power—so, when the ointment has been poured out of the vessel in which it was enclosed, it is said to be diffused far and wide.

In the same way, before his coming, the name of Christ was enclosed among the people of Israel, as though in a vessel, within the minds of the Jews: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:1). This name, then, which the vessels of the Jews contained and confined within their narrow limits, was indeed a great name even then, when it remained within the narrow confines of the weak and the few; but it had not yet poured out its greatness through the hearts of the nations and to the ends of the whole world.

Afterward, however, through his coming, it shone throughout the whole world and extended that divine name of his throughout every creature—not because anything had been added to it, for fullness knows no increase, but because it filled what was empty, so that his name might be wondrous throughout the whole earth. [Col. 1857B] The pouring out of this name therefore signifies a certain abundant overflow of graces and an abundance of heavenly blessings; for whatever is poured out overflows from abundance.

[Note: [Col. 1857D] On Isaac, chapter 3.] “Therefore the maidens loved you.” “Good,” he says, “is prudence, but mercy is sweet.” Few attain the former, but the latter reaches everyone. “Because of this indulgence of yours,” he says, “souls renewed by the Spirit love you.”

10. (Verse 3.) [Note: [Col. 1857D] Letter to Irenaeus.] “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” The holy soul, having already kissed the Word of God, does not know moderation and is not satisfied, saying: “You are sweet, O Lord, and in your delight teach me your ordinances” (Ps. 118:12).

Having kissed the Word of God, it desires him above every beauty, loves him above every joy, delights in him above all spices, longs to see him frequently and gaze upon him often; it longs to be drawn so that it may follow. “Your name is an ointment poured out,” it says; “therefore we maidens love you. Therefore we strive, but we cannot grasp you. Draw us, so that we may run; so that through the fragrance of your ointments we may receive the strength to follow.”

It also hastens to see the inward mysteries: the very repose of the Word, the dwelling of that supreme good, and his light and splendor in that paternal bosom and retreat. It hastens to hear his words, and when it has heard them, it receives something surpassing every sweetness.

11. Let the prophet who tasted teach you, saying: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118:103). For what else does the soul desire once it has tasted the sweetness of the Word, once it has seen his glory?

Moses, stationed on the mountain and receiving the Law for forty days, did not seek bodily food. Elijah, hastening toward that rest, asked that his soul be taken from him. Peter, likewise seeing the glory of the Lord’s resurrection on the mountain, did not wish to descend, saying: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4). How great, then, was that glory of the divine substance; how great were the gifts of the Word, into which angels long to look!

12. The soul, therefore, which sees that reality does not seek this body and understands that it ought to have only the slightest association with it. It renounces the world, withdraws itself from the bonds of the flesh, and strips itself of all the ties of these pleasures.

Finally, Stephen was seeing Jesus and was not afraid to be stoned; indeed, while he was being stoned, he prayed not for himself but for those by whom he was being killed. Paul, too, having been caught up to the third heaven, did not know whether he was in the body or outside the body—caught up, I say, into paradise. He no longer experienced the use of his own body, and, hearing the words of God, he was ashamed to descend to the weaknesses of the body.

Therefore, knowing what he had seen or heard in paradise, he cried out, saying: “Why, as though you were still living in the world, do you make judgments? Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste—things which all lead to corruption by their very use” (Col. 2:20–21). For he wanted us to be in the likeness of this world, not in its possession and use, so that we might use this world as though we did not use it—as passing through, not as settling in it; walking as in an image of the world, not in desire, so that with the utmost speed of reasoning we might pass through the very image of this world.

Finally, walking by faith, not by sight, he was a stranger to the body and present with God. Though he was on earth, he lived not in earthly things but in heavenly ones. Therefore, if our soul wishes to draw near to God, let it raise itself above the body and cling always to that supreme good—to that good which is divine, which always is, which was in the beginning, and which was with God (1 John 1)—that is, to the Word of God. He is that divine reality “in whom we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28).

13. “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” The soul begins to breathe this fragrance when it begins to open itself to Christ, so that it may first receive the fragrance of the Lord’s burial and believe that his flesh did not see corruption or wither in any smell of death, but rose seasoned with the fragrance of that eternal and ever-flourishing flower.

For how could the flesh wither when his name is “an ointment poured out”? He emptied himself so that he might breathe fragrance for you. This ointment always existed, but it was with the Father, it was in the Father; it gave fragrance only to angels and archangels, as though within the vessel of heaven.

The Father opened his mouth, saying: “Behold, I have appointed you as a covenant for my people, as a light for the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49:6). The Son descended; everything was filled with the new fragrance of the Word. “The heart of the Father uttered a good Word”; the Son gave forth his fragrance; the Holy Spirit breathed it out and diffused it through every heart. For “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 5:5).

The Son of God, in the body as in a vessel, at first held back his fragrance, awaiting the proper time, as he says: “The Lord gives me a learned tongue, so that I may know when it is necessary to speak a word.” The hour came; he opened his mouth; the ointment went forth, when power went out from him.

[Note: [Col. 1858D] On Isaac, chapter 3.] Therefore this woman hastens to the Word and asks to be drawn, lest perhaps she be abandoned, because the Word of God runs and is not bound. Finally, “he rejoices like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6). And because “his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course reaches to its highest point” (ibid., 7), seeing herself unequal to such speed, she says: “Draw us.”

14. Good is the soul that asks not for itself alone but for everyone: “Draw us,” I say. We have the desire to follow, which the grace of your ointments inspires; but because we cannot match your running, “draw us,” so that, supported by your help, we may be able to follow in your footsteps.

For if you draw us, we too shall run and catch the spiritual breezes of speed. The burden is laid down when your hand is our support; and your oil is poured in, by which the man wounded by robbers was healed.

15. But lest what she says—“Draw us”—seem impudent to you, hear him saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). You see that he willingly draws us, lest we lag behind in following him. But whoever wishes to be drawn should run in order to grasp him; let him run, forgetting what lies behind and reaching toward what lies ahead. In this way he will be able to grasp Christ. Hence the Apostle also says: “Run in such a way that you may obtain.”

This woman, too, wishes to reach the prize, which she desires to grasp. Wisely, therefore, she asks to be drawn, because not everyone can follow. Finally, when Peter asked, “Where are you going?” the Word of God answered him: “You cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward” (John 13:36; cf. Matt. 14:30). He had entrusted to him the keys of the kingdom of heaven, yet judged him unequal to following him. Nevertheless, he did not delay this soul, because it did not presume but asked. Finally,

[Col. 1859C] 16. (Verse 3.) [Note: [Col. 1859D] On Isaac, chapter 3.] “The king brought me into his chamber.” Blessed is the soul that enters the inner chambers of the Word. Rising from the body, it becomes more remote from everything; and it investigates and seeks whether it can somehow attain that divine reality which is above itself. When it has been able to grasp it, having surpassed intelligible things, it is established in it and nourished by it.

Such was Paul, who knew that he had been caught up into paradise, but did not know whether outside the body or in the body. His soul had risen from the body, withdrawn and lifted itself away from the bowels and bonds of the flesh. Having become alien to himself, he held within himself the unspeakable words that he had heard and could not disclose, because he understood that it was not lawful for a human being to speak them.

The good soul therefore despises visible and perceptible things; it does not remain in them, nor linger and settle in looking at them. Rather, it ascends to those eternal and invisible things, full of wonders, lifting itself with a pure understanding of the devout mind. For, striving toward perfection, it fixes its attention upon that one good of divinity and considers nothing else worth seeking, because it holds what is supreme.

17. [Note: [Col. 1859D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 1, nos. 5 and 16.] “The king brought me into his chamber.” The kiss is simple, but the secret of the chamber is demanding. In this passage she testifies that she wishes to know the mysteries more fully, so that she may enter the inner chambers of heavenly mysteries and that the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ may be opened to her. To accomplish this, she perhaps says what appears above: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”

It signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit coming upon her, just as the angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

When, however, the king brought her into his chamber, the time of the Passion is indicated by the piercing of his side, the pouring out of blood, the ointment of burial, and the mystery of the resurrection; so that she received the kiss as a bride. The Church was brought into Christ’s chamber, no longer merely betrothed but also as though married—not only entering the bridal chamber but also receiving the keys of a lawful union.

Therefore, as though situated in the bridal chamber, she says: “My brother is a bundle of myrrh to me; he rests between my breasts” (verse 12).

18. But if we seek the chamber, he himself teaches us, saying: “When you pray, enter your chamber, and, shutting the door, pray to your Father in secret” (Matt. 6:6). The chamber of the Church is the body of Christ.

The king brought her into all the inward mysteries; he gave her the keys so that she might open the treasures of knowledge for herself, throw open the doors of the sacraments that had previously been closed, and know the grace of the one who rests, the sleep of the deceased, and the power of the one who rises.

In that chamber the bride found the justifications of the Lord Jesus. What are those justifications? Certainly the sacraments of baptism, as we read. When John said to the one coming for baptism, “I ought to be baptized by you, and are you coming to me?” Jesus answered: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:14–15).

In that chamber she learns the Lord’s ordinances and knows the counsel of God, than which nothing can be more sublime. For this is the divine reality in which the forgiveness of sins takes place.

19. [Note: [Col. 1859D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 2, no. 28.] She seeks from the Lord to learn those things which human beings could not teach unless God had first taught them. After the apostles had learned these things from Christ, the Church says: “The king brought me into his chamber”—that is, into that secret place in which are all the treasures of his knowledge and understanding.

Therefore it is said to you: “When you pray, enter your chamber” (Matt. 6:6), which signifies the secret place of the mind and soul. In this chamber the bride asked to be brought into the possession of righteousness, after she had run after the fragrance of the ointment, which always flows and never fails.

[Col. 1860D] 20. [Note: [Col. 1860D] On the Sacraments, book V, chapter 2.] “The king brought me into his chamber.” In Greek, it reads “his storehouse” and “his wine-cellar,” where there are good libations, good fragrances, sweet honey, various fruits, and different foods, so that your meal may be seasoned with many dishes. Finally, brought into the secret place of that divine bridegroom:

21. [Note: [Col. 1860D] On Isaac, chapter 4, no. 13.] “Let us exult and rejoice in you,” she says; “let us love your breasts more than wine.” For she does not rejoice in riches or treasures of gold and silver, in the produce of possessions, in powers, or in banquets, but in God alone, saying to him:

[Note: [Col. 1860D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 2, no. 7.] “Let us love your breasts more than wine.” Yet she drank in such a way that she was not swallowed up by wine, but drew the joy of the heart from its grace and did not stagger through bodily drunkenness.

Finally, while drinking this wine, she opened her eyes and saw the straight way; she abandoned crooked paths, saying: “Righteousness has loved you.” That is, they do not follow you along winding paths; only the path of righteousness can reach you. For whoever loves righteousness does not turn away from Christ.

How, indeed, could an innocent conscience fear the judge of righteousness and the rewarder of merits?

[Note: [Col. 1860D] On Isaac, chapter 4, no. 13.] Yet the same soul, recognizing that it has been darkened through association with the body, says to the other souls—or to the other heavenly powers who are closely joined to the sacred mystery: “Do not look at me, for I am darkened, because the sun has not looked upon me.”

22. (Verse 4.) [Note: [Col. 1861D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 2, nos. 8ff.] “I am dark and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.”

[Col. 1861B] Imagine the Lord Jesus reclining at a banquet, with John leaning upon his breast, while the others marvel that the servant should recline above the Lord, that sinful flesh should recline above the temple of the Word, and that the soul bound to the ties of flesh should investigate the court of divine fullness.

As the others marvel, John’s soul answered: “I am dark and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem”—dark through guilt, beautiful through grace.

The flesh also says: “I am dark and beautiful”—dark with the worldly dust that it gathered through struggle, beautiful through the spiritual eye with which it wiped away the dust and filth of this world; dark through vice, but now beautiful through the bath that washes away every offense; dark because I sinned, beautiful because Christ now loves me. For the one whom he had banished in Eve, he receives again in the virgin; he takes her up from Mary.

23. The Synagogue also speaks, whose mysteries many seem to find expressed in this passage. When it saw itself rejected because of the impiety of the whole people, it nevertheless consoled itself, [1553] because it saw not only Christ himself from its people but also Peter, John, and James clinging to Christ, and because it possessed the utterances entrusted to it.

Therefore it said: “I am dark and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem”—dark through unbelief, beautiful through the Law; dark through my fall, beautiful because the sun loved me, and I became the first congregation of God.

Do not shun me because I am dark. I am dark because the sun of righteousness has left me, the sun that formerly used to illumine me. I have lost the color of my face; the sight of my eyes, with which I formerly saw the sun, has become dull. I walk in darkness, because I do not know the day of Christ.

Nevertheless, do not despise me, because the one who left me can look upon me again. He is accustomed once more to have mercy, to gather the dispersed, to seek the abandoned, and to collect the forsaken.

All the tribes of Israel, come together; look at me, beautiful before my offenses. Do not look at me, because I am darkened—that is, do not look only at the fact that I am darkened. “The sun has not looked upon me,” and therefore I am darkened.

But the sun shines upon the just and the unjust: upon the just through grace, upon the unjust through mercy; granting the just the reward of their merits and forgiving the unjust their sins. Formerly it did not shine upon the nations; now it shines, now it rises for them—the one who used to rise for me. The one who forgave them will forgive me also.

Do not suppose that, because I am darkened, the sun has entirely abandoned me and no longer looks upon me or seeks the sick woman. It turned away from me because I did not keep its commandments; it will be reconciled when it sees the repentance of my offenses.

The sun did not see me because I did not receive the one who came; I did not open the windows so that the light of life might enter. When I open them, he will illumine my eyes—the one who came to illumine the whole world—so that even those who do not see may see.

24. Or the Church speaks from among the nations: “Do not look at me, because I am dark, for the sun did not look upon me.” For, as though bound by the winter frosts and ice of pagan error, the sun of righteousness long considered the congregation of the nations unworthy to be brightened by the serene light of his face.

Did not the severity of wintertime seem to be present when God was known only in Judea? But now the fullness of summer light shines, when Christ is all things and in all. Is not “the earth the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1)? And truly the whole world is in the Church, because “there is neither Jew nor Greek, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all” (Col. 3:11). The sun shines for everyone; the day gives light to everyone.

[Note: [Col. 1862D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 18.] “I am black and beautiful.” He placed “black” first in order to increase the beauty. He did not say, “I am black-beautiful,” lest what is black be considered beautiful; rather, he said: “I am black through former sin, but beautiful through confession of sin, the pursuit of correction, and the love of virtue.”

Although the syllable “and,” as grammarians call it, is connective, it nevertheless introduces a distinction by which things are differentiated and separated. Thus, if you say, “Ambrose Bassus is inside,” one person is thought to be meant; but if you assert, “Ambrose and Bassus are inside,” two are certainly understood.

25. [Note: [Col. 1862D] On the Holy Spirit, book I, chapter 11; on Psalm 118, Sermon 2.] “Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.” For tents are made from the hides of dead animals. Therefore she who said this was dead to sin and alive to God. Let us therefore also die to sin, so that we may live to God.

Filled with the Spirit, with joy and the sweetness of gladness, we shall become spiritual hides, stripped of bodily weakness and preserving in the intact bosom of the mind the grace of divine mysteries poured into us.

It is clear from many passages that the tents of Kedar, or the skins of Solomon, refer to this body. Yet understand it also from this: when Adam and Eve laid aside the image of heaven that they had previously borne and, putting on the image of the earthly human being, were said to have been clothed in tunics of skin, the sin committed had made them corporeal from being spiritual.

26. Nor is it absurd to understand that the bride says she has become like skins scorched by the sun’s heat, because, although placed amid the harshness of tribulations, she nevertheless mortified her body so that it could not feel that harshness. For just as the tent-skin does not feel the sun’s heat, because it is the skin of a dead animal, so she, dead to sin, could not feel the heat of sin—either because she was not broken by necessities, or because “we are the body of affliction” and must always carry the death of the Lord Jesus in our body.

27. (Verse 5.) [Note: [Col. 1863D] *On Isaac*, book 4, chapter 4, no. 13 and following.] “The sons of my mother fought against me”; that is, the passions of the body attacked me, and the allurements of the flesh discolored me. Therefore the sun of righteousness did not shine upon me, because, deprived of the protection of devotion, I was unable to preserve my dedication and observance intact. This is what is meant by “I did not guard my vineyard,” because I brought forth thorns and not grapes—that is, I produced sins instead of fruits. And when she speaks of the Word, with the splendor of the Word shining upon her, she turns to him and says:

28. (Verse 6.) “Where do you pasture, where do you rest at midday?” She rightly says “where do you pasture,” because the Word of God is royal; “where do you rest,” because it is moral; “at midday,” because it is mystical. For at midday Joseph, seated at table with his brothers, revealed the mysteries of future times. David also says: “Commit your life to the Lord and hope in him, and he himself will act; he will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like midday” (Psalm 36:5). Paul himself declared that a light had shone around him at midday, when he was converted from persecution to grace.

29. She therefore asks why she has been abandoned, why she, who was poor after having been rich, has been forsaken. For she had abounded in the gift of graces; but she began to be needy when the abundance of the divine presence was denied her. And so she asks to be regarded, as it were, as a hired servant, although formerly she claimed for herself the grace of a more precious union.

30. [Note: [Col. 1863D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 2, no. 10.] “They made me keeper of the vineyards; I did not guard my own vineyard” (verse 5). Some think this is said of those who subject the Synagogue to the precepts of the Law, so that it might keep the Law and protect its vineyard, which it was unable to guard. In the end, it guarded it in order to produce grapes, but it produced thorns. David comes to testify to us what the vineyard is, saying: “You brought a vine out of Egypt, you drove out the nations, and planted it” (Psalm 79:9).

The sons of her mother may also be the apostles, who truly attacked the Synagogue, saying: “Behold, we are turning to the nations”; and they began to sow the word of God among the Gentiles. The prophets may also be understood, for although they admonished and warned the Synagogue to guard its vineyard, they accomplished nothing. It produced the thorns of wickedness, although it ought to have brought forth abundant fruits of virtue. Therefore she confesses that she could not guard her people, and rightly seeks late to hold the one whom, while she held him, she lost. In this she is very unlike the woman who says: “I found him whom my soul loves; I held him and will not let him go” (Song of Songs 3:4). Indeed, the latter invites the bridegroom into her garden; but this woman, asking where he pastures, says to him:

[Col. 1864A] 31. “Tell me whom my soul has loved.” Why do you say “whom my soul has loved,” and not “whom it loves”? Why did you let go of the one you held? You loved him through the faith of the fathers; you lost him through unbelief. You held him with the bonds of charity; you lost him through the long rope of faithlessness. Therefore you do not know where he pastures or where he rests; for if you knew, you would not ask.

You say: “Where do you pasture, where do you rest at midday?” You know that midday is the Church, which holds Christ, while you seek him in the nights. “Tell me,” she says, “Christ; answer me, if only because you were formerly dear and beloved to me. Although I have lost the privilege of such great love, still, as one who is merciful, answer me: Where do you pasture, where do you rest? You left me; you went away to the Gentiles; you withdrew far from me and became nearer to those from whom you had been far away. But you became near to them because they believed through your blood. You withdrew from me because I did not receive the cross as the redemption of the world, but as the condemnation of one who was guilty. Those, however, who received it as the author of salvation are at midday. For them you shine; upon them you radiate; for them your grace is warm like midday.

“You were morning to me when I still believed, but I did not believe fully, because I was not found at midday, like Joseph with his brothers, who held midday. You became midday for those who are nourished by your riches and hope in you. Therefore, as David said: ‘You will lead forth their righteousness like the light, and their judgment like midday’” (Psalm 36:6).

32. You therefore seek as foreign what was near to you, and as poor what you once were when rich. You wish to follow those whom you preceded—and would that you might at least follow those whom you ought to have preceded! You desire to be a hired servant, although formerly you gathered hired servants. This, then, is the voice of the hired servant who says: “Lest perhaps I become one wrapped around the flocks of your companions.” You formerly received proselytes from the nations; now you yourself wish to be received among the nations on behalf of proselytes and to be gathered as a stranger. The Word of God answered the soul that desired this:

33. (Verse 7.) [Note: [Col. 1864D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 10, no. 10.] “Unless you know yourself to be beautiful among women.” “Know yourself,” human being: this is said to your soul—unless you recognize yourself as beautiful among women. Know yourself, soul, because you are not from earth, not from clay, since God breathed into you and made you a living soul. You are a magnificent work, formed by God’s inspiration. “Pay attention to yourself,” as the Law says—that is, to your soul. Let worldly and earthly things not hold you; let terrestrial things not delay you. Hasten with complete attention toward the one from whose inspiration you exist.

“Great,” he says, “is a human being, and precious is a merciful man; but a faithful man is difficult to find” (Proverbs 20:6). Learn, human being, in what respect you are great and precious. Earth shows you to be worthless, but virtue makes you glorious, faith makes you rare, and the image makes you precious. For what is as precious as the image of God? It ought first to pour faith into you, so that some likeness of the author may shine in your heart, lest the one who questions your mind fail to recognize its author.

Or what is as precious as humility? By perceiving the nature of your body and soul, you subject yourself through the one and recognize yourself through the other. The flesh’s inclination toward vice urges mercy, because what you bestow upon another you repay to yourself; whatever proceeds from you returns to you; whatever you do, you repay to yourself; and whatever good you accomplish benefits you. The vigor of a living soul, the sense of reason, and an intellect capable of understanding and judgment should not lose the privilege of its nature, so that it may appear a worthy dwelling for so great an inhabitant.

[Note: [Col. 1865D] *On Isaac*, book 4, chapter 4, no. 15.] “Unless you know yourself, beautiful among women.” You complain that you have been abandoned; but unless you know yourself, unless you repent of your fall, unless you approve the purpose of your devotion, unless your faith and sincerity increase, your complaint will accomplish nothing. Or understand it this way: unless you know yourself to be beautiful, unless you preserve the beauty of your nature and do not allow the allurements of the body to drag you down, nor obstacles to hold you back, the nobility of a better creation will provide you no support.

34. Know yourself, then, and the beauty of your nature. Go out as though freed from the bonds of your feet, and advance with your foot unshod, so that you may not feel the coverings of the flesh. Let bodily bonds not entangle the step of your mind, so that your foot may appear beautiful. Such are those whom the Lord chooses to proclaim the kingdom of heaven, of whom it is said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace” (Isaiah 52:7).

Such was Moses, to whom it was said: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exodus 3:5), so that the one who was going to call the people to the kingdom of God might first cast off the coverings of the flesh and walk with an unshod spirit and the foot of the mind. This, then, is what he says: “Go out in the sandals of the flocks, and pasture your young goats in the tents of the shepherds.”

35. By “flocks” we understand the kingdom, because it belongs to power to preside over flocks. Each person presides over himself with a certain royal power if he restrains the body’s luxury within himself and reduces his flesh to servitude. Hence it is said: “The kingdom of God is within you.”

Therefore he beautifully says to the soul: “Go out”—that is, go out from servitude; go out from the rule and dominion of the flesh; go out not in the flesh but in the spirit; go out to the exercise of authority. For this reason he adds: “Pasture your young goats”—that is, rule what is on your left, for if they are not ruled, they easily fall.

Restrain the wantonness, lust, and irrational luxury of your body; tame its frivolous impulses. Pasture them not in bodily tents, but in the tents of shepherds who know how to govern a flock. For the tents of Israel are lovely, like groves casting shade over a river. In them the soul, as though stationed in battle array, practices good warfare and scouts the enemy’s attacks.

36. [Note: [Col. 1866D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 2, no. 13 and following.] “Unless you know yourself, beautiful among women.” What does it mean to know oneself, except that each person should know that he has been made in the image and likeness of God and is capable of reason; that, like a good farmer, he ought to cultivate his own land with a kind of plow and sickle of wisdom, so that hard things may be split and luxuriant growth cut back; and that he ought to govern his inner self by the rule of the soul?

Hence it is also written in the Law: “Pay attention to yourself, lest there be a hidden word in your heart” (Deuteronomy 15:9). “Pay attention to yourself,” he says—not to your money, not to your possessions, not to the strength of your body, but to your soul and your mind, from which all plans, deeds, and thoughts flow. Pay attention to yourself, therefore, in that place where you know yourself to be superior.

“Know yourself,” which pagan writers attribute to the Pythian Apollo, as though he himself had been the author of this saying. They have taken what was ours and transferred it to their own tradition, although Moses, who wrote the book of Deuteronomy, lived much earlier than the philosophers who invented these things.

37. Therefore Solomon too, following a divine oracle, wrote in the Song of Songs: “Unless you know yourself, beautiful among women.” That is, unless you recognize yourself as mortal and rational and quickly confess your sins; unless you quickly declare your iniquities so that you may be justified; unless you turn back and accuse your offenses first, the day of death comes, and there is no remedy of conversion. You are overtaken while you are still deliberating.

Light your lamp before the bridegroom’s door is closed to you, for he does not usually wait long for the negligent. “Unless you know yourself,” he says, “beautiful among women,” and say: “I am dark and beautiful.” I am dark because I have sinned; beautiful because I am loved, because I am of the race of Abraham, an elect race, beloved by God. The favor of your ancestors will profit you nothing: “For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3:9).

Elsewhere in the Gospel you read that the devil had bound a daughter of Abraham with the bonds of his wickedness, and that the Lord released her on the Sabbath day. Unless, then, you know yourself, nothing will profit you. Even if you say, “I am a daughter of Abraham,” while you do not believe and do not correct your error, Abraham is indeed saved, but the nobility of your lineage will not help you unless faith saves you.

Let the promise made to your ancestors not deceive you. I do not accept the person of a human being; I do not accept the privilege of lineage. Unless I see a nobility of conduct corresponding to the lineage, I will not make a choice in favor of noble descent.

38. But if you know yourself and recognize that you are subject to sin, you must go out in the tracks of the flocks. Go out, then, with your foot bare, and pasture your young goats in the tents of the shepherds. The one who is without sin pastures lambs and sheep; but the one subject to sin should pasture young goats, which are on the left, for she cannot be on the right hand of the good shepherd.

Rather let her follow the one who says to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:33). By following, Peter deserved to be placed on the right; therefore it is said to him: “Pasture my little lambs” (John 21:16).

But hear where she is to go: “To the tents,” he says, “of the shepherds”—that is, to the nations, to the dispersion. Therefore he said: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7), so that the whole world might be filled with Christ’s flock. This signifies that the Synagogue will then be saved when it too joins this dispersion, which has filled the world. For the tents of the shepherds are the kingdoms of the earth.

[Col. 1867A] 39. (Verse 8.) [Note: [Col. 1867D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 2, no. 32.] “I have compared you, my companion, to my mare among the chariots of Pharaoh.” Here, while the Church seems to be compared to the course of swift horses, the richness of her grace is indicated. Do not understand this as one mare belonging to a rich king, but, by an understood reference to the cavalry—as we have often said—understand it as “sheep” for a flock of sheep.

Pharaoh, therefore, as a most powerful and exceedingly wealthy king, possessed strong horses. Hence Scripture says: “The chariots of Pharaoh” (Exodus 14:9), as a most powerful force for warfare and a means of military support. Indeed, with these chariots Pharaoh easily overtook the fleeing Hebrews.

Just as horses yoked together easily draw a chariot, patiently accept the yoke, carry it gracefully, and are tamed by bearing that yoke, so the congregation of the nations formerly displayed itself as untamed in its ways. But when it accepted the yoke of the one who says, “Take my yoke upon you, for it is light, and my burden, for it is sweet” (Matthew 11:29–30), the bride of Christ began to be exalted through the harmony and gentleness of the peoples and to be carried throughout the whole world. Like a chariot drawn by swift horses, she was lifted above the world and mounted up to the bridegroom.

40. Christ has his own horses, of whom the prophet says: “You sent your horses into the sea, disturbing many waters” (Habakkuk 3). For the apostles, by preaching, stirred up the peoples of the nations, who are moved like many waters and raised into waves, so that, rising from the earthly rites of idols, they might believe in Christ.

Above he also says: “You mounted upon your horses; your riding is salvation.” O great and wondrous team of two tens of good horses, whose bridles are peace and whose reins are charity! Bound together by the bonds of harmony and subjected to the yoke of faith, carrying the mystery of the Gospel on four wheels to the ends of the whole world, they bear the good charioteer, the Word of God. By his whip the allurements of the world have been driven away; the ruler of this world has been destroyed; and the course of the righteous has been completed.

O great contest of rational horses! O wondrous mystery! A wheel was running within a wheel, and it was not hindered: the New Testament was running within the Old Testament, within that through which it was proclaimed. The wheels went in four directions and did not turn back, because the spirit of life was in them, running in the four directions of the whole world. It ran without stumbling because the good life of the horses was well ordered. The horses therefore ran because the one who had mounted the horses did not sleep.

41. Jesus is therefore the charioteer of our souls. He also wishes us to mount our horses—that is, our bodies—and to remain always vigilant, lest it be said of us: “They slumbered who mounted the horses” (Psalm 75:7). This sea must be crossed without delay; it is scarcely crossed by the vigilant. If anyone sleeps, he will not be able to cross it, but will be drowned, like the Egyptian, whose soul and body alike perished.

For he cast horse and rider into the sea—those who did not follow the Law but persecuted it (Exodus 15:1).

42. “I have compared you to my mare among the chariots of Pharaoh.” [Note: [Col. 1867D] *On Isaac*, book 4, chapter 4, no. 17.] The labor of virtue seeks victory, so that the mare belonging to Solomon cannot be compared with that one: she is swift in running and capable of bearing offspring, since the fruitfulness of the soul is desired and sought.

This mare, then, is precious, and the chariots of Pharaoh are swift. But in this passage we have undertaken to speak of the soul, of this mare that is considered similar to the soul—that is, to prophetic or apostolic virtue—because she is counted among the flock of those who, through the fruitfulness of their preaching, filled the expanses of the whole world.

Although they were established in the body, they felt no hindrance to their spiritual course. Therefore she is praised because, with a heavenly command illuminating her, she is already beautiful and lovely, displaying the beauty of chastity in her countenance and wearing the necklaces about her neck, in which are the insignia of patience and humility. And for this reason, praising his bride, he said:

43. (Verse 9.) [Note: [Col. 1868D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 3, no. 6 and following.] “How beautiful your cheeks have become, like those of a turtledove; your neck like necklaces.” The face is freer where there is the conscience of charity; and it is pleasant to bear Christ’s yoke if you consider the ornaments of your neck, not its burdens. Therefore always lift your eyes toward your Lord and seek God, so that you may find him.

Raise your neck: you bear necklaces, not chains. Even mute animals delight in necklaces and seem to take pleasure in being adorned rather than bound. Let your cheeks, like those of a turtledove, bear the insignia of modesty. Let the necklaces of your neck lift the confidence of freedom; for Christ’s yoke is light, and therefore the neck is not weighed down by it but lifted up.

44. (Verses 10–11.) “We will make likenesses of gold for you, with silver inlays, until the king is at his reclining place.” For those who are from the Law and the prophets had previously believed only moderately in the glory of the Lord Jesus; and his inheritance, spread throughout the peoples, has been tested more frequently and therefore approved more fully.

The frequent persecutions of the Church have produced for us the honors of the righteous and the victories of martyrdom. Therefore, just as good gold suffers no loss when it is used, so the Church suffers no loss but rather increases in brilliance, until Christ comes into his kingdom and reclines his head upon the faith of the Church.

When he came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, he had nowhere to recline his head. But now faith already gives forth its fragrance; therefore the Church says: “My nard gave forth its fragrance.” She says this confidently, awaiting her reward. The ointment of grace gives off its fragrance, in which the Virgin gave birth and the Lord Jesus assumed the sacrament of the incarnation.

45. (Verses 12–13.) “A cluster of drops is my brother to me; he will remain, or dwell, in the midst of my breasts.” Earlier she had said that her nard had given the bridegroom its fragrance, and that through the ointment with which she had anointed him she had received the fragrance of his perfume. Now she says: “My brother gives forth the fragrance of a drop,” and this drop is not diffused or scattered as it pleases, but gathered together and bound, so that the scent of its sweetness may be made denser and more powerful.

“And here,” she says, “when he is such, he dwells and remains in the midst of my breasts; there he makes his rest and dwelling in the place of my heart.”

[Note: [Col. 1869D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 3, no. 8 and following.] “A cluster of drops,” he says; “my kinsman, a cluster of henna, is my brother to me; he will rest between my breasts.” For in assuming a body, the Lord Jesus bound himself with the bonds of charity. He joined himself not only to our limbs and natural sufferings, but also to the cross. Therefore, like a cluster of grapes, he rests in the faith of the Church and in moral grace.

46. “My kinsman is nard of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.” If we are seeking the name of a particular region in Judea, this is the place where balsam is produced. If we seek the interpretation, the name means “temptation” in Latin.

In those vineyards there is a tree which, if someone pricks it, releases ointment; this is the fruit of the tree. If the tree is not cut, it does not give forth such fragrance; but when it has been pierced by the hand of the craftsman, then it drips a tear.

So Christ, crucified on that tree of temptation, wept over the people in order to wash away our sins, and from the depths of his mercy poured forth ointment, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Then, pierced on the tree by the lance, blood and water came forth from him, sweeter than every ointment: an offering accepted by God, spreading the fragrance of sanctification throughout the whole world. And just as balsam comes forth from a tree, so power came forth from the body. Hence he said: “I perceive that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:46).

For this reason it is called *opobalsamum* more precisely, because through the piercing of the tree the balsam bursts forth through the opening of the wound.

47. Jesus, therefore, when pierced, poured forth the fragrance of the forgiveness of sins and redemption. For he was also bound, although he was the Word made human; he became poor, although he was rich, so that we might be enriched by his poverty; he was powerful, yet presented himself to be despised, so that Herod scorned him and mocked him; he moved the earth, yet hung upon the tree; he covered the heavens with darkness and crucified the world, while he himself was crucified; he bowed his head, and the Word went forth; he was emptied, and he filled all things; God descended, and the human being ascended; the Word became flesh, so that flesh might claim for itself the throne of the Word at God’s right hand; he was a wound, and ointment flowed; the beetle was heard, and God was recognized.

Christ also answered:

48. (Verse 14.) “Behold, you are beautiful, my companion; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like those of a dove.” Because the Church had understood the mystery and proclaimed the Lord Jesus crucified for the redemption of the whole world, she deserved to hear: “Behold, you are beautiful,” you who call me good; “behold, you are beautiful,” you who have seen the beauty of my glory, and you yourself are lovely and beautiful.

What does it mean for Christ to say, “You are good,” or “You are beautiful,” except what the Gospel says: “Take courage, daughter; your sins are forgiven” (Matthew 9:22)? Therefore, to the one whose sins Christ has forgiven, he rightly says: “Repay your servant, that I may live and keep your commandments” (Psalm 118:146).

Such a person has nothing in the reward to make him despair, because the Lord Jesus came to save the world, not to destroy it. Therefore he forgets the injury and remembers grace, as he himself testifies in the prophetic book, saying: “I am, I am the one who blots out your iniquities, and I will remember them no more. But you remember, and let us be judged; speak first of your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:25–26).

Whoever therefore declares his iniquities to God is justified; and whoever is justified does not fear a reward but asks for it. Whoever does not fear a reward lives.

49. (Verses 15–16.) [Note: [Col. 1870D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 4, no. 18 and following.] “Behold,” she says, “my kinsman is beautiful, and indeed lovely. Our shaded resting place, the beams of our houses are cedars, our ceilings are cypresses.”

The Church praises the beauty of the bridegroom, whom each person praises even more through silent affection, and whom the faithful interpreter of mysteries proclaims more fully through silence. For one who divulges secrets diminishes Christ’s beauty. Therefore let no one cast his pearls before swine, lest he cause precious ornaments to be trampled.

Christ therefore does not recline in the tent of the talkative and chattering, because sin is committed through excessive speech. Rather, he reclines in the tent of a serious man who is sparing in conversation, not immoderate in speech, and who avoids the drunkenness of loquacity through sobriety of words.

50. And rightly she signifies a shaded resting place, because the power of the Most High overshadows those established in the Church. David asked to be protected by this shade, so that the sun would not burn him by day or the moon by night (Psalm 120:6). Spiritual grace supplies this shade to those fleeing the torrid summers of this age and world.

The shaded resting place, then, belongs to Christ and the Church, upon whom that eternal rest of God the Father breathes. In this shade, therefore, let us rest, wearied by the heat of our sins. If lust has scorched some, let the Lord’s cross, upon which he reclined in order to take upon himself our debts, refresh them. If guilt has wearied others, let Jesus receive them into his embrace and cherish them in a gentle embrace. Hence I dare to say that the flesh of Christ is the resting place of the Church.

51. “The beams of our houses are cedars.” By the appearance of cedars, the glory of the ancestors who were righteous is signified. “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree and multiply like the cedar that is in Lebanon” (Psalm 91:13). For just as the cedar does not decay, so the glory of the ancestors is not corrupted by any old age.

52. “Our ceilings are cypresses.” This kind of tree never loses its greenness. In winter as in summer it nourishes its foliage and does not change into a different color. Of all trees, it alone is never stripped of its honor by the wind; alone it is never divested of its old covering or clothed in a new blossom.

So apostolic grace also knows no decline, but flourishes through the endurance of its age. The soul, therefore, does not know how to decay when it flourishes in its limbs and always sustains the heights of justice and the other virtues with patient greatness of spirit. Thus it does not flow away or fail, because there is nothing cracked or slack in it, nothing changeable, nothing slippery, nothing that could be poured out from it through a defect of speech.

The Church, or the faithful soul, follows. I say “soul” because nothing is so truly human as the soul.

## CHAPTER TWO

1. (Verses 1–2.) [Note: [Col. 1871D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 5, no. 7.] “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys, like a lily among thorns.” For the faith of the believing people has gone out into the whole earth, and Christ has set his feet in the broad expanse. Therefore he beautifully says that he is the flower of the field.

Paul was also a flower, saying: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God” (2 Corinthians 2:15). And truly he was a flower, since he could bring forth new and old things from the treasure of his heart.

[Note: [Col. 1871D] Book 7 on Luke, on chapter 12.] “I am the flower of the field.” And rightly the Church is a flower, since she announces the fruit—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—of whom it was said to Mary: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42).

2. In another sense also I show you a flower to be plucked, the one who said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” Many think that this comparison is especially appropriate according to the nature of the flower and the use of the plant in question, because lilies require no cultivation for annual use. Nor, as happens with the production of other fruits, does the labor of the farmers return anxiously each year for the generation of this flower.

Regardless of the droughts of the fields, everything that is nourished into a flower is animated by a certain generative power from itself and within itself, by the sap that is always green. Thus, even when you see the stem of the tender leaves wither, the nature of the flower nevertheless remains green. Its greenness is hidden, not lost. But when it has been summoned forth by the springtime’s gentle influences, it resumes the clothing of its growth, the foliage of the flower, and the adornment of the lily.

3. It is also pleasing to observe that lilies are not produced amid the harshness of mountains and uncultivated forests, but in the pleasantness of gardens. For there are certain gardens bearing the fruits of various virtues, in accordance with what is written: “A garden enclosed,” and so forth (Song of Songs 4:12). Where there is integrity, chastity, religion, and faithful silence concerning secrets, there is the splendor of angels; there are violets of confessors, lilies of virgins, and roses of martyrs.

Christ is rightly a lily, because where there is the blood of martyrs, there is Christ, the lofty, undefiled, innocent flower, in whom the harshness of thorns does not wound but an overflowing grace shines. For there are thorns of roses, which are the torments of martyrs. Divinity that has not been offended has no thorns, since it did not suffer torments.

4. [Note: [Col. 1871D] Book 1 *On Virgins*, chapter 7, no. 43, and chapter 8, no. 44.] “Like a lily among thorns.” This clearly indicates that virtue is besieged by the prickles of spiritual wickedness, so that no one can bring back fruit unless he approaches cautiously.

Take wings, therefore, virgin—but wings of the spirit—so that you may fly above vices if you desire to touch Christ, who “dwells on high and regards the lowly” (Psalm 112:5).

His appearance is like the cedar of Lebanon, which inserts its foliage into the clouds and its root into the earth. Its beginning is from heaven, its later parts are on earth, and it has produced fruits close to heaven.

Search more diligently for so good a flower, to see whether you may find it in the valley of your heart; for it is often inhaled by the humble. It loves to be generated in gardens, where Susanna found it while she was walking, prepared to die rather than be violated.

5. [Note: [Col. 1872D] *On Virginity*, chapter 9, no. 51.] Another interpretation: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys, like a lily among thorns.” Behold another place in which the Lord is accustomed to dwell—or rather, not in one place but in several: “I,” he says, “am the flower of the field,” because he frequents the open simplicity of a pure mind.

[Col. 1872B] “And the lily of the valleys.” Christ is the flower of humility, not of luxury, pleasures, or wantonness, but the flower of simplicity and the flower of humility.

[Note: [Col. 1872D] Book 2 *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 5, no. 39.] A flower preserves its fragrance even when cut, and increases it when crushed; it does not lose it when plucked. So too the Lord Jesus, on the gallows of the cross, neither withered when crushed nor vanished when plucked. Cut by the piercing of the lance, he blossomed more beautifully through the sacred color of the blood poured forth: himself ignorant of death, yet breathing upon the dead the gift of eternal life.

6. (Verse 3.) [Note: [Col. 1872D] *On Virginity*, chapter 9, nos. 51–52.] “Like a lily among thorns.” Does not the good flower of fragrance rise amid the harshness of labors and the crushing of souls, since God is pleased by a contrite heart?

This is the desert, daughters, that leads to the kingdom. This is also the desert that flowers like a lily, in accordance with what is written: “Rejoice, barren one, and exult, desert, and let it flower like a lily” (Isaiah 35:1).

In this desert, daughters, that good and fruitful tree which produces good fruits begins to spread the branches of its deeds and to lift the crown of its divinity; beside it the trees of our forest put forth shoots. For just as the apple tree is among the trees of the forest, so is my brother among the sons. Seeing this, the Church, already rejoicing in the success of our faith, says: “I desired and sat in his shadow, and his fruit was sweet in my throat.”

7. (Verses 3–4.) [Note: [Col. 1872D] *On Isaac*, book 4, chapter 4, no. 27.] Observe that throughout this book of the Song of Songs Solomon clearly expressed that threefold wisdom—moral, natural, and mystical—just as he had said in Proverbs, so that the one who wished to hear his wisdom might write it for himself in three ways.

Thus in the Song the bride says of the bridegroom: “Behold, you are beautiful, my kinsman; behold, you are beautiful and lovely; our shaded resting place, the beams of our houses are cedars, our ceilings are cypresses” (Song of Songs 1:15–16).

We can understand this morally. Where do Christ and the Church rest except in the works of their people? Indeed, where there was impurity, pride, and iniquity, the Lord Jesus said: “The Son of Man has nowhere to recline his head” (Matthew 8:20).

What shall we understand naturally? “In his shadow,” he says, “I desired and sat, and his fruit was sweet in my throat.” For the one who rises above earthly things and for whom worldly things die—for the world is crucified to him, and he to the world—flees and despises everything under the sun.

Mystically also he says: “Bring me into the house of wine; establish charity in me.” For just as a vine embraces its vineyard, so the Lord Jesus, as an eternal vine, embraces his people with certain arms of charity.

8. Consider each point separately. Morally, the flower is a lily among thorns, as he himself says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (above, verse 1). Morally, then, he is a flower; naturally, he is the sun of righteousness, who, rising and rising again, illuminates, and, setting, casts a shadow.

Take care that he does not set for you, because it is written: “Let not the sun set upon your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). Mystically, he is charity, because Christ is the fullness of the Law. Therefore the Church that loves Christ has been wounded by charity.

9. [Note: [Col. 1873D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 5, no. 7 and following.] The Church is also beautifully called a lily. Just as the lily shines, so the works of the saints also shine. It is most beautifully said: “The lily of the valleys,” because grace shines more brightly among the humble.

But this lily is among thorns—that is, among Jews and heretics, and among the cares of this age, which prick the mind and spirit of the human being. We can also understand it in another way: just as the lily rises above the thorns, so the Church of God shines above all assemblies.

10. It is also worth considering that this lily is surrounded by radiance, while what it contains within is red and itself of good fragrance. This is because the flesh of Christ, as though surrounded by the moral splendor of divinity, possessed heavenly protection through grace.

Indeed, later he says: “My kinsman is white and red” (Song of Songs 5:10): white in divine radiance, red in the appearance of human color, which he assumed through the sacrament of the incarnation. And rightly even what is red smells good, because the flesh of Christ is without sin. The faithless, handling it, defiled their hands; the saints, venerating it, gave forth the fragrance of devotion.

11. The Lord Jesus received this fragrance from his fragrant Church and said: “Behold, my companion, you are good.” And the Church says to Christ: “Behold, my brother, you are good; behold, you are good, like an apple tree among the trees of the forest.”

A most beautiful comparison! What could be said more beautifully or appropriately than to compare the bridegroom to an apple tree? Such a fruit has a pleasing fragrance, surpassing the fragrance of other fruits. And Christ, fastened to the tree like an apple hanging from a tree, poured forth the good fragrance of the world’s redemption. It wiped away the heavy stench of sin and poured out the ointment of the drink of life.

12. “Like an apple tree,” he says, “among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman among the sons,” because above prophets and apostles he soothed the innermost hearts of human beings with the sweetness of his words. But an apple contains not only fragrance; it also contains sweet food. Therefore Christ is sweet food.

13. “I desired the shade of it, and I sat down”; for he had received the law, followed it, and ran along this road. Thus, resting in the law, he was resting in the shade of Christ. A good shade, which defends us from the sun of iniquity! Who can doubt that the law of God is a shadow of Christ? What is the law concerning feast days, the new moons, and Sabbaths, except a shadow of things to come? What are the days according to the law of Moses: “That I may see six days, and again the seventh day,” and so throughout the everlasting ages? What is the month according to the law of Moses, so that, knowing the month, I may know the new moon at the beginning of the month, and what truly holy offerings are to be made at the new moons? What is the year according to the law of Moses, [Col. 1874B] consisting of those six days concerning which it says: “For six years the Hebrew shall serve, and in the seventh year he shall be released” (Deut. XV, 12)—so that there may be six years in which one cultivates the land, but in the seventh year one grants it respite for proselytes, the poor, and the beasts of the earth? What is the seventh year, in which all debts owed to Hebrews are remitted?

14. In this shade rested the faith of the Fathers and the holy devotion of the prophets. Let the religious assembly, or the holy soul, therefore say: “I desired the shade of it, and I sat down.” The jubilee year is a shadow: for who perceives its mysteries so as to know face to face what the Law prescribed for completion in the five-hundredth year? The feast days according to the Law are a shadow, from the first month’s tenth day through the fourteenth, [Col. 1874C] and from there through the twenty-first day of the month. What shadow is that celebration between the first and seventh months in that unnamed period? The sanctified freedom of the Sabbath is a shadow. The feast day of the seventh month’s new moon is a shadow, as are the memorial of trumpets, the tenth day of the seventh month, and the Day of Atonement. You see that the monad and the decad are two feast days. Likewise, the fifteenth day is the Feast of Tabernacles, lasting eight days: all these things are in shadow. In shadow are the first day called, and the eighth day called in shadow, prescribed according to the Law for the Feast of Booths.

15. Imagine some believers from the circumcision, instructed in the Law, men zealous for careful observance, and now enlightened by the knowledge of the Gospel and spiritually fattened by grace. The Church, which sees Christ, receives the Bridegroom, and is nourished by his food, says in them: “I desired the shade of it, and I sat down, and its fruit was sweet in my throat.” What is its sweet fruit except the preaching of the Lord’s Passion? As he himself says: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: children are the fruit of the womb’s reward” (Ps. CXXVI, 3). For what fruit could be sweeter in our throats than the forgiveness of sins?

16. [Note: [Col. 1874D] Letter to Irenaeus, on Exodus XVI.] “And its fruit was sweet to my throat.” It is the spiritual manna, that is, the spiritual rain of wisdom, which is poured from heaven upon the gifted and the seekers, [Col. 1875A] moistens the minds of the devout, and sweetens their throats. Whoever, therefore, has understood the infusion of divine wisdom delights in it and seeks no other food; he does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God. Whoever is more inquisitive asks what that thing is which is sweeter than honey. The minister of God answers him: “This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat.” Hear what this bread is: “The word,” he says, “which God ordained.” 1562 This ordinance of God, then, this nourishment, feeds the soul of the wise, enlightens it, and sweetens it; shining with the flash of truth and soothing it as with a honeycomb, through the sweetness of diverse virtues and through the discourse of wisdom. For words of goodness are honeycombs of honey, as it is written in Proverbs. Therefore, when she has tasted the fruit of sweetness, impatiently she hastens toward greater things, saying:

[Col. 1875B] 17. (Verses 4–7.) [Note: [Col. 1875D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 5, no. 13 and following.] “Bring me into the wine-house; establish love in me; strengthen me with perfumes; surround me with apples, for I am wounded by love. His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field: if you awaken and revive love, as long as it wills.” Rightly does she seek him, rightly does she desire him, because our commander has ordered everything well along this course and journey. First of all, he considered that this tabernacle must be established on the foundation of faith. Then, if we have some harsh, dry, and precipitous dwelling place, this Commander nevertheless distinguishes what is disturbed, waters what is dry, and makes the wilderness fruitful. If there is any bitterness, temptation, or weakness, our leader both tempers what is bitter and softens what is troubling; he loosens what is hard and strengthens what is weak.

18. Whenever the king of the earth wishes his army to rest, he chooses neither an undistinguished village lacking provisions, nor sandy and barren ground, but a city renowned for its buildings, restored and rich in supplies; or a pleasant field; or land green with pastures; or wooded and level country suitable for encampments. Therefore, if earthly kings know how to provide what benefits those who follow them, how much more does God, who is good, know how to arrange what will benefit those who love him? And first, if an unfamiliar road must be traversed, guides are chosen for the roads to go ahead of the column; but these commanders consider that beneath their dignity. God, however, went before when the Hebrews were making their journey. Indeed, he spoke to them in a pillar of cloud. And so that you may know that God went before them, he says: “By day he went before them in a pillar of cloud, showing them the way; but by night in a pillar of fire, and the pillar of cloud did not fail by day” (Exod. XIII, 21–22). Following this pillar that goes before us, the Church, so that she herself might not fail, was refreshed by its shade; and therefore she says: “I desired the shade of it, and I sat down, and its fruit was sweet in my throat” (above, v. 3), because she was fed by the Lord and led into a place of pasture and waters of refreshment.

[Col. 1876A] 19. “Bring me into the wine-house.” From the provisions prepared, she seeks to advance to another dwelling, where she may receive the sweetness of the grace and joy of the mysteries. Advancing from there along the true road, she says: “Order love in me.” Good is the encampment where there is the fullness of charity. [Note: [Col. 1875D] On Virginity, chapter 9, no. 53.] Charity cannot exist without faith. For hope, faith, and charity are, as it were, three sureties of the Church: when hope has gone before and faith has been established, charity is ordered and the Church is joined together.

20. [Note: [Col. 1876D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 5, no. 16.] “Strengthen me,” she says, “with perfumes; surround me with apples.” You have other dwellings, to which the Church advances with delight. These dwellings are the cross of Christ and the tomb, in which the Church was wounded—but by the wound of charity. For there is the wound which Christ received, but the perfume which he poured forth. [Col. 1876B] It is the apple that hung there; the Church tasted this apple and said: “And its fruit was sweet in my throat.” And so that you may know that the Lord is the apple, you read above: “As an apple among the trees of the forest, so is my kinsman.” We also acknowledge the wound when we preach Christ crucified, but we are a good odor to God; for the cross of Christ is a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks, but to us it is the power and wisdom of God. The Church is wounded by this wound when she preaches the death of her Savior, but this wound is charity. In the end, the one who does not believe denies; the one who loves confesses. The Manichaean denies; the Christian confesses. Therefore it is written: “The wounds of a friend are better than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Prov. XXVII, 6). Beautifully, then, the Church says: “For I am wounded by love.”

21. Let us bare our limbs to the good wound; let us bare them to the chosen arrow. This arrow is Christ, who says: “He made me like a chosen arrow” (Isa. XLIX, 2). It is good, therefore, to be wounded by this arrow. This is no ordinary advance to a dwelling; not everyone can say that he has been wounded by love. 1563 The apostles said this when they were being stoned for Christ and preaching Christ; Paul said it when he was beaten three times with rods and argued day and night that Christ must be worshiped by the nations; the martyrs say this, those who are wounded for Christ. And because they were found worthy to be wounded for his name, they love more deeply. Coming, therefore, to this dwelling, advancing to the point of offering her children for Christ and receiving the wounds of charity—as though she had found good nourishment for faith—the Church herself tasted the fruit of devotion and began to exhort the others, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.” And the Church added:

22. [Note: [Col. 1876D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 5, no. 19.] “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” These too are the dwellings of the Church as she proceeds along the royal road. “For there are many dwellings with my Father” (John XIV, 2). The Lord Jesus bears witness: “And behold, I am coming, and I summon you” (ibid.). The dwelling of wisdom is good, and whether it is in his left hand or in his right, it is a good dwelling, because it is the royal road. Therefore [Col. 1877A] the wise messengers say: “We will go by the royal road; we will not turn aside to the right or to the left until we have passed beyond your boundaries” (Num. XX, 17). The messengers sent by Moses said this to the king of Edom, that is, to the earthly king; for all earthly things, whether on the right or on the left, are evil. Folly is an evil dwelling; self-indulgence is an evil dwelling. Therefore the Hebrew passes through these dwellings: he does not turn aside to them, but passes through, so that he may arrive at the left and right hand of wisdom and remain in them, where there are the riches of simplicity, glory, and length of life. For “length of life is in her right hand,” as Solomon says, “but in her left hand are riches and glory” (Prov. III, 16): life is in the right hand, rest in the left. Would that I might rest upon her left hand and not seek cushions! For woe to those who sew cushions, as Ezekiel says (Ezek. XIII, 18). The good leader prepares these dwellings for his Church and directs her journey along the ways of wisdom. Finally, the wise man praises her ways: “Her ways are good ways, and all her paths are peace” (Prov. III, 17).

23. [Note: [Col. 1877D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 14, no. 31 and following.] “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” The bride speaks this concerning Christ, the soul concerning the Word of God. Christ, however, is himself the Word of God and Wisdom. Blessed, therefore, is the soul whom wisdom embraces. Great is the hand of wisdom, great is the right hand that embraces the whole soul; for the soul betrothed to the Word of God is wholly fortified. For the fullness of wisdom is to fear God; therefore the soul that fears God fortifies itself with complete protection. Wisdom sends her left hand beneath its neck, but her right hand into its embrace. Both arms extend toward what is beneficial; yet each hand of wisdom has its own particular function: “In her right hand is length of life, but in her left hand are riches and glory.” Both hands are good, endowed with good gifts; yet they differ in the distribution of their functions because they encompass both present and future times: the left hand is the rewarder of present things, the right hand of future things.

24. We can also understand this from the prophecy of the holy patriarch Israel. When he had placed his right hand upon Ephraim and his left upon Manasseh, and Joseph wished to reverse them out of consideration for age, so that the father’s right hand might be placed upon the head of Manasseh, the elder son, he refused and said: “I know, my son, I know; he too shall become a people, and he too shall be exalted, [Col. 1877D] but his younger brother shall be greater than he” (Gen. XLVIII, 19). In what way greater? Certainly in this: he was preferred in blessing, as Ephraim’s descendants said: “May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh” (ibid., 20). Or because his seed is the multitude of the nations, which chose labor in this world, believing in the Lord Jesus, so that it might have the consolation of future things. Manasseh, however, is the seed of the people of forgetfulness, who, having forgotten their own Creator, were exalted for a time in this world but will thereafter pay heavy penalties, because they denied their God and Lord.

[Col. 1878A] 25. We have said this to prove that future things are more excellent. In the end, wisdom’s left hand is beneath the bride’s head, but the right hand is higher and embraces the whole bride. Thus the left hand is, as it were, the support of present rest, upon which the soul leans and rests. It has a place on which to recline its head, because the riches and glory of wisdom are in her left hand. For a time these things soothe and provide partial consolation. Therefore, “the Son of Man had nowhere to recline his head” (Matt. VIII, 20), because “though he was rich, he became poor” (II Cor. VIII, 9). Nor did he seek any glory of this world, because he had come not to help one portion but the entire human race, saying: “Are you angry with me because I made the whole man sound on the Sabbath?” (John VII, 23)—that is, the whole man; not to enrich him by an increase of possessions, nor with the insignia of honors, nor with an accumulation of worldly glory. For these things do not possess the fullness of blessedness and grace. Rather, “the whole” means that which embraces the length of eternal life. For the life in wisdom’s right hand is not like ordinary life, but is length of life, so that whoever receives life from wisdom may attain not a brief life but perpetuity and the length of eternity.

26. Eternity of life is a good garment.
