[Note: [Col. 1877D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 19, no. 26.] Therefore the bride, supported by the riches that are around the bridegroom’s left and right hands—riches of good pomegranates, that is, of diverse and innumerable fruits, and especially of the fragrances of faith, grace, wisdom, glory, and eternal life—rouses Christ through the applause of holy souls gathered in congregations, saying:

27. [Note: [Col. 1878D] Book II on Jacob and the Blessed Life, chapter 1, no. 3.] “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field: if you awaken and revive love, as long as it wills.” That field which the Lord blessed is not this earthly field, either dreadful with forests, broken by torrents, useless for vines, stony with barren gravel, cracked and dry from drought, soaked with blood, or uncultivated and covered with thorns. It is that field of which the Lord says: “And the beauty of the field is with me” (Ps. XLIX, 19). In this field is found that vine which, when pressed, poured forth blood and washed the world; in this field is that fig tree beneath which the saints will rest, refreshed by the sweetness of spiritual grace; in this field is that fruitful olive tree, from which the ointment of the Lord’s peace flows; in this field bloom [Col. 1878D] pomegranates, which shelter many fruits under the single protection of faith and cherish them in a kind of embrace of charity.

28. [Note: [Col. 1878D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 5, no. 20.] Since wisdom and honorable splendor are perfect in this way when they possess charity—for “the fullness of the law is charity” (Rom. XIII, 10)—she wishes charity to be awakened and revived: awakened in the Old Testament, revived in the New. Charity is God, as we read; charity is Christ (I John IV, 8). He is awakened like a lion and a lion’s cub, so that Judah may arise from the offspring (Gen. XLIX, 9); he is revived like one sleeping, like one reclining, because he was raised from the dead not by human majesty but by his own and the Father’s majesty. Hence Scripture says: “Who will raise him up?” For neither an angel nor an alien Power could raise him, since he himself raised others. Therefore, when he says here, “If you awaken and revive love, as long as it wills,” he speaks of those who can fittingly preach his resurrection, so that they may kindle the heat of faith and devotion in their hearers. Or Christ is awakened in those who approach him for the first time, and revived in those who, after approaching, have fallen asleep. Christ therefore sleeps in the negligent and is awakened in the holy.

29. [Note: [Col. 1879D] Book on Isaac, chapter 4, no. 31.] She awakens and revives this charity until she hears his voice and summons his presence, because when sought he not only comes but comes leaping. But the bridegroom was already present, to prove what he tells us even while we are still speaking: “I am here.” [Note: [Col. 1880D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 6, nos. 5–13.] He is present because he was awakened by the daughters of Judah, as though revived by the daughters of Jerusalem. The Church hears the sound of his voice and says:

30. (Verse 8.) “The voice of my kinsman! Behold, he has come, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.” This book is like a sheaf containing many noble persons, like a triumphal sheaf, signifying many actions which we can understand more readily than express. For when the bride seems to have heard the bridegroom coming and speaking with some fellow travelers, she says: “The voice of my kinsman.” While she is speaking with the daughters of Jerusalem and asking them to awaken and revive the bridegroom, suddenly, as though sensing from afar the sound of a voice sent forth, she says: “The voice of my kinsman,” announcing the one whom she had previously sought to have announced to her. The one whom she had desired others to awaken, now believing that he had been revived by her prayer and was coming from the Father, she joyfully calls “the voice of my kinsman.” She rightly added “my kinsman,” so that no other woman but the one kinswoman might claim his coming for herself.

1565 31. “Behold,” she says, “he has come.” I am still seeking him, and he has already come; I am still gathering support so that he may come, and he is already near; I desire love to be awakened for me, I consider myself wounded by love, and love itself hastens more eagerly toward me. I said, “Come”; he leaps and bounds. I ask him to come with grace; he brings about an increase of graces; and as he comes, he carries increases of grace with him, gaining them by coming, because he too is eager to please his beloved. He leaps over lofty places so that he may ascend to the bride; for the bride’s bridal chamber is Christ’s tribunal. He leaps over Adam, bounds over the Synagogue; he leaps over the Gentiles, bounds over the Jews.

32. Let us see him leaping. He leaps from heaven into the Virgin, from the womb into the manger, from the Jordan to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, and from the tomb into heaven. Prove to me David’s leaping; prove to me his running. For you said: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to its highest point, and no one can hide from his heat” (Ps. XVIII, 6–7). Even now he leaps, even now he runs, from the Father’s heart over his saints, from east to west, from north to south. He is the one who ascended over the setting sun; he himself ascended over the heavens of heavens toward the east; he himself ascended over the mountains; he himself over the hills.

33. Would that I, wretched man, might say this, and that my soul might say: “Behold, he has come”—and has come not over earthly things, not over valleys, but has come “leaping over the mountains.” For God is the God of mountains, not of valleys; therefore, wherever he leaps, he leaps over mountains. If you are a mountain, he leaps over you; he leaps over Isaiah, he leaps over Jeremiah, he leaps over Peter, John, and James. “The mountains surround him” (Ps. CXXIV, 2). If you cannot be a mountain and do not prevail, at least be a hill, so that Christ may ascend over you; and if he bounds over you, may his passing preserve you.

[Col. 1880B] 34. We have spoken of Christ and the Church; let us speak of the soul and the Word. The soul of the righteous is the bride of the Word. If she desires, longs, prays and prays constantly, prays without any doubt, and directs her whole attention toward the Word, suddenly she seems to hear the voice of the one whom she does not see; and in fear her perception recognizes the fragrance of his divinity, as often happens to those who believe well. Suddenly the soul’s nostrils are filled with spiritual grace, and she feels the breath of his presence breathe upon her, the one whom she seeks, and she says: “Behold, this is the very one whom I seek, the very one whom I desire.”

35. When we think about something in the Scriptures and cannot find its explanation, while we doubt and search, does not the Word suddenly seem to us to ascend over the mountains—that is, over the loftiest doctrines? Then, appearing to us as though upon the hills, he enlightens the mind, so that he may pour into our understanding what seemed difficult to discover. Thus the absent Word becomes present in our hearts. Again, when something is obscure to us, the Word seems to withdraw, and we desire the coming of the absent one; then he appears again and shows himself to us as though he were present, so that we may understand the things we seek.

36. He therefore frequently leaps in the heart of each person, bounds over, goes out, and returns. Follow him, seek him, and ask that, through the welcome discourse of faithful teachers, the Word that had gone out and passed by may be revived for you, as did she who sought and found and said: “My brother passed by; my soul went out at his word” (Song V, 6). Even if he leaps over the mountains, follow him; even if he bounds over the hills, follow him. For the Lord’s hunters are found in the mountains and hills, investigating those who are captured for life. Thus God said through Jeremiah: “Behold, I am sending many fishermen and many hunters, and they will hunt them over every mountain and over every hill” (Jer. XVI, 16). Let the people of God therefore be sought and found there, in the teaching, grace, and discipline of Peter and Paul, so that they may not be in the valley, where there is weeping, but on the mountains, from which Christ enlightens each person. When we read Peter, Christ enlightens us; when we read Paul, Christ enlightens us. Paul healed, Christ enlightened, because, when the name of the Lord Jesus was invoked, he rose again, having been healed by his gift. Peter raised the dead woman; Christ enlightened. Therefore he says: “You enlighten wonderfully from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. LXXV, 5).

37. We, then, who cannot be mountains, let us stand upon mountains or hills, so that when the Lord sends his fishermen and hunters to hunt those who are upon every mountain or every hill—that is, in the precepts of the Law and the prophets—and those who possess the whole manner of life in the knowledge of the New and Old Testament, they may find us ready. Like good ears of grain, may the reapers sent at the proper time gather us. For if anyone is found outside a mountain or hill, he cannot be gathered like a good ear of grain by those who—as we may mention another comparison—are sent to separate wheat from chaff. The Lord therefore has ministers skilled in very many operations: they are fishermen, hunters, and reapers alike. If, at the harvest season when they are sent to reap, you await the harvest ripe, you will be able to behold him leaping upon the mountains, and you will see the Lord Jesus like a young gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel. For he leaps over the Church, which is the house of bread, because he strengthens the hearts of the faithful. Hence the bride also says of him:

38. (Verse 9.) “My kinsman is like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel.” For he leaps over the Church, which is the house of God, because he strengthens the hearts of the faithful. Rightly is he like a young gazelle, because the goat grazes in high places. *Dorcas* is said to derive from “seeing,” for *dorkadion* denotes sharper vision. What is more suitable to Christ, who saw the Father whom no one has seen? Or, if anyone has seen him in Christ, the Son himself revealed him. Rightly is he like a fawn of the deer: a fawn, as though a son in whom the power of his father’s nature has grown, so that hidden things do not escape him, serpents flee from him, and poisons do not harm him. In the end, the serpent drawn out from his hiding places—the one being driven out of the man—said: “Why have you come to torment us before the time?” (Matt. VIII, 29). Let us therefore watch this leaping fawn, so that we may be unable to fear the serpent.

39. [Note: [Col. 1881D] Book on Isaac, chapter 4, nos. 32–33.] “Behold, he himself stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice.” He comes, therefore, and at first is behind the wall, so that he may dissolve the hostility between soul and body, once the wall that seemed to create an impediment to harmony has been removed. Then he looks through the windows. What the windows are, hear the Prophet saying: “The windows have been opened from heaven” (Isa. XXIV, 18). He therefore signifies the prophets, through whom the Lord looked upon the human race before he himself descended to the earth. And today, if any soul seeks him greatly, she will merit great mercy; for whoever seeks greatly is owed much. If, then, any soul seeks him more diligently, she hears his voice from afar; and although she seeks him through others, she hears his voice before those through whom she seeks him. She sees him leaping toward her, that is, hastening, running, [Col. 1882A] and bounding over those who cannot grasp his power with a feeble heart. Then she sees him looking through the riddles of the prophets, reading them and retaining their words. She sees him looking forth, but as through a window, not yet as though he were present. She sees him rising above the lattice. What does this mean? Perhaps that those lattices are ours; they are not lattices to him, since that soul is still within sensible and worldly things, which are accustomed to seize the human mind and enfold it, as it were, in their own bosom.

40. “Behold, he himself stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice.” [Note: [Col. 1882D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 6, nos. 18–26.] The Church, or the soul of the righteous, had seen him leaping like a fawn over the mountains; and suddenly, seeing him first looking behind the wall of her house, gazing through the windows, [Col. 1882B] and rising above the lattice, she rejoices and exults because she too is loved by the Bridegroom. As though he too were wounded by the beauty of love, he came, when first absent from his beloved, at her request for kisses—for he is requested when she says, “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (Song I, 1). Then he did not reject the bride’s prayers and endearments, when she offered him her breasts, beloved by him; and in his kindness he led her into the inner parts of the house. Then, as though playing in sportive love with one who was in love, because he wished to test the feelings of the lover, he often went out so that the bride might seek him, and often returned so that she might invite him to kisses. He stood behind the wall, looked through the windows, and rose above the lattice, so that he might neither be wholly absent nor enter as though wholly present, and that he might call the bride to himself, so that the exchanges of their coming to one another might become more pleasing and they might kindle love through mutual words.

1567 41. (Verse 10.) “Rise, come, my kinswoman, my beautiful one, my dove.” And you too, if you have a firmly established wall—not that partition which separates the members of one house, but one built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, so that its joined structure may grow into a temple and not divide its inner parts but fortify them—if, then, you have within you the building of God, and your windows always open toward the East, the Word comes. “He stands behind your wall” (Song II, 9), for “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII, 16); he looks through your windows (Song II, 9).

42. What are these windows? We read of windows concerning which Jeremiah says: “Death entered through the windows” [Col. 1882D] (Jer. IX, 21); through them greed entered, lust entered. Your eye is a window. If you look upon a woman in order to desire her, death has entered through your eye. If you look upon a widow’s property or a minor’s treasures and stir up your desires, death has entered through the window. Thus, just as death enters through these windows, so does life enter. If, looking upon the beauty of a young girl consecrated to the sacred life, you revere the Lord Jesus because old age has come in tender years, a life without blemish, and if you offer your own daughter so that she may be consecrated with a devout veil; if you do not look upon a minor’s property as an anxious invader but, like a watchful parent, protect it with religious affection—through these windows Christ looks forth, so that he may call the bride.

43. “Rising above the lattice.” He rightly rises above it, because he alone is not entangled in the lattices of sins. We were all within the lattices; indeed, we are still within them, because no one is without sin except Jesus alone. The Father made him who knew no sin to be sin for us; indeed, he delivered him to snares and handed him over to nets—not sending him in the sin in which all human beings were, but in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that from sin he might condemn sin in the flesh. The flesh was sin, according to the fact that it had been condemned by an inherited curse; sin was the enticement and instrument of sin. The Lord Jesus came, and in flesh subject to sin he exercised the warfare of virtue. Our members became no longer weapons of lust but weapons of virtue; for where the provocations of lust had been, there are now dwelling places of chastity. He therefore came to the snares, but willingly; he came to the nets, but unharmed. Everything was full of nets and crowded with snares. Hear him saying: “Along the way by which I walked, the proud hid a snare for me” (Ps. CXLI, 4). And in the book of the wisdom of Sirach you are warned to recognize that “you walk in the midst of snares” (Sir. IX, 20). As many vices as there are, so many nets; as many sins as there are, so many snares.

44. Hereditary bonds already held you; Jesus came to the snares in order to release Adam. He came to free what had perished. We were all held in nets, and no one could rescue another, since he could not rescue himself. Such a one, therefore, was necessary—one whom the bonds of human generation, subject to sins, would not hold; whom greed would not capture; whom deceit would not bind. That one was Jesus alone. Although he had surrounded himself with the bonds of this flesh, he was not captured and was not bound. Rather, breaking and dissolving them, he called the Church more fully to himself: looking through the snares and rising above the nets, so that she too might learn not to be held by bonds. In the end, he was not so far from the bonds that he did not undergo death for us; yet he did not become death’s slave, but was free among the dead. For he was free, since he possessed the power to lay down his death. Let him teach you this himself, who says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19). Let us therefore hear what he says:

45. (Verses 11–13.) “Rise, come, my kinswoman”—that is, rise from the dead, rise from the bonds with which you were surrounded. Rise, because I have risen for you; loose the bonds of iniquity, because I have already loosed them for you. Come, because the nets have already been loosed; the Virgin has given birth, a child has been born from a virgin, owing nothing to woman’s inheritance and not held as a woman’s son. See the middle wall of the partition already dissolved, the wall that divided the harmony of inward affections and stirred up dissensions among bodily passions. Come, therefore, without fear. I desire to see your face and hear your voice. Come, so that you may no longer see me through nets, but may enjoy me, beloved, face to face in the countenance of the lover.

46. Let these matters here be passed over in their ethical sense. But if we can, let us also glance at the outermost line of those mystical matters. The bride, devoted to the Lord, sat within the house, within the wall of the Law and the prophets, founded upon the construction of spiritual stones. It enclosed and fortified the royal house, full of delight and joy. She marveled at the royal treasures and gazed upon them attentively, desiring to acquire the wisdom that would reveal these riches to her. She was in a secret place, but she sought an interpreter of that very secret. The Lord Jesus came, leaping over the mountains. To us he seemed slow to come, but he was hastening. Indeed, he leaped and bounded over them so as to pass beyond the bodily and stony doctrines of the Jews. He stood behind the wall of the house that existed in the Old Testament, looking through the window of the Law and the caverns of the prophets.

[Col. 1884B] 47. The vestibules of that house were not yet open, nor had the keys of wisdom opened the bars of the gates by which the inner things of the Law were closed. Yet, looking forth from above—that is, from the spiritual part—he calls the Church, so that, rising exalted through the Law and the prophets to the summit of the Gospel, she may trample with fearless step upon the nets of Jewish interpretation and its knots. Therefore she is called “Kinswoman,” so that she may cling to Christ and not seek worldly things; “Beautiful,” so that she may bear the beautiful feet of those who proclaim the Gospel; “Dove,” so that she may seek spiritual things and abandon earthly ones.

48. “Behold,” he says, “the winter has passed, the rain has gone away, it has departed; flowers have appeared on the earth, the time for cutting has come.” Before Christ’s coming there was winter; Christ came and made summer. Then everything was lacking flowers, naked of virtues; Christ suffered, and everything began to be made fruitful with the shoots of new grace. The rain of overflowing wantonness has gone away, and the clouds arising from dark crimes are now dispersed by the summer brightness of a pure conscience. Therefore those whose flight takes place in winter do not escape, because they do not follow the Lord’s Passion, do not take up their cross, nor follow Christ.

49. Rain hinders the flowers, but now flowers appear on the earth. The good flowers are the apostles, who poured forth the fragrance of their various writings and works. The time for cutting has come, when ripe grain is stored in the granaries and the one who reaps receives a reward. The voice of the turtledove has been heard, because it has found a nest for itself; for the Church is the house of chastity. The fig tree that, because of its barrenness, was ordered to be cut down has now begun to bear fruit. The vine transplanted from Egypt is now, its fences having been cast down, assailed by beasts; nor is it shapeless with thorns, but now fragrant with flowers.

50. [Note: [Col. 1883D] From *The Final Apology for David*, chapter 8, sections 43–44.] “Arise,” he says, “come, my close companion, my beautiful one, my dove, my perfect one”: close companion, certainly, in the desire of faith; beautiful in the adornment of virtue; a dove in spiritual grace. For the silvered wings of the dove signify that eternal power, and the dove’s flight declared the presence of the Holy Spirit. Christ therefore calls her to himself to come, since she was coming already endowed with spiritual gifts.

“For behold,” he says, “the winter has passed, the rain has gone away, it has departed of itself, and flowers have appeared on the earth.” See how the holy Church is invited. “The winter,” he says, “has departed of itself,” so that she need not fear winter while naked—not winter as a season, but the winter of weakness, which strips the fruitful field of the soul of every flower. There is indeed a winter that is not the winter of the earthly sun, but of the mind: when cold seeps into the spirit; when the mind’s vapor evaporates; when the vigor of understanding is dissolved; when excessive moisture overflows and weighs down the mind; when the inward vision grows dark. And therefore the Lord says: “See that your flight does not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew 24:20). For it is good that the day of judgment or of death should come when the mind’s gentle temper is vigorous, when the heavenly mystery shines with serene light, when our heart burns within us. For then Christ is present, as Emmaus and Cleopas testify in the Gospel, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

The spirit is vigorous, moreover, when a flower also appears on the earth. What is this flower of good fragrance except the one who said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (above, verse 1)? Of him it is also written in Isaiah: “A shoot will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a branch will rise from the root, and a flower will come forth from the branch” (Isaiah 11:1). The root, certainly, is the family of the Jews; the branch is Mary; the flower of Mary is Christ. When he shines upon our earth, and gives fragrance in the field of the soul, or blossoms in his Church, we can neither fear the cold nor dread the rain, but must await the day of judgment. And therefore, so that the Church might see this flower, she hastened with every effort, as she herself testifies later, saying: “At night, on my bed, I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:1).

50. [Note: [Col. 1885D] Book VII, *On Luke*, on chapter 13.] “The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs.” This tree is aptly compared with the Synagogue. For just as this tree, overflowing with spreading leaves, deprives its owner of hope through the empty expectation of anticipated produce, so also in the Synagogue, while its teachers—unfruitful in works—boast only in words overflowing like leaves, the empty shadow of the Law prevails; meanwhile the false hope of an expected harvest mocks the hopes of the believing people.

51. There is also something in the nature of the tree that may make you believe even more strongly that the appearance of the Synagogue has been represented by this comparison. For if you investigate carefully, you will find that the nature of this tree follows a pattern distinct from that of other trees. Other trees bear flowers before fruit, and by the announcing sign of their flowers indicate the fruits that are to come. This tree alone produces fruit from the beginning in place of flowers. In other trees the flower falls away and fruits are born; on this tree the fruits fall away so that fruits may follow. Thus those first, empty products take the place of flowers: through a certain premature manner of birth, things that do not know the order of nature cannot preserve nature’s gift.

For from the place where a bud is accustomed to push itself out from the bark, the very smallest fruits of this kind burst forth. Of these we read in the *Song of Songs*: “The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs.” Thus, while other shrubs grow white with blossoms in early spring, the fig tree alone does not know how to become white with its own flower—perhaps because none of these fruits has a more mature use. For when others succeed them, as though they were degenerating, they are cast off; and those weak with a withering root are stripped away, while those renewed with more beneficial sap take their place. Some, however, exceptionally rare, remain and do not fall away; when this yield has smiled upon them, they emerge from the midst of two branches through a short-shooting stalk. Covered, as it were, by a double protection and nurtured in the lap of their mother, nature, they grow strong through an abundance of sap. Invigorated by the temperate air, and matured over longer periods, once they have shed the wild character of their earlier sap, they surpass the others in appearance and in the grace of ripeness.

[Col. 1886B] 52. Consider now the conduct and disposition of the Jews, who, like the first fruits of the poorly fruitful Synagogue, fell in a likeness to something slipping away, so that fruits of our race that would endure beyond the ages might take their place. For the first people of the Synagogue, weak as to the root of their works and withering, could not draw up the abundance of natural wisdom. And therefore the fruit fell away like something useless, so that, as it were, from the same short shoots of the fruitful tree, a new people of the Church might emerge from the richness of the ancient religion.

Thus the one who existed ceased to exist, so that the one who did not exist might begin. Yet the first among Israel, whom the branch of stronger nature had raised up, colored by a double sap beneath the shadow of the Law and the cross, in the bosom of both, surpassed the others by the beauty and grace of most excellent fruits, in the likeness of the ripening unripe figs. To them it is said: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

53. [Note: [Col. 1886D] Book IX, *On Luke*, on chapter 20.] “The flowering vines have given their fragrance” (above, verse 5). The Church is aptly represented by the vine. For just as the vine is married to trees, so the body is joined to the soul, and the soul likewise to the body. As the vine, when bound, is raised up, and when pruned is not diminished but increased, so the holy people, when bound, are stripped; when humbled, they are lifted up; when pruned, they are crowned.

Moreover, just as a tender shoot, cut from an old tree, is grafted into the fertile rootstock of another, so this holy people, with the scars of the old shoot untied, grows strong in that new sign of the cross, as though in the lap of a devout mother. And the Holy Spirit, poured into this prison-like body, as though sent down into deep trenches of the earth, washes away whatever is foul with a life-giving irrigation; and he raises the condition of our members into heavenly discipline.

54. The diligent cultivator is accustomed to dig, water, and tend this vine. Having cleared away the embankments of the earthly mass, he is accustomed to make the work of our body endure now the heat of the sun, now the soaking of rain; he packs the soil around the field so that no thorn may injure the bud, and so that the unproductive boastfulness of words may not luxuriate in the shadow of leaves and, by overshadowing the virtues, hinder the maturity of our natural disposition.

[Col. 1887A] 55. (Verse 14.) [Note: [Col. 1887D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 6, section 33.] “And come,” he says, “my dove, in the shelter of the rock, beside the fortification.” That is: come near the Gospel. The strongholds of your faith are the deeds of Christ; the supports of your walls are the words of the Lord; the passion of the Lord’s body is your strength.

56. “Show me your face and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.” Your voice is sweet because confession with the mouth leads to salvation; and your face is beautiful because she who is not ashamed of her author is not put to shame by her redeemer. She therefore shows her face, bearing the sign of the cross before her; and she lets her voice be heard, assuming the authority of preaching. In the shelter of Christ’s body, by which she has been redeemed from sin, she finds the protection of spiritual grace, so that she both perceives and speaks what is beneficial for her salvation. Sweet, therefore, is the voice that spoke in the divine testimonies; beautiful the face that was not put to shame in the presence of kings.

57. [Note: [Col. 1887D] *On Isaac*, chapter 4, sections 34 and following.] “Arise,” he says, “come, my close companion”—that is, arise from the pleasures of the world; arise from earthly things and come to me, you who are still laboring and burdened, you who are anxious about the things of the world. Come above the world; come to me, because I have conquered the world. Come near me, now beautiful with the beauty of eternal life; now a dove, that is, gentle and meek; now wholly filled with spiritual grace.

Rightly, therefore, she need no longer fear nets, since the one who calls the soul to himself could not be caught by the temptations and nets of the world. For while we human beings walk in the midst of snares, through our appetite for food we are subject both to nets and to traps. He, placed in the body, did not fear the nets, but rose above them—that is, above the temptations of the world and the passions of the body. Indeed, he also caused others to rise above them.

58. “Arise, come, my close companion; do not fear the nets. The winter has already passed. Easter has come; indulgence has come; forgiveness of sins has come; temptation has ceased; the rain has gone away; the storm and the shaking have gone away.” Before Christ’s coming there was winter; after Christ’s coming there are flowers. Hence he says: “Flowers have appeared on the earth.” Where there were thorns before, there are now flowers. “The time,” he says, “for pruning has come.” Where there was a desert before, there is now a harvest.

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” The prophet rightly added “our,” as though marveling that where there was immodesty before, there is now chastity. “The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs.” What was ordered to be cut down as though fruitless has now begun to bear fruit. But why do you hesitate because he said “unripe figs”? He shakes off the earlier ones so that he may bring forth later, better ones—just as the fruit of the Synagogue is cast away, while that of the Church is renewed.

59. And although complete tranquility exists and the mysteries have matured, he nevertheless says again: “Arise securely in the shelter of the rock”—that is, safe under the protection of my passion and the defense of faith. “They sucked honey from the rock and oil from the firm rock.” Souls clothed in this shelter are no longer naked, and this is their fortification.

Therefore he also says to this soul: “And come, my dove, in the shelter of the rock, beside the fortification; show me your face and let me hear your voice.” He urges her to confidence, so that she may not be ashamed of Christ’s cross or of his sign. He urges her to confession; he wishes all ambushes to be removed, so that the good fragrance of faith may breathe forth, so that the day may shine, and so that the shadow of the hostile night may do no harm. For the one who is beside Christ says: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Romans 13:12). There is also the shadow of worldly things, which passes away, and the day of heavenly things, which is Christ, who shines upon his saints.

60. (Verse 15.) [Note: [Col. 1887D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 11, section 29.] “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, so that our vineyards may flower.” Scripture calls a human being one who is made in the image and likeness of God. But it is accustomed to call the sinner not a human being, but either a serpent, or a horse neighing after females, or a little fox, or a beast of burden. Concerning one of these the Lord says: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke 13:32)—that is, concerning Herod. And elsewhere, when he perceived that they were questioning him deceitfully, he said: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the air have nests where they may rest” (Matthew 8:20), because they linger deceitfully in certain hiding places of earthly passions.

61. Hence Samson also tied the foxes together in pairs, fastened torches to their tails, and released them among the crops of the Philistines (Judges 15). By this figure he signified that wicked and deceitful people, especially heretics, have a free tongue for barking, but obstructed outcomes or contentious beginnings, while the end of their deceit is appointed for burning.

And therefore he also released three hundred foxes, because the faithless desire to commend themselves through the preaching of the cross, but cannot hold its mystery. Having composed this preaching—false and simulated—they try rather to burn up the fruits of others; whereas the true cross of the Lord does not burn up the merits of others, but makes them fruitful.

62. Rightly, therefore, it is written: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, so that our vineyards may flower.” This shows that either the Lord Jesus or the Church commands that the deceits of the fraudulent be driven out of his vineyards, lest they harm the little vineyards, since they cannot harm the already mature vines. For a heretic can attack the imperfect, but cannot overthrow the perfect.

63. (Verse 16.) [Note: [Col. 1888D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 16.] “My brother is mine, and I am his.” This is the voice of a virgin. To preserve an undefiled body from intercourse with a man, and to raise the palm of chastity in a body of clay all the way to the fellowship of angels by guarding one’s integrity, is a private benefit and a public praise.

How rare on earth is the one who can say this; how free from vices, how separated from every stain of sin, the one who has nothing in common with the world, saying: “My beloved is mine, and I am his; he will dwell among my breasts.”

[Note: [Col. 1888D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 8, sections 3 and following.] Certainly, nothing of this world may claim as its own the one who is not possessed by bodily desires; whom lust does not inflame, greed does not goad, licentiousness does not make effeminate, luxury does not stain, ambition does not overthrow, envy does not waste away, and no concern of worldly business troubles. He is the true minister of the altar, born for God, not for himself.

For “Levi,” as the interpretation has it, signifies: “He has been taken for me”; it signifies: “And he is mine”; it also signifies simply: “Taken”; it signifies: “And taken for me.”

64. He himself is both Levi for me and for God. How is he at once priest for me and for God? He is my advocate and the Lord’s intercessor: offering sacrifice for me, and offering himself to the Lord. Finally, elsewhere Levi is also said by interpretation to mean “for me.” For if Levi is named from me, Levi is “for me”; if he offers “for me,” he is “for me”; if he intervenes “for me,” he is “for me.” But if he is called by the Lord, he is said to be mine—that is, tributary to no one else, paying tithes to no one else, generous from no possession.

“He is mine”: that is, as one who is abundant for all his own. I do not seek tithes from him, nor produce, gifts, or offerings; he himself is my gift, he himself is my tribute. He is not generous to me from his possession; he himself is my possession, my fruit, my understanding. “Taken by me,” or “taken for me,” cannot occur without divine grace. For just as a possession cannot be mine unless I have bought it, so Levi cannot exist unless he has been taken by the Lord. Once he has been taken, he is rightly called mine.

Finally, when Moses had been commanded to divide the dwelling-place among the Jewish people by their individual tribes and to distribute a portion to each tribe, God excluded the tribe of Levi, saying to the sons of Levi: “He shall have no portion or lot among his brothers, because the Lord God is their portion” (Deuteronomy 10:9); and elsewhere: “I, the Lord, am their portion” (Numbers 18:20).

65. An earthly division is denied to these people so that, while they claim no worldly portion for themselves, they may become a heavenly possession—or may know that they possess only this: the service of faith and devotion. They are much richer than those who spread out the broad extent of their possessions. For however far they extend their boundaries, the earth comes to an end, the sea confines their mad desires, and they pay greater taxes than their harvests amount to.

But this man, possessing nothing, serves no one except God. His portion is above the earth; it does not end when the earth ends, nor is it enclosed by the sea. He whose portion is God is possessor of the whole of nature.

Instead of fields, therefore, he himself is sufficient for himself, possessing a good fruit that can never perish. Instead of houses, it is enough for him to be the dwelling place of the Lord and the temple of God, than which nothing can be more precious. For what is more precious to God? Or what does this man lack who can say: “Let it not happen that I should glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14)?

66. The prince of this world cannot claim fellowship for himself with the one in whom he finds nothing belonging to him. Therefore the Lord, who came to teach that God should become our portion, says: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has found nothing in me” (John 14:30).

And wishing us to be his imitators, he says: “Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money” (Matthew 10:9). Hence Peter, showing that his portion is in God and not in the world, says: “I have neither silver nor gold, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). That is: this is my portion; Christ is my portion. “In the name, therefore, of Jesus Christ, rise and walk” (ibid.).

That is: in my portion I am rich; in my portion I am powerful. Rightly do I anticipate such fruits from this portion that salvation and life may be given, because this is the inheritance of the portion that I have chosen for myself: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.”

67. “Who feeds among the lilies.” The lily signifies chastity. The good shepherd therefore knows where he should feed his flock and what pastures are suitable for his sheep.

[Note: [Col. 1889D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 14, section 2.] What are our pastures—that is, the pastures of the faithful—except Christ? The Prophet rejoiced that he had been placed in his pastures, saying: “He placed me in a place of pasture” (Psalm 22:2); for there he feeds and refreshes us.

Good pastures are the divine sacraments. There you pluck the new flower that gave the good fragrance of resurrection; you pluck the lily in which there is the splendor of eternity; you pluck the rose—that is, the blood of the Lord’s body.

Good pastures are also the books of the heavenly Scriptures, in which we are fed by daily reading, in which we are restored and refreshed, when we taste what has been written or repeatedly ruminate upon it after having lightly sampled it with our lips. With these pastures the Lord’s flock is fattened.

The mountains of the valleys are also good pastures of Christ, for Christ feeds even among them like a young goat or a fawn of the deer—that is, amid the splendors of the saints.

68. (Verse 17.) [Note: [Col. 1890D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 3.] “Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree in order to see Christ; Jesus also stretched out his hands for us, so that he might overshadow the whole world. How are we not in the shadow, when we are protected by the covering of his cross? How are we not in the shadow, when the crucified one protects us from the wickedness of the world and the heat of the body?

Or do we not know that the Word of God, when he came into this world, did not come as he was in the beginning, as he was with God, but “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). He came in a light cloud, and although he was the power of the Most High, he overshadowed Mary, so that he might transform the body of our humility and make it conform to the body of his glory.

Thus, just as he changed his form when he was born from the Virgin, so the words of God also seem to us to be transformed when they are read in the Gospel, when their appearance is seen in the Scriptures as though in a mirror. For the whole truth cannot be comprehended here. But when that which is perfect has come, they will no longer shine through examination or appearance, as though transformed, but in complete and expressed truth.

[Col. 1891A] 69. [Note: [Col. 1891D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 5, section 35.] Let the soul therefore bend beneath the yoke of the Word and let him guide it with his reins, so that by God’s will it may be led away from vices and receive the fragrance of eternal life. For this life is not perfect; this life is in shadow.

Therefore, so that Christ Jesus might be born from the Virgin, the power of the Most High overshadowed the mother who was to bear him. He descended in shadow, beginning to work the salvation of humanity from shadow, and destined to bring it to completion in the brightness of the eternal sun.

This life, then, is a shadow. Hasten to the sun, so that he may protect you from the cold of this shadow and pour summer’s warmth over you. And therefore he urges us to pray that our flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath—not signifying a time and a day, but preventing us from growing cold in merits and from being without good works.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 1891B] 1. (Verse 1.) [Note: [Col. 1891D] *On Isaac*, chapter 5, section 38.] “On my bed, at night, I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him. Therefore I will rise and seek in the city, in the marketplace, in the streets, him whom my soul loves.”

This soul had already received good pledges of love. But because we must always be vigilant, always attentive, and because the Word of God leaps forth like a young goat or like a fawn of the deer, let the soul always keep watch and hold before itself the one whom it seeks and whom it desires to hold.

Therefore, lamenting as though he had slipped away from her, she says: “On my bed, at night, I sought him whom my soul loves.” Let the one who seeks well seek on a bed; let him seek at night. Let there be neither a day free from labor nor nights without it; let no time be empty of the duty of piety. Even if he does not find him at first, let him persevere in seeking. And therefore she says:

[Col. 1891C] 2. (Verse 2.) “Therefore I will rise and seek in the city, in the marketplace, in the streets.” And perhaps she has not yet found him because she sought in the marketplace, where there are disputes; in the streets, where there are markets of things for sale. For Christ is not purchased with money.

[Note: [Col. 1892D] *On Psalm 118*, sermon 7, sections 31 and following.] Let holy devotion allow no time free from preaching to pass. If students of worldly teachings indulge sleep very little, how much more should those who desire to know God not be hindered by bodily sleep, except insofar as nature requires?

David washed his bed with tears every night; he also rose in the middle of the night to give thanks to the Lord. And do you think that the whole night should be assigned to sleep? It is then that the Lord must be prayed to more earnestly; then that protections must be requested and guilt avoided, when the night seems to possess privacy.

Especially then, when darkness surrounds me and walls cover me, I must consider that God sees all hidden things. Therefore, do not say, surrounded by darkness, “Who sees me?” And whom do I fear when enclosed by walls and shut in? For “the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil” (Psalm 33:17).

Finally, if you do not see the judge, do you not see yourself? Do you not fear the testimony of your own conscience? Do you not know that the darkness of night is not a covering but an incentive to sin? When bodies are heated by sleep and food, then the vigor of the mind is also loosened by drowsiness and dissolved in sleep. Then impure sexual desire creeps in; then the heart is disturbed by the squalor of uncleanness. Chastity is not seen, purity is not considered, and the glory of modesty is not remembered.

3. It was night when Judas betrayed Christ, when Peter denied him. At that time above all, therefore, God’s ordinances must be unfolded in the mind, and the exhorting commandments reread. Let those precepts concerning chastity not be absent, so that the mind, occupied with them, may extinguish the blaze of lust and the heat of the flesh.

Keep this in mind: “Every night I will wash my bed” (Psalm 6:7). For who, devoted to adulteries and entangled in crimes, washes his bed every night? The one who commits things to be mourned does not know how to weep; and though he himself is worthy of tears, he has no tears for his punishment.

But the one who disciplines his body, who is a careful governor of himself, and who groans and grieves over the offense of an earlier fall, seeks how to wash it away with the tears of repentance. He washes his bed every night.

Let us therefore not sleep through the entire night, but assign most of it to reading and prayers. Hear the voice of the Church seeking Christ even at night: “On my bed,” she says, “at night I sought him whom my soul loves.”

4. Understand this according to the literal sense: she sought him at night by praying, pleading, and also mourning with tears. She sought him at night because “he made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17:12), so that we might learn to seek him more earnestly.

The Church, gathered from the Gentiles, therefore sought him in the prophets, and for this reason believed. Finally, the Evangelists and Paul set forth from the prophets the testimonies concerning the Lord’s coming. Hence it is written: “Night reveals knowledge to night” (Psalm 18:3).

She sought him at night—in persecutions and adversities, in tribulations and severe sufferings. It is night for all those who do not possess perfect security. Hence the Lord says: “The night will come when no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9:4). Let us therefore not work in darkness. For if our works shine, we do not work in darkness but in the light.

5. It is day for those among whom Christ is present; it is night for those to whom he denies himself. It is no great thing for you to give thanks to the Lord when you are in prosperity and favorable circumstances. But remain attached to Christ when persecution harasses you, when some storm troubles you.

Have you lost a son? In that grief, in that night, in that abandonment, remember the Lord your God, lest, as though you had not been heard, you become ungrateful and transgress in your misery.

Have you been driven into exile? Remember the Lord your God, lest you prefer love of your forbidden homeland to God.

Have you been oppressed by the power of some rich man, lost your own resources, and fallen into need? Remember the Lord your God, lest the night of poverty draw you away from the devotion of your heart.

For this is the commandment of the Law: seek him more earnestly at night, when you are more readily heard by the Lord, and can say: “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and the Lord answered me in spaciousness” (Psalm 117:5).

6. But it is not enough to seek casually for the sake of grace; you must persist and devote yourself to the gift. Finally, this woman—whether the Church or the soul—who sought on her bed and sought at night did not find him at first, because perhaps she sought on her bed.

1574 But afterward, when she rose and went into the city—see whether it was that city in which the Lord was about to celebrate the Passover and to which he sent his disciples, saying: “Go into the city to a certain man” (Matthew 26:18)—afterward, when she sought in the marketplace, as I said, where the oil is sold that those awaiting the Bridegroom are accustomed to buy; where there is law and legal judgment.

For if the law is spiritual, then the marketplace is also spiritual, where experts in the eternal law debate. This marketplace is not tumultuous with lawsuits, but glorious with the tribunals of Christ.

Where did she seek, I ask? In the marketplace. And afterward she sought in the streets, from which those who were to gather for the banquet of the Gospel householder were collected—those who had been invited and did not consider themselves obliged to excuse themselves from such a feast.

After she sought in the marketplace, I say, and in the streets, she encountered those who go about the city. Only then was she able to find what she was seeking—perhaps because, placed in tribulation and fear, she found grace more readily. Finally, she says later:

7. (Verse 3.) “Those who go about the city found me; they took away my cloak.” She therefore had a struggle. But for what reason they did not take away her cloak here, I am at a loss to discover—unless perhaps it was because she said that there she had asked: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” She who was speaking of Christ was not stripped of her cloak and found the one whom she was seeking.

Learn how Christ is to be sought: by those who do not seek casually, but hold him with force, like the woman who says: “I held him and will not let him go.” By faith she found him; by meditation she bound him fast.

8. If we understand the good guards to be angels, then the one who passed beyond the angels found the Word. Therefore there was not much distance when she passed beyond them and found Jesus.

How, then, did they take away her cloak below? Perhaps because, as the offense against faith progressed, the Church, while being stripped, is loved more by the Lord: she strips off the old human being in order to put on the new, whom sins do not cover but whose inward secrets are made bright. Or perhaps she laid aside the garment of secular wisdom as she came to Christ. She was not stripped of the cloak after she had begun to become more perfect.

9. Let us therefore remember the heavenly ordinances, so that, while we sing them with the secret voice of the mind, we may remember the name of the Lord at night and say, as it is written: “This happened to me because I sought your ordinances” (Psalm 118:56).

That is: this remembrance came to me, so that I might remember your name even at night—not sunk into sleep through drunkenness, not relaxed into sleep by banquets, not occupied with worldly cares, lest forgetfulness of your worship creep upon me; but disciplining my limbs by daily meditation and exercising the concentration of my mind.

Thus, through constant practice, this solemn course may become ours, so that we may worship the Lord Jesus with our whole devotion even at night.

10. [Note: [Col. 1893D] *On Isaac*, chapter 5, section 39.] “On my bed, at night, I sought him whom my soul loves.” We can also understand it in this way. He seeks Christ on a bed who seeks him in tranquility and peace. He seeks him at night because Christ spoke through parables. For “he made darkness his hiding place,” and “night reveals knowledge to night” (Psalm 17:12; 18:3).

Moreover, whatever we say in our heart ought to pierce us in our chambers.

11. Yet even in this way she does not find him, and therefore says: “I will rise”—that is, I will raise up and lift my concentration, so that I may seek diligently and seek attentively. “I will enter the city.”

There is also a soul that says: “I am a fortified city; I am a besieged city” (Isaiah 27:3). There is a city fortified through Christ; there is that city, Jerusalem in heaven, in which interpreters of the divine law and experts in disciplines abound, through whom the Word of God is sought.

[Col. 1894B] “I will seek,” she says, “in the marketplace of that city,” in that marketplace where legal experts discuss laws, where the oil is sold that the virgins of the Gospel buy, so that their lamps may always shine and the smoke of iniquity may not extinguish them.

“I will seek,” she says, “in the streets in which waters overflow, bursting forth from those fountains from which Solomon says one ought to drink.”

12. “Those who guard the city and go about it found me,” she says. While she seeks Christ, therefore, she finds the guards who are engaged in service, and asks them: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”

But the soul that seeks God passes even beyond the guards. For there are mysteries that even the angels desire to see. Hence Peter says: “They were announced to you through those who preached the Gospel to you, by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven—things into which angels desire to look” (1 Peter 1:12).

13. (Verse 4.) “When I had passed beyond them only a little, I found him; I held him and did not let him go.” Therefore the one who passes beyond the guards finds the Word. John passed beyond them and found the Word with the Father.

There are also many others who seek Christ in leisure and do not find him, but seek him in persecutions and find him. And therefore, as though after temptations, because he is present in the dangers of his faithful, she says: “When I had passed beyond them only a little, I found him; I held him and did not let him go.”

For everyone who seeks finds; and whoever finds must cling to him, lest he be able to lose him.

14. And since through the Gospel we see heavenly mysteries represented on earth, let us come to Magdalene; let us come to the other Mary. Let us consider how they sought Christ in the chamber of his body, in which he lay dead, at night, when the angel said to them: “You seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen. Why then do you seek the living among the dead?” (Matthew 28:5 and following).

Why do you seek in the tomb the one who is already in heaven? Why do you seek in the bonds of burial the one who releases the bonds of all? The tomb is not his dwelling place; heaven is. Therefore one of them said: “I sought him and did not find him” (Song 3:1).

Yet as they went to report this to the apostles, Jesus, taking pity on those who were seeking, met them and said: “Greetings.” They approached, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.

15. Jesus is therefore held, and he takes delight in being held in this way, because he is held by faith. Finally, he was also pleased by the woman who touched him and was healed of the flow of blood, concerning whom he said: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:46).

Touch him, therefore, and hold him by faith; clasp his feet faithfully, so that power may go out from him and heal your soul. And if he says: “Do not touch me”—for he said, “I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17)—you hold him nonetheless.

He said “Do not touch me” only once, when he had risen; or perhaps he said it to her because she thought that he had been taken away by theft and not raised by his own power. Finally, in another book you have it that he said to those who were holding his feet and worshiping him: “Do not fear” (Matthew 28:10).

16. Hold him, therefore, you too, O soul, as Mary held him, and say: “I have held him, and I will not let him go”—to whom both women said, “We hold you.” Go to the Father, but do not abandon me, lest I fall again. And, together with Mary, who did not go astray but held the tree of life, carry me with you, clinging to your feet.

I will ascend with you. Do not let me go, lest the serpent again pour out his poisons, lest he again be able to bite the female foot and overthrow Adam. Let your soul therefore say: “I hold you, and I will bring you into the house of my mother and into the secret chamber of the one who conceived me” (Song 3:4), so that I may know your mysteries and draw in your sacraments.

17. [Note: [Col. 1895D] *On Virginity*, chapter 13, section 78.] “I held him and will not leave him until I bring him into the house of my mother and into the chamber of the one who conceived me.” What is the house of my mother and her chamber except the inner and secret place of your nature?

Guard this house; cleanse the inner rooms of this house, so that, when the house has become undefiled and unpolluted by the stains of any adulterous conscience, the spiritual house may rise up, joined together by the cornerstone into a holy priesthood, and the Holy Spirit may dwell in it.

The one who seeks Christ in this way, who entreats Christ in this way, is not abandoned by him; indeed, he is frequently visited by him.

18. [Note: [Col. 1895D] Sermon 17 on Psalm 118.] Or perhaps “the house of my mother” is the house in which the discipline of moral conduct shines forth; while “the secret chamber” is that in which the higher mysteries reside, mysteries fragrant with the honey of divine grace. Is not the forgiveness of sins sweeter than every honey? Is not the resurrection of the dead more delightful than every flower?

[Note: [Col. 1895D] *On Isaac*, chapter 5, no. 43, at the end.] Receive, therefore, Eve—not now covered with fig leaves, but clothed with the Holy Spirit and glorious with new grace; for she is no longer hidden as one stripped naked, but appears as one surrounded by the splendor of a shining garment, because grace clothes her. Yet Adam, too, was not naked at the beginning, when innocence clothed him. Thus, when the daughters of Jerusalem see her clinging to Christ and still ascending with him—for he deigns frequently to meet those who seek him and to stoop down to them in order to raise them up—they say:

19. (Verse 6.) [Note: [Col. 1896D] Letter 63, to Irenaeus, nos. 4 and following.] Who is this who comes up from the wilderness?

Be like that soul which awakens within itself love for Christ, and which the heavenly powers marvel to see ascending—ascending without stumbling, and ascending from this world with joy and gladness, like a vine-shoot, and rising upward like smoke, fragrant with the scent of a holy resurrection and the sweetness of faith, as it is written: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, like a vine-shoot, perfumed with the smoke of incense, with myrrh and frankincense from all the powders of the perfumer?” He aptly expressed its subtlety by comparing it with powder and by mentioning perfume, because in Exodus we read of a finely ground incense compounded from many ingredients: that prophetic incense which is the prayer of the saints, so that it may be directed in the sight of the Lord, as David also says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140:2).

20. [Note: [Col. 1896D] *On Isaac*, chapter 5, no. 44.] Who is this who comes up from the wilderness? This wilderness appears to be a desolate and uncultivated place, overgrown with the thorns and briars of our sins. They marvel, surely, at how the soul that was formerly left in hell clings to the Word of God and has ascended like a vine-shoot, raising itself toward the heights like smoke born from fire and seeking what is above, while also exuding good fragrances. That fragrance gives off the sweetness of holy prayer, which is directed like incense in the sight of the Lord (Psalm 140:2). And in the Apocalypse we read that “the smoke of the incense rose from the prayers of the saints” (Revelation 8:4). These prayers are presented as incense through the prayers of his angels, namely upon that golden altar which is before the throne of God. And it gives off the fragrance of an ointment, like the sweetness of devout prayer, because it is composed not from requests for bodily things but from requests for eternal and invisible things. Above all, however, it smells of myrrh and frankincense, because the person has died to sin and lives to God. Hence, later on, he says: “I will go for myself to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.” It continues:

21. (Verse 7.) [Note: [Col. 1896D] Book I, *On Duties*, chapter 38, no. 189.] Behold, sixty mighty men surround his vine-shoot, armed with drawn swords and trained in the disciplines of war.

Observe who these strong men are, trained in the disciplines of war. It is characteristic of a strong and ecclesiastical man not to disregard danger when something threatens, but to anticipate it and, as though keeping watch from a lookout tower of the mind, to confront future circumstances with prudent forethought, lest he later say: “I fell into this because I did not think it could happen.” Indeed, unless dangers are examined beforehand, they quickly seize us. Just as an unforeseen enemy is scarcely resisted in war, and easily overwhelms those whom he finds unprepared, so evils that have not been examined beforehand break the spirit all the more.

In these two matters, therefore, the excellence of the soul consists: first, that your soul, trained by good thoughts and possessing a pure heart, should see what is true and honorable—for “blessed are the pure in heart, because they shall also see God”—and should judge only what is honorable to be good; then, that it should be disturbed by no occupations and fluctuate under no desires.

[Col. 1897A] 22. No one, however, accomplishes this easily. For what is more difficult than to discern, as though from some citadel of wisdom, riches and all the other things that seem great and exalted to most people? Then, having confirmed your judgment by stable reasoning, to despise as useless those things that you have judged insignificant? And then, if something adverse occurs and is considered grievous and bitter, to bear it in such a way that you think nothing has happened contrary to nature, when you read: “Naked I was born, and naked I shall depart; the Lord has given, and the Lord has taken away” (Job 1:21)—although he had certainly lost both his children and his possessions—and in everything to maintain the character of a wise and just man, as that man maintained it who said: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (ibid.). And later: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks: if we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (ibid., 2:10).

23. [Note: [Col. 1897D] Ibid., chapter 39, no. 202.] The courage of the soul that wages war alongside the virtues is therefore neither mediocre nor undistinguished from that of others. Rather, it is the courage that alone defends the adornments of all the virtues, guards their judgments, and wages an unrelenting battle against every vice—unconquered in hardships, strong in dangers, sterner toward pleasures, harsh toward enticements, refusing to lend them an ear or, as the saying goes, even to bid them “hail.” It disregards money and avoids greed as a kind of stain that makes virtue effeminate; for nothing is so contrary to courage as being conquered by gain.

Often, after the enemies have been driven away and the opposing battle line has been turned to flight, while the soldier is seized by the spoils of the slain, he has perished pitiably among those whom he himself had struck down. And while legions that had been cast down in their triumphs are occupied with plunder, they have recalled against themselves the enemy who had fled.

24. Courage, therefore, must drive away and crush so monstrous a plague. It must neither be tested by desires nor broken by fear, because virtue remains true to itself: it pursues every vice with courage as though vices were the poisons of virtue. It must repel anger with weapons of a kind, since anger removes sound judgment, and must avoid it as though it were an illness. It must also beware of the desire for glory, which has often done harm when sought immoderately, and which is always an act of self-appropriation. To be softened by flattery seems not only unworthy of courage but also characteristic of cowardice.

Seeing in spirit the camp of these strong men, Jacob says: “This is the camp of God” (Genesis 32:2).

25. [Note: [Col. 1897D] Letter to Horontianus.] But what are the sixty? We know that the week belongs to the Old Testament and the octave to the New Testament, namely to the time when Christ rose again and the day of the new salvation dawned for all—when the radiance of a full and perfect circumcision poured itself into human hearts. Seven and eight make fifteen. These, then, are the seven and the eight, that is, the fifteen, for which Hosea acquired the prostitute whom the Lord had commanded him to acquire. The week and the eighth day therefore signify the completion of the two Testaments [Col. 1898A] and the fullness of faith. The number fifteen multiplied by four, which is sixty, signifies the perfection of the Gospel.

26. [Note: [Col. 1897D] *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, chapter 10, no. 41.] But what is the vine-shoot around which these mighty men stand? “Naphtali,” he says, “is a vine-shoot set free, extending beauty in its growth.”

One branch of the vine is cut away because it seems useless, lest the empty vine grow wild in the exuberance of its branches; another is cut back for a while and then released so that it may bear fruit, whose beauty extends through its growth. For as it raises itself toward the heights, it embraces the vine, and, ascending to the summit, clothes the necks of the vines with a kind of necklace of the precious branch. It is also beautiful in its growth because, with its full branches, it pours forth many fruits.

This beauty is admirable, but far more beautiful is that which signifies the branch clinging to the spiritual vine, whose branches we are and from which we can bear fruit if we remain in the vine; otherwise, we are cut off. The holy patriarch Naphtali was a fruitful branch, and therefore Moses says: “Naphtali is the abundance of those who receive; he will be filled with blessing from the Lord; he will possess the sea and the south” (Deuteronomy 33:23). He explains what Jacob had said concerning the meaning of “a vine-shoot set free”: that is, one released from the bonds of death through the grace of faith. In this is signified the people of God, called to the freedom of faith and the abundance of grace, spread throughout the whole world. It clothes the yoke of Christ with good fruit and embraces the wood of that true vine—that is, the mysteries of the Lord’s cross—nor does it fear the danger of confessing him. Rather, even when placed amid persecutions, it glories in the name of Christ.

27. [Note: [Col. 1898D] Book X on Luke, on chapter 22.] These mighty men hold swords in their hands, swords which, for the sake of Christ’s name, they do not reject, and by which they distinguish bodily things from spiritual things and shadow from truth. For “the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews 4:12–13). The word of God is indeed a two-edged sword.

There are also two other swords in the Church, concerning which it is said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords” (Luke 22:38)—namely, ecclesiastical authority and worldly authority, by which false mercy is opposed.

28. [Note: [Col. 1898D] Sermon 8 on Psalm 118, nos. 25 and following.] There is a just mercy, but there is also an unjust mercy. Thus, it is written in the Law concerning a certain person: “You shall not pity him” (Deuteronomy 19:13). And in the Books of Kings you read that Saul incurred offense for this reason: he pitied Agag, king of the enemies, whom the divine sentence had forbidden to be spared (1 Samuel 15:9).

Suppose someone, moved by the entreaties of a robber’s children and softened by the tears of his wife, should think that the robber ought to be released, although he still desired to commit robbery. Would he not hand the innocent over to destruction, who frees one intending the destruction of many? Certainly, if he restrains the sword, dissolves the bonds, and relaxes the exile, why does he not remove the opportunity for robbery by the more merciful means available, since he was unable to extort the man’s will?

Again, when two men—that is, an accuser and a defendant—are contesting a capital case at equal risk, if the one has not proved his charge and the other has not been convicted by the accuser, the judge should follow what justice requires, rather than, through pity for the defendant, condemn the one who proves the charge, or, by favoring an accuser unable to prove it, acquit the innocent. This, therefore, cannot be called just mercy.

29. In the Church itself, where it is especially fitting to show mercy, the rule of justice must be observed most carefully, lest someone excluded from the fellowship of communion extort communion from the priest’s leniency by means of a brief and temporary display of tears, or even by more abundant weeping, although he ought to seek it for a very long time.

When he shows indulgence to one unworthy person, does he not incite many others to the contagion of falling away? Leniency in granting pardon gives an incentive to sin. This has been said so that we may know that, according to the word of God and according to reason, mercy must be administered to those who are debtors; otherwise, the sword must carry out what belongs to it.

30. (Verses 9–10.) [Note: [Col. 1899D] Book III, *On Virginity*, chapter 5, no. 21.] King Solomon made himself a couch from the wood of Lebanon; he made its columns of silver, its backrest of gold, its ascent of purple, and its back covered with gems.

What is this couch except the form of our body? For in the gems the air is shown by the appearance of brilliance, in gold fire, in silver water, and through wood earth. The human body consists of these four elements, and in it our soul reclines—provided it does not remain without rest on the roughness of the mountains or the dry ground, but, raised above vices and supported by the wood, rests.

Hence David also says: “May the Lord assist him upon the couch of his pain” (Psalm 40:4). For how can it be a couch of pain, when one who has no sensation cannot feel pain? The body of pain is like the body of death: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24).

31. Since we have introduced the verse in which we mentioned the Lord’s body, lest it perhaps disturb the reader that the Lord assumed a body of pain, let him remember that he both grieved and wept over the death of Lazarus, was wounded in his passion, and that blood and water came forth from the wound, while he breathed out his spirit (John 11:35).

Water is for the washing, blood for drinking, and spirit for resurrection. For Christ is one for us: hope, faith, and love—hope in the resurrection, faith in the washing, love in the sacrament. Yet, just as he assumed a body of pain, so also he experienced a bed in weakness, because he turned it to the benefit of human flesh: through passion, weakness was dissolved; through resurrection, death.

Nevertheless, you ought to grieve for the world and rejoice in the Lord; to be sorrowful for repentance and joyful for grace, although the Teacher of the Gentiles prescribed in a salutary command that we should also weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15).

32. [Col. 1900A] [Note: [Col. 1899D] *On the Good of Death*, chapter 10.] He paved its midst with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.

Who are these daughters? It should not be obscure that those who came earlier appear to be superior, while those who came later are weaker. For they are compared with the womb and the births of this world, since those born in the strength of youth are stronger, while those born in the time of old age are weaker. This world has grown feeble through the multitude of its births, like the womb of a woman giving birth; and, like a creature growing old, it lays down the strength of its youth, as though the vigor of its powers were already withering.

These, then, are the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the more tender and weaker souls. He presents himself to them so that his image may shine in their confession, shine in their love, and shine in their works; and, if possible, so that his entire appearance may be expressed in them.

33. [Col. 1900B] [Note: [Col. 1900D] *On Isaac*, chapter 5, no. 45.] These daughters of Jerusalem therefore see the bride ascending and not resisting; they delight in the fragrances of her merits and recognize that she is the bride of that peaceful Solomon. They diligently follow her even to Solomon’s couch, since true rest is owed to her in Christ.

For Christ is the couch of the saints, on which the hearts wearied by all the battles of the world find rest. On this couch Isaac rested and blessed his younger son, saying: “The elder shall serve the younger.” Reclining on this couch, Jacob blessed the twelve patriarchs. Reclining on this couch, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue rose from the dead. Lying on this couch, the only son of the widow, who had died, dissolved the bonds of death when summoned by Christ’s voice.

When the bride has therefore been led to the bridegroom’s rest, they sing a nuptial song, saying to the daughters of Jerusalem:

34. (Verse 11.) Come out and see, O daughters of Zion, King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding.

They sing an epithalamium and call upon the other powers of heaven or the souls to see the love that Christ has for the daughters of Jerusalem. Hence he deserved to be crowned by his mother as the son of love, as Paul shows when he says: “God has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians 1:13). He is therefore the Son of love and himself is love—not possessing love as an accidental quality, but possessing it as his substance, just as he possesses the kingdom of which he says: “For this I was born” (John 18:17).

35. Therefore he says, “Come out”—that is, come out from the anxieties and thoughts of the world; come out from bodily confinement; come out from the vanities of the world; and see what love the peaceful king possesses on the day of his wedding: how glorious he is, because he has given resurrection to bodies and joined souls to himself.

This is the great crown of the contest; this is the splendid gift of Christ’s wedding—his blood and passion. For who could have given more, when he did not even spare himself and laid down his life for us?

36. [Note: [Col. 1900D] Sermon 15 on Psalm 118, no. 11.] What crown of glory is there except the Church, which crowns Christ, its head? What is the joy of the whole earth except the house of the Christian people, the hall of the saints, concerning whom it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm 18:5)?

Therefore, because the Church is the crown of glory, it is said: “Come out, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding and on the day of the joy of his heart.”

37. This is said to souls, so that they may come out from their bodily shelters and enclosures, come out beyond bodily thoughts, depart from desires, anxieties, and all the other passions of this flesh and its slippery affections. Let them ascend above the world, come out from this world, and meet Christ, prepared and present with shining, burning lamps.

As though Christ’s angels are saying these things: “You cannot see his brightness and glory unless you come out from the cares of human weakness, daughters of Jerusalem.” It is as though they were saying: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” (Luke 24:5). Christ is not to be sought within this world, since he willed his disciples to be above the world.

38. What is the crown with which Christ is crowned except the crown of glory? Joseph had the crown of chastity, Paul that of justice, Peter that of faith. Each virtue has its own crown. Christ alone possesses the crown of glory with which the Church crowned him. In this crown are all crowns, because glory is not the portion of one crown but the reward of all crowns.

# CHAPTER FOUR

[Col. 1901C] 1. (Verse 1.) Now the Bridegroom, turning to praise the bride, says: “How beautiful you are, my beloved, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are like doves, beyond silence.”

Beautiful in preaching, beautiful in conduct.

[Note: [Col. 1901D] In the same place as above, no. 13.] “Her eyes also,” he says, “are like doves.” The eyes are men—that is, men adorned with spiritual senses, sharp for seeing mysteries and prepared to penetrate the divine secrets of Scripture, shining with rational milk. In them there is no stained confusion of deceit, but the pure and unstained simplicity of a sincere affection. Therefore he later mentioned these doves, washed in an abundance of water, in milk.

2. We understand the remaining features—the teeth and cheeks, and the lips of the bride like a scarlet thread—to be the virtues of souls and the various kinds of teachers. Some, through diligent stewardship, supply spiritual nourishment to the mind; others bind the hearer by preaching the Lord’s cross, as though with a kind of thread of the Word; others are most pleasing in the modesty of chastity and the flower of youth.

Although they may be restrained from touch by modesty, the fragrance of Christ nevertheless emanates from them. And just as ointment descends upon the cheeks from the priestly head, so the beauty of teaching shines forth in them.

3.
