[Note: [Col. 1901D] Sermon 16 on Psalm 118, no. 20.] “Your eyes are like doves beyond your silence”: this means that she sees spiritually and knows that there is a time for silence and a time for speaking, so that she may bring forth her word at the proper time and not incur sin through speaking inopportunely.

4. “Your eyes are like doves.” Here the simplicity and grace of the dove—that is, of the Church—are revealed. Consider, therefore, the simplicity of the eye. Whoever sees a just person and rejoices also wishes to be just himself. It is beautiful to delight in others in what one wishes to preserve in oneself, if possible. It is innate in the good that the modest person should love the chaste, the wise the prudent with devoted affection, and the merciful the generous; they love their own virtues in others.

For many people, the sight of a just person is an admonition to correction; for the more perfect, it is a source of joy. If there is such power in natural things that the sight of an animal benefits those suffering from jaundice—so much so that even the body of the dead animal is said to benefit those who have fallen into this illness, if it is shown to them—can we doubt that the sight of a just person heals, when his eyes are like doves, simple and chaste?

A lowly irrational animal has such power that it can heal a human being in the brief moment in which it is seen. Will a just person, provided he is seen with faith by one who desires to receive benefit from him, contribute nothing? How beautiful, then, it is to be seen and to do good!

5. [Note: [Col. 1902D] Sermon 10 on Psalm 118, no. 23.] A just man is therefore a good thing. For this reason the apostle Paul went up to Jerusalem in order to see the just, and he remained with Peter for fifteen days so that he might gain something from living with him (Galatians 1:18).

For this reason Paul himself and Barnabas, when they entered Jerusalem, were received with great honor by the Church, the apostles, and the elders. When they wished to depart, they were entreated not to leave; and later, as we read concerning Paul, he was escorted with tears.

Do not even the rays of the eyes themselves seem to infuse some power into those who faithfully desire to see him?

6. But just as the just person gladdens the heart of the innocent when he is seen, so the wicked are tormented by knowledge of the just, because they are convicted even by the silent conduct of the saints. Chastity torments the incontinent, generosity torments greed, and faith torments impiety.

Let us take another example from a lowly animal. Just as we said that a mute animal can benefit when it is seen, so we understand that a wolf can do harm if it has seen someone first; for those whom the wolf sees first are said to lose their voice. The basilisk also—this is a harmful serpent—is said to kill any animal that it sees first; and it is said that anyone who has been seen beforehand by such a serpent is immediately killed. The serpent itself, too, is said to die if it is seen first by a human being.

If there is such power in the eyes of a serpent or in the eyes of a human being that, if one sees the other first, it can kill him, is there no power in the eyes of a just person, who is filled with the grace of virtue—especially when faith accomplishes so much that the woman who touched the fringe of the Lord was healed, and the man upon whom the Lord Jesus looked immediately drew the grace of healing from his eyes (Matthew 9:22)?

7. But the person who sees a just man must know what he is seeing. He does not see him in his body, in his clothing, in his property, or in his face; he sees him inwardly. I say that he does not see him unless he has seen his mind, unless he has attended to his speech, unless he has been able to grasp his understanding and take wisdom from his teaching.

Then he will rejoice, when he has perceived and understood these things. Thus, wherever we hear that a just person is present, let us hasten to see him, like the woman who heard that the Lord Jesus was reclining in the house of the Pharisee; she entered and bathed his feet with ointment (Luke 7:37–38). Let us imitate her, for who could doubt that she represents the Church?

Wherever, then, a just man sits or reclines, let us hasten to see him. It is precious to see a just man, so that you may see him according to the image of God. What is outward contributes nothing; what is inward heals.

Yet even in the person who is outward, we frequently look upon the one who is inward: when we see a poor person, we honor in the poor the one according to whose likeness he was made. Concerning this person he says: “You gave me food, because whatever you gave to one of them, you gave to me” (Matthew 25:35, 40).

8. “Your hair is like a flock of shorn sheep, which have been revealed from Mount Gilead.”

He says “hair” because the power of all the senses is in the head: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Ecclesiastes 2:14). It signifies, therefore, the profound wisdom of teachers, which can reveal obscure things and disclose the heights of understanding.

9. (Verse 2.) [Note: [Col. 1903D] Sermon 16 on Psalm 118, nos. 23 and following.] “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn goats that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and none among them is barren.”

What is said literally about goats must be understood mystically about the flock of the Church. Do not consider these animals worthless. You see that this flock grazes in high places and is bold upon the mountain. Where there is precipitous danger for others, there is no danger for the goats; where there is danger for others, there is the nourishment of that flock, sweeter food, and a more excellent fruit.

They are watched by their shepherds as they hang from wooded crags, where the attacks of wolves cannot reach them; there fruitful trees supply sound fruit. You may see them swollen with abundant milk and solicitous for their tender offspring with maternal devotion. Therefore the Holy Spirit chose them as the animals with which to compare the union of the venerable Church.

10. And if you hear it mystically, the hair of the Word is its height and a certain eminence of righteous souls, since “the understanding of the wise is in his head.” Wisdom is certainly found in the height of human thought.

And just as goats are shorn so that they may lay aside what is superfluous, so holy Church possesses a flock of shorn souls—that is, the virtues of many souls—in which you can find nothing insensible and nothing superfluous. Faith has made them wise, while spiritual grace has cleansed them from every stain of what is superfluous.

11. Rightly, therefore, the souls of the just have been revealed, and revealed from Mount Gilead—that is, from the “transmigration of testimony”—because the heavenly testimony has migrated from the Synagogue to the Church.

On this mountain, then, incense, resin, and the other fragrances are born, which those Ishmaelite merchants, as you have it in the first book of the Old Testament, were carrying (Genesis 37:25). Thus, just as goats, refreshed by good foods and blooming in the warmth of the sun, wash themselves in the river and rise rejoicing and clean from the river, so the souls of the just ascend from the spiritual washing.

12. These are truly the ones who bear twins; in them there is no barrenness of virtues or sterility of merits. They bear twins well because they make their understandings twofold. Hence you have it written in Proverbs: “And you write these things for yourself three times, for counsel and for knowledge” (Proverbs 22:20).

He first mentioned writing three times and then supplied two things: counsel and knowledge. But knowledge is twofold: one knowledge of incorporeal things and another of corporeal things. Hence later you also have: “Your two breasts are like two young twin fawns, which feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (verse 5).

13. We have spoken of fertility; let us speak of teeth. Many travelers by sea and many hurrying along a land journey, when they see some beautiful place, linger there for the sake of delight; they feed their eyes and refresh their minds. No delay in traveling is thought to have occurred, but rather a pleasure has been gained.

So it is also our desire to consider the most beautiful teeth of righteous souls. Scripture taught that the teeth of the just are most beautiful when it said—literally concerning the patriarch Judah, but spiritually concerning Christ: “His eyes are bright with wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk” (Genesis 49:12). Here he certainly praised not the functions of human flesh but the gifts of divine grace. The example therefore teaches that teeth should not be passed over when we have discussed the eyes.

14. What, then, are the teeth of righteous souls except those which, receiving food that is formless and hard, often cold or excessively hot, now break it up, now warm it, now temper it, according to the nature of the nourishment?

They break up hard things, lest the harshness of the letter in the Old Testament and the rigidity of secular understanding, unless dissolved by a spiritual tooth, should obstruct the vital passages of the salvific books and, through the careless greediness of the soul, choke its throat.

It is therefore fitting first to divide the food if what you take seems solid to you, and to distinguish it; then, when it has been softened, to distribute it without harm to the soul among all its members by a natural division, so that the whole body may feed on its life-giving juice. Let nothing corpse-like and nothing dead enter your mouth, lest it be said: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Psalm 13:3). Rather, draw in the living word, so that it may work in the inward parts of your mind.

These teeth are whiter than milk, because they are the teeth of the just.

15. Finally, although all our fathers who were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea “ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Corinthians 10:2–4), it was not without purpose that it was written in order that a greater brightness might be added to these teeth of the saints.

After the crossing of the Red Sea, they were cleansed by the bitterness of the spring, tempered through the grace of the wood (Exodus 15:25); then by the drink from the twelve springs; and finally by the irrigation of the rock that poured forth spiritual water—“for the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

Therefore they also ate manna (Numbers 20:11), so that, washed so many times, they might eat the bread which is written to be “the bread of angels” (Psalm 77:25).

Now also, in the mysteries of the Gospel, you recognize those who have been baptized: although they have been washed over their whole body, they are afterward cleansed by spiritual food and drink. That is the true brightness of the teeth, where the melodious confession of a good conscience resounds.

That is the pure eye which no beam of grave sins has weighed down and no speck of minor impurities has disturbed.

16. [Note: [Col. 1905D] *On the Mysteries*, chapter 7, no. 38.] “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn goats that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and none among them is barren.”

This is no ordinary praise, first because the comparison with shorn goats is appropriate. We know that goats graze safely in high places and feed securely on precipitous ground; then, when they are shorn, they are relieved of what is superfluous.

The Church is compared with their flock, possessing within herself many virtues of souls. Through the washing, these souls lay aside their superfluous sins; they bring to Christ mystical faith and moral grace; they proclaim the cross of the Lord Jesus.

In these things the Church is beautiful. Hence God the Word says to her: “Behold, you are beautiful, my companion; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like doves. You are wholly beautiful, my companion, and there is no reproach in you,” because guilt has been submerged.

“Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon, and you shall pass through from the beginning of faith.” For, renouncing the world, she has passed through this age and passed over to Christ.

17. (Verse 3.) [Note: [Col. 1906D] Sermon 18 on Psalm 118, nos. 22 and following.] “Your lips are like a scarlet thread.”

In scarlet, the appearance of fire and the blood of the Lord’s cross shine forth. The Lord’s lips are scarlet because he spoke of his own passion. Thus, in Exodus, scarlet is assigned to fire (Exodus 25:4).

The world does not consist of scarlet but of four elements. Yet in scarlet the figure of fire is expressed; unless its heat penetrated heaven, air, seas, and lands, everything would dissolve as though its powers had been exhausted.

Through the thread, therefore, we recognize the bond of persuasion; through scarlet, either the ardor of desire that sparkles in the souls of hearers or the sign of passion.

18. (Verse 4.) “Your neck is like the tower of David, built in Thalphioth; a thousand shields hang upon it, all the weapons of the mighty.”

The neck is raised toward God and suited to Christ’s yoke; it is not bent toward earthly things by any allurements. It is like Christ’s royal tower, upon which Nebuchadnezzar cannot impose his yoke.

That tower was founded by David, the man strong of hand, who built lofty structures above the walls so that the tower might be both a protection and an ornament: a protection because it foresees and drives away the enemy; an ornament because it rises above not only lowly things but also lofty things.

It is a protection and an ornament, however, only if it possesses within itself the doctrines of the Word, like jewels in some kind of harness; and if it also possesses the weapons of the mighty prophets, which, against every height that exalts itself, are directed by certain muscles of faith.

19. Do not, therefore, bring your soul down into the dust of death. The Lord has given it natural height and vigor, by which it may rouse and raise itself.

Hence what has been said about this union of soul and body is appropriately understood: in the mystery of our natural life, the soul joined to the body crawls as though upon the ground and clings to the pavement, partly because of this earthly dwelling and partly because this body is from the earth.

Both the lodging of the region and the very material of our body contribute to this interpretation. Therefore the Apostle beautifully desires to be freed from this body of death, because we are confined in a kind of prison and, situated in a certain den of luxury, are enveloped in the darkness of sins.

20. Therefore let us walk according to the will of God, so that we may be said to cling to God. For whoever lives according to the appetite of the body is flesh; whoever lives according to the commandments of God is spirit. Let our soul, then, not become flesh—that is, let us not be called flesh—as were those who perished in the Flood, of whom it was said: “Because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3). Rather, obedient to the soul’s governance, let our flesh become soul and deserve to be called by that name, just as the household of the patriarch Jacob and his holy posterity were so called. For it is written: “These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel; she bore these to Jacob—seven souls.” And in the same place: “All the souls who entered Egypt with Jacob, who came forth from his loins, apart from the wives of his sons, were sixty-six” (Genesis 46:25–26). At the beginning of Exodus also we read: “All the souls who came forth from Jacob were seventy-five” (Exodus 1:5).

**21.** Therefore those who lived with Joseph and went out from Egypt are souls. But those who, although they were angels of God—that is, who imitated the grace of angels through the uprightness of their lives (for “those who do not marry and those who are not given in marriage will be like the angels of God in heaven,” Matthew 22:30)—were captivated by feminine beauty: these are flesh, as the Lord God said: “My spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3). And rightly those who are free from lust are compared with angels: they are not flesh, because they are not in the flesh but in the spirit. Such were those who followed the Apostle as teacher, to whom he said: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Romans 8:9). Those who are seized by bodily lust for women are flesh—and would that they were flesh only, and not also neighing horses! For, he says, “They neighed after the wife of their neighbor” (Jeremiah 5:8).

**22. (Verse 7.)** [Note: [Col. 1907D] *The Book on Virginity*, chapter 7, no. 37 and following.] “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.” What greater beauty can one imagine than the beauty of her who is loved by the King, approved by the Judge, dedicated to the Lord, and consecrated to God? Always a bride, always unmarried, so that neither love may have an end nor modesty suffer loss. This is truly perfect beauty, lacking nothing, which alone deserves to hear from the Lord: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.”

**23. (Verse 8.)** “Come here from Lebanon, come here from Lebanon; you shall pass and pass beyond from the beginning of faith, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the hiding places of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” By these indications the perfect and irreproachable beauty of the virginal soul is shown: consecrated to the divine altars, and, amid the attacks and hiding places of spiritual beasts, not bent toward mortal things but intent upon the mysteries of God. She has deserved to win the beloved, whose breasts are full of joy—for “wine gladdens the heart of man.”

**24.** [Note: [Col. 1907D] *The Book on Virginity*, chapter 12, no. 69.] “And the fragrance,” he says, “of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon. Come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon: you shall pass and pass beyond from the beginning of faith.” You shall pass into the world to contend; you shall pass beyond to Christ, triumphing over the world. You have heard that he separated you from lions and leopards—that is, from the assaults of spiritual wickedness. You have heard that the beauty of your virtues pleases him.

**25.** [Note: [Col. 1907D] *The Book on Isaac*, chapter 5, no. 47.] “Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon: you shall pass and pass beyond from the beginning of faith, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the caves of lions, from the mountains of leopards”—that is, come forth from the body and strip yourself entirely of it. For you cannot come to me unless you have first become a pilgrim away from the body, since those who are in the flesh are pilgrims away from the kingdom of God.

“Come here,” he says; “come here.” He repeated this appropriately, because whether present or absent, you must be present to and pleasing to the Lord your God. Be present when present; be present when absent—even if you are still in the body. For to me all are present whose faith is with me. He who has departed from the world is present to me; he who thinks of me, looks upon me, and hopes in me, to whom I am a portion, is present to me. He is present to me who has become absent from himself; he is with me who is not within himself, because whoever is in the flesh is not in the spirit. He is with me who goes forth from himself; he is near me who has gone outside himself. He is whole for me who, for my sake, has lost his soul. Therefore: “Come here, come here, bride; you shall pass and pass beyond from the beginning of faith.”

She who reaches Christ passes and passes beyond all others: she passes by the merit of faith and the brilliance of her works, which shine like Sanir and Hermon—that is, like the way of a lamp. She passes after conquering the temptations of the world and overcoming spiritual wickedness, seeking the crown of a lawful contest.

**26. (Verse 9.)** [Note: [Col. 1908D] *Commentary on Psalm 118*, sermon 11, nos. 7–8.] “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.”

These are the eyes of the mind, the eyes, namely, of the inner person—not those eyes that perform the service of sight. There is an eye both of the mind and of the flesh; but that eye is blind which does not see divine things, though it is vainly puffed up with a carnal mind. There is also another eye, the sense of Christ, by which the Church sees Christ, just as he says to the Bride: “You have captivated us in heart with one of your eyes.” Christ is rightly seen with one eye, either because he is not seen with a bodily eye, or because, although the Church has two eyes—the moral and the mystical—it sees Christ more fully with the eye of faith. For the mystical eye is sharper, while the moral eye is gentler.

**27.** Perhaps these are the eyes with which Paul saw eternal things, when he began no longer to see temporal things. Indeed, he who did not see Christ before losing his eyes saw him after he had lost his bodily sight. He saw him, for he said: “Who are you, Lord?” (Acts 9:5). Certainly he saw Christ, whom he also acknowledged as Lord. And afterward he said: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” Was he not therefore seeing the one whose command he awaited?

With what eyes, then, did Paul begin to see more clearly, unless with those that he himself showed us when he said: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14:15)? Finally, so that you may know that he saw while praying, he says: “It happened, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, that I fell into a trance and saw him saying to me: ‘Hurry, leave Jerusalem quickly, for they will not accept your testimony about me’” (Acts 22:17–18).

**28.** [Note: [Col. 1908D] Ibid., no. 10.] These eyes, then, grow faint for the word of God and say: “When will you comfort me?” It was through these eyes that the prophets were called seers, because by revelation they perceived in their minds what had been hidden.

But since the eye of the mind and the eye of the flesh are one eye, and a person is then supported by consolation when flesh and mind do not desire different things but desire and seek one thing, they are therefore intent upon him who says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). These eyes likewise confess themselves to be one, because they perform one and the same function with one and the same desire.

**29. (Verse 10.)** [Note: [Col. 1908D] Book 1 *On Virginity*, chapter 7, no. 39.] “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.” And below: “The fragrance of your garments is like Lebanon.”

See what progress you assign to us, virgin! For your first fragrance surpasses all the spices that were brought to the burial of the Savior and gives off the scent of having put to death the pleasures of bodily movement and the limbs. Your second fragrance, like the fragrance of Lebanon, breathes forth the integrity of the Lord’s body and the flower of virginal chastity. Let your works, then, form a honeycomb. The fragrance of your garments is also the fragrance of our deeds.

[Col. 1909A] [Note: [Col. 1909D] *The Book on Virginity*, chapter 12, no. 73.] Bring your hands, then, to your nostrils, and examine the fragrance of your deeds with tireless and wakeful eagerness of mind. The fragrance of your right hand will delight you, and your limbs will give off the perfume of the resurrection; your fingers will sweat myrrh—that is, spiritual deeds will exhale the grace of true faith. Thus, virgin, you receive pleasure from your inner self, and you yourself are sweet to yourself, you yourself are pleasant to yourself; indeed, as often happens to sinners, you do not begin to displease yourself.

**30. (Verse 11.)** [Note: [Col. 1909D] Book 1 *On Virginity*, chapter 7, no. 40.] “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb.” Let your works, then, form a honeycomb. Virginity is worthy to be compared with bees: so industrious, so chaste, so self-controlled. The bee feeds on dew, knows no sexual intercourse, and forms honey. Dew is likewise the divine word for the virgin, because the words of God descend like dew. The virgin’s modesty is her undefiled nature; the virgin’s childbirth is the fruit of her lips, free from bitterness and fertile in sweetness. The labor is shared, and the fruit is shared.

How I would wish you, daughter, to imitate this little bee, whose food is a flower, whose offspring is gathered by the mouth and formed by the mouth. Imitate her, daughter. Let your words display no veil of deceit and contain no covering of fraud, so that they may possess purity and be full of gravity. May the eternal posterity of your merits also be born for you through your mouth, and may you gather it not for yourself alone but also for many—for who knows when your soul may be required of you? Do not leave behind storehouses heaped with grain and then be seized and taken away to a place where you cannot carry your treasure, which will benefit neither your life nor your merits. Therefore be rich—but for the poor—so that those who share your nature may also share your resources.

**31.** “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb.” Tell us, Solomon, what the honeycomb is. For you said: “Good words are a honeycomb” (Proverbs 16:24). And truly it is a good honeycomb, which the Church eats, fragrant with honey gathered through the spiritual abundance of many prophets, as though they were bees. This is the honey of which he says: “I ate my bread with my honey” (Song of Songs 5:1).

The lips of the preacher drip honey when the members of a fallen soul, bruised by harsh misfortunes or collapses, are restored and strengthened. “Your lips, bride, drip honey; honey and milk are under your tongue.” For “the mouth of the righteous drips wisdom”; from the mouth of the righteous flow the honey of sweetness and mercy. In the mouth of the righteous there is no deceit, no treachery, and no bitterness of sin.

The Church hears the words of the righteous; the people of God hear the words of the wise. It delights in the sweetness of his address and is soothed by the pleasure of moral discourse, saying: “How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Psalm 118:103). For the honey of bees delights for a time, but its flavor soon vanishes, and often diseased entrails are harmed by it. The honey of moral words, however, even when it stings, does not injure.

**32.** Nevertheless, recognize to whom those words are entrusted. For it is written: “Say nothing in the ear of a fool, lest he mock your prudent words” (Proverbs 23:9). The fool, who cannot perceive their sweetness, will vomit out and reject your word.

How can the words of God be sweet in your throat when the bitterness of wickedness is there? How can honey and milk be under your tongue when your tongue constructs deceit—when you conceive one thing in your heart but present another in public speech in order to deceive the unwary?

The Apostle Peter tells you to lay aside all malice and reject the disguise of hypocrisy, saying: “Like newborn infants, desire rational and guileless milk” (1 Peter 2:2). By showing us what it means to have honey and milk under the tongue, he teaches us not to curse those who curse us but to return a blessing. We must know how to hate only the way of iniquity, so that, even when our feelings resist, we may avoid doing what we condemn.

**33. (Verse 12.)** [Note: [Col. 1909D] Book 1 *On Virginity*, chapter 8, no. 45.] “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain. Your streams…” Because in gardens of this kind the image of God, impressed with seals, shines forth in the water of a pure fountain, and the streams are not disturbed by the mud scattered by the wallowing of spiritual beasts.

Hence modesty, enclosed by a spirit fortified as by a wall, is shut in so that it may not lie open to plunder. Thus, like a garden inaccessible to thieves, it smells of the vine, breathes the fragrance of the olive, and gleams with the rose, so that devotion may grow in the vine, peace in the olive, and the modesty of consecrated virginity in the rose.

This is the fragrance exhaled by the patriarch Jacob when he deserved to hear: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field” (Genesis 27:27). Although the field of the holy patriarch was full of almost every kind of fruit, it produced those fruits through greater labor of virtue, whereas this one produces flowers. Gird yourself, then, virgin; and if you wish such a fragrance to rise from you as from a garden, enclose it with prophetic commandments: “Set a guard over my mouth, and a door around the circumstances of my lips” (Psalm 140:3).

**34.** [Note: [Col. 1910D] *The Book on Isaac*, chapter 5, no. 48.] “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain. Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruit of Cyprus.”

The Bride is praised because she is a garden, bearing within herself the fragrance of that full field of which Isaac says: “The fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field” (Genesis 27:27). Thus the good soul gives off the fragrance of righteousness.

Perhaps the field is the patriarch, while the garden is the soul of someone of lesser rank, as though a portion of the field. It is an enclosed garden so that it may not be invaded by beasts; and a sealed fountain because, through the integrity of its seal and perseverance in faith, it has washed away its own sins.

For whoever has received from the Church has something that may be related to the grace of virginity: placed in the paradise of delight, he gathers spiritual fruits without labor, so that the souls of the patriarchs may contribute their fruits to him through a kind of rural labor of their souls, enabling him to receive everlasting sweetness. He is rightly called a sealed fountain because the image of the invisible God is impressed upon him.

**35.** [Note: [Col. 1910D] *Letter to Sabinus*.] “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.”

All the teachers agree concerning paradise, in which the tree of life is rooted, and the tree of knowledge, by which one distinguishes good and evil, as well as the other trees, full of vigor and full of life, breathing and rational. From these things it is gathered that the earthly paradise itself may be understood to exist not in some particular place but in our ruling faculty, by which the soul is animated and given life through virtues and the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

Solomon clearly declared in the Spirit that paradise is in the human being. And because he expresses the mysteries either of the soul and the Word or of Christ and the Church, he says of the virginal soul or Church—which he wished to present to Christ as a chaste virgin: “A paradise enclosed, my sister, my bride; a paradise enclosed, a sealed fountain.”

*Paradise* is called *garden* in Latin. Thus Susanna was in paradise, as it is read in Latin; and Adam was in paradise, as we read. Therefore do not be troubled by the fact that some Latin codices have *garden* and others *paradise*. The chaste wife is there, then, where the virgin also is. Although the virgin, in her exceptional state, has her own enclosures and seals, both are in paradise, so that they may be cooled by the shades of virtues against the heat of the body and the burning of the flesh.

**36.** Paradise, then, is in our ruling faculty, growing wild with plantations of many opinions, in which God principally established the tree of life—that is, the root of piety. For this is the substance of our life: to offer the worship owed to our Lord and God.

He also established there the seedbed of the knowledge of good and evil. For among all earthly living creatures, the human being alone possesses knowledge of good and evil. There are other diverse plantations there as well, whose fruits are virtues.

But because God knew that the human will, capable of knowledge, would incline more quickly toward cunning than toward the highest prudence—and because the quality of his work could not escape the notice of the Judge who established definite boundaries in our soul—he wished to expel cunning from paradise, as the provident author of our salvation, and to infuse a devotion to life and a discipline of piety.

Therefore he commanded the human being to taste from every tree that is in paradise, but not to taste from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Yet because every creature is subject to passion, pleasure slipped like a serpent into human affections.

**37.** Thus holy Moses did not inappropriately represent pleasure by the likeness of a serpent. For it lies prone upon its belly like a serpent, not walking on feet or raised upon any legs, but slippery through the winding curve of its whole body. Earth is its food, as it is the serpent’s, because it knows no heavenly nourishment. It feeds upon bodily things, changes into various forms of desire, and twists through winding turns.

It has poison in its teeth, with which every pleasure-seeker tears himself apart, the glutton destroys himself, and the debauched man perishes. How many have wine burst apart, drunkenness dissolved, and indigestion distended!

Now I understand why the Lord God breathed into the face of the human being. There are all the senses; there is the seat and allure of pleasure—in the eyes, ears, nostrils, and mouth—so that he might make our senses stronger against pleasure.

Thus pleasure infused cunning into us like a serpent. Perfect prudence is given not by pleasure but by labor and prolonged meditation together with the grace of God. Nevertheless, because the inheritance of the human race is wrapped in the serpent’s deceits, let us imitate the serpent’s cunning in this respect: let us not cast our head into dangers, but guard it intact above all else. Our head is Christ.

Let it remain unharmed, so that the serpent’s poisons cannot injure us. For wisdom is good with an inheritance—that is, with faith—because faith is the inheritance of those who believe in the Lord.

**38.** If the first human being, who spoke with God while placed in paradise, could fall so easily, although created from virgin earth, which had only recently been formed and created at God’s word, not yet compacted with the murderous blood of others, polluted by crimes and disgrace, nor yet our flesh condemned by the curse of an inherited condition—how much more easily, afterward, did the slippery path to sin bring a greater precipice upon the human race, when through successive generations a worse condition succeeded a more tolerable one!

For if the magnet has such power of nature that it attracts iron and communicates itself to the iron’s form, so that, as many have discovered by experiment, when several iron rings are brought near the stone it holds them all in the same way—and if, after one ring has adhered to the stone, you bring another ring to it and then substitute each one in turn, so that although the natural force from the stone penetrates through them all in succession, it binds the earlier rings with a stronger bond and the later ones with a weaker one—how much more has the condition and nature of the human race fallen from a purer state into a worse one, reaching an ever more wicked condition!

For if nature is diminished through forms that are not capable of guilt, how much more is its strength weakened through minds and limbs stained by the pollution of crimes! Hence, when wickedness had prevailed and innocence had been destroyed, there was no one who did good—not even one. Therefore the Lord came to restore, indeed to increase, the grace of nature, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound even more.

**39.** It is therefore clear that God is the author of the human being, and that there is one God—not many gods—but one who made the world, and one world, not many worlds as the philosophers say.

First, then, he created the world; afterward, the inhabitant of the world, for whom the whole world would be a homeland. If today a wise person goes anywhere, he is a citizen everywhere, understands everything as his own, and considers himself nowhere a stranger or a guest, how much more was that first human being an inhabitant of the whole world! As it is said in Greek, he was a *cosmopolites*—a citizen of the world—one newly conversant with God, an assiduous fellow-citizen of the saints. Planted together with virtues and placed over all earthly, marine, and flying creatures, he considered the whole world his possession. The Lord protected it as his work and, as a good parent and author, did not abandon it.

Indeed, he nurtured the one he had created to such an extent that he redeemed him when disowned, received him when expelled, and raised him from the dead through the passion of his only-begotten Son. God, then, is the author of the human being, and the good Creator loves his work. The good Father does not abandon the one whom, like a wealthy head of a household, he has redeemed with the resources of his own inheritance.

**40.** Let us therefore beware lest that woman—that is, the passion of our senses—herself deceived and mocked by pleasure, effeminate this human being, namely the *νοῦς* (*nous*, the mind), and draw him, once ensnared, into her own laws and judgment.

Let us flee pleasure like a serpent. It has many arts, especially in the human being. Other living creatures are captured by eagerness for food; but the human being, possessing more senses—of sight and hearing—faces correspondingly greater dangers.

[Note: [Col. 1913D] *The Book on Isaac*, chapter 1, no. 2.] Therefore beware lest the strength of your mind, bent by a kind of intercourse with bodily pleasure, become softened and dissolve into all its embraces, opening its fountain, which ought to be closed and fortified by the diligence of intention and the consideration of reason: “For a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.”

When the mind’s sense has been loosened, bodily pleasures pour themselves out—exceedingly destructive—and flow into a full appetite fraught with grave danger. If the watchfulness of the living mind had remained attentive, it would have restrained them.

**41. (Verses 3–4.)** [Note: [Col. 1913D] *The Book on Isaac*, chapter 5, nos. 48–49; and chapter 6, no. 50.] “Your streams,” he says, “are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruit of choice trees; Cyprus with nard, nard and saffron, cane and cinnamon with all the trees of Lebanon, myrrh and aloe with all the finest ointments.”

The gifts of the soul are praised—gifts sent by the Bridegroom, with which she came endowed. For to God, pious souls are good fragrances: myrrh, aloe, saffron, and the other substances by which the grace of gardens breathes forth and the stench of sins is abolished.

Therefore, with such a secure proclamation, she asks the harsh north wind to rest, lest it scatter the flowers; and she asks the south wind to blow—that is, as though winter were passing and the mildness of spring were coming with gentler breezes.

She invites the Bridegroom into her garden. The bridegroom descends, and, delighted by the variety of its fruits, rejoices that he has found stronger food and also sweeter food. There is, as it were, a kind of bread of the Word and honey: one word is more forceful, another more persuasive. There is also one kind of faith more fervent, like wine, and another brighter, like the juice of milk. Christ feasts upon this food in us and drinks this cup; and by the intoxication of its drink he urges us to pass from inferior things to better and best things.

**42.** Hearing these things, the soul drank deeply of the intoxication of heavenly mysteries and, as though drowsy with wine, placed in a kind of ecstasy or stupor, says: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2). Then, struck by the light of the present Word, it is awakened by the Word.

This is the soul’s fourth advance. At first, unable to endure the delay of love and the Word, it asked to deserve kisses and deserved to see the one it desired. Second, after being brought into the king’s chamber, while exchanging mutual words, it rested in his shadow; suddenly the Word departed from it in the midst of speech. Yet, when it sought him, he was not absent for long, but came leaping over the mountains and bounding over the hills. Not long afterward, like a young stag or a fawn of the deer, while addressing his beloved, he sprang away and left her.

Third, when she did not find the one she sought in the bedroom or at night, in the city or the marketplace or the streets, he sometimes recalled her, seeking grace through her prayers, even to the point that she was called nearer by the Bridegroom.

Fourth, now sleeping, she is awakened by him, although her heart was awake, so that she might immediately hear the voice of the one knocking. But while she delayed as she rose—for she could not grasp the speed of the Word—and while she opened the door, the Word passed on, and she herself went out in his Word. Sought through wounds—wounds of love—she scarcely found him at last and held him, so that afterward she would not lose him.

In brief, I have touched upon these matters in a condensed account; now let us examine them individually.

**43. (Verse 15.)** [Note: [Col. 1914D] *The Book on Isaac*, chapter 4, no. 23 and following.] “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters that flow forcefully from Lebanon.”

You have these things in Solomon, because his Proverbs are moral, Ecclesiastes is natural, in which he despises, as it were, the vanities of this world, while his Song of Songs is mystical.

You have them also in the prophet: “Sow for yourselves according to righteousness; reap according to the fruit of life; enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge” (Hosea 10:12). For this is the light of knowledge: to possess the perfection of love. Therefore it was said: “Do not fear” (John 12:15); for love casts fear out.

**44.** To understand that Solomon interpreted in this way the three wells dug by Jacob, relating them to moral, natural, and mystical teaching, he placed these wells in each of his books, which he wrote concerning moral, natural, or mystical matters.

In Proverbs, when he spoke of avoiding the appearance of worldly allure, he said: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your wells, and let waters flow over for you from your own fountain” (Proverbs 5:15). And below: “Let the fountain of your water be your own, and rejoice with the wife of your youth” (ibid., 18). This means that true wisdom is our remedy against the temptations of the world. Moral teaching likewise washes away, through its own irrigation, the image of worldly pleasure smeared with certain harlot’s cosmetics and cleanses it with the stream of its fountain.

**45.** Concerning natural things you have the same in Ecclesiastes: “I made pools of water for myself, to irrigate from them a wood producing trees” (Ecclesiastes 2:6). Nor should it trouble you that he put *pools* in place of a well, because Moses too spoke of a well of breadth, since the person who transcends this world with a pious mind is released from every anxiety and narrowness.

Ecclesiastes rightly has pools, since he saw that there is no abundance under the sun. But if anyone wishes to abound, let him abound in Christ.

**46.** Concerning mystical matters, a well still remains for us, and we find it also in the Song of Songs, where Scripture says: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living water, and a stream descending forcefully from Lebanon.”

If you pursue the height of the mysteries, the well seems to you to be mystical wisdom situated in the depths. But if you wish to draw the abundance of love—which is greater and richer than faith and hope—then it is a fountain for you. Love overflows, so that you can both draw from it nearby and irrigate with its abundance your garden, which teems with spiritual fruits.

And because the person who possesses love is himself a well of breadth, it says that where love is, there a great stream descends from Lebanon.

**47.** But so that it may not trouble you that he called it both a well and a fountain, let the Gospel also instruct you. It is written: “Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate that Jacob gave to his son Joseph” (John 4:5–6). “Now Jacob’s fountain was there.” And, being wearied, he sat there by the well.

From this we also understand that this well is related to mystical teaching, because there the Samaritan woman—that is, the guardian (and a guardian of heavenly commandments)—drew divine mysteries from that well, learning that God is spirit and is worshiped not in a place but in spirit, and that the Messiah had come, who is Christ.

When she heard these things, the woman who bears the figure of the Church understood and believed the mysteries of the Law.

**48.** [Note: [Col. 1915D] *Commentary on Psalm 118*, sermon 17, no. 31 and following.] “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and a stream descending from Lebanon.”

The Church drew these streams down from Lebanon. By this stream sins are washed away; by this stream the Bride, a pure fountain of the Holy Spirit, came from Lebanon, passed through the world from the beginning of faith, and passed beyond into the kingdom.

For some, spiritual grace is a fountain; for others, according to their capacity, it is a well. For some it is a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain; for others, a fountain of gardens, which is counted among the Church’s dowry. For others it is a stream descending from Lebanon, a great stream that never fails.

For breasts do not fail from the rock, nor snow from Lebanon, nor the water carried by a mighty wind to the virgin Jerusalem.

**49.** The stream descends from Lebanon when, with the apostles and many believers gathered together in one place, suddenly there came from heaven a sound as though a mighty force were carrying the Spirit, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, who granted diversity of languages (Acts 2:1, 3).

It is a good stream that knows not how to injure but knows how to fill. If anyone wishes to deserve this stream of grace coming from heaven, let him also descend with his eyes into the channels of water. Whoever pours forth this first stream will deserve it.

She descended with her eyes into these channels of water, she who watered the Lord’s feet with her tears in the Gospel (Luke 7:38). Therefore, at the price of her faith, she purchased health for her soul and body—no longer the outpouring of blood but of spiritual grace.

**50.** [Col. 1589] The prophet David, therefore, descended and for that reason brought back grace from sin. He descended into the channels of water—that is, he filled them and heaped up their streams with the tears of the flowing waters; or he filled channels that were empty and void with tears alone.

Or, as a moral mode of expression reveals certain meanings, he descended into the channels of water and crossed them. We could say that he crossed above them and surpassed them; but the force of the expression is diminished, since it expresses a greater force of descending abundance than of ascending.

Consider, I ask, what force words possess through usage, so that prophetic speech does not lose its momentum, although usage itself ordinarily serves the meaning of writers with greater elegance.

**51.** [Note: [Col. 1915D] *The Book on Naboth*, chapter 12.] “A well of living waters.” For if you draw nothing from a well, it is easily corrupted by sluggish idleness and degenerate stagnation; but when worked, it shines in appearance and becomes sweet for drinking.

So too a heap of riches, sandy through accumulation, is beautiful when put to use but is considered useless in idleness. Therefore draw something from this well: “For water extinguishes a burning fire, and almsgiving resists sins” (Sirach 3:33). Standing water quickly breeds worms. Do not let your treasure stand still, lest your fire stand still. It will remain in you unless you divert it through works of your compassion.

**52. (Verse 16.)** [Note: [Col. 1915D] *The Book on Virginity*, chapter 10, no. 54.] “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let my spices flow forth. Let my brother descend into his garden and eat the fruit of his fruit trees.”

You have heard, Bride of Christ, that the beauty of your virtues pleases him. You have heard that he preferred the spices of your garments—that is, the good fragrance of integrity—to all other fragrances. You have heard that you are a garden enclosed, filled with the fruits of sweet-bearing trees.

Ask, then, that the Holy Spirit blow upon you, that he blow over your couch and increase the fragrance of a pious mind and of spiritual grace. Awaken the Holy Spirit, saying: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let my spices flow forth. Let my brother descend into his garden and eat the fruit of his fruit trees.”

The garden of the Word is the flourishing disposition of the soul, and in its fruit trees is the fruit of virtue. He comes, therefore; and whether you eat or drink, if you invoke Christ, he is present, saying: “Come, eat my bread and drink my wine” (Proverbs 9:5).

**53.** [Note: [Col. 1916D] Book 1 *On Virginity*, chapter 8, no. 47.] “Arise,” he says, “north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let my spices flow forth.”

For the fragrance of sacred religion has grown throughout all parts of the world, and by it the limbs of the beloved virgin have given forth their perfume. Hence the Church, preserving the height of the heavenly mysteries, rejects from herself the heavier storms of the winds and invites the sweetness of flourishing grace. Knowing that her rising cannot displease Christ, she calls her Bridegroom: “Arise,” she says, “north wind, and come, south wind.”

[Note: [Col. 1916D] *Commentary on Psalm 118*, sermon 12, no. 24.] Many understand this as though the north wind were cast out and the south wind invited. If they understand it in this way, the icy harshness of unbelief is driven out of the Church, so that our flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath, and the springlike mildness of the southern wind is invited.

**54.** Or certainly: “Arise, north wind”—that is, “Rise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead” (Ephesians 5:14). People of the nations, who have long slept beforehand, wake at last, and Christ will shine upon you.

Finally, all are invited to the Church, both the people of the Synagogue and the Gentiles; but the Synagogue first, because the apostles, who were the first, believed from the Jews, and afterward the peoples of the nations were gathered through them.

See, then, our sun coming toward the south and afterward turning toward the north. “Jerusalem, Jerusalem”: he certainly came to her, whom he also deigned to call. But this is the earthly Jerusalem, which killed the prophets—that is, the synagogue of the Jews: “How often,” he says, “I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house will be left desolate” (Matthew 23:37–38).

He therefore turned toward the nations. In turning, the Spirit of God made its circuit and returned into its own courses, so that God might become all things in all.

# CHAPTER FIVE.

1. (Verse 1.) [Note: [Col. 1917D] *On the Good of Death*, chapter 5, no. 19.] “Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his apple trees.” From this Plato fashioned that garden for himself, which in one place he called Jupiter’s garden and in another the garden of the mind; for he said that Jupiter was both god and mind. He represented the soul, whom he calls Venus, as having entered this garden in order to fill herself with its abundance and riches, and as lying there, filled with drink—a drink that poured forth nectar. Thus he composed this from the Book of the Song of Songs, because the soul clinging to God has entered the garden of the mind, in which there is an abundance of different virtues and flowers of discourse. Who, moreover, does not know that from that paradise which we read about in Genesis—containing the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. II, 8), as well as the other trees—he thought that an abundance of virtues was to be transferred and planted in the garden of the mind?

2. The garden in the Song of Songs signifies the soul’s garden, or the soul itself; for it is written: “[Col. 1917C] A garden enclosed is my bride, my sister; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.” And below the soul says: “Rise up, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let your perfumes flow; let my brother descend into his garden” (Song IV, 12 and 13). How much more beautiful is it that the soul, adorned with the flowers of virtues, should be a garden—or should possess within itself a paradise in bloom—into which it invites the Word of God to descend, so that that soul may bear fruit, watered by the heavenly rain of the Word and refreshed by its abundance! The Word of God, moreover, feeds upon the soul’s virtues whenever it finds the soul obedient and richly endowed; it plucks its fruits and delights in them. But when the Word of God has descended into it, perfumes of wholesome words flow from it, and fragrant breathings of various graces spread their scent far and wide. Hence the Bridegroom says (the Bridegroom of the soul is God the Word, to whom the soul is joined by a certain lawful covenant of marriage):

3. (Verse 2.) “I have entered my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my perfumes; I have eaten my bread with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, my neighbors, and drink; drink deeply, my brothers. I sleep, but my heart is awake.” Let us learn what fruits or foods God feasts upon, and in what he delights. He delights in the one who puts his sin to death, erases his guilt, buries and destroys his iniquities; for myrrh is used for the burial of the dead, while dead sins are those that cannot possess the sweetness of life. Certain wounds of wrongdoing are drenched with the perfumes of divine discourse and healed with the stronger food of the word, as with bread, and with sweeter speech, as with honey. Solomon also teaches elsewhere that words are food, saying: “Good words are honeycombs” (Prov. XVI, 24). In that garden, therefore, there are good words: one that restrains guilt, another that rebukes iniquity, another that puts arrogance to death and, as it were, buries it, when someone, reproved for his errors, renounces them.

4. There is also a stronger discourse that strengthens the human heart with more powerful nourishment from heavenly Scripture. “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.” There is a persuasive discourse, sweet as honey, yet piercing the sinner’s conscience amid that very sweetness. There is also a discourse of more fervent spirit, which intoxicates like wine and gladdens the human heart. Finally, there is a milky discourse, pure and white. The Bridegroom tells his neighbors to feast on these foods of sweet and beneficial words: “Eat, my neighbors, and drink; drink deeply, my brothers.” His neighbors are those who follow him and take part in his wedding feast. When the soul has been filled and intoxicated by this food and drink—for “each person drinks water from his own vessel and from the springs of his own wells” (Prov. V, 15)—it slept with respect to the world and remained awake for God. Therefore, as what follows teaches, God the Word asked that the door be opened to him, so that he might fill the soul by entering it.

[Col. 1918C] 5. Hence those Platonic feasters, hence that nectar made from prophetic wine and honey, hence that sleep, and hence that perpetual life which he said his gods feasted upon—all this was transferred from here, because Christ is life. Therefore, the belly of his soul was filled with the seeds of such words, and the soul itself went forth in the Word; but when the soul goes forth from this servitude and raises itself above the body, it follows the Word. Alternatively, to repeat briefly what was said above (above, chapter 4): [Note: [Col. 1918D] *On the Mysteries*, chapter 9, no. 55.] “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.” By this he signifies that the mystery ought to remain sealed within you, lest it be violated by the works of an evil life and by adultery against chastity; lest it be disclosed to those for whom it is unsuitable, or scattered among the faithless by garrulous speech.

[Col. 1918D] 6. Your faith’s guardianship must therefore be good, so that the integrity of life and silence may remain undefiled. Hence the Church, preserving the height of heavenly mysteries, drives away from herself the harsher storms of the winds and invites the sweetness of springtime grace. Knowing that her garden cannot displease Christ, she summons the Bridegroom himself, saying: “Rise up, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let my perfumes flow” (Song IV, 10); “let my brother descend into his garden and eat the fruit of his apple trees” (Song V, 1). For she has good and fruitful trees, and roots that she had steeped in the irrigation of the sacred font, so that they might sprout with the bud of a new fertility into good fruits; so that they might no longer be cut down by the prophetic axe, but be made fruitful by evangelical abundance. Finally, pleased by their fertility, the Lord replies:

7. “I have entered my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my perfumes; I have eaten my bread with my honey; I have drunk my drink with my milk.” The faithful understand why I have spoken of bread and wine. There is no doubt, however, that he himself eats and drinks in us, just as you have read that he said he was in prison (Matt. XXV, 36). Therefore the Church, seeing such great grace, exhorts her children, exhorts her neighbors, to hasten to the sacraments, saying: “Eat, my neighbors, and drink; drink deeply, my brothers.” What we should eat and drink, the Holy Spirit elsewhere expressed to you through the prophet, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. XXXIII, 9). Christ is present in that sacrament, because it is Christ’s body; it is therefore not bodily food but spiritual. Hence the Apostle says concerning its type: “Our fathers ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink” (I Cor. X, 3). The body of God is spiritual body; the body of Christ is the body of the divine Spirit, because Christ is Spirit, as we read: “Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face” (Lam. IV, 20). And in Peter’s letter we have: “Christ died for us” (I Pet. II, 21). Finally, this food strengthens our heart, and this drink gladdens the human heart, as the prophet recalled [Col. 1919C] (Ps. CIII, 25).

8. [Note: [Col. 1919D] *On Virginity*, chapter 13, no. 80.] “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain”—so that she may not readily open her mouth or surrender it to ordinary conversation. For it is not fitting, when speaking of divine things themselves, that you should answer unless addressed by the word of God. What have you to do with others? Speak to Christ alone; converse with Christ alone. If it is written that women should keep silence in the Church (I Cor. XIV, 34), how much more is it unfitting for a virgin’s door to stand open, or for a widow’s gates to stand open! The assailant of modesty quickly creeps in; quickly he catches a word that you may wish to recall. If Eve’s door had been closed, neither would Adam have been deceived nor would she have answered the serpent when questioned. Death entered through a window—that is, through Eve’s door. Death enters through your door if you speak falsely, shamefully, or brazenly, and finally if you speak where you ought not. Let the doors of your lips therefore be closed, and let the vestibule of your voice remain barred; perhaps it should be opened only when you have heard the voice of God, when you have heard the word of God. Then myrrh will sweat for you; then the grace of baptism will breathe upon you, so that you may die with Christ to the elements of the world and rise with Christ. “Why,” he says, “as though living in the world, do you still make decrees? Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste the things that perish by their very use” (Col. II, 20 and following).

9. [Note: [Col. 1919D] Book V *On the Sacraments*, chapter 3, no. 14.] “Let my brother descend into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple trees.” What are these apple trees? You became a dry tree in Adam, but now, through the grace of Christ, you have sprouted as a fruit-bearing tree. The Lord Jesus willingly accepted this and, in heavenly condescension, answered his Church: “I have descended,” he says, “into my garden; I have gathered my myrrh with my perfumes; I have eaten my bread with my honey, and I have drunk my wine with my milk.”

10. “Eat,” he says, “my brothers, and drink deeply: I have gathered my myrrh with my perfumes” (Ps. LXXIX, 9). What is this gathering? Recognize the vine, and you will recognize the gathering. “You brought a vine,” he says, “out of Egypt”—that is, the people of God. You are the vine; you are the vintage. Planted like a vine, you have yielded fruit like a vintage. “I have gathered my myrrh with my perfumes”—that is, into the fragrance which you received.

11. “I have eaten my bread with my honey.” You see that there is no bitterness in this bread, but complete sweetness. “I have drunk my wine with my milk.” You see that this is a joy undefiled by the filth of any sin. For whenever you drink, you receive remission of sins and are intoxicated with the Spirit. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine . . . but be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Eph. V, 18). One who is intoxicated with wine staggers and reels; one who is intoxicated with the Spirit is rooted in Christ. Therefore it is an excellent intoxication that produces sobriety of mind.

1592. 12. [Note: [Col. 1920D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 8, no.] “Eat,” he says, “my friends, and drink; drink deeply.” Good is the intoxication that produces a certain ecstasy of mind toward better and joyful things, so that our spirit, forgetful of its anxieties, may be cheered by the wine of gladness. Good is the intoxication of the spiritual table; indeed, how excellent is the cup that intoxicates! (Ps. XXII, 5). Elsewhere you have: “Make its streams drunk; multiply its generations” (Ps. LXIV, 11), because the earth, when it has been made drunk with heavenly rain, customarily awakens seeds and multiplies fruits. Therefore, when the Word—which descends from heaven like rain—has intoxicated the veins of our earth, that is, of soul and mind, with divine preaching, the aspirations of various virtues are awakened, and the fruits of faith and chaste devotion grow. Rightly, therefore, it is said to it: “You visited the earth and intoxicated it” (Ps. LXIV, 10). For he visited it by assuming a body, in order to heal the weak; he intoxicated it with spiritual grace, in order to soothe the anxious with joy.

13. [Note: [Col. 1920D] Letter to Anysius, no. 54.] “I sleep, but my heart is awake.” There is also a sleep of the saints that is active, according to what is written: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.” Likewise, when holy Jacob was asleep, he saw divine mysteries that he had not seen while awake: the expanse of air extending from heaven to earth, with the Lord looking down and promising him possession of the land. Thus, sleeping in a brief sleep, he obtained what he later acquired through great labor; for the inheritance of the saints is sleep, resting from all the pleasures of the body, [Col. 1921A] from every disturbance of the spirit, bringing tranquility to the mind and serenity to the soul, so that, as though released from the body’s bond, it may lift itself up and cling to Christ. This is the sleep of the saints’ life.

14. [Note: [Col. 1921D] *On Isaac*, chapter 5, no. 51.] “The voice of my beloved as he knocks: Open to me, my sister.” Even if you sleep, provided that Christ recognizes the devotion of your soul, he comes and knocks at its door and says: “Open to me, my sister.” He rightly says “sister,” because the marriage of the Word and the soul is spiritual; for souls do not know the bonds of marriage or the practice of bodily intercourse, but are like the angels of God in heaven. “Open to me,” he says, “but close yourself to strangers. Close yourself to the age; close yourself to the world. Do not yourself go out toward material things, nor, abandoning your own light, seek another’s; for material light pours in a murky darkness, so that the light of true glory may not be seen. Open to me, therefore; do not contract yourself, but enlarge yourself, and I will fill you. And because, after traversing the world, I have found more troubles and offenses and have not easily found a place where I could rest, open yourself, so that the Son of Man may recline in you—for he has no resting place except upon one who is humble and gentle.”

15. [Note: [Col. 1921D] *On Virginity*, chapter 12, nos. 70 and following.] “Open to me, my sister; rise, my neighbor, my dove, my perfect one.” Near through charity, a dove through simplicity, perfect through virtue. “For my head is full of dew.” Just as the dew of heaven removes the night’s dryness, so the dew of our Lord Jesus Christ has dripped the moisture of eternal life into the night and darkness of the world. This is the head that did not know how to wither in the world’s heat. Hence he says: “For if they do these things in the green wood, what will they do in the dry?” (Luke XXIII, 31). This head therefore drips upon others and abounds for itself. Christ’s head rightly abounds, because Christ is your head: he is always full and is not drained by his generosity or exhausted by his continual giving. Iron has not risen upon this head—the instrument of war and emblem of discord. Now look and see what kind of dew it is: surely it is not ordinary moisture.

16. “And my locks with drops of night.” Do not, my neighbor, understand locks of bodily hair: those are not ornaments but sins, enticements of beauty, not commandments of virtue. The Nazarite has other locks, upon which iron has not risen and which no one has cut. They are not arranged by curling irons or ordered by art, but gleam with the grace of many shining virtues. Learn from the narrative what kind of locks the Nazarite has: as long as Samson possessed them intact, he could never be conquered. He lost his locks and lost the merit of his virtue (Judg. XVI, 17).

17. (Verse 3.) Having heard the voice of the Word, you who had put off your tunic at night—do not seek how to put it on again; for it is shown and repeatedly offered through spiritual wickedness how, I say, you might put it on again: forget and do not know how. As though the Lord were already present, rise up, freed from bodily bonds but troubled, and prepare your inner mind with prayers as you rise, so that you may strive upward from lowly things to those above and endeavor to open the doors of your heart. As you extend your hands toward Christ, your deeds will breathe forth a faithful fragrance.

18. [Note: [Col. 1921D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 22, no. 12, middle.] “Open to me, my sister.” When you desire to meet one of the chief men, do you not first approach his house? Then you seek to be informed and instructed, so that you may learn the mind of the head of the household; then, in order to enter his house, you implore that no one reject or exclude you. You too, therefore, knock at that royal heavenly palace—not with the hand of the body, but with a certain right hand of your prayer. It is not only the bodily hand that knocks; the voice also knocks, for it is written: “The voice of my brother knocks at the door.” We knock with a finger as well. Indeed, Thomas also deserved to open the door of the resurrection with his finger; and Jesus says to you: “Put your finger here, and place it in my hands and my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John XX, 27). Knock, therefore, with your finger if you cannot with your whole hand; knock at the door. Christ is the door, who says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X, 9).

19. When you have knocked at this door, consider how you should enter, lest perhaps, even after entering, you remain outside the king’s sight. Many enter palaces and do not immediately see this earthly king; rather, they wait attentively so that they may at some time deserve to see him. They do not presume upon the opportunity to see him, but are presented by command and pour out their request, so that they may be received with goodwill, taking care over the first words of their address, lest anything stumble or give offense. How much more must God be entreated, so that our prayer may enter the door of his mercy!

20. [Note: [Col. 1922D] *On Virginity*, chapter 13, no. 80.] “The voice of my brother knocks at the door.” Learn also, O bride of Christ, to bar your door during the hours of night, lest anyone easily find it open. The Bridegroom himself wants it to be closed when he knocks. Our door is our mouth; it ought to be opened almost only to Christ, and it should not be opened unless the Word of God has first knocked. “The voice of my brother knocks at the door.” Hear him knocking; hear him desiring to enter.

21. [Note: [Col. 1922D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 12, no. 14.] (Verse 2.) “Open to me, my sister, my bride, my dove, my perfect one; for my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of night.” Consider when God the Word knocks most forcefully at your door: when his head is filled with nighttime dew. For he deigns to visit those placed in tribulation and temptations, lest anyone perhaps succumb, overcome by hardships. His head is therefore filled with dew or drops when his body suffers. At such a time you must keep watch, lest, when the Bridegroom comes, he depart because he has been shut out. If you sleep and your heart is not awake, he departs before he knocks; if your heart is awake, he knocks and asks that the door be opened to him.

22. We therefore have a door for our soul, and we also have gates, of which it is said: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will enter” (Ps. XXIII, 7). Heaven, therefore, is also present in those who possess eternal gates. If you wish to raise up these gates of your faith, the King of glory will enter you, bearing the triumph of his own Passion. Righteousness also has gates, for we read of them as well, when the Lord Jesus says through his prophet: “Open to me the gates of righteousness” (Ps. CXVII, 19). And below the prophet David says: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. CXLVII, 12).

23. There is therefore a soul that has a door, and one that has gates. Christ comes to this door and knocks; he knocks at the gates as well. Open to him, therefore: he wishes to enter; he wishes to find his Bride awake. Do not therefore delay the good lover—he quickly departs—and by the sleep of your body you may seem to have shut out the one who knocks. You shut him out when you are negligent, lazy, and drowsy. Christ is excluded by these barriers. If you are chaste and sober, take care not to be careless. The one who repels Christ when he comes does him the greater injury.

24. [Note: [Col. 1923D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 1, nos. 11 and 12.] “Open to me, my sister, my neighbor.” He knocks at the door even when you sleep—provided that, when awakened or summoned, you wake up and open the door of your heart, he will enter. But if you flee prophetic reading, if you do not read at home and refuse to hear in church, are you not like one who, turning his gaze away, closes his eyes so as not to see what he could see—or like those who, in fury, have thrust their hands upon their own eyes? So you too first turn away with a blinking evasion rather than with outright resistance. For when you come to church and assert that you are a Christian, you appear sound and open your eyes so that you may see; but while you pretend not to hear what is read, you close them so that you may not see for yourself, even if you seem to others to see. You also place certain hands of faithlessness and intemperance upon the eyes of your soul and bring voluntary blindness upon your heart—which is more serious—so that, seeing, you do not see, and hearing, you do not hear.

25. Do you think you are alone when you fornicate, and do you not remember that the eyes of the Lord see the whole earth? Do you not hear him saying: “Behold, the hour is coming when you will be scattered, each one to his own, and you will leave me alone; yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John XVI, 32)? The Father is therefore present; the Son of God is present; the ministers are present; the Cherubim and Seraphim are present, saying: “Holy, holy, holy; the earth is full of your majesty” (Isa. VI). The world is full of virtues, because it is full of wickedness; the whole earth is full of remedies, because it is full of snares.

26. (Verse 3.) [Note: [Col. 1923D] *On Virginity*, chapter 10, no. 55.] “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” In this night of the world, you must first put off the garment of bodily life; for the Lord stripped himself of flesh in order to triumph for your sake over the dominions and powers of this world. “How shall I put it on?” See what the soul devoted to God is saying. [Col. 1924A] It has put off the deeds of the body and earthly ways so completely that it does not know how, even if it wished, it could put them on again. “How shall I put it on?” That is: with what shame, with what modesty, and finally with what recollection? The habit of good has lost the practice of its former perversity.

27. [Note: [Col. 1924D] *On Isaac*, chapter 6, no. 52.] Hearing, “Open to me,” and having its head full of dew—that is, of worldly temptations—the soul was suddenly troubled and, as though about to rise when commanded to rise, said, while it smelled of aloe and myrrh, the emblem of burial: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” For it fears rising again into temptations, returning again to guilt and sin, and beginning to soil its departures and progress in virtue with earthly footprints.

[Col. 1924B] 28. In this way, certainly, it also indicates the perfection of its virtue: it has merited such great love from Christ that he comes to it, knocks at its door, comes with the Father, and sups with that soul, and it with him, as the Apostle John said in the Apocalypse (Rev. III, 20). For when earlier it had heard, “Come here from Lebanon,” and realized that it could not be present with Christ in the flesh, but could be present if it were present in the spirit, conforming itself to his will so that it too might be conformed to the image of Christ, it no longer feels the garments stripped from the flesh. As though stripping off the body’s union, as though forgetful and unable, if it wished, to remember that union, it says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” For it has taken off that skin tunic which Adam and Eve received after their sin, the tunic of corruption, the tunic of passions. “How shall I put it on?” It does not seek to put it on, but signifies that it has cast it away so completely that it could no longer serve as clothing.

29. (Verse 3.) “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” That is, I washed my footprints when I went out and raised myself above the body’s companionship, above that connection and intimacy of carnal embrace. How shall I soil them by returning to the body’s confinement and to that dark prison of its passions? We bury the passions if we do not loosen the cross of this body; if we do not rewrite on Christ’s cross the record of sin that has been erased; if we do not put on again the garment of the old person that we have stripped off. For it is written in the Song of Songs: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” If the members of the body have therefore been put to death, why do its vices sprout again? For this reason the law did not prevail: it did not put the flesh to death. For this reason it passed away like a shadow: it did not change its color. And for this reason it overshadowed us from the sun of righteousness: it heaped up sins.

30. [Note: [Col. 1924D] *Apology for David*, chapter 9, no. 45 at the end and no. 46.] Sometimes being naked is an indication of virtue, because it is written: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” What tunic, then, did she take off, without finding how to put it on again? Let us reveal it from the Scriptures, if we can. There is a bodily tunic, and there are woven coverings of various desires; therefore at times it is better to be naked in body than veiled in heart. Hence Paul also admonishes us that being stripped is much better than being clothed over, saying elsewhere: “Strip off the old person with his deeds, and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him.” Therefore she who has been stripped and has washed her feet does not know how they could be soiled; for through grace she forgets what she had drawn in through nature.

31. [Note: [Col. 1925D] *On Virginity*, chapter 10, no. 57.] “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” You have learned from the Gospel that washing the feet is a mystery of faith and an emblem of humility, according to what is written: “If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet?” (John XIII, 14). But this pertains to humility. As for the mystery, the one who wishes to have a share with Christ must wash his own feet: “If I do not wash your feet,” he says, “you will have no share with me” (ibid., 8). When this is said to Peter, what is judged concerning us? Therefore the one who has washed his feet need not wash them again, and for this reason must take care not to soil them.

32. The holy Church rightly says: “I have washed my feet.” She does not say, “How shall I wash them again?” but, “How shall I soil them again?” As though forgetful of the former stain and contagion, she teaches how, in bodily ministry, we ought spiritually to wash away the trace of our deeds. Therefore, when you have once washed your feet with the irrigation of the eternal fountain and cleansed them through the sacrament of the mystery, beware of the filth of bodily desire, lest muddy deeds be soiled by earthly stains. These are the feet that David washed in the Spirit, teaching you how you cannot soil them when he says: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” (Ps. CXXI, 2). Understand that these are not bodily feet but those of the soul; for how could an earthly human being have bodily feet in heaven? Jerusalem, as Paul taught you, is in heaven; and he likewise taught you how you can stand in heaven when he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil.
