III, 20)—a citizenship of conduct, a citizenship of deeds, a citizenship of faith.

33. [Note: [Col. 1925D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 16, no. 14 at the end.] “I have done judgment and righteousness; do not hand me over to those who slander me.” Where there is righteousness, there is mercy. Mercy frees from sin. How, then, am I handed over to sinners? The following passage in the Song is similar: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” I have stripped off the sinner’s tunic and the earthly covering; why am I judged as though I were sinful and earthly? I have washed my feet so that no portion of sin could cling to my footprint; why do you give those who transgress power against me?

34. [Note: [Col. 1925D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 22, no. 4.] Jeremiah says in his Lamentations: “Your iniquity has come to an end, daughter of Zion; he will not continue to exile you. He has visited your iniquities, daughter of Edom; he has exposed your sins” (Lam. IV, 21). Do you perceive that iniquity could not come to an end without God’s visitation, nor correction be complete except through the grace of the Lord Savior? But hear how iniquity comes to an end, as the Church says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” The garment of the old person, woven from the vices of error and laid aside in the washing of regeneration, does not know how it could put itself on again; for through the zeal of correction forgetfulness of sins had grown strong. Such is the power of completed amendment that it returns to a kind of spiritual childhood, which does not know the ways of error; even if it wished to, it could not commit a crime, because the habit of sinning has ceased to know how to sin.

35. (Verse 4.) [Note: [Col. 1926D] On Psalm CXVIII, sermon 12, no. 16.] “My brother sent his hand through the opening, and my belly was troubled for him. I rose to open to my brother. My hands dripped with myrrh; my fingers were full of myrrh.” First, therefore, he sends his hand, as it were, through a window, when God is understood from his works; hence he says: “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John X, 38). Then love increases, and what has been conceived grows within the innermost entrails. From the intelligible womb, in which the Word is received, once his seeds have been infused, our soul desires to drink in his fullness as dwelling bodily in him; for a woman’s womb is troubled only when she is heavy with child. The soul therefore rises to open to the Word of God; but as it expands and opens, so that through the reception of the Word it may put to death the works of this world, like the one who says: “We carry in our body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus” (II Cor. IV, 19). Thus, while it opens, the Bridegroom passes through; for he always wishes to be sought, and to be found more often. If he finds the door closed, he knocks; and if he is shut out by delay, he departs. But he quickly returns and knocks again, so that at last he may find his Bride prepared.

36. This can indeed also be understood as: “My brother passed through,” just as we read that he penetrated the beloved’s innermost marrow, as it was said to Mary: “And a sword will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke II, 35). Finally the Bride added that her soul had gone forth in his word, which happens when the soul is a pilgrim away from the [Col. 1926D] body and is present with God. Hearing this, the Bridegroom sent forth his work, the Word, as through a cavern—not yet face to face. He sent it as a hand. “And my belly,” she says, “was troubled for him.” Whoever lives in this way can say:

37. [Note: [Col. 1926D] *On Virginity*, chapter 11, no. 60.] “My brother sent his hand through the opening, and my belly was troubled for him; I rose to open to my brother.” It is good for one’s inner parts to be troubled at the Lord’s coming. If Mary was troubled at the coming of an angel, how much more are we troubled at Christ’s coming! When divine influences flow in, bodily desire becomes a pilgrim, and the practice of the outward person grows obsolete. You too, then, be troubled; you too, hasten. Those who hasten are commanded to eat the lamb. Rise, open: Christ is at the door; he knocks at the vestibules of your house. If you open, he will enter, and he will enter with the Father. Nor does he leave a reward only after he has entered; even before he enters, he sends the reward ahead. The soul is still troubled; it still feels along the walls of its house; it is still looking for the door where Christ is; it is still loosening the bond of flesh and the body’s confinement; Christ is still knocking outside.

38. [Note: [Col. 1927D] *On Virginity*, chapter 13, no. 78.] What is our window except that through which we see Christ’s works—that is, the eye of the soul and the gaze of the mind? Therefore, virgin, let Christ enter through your window; let Christ send his hand. Through the window, let the love of the Word come to you, not bodily love. If, therefore, the Word of God sends his hand through your window, see how you should prepare your windows; see how you ought to wipe them clean of every speck of sin. Let the virgin’s windows contain nothing foul, nothing adulterous. Far from them be antimony and the other trifles of affected adornment; far from them be the enticements of adulterous love. The ears have a similar closure: burdens are not to be hung upon them, nor wounds inflicted in them; their one adornment is to hear what is beneficial.

39. (Verse 6.) [Note: [Col. 1927D] *On Virginity*, chapter 11, no. 67, and a little below.] “I opened to my brother; my brother passed through.” How did he pass through? That is, he penetrated the inner depths of the mind, as it was said to Mary: “And a sword will pass through your own soul.” For the living word of God, like a sharp sword penetrating the barriers of bodily thoughts, searches out the inner recesses of the heart. Established in your chamber and in the nighttime, meditate continually on Christ, and hope for his coming at every moment. If he seems to you to delay, rise. He seems to delay when you sleep for a long time; he seems to delay when you are absent from prayer; he seems to delay when you do not raise your voice in psalms. Dedicate the first fruits of your vigils to Christ; offer the first fruits of your deeds to Christ.

40. (Verse 5.) [Note: [Col. 1928D] *On Isaac*, chapter 6, no. 53.] “I rose to open to my brother; my hands dripped with myrrh; my fingers were full of myrrh upon the handles of the lock.” Let us consider what this signifies. At first, as I said, God the Word appears through his works, as though through a cavern, not fully and perfectly; then love increases and what has been conceived grows, and from his seeds, which the soul has received in a kind of intelligible womb, it desires to see the whole fullness of his divinity dwelling bodily in him, as we read. It rose in order to see that Word of God more closely, and in this very movement its progress is signified: it rose through vigor and strength. For the presence of the Word drew out the soul’s strength, just as Mary’s presence, when she was pregnant, instructed John while he was still in the womb, so greatly that he leaped from the womb and rejoiced, recognizing the presence of the Lord.

[Col. 1928A] **41.** She rose to open, and her works and deeds have been put to death for the world. For such must be the soul that is about to receive the Word: it must die to the world and be buried with Christ; for thus Christ is found, and such a lodging-place he seeks for himself. Then the very instruments of action—that is, the hands and fingers by which Christ is grasped—are put to death. We may regard these fingers as the outstanding works of our deeds. Thus, as she was already extending her intelligible hands and fingers from her embrace in order to grasp the Word, the devout soul says that he passed through her, though he has not yet completely passed beyond her. The Word of God undergoes this progression when he passes through and traverses the soul, because it is written: “And a sword will pass through your own soul also, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35). Here he is still passing through, not passing beyond; perhaps he passes beyond in the case of Mary later on, where the Lord Jesus is placed like a seal in her midst.

**42.** Finally, there is immediately another advance of the Word as he passes beyond, because the soul went out in his Word. That is, following his Word, she went out from the body, raising herself from its dwelling-place and making herself a stranger to it, so that she might be present with God and be a citizen of the saints. For we cannot at the same time belong to the household of the flesh and to God. Therefore, in this passage “to go out” signifies, as I have said, the soul’s withdrawal from bodily pleasures. Thus it is written: “Go out from Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldaeans” (Isaiah 48:20). This does not mean that the Hebrew should flee the regions of Babylon, but its ways, as he is admonished by the prophetic address [Col. 1928C]. For there are Hebrews who are in Babylon and who show by their conduct that they have gone out from Babylon. Indeed, those of whom the prophet says that they sat beside the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 136:1) were sitting in the region of Babylon, but they were not in its vices and confusion. For how could they have been in that confusion of vices, when they were weeping and doing penance because they had fallen away from the ark of devotion and faith and from the merits of their ancestral virtue? But when the soul goes out in the Word, she seeks the Word; hence, while seeking him, she came upon the watchmen who go about the city.

**(Verse 7.) [Note: [Col. 1928D] As above, consecutively.]** “The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me and wounded me, and the watchmen of the walls took my cloak away from me.” Properly, as though a bride, she came wearing a cloak with which to cover her head when the bridegroom met her—like Rebecca, who, when she learned that Isaac was coming to meet her, descended from the camel and covered herself with her cloak. So this soul was sending ahead the signs of bridal clothing, lest she be rejected as one not wearing a wedding garment—or so that she might veil her head because of the angels. But they struck her so that she might be tested more fully; for souls are exercised by temptations. They took away her cloak, seeking to discover whether she could bring forth the true beauty of naked virtue, or because one ought to enter that heavenly city without covering, carrying with oneself none of the disguises [Col. 1929A] of false adornment. There are also those who inquire whether a soul is carrying with her the cast-off garments of carnal allure and bodily desire. She is stripped of her cloak when her conscience is laid bare. Yet she is well stripped who is permitted to imitate him who says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14:30); for certainly he found nothing in that one alone who committed no sin.

**44.** Blessed also is she in whom he finds nothing grievous or excessive, but finds the garment of faith and the discipline of wisdom. Thus, without suffering loss—for even if someone wishes to do so, he cannot take away true wisdom—even if the adversary raises an outcry, where the integrity of an innocent way of life shines forth, she passes by the watchmen, is joined to the daughters of that heavenly city, and seeks the Word [Col. 1929B]. By seeking him, she awakens his love within herself, and recognizes where the Word is to be sought.

**[Note: [Col. 1929D] *On Virginity*, ch. 10, no. 47.]** It is not merely an injury not to have found the one whom you seek; often, even to have sought where one ought not is a wound: to have sought in the houses of men who falsely assume the name of teachers, to have sought more boldly than modestly. Therefore, let us beware, following her example, lest the watchmen who go about the city find us.

**45.** “The watchmen who go about the city found me,” she says; “they struck and wounded me, and the watchmen of the walls took my cloak away from me.” It is not in herself, daughters, but in us that the Church is wounded. Let us therefore beware lest our fall become a wound to the Church, lest someone take away our cloak—that is, the covering of prudence, the badge of patience, by which the ambition of softer clothing is stripped away: “Those who wear softer clothing are in the houses of kings” (Matthew 11:8). But Christ gave us a cloak with which he himself clothed his apostles and his body; finally, he commands you to give it if someone asks you for your tunic, so that you may let him have your cloak also (Matthew 5:40)—that is, hand over the distinguishing mark of your philosophy and, as though with the cloak of your prudence, wrap around the one who had previously been naked.

**46.** There, then, daughters, let us seek Christ where the Church seeks him: on the mountains of good fragrance, which, by the height of their lofty deeds, exhale the sweet odor of life in proportion to their merits.

**[Note: [Col. 1930D] *On Virginity*, chapters 13 and 14, nos. 83–92.]** She who seeks Christ must not be common, must not be in the marketplace, nor in the streets, with a plaintive voice, an unsteady step, easy of access, cheap in appearance. The Apostle denies you earthly companionship and teaches that you must fly beyond almost the boundaries of nature, on spiritual wings, to heaven. “Set your minds,” he says, “on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth” (Colossians 3:2). But because this was impossible for those confined within this bodily prison, and because, once the body is dead, the soul is borne back to the heights, while we live it is bound by a certain law of our nature; therefore he added: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (ibid., 3). If it is hidden with Christ in God, let it not appear to the world, for Christ died to the world and lives to God.

See now how Christ loves to be desired, but does not love idle conversation. That virgin opened her doors to the Word of God; but, she says, “my soul went out when he spoke” (verse 6). She went out from the world, she went out from the age, and remained in Christ. “I sought him,” she says, “and I did not find him.” For Christ loves to be sought for a long time.

**47.** “The watchmen of the walls found her.” Perhaps there are other watchmen whom we ought to understand more fully. There is a city whose wall-gates are not closed, of which it is said: “Its gates will never be shut by day” (Revelation 21:25); for there will be no night there, and the nations will bring their glory and honor into it. That, then, is the city of Jerusalem which is in heaven, within which you are already preserved as though perfected and immaculate; for nothing common enters it. There is no common chastity, no common modesty, which is written in the book of life.

**48.** If, then, we have found the city, let us enter it; let us see its light, see its walls, see its mural foundations, and also see the watchmen of the walls. But how shall we enter it? In this city there is life, and there is one way that leads to life. The way, therefore, is Christ; so let us follow Christ. But the city itself is in heaven; how, then, shall we ascend to heaven? The Evangelist teaches us, saying: “And in the spirit he carried me away to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem descending out of heaven” (Revelation 21:10). Let us ascend in spirit, then, since flesh cannot ascend to it. For the present let us ascend into heaven, so that afterward it may descend from heaven to us. Its light is like a most precious stone, like jasper and crystal; it has a great and high wall.

**49.** You have learned about the light; you have learned about the wall. Learn the gates; learn the watchmen. “It has,” he says, “twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, on which are inscribed the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel” (ibid., 12). The names of the patriarchs are contained in the gates, and those of the apostles in the wall; for the apostles are the foundations of the city, and Christ is the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure rises. God is outside, God is within, God is everywhere: “The city,” he says, “has the glory of God” (ibid., 11). Therefore you also, holy virgins, and all who are righteous and bear the undefiled chastity of the soul, are citizens of the saints and members of God’s household. But you will possess this nobility of your homeland only if you seek Christ within the boundaries of this city, having entered through faith and precious deeds, made glorious by the light of the patriarchs, founded upon the apostles, and dwelling among the angels.

**50.** How, then, are these watchmen angels, who take away the cloak of the chaste soul? One cloak belongs to virgins, another to the young woman who goes about the marketplace. She who seeks Christ in the marketplace has lost even the cloak she possessed. For prudence is possessed not in the marketplace or in the streets, but in the Church.

And perhaps, so that we may also come into favor with them and teach that God is merciful to all—for they too sometimes find Christ, provided that they seek him continually—this cloak is the covering of the body. Therefore, one who sought Christ in the bedchamber, provided that she sought him as did the one who said, “Thus I remembered you upon my bed” (Psalm 62:7); if she sought him in the nights, according to what is written, “In the nights lift up your hands to the holy places” (Psalm 133:2); if she sought him in the city, in the marketplace and in the streets, in the city of our God; perhaps in the marketplace where that judge of divine law sits, in the streets from which those invited to the Lord’s supper were gathered—such a person may, while seeking for a long time, encounter the angels who guard the city of God. Indeed, from the heavenly nature of the watchmen we can understand a heavenly city, a heavenly marketplace of eternal justice—not cheap streets, but perhaps those in which that fountain is accustomed to overflow, of which it is written: “Let your waters overflow from your own fountain, and let your waters be poured out in your streets” (Proverbs 5:16). Whoever therefore seeks Christ in this way reaches the angels.

**51.** But if good merits bring one to the angels, why is the one who reaches them wounded? There is also a good sword, whose wound is good. The Word of God wounds, but does not ulcerate. There is the wound of good love; there are the wounds of charity. Therefore she said: “I am wounded by love” (Song of Songs 2:5). She who is perfect is wounded by love.

The wounds of the Word are therefore good; the wounds of the one who loves are good: “The wounds of a friend are more useful than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6). Rebecca is wounded by love: she left her parents and migrated to her bridegroom. Rachel is wounded by love: she was jealous of her sister and loved her husband. She envied her sister because the latter abounded in children while she herself was still barren, for she bore the figure of the Church, to whom it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail” (Isaiah 54:1).

**52.** The watchmen therefore found her and wounded her, and took away her cloak—that is, they removed the covering of bodily deeds, so that the naked simplicity of the mind might seek Christ; for no one can see Christ clothed in the cloak of philosophy, that is, in the garb of secular wisdom. Properly the cloak of philosophy is taken from her, lest someone plunder her through philosophy. Properly her cloak is taken from her as she draws near to Christ, so that, about to see God, she may walk with a pure heart: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Finally, when she had cleansed her heart, she found the Word and saw God.

Seek him, therefore, virgin—indeed, let us all seek him; for the soul has no sex. Perhaps it has received a feminine name because a more violent heat of the body drives it; yet it soothes the impulse of the flesh and of its own love with a certain gentle and persuasive reasoning. Therefore, by prayers and supplications we ought to invite God, so that, like a favorable south wind, he may deign to breathe upon us. May the breeze of the heavenly Word blow upon us—he who is accustomed to stir fruitful trees not with a heavy wind, but with a gentle breath and soft breeze.

[Col. 1932A] **53. [Note: [Col. 1931D] On Psalm 118, sermon 14.]** “They took my cloak from me.” The cloak of eternal life is a good covering. The watchmen of the walls wished to take away this cloak of the Bride, of which the first man had been stripped. But the soul devoted to God, holding fast for a long time to what she had sought and not letting go of her beloved, clothed herself in the precious covering of divine charity. Blessed, then, are those who are clothed in such a cloak and have merited such a covering by observing the law; for they have not forgotten the law, but have done the things that belonged to the law.

**54. (Verse 8.) [Note: [Col. 1932D] On Psalm 118, sermon 8, no. 17.]** “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love.” But what is this sickness of the soul? The moral meaning of the ancient history reminds us of holy Moses, who asked God to reveal himself to him, so that he might see him face to face. The holy prophet of the Lord certainly knew that he could not see the invisible God face to face. But holy devotion surpasses measure, and he thought that even this was possible for God: that what is incorporeal might be grasped by bodily eyes. This was not a blameworthy error, but a welcome and insatiable desire: he longed to hold his Lord, as it were, in his hand and to see him with the gaze of his eyes.

For he knew that man had been made in the image and likeness of God. When he had been chosen by the Lord God to deliver the people and had been filled with the spirit of wisdom, he had seen that angel and his face in glory. Finally, terrified by the brilliance of his light, he saw the bush burning without being consumed. He began with the sight of the radiance, and approached in wonder; urged on by desire and grace, he wished to examine that radiance in the bush more closely. If, then, he received so great a burning and was seized by so great a desire when he saw the angel in the flame of fire from the bush—so that, although overcome by fear, he did not dare to examine it, yet still wished to do so—how much more did he desire to see the Lord’s face bodily, saying within himself: “What shall I call that face full of light, full of grace, full of power, full of divinity?” I cannot say or think more about God; for when a human being has finished, then he begins, and when he has ended, then he will be perplexed, as it is written, because the eternal majesty of God is incomprehensible (Ecclesiasticus 18:6).

**55.** The result of his request was indeed fruitless, but the servant’s affection was commendable; for, advancing beyond his own nature through devotion, he estimated from the Lord’s angels how much more he desired the Lord’s face, in order to satisfy his longing [Col. 1932D]. He knew that another glory and another splendor awaited the human being after death: “As star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption, but it will rise in incorruption; it will rise in glory, it will rise in power, it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:41–44).

Since, then, he could know these things, he rightly presumed that he might desire to see the Lord’s face, since he would see it after the body had undergone death. Certainly he had already assumed such a form, and the Lord was already approving such a heavenly minister and executor of the oracle, as one who would not differ from the angels. And because he knew that “the angels of the little ones continually see the face of the Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10), he thought that he could and ought already to see it, as though he had forgotten the body and laid aside the flesh—like the one who, while still in the body, was caught up into paradise and said that he did not know whether he had been caught up to the third heaven in the body or outside the body (2 Corinthians 12:3).

For even when the saints bear a body, they are nevertheless not in the flesh but in the spirit, because those who live in carnal desire and conduct cannot please God. The saints, however, are not in the flesh in their conduct, but in heaven.

**56.** From these things, then, let us understand the feeling of the languishing Bride. Like an innocent person, she desired to see the face of God, as though with the face of her conscience; she longed to open to him the face of her inner mind and to be known more fully. Impatient love, knocking day and night at a prostitute’s doors, if the desire of possession is deferred too long, itself fails through waiting while it hopes; yet in this there is not an end of love, but an increase.

Whatever is desirable, if it does not come to the one who desires it, the desirer fails into it and, as it were, lays down his very soul—provided that a nearer hope does not arise. A hope that is close gives strength; but if the beloved is absent, by the very fact that she desires the absent one, the soul suffers the weakening of what it has longed for. Therefore, the farther away the desired object is, the more the one who desires grows weak.

This weakening, then, means that each person migrates with all his efforts into the one whom he loves: he thinks of him, clings to him, echoes him, and is poured into the one whom he has received as worthy of love, through a certain failing-away of the soul. Thus, if a mother were awaiting the presence of her son, as Tobias’s wife awaited her traveling son, she would appear weakened by desire, distressed, and as though dissolved (Tobit 10:3 ff.). For what else do her words signify but a certain weakening?

Yet the more the affection is wearied, the more love grows; and the longer the desired one is absent, the more powerfully the desires of the one waiting are kindled by love. The flesh grows weak, but desire is nourished and increased.

**57.** Thus the holy soul knows how to desire no one else but the Bridegroom, who is Christ Jesus. She longs for him, desires him, directs all her strength toward him, cherishes him in the embrace of her mind, opens and pours herself out to him, and fears only that she might lose him.

Therefore, the more intense the desire with which the soul is aroused, longing to cling to her saving God, the more she grows weak. This weakening consequently produces a diminution of weakness but an assumption of strength. She longed, she desired, she grew weak, she was wholly dissolved in affection, so that she might become wholly the possession of the one whom she desired, just as David himself says: “I pour out my prayer before him, and I declare my distress before him, when my spirit fails within me” (Psalm 142:3–4). His spirit failed—indeed, the spirit failed him who denies himself in order to cling to Christ.

**[Note: [Col. 1933D] *Apology for David II*, ch. 9, no. 47.]** Thus, as though impatient with love, she ran about and sought the Word of God everywhere, because she was wounded, because she was naked; and she sought the assistance of someone through whom Christ might be asked to come. See her burning, see her longing: “I adjure you,” she says, “daughters of Jerusalem,” and so forth. Then, joined to the daughters of that heavenly city, she seeks the Word; by seeking him and contemplating his appearance, she awakens his love within herself.

**1601 58. (Verse 10.) [Note: [Col. 1933D] Book I *On Virgins*, ch. 8, no. 47.]** “My brother,” she says, “is white and red, chosen from among thousands.” It is fitting, virgin, that you should fully know the one whom you love and recognize in him the whole mystery both of his innate divinity and of the incarnation he assumed [Col. 1934B]. He is rightly white because he is the Father’s splendor; red because he is the offspring of a virgin. In him the color and radiance of both natures shines and glows. Yet remember that the signs of his divinity are more ancient in him than the mysteries of his body, because he did not begin from the Virgin; rather, he who already existed came into the Virgin.

**59. [Note: [Col. 1934D] On Psalm 118, sermon 5, no. 8.]** “My brother is white and red.” White with eternal brightness, red in the appearance of human color, which he assumed in the mystery of the incarnation. And what is red in him also gives off a good fragrance, because Christ’s flesh is without sin. When the impious handled it, they defiled their hands; when the holy venerated it, they blazed with the fragrance of devotion.

**60. [Note: [Col. 1934D] *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, ch. 11, no. 56.]** “Chosen from among thousands.” “Ten thousands,” Jacob says, “of Ephraim, and thousands of Manasseh”; that is, let him rule over both Jews and Gentiles, and acquire for himself from both peoples the fullness of the Church. Therefore holy Jacob placed his right hand upon Ephraim, because of what the Church says in the Song of Songs: “My brother is white and red, chosen from among ten thousand.”

Finally, David also proclaimed in tens of thousands the author of the young woman Mary, from whose succession Christ was born through the Virgin’s childbirth; Saul, however, was proclaimed in thousands, although they ought rather to have shown greater reverence toward the king.

**61. (Verse 11.) [Note: [Col. 1934D] On Psalm 118, sermon 15, nos. 12–13.]** “His head is gold, Cephas.” This signifies steadfast and eminent wisdom. The body of Christ is the Church; its head is like gold, because the precious wisdom of the saints is found in it—that is, righteous and prudent men.

[Col. 1934D] **62.** “His locks are like fir trees, black as a raven.” Elsewhere he said of this: “Your hair is like a flock of shorn sheep.” It is called hair because the power of all the senses is in the head: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Ecclesiastes 2:14). The profound prudence of teachers, therefore, can reveal what is obscure and open the heights of understanding. Such interpreters are the hair of the Church, like the young of ravens to which the Lord gives food, as he gave it to holy Jacob and fed him from his youth. The Lord feeds these others, deep and rich in the abundance of their teaching, with heavenly mysteries.

**63. (Verse 12.)** “His eyes also are like doves.” The eyes are men adorned with spiritual senses, sharp for seeing the mysteries and ready to penetrate the divine secrets of Scripture, shining with rational milk. In them there is no defiled confusion of deceit, but the undefiled sincerity of a simple affection. Therefore he mentioned these doves, washed in the abundance of waters, in milk, saying:

**64. [Note: [Col. 1935D] On Psalm 118, sermon 16, no. 21.]** “His eyes are like doves beside an abundance of waters, washed in milk, sitting upon fullness.” The Lord baptizes in milk, that is, in sincerity. Those are truly baptized in milk who believe without deceit and bring pure faith, so that they may put on undefiled grace [Col. 1935B]. Therefore the white Bride ascends to Christ, because she has been baptized in milk. Therefore the powers marvel at her, saying: “Who is this who ascends, made white?” (Song of Songs 8:7). A little earlier she said, “I am black” (Song of Songs 1:5); now she is seen made white, and she ascends to heaven, and, leaning upon the Word of God, already penetrates the heights.

**65.** Nor is it without reason that there is an abundance of waters where Christ is, from whom the human mind desires to be filled. The stag thirsts for these waters, and after drinking them cannot cease to thirst. The Prophet thirsted for these waters when he said: “My soul thirsted for you” (Psalm 42:3). Christ therefore sits upon the abundance of waters and upon fullness; and for this reason the one who baptizes in water says: “We have all received from his fullness” (John 1:16).

Hence the “eye of punishments” (*oculus suppliciorum*; reading uncertain) is not foreign to the Church; for although John baptized at Aenon, he baptized near Salim, where there was an abundance of water, with twelve springs and seventy palm trees. The Church possesses these springs: in the Old Testament, the twelve patriarchs; in the New, the twelve apostles. Therefore it is said: “Bless the Lord God in the churches, from the springs of Israel” (Psalm 68:27).

Everyone who receives the holy mysteries is first drenched by these springs; for these springs, flowing from the eternal fountain, have spread throughout the whole world. Where these springs are, there is the ascent of souls. Finally, they interpreted Salim as “the one ascending”; for he truly ascends who lays aside his own sins. This expression, therefore, conveys the use of purifying sanctification.

**66. (Verse 13.) [Note: [Col. 1935D] On Psalm 118, sermon 15, no. 14.]** “His cheeks are like bowls of spices, producing perfumes.” We now understand the cheeks and the other features as the virtues of the soul and the various kinds of teachers: those who either supply spiritual nourishment to the mind through careful stewardship, or bind the hearer by their preaching of the Lord’s cross, as by a certain line of the Word, or are most pleasing through modesty, reverence, and the flower of youth. Although modesty keeps them from touch, the fragrance of Christ nevertheless rises from them. And just as ointment descends upon the cheeks from the priestly head, so in them also the beauty of teaching shines forth.

**67. [Note: [Col. 1936D] On Psalm 118, sermon 18, no. 22.]** “His lips drip with flowing myrrh.” By myrrh the ointment of the Passion and the grace of the resurrection are revealed; this pours the renewed fragrance of life into the limbs of the resurrected dead. Let the doors of your lips therefore be closed, and let the vestibule of your voice remain shut—perhaps to be opened when you hear the Word of God. Then myrrh will ooze for you; then the grace of baptism will breathe upon you, so that you may die with respect to the elements of the world and rise with Christ.

**68. [Note: [Col. 1936D] On Psalm 118, sermon 11, no. 11.]** “His lips drip with flowing myrrh.” We, however, think ourselves idle if we seem to devote ourselves only to the Word, and we value those who work more highly than those who exercise themselves in the pursuit of knowing the truth. Many say: “Behold the man and his works,” as though the one who studies the Word does not work, although this is a greater work than the others.

For if justice is a work, if temperance is a work, if courage is a work, then wisdom also is certainly a work; for these are considered the four principal virtues. If Christ works according to what he is as justice, then he certainly works according to what he is as the Word. He was working when he was in the beginning with the Father. Finally, all things were made through him, so that you may know that he is the worker of all things and that Christ Jesus is our work.

Indeed, insofar as he is the Word, the Word is a great work for those who seek the Word. Hence, when Martha was hurrying about her service while Mary was listening to the Lord’s Word, the one who was listening deserved to be preferred to the one who was serving. For when Martha said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me,” the Lord replied: “Martha, Martha, Mary has chosen the good portion, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:40–42). Thus, by the authority of the divine judgment, it is established that knowing the Word is a greater work than serving.

**69.** But perhaps someone might say that the Apostle declared: “The kingdom of God does not consist in speech but in power” (1 Corinthians 4:20). I do not deny that this is written, but I understand what kind of speech he means: the speech poured forth by one who is puffed up, a speech unable to benefit its hearers, lacking the manifestation of spirit and power. Paul does not wish to acknowledge this kind of speech; rather, he wishes the power of speech to be commended.

Finally, the Apostle wanted his own speech to be of such a kind that it came in weakness, in order to make others stronger; in fear and trembling, so that those who feared would fear nothing except the Lord Jesus, and those who trembled would preserve his peace and tranquility. Hear, then, what kind of speech the Apostle had: “My speech and my proclamation were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Corinthians 2:4); for faith is established not in the forensic speech of wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and in the power of God.

**70.** Therefore, in the speech of the saints there is power; but in this forensic and philosophical speech there is the vanity of the world. That there is power in the speech of the saints, this prophet also teaches you when he says: “The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the gospel with great power” (Psalm 68:12)—that is, so that they may preach the Gospel with great power.

It has therefore been proved that there is power in the preaching of the Gospel; and the preaching of the Gospel is the speech of the saints. Thus no doubt remains that there is power in holy speech. This is the myrrh dripping from the lips of the Bridegroom, through which vices are put to death.

**71. (Verse 14.) [Note: [Col. 1937D] On Psalm 118, sermon 10, no. 17.]** “His hands are wrought, golden, full of hyacinths.” Consider what hands made the human being, and what human being they made: the one whom “we have put on according to Christ,” stripping off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him, “where there is neither slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all” (Colossians 3:9–11).

We have therefore put on Christ, as it is also said elsewhere: “You have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). We have received the Holy Spirit, who not only forgives our sins, but also makes us his priests, so that we may forgive the sins of others. Therefore the Prophet says: “You fashioned me and placed your hand upon me” (Psalm 139:5): he fashioned through clay; he placed his hand through spiritual grace. Although many understand this psalm to have been spoken in the person of the Savior, hear that the hand of the Lord is also called the Spirit. Job cries out: “The divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33:4). These, then, are the hands that prepared humanity: Christ and the Spirit.

**72.** The Lord Jesus is therefore also the author of our body. First he made the human being in his image; afterward he fashioned him from clay and wished to save what he had made, to save what he had formed, so that he might save the whole human being. These are the turned-work hands of God—that is, perfect hands—golden because of the wisdom that is Christ, full of hyacinths because of the Holy Spirit and the fullness of his gifts of grace.

**73. (Verse 14.) [Note: [Col. 1937D] *On the Incarnation of the Lord*.]** “His belly is ivory, variegated with sapphires.” The Apostle says: “And although he was crucified from weakness”—behold the belly, that is, the weakness of the flesh—“yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4)—behold the sapphire ornamentation. For sapphire, because it bears the appearance of a clear sky, signifies the works of divinity.

Ivory, because of its purity, brightness, and permanence, signifies the Savior’s flesh, of which the same Apostle says: “Although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Corinthians 5:16).

**74. (Verse 15.) [Note: [Col. 1937D] On Psalm 118, sermon 5, no. 38.]** “His legs are marble columns, founded upon golden bases.” The columns of the Church signify the apostles, who are founded in holy fear. For just as Peter, James, John, and Barnabas seemed to be columns of the Church, so also whoever conquers this world becomes a column of God, whom the one who says, “I strengthened its columns” (Psalm 75:4), confirms.

Thus the golden base is fear filled with discipline, because “the beginning of wisdom is fear.” Therefore apostolic preaching, like a column, is firmly established in the fear that is the beginning of wisdom, upon a golden base in Christ. Accordingly, for eloquence and apostolic speech the tribunal is the fear of the righteous, and the golden base is full of prudence; while the good likeness, as an image of truth, is the speech of the saints.

**75.** And observe that the fear of the saints is like a golden base. Read Isaiah; see how many things he subordinated to fear in order to make fear irreproachable and good: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and power, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isaiah 11:2). He placed fear beneath so many things, so that it might have something to follow. It is shaped by wisdom, instructed by understanding, directed by counsel, strengthened by power, governed by knowledge, and adorned by piety.

Take these things away from the fear of the Lord, and it is irrational and foolish fear, one of those of which it is said: “Outside are battles, within are fears” (2 Corinthians 7:5)—fears by which Paul too would have been afflicted, had he not had the Lord comforting him.

**76. (Verse 15.)** “His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen like the cedars.” He dwells in high places and looks upon the lowly, because his appearance is like the cedar of Lebanon, which spreads its crown among the clouds and fixes its root in the earth. Its beginning is from heaven, while its later branches on earth produce fruits close to heaven.

**[Note: [Col. 1938D] On Psalm 118, sermon 4, no. 21.]** This kind of tree never loses its greenness; in winter as in summer it nourishes its foliage and does not change into another color. The wind alone never strips this tree of its honor; alone it is never divested of its old covering or clothed in a new blossom. So apostolic grace knows no decline and flourishes in perpetual beauty.

The soul, therefore, does not know corruption when it flourishes in its living members and with patient greatness continually sustains the heights of justice and the other virtues. For this reason it neither flows away nor grows weak, because there is nothing ruinous or slack in it, nothing unstable, nothing slippery, nothing that could be poured out from it through a fault of speech.

77. (Verse 16.) “His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable.” “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone” (Psalm 18:10–11). [Note: [Col. 1938D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 5, no. 43.] What is severe in others is sweet in Christ, pleasant in Christ, because he himself is sweet: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9). His judgments are sweet to the one who confesses, because he himself says: “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will remember them no more; but you remember, and let us be judged. Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:25–26). His judgments are sweet to the one who does penance, because he said: “There will be joy over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance” (Luke 15:7).

If, then, the judgments of the Lord are sweet, let us labor to receive the fruits of his sweetness. Do you wish to know how sweet the judgments of the Lord are? “Whoever believes in him is not judged” (John 3:18). His judgments, therefore, are sweet to believers. Those who do not believe, however, are not condemned by Christ’s judgment—he came not to judge the world but to save and redeem it—but they have undergone the judgment of their own ungodliness, because they were unwilling to believe in the remission of sins. For they cannot share in the benefit of one whom they refused to acknowledge. Therefore those who did not believe in him appear unworthy of his judgment. Learn what his judgment is from his own words: “This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world” (ibid., 19). Sweet, therefore, is that which is light; sweet is the judgment that is preceded by mercy. Thus it is written: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm 100:1). His throat, too, is sweet and most pleasant, from which this mercy proceeds before the judgment.

78. (Verse 16.) “And altogether desirable.” [Note: [Col. 1939D] Letter 46, to Sabinus, no. 7.] “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3). He was indeed human according to the flesh, but beyond a human being according to divine action. Thus, when he touched the leper, he appeared to be human; but he was beyond a human being when he cleansed him. And when he wept over Lazarus who had died, he wept as a human being; but he was above a human being when he commanded the dead man to come out with his feet bound. He appeared to be human when he hung upon the cross; but he was above a human being when, after the tombs had been opened, he raised the dead.

Let not the venom of Apollinaris flatter itself with the passage that reads, “And being found in appearance as a man” (Philippians 2:7). Jesus was not denied to be human, since Paul himself elsewhere says of him: “The mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5); rather, this was confirmed. For it is the usage and custom of Scripture to express itself in this way, as we also read in the Gospel: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1). Just as he is called “as the only-begotten” without denying that he is the only-begotten Son of God, so he is also called a human being, without denying that the perfection of humanity existed in him.

79. Although, therefore, he was in the form of a servant, humbled even to death, he was nevertheless in the glory of God. What harm, then, did servitude do to him? He is read to have been made a servant because he is read to have been made from a Virgin and created in the flesh; for every creature serves, as the prophet says: “Because all things serve you.” This is Christ’s glory: that he accepted servitude in his body in order to restore freedom to all. He bore our sins in order to take away the sin of the world. He became a servant, sin, and a curse so that you might cease to be a servant of sin and so that he might release you from the curse of the divine sentence.

He therefore accepted your curse: “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree.” He became a curse upon the cross so that you might be blessed in the kingdom of God. He was dishonored, devalued, and counted as nothing. He said, “I have labored in vain”; through him Paul deserved to say, “I have not labored in vain” (Philippians 2:16). Thus he bestowed upon his little servants the fruit of good works and the glory of evangelical preaching, through which the burden of labor was removed from all.

80. (Verse 17.) [Note: [Col. 1939D] The Book on Isaac, chapter 6, no. 56.] “Such is my beloved, and such is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.” Thus the Church, or the holy soul, joined to the daughters of that heavenly city, seeks the Word and, by seeking him, arouses his love within herself. Those daughters, meanwhile, seek him and say: “Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned, so that we may seek him with you?”

## CHAPTER SIX

1. (Verse 1.) [Note: [Col. 1940D] The same work, in the place cited above.] “My beloved,” she says, “has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.” She recognizes where the Word seeks to be: she knows that he dwells among the prayers of the saints and clings to them; she understands that he pastures his Church, or the souls of his righteous, among lilies.

He demonstrated this mystery to you in the Gospel when, on the Sabbath, he led his disciples through the sown fields. Moses led the Jewish people through the desert; Christ leads through sown fields, Christ leads through lilies, because through his passion the desert blooms like a lily. Let us therefore follow him, so that on that great Sabbath, in which there is great rest, we may gather fruits.

Do not fear that the Pharisees will accuse those who gather from the sown fields. Even if they accuse, Christ excuses, and makes those souls who follow him like that David who, above the Law, ate the bread of the Presence, already conceiving in his mind the sacraments of the new grace.

2. (Verse 2.) “I belong to my beloved, and my beloved belongs to me, who pastures among the lilies.” [Note: [Col. 1940D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 12, no. 37.] The expression seems easy and common, but it belongs to few. For it is quite rare for someone to be able to say: “I belong to my beloved, and my beloved belongs to me.”

What does it mean to say, “I am yours”? The one who clings to God with all his faculties says this; the one who knows how to think of nothing else uses this expression; the one who can say to the Lord, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8). Does the lover of money, honor, or power use this expression? For many—and indeed for very many—it is not enough to know God. So many peoples, so many nations, so many rich men consider serving the Lord to be poverty; and he who is above all things is, in their eyes, small and confined. For them the Son of God, in whom all things exist, is not enough.

Thus the rich man in the Gospel, to whom it was said, “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you possess and give to the poor” (Matthew 19:21), judged that God was not sufficient for him. He was also saddened, as though he were being ordered to abandon what was more valuable and choose what was less valuable. Therefore the one who can say, “I am yours,” is the one who can say: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (ibid., 27).

3. This is the voice of the apostles, though not of all the apostles. Judas too was an apostle, and he reclined among the apostles at Christ’s banquet. He also said, “I am yours,” but with his voice, not with his heart. Satan came and entered into him, and began to say: “He is not yours, Jesus; he is mine.” Indeed, he thinks about what is mine; he turns over in his heart what is mine. He feasts with you, but feeds with me. From you he received bread; from me, money. He drinks with you, and sells your blood to me. He is your apostle, but my hireling.

The worldly person cannot say, “I am yours,” for he has many masters. Lust comes and says, “You are mine,” because you desire the things that belong to the body. You sold yourself to me in love for that young woman; in intercourse with that prostitute I counted out the price for you. Avarice comes and says: “The silver and gold that you possess are the price of your servitude. The property you hold is the purchase of your rights and the sale of your freedom.”

Luxury comes and says: “You are mine. A banquet lasting one day is the price of your life. That expense on food is the auction of your head, the total amount of your contract. And what is worse, you were bought at a dear price: you are worth less than your food. The table of one day is more precious than the life of all your time. Among cups I redeemed you; among banquets I acquired you.”

Ambition comes and says to you: “You are plainly mine. Do you not know that I made you rule over others so that you yourself might serve me? Do you not know that I bestowed power upon you so that I might subject you to my power? Or do you not know that the ruler of this world said to the Lord and Savior, when he had shown him all the kingdoms of the world: ‘I will give all these things to you, if you fall down and worship me’ (Matthew 4:9)?”

Before anyone else, therefore, the one who wishes to have others subject to him is himself subjected. All vices come and each says: “You are mine.” How vile a slave is the one claimed by so many! How, then, can you, being such a person, say to Christ, “I am yours”? He will answer you: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21); not everyone who says to me, “I am yours,” belongs to me.

4. You are truly mine if conscience does not contradict your voice, if your mind or your works do not reject your words. I do not deny that person to be mine who does not deny himself to be mine—or, at least, if for my sake he denies himself to himself. I do not want to possess a little servant who serves many masters.

For how is he mine if he says to me in words, “I am yours,” but denies it in his works, and by his deeds assigns and binds himself to the devil? He is not mine whom lust inflames, because chastity is mine. He is not mine whom anxiety to strip the weak torments, because generosity is mine. He is not mine whom the breath of fickleness disturbs, because tranquility is mine.

He is not mine who is drunken with wine, impure through the filth of ambition, desirous of worldly glory, drunk unto danger, and unable to preserve the mark of sober moderation. I am peace; I do not know how to quarrel. Why should I possess someone from whom the devil may come and say, “He is mine”? For he has bent his neck to me; I find more of mine in him. He claims your name for himself, but my gift.

He therefore does not belong to Christ unless he is a stranger to sin. He does not belong to Christ unless he can always show himself to be Christ’s little servant.

5. [Note: [Col. 1941D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 2.] “I belong to my beloved, and my beloved belongs to me, who pastures among the lilies.” She seems, among the beloved things of her beloved, to say: “My secret is mine, my secret is mine.” For in the ecstasy of her love she had understood certain hidden mysteries of faith, which she judged ought not to be disclosed even to the daughters of Jerusalem.

“It is good to conceal the mystery of a king”; for he sins against God who thinks that the mysteries entrusted to him should be made public to the unworthy. It is therefore dangerous not only to say what is false, but also to say what is true, if someone reveals it to those to whom it ought not be revealed.

This fault has four forms: flattery, greed, boasting, and careless loquacity. When someone wishes to flatter, he pours out the mystery to the person with whom he is speaking. Some, also, out of a desire for profit, pursue the reward of betrayal, selling by speech what ought to be guarded in silence. Others reveal what they ought to conceal so that they may appear to know more and boast of their knowledge. Many, while speaking without judgment, utter a word that they cannot recall.

For this reason a man is praised when he is deliberate and not idle. He was a man who concealed his words, like the apostle Paul, who knew what to say to each person and when he ought to say it.

6. (Verse 3.) [Col. 1942B] “You are beautiful, my sister, pleasing as Jerusalem, awe-inspiring as one arranged in order.” The truth of love is proved by its permanence. [Note: [Col. 1941D] The Book on Isaac, chapter 7, no. 57.] The Bride is therefore praised by the Bridegroom because she has sought him so well and so steadfastly. For this reason she is now called not only “sister” but also “pleasing,” as one who has pleased him, because she pleased the Father; and “beautiful as Jerusalem, awe-inspiring as one arranged in order,” because she possesses all the mysteries of the eternal city. She is an object of wonder to all who see her, because she is full and perfect like righteousness. Having borrowed brilliance from the light of the Word, and always directing her attention toward it, she is also made terrible by a certain order, advanced to the summit of the virtues.

7. [Note: [Col. 1941D] Letter to Irenaeus.] “You are beautiful,” he says, “my friend, sweet and lovely,” and so forth. She is truly beautiful who directs her attention toward him of whom it is said: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3). Let us therefore direct our minds toward him as far as we can, and let us be in him. Let us hold in our minds what is beautiful, lovely, and good, so that through his illumination and brilliance our soul may become beautiful and our mind radiant.

For if our eyes, when some mist is drawn over them, are refreshed by the greenness of the fields, and the beauty of a grove or shady hill drives away every irregularity from a sickly gaze, so that the pupils and orbs themselves seem to be colored by a certain healthful beauty, how much more does this eye of the mind shine and gleam when it gazes upon the highest good, dwells in it, and is nourished by it?

[Note: [Col. 1942D] Book 1 on Virgins, chapter 8, no. 47.] “Beautiful as Jerusalem.” This, then, is not the fleeting beauty of the body, destined to perish through sickness or old age, but beauty subject to no misfortune and never to perish in the esteem of good people on account of its merits, since it is worthy to be compared not with human things but with heavenly things, whose life it lives on earth. Therefore the Bridegroom says to the Bride, now as though she were perfect:

8. (Verse 4.) [Note: [Col. 1942D] The Book on Isaac, chapter 7, no. 57.] “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me flee.” Do not direct yourself toward me with excessive devotion and faith. You have surpassed the capacity of your nature and condition, because it is difficult to gaze directly upon inaccessible light. “Turn your eyes away from me,” he says, because she cannot bear the fullness of his divinity and the splendor of the true light.

9. [Col. 1943A] We can nevertheless understand it in this way as well: “Turn your eyes away from me.” Even if you are perfect, other souls still need to be redeemed, and others still need to be strengthened. You raise me up by seeing me, but I descended for this reason: to raise everyone up. Even if I have risen and possess the Father’s throne, I will not leave you orphans, deprived, as it were, of your father’s protection; rather, I will strengthen you by my presence.

You have this written in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the world” (Matthew 28:20). Turn your eyes away from me, then, because you raise me up. For the more someone directs his attention toward the Lord, the more he raises up the Lord, and he himself is raised up. Hence he also says: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me” (Psalm 29:1). The holy person exalts the Lord; the sinner humbles him.

He therefore wishes her to turn her eyes away, lest, considering her, he himself be raised up because she can now follow what is above and leave the other souls behind. For this reason, in the Gospel, he demonstrated his glory not to all the disciples but to the more perfect ones (Matthew 17:1).

Imagine, then, a teacher who wishes to explain an obscure matter to his hearers. Although he himself may be powerful in speech and knowledge, he nevertheless accommodates himself to the ignorance of those who do not understand, and uses simple, plainer, and familiar speech so that he may be understood. If, then, someone among the hearers is more lively in understanding and can easily follow, he raises him up and stirs him onward. Seeing this, the teacher calls him back, so that he may allow the teacher to dwell upon matters lower and plainer, by which the others too may be able to follow.

10. (Verses 5–7.) [Note: [Col. 1943D] The Book on Isaac, chapter 7, nos. 59–61.] The Bride is also praised as faithful, powerful in speech, fruitful in various fruits, and as one dove possessing unity of spirit, in which there is peace that makes both into one. She is not composed of diverse elements of a separated and mutually hostile nature.

For what is as different as fire and water, air and earth, from which the constitution of our body is formed? But the blessed soul is entirely simple, imitating the one who says: “That they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be one in us” (John 17:21). This is the consummation and perfection. Hence he added: “That they may be one, just as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected in one” (ibid., 23).

This, then, is the one and perfect dove, simple and spiritual, which is not disturbed by the passions of this body, in which there are “battles outside, fears within.” Finally, Scripture teaches us that harmony and peace are signified by this word “unity,” saying: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and there was no division among them” (Acts 4:32).

11. The soul is not praised for its fruitfulness without reason—not only because it is fruitful in virtues, but also because it contains no evil within itself. For that is beautiful and lovely in which there is no evil. What is beautiful is good; what is unbeautiful is evil. Fruitfulness in good works is beautiful; sterility is therefore contrary to beauty. For whoever is deprived of beauty or loveliness possesses every evil; and whatever is evil is sterile and fruitless.

What gives clearer evidence of this than the earth? The earth that is good is fertile and fruitful; the earth that is bad is barren and sterile. Whatever is fertile is also beautiful. For what is more beautiful than a full field when the grain billows, when the apples glow red, when garlands of grapes hang down, when the olive tree, loaded with berries, bends beneath its burden, or when the mountain peaks are clothed in green grass and the low valleys are covered?

12. God is the author of all good things. Whatever belongs to him is entirely good, and there is no evil anywhere in it. If our mind remains in him, it knows no evil. The soul, therefore, that does not remain in God is itself the author of evils, and so it sins. But the soul that sins will die. Released from the golden bonds of the virtues, it is carried headlong down the precipice and slips toward lower things.

The soul is blessed, however, which no hostile battles of the body overcome. This soul flies away like a sparrow when the snare has been broken. Bodily pleasures are the food of evils; whoever directs his attention toward them ensnares his soul in the trap. But whoever abstains from its food and comes out of its darkness has a soul that shines like the dawn. Of this soul it is said:

13. (Verse 9.) “Who is this that looks forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon?” She looks forth as if from a free house. She does not say: “Darknesses cover me, and walls surround me; who knows whether the Most High sees?” (Sirach 23:26). Rather, she herself seeks the light as though she were in the upper rooms of her house—that is, of her body. Set above the world, she gazes upon divine things and raises herself toward the eternal, so that she may be present with God, already carrying the light of her works throughout her whole sphere like the moon.

14. (Verse 10.) “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the growth beside the torrent, to look upon whether the vine had blossomed and the pomegranates had budded.” [Note: [Col. 1943D] The Book on Virginity, chapter 16, no. 98.] The Word of God is finally invited into the garden of nuts, in which there is the fruit of prophetic reading and priestly grace—bitter in temptations, hard in labors, but fruitful in inner virtues. Thus Aaron’s rod also blossomed as a nut tree, no longer by its own nature but by a hidden power.

Let him therefore descend into the garden, so that he may harvest faith, receive fragrances, find heavenly food, and feast upon the sweetness of our honey.

15. [Note: [Col. 1944D] The Book on Isaac, chapter 8, no. 64.] For while she is praised by the Bridegroom, she modestly withdraws from being praised before him; then, recalled by love for the Bridegroom, she says: “I went down into the garden of nuts to see the growth beside the torrent.”

For where is the Church, if not where the rod and grace of the priesthood bloom? She is frequently there, so that she may be tested amid bitterness and temptations. By the nut we understand bitterness; by the torrent, temptations—but temptations that can nevertheless be endured, because it is written: “Our soul has crossed the torrent” (Psalm 123:5).

She therefore descends into a place of bitterness, where the vine blossoms and there is a varied and manifold fruit in the likeness of pomegranates, protected, as though by a single covering, by the faith and love of the whole body.

1608 16. In that bitterness, therefore, the soul did not know itself. “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling is quickly bent down” (Wisdom 9; reading uncertain). Yet it ought always to know itself.

Peter was tempted, but Peter did not know himself. For if he had known himself, he would not have denied his Master. But Christ knew him. Indeed, he knew him because he also looked upon him; “the Lord knows those who are his.” And, like a good charioteer, with the reins of his mercy, he recalled him from his fall. Christ, therefore, is our charioteer. Hence it follows:

17. (Verse 11.) [Note: [Col. 1945D] The Book on Virginity, chapter 15, no. 94.] “The chariot of Aminadab placed me,” because the soul is joined to the body and, like a chariot of neighing horses, seeks a charioteer to guide it.

Aminadab was the father of Naasson, as we read in Numbers (Numbers 1:7). He was prince of the people of Judah, whose figure refers to Christ. Christ, the true prince of the people, mounts the soul of the righteous like a charioteer mounts a chariot and governs it with the reins of the Word, lest it be carried headlong into precipices and abysses by the fury of violent horses.

His four horses are, as it were, the four affections: anger, desire, pleasure, and fear. When the soul begins to be driven by these in their fury, it no longer knows itself. “The corruptible body weighs down the soul,” and, like a chariot drawn by irrational animals, it drags the unwilling soul along, as though rushing forward by some impulse amid swirling cares, until the aforesaid passions of the body are calmed by the power of the Word.

18. [Col. 1945C] This is the providence of the Word, like that of a good charioteer: lest the mortal body joined to the soul, which is not subject to death in itself, make its movement difficult. First, therefore, let him master these swift movements of the body and bridle them with the bond of reason. Then let him take care that they do not become entangled with one another through unequal movement, so that the good horse is not disfigured by the wicked, the slow horse does not hinder, or the turbulent horse does not unsettle.

The horse of wickedness neighs and, by throwing itself about, damages the chariot and weighs down its yokemate. The good charioteer soothes it and sends it out into the field of truth; he avoids the winding paths of deceit. The course toward higher things is safe; the descent toward lower things is dangerous.

From there, like horses that have performed their service well and have borne the yoke of the Word, they are led even to the Lord’s manger, in which the food is not hay but the bread that came down from heaven. The wheels of this chariot are those of which the Prophet said: “And the spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezekiel 1:20), because the chariot of the soul rolls smoothly and roundly without any obstacle.

19. [Note: [Col. 1945D] The Book on Isaac, chapter 8, no. 65.] “The chariot of Aminadab placed me.” The soul, therefore, is a chariot that supports a good charioteer. If the soul is a chariot, it has either good or bad horses. The good horses are the virtues of the soul; the bad horses are the passions of the body.

The good charioteer restrains and recalls the bad horses, and urges on the good ones. The good horses are four: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The bad horses are anger, desire, fear, and iniquity.

Sometimes the horses themselves disagree with one another, and either anger or fear stretches itself forward. They hinder one another and delay their course. But the good horses fly and rise from earth toward higher things, lifting up the soul—especially if they have the gentle yoke and light burden of the one who says: “Take my yoke upon you; for my yoke is sweet and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29).

20. He himself is the charioteer who knows how to govern his own horses, so that the course of all may be equal. He restrains the swifter by prudence; he admonishes the slower with the proper whip of justice. He makes the gentler through temperance and the harder through fortitude. He knows how to join together those who disagree, lest they perhaps destroy his chariot.

Thus it is a beautiful spectacle for the understanding to see each soul carried up to heaven amid the greatest struggle, with horses hastening to reach first the prize of Christ, whose necks will first bear the palm. These are the horses subjected to the yoke of faith, bound by the bond of love, and controlled by the reins of justice and the restraints of sobriety.

21. He therefore says beautifully: “The chariot of Aminadab placed me,” that is, of the father of the people. He who is the father of the people is also the father of Naasson, that is, of serpents. Now recall who, like a serpent, hung upon the cross for the salvation of all, and understand that soul to be peaceful over which God the Father presides and Christ is the charioteer. For this name too is written among our Scriptures: “Father, father, charioteer of Israel” (4 Kings 11:12).

This charioteer therefore says:

22. (Verse 12.) “Turn back, O Shulamite, turn back.” He speaks fittingly both as a charioteer and as one speaking to a chariot: “Turn back, O Shulamite,” that is, “peaceful one.” For the peaceful soul quickly turns back and corrects itself, even if it previously sinned.

Christ also mounts her, and deigns to govern her, to whom it is said: “Mount your horses, and your riding is salvation.” And elsewhere: “You sent forth your horses into Tharsis” (Habakkuk 3:8). These are Christ’s horses.

Christ therefore mounts his horses; the Word of God mounts pious souls. When our soul is peaceful, so that it may be told, “Turn back, turn back, O Shulamite,” which signifies “peaceful,” then it will receive Christ within itself as a seal—that is, the image of God—so that it may exist according to the image. For “as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones,” and “we ought to bear the image of the heavenly one” (1 Corinthians 15:48), that is, peace.

And so that we may know this to be true, in the same Song of Songs we find it said at the end to the perfected soul—and may the Lord Jesus say it also to me: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song of Songs 8:6), so that Christ may shine in the peace of my heart and in my works, and wisdom, justice, and redemption may be formed in me.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

1. (Verse 1.) [Note: [Col. 1946D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 17, nos. 14 and following.] “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of Aminadab! The contours of your thighs are like necklaces, the work of an artisan.”

There is no doubt that here too the progress of the Church or of the soul is signified. “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things” (Isaiah 52:7)! He plainly calls beautiful the progress of evangelical preaching and discussion, as it is said elsewhere: “Cross over the rivers” (Isaiah 47:2), that is, pass through the streams and slippery places of this world with a steady tread of mind.

David clearly shows that this is said of the soul’s progress when he relates that his soul crossed a torrent of iniquities (Psalm 123:5).

2. But what does it mean that he says the steps of the Church are beautiful in sandals? We read that Moses was told: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exodus 3:5), by which he seems to have been warned not to remain bound by bodily ties.

Therefore, in the Song of Songs he signifies the beauty of the soul that uses the flesh as a sandal and, in that sandal, suffers no impediment but surpasses others in the beauty of its gait. Let the soul therefore put on ecclesiastical grace as its sandal, so that it may pass through the course and passage of this life with beauty.

This happens if it does not soil its sandal with bodily mud, nor plunge it into the abyss of vices; if it chastises its flesh, so that it does not delay its course or become weighed down by the heavy burden of fat. The soul’s good sandal is modesty; a good step is one that proceeds in the path of chastity.

Wisdom, however, is the soul’s garment, as it is written: “Honor her, and she will embrace you” (Proverbs 4:8). Let us therefore use the body as a sandal for the lower works of virtue: for service, not command; for obedience, not pleasure; for compliance, not dissent. Let us place our footprint on the way of wisdom, lest some force of the torrent block our steps.

3. For this reason Moses was told: “Remove the sandal” (Exodus 3:5). Jesus son of Nave was told the same (Joshua 5:16). But this was not said of Christ. Rather, the Baptist says of him: “After me comes a man whose sandals I am not worthy to carry” (Matthew 3:11).

For those who could not be without sin are rightly admonished to remove their sandal. But he not only did not remove his sandal; he also removed the sandals of others, because he not only kept his own body free from sins but also granted forgiveness of sins to everyone.

4. The Church, therefore, is beautiful in imitation of Christ and washed clean of every offense in her sandals. Perhaps, when she speaks wisdom among the perfect, she is beautiful in her higher members. But when people of a lower rank or less advanced teaching also follow the Word, do not forget the order of faith, and keep the commands of the priest, she is beautiful in her sandals.

Often the clergy have gone astray, the priest has changed his judgment, the rich have sided with the earthly ruler of this world, and the people have preserved their own faith.

5. Therefore we can also rightly say of the Lord Jesus that the Word has beautiful steps even in those matters that are bodily, when moral questions are being discussed. Perhaps for this reason the apostles are sent barefoot, so that their discussion may not be overshadowed but may shine forth.

Thus the Church is the daughter of Aminadab, that is, of the willing one or of the well-pleased one, because the willing or well-pleased one gathered her; and she is beautiful in her sandals. And fittingly it is added:

[Col. 1948A] 1610 6. “The contours of your thighs are like necklaces, the work of an artisan’s hands,” so that the adornments of the Church’s posterity might be sung.

By the thigh we recognize the emblem of generation, according to the passage: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Psalm 44:4). This signifies that, when the Son of God had emptied himself, girded with the divinity of the Word and shod with human generation, he came forth from the Virgin to give salvation to all.

The contours are called precious ornaments of the sort customarily hung around the necks of matrons. The progress of the Church is therefore signified as compared with the most precious ornaments and with the necklaces of triumphant warriors, for these are the ornaments of soldiers. Hence Symmachus used the Greek term Epitrachelia, that is, things worn around the neck.

Whether, therefore, we understand the generation of Christ from the Virgin or the propagation of the Church, in appearance—like necklaces adorned by the hand of an artisan—he has adorned the necks of the faithful with spiritual ornaments distinguished by true virtue. Indeed, the whole description of the members of the Church is full of beauty and praise. For it is also said:

7. (Verse 2.) “Her navel is proclaimed as a turned bowl, never lacking mixed wine,” because in every teaching she is fashioned and perfected, full of knowledge, and does not lack spiritual drink.

Her belly is not only fattened with a heap of wheat—that is, with the stronger foods of the heavenly mystery—but also filled, as with lilies, by the sweetness of moral virtues. Therefore, as a queen who has served well, she is crowned with the blood of Christ, as it is written: “And the adornment of her head was like purple.” The blood of Christ is purple. It stains the souls of the saints, shining not only in color but also in power, because it makes them kings, and better kings, to whom it gives an eternal kingdom.

8. [Note: [Col. 1947D] Letter to Irenaeus.] “Your navel is like a turned bowl, never lacking cups.” The navel of the soul and its belly are subtle in the soul that ascends to Christ. Therefore the Bridegroom praises it, saying: “Your navel is like a turned bowl, never lacking mixed wine; your belly is a heap of wheat protected among lilies.”

For in every teaching it is fashioned and perfected, and spiritual drink does not fail it, because of the fullness of its knowledge and its understanding of heavenly secrets. The belly of the soul is also mystical, like the navel. Through this belly the soul not only takes strong food by which hearts are strengthened but also food that is sweet and flowering, by which they are delighted.

9. (Verse 4.) [Note: [Col. 1947D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 16.] “Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, at the gates of the daughter of many peoples; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.”

What are the pools in Heshbon except abundance in rational thoughts, which is found at the gates of the Church, to which a multitude of teaching is rightly attributed? For the daughter of many peoples is the posterity and effect of many teachings, whose nose is the fragrance of sacrifices, surpassing all flowers.

10. [Note: [Col. 1948D] On Psalm 118, Sermon 5, no. 34.] “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon”: exceedingly lofty, and therefore it looks toward the face of Damascus, that is, smelling the gentile people and the faith by whose grace it would wipe away the stench of its sins.

The face of Damascus, therefore, is the faith of the nations, shaded by no covering, concealed by no garment, naked and free, directed more toward heaven than toward earth. The nose of the Church observes and beholds this face, gathering from it what is sweet, both the breath of fragrance and of grace.

11. And rightly it says, “Her nose is like the tower of Lebanon,” because in sacrifices the Church possesses a sweet fragrance, in which the offering of good odor is the remission of sins.

Take these noses, therefore, O human being, so that you may distinguish what is flower-filled from what is foul-smelling; then the Lord will bring you to life. For when he perceives what you ask of him, so that he may turn the eyes of your mind away from vanity, he cooperates with your soul.
