If it is captivated by some outward appearance, or is not bent by hardness or weakness, he bends it beneath the yoke of the Word and guides it with his reins, so that by God’s will it may be led away from vices and receive the fragrance of eternal life.

12. (Verse 8.) [Note: [Col. 1949D] *On Isaac*, chapter 8, no. 67 and following.] “I will ascend the palm tree and grasp its height.” Hence understand that she too ascended and brought her to the place of the palm when he also says to her: “How beautiful and sweet you have become, love, in your delights! Your stature has become like a palm tree” (*Song* VII, 6). And she herself says: “I said, ‘I will ascend the palm tree.’” But love itself is also a palm tree, for it is the fullness of victory; indeed, love is the fullness of the Law. Let us run, then, so that we may seize it; let us run so that we may conquer. Whoever has conquered ascends the palm tree and eats its fruit; whoever has conquered no longer runs but sits, as it is written: “To the one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne” (*Rev.* III, 21). From this the philosophers expressed in their books those contests of the soul’s races, yet they could not reach the palm, because their souls did not know the sweetness and loftiness of the Word. “I will ascend,” she says, “by conquering the world, so that I may grasp the height of the Word,” which this soul knew, in which there was the Word’s conversion; for thus she says:

13. (Verse 10.) “I belong to my brother, and his turning is toward me.” This meaning he repeated a third time, in different words, in the *Song of Songs*. At the beginning he says: “My brother is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows bend” (*Song* II, 16). Then he says: “I belong to my brother, and my brother belongs to me, who feeds among the lilies” (*Song* VI, 2). At the end he says: “I belong to my brother, and his turning is toward me.” The first refers to the soul’s instruction; therefore he prefaced it with: “My brother is mine,” since, by his revealing himself, she acquired the desire to cling to God. What follows refers to progress; the third, to perfection. In the first, as though still at the stage of instruction, the soul sees shadows, not yet stirred by the revelation of the approaching Word; and therefore the day of the Gospel did not yet shine upon her. In the second, without the confusion of shadows, she gathers pious fragrances. In the third, now perfected, she provides within herself a resting-place for the Word, so that he may turn toward her, recline his head, and rest; and she invites him into her field, saying:

[Col. 1950A] 14. (Verse 11.) “Come, my brother; let us go out into the field, let us rest in the villages.” Above she invited him into a garden; here, into a field possessing not only the grace of flowers but also wheat and barley—that is, the solid foundation of virtues—so that he may behold its fruit. “Let us rest,” she says, “in the villages,” to which Adam had been banished when he was expelled from paradise. In these he rested, but he worked the earth.

15. The reason why she wishes him to go out into the field is clear: so that, like a good shepherd, he may feed his flock, raise up the weary, and recall the wandering. For even if this soul has preserved both new and old things, there are still those who are like lambs and must be nourished with milk. Thus, as one perfected, she intervenes not for herself but for others: that he may come out from the Father’s bosom, that he may go forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber; going out, let him run his course so that he may win the weak. Let him not remain in that secret throne of the Father, nor in that light which feeble horses cannot ascend, but let him be taken up and led into the Bride’s house and inner chamber. Let him be outside for himself, so that he may be within for us; let him be among us, even if he is not seen by us. Hence she says: “Who will give you to me, my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother? When I find you outside, I will kiss you” (*Song* VIII, 1). Good is the soul that is outside, so that the Word may be within; she is outside the body, so that the Word may dwell in us.

16. “I will take you up,” he says, “and bring you in” (*ibid.*, 2). The Word of God is rightly taken up and brought in, because he knocks upon the soul so that the door may be opened to him; and unless he finds the door opened to him, he does not enter. But if anyone opens the door, he enters and dines. Thus the Bride takes up the Word, so that by taking him up she may be taught. Hence she rightly ascends to him, to the higher dwellings, and continually receives an advance in virtue.

17. [Note: [Col. 1949D] *On Virginity*, chapter 6, no. 34.] “Come, my brother; let us go out into the field, let us rest in the villages; let us rise early in the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed.” Many fields bear fruit, but that field is better which abounds both in fruits and in flowers. The field, then, is the Church, fertile in diverse riches. Here you may see the shoots of virginity blooming with flowers; there, as in woodland meadows, widowhood strong in dignity; elsewhere, like a rich harvest of the Church, the grain of marriage filling the world’s granaries, and, as though they were married vines, the presshouses overflowing with their produce—the Lord Jesus’ presshouses—in which the fruit of faithful marriage flourishes abundantly.

18. [Note: [Col. 1950D] *On Psalm* CXVIII, sermon 19, nos. 23 and following.] Having obtained the abundance of her desire, the Bride speaks to the Bridegroom: “Come, my brother; let us go out into the field, let us rest in the villages; let us rise early for the vineyards.” Do you see how the Bride invites the Word of God to come to the earth and take away the sins of the world? This field had previously been deserted, made desolate by the thorns of our sins and bristling with briars. It was a village in which Adam, confined there, held the heirs of his whole posterity in perpetual exile. The Church therefore leads Christ there so that he may free Adam. Then, after the exiles had been released, this world’s field began to have suitable cultivators; and what had previously been barren became fertile through the planting of the eternal vine. Yet even so she does not spread joyfully among spiritual branches, but calls Christ to these vineyards where people sing psalms and pray, and where harmless fruit endures night and day.

19. (Verse 12.) “There,” she says, “I will give you my breasts; there the mandrakes gave forth their fragrance.” Many distinguish a certain sexual difference among mandrakes, believing that there are male and female plants, with the females having the stronger odor. He therefore signifies the nations, which formerly stank but, after believing in the Lord’s coming, began to bear the fruits of good odor, although previously they had been weaker, emasculated by a certain feebleness of unbelief. We also read that holy Rachel received mandrakes from her sister Leah so that Leah would grant her permission to sleep with holy Jacob that night. Reuben, the firstborn, had brought mandrakes to his mother Leah, who, with bleary eyes, took on the figure of the Synagogue because, with the sight of her mind weakened, she could not see the grace of Christ. This makes clear that the fruits which the Synagogue had earlier received from the firstborn Son of God, she granted to the Church. But because Leah conceived and bore an heir of her posterity from the intercourse requested for that night, she fulfilled the mystery: when the apostles believed, the remnant of the Jews was saved through the election of grace. Hence the Church says:

20. (Verse 13.) “The new and the old things, my brother, I have kept for you. Who will give you to me, my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother? When I find you outside, I will kiss you, and indeed they will not despise me. I will take you up and bring you into the house of my mother, and into the inner chamber of her who conceived me; there you will teach me.” Possessing, therefore, the instruction of the new and old Scriptures, and not considering herself contemptible, she holds the Word not only in the secret prayers of her heart but also with the voices of the psalm-singing choir, kissing him, as it were, with certain kisses of grace.

21. [Note: [Col. 1951D] *On Psalm* CXVIII, sermon 22, no. 33.] “The new and the old things, my brother, I have kept for you”—that is: “I hold all the commandments of the New and Old Testament.” The Church alone can say this. No other assembly says it; neither does the Synagogue, which holds neither the new according to the letter nor the old according to the spirit. The Manichaean heresy does not say, “I have kept the old things for you,” since it does not accept the prophets. Rightly, therefore, she is called whitened, whose radiance is the grace of both Testaments.

[Col. 1951D] 22. “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you awaken and stir up love until it wishes.” She still seeks one who will awaken her, and asks that she be awakened for him by the daughters of Jerusalem, through whose agency—that is, through the agency of faithful souls—she desires the Bridegroom to be stirred to a fuller love of her. Thus those virtues which guard the gates of heaven say:

## CHAPTER EIGHT

1. (Verse 5.) [Note: [Col. 1951D] *On Psalm* CXVIII, sermon 14, no. 34.] “Who is this who comes up, white, leaning upon her brother?” Consider how she who placed her head upon the left hand of Wisdom, so that she might open her hand to the poor and assist the needy; who, having things distributed or left to her, used wealth rather than invading and plundering it; who, desirous of glory, acquired it even through good works, and did not pursue the empty ostentation of worldly dignity—that is what it means to place her head, the governing principle of the senses, above the hand of Wisdom. This soul, I say, ascends with whitewashed merits from this desert of the present life, as many understand it, to that ever-flourishing place of eternal delight.

2. These are the virtues that also say in the book of Isaiah: “Who is this who comes from Edom, the redness of his garments from Bosor, so beautiful in his robe?” (*Isa.* LXIII, 1). These, I say, are the ones who marvel that from this rough and rocky desert any soul could ascend without the stain of great vices. Therefore they rejoice to find one who has not defiled the garments of natural innocence with the ink of worldly foolishness, but has rather cleansed them with the whiteness of spiritual wisdom and grace. The daughters of Jerusalem—the holy souls of the patriarchs and prophets and of the ancient righteous—or the heavenly powers marvel and say: [Note: [Col. 1952D] *On Psalm* CXVIII, sermon 19, nos. 27 and following.] “Who is this who comes up whitened, leaning upon her brother?” That is: the Church shines with such solemnities; she who previously was dark by day now shines and gleams in the nights. The Lord himself, delighted by such a great gift of those singing psalms, says:

3. (Verse 6.) “Set me as a sign upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, and your jealousy is hard as the underworld.” [Col. 1952C] “Its wings are wings of fire and flame. Many waters cannot drive out love, nor will rivers overwhelm it.” Because the Church saw such devotion, she considers the peoples now suitable to bear his sign upon our heart and arm. For God the Father himself sealed him; and whoever received his testimony has set his seal that God is true. Therefore those who work for food that endures to eternal life have been sealed according to the image and likeness of Christ, who is the image of the invisible God.

As God, then, is truthful, so also mark truth in your understanding and conduct, so that your mouth may not speak falsehood, nor your hands perform the works of human beings, which belong to this deceptive world; but let them perform the things that belong to God, so that they may give generously to the poor, raise up the weak, and honor the dead with the burial of tombs. Through such works love is sought, so that no one may be torn away from Christ even by the danger of death. Hence he says: “Who will separate us from Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?” (*Rom.* VIII, 35). And further: “For I am confident that neither death nor life nor angels …” (*ibid.*).

4. In this respect, too, jealousy is a harsh quality of love, and its wings are wings of fire. It has wings like a dove, for “the feathers of the dove are silvered”; with these the one who loves flies away, saying: “Behold, I have fled far away and remained in solitude” (*Ps.* LIV, 8). But the wings of love are wings of fire, with which it kindles the ardor of affection. [Col. 1953A] With this vapor the Lord made his angels fervent spirits and his ministers a burning but not consuming fire. We also read of the wing of the temple, above which the devil, when tempting him, made the Savior ascend; it was at the summit of the temple (*Matt.* IV, 3). There are, therefore, heights of piety and summits of love, which customarily burn the vapor of grace into human breasts, so that much water cannot extinguish or drive out love, nor can rivers of worldly storms confine it. We said that love drives out fear; we did not say that it drives out every disturbance. Indeed, whoever loves God possesses the deep tranquility of a mind made firm.

5. (Verse 7.) [Note: [Col. 1953D] *On Psalm* CXVIII, sermon 21.] “Many waters,” he says, “cannot drive out love, and rivers will not flood it.” The many waters are the various passions, and the rivers are worldly desires stirred by bodily impulses; nevertheless, they cannot overthrow the wall of love. Therefore the one founded upon love says: “Our soul has passed through the torrent” (*Ps.* CXXIII, 5). Could the water of the sea drive out Moses’ love? And, so that the sequence of the psalms may support you according to the letter, surely the one who loved God believed the way through the seas to be safe; but those who did not love God were submerged by the waves and suffered an end worthy of their sacrilege.

6. (Verse 5.) [Note: [Col. 1954D] *On Isaac*, chapter 8, no. 72 and following.] “Who is this who comes up, leaning upon her brother?” Above they said: “Who is this who looks forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” Here something more has been found to add: she had ascended leaning upon the Word of God. For the more perfect recline upon Christ, just as John reclined upon Christ’s breast. Thus she too either leaned upon Christ or reclined herself above him; or, since we are speaking of a wedding, now as one given into Christ’s right hand, she was being led into the bridal chamber to the Bridegroom.

And because the bond of love already exists, the Bridegroom caresses her and says:

7. “Under the apple tree I raised you up; there your mother went into labor with you; there she went into labor who bore you.” Good is the soul that rests beneath a fruitful tree, and especially beneath one of good fragrance. For if Nathanael, in whom there was no deceit, was seen beneath a fig tree, then surely the good soul is one that was raised up by her Bridegroom beneath an apple tree. To be raised up is more than to be seen; to be raised up by the Bridegroom is greater still. Although Nathanael was seen beneath a tree, his soul was not a bride, because he came to Christ secretly, since he feared the Jews. She who was in the shadow was not “beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun,” because the bride who marries by day makes public confession. Therefore one is beneath an apple tree and the other beneath a fig tree: the former spread the fragrance of her confession farther, while the latter possessed the sweetness of purity and innocence but did not possess the fervor of the spirit.

8. “There,” he says, “your mother went into labor with you; there she went into labor who bore you.” For there we are born and there we are reborn. Those in whom the image of Christ is formed are brought forth; hence Paul also says: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (*Gal.* IV, 19). The one who receives the spirit of salvation in the womb and pours it into others has gone into labor. Therefore, since Christ had already been formed in her, she says:

9. (Verse 6.) “Set me as a sign upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.” The sign of Christ is on the forehead and the sign is on the heart: on the forehead, so that we may always confess him; on the heart, so that we may always love him; the seal is on the arm, so that we may always act. Let his image therefore shine in our confession; let it shine in our reading; let it shine in our works and deeds, so that, if possible, his whole form may be expressed in us.

Let him be our head, because “the head of the man is Christ”; let him be our eye, so that through him we may see the Father; let him be our voice, through which we may speak to the Father; let him be our right hand, through which we may offer our sacrifice to God the Father. He is also our seal, the distinguishing mark of love and perfection, because the loving Father sealed the Son, as we read: “The Father, God, has sealed him” (*John* VI, 27). Christ, therefore, is our love. Good is the love that offered itself to death for those it loved; good is the love that forgave sin.

10. Therefore let our soul put on love, and such love as is strong as death; for just as death is the end of sins, so also is love, since whoever loves the Lord ceases to sin. “Love does not devise evil, nor rejoice over iniquity, but bears all things” (*I Cor.* XIII, 5). For one who does not seek what is his own—how could he seek what belongs to another? There is also that strong death through the washing by which every sin is buried and guilt is forgiven. Such was the love borne by that woman in the Gospel, of whom the Lord says: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (*Luke* VII, 47). There is also the strong death of the holy martyrs, which removes previous guilt; and therefore strong is the love equal to it, which corresponds to the martyrs’ suffering so as to take away the merit of sins.

11. Jealousy is also like the underworld, because whoever possesses zeal for God does not spare even himself for Christ’s sake. Thus love has death, love has jealousy, and love has wings of fire. Indeed, Christ, loving Moses, appeared to him in fire. And Jeremiah, possessing within himself the gift of divine love, said: “And there was a burning fire in my bones, and I was utterly weakened, and I cannot endure it” (*Jer.* XX, 9). Good, therefore, is love possessing wings of burning fire, which flits through the breasts and hearts of the saints and consumes whatever is material and earthly; whatever is sincere, however, it tests, and whatever it touches it improves with its own fire.

12. The Lord Jesus sent this fire upon the earth, and faith shone forth, devotion was kindled, love was illumined, and righteousness gleamed. With this fire he inflamed the hearts of his apostles, as Cleopas testifies, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us when he opened the Scriptures?” (*Luke* XXIV, 32). The wings of fire in the flame are therefore the divine Scriptures. Indeed, he was opening the Scriptures, and fire came forth and penetrated the hearts of those listening. They are truly wings of fire, because “the sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire” (*Ps.* XI, 7).

When Paul also was taken up by Christ, he saw a light shining around him and around those who were with him; he fell from fear and rose more approved. Thus the one who had come as a persecutor became an apostle. The Holy Spirit also descended and filled the whole house in which many were sitting, and tongues divided as though of fire appeared. Good wings, the wings of love—truly wings that flitted through the mouths of the apostles—and wings of fire, because they spoke purified speech.

13. On these wings Enoch flew away, carried up to heaven; on these wings Elijah flew away, transported above in a fiery chariot and fiery horses. On these wings the Lord God led the people of the fathers by the pillar of fire. The Seraphim had these wings when he took fiery coals from the altar, touched the prophet’s mouth, removed his iniquities, and cleansed his sins. By the fire of these wings the sons of Levi were purified, and the peoples of the nations were baptized, as John testifies when he says of the Lord Jesus: “He himself will baptize you in Spirit and fire” (*Matt.* III, 11).

Rightly David wished to burn his kidneys and his heart, because he knew that the fiery wings of love were not to be feared. Rightly the Hebrew boys did not feel the burning of the fire in the blazing furnace, because the flame of love cooled them. And so that we may understand more fully that perfected love has wings, you recently heard him saying: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings” (*Matt.* XXIII, 27).

14. Let us therefore take up these wings, which, like flames, direct us upward. Let each person strip his soul of its more filthy wrappings and, like gold, have it tested by fire after being cleansed of mud. In this way the soul is purified, like the finest gold. The soul’s beauty is sincere virtue and adornment, a truer knowledge of heavenly things, so that it may see that good from which all things depend, while it itself depends upon nothing. By this it lives and receives understanding. For the source of life is that highest good, whose desire is kindled within us, and to which it is a delight to draw near and be joined. To one who does not see it, it is an object of desire; to one who sees it, it is life. Therefore he despises all other things, is soothed by this alone, and delights in it. This is what supplies all substance; while remaining in itself, it gives to others, but receives nothing from others. Of it the Prophet says: “I said to the Lord: You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (*Ps.* XV, 2).

15. “His wings are wings of fire.” [Note: [Col. 1955D] *On Psalm* CXVIII, sermon 20, no. 12.] All who desire to return to paradise must be tested by fire. For it was not written without purpose that, after Adam and Eve had been expelled from paradise, God placed at the exit of paradise a turning, fiery sword. All must pass through flames, whether that person is John the Evangelist, whom the Lord loved so greatly that he said of him to Peter: “If I want him to remain, what is that to you? You follow me” (*John* XXI, 22). Some have doubted his death, but we cannot doubt his passage through fire, because he is in paradise and is not separated from Christ.

Or whether it is Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and walked upon the sea, he must say: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” (*Ps.* LXV, 12). Yet the fiery sword will quickly turn toward John, because no iniquity is found in him whom equity loved. If there was anything of human fault in him, divine love boiled it away, for “his wings are like wings of fire.” Whoever has possessed the fire of love here will not be able to fear the fire of the sword there.

To that Peter who so often offered his death for Christ, he says: “Cross over; recline.” But he says: “He tested us by fire, as he himself tested silver.”

16. “His wings are wings of fire.” [Note: [Col. 1955D] *On Virginity*, chapter 18, no. 116 and following.] Since the opportunity to fly has therefore been given to us, let each person stir up God’s grace within himself; forgetting what is behind and desiring what is ahead, let him press toward the appointed goal. Far from military honors, far from the world’s heat—lest what the myths relate should happen: that, with the heat of the sun melting the wax, the feather slipping from the Icarian [*Icareos*] flight should leave him without support. For although the seriousness of the subject may be an obstacle, they nevertheless wished by poetic wit to show that flights through heaven are safe for the mature wisdom of the prudent, whereas youthful fickleness, subject to worldly desires, with its wings falling away and the structure of its merits dissolved through forgetfulness of truth, falls back to earth with greater ruin.

17. Flight is not easy for everyone, and the course of human life is difficult even for animals that are at odds with one another on earth. But if the order of our actions corresponds to you, the prophet will also see in us that one wheel upon the earth joined to the four living creatures. Ezekiel will therefore see it again—for he still sees, remains alive, and will continue to see (*Ezek.* I, 15–16)—he will see, I say, a wheel within a wheel gliding harmlessly upon the earth.

The wheel upon the earth is the life of the body adapted to the soul’s virtue and formed, in a coherent course, according to the Gospel commandment. The wheel within the wheel is, as it were, life within life, because the life of the saints does not disagree with itself: as the earlier age has been, so also is the succeeding one; or because, in this bodily life, the practice of eternal life is set in motion. When these things correspond, then the divine voice resounds; then, above the likeness of a throne, a likeness appears resembling the form of a human being. This human being is the Word, because “the Word became flesh” (*John* I, 14). This human being is the driver of our living creatures and the ruler of our conduct; according to the measure of our merits, he usually ascends either a chariot, a mountain, or a ship.

18. “Set me as a sign upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm,” you who have kept the new and old things for me. You are my seal; you are in my image and likeness. The image of justice, the image of wisdom, and the image of virtue shine in you. And because the image of God is in your heart, let it also be in your works. Let the likeness of the Gospel be in your deeds, so that in your conduct you may keep my commandments. The likeness of the Gospel will be in you if, when struck on one cheek, you offer the other; if you love your enemy; if you take up your cross and follow me.

Therefore I carried the cross for you, so that you would not hesitate to carry it for me. The daughters of Jerusalem heard that the Lord God was already joining the Church to himself; and because, considering the greatness of the Word, they judged themselves unequal to such a marriage, lest perhaps they be unable to bear the weight of so great a union, they excuse themselves, saying:

[Col. 1957B] 19. (Verse 8.) “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts.” Those who wish to postpone a wedding customarily excuse themselves in this way, alleging the weakness of immature age and asserting that they have no breasts, which signify the age suitable for marriage. This is a common sign among all virgins who are to marry: when their breasts begin to protrude, then they are judged fit for union. Troubled, therefore, because the Bridegroom presses the wedding forward with the zeal of love, they say:

20. “What shall we do for our sister on the day when one speaks concerning her, or, according to Symmachus, ‘on the day when one speaks to her’?” That is, at the celebration of the betrothal, a conversation and confirmation of the marriage customarily take place. “What shall we do,” they say in their confusion, “because the spiritual union presses upon us?” They cannot excuse themselves from so great a wedding, for no one thinks the union either of soul and spirit or of Christ and the Church anything but blessed. But because the fullness of the Word or of the Holy Spirit flashes and shines, and nothing can be compared with them, they desire to postpone it, so that by that delay either the soul or the Church may become more perfect. Therefore they say:

21. (Verse 9.) “If she is a wall, let us build silver enclosures upon her; and if she is a door, let us carve cedar panels upon her.” The soul of the saint is a wall. The Church also has her walls, and, now more perfect, says: “I am a fortified city” (*Isa.* XXVII, 3). This is the wall that has twelve apostolic gates, through which entry into the Church is open to the people of the nations.

But although a wall encloses the circuit of the whole city, it is more strongly fortified when it has prepared enclosures in which the city’s defenders may have a secure means of observing and protecting it. Since this city is rational and all its hope is in the Word of God, it requires not iron but silver defenses, accustomed to repel hostile attacks more by heavenly utterances than by bodily pleasures.

22. Supported by this defense and shining with this splendor, she is judged more suitable for union with Christ. And because Christ is the door, who says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (*John* X, 9), the Church is also called a door, because through her the way to salvation lies open to the peoples.

But lest she be corrupted by the moths or worms of heretics, the daughters of Jerusalem—or angels, or the souls of the righteous—say: “Let us build cedar panels upon her,” that is, the good fragrance of sublime faith. This material has a sweet fragrance, which neither worm nor moth can corrupt. Therefore this material is chosen for raising and shaping the heights of roofs and for forming the elements of letters, by which childhood is instructed in the pursuit of liberal learning.

This material, then, is lofty for grace, light for carrying, sweet in fragrance, useful as an instrument of knowledge, and suitable for the service of eternal understanding. But just as Christ, loving his Bride, pressed her toward the solemnity of spiritual union, so the Church, already captivated by the beauty of the Word, hastened toward the wedding. Therefore, unable to endure the delays which the daughters of Jerusalem were eager to impose, she says:

23. (Verse 10.) “I am a wall, and my breasts are towers.” That is: “Do not doubt whether I am a wall. They said, ‘If she is a wall’; but I am a wall, and I do not have small breasts: my breasts are like towers. How can you say that I have no breasts?” I possess understanding like the towers of wisdom, in which there is abundance, as it is written: “And abundance in your towers” (*Ps.* CXXI, 7). With these breasts—that is, with these understandings—she judged herself suitable for so great a wedding. But the daughters of Jerusalem still could not judge this, because they did not see the abundance of her understanding. And she added:

[Col. 1958C] 24. (Verse 11.) “I was in his eyes as one who finds peace”—that is, after considering my understanding, when I found the peace of God, which surpasses every mind and guards hearts and thoughts in Christ Jesus. “Such,” she says, “was I in the bridegroom’s eyes as one who possesses peace.” For it is written: “Those who seek peace rightly will rejoice.”

1617 25. (Verse 12.) [Note: [Col. 1957D] *On the Good of Death*, chapter 5, no. 18.] “I,” he says, “am a fortified city; I am a besieged city” (*Isa.* XXVII, 3). With these walls she is fortified; besieged, she is defended by them. Truly the soul is a wall, one displayed in the camp. Hence she herself says in the *Song*: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers” (verse 10).

Good is the wall that the Lord painted, as he himself says: “Upon my hands I have painted your walls, and you are always before me” (*Isa.* XLIX, 16). Good is the soul that has God as its watchman and is in his hands, like the prophetic soul that is commended into God’s hands as a spirit (*Ps.* XXX, 6), and that is before God’s sight: “For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.” Thus she herself says: “I was in his eyes as one who finds peace.” She has good towers who possesses both a word concerning intelligible realities and discipline concerning moral matters.

[Note: [Col. 1957D] *On Psalm* CXVIII, sermon 22, no. 40 at the end, 41 [Col. 1958D] and following.] Since the beloved and the beloved woman were hastening, the spiritual union was celebrated, sought by mutual consent. Therefore, as though singing a nuptial song, the Spirit exulted in the prophet, saying:

[Col. 1959A] 26. (Verse 11.) “A vineyard was planted for Solomon in Beelamon; he gave his vineyard to those who keep it.” The Spirit therefore cries out: “The assembly of the peoples has been planted, founded upon the root of the eternal vine, and it has subjected spiritual hearts beneath the yoke of the Word with a gentle heart. It has been planted among the multitude of the nations.”

This is what *Beelamon* should be understood to mean, as Symmachus, Aquila, and the other translations taught in the Greek language. The former union, which could not bear fruit, was rejected; the vineyard was given to new and faithful cultivators, who could not only produce fruit but also guard it.

One sheep therefore went astray, but when recalled filled the whole expanse of the world. Error had led away one sheep, but the grace of the Lord gathered a multitude of peoples. The human being went astray, but in the Church he is now a wall, and a strong wall. Adam went astray, but David is a wall, for he did not forget God’s commandments.

This vineyard, therefore, guarded and enclosed by spiritual protection, gives Christ a thousand fruits, but two hundred fruits to its keepers. Hence the Church says:

27. (Verse 12.) “My vineyard is before me: a thousand for Solomon, and two hundred for those who keep its fruit.” The portion of the little ones is Christ’s perfection and fullness. You have this mystery in Genesis, where Joseph assigns five portions to Benjamin, his younger brother, and single portions to the remaining brothers (*Gen.* XLIII, 34). The portion and privilege of the five senses, therefore, is given to the Lord; and it is given to him by the one whom he loves, just as he loved Paul and gave him primacy in wisdom for calling the nations.

[Note: [Col. 1959D] Book I *On Virgins*, chapter 8, no. 49.] Let fear depart from the sacred virgins, to whom the Church first grants such great protections. Concerned for the growth of tender offspring, she herself rises like a wall, her breasts swelling abundantly like towers, until, once the enemy’s assault of the siege has been broken, she obtains peace for vigorous youth through the protection of maternal virtue. Hence the Prophet also says: “Let there be peace in your strength and abundance in your towers” (*Ps.* CXXI, 7).

28. (Verse 13.) [Note: [Col. 1959D] *On the Good of Death*, chapter 5, no. 18.] “You who dwell in gardens, friends attend to your voice; make your voice known to me.” Therefore this soul, possessing the grace of her breasts, enters the gardens and, finding the Bridegroom sitting there and conversing with his friends, says: “You who dwell in gardens, make your voice known to me”—“to me,” she says, “not to the friends.”

29. [Note: [Col. 1959D] *On Psalm* CXVIII, sermon 22, nos. 43 and following.] “You who dwell in gardens, friends attend to your voice; make your voice known to me.” She rejoiced that Christ was sitting in the gardens and that the friends placed in the gardens were attending to his voice. But because those friends were heavenly beings—Archangels, or Dominions and Thrones—for human beings had been expelled from paradise because of disobedience to the heavenly commandments and therefore the Church still could not hear the voice she desired to hear, she says: “Make your voice known to me.”

Hence, if we too wish him to sit within us, let us be enclosed and fortified gardens; let us bear the flowers of virtues and the sweetness of grace, so that we may be able to hear the Lord Jesus conversing with the angels. But because it was destined that, when the Church had reached her fullness, she would be tested by various persecutions, therefore, while she rejoiced in the grace of the Word, she suddenly perceived the plots of her persecutors. And because she feared more for the Bridegroom than for herself—or because Christ is more eagerly sought by persecutors in us—she says:

### 30. (Verse 14)

“Flee, my brother, and be like a young doe or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of spices.”

For the sake of the weak he flees, who could not endure more severe trials. Therefore it is written that we should flee from cities to cities: and if they persecute us in this city, let us flee into another. For the sake of the weak, then, as we have said, let him flee from those who pursue him; or let him flee from lowly things and pass over to the mountains of spices, [Col. 1960B] which, in place of martyrdom, can bring the fragrance of the blessed resurrection. The mountains of spices are the saints. Christ flees to them, because “His foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 86:1). He therefore flees to those who are His firm foundations. In us He flees; in them He abides in a secure station. Thus Paul is a mountain of spices, who can say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15). David is a mountain of spices, whose prayer’s fragrance rose up to the Lord; and therefore he said: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in Your sight” (Psalm 140:2).

### 31

Symmachus and Aquila, however, interpreted the passage as Christ’s saying to the Church: “You who sit in the gardens”—that is, “you now sit in the gardens, worthy of the heavenly paradise”; and therefore, “Make your voice known to me; your friends are listening: I too desire to hear it.” The Church began to be in the gardens after Christ was seized in the gardens.

### 32. [Note: *On Virginity*, chapter 9, no. 49.]

“Flee, my brother, and become like a stag or a fawn of a stag, into the mountains of spices.”

For, hated by serpentine snakes, fleeing from dogs, and hostile to creeping serpents, he knows how to dwell only in the heights of the virtues; he knows how to remain only with such daughters of the Church as can say: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15). But to some we are “the fragrance of death unto death,” namely, to those who are perishing; to others, “the fragrance of life unto life,” namely, to those who hope with living faith for the fragrance of the Lord’s resurrection. These are the mountains of spices, which received the body of the Lord Jesus and wrapped it in linen cloths with spices. For all who believed that Jesus died, was buried, and rose again have raised the lofty summit of true faith upon the pinnacles of the virtues. Where, then, is Christ sought? In the breast, surely, of the prudent priest?

### 33. [Note: *On the Good of Death*, chapter 5, no. 18.]

“Flee, my brother.”

He urges the Bridegroom to flee, because she herself will then be able to follow Him who flees from earthly things. He says that she should be like the doe that escapes from the nets; for she too wishes to flee and soar above the world.

[Note: *On Isaac*, chapter 8, no. 78, near the end, and following number.]

Let us therefore flee into our truest homeland. There is our homeland, and the Father by whom we were created; there is Jerusalem, the city that is the mother of all. But what is this flight? Certainly not a flight of the feet, which belong to the body; for wherever they run, they run upon the earth, passing from one piece of ground to another. Nor should we flee in ships, or chariots, or upon horses that are harnessed and fall. Rather, let us flee in mind and with our eyes; or let us accustom our inner feet to make our eyes see what is bright and clear, to behold the face of self-restraint and moderation, and all the virtues—in which there is nothing rough, nothing obscure or crooked. Let each person also look upon himself and his conscience, and cleanse that eye, lest it contain anything filthy. For what is seen ought not to be discordant with the one who sees, since God willed us to be conformed to the image of His Son.

[Col. 1961B] ### 34

That good, then, is known to us, and it is not far from any one of us: “For in Him we live, and move, and have our being; for we are also His offspring” (Acts 17:28), as the Apostle wished to teach the Gentiles. He is the good that we seek, and the only good; for “no one is good except God alone.” This is the eye that beholds that great and true beauty. The sun is not seen except by a sound and healthy eye; nor can the good be seen except by a good soul. Let the one who wishes to see the Lord and what is good therefore become good. Let us be like this good, and act according to it in the things that are good. This is the good that is above every action, above every mind and understanding; it is that which always remains, giving life and being to all, because Christ is the source of all life. Concerning Him the prophet says: “In His shadow we shall live.” For now our life is hidden in Christ; but when Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with Him in glory.

### 35

Therefore let us not fear death, since it is rest for the body, but for the soul either freedom or release. Nor let us fear the one who can kill the flesh but cannot kill the soul; for we do not fear the one who can remove our garment, nor do we fear the one who can steal what belongs to us but cannot steal us. Let us therefore be souls, if we wish to be Hebrews, that is, among those who are companions of Jacob and imitators of him. Let us be souls; our limbs, however, are garments. The garments must indeed be preserved, lest they be torn or grow old; but the one who uses them must preserve and guard himself still more.

# APPENDIX TO THE FIRST VOLUME OF THE BENEDICTINE EDITION

[Col. 1961C]

# APPENDIX TO THE FIRST VOLUME OF THE BENEDICTINE EDITION. EDITORIAL NOTICE

[Col. 1961]

Whoever reads the preface that the Benedictines placed before the later volume of their edition will immediately discover that those most learned men deliberately omitted works of various kinds which, although inscribed in the name of Ambrose, seemed to them—though unjustly so—to bear that name. We, however, whose foremost concern is to reprint the edition of each Father complete in every respect, intend to present to the reader whatever works—whether doubtful or even unquestionably apocryphal—which we have been able to investigate and which the Benedictines either rejected or did not even mention. We shall omit only those works which, according to the rules of sounder criticism, are attributed to Fathers other than our Ambrose and are found among their works.

When we first undertook this task, our intention had been to gather at the end of the Works into a single body everything that we had added to the Benedictine recension. But later, when the abundance of material required a four-volume work, necessity arose to append part of our additions to the first volume of the Benedictine edition and to reserve the remainder for the second, lest the volumes differ in excessively unequal size. Having weighed these considerations, we have therefore arranged for the books *On the Jewish War* to be published here. The Benedictines deny them to Saint Ambrose, but Schaenemann attributes them to him, in accordance with the recent vindications of Mazochius and Gallandi.

[Col. 1961D]

# FIVE BOOKS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE DESTRUCTION OF THE CITY OF JERUSALEM (G, S)*

[Col. 1961]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1961B] The four Books of Kings contained in Sacred Scripture I have already treated in concise style, composing them in the manner of history down to the captivity of the Jews, the destruction of the wall, and the triumphs of Babylon. The prophetic account briefly concludes the deeds of the Maccabees as well. For the remaining events, down to the burning of the Temple and the spoils of Titus Caesar, the distinguished historian Josephus is the narrator in historical style—if only he had been as attentive to religion and truth as he was to investigating events and maintaining sobriety of expression.

For in the very account by which he revealed their punishment, he displayed himself as an associate of the Jews’ faithlessness; and although he abandoned their weapons, he did not abandon their sacrileges. He lamented their misery tearfully, but did not recognize the cause of that misery. Therefore it was our concern, relying not upon the resources of talent but upon the purpose of faith, to proceed a little farther inward into the history of the Jews beyond the sequence of Sacred Scripture, so that, as though seeking a rose among thorns, amid the savage deeds of the impious—which were paid out with the fitting price of impiety—we might draw forth something either concerning reverence for the sacred law or concerning the marvel of holy religion and its constitution. These things, though they may have served their heirs either as a spectacle in adversity or as an honor in prosperity, are of greater significance here.

At the same time, let it become clear to all—as evidence of domestic wickedness—that they themselves were the authors of their own disaster. First, while attending to other matters, they turned the Romans against themselves and invited them to investigate their kingdom, when it would have been better for them to remain unknown. They sought friendship without intending to keep faith. They violated peace although unequal in strength. Finally, they made war upon those whose entire hope lay in walls, not in strength, although nothing is more pitiable than to be shut in by a siege; and even when it proceeds well, a siege more often increases than diminishes dangers.

But lest anyone think that we have undertaken a task empty of faith or superfluous, let us therefore consider the whole Hebrew people as traced through its leaders, so that it may be clearly evident whether the succession of its generation from the loins of Judah ever failed; [Note: The older editions read “thighs,” incorrectly. The restored reading is confirmed by Genesis 49:10. Gallandi.] or whether it stumbled in the succession of its rulers but remained in the one in whom all things were reserved. He was “the hope of the nations” (Genesis 49:10). From this point, then, I shall begin.

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE

The Parthian War, which was prolonged and frequent and marked by varying victory between the Maccabean leaders and the people of the Medes, had as the spark and beginning of its sacrilege the grief caused by this fact: King Antiochus, surnamed the Illustrious, son of King Antiochus, after he had also brought Egypt under his rule, was lifted up in pride because the uncertain fortunes of war had favored him. He ordered that the rites of the Hebrews be neglected and their religious services profaned, and he dared to establish this at the request of many of the Jews.

The priest Mattathias could not endure this. Not only did he himself abstain from sacrilege and refuse to obey the royal decree; when he found one of his countrymen sacrificing victims to idols, he pierced him through with a sword. Gathering a band of men and admitting the Hasideans into his alliance, he and his sons killed those who violated ancestral custom and the ordinances of the Law, expelled many others, and became the author of beginning battle on the Sabbath. Otherwise they too would have been deceived by the same stratagem, since already many of them had fallen when they refused to undertake battle on the Sabbath and enemies attacked them.

The success of his actions gave him power, and the strength of his defense and devotion gave him the determination to persevere in the man’s cause until the end of his life. But when he understood that his final day was approaching, he summoned the citizens and his sons who stood around him and exhorted them to defend their homeland and the religion of the Temple. He left Judah Maccabee as leader and successor to his care and responsibility.

Judah, vigorous in war, wise in counsel, and more ready than the others in faith, often defeated countless forces of the enemy with a small band. To recount this is not part of our present task, although it can be summarized briefly. Having often enjoyed successful outcomes, he drew a great multitude of enemies against himself. While surrounded on every side and considering it shameful to retreat, he rushed into battle as his companions fled. After killing those against whom he had advanced, he was surrounded from the side, but, having nevertheless avenged his own death, he was killed.

Jonathan succeeded him, equal to him not less in likeness of courage than in brotherhood of nature. After accomplishing much in military affairs and carrying out religious duties that were observed and approved in connection with the purification of the Temple, [Note: Variant: “previously attempted.” Barr.] he was shut up inside the enemy city after they had pretended friendship through deceit. Not long afterward he too was killed.

John, the elder brother by birth, and Eleazar, the younger than the others, likewise did not refuse death for the sake of religion. After them Simon took control of affairs. He approached it not as an inexperienced man but as a brother already proven by the triumphs of their common cause.

[Col. 1964C] If only he had been as perceptive in guarding against fraud as he was strong of hand and sufficiently distinguished in the arts of war. For after, through his courage, he had established alliances with Roman commanders and the kings of foreign peoples, he was invited to a banquet by the treachery of Ptolemy, his son-in-law. There, amid tables and cups, he was surrounded and disarmed with the two sons who were present, and impiously handed over to death.

John, born from Simon and surnamed Hyrcanus, had wisely anticipated the plot. He hurried to the walls of a neighboring city, where the people were awaiting him because of his father’s outstanding merits and also out of hatred for the enemy’s crime. He had scarcely entered the city when Ptolemy was already there. But when Ptolemy attempted to enter through another gate and was repulsed, he judged that he must yield to the multitude.

Jonathan immediately assumed the office of his father’s priesthood and, proceeding to the worship of divine things, at once carried out the duties of piety and his concern to preserve the bonds of kinship, wishing to rescue his mother and brothers from danger. Having gained the upper hand in the encounter, he was overcome by the emotion of righteous affection, which prevented him from taking the fortress in which they were confined. For when Ptolemy saw himself hard pressed, he placed Jonathan’s mother and brothers upon the walls, intending to cast them down immediately unless Jonathan desisted from the war he had begun.

The young man was overcome by fear for his piety, which conquered his assumption of courage; and he recalled his anger against the enemy through compassion for his own people. His mother, however, ready for torture, stretched out her hands, asking not for help toward safety but for the consolation of vengeance. For she feared that her son might fear more for his mother than he would devote himself to avenging his father. She declared that this death would take the place of immortality for her, by which her husband would be avenged and her impious son-in-law would pay the penalty for his monstrous crime.

But the young man fought more within himself than against the enemy. Whenever he thought of his father, he was inflamed. Again, when he saw his mother beaten and prepared for death, he made an attempt; then he recalled his assault and withdrew his step, because grief held him back.

During the delays of the siege, while he was keeping the Sabbath according to the Law, the year that was the seventh arrived. Piety yielded to religious observance, and the siege was lifted. But Ptolemy’s savagery was stirred all the more, so that he ordered those whose presence had enabled him to escape punishment to be slaughtered. He immediately removed himself from the vengeance by fleeing to Zeno, surnamed Cotylas, king of Philadelphia, so that he might protect himself with his aid.

Nor did Antiochus remain inactive. He was indignant that his armies had been made a laughingstock by Simon, Jonathan’s father. Wishing still to extinguish Jonathan’s rising first fruits, he came with a large force against Jerusalem and besieged Hyrcanus.

Hyrcanus overcame with gold the one whom he could not overcome with iron. Having opened David’s tomb—as Josephus relates—he removed three thousand talents of gold. Of these he paid three hundred to Antiochus so that he would abandon the siege and depart after having been bought off. And, to lessen the odium of the act, Hyrcanus is said to have been the first to establish hostels with that money, in which he could receive poor foreigners upon their arrival.

He also took advantage of Antiochus’ difficulty, since Antiochus was waging war against the Medes, and avenged the loss he had suffered. He added very many cities of Syria to his own territory. He also surrounded Samaria—which was later called Sebaste—with fortifications and entrusted its capture to his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus.

Their siege continued slowly until the defenders were driven by dreadful hunger to consume the loathsome food of human corpses. Compelled by this necessity, they decided to seek help from Antiochus, surnamed Aspondius, but involved him in sharing their distress. For, defeated by the brothers in battle, he escaped death by flight.

The Samaritans, however, were besieged again; once the city had been captured and destroyed, they were delivered into slavery. Stirred by this succession of successes, Aristobulus and Antigonus did not slacken their attacks. They considered it necessary to compel neighboring peoples to join them by war, until jealousy arose and a savage war broke out, with the inhabitants of the region conspiring and a strong force being assembled.

That force was nevertheless defeated, bringing deep tranquility thereafter to John and leisure to himself. Hyrcanus, having enjoyed thirty-one years of prolonged peace, ended his final day with five children surviving him, a condition that many count as blessedness. He was an outstanding governor and admirably temperate; no chance event had ever left anything by which his conduct might be darkened. He entrusted the affairs of supreme power to his wife, thinking that she would govern public affairs more wisely, while, with a certain prescience of mind, he considered that his sons would not live long. His judgment did not deceive him.

For Aristobulus, the older among the brothers and the more energetic in mind, turned the high priesthood into royal power and was the first to claim the right to place a diadem upon himself—four hundred and seventy-five years and three months after Israel, returning from Babylon, had been freed from slavery and had come back to its own land.

In his arrogance, and unwilling to assign even a portion to his remaining brothers, he soothed only Antigonus, whom he seemed to love, with the appearance of honor. Because his mother complained that she had been deprived of power and cheated of her husband’s judgment, he bound her in chains. He went so far in the savagery of a parricidal spirit that he held both her and his brothers, similarly bound, in close confinement, so that they were nearly forced to die of extreme hunger—unless Aristobulus had sooner paid the penalty owed for his wicked parricide.

At first his savage spirit was enraged against Antigonus himself, and love was changed into hatred, so that he killed before all others the one whom alone he had promised himself as a partner in rule. So worthless is affection among the wicked that it is quickly torn away by wicked suggestions.

## CHAPTER TWO

It is therefore fitting that we not pass over the sequence of his cruelties, so that John’s judgment may be vindicated even after his death. He certainly did not think that the supreme direction of public affairs should be entrusted to his older son, whom he foresaw would depart so far from the law of piety and the norm of justice in his madness.

I do not know whether this arose from regard for his character, or from the natural favor shown by priests toward rulers, so that certain things that were going to happen might be infused even into men less worthy. It was a pitiable crime that they envied the love of brothers for one another: from this the first stain of evil arose. The inventions of envy that followed were of this sort.

## CHAPTER THREE

At first they devised other accusations, to which Aristobulus did not give credence, and he softened the slander through the grace of affection, attributing the bitterness of the report to envy. Therefore they mixed falsehoods with truths, so that by means of what they had adopted for the appearance of truth they might surround the man who resisted them.

## CHAPTER FOUR

Meanwhile the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles was being celebrated in the land according to the Law—a festive day, namely, and one full of reverence, on which the solemn sacrifice was offered.

On that day Antigonus, distinguished by his military achievements, returned home, and it happened that, when he arrived, he found his brother in an altered condition. He went immediately to the Temple—for what would he place before religion?—and, girded in military dress and surrounded by an escort, he proceeded there. There he offered many prayers to the Lord for his brother’s safety, and from there hastened diligently to his brother.

From this, the slander was composed out of bitter gall, and an even more bitter outcome was prepared.

## CHAPTER FIVE

Immediately the most wicked men approached the king and aroused his envy, alleging that he had sent a more elaborate display of armed men than was customary for private persons, one that would become an ostentation before the people, so that no one would dare oppose his efforts. Such an impressive display, they said, sought nothing other than the king’s death and the power to usurp the rule.

A sick mind, weakened by an infirm body, was not difficult to drive into believing what was asserted as truth—especially since the day was consecrated to religion and excluded suspicion of falsehood; the display aroused envy; weakness added fear; and the cohort of armed men supplied confidence that the crime could be carried out.

Before any trial of parricidal wickedness had been established against him, therefore, he ordered his guards, with their weapons, to be stationed in a dark underground passage. They were to kill Antigonus by deceit when he arrived [Note: “They should tear him open” (*diloricarent*) is read more correctly; the author himself uses this verb in chapter 25 of this book and in Book IV. Barr.] and were not to wait for the king’s command but to destroy him on their own.

After sending word through messengers that Antigonus should come unarmed, Aristobulus’ wife changed the nature of the message to the opposite effect. Through the conspirators she had it conveyed that the king had been pleased with the splendor of his brother’s arms, in which he had recently appeared equipped, but that, because of his illness, he had not considered the matter carefully enough. He now requested that Antigonus bring him all the military adornment he had prepared for himself [Note: “Compare.” ID.]; this would please the king, if he came armed.

Antigonus did not foresee the trick. He obeyed the order all the more eagerly because he desired equally to please the king and his brother. Aristobulus was lying ill in the fortress that was first called Baris and later Antonia, receiving that name and its dignity from Antony the triumvir, who had bestowed it.

When Antigonus approached and came near that dark passage, the king’s guards saw that he had arrived armed, attacked the young man suddenly, fulfilled the order, and overwhelmed him while he was unaware.

This place was called Strato’s Tower. Because of the similarity of the name, there is a widespread opinion that the Judas who was an Essene by birth was deceived there; ancient history relates that he often foretold what was to come, whether because of the integrity of his life or because of his mystical observance.

## CHAPTER SIX

As we have learned, when he saw Antigonus passing by in order to visit his brother, he said to those who were attached to the number of his disciples:

“Alas! It is now good for me to die, when truth has died for me. Antigonus lives, and he must be killed today. The place appointed for his death is Strato’s Tower, which is six hundred stades from here. It is already the fourth hour of the day.”

Thus the timing appeared to exclude the reliability of the predestined death. When he had said this, he began to consider more intently within himself how his prediction had deceived him.

Not long afterward word was brought that Antigonus had been killed in the underground passage at Strato’s Tower, a place which, because of the same name, was also accustomed to be called by the name of the place on the coast at Caesarea.

After this crime had been committed, Aristobulus, reflecting with himself on what a crime he had perpetrated, fell ill himself. The parricide was before his eyes; there was turmoil in his mind; and he gave no room anywhere for concealment. Pain was fixed in the depths of his entrails. Envy had been turned into pity because he had killed an innocent man against the law of brotherhood. The enormity of so great a crime ulcerated his mind. Neither sleep was granted to his eyes nor rest to his spirit. The wound spread with hidden pain; his sick heart was consumed; harsh anxieties weakened his limbs; and, with frequent groans, excessively deep sighs struck him.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

The force of his illness therefore advanced through immoderate grief to such a degree that, [Note: “With his entrails convulsed.” ID.] with his entrails torn apart, he expelled blood from his mouth in vomiting. A palace boy, who was performing service for the king, carried it outside and, unaware of what he was doing—which happened by chance rather than design—came to the place where Antigonus had been killed.

There, above the spots still wet with his brother’s blood, he poured out the blood of the murderer. Suddenly a cry and groaning arose among those who witnessed it, because the blood of the most wicked parricide who had been slain seemed, by some profound ordering of the Lord, to have been offered as a libation.

Aristobulus was roused by the sound and asked the reason. When they kept silent, he drew the truth out of them through persistent questioning and fear of his anger. On learning what had happened, his eyes filled with tears, and he groaned as deeply as his strength allowed:

“An exchange corresponding to my deserts is not being exacted from me. I could not escape the eye of God, though I devised so impious a crime. The vengeance of my wickedness is at hand, and I am already being confronted with the fitting price of my parricide.

“Farewell, body! How long will you hold back the soul condemned for its brother and mother? Why do I offer them my blood in portions? Let every hand, if there is any piety in it, turn its weapon against me; let all my sons and brothers pierce me with the sword of avenging piety. Let the parricidal victim be slaughtered and sacrificed to violated kinship. Let guilty flesh disgorge all its blood at once.

“Let the demon that drove me into such wicked acts of savage crime not be satisfied by the tortures of my entrails and a lingering wasting disease.”

After saying these things, he brought an end to his rule and his life. He had held royal power scarcely a year, for the sake of which he had not escaped parricide.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

The woman immediately released the dead man’s brothers and freed them from their chains. She established Alexander as king, since his mature age and moderation were thought likely to support him.

As soon as he obtained the kingdom, he immediately killed the brother whom he had recognized as a rival to the throne. He spared the remaining brother, who was concerned more with life and safety than with kingship, leaving him free from public affairs.

Immediately—as is characteristic of an unsettled disposition—he changed peace into war. In an engagement against Ptolemy Lathyrus, he killed very many of the enemy, but victory slipped away to Lathyrus. Nevertheless, his mother Cleopatra deprived him of the fruit of that victory, being forced to withdraw into Egypt in order to escape the death threatening her.

Alexander took advantage of her absence. While he sought to invade parts of her kingdom, he also turned Theodorus against himself, because he had appropriated to himself the most important portions of Theodorus’ possessions. Theodorus therefore seized the royal treasures in a sudden attack and also defeated ten thousand Jews in battle. But Alexander, not broken by the blow, added still more of the enemy’s territories to his own rule and reduced the populations of the captured cities to slavery.

Domestic sedition interrupted these military successes, and a quarrel that arose at banquets progressed all the way to war. It was a familiar plague among Jewish men to stir themselves from an entertainment into arms; and unless foreign auxiliaries had been available to the king, the rebellion would have prevailed. But although it was suppressed with difficulty by the force brought in from elsewhere, it was suppressed nonetheless, with approximately eight thousand Hebrews killed.

From there Alexander directed his march into Arabia, and some of its cities were subdued. Tributes were also assigned by right of victory to the Moabites and the Gileadites. Returning from there to Amathus, and finding Theodorus stunned by the extent of his successes, he discovered a fortress empty of defenders and captured it without delay.

The Arab king Obedas, however, was not wholly idle, nor [Note: Variant reading placed before “not.” Barr.] did he long tolerate the losses inflicted upon his kingdom without retaliation. For, having opportunely laid an ambush, he destroyed Alexander’s entire army, which had been trapped in a valley and crushed by a deep and numerous mass of camels.

Alexander nevertheless escaped and, fleeing from the battle, sought the defenses of Jerusalem. He was hated by his own people because their hatred of his misery had grown more bitter, since they were oppressed by fear of his great power. The discord of their minds was not concealed in silence or exercised only in words; battle was fought not once but many times.

In these conflicts nearly fifty thousand Jews were killed by Alexander. He was more destructive to his own people than to the enemy and, though the greater victor, suffered the greater loss, because by conquering he had worn away the strength of his kingdom.

Therefore he no longer took pleasure even in his own victories. Turning away from battle, he dealt with his subjects by policy, so that he no longer oppressed them with arms but pressed them with words, seeking to dissolve the causes of offense by speech alone. He achieved nothing in winning their favor, because his crimes outweighed his pretenses, and the very suddenness of his conversion to repentance, together with the inconsistency of his character, was everywhere regarded with cruel suspicion.

## CHAPTER TEN

Finally, when they thought that they were being surrounded by his feigned gentleness, they stirred up King Demetrius to war, intending him to assist them against Alexander. The battle was joined immediately and was not postponed, although one man had to fight against two armies while inferior in numbers.

He was accompanied by one thousand cavalry and six thousand infantry whom he had hired for pay. He also summoned ten thousand Jews who had conspired with him and met the enemy near the city of Sichem. The opposing forces had three thousand cavalry and forty thousand infantry.

After both sides had tested their battle lines, when Demetrius saw that the men hired for pay were not abandoning their loyalty, and Alexander learned that none of the Jews who had joined Demetrius had laid aside their hatred of him, they decided that the matter must be settled by arms.

Demetrius proved superior in the war, though at the cost of much of his own blood. For those who had come from the opposite side as hired troops fought brilliantly, contending with such courage and loyalty that they persisted even unto death.

Seeing himself abandoned, Alexander withdrew into the mountains after his forces had been cut down. But, contrary to the expectations of both sides, the appearance of victory came to one of them while its benefit accrued to the other. Demetrius was stripped of the Hebrews who had invited him into their alliance, while six thousand of them joined Alexander, following a certain habit of human nature in which adverse circumstances encourage compassion.

Demetrius therefore yielded to the man whom he had defeated in war when he saw that, with Hebrews gradually flocking to him, Alexander was now fit for battle and that Demetrius himself had been left with only a few.

His victory stirred in those accustomed to liberty a fear of condemnation. [Note: Variant: “of domination.” ID.] Alexander’s savagery returned with security, and rule over his own people and the practice of war were restored.

When he asked them what he should do to reconcile the minds of the populace to himself, they replied: “If he were to die.” For, once he was dead, they would scarcely be so deeply afflicted that they would return to friendship and lay aside their hatred of the deceased.

Provoked by this answer and accustomed to rebellion, he killed many of them and forced the rest into the city called Besemelel. Its capture brought in a plague more bitter than usual. He advanced in such savage cruelty that he crucified eight hundred of their number in the middle of the city. In their presence he ordered their wives and children to be slaughtered.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

He watched this while reclining in the midst of his concubines, joyful amid food and drink, but intoxicated more by blood than by wine. By this single deed he terrified the people more than he had by war, so that on the following night eight thousand Jews departed beyond Judea. Their flight ended only with Alexander’s death, and such horror of evil brought peace to the kingdom.

But when, after a respite from civil battles, a cause of anxiety arose for him—the expedition of Antiochus against the Arabs, which he considered terrifying and dangerous to himself—this was the Antiochus who was also called Dionysius, the brother of Demetrius and the last of the Seleucids.

Wishing to prevent him from passing through, Alexander obstructed him between the city of Antipatris and the shores of Joppa by digging enormous trenches, erecting a very high wall, and placing wooden towers upon it. He frustrated the undertaking through great labor on the part of his own men, but without any impediment to the enemy.

For the trenches were easily filled, the towers were burned, and Alexander himself secured his safety by flight. He was safer because he was not considered important enough [Note: Variant: “esteemed”; and shortly afterward, “in the position of a leader.” ID.] for the victor to pursue him as a leading figure. He had been reserved for a later occasion, so that he might avenge the injury he had suffered when his route was blocked.

He then directed his march straight against the Arabs, whose king had withdrawn to places suitable for battle. Then, suddenly turning his cavalry, they attacked the enemy’s troops, which had spread out in great force and numbers and were rushing forward without order.

They fought fiercely as long as Antiochus resisted—for he did resist—even though his army was being slaughtered like herds of animals. But when he too fell—for he was accustomed to expose himself to danger more than the others—all the enemy forces were destroyed. Most of them perished scattered in a confused flight; the remainder were driven into a village called Annana and, deprived of food, were consumed. Scarcely any of them survived such a disaster.

## CHAPTER TWELVE
This success also led the Damascenes to seek Aretas as their king, so that he might rule Coele-Syria and Syria, in order to exclude Ptolemy, whom they were pursuing with the bitterest hatred. Nor did he leave Judaea free from invasion. After his victory there, although Alexander had been defeated, he nevertheless departed according to the agreement made between both sides [Col. 1971B] and returned to his own territory.

Alexander, however, destroyed Pella and marched against Gerasa, preparing to add to his possessions certain territories belonging to Theodorus; he claimed it for himself by force of arms. From there he advanced into Syria and destroyed Gaulanitis, Seleucia, and Gamala, taking revenge for the humiliation suffered in the earlier war; he also demolished the fortifications of Antiochus. From these places he turned his march toward Judaea and, contrary to expectation, was received with joy by the entire nation because of the remarkable success of his achievements. There, when the rest gained from warfare gave rise to illness, and he had been somewhat afflicted by recurrent quartan fevers, he experienced a brief alleviation of his condition and resumed his military affairs. Since he observed no moderation, being stronger in spirit than in body, he weakened all the vigor of his health and exhausted his strength [Col. 1971C], and thus died.

He had therefore held the kingdom for twenty-six years amid varied turns of fortune and against countless disturbances of war. He died leaving two surviving children, whom he considered unequal to the direction of the kingdom, and entrusted the supreme power to the care of his own wife, since he knew that she was more acceptable to the people. For this reason she found favor with everyone: she had always considered it necessary to show herself wholly opposed to her husband’s savagery, so that she not only avoided sharing in his crimes but also, by resisting his injustices, turned the goodwill of the entire populace toward herself.

Nor was her husband’s judgment misguided. The woman exercised the right of kingship without opposition and, without any hindrance arising from her sex, gained the people’s approval in governing through her observance of the sacred law. For while more attentive care was devoted to the temple and the ministers of fraud were dismissed, the power of the government grew stronger; yet maternal affection did not weaken her desire for the kingdom. From her two children she selected one [Note: [Col. 1971D] “For appearance,” as below, chapter 42. ID.] as a prospect for kingship, not as its possessor: Hyrcanus, the elder by birth, milder in character. Aristobulus, on the other hand, more vigorous in spirit but deprived of power, she softened by the humiliation of private life.

The Pharisees attached themselves to the woman. They were a class of men trained according to the teaching of the law, but crafty in the quality of their ambitions, eager for affairs and desirous of money. Seeking to flatter the haughty little woman, they made themselves her authorities by exalting her according to their knowledge of divine law, with the result that she entrusted many affairs of the kingdom to them. They admitted whomever they wished, excluded whomever they wished, and stripped men of court office. What more need be said? They insinuated themselves so successfully that the profits of every advantage came to them, while the expenses and burdens affected the woman alone.

The woman was no ordinary spirit, but dared the greatest undertakings and organized wars beyond the condition of her sex. She assembled an outstanding force from her own people and gathered huge contingents of foreign armies, so that she would be secure at home in every matter relating to the safety of her rule and would also be feared by foreign powers. Yet although she surpassed everyone else, she obeyed the Pharisees as though she were inferior to them.

There was a certain Diogenes in her kingdom, who had attached himself to her intimacy as one of the most powerful of Alexander’s friends [Col. 1972B]. They attacked and killed him, recalling that, on his advice, Alexander had crucified those eight hundred men in the middle of the city. Orders were also given that vengeance should continue against the other perpetrators of the crime [Note: [Col. 1971D] This expression is absent from the manuscript. ID.]. Thus those whom the Pharisees commanded were killed, not those whom participation in the crime had implicated.

Terrified by this fear, many of those threatened with such dangers—and especially those most distinguished by wealth or rank—begged Aristobulus to intervene, so that he might turn his mother away from carrying out the harsher decree and incline her toward better measures. Wishing to gain favor for himself, he did not refuse. Although reluctantly, the woman nevertheless yielded to her son’s request: out of regard for the honors those men had held, and for which they were being brought under suspicion, the sentence of supreme death was softened. She ordered only those whom she suspected of having been instigators of the crime [Col. 1972C] to leave the city [Note: [Col. 1972D] “Of the crime committed.” ID.]. Having received security for their lives, they scattered through the countryside.

## CHAPTER XIII

At the same time circumstances arose requiring that troops be sent toward Damascus, because Ptolemy was terrifying the inhabitants of that city with repeated incursions. The necessity of this undertaking occupied a strong force from the army at Alexandria. Cleopatra, too, had been shut up under siege in the city called Ptolemais by Tigranes, who ruled the Armenians; Alexandra sought to placate him with gifts so that he might be turned away from her. Lucullus, however, having invaded the Armenian territories, compelled him to return without accomplishing his purpose, since he judged it more prudent to protect his own possessions than to add those of another [Col. 1972D].

While Alexandra was occupied with such extensive affairs, she fell ill. Aristobulus seized this opportunity for his own schemes. Gathering a force and joining with those whom the ardor of their nature, eager to attempt every rash undertaking, had drawn to him, he seized the treasuries. With their resources he invited volunteers into military service and hired them for pay, so that they would pledge their loyalty to everything he wished. He put on the royal headband.

Hyrcanus, disturbed in spirit, approached his mother with tears. But she, breathing ferocity, shut Aristobulus’ sons and wife in the fortress called at first Baris and later Antonia [Col. 1973A], which we mentioned above. Alexandra’s plans were cut short by her swift death. Hyrcanus succeeded to the whole inheritance; while his mother was still alive, he had assumed the dignity of the priesthood.

Aristobulus excelled in courage and wisdom. Matters were brought to the point of confrontation and battle, and when the fighting began, most of those who had abandoned Hyrcanus followed the other brother, considering him the better in war. Hyrcanus, accompanied by those who had remained with him in the war, fled to Antonia.
