There he found Aristobulus’ sons and wife and secured his safety through hostages, since Aristobulus, by agreement, took care that nothing harsh should be done to his own family [Note: [Col. 1973D] An old manuscript reads *conventus*. BARR.].

The agreement between the brothers was as follows: Hyrcanus would yield the kingdom, and all authority would pass to Aristobulus; yet Hyrcanus would not be left without honor, but would be permitted to hold another dignity, which Aristobulus himself would confer upon him, though he would have no share in the kingdom [Col. 1973B]. This settlement, also sanctified by the religious authority of the temple, secured the voluntary assent of both. They then departed amicably, and after greeting one another, Aristobulus withdrew to the royal palace, while Hyrcanus peacefully went to Aristobulus’ house.

## CHAPTER XIV

But there were some whom fear and the change in circumstances had unsettled, who remembered that they had acted against Aristobulus, especially Antipater. He was an Idumaean by birth [Note: [Col. 1973D] “By his ancestors.” ID.], distinguished among his people for his character, possessed of no small wealth and therefore of very great power. By remarkable skill he had learned to despise money in order to win favor.

He frightened Hyrcanus with his counsels, arguing that he had no secure hope of safety after having withdrawn from power unless he protected himself by defection. When he had inclined him toward his own schemes, Antipater suggested to King Aretas that a man who had been surrounded and forced to yield the kingdom should be supported with aid. It would be honorable for a king to become the arbiter who restored the kingdom; and it would be far more glorious if he ordered the wrongful removal of the man to whom the kingdom originally belonged to be corrected by stratagem. Aristobulus, he said, was crafty and cunning and therefore suspect to his neighbors; Hyrcanus was gentle and peaceful and would accept as the greatest favor whatever an outsider might grant him, especially since his brother had deprived him of his right to rule.

Having announced to Hyrcanus that Aretas’ favor had been secured, Antipater offered him the hope of escape and showed him the route, so that he might go with him to Petra, situated on the borders of Arabia, where they could approach the king. Aretas, persuaded by the entreaties and gifts of Antipater [Col. 1973D], attached a very large force of warriors to Hyrcanus in order to restore him to the kingdom.

There were nearly fifty thousand infantry and cavalry. Aristobulus, driven back at the first encounter, fled to Jerusalem and remained there, unable to withstand such a great multitude of enemies. They would have captured the city, had not Scaurus, commander of the Roman army, lifted the siege on the occasion of another war being waged against Tigranes. He had been sent by Pompey, whose anger over the recovery of Mithridates was intense and who had become eager to transfer the war against his father-in-law. For this reason he had ordered Syria to be harassed through Scaurus, while he himself pressed Tigranes and Armenia [Col. 1974A].

When Scaurus arrived at Damascus—which Metellus and Lollius had completely destroyed—the envoys of the brothers met him, each asking for Roman assistance on his own behalf. Although Aristobulus was inferior in strength, he nevertheless prevailed through the offer of money. The outcome of the entire armed conflict was sold for three hundred talents, and the justice of the petition was weighed out against its price.

After the money had been paid to him, Scaurus ordered Hyrcanus and the king of Arabia to withdraw from the siege; if they persisted, they were to understand that they would have to wage war against Pompey and the Romans. Terrified by this threat, they abandoned the siege. Aretas went to Philadelphia, while Scaurus returned to Damascus.

Aristobulus, scarcely yet able to gather a force sufficient to ward off danger, pursued the enemy. At Paparion—this is the name of the place [Note: [Col. 1974D] “Papyrenus,” Josephus, book I, chapter 5, *On the Jewish War*. ID.]—he routed in battle six thousand of the enemy, together with Phallion, Antipater’s brother [Col. 1974B]. The hopes of Hyrcanus and Antipater collapsed, since all their confidence had rested on the strength of Arabia.

## CHAPTER XV

But when the great Pompey began to approach Syria and arrived at Damascus, they—having been weakened by the Roman auxiliaries and having lost victory from their grasp—asked for help and approached Pompey as a just arbiter and one by no means greedy for money.

They therefore began to rely on arguments rather than gifts, as before. His upright mind could not be caught in the snares of avarice or corrupted by money, and he could hate without payment the man who had plotted against his brother’s honor. They accordingly attacked him with complaints which both aroused hatred against Aristobulus, since he had unworthily seized what belonged to another, and won Pompey’s favor for Hyrcanus, to whom the right of ruling belonged either by the merit of his life or by the support of age, especially with the authority of his mother, who had possessed both the power to choose and the right to confer the kingdom.

Aristobulus was not long absent, although he saw nothing in Pompey’s great spirit that suited his own methods. Nevertheless, he relied upon the redemption arranged by Scaurus and boasted of his association with him. He came dressed in royal attire and surrounded by a display more elaborate than usual, as though one who disagreed with the judgment being rendered could exclude any presumption of submission and deny any expectation of obedience.

Yet he could not long endure the superiority of the Roman consul, whose custom it was to command kings who had obtained a kingdom. When they reached the city called Diopolis, Aristobulus withdrew elsewhere, disdaining the arrogance of Roman dignity [Col. 1974D] through the pride of kingship.

Aristobulus’ withdrawal provided a considerable cause for offense. The consul was so deeply angered that he immediately turned the Roman arms toward Judaea, with many of Syria’s auxiliaries also joining him. When Aristobulus learned that Pompey was approaching the city of Scythopolis and from there the place called Coreae, where the possession of Judaea began, he fled to the strongly fortified castle of Alexandrium, situated on a very high mountain.

When Pompey learned this, he ordered him to descend. Aristobulus, however, considering it dishonorable to obey as though responding to a master’s command, judged in his unrestrained spirit that it was better to face danger than to obey authority. But when he looked down upon the Roman camp crowded with people, and was at the same time warned by his own men not to provoke those to whose name and power almost the whole world had submitted, he descended. He made extensive use of arguments by which he tried to establish that the kingdom had been lawfully conferred upon him: by hereditary obligation, by the judgment of the army, which had followed the stronger and abandoned the cowardly, or by the outcome of battle and the terms of the agreement. He then returned to the fortress.

When Hyrcanus again approached the consul, Aristobulus, summoned to judgment, presented himself. But when he saw that the hearing was still being postponed, he returned to the fortress. Caught between hope and fear, he thought that by obeying Pompey’s commands he might incline him toward his favor. Yet, lest he should again be compelled by force to yield, he withdrew to Alexandrium.

The Great One did not overlook the king’s cunning. He ordered Aristobulus to depart from the fortifications and required him to bind himself to do so by giving written orders to each of the fortress guards. Aristobulus obeyed the commands, which he did not dare reject, but immediately concealed himself within the walls of Jerusalem and began preparing for war against the Romans.

Pompey pursued the fugitive, pressed the besieged, and allowed no time for preparations of war. A messenger redirected the Great One’s attention to Mithridates, announcing that he had ended the war by his death. Pompey was holding Jericho in its surrounding territory when news of this event arrived. Near the city was a place where balsam grows and springs up among shrubs. The farmers’ boys cut these plants with stones, and through the cuts a liquid drips like beautifully glistening tears [Col. 1975C].

Then the veteran soldier, having arranged his ranks, moved camp at evening. At first light he stood before the walls of Jerusalem and, taking them by surprise, poured armed battalions into the city.

## CHAPTER XVI

Astonished by the appearance of the army’s formation, the strength of its men, and the eagerness of its soldiers, Aristobulus came forward voluntarily, begging pardon and offering money, the city, and himself. With soft and submissive words he had moderated the consul’s indignation; but his petition was useless because his promise lacked fulfillment. Not only did he refuse to provide the money, but Gabinius, who had come to receive what was being offered, was also excluded from the city [Col. 1975D], and war descended upon it.

Pompey, having stationed guards over Aristobulus, began to inspect the city walls and carefully investigate the places where he might attempt a breach. But when he observed both the strength of the walls, which could not easily be stormed, and the temple, surrounded within the city by fortifications no weaker than the walls, he hesitated in uncertainty for some time, since the attack would involve a double danger—from the temple’s defenders and from those who guarded the wall’s battlements [Note: [Col. 1975D] Gronovius, *Monob.* p. 67, restores: “He remained uncertain in mind and undecided in judgment for some time.” GALLAND.].

Suddenly a sedition arose within the city. Hyrcanus’ supporters wished to admit Pompey, while Aristobulus’ defenders resisted. The former opened the gates to Pompey; the latter barred them and brought on war so that they might not surrender the king. But the weaker party yielded to the larger number, whom fear of Roman power had strengthened, and withdrew into the temple after the bridge had been destroyed—the bridge that provided a pass and joined the city and temple in the middle.

Thus the Roman army was received into the city, and the Jews themselves opened the gates for them, soon to become the conquerors of the city and temple. The saying of David was fulfilled: “God, the nations have entered your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple” (Psalm 77:1).

They therefore surrendered their royal insignia of their own accord and yielded to the court officials. The task of protecting the royal palace and the rest of the city with a strong force was entrusted to Piso, a distinguished man among his people and trained by military service [Col. 1976B]. He carried out this duty carefully, as though he had led the Roman army to defend those places rather than to seize them.

Because the temple was being stubbornly defended, Pompey prepared Jewish allies—namely, the followers of Hyrcanus—so that, if possible, the Romans would not profane religious rites belonging to others. At the same time he made the Jews fill the ditches with their own hands. Their hands served in an impious task and shameful obedience, “their hands in the basket, their minds in sacrilege” (Psalm 80:7). Yet the work of piling up earth achieved nothing, since Aristobulus’ supporters resisted from the walls and hurled obstacles down from above.

Pompey’s initial efforts would have been fruitless had not the sacred religious days intervened [Note: [Col. 1975D] “By intervening.” BARR.]. On those days ancient Jewish observance required them to abstain from every kind of work. Pompey therefore ordered his men to continue raising their mounds of earth. The Jews considered it permissible to take up arms only in the act of joining battle, when battle had been initiated and the ultimate danger threatened their safety; all other conflicts they regarded as contrary to religion [Col. 1976C].

The rampart had already risen; the siege engines had already been brought up. The king’s men, made more aggressive by the height of the walls, resisted and did not yield even when the fighting brought Pompey closer. Pompey marveled at the fierce spirit of the men, the beauty and size of the walls, and the priests’ duties, which were nowhere relaxed amid the fury of war. It was as though profound peace prevailed: nothing was lacking from the solemnity of the sacrifices. The blood of the sacrificial victims flowed among weapons and the deaths of combatants. A victim was placed upon the altars; men were struck down before the altar.

The third month now held the still-undecided struggle [Note: [Col. 1975D] “Held … the tower of the walls.” ID.]. First came Sulla, born of Cornelius, Faustus, and two centurions, one named Furius and the other Fabius. After lowering the earthworks by the walls, they burst into the temple. Rank after rank followed them, and surrounding the temple’s interior on every side, they pierced with swords all whom they found. Some fugitives were cut down; others who resisted were slaughtered.

There was no restraint in sparing anyone, yet this savagery among the combatants did not interrupt the services of the priests [Note: [Col. 1976D] “Of the prophets,” that is, the priests, as is clear from the context. The distinguished Mazochius discusses this passage at length in his *Commentary on the Neapolitan Church Calendar*, vol. III, p. 771. GALLAND.]. The enemy threatened them with drawn swords, but they performed their customary service without any disturbance. No part of the ritual was interrupted. Everything that could pertain to the solemnity of purification and the observance of sacred worship was fulfilled.

Such was their care in performing the ministry—and would that it had been for the sake of true devotion and faith! Still greater dangers arose from their own people than those inflicted upon them by the Hebrews against one another. The internal battle became more violent, and the danger from the rebels was nearer and more uncertain: in front was the external enemy, behind and on the sides, enemies from within.

## CHAPTER XVII

Thus, surrounded on every side, some threw themselves down, while others were consumed in the fires of their homeland. The priests nevertheless persevered in their office to the very end, encouraging one another not to place the duty of religion behind the defense of their lives [Col. 1977B]. They said that they would be treated rightly if they devoted to piety what necessity demanded, and that it would be most glorious if they could be buried in the bosom of their homeland.

What benefit would it be to escape and live on after religion had perished? It was better to die in the performance of one’s sacred office, a noble deed. If anyone abandoned it through fear of danger, that was sacrilege; if anyone fulfilled it, that was sacrifice and the victory of a pious suffering.

Thus the priests, wearing their sacred headbands, were sacrificed among their own victims, and clothed in priestly robes they lay upon the ground among the corpses of the slain. Twelve thousand Jews were killed there; only a few Romans perished, though many were wounded.

Yet amid that misery the Jews lamented nothing more deeply than that the mysteries of their sanctifications, previously concealed, had been uncovered and revealed to the gentiles. Finally, Pompey, avoiding such unnecessary concerns while seeking rather the glory of a triumph, saw, with many of his men following him, the tent that was open only to the high priest on his ceremonial entrance. He looked inside and saw the lamp, the table, and the incense vessels [Note: [Col. 1977D] Alternatively, *thymiamateria*. The author writes below, book V, chapter 9: “Inside, the incense vessel; inside, the table; inside, the lamp.” That reading seems to belong here as well. The word *thymiama*, that is, incense, has no place here, since after the lamp and table there remained the golden altar of incense, namely *θυμιατήριον* (*thymiaterion*), which should have been mentioned. Moreover, *thymiaterion* ought to have been written rather than *thymiamaterion*. See Mazochius, cited above, p. 794. GALLAND.], the tablets of the Testament, and above them the cherubim, together with a quantity of scattered spices and two thousand talents of sacred money.

Although there was a great amount of gold among these objects, Pompey, wholly free from every desire for wealth, ordered that both it and any sacred vessels that might be found should remain untouched. On the day after the destruction, he ordered Theocorus [Note: [Col. 1978D] Perhaps *Neocorus*. ID.] to cleanse the inner parts of the temple and restore the customary sacrifices.

He also granted Hyrcanus the dignity of the priesthood, making use of his ready assistance during the necessity of the siege. For although he was unfaithful to his own people, he was faithful to the Romans, so that his own homeland might be conquered. Yet I think no one can be called faithful who has been hostile to his own people.

Thus he had not merely offered passing assistance to the enemy in the very battle itself, either by withdrawing from Aristobulus’ alliance the multitude of the people beyond the walls who were supporting him, or by providing everything Pompey, as an outstanding commander, required either to forestall Aristobulus and guide his authority or to bring the war swiftly to an end [Col. 1978A].

Pompey added this notable quality: in victory he maintained restraint. Finally, he won those whom he had conquered more by kindness than by terror, putting to death only the leaders of the war. He also imposed tribute upon the defeated, appointed a governor, and fixed the boundaries of Judaea.

Thus Judaea was confined within its own borders. He also restored Gadara, which the Jews had destroyed, at the request of Demetrius, who had asked this favor for his homeland from his patron. In this matter, and in many others, Demetrius surpassed the status of a freedman to such an extent that he became an object of envy.

Pompey ordered Aristobulus to be taken captive to Rome together with his sons and his father-in-law. But one of the royal offspring escaped from the guards during the journey and returned home. His name was Alexander; he was older than his brother, and there were also two sisters. Antigonus, younger in age, was brought to the city together with his sisters. Pompey then proceeded through Cilicia [Col. 1978B] and afterward to Rome.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Meanwhile in Syria, Scaurus, who was in command, recovered the inland cities that the Jews had invaded: Scythopolis, Hippo, Pella, Samaria, Jamnia, Marisa, Azotus, and Arethusa. Among the coastal cities were Gaza, Joppa, Dora, and the place formerly called Straton’s Tower, later named Caesarea, under the rule of Herod, who both added to its ornamentation and changed its name.

Scaurus was preparing war against the Arabs, with Judaea lying between the Euphrates and Egypt. He also restored Syria within its proper boundaries and restrained it by his judgment and from the desire to plunder—which, I think, was the more likely motive rather than any wish to extend the empire.

He wished to invade Petra, the capital of the Arabian kingdom, but was prevented by the difficulty of the terrain and could not force his way in. Nevertheless, he devastated many places, some near the city and others far away. His army was delayed in those regions and suffered from hunger. A deplorable crime would almost have occurred had not Hyrcanus, through Antipater, supplied provisions to the Romans in their distress. On Scaurus’ advice, Antipater also urged Aretas to end the war by payment.

At last the Arab freed himself from the enemy for three hundred talents and bought off Scaurus. This was the price of his withdrawal. The event strengthened Hyrcanus’ loyalty with the Romans and fostered alliance and security in profound peace, since, in hostile territory, his efforts relieved the Roman army from severe want by providing an abundance of grain and ready assistance.

## CHAPTER XIX

But when Alexander escaped from Pompey’s chains, at first secretly gathering a force suitable for himself, and then began openly to travel through Judaea, Hyrcanus became troubled and distrustful of his own position. The Romans were urgently concerned that the war should not grow. Alexander had even decided to rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, which Pompey had destroyed, and had nearly begun the work when Gabinius, who succeeded Scaurus, judged that Alexander’s attempts had to be opposed. He had energetically settled the other matters by which he had spread fear of his name [Col. 1979A].

Alexander did not think he should retreat. He dared to decide the matter in battle with ten thousand infantry and one thousand five hundred cavalry. He also repaired the fortresses of Alexandrium, Hyrcanium, and Machaerus, intending them to serve as refuges for himself if circumstances demanded, or as obstacles to his enemies, since Arabia, which was not sufficiently loyal to the Romans, lay nearby.

To meet him as quickly as possible, Gabinius sent Marcus Antonius ahead with part of the army, so that the enemy’s march might be obstructed until he himself arrived with the entire force. Antipater came with picked troops, while Malichus and Pitholaus, supported by separate bands of Jews, joined their strength to Antony’s.

When Alexander saw them massed together—for Gabinius was now also present—he changed his plan and began to retreat. But when they were already not far from Jerusalem, he was forced to join battle. Defeated, he fled. Nearly three thousand of his men were killed, while the rest were captured or scattered. Only a few survived with Alexander, more for companionship in flight than from any courage to rebel.

Finally, seeking peace from Gabinius, he also surrendered the fortresses to the Romans so that they would not regard anything as suspicious. In that war Antony’s courage shone brilliantly, although everywhere he gave outstanding proof of his bravery.

Gabinius divided Judaea into five administrative districts in order to reduce the power from which excessive insolence in public affairs arose. Because of his mild character, Hyrcanus retained the honor of the priesthood. But responsibility for the affairs of the entire region was assigned by Gabinius not to one man but collectively to the inhabitants of Jerusalem [Col. 1979C]. The other districts were likewise assigned in the same manner, being divided among Gadara, Amathus, Jericho, and the people of Sepphoris—that is, the more important cities—so that nothing would remain for the power of individuals and the administration of the regions would not falter while awaiting public oversight.

This arrangement was welcomed both by the Romans, because it revealed and diminished the fear of rebellion, and by the Jews, because it removed the cause of resentment with their approval. The Hebrew people would live not under a king but under leading men, in imitation of the Roman republic, in which no single person ruled but the best men in turn administered the offices that had fallen to them by lot. Though excluded from kingship, they were the arbiters of kings. This arrangement was prudently judged suitable for restraining the restlessness of the nation.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 1979D]

But Aristobulus’ flight and return to Judaea had aroused considerable disturbance among many people. Those whom old friendship had attracted to him, or whom desperate circumstances had led to seek a remedy in public discord, flocked back to him. They wanted to mix the lowest things with the highest, especially since their other hopes had failed.

After returning, Aristobulus began to build fortifications and repair Alexandrium. When Gabinius learned this, he sent Sisinnius, Antony, and Servilius with part of the army and stopped the work that had begun. Aristobulus abandoned the fortifications and prepared for war. Since he was leading a force larger in number than usefulness, he relieved the multitude of the people of their weapons and gathered only eight thousand armed men. Pitholaus also joined him, having come voluntarily from Jerusalem with one thousand men [Col. 1980A].

Then battle broke out, with the Romans pressing upon his heels. The Jews fought bravely for some time, but Roman valor prevailed, and five thousand Jews were killed. Aristobulus broke through the line with one thousand men and withdrew into the defenses of the fortress of Machaerus. Two thousand others scattered elsewhere; nevertheless, the Romans who attacked the fortress were delayed for nearly two days, since Aristobulus was fighting with all his strength in this final peril.

He could not hold out any longer. He was captured with his son Antigonus, whom he had taken with him when escaping from captivity, and they were sent to Gabinius. Gabinius sent them on to Rome. The Senate placed Aristobulus under guard and sent his sons to Bithynia. They say that Gabinius had indicated in letters that this had been promised to Aristobulus’ wife as a reward for her diligence in handing over the fortifications to him [Col. 1980B].

## CHAPTER XXI

After these events had taken place in Judaea, Gabinius thought that he should attempt something and prepared an expedition against the Parthians. But suspicions concerning the faction of King Ptolemy recalled him from his undertaking. Gabinius therefore turned his march from the Euphrates toward Egypt. In everything he made use of the necessary services of Antipater and Hyrcanus—though Hyrcanus acted through Antipater. They assisted the army with money, grain, weapons, and auxiliary troops. They especially helped with the engagements around Pelusium; unless Jews familiar with the region and with every aspect of the war had arranged everything, those encounters would easily have deterred Gabinius.

While the army was again delayed, Alexander, the son of Aristobulus, attempted to plunge into Syria as though it were a vacant province. Gabinius, however, was roused by reports and hastened his return. He sent Antipater ahead, who recalled many Jews from Alexander’s alliance. Relying on their numbers, Alexander was preparing to send all Romans whom he encountered in the region into exile.

Although most of the Jews dispersed through Antipater’s intervention, Alexander did not abandon his boldness. He joined battle with thirty thousand men, but near Mount Itabyrion ten thousand were routed and he fled. The dispersal of the rest brought the war to an end.

Gabinius, having arranged the affairs of the Jerusalem republic according to Antipater’s wishes, departed from there and defeated the Nabataeans in battle. He secretly allowed Mithridates and Tigranes, who were fleeing from Persia, to escape, but publicly told the soldiers that they had slipped away in flight.

Gabinius was succeeded by Crassus. As he was about to depart for the Parthian war, he took all the gold that was in the temple at Jerusalem. In addition, he ordered two thousand talents to be removed, which Pompey had left untouched. He did not enjoy this for long: when he crossed the Euphrates, he lost his army and was himself killed.

The Parthians, made more confident by this success, believed that they should cross into Syria. Cassius received them bravely in an ambush and drove them back beyond the boundaries of the province entrusted to him, not without serious loss to the enemy. The Parthians had advanced in a disorderly manner because they thought no one would dare oppose them, but Cassius had occupied the narrower places in advance. Finally, after many of their men had been routed, they abandoned the war.

Cassius, having repelled the enemy and feeling secure in the province [Col. 1981A], invaded Judaea. After destroying Tarichaea, he sold thirty thousand Jews into slavery. He also ordered Pitholaus to be executed, suspecting him of treachery because he was supporting Aristobulus’ faction.

Antipater was not free from responsibility for this decision either, since he wished above all to exclude a rival to his power.

## CHAPTER XXII
Antipater had married a woman named Cypris, born into the most distinguished rank among the women of Arabia, and by her he had four sons and one daughter. The names of the males were as follows: the first Phasaelus, the next Herod, the third Joseph, the fourth Pheroras, and the daughter Salome. By this means, having become a man of exceptional ability in winning the alliance of powerful men through gifts and friendship, he had secured for himself, above all others, the favor of the king of the Arabs, since he claimed kinship through the region of Arabia from which his wife came. Finally, when preparing to engage Aristobulus in battle, he sent his sons to the aforementioned king of the Arabs as pledges of mutual affection. The king received them as an inviolable deposit, treated them with the same regard that he showed his own children at home, and later returned them to their father when they were reclaimed.

But while Aristobulus, defeated in war, was being held in chains, and his son Alexander was abstaining from battle in accordance with the terms of the peace by which Cassius had bound him when he was returning to the Euphrates; while the borders of Persia were being disturbed by no suspected passage of the Parthians, and the appearance of a seductive tranquility in the East was relieving human anxieties—Caesar, pouring into the transalpine regions of Gaul and into Italy, drove Pompey and the Senate beyond the Ionian Sea. Excluded from Italy, Magnus made for Aemathia and ordered Roman armies to follow him there from various regions, because he was preparing for war in that place.

While Caesar was occupied with these operations, Caesar—who was between the city of Rome and Pompey, since he was following Magnus by shortcut routes from the Via Flaminia to the Via Appia—released Aristobulus, whom he had left bound at Rome, from his chains, assigned him military forces, and sent him into Syria so that he might attach Judaea to himself and press Pompey from the rear, either by receiving Pompey himself or by intercepting his army. But at the outset of his undertaking, when he had reached the appointed place, Aristobulus was killed by poison and left the enterprise unfinished.

The belief that he had been murdered was attributed to Pompey’s supporters. Thus Caesar’s plans and Aristobulus’ ambitions were thwarted by a remarkable succession of changes, so that he had been safer as an exile among enemies and as a captive in chains than as a citizen among his own people, a master in his chamber, and a king at table.

When Pompey learned this, since Aristobulus had attempted to renew the wars in Judaea for himself,

[Note: Thus also the author below, Book III, final chapter, uses *recidiva praelia* for wars revived—imitating Maro, for whom in *Aeneid* X and elsewhere *recidiva* means “arising again.” Tertullian likewise often uses the word in this sense; for example, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 18: “The Scriptures,” he says, “promise the revival (*recidivatum*), that is, the resurrection, of the flesh.” MAZOCH.]

he ordered his son Alexander also to be put to death, because he was regarded as excessively favorable to Caesar’s party. Scipio, obeying the orders of Gnaeus, brought the accused before the tribunal so that the appearance of a trial might be maintained; accusers were also introduced, and a sentence was pronounced against the man who had disturbed the Roman state with arms, so that he might be considered to have been struck down by the executioner under the authority of the law rather than in the execution of an order—according to the practice by which enemy commanders convicted of rebellion were believed to be put to death.

## CHAPTER XXIII

When the deaths of both men became known, Ptolemy, who had received Aristobulus’ brothers and Alexander’s wife, sent his son Philippion to the city of Ascalon to summon the brothers. On his arrival, Philippion received Antigonus and his sisters in order to escort them to their father. Through association and the habit of affection, a spark of love crept upon the young man—an occurrence surely pardonable, if tyrants knew how to pardon—and he took one of the sisters in marriage.

His father Ptolemy could not endure this. After killing his son, he openly took his daughter-in-law as his own wife: an excellent censor of morals, who condemned in his son a union so unforgivable, while he himself polluted himself with parricide and incest.

After Pompey was killed—when, fleeing Caesar’s arms, he offered his head to be severed by an Egyptian eunuch—the situation changed. Yet he offered his head with the patience becoming one who had so often conquered so many peoples: contemplating, in the lot of the defeated and the condition of an exile, the mockery and instability of human affairs, he offered his neck to the sword, about to receive death as a favor from the man to whom he had given a kingdom.

After his death a change occurred, with most of Magnus’ associates seeking Caesar’s friendship, and Antipater in particular displaying an extraordinary aptitude for winning the friendship of everyone whose alliance he desired. For resources are necessary to all, especially in the preparation of wars, where enemies and adversaries are very often made dearer than friends. Indeed, because Ptolemy, king of Egypt, had violated his good faith, Caesar himself was pressing him with the most serious wars.

## CHAPTER XXIV

The Pergamene Mithridates, repulsed by the obstacles at Pelusium with all the forces he had led with him, had settled at Ascalon. Having despaired of passage and failed in his attempt, he no longer dared to commit himself to battle, since the ground was unfavorable and he was inferior in strength.

Antipater first summoned Arabians to his aid, and then led with him three thousand Jews, a powerful force equipped with arms. He also stirred up the leading men of Syria to support him: Ptolemy, who lived in Lebanon, Jamblichus, and another Ptolemy. Relying on their alliance, other peoples too were inflamed for war.

Strengthened by these additional forces, Mithridates approached Pelusium. When he was prevented from crossing, he undertook a siege. There Antipater gave a remarkable demonstration of military skill. While the townspeople resisted and the battle raged on both sides with the utmost force, Antipater was the first, with his men, to break through the section of the wall where he himself was fighting, burst into the city, and capture it.

Nor was this the end of his exertion and assistance. When the army advanced inland, the Judaeo-Egyptians in the region called Onias wished to resist and cut off its route. Antipater not only removed the obstacle of battle but also compelled those who had prepared to take up arms against the army to provide whatever was necessary for human use in support of it.

As a result, the Memphites too abandoned their intention of fighting and willingly surrendered themselves to Mithridates’ alliance. Passing by the more suspect districts, Mithridates decided to engage the remaining Egyptians in battle, on more open ground but with stronger men, in the very region whose Jewish inhabitants were called the army. He fought vigorously, to the point of exposing himself to extreme danger and nearly being killed. He would have perished if Antipater, seeing the entire force with Mithridates pressed on the right flank by a cohort and enclosed on the other side by a river, with no means of escape for the men, had not charged from the left wing against those who were pursuing Mithridates as he retreated. Antipater pursued them until the entire enemy population was destroyed.

In that battle Antipater lost only eighty of his own men, whereas Mithridates lost more than eight hundred, though he himself escaped contrary to expectation. This disaster followed in a single moment.

Antipater, having received many wounds in his body, found in Caesar an outstanding witness to his valor. Mithridates in particular not only testified to his acquittal but also proclaimed his courage. Caesar was greatly pleased by these circumstances and, as was proper, received Antipater among his friends in his honor.

Then, after arranging what had to be settled in Egypt and proceeding into Syria, Caesar bestowed upon him honors belonging to the Roman state. He also presented him with a talent and granted him other pledges of his favor, as to a man whom he approved. He likewise confirmed Hyrcanus in the high priesthood, following Antipater’s advice.

## CHAPTER XXV

Antigonus too met Caesar in Syria. He had undertaken, more from resentment than grief, to lament either the misfortune of his father, who had been killed by Pompey’s associates with poison, or the punishment inflicted upon his brother, whom Scipio had struck down with an axe in the height of cruelty. He accumulated the gravest complaints against Hyrcanus and Antipater, alleging that they were laying claim to what belonged to others—things that had been criminally snatched from him and his brothers; that he had been driven from his ancestral dwelling; that the land in which he had been born was denied to him.

Yet he claimed that his own injuries seemed more tolerable than those much more bitter injuries inflicted upon the entire Jewish people by Hyrcanus and Antipater. He further argued that they were claiming gratitude for the achievements in Egypt, although no diligence in assisting Mithridates had been offered from any innate goodwill toward Caesar; rather, fear arising from their known association with Pompey had extorted it from them, so that it could serve as a pretext for avoiding offense.

Against these charges Antipater did not answer with words but with a demonstration of facts. He tore his garment and, stripped of clothing but covered with wounds, exposed to the eyes of those standing around him, through his torn and disordered cloak, the proofs of his tested valor.

“Behold,” he said, “the evidence of my ill will toward Caesar. Let these wounds, which shine like the lights of my soul, defend the accused. To you, Caesar, I offer these scars as pledges of my inward loyalty. These I deposit as tokens of my faith, and I bear upon my heart letters engraved there. If citizens are not believed, let the enemies be questioned for whom I received those wounds. What else were they pursuing in me except the loyalty that I was bringing to you?

“But he charges me with gratitude toward Pompey. I confess, Caesar, that I was a friend not of a man but of the Roman name, and that I strove earnestly to make my services available to your state. Thus I served not one man but all. Pompey may have been dear to me, but he became my friend before he became Caesar’s enemy. He was your son-in-law, and you were his father-in-law. When he was in the regions of Judaea, I assisted him as a Roman commander; yet I did not receive such wounds for him as I did for you. For you I offered guarantees of death and received the blows of enemy weapons.

“What wonder is it, however, if a captive does not understand the honor of wounds, or a fugitive does not know what loyalty is? What else could a perpetual enemy charge me with except your friendship? It is surely astonishing that Antigonus should approach Romans whom he habitually attacks in war, and complain before them that he has been stripped of the power whose use and administration he desired not for his own authority or domestic distinction, but to provoke Roman arms and avenge the deaths of his father and brother.

“Let an ingrate who does not fear the Roman tribunal of salvation even dare to attack it openly, although he knows that there his accomplice in rebellion has paid the penalty. Let him not be afraid!”

When Antipater had finished speaking, Caesar declared that Hyrcanus seemed more worthy of the priesthood. To Antipater he granted the choice of authority. Antipater then sought him as the arbiter of honor and the governor of his own distinction, making the measure of his honor depend upon the one who bestowed it. In this way, with considerable cleverness and modesty, he secured both honor and an increase of power.

For Antipater was made procurator of all Judaea. He also requested that the walls of Judaea, which had been destroyed in the war, be rebuilt. Confident in the guarantee that had been given him, he both requested and obtained this. In accordance with the custom of Roman commanders, whatever Caesar judged should be conferred upon Antipater as marks of honor was recorded in the Capitol by Caesar’s authority, so that evidence of his justice and of the man’s merits might remain for the knowledge of posterity.

After accompanying Caesar from Syria, Antipater turned his journey toward Judaea. First, he restored to its former condition the wall that Pompey had destroyed. Then he suppressed disturbances, visiting each person with parental affection—sometimes with gentler admonitions, sometimes with threats—so that they might judge that what belonged to peace rather than war ought to be pursued and that they should not provoke the king’s temper.

If Hyrcanus remained unoffended, Antipater said, he would prove a citizen; if he were angered, he would show himself a tyrant. Even if Hyrcanus were gentle by nature, they should nevertheless take care not to embitter him by insult. Antipater himself was also eager to act for the common good, out of dutiful concern rather than authority. But if they attempted any acts of violence, he would not lack the will to punish them, and they would learn to value the friendship of the Romans rather than domination.

For who could doubt that his friends would burst into arms if they learned that the man whose kingdom they themselves had secured had been stripped of his kingdom?

At the same time, because he knew that Hyrcanus, owing to the sluggishness of his disposition, was slow to carry out the duties required by public affairs, Antipater thought that the responsibility for protecting the region should be divided among his sons, since Hyrcanus was unequal to so great a burden of rule and authority.

Accordingly, he appointed Phasaelus, the elder of his children, governor of Jerusalem and commander of the army. He also placed Herod, younger in age and still very much a young man, over Galilee with equal honor. As soon as Herod had acquired authority, his naturally energetic disposition for undertaking business immediately found material for its exercise.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Syria was suffering from the incursions of the brigand Hezekiah. As leader of a predatory band, he was ravaging the entire province and hostile everywhere. Herod seized him and ordered him to be put to death, and he killed many of the brigands. This brought him great glory for valor and earned him favor among the Syrians. As a result, he was celebrated in the cities and villages by the voices of singers, as though after a long period he had restored public peace and quiet.

This report, carried along by the favorable rumor of the common people, aroused in Phasaelus a noble rivalry in his younger brother’s praise. Phasaelus sought to equal him in generosity of spirit by attracting to the foremost place men distinguished for their goodwill, whose severity he tempered with kindness. Hence the greatest honor was also paid to Antipater, as though he were the father of the state. Yet Antipater himself changed nothing in the goodwill and loyalty with which he had been accustomed to honor Hyrcanus.

But it is difficult to escape envy in prosperity. At first Hyrcanus was quietly provoked by the young men’s praises; more forcefully, however, he was irritated by the brilliant achievements reported of Herod’s actions. He saw that Herod had advanced beyond the laws of the Jews and beyond the limits proper to a private citizen, claiming all power for himself, together with his brother and father, and stripping the king of every honor except the name—a hollow appearance that presented an empty semblance of authority.

Finally, without consulting Hyrcanus, many men had been put to death without royal orders, although the law of the fathers did not permit them to perish. Hence many said that Herod ought to be summoned to trial so that he might give an account of why he had violated the law that forbade the execution of persons without a hearing. Hyrcanus ought to rise up, they said, and determine by this whether Herod was conducting himself as a king or as a private citizen.

If Herod, when summoned to court, failed to appear, it would be clear how far his arrogance was aspiring. By such words and others like them from the king’s attendants, Hyrcanus was gradually inflamed by envy. They reproached him with an excessive shame born of indolence, because he had abandoned the rights of royal business and transferred authority to Antipater and his sons, whom he had made masters while diminishing for himself the freedom to reign.

Stirred by these accusations, Hyrcanus resolved that Herod would not fail to appear before his court, where he would clear himself of the charges that he had usurped powers contrary to the laws.

Although Herod was indignant at being summoned to trial, he nevertheless approached, either because of his father’s admonitions or on the advice of more peaceable counselors, after securing the fortifications of Galilee. Yet he came neither with an ostentatious procession, which might seem to threaten war, nor with a secure military escort, which would reveal his fear for his safety. He was also supported by Sextus Caesar, who was favorably disposed toward him. Fearing that an ambush might be laid for the young man, Sextus had issued strict orders to Hyrcanus that he should avoid the danger of a harsher trial.

Thus Herod owed the acquittal of the trial more to Sextus than to Hyrcanus’ will, although Hyrcanus, despite having yielded to those who accused Herod and wished to summon him to trial, acquitted him willingly at that time, since he preferred to preserve the young man rather than prosecute him.

But Herod, grieving the insult with youthful ardor and ungrateful for the acquittal, proceeded to Sextus with the deliberate intention that, if he were summoned again, he would not obey. He thus gave his detractors an opportunity to bring accusations against him. Although Hyrcanus did not rise up for revenge when he saw that Herod was the stronger, Herod, nevertheless stirred by the recollection of the insult—which grows stronger through deliberation—gathered an army and marched toward Jerusalem to abolish all Hyrcanus’ authority.

He had nearly achieved this, except that the force of his attack was broken and gradually subsided through the counsel of his brother and father. They begged him to consider that he had already risen up sufficiently and to put an end to threats of revenge. They urged him to refrain from bringing about the death of the commander, under whom he had attained no insignificant favor, enabling them to acquire so great a power.

It certainly seemed an injury that he had been summoned to trial, they said, but on the other hand he had been treated with favor because he had been acquitted. It would be excessively harsh to pursue an injury and be ungrateful for his own safety. The outcome of wars was uncertain and precarious. There would also be a heavy burden of envy if he brought arms against his own commander and against one who had cherished him with paternal affection, had often assisted him, and had never harmed him except when, by employing bad counselors, he had raised against him the shadow of an injustice under which Herod believed himself deceived.

## CHAPTER XXVII

By these and similar arguments they broke the young man’s attack. The civil war was removed from Judaea, but through Roman intervention it was transferred and turned against the Romans themselves.

For Sextus Caesar was treacherously killed by Caecilius Bassus. Later Julius Caesar, after exercising perpetual power for three years and seven months, paid a heavy penalty in the Senate because he had gone beyond the status of a private citizen, with Cassius and Brutus as the instigators.

Accordingly, when the cities had assembled, and Julius Caesar’s adopted son had resolved, with Antony joined to him, to avenge his father’s death, Herod was believed to have provided the greater part of the war effort through the forces he sent. The responsibility for governing all Syria was therefore entrusted to him.

This became the cause of Antipater’s fatal death.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Malichus feared the power of Antipater, which was being increased by Herod’s valor. He corrupted one of the royal servants and prepared poison for Antipater. After drinking it, Antipater died immediately after the banquet—a man energetic in every other matter and especially vigorous in seeking and strengthening Hyrcanus’ rule.

Herod took his father’s death very hard. Having gathered an army, he promised to avenge it. But his brother’s counsel recalled him, lest Judaea be ravaged by civil war between Herod and Malichus, who was preparing to resist and was especially concealing his knowledge of Antipater’s murder.

Herod was easily diverted to another form of revenge. After accepting an assurance that Antipater had died without any deceit on Malichus’ part, Herod invited Hyrcanus and Malichus to dinner, following the decision of Cassius, who had also assigned this task to his own men sent to carry out the revenge.

Centurions and commanders of the Roman army, prepared to meet Hyrcanus and Malichus as they came ashore, surrounded both men with drawn swords. They killed only Malichus, however, stabbing and mangling him with many wounds until he met his final end.

Overcome by the terror of this event, Hyrcanus lost consciousness and collapsed, deprived of all strength of mind and body. After recovering somewhat, he asked Herod who had ordered Malichus to be killed. When he learned from the commanders that Malichus had been killed by order of Cassius, the Roman commander, he immediately replied:

“Then Cassius has been the savior of both me and my country, since he destroyed the plotter against us both.”

Whether Hyrcanus said this out of fear or truly thought so is not clearly evident and cannot be determined by our judgment.

Elichus had risen up, wishing to avenge Malichus’ death because of their brotherly relationship. But because he did not dare to attack Herod, he thought that Herod’s brother Phasaelus should be attacked. When Herod learned this and wished to take action, illness prevented him.

Meanwhile Elichus occupied certain fortifications, especially Massada, by placing garrisons there. But when Herod’s health and strength returned, he recovered everything and dismissed Elichus himself, who had pleaded with Herod at the fortress of Massada.

Antigonus, the son of Aristobulus, had also challenged Herod’s power, aided by his father-in-law Ptolemy. Herod defeated them in battle, drove out Antigonus, and returned victorious to Jerusalem.

He enjoyed great favor because of his recent triumph and, especially, because of his new marriage. At first Dosis had been his wife, by whom he had a son, Antipater. Later he had married Mariamne, daughter of Alexander son of Aristobulus, in a second marriage. She was closely related to Hyrcanus and possessed royal nobility on that account.

Yet he did not escape the resentment caused by his ambition to wrest the kingdom from Hyrcanus. When Caesar and Antony defeated Cassius and Brutus in the Macedonian war, the victors proceeded in opposite directions: one hastened to return to Italy, while the other believed that he should hurry into Syria.

Many deputations arrived, and the leading Jews gathered before Antony and proceeded into Bithynia, accusing Herod and his brother Phasaelus on the ground that they had violently seized control of everything and had left Hyrcanus only the name as an appearance of honor.

But Herod’s presence and influence prevailed. He had bound Antony’s spirit to himself not merely with a considerable sum of money but also with splendid gifts. As a result, Antony did not even reproach him in speech and neutralized the resentment directed against him by the deputation.

Again, nearly one hundred Jewish men proceeded as far as Antioch with no less determination to bring accusations. At Daphne they encountered Antony, who was already wholly devoted to Cleopatra’s love and serving her desires. There they began to denounce the brothers’ intolerable power.

Messala, on the other hand, refuted them while standing beside Hyrcanus. He condemned the arrogance of the people, who, stirred up by the faction of a few, rejected their own men, sought outsiders, and used Hyrcanus’ injury as a pretext, although Hyrcanus had preferred what was advantageous to his fellow citizens.

After hearing the allegations of both parties, Antony asked Hyrcanus which men he thought more suitable. When Hyrcanus’ preference agreed with Herod and his brother, Antony was greatly pleased that the answer corresponded to his own wishes. He was bound to the brothers by the relationship of their father’s hospitality, since Antipater had received him most graciously as a guest when he arrived in Judaea with Gabinius and had honored him with many services.

Antony appointed Herod and Phasaelus tetrarchs and ordered them to administer all Judaea.

The number of those bringing complaints increased from this point. Although Antony had received some of the envoys into custody and had treated others with insult, those who remained nevertheless later went as envoys to Antony, who was staying in the city of Tyre. After a revolt had broken out at Jerusalem, he ordered them to go, and they did not fail to carry out the wishes of their fellow citizens.

Although severe punishment had been inflicted upon those who protested, they nevertheless dared to raise the uproar again. Antony sent the governor of Tyre to seize the guilty men for their arrogance. Both Herod and Hyrcanus sought to prevent this, lest the most serious punishments, disturbances of the homeland, and causes of war arise there.

When nothing was accomplished and everything began to be thrown into confusion by irrational contention, Antony sent armed men. Some of the protesters were killed and others severely wounded. Hyrcanus, however, granted burial to the dead and medical care to those who had been able to escape, providing a twofold opportunity for humane conduct by which his goodwill toward his fellow citizens was made evident.

The rest who had escaped so exasperated Antony by their agitation of the city that he ordered the ultimate penalties even against those whom he held in chains.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Arrogance had yielded to severity. But over the course of nearly two years, the Parthian army poured into Syria, led by Pacorus, the king’s son, and Barzapharnes, satrap of the Persians, who commanded the barbarian host.

They were joined by Lysanias, son of Ptolemy, whose father had died and who had borne the surname Mennaeus. Having already been stripped of power by the aforementioned satrap, Lysanias enticed Pacorus with promises of a thousand talents of silver and five hundred women, in order that Pacorus might give the kingdom to Antigonus and remove Hyrcanus from the priesthood.

Pacorus gave part of his cavalry to the royal minister—for he himself was detained by rebellions within Syria—so that the minister might cross into Judaea, conduct the affair on behalf of Antigonus, and assist his cause.

Yet this would not have advanced even so far if the Jews, divided against one another, had not taken up arms—Herod and Phasaelus on one side, Antigonus on the other—and if the leaders, following Antigonus’ judgment, had not proposed that they receive Pacorus as a mediator of peace.

Phasaelus, with his naturally accommodating character and against Herod’s opposition, approved this course at the wrong moment and soon discovered it to be destructive to himself. He learned that barbarians are naturally faithless. Sent to Barzapharnes as though to an executor of peace, he went with Hyrcanus to meet the satrap, who skillfully concealed an ambush beneath a show of kindness.

Finally, as they were preparing to depart, Barzapharnes gave them gifts while arranging how they might be surrounded by his plans. Guards accompanied them more for the purpose of custody than as companions in danger.

Messages were brought that the Parthian had been bribed with a thousand talents to bring about the destruction of the men mentioned above. Ofellius also urged flight, because he had learned from Saramalla, the most savage of the Syrians, that a plot had been prepared against them.

Yet even then Phasaelus was not persuaded to abandon Hyrcanus and provide for his own safety. Instead, he attacked the satrap with severe insults, accusing him of betraying his trust for a price, of valuing money more highly than justice, and of offering more for his own safety than Antigonus was paying for the kingdom.

The Persian, attempting by perjury to reconcile to himself the trust he had betrayed and to dispel every suspicion, perpetrated the deception not long afterward. For when he had departed to Pacorus, those to whom the task had been assigned seized Phasaelus and Hyrcanus, who—since they could no longer do anything else—cursed the barbarians and desired to avenge their perjury and treacherous betrayal.

[Note: Some copies read *vini* (“of wine”); for the name Ninus is not found in Josephus. BARR.]

Ninus’ minister, sent into Judaea, had also used deception as a pretext for capturing Herod. But Herod, who had long suspected the barbarians’ ambushes, was kept intensely alert by the need for caution and remained within the fortifications.

When Pacorus sent false orders for him to meet his brother concerning Phasaelus and his arrogance, Herod did not think that he should leave the walls and expose himself to the enemy’s words. When he learned that his brother and Hyrcanus were being held, he sent his own men into Idumaea by night, while he himself attacked and routed the pursuing barbarians.

After killing many, he hurried to Massada. Yet he found the Jews who had fallen upon him in flight more dangerous than the Parthians. He placed his own men within the fortifications and took revenge upon his pursuers.

He himself, however, left garrisons to protect his mother and younger brothers and hastened into Arabia Petraea.

The Persians poured into Jerusalem, rushing into the houses of the fugitives. Everything was turned to plunder, war, and disorder. Their violence went so far that the kingdom was handed over to Antigonus, while Phasaelus and Hyrcanus were delivered into his power to undergo whatever he wished.

Antigonus, however, could not restrain himself for long. He immediately attacked Hyrcanus and bit off his ears with his own teeth, so that no reversal of circumstances might ever open for him a return to the priesthood. For it is necessary that the high priest be physically uninjured, and it is clear that the law does not permit anyone with a mutilated body to perform the supreme office of the priesthood.

Phasaelus forestalled the insult by hastening his own death. He dashed his head against stones that happened to be nearby, scorning to be preserved for mockery, or to die at another’s command when, even with his hands bound and deprived of iron, he could find a way to end his life.

There was, however, another account of his death: that Antigonus, after he had been wounded, brought in a physician who poured poisons into the wound as though they were medicine.

Whatever the outcome of these events, they originated in a spirit of exceptional fierceness. It is also reported that Phasaelus added the following at the end of his life, when he was already breathing out his spirit. Having learned that Herod was alive and had escaped the ambushes prepared during his flight, he said that he was dying with gratitude, because he was leaving behind a survivor who would avenge him.

Herod hurried into Arabia, hoping to obtain money, since he believed that only money could bend the barbarians’ greed and enable him to ransom his brother’s captivity. If he encountered an Arabian who had forgotten his father’s affection or was reluctant to return the gifts he had received, Herod intended to request a loan as the price of the ransom, pledging as security the son whom he had brought with him for this purpose, a seven-year-old boy.

But the pious effort of brotherly affection was forestalled by Phasaelus’ death, and Herod was carrying out the duties of fraternal devotion with such diligence in vain.

Before learning of his brother’s death, however, he found Bocchus, king of Arabia, to be unlike the friend he had believed him to be. Bocchus changed his allegiance with the circumstances and, when Herod was already approaching the borders of Arabia, forbade him to enter. He had been told by messengers of the Parthians that he should not receive their fugitive into the kingdom of Arabia, lest he create for himself the cause of a very serious war.

Offended by this, Herod immediately replied with the words that grief had prompted in a just outburst of anger, and from there turned toward Egypt.

Soon afterward Bocchus regretted his violation of their former goodwill and sent men to recall Herod, but Herod had already gone on ahead. When he entered the regions inhabited by the Rhinocolurae, he learned through reliable reports both of his brother’s death and of Hyrcanus’ captivity—Hyrcanus had been taken under guard into Parthia. He was overcome by as much grief as he had laid aside anxiety, and therefore prepared flight rather than war.

Finally, he hastened with the greatest determination to Alexandria. There Cleopatra received him with honor, believing that a man of such distinction should be sought as a military commander for her cause.

He therefore set aside the queen’s requests and sailed for Rome. He judged the lesser storms of winter and the disturbances of Italy, which he knew, less serious than the waves that he feared would be more dangerous than all shipwrecks in Cleopatra’s fickleness.

At last, having departed despite unexpected blasts of wind, he encountered danger near Pamphylia but nevertheless escaped. Changing ships, he reached Brundisium first and then Rome.

There he approached Antony on the strength of their fathers’ friendship. He lamented his own misfortunes and those of his close relatives, for whose sake he had come to Rome to plead while they were under siege.

He moved Antony to pity, since such a great reversal of circumstances had occurred: a once extremely powerful king, who had repeatedly brought assistance to the Roman state, had suddenly changed his position and, like a shipwrecked man deprived of everything and lacking all aid, was humbly imploring help for his people placed in danger.

In this matter Antony was already strongly inclined toward him by gratitude for the hospitality he had shared with his father Antipater, especially because Antipater

[Note: “Idumaea”; another reading is “into Idumea.” BARR.]

had left him as tetrarch of Idumaea, destined for the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXX
Caesar, however, being more expansive in his natural benevolence, held dear both Antipater’s military service, endured in Egypt and in all the battles of his father Caesar, and their hospitable alliance, as though fresh pledges of gratitude had renewed it. Yet he suspected the king’s crafty character, perversely directed not toward equity and goodness but toward the interests of his own affairs. When permission was granted to approach the Senate, Messala and Atratino commended the good services of his father, as well as Herod’s own services to the Roman commonwealth; and by authority of the senators it was decreed that Herod’s kingdom appeared useful to the Roman empire. With Antonius supporting the motion, it was judged advantageous, in the war then being waged against the Parthians, to join the alliance of the aforesaid king to the Romans.

When the Senate had been dismissed, Caesar, Antonius, and Herod emerged together from the curia and were escorted by the official services of the magistrates. On the first day on which Herod’s kingship had been conferred by decree of the Senate, Antonius prepared a banquet and invited the king. At almost the same time, Herod’s brother Josippus had arranged to flee by night because of the lack of water. But suddenly such a great quantity of rain poured upon the land that it filled all the watercourses. Thus, abandoning the defection he had been planning to the Arab people, he routed the forces of Antigonus, who was besieging him, partly by ambush, partly by engagement and open battle; yet he himself, often meeting with an unfavorable outcome, withdrew into the fortress.

By now Herod had arrived unexpectedly from Italy at Ptolemais, a city of Syria. He quickly departed by ship and, with a great force of citizens and foreigners, moved against Antigonus. The commanders of the Roman army, Ventidius and Silo, came to meet him; Antonius had ordered them to be present in escorting Herod. Gellius, although opposed to the purpose for which Antonius had sent them—since Antigonus had turned both of them aside by bribery—had nevertheless advised them, under the pretext of meeting at close hand, to join Herod. Ventidius was indeed staying in the neighboring cities to suppress the disturbances of the Parthian war, while Silo, stationed within Judaea, was arranging an open alliance with Antigonus through money.

Yet Herod did not need their assistance, for all except a few Galilaeans had joined him. Since his intention was to rescue his people from the siege at the earliest opportunity at Massada, he captured Joppa, situated midway and crowded with the enemy’s forces, by fighting, so that if he advanced farther he would not leave the enemy behind him. Although Antigonus wished to impede his march, Herod nevertheless recovered Massada with little difficulty and rescued his people from danger.

Then he set out for Jerusalem. He had done everything to avoid being forced to fight, asserting that he had taken up arms on behalf of his fellow citizens against rebellion, not against his own people. But when he was attacked by the supporters of Antigonus, he drove them into flight with arrows and light javelins as they opposed him from the wall. There would have been no delay in the victory had not Silo, commander of the Roman army, secretly arranged for soldiers to complain of scarcity, to allege that everything around the walls had been devastated and that supplies were difficult to obtain and provisions insufficient, and to threaten that, since the time had already come when they ought to withdraw to winter quarters, they would break his authority unless their demands were satisfied.

The mutiny had already gained strength, had Herod not placed himself between the Roman centurions and soldiers and entreated them not to abandon one whom Caesar, Antonius, and the Senate had entrusted to their protection, especially since he promised that nothing necessary for their needs would be lacking. After completing his speech, he went out into the region and suddenly caused an abundance of everything to be supplied to the army, so that Silo had no complaint left. Then, with the courage of all raised, he recovered Idumaea with two thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry.

When the Roman army had become quiet and had been stationed in winter quarters, Josippus, the leader of the undertaking, was chosen for the easier task, since he thought that nothing should be attempted against Antigonus at greater risk. Herod himself, after transferring his people from Massada, remained in Samaria, having made provision for whatever he believed would serve for defense and use. In the freezing winter, when every place was filled with snow, he anticipated his arrival by sending a messenger to Sephorim—an ancient name, later changed to Diocaesarea—and entered it without any battle. He judged it suitable for restoring those whom the winter frosts and the harsher frozen roads had exhausted; for there was also a great abundance of provisions there.

When the soldiers had been restored by food and by a pause in their stationing, he decided that battle should be undertaken against the brigands who ranged throughout the whole region and afflicted its inhabitants no less than by a military incursion. Accordingly, he first sent part of the cavalry and infantry ahead to the village of Arbela, and he himself arrived with the rest of the force after forty days.

The brigands were not, however, terrified by the appearance of the army. Thinking that they should meet it with weapons, they displayed both military discipline and the boldness of brigands. After the engagement had taken place, Herod’s left wing gave way. But Herod quickly repaired the situation; bringing up reinforcements, he restored his men, routed those who pursued them, and broke the force of their attack. They could not endure Herod fighting at close quarters. As they withdrew as far as the Jordan, he pursued them and delivered them to death. All the rest were scattered above the river, so that Galilaea might be freed from all fear of their incursions. Only those remained who, concealing themselves in hiding places and, as it were, burying themselves in caves, delayed the victory.

There were, in the precipitous mountains, in the hollow sides of the rocks, terrifying caverns among jagged crags, inaccessible from every direction except to the inhabitants of the region. By means of crosswise paths and narrow tracks, by which alone they were accustomed to be approached, they had made themselves secure through familiarity with danger, so that they might be safer when danger was detected. Inside were blind recesses of caves; at their entrance a rock, projecting like a continuous ridge over the deep gatherings of water, excluded the hope of access. Everywhere the footing was slippery; waters fell from the mountain brows, and the broken course of streams made the precipice of the rushing waters seem to collapse, while the overhanging rock, crashing down, added still more terror.

For some time afterward the king remained uncertain, unable to discover how he might overcome nature. Later, however, he used the following stratagem: he enclosed the strongest men in fortifications fashioned in the manner of chests. He lowered armed men by means of certain ropes to the very mouths of the caves. These men began easily to force out the unarmed and to kill them together with all their families and children; and if any dared to resist, they burned them by casting fire upon them.

There was no room for pity. Indeed, although Herod wished to rescue many from death and give them confidence to take refuge with him, he achieved the opposite, so that no one voluntarily joined Herod; and if any were compelled to do so, they preferred death to captivity.

Finally, one of the elders, who had with him seven sons and a wife whose safety he might have sought to preserve, killed them all in the following manner. Ordering each one in turn to come forward, he himself stood at the entrance and killed each son as he advanced. Herod, looking down upon so dreadful and pitiable a deed and moved by paternal sympathy, restrained him with his hand and begged him in words to spare his children, promising him impunity. But the man was in no way softened by any appeals; indeed, he heaped insults upon the king. In addition to his sons, he killed his wife, throwing the bodies of his children down from the height, and finally hurled himself headlong into the depths.

Antigonus was terrified by this, since Herod had then easily overcome both the multitude of brigands and the difficulty of the terrain. He avoided Herod’s presence, but turned against Ptolemy, whom Herod had placed in command of part of the army. Antigonus, a man highly suited to the stratagems of war, unexpectedly compelled Ptolemy to be slain by those accustomed to disturb Galilaea. He also destroyed Josippus, Herod’s brother, who was vigorously resisting while his brother was occupied in other regions, together with the Roman soldiers who had rashly gathered and come to his aid.

Not content with so great a triumph, he added a grievous insult to the dead man: he ordered his severed head to be left behind. In return for it, Pherora, the slain man’s brother, offered fifty talents, but could not obtain it. As a result of this victory, the allegiance of many throughout Galilaea was again turned toward Antigonus, and the business of war was renewed.

Herod had hastened to Antioch and was resting there in a pleasant place called Daphne. When he received news of his brother’s death, he groaned briefly over his suffering, set aside his grief, and prepared vengeance. Antigonus could not endure the man raging with grief but hid himself within the fortifications. Herod burst in to pursue the authors of so great a crime and easily drove back the forces that met him. There was a great slaughter of many; the roads were blocked by fallen corpses, so that the very routes were filled with the funerals of the slain.

The battle would have been completed, with everyone turned to flight, if Herod had judged that he should immediately direct his march toward Jerusalem. Antigonus had thrown down his spears, fearing the ultimate punishment. All were thrown into confusion by fear. Thus, when Herod had been recalled from the pursuit by the severity of winter, and had entered a bath after laying down his arms, accompanied by only one servant, three men with drawn swords came upon him. Then there were more, men who had fled from the battle and were seeking hiding places. When they saw the king, they were so disturbed by fear that they hurried past him toward the exit of the bath, in order to escape—men who had been able to undertake the killing of the king and bring the war to an end.

In the end, no one seized the fugitives. From this Herod inferred how great a dread was present in the enemy. He threw himself into battle and killed Pappus himself, the commander of the opposing force, ordering that his head be cut off because his brother Josippus, the king’s brother, had been killed by him.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Meanwhile Antigonus delayed the flight he had planned. While he lingered, Herod surrounded and besieged him with his army. He attacked on the side facing the Temple, the same side on which Pompey had once stormed the wall. The king’s confidence in victory had by then become so great that, even after the siege had begun, he turned aside to marry the daughter of Alexander, changing the trumpet-call of war into a wedding trumpet and mingling marriage with warfare. Having found an opportunity for the union during the battle, he returned from the festivities to the war.

Sosius also arrived, sent by Antonius to aid the king. With their forces joined, and with the Romans superior in military experience and discipline while the king’s men exerted themselves in their eagerness to please him, an assault was made only in the fifth month, when Herod’s men dared to climb the wall.

When the Roman centurions rushed into the town, innumerable massacres took place, and everything around the Temple was devastated. Some fugitives were slaughtered at the Temple; others, gathered inside their houses, were cut down. There was no pity for old age, none for infancy or feminine weakness.

Antigonus presented himself and, forgetting where he was, threw himself at Sosius’s feet. But Sosius, whom so great a reversal of fortune ought to have reminded of mercy, insulted the prostrate Antigonus and called him a woman; yet he did not spare him as one would spare a woman, but bound him and thrust him into prison.

Herod was torn between two concerns: how he might rescue his homeland from Roman hands and how he might preserve the Temple undefiled by foreigners. For the Romans were hastening to see the inner mysteries and profane the Holy of Holies. The king, now by entreaty and now by threats, tried to restrain them individually. He judged a victory worse than flight if any of the sacred rites were disclosed.

The Romans pressed on toward the plunder; Herod resisted, lest they leave him an empty city and leave only a deserted kingdom for him to rule. Sosius, on the other hand, maintained that the plunder of the captured city was owed to the soldiers. But the king personally promised the soldiers that he would give them money. In this way he redeemed with money what remained of his homeland. To fulfill his promise, he received the soldiers with the utmost humanity, treated the commanders reasonably, and rewarded Sosius himself with royal generosity. No one departed ungrateful.

Sosius offered a crown to God and departed, taking Antigonus with him to Antonius. Antonius struck him with an axe, as though he were a man of degenerate spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXII

Herod also gave very generous gifts to his own people and presented many gifts to Antonius and his friends. Yet he could not purchase his own safety from Antonius. For Antonius had by then become enslaved to Cleopatra’s love and served in submission to her desire. But he could not overcome feminine greed—especially the greed of a woman practiced in the murders of her relatives, whose possessions she had added to her own as spoils after destroying them.

With the same greed and cruelty, whenever she learned by reputation that anyone in Syria was especially wealthy, she killed him. And now that Antonius had become subject to her desires, she thought that the kingdoms of Judaea and Arabia could also be added to her greed once those who ruled each nation had been destroyed.

Although drunk with lust and weighed down by sleep, Antonius nevertheless came to his senses in this matter, refusing to destroy such men and such powerful kings for the sake of an exceedingly insolent woman’s dominion. Yet, so as not to send them away untouched, he struck at their friends and deprived them of the greater part of their possessions, especially the territory that produced balsam. He also assigned to Cleopatra’s desire all the cities lying within the Eleutherus River, except Tyre and Sidon.

Won over by such payment from her husband, Cleopatra accompanied Antonius as he departed for the Parthians as far as the Euphrates, then returned through Judaea. There Herod did not fail to win the queen’s favor by the greatest gifts and presents. His prosperity increased his arrogance, so that feminine insolence raised itself beyond measure.

Indeed, not long afterward the Parthian king Artabazes, son of Tigranes, a most powerful king, was given to her as a gift. Antonius held him captive, though he was entitled by triumph to all Persian booty and spoils, and assigned him to the woman as though he were a worthless slave. Thus, the more illustrious the victory had been, the more disgraceful was the gift that dishonored a king with such mockery.

Yet he did not long enjoy prosperity, since he did not know how to use it. Through feminine arrogance he roused Augustus against himself. Accordingly, the Actian War was being prepared with great exertions on both sides.
