The king was extremely eager to undertake the war with Antonius, since Judaea was free from enemy disturbance and he had recovered Hyrcania, which had long been held by Antigonus’s sister. But in this too Herod was most fortunate, in that he was spared involvement in the dangers of others.

Therefore Cleopatra, wishing to estrange and turn his mind away from the kings, advised her husband that Herod should wage war against the Arabs. If he were victorious, Arabia would fall to the queen; if he were defeated, Cleopatra’s rule would be extended over Judaea. Whichever of the two won would undo the other.

This plan, not because of its design but because of its outcome, worked against Herod. As soon as he undertook battle, he turned the enemy back because of his superior cavalry. At the end of the engagement, however, he was overcome by the multitude of the enemy and surrounded by their numbers.

When the enemy forces had gathered at Canatha, Herod wished to mass his line against them. His men’s spirits had been raised by their earlier successes, and for that reason they rushed upon the enemy. But he was abandoned, especially through the treachery of Athenion, whom Cleopatra had attached as commander—not to assist Herod, but to abandon him in the very crisis.

Finally, after attacking his abandoned army in rocky and inaccessible places, the Arabs laid it low in a heavy slaughter and routed it. Pursuing the fugitives as far as their places of refuge, they delivered them to destruction. Herod arrived later than necessity demanded; nevertheless, having avenged his distress, he afflicted the Arabs in subsequent battles so severely that they lamented that single victory of theirs again and again.

A serious collapse of morale also occurred because of an earthquake, in which a great number of animals and nearly thirty thousand human beings were destroyed. The entire military force, however, because it was living under the open sky, remained unharmed.

This too raised the spirits of the enemy, so that they thought they could more easily invade Judaea now that it had been deserted and overwhelm those shaken by such portents. Herod therefore thought that he should strengthen them for his defense, especially because he had learned that the ambassadors he had sent to Arabia had been treacherously killed.

He addressed the trembling men in the following speech:

“Although in so many successive battles of our people the fortunes of the enemy have been broken to the point of their own admission, those men, driven by mad grief, have killed our ambassadors as though they had been defeated. I am astonished that irrational fear has so shaken you that you prefer the accidental signs of the elements to the established successes of our valor.

“There was no engagement in which the Arabs did not immediately yield and, turning to flight, consider that they ought to give way. As the chances of war commonly proceed [Note: [Col. 1995D] I would indeed prefer *fata belli* (“the chances of war”). GALLAND.], they sought remedies by treachery and ambush—not to conquer themselves, but to delay our victory.

“Although these things ought to have given you confidence, there has arisen an agitation as if a terrifying war were approaching, because the earth trembled while you alone were unharmed, since you were engaged in battle. Or, if we wish to consider whom the earthquake harmed, we shall judge that it harmed the Arabs more, since it brought them back to war and prevented them from withdrawing by flight from their stronger opponents.

“I see that they have returned to the battle relying not on arms or strength but on the loss of our cattle. Fragile is the hope that depends not upon confidence in one’s own valor but upon another’s misery, since nothing on earth is so changeable as prosperity or adversity. Human circumstances are altered by very slight moments. Prosperity is not lasting, nor is hardship persistent. Thus neither misery nor its opposite is perpetual; rather, circumstances frequently alternate, and their changes vary among the same people.

“Finally, we may take an example from ourselves. In the previous engagement we were the stronger, but as the battle progressed, fortune changed, so that we were defeated by those whom we had defeated. Therefore we too may hope that those who defeated us will be defeated by us.

“Excessive confidence is always careless and neglectful of itself. Fear, however, warns us to look to the future and teaches diligence. In prosperity, boldness creeps in, and rashness without counsel does not know how to await the commander’s decision. In the end, when you advanced against my advice, Athenion’s wickedness found an opportunity to harm you.

“Now let your trembling purchase for you a privileged victory. Therefore raise your spirits and lift up the ancient courage of the Jews. Do not let the movements of insensible things terrify you, and do not consider earthquakes judges of another misfortune. The sufferings of the elements have their own harm; fear nothing except what lies within those very injuries.

“For an earthquake and a plague among living creatures are not signs of dangers but the dangers themselves. There is nothing for us to fear, as though we were going to endure severe things, since we have endured the severest. He who has taken vengeance may now be favorable, and more gentle than if he had not taken vengeance. What remains after an earthquake and pestilence except mercy? For we have paid a double penalty.

“Nevertheless, we retain what is useful for war. The pestilence carried off those who were outside the war; but our victory deprived the enemy of what they had selected as fit for battle. We have dead cattle; they have a scheme, those men who thought that the ambassadors we sent should be slaughtered contrary to human and divine law.

“They have violated the law of all human beings, even of the barbarians themselves. For among them too, though they do not know humanity, ambassadors are held inviolable, since the vengeance of heaven is feared and God, the avenger of so great a crime, is dreaded.

“This, then, is what our opponents have done: a deed that neither human nor divine laws leave unpunished. Let us therefore go forth to fight, not for boundaries or spoils but to avenge a wrong against the divine. Let us be urged to war not by love of marriage or offspring but by the protection of God already promised. We are carrying out not our own judgments but the commands of divine law; we are performing sacred rites so that we may demand vengeance for those whom religion orders to be inviolable.

“Amid hostile arms, an embassy alone stands apart as the representative of peace. The man who performs an embassy lays down the arms of an enemy; now the blood of these men cries to God and demands vengeance. Let us therefore hasten to battle while we have God as the avenger and defender of the slain. They fight better for us and, surrounded by legions of angels, stand before us in the line of battle.”

After encouraging the soldiers with such words, he rushed against the enemy, seeking every opportunity for battle. The Arabs were superior in number but weaker in spirit. When the engagement took place, nearly five thousand of them fell. The rest withdrew into a fortification and were worn down by lack of water, so that they sent an embassy to request peace at a price.

But when they saw that the matter was being prolonged, and when their thirst grew greater as their water ran out, many of them came out and offered themselves to the enemy, preferring to perish by voluntary steel rather than by thirst. Herod kept them bound, lest there be some ambush.

Thus, over five days, about four thousand were captured. When the others came out to battle, about seven thousand men were again killed. By this blow the Arabs were humbled by the king. Although inferior to him in valor, they were superior in strategy: they regarded the enemy they faced as though he were their defender and sought him out for their own protection and assistance.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

But a greater anxiety struck the victor, since the man who had subjected others now feared the danger threatening not merely his borders but his entire kingdom, once Antonius—joined to him by faithful friendship—had been defeated.

Indeed, after Caesar Augustus had triumphed in the Actian contest, he did not yet consider Antonius defeated while Herod remained to the victor. Therefore, when the anxious king learned from reliable information that Caesar had arrived at Rhodes, he sailed to him, lest rumor precede him by land.

On arriving, he laid aside his diadem and presented himself in private attire, but with a kingly mind. In the end, withholding nothing from the truth, he maintained his steadfastness and preserved his authority.

“I confess, Augustus,” he said, “that I was Antonius’s faithful ally, since I received my kingdom from him, and I do not deny that I remain his debtor. I would have proved this by arms if Cleopatra had not been jealous and the Arabs had not hindered me.

“I did not take up arms against you because of that necessity—not as a deserter of a friend or as one fearful of battle, but as one occupied with affairs at home. Yet Antonius did not judge me ungrateful to him, since, though absent, I sent him both military assistance and countless supplies of grain.

“And you too, Caesar, would have judged me not ungrateful for his benefits if I had taken part in the Actian War. See how I conceal nothing. I fear more that I may appear ungrateful to your enemy than that I may appear your enemy. Your judgment is more serious to me than war, before you, in whose presence not the merits of my virtues but my faults are at risk.

“Therefore I prefer to plead my case before you concerning loyalty rather than treachery. See, Caesar, how I did not abandon Antonius while he was still whole, nor avoid him after he was defeated. You conquered Antonius, Caesar, with your great legions; you conquered him by your counsels; you conquered him by the strength of the Roman command, which he abandoned and denied. He was truly defeated by your virtues, but more by his own character.

“Cleopatra, his wife, conquered him; Egyptian love conquered him; the luxury of Canopus conquered him. He was defeated because he preferred to be defeated with Cleopatra rather than to conquer without her. A woman more hostile to her own people than to her enemies conquered him.

“I had advised him to put the woman to death if he wished to take care of himself. I had promised assistance with which I would restore his fortunes; I had promised forces with which I would protect him in flight; I had offered myself as his companion in war. But Cleopatra’s desires had bound his mind. He was defeated because he would not listen to me.

“I too was defeated with Antonius, though with the lesser disgrace, because Cleopatra conquered him while Antonius conquered me. He did not abandon the foreigner; I did not abandon my friend. I laid down my diadem together with him. But, fearing to come to you, I laid aside the insignia of my kingdom in the capacity of a faithful friend, though I did not cast away the consciousness of my courage. Judge me as you wish.

“Whatever the outcome of your judgment, I shall nevertheless carry away with me the fact that my character as a friend will be assessed according to what kind of friend I was.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Caesar replied to this:

“Greetings,” he said, “and now make even greater use of your kingdom, since we do not envy your virtues but delight in them. You are worthy to rule over more people, since you so well protect friendship, refusing to disown a friend when he is in adversity and not being ashamed to acknowledge that he is your friend.

“But it is desirable to attach oneself to the more fortunate and to preserve loyalty in prosperity; in adversity you have already proved it sufficiently. Antonius may have conquered you, but I did not regard as defeated a man whom friendship made equal to his conquerors.

“For this reason you are sought by us: no outcome of war changed you. It was not you who deserted Antonius, but Antonius who deserted you, trusting Cleopatra more than you. His folly acquired you for us, because he chose the most destructive woman for himself and rejected the faithful man.

“And it is no wonder that Antonius, conquered by Cleopatra, clung to her, since he had been captured by her when he was victorious. Why are you surprised that Cleopatra made Antonius abandon you, when she separated him from me and turned him from a partner in command into an enemy?

“Therefore, because you were rejected along with us and for that reason now reign with us, this too is not without its benefit: while we were occupied in civil wars, you subjected the untamed nation of the Arabs, since we regard the enemies of the Jews as our own enemies. Those who attack you bring arms against us.

“You therefore served us when you won for yourself. For this reason we shall reward you, so that your kingdom may be confirmed by our gift. In the meantime, the fact that we have diminished nothing is no small favor. For the future we shall undertake to ensure that you do not miss Antonius. It is not fitting that the man whom we conquered in war should not be conquered by our benevolence.”

When Caesar had said this, he placed the diadem on Herod’s head, adding personal attentiveness to the gift.

Encouraged by this distinction shown by Caesar, Alexander, one of Antonius’s friends, wished to save from punishment a man with whom Caesar was especially angry. He pleaded at length and with many entreaties, but excessive indignation left no room for pardon.

From there, as they departed for Egypt, Herod accompanied Caesar’s journey and supplied everything that would be useful either to Caesar himself or to the army. By this he won the commander’s favor for himself to the greatest degree, especially because, through royal provision, he supplied an abundance of water in the arid regions all the way to Pelusium. By these services he poured such love for himself into everyone that he seemed to have deserved more than he had received.

Even the power of his kingdom was judged less highly than the generosity of his humanity. Therefore, after affairs in Egypt had been settled according to his wishes and Antonius and Cleopatra had died, Caesar not only restored to Herod what had been taken from him but, beyond what Cleopatra had carried away, also granted him Gadara, Joppa, and Samaria. He likewise gave him the coastal cities—Gaza, Arithedana, Joppa, and Straton’s Tower—as well as the four hundred Gallic bodyguards who had surrounded Cleopatra when she traveled, and many other things.

But the king valued all these less because Caesar loved him above everyone except Agrippa, and Agrippa loved him below Caesar alone.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Accordingly, in the fifteenth year of his reign, to correspond to his prosperity and gratitude, he was lifted up by such a great succession of favorable circumstances and turned his attention to piety. To show himself grateful for the heavenly benefits that were flowing upon him beyond measure, he adorned the Temple. He enclosed the entire area around the Temple with a wall and surrounded it with doubled spaces, at immense expense of construction and with elaborate beauty.

The great colonnades around the sanctuary that he built from their foundations were evidence of this. His concern for protection was no less than his concern for adornment. Indeed, he fortified the citadel lying to the north, which he called, in honor of Antonius [Note: [Col. 1999D] It seems that *Antonii castrum* (“the fortress of Antonius”) should be read; or, if preferred, *Antonium* or *Antoninum castrum*, in honor of Antonius. BARR.], inferior to none of the upper palaces.

He also added, in the very citadel, two royal residences of immense size and remarkable beauty, whose splendor one might think impossible to surpass. One of them was called Caesarium and the other Agrippium, so that the enduring memory of such great friends might be celebrated in their buildings.

He also built the city of Sebaste and filled it with inhabitants. And, not to pursue each individual example, he scarcely passed by any site of an ancient city without restoring what was falling into ruin or adorning it with buildings added to supply what seemed to be lacking.

He extended his generosity even to the quinquennial contests, and thus enriched that class of people with lavish wealth.

He also built a temple of white marble for Caesar at the sources of the Jordan, becoming so forgetful of religion that he dedicated a temple to a human being and introduced the practice of the nations into Judaea. The place is called Panium. There a mountain rises high into the sky, reaching upward with its lofty summit; on its side an overshadowed cavern opens, through which the depth of a foul-smelling precipice exhales a savage vapor. Inside there is a gathering of waters and a great mass of water without any visible movement, so that the estimation of its profound depth cannot be grasped.

Outside, around the very roots of the cave, springs burst forth. For this reason many have judged that the Jordan rises there; but for us it seems that what the truth is must be disclosed later.

On the coast there was a city called Straton’s Tower, already weakened by frequent wars and itself sinking into ruin through age. Yet it surpassed other places in convenience and attractiveness of situation. Herod restored it with white stone, adorned it with various buildings, and displayed in it both the power of his generosity and the elegance of his workmanship.

For it lay midway between the two coastal cities, Dora and Joppa. On either side it was bordered by an unfavorable shore, so that all who wished to pass from Egypt through Phoenicia were tossed about on the open sea, because the sea there is frequently stirred by the winds, especially by the Libyan blast, whose moderate breath is enough to raise the waves. At last, striking against the rocks that lie before them and thrown back after their force has been broken, the waves make the savage sea more violent as they fall.

Therefore the king set no limit to his expenditure. By his magnanimity he overcame nature and constructed a harbor larger than the Piraeus. There, by penetrating and removing an immense mass of rock, he arranged safe anchorages.

He also measured out a space suited to the size of the harbor and threw enormous rocks into the sea, some of which reached a depth of fifty feet, while others were even higher. He marked out the harbor with immense towers, one of which he called Drusion, so that he might weave into the insignia of his work the name of Drusus, who belonged to Caesar’s ancestors.

He also inserted shorter steps at frequent intervals, by which ships could be hauled up without great labor. With three enormous colossi he further beautified the entire splendor of that harbor.

Again, he laid the foundation of a temple to Caesar on a higher site, and in the middle of the temple he placed a colossus in the name of Augustus, as though it were his image, no smaller in size than the statue of Olympian Jupiter or Argive Juno.

One would not know whether to admire the beauty amid such difficulties or the strength of the workmanship; indeed, one might judge the fortification to be even more remarkable than the beauty, since the work remains unbreakable against both the sea and the passage of time.

Thus the work acquired a manifold distinction. The city grew greatly within the province; it provided a harbor for sailors; and it honored Caesar, whose name gives the city its present name, Caesarea.

## CHAPTER XXXVI
[Col. 2001B] This royal power, flourishing in the prosperity of success, was brought low by the desired companionship of one woman; and it was broken by grievous sorrows, after he had judged a marriage contrary to human and divine law to be measured by the rank of the family rather than by affection, according to a certain royal custom. He had as his consort a woman named Dosis, a Jerusalemite, previously joined to him in a private marriage; she ought to have been dearer to him precisely because she had been fortunate with her husband, with whom he had attained royal eminence. But, forgetful of gratitude, he cast Dosis aside and joined himself to Mariamne, the granddaughter of Aristobulus and daughter of Alexander.

Thus, while pursuing nobility, he fell into a disorder in which his own household could not be harmonized with the rule of a kingdom obeyed by a people drawn from many different provinces. And, lest the eyes of his new wife be offended by the sight of the son whom Dosis had borne, through the hatred of a stepmother maintained within the house, Antipater—for that was the young man’s name—was expelled not only from his father’s home but from the entire city. He thereby made room for an ill-omened marriage, which the father celebrated by exiling his only son, and to which Antipater was scarcely summoned even for the solemnities of festival days.

When the woman saw that her husband was accommodating himself to her, she was also turned toward arrogance by the reproach of filial devotion. A further cause was added, by which her spirit was rightly inflamed: she knew that her grandfather Hyrcanus had been killed through the treachery of her husband, having been falsely suspected because of his desire for the kingdom. He was the man whom we mentioned above: when Barzapharnes, who ruled the Persians, had occupied Syria, he carried Hyrcanus away captive; at first he was detained in Parthia, but later, when the Jews living beyond the Euphrates requested him, Barzapharnes took pity on his fallen fortunes [Col. 2001D] and allowed him to depart. Would that, just as he had yielded to those who pleaded for him, he had also believed those who warned him not to let the delay characteristic of the human mind, together with the power of his relatives, trouble him—namely, that he should make his way to Herod, since this would expose him to danger, for the desire to preserve a kingdom harasses no one more than one’s closest relations, and one must beware of relatives.

But, wearied by exile and longing for his own people, he crossed the Euphrates and returned to Judaea. This sank more deeply into Herod’s heart than anyone had supposed—not because Hyrcanus had sought the kingdom, but because, as a man of royal lineage and long exercised in the privilege of power, it was uncertain whether he could restrain himself from it. Thus the marriage of his granddaughter became Hyrcanus’s snare of death, for whose sake he had hastened to Herod, unaware that it was safer to live as a captive among enemies than as a relative among kings.

He was therefore killed without even the slightest suspicion that he desired to reign, solely because it seemed that kingship might befit him. Meanwhile Herod loved Mariamne with extraordinary devotion and did not wish to offend her. The woman had increased her claim upon his affection by bearing numerous children. She had given him five sons, but one of the three boys died at Rome while being educated in the liberal arts. The remaining two were honored with royal splendor beyond the measure of private citizens. The young men had the support of their mother’s nobility and of their own birth in a kingdom, since they had been born while their father was already ruling [Col. 2002B]. But Mariamne’s chief support was the love with which the king was daily becoming more and more inflamed. Thus, although she returned no corresponding affection to him, he nevertheless took care not to distress the woman’s spirit in any way.

The woman’s hatred and the man’s love contended against each other on equal terms. Yet Mariamne hated the man who loved her more justly than Herod loved Mariamne, who did not love him. The woman’s hatred was supported by the outrage committed against her; her confidence, by his love. By the one she opposed him because of the wrong done to her grandson; by the other she was exalted through the obedience of her lover.

Therefore she did not even refrain from reproaching him with the crimes of which she accused him: that he had wickedly taken from her both her grandfather Hyrcanus and her brother Jonathan, one her grandfather-in-law and the other her kinsman; the former ought to have been preserved because of the weakness of old age, [Col. 2001D] the latter at least because of his youth.

[Note: In the first Ascensian edition we read *propter senectutis infirmum* (“because of the weakness of old age”), in place of which later editors wrongly substituted *infirmitatem* (“weakness”). Mazochius, cited work, p. 826.]

He had entrusted the supreme priesthood to a young man of seventeen; yet he immediately bestowed the honor upon him and brought about his death. As we have learned, there was no other reason than this: when the young man, dressed in priestly garments, first approached the altars on a sacred and solemn day, the people suddenly burst into tears. Herod suspected this so deeply that, in the midst of his joy, he believed that the people had wept and had thus revealed their affection for the youth—those tears being evidence of their hopes, and the attachment of his people a danger, since they had shown from the depths of their hearts how devoted they were to honoring the young man. He imagined that this noble royal grandson, son of an overbearing woman and brother of a presumptuous queen who scorned the king as her husband, would break out into a bid for power unless he were removed from their midst at once; he possessed beauty and such grace of appearance that he might rightly be judged preferable to all others.

He therefore resolved to kill the young man. The young man’s mother harassed him: she was both more determined to investigate and more vehement in seeking vengeance, allowing nothing to remain hidden and nothing to go unpunished; she was thus resolved to recall him to his senses and restrain him. Again he was harassed by the steadily increasing love of everyone for the young man and by the danger to the kingdom. Driven by this precipitous fury, he decided to protect himself by whatever means he could.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

[Col. 2003A]

The young man was sent at night to the city of Jericho. There he was accustomed to amuse himself by swimming; while many others joined him as though for sport, he was repeatedly plunged beneath the water beyond measure and drowned in the pool.

His sister could not keep silent about this. Moved by sisterly affection, she revealed it through reproaches and accused her husband of having taken her brother from her by his command. She declared that she had been left deprived of everything, that her husband’s house had become a house of mourning for her: first he had taken away her grandfather, then he had killed her brother, and she herself had brought ruin upon her own family. She invoked dreadful curses upon the man, his mother-in-law, and the king’s sister; she called it a crime shared by them all. She appealed to God as avenger, asking that so great a deed not be left unpunished.

Herod endured these reproaches as though captured by love and subject to her every gesture. But womanly anger raged, and he could not bear [Col. 2003B] the curses and the arrogance of the woman who denounced him, especially because, overcome by her native eloquence, Herod could not bring himself to rise against her despite her disregard for him. Therefore, so that he might be provoked still more, as though by a lover, a scene of adultery was contrived, and a charge of this kind was fabricated against the woman: that she had sent her likeness to Antony in Egypt.

What intemperance this would have displayed—that, to a man absent and ready for lust, and moreover a powerful man who used his power as though it were law, she should have offered her beauty for sale so that he might be enticed by her appearance; that, through the commerce of a new auction, she, a woman, could have put herself up for sale, whether through the force of love or through hatred of her husband, whose death she would have demanded as the price of her adultery?

This fabrication of the women—Mariamne being the more deeply loved by Herod, and therefore the more fiercely assailed—was not, however, entirely devoid of truth, although it came from enraged women. For it was probably true that Alexandra, raging because another was preferred to her son Aristobulus in the priesthood—for she preferred that her own son be called Jonathan, so that the name might recall that his grandfather had been king—had asked Antony through a certain Musurgas, an intermediary in correspondence, to grant the priesthood to her son.

Then, when Gellius, a friend of Antony, arrived in Judaea, it became known that the young man was regarded with wonder because of the excellence of his appearance. Mariamne was no less so: the brighter her rank, the more illustrious her reputation. It may also have been discovered that, according to a certain tendency of human nature, men wish to show themselves dearer to their intimate friends by indulging even their present relations with the fellowship of hospitality [Col. 2003D]. There, too, Alexandra, as a freer widow, was given the opportunity to converse with Sosius, and she could not have lacked other opportunities for learning about the guest, especially since circumstances and persons of this kind invited it.

Then, after counsel had been exchanged on both sides, they decided that the likenesses of both of them should be sent to Antony. Struck by the brilliance of the portraits, and especially by the testimony of Sosius—who asserted that he had never seen anything like them anywhere on earth and that they possessed a beauty not human but divinely alluring, calculated to arouse the least sober desires of a man—Antony wrote [Col. 2004A] to Herod that he should send Aristobulus to him without delay. As for Mariamne, Antony omitted mention of her because [Note: Herod, naturally, was the person to whom the phrase refers. BARR.] she was joined to Herod.

This was not because Antony was accustomed to conceal his lusts, or to restrain himself from married women in their husbands’ presence—for he could gratify himself without danger and commit outrage without shame—but because he wished to avoid Cleopatra’s anger. She was offended by a rival of either sex, but especially if she discovered a woman joined to a husband, since she believed that she surpassed all women in beauty.

After reading the letter, Herod excused himself on the ground that he could not remove a noble young man from his people without causing a popular uprising and disturbing the entire nation. To satisfy Alexandra, he promised Aristobulus the priesthood. But when he saw that the fulfillment of the promise was being delayed and thought that he was being mocked by a trick, Alexandra prepared a ship; when her preparations for flight became known, she was recalled, together with her son, through the intervention of Sabion.

Moved by this, Herod concealed his injury for the time being and hastened to confer the priesthood upon Aristobulus, so that the odium of a planned murder might be concealed beneath the appearance of an honor. Once this had been done, as we have said, he was shaken as though struck by lightning. At the same time he was tormented by the charge of alleged adultery, fabricated by his own people, knowing Antony to be eager for lust and, because of the extent of his power, to inflame desires of every amorous kind.

He feared that Cleopatra’s implacable grief and especially her savagery in rivalry threatened him. She had killed many men whom she had found, as older men, restraining the excesses of their wives. He therefore dreaded not only the loss of his wife but also the necessity of undergoing death himself.

[Col. 2004C] He therefore resolved to make his way to Egypt, in order to divert Antony or Cleopatra, whom he feared above all. Others report that, summoned there by a letter from Mark Antony, he went in order to give an account of the young man’s death.

Before departing, however, he secretly disclosed to his kinsman Josephus—whose wife was Salome, the king’s sister—that he suspected that his death was desired because of his wife’s beauty, which the woman was alleged to have revealed by sending an image of her appearance. He entrusted this matter to his kinsman as follows: if he himself were killed by Antony, Josephus was to kill Mariamne, so that no reward for the outrage would remain.

Josephus, as I think, did not disclose the command from a desire to betray Herod, but in order to quiet the woman’s complaints against her husband, by which she said that she was tormented and burning with hatred of him. He reported the order and interpreted it in the spirit of a lover, saying that Herod would not tolerate being separated from his wife’s companionship even after death.

But the woman understood this quite differently from Josephus. She took it as evidence of cruelty still directed against her, since Herod had entrusted the execution of his cruelty even after his death to his own kinsman. She complained that he was hostile to her without justification, since he did not test his suspicions by any argument of truth but pressed her toward a violent death; there would be no end to his hatred, since it extended beyond the limits of his own life and safety.

But Josephus, forgetful of his own domestic trouble, while eagerly seeking to reconcile another man’s wife, inflamed the suspicions of his own wife against him [Col. 2005A]. She could not tolerate without resentment the conversations between her husband and Mariamne, or the time he spent at the royal court.

Finally, when her brother returned, she did not delay her accusations. Adding her own injury to the royal insults, she declared that Mariamne had also taken her husband from her. Although Herod was stunned, he was not at first seriously provoked and did not show himself hostile to his wife. Indeed, still overcome by the power of love, he began one day to swear to the woman that he loved her with such devotion that he had never burned with desire for another woman; he had cast all others from his heart in order to remain faithful to his wife.

But she replied: “You have sufficiently revealed your love for me by the instructions you gave Josephus, ordering him to kill me. How can one who can kill love?”

At once the king went mad when he heard that his secret had been disclosed. He began to think that Josephus would never have betrayed him unless, captured by love of the woman, he had sought the reward of his betrayal through sexual intercourse. What had long been hidden was now revealed as an open crime, established by unmistakable corruption. It was not without reason, he thought, that his sister had been aroused, since she had detected the domestic injury before anyone else.

Raging with excessive indignation and no longer master of himself, he leapt from his bed, fleeing the shameful contagion of corruption; the palace could not contain him in his frenzy. His sister heard him shouting and immediately seized the opportunity as evidence for an accusation and as an occasion for inflicting harm. She confirmed the suspicions of the enraged man.

Driven by the pain of the injury and by his sister’s accusation, he ordered both of them to be killed. Not long afterward, however, remorse for his actions followed. When his anger subsided, love took its place and his passion was revived. The ardor of his desire blazed so fiercely that he refused to believe she was dead; beside himself, he addressed her as though she were alive. Just as he had sent children to her while she lived, he now begged her to lay aside their quarrels, come to him, and restore herself to his married affection.

At last, only after a long interval and after much testimony, did he believe that she had died. Out of love he had thought that a woman of such beauty, almost immortal, could not have died. Such was his affection for the dead woman.

Finally, he became savage and is said afterward to have been so exasperated by hatred of those around him that he brought death upon many. He suffered not only from an illness of the mind but also from a severe bodily disease, which they said he had contracted from the corruption of the air as well. For an unhealthy atmosphere caused pestilence among many.

Having therefore consulted physicians, he hid himself in the seclusion of the forests. As his strength gradually returned, he recovered the health of both body and mind through hunting [Note: The manuscript reads “sobriety.” BARR.].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

He also added this to the marvels by which he imagined that the dead woman’s beauty had been avenged: he said that he had paid the penalty for an unjust crime and that the death of such beauty had been expiated by the sickness of the elements; that, amid the destruction of the world and the pestilence of nations, one woman’s death had nevertheless been avenged by an unequal fate, since the earth refused its fruits and famine increased the pestilence.

Such was the end of Mariamne. She was temperate toward her husband and chaste, but insolent because she was conscious of her beauty. She possessed more courage than was needed, but lacked attentiveness, so that she scorned her husband’s caresses, confident that she could suffer no destruction at the hands of one who loved her beyond measure. She thus found not only present vengeance but also transmitted hereditary hatreds into the future.

Her sons succeeded her as avengers of their mother’s grief, acting with pious affection toward their mother but with impiety toward their father, although the law of nature required them to discharge an equal duty toward both parents. Their grief did not find them unprepared. For, having long been educated at Rome in both Latin and Greek literature, they had acquired no ordinary cunning. While absent, they had learned of their mother’s death and, with very many people inciting them to hatred of their father, grew embittered.

[Note: Having learned of their mother’s death, they believed that very many people would be driven to hatred of their father; and, upon their return, not even the sight of their father instilled reverence and dutiful attentiveness in them. ID.]

Even after their return, not even the sight of their father instilled reverence or dutiful attentiveness in them; their wickedness grew with their age. A further presumption arose from their marriages: one had married the daughter of Salome, a niece of Herod; the other had married a daughter of Archelaus, who held the kingdom of Cappadocia. The nobility of these unions gave authority to their hatred.

Herod was therefore offended by the sons’ intelligence, more acute even in silence than paternal affection could endure—for even a countenance frequently gives offence. Those who warned him repeatedly to beware of his sons’ plots added further goads, declaring, as though out of concern, that the young men were arming their hands to avenge their mother’s death.

Terrified by these warnings, Herod began to prefer Antipater, the son of Dosis, to his brothers, and to court him with a more abundant [Col. 2006C] affection [Note: “Effect” or “affection.” ID.]. The royal court burned with still greater hatred and was shaken by the rivalry of the brothers. They were indignant that the son of a private woman was preferred to them, although they had been born to the kingdom. He, crafty in flattery, saw that he was inferior to them on his mother’s side and therefore worked all the more diligently to recommend himself to his father. Through contrived accusations he never ceased attacking his brothers, until, by his own efforts and through others whom he had enlisted, he excluded them from their father’s affection.

Finally, he deprived them of all hope of ruling, so that, when a will had been publicly drawn up, he alone was designated heir to the empire. He was sent to Caesar at Rome and was supported with every ornament and form of royal dress, except the distinctive diadem.

After returning to Judaea, he increased the favor shown him by Caesar and by many distinguished men. In a very short time he gained such power that he even induced his mother to be added to his father’s marriage [Note: “Restored” or “returned [to him].” ID.]. Armed with two weapons—flattery and the cunning of dissimulation—he began to press his brothers upon their father so forcefully that the son prepared death for his father.

Finally, driven mad, he went to Rome, taking Alexander with him; before Caesar he accused Alexander of practicing magic against him. Alexander was given an opportunity to lament his misfortune and all his sufferings. Seeing that he possessed the authority of so great a judge, one who could neither be swayed by Herod through favor nor deceived by Antipater, he thought that nothing should be omitted. He touched upon his father’s crimes with a certain restraint, so that he would not appear to press the charge like an accuser, but would not allow the crimes to remain hidden. His case would be greatly strengthened if he could show that his father’s hatred was directed against him because of grief over his mother’s death.

In such trials, nothing weighs more heavily against children than filial devotion and the authority of filial affection. If these are somewhat discredited by wrongdoing, the prejudice is reduced and the privilege is excluded.

When the charge brought by his father was reached, Alexander refuted it with powerful arguments. First he showed that his brother was foreign to the crime, although he shared the dangers confronting his family, and he lamented that an innocent man was being summoned into the accusation. His right to speak and act on the testimony of a pure conscience supported him. He declared that no honor had been left to himself or to his brother: everything had been taken from them through his brother’s crime and their father’s weakness.

He bitterly lamented that death was being inflicted upon him, and that his father pursued it so far as to add accusation to crime and outrage to wrongdoing. By these words he moved everyone to tears and brought the judgment to such a conclusion that Caesar did not accept the accusation and the father embraced reconciliation.

This was exceedingly pleasing and glorious to the Roman prince: not only had he granted a kingdom to a renowned king, but he had also restored his children to him. The case was therefore settled after a just examination, so that respect for the father’s authority might remain inviolate and the sons’ innocence secure. The sons were to obey their father as was proper. He himself was to show his undiminished natural affection toward his sons [Note: That is, as I suppose, he was to display it equally and jointly toward them. GALLAND.], though he might leave the kingdom to whichever of them he wished.

Alexander returned from Rome with his father, acquitted more by the judgment than by the absence of suspicion. For Antipater did not allow Herod’s mind to be free of hatred toward his sons. He himself was the source of the hatred. Yet he restrained his own ambition under the appearance of reconciliation, lest he reveal the theater of his pursuit of brotherly affection and expose his plots.

When they reached Cilicia and, while sailing, put in at Eleusa [Note: Rufinus, the translator of Josephus, reads “Eleusa.” BARR.], Archelaus received them with a splendid banquet. He gave thanks on account of Alexander, his son-in-law, because Herod had judged him worthy not only of being rescued from danger but also of reconciliation. Archelaus had also sent letters through his own people, asking his friends to aid his son-in-law in his defense. As Alexander departed, he presented him with thirty talents as a gift of hospitality and escorted him as far as Zephyrium.

When the king returned home, he immediately summoned the people and addressed them in these words.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Col. 2007D]

“Just now, fellow citizens and Hebrews, I had a cause both useful and fruitful for going to Rome: namely, that Caesar should judge the case of my sons. So that I alone, who was angry, would not be the one to decide, I went to Caesar, asking the man who had restored my kingdom also to pronounce upon my successor.

“He added this to his benefits: what was difficult, he restored to a father—sons who had almost been lost; and to brothers, he restored what is above a kingdom, namely, harmony. I therefore return richer than I departed. Through Caesar’s benefaction I have learned to be a better father, because my sons have learned to be better children.

“He decreed that the succession of my sons should depend upon my judgment, lest the privilege of succession produce arrogance. I myself am to choose my successor: the one who deserves it, the one who has honored his father more.

“I shall imitate Caesar. By acquitting my younger sons, he made them equal to the elder son. Therefore today I establish all three of my children as kings at once. Age supports one; nobility supports the others. Let no one be troubled by their number: the greatness of the kingdom is sufficient for more than one.

“Let God first be the judge of my decision; then let you also participate. Those whom Caesar has joined and the father has established, honor with an honor suited to them, so that it be neither excessive nor too little. The one inflates; the other exasperates. Let each receive whatever the merits of his portion require.

“For a man does not please the one whom he honors beyond measure as much as he injures the one to whom he denies what is owed. Often both are offended when flattery takes the form of preference.

“I am certainly the father of all. The honor shown to sons is unquestionably the father’s glory [Note: The old manuscript reads *gratia*, “by the father’s favor,” that is, by the father’s permission—so that the sons are honored only as far as the father permits. GUAL.]. Yet if anyone exalts my children beyond measure, he is answerable to me even on behalf of my children, since he becomes the author of their downfall. Excessive honor is an investment in boldness.

“Do I begrudge my children? Far from it. But I would rather that they possess less with favor than much amid sedition. What rests upon arrogance or seizure soon collapses; what rests upon favor endures for a long time.

“Therefore I shall take care to join to my children as guarantors of harmony their parents’ friends, at whose urging they may adopt mutual affection. For although every evil word easily infects the mind of its hearer, continual conversations and long association are especially accustomed to pour corruption into the spirit, so that, as if by contagion, it quickly passes into the character of those who live together. Even when the disposition is tranquil, a calm pool can rise into waves if the winds agitate it; so a good nature is tossed about by wicked advisers.

“I therefore think that each of you ought to place his greatest hope in me. Whatever is added to my children is not lost to me. Every tribune or soldier ought to reverence the father of the commanders more deeply. I—I am the one who will repay all of you, even for the honors you bestow upon my sons.

“If I find your devotion upright, I shall reward it by your deeds. Malevolence will receive its own recompense, so that even with the man whom it thought worthy of flattery it will lose the fruit of its efforts.

“But you, good sons, consider first the sacred bond of nature. Through it even beasts are bound together, and it compels wild creatures to love their kind. Mutual affection remains among untamed animals, and beasts redeem their own at the cost of their own danger.

“Revere Caesar also, who has made you friends from enemies. Thirdly, revere me, who prefer to ask when I could command. Remain brothers; do not forget what you were born as [Note: Perhaps *exuere*, “to cast off,” that is, “to forget.” GALLAND.].

“I give you imperial clothing and rank. But more precious is what I urge upon you: the unbroken seal of your mutual love. If filial devotion remains, kingship is a delight; if affection is absent, sovereignty is worthless and often harmful.

“Therefore, while I test you, for the present you shall have not the kingdom itself but the honor of the kingdom. If you love your father, authority will follow. Yet prove your love for me among yourselves; you will possess all those things by which royal power is accustomed to delight its rulers.

“The burdens of empire and the weight of affairs will remain with me alone—and, even if I should not wish it, they will remain with me. Therefore it benefits you to desire what I desire, because I both wish for what belongs to you and regard it as my own.”

After saying this, he kissed his sons, so that with a single kiss of affection he might bind them to one another. Having done so, he dismissed the assembly.

## CHAPTER XL
Most departed rejoicing, pleased by the reconciliation of the brothers; but dissension returned with the brothers, and all the more grievously because the one whose rank was higher was envied more and possessed greater power to do harm. The sons of Mariamne were distressed that the son of a private woman, who knew nothing of the royal lineage, had been made their equal.

**[Col. 2009D] Note:** “And from his brothers.” *Barr.*

Antipater, on the other hand, scorned the hope of the kingdom that had been distinguished for him from that of his brothers; and he envied his brothers, for whom only the later places would scarcely be reserved instead of the first. Yet he concealed and veiled himself, pretending affection in place of hatred, offering them every piece of advice in conversation, even when they did not seek it. His tongue was ready and lavish with secrets: whatever they had said in Alexander’s presence immediately reached Antipater; many things they had not said were fabricated as well. The intermediary added most things with exaggeration.

Antipater was the architect of every scheme by which the brothers were attacked. His life was nothing other than a kind of gathering-place of cunning, a stage of wickedness, a plot of crimes, a ministry of outrages.

**[Col. 2009D] Note:** “Mystery.” *Idem.*

He put forward judges, suborned witnesses, and pretended to defend them, as though carrying the part of a brother about on the stage: he would shake off the lesser charges and yield to the more serious ones, so that he might deceive his father more completely and turn him more violently against the brothers. Above all, by his skill he sharpened resentment over the alleged preparation of the father’s murder, on the grounds that the kingdom was to be seized—for kings are especially suspicious of threats to their safety. But lest the charges appear less credible to the king without someone to refute them, he himself first attempted to rebut them, and then wished to seem constrained by manifest evidence of the facts. Thus, when the case had supposedly been pleaded on both sides and nothing further seemed lacking from the judgment, the father would be stirred up against his sons as though they had been convicted. For nothing lent greater credibility to the allegations than the fact that Antipater was regarded as the brothers’ defender.

By this fraud he won the favor of many and also inclined his father’s mind toward himself. Whatever was daily taken away from the brothers was transferred from their father’s affection to him. He drew away the king’s friends and relatives, especially Pheroras, the king’s brother, and his sister Salome; he made them hostile to the nephews, so that they not only failed to defend them but also attacked and hated them.

There was added to the material for hatred Alexander’s wife Glaphyra, who had begun, with sufficient feminine arrogance, to exalt herself above those around her with proud disdain, because she surpassed them all in the splendor of her ancestry. Thus, as though she were mistress of all who were in the royal court, she placed herself before them, boasting that her father and grandfather had been kings,

**[Col. 2009D] Note:** The old codex reads, “kings.” *Idem.*

and especially that Darius Hydaspes was the summit of her maternal lineage. She was accustomed to insult Salome, the king’s sister, and Dosides, his wife, by imputing low birth to them; this caused them grief and hatred toward her. She likewise exasperated the other women who were joined to the king more for their beauty than for the nobility of their lineage.

For Herod, contrary to royal custom and even to Jewish practice, took pleasure in a kind of license of error: they use the forms of their ancestors as a screen for their own vices. Alexander was therefore burdened by his wife’s arrogance. Aristobulus also reproached his wife with the same arguments that Glaphyra used: she was of an inferior station and could not be compared with royal offspring; it was an insult that she was Glaphyra’s equal and his own, since his brother had obtained a marriage into a royal family while he himself had degenerated into the companionship of a private woman. He was mad, he said, to disturb his own family relationships with such abuse.

**[Col. 2010D] Note:** “Family relationships.” *Idem.*

**[Col. 2009D] Note:** She had begun. *Idem.*

The wife of Aristobulus, wounded by these insults, reported everything to her mother with tears. Salome, having learned of it through her daughter, informed King Herod. But he thought it more expedient to admonish his sons than to destroy them. He summoned them, partly terrified them in an imperial manner and partly exhorted them with paternal affection, urging them to love their brother and not to quarrel like enemies. He granted pardon for the past while announcing correction for the future.

But they, lamenting that they were being attacked by numerous fabricated accusations, both begged and promised that in future they would entrust their loyalty to their own defense by their actions themselves. They asked only that their father await what they had done and not believe rashly what he heard: wicked informers would not be lacking so long as a credulous listener supplied them.

By these and similar arguments they softened their father. Although they had at that time driven away the immediate danger, they nevertheless accumulated sorrow, because they saw themselves being pressed by Pheroras and Salome. The one was their uncle, the other their father’s sister—people who ought to have defended them—yet they were plotting against them. A grave fear was added, since both possessed great influence with their father.

After receiving the diadem, Herod had shared almost the whole power of the kingdom with his brother and had conferred considerable wealth upon both of them, especially upon Pheroras. In the end he set aside for them a hundred talents each year, apart from the region beyond the Euphrates, which multiplied the abundance of its revenues. At Herod’s request to Caesar, Pheroras had also been appointed tetrarch. He had even been endowed with the connection of a royal marriage, since he had taken the sister of the royal wife as his bride. After her death, the king’s elder daughter, who had been betrothed to him, succeeded her as his wife through the favor shown to the son-in-law—unless, captivated by love for a little maidservant, he had rejected marriage with the royal girl. Angered by this insult, Herod gave him a daughter, who later died in the Parthian war.

**[Col. 2010D] Note:** “A daughter.” Josephus, *Jewish War*, book I, chapter 17; *Antiquities*, book XVI, chapter 11. *Barr.*

Yet Pheroras was accused before Herod of having sought his brother’s life with poison. His wife, too, had not been free from this suspicion while she lived. Her case was investigated first by many people and finally by his friends; when she was found innocent of the crime of which she had been accused, Herod willingly acquitted her, even granting permission for her flight. For the maidservant whom Pheroras loved had been carried off, and, after an arrangement had been made for her removal so that she might flee to the Parthians, she revealed the extent of the affair through the confessions of her companions.

**[Col. 2010D] Note:** Of the arrangement that had been made. *Barr.*

Alexander had breathed somewhat more freely while Pheroras was under accusation and attack. He himself then attacked Salome, because she had promised herself in marriage to Syllaeus, who was Obodas, king of Arabia’s procurator and Herod’s bitterest enemy.

**[Col. 2011D] Note:** I restore this from Josephus: “because she had promised herself in marriage to Syllaeus, who was Obodas, king of Arabia’s procurator.” *Barr.*

But when the accusation was withdrawn on both sides, the storm within the household descended upon Alexander and involved him in grave danger. A savage plague was raging, and Antipater was the storm of the entire court. By every means, and even through the assembly of their relatives, he pressed his brother so heavily that, when his sober state of mind had been disturbed, the father loudly protested that Alexander was threatening him with a sword.

**[Col. 2011D] Note:** The manuscript reads, “through concert.” *Idem.*

The following scene was then brought forward. Alexander had lured three eunuchs—one accustomed to serve the king’s cups, another to bring in the dishes for dinner, and the third to watch over the royal bed and never leave it once Herod had settled upon his couch—with lavish gifts into favor toward himself and into complicity in a shameful crime. When this was exposed, the eunuchs, compelled by punishments, revealed the obscenities of their lustful mockery. Unable to conceal the amorous promises by which they had been enticed, they also disclosed the price of the sexual act at which they had been solicited: Alexander had told them that youth, beauty, and the strength of his age were on his side, whereas Herod was weak and weighed down by old age; that Herod dyed his hair so as not to reveal his age; that, whenever Alexander wished, Herod would transfer to him the right to rule and promise immense rewards. Therefore, they ought to place their hope in a young man, not in an aged old man whose very nature was hastening his end.

These things deeply disturbed Herod. But what disturbed him above all was that, as he learned from the eunuchs’ information, military forces, army commanders, and centurions were conspiring with Alexander. At last he was so agitated that he thought no form of savagery should be omitted. He trusted no one and suspected everyone.

Punishments moved more quickly than inquiries into the crimes, and judgment anticipated the condemned men’s end. Those against whom any suspicion pressed were dragged everywhere to execution. Calumnies boiled over. Many, wishing to please the king, denounced the accused; but immediately those who had denounced others were themselves denounced and led with their victims to the place of punishment.

Thus Herod had become savage toward everyone, so that, if any one of them survived, he would be suspect.

**[Col. 2012D] Note:** Read “so that if.” *Idem.*

The king thought himself secure in no other way than by the destruction of the human race. He accused those with whom reconciliation was impossible, distrusted his friends, was arrogant toward his intimates, merciless toward the accused, and fearful of everything. He frequently changed his residence and passed nights without sleep.

Having been provoked against everyone, he suddenly bound Alexander in chains, shut him under guard, and summoned his friends for interrogation. Those who denied the charges died amid tortures. Those who remained silent, because they confessed nothing consistent with the suspicions, were likewise tormented to the point of death.

**[Col. 2012D] Note:** I think the text should finally be emended thus. *Galland.*

Nevertheless, some, overcome by the force and severity of the tortures and punishments, asserted that the young men had planned to kill their father while he was occupied with the hunt and then immediately go to Rome, in order to escape the punishment of flight. Although this was supported by no evidence, the father turned it into consolation for his savage purpose, wishing to have just grounds for the son’s imprisonment.

Alexander therefore perceived that his father’s ears were closed to every defense of him, and that the matter could not in any way be brought to a point at which he might presume upon his innocence, since he was being attacked by such enormous heaps of calumny. He decided that he must meet the most wicked informers by a similar art, surround the contrivers of fraud and calumny with their own devices, and summon to trial those by whose accusations he believed himself oppressed.

He therefore wrote four little books in which he confessed the fabricated crime by which he was alleged to have attacked his father’s safety. He exposed as accomplices in such plots many of those by whom he himself was attacked, and he inscribed the same books especially with the names of Pheroras and Salome. He alleged that, in the dead of night, they had broken into the room in which the young man lived, enticed him against his will, and compelled him, despite his resistance, to commit incest.

**[Col. 2012D] Note:** Having broken into it. *Barr.*

He sent the little books to the king as records of his own crimes, implicating in them the most powerful of the king’s companions and friends.

At that time Archelaus arrived in haste in Judaea, intending, if possible, to bring help and support to his son-in-law and daughter. But foreseeing that, in the presence of the most hostile father, the avenues of legitimate defense were closed to him, he restrained Herod’s agitation by the art of lawful defense.

As soon as he entered the royal court, he began shouting in a loud voice, as though out of his mind—Herod could already hear and see him:

“Does that poisoner, my son-in-law, still live and enjoy the light of day? Where is he, I ask? Where shall I find that parricidal head, so that I may tear it apart with my own hands?

**[Col. 2012D] Note:** “Tear apart.” *Idem.*

He who wished to commit parricide ought to perish by parricide. What will he do to his father-in-law, who did not spare his father? Who will point him out to me? I will first tear out the entrails of the criminal, and I will add his daughter to the worthy husband. Even if she was not conscious of the crime, she is not free from its contagion, since she enjoyed marriage with a parricide.

“I do not acknowledge as my daughter the woman who failed to detect her husband’s schemes and did not show herself to her father-in-law as a daughter-in-law who would restore his son to his father. I joined her to him not for the service of crime but for partnership in marriage, to make her a co-heiress of favor, not an accomplice in guilt.

“I marvel at you, Herod, if that Alexander, the plotter against his father, is still alive. I thought he had already suffered the deserved punishment, since he ought not to have been denounced. Why should a confessor or such a parricide be preserved any longer? But perhaps this too has been arranged by divine providence, so that he might be condemned by the judgment of both parents, since he has violated the filial devotion owed to both of you.

“I will not deny that I am the avenger, since I had prepared myself to proclaim the vengeance exacted. Yet I will not spare my daughter, whom I myself betrothed in an ill-fated marriage after following you as her sponsor. I did not entrust her to her husband’s character but to your loyalty. Let her give an account of why she concealed her guarantor and loved her husband.

“The judgment concerning both of them now rests with you. If you are a steadfast executor of so great a grief, gird yourself, father, and set filial affection aside. The duty is certainly not one that fathers should desire, but it must not be evaded. If filial affection softens you and nature bends you, let us exchange roles: let me be the executor against your son, and you against my pledge, in a mutual discharge of duty.”

With such a speech, Archelaus roused Herod and gradually softened the force of his anger, so that Herod believed him to be sharing his grief and united with him in feeling. He therefore gave him the little books that Alexander had composed to read.

But Archelaus, examining each point carefully, realized that the charges had been piled up more from grief than supported by truth. With profound deliberation, he began gradually to diminish the resentment aroused by the alleged attempt at parricide and to transfer the causes of the accusations to those who had been named, especially Pheroras.

When he noticed that the king was not hostile to his view, he said:

“It must be considered whether the young man has been attacked in your presence more by the plots of so many wicked men than you by the young man. What reason did he have to seek your life, when you had granted him the honor of the kingdom, reserved for him the right to rule, and held out the hope of succession? What could he seek that he already possessed? How could he be ungrateful for such great gifts? What else would he accomplish by your death except to expose himself to danger—to a danger he could not fear while you lived but would fear once you were dead—from those very men whose destruction of his own safety he dreaded even while he lived under his father?

“This age is open to deception, easily misled and surrounded by the plots of fraudulent men. Old age scarcely withstands such trickery; yet even the prudence of the old is often entangled in the cunning snares of those who plot against them. Therefore, if mature experience has often been shaken, what wonder is it if an immature age could not protect itself when it was being pressed by whole bands of plotters?

“Those men, then, are the disturbers of the royal household; they are the instigators of the young men and sowers of discord. They drove the young man to despair of his safety, so that he indulged his anger more than was proper, aimed at vengeance rather than acquittal, and yielded something even to agitation.”

By such arguments Herod gradually began to bend and soften his indignation toward Alexander. But he became much more agitated against Pheroras, because in those four books Pheroras was exposed as the agent of all the crimes and the architect of the entire scene.

Seeing that Herod had inclined his mind toward Archelaus and that the favor of their intimate friendship weighed more heavily in his case than in anyone else’s, Pheroras went to him, begging him to restore the king’s favor toward himself.

Archelaus replied that Pheroras was entangled in so many bonds of crime that it was clearly proved that he had prepared plots against the king and attacked the young man. He said that he had no hope of pardon unless he abandoned the cunning with which he denied the charges brought against him, confessed them to his brother, who loved him, and did not hesitate to ask that brother for forgiveness. Archelaus promised that he would support such an action with all the effort he could provide.

Pheroras therefore changed his clothing, covered himself with tears, and clung in a pitiable manner to his brother’s feet. He begged pardon, confessed his wickedness, and did not deny the charges brought against him but acknowledged them, saying that madness had been the cause of his great fall, because excessive passion for the woman he loved had boiled over within him.

Thus Archelaus represented Pheroras both as the originator and the witness of his own outrages, as though he had arranged matters for a reward and were offering evidence that would serve his own interests. He begged Herod to soften his anger in consideration of nature and forgive his brother, setting the law of nature above vengeance.

“It is not surprising,” he said, “if in great kingdoms, as in great bodies, some limbs are often inflamed; they should not be cut off but treated with gentler medicines.”

**[Col. 2013D] Note:** In the old manuscript: “often some part is inflamed.” *Barr.*

He added that much more serious plots had also been contrived against him by his brother, but that he had remitted to family affection what was owed to grief; the more he had lightened the punishment of an ungrateful man, the more he had aggravated the offense.

By adding these and similar arguments, Archelaus indeed softened Herod so that he forgave his brother, but he himself remained apparently inexorable toward his son-in-law. Finally, he threatened to tear his daughter away from him and raged with such movements of indignation that Herod thought his son’s crime against him had been sufficiently expiated. He begged Archelaus to avenge his injuries and himself intervened for the accused man before his father-in-law, so that the marriage might be renewed.

Archelaus persisted in asking that Herod join his daughter to any other man he wished, except Alexander. He insisted that the wife’s case should also be brought forward, and by this strategy he urged Herod much more strongly to believe that his son had been restored to him if the marriage were not dissolved.

“Alexander dearly loves his wife,” he said, “and has children by her, dear to their grandfather and pleasing to their parents. This will be the gift by which your son is restored to you, because a good wife in no small measure restrains her husband’s errors or compensates for the resentment caused by his crimes through her services. If she is torn away from him, no remedy will remain for her husband; he will plunge headlong into every form of wickedness. Suspicions of crime usually become gentler when domestic affections call them back.”

At last Archelaus was scarcely persuaded to reconcile himself with his son-in-law and to reconcile the father with him. By this plan he rescued his son-in-law from death, receiving his acquittal as his reward while pretending rather to condemn him than to intervene. Had he thought it necessary to intercede openly, he would undoubtedly have obtained nothing.

He added that Alexander ought to go to Rome to clear himself of the suspicions his father had formed against him, since Herod himself had written everything to Caesar. I think this too was contrived, so that Alexander, once he had cleared himself in this manner, might be commended to Caesar and the plots that Antipater had prepared against his brothers might be exposed.

## CHAPTER XLI

By this plan the faction was dissolved and the change turned into rejoicing. A banquet was renewed as a sign of the reconciliation that had been undertaken. Its authors were Archelaus, who gave seventy talents and a golden couch adorned with jewels. Eunuchs were also selected and presented with royal magnificence, and a concubine—whose name was Panichis—was given and accepted as a gift.

**[Col. 2015D] Note:** The old manuscript reads, “to the author, Archelaus.” *Barr.*

**[Col. 2015D] Note:** The old manuscript reads *Panuchis*. Josephus has *Pannichis*; it should be written with *y*, since it comes from the Greek word signifying spending the night. *Idem.*

Likewise, at the king’s suggestion, the relatives presented Archelaus with splendid gifts, and none of his household was excluded from receiving a present. Herod distributed very substantial gifts to all according to each man’s merits.

He also accompanied Archelaus with his powerful associates as far as Antioch, the splendid city of Syria, while Archelaus was returning to his kingdom.

Alexander would have escaped, had there not come into Judaea a man far more practiced than Archelaus in the arts of intrigue: a Laconian named Eurycles, excessively greedy for wealth and contemptuous of it whenever the hope of obtaining something greater shone before him. Not content with the resources of Laconia, he turned his mind toward royal extravagance. By hunting Herod with lavish gifts of ancient magnificence, he prepared a place for an even greater reward; and although he obtained gifts far richer than those he had offered, he was not satisfied unless he could purchase the king’s favor through bloody and impious factions.

**[Col. 2016D] Note:** This word is absent from the manuscript. In some copies *Archelaus* is repeatedly found in place of *Antipater*. *Idem.*

Thus, following a custom and practice familiar to the Greeks, he reached Herod’s intimate friendship in a short time by flattering him and praising everything about him—not only what was worthy of praise but also what was entangled with vices—until he was chosen among the foremost arbiters of the king’s secrets. His claim by nationality also assisted him, since the Jews regard the Spartans, joined to them by kinship of race, as brothers.

When he learned the vices of the royal household, the father’s suspicious disposition, and the hatred between the brothers, he adopted new methods. He pretended to be dear to everyone at once and was regarded as faithful by each of them; but he shaped his efforts according to the king’s character and the value of the gifts, so as to attach himself more closely to Antipater and surround Alexander with plots and snares. Under the appearance of friendship he inflamed both men against each other, representing Antipater as entitled to the kingdom by the prerogative of age, and Alexander as superior by right because he possessed the nobility of maternal descent; he added that Alexander could have no equal partnership with one who possessed only the pledge of the basest corruption.

Alexander, captivated by these words—for he was the younger and delighted in what was said to him without weighing what was in turn fabricated about him before Antipater—opened himself to Antipater’s hired agent and betrayer. With an unstable character and imprudent affection, he revealed his mind, complaining that his father was the author of his misfortunes: he had taken his mother from him, disfigured the kingdom, and wished to divert from him what was owed to him through his grandfather and the insignia of his ancient lineage. The legitimate heirs were being cheated of their right of succession, while a bastard was preferred as the reward of sexual misconduct. Yet, he said, the judgments of the gods would not remain quiet for long: the man who had killed an innocent wife would not himself quickly be deprived, through his wife, of the authority he had prepared.

The Laconian immediately reported these words to Antipater. He also ensnared Aristobulus, so that he too might be caught in the same net of complaints; then, after accumulating his reward, he insinuated them to the king. He said that he could not suppress such an enormous crime in silence and that, in return for the hospitality he had received, he was bringing the king the favor of daylight: the sons were preparing to snatch it away, and unless he himself had recalled them by pretending to offer more faithful counsel, they would long ago have killed their father with Alexander’s sword and emptied the kingdom for unworthy heirs.

Alexander, he added, felt no religious scruple about the atrocity of parricide, since he regarded it as a grave crime that the deaths of his grandfather and mother still remained unavenged. He was being summoned and pressed by the complaints of the murdered, so that he might avenge so enormous an outrage. The funeral offerings owed to the dead had to be exacted, and their succession ought not to be polluted by allowing the kingdom to pass to the man who had killed their ancestors. He would reopen Caesar’s judgments—not with the reverence he had shown before, but so that Caesar himself might learn all the king’s secrets, the wealth acquired through bloodshed, and the province that had been undermined. He would bring his grandfather back from the underworld and reveal the mother’s most bitter death, so that an alien successor might be installed in the royal kingdom.

**[Col. 2016D] Note:** He would reopen them. *Barr.*

Eurycles had stirred up the king. Nevertheless, judging the suggestion of one man insignificant, Herod suborned other accusers against the brothers. They said that the brothers had once entered into conversation with Jocundus and Tyrannus, commanders of the cavalry, and had contrived plots against the king out of resentment over their being set aside; danger threatened his neck unless he took precautions promptly.

**[Col. 2016D] Note:** The old codex had added “of the succession.” *Idem.*

Herod did not delay. He immediately seized the men and interrogated them severely. Yet they were found to have confessed nothing of the crimes of which they were accused. Since such serious charges were fabricated with impunity before a man who claimed to be the avenger of crimes while neglecting to punish calumnies, there were always people ready to devise plots of this sort, believing that they would be more pleasing to the father.

A letter was also produced, supposedly written by Alexander and Aristobulus to the commander of a fortress, granting them the opportunity to take refuge there after killing the king, until they could arm themselves against those who pursued them and prepare their defense with other resources. The commander of the fortress was tortured but confessed nothing.

Nevertheless, although no evidence of the alleged crime appeared, Alexander and Aristobulus were treated as guilty and handed over to custody. Eurycles, rewarded with fifty talents, was regarded as the author of their safety and life.

It is proper not to pass over the man who, at the time of Eurycles, had been sent to Judaea as Alexander’s most trusted friend. The king thought he should be interrogated as though he were an accomplice in Eurycles’ schemes: whether the things the Spartan had reported about the young men were consistent with the truth.

But he swore that he knew nothing whatsoever of such things and thus established his credibility. Yet this did not help the young men. He avoided questioning himself, lest he diminish the resentment against the accusation and expose Eurycles’ fraud if, interrogated more severely, he denied it. Herod therefore dismissed him as unworthy of belief.

For Herod was a good father who gladly listened to accusations against his sons but did not permit them to be defended. He took pleasure when they were attacked and was offended if they cleared themselves.

Finally, when Spartes had been enriched with royal rewards, he reached Achaia and paid the price of his calumnies.

**[Col. 2017D] Note:** “The Spartan.” *Barr.*

Salome was unable to clear herself of the charge that she had arranged a marriage with Syllaeus the Arab. When she disclosed the secret to her son-in-law, he advised her to look to her own safety and escape her brother’s anger, since, because of the hope of a future union, she was suspected of having obtained and reported the plans of the Arab king. She thereby earned pardon for her offense and turned the whole storm of royal savagery against the young men. In the last and unavoidable shipwreck, they were overwhelmed and paid the penalty.

They were therefore convicted; and what was harder for them than their chains was that the brothers were separated from one another. Volumnius, the commander of the army, and Olympius, a man among the king’s friends, were sent to Caesar to accuse them before him.
