Although Caesar was offended that a father should demand the punishment of his sons, he nevertheless did not think he should deny the father authority over his own children. He therefore granted Herod permission, but added advice: he would make a better decision if a council of the king’s relatives and of those who governed the provinces were assembled, and the interrogation proceeded by common judgment. They should determine whether the sons had prepared any plots against their father; if they were convicted of an attempted parricide, they should be struck down, but if they were accused only of flight or some lesser offense, the punishment should be more moderate.

Herod thus received the power to punish parricide, but, through the condition that it be judged, was also reminded to exercise moderation. He immediately hastened to the city of Berytus, which Caesar had designated for the trial.

The provincial governors assembled according to the written instructions sent to them by the Roman prince Caesar. Saturninus and the legates took their seats, among them the procurator Volumnius. Then came the king’s relatives and friends, including Salome and Pheroras, as well as the leading men of Syria.

Archelaus alone was excluded.

**[Col. 2017D] Note:** The king of Cappadocia. *Idem.*

He had been summoned from Cappadocia because his favor toward his son-in-law was suspect, while the accusers and plotters against the young men were presenting the case before the court.

But what sort of trial was it when the accused were not permitted to be present and were accused in their absence? Herod understood that if they were merely seen, people’s natural inclination toward mercy would immediately acquit them, especially since the privilege of natural affection would favor them. He also understood that, if Alexander were granted any opportunity for defense, he could easily dissolve the charges.

He therefore relegated them to a village belonging to the Sidonians, while the accusation was directed against them as though they were present. Their father brought forward the charge that they had prepared plots against him; no proof was offered, no evidence of the alleged attempts, and the accuser stood firm because no one contradicted him.

**[Col. 2017D] Note:** Another reading is *destitutis*, “when they had been abandoned,” or, if preferred, *in destitutos*, “against those who had been abandoned”; the sentence would then be less objectionable. *Idem.*

Herod heaped upon those abandoned on every side the odium arising from insults and injuries—forms of mistreatment that those who considered them would judge worse than death. But no one examined them, and no one dared investigate what was alleged by the father and commanded by the king. The appearance of filial devotion prejudiced the case; the law of royal power terrified everyone. He asked for their judgments secure in victory, unaware that in such a trial the one who won would be more wretched than those who were condemned with such cruelty.

Saturninus condemned the young men, because no other course was permitted. But he moderated his sentence, asserting that care should be taken lest, when two of the three brothers had been killed, the death of the two be attributed to the third brother. He spoke timidly, but he did state the case: that man, he said, was the source of danger to his brothers. A few of the many followed him.

Volumnius, however, muttered a fatal sentence, and after him everyone, with the king’s approval, declared their verdict. They weighed the death sentence with different feelings but an equal outcome. Some had been compelled by flattery, others infected by hatred, so that they might either seek the king’s favor or inflict a harsher penalty upon the cruelty of the parricide, who, in his victory, had carried away such a bitter triumph over himself.

**[Col. 2017D] Note:** The manuscript reads *volentiam regis*, “the goodwill of the king.” *Barr.* — Gronovius, in *Monobiblos*, p. 115, has most correctly restored *volentia regi* from his manuscripts. The same phrase occurs again below, in chapter 44: “he therefore believed more in what was pleasing to the king.” The author of the *Excidium*, Ambrose, uses the same phrase in *Epistle* 24, to Valentinian, §1: “For it was sufficiently clear from the very fact that I was detained for several days within Gaul that I had not returned through the goodwill of Maximus,” and so forth. Ambrose owes this usage to both Sallust and Tacitus: the former says, “to do what is pleasing to the people”; the latter, “they were pleasing to the people,” and elsewhere, “they wrote back what was pleasing to Mucianus.” *Mazo[ch].*

Nevertheless, no one shuddered at what had been done or pronounced judgment as though moved by indignation. It was a theatrical spectacle, not the discipline of a trial: to condemn absent men, to condemn without a witness or an informer, solely by the privilege of nature—which ordinarily tends toward safety rather than danger.

All Syria and all Judaea were stunned, and with minds overwhelmed they awaited the end of so great a tragedy. Although Herod’s cruelty was known, no one could believe that he would persist all the way to parricide. But the savage force of his spirit was restrained neither by sea nor land.

Therefore, as though following the custom of triumphant generals, he sought the famous city of Tyre, dragging his sons through different places. From there he crossed to Caesarea by ship, carrying the miserable spectacle of parricide with him until some form of the most bitter death could be found for his sons.

The whole army was agitated, but fear suppressed their indignation. In the royal army was a veteran soldier named Tyro, who had a son attached to Alexander. He was an exceptionally loving father and, for that reason, dear to his son; for there is a kind of popular affection, especially toward one’s own people, that draws love to itself. He was particularly devoted to the king’s sons because his own son was loved by them.

Having conceived an indignation beyond measure, he became disturbed in mind and began to shout that justice was being crushed, truth excluded, religion abolished, the laws of family bonds confused, natural affection cast aside, and injustices allowed to overflow.

Finally, advancing to the king’s very face, he declared that Herod was wretched if he thought that the most wicked men should be believed against his sons—Pheroras and Salome, the king’s advisers. What trust, he asked, could be placed in those who repeatedly acknowledged that they themselves had been condemned to death by the king? What else could they be doing except arranging vengeance, so that, when the king had been deprived of worthy successors, he might incline toward the one who was weaker than the others? That man could easily be removed, since the royal army itself would pursue with hatred the one to whom the death of his two brothers had opened the way.

There was no one whom the mercy owed to innocent youth did not touch. Many of the commanders were no longer suppressing their indignation but spreading it openly. After naming them, he ended his speech.

They were immediately seized together with Tyro. Then Tryphon, one of the servants of the royal court, whose skill and practice in cutting hair were at hand, suddenly, through a kind of vanity of spirit, made an accusation, claiming that it had been devised by Tyro. He said that Tyro had persuaded him, when he shaved Herod’s beard as usual, to press the razor to Herod’s throat and complete the murder. He asserted that this would bring Tryphon the greatest profit, since Tyro had promised him gifts from Alexander.

Tyro was placed under guard with his son, and both were then interrogated together. They denied everything, while Tryphon reported nothing further. Since there was no manifest proof of the facts and no argument or evidentiary indication, Tyro was ordered to be tortured with harsher torments.

Then, pitying his father’s sufferings, the son promised to reveal everything if his father’s life were granted to him. He suggested that the king had promised pardon and claimed that, incited by Alexander, his father had prepared the king’s murder.

Many thought this had been fabricated temporarily so that Tyro might be spared through such evidence concerning his son; others declared that it had been stated as true. But Herod judged doubtful matters as certain, as though he feared that the opportunity for parricide would slip away from him.

He therefore summoned the people and assembled the commanders. With the gravest agitation, he brought forward a complaint concerning the plots that had been discovered and stirred up the people against their deaths. There Tyro, his son, and the barber were all killed with stones and clubs.

## CHAPTER XLII
[Col. 2019D] Alexander and Aristobulus too, sent to the city of Sebaste, which was not far from the city of Caesarea, were strangled by order of their father. Such was the end of Mariamne’s sons. Antipater did not long rejoice in their destruction; without doubt he was already flattering himself with the succession once they had been removed. But soon a considerable hatred of him blazed up among the entire people, because it was clear to everyone that the brothers had perished through his faction.

[Col. 2020A] There followed also no slight fear in those who considered how numerous the offspring of the murdered men were becoming day by day. Alexander had left behind two sons, Tigranes and Alexander, born of Glaphyra; Aristobulus, by Bernice, Salome’s daughter, had left Herod, Agrippa, and Aristobulus as survivors. There were also Herodias and Mariamne, daughters whose sex would not prevent them, if driven on by desire for the kingdom. Terrified by these circumstances, Antipater placed his hope in fraud and cunning. By gifts and presents he increasingly bound each person to himself, and even tried, by means of money, to entice Caesar’s friends and household into his favor.

But those who were at home also stood opposed to him. For, as time gradually passed, the king was becoming gentler toward the grandchildren born to his sons Alexander and Aristobulus, and he displayed repentance for what he had done, pitying those whose parents he had killed. Finally, one day, after gathering his friends and relatives, his face suffused with tears, he said to them:

“I see that my life is advancing, and I cannot look without tears upon these little shoots of unhappy fathers, whose grief I have caused, lest I leave them in a worse condition than that in which I deprived them of their parents. A certain calamity took those parents from me; nature and compassion commend these children to me more and more—nature, because they are my grandchildren; compassion, because they have been deprived of their parents. [Col. 2020B] The sons went astray against their father; what have the grandchildren done against their grandfather? I was an unhappy enough father; as a grandfather I ought to be more solicitous. I shall try to provide for my grandchildren after my death; would that I had also provided for my sons! But the fraud of a common enemy and foe has crept in against them. We must also take care lest their dangers engulf these children, and lest by one wound I lose both sons and grandchildren. [Note: [Col. 2019D] ‘Strike down.’ BARR.]

“Let us provide these children with protectors from whom we have taken their parents. [Col. 2020C] I shall therefore betroth your daughter, my Pheroras, to Alexander’s elder son, and appoint you as his father. To your son, Antipater, I shall give Aristobulus’s daughter, so that in this way you may become the father of an orphan girl. Herod, my son born to me by Mariamne of Hyrcanus, shall also take her sister as his wife. This is my decision: that, through marriages contracted with one another, the succession of my descendants may be joined together; so that no one may be suspicious of another, and so that I myself may look upon my grandchildren with calmer eyes than I looked upon their parents.”

Having spoken these words, he joined the right hands of those he had named, kissed each of them, and wept. Antipater, while the others rejoiced, took this so gravely that he immediately revealed his distress even in his expression, gripped by no slight anxiety. [Col. 2020D] He saw that the sons of Alexander had the support of King Archelaus and of Pheroras, who held the tetrarchy—support stronger than that of the others. He observed that hatred of himself was increasing, while compassion was favoring the grandchildren.

Nor could he receive Aristobulus’s daughter into his household, lest the repeated sight of her offend him as a perpetual reminder of his crime. He did not dare approach his father, lest he stir universal suspicion by appearing to think that the agreed marriages should be dissolved. Nevertheless, he craftily presumed to ask his father to take thought for him, lest, against the power of two influential men, the king and the tetrarch, he should be exposed helpless, with only the empty title of royalty. He urged him certainly to protect the honor of the son whom he judged should be joined in alliance with his own, lest the appearance of kingship come to him while the power passed to those others.

[Col. 2021A] Nor did he regard only Alexander’s and Aristobulus’s sons as threats; he believed that everyone was standing in his way. Whoever, from the various marriages of Herod, seemed—even silently—to be eligible for succession to the kingdom was a danger to him, and their number was large.

For nine women possessed the royal marriage-bed. Of these, only two were childless; the others had children. Antipater, son of Doris, was the eldest; Herod was Mariamne’s son; Antipas and Archelaus were the sons of Malthace the Samaritan, as was their sister Olympias, who was married to Joseph. Cleopatra of Jerusalem had also borne Herod and Philip to Herod; Pallas had borne Phasaelus. There were also other daughters of the king, Roxana and Salome: Phaedra was the mother of one, and Helpis of the other. The full sisters of Alexander and Aristobulus also survived, whom Mariamne had borne to Herod, as we mentioned above.

Thus Antipater feared Herod’s numerous offspring. Although reluctantly, and after his first attempts had greatly agitated the king, who resented Antipater’s opposition to the marriage arrangements made for grandchildren deprived of their father’s support, he finally achieved only this: [Col. 2021B] that Aristobulus’s daughter was joined in marriage to him, and that one of his own sons was joined to the daughter of Pheroras, his kinsman. [Note: [Col. 2021D] “Nevertheless.” BARR.] His influence through flattery was so great that he caused the marriages that had been arranged to be dissolved.

Salome, however, when she wished to marry Syllaeus, could not obtain this from her brother even through the intercession of Livia. [Note: [Col. 2021D] Livia’s. ID.] Livia was Caesar’s wife. Instead, against her will, she married one of the king’s friends named Alexander.

[Col. 2021C] With the king’s arrangements thus overturned, Antipater exulted in spirit, as though he had provided for himself exactly as he wished, and he surpassed everyone in cunning. Yet he could not in any way suppress hatred; rather, he inflamed it, because he sought to build a defense for himself through terror.

He had joined to himself as an accomplice in his factions Pheroras, his father’s full brother. Not long afterward Herod separated Pheroras from his own wife, toward whom he was especially hostile because of the injuries that woman had inflicted upon Doris, Pheroras’s wife, and he drove her from the household. Pheroras, embracing this insult, went over to Antipater’s party, over which he presided as tetrarch, with the firm intention never to return to Herod while Herod lived.

Indeed, even when he learned that Herod was afflicted by a serious illness and that Herod repeatedly begged him to come to him, judging that there were certain matters he wished to entrust to him as though he were dying, Pheroras did not think it necessary to visit him. Although wounded by this insult, when the king unexpectedly recovered from his illness, he nevertheless went to Pheroras out of brotherly affection. When he found him ill, he showed him attentive sympathy, and, when he died, he transported his body to Jerusalem and arranged his funeral with great mourning and elaborate ceremony.

Yet these signs of devoted affection did not remove the suspicion that had arisen that his brother had attacked him with poison. Herod was so cruel even toward his own family, and it was not difficult to believe that he could have killed his brother, since he had killed his sons.

## CHAPTER XLIII

[Col. 2022A]

Thus one of the men responsible for the murder of Alexander and Aristobulus met the end of his wickedness; from him the punishment passed to Antipater, the author of the crime. Herod had been provoked by the complaints of freedmen who asserted that their patron had been killed by poison. While investigating the matter with increased care, he learned that Pheroras had received from his wife a potion made from Arabian juices, which was thought to be a love potion but had in fact been poison, given to her at the request of Syllaeus and immediately turned into a deadly substance. He then subjected many people to examination under torture.

During the torture, one of the maidservants cried out that Almighty God would transfer every punishment to Antipater’s mother, the author of all their crimes. Through her, Antipater and Pheroras had held secret meetings and practiced drinking together day and night until they were drunk; after withdrawing from the king’s banquets, they would drink throughout the entire night.

This was rightly suspected to be neither an idle experiment nor free of conspiracy, especially since the servants and attendants had been dismissed. It was a powerful bond and indication of so prolonged a connection and conspiracy—a delay all the more suspicious to kings when it occurs in the solitude of secrecy and the silence of night.

There it was arranged that Antipater should go to Rome and Pheroras to Petra. [Note: [Col. 2021D] The old manuscript reads “into Peraea,” more correctly; for Josephus writes that Peraea is beyond the river in *The Jewish War*, Book III, chapter 2, [Col. 2022D] and the author himself does so below, Book II, chapter 9. ID.] They were reported to have frequently discussed this among themselves, because, after Alexander and Aristobulus, Herod would turn against them for their destruction. They said that they were wretched to have believed that Herod hated parricidal thoughts in them, when he was persecuting the heirs of the kingdom; that the murdered men had not been removed as rivals for power, but as partners in misery; that every danger and hatred had passed over to themselves [Note: [Col. 2022D] “All danger.” ID.]; and that Herod would not spare even women, since he had not spared his beloved Mariamne or the children born from her. They had no other remedy than to withdraw somewhere farther away, so that they might escape the fury of such a beast, at least by flight.

Frequent complaints were also made to Antipater’s mother. He lamented that he was burning with jealousy over the royal succession, since the savagery of the kingdom bore down upon him above all. He could no longer endure it, though he had devoted himself to the ultimate forms of obedience [Note: [Col. 2022D] “Owed.” And shortly after, “the courses having run out.” ID.] and was being pressed by the most extreme dangers. Not only had the right to rule been taken from him, but the course of his life had also been brought to its end. He was reaching a more mature age; his head had already grown gray. His father, on the other hand, was growing younger. It was futile to hope for the inheritance of one who might perhaps be kept alive so long that he would outlive even his heir.

And what benefit would succession bring him when the heir was long-lived, while Alexander’s and Aristobulus’s numerous offspring, like a kind of Hydra, sprouted again with new heads in place of those that had been cut off? By his father’s will he had already been deprived even of their common right: after being given the hope of ruling, but only as a temporary deputy, he would not be permitted to keep any of his own sons in authority; rather, he would be forced to hand the kingdom back to Herod, Mariamne’s son. [Note: [Col. 2023D] “He would substitute him.” BARR.]

Thus hope of the kingdom had not been given to him for its enjoyment, but for his danger, so that he would be suspect to his predecessor and burdensome to his successor. Finally, the king himself, vigorous and intent upon killing his own family despite his advanced old age, was the executor of his own will: he was driven by a heavy hatred of his sons, and by no lighter a hatred of his brother, who had given him one hundred talents. He would not even speak with his uncle. [Note: [Col. 2023D] “Who had given it to him.” ID.]

When Pheroras replied, “In what way have we injured him? Am I also his successor?” Antipater answered that Herod had several reasons for taking offense at him.

“Would that, after all the others had been lost, I might make myself fit for his displeasure! He is a savage beast, which is not satisfied even with deaths and cannot endure that any affection should remain among his relatives. Would that, after everything had been lost, we might at least escape him alive and stripped of everything—but that is impossible. Therefore we need secret conversations for the time being. The time will come when we must use the vigor of a manly mind, the liveliness of counsel, and the service of an avenging hand.”

These things were reported by slaves placed under torture, and Herod believed the slave, especially because he had spoken only of the hundred talents given to Antipater, and there had been no interpreter of his words. Inflamed with indignation, Herod seized most of them for punishment, including many innocent people, so that none of the guilty might be left behind.

Antipater the Samaritan was summoned to torture because he had been Antipater’s procurator, and he was tormented in various ways. The interrogation revealed that poison had been sent from Egypt through a certain companion of Antiphilus. Antiphilus had given it to Theudion, Antipater’s friend, and Theudion had handed it over to Pheroras, to whom Herod’s son Antipater had entrusted its execution, so that while Antipater himself was staying in Rome, his father Herod might be destroyed.

[Col. 2023C] At that time no suspicion of the planned murder would arise against Antipater while he was absent. [Note: [Col. 2023D] “Accomplished.” ID.] But when Pheroras had entrusted the poison he had received to his own wife, suspicion of the poison fell upon Pheroras’s wife in turn. The king immediately ordered her to produce the poison.

The woman went out as though she were going to bring what had been requested, then threw herself from the height of the buildings, in order to escape the double burden of the accusation and to forestall, by her death, both the discovery of the matter and the severity of the interrogation. But because the fatal vengeance for parricide was being hastened against Antipater, she did not fall upon the top of her head, where she would easily have died; instead, she fell upon another part of her body, so that death might be prolonged. She was nevertheless unconscious and stunned, since she had fallen from a great height.

Herod ordered that she be allowed to recover for a little while, until she returned to herself. He promised pardon if she would plainly disclose the sequence of events. Her leap, he said, had not been without cause: she was conscious of a great crime and had sought to shorten her punishment. All crimes would be pardoned if she confessed; but if she denied them, her punishments would be heaped up, and she would be denied burial as well.

When she had recovered somewhat, she said:

[Col. 2024A] “And for whom, now that Pheroras is dead, shall I continue to keep the secrets in silence? [Note: [Col. 2023D] “Silence.” ID.] I owed him the loyalty of silence, for whom I would not have refused punishment if it had been necessary. But he is now free from torments and, if an error deserving pardon can be corrected, free from guilt. [Note: [Col. 2023D] For *venialis* (“pardonable”), as in Macrobius. ID.] Why, then, should I think of concealing the truth with lies in order to comply with Antipater? [Note: [Col. 2023D] “Does [this] compel [me]? Or, ‘that I may comply with Antipater’?” ID.] Shall I spare him and not spare myself? We owe an extraordinary reward to the man who by his crimes has brought us all to these punishments.

“Listen, O king, with God as my guardian, for he alone is the judge of my truthfulness. I have resolved to deceive in nothing. Listen, I say—but first recall how you sat weeping beside your brother in danger, and how you fulfilled every duty of a loving brother toward Pheroras. [Note: [Col. 2024D] “Of pious brotherhood.” ID.]

[Col. 2024B] “Moved by these things, as soon as you had departed he called me to him and said: ‘Not a little, woman, have I strayed from my brother’s affection and devotion. I hated one who loved me so much, and I wished to kill one who could not bear the distress of my dangers. He cannot endure what is accidental, while I was pressing what was not owed. I admit that I have been surrounded by Antipater’s treachery, but I am paying the price of his plan. [Note: [Col. 2024D] The old manuscript reads “contagion”; shortly afterward, however, “I am paying the price.” ID.] Bring me quickly the poison that you have received from him and pour it out before my eyes, so that I may not carry a parricidal intention even among the dead. Let repentance for the correction of my conduct be the consequence of having prepared what was criminal. Quickly, woman, I say, so that I may at least forestall death, since I could not forestall guilt.’

“Then I brought the poison and emptied it in his presence, though I kept a small amount for myself, because I feared you, so that the poison might be ready as a remedy for these purposes if I were exposed.”

[Col. 2024C] When she had said this, she produced the box containing what remained of the poison.

The mother of Antiphilus and his brothers were subjected to interrogation. [Note: [Col. 2024D] “Brother” is more correctly read, according to the old manuscript and Josephus, *Jewish War* I.19. ID.] They confessed that Antiphilus had brought from Egypt a box full of poison, which he had received from a brother who lived in Alexandria under a teacher of medicine.

Mariamne, the daughter of the high priest, was also discovered to be aware of the plots being prepared against her husband; this was revealed when her brothers confessed it under torture. Consequently, the younger Herod paid the price for his mother’s boldness. Although Antipater had substituted him as heir to the kingdom, the same man who had appointed him—his father—decided that he should be erased from the will. [Note: [Col. 2024D] “The same man who had appointed him.” ID.]

[Col. 2024D] This was certainly no slight error on the part of the elder Herod: when a further crime had been discovered, another man was punished. Yet the younger Herod’s punishment was not unjust either. For it seems to have been divinely provided that, although not yet because of the merit of an act already committed, he should nevertheless be deprived of the kingdom as the price of future wickedness. For who could have endured him as king, when he had been so insolent as tetrarch that he could not be tolerated?

[Col. 2025A] Another kind of poison was also added to the charges. Bathyllus, Antipater’s freedman, brought it to Pheroras and his wife. It had been compounded from the juices of serpents and the venom of asps, so that, if the first poison did not succeed in killing Herod, they might use the second.

## CHAPTER XLIV
Letters are also found composed against the brothers Archelaus and Philip. They were the king’s sons, being educated at Rome, whom Antipater was especially eager to discredit because he saw that they possessed no ordinary intelligence and that the king leaned toward them with paternal affection. Finally, he had summoned them by letter to return home as soon as possible. Antipater therefore judged that they obstructed his own interests and applied himself to his usual schemes, so that, under the pretext of the young men’s pretended hope, all the efforts of his faction might be concealed.

Accordingly, he composed letters in the names of powerful men [Col. 2025B] whom he had enticed at Rome into his friendship [Note: [Col. 2025D] “Placed” there. BARR.]. He also forced others by payment to write that the young men were assailing their father with hostile hatred and lamenting with excessive complaint the deaths of Alexander and Aristobulus. When, by secret devices and through courtiers who were ministers of his crime, he presented such letters to his father, he employed the same trickery by which he had earlier pretended to intercede for his brothers, so that, under the supposed protection of filial devotion, he might conceal parricide.

When all these matters had been brought into the open by examination, and his father’s life, the letters, and the desire for his brothers’ death had been revealed with the utmost clarity, a decision was reached [Note: “In council”; and shortly afterward. ID.]: punishment was to be inflicted on the author who had exposed the later facts, because he had persecuted his brothers not as parricides but as rivals for the lawful succession [Col. 2025C]—not because he was defending his father, but so that he would not have a partner in the kingdom.

Meanwhile, while seven months passed amid the evidence of his crimes and the return of Antipater, no indication of what had happened became known to Antipater, so fiercely did universal hatred boil around him. Uncertain of everything, therefore, he wrote from Rome that he would immediately be present and that Caesar had dismissed him with the highest honor. After reading this letter, Herod wrote back that he ought to hasten his return, confident in his father’s affection: his standing had not merely suffered no diminution through his absence; indeed, such favor had been added to it that his presence would lessen his mother’s offense.

For Herod had once again caught her at home consenting to her son’s schemes, and, stripped of her association with him, had expelled her from the benefits and advantages of royal generosity. He now made it evident, under the appearance of his written words, that he would set aside his anger toward her, fearing that, upon learning of his mother’s expulsion, Antipater might be stirred to take precautions against his suspicions.

On arriving, therefore, Antipater first learned at Tarentum of Pheroras’s death, and there he displayed profound mourning. Some attributed this to filial devotion, because he was grieving impatiently over the death of his uncle. But he was lamenting that the agent of his attempted parricide had been removed, and he was terrified that not only had the preparations for the crime failed to advance, but that he himself had given the poison away, lest it somehow come to the king’s knowledge and the king disclose the whole scene of the crime [Col. 2026A] [Note: “By any means whatever.” ID.].

He therefore proceeded to the harbor of Caesarea by no means free from a heavier burden of care and anxiety, since his mother too supplied no slight prejudgment against her already condemned son [Note: “And expelled.” ID.]. But his friends pressed him, judging that everything else should be subordinated to the interests of his native land and that whatever benefited Antipater ought to be pursued. Finally, they relied on his accustomed cleverness: he had usually been able, by his counsels, easily to bend even an estranged father back toward his favor. They urged him to present himself quickly to his father and to the kingdom already destined for him, since no one would dare to oppose him while he was present. Only his absence had provided an opportunity, so that it could be judged possible to turn the king’s mind away from him.

[Col. 2026B] He therefore had to forestall matters promptly, lest delay either offend his father, who was longing for him, or aggravate his suspicion, since delay would reveal distrust of himself. Antipater consequently trusted inclination more than necessity, as his advisers urged [Note: Thus the manuscripts of Gronovius correctly. The first edition, however, reads *volenda* with what follows; later editions alter the margin to *violentia*, as though it derived from *violens*. But there is no place here for *violentia*. MAZOCH. See what was noted above concerning this word at chapter 41. GALLAND.].

But when he entered the harbor, he looked around and saw no one coming to meet him. He sensed, as though some pestilence were present, that his arrival was being shunned. In the midst of the greatest crowd of people, he experienced the deepest solitude, since no one dared to come forward: some were afraid, others hostile. For at that time even hatred had acquired authority enough that people no longer concealed it. He began to reflect upon his crimes and to be tormented by the goads of conscience. No avenue of flight or means of escape remained to him. He was surrounded and held captive, as if by certain nets.

He derived all his confidence from shamelessness, so that, concealing everything, he might present himself unexpectedly to his father, rush into his embrace, and put forward the services of filial devotion. But Herod extended his hands, repelled him as he thrust himself forward, and leaned back his head so that it would not be touched by a parricide’s kiss. He cried out:

“This too is the madness of a parricide: to seek the embrace of one whom you recognize as hostile to you; to infect your father with horror at your presence; and by contact with your guilty body to rob him of the sweetness of life. Do not, then, touch me; do not lay hands upon one whom you sought to destroy by crime. First clear yourself, if you can; explain away the facts that have been discovered. I will not refuse judgment, nor will I allow you to be denied a hearing. I will not take the investigation upon myself, nor leave you any opportunity for argument. Varus is conveniently present; prepare your defense before him. There is no opportunity for delay. Tomorrow, although you are equipped with deceit and fraud, you will have the chance to clear yourself.”

Struck dumb with terror at such an upheaval, Antipater dared neither to answer nor was he able to do so. He went outside, wavering in mind, because he had learned nothing at all of the events that had occurred and had been disclosed to his father. Later, his mother and wife came to him and revealed everything.

Once he understood these matters, he began to collect himself and prepare his mind, considering how he might meet the accusation and weaken the force of the confession. The next day all the king’s relatives and Antipater’s friends assembled; everyone attended the examination. Those who had disclosed different matters concerning Antipater were ordered to be brought in.

The letters of Antipater’s mother were also read. In them she had written to her son that he should realize that the scene of his crimes had been betrayed to his father. He should by no means appear unless some force were summoned from Caesar, with whose protection he might surround himself. He should not submit himself to the judgment of one who was being attacked by the confessions of so many, but should fortify himself with arms.

When these matters had been added to what had already been presented, Antipater entered and threw himself at his father’s feet. He begged him not to regard him as already condemned. He said that, if a hearing were granted him, he trusted that he would be found free of crime—if his father were willing.

His father ordered him to be silent and forestalled him with the following speech:

“It is sufficiently certain that Antipater’s wickedness can appear pardonable to no just man; but for that very reason I think that I am all the more burdened before you, Varus. For I fear that you may also hate me, since I fathered sons who were parricides, sons whom even a father could not spare. Yet I am perhaps more deserving of pity because I loved such men as well.

“But I shall say nothing about those whom I myself provoked and whose just accusations against this man I rejected. They had no cause for resentment against me except that Antipater was preferred to them and had received the privilege of royal association, although he had not been born to royal rank [Note: “In the kingdom.” BARR.]. I thought, nevertheless, that I was bringing an elder son into association with the younger ones for their protection.

“But I introduced an enemy who envied the nobler men, stirred up the boys, surrounded the weak, and betrayed the unsuspecting. I do not deny that they fell, but they ought to have been excused rather than pressed. Antipater was the one who took them from me; Antipater was the one who compelled them to become plotters against me.

“I grieved, I admit, that those to whom I had given hope of the kingdom, to whom I had reserved the succession, were plotting wickedly against me. But now they hated not their father, but Antipater. They perished, therefore, to their father’s grief but for Antipater’s advantage.

“You ask, Varus, who killed them? Learn whose interests their death served. The household lay open to the stepmother’s son; the palace was opened to a single successor, although it had possessed many successors. Nor was his bloodthirsty spirit and wicked mind satisfied by the death of his brothers. When he had no brothers left to hate, he persecuted his father.

“I reflect with myself: I was the one who prepared for this man the protection of an inheritance. I seemed to live too long to one who was impatient for my departure [Note: ‘To him . . . as successor.’ ID.]. I taught him what he wanted, since I had removed his competitors for the succession. He could not endure the delay; he did not await the kingdom except in order to obtain it through parricide.

“He repaid me because I had gathered him up when he was cast aside and had preferred him to nobler men. For to whom among them did I grant as much as I granted him? To whom had I yielded power while still alive? Whom had I named heir in an opened will—something that is usually dangerous for kings, since it allows someone to know that he will succeed?

“I granted him fifty talents in annual revenues [Col. 2028A]. When he departed for Rome, I gave him three hundred. I commended him to Caesar as though he were my only son. I kept nothing back that could have made me fear a parricide. Yet this armed him all the more for parricide: he saw himself made greater than I by my benefits.

“What such crime had his brothers committed, whom he drove to death? What evidence of that kind had been discovered against them, such as has been discovered against him? And yet this parricide dares to interrupt and protest, attempting by deceit to obscure the truth?

“Beware, Varus, I warn you; beware of his feigned tears and artfully composed groans, expressed by no genuine grief. This is the man who deprived me of the affection of my sons, when he warned Alexander that he must beware of a fictitious fear, asserting that many minds were in agreement with him and that my presence should not rashly be entrusted to everyone.

“He pretended to watch over everything, to escort me even to my bed, to search out and examine each person. He was the manager of my sleep and the minister of my security. In him I placed my consolation, and through his services I eased my grief over those who had been killed. I thought that he would restore them to me, take away my sorrow, and display filial devotion.

“He was my protector; to him I entrusted the guardianship of my aged body. I do not know how I shall live, or how I escaped so great a plotter, by what blandishments he surrounded me, by what frauds he held me bound, so that I entrusted myself to this one man, when I ought to have guarded myself against him alone.

“It seems incredible to me that I escaped, and I do not seem to myself to be alive; I think it a dream. Who would have believed either that he would prove so ungrateful, to whom I had entrusted all power over me, or that I could escape if Antipater did not wish it? Yet I thought myself made safer by his favor.

“But what misfortune—good heavens!—that I should either make hostile or rouse against me those whom I had loved most. I lament the misery of my household, Varus; I mourn its solitude; I groan under the force of such great grief. Yet the bitterness of parricidal crime is so great that I will allow no one to escape me who has thirsted for my blood, even if evidence of attempted parricide is brought against all my sons.

“As he said these things, his voice was broken by indignation and grief. Immediately Antipater raised his head. He had been lying at his father’s feet as though struck down and wounded by a blow, and he did not dare to rise. Crying out, he said:

“‘You, father, accuse me as an angry man; but I have no greater defense than the testimony of your accusation, because I have always been the guardian of your safety. In my favor, therefore, you have supplied a defense through the very words of my accuser.

“‘For how could I be a parricide, when you yourself confess that I was your protector? Or how could I be cautious and crafty, when you accuse me of devising parricide? It would be the height of folly to have conceived such a thought, since it is detestable among men and cannot remain unpunished before God.

“‘I could have been instructed even by the example of my brothers that there is no escape from so great a crime, since such a crime finds neither hiding place nor exemption from punishment, seeing that they paid the penalty for such hostility toward you. But, as you say, a certain envy drove them to parricide, because they saw me preferred to them. The nobility of their maternal descent gave them confidence to claim the kingdom as though it were owed to them by maternal succession, and to demand back from you what you had taken from them.

“‘What of me? I knew no hope of the kingdom except through you; I sought your judgment and desired to please you alone. What, then, could have driven me to dare anything against your safety? Was it desire for the kingdom? But I was already reigning. Was it suspicion of hatred? But I was loved. Was it resentment over an injury? But I was preferred.

“‘If fear of my advancement alone armed them for parricide, I am acquitted, because those who are preferred do not know how to conceive parricide, but only how to hate [Note: “Nor hatred.” BARR.]. Unless perhaps some fear of you compelled me. Yet, as your own voice testifies on my behalf, I knew nothing except how to fear for you.

“‘For what should I fear for myself, when I was the minister of your security and the manager of your peace? Or did lack of money and poverty compel me—circumstances that usually persuade the needy to robbery? But you had given me enough not only for the present but for all time, and you had sent me to Rome a rich man, so that the kings of kings might declare that, among themselves, the preeminence of rule lay in power, not in wealth.

“‘Finally, I captured Fabatus, that administrator of Roman affairs and intimate of Caesar, for you. Though he had been won over by a great sum of money from Syllaeus [Note: “Courted.” ID.] to attack you, I so transformed him that he became your defender and betrayed the man who had solicited him.

“‘Through whom were other plotters against your safety exposed to my father? How, then, could I be a parricide, when I discovered Corinthus, a guard of your body, hiding? When I removed him while he was plotting? When I led those who denied the matter to confessions? I could have refrained from thinking of parricide and still have obtained the benefit of parricide, if I had kept silent.

“‘But even if I possessed the savagery of beasts and the fury of savage animals, I could nevertheless have been softened by such great benefits from you, so that I would establish no protection except for the defense of your safety; so that, in return for everything, I would offer you at least my affection; so that I would protect you with my body and, if it were possible, enclose you within my inmost entrails.

“‘You had preferred me to your nobler sons, although I was less noble by my maternal descent. You had even called my mother, an exile from the kingdom, back into the kingdom. You no longer treated me as the successor to the empire but almost as your partner.

“‘Wretched that I am, upon whom your generosity had poured out so many blessings that envy followed! Most foolish that I am, who abandoned you, father! Thus room and power were given to envy and to plotters against you. For while I lingered long in the defense of your safety, I betrayed my own; and yet I have nothing to attribute to myself.

“‘You, father, ordered me to depart. I was traveling abroad for you, father, so that Syllaeus would not ensnare your old age, deprive you of the kingdom while you were still alive, or seek your destruction before Caesar.

“‘Rome is my witness to my filial devotion; Caesar too, the governor of the world, the judge of all things and arbiter of my heart, who used to call me one who loved his father. Bear witness, Caesar, to what I said about my father before you, the only man before whom I could have done harm. Bear witness, I say, you who had given judgment concerning the others. You did not think that parricide should be concealed, but investigated.

“‘Would that your presence were available to me! But you are absent and far away, and I am judged by my father without you. Yet you are present in your letters. I offer your writings, which parricides usually fear. I carry your letter, which those who want parricide not to remain hidden usually bring forth.

“‘Receive, father, Caesar’s letter. Let him himself instruct you—the man who recently avenged you. Receive Caesar’s writings, stronger than every argument. Use them now for my salvation, as you used them earlier for vengeance.

“‘I bring these documents as witnesses to my innocence. That right hand never deceived you. That right hand placed Caesar’s diadem upon your head; it did not take it away. That hand restored to you Caesar’s kingdom, which you had cast aside.

“‘Caesar could have hated me earlier if he had discovered me to be like my brother [Note: “Of the brothers.” ID.]. But he recognized and declared me an interpreter; had I not been at Rome, Syllaeus would have prevailed. Today I am handed over to him; wretchedly I pay the penalty to him.

“‘Remember, father, that I did not sail away voluntarily. I saw that traps were already being prepared for me by plotters. Nevertheless, father, I preferred that I myself should be endangered rather than you. Yet I do not shrink from the danger to my safety; I grieve that, before you, father, I am endangered as though I were your enemy.

“‘I am endangered, nevertheless, if the testimony of Caesar is endangered before you. I use these documents as evidence for my defense. I do not appeal to Caesar as though he must hear me, but implore him as though I must be acquitted.

“‘And if you think that judgment must be exercised, behold, my father: after Caesar I have come to you; from Caesar I hastened to you. Would indeed that I had never departed from you. But you, father, unknowingly exposed me to dangers when you ordered me to go.

“‘I am present, father. I do not think that the truth necessary for your safety should be sought perfunctorily from lesser witnesses. Let neither those who may fear torture nor those who may despise it prejudice the case. “Every man is a liar,” Scripture says (Psalm 115:11).

“‘I offer the incorruptible testimony of the elements. I come to you across seas and lands, having suffered nothing anywhere. If I were guilty, a parricide should not have escaped. Let heaven, which did not strike me with lightning; the sea, which did not swallow me; and the earth, which did not engulf me, acquit me before you, father. Through these I come safely to you—though even those who are not parricides of their natural fathers do not usually escape through them.

“‘The earth’s chasm swallowed Dathan and Abiram, although they had not sought the life of their natural father. The tree’s branches suspended Absalom as he fled, so that he could not reach his father; if he had reached him, he would have escaped. I have come to you, and I am still in danger.

“‘David avenged his parricide because he could not preserve him. I do not ask to be avenged upon my enemies and accusers by summoning them to torture; let them reap the punishment of their accusation. I ask one thing, father: do not trust the torture of others. Seek punishment from me, against myself.

“‘Hang your accused man. Let the examination of truth proceed into my entrails; let the cords of interrogation descend into my body and inward recesses; let blood flow—the blood that usually cries out against parricide; let fire be carried into my guilty limbs.

“‘Why do you hesitate, father? If you spare me, you declare me innocent; if you refrain from torture, you acquit me of the crime. A man who is judged worthy of a simple death is not a parricide.

“‘Or, if you spare me as a son and feel compassion for limbs born from you, those are not your limbs that serve as instruments of cruelty.’”

When he had spoken these words, he ended his speech with abundant weeping and lamentable groaning. With the loudest wailing, he moved Varus and everyone else to pity. Herod alone was moved by no tears; he himself refrained from weeping, unyielding toward forgiveness, pressing for the investigation and demanding vengeance.

## CHAPTER XLV.

Nicolaus followed Antipater’s speech by order of the king. He skillfully answered Antipater’s tricks and drew those who had been bent toward pity away from compassion, by bringing up the odium of Antipater’s fratricidal killing and arguing that, if anyone was moved by pity, pity ought to be shown to those who had been killed by his frauds and who were demanding vengeance.

If they acquitted one man, he said, the entire royal household would be exposed to danger: his brothers, relatives, parents, and the king himself, whose safety Antipater had not spared. Thus, turning to the trickery of the speakers, he seemed, in a certain epilogue [Note: The words enclosed in parentheses are superfluous. BARR.], to summon the murdered men’s souls from the underworld in a narrative designed to arouse pity. They filled the benches with lamentable complaints, saying that they had perished innocent, surrounded by fabricated witnesses, composed letters, and fraudulent speeches; that their father had been deceived because he had trusted a son whom he did not think capable of lying about his brothers.

Now the man who had not believed his brothers’ tortures offered his own torments [Note: “Now he offers his punishments.” ID.]. He had loaded them with chains and bound them so that they could not attend the investigation. Judgment had been passed upon men who were absent, since they had been killed while far away, lest their father pity them.

If this man escaped, no one would be left safe, for he was skilled at pouring parricidal poisons into the bowels of his own family and at changing men’s minds. He had even stirred up Pheroras, who had always been most devoted to his brother, to undertake the fatal parricide of Herod.

After Nicolaus had added many other points to excite emotion, he finished his speech. Varus then asked Antipater whether he wished to reply. He answered nothing except: “God is my witness: I have harmed no one.”

Varus ordered the poison to be brought forth and given to one of those who had already been condemned to death. After drinking it, the man immediately died. The matter was reported to Caesar, and by order of his father Antipater was led away in chains.

Yet he was not free from plots. He was then especially attempting to endanger Salome by means of letters. Antipater had composed them in Salome’s name, full of insults against the king, and had ordered them to be delivered through Antiphilus’s servant to Acme, a maidservant of Julia, who was Caesar’s wife. He intended Acme to return them to the king. The deception had almost brought about the woman’s ruin, had not a letter from Acme to Antipater been discovered, exposing the plot. It was written as follows:

“As you wished, I wrote to your father, and I sent those letters. I have no doubt that the king will rise up to endanger his sister. Now repay me when you have obtained the desired result.”

When these letters were discovered, the king was led to suspect that Alexander too had been attacked by letters composed by his brother through the same device. Deeply agitated and embittered, he contracted a serious illness.

Seeing himself pressed by danger, he named Antipas, one of his sons, heir to the empire [Note: The old manuscript says, “He wrote in his will.” ID.], preferring him to Archelaus and Philip, his older children, because Antipater had also made them suspect to their father through his plots and deceptions.

He bequeathed a thousand talents to Caesar, with gifts and presents added. He granted fifty talents to his wife and sons, freedmen, and friends; nor did he leave his sister Salome without a share of his gifts.

His illness grew worse and intensified with the passage of time [Note: “Was aggravated.” ID.]. His feeble old age aggravated it daily with its own troubles. Indeed, his body, weighed down by more than seventy years, was also repeatedly afflicted by grief of mind, wounded by so many parricides [Note: Thus the first edition. Others read *conulceratus*, “covered with sores,” or *vulneratus*, “wounded.” The same author, Ambrose, writes in Letter 43 to Horontianus, no. 5: “He wounded all spiritual wickedness together.” MAZOCH.].

It was an incurable fever of illness, because Antipater’s survival was feared. His contempt also increased day by day, because the images of Caesar and likenesses of animals that had been placed in the temple contrary to the law were being torn down [Col. 2032C], chiefly at the instigation of Judas and Matthias, teachers of the young men. They said that, since they had learned of the conspiracy and were acting in agreement, the time had come for vengeance upon the outrage of the violated law.

The sacrilegious man, they said, was paying the penalty: he had thought that whatever power permitted was lawful, and, not restrained by religion but lifted up by pride, he had exercised his desire to do whatever he wished in the temple’s inner sanctuary as though it were a legal right.

Although divine vengeance was hastening his death, they nevertheless thought it glorious if they also demonstrated the temple’s sacred freedom [Note: Read “the freedom of the sacred temple.” ID.] by defending the observances of their ancestral rite. No one ought to be deterred by fear of danger, since even to die for the ancestral law was a mark of immortality.

They were the first to attempt to tear down the golden eagle fastened above the gateway. They were arrested and brought before the king. When asked whose authority they wished to obey in undertaking so great a deed, they replied: “Our ancestral law.”

When he asked again what gave them confidence to appear so cheerful, although they were being called to the danger of death, they replied: “The rewards of piety and devotion, which are paid to those who seek death according to the ancestral rite.”

He could no longer endure the steadfastness of their answers. Indignation added to his illness and overcame his weakness. He went out into the assembly of the people, and there began to accuse them before the populace as guilty of sacrilege, alleging that they were suspected of planning still greater deeds.

Even if these charges were not proved, each person, fearing for himself, begged that the punishments of the captured instigators not be extended to the others. He was therefore asked to pronounce judgment upon those present, and ordered that they be burned alive, rather than proceed against the rest, lest the investigation disturb more people—strangers and innocent men alike.

As a result, his illness increased, and the force of a more serious disease consumed his whole body with various afflictions. There was a violent fever, unbearable itching, continuous pains in the inner organs without any interruption, and a disorder affecting the middle of his neck. His feet were swollen with dropsy; hidden parts of his body swarmed with worms; there were spasms throughout the body [Note: “Spasms.” BARR.], heavy breathing, and deadly sighs. The condition indicated that punishment was being exacted for unjust parricide and sacrilegious condemnation.

Yet he did not yield in spirit. His desire to live struggled against his illnesses. He requested the hot springs beyond the Jordan, but they provided no benefit. The Asphaltite Lake, medicinal for many, held the sick man without producing any improvement.

While he was being fomented with a great quantity of oil, his body relaxed and collapsed. He turned his eyes upward as if he were dying; his voice failed, and his senses no longer remained. But the shouting of those crying aloud roused him [Note: “Or, once aroused?” GALLAND.]. Wishing to return to his own affairs, he reached the region of the place called Jericho. Agitated by black bile and, in a certain sense, threatening death itself, he conceived a monstrous deed [Col. 2033C] by which, as though funeral offerings were being sent to him, the people might serve as his funeral rites.

For some time earlier he had ordered all the more distinguished people from throughout Judea to be gathered, so that a group from each village might assemble in one place. When his order had been obeyed, he commanded that they be shut inside the hippodrome. He summoned Salome and her husband Alexas [Note: “Alexander.” BARR.] and entrusted them with a bloody commission. He declared that his death would be a source of joy to the Jewish people; therefore, he said, he had devised a plan by which his epitaph might be celebrated with the greatest distinction.

He asked his relatives that, as soon as he breathed his last, they should order all those being held inside to be killed. In this way, no one throughout Judea and no household would remain whose grief over his death could be shed without tears, since he would have left the inheritance of mourning to all their families. While they mourned the death of their own people, they would seem to be paying the proper honors to the king; thus the joy of the public would be obstructed by private grief.

And lest some criminal reluctance to execute the orders frustrate his wicked commands, he ordered fifty drachmas to be given to each soldier. By imposing such payment for the crime, he ensured that the soldiers would not refuse the funeral service, compensating the horror of the execution with the gain of the reward.

His illness was now almost yielding to the punishments it had inflicted, but he awaited the grim report of the delegation. It reported that Acme had been punished at Herod’s complaint; that Antipater too had been convicted of parricide and condemned to death; but that, after depriving him of his fatherland and kingdom, Caesar had ordered that his father might grant him leave to flee, if he wished, thus passing sentence on the crime while leaving the decision to filial affection.

Nature had relieved him of the necessity of parricide. For, after recovering somewhat and having been granted the power to punish as he wished, he became occupied with considering the manner of death. Overcome by pains, he had eagerly desired that the day of his death should arrive quickly [Note: Others read “of his own”; and shortly afterward, “to forestall.” ID.].

He therefore asked for an apple and, at the same time, a knife, so that he might cut the apple with it and take some refreshment. Raising himself slightly and leaning on his elbow, he lifted his right hand, wishing to strike himself. But Achiabus came forward and prevented the blow. The whole household resounded with mourning, so that those outside thought that Herod had died.

Antipater rejoiced at the sound of lamentation and asked the guards who had been assigned to him to release him from his chains. But the officer in charge not only refused his request; he also reported it to the king.

Herod cried out that he was still being mocked while alive. He sent men to kill Antipater, ordered that he be buried at Hyrcania, and altered his will once again. He established Archelaus as king, the eldest of the brothers, and left the tetrarchy to Antipas.

He survived Antipater by five days and died after possessing the kingdom for thirty-seven years from the time he had been ordered by the Romans to rule. From the time he removed Antigonus, his rival for the kingdom, he had exercised power for thirty-four years—if only he had been as fortunate in his household as in his public successes.

For fortune favored him abroad so greatly that, although a private citizen, he was raised to the kingdom and enjoyed it for many long years. It is difficult for anyone to relinquish power while still safely possessing it, yet he left his children the succession to the empire, which he himself had not received from his own family.

But within his household he was most wretched. He filled it with the bitter blood and mourning of his own people. Nevertheless, he did not carry out the final act of cruelty. Salome alone erased the earlier mockery of his crimes by releasing all those whom the king had ordered to be struck down. She said that the king had later repented of the fatal command and, withdrawing his earlier orders, had instructed that everyone be sent back to his own home.

## CHAPTER XLVI.

Afterward, an assembly of the soldiers and the remaining people was held in the amphitheater, and proceedings were held concerning the king’s death. Ptolemy came forward. He had remained among the most faithful of the king’s friends to the very end. Carrying the ring that he had removed from the dead man’s finger, he praised the king, urged the people to remain calm, and opened for them a letter in which the king, addressing his most faithful soldiers, had urged them to show goodwill and favor toward his successor.

The will was also read from the opened tablets. Philip was named heir of the region of Trachonitis and the neighboring territories; Antipas was appointed tetrarch; Archelaus was appointed king, but with the provision that his ring should be taken to Caesar and that Caesar should retain the authority and confirmation of all his arrangements. His will was to be valid only if Caesar approved it. He ordered the remaining provisions to be preserved according to his earlier wills.

Immediately the soldiers acclaimed Archelaus with applause. He was at once surrounded by a circle of guards; they promised goodwill and pledged loyalty.

After this, the funeral was suitably and magnificently arranged. All the splendor of royal wealth was displayed for the solemnity of the funeral procession. The bier was entirely covered with gold and adorned with jewels; its brilliant covering was dyed with purple; the body was covered by a purple double garment, fastened with a brooch sparkling with precious stones. A diadem clung to his head, above it was a golden crown, and he held a scepter in his right hand, so that one might think him alive.

A Thracian contingent led the procession. German and Gallic guards [Col. 2036A] maintained the royal military order. They were girded with weapons in the same manner as though they were marching out to war [Note: “But with faces sorrowful and resembling mourners.” BARR.]. Their faces, however, were full of sadness, and they accompanied him like men in mourning.

The remaining force followed in its customary dress and accustomed attire, accompanied likewise by commanders and centurions. Five hundred servants and freedmen of the royal household sprinkled spices, so that the whole road might be fragrant with a pleasant smell. A great multitude of the king’s sons and relatives surrounded the bier.

He was buried at Herodium, as he himself had ordered, two hundred stades from the place where he had met the end of his life. All escorted him over this great distance with solemn service, but not all with equal feeling: fear had extorted the outward duty, not the inward wish; grief at least retained freedom of judgment within itself.

Such was the end of Herod.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 2035]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 2035B]

After Herod had been buried, the people gave free expression to their judgments, as is customary regarding the dead: that he had been a harsh and intolerable man; that he had exercised unjust commands over his fellow citizens; that he had been a tyrant, not a king, of his subjects; a domestic parricide; a public plunderer; that he had left nothing to anyone; that everything had been exhausted by taxes; that foreigners had been enriched while the Jews had been impoverished, because he had brought an enemy into the Temple and polluted all that was sacred with sacrilege [Note: [Col. 2035D] Sacred things, or holy things. BARR.]; that those who had defected from him were fortunate, since the living had not been without torments; that Judaea had endured more evils in a few years under Herod’s rule, after its captivity had been removed, than it had suffered during the captivity itself under a barbarian enemy; that, when the kings of Babylon ruled over them, their exiles had been more tolerable than a domestic dwelling under Herod; that under the former they had been sent back to their own, whereas by the latter they had been driven into flight; that he had been more savage than Darius, more arrogant than Artaxerxes, and more rapacious than the Medes.

They had hoped for an end to their evils, so that they might be permitted to leave their exile if he closed the day of his life; but Archelaus had come as a voluntary successor to the misery of servitude, one who both resembled Herod and added new evils. It was miserable in kingdoms that a ruler should be chosen; more miserable that one should be imposed upon unwilling subjects. Servitude seemed to offer some consolation if they chose their own master, because authority became milder when it was conferred, but more arrogant when it was usurped. Archelaus, therefore, would be far more intolerable than Herod, since the latter had taken up the kingdom, whereas the former had received it.

These things were discussed not only frequently in Judaea, but also at Rome [Note: [Col. 2035D] With Archelaus in attendance. ID.]. While Archelaus was present, the accusers delivered their speeches and cast these charges in his face before Caesar and the Senate, where a long dispute was waged over confirming or abolishing Archelaus’s kingship. Finally, when a hearing was granted in the Temple of Apollo, which Caesar had founded and adorned with many embellishments, Antipater, the son of Salome, forcefully pursued the matters mentioned above and many others. He expressed his amazement that Archelaus should pretend that the kingdom had to be requested from Caesar, when by rash usurpation he had long since exercised kingship within Judaea without consulting Caesar.

For what else were the golden throne and the diadem that had been brought to him, if not insignia of kingship? With what presumption had he dared to sit upon the royal throne; from the lofty seat to greet the surrounding people, while they were flanked by military arms [Note: [Col. 2035D] “Numbers . . . to be placed.” ID.]; and, after the manner and practice of emperors, to bring forth the diadem, which ought to have been reserved for Caesar’s judgment—not only by virtue of the power of the Roman Empire, but also by the authority of the will?

Herod could not have snatched from Caesar or the Senate what he himself had received from the Senate; and in his earlier will he had sufficiently expressed the judgment of his own will, declaring with sound mind and deliberate counsel that Antipas should succeed him in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 2036D] Other manuscripts: Antipater. ID.]. Finally, he had reserved everything for Caesar’s judgment, although, with his body already failing and anxious in the face of supreme danger, incapable of any further perception or deliberation, he had dictated—not what he thought, but what was thrust upon him.

Thus he had pronounced himself the teacher of imperial authority by declaring that one who did not deserve it was to be substituted in the kingdom by Caesar’s judgment. For if he had been conscious of his own merits, he would have hastened to request the kingdom rather than to usurp it. By not requesting but usurping it, he was accustomed to prejudge matters that would otherwise depend upon a petition, even in financial affairs [the text here is corrupt or incomplete; the parenthetical material that follows is absent from some manuscripts]. “And yet I have taken for you that Fabatus, administrator of Roman affairs and Caesar’s intimate, and from Syllaeus an enormous sum for bribery, so that they might oppose”—so that litigants who bring their case in the wrong order may lose their cause [Col. 2037A].

But here it was not financial gain that was being charged as a crime; rather, the law of Roman authority had been violated, reverence had been despised, power had been scorned, and the Senate of the Roman Curia—which was accustomed to grant and take away kingdoms—had been judged unworthy, together with Caesar, of retaining the ancient prerogative of conferring authority.

What would he do once he had begun to rule legitimately, when, before he had obtained the kingdom, he had most arrogantly killed so many who had sought aid in their distress and relief from taxation? When war had been inflicted upon those requesting a remedy; when nine thousand Jews had been killed amid the very solemn celebration of Passover, revered among their people; when human beings had been sacrificed like cattle; when the blood of those who had gathered for the festivals of the sacred Temple had been shed as a pitiful spectacle—if someone were to count the slaughter of the slain, would he not think that the Babylonians had returned [Col. 2037B]? How much more cruel were acts committed by a fellow citizen that, if committed by a barbarian enemy, would be judged full of savage ferocity and impiety? This was the dole given to the citizens; this was the sacrifice by which Archelaus commended the beginning of his reign.

Caesar and the Senate ought to take pity on the remnants of Judaea, which once had been supported by free peoples and would now prefer servitude, provided only that it were permitted to endure it under a just king [Note: [Col. 2037D] Unjust. BARR.]. For among the Jews kingship could belong to no one except one descended from the Jewish line, as the law declared. But this man, an Idumaean by birth, whom no royal origin touched, had insinuated himself into an undeserved position of honor.

For although Antipater had been the grandfather both of himself and of Archelaus, distinguished by wealth and powerful in other abilities, especially through his friendship with the Romans and the favor he had won from the elder Caesar in war, yet, although he could have claimed the kingdom for himself, he had never sought it. Indeed, he had preferred to defend it for others rather than secure it for himself. He had rightly been regarded as an excellent father, since he had restored Judaea to freedom through his own wounds and had not led it into servitude.

Herod, relying on the testimony of Antony, who had been his host by hereditary friendship, had aspired to the kingdom; from that point onward he had diminished Jewish affairs and had treated the Jews as an enemy, not as a ruler. Since he himself had been an adulterer of the kingdom, how could he have created a legitimate king? They did not, however, ask that the Jews be spared rule altogether; they demanded that they be governed under Roman authority, whose favor they had earned for themselves from the time of the Maccabees, but from which they had later degenerated so far through the usurpation of the kingdom that they were now much inferior to those against whom they had sought Roman alliance [Note: [Col. 2037D] Alternatively: nevertheless. ID.].

Finally, he asked that Judaea receive from them a provincial administration under the same conditions as Syria, so that the sincerity of their devotion might be tested: whether those who were called seditious and rebellious could obey moderate judges.

In reply, Nicolaus, speaking for Archelaus, asserted that the most restless nation had paid the penalty for its arrogance. Archelaus should not, above all, be exposed to the charge of an inexcusable crime if they disturbed the peace through sedition and withdrew in spirit and arms from the alliance of the Romans [Col. 2038A]. As for the precedence of the wills, who could doubt it, since a later will is ordinarily preferred to earlier ones? This one ought to seem much more authoritative than the others, because in it the prerogative of confirming the royal judgment had been preserved for Caesar. The reverence due to the Roman name would thereby be increased rather than diminished, if Caesar were not deprived of what private individuals were permitted to do: to make their wills valid and to write in their final document whom they most wished to succeed them. Furthermore, that honor should again be reserved for Caesar, so that confirmation of the judgment might be requested from him, and the one whom the father had chosen and Caesar had approved might succeed [Note: [Col. 2038D] “Be preserved.” A little later, *servavit* should be read instead of *servaverit*. ID.].

When, then, was Herod wiser: when he preserved the prerogative for you, Caesar, or when he disregarded it? When Antipas is substituted, Caesar is disregarded. When Archelaus is appointed in his place, Caesar is brought in. Without a foundation nothing is stable. Thus, where justice was lacking, the foundation was absent either for pretense or for intention. But where equity was available for examination, strength was sought so that the judgment might be confirmed.

Consider, therefore, whether the man who chose you did you an injury, or whether what he left to you, the master of all things, to establish as arbiter should be annulled—for by right even kings yield to your authority. The man who knew whom to choose for confirmation certainly knew whom to choose for rule; and the one who was not mistaken in the confirmer could not have been mistaken in the successor. For the man who appointed you as arbiter thereby recognized that he ought to appoint as his successor one who would not displease you, the person whom you would appoint.

After hearing both sides, Caesar postponed his decision. Then, after consulting with the Senate, he placed Archelaus at the head of the nation, so that he might perform the office of governor, not possess the dignity of a king. He nevertheless promised to grant him the kingdom if he conducted himself in such a way as to win approval. For reports were already announcing the first attempts at dissension among the Israelite people.

He appointed two of Herod’s sons, Philip and Antipas—the latter of whom had contended with Archelaus for the kingdom—as tetrarchs. To Herod’s sister, whose name was Salome, he preserved the estate that had been assigned to her [Note: [Col. 2038D] A legate. ID.], and he himself added other possessions. He also decided that the thousand talents left to Herod’s two daughters should be distributed between them; he added another six hundred thousand and decreed that this sum should be joined to the property of Pheroras’s children.

## CHAPTER II

Meanwhile, a certain young man, pretending to be Alexander, and claiming that, out of pity, those to whom Herod his father had entrusted the task of killing him had substituted others in their place and released him together with his brother Aristobulus, went to Miletus and from there to Rome, where it would be more difficult for strangers to recognize him. There he easily stirred up the Jews, who were exceptionally ready for political novelty, unless Caesar, after discovering who he was, had quickly ordered him to be brought before him by a certain Celadus, who knew Alexander thoroughly.

When Celadus saw the young man, he hesitated, deceived by the resemblance. But when he examined the remaining indications and found that they did not agree, he asked where Aristobulus was. The young man replied that Aristobulus was living on the island of Cyprus, taking care to avoid ambushes, since the brothers, if united, could more easily be destroyed.

Then, after he had been brought before Caesar, he immediately confessed, once immunity had been promised, that he had relied upon the resemblance of his appearance and pretended to be Alexander so that, as the king’s son, he might receive innumerable gifts from the Jews. Caesar laughed at the deception, but ordered the young man himself to be released without punishment. He declared that those who had treated him as though he were the king’s son, beyond the limits appropriate to a private person, had been sufficiently punished by having to endure immeasurable losses through their needless expenditures.

Archelaus, however, having gone to Judaea, was accused before Caesar of obscenity in his conduct and arrogance. After the case between the parties had been investigated, he was banished to Vienna, and his wealth was added to Caesar’s treasuries [Col. 2039B]. This was the fitting price he paid, since he had not restrained his desires even from the wife of his own brother.

For when Alexander died, having been handed over to execution by his father’s command, his wife Glaphyra—whose father was Archelaus, king of Cappadocia, as we have related above—was married in a second marriage to King [Note: [Col. 2039D] An old manuscript reads “Tobas.” Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book II, chapter 6, has “Juba, king of Libya”; and *Antiquities*, Book XVII, chapter 18, has “Juba, king of Mauretania.” BARR.] Juba of Libya. When he too had died, she returned to her father. There Archelaus saw her and, considering that he, as her husband’s brother and the paternal uncle of her children, ought by no means to be shunned as impious, he began to love her so passionately that he divorced Mariamne and put Glaphyra in her place.

Not long afterward, when the woman had returned to Judaea, she saw Alexander in a dream and desired to embrace him. But he, appearing angry and seeming to shrink from her embrace, said:

“Is this, Glaphyra, the faithfulness you promised? Is this how you have preserved your love for me, of which you ought to have remained mindful? But let it be so: as a young woman, you did not refuse a second marriage. Yet should you also have desired a third? Should you have desired the brother of your husband?
