Did my injury delight you so much that, married for the third time, you were not ashamed to return to my household as a wife? But I am concerned that my dishonor and your pollution should remain no longer. The marriage contracted in incest with your husband’s brother will not bring you joy for long.”

The woman arose and told her attendants about the dream. Two days later she herself died, thereby proving that such marriages are neither unpunished by the laws of the living [Note: [Col. 2039D] “Unpunished.” ID.] nor overlooked by the wishes of the dead.

## CHAPTER III

Archelaus himself also saw in a dream nine ears of grain, full and large, being devoured by oxen [Col. 2039D]. When he asked about it, the interpreter replied: “The nine ears signify the nine years during which he exercised the greatest and most extensive power. Therefore, in the ninth year of his rule, a change will come upon him, because oxen, which are accustomed to turn over the fields with the plow, signify a laborious change that will devour and swallow up his former achievements.”

After learning this, on the fifth day a man came from Caesar to take him to Rome for trial. There he was condemned and driven into exile, and he also fulfilled his dream through his death [Col. 2040A].

The principate of the nation, which had belonged to Archelaus, was converted into the name of a province. By this name the Romans called provinces those distant regions which they brought under their own jurisdiction by conquest. The tetrarchs nevertheless remained, as they had been: Philip and Herod, the latter having changed his name, since he had previously been called Antipas.

When Salome died, she left to Livia, the wife of Caesar [Note: [Col. 2040D] He means Livia, the mother of Tiberius. ID.], the places she had possessed and the authority over her people. Such was the condition of Judaea when Caesar died, leaving Tiberius, his stepson and the son of his wife Libya by a former husband, as successor to the Roman Empire. In his honor Herod founded Tiberias. Philip likewise decided that a city should be called Livia, after his mother.

Since it is our purpose to disclose the causes by which the Jewish people revolted from Roman rule and hastened their own destruction, events indicate that Pilate, governor of the province, gave the beginning to their ruin. For he was the first of all who did not hesitate to bring images of Caesar into the buildings of Jerusalem. When the people, moved by this, resisted and he judged that the images had to be received, he forced many to their deaths.

While these things were happening in Judaea, Agrippa, the son of Aristobulus, arrived at Rome, wishing to contend in court before Tiberius against Herod the tetrarch. But, having been despised by Tiberius, while he remained in Rome he cultivated the friendship of many men, especially Gaius, the son of Germanicus. Whether he regarded Gaius as beloved by the people because of his father’s name, or as close to imperial power because of his royal descent, or whether he cultivated him with greater devotion because of some presage, beyond what his age or rank warranted [Col. 2040C], he once raised his hands and prayed that, after Tiberius’s death, he might see Gaius become emperor.

When this was disclosed by his freedman Eutychus, Agrippa was taken into chains by order of Tiberius and subjected to severe tortures. He was not released until Tiberius closed the day of his life. The years of Tiberius were foul with mockeries [Note: [Col. 2040D] So the printed editions read. But *in the retreat of Capua* seems to be the correct reading. GALLAND.] and retreats among goats, and his idleness was intolerable. Nevertheless, they did not arouse any man of effective action to kill him, either because of the recent reverence for Roman rule, or from fear of his most savage cruelty, since harshness is often safer the more severe it is.

## CHAPTER IV

While Tiberius ruled, the notorious disgrace of Paulina, a woman of exceptionally distinguished birth, became widely celebrated at Rome. She had an outstanding reputation for chastity among everyone, and she was also remarkable for her beauty and eminent grace. When she was tested by the advances of Mundus, commander of the equestrian forces, and did not yield, she nevertheless became open to error through excessive superstition.

For Mundus, having suborned priests of Isis, arranged for them to approach her as though they were Anubis and to announce that the god invited her to the Temple. He was delighted by her devotion and chastity; he requested the night, since he had something he wished to entrust to her in secret.

She received the message joyfully and reported it to her husband: her god was present to answer her prayers; he was asking for her presence; she could not refuse obedience. Therefore, with the approval both of herself and of her husband, she went to the Temple of Isis and demanded the night. With all witnesses removed far away, as though she were about to learn the knowledge of a sacred mystery, she arranged herself upon the couches, believing that her god would come to her in dreams and reveal himself to her in a vision.

But when part of the night had passed, so that the woman, full of sleep [Note: [Col. 2041D] “Sleep.” BARR.], might more easily be deceived, Mundus arrived wearing the face and clothing of Anubis. He lifted her garments and rushed to kiss her. When the woman awoke, he told her that he was Anubis and presented the face of Anubis. She believed him to be the god and declared herself blessed that her god had deemed her worthy of a visit.

When he sought her embrace, she did not refuse it. Yet she asked whether a god could unite with a human being. He produced examples: that Alcmena had received Jupiter, the highest of the gods; that Leda had enjoyed intercourse with him; and that many other women had given birth to gods. He persuaded her that a god was also to be born from her and himself. He united with the woman, who then returned to her husband more joyful, saying that she had been joined with a god and, according to his promise, would give birth to a god.

An enormous delight arose in both the woman and her husband over the adultery. Later Mundus met her and said:

“Blessed Paulina, through intercourse with a god: the great god Anubis, whose mysteries you received. But learn that you should not deny to human beings what you do not deny to the gods, since the gods grant us what you refused. They do not disdain to give us either their forms or their names. Behold, the god Anubis called Mundus also to his sacred rites, so that he might unite with you. What benefit did your stubbornness bring you, except that you deprived yourself of the twenty thousand that I had offered? Imitate the more indulgent gods, who grant us without payment what cannot be obtained from you except at a great price. And if human names offend you, I was pleased to be called Anubis, and the affection associated with that name delighted me.”

Struck by these words, the woman understood that she had been deceived. Grieving over the violation of her chastity, she confessed the fraud to her husband. He had no reason to be angry with his wife, since he himself had permitted her to lie in the Temple and knew the purity of her marriage. He nevertheless brought the complaint before the emperor.

Moved by the insult done to a powerful man and by the invention of such an atrocious outrage, the emperor seized the priests from the Temple, subjected them to interrogation, and, after they confessed, killed them. He threw the image of Isis into the Tiber. Mundus was granted the opportunity to flee, because he was judged to have been overcome by the force of love and the attraction of beauty and therefore to deserve a lighter penalty for his offenses.

## CHAPTER V

I have therefore not thought that the disgrace which occurred while Tiberius ruled should be passed over, so that from it the emperor’s deformity may be understood. For just as the life of a good ruler is a kind of prescription of uprightness and a model of living for everyone, so the corruption of an emperor is a law of wickedness [Col. 2042A].

Pilate, an evil man, was sent by him to Judaea. Treating a small matter as though it were insignificant, he deceived the Samaritans into going to the mountain called Gadir. It was sacred to them, since he wished to learn their mysteries. When he ascended, he forestalled the people with cavalry and routed them with infantry, attaching to them the charge that they had been preparing to withdraw from the Romans and seek a gathering-place for themselves.

For what would he not dare, when he even crucified Christ the Lord, who had come for the salvation of the human race and, through many divine works, poured out upon humanity the grace of his mercy, teaching nothing other than that peoples should be obedient first to God and then to the emperors? What a madman he was, to serve sacrilegious [Col. 2042B] fury by killing the author of salvation!

From that point onward the affairs of the Jews were betrayed; from that point onward the destruction of the nation and the Temple was hastened. For if Herod, who handed John over to death, paid the price for his treachery and cruelty by being deprived of his kingdom and sent into exile, how much more clearly must the man who killed Christ be understood to have been driven on by headlong madness?

I shall briefly explain the cause of John’s death. We have shown above that Philip and Herod, who had previously been called Antipas, were brothers. Herod unlawfully and impiously joined himself in marriage to Herodias, Philip’s wife. John did not tolerate this and said to him: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Matt. VI, 18). Then Herod, angered, threw John into prison. Not long afterward he killed the just man [Col. 2042C], the steadfast executor of the divine Law.

For he rebuked the incest of his brother’s bed not only as a preacher of the Gospel, but also condemned the transgressor of the Law as its executor: Herod had taken his brother’s wife while his brother was still alive, especially since she had offspring by Herod’s own brother.

From this arose the hatred of nearly all the Jews against Herod and the hastening of his punishment. Herodias, seeing that Agrippa had gained great influence with Caesar, compelled Herod to go to Rome so that he might win the emperor’s favor. She reproached him for indolence, saying that while he avoided hardships and remained at home, he allowed people unworthy of him to be preferred.

For if Agrippa had become a king from a private station, how much more would Caesar not hesitate to confer a kingdom upon Herod, who had long been a tetrarch? Unable to endure the woman’s reproaches, he went to Rome. While seeking the friendship of Gaius, he was accused by Agrippa and even lost the tetrarchy that he had received from Julius Augustus. Fleeing to Spain with his wife Herodias, he was consumed by grief.

After Tiberius died, Gaius succeeded him. Wishing to appear and be called lord and god, he gave the Jews cause for the most serious sedition; and, unless he had brought his rule to an end by a swift death, he would have hastened the destruction of the Jewish nation. For he not only failed to restrain his subjects from unlawful acts, but also, after sending orders to Judaea, threatened the ultimate punishments unless they accomplished everything contrary to religious law and right by force of arms.

Agrippa had great power. But while he wished to surround Jerusalem with a massive wall, so that it might be impregnable to the Romans—for he foresaw the ruin that was approaching—he was overtaken by death and left the work unfinished.

He also exercised no lesser power during the reign of Claudius, since he took part in the very beginning of Claudius’s rule. When Gaius had been killed, Claudius himself had been taken up by the soldiers, despite the Senate’s resistance. Because he was weary of kingship, he sent Agrippa as an envoy. Through Agrippa as interpreter, an agreement was reached concerning the limits of the ruler’s authority, the terms of favor were defined, and peace was established. In place of Agrippa’s father, his son Agrippa was appointed king by Caesar Claudius.

## CHAPTER VI

When Claudius himself was failing after thirteen years [Col. 2043B], he appointed Nero as ruler of the Roman Empire. He had been won over by the persuasions of his wife Agrippina, who possessed such power through her intrigues that she deprived Britannicus, the emperor’s son and designated successor, of the principate by the very law of nature.

She soon regretted this stratagem, because, while she had acted for the ruler’s sake in favor of the son born from her, she had disowned her own son, not realizing that once elevated to imperial power he would not acknowledge his mother and would turn the reward for her benefaction into her destruction. Nevertheless, he kept Octavia, the daughter of Claudius, as his wife: a son-in-law was preferred to a son in perverse order, because the evils of the state outweighed everything else. It was owed a parricide, a sacrilegious man, and an incestuous man, so that crimes, not any merits of good conduct, might rule in him.

Under such an emperor—whether because of the character of his conduct and contempt for his indolence [Col. 2043C], or because, on account of their grave sacrileges and with the protection of the supreme God withdrawn, the final destruction of the Jews was being prepared—serious seditions, robberies, and dissensions broke out. The insolence of those whom Eleazar, the leader of the brigands, had grievously ravaged for twenty years broke out in these disturbances. At last he was captured by Felix, who governed Judaea, and sent to Rome, where he suffered severe punishment.

Even this did not break the spirit of the people inhabiting Judaea, despite the great number of those who had been slain. Rather, in Jerusalem itself another kind of brigands arose, who were called *sicarii*, “dagger-men.” They were no longer hidden in secret or lying in wait in the darkness of night. They struck down anyone they approached in broad daylight, in the middle of the city and amid the protection of the crowd.

Carrying short swords in their hands and mingling with the tightly packed populace, they stabbed those to whom they drew near. Once the weapon had been fixed in the victim, the unsuspecting person fell from a hidden wound before he could utter a complaint. The funeral was immediately visible, but the attacker remained concealed. If anyone was stirred by another’s wound, he soon became part of the number of the slain through his own wound.

Thus, whether because of fear of danger or because the crime was concealed, the *sicarius* was not apprehended. Such was the speed of the ambushers and their skill in hiding themselves. The priest Jonathan was killed. Many others were added each day, and the fear of the living became heavier than the misery of those who had been murdered.

Each person went out daily as though to battle, but under a more grievous condition: the enemy can be foreseen, whereas the *sicarius* lay concealed; death was before their eyes and fear in their hearts. No one believed that he would return, and trust was not extended even to friends while the *sicarius* was feared.

Terrified by this, many men, innocent indeed of the crime of brigandage and of association with the *sicarii*—though harmless in hand, yet weaker in resolve—sought the desert. But while they were looking to their own safety, they caused panic through their departures [Note: [Col. 2043D] An old manuscript reads “withdrawals.” BARR.]. From this arose first the suspicion of war against the Romans and then open hostility. Because of this fear, the governor of the province sent cavalry and infantry and inflicted a great slaughter upon the multitude.

## CHAPTER VII

An Egyptian pseudo-prophet also arrived. Trained in magical arts, he boasted that he announced heavenly oracles through the prophetic spirit. He gathered nearly thirty thousand Jews around himself and, assembling them on the Mount of Olives, repeatedly made incursions toward Jerusalem. He even attacked the Roman guards stationed before Jerusalem so that nothing might be stirred up by the people [Col. 2044B].

When this arrogance too had been suppressed, it was as though another part of a sick body had become more severely inflamed. For many openly shouted that they should withdraw from the Romans and that liberty ought to be preferred to servitude. They proceeded into the countryside, where food was lacking, and sought it by force.

## CHAPTER VIII

Finally, in the city of Caesarea, a serious sedition arose between the Jews and the Gentiles. The Jews claimed possession of the entire city, as though it had been founded by Herod the Jew. The Gentiles resisted, arguing that although its founder had been a Jew, he had designated it in Caesar’s name.

Finally, they added that he had built a Temple within it and set up statues, so that it appeared to have been devoted more to Gentile uses [Col. 2044C]. The conflict arising from these disputes turned into armed sedition. The leading Jews could neither restrain their own people, who had devoted themselves to sedition, nor could the Gentiles tolerate the idea that they should yield to the Jews.

Therefore they stirred up Felix, so that, while he was eager to suppress the multitude of either side that refused to submit—especially by arms, since it could not otherwise be restrained—the matter might be settled. Festus succeeded him. After arresting many brigands, he put a considerable number to death.

Albinus too, exercising the same authority entrusted to him by the Romans, omitted no kind of wickedness. He was a shameless plunderer and robber: anyone who did not pay money was dragged into chains, even if innocent; anyone who paid was acquitted, even if guilty.

Avarice gave birth to arrogance, so that he presented himself as a tyrant to the poorer and as a slave to the richer [Col. 2044D]. Although he surpassed the wickedness of his predecessors [Note: [Col. 2044D] “Yet in such a way that he surpassed.” ID.], he was nevertheless so far surpassed and left behind by his successor Florus—Albinus appearing, by comparison, almost inactive and slow in his crimes—that he was judged upright when compared with the worse man.

Those who had first complained as victims later longed for Festus as though he had been a good judge. Festus had stripped individuals; Florus plundered cities. He was utterly defiled in his obscenities, most savage in his cruelty, throwing everything into confusion with arms and sowing battles upon battles. Neither entreaties moved him to pardon, nor satiety to spare.

In the presence of Berenice, the sister of King Agrippa, who had come to the Temple for the sake of religious observance, he savagely raged against the people in a most bitter slaughter. He did not think that her entreaties deserved consideration, although he saw her standing barefoot in attendance upon religious worship and praying, and regarded her prayer with disdain.

For this reason she herself wrote to King Agrippa, and the Jewish people sent a delegation to beg for aid to preserve their liberty. When Agrippa came out of Egypt, many went out to meet him, proceeding more than sixty stadia from Jerusalem. They escorted him through the city; and, when he approved the truth of their complaints, they began to press him to send envoys to Nero.

But Agrippa himself pitied their grief as that of fellow citizens. Yet with profound prudence he perceived that attempts at war against the Romans were being set in motion. He saw that this would create the ultimate danger both for himself and for the people. Therefore, after gathering the people together in the place called the Xystus, which was close to the Temple and divided from it by a bridge, he delivered the following speech.

## CHAPTER IX
Although grief may make many people, unprepared to deliberate and impatient of restraint, seethe with heavy complaints, nevertheless, once counsel is taken, the emotion of grief is set aside. For if I had discovered that all of you were eager to avenge injuries and wage war against the Roman Empire, rather than that the better and more peaceable party preferred what belongs to peace and valued what belongs to tranquillity, I would have dared neither to come before you nor to offer counsel. It is pointless to advise what ought to be done when the assent of those listening is directed toward worse things.

But since some are inexperienced in the evils of war, while for others the superficial hope of liberty is exceedingly sweet to seek but generally burdensome to obtain—for while many seek liberty, slavery is increased, and often everything is taken away from those who had retained at least the name of liberty—and since novelty attracts others who are displeased with the usefulness of their present circumstances, so that, if affairs are thrown into confusion, profit is thought to have been made, I therefore decided to confer counsel with you, lest either the sobriety of the wiser be forestalled by the boldness of the more insolent, or those who do not know how to think correctly may at least learn from my admonition that they ought to yield to wiser counsel.

I therefore think that silence should be granted, so that we may disclose what we believe to be advantageous for you and so that none of you may be disturbed if he hears something contrary to his own will. No one can judge what is being said unless he has first heard it, since he himself is to be its judge: whether he approves or rejects it, he is needlessly disturbed if he refuses to listen. For even afterward each person may retain whatever opinion he holds; and if, after sober admonitions, withdrawal seems preferable, he may still preserve the judgment of an ill-considered will.

But someone may say: Why should they wish to be heard in vain, if those who listen will not yield? Because, if they refuse to yield after hearing me, only a portion of the assembly will be endangered, not the entire people; but if they refuse to listen, even when a part of the people disturbs the hearing, the benefit of listening will be snatched from the whole people. [Note: “It is snatched away”; shortly afterward: “if they refuse.”—BARR.] Thus my speech will arise among those who wish to listen, if only some degree of silence is granted me; for the entire speech will be interrupted and will, as it were, become wholly ineffectual if the noise of the assembly and its restless uproar are allowed to impede it.

There are therefore two matters to which I think I must first reply, since they bear the greatest weight of complaint: that many loudly complain of the injuries inflicted by the governors, and that many lament that their liberty has perished. I think these two propositions must be separated. For if the governors are wicked, why bring liberty into the discussion? Otherwise you may seem to accuse the governors not because of their deserts, but out of disgust with slavery, as though they were the ministers of domination. Or, if slavery is intolerable, then complaints about the governors are superfluous. For even if it is more moderate under them, slavery is nevertheless disgraceful.

Let us therefore consider whether, in either of these matters, there may not be a serious ground for war. For what is more foolish than to complain of injuries, then add war to them, and exchange insults for dangers? While fleeing from a judge, you introduce an enemy, although a judge, even when unjust, is generally an interpreter of the law, whereas an enemy, even when just, always seeks your destruction. A judge ought therefore to be moderated, not exasperated; an enemy ought to be avoided, lest you make one more bitter and summon the other, since the former may be softened by appeasement, while the latter must be evaded so that he cannot do harm.

Care must therefore be taken regarding judges, lest the complaint be greater than the injury, and lest the resentment over accusations be more serious than the penalty for the offenses. Often those who at first transgressed more bashfully become more insolent when accused, and those who previously stole secretly afterward commit robbery openly. Nothing therefore inflames the heat of a wound so much as impatience in bearing it. Indeed, even among wild beasts, the tightest bonds are applied when they struggle, but loosened when they are still; the severe force of fevers is likewise diminished by endurance and increased by restlessness.

If even wild creatures know how to care for themselves by forgetting their nature in order to lessen their pain, how much more has common experience taught human beings that what the injured must endure becomes a matter of shame to those who inflict the injury, so that they correct without an accuser what, once accused, they would not have corrected. [Note: “Endurance … shame.”—ID.]

But suppose the insolence of the Roman judges has been intolerable. What, then, is more tolerable: to suffer the rule of all or of one? And what justice is there in bringing war upon everyone when one person has inflicted an injury? Are all Romans responsible for the injury? Is Caesar himself? Or was an evil man deliberately chosen and sent to you? Yet those across the sea [Note: Overseas.—ID.] cannot keep watch, fixing their eyes toward east and west to see there what is being done here; nor can they easily hear what has happened, even though concern demands it, because distance prevents the matter from being verified.

Thus the fault of one man would create division throughout the Roman world, even though swift correction can take place without your complaints, without the odium of an accusation, and without the labor of a journey. Roman magistrates, after all, are changed at regular intervals. Consequently, an insolent man does not remain long, and a more moderate one soon succeeds him. It will therefore do no harm to have remained quiet, since a remedy is brought even to those who remain quiet.

But it is destructive to weave the causes of war into the matter, because war is a harsh condition against everyone and a final one against the Romans. If you wish to flee them while unable to overcome them, you must abandon the whole world. But you claim the desire for liberty? That deliberation comes too late. You ought first to have fought so as not to lose your liberty, rather than demand it back after it had been lost. The experience of slavery is harsh, and for that reason it ought not to have been undertaken at the beginning, or, once undertaken, it ought to have been borne with equanimity. You should have resisted when you were being summoned into slavery. That would have been the more just struggle. But whoever has once surrendered himself into slavery, even if afterward he wishes to withdraw himself, is not upheld as a lover of liberty, but condemned as a rebellious slave.

Where was this defense of liberty when Pompey descended upon your territories? When the master entered the city, where were the weapons for liberty? Why were they laid down by our fathers? Certainly they were stronger than we are: they were vigorous in spirit, rich in resources, and eager to resist. Yet they could not withstand even a small part of the Roman army. They were defeated, but those who were spared recognized the yoke of slavery, lest they endure the punishment of captivity.

What do you, as heirs, refuse—what you owe by right of succession? Your fathers’ affairs bind you. How do you refuse obedience, so much inferior to those who obey? Or what will remain for you, when you set Caesar and all Roman valor in motion against yourselves? How can you withstand those who have triumphed over all peoples and are now aided by all who serve them?

The Athenians, indeed, surrendered their homeland to fire for the liberty of all Greece, exchanging their homes for exile so that Xerxes might not rule them. He traversed the earth in ships and the waves on foot; neither the seas could contain him nor the land support him, since the vast extent of all Europe confined the course of his journey within narrower territorial bounds than the army’s supply train. They pursued him as he fled, until he barely escaped captivity on a single ship and in need of assistance. Yet those same men who broke all Asia, because of little Salamis and Xerxes, who commanded the waves and subdued the seas, most gloriously defeated and drove him into flight on the very element that he thought subject to himself.

Now they serve the Romans, and the leading people of all Greece obey Italian commands. Athens herself, once giving laws to others, now serves under foreign laws. The Lacedaemonians too, after Thermopylae and the triumphs of the deceased Leonidas, after Agesilaus, the savior of Asia, now love their masters.

Macedonia and Africa likewise, which through their most powerful commanders had transferred the dominion of the whole world into their own laws and possessions, do not resent the power they transferred from themselves. Content with so great a change of circumstances, they desire masters whom they had sought to reduce them to slavery. [Note: “Two”; shortly afterward, the word “masters” is absent in an old manuscript.—BARR.]

The Macedonians are not stirred by the wealth of Philip or the triumphs of Alexander, whom they rightly considered the wisest of all commanders and unconquered: one held himself within Greece, while the other, fleeing Roman arms, reached victorious as far as the Caspian kingdoms and the remotest regions of conquered Persia and the hidden lands of the Indians. [Note: “Within Greece.”—ID.] He acquired a great name because he did not challenge the greatest of all. Although premature death removed him from a Roman triumph, even he serves in his descendants, for whom the spoils of the East were sought not as a support for domination but as the price of slavery, so that the nobility of those who served might reach the wealth of the victor.

Great was Alexander’s valor. Yet what is surprising? He extended his victory as far as the ocean; the Romans extended theirs beyond the ocean. Britain, situated beyond the known world but brought within it by Roman valor, is a witness to this. [Note: A similar passage occurs below, Book V, chapter 15: “What should I add about Britain, separated from the whole world by the intervening sea, yet brought by the Romans into the compass of the world? Surely the author imitates Virgil, whose words are: “[lacuna] Britons separated from the whole world.” —MAZOCH.]

Those whom the earlier age did not know learned of Roman victory. They too serve, although they did not know what slavery was: born only for themselves and always free to themselves, because, separated by the intervening ocean from the power of their superiors, they could not fear those whom they did not know. [Note: “Who.”—BARR.] It was therefore a greater achievement to cross over to the Britons than to triumph over the Britons.

For what could they do once the elements themselves had been subjected to Roman rule? The ocean taught them patience in slavery after they themselves had recognized an unfamiliar slavery when Roman ships crossed it. [Note: “Itself had recognized it,” referring to the ocean.—ID.] For why should I reopen the story of Hannibal, who, victorious over so many regions, himself served in Roman triumphs, opened the Alps, paved the way, and subdued cities to be acquired by the victors? Though he frequently prevailed over the Romans, he never deprived the defeated of hope of victory; once defeated, however, he was unable to recover himself. He voluntarily yielded to the victors whom, when victorious, he had not been able to withstand; casting aside his victorious arms, he betook himself to King Prusias: from commander, a mercenary; from triumphant general, a fugitive.

Let us come to the inhabitants of Gaul, peoples fierce by nature and made fiercer by their natural barriers. They are guarded not by walls of masonry but by the ridges of the Alps from the rising sun; from the setting sun the ocean encloses them; to the south the rugged Pyrenees; to the north the streams of the Rhine and the immense Germans, who considered themselves made unconquerable and inaccessible by the protection of these barriers. Yet, when the Romans traveled above the clouds and extended their dominion beyond the Pillars of Hercules, nothing was inaccessible. By such good fortune was the enemy found when hidden and conquered when resisting. [Note: “With such ease.”—ID.]

At the Romans’ unexpected arrival, Germany believed that the mountains had sunk and the Rhine dried up. Those peoples, stronger than the rest in the size of their bodies and their contempt for death, had previously regarded the Rhine as a restraint before them; now they regard it as a defense of their safety. Thus the Rhine is no longer filled with German forces but with Roman liburnian ships, which, roaming through all its waters as far as the sea, press into slavery free peoples who had once presumed upon dominion over the whole world and now pay the price of their own slavery.

What did it profit the Illyrians that gold was dug from the veins of their own lands, when they did not possess enough of it to purchase liberty? How much more precious is the Roman iron, to which the gold of Pannonia serves! Pannonia therefore pays tribute in gold and willingly transfers its wealth to the Roman treasury, so that it may be safer in slavery.

Nor has the murky stream of the Pactolus lifted its inhabitant into arrogance: he willingly serves those whom he sees ruling over others. Nor does the Indian marvel at his gem, or the Serian at his wool. Those things are produced for the use of their masters, not as the price of merchandise but as the duties of tribute.

[Note: I prefer to think that both expressions were written by the author in the ablative of price: “not by the price of merchandise, but by the duties of service.” In both manuscripts the word *functiones* commonly denotes the payment of tributes. Moreover, *munia* is used in the sense of “duties,” as in *altaria* and several similar words favored by a later age. A single *munium* is indeed recognized by the old glossaries as a synonym of *functio*; both are rendered by λειτουργία (*leitourgia*), a word relating to the payment of tributes.—MAZOCH.]

We hear of the proud rule of the Persians, but we have also seen their hostages. [Note: “We have heard.”—BARR.] Though they rule many nations, they nevertheless offer their children and their nobility. They rejoice to serve the Romans in pledge of peace, so that by serving they may learn to command their own subjects. They offer the Romans garments, jewelry, even elephants—the kings impose one tribute.

Let us add Egypt, abounding in her own resources and not needing heavenly rain. She herself generates her showers and produces an abundance of rain. Since she is hotter than all other regions, she alone does not complain of drought; what is supplied to no other place, she provides for her crops through irrigation. One sails over the sands; one sails through the fields, where rain is unknown.

Yet Egypt’s remarkable natural fertility serves the Romans, feeding her masters for four months. What shall I say of the city itself, named after a most powerful king, which, enclosed by a river as by a wall, knows no siege? The greatest of all rivers, spreading its channel across vast stretches of land, both removes the obstacles of siege and supplies what is necessary for the use of affairs. [Note: “Remedies.”—ID.]

What country could be more provoked to rebellion than Egypt, which counts ten million seven hundred and fifty thousand people, apart from the inhabitants of Alexandria, enrolled under the Roman fasces? Yet, although she possesses so great a multitude, she prefers to occupy herself with the taxes of the Roman Empire rather than serve under her own military pay.

I shall not pass over the Cyrenaeans, a people of Lacedaemonian stock, who once contended with the Carthaginians over territory and dominion, offering death as the end of their struggle. Defeated by that offering, they nevertheless avenged the injury done to their brothers, the Philaeni. [Note: “Philaeni.”—ID.] They conceded victory to them.

Nor shall I pass over the terrible Syrtes, even in name, because they draw everything toward themselves and whatever approaches becomes stuck in their shallow sea. Experts in geography assert that they define a third of the whole world, from the Atlantic Sea and the Pillars of Hercules to the Red Sea and the Ethiopians.

Who could count by number the peoples of so many nations, supported by whom Carthage could not withstand Scipio’s right hand, and preferred to feed Rome at its own expense for two parts of the year rather than rely on the resources of others and rebel against the Romans?

Crete too, famous for its hundred cities and displaying exceedingly fertile kingdoms, surrounded on every side by sea and waves as though by walls with which she was accustomed to repel the enemy, fears a single consular official, and many peoples bow in fear before six rods of fasces.

Asia, Pontus, the Eniochi, the nomadic Scythians, the Tauric Scythians, and the kingdoms of Maeotis, together with all the Bosporans, are subject to Roman rule; and that sea, previously unnavigable, is now patrolled by forty ships in the service of peace.

For what should I say of Armenia? She not only preserves the peace of her own frontier, but also, intent upon guarding her gates, carefully investigates whether anyone might enter to disturb the peace.

All therefore desire to serve the Romans. Are you alone disdainful of being subject to those to whom all peoples are subject? On what arms do you rely? With what proud army? Where is the fleet of your ships that could blockade the straits and range across the seas of the Romans?

For even the elements have passed into their name, and the whole world has passed to them; it is enclosed and defined by Roman rule. Indeed, most people call it the Roman world. For if we seek the truth, as I said above, the earth itself lies beneath Roman authority, and Roman valor has advanced beyond the ocean, seeking another world for itself and finding in Britain a new possession remote from the boundaries of the lands.

Indeed, those to whom not only Roman citizenship but almost participation in human society itself is denied are sent there to dwell, as exiles from the world. The ocean has yielded its boundaries; the Roman knows how to penetrate its inner secrets. You will be at war with those against whom nature itself possesses no rights of its own.

That previously inaccessible Euphrates, except to its own inhabitants, is now Roman on both banks, and under Roman rule signifies that the entire East belongs to Rome. The Ister, flowing in the northern regions amid savage and countless peoples, receives hostages and restrains enemies.

The southern region, as far as it can be inhabited, plows for the Romans and gathers its own harvest for them. At the western extremity of the world, the Gaditanian shore receives new guests who bring their tributes to Roman rule. It too has somewhere to direct its merchandise: where it previously thought there was only shipwreck, it now practices commerce.

Since everything belongs to the Romans, from where will you seek assistance against the Romans? From what uninhabitable region will you request allies? Whoever exists in the world is Roman.

Will you send an embassy beyond the Euphrates to the Adiabenes? They themselves have no leisure to abandon what is theirs, nor does the Parthian permit the peace requested of him to be interrupted, lest he himself be held responsible for rebellion among neighboring peoples.

Do not think that this war will resemble one waged against the Arabs or Egyptians. Roman arms are of another kind, and their resources have been gathered from the entire world. Nor should the fortifications of Jerusalem flatter you: the Romans have broken through a stronger wall, the ocean.

Or do you rely upon the aid of religion, when the disciples of Jesus have already filled the Roman world? Can we suppose that this religion has grown without the will of God, and that the city of Rome has extended its dominion above all religions? [Note: Certainly.—ID.]

Our own religion abandoned us long ago because we abandoned faith, and repeatedly returned to what had been forbidden by the commands of heaven. How did the Egyptian come against us? How did we become captives of the Assyrians? Did Scripture not say that these things would occur? Was it not written that all the sacred things of the Temple would be profaned? These things, already profaned so many times, no longer display their power or the whole grace of the divine mysteries.

The Temple has been polluted with human blood; the sacred couches have been filled with corpses; the altars have been drenched with Roman blood; battle has been waged on the Sabbath. Transgression has occurred, since the Temple is defended not by observance of its own festivals and solemnities but by bloody battle.

And this will certainly happen again. How, then, can we deserve divine assistance as though we were contending against enemies and opponents of religion, when we ourselves bring transgression upon our religion? What remedy remains, when neither human resources support us nor divine grace assists us? Either one of these ordinarily invites some people to war; you lack both.

What therefore remains except evident destruction? You do not avoid it while it is still possible to beware. You yourselves will burn your own homeland and set fire to the Temple; you will also deliver your wives and children to death, becoming the authors of their final loss, since the increase of all the evils we endure will be attributed to our fault.

Added to this is the fact that wars in other cities are brought to an end by the destruction of their inhabitants; your rebellion will be the destruction of the entire religion, which, spread throughout the world, will scatter our people everywhere, and in every city there is a portion of our people. [Note: “Of the region.”—ID.] All Jews, therefore, will be implicated in your war, and no region will be free from our blood.

Or, if the Romans are such that they do not persecute Jews who have not provoked them in war, how unjust is the war brought against those whose humanity you hope for?

It is good, dear friends, it is good, while the ship is still in harbor, to foresee the storm that is coming, and not to expose oneself to imminent dangers, lest, once you have gone out to sea, you be unable to avoid shipwreck. Often, indeed, a sudden squall arises, and war is encountered even if it is not initiated. But there is a difference between provoking an enemy and meeting him. He is more sparing when not provoked, and necessity excuses insolence; but when someone plunges himself into precipitous danger, he is also burdened with reproach.

This is not an enemy whom you can avoid by flight. Wherever you go, danger will follow; indeed, everywhere you will find an enemy. For all are friends of the Romans, and whoever stands outside the friendship of the Romans is the enemy of all.

Let love of your homeland move you. If the thought of your children and wives does not call you back, let the sight of the most sacred Temple call you back. At least spare religion; spare the most sacred priests, whom the Romans now do not spare, nor the Temple itself, although they regret having spared them. For all nations have long desired to extinguish our religion, yet Pompey spared it when he could have destroyed it.

I have omitted nothing; I have warned you about everything that concerns your safety. I advise you to do what I choose for myself. Consider what is useful for you and for me. I desire that you and I may have peace with the Roman people. If you refuse, you yourselves deprive me of association with you. Either favor will be shared, or danger will be faced without me.

Having said this, he burst into tears, as did his sister Berenice, for she too was in the upper part of the Xystus. Agrippa moved them greatly by his tears, so that the Jews said: “We are not waging war against the Romans; but we think that war ought to be brought against Florus, who has committed deeds worthy of war.” [Note: “We are not rebelling.”—ID.]

Agrippa replied: “But to bring war upon Florus is to bring Roman war. Your actions seek injury against the Romans. It is not Florus but the Romans; it is not Florus but Caesar to whom tribute is being denied. It is not Florus but a Roman garrison that is in the fortress called Antonia, from which you separated the Temple by demolishing and dividing the colonnades, so that the guard might be kept apart.

“Restore the established arrangement of former times. Let the tribute owed to Caesar be paid to Caesar, lest Florus report that it was not himself whom you rejected, but Caesar’s authority.”

The people had been persuaded by these words. When they went up into the Temple with Agrippa, they began rebuilding the colonnades as they had been, and they collected the tribute. Indeed, by sending out diligent collectors for this purpose, they gathered the forty talents lacking for the payment of the tribute. [Note: “Service”; see above, column 2049, the note on *functionum munia* from Mazochius.—GALLAND.]

The whole tumult of war had been suppressed. But Agrippa wished to add that they should obey Florus until a successor came to him from Caesar. This so exasperated the people that they did not even restrain themselves from insulting him. They drove him from the city, throwing some stones, though it is uncertain whether they struck him.

Moved by this insult, the king seized those responsible and sent them to Florus. He himself withdrew to his kingdom.

## CHAPTER X

After he had departed, the instigators of war, having prepared an ambush, seized the fortress of Masada, killed the Roman guards, and installed their own men. Eleazar too, the son of the high priest, a man of reckless courage, urged that no gift or sacrifice from any foreigner should be accepted. This disturbance became a cause of war against the Romans and stirred everyone into turmoil.

When the leading men saw that this action was being undertaken as a cause of dissension, they argued with the people that not only was war being declared against Caesar, but the institutions of religion were also being violated and reverence for the Temple diminished. The traditions of their fathers were being accused and condemned, although those fathers had adorned the Temple with gifts from foreigners, and much greater wealth had entered it through the contributions of nations and the gifts of various and innumerable peoples. The sacred customs of the ancestors were being obliterated and the holy rites altered. [Note: The old manuscript reads “denied.”—ID.]

What would become of the gifts already contributed, if gifts from the nations were likewise prohibited in the future? Or, if what was permitted to everyone were forbidden only to the Romans, what encouragement to war would that provide? Finally, it would be impious if foreigners alone were not permitted among the Jews either to sacrifice or to bring offerings.

They ought to consider that Caesar’s peace would be dissolved, and that Caesar, undoubtedly offended by such an upheaval, would deprive the Jews of every use of sacrifice. They would then be unable to sacrifice even for themselves, since they had rejected Caesar’s sacrifice. [Note: Mazochius supplied this passage from the Ascensian edition. Another edition reads: “so that they would not have refused Caesar’s sacrifice even on their own behalf.”—GALLAND.] This had to be forestalled in time.

For if such resolutions reached Florus and from him, as was certain, Caesar, they would bring destruction upon the Jewish people. [Note: “Would bring.”—BARR.] At the same time, wishing to establish these points by the testimony of the priests, they asked whether the ancestors had ever renounced the sacrifices of the nations. To prevent the matter from becoming clear, those prepared for sedition shouted over them. Even the ministers of the altar did not dare to insert themselves into so great a conflict among the dissenting parties.

One remedy seemed to remain: Florus and King Agrippa should be present with a military force, so that at least fear might stop those whom reason could not recall. But Florus, who wished the sedition to increase so that the Jews would have no opportunity for pardon—[Note: The old manuscript reads: “for, unless they were involved in war, every opportunity to press charges against him concerning his plunder and more serious offenses would be extinguished.”—ID.]—allowed the fury of war to grow and returned no answer to the envoys.

Agrippa, however—[Note: Something appears to be missing; perhaps: “Agrippa, however, who was most eager … sent,” etc.—GALLAND.]—was most eager to secure the embassy of Scylus, Antipas, and Custobaris, his relatives, for the common good, so that he might preserve the Jews for the Romans, religion for the Jews, the ancestral Temple, the city for its citizens, and for himself the dignity of his authority and the tranquillity of his kingdom. He sent three thousand cavalry under Darius and Philip, commanders of troops, so that, relying on their assistance, the advocates of the sounder party might strive with greater confidence.

From this arose confidence among the good and indignation among the wicked, and the war grew. Since the former were inflamed by the more just cause, which nevertheless gained nothing from armed conflict, and the latter by fury and the size of the multitude, the battle lines of the combatants were divided.

The high priests and that part of the common people who desired peace occupied the upper part of the city with the king’s cavalry. The others, stationed in the lower parts, claimed the Temple and the neighboring sacred areas for themselves.

At first they provoked war on both sides with stones, rocks, and the casting of missiles; they fought with arrows. Later, when the necessity of fighting arose, they engaged hand to hand. The king’s troops had the advantage in skill and experience, wishing to prevent the instigators of war from approaching and defiling the Temple. Eleazar and his followers, by contrast, sought to invade even the upper city called Zion.

For seven days they fought without interruption. The eighth day, the feast on which everyone customarily placed wood upon the altars so that the fire, which had to remain unextinguished, might never fail, added to the fury, with the result that all the ministers were excluded from the Temple.

When the Sicarii burst forth with greater boldness than usual, the king’s troops withdrew, not daring to remain in the upper districts. The houses of Agrippa and Berenice were burned, and all the royal equipment was plundered. Fire was carried about so that the debt records kept in the public archives might be burned. [Note: Publicly.—BARR.]

Thus the poor rose more insolently against their creditors, thinking themselves freed from every obligation. They set fire to the city with their own hands; the sinews of the state were burned. The fortress called Antonia was stormed, all the guards found there were killed, and afterward the fortress itself was burned.

Manahem, son of Judas the Galilean, an impetuous and able sophist experienced in disturbing affairs, also burst into Masada, seized the arsenals of weapons, and armed the unarmed. Returning to Jerusalem with bodyguards accompanying him as though he were a king, he had grown monstrously arrogant, so that, going beyond the limits of private life, he thought he need not refrain even from unlawful actions that free peoples could not tolerate.

When many rose against him, reproaching him for having assumed royal clothing and imposed himself as tyrant and master upon the liberty of the citizens, he paid a severe penalty. First he was afflicted with tortures and then put to death, yet the dissension was not removed. For a much more serious disturbance arose.

Finally, Metilius, together with the Roman soldiers, pleaded that they be allowed to depart. After a pledge had been given and oaths exchanged, once they had laid down their arms according to the agreement and were leaving without fear, many were slaughtered by Eleazar and the members of his faction. They thought that they should neither resist force nor plead for mercy, but merely shouted that the faith pledged had been violated and that the treachery of the faithless was perjury.

All were therefore killed. Metilius himself, the commander of the soldiers, was spared alone because he pleaded and begged, while at the same time promising that he would become a Jew even to the point of circumcision.

## CHAPTER XI

All Judaea was in flames; the entire province of Syria too was aroused to war. [Note: “Was aroused.”—BARR.]

Finally, the people of Caesarea killed all the Jews they had among them. Stirred by this grief, the Jews attacked and defeated many cities of Syria. Nowhere was there justice, nowhere religion. The more a man had plundered, the nobler he was considered, as though he were amassing rewards for courage.

It was a pitiable spectacle when unburied bodies lay scattered through the cities: old men mingled with children, and women too, having abandoned even the coverings that decency required for the protection of their nakedness from the gaze of onlookers. Everything was foul and filled with a pitiful appearance. Although these sights surpassed the grim horror of grave and impious cruelty, they nevertheless threatened one another with still greater horrors.

There was a monstrous brigandage between Jews and Syrians, since no hope of safety remained except to forestall one another. What city was there that did not contain Jews and Syrians mingled together? Days were passed in blood, nights in terror; there was no limit either to hatred or greed.

For, apart from the diversity of sects and worship, which had burst forth into public disaster so that each side wished the other destroyed, greed for possession and the desire to seize had so invaded their minds that they thought no one whom they had marked for death in the pursuit of plunder should be spared.

Why should I speak of the smaller number of those killed? Apart from the Antiochenes, Sidonians, and Apameans, scarcely any people failed to persecute the Jews living among them.

[Note: The Gerasenes.—ID.]

The Gerasenes, however, escorted those who wished to leave as far as their own borders, so that they might depart without any deception.

At Alexandria, a dispute arose between the non-Jews and the Jews. While the Hebrews demanded vengeance and, having seized the fasces, threatened to burn the assembled Gentile population in the amphitheater, Alexander Tiberius, the prefect of the place, turned his attention to them. At first he tried by peaceful speeches to restore public harmony.

But when he realized that they were mocking the things he earnestly urged and that so great a sedition could not be ended in any other way, he gave the soldiers permission to attack them. The soldiers, assaulting the people who surrounded them, inflicted a tremendous slaughter throughout the city: they killed some who resisted, others who fled, and others who hid in their houses. No mercy was shown to children, no reverence to the old, and no regard for the modesty of women.

Nearly fifty thousand Jews were killed. The streets swam with blood; everything was filled with corpses. Flames crackled in a savage fire throughout the city, consuming the neighboring buildings as well as the Jewish houses into which they had been set alight (Matt. XIV.4). [Note: “Set alight.”—ID.]

Alexander nevertheless relented and finally ordered the soldiers to stop and sound the retreat. But the anger of the common people, once it had advanced to the power of killing, was in no way appeased.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 2056A]

For they were paying the penalties for their crimes: after crucifying the Lord Jesus, the judge of divine things, they afterward persecuted his disciples as well. Yet many of the Jews, and very many Gentiles, believed in him, drawn by his moral precepts and by works flowing beyond human power. Not even his death brought an end to their faith or devotion; rather, it increased their devotion.

They therefore laid murderous hands upon him and led the author of life to Pilate to be put to death. They began to press the reluctant judge; yet Pilate was not thereby excused, but the madness of the Jews was heaped up. For neither ought he to have condemned one whom he had found in no way guilty, nor ought they to double sacrilege with murder, so that he might be slaughtered by those for whose redemption and healing he had offered himself. Concerning him the Jews themselves also bear witness, as Josephus, the historian, says [Note: Antiquities, book XVIII, chapter 3, §3]: that at that time there was a wise man—“if indeed,” he says, “one ought to call him a man”—a doer of marvelous works, who appeared alive again to his disciples after the third day of his death, in accordance with the writings of the prophets; and that the prophets foretold these and countless other things concerning him, filled with miracles [Note: The old codex reads: “the God-filled miracles of the prophets.” ID.]; that from this the assembly of Christians began and spread among every race of humanity, and that no nation in the Roman world remained without being left ignorant of his worship.

If the Jews do not believe us, let them believe their own people. Josephus said this, the man whom they themselves regard as preeminent. Yet, although he spoke the truth in this very matter, he was so mentally astray that he did not believe his own words. He spoke them for the credibility of his history, because he considered it wrong to deceive; he did not believe them because of the hardness of his heart and the obstinacy of his unbelief. Nevertheless, the fact that he did not believe did not prejudice the truth [Note: Does not prejudice it.]; rather, it added to the testimony, since he denied it neither as an unbeliever nor unwillingly.

In this the eternal power of Christ Jesus shone forth: even the leaders of the synagogue, who had seized him for death, confessed that he was God. And truly, speaking as God, without respect of persons or any fear of death, he also announced that the temple would be destroyed. Yet they were not moved by the insult to the temple, but because he reproved them for their crimes and sacrileges; hence their anger blazed up, so that they might kill the one whom no age would have possessed.

For whereas others earned by prayer the ability to do what they did, this man had the power to command everything he wished to be done.

Before the death of Jesus, John the Baptist, a holy man, had been killed; he had never placed the truth of salvation in worldly possessions [Note: In temporal things.]. Indeed, in all that he taught, full of justice, by which he invited the Jews to the worship of God, he had also instituted baptism for the purification of soul and body.

The cause of his death was his freedom of speech: he could not endure that Herod had violated the rights of his brother’s marriage and taken away his brother’s wife [Note: His brother’s.]. For when that same Herod was going to Rome, he entered the house of his brother for the sake of hospitality. His brother’s wife was Herodias, daughter of Aristobulus and sister of King Agrippa. Forgetful of nature, Herod dared to solicit her to leave her brother and marry him. When he had returned from the city of Rome, an incestuous agreement was made with the woman’s consent.

News of this affair reached Aretas’s daughter, who was still married to Herod. Indignant at her rival, she suggested to her returning husband that he should go to the town of Machaerus, which lay on the frontier between King Aretas and Herod. He suspected nothing; and since his affection for her had already greatly diminished, he readily agreed to her suggestion, so that he might more easily fulfill his pledge to Herodias if he sent his wife away.

But when she approached her father’s kingdom, she disclosed to her father Aretas what she had learned. He set an ambush and destroyed Herod’s entire army, which had been challenged to war, after the betrayal had been carried out by those who, from the people of the tetrarch Philip, had joined Herod.

Therefore Herod brought a complaint against Caesar. But the vengeance ordered by Caesar was taken away by the judgment of God. For while preparations for war were being made, news arrived of Caesar’s death. We learn and understand that the Jews regarded and believed—Josephus being a trustworthy witness against himself—that Herod lost his army not through human treachery but through God’s anger, and justly, on account of the vengeance exacted for John the Baptist, a righteous man, who had said to him: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18).

Yet we have woven these matters together as though the Jews had preserved legitimate institutions among their own people, although among them the right of the high priesthood had perished, either intercepted by greed or seized by the arrogance of powerful men, who thought that the right to do whatever they wished constituted law.

From the beginning, Aaron was the high priest. By God’s will, through legitimate anointing, he transmitted the privilege of the priesthood to his sons, from whom, by succession in due order, those who held the office and supremacy of the priesthood were appointed. Hence, according to ancestral custom, the rule prevailed that no one could become high priest unless he was descended from the blood of Aaron, to whom this kind of priestly right had first been entrusted. A man of another lineage could not succeed, not even as king.

Thus Uzziah, because he usurped the priestly office, was covered with leprosy, expelled from the temple, and spent the rest of his life without authority. Certainly he had been an excellent king, but he was not permitted to usurp the religious office.

## CHAPTER XIII

From the time when the ancestors came out of Egypt until the building of the temple constructed by Solomon, there were thirteen high priests, covering 212 years [Note: The manuscript reads “612,” as does Eusebius in the *Chronicle*. BARR.]. At first, the high priest who held the office remained in it until death, and no one was appointed in the place of a living man. Later, successors were also appointed while their predecessors were still alive.

These thirteen, then, obtained the priesthood by succession. During their period there existed both aristocracy and monarchy, the authority of the Judges and of the Kings.

Again, from Solomon until the time of the captivity, when the people migrated into Syria, after the city had been captured and the temple burned, there were eighteen high priests over 460 years, six months, and ten days. For seventy years afterward the people remained in captivity [Note: This phrase is absent from the manuscript.].

Later, when Cyrus released the ancestral people from the land of the Assyrians and granted permission for the temple to be rebuilt, he also allowed Josedech, the high priest who had been taken away with them, to return, so that the rites of the ancient solemnity might be restored through the knowledge of the accustomed priest.

He and his successors—fifteen men in all—served in succession from the return of the people until Antiochus Eupator, and represented the high-priestly office for 414 years.

The first Antiochus whom we mentioned above, and his commander Lysias, after killing Onias, the high priest, installed Alcimus in his place. Although he was of the family of Aaron, he did not belong to that particular house.

Therefore Ananias, the brother of Onias, went to Egypt and asked Ptolemy Philometor and his wife Cleopatra—who had incorporated observances resembling the rites of the Jerusalem solemnity into the worship of Alexandria—that he might be appointed high priest there, because Alcimus did not possess a legitimate succession to the priesthood. Yet, when Alcimus died after completing three years, he did not deserve to have a successor, since he had abolished the solemnity of legitimate succession.

Thus the city was without a high priest for seven years.

Up to this time, from the return [Note: “Return.” ID.] of the ancestors from the lands of the Assyrians, democracy had prevailed, because the Jewish people recognized that they had been led into captivity through the injustice of kings.

Later, when the Hasmoneans obtained authority to govern the people, they appointed Jonathan high priest. He held the office for seven years, but met the end of his life through the treachery of Trypho. His full brother Simon succeeded him, as though by hereditary right, though in fact by election. We are told that Simon was killed by treachery during a banquet; from him the priestly privilege passed to his son Hyrcanus, whom flight had rescued from danger.

Aristobulus succeeded Hyrcanus and added the kingship to the office already mentioned, so that he possessed both. Alexander succeeded Aristobulus. In Alexander’s hands both the kingship and the priesthood remained supreme until the day of his death, for twenty-seven years, though often in an uncertain condition. Victory between him and Demetrius was doubtful, and he was also hated intensely by his fellow citizens.

When Alexander was dying and saw that his sons would inherit the dangerous burden of his hatreds, he wished his wife Alexandra—experienced in government and accustomed to their common counsels, yet more acceptable to the people because she had often protected those endangered by her husband’s severity and had moderated her husband—to preside over the royal government. He also appointed her arbiter of which of his sons should chiefly receive the high priesthood.

She appointed Hyrcanus to the priesthood in place of his father, either because of the privilege of his greater age or because, being gentler in character than his brother, he seemed unlikely to cause his mother any trouble in royal affairs. She entrusted Aristobulus with no public office.

But even while his mother was alive, taking advantage of her illness, he acted as king in distant and more fortified places. His mother was offended by this, and troubled by Hyrcanus’s complaints. She prolonged the effects of her illness and, after not advancing beyond nine years of rule [Note: Fourteen.], left Hyrcanus heir to everything—not because she expected him to preserve it, but so that she might neither assist an unworthy man nor, by a more favorable judgment, inflame the insolence of a usurper.

Yet Alexandra’s death deprived Hyrcanus even of the priesthood and kingship. Defeated in war, he withdrew to stronger positions. After retaining Aristobulus’s wife and children, whom he had found in the fortress, he resolved to alter the arrangement so that all authority and the priesthood would pass to Aristobulus, while he himself, as a private citizen, would withdraw into Aristobulus’s household.

Nor was he long content to have exchanged the royal palace for a private home. Stirred up by Antipater, he first went to Arabia, as though intending to challenge the injustice of the agreement [Note: To protest.]. Then, when he realized that he was weak against the Romans, whom Aristobulus had drawn into his alliance through Scaurus, he sought the aid of the king of Arabia and brought his complaint to Pompey as he was approaching.

Pompey, after Aristobulus had already ruled for three years and was mocking him, struck him in war, captured him through his authority, and placed him under guard even before achieving victory. After defeating his people and capturing the city, he ordered Aristobulus himself and his sons to be sent as prisoners to Rome. He restored the dignity of the priesthood to Hyrcanus and appointed him governor over the citizens, though without the diadem or the insignia of kingship [Note: To preside.].

He was generous with honor but mindful of peace, lest tranquility be disturbed by the spirit of his brother’s arrogance.

Thus, although Aristobulus had been captured, Hyrcanus was nevertheless deprived of the kingship. He afterward spent twenty-four years in power, more in practical authority than in name. Yet this was not the end of Hyrcanus’s life, as it was of his power. For the remainder of his life became a disgrace, as we have related above. After being defeated in battle, when the Parthians crossed the Euphrates, he was captured and handed over to Antigonus, the son of Aristobulus. His ears were cut off, but even this did not complete the bitterness of his wretched suffering.

For afterward he was also taken into Parthia as an exile. Feeble and aged, he became a spectacle for the barbarians. Later, when he learned that Herod was ruling and that his granddaughter Mariamne was married to him, he returned to Judaea.

There he was initially received with every appearance of honor, which concealed a plot. Not long afterward, accused of wishing to recover power, he was killed.

Herod, therefore, having obtained the kingship—which he had received from the Romans as a reward for attacking or betraying his homeland—appointed successors to the priesthood in place of Antigonus, who had held power for three years and three months. They were not of the Hasmonean family, which we understand to have been of more distinguished ancestry, but men of low birth, whom either desire or chance had supplied.

Yet, worn down by the pleas of his mother-in-law Alexandra, or frightened by her accusations, he made Jonathan, his wife’s brother, a seventeen-year-old, a priest. Soon afterward he himself brought about Jonathan’s death, suspecting his power because he saw the favor of the entire people toward him growing day by day.

He therefore set aside Ananelus, whom he had already appointed high priest before Jonathan from among men of low birth, and chose the others in succession according to this pattern, selecting men concerning whom he had no suspicion. For if he had been unable to tolerate such a thing in a relative, how could he fail to guard against similar things in strangers?

In arrangements of this kind, Archelaus followed the appearance of his father’s practice and adopted the view of a narrower mind. It is a custom inherent in mortals that among them the dullness of inferior men is less suspect than the favor of good men, since a weak mind is more arrogant in prosperity, whereas a prudent mind knows how to return benefits.

From Herod’s reign until Roman rule—which, after the removal of Archelaus, joined Judaea to the remaining provinces—and from that time until the destruction of the temple and Titus’s triumph, there were twenty-eight high priests over 170 years [Note: “Of the Romans.” BARR.].

Among most of them, only the exercise of the dignity belonged to them; in the case of a few, the right of authority also belonged to them.

It is therefore clear that legitimate hereditary succession did not persist among the high priests, since not all were descended from Aaron or from his sons, who, when appointed in his place, left to the others the pattern of the prescribed succession.

Thus, when the institutions of the ancestors had been corrupted by the greed or treachery of their own people, the rights of religion violated, and the supports of justice shaken, divine assistance rightly abandoned them. As though the people had been left empty and exposed, every kind of injury advanced against them: they turned their hands against one another in domestic seditions, were afflicted by serious brigandage, and received the most wicked judges, so that the more depraved succeeded the wicked.

Finally, Albinus was regarded as the worst of his predecessors. But when Florus succeeded him, Albinus was counted among the good, because Florus raised the torch of war and kindled battle between the Jews and the Romans. This became the cause of the final destruction of the temple and the city.

## CHAPTER XIV

When Cestius learned that the Jews were burning with the fury of war, he—who had received from the Romans the supreme command of the army in the Syrian region—took up arms in the twelfth year of Nero’s reign, to avenge the killing of the Roman soldiers who had been entrusted with maintaining order and preserving peace.

After assembling auxiliaries from the allies as well, he entered Judaea. The inhabitants of the city called Zabulon had scattered in fear, leaving it full of the wealth that its owners, fleeing to the upper mountains, had been unable to carry away. Cestius allowed the army to plunder it.

He also admired the beauty of the public buildings and ordered them burned. As though this were insufficient for vengeance, he occupied Joppa after sending an army in advance, so that no one might escape destruction by flight. Those assigned to the task burst in by land and sea; about eight thousand four hundred men were killed, and once the plunder had been carried off, the city was burned.

He also ravaged the area near Caesarea, plundered what he found, and burned the villages. Sepphoris broke his advance: all its inhabitants came out to meet Cestius, and, winning his favor and goodwill, they caused him to leave the city unharmed.

A band of brigands was active in these regions, but when the army arrived, they withdrew into the mountains. They boldly attacked Gallus, commander of the Twelfth legion, as he was advancing with his standards, and killed nearly two hundred Romans.

But when the brigands seized the higher ground and could not endure close combat with the infantry, they were easily surrounded and killed by the cavalry as they fled. More than two thousand were killed; a few escaped, able to hide in the steep mountain terrain.

After the whole region had been cleared of brigandage, Gallus returned to Caesarea.

Cestius proceeded with his entire force to Antipatris, where the Jews assembled a considerable multitude. But before they joined battle, they scattered in different directions and abandoned the region and villages to plunder and fire.

Lydda was also found empty of inhabitants. Gabaon, which lay fifty stadia from Jerusalem, was burned. When the Roman army appeared there in full view, the Jews took up arms.

They set aside the observance of the Sabbath—a day on which they initiated their ancient and solemn worship—and rushed upon the Romans with such force that they would have turned the entire army back, had cavalry not come to the aid of the hard-pressed infantry.

Five hundred and fifteen Romans were killed, though all were in serious danger. Twenty-two Jews were lost in the battle.

On this occasion the courage of Monobazus and Cedeus shone forth. When they learned that the Jews were attacking the Roman lines, they assaulted the Romans from the front, drove back most of them, and forced them to return to the city.

## CHAPTER XV

Simon also stripped the Romans, as they were ascending, of the obstacles presented by the neighboring city. Consequently Cestius remained in the region for three days.

During this delay, the enemies surrounded him and occupied the higher ground. He watched the approaches, to ensure that no one might break in with impunity.

Considering that an attempt could not be made without great losses on both sides [Note: This word is absent from the manuscript.], King Agrippa sent Lorcius and Phoebus to say to the people that whatever crime they had committed against the Romans could be forgiven, provided that, laying down their arms for the future, they took thought for their own welfare. He supposed either that he should persuade everyone to renounce battle or that he might separate one faction from the rest.

But the rebels, fearing that one of the two envoys might advance, attacked the ambassadors and killed Phoebus. Lorcius, having received a wound, barely escaped.

When Cestius saw these divisions in the city—some attacking the envoys, others urging that the Romans be admitted—he attempted to break in and drove back the resistance as far as Jerusalem. He himself approached the city mentioned with his army to within three stadia and remained there for three days.

On the fourth day he launched an assault, entered Bethesdam, and immediately burned it, as well as Cenopolis. As he climbed to the upper part of the city, the rebels fled into the interior. If he had thought that he should break into the city, the whole war would undoubtedly have been ended [Note: “Pressing forward.” ID.].

Indeed, Ananus, son of Jonathan, had stationed many men to invite the Romans by their shouts, as though they were about to open the gates. But while Cestius was either recalled by Priscus and by many centurions who, having been corrupted by Florus, wanted the war to grow, or was insufficiently trusting, Ananus and his men were thrown down from the wall.

When they fled to their own people, the rebels occupied their position. For five days the Romans tried various approaches. Seeing that they could not break in, they chose their strongest men and archers and attacked the temple from the northern side.

The Jews were not idle either. They fought bravely, and, repeatedly driving back the enemy, grew more confident. Finally [Note: This word is not recognized by the manuscript. BARR.], however, some were wounded by the mass of arrows, while others were struck and terrified, and they withdrew. The Romans began to undermine the wall and set fire to the gate of the temple.

Great fear and a kind of mental panic seized the rebels. Many, as though the destruction of the city were immediately at hand, withdrew in flight. Not daring to stand firm, they gave the people confidence. As those whose multitude had surrounded them departed, the people, now as though free and released from the siege imposed by the wicked, poured toward the gates, intending to admit Cestius—as though he had come not to attack the city but to defend it.

But Cestius himself was suddenly seized by stupefaction, so that he perceived neither the despair of the wicked nor the eagerness of the common people. Had he persisted in his undertaking even briefly, he would have driven away the war and captured the city.

But God’s will, as far as can be understood, was adverse to the Jews and postponed the impending end of the war until it had engulfed many, almost all, in the ruin of the Jewish race. It was expected, I think, that every enormity of crime and every impiety should grow and, through the increase of wickedness, reach the measure of the final offenses.

What was it that, when Cestius ought to have pressed forward, suddenly caused him to recall the army and raise the siege? Through an unexpected and sudden change of circumstances, the courage of the respectable was broken and the brigands were emboldened. Returning from flight to pursuit, they attacked the rear of the column and killed many cavalrymen and infantrymen who were rushing about in confusion.

The day was already declining. Fearing the approach of night and the darkness, which would give greater confidence to those familiar with the region and enable them to press him from every side in uncertain terrain, Cestius built a rampart before the city.
