On the following day, while leaving the enemy behind, he armed himself against them, so that they might suppose fear to be the reason for his withdrawal.

The brigands, surrounding [Note: This word is likewise absent from the manuscript. ID.] them from the sides and rear, cut down the last in the column; they harassed the advancing army with javelins. The force of missiles hurled into the packed ranks could scarcely fail to strike. If anyone dared to strike back, he exposed himself to a wound; if anyone turned toward his assailant, he was abandoned by his own men and hemmed in by the enemy.

For the man who follows is always in a stronger position than the man who leads: the former covers his chest, while the latter exposes his back to the enemy.

The Romans were therefore hard pressed, like besieged men who had come to besiege. They could no longer endure or withstand the weight of their armor, which burdened them, while the enemy was more nimble. It was not easy to overtake the enemy, and they were in great fear that their line might be broken. Under these unfavorable conditions of combat they could not harm the enemy, while they themselves were suffering severely.

Cestius remained uncertain what to do as he saw his men being worn down along the entire route. Even after many of the leading officers had been afflicted, he halted for two days, as though to restore the exhausted.

But when he saw the number of the enemy increasing more and more, and everything around filled with adversaries, and recognized that his delay harmed him because more men were gathering, on the third day he sought a shorter route and an easier passage. He ordered the baggage of the column to be moved [Note: “To be put in motion.” ID.].

He had the pack animals killed, most of the vehicles broken up, and other things of this kind—more burdensome than useful in danger—destroyed or thrown over precipices. These included siege equipment and kinds of missiles, by which they were further alarmed, lest they arm the enemy against themselves with their own resources.

When the Jews noticed this, they understood that the Romans were preparing flight rather than battle. They occupied the narrowest parts of the route; in the more open areas they pressed less closely, blocked the front, constricted the sides, harassed the rear, and forced the Romans toward a precipice into which those enclosed on every side either slipped or were thrown down.

Many covered the sky with javelins and showered the column with arrows, never relaxing their attack, but aiming solely at the destruction of their adversaries.

The infantry could no longer stand firm. The cavalry faced even greater danger: their horses slipped and fell over steep rocks and treacherous ground, and the riders could not maintain their formation, hindered by the narrow path. On one side there were cliffs, on the other precipices; they allowed neither a place for flight nor a position for defense.

The Jews, by contrast, were inflamed still more by hope of victory. They loomed over the exhausted, pressed upon those who were stuck, mocked the despairing, and would have destroyed almost the entire strength of the Roman army had night not come to their aid.

The darkness of night interrupted the battle, which the Romans fought at a nearby place called Bethoron. The Jews surrounded them on every side and watched the exits, lest the Romans escape.

Cestius, distrustful of an open route, attempted flight by deception. He therefore selected forty men whose despair of escape had filled them with contempt for death. He stationed them in the fortifications and ordered them to make the defenses resound throughout the night with the greatest possible noise, as though carrying out the usual duties of those guarding the rampart.

Thus the preparations of the departing army would not be revealed to the Jews by the customary signs, by which men in confusion usually betray themselves. All the Romans were to leave in silence, while the Jews suspected nothing. Hearing the customary sounds of the guards, they would suppose that all the Romans remained in position.

By this deception Cestius led out the army. He had already covered thirty stadia, relying in this uncertain matter on the loyalty of a few men who preferred, when doomed to die, to repay their companions’ dangers with their own rather than abandon them.

The night concealed the deception, but daylight exposed it. When the light spread and the facts became clear, and the entire place where the Romans had stayed appeared empty, the Jews attacked first those whom they had been deceived by the simulated duties into sparing. They easily killed the forty men and pursued the army, which had covered a great distance during the night and now hurried more quickly by day, lest it be caught up in the dangers of another night.

The road was full of baggage abandoned by the fleeing Romans, so that no one might be delayed beneath an unjust burden. Vessels, utensils, and even objects necessary for war lay scattered everywhere: crossbows, battering rams, and other equipment brought for the destruction of the city. The pursuing Jews passed these by so as not to be delayed; those returning gathered them up, intending to use them against the Romans, whose companions had abandoned them [Note: “Who had distributed them.” ID.].

They pursued the Romans as far as the city of Antipatris. When they realized that they had failed to overtake the entire Roman army and had lost hope of capturing it, they turned back. Gathering the spoils of the slain, they returned to Jerusalem in triumph and with hymns.

Their joy was so great that, having lost only a few of their own men, they had destroyed five thousand Roman infantrymen and three hundred cavalrymen.

This occurred in the twelfth year of Nero’s reign, as we mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XVI

But not all the Jews shared that rejoicing. Some longed, after that event, to escape not merely from Cestius’s battle but from misery itself, as though rescued from the utmost peril of a sinking ship; they wished to swim out of the shipwreck of the state.

Among them were Custobarus and his brother Saul, together with Philip, commander of King Agrippa’s forces. These men fled to Cestius and asked to be sent to Nero in Achaia.

Cestius willingly accepted their request and did not refuse what they asked, so that through them Caesar might learn that Florus had been the cause of the war; that Cestius himself had been compelled by the force of necessity to undertake the war, since the army had been surrounded by the unexpected multitude of the conspirators; and that he had left it rescued from danger by the commander’s judgment rather than entangled in it.

Cestius had attempted to calm the hatred aroused against Florus, but he had been unable to do so. Thus, he would say, war had broken out, not been initiated by him.

These, then, were the instructions given, so that, by arousing Caesar’s entire anger against Florus, he might hope to lessen Caesar’s displeasure toward himself, which he feared because he knew that the matter had been badly handled.

The Romans were so terrified by the army’s defeat that the Damascenes, fearing the contagion of a suspected alliance, killed the Jews who lived with them in the city and had gathered in the gymnasium. They did this because the Jews had long before arranged the matter, whether through suspicion or by deceit, so that they might be separated from the assemblies of the Gentiles—either lest they undertake some new action during the night or so that they alone might be exposed to exile.

The plan was carried out with the deepest secrecy, so that not even their wives learned of such an attempt, since most of the women themselves participated in Jewish observances.

## CHAPTER XVII

They therefore attacked them all in a confined place and killed ten thousand Jews. This was easily done, since unarmed men were overcome by armed men who had taken them by surprise.

A recent example of such savagery had also occurred on an even greater scale at Scythopolis, and I believe it encouraged the Damascenes. When the Jews were ravaging all the neighboring areas, they came to Scythopolis. There they attempted to test the Jews who lived in the city and discovered that they were adversaries whom they had thought loyal to them.

For, as is customary in human character, concern for safety outweighs kinship among such people [Note: “Prevails.” BARR.]. Therefore, when they had formed a council with their fellow tribesmen, they preferred the fellowship of those living in the city and threatened their fellow tribesmen with destruction.

The Gentiles became suspicious, because the Jews’ eagerness seemed directed toward carrying out hatred against their own people. They feared that, under the appearance of a pretense, some deception was being prepared, and that the Jews would attack the city’s unwary inhabitants by night. After overthrowing all the Gentiles, they might then restore themselves to favor among the Jews.

Accordingly, if the Jews wished to prove their loyalty even toward the Gentiles, they were to leave the city with all their families and go to a nearby grove.

After this had been done, the people of Scythopolis remained quiet for two days, so that the Jewish group might lay aside suspicion and adopt a sense of security.

On the third night, when the confidence presumed by the Gentiles had removed their concern for guarding themselves [Note: Or: “when the assumed confidence had removed the anxiety of the guard.” ID.], force was brought against the unsuspecting and sleeping Jews, and thirteen thousand people were killed. Everything they possessed was also plundered.

## CHAPTER XVIII

The bitter suffering of Simon calls for explanation. It was pitiable to see and hear, but memorable because of the novelty of the event.

He belonged to the Jewish people and was born to Saul, a father of no mean standing. He possessed both boldness of spirit and bodily strength. He exercised both of these qualities to the destruction of his fellow tribesmen. By repeated attacks he killed many of the immigrant Jewish population. If they happened to gather in conspiracy, he alone held the battle line; when they formed a mass, he was accustomed to drive them back. He was the knot and hindrance of the whole war, and often its reversal when matters seemed desperate.

The Jewish inhabitants of Scythopolis had already rendered military service against their own people [Note: “They displayed.” ID.], but vengeance owed to kindred blood did not long fail. When their loyalty was broken and the Scythopolitans who had withdrawn by agreement to the grove were surrounded, they began to press the war and attack.

They also attacked Simon’s children and parents from a distance with missiles and weapons, after the rest of the multitude had been destroyed.

Simon saw that the innumerable multitude was easily superior and that he could not endure much longer. He drew his sword, turned toward the enemy, and cried:

“I am receiving, Scythopolitans, what my deeds deserve. I am receiving, Scythopolitans, what my deeds deserve: I who made the slaughter of my kinsmen a testimony of the goodwill I owed you [Note: A variant reads: “by the slaughter . . . goodwill”; shortly afterward, “brotherly blood.” ID.], and gave you my brothers’ blood as a pledge of favor—though perfidy would more justly have been assigned to you.

“Now, while I offer loyalty to foreigners, I have lost it among my own household. I have betrayed my children and parents, whom you nevertheless ought not to have killed [Note: “They ought not to have been killed.” ID.], if you judged the reward of crime correctly.

“I shall therefore die, angry with everyone and a friend to no one. I have betrayed my own people, and with my own hands I shall first demand vengeance from myself. I killed companions in religion and fellow believers; I acknowledge the penalties owed for my crime.

“I shall pay the penalty of parricide worthy of so great a sacrilege, so that it may be both punishment for my offense and glory for courage. Let no one else boast of my wound [Note: “My wound.” ID.]; afterward my right hand will turn against myself, so that it may appear that I die through madness, not weakness.

“Let no one insult me as I fall. Let clemency be the avenger of parricide, and let parricide be the avenger of sacrilege.” [Note: Another reading: “Let madness be the witness of parricide.” ID.]

After speaking these words, he turned his gaze upon his children and parents. His eyes expressed indignation, but as mercy now mingled with his anger, he seized his father from the midst of the group and pierced him through with his sword.

After him his mother was brought forward, so that no one might intervene for her grandchildren. His wife willingly offered herself in turn, lest, cast down by the death of her husband, she should survive him.

His sons came forward, lest they be judged degenerate from so great a father even in death.

He himself hurried to anticipate the enemy with a swift blow. When his entire family had been killed, he stood amid the funerals of his own people. And, as though triumphing over his domestic sufferings [Note: “Over those who had been triumphed over.” ID.], because he had seen none of his family perish by another’s sword, he raised his right hand so that all might see it and, imposing upon himself a death fearful to everyone, victoriously pierced himself with his own blade.

He was a memorable young man because of the exceptional strength of his body and the greatness of his spirit. But because he offered loyalty to foreigners rather than to his own people, he deserved such an end.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 2065D]

After these things had been reported to Nero, who was then in the regions of Achaia and had been striving, through the practice of tragic songs, to carry away the scenic crown from many contests, one could not say which was more disgraceful: that the emperor should come upon the stage, or that he should fill the stage with his crimes—he who disgraced Orestes by his singing and represented him through parricide. Grave fear seized him. [Col. 2066D]

He feared not spectacles resembling those games, but the ultimate disasters of war; and he feared them so that at last he might recover from the obscenity of theatrical pleasures and the madness of parricide, turn back to concern for the state, and rage and seethe within himself because the Roman state had suffered so great a calamity more through the negligence of its commander than through the valor of its adversaries. [Col. 2067A]

He did indeed try to feign boldness, but fear exposed him; and he attempted to assume the appearance of magnanimity, so that his mind might rise above the distress of affairs. Yet he was distracted by anxiety of mind as he considered what commander he should choose to remove the disgrace and bring the war to an end. The impending destruction of Judaea, the final ruin, pressed upon him, so that Nero put on the character of a king and, in the voice of a prudent counselor, expressed a salutary judgment.

Vespasian alone was the man to whom the supreme command of the armies in the East could rightly be entrusted: a man seasoned from youth in military service and triumphal campaigns, who had brought to lasting peace the Gauls, unsettled by the tumult of the Germans and thrown back into war by the native ferocity of their recklessness. He had also acquired Britain for the Roman empire by arms, though it still lay hidden among the waves. [Note: [Col. 2067D] This word is absent from the manuscript. ID.] Through the wealth of that conquered land Rome was considered richer, Claudius more prudent, and Nero more courageous. Thus they celebrated the trophies of nations whose wars they had not witnessed.

Under this commander—I say it again—Nero was terrible, Nero was feared, powerful abroad and secure at home, Vespasian’s loyalty and courage being matched against each other. How great was this man, by whose arms Nero’s vices were concealed among foreign peoples, so that, as a mockery of human affairs and a reproach for impurity renounced, he might even be glorified by triumphs! Whenever war had to be waged at the farthest boundaries of the Roman world, Vespasian was chosen from among all others. Whenever the war had been brought to an end, Vespasian was joined to the enterprise above all others, lest either a public enemy remain or a domestic plotter creep in. He was worthy to precede a kingdom through the service of a soldier. He taught loyalty and displayed valor.

Nero sent him unwillingly, since he was taking away his own protection; but he was constrained by the future punishments of his crimes, so that he might leave himself deprived of so great a commander’s company and without arms. Galba would never, surely, have undertaken his efforts to aspire to imperial power had he not discovered that Vespasian was absent.

But God arranged this, so that a man might be sent to Syria who would both weaken the insolence of the Jews through the ultimate destruction and disgrace of captivity inflicted upon the nation, and deprive Nero of assistance—although no human valor can obstruct the decrees of heaven. Yet foolish Nero, when he learned that the strong arm of the Roman army had been weakened by the Jewish war, rose up against the Christians, so that the end appointed for him might draw near. [Note: [Col. 2067D] The learned Mazochius discusses this and what follows at greater length in his commentary on the Neapolitan marble calendar, vol. III, p. 854.]

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 2068A]

At that time Peter and Paul, teachers of the Christians, were in Rome—distinguished by their works and renowned for their teaching. By the power of their works they had made Nero hostile, after he had been captivated by the soothing arts of the magician Simon, who had won his favor. Simon promised him, through deadly arts, the subjection of nations, long life, and the preservation of health; and Nero believed him, since he did not know how to examine the nature of things. In the end Simon held the highest place in Nero’s friendship, since Nero even regarded him as the guardian of his health and life.

But when Peter exposed his vanities and crimes, and demonstrated that he was lying about the appearance of things and could accomplish nothing substantial or true, Simon was treated with ridicule and consumed by a fitting grief. Although he had experienced Peter’s power in other parts of the world, he nevertheless arrived in Rome and dared to boast that he could raise the dead.

At that time a noble youth, a relative of Caesar, had died at Rome, to the sorrow of all. Many urged that it should be tried whether he could be restored to life. Peter was regarded as most famous in such works, but among the Gentiles no confidence in an act of this kind was granted. [Note: [Col. 2068D] I think a syllable has fallen out of this word, and that Ambrose wrote FACTIS, not facti, for that case is joined with this expression. ID., same place, p. 859.] Grief demanded a remedy, and they went to Peter.

Some thought that Simon should also be summoned; both men appeared. Peter said that he would give precedence to Simon, who boasted of his own power, so that, if he could, he might raise the dead. If Simon did not raise him, Peter would not fail to bring Christ’s aid to the dead man, so that he might rise again.

Simon, supposing that his arts would have greatest force among the city’s Gentiles, proposed this condition: if he himself restored the dead man to life, Peter should be killed, because by challenging the one called “Great Power”—for that was his title—he had offered an insult; but if Peter prevailed against Simon, Simon should be punished in the same manner.

Peter agreed. Simon began, approached the dead man’s bed, and, as soon as he began to chant and mutter dreadful spells, the dead man appeared to shake his head. There was a great outcry among the Gentiles that he was already alive and speaking with Simon. Anger and indignation were directed at Peter, because he had dared to compare himself with so great a power.

The holy Apostle asked for silence and said: “If the dead man is alive, let him speak; if he has been restored to life, let him rise, walk, and speak. What appears to have moved his head is an apparition, not reality.” Finally he said: “Let Simon be separated from the bed; then not even this will remain as a spectacle.”

Simon was led away from the bed. The dead man remained without any appearance of movement. Peter stood at a distance and, for a little while, devoted himself inwardly to prayer; then he said in a loud voice: [Col. 2068D]

“Boy, arise; may the Lord Jesus heal you.”

[Note: [Col. 2068D] The formula is the same as that which the same Peter uses in Acts 9:34: “Aeneas, the Lord Jesus Christ heals you” (ἰᾶται, “heals”); “arise and spread your bed.” From this passage in Acts it appears that Ambrose too wrote sanat, “he heals,” rather than the merely optative sanet, “may he heal.” Moreover, unless Christ had already restored health, there would have been no reason for Peter to command, “Arise.” And since Abdias expressly wrote the indicative sanat, this is certain proof that he found it written no differently in his copy of Exosippus. Mazochius, same place, p. 861.]

Immediately the youth rose, spoke, walked, and took food; and Peter gave him to his mother. When he was asked not to depart from him, Peter said: “He will not be abandoned by him who caused him to rise, whose servants we are. Be at peace about your son, mother; do not fear—he has his guardian.”

When the people rose up against Simon to stone him, Peter said: “It is punishment enough for him that he recognizes his arts to be powerless. Let him live and, unwilling though he may be, see the kingdom of Christ increase.”

The magician was tortured by the Apostle’s glory. He gathered himself, summoned all the power of his spells, and assembled the people. He declared that he had been offended by the Galilaeans and would leave the city that he had been accustomed to protect. He appointed a day and promised that he would fly and be carried up to the heavenly seats, where heaven would be open to him whenever he wished.

On the appointed day he climbed the Capitoline Hill and, throwing himself from the cliff, began to fly. The people marveled and worshiped him, many saying that this was the power of God, not of a human being, who was flying through the air with his body; and they said that Christ had done nothing of the kind.

[Note: [Col. 2069C] So the common editions print it. Yet Gualtherus testifies that he found somewhere in his notes, “not of a human being,” which in my judgment is the finest reading and the only true one. Since Simon persuaded the credulous that he was the power or virtue of God, as is clear from Acts 8:10, the people, seeing him flying, rightly shouted, “the power of God, not a human being.” Therefore the entire period should be corrected and punctuated as follows, unless I am mistaken: “The people marveled and worshiped, many saying that he was the power of God, not a human being, since he was flying through the air with his body.” ID., same place, p. 863.]

Then Peter, standing in their midst, said: “Lord Jesus, show him that his arts are empty, lest this people, who will believe, be deceived by this appearance. Let him fall, Lord—but in such a way that, while alive, he may recognize that he was able to accomplish nothing.”

Immediately, at Peter’s word, the pinions of the wings he had assumed became entangled; he fell and was not killed, but, with his leg broken and weakened, he withdrew to Aricia, and there died.

When Nero learned this, he grieved that he had been deceived and deprived of such a friend, and, indignant that a useful and necessary man had been taken from him and from the state, began to seek reasons for killing Peter. [Note: [Col. 2069D] Mazochius, same place, p. 465, punctuates this passage in this way; Abdias confirms his punctuation, for he sometimes alters the text of Exosippus in such a way that he nevertheless makes sufficiently clear what he found in his copy. The common editions differ. Moreover, the same learned man, following Gualtherus, who read it in an old manuscript, thinks that the entire passage should be restored as follows: “When Nero learned this, grieving that he had been deceived and deprived by the death of such a friend, and indignant that a useful man had been taken away ... he began to seek,” etc. GALLAND.]

Now the time had come when the holy Apostles Peter and Paul were to be summoned. Accordingly, after an order had been given for their arrest, Peter was urged to withdraw elsewhere. He resisted, saying that he would certainly not act so as to retreat as though terrified by fear of death; that it was good to suffer for Christ, who had offered himself to death for all; that this would not be death but immortality; that it was unworthy for him to flee the passion of his own body, since by his teaching he had compelled many to offer themselves as sacrifices for Christ; and that, according to the Lord’s word, it was owed to him that he too should give Christ glory and honor in his own passion.

Peter advanced these and other arguments. But the people pleaded with tears that he should not abandon them or leave them wavering amid the storms of the Gentiles. Overcome by their tears, Peter yielded and promised to leave the city.

On the following night, after greeting the brethren and celebrating the prayer, he began to depart alone. [Note: [Col. 2069D] There can be no doubt that by “celebrating the prayer” Ambrose means performing the sacrifice of the Mass. In the Acts of Saint Pionius the Martyr, in Ruinart, section 5, it is related that “after the solemn prayer, when on the Sabbath day they had tasted the holy bread and water, Pionius and his companions were arrested.” In canon 13 of the Synod of Laodicea, according to the interpretation of Dionysius: “The priests of the countryside, when the bishop is present, or the priests of the city itself, may not offer, nor give the consecrated bread” (the latter phrase in Greek is οὔτε μὴν ἄρτον διδόναι ἐν ΕΥΧΗ, “nor indeed give bread in prayer”) “or present the cup. But if these men are absent and are summoned to give prayer (εἰς εὐχὴν), they alone shall be permitted to give it.” Zonaras, commenting on this canon, interprets ἐν εὐχῇ as ἐν ἱερουγίας καιρῷ, “at the time of the sacrifice.” Hence, in the Greek liturgical books, Μυστικὴ εὐχὴ, “mystical prayer,” is what we call the Mass. Balsamon, commenting on Gregory of Nyssa’s letter to Letoius, explains μυστικῆς ἐπιτελουμέμης εὐχῆς, “the mystical prayer being performed,” as referring to the consecration of the bread and cup, preceded by the secret prayer of the priest, so that the bread and cup may be sanctified. MAZOCHIUS, same place, p. 993.]

When he had reached the gate, he saw Christ coming to meet him. He worshiped him and said: “Lord, where are you going?”

Christ said to him: “I am coming again to be crucified.”

Peter understood that this referred to his own passion: Christ appeared to be about to suffer in him who suffers in each person—not through bodily pain, certainly, but through a certain compassion of mercy, or through the celebration of glory. [Note: [Col. 2070D] I would not at all understand what Ambrose calls here “the celebration of glory” unless the examples of the first martyr Stephen—whom the Son of Man, standing at the right hand of the power of God, that is, in the glory of the saints, showed himself to be seeing in his final struggle—and of other champions, to whom something ἰσοδυναμοῦν, “equivalent,” often occurred, taught me what this was. ID., same place, p. 867.]

He turned back and returned to the city. When he was captured by the persecutors and condemned to the cross, he asked to be fastened to it with his feet turned in the opposite direction, because he was unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as the Son of God had suffered.

This request was granted—either because it was ordained in this way, as Christ had foretold, or because the persecutor was not unwilling to grant an increase in his punishment. Thus both he and Paul were killed: the one on a cross, the other by the sword.

## CHAPTER III

But, to return to the subject: Nero, disturbed by the grave report and by the less successful course of affairs in Judaea, appointed Vespasian, a man experienced in war, over all the forces that were in Syria. Vespasian hastened on, for there was no time to delay. He sent his son Titus to Alexandria to lead from there a portion of the troops stationed in that region; he himself, having crossed the Hellespont, made for Syria on foot.

Meanwhile, the Jews, elated by their successes, chose commanders for the war. They assigned districts, determining who should preside over each, what duties each should perform, what ranks they should hold, and what office each should discharge. They appointed Joseph, son of Cution, and Ananus the chief priest to administer the affairs of Jerusalem, especially the restoration of its walls. [Note: [Col. 2071D] An old manuscript reads Gurion. Josephus, son of Gorion. BARR.]

Eleazar, son of Simon, burned with desire that some public offices should be entrusted to him. Although he had brought under his own authority all the booty they had captured from the Roman army—especially the rich and abundant wealth amassed through the greed and excessive plundering of Cestius—nevertheless they judged him to be more intent on acquiring power for himself than devoted to the common good, and thought that he should be avoided. But by gradually courting individuals, giving and distributing gifts, he brought it about that the supreme control of everything was entrusted to his discretion.

Jesus, one of the priests, and Eleazar, the son of a priest, having been appointed commanders of the army, also took charge of the defense of Idumaea. They reserved, however, every authority over the whole of Idumaea for Niger, who held the highest command. Joseph, son of Simon, received Jericho; Manasse was entrusted with the region of Peraea, situated beyond the Euphrates. [Note: [Col. 2072D] An old manuscript reads Petraea. ID.] It received its name from the fact that, for those traveling in that direction, the Euphrates must be crossed.

John the Essene, another John the son of Ananias, and the others were assigned the remaining districts, which they were to protect by their own diligence. Thus each attended to the duties entrusted to him: they restored the walls and recruited a fighting force. Joseph, descending into Galilee, diligently worked to fortify the forts, restore the defenses, and enlist the strongest and most war-ready men. He prohibited banditry, appeared daily in the camps, trained the soldiers according to Roman military practice, divided them and distributed them by ranks, and appointed many centurions, so that discipline might more easily be demanded from all and no one who had abandoned his proper duties might remain hidden.

He also trained them to recognize the signals and reversals of the trumpets, to keep ranks, draw up the battle line, and cover themselves with their shields, so that, like a wall, they might defend themselves against attacking forces if a great mass of the enemy should descend upon them; to assist those in difficulty, sympathize with the weary, and take upon themselves the dangers of others.

He taught them not only the arts of war after the fashion of Roman military practice, but also, before the war, the measures by which they could better aid those fighting: he ordered the soldiers to carry their own food and weapons, fortify themselves with rampart and ditch, anticipate the enemy by establishing camps, obey orders, grow accustomed to abstaining from theft and plunder, and regard it as a personal gain if no loss were inflicted on rural cultivators.

“For what,” he said, “distinguishes a man from the enemy if he himself takes things away in an enemy’s manner? Except that it is more serious to attack one’s own people than another’s, and to despoil allies rather than adversaries. A good conscience has the greatest power in war, because the man who recognizes himself as associated with no crime has greater confidence in divine assistance.”

But in these matters he soon discovered that envy had harmed him more among the wicked than favor had benefited him among the good. For when he had gathered nearly sixty thousand infantry, very few cavalry, four thousand men who practiced war for pay, and six hundred chosen guards for his own person, he suffered so much from the Jews that before the war he feared dangers from his own people more than, during the war itself, from the Romans.

I omit what sedition was stirred up, because he was suspected of returning the property recovered from banditry to those who had lost it—and especially the property of Agrippa and Berenice, which ought justly to have been restored, lest they make the king more hostile.

Nevertheless, in order to soften the people’s anger, he maintained that the money should be reserved for building the walls rather than for compensating the owners. He said that the Taricheans ought to assess everything that had been taken from Ptolemy, who had carried away the royal gold, clothing, and other gifts; for the question before them was whether they thought it should be preserved for the restoration of their walls or brought out to be plundered by bandits. It certainly seemed disgraceful that he should suffer punishment for having given better counsel.

Thus, by turning them toward his favor, he escaped both their envy and the danger.

Again, when he requested the favor and alliance of King Agrippa and Tiberias, Joseph withdrew from the city mentioned above and closed the gates of Taricheae, lest any messenger proceed to Tiberias and report that Joseph lacked military support.

He himself gathered from the lake whatever fishing boats he could find in the time available and approached Tiberias with oars. When he came to a place from which the boats could indeed be seen clearly by those in the city, yet it could not be discovered whether they were empty of fighting men, he ordered them to be scattered across the whole expanse of the lake, so that their number might appear greater, lest anyone judge them empty rather than filled with warriors.

Terrified by this, and thinking themselves weak against so great a multitude, they threw down their arms, opened the gates, and poured out as suppliants before Joseph, who had drawn nearer like the commander of an army. He asked with what madness they had finally conceived the idea of abandoning their cause, under whose instigators they had been driven to surrender themselves to their enemies. At the same time, as they came toward him, he ordered the helmsmen to bring them to Taricheae; and there he seized nearly three hundred members of the council and many persons from the common people, throwing them into chains.

He also summoned Clytus, the principal author of this crime, and ordered him to pay the penalty by having his hands cut off. When Clytus asked that at least one hand be left him, Joseph ordered him to cut off whichever one he wished himself. Clytus then seized a sword in his right hand and cut off his left.

Thus Tiberias was recovered. Sephoris too had attempted to defect, but through Joseph’s vigilance it was nevertheless retained among the allied cities of the Jews. For he preferred to defend what was his through calmer counsels rather than attack what belonged to others.

## CHAPTER IV

But Petates Niger, the Babylonian Syllas, and John the Essene, gathering together all the able-bodied youth in Judaea, marched against Ascalon—a large city, indeed, and supported by strong walls, but lacking assistance and resources. It lay seven hundred and twenty stadia from Jerusalem, and was separated from it by immense hostility. Therefore the Jews, wishing to destroy the city that was hostile to them, gathered their forces and attacked.

Antonius commanded the city with a smaller number of Roman troops than the Jews thought sufficient for resistance. But he was a man of sharper intelligence and an equally prudent soldier. He drew out his cavalry and allowed the Jews, spread out and relying more on their numbers than on their courage, to cross toward the city. Then, when they had advanced in their charge, he tired those who followed, broke up the compact ranks, put the disordered to flight, and pursued them as they scattered across the whole field. Some were driven back toward the walls, with their escape cut off; others sought different routes, but were surrounded by the cavalry and cut down.

Many fell upon those above them and trampled one another in their rush. Thus, after being slaughtered until evening, they lost ten thousand of their men, with their commanders John and Syllas killed alike. Few of the Romans were wounded in the battle; yet the rashness of the Jews was not checked but inflamed. For grief kindled boldness, and their defeat aroused a desire for revenge.

They therefore armed themselves with far greater fury, before the wounds of the wounded had yet healed, and, having gathered more men than before, attacked again. But Antonius received them with arranged ambushes and, before they came to blows, enclosed them by surrounding them with cavalry. He ordered the surrounded men to be cut down: nine thousand were killed and the rest put to flight.

Niger himself escaped and took refuge in a fortress. There was a tower enclosed on every side by strong stonework. Since the Romans could not cut it down, they surrounded it with fires. When it caught fire, Niger crossed from the tower into a sort of cave, concealed himself from the enemy, and escaped the flames.

The Romans, assuming that he too had been consumed in the fire, were unconcerned. On the third day, when his men were seeking his body for burial, he was restored to them alive and vigorous. Thus he was preserved to the Jews’ great joy and brought back from the enemy.

## CHAPTER V

Meanwhile Vespasian, having crossed the Hellespont and passed through Bithynia and Cilicia, reached Syria and led the legions and the other military forces that he found there to Antioch.

That city is unquestionably the first of Syria and is therefore regarded as its metropolis. It was founded by those who joined Alexander the Great in war and was named after its founder. The city stretches to an immense length; it is narrower at its upper end, because on the left it is confined by the steep face of a mountain, so that the space for extending the city could not be measured farther.

Necessity marked out the site. For if the Parthians broke in through hidden and difficult paths, the higher mountain would provide a hiding place from which they could pour unexpectedly and with a more ready assault into unprepared Syria—unless the city, like a barrier, were placed against the mountain and blocked the approach of those arriving. Thus, if any barbarians climbed up, they could immediately be seen from the heart of the city.

Indeed, when theatrical games were being celebrated in the city, they say that a certain author of mimes, lifting his eyes toward the mountain, saw the Persians approaching and immediately said: “Either I am seeing a dream, or there is great danger: behold, the Persians!” The mountain rises so high that even the height of the theater does not obstruct the view of it.

A river divides the city through its middle. Rising where the sun rises, it empties into the sea not far from the city. Because of the course of its source, the ancients called it the Orontes, so that it is commonly thought to have given its name to the place, although it received its own name from there.

Because its waters are cooled by their very current and because west winds continually blow through that region, the entire city is almost constantly refreshed, so that the Orontes conceals the East in the regions of the East. Within the city are sweet waters; outside is a neighboring grove woven thickly with cypresses, abundant springs, and waters. They call it Daphne because it never lays aside its greenery.

The population is numerous and cheerful, like most of the peoples of the East, and almost universally more witty, but also more inclined to wantonness. The city was formerly judged third among all the cities in the Roman world; now it is fourth, after Constantinople, the city of the Byzantines, had grown. Rome is first, Alexandria second, Antioch third, Constantinople fourth. Formerly the capital of the Persians, Constantinople is now the city of those who have been driven back.

I think enough has been said about the site of the city. There is no need to linger over a description of its buildings, since, when I have said that the East lies behind it, it is clear enough that the south lies to its left, Europe faces it, and the northern peoples dwell on its right; there also lie the Caspian kingdoms, which formerly were especially ready to invade Syria.

But after Alexander the Great placed the Caspian Gate at the steep pass of Mount Taurus and closed the route to all the peoples of the interior, he rendered the city peaceful, except insofar as it remained suspicious of Persian movements.

In that city King Agrippa, with all his forces, awaited the arrival of Vespasian. Since Vespasian did not remain there long, Agrippa joined his retinue, and together they began to travel toward Ptolemais.

The inhabitants of Sephoris came to meet them at that city, asking Vespasian to confirm the peace that they had long ago made with Cestius Gallus. Their prudence was praised, because they had provided for their own safety by not provoking the Romans. After receiving their pledge, Vespasian both accepted them into friendship and, adding infantry and cavalry auxiliaries, supported them with protection, lest they should be driven by the pain of abandonment to rise against the instigators of the war.

For, as Sephoris offered itself to the Roman empire like a kind of barrier of Judaea, the way into Judaea was opened to the enemy at that point which had been placed in the enemy’s path as a suitable defense for the whole nation. It was, contrary to expectation, the most strongly fortified city in Galilee. This fact led me to distinguish one Galilee from the other, since there are two Galilees, one upper and the other lower, though they are joined and connected with one another. But first we must speak of both.

## CHAPTER VI

Both Galilees border on Syria and Phoenicia. On the west they are separated from it by the boundaries of the territory of Ptolemais and by Mount Carmel, which formerly belonged to the Galileans but is now joined to the territory of the Tyrians. The city of Gabaa is connected with this mountain; it once became a grave cause of destruction for the Jews.

On the east, Hyppena and Gadara cut them off with their own boundaries. In ancient times they also shared prescribed borders with the region of Gaulanitis and the kingdom of Agrippa. On the southern side, Scythopolis and Samaria receive both Galilees within their territories and do not allow them to extend beyond the waters of the Jordan.

Tyre closes off their northern side on the right, together with the entire region of the Tyrians, whose position defines the extent of Galilee.

The two Galilees are distinguished from each other in this way: lower Galilee, as it is called, extends in length from the city of Tiberias to the city named Zabulon, above the maritime territory of Ptolemais. Its width unquestionably runs from the village of Zaloth, which lies in the great plain, to Beersheba.

From there the beginning of upper Galilee opens, extending as far as it reaches the boundaries of the village of Bathatae. The boundaries of Tyrian territory are also determined by that village. The beginning of its length is the village of Thalla, and its end is Rothala, neighboring the Jordan. From this it may be understood how far the territories of upper Galilee extend, whose beginning is the Jordan or its boundaries.

Thus the two Galilees are distinguished according to this measurement of their extent.

The land is rich and grassy, flourishing through varied kinds of cultivation and marked by trees, so that it attracts anyone to appreciate it and invites and stimulates even those who shun labor to undertake cultivation. Indeed, no part of the land there, however small, lies unused; it is densely inhabited. Cities are numerous, villages frequent, and the multitude of people beyond counting, so that a small village within its territory has twenty thousand inhabitants. [Note: [Col. 2075D] An old manuscript reads fifteen thousand. Josephus likewise, same work, book I, chapter 2. BARR.]

Both Galilees are surrounded by foreign nations, and therefore their people are warlike: trained from their earliest age in exercises of battle, numerous, ready for bold action, and prepared for every art of war.

The region of Petraea, however, surpasses it in size, as we explained above when discussing the origin of its name. It is larger, but Galilee is more useful, because it is cultivated throughout and no part of it is barren of produce; its entire land is rich and fertile.

Petraea is more extensive, but for the most part deserted and harsh. It does not know how to submit to the plow, nor is it easily able to tame its rougher juices. Yet one part of it is soft enough for cultivation, fertile for use, pleasing to the eye, gentle for working, useful for grafted fruit trees, and productive of everything. Trees line its fields in the foreground and beautify the middle; for the most part they protect the crops from excessive heat or cold. The land is especially clothed with olive trees, woven with vines, or marked by palms.

It is indescribably beautiful when rows of palms, stirred by the wind, rustle and spread the scents of dates, sweeter than usual.

Nor is it surprising that the whole region possesses such charm of greenery, where the land is watered by the pleasant courses of rivers descending from the higher mountain ridge and is occupied by abundant snowy springs, envied when possessed and desired when absent.

Its length runs from Machaerus to Pella—that is, from the southern side to the north. Its width extends from Philadelphia to the Jordan River, that is, from the rising of the sun as far as Arabia. [Note: [Col. 2075D] An old manuscript reads: “from the rising of the sun it is bordered as far as Arabia.” BARR.]

To the west, its extension from the city to the Jordan River is apparent. [Note: [Col. 2075D] Or, “the river”? But I have changed nothing. GALLAND.]

The Samaritan region lies between Judaea and Galilee. It begins at a village named Elas and ends in the land of the Acrabathenians, similar in nature and in no way different from Judaea. [Note: [Col. 2076D] The Barrensis edition does not contain “in no way”; perhaps it is more correct. GALLAND.]

Both regions are mountainous and level, according to the diversity of their places. Neither is spread entirely across plains, nor is every part split by mountain crags; each possesses the charm of both qualities. The soil, loose and soft enough for cultivation, is useful for grain and, in the fertility of its soil, scarcely inferior to any region; certainly, in the ripening of its fruits, it is earlier than all others. For while grain is still being sown elsewhere, it is harvested there. The appearance and very nature of the grain are considered superior nowhere else.

The water is sweet, beautiful to look upon, and pleasant to drink. Thus, judging from the excellence of the elements, the Jews considered it the land promised to the fathers, flowing with milk and honey, when God had promised them the privilege of resurrection.

God’s mercy had indeed granted both, if they had kept faith; but both were taken away from faithless minds: here, by the yoke of captivity; there, by the bond of sin.

The region is wooded and therefore rich in livestock and abundant in milk. Nowhere, indeed, does livestock bear udders so swollen with milk. Its wild and grafted fruits surpass the abundance of all other regions.

Both Judaea and Samaria are filled with such a multitude of people that it seems to me the Jews interpreted from this the statement that there would be nothing barren or unproductive in these places, although the Law prescribed this concerning the fruitfulness of merits and the fertility of virtues.

Samaria begins at the borders of Arabia, at a village named Jordan, and ends to the north at the village of Borceus. The width of Judaea extends from the Jordan River to Joppa.

It begins at the springs of the Jordan and at Mount Lebanon and stretches as far as the lake of Tiberias. The beginning of its length is also the village of Artha, and it extends to the village of Juliades, where Jews and Tyrians share a common settlement.

In the middle of Judaea lies the city of Jerusalem, called, as prudent men have judged, almost the navel of the entire region. It abounds in inland resources and is not deprived of maritime ones, since it extends as far as Ptolemais and stretches its shores along the whole of that sea.

There are many cities, but Jerusalem rises above them all, so that, like the head in a body, it does not overshadow its members but governs them and serves as their protection and beauty.

Thus, concerning Judaea and the neighboring regions, I have not omitted, even in this conveniently brief account, those matters that needed to be indicated.

## CHAPTER VII
Sephoritans [Note: [Col. 2076D] The old manuscript reads: “the military subsidies assigned to the Sephoritans were raiding the neighboring region.” BARR.] also collected taxes and military subsidies and raided the neighboring regions, arrogating to themselves, under the pretext of war, the unrestricted authority to plunder what was being imposed upon the Jews by the Roman Empire. Therefore Josephus, eager to avenge the injury of the bitterness he had suffered, marched against the city of Sepphoris with a considerable number of men, intending either to recall them into alliance with Judaea [Col. 2077A] or, if they resisted, to weaken them with total destruction, if he could. But neither attempt achieved its purpose: he could neither dissuade them from choosing alliance with Rome nor overthrow the city, which he himself had strengthened with such fortifications that it could not be captured even by Romans far superior in number.

He therefore sounded the trumpet for battle; and when his attempted assault had produced no result, he stirred up war throughout the entire region. They ravaged everything, burning buildings day and night, plundering estates, killing everyone capable of fighting whom they captured, and subjecting the weak to slavery. All Galilee was filled with fire, blood, and brigandage; no one was exempt from misery, and everything presented a [Note: [Col. 2077D] Deplorable. ID.] deplorable appearance, since whatever had escaped fire or death was reserved for captivity. This [Note: [Col. 2077D] Evil. ID.] evil was preferred to those things that shortly before had been judged more bitter. [Col. 2077B]

## CHAPTER VIII

This was a kind of prelude to the war, before Titus arrived. As soon as he had crossed from Achaia to Alexandria, he brought the soldiers in accordance with his father’s command and came to the city of Ptolemais. There, having joined the ranks of the fifth and tenth, with the fifteenth also added—units that were exceptionally distinguished—and having assembled both Roman and allied forces, they began a savage and memorable war.

For when the opening operations had gone well under a commander of calm disposition, subsequent events turned against them. Vespasian, now more hostile, advanced with his son from the territory of Ptolemais and plunged into Galilee. When he learned that those to whom he had offered the opportunity of abandoning their [Col. 2077C] dissension [Note: [Col. 2077D] Secession. ID.]—if they thought it advisable to look to their own interests—were refusing peace, he utterly destroyed Gadara. He found it empty of fighting men, since all the stronger inhabitants, distrustful of its weaker defenses, had withdrawn to more secure fortifications.

He spared none of those whom he found, but ordered all to be killed, without regard for age and without mercy toward weakness. He was carrying this out not so much according to the right of war as from resentment over the battle with Cestius and from the hatred he had poured out against the Jews. Finally, he ordered not only the city but also its villages and municipal towns to be burned. His anger was not unjustified, since after such great insolence he had offered them the opportunity to correct their error, and they had not obeyed.

Josephus had crossed from that city to Tiberias before the Roman army approached. But the flight inspired more fear than his presence inspired confidence: they were terrified precisely because Josephus considered himself unequal to waging war against the Romans. Nor did he place his hope in anything else, unless perhaps the Jews should lay aside their eagerness for war. His earlier judgment had been that, if they chose war, he would rather prove his loyalty to his fellow citizens by sharing their danger than, by avoiding it, prove himself a traitor. For he was especially anxious not to disgrace the military command entrusted to him.

Accordingly, he wrote to the city of Jerusalem that war had descended upon them, and urged them to reply promptly whether they preferred peace or battle: the matter had to be considered in good time. He conveyed this briefly, showing no preference for either side, lest he be judged either a timid warrior or a stubborn rebel.

## CHAPTER IX

Again he set out from the city of Tiberias for Jotapata, either because it was more strongly fortified than the others and therefore many of the men most eager for battle had gathered there, or because Vespasian had sent many of his own men there to secure the route, which was difficult and rocky through the mountains, rough for infantry, and inaccessible and impassable for cavalry.

Finally, over four days, the roads were cleared so that the narrow passages would not impede them; a route was prepared by which the entire army could cross more easily. On the fifth day Josephus crossed by that route and restored the courage of the Jews. When Vespasian learned that Josephus had gone there, this gave him an additional incentive to hasten his march, since he thought that he could bring the war to a swift conclusion if he intercepted both the commander and the people, who were more ready for battle.

He therefore arrived with his army. On the first day he gave the soldiers time to attend to their food, so that concern for the battle would not overtake them while they were exhausted from the march. On the following day he surrounded the city with a double line, and on the third day with a cavalry formation as well.

When the Jews saw that they were enclosed and besieged on every side, with no place of [Note: [Col. 2078D] Escape. ID.] refuge, they took courage from the very desperation of their situation. Nothing makes a soldier readier for battle than the necessity of fighting and the imminence of danger.

Vespasian pressed them with javelins and arrows. Many of the Jews, advancing beyond the walls with missiles, were wounded by the carefully aimed shots; nevertheless, they remained undaunted. Roman courage attempted everything; and wherever it noticed that the walls’ defenses were weaker, it applied a greater force there. Shame armed some, while others were armed by their last hope, as they desired to open a path to safety with the sword.

The Jews endured severe assaults and returned no less daring attempts. Roman skill contended with courage, and Jewish fury with recklessness. Thus, after the Jews had fought all day for their lives and the Romans for triumph, night brought the battle to an end.

They fought similarly on the following day, and on the third and fourth days; on the fifth they fought fiercely. But, as usually happens in such battles, more wounds than deaths were inflicted, although the Jews often attempted sorties and the Romans breakthroughs. The Romans were provoked to anger by shame, because the conquerors of Hannibal, Antiochus, and all nations were being detained by Jewish battles.

So great was the constancy of Roman courage [Note: [Col. 2078D] Conviction. ID.] that the defeated side was not considered to have been quickly overcome; rather, their struggle was more against nature than against the enemy. For the city was almost completely enclosed on every side by precipitous cliffs. It was surrounded not by rampart and ditch, like other cities, but by deep precipices which neither human sight could encompass nor human use explore; and the anxious [Note: [Col. 2078D] Apprehensive. ID.] terror of the scene increasingly overwhelmed anyone who looked upon it more closely.

Only on the north, where the mountain declined, was there one approach to the city, though it was open only by a steep ascent. Josephus blocked this with a wall and fortified it with defenders, so that a dangerous [Note: [Col. 2079D] Breach. ID.] assault would face the besiegers between the lower wall and the upper city, while anyone looking upward would have an immeasurable view of the heights.

The city itself was situated on the brow of the mountain and was surrounded on all sides by the neighboring mountains, enclosed as if by a natural rampart and hidden behind a native barrier, so that no one could realize that a city was there until he had entered the city itself.

## CHAPTER X

Since Vespasian could not overcome nature, he summoned it to his own aid, intending by a prolonged siege to compel the besieged to surrender through shortage of food and drink. But a supply of grain, stored up long beforehand, warded off the danger of famine.

Water was in extremely short supply, because there was no spring in the city, and the customary dryness of the region, together with its infrequent rains, had reduced the available supply for drinking. He had blocked all the channels by which water could flow into the city. Scarcity increased their thirst, while nature resisted their efforts.

Josephus devised a stratagem: garments soaked with water were hung over the wall, so that, as the water slowly dripped and ran down, the Romans would believe that the inhabitants did not lack for drinking water what they possessed in abundance for washing their clothes.

## CHAPTER XI

Defeated in this attempt, Vespasian was again roused to capture the city and gathered his entire army around it. With siege engines he battered the wall; the battering ram pounded it.

This name was given to the machine because the head of a strong, knotty tree was sheathed in iron and projected like a ram’s forehead, which bulges and protrudes beneath its covering plates. From its middle extended something like a horn made of solid iron. The tree was as large as a ship’s mast, which neither a storm’s blast nor the curve of sails could bend.

Suspended by ropes fastened to the upper and strongest parts of trees, it was driven forcefully against the wall by the hands of many men. Then, drawn backward and supported by restraining ropes like a balance beam, it was directed forward with greater force, so that the side of the wall, weakened by repeated blows, might yield and, hollowed out by the impact, give the breach [Note: [Col. 2079D] To those about to break through. ID.] through which the Romans could gain a way into the interior of the city.

At the first blow the wall was shaken, and the whole city trembled. Immediately there arose a clamor from everyone, as though those terrified by the city’s imminent capture feared that the wall, struck by the rebound, would collapse.

But Josephus ordered sacks filled with straw to be thrown down into the place where the Roman ram was being hurled, so that the loose folds of the sacks would absorb and soften the entire force of the ram’s blow. When solid objects strike solid objects, they cause harm; against softer substances, their force is dissipated. In general, solid things yield more easily to soft ones than soft things to solid ones.

Thus rocks are worn away by the washing of water, while the collapse of a cliff does no harm to water. When masses are thrown into the sea, the water retains its customary function; but rock cannot retain its own amid the waves. Nor does the fall of marble shatter sand, whereas the fall of sand breaks marble into fragments.

The Romans, however, devised a countermeasure to defeat the Jews’ stratagem: they fastened hooks to the ram, with which they could cut the lowered sacks, since once the straw had been emptied they would no longer be able to avoid the ram’s blows.

When the machine’s assault had been restored and the Jews saw themselves under pressure, one of them, Eleazar, lifting a huge stone from the wall, hurled it upon the ram with such force that he shattered the head of the machine. He also leapt into the midst of the enemy, seized the stone, and carried it fearlessly back to the wall in full view of his adversaries, exposing himself to their weapons.

Finally, he was struck by five javelins; but he did not turn his attention to his wounds. Rather, he watched how he might envelop the enemy in the collapse of the stone. He climbed the wall and stood there, victor over pain, conspicuous for such audacity; then he threw himself and the stone down upon the ram, and fell with it.

Defeated by death but victorious over the machine, he [Note: [Col. 2079D] Perhaps one should read: “he alone had departed.” BARR.] died alone for his homeland, while by destroying the machine he saved the whole city from destruction.

Netyras and Philippus also threw themselves into the midst of the enemy ranks to drive back those whom they [Note: [Col. 2080D] Were able to drive back. ID.] had attacked. Josephus, however, set fire to the machines and soon destroyed many of them, but those that were destroyed were replaced.

## CHAPTER XII

Vespasian pressed on and attacked so fiercely that he was struck in the heel by an arrow. The Romans were thrown into confusion when they saw the blood flowing from their commander. His son, distraught, ran to his father. But Vespasian, displaying courage of spirit greater than the violence of the wound, prevented his son from panicking and instead incited the soldiers more fiercely to battle, so that they might avenge the injury to their commander.

He himself, acting as standard-bearer, recalled the army and drove it toward the walls. He himself urged the others into battle. Some pressed the enemy with arrows, others with spears, others with ballistae.

The force of this engine, by which stones were hurled against the enemy, was so great that one of Josephus’s allies who was standing nearby was struck and fell with his skull shattered; the back of his head was thrown as far as a third stadium [Note: [Col. 2080D] Beyond. Immediately afterward: “womb.” ID.]. A pregnant woman was also struck in the abdomen, and the infant was expelled from its hidden generative seat to a distance of more than half a stadium.

At last, when the Roman soldier had already gained the wall and a fierce struggle was taking place on both sides at the very entrance, Josephus ordered boiling oil to be poured over the Romans while they were locked together. It flowed easily from the crown of the head down to the feet. The heat of the oil consumed all their limbs no less than the blaze of a burning fire.

Others continued to advance, and for many even the profuse sweat flowing from them cooled the force of the oil. Although oil is naturally quick to heat but slow to release the heat it has acquired, they concealed their suffering out of zeal for victory. Their spirits burned so fiercely that they did not feel the fire consuming their bodies; nor did they value the pain of the burning punishment as highly as the loss of glory, if they should abandon the battle as men excluded from triumphs—men who had been leaders in dangers.

They even contended to extinguish the burning oil with their own blood.

## CHAPTER XIII

During this delay in the siege, the people of the nearby city of Japhia had also grown insolent, since the conflict was continuing for so long. Therefore Vespasian, angered by this, sent Trajan, who commanded the fifteenth unit, in the capacity of leader, with one thousand cavalry and two thousand infantry.

Trajan set out without hesitation. A vigorous man, skilled in the arts of war, he found an outcome corresponding to his eagerness for battle. The city was protected both by the nature of the site and by a double surrounding wall. Yet its people, unwilling to rely solely on their fortifications, thought that they should meet the Romans in the open.

After daring to resist for a short time, they wished to withdraw within the outer wall, but they brought the enemy in with them. For as the inhabitants rushed inside, the Romans entered alongside them. When the inhabitants fled toward the inner wall, the gates were closed so that the Romans could not burst in again with them.

Thus the Jews fought with God’s aid turned away from them, though previously they had usually conquered by it. But they had offended by their wicked crimes, and therefore the punishment they deserved was being exacted from them, so that their punishments might be given over to the nations.

In the end, more of them were crushed in wars among their own people than by the enemy. The people of Japhia provide an example: they opened the gates to the Romans and closed them against themselves. When the Romans first burst through the outer wall, the Jews themselves opened it; so that the Jews could not pass through the second wall, the Jews themselves closed it.

The enemy was therefore admitted, while their compatriots were shut out. The former was admitted so that an executioner might not be lacking; the latter was excluded so that [Note: [Col. 2081D] He who was about to perish. ID.] he might not escape altogether.

The Jews were therefore slaughtered between the two walls, some at close quarters by hand, others from a distance down from the wall. Many Roman soldiers, hemmed in by the narrow passages, climbed the wall and from there hurled weapons at those below.

The Galileans, more hostile to their own people than to the enemy, begged to be received at the entrance of the inner wall, but their own people resisted them. Fighting took place at the threshold of the gate, with Jews battling among themselves: some received the advancing wedge with their swords, while others died as they resisted.

They cursed one another savagely and declared in their last cries that they were suffering less than their crimes deserved. Thus twelve thousand men [Note: [Col. 2081D] Twelve thousand; Josephus, Book III, chapter 11. ID.] in all who had taken part in the fighting were killed.

Trajan, thinking either that no one would now resist him or that the city would easily be captured, a veteran soldier of discipline, reserved the final victory for Vespasian. He sent to him, requesting that he dispatch his son Titus to bring the battle to an end.

When Titus approached, an assault was launched, and many people were killed; yet victory came to the Romans only with difficulty and danger. Once they had entered the inner wall, all who were fit for battle and had been placed in the narrow passages opposed themselves to them [Note: [Col. 2081D] They placed themselves in the way. ID.]. They made the battle uncertain for the victors, with men and women fighting down upon them from above, and often hurling stones and every kind of weapon that happened to be at hand even at their own people.

For six hours they fought at the very end as though from the beginning. At last, after those who had stood ready to fight had been killed, the others were attacked without order, measure, or mercy. Old men were slaughtered with young men; women with their little children were spared—not for pardon, but for slavery. All the males were killed except those whom childhood or infancy protected.

Two thousand one hundred and thirty slaves were carried away as spoil, masters and servants [Note: [Col. 2081D] Reduced to equality. ID.] now equal in condition, because captivity had made them alike.

## CHAPTER XIV

Nor were the Samaritans exempt from misery. For when, according to their custom, they had [Note: [Col. 2082D] Gone up in a gathered body. ID.] gone up to Mount Gerizim, which had been consecrated to them and where they were accustomed to worship—for this reason the Samaritan woman also says in the Gospel, “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain” [Col. 2082B]—she received the answer: “The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” (I John IV, 20–21).

It was necessary that superstition should cease and true religion take its place; that the shadow should be emptied of meaning and the truth should come. Thus no longer on a mountain, as the Samaritans did; nor in Jerusalem three times a year, as the Jews did; but in spirit, in every place, every human being would worship God with pure hands lifted up and bend the knee in the name of Jesus.

When, therefore, as we have said above, they had gathered on the mountain and remained there according to their rites, the appearance of their assembly—or the attitude of those who had not learned from the misfortunes of their neighbors—seemed to display the threat of war. They were even more strongly stirred by envy at the Romans’ increasingly successful progress, and matters were close to an uprising.

It was therefore judged wiser to forestall them, lest they break out into a greater disaster. Vespasian summoned the prefect of the fifth unit and sent him there with three thousand men of both branches of the army [Col. 2082C] [Note: [Col. 2082D] This pronoun is absent from the manuscript codex. BARR.]. But the prefect—his name was Cerealis—thought it dangerous at the outset to ascend the mountain, since a large crowd of people was simultaneously joined to the terror of the situation and to the steepness of the terrain.

He surrounded the approaches to the mountain with his army and throughout the day had guards posted so that no one could come down for water. When thirst afflicted so great a multitude of people, growing more and more intense in the heat, and many preferred to surrender themselves either to slavery or even to death rather than perish from hunger or thirst, Cerealis judged that all those who were descending were exhausted.

He surrounded the mountain and, in military fashion, promised safety if they laid down their arms; those who refused he ordered to be struck down. Thus eleven thousand six hundred men were killed there.

## CHAPTER XV

On the forty-eighth day at Jotapata, an assault was made at first light, while the inhabitants were still resting, exhausted by the heavy labor of the previous day. Titus, entering first of all with Sabinus, opened the way for the others.

After the higher positions had been seized, the inhabitants were struck down throughout the narrow streets, still unaware that the assault had taken place. Some were killed in their beds, others after being awakened, and others while still keeping watch but weakened by hunger and sleep. Yet the full force of the disaster still remained hidden from the entire city.

But when the army entered with a military roar, they rose up, almost all possessed by the feeling that they must face death. Those who attempted to reach the higher ground were driven back and killed; those who might have possessed the strength to avenge themselves had their opportunity for vengeance taken away by the confinement of the place; and those who were preparing to resist the attackers were concealed by others rushing upon them from above.

Others, exhausted by prolonged struggle, offered themselves to the wound with lowered hands, so that death might rescue them from the spectacle of such savage disasters.

Deceived by this apparent security among the dying, the centurion Antonius was asked by a man who had taken refuge in a cave to give him his right hand as a pledge and guarantee of pardon and safety. He immediately extended it, heedless of deceit—and, wretched man, excessively confident of triumph. But the other struck him while he was off guard with a dagger and immediately pierced him, so that the Romans’ victory would not be entirely bloodless.

On that very day all who were found were killed. In the following days, people were also dragged out of underground chambers and other buried caves, or were killed where they lay, except for children and women.

Forty thousand were killed, as the total was reckoned; one thousand two hundred were led away into captivity. The city was overthrown and burned with fire, together with all its forts, in the thirteenth year of Nero’s reign.

Meanwhile Josephus was hiding among the ashes of the city in a certain cistern, well aware that, as the leader of the opposing army, he would be sought with special determination. On the second day he came out, but when he saw that everything was surrounded, he returned to the cistern.

On the third day a woman was found who, knowing Josephus’s hiding place, revealed it to those who were searching. Forty men [Note: [Col. 2083D] Forty-two men. ID.] were hiding in the cistern with him. When they saw Josephus first being summoned by Paulinus and Gallicanus, sent by Vespasian to offer him hope of safety, and afterward by Nicanor—who was connected with Josephus by an old friendship and had therefore been sent to extend his right hand, carrying out the duty entrusted to him with particular readiness—they surrounded Josephus and addressed him in words such as these:

## CHAPTER XVI

“Now the ruin of the Jewish name is being tested in its fullest measure; now an even darker ash is at hand to bury and conceal the teaching of a most illustrious lineage and to overthrow all its glory, since Josephus is ordered to be kept alive as a captive for the triumph.

“What do these sudden, persistent entreaties of the enemy mean? What do these voluntary gifts of safety mean? They spared no one else who begged for life. Josephus is summoned; Josephus is begged to live. Clearly they fear losing the spectacle of their triumph; they fear that there will be no one for Rome to watch as a captive, no one whom Vespasian can lead in chains before his chariot.

“Are you being preserved for these mockeries? And from whom will they triumph if their commander is absent from those over whom they triumph? Or what sort of triumph is it if friendship is granted to the defeated?

“Do not believe them, Josephus. Life is being promised you, but things worse than death are being prepared. Roman arms have conquered you; let deception not capture you. Their gifts are more atrocious than their wounds. The former threaten captivity; the latter preserve freedom.

“You are yielding, Josephus, and, broken by a certain softness of spirit, wish to survive your homeland? Where is the teaching of Moses, who asked to be erased from the heavenly book rather than outlive the people of the Lord? Where is Aaron, who stood between the living and the dead so that death might not consume the living people with savage contagion [Note: [Col. 2083D] Consume. ID.]?

“Where is the devoted spirit of King Saul and Jonathan toward their homeland—that death undertaken for their fellow citizens and bravely and gloriously sought? The son invited his father by his example, and the father did not abandon his son in his resolve to die. Though he could have lived, he preferred to be killed rather than be led in triumph by the enemy. [Col. 2084A]

“He urged his armor-bearer, saying: ‘Strike me, lest these uncircumcised men come and strike me and mock me’ (1 Samuel 31:4). Because the armor-bearer was afraid, Saul pierced himself with his own sword.

“He was worthy for David to vindicate him in prophetic spirit, since a degenerate Amalekite had falsely boasted of his death and thought that the glory of the man who had removed himself from the enemy ought to be diminished by claiming that he had killed him.

“He was also worthy for so great a prophet to praise him, saying: ‘Saul and Jonathan, beautiful and beloved, inseparable in life, and in death they were not divided; swifter than eagles, stronger than lions’ (2 Samuel 1:23).

“David himself, when he saw the people being struck by the angel, wished the heavenly vengeance to be diverted onto himself, so that he would not be spared while the people perished.

“Finally, where is the divine law, whose interpreter you have always been, which promised the righteous perpetual immortality in place of this brief life? Where is the God of the Hebrews, who teaches the righteous to hold death in contempt? He teaches them also to flee their earthly dwelling, [Note: [Col. 2083D] To fly back. Shortly afterward, the reading is ‘consecrated’ for ‘preserved.’ [Col. 2084D] BARR.] to yearn for the heights, for the region of paradise, where God himself has preserved pious souls.

“Only now, Josephus, do you desire to live, when you ought not—indeed, when you are not permitted to—indeed, what is more, when it is not fitting? And you desire, I dare say, to grasp that light [Note: [Col. 2084D] To seize. ID.] of slavery, which is in another’s power, so that the Roman may take it away whenever he wishes and cover you with the darkness of prison whenever he chooses; so that you may desire to flee from here but may not be permitted to die.

“With what shame will you go to those whom you persuaded to die for their homeland? What excuse will you have for having remained so long? They are waiting to see what you will do. They will surely say: ‘Why does Josephus delay, when he ought to have gone before us? Why does he follow so late? Why does he refuse to imitate his disciples, whom he urged to die for freedom?’

“Certainly we shall have to endure the fact that you, the defender of the law and of freedom, chose slavery; that you sold yourself as a slave to the Romans; that you preferred captivity to freedom.

“But suppose that you wish to live. How will you obtain this from those against whom you have fought so many times? How will they look upon you? With what eyes? With what feelings? How will you wish to live among angry masters, even if you are permitted to?

“Who will not believe that the traitor to his homeland was the man whom he sees receiving payment for his treachery? Choose which you prefer; one of the two must be the case. Your life will either be the reward of treachery or the punishment of slavery.”

With these words they brandished their swords, adding: “If you consent to die, we offer you the service of friends; if you refuse, we shall exact vengeance from you as from a traitor.”

## CHAPTER XVII
To this Josephus replies:

“And who would wish to survive so great a death? Who would choose to become the heir of suffering? Who would not wish, if it were permitted, to release his soul from the very body of death? But it is not permitted to release it except to him who bound it. The soul is joined to the body by the bond of nature. And who is the author of nature except almighty God? Who would dare to interrupt and separate this lodging of our soul and body, which is pleasing to God?
