If someone were to remove with his own hands the bonds imposed by the command of a master, without the will of his lord, would he not be condemned as having inflicted a grave injury upon his master? We are God’s possession; we owe God our service. Like servants, let us await his commands; like prisoners, let us preserve our bonds; like faithful stewards, let us guard the good deposit entrusted to us.

“Let us not refuse the gift of this life which he gave us; let us not reject the heavenly gift. If you reject what a human being has given you, you are insulting; how much more ought we to preserve what we have received from our God? From him, therefore, we have received the fact that we exist; it ought also to belong to him that we exist as long as he wills. For both are acts of ingratitude: to depart sooner than he wills, and to live longer than he himself, who gave life, wishes.

“Did Abraham hasten to depart beforehand? Did Moses ascend Abarim before he was told, ‘Ascend Mount Abarim’ (Deut. 32:49)? But he was told, ‘Ascend’; and he ascended, and he died—like a good little servant, he awaited his Lord’s command. Job himself, who said, ‘Let the day perish on which I was born’ (Job 3:3), nevertheless, though placed amid wounds and pains, did not break the bonds of this life; rather, he asked to be released, saying, ‘Why was light given to those in bitterness, and life to those whose soul is in pain?’ (ibid., 20). Thus he praised death when he said, ‘Death is indeed rest’ (Job 17:16), yet he did not seize it in advance; he asked for it, as it is written: ‘I am shaken in all my limbs; and since I am impious, why am I not dead? Why did I not fall from my mother’s womb directly into the grave? Or is not the time of my life short? Leave me to rest a little while’ (Job 10:18–20).[¹] [Note: Col. 2085D: “For man.” ID.]

“Another holy man also says, ‘Bring my soul out of prison’ (Ps. 141:8). He asks to escape; he asks to be released from this body as from a certain prison. Yet none of the saints takes death for himself; none anticipates it. If it is a gain to die, it is theft to seize death before it is expected. If it is good to live, it is sacrilege to reject life before it is reclaimed.[²] [Note: Col. 2085D: “Sacrilegious.” ID.]

“But do you think it glorious to die in war? Nor do I deny that it is good to die in war for one’s country, good for one’s fellow citizens. But under the law of war I offer my throat if the enemy demands it—if the Romans strike, the Romans to whom God has given victory over us, to whom he has handed us over because of our sins. Nor do I flatter myself with the promise that they will spare me. Would that they deceive me! Either I shall gain this much—that they feared me so greatly that they deceived me—or I shall obtain this revenge, because they break faith. I would rather perish through their brigandage than through my own. It is my brigandage if I lay hands upon myself; if the enemy does so, it is a benefit.

“Thus, when they could have granted that benefit by killing me, they decided to preserve what lay in their power, so that they might kill a captive: they committed brigandage. But you promise me the service of your hands. In truth, we have lacked an executioner, so that we might perish by our own crime. I do not wish to perish by my crime; I do not wish to perish by yours, which is worse than mine; I do not wish us to perish by a mutual crime. For this is what it means for each of us to lay hands upon himself: to pay the price of another’s death, so that each may now be guilty not only for his own blood but also for that of another.

“Yet the example of King Saul is brought forward—certainly of one who had been demanded as king against the divine will and had incurred God’s displeasure. Hence, while he was still alive, he was given a successor. An outstanding example is offered of a man who lacked God’s grace and yet wished to die because he could no longer live. He himself wished his companion to kill him; but the other considered it a crime and refused the service. Thus, not having acted on counsel but being denied the service, Saul turned the sword upon himself. If he did it out of fear that he might be mocked, why do you praise what arose from fear? If he was not afraid, why did he first choose another course? I fear neither Romans who mock nor Romans who lie. Saul alone killed himself; neither Jonathan nor anyone else in our Scriptures did so.

“What is surprising if he could kill himself, when he could even kill his son? Aaron stood between the living and the dead; and this was an act of courage, not recklessness. He did not bring death upon himself, but he did not fear death: he repelled it with his own body and stood in the way of the serpent [Note: [Col. 2086D] ‘Against all.’ ID.]. I am not Aaron, certainly, but I am nevertheless not degenerate from him. I offer my hands; let them strike as they wish. If I can fear their hands, I deserve to perish by my own hands. If they perish at the hands of an adversary, why should I not perish at my own? If you ask why they wish to spare me, it is because they admire courage even in an enemy. So great is the appeal of courage that it often delights even an enemy.

“You yourselves know how much destruction I inflicted upon the Romans, and how, though they were conquerors of all nations, I diverted them from the destruction of Jerusalem by the prolonged siege of the insignificant city of Jotapata. I gambled with the fate of the entire war at the cost of a brief loss. Others learned, through my danger, to desire peace. Perhaps I am being kept alive for this purpose: not so that the others may be deterred, but so that they may be provoked.

“But you assert that it is sweet to die for freedom. Who denies that? Yet it is also sweet to live for freedom. For the one who offers friendship promises freedom. But if he imposes slavery, then certainly the desire to die will be more timely, if death is required. For now they offer life; they do not wish to kill. A coward is both the man who does not wish to die when it is necessary and the man who wishes to die when it is not necessary. For who does not know that it is womanly fear—and feminine courage—to wish to die in order not to die?[³] [Note: Col. 2087D: “Of fear.” BARR.] In the end, timid women, whenever they learn that some danger threatens them, are accustomed to throw themselves from a height. For they cannot bear the burden of fear and the dread of death in their narrow minds.

“But a man who is steadfast, who does not fear the present and considers the future, does not know how to tremble where there is no fear. Thus it is written, ‘The souls of the effeminate shall hunger’ (Prov. 18:8)—that is, because they lack the food of courage, they hunger; and therefore they hasten to death before the proper time. For one who is filled with the food of spiritual grace does not lay hands upon himself, since it is written, ‘The mouth of the foolish calls for death.’ And Scripture says again: ‘He who does not care for himself in his deeds is a brother to him who destroys himself’ (ibid., 9).[⁴] [Note: An old codex reads: “is a brother of one who destroys his own works.” ID.] Therefore the man who strikes himself is condemned.

“For what is so contrary to the law of nature? What is so contrary to the nature of all living creatures? Every wild and untamed animal has been endowed with a love of itself. For the law of nature is strong: to wish to live and not to take death upon oneself. Indeed, no species of living creature can arm itself with iron against itself, even if it wished to do so. Human beings invented the shapeless noose of death; wild animals do not know it. The bites of wild beasts are their weapons, their teeth are their swords. Yet who has ever heard that some wild beast removed a limb from itself with its own bite? Against others they use the weapons of their jaws; against themselves, their mouths are used for caresses.

“What is as sweet to us as life? What is as hostile as death? In the end, the one who protects life is its defender; the one who attempts to seek death is an assailant. If, then, we ourselves seek what we curse in others, we wish to inflict it upon ourselves; and what we demand from others as punishment, we inflict upon ourselves as a favor. We prosecute a helmsman if he drives the ship entrusted to him onto a rock; shall we extinguish with the sword the helm of our own body entrusted to us, and surrender ourselves to voluntary shipwreck?

“But you object that I face an early death once I have been delivered into the power of the enemy. What gain shall I make, then, if I myself inflict what I fear from the enemy, when it may happen that the enemy will not do what you urge me to do? This would be like a helmsman who, seeing a storm in the future, sank his ship into the waves in order to avoid the storm.[⁵] [Note: “To violate.” ID.] Do you think that the enemy’s harsher punishments must therefore be anticipated? Or do you think it courageous that we ourselves should use the sword against ourselves? That is a refuge of weakness, not a trophy of courage: to grasp at the gain of punishments.

“Thus we cling to this conclusion: the act possesses neither the marks of courage nor any useful advantage. What more shall I add concerning the sanctity of a violated deposit?[⁶] Almighty God gave us a most precious treasure and, enclosed and sealed within this earthen vessel, entrusted it to us to guard until it should please him himself to reclaim it. Is there not guilt in either case: in rejecting the deposit when the giver has not reclaimed it, or in refusing it when he does reclaim it? If violating a human deposit is punishable by disgrace, how much more is it to violate God’s deposit! [Note: Perhaps the preposition should be deleted, and the reading should be: “God’s deposit, the soul, is in this body.” GALLAND.]

“God’s deposit is the soul in this body—the soul which is not made subject to this death. For it is not bound and fastened by any bond of death; rather, it seems to await death when it is released from the body and separated from the lodging entrusted to it. Why, then, do we inflict death before the deposit is reclaimed, send back the soul to us as though it were useless, exclude it from our house, and dissolve the body into the earth without its dignity and grace? Why do we not await the command to depart from here?

“A soldier awaits the password; a servant awaits the command. If either leaves without orders, the one is a deserter, the other a runaway. The man who flees from a human being is liable to punishment, even if he has fled an unjust master. Can we, fleeing from the best of all masters, fail to be bound by the crime of impiety? Is it also beyond our understanding that ‘God has placed an angel around those who fear him’ (Ps. 33:8)? Is there, then, someone to prevent us unless he has received the command? If there is no command, there is no provision for the journey. And how shall we arrive without provisions for the journey? Who will receive us into that pure and secluded place? Who will admit us into the fellowship of those holy souls?

“Adam hid because he had transgressed God’s command; he was expelled from paradise because he had not kept the commandment. He is told, ‘Adam, where are you?’ (Gen. 3:9)—as to one who has fled, as to one who is not present before God. Will it not also be said to me, ‘Where are you?’—to me who have come without the command, whom I have not released from the natural bonds? ‘Take him away into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth and pain’ (Matt. 22:13).

“We have received these prohibitions not only in human customs but also in laws. Some order that those who have thrown themselves upon a sword be cast out unburied. For it is fitting that those who did not await their father’s command should be deprived, as it were, of the earth’s grave, their mother’s womb. Others cut off the right hand of the dead, so that it may be separated from the limbs of the body against which it had fought in mad fury.[⁷] [Note: “Which.” BARR.] But sacrilegious men, traitors, or murderers of their parents suffer this end—those who did not acknowledge their true father and do not recognize themselves. Therefore they are either forbidden burial altogether or are not buried whole.

“Their souls also are not received by paradise, but by the darkness of the underworld and savage punishments. As I reflect upon these things, although everything else has been taken from me, these alone terrify and cause me dread.[⁸] [Note: “That I should not [inflict them] upon myself.” ID.] I shall not inflict upon myself what even the enemy cannot inflict, nor shall I tear away from myself those things of paradise which the Roman has not yet been able to take away. Certainly he could hasten my end; he cannot take away what alone I desire impatiently.

“For no desire for this life holds me, since I have found nothing delightful in it either among my fellow citizens or among my enemies. These denied me peace; those took my country from me. Amid so many evils, what sweetness can remain in this life? You alone, almighty Father, author and ruler of nature, grant me an honorable end; you break this natural bond; restore my soul to its secluded dwelling. Let the people be destroyed, let right be taken away, let freedom be broken; nevertheless I shall not transgress your law by dying without your command. I await your order; I await your command to free me when I am willing. You have many executors of your authority: from you I await the command, from the executor the service.

“It is good to die; but I shall die as a Hebrew, not as a brigand, not as an executioner, not as an enemy. Though defeated in war, I shall nevertheless remain what I was born to be, and I shall not abandon the inheritance of Abraham my father. I shall not pass into the number of the enemy, so that I myself become my own executioner. I can offer myself to the enemy to be struck without loss of piety; I cannot turn my hands against myself without crime.[⁹] [Note: “Against myself” for “upon myself.” Another reading: “against the enemy.” BARR.] Is there truly fear that we shall not be permitted to live according to the law? In fact, there is now great freedom for those who are permitted to die according to the law.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

Josephus argued these points in order to eliminate the attraction of voluntary death.[¹⁰] [Note: “Assertion.” ID.] But those who had once devoted themselves to death, since they could not resist him with words, surrounded the man as though they were about to strike him immediately with their swords, unless he thought he ought to yield. Surrounded by them, he recalled one by the authority of a commander and the steadfastness of courage; he confronted another with a stern look. He restrained one man’s right hand, bent another’s anger, and soothed them with the salutary wisdom of his counsel. In different ways he wrested from each his irrational fury.

For although their defeat had wrested away their dignity as their final lot, it had not entirely abolished their reverence. Gradually, therefore, hands were lowered and swords were sheathed, though their purpose persisted. When he saw himself surrounded and held by the many, whether by some accident or by a plan he had devised,[¹¹] [Note: “Having devised it.” ID.] he contrived to reduce the number of those resisting him.

“Let us entrust the order of dying to chance,” he said, “so that no one may withdraw when the lot falls upon everyone. Let the condition of the lot be this: that the one who is chosen by lot shall be killed by the one who follows him. Thus the lot, not his own will, will assign each man to death. Let each man, then, stand beneath the lot as judge, free from crime and free from captivity, so that he neither hastens the death that awaits him at another’s decision nor avoids it by his own. No one will be able to reject the outcome which either chance has brought about or God’s will has marked.”

His offer secured their trust, and everyone agreed to submit to the lot. Each was designated by lot and offered himself for the death of the next man. It happened, therefore, that after the others had been killed, Josephus and one other remained to face death. It necessarily remained for him either to be condemned by the lot or, if he survived the slaughter, to be stained by his companion’s blood. He persuaded the other to abandon the agreement of the lot. Thus the internal battle came to an end, and Josephus was led by Nicanor to Vespasian.

A crowd gathered to witness his arrival, with almost all the Romans assembling. Some wished to see the fallen man whom they had recently observed placed in the highest honor and commanding the supreme enterprise; others competed in mocking the captive; others marveled at the many and shifting reversals of human affairs. Most, with greater foresight, groaned because they considered that the same things could happen to themselves in the misfortunes of others.

Titus was moved above all by his inborn gentleness of spirit: he saw the proud warrior of a little while before suddenly subjected to the power of alien enemies, awaiting the outcome of life’s shipwreck, exiled from hope, uncertain of safety. So powerful are the turns of battle that a brief accident makes men unlike themselves, when either the powerful are cast down or the afflicted are raised up.

Accordingly, the better part—namely, those who possessed authority—gave milder counsels. Yet Titus was Josephus’s principal means of safety with his father. Vespasian ordered that he be kept under guard, lest he should somehow escape.

## CHAPTER XIX

A few days later he returned to Ptolemais and from there hastened to Caesarea, the largest city of Judaea, though more densely inhabited by Gentiles. They received the Roman army there with applause and joy, not only because they desired the benefits of Roman alliance but also because of their innate hatred of the Jewish populace. With the loudest cries they demanded that Josephus, their leader, should be punished.

Vespasian dissolved the anger of the crowd, which had arisen without judgment, by silence. Since the city was suitable both for winter quarters and for the season, he established two divisions at Caesarea and the Tenth and Fifteenth legions in the city of Scythopolis, so that Caesarea would not be worn down by bearing the burden of the entire army.

The city mentioned above was consecrated to Scythian Diana, as though it had been founded by the Scythians; it was called the city of the Scythians, just as Massilia is called a city of the Greeks. The character of the place reveals the innate harshness of its founder: he chose expanses more suited to endurance than to the usefulness and comfort of habitation. For the open and rugged winter and the scorching summer season there involve more hardship than pleasure,[¹²] [Note: “For winter is open and harsh, and the season of summer scorching.” ID.] since in winter they are more exposed to the cold, while in summer the heat is more oppressive in those places, where they receive the whole sun without any charm of green farmland. Thus the level, coastal region of the city mentioned above was made still hotter by the heat of the sea.

## CHAPTER XX

Nevertheless, Vespasian was not free from military affairs. When he learned that many people from various places had gathered at the city of Joppa, that they had repaired the buildings destroyed by Cestius, and had restored the city for their own use in pirate raids—for, since the region had been devastated, they sought supplies of food from the sea—he carefully investigated everything.

They constructed vessels of the kind suitable for pirates and, watching the routes of passing ships, plundered nearly all the commerce of Phoenicia and Egypt. They caused such terror through repeated raids that they closed off that entire sea, and the use of navigation was interrupted by fear of certain danger.

When he learned this, Vespasian ordered a force of infantry and most of the cavalry to proceed to Joppa and enter it by night. This was easily done, since no guard had been placed before the city: the city’s reputation had been ruined, and it was thought unlikely to arouse any concern in the Roman commander. Nevertheless, the inhabitants were present. But they did not dare to resist or deny entry to the approaching Romans. They boarded their vessels and, advancing beyond the range of an arrow’s cast, spent the night at sea.

The circumstances seem to require a brief description of the position of the coast before Joppa, so that it may clearly be shown how the city mentioned above suffered a second disaster without any battle.[¹³] The city is naturally without a harbor. [Note: “It is harborless.” BARR.] From the seashore the coast runs straight and rugged, but at both ends it curves slightly like horns. There are deep cliffs and enormous rocks there, which project into the sea; although they rise from the bottom of the sea, they nevertheless extend outward into it. Hence, when people say that Andromeda was once exposed there with the sea monster, the shape of the place and the very appearance of things seem to give no slight credibility to the ancient stories.

When the opposing blasts of the north wind strike the shore, the waves rise to an extraordinary height. They crash against the rocks with a tremendous roar and, falling back into the waves, make that bay of the sea restless, so that there is more danger in the harbor than in the open sea.

While the boats from Joppa, which we have said were brought out from the city, were tossing there, a violent wind arose toward morning. Sailors in those waters call it the Melamborium. Immediately, as the waves drove against one another, it mingled and entangled the boats. Some, after their anchors had broken, it drove against the rocks. Others, when they were violently lifted against the opposing sea, met disaster either from the danger of the rocky shore or from the Romans who had surrounded the coast, while the sailors attempted to flee. A towering wave rose over them and overwhelmed and submerged them.

There was nowhere to flee and no hope of remaining, since the wind drove them in from the sea while the Romans excluded them from the city. The noise of the vessels was terrible as they collided with one another; the groans of the men were unbearable as the boats broke apart. When they saw the sea rushing into their unsteady hulls, some threw themselves into the water, trusting their skill in swimming; others, while leaping into boats that were approaching, fell into the sea and were crushed beneath the collision of the hulls.

Most sank into the depths together with the small vessels, the myoparones, when their confidence in swimming failed them. For those who lacked the skill—or any hope of trying—death pierced them with lesser torment. Those who attempted to swim struck the broken fragments of the ships repeatedly with convulsive blows; these battered the wretched limbs against their sides and cruelly punished them. Others, driven against the rocks, were overtaken by death even as they longed to embrace the shore, though they possessed whatever consolation there might be in having perished on land.

The spectacle was therefore pitiable: the rocks were spattered with the brains of the unfortunate, and the shores were soaked with blood. One could see the sea stained with gore and everything filled with corpses. Any who happened to escape were killed as they approached the shore. The Romans judged that the storm did not rage in those places with such violence merely because of the roughness of the location and the customary winds; rather, they thought that, by divine indignation, the winds had conspired beyond their usual manner and that the sea had been enveloped so that the Jews could not escape. For that reason they feared to spare those whom God had not spared.

Some killed themselves with the sword, judging it more bearable to perish by the sword than in a shipwreck.[¹⁴] [Note: “Some.” ID.] Others, wishing to drive the vessels away with poles, pierced them. Some, when those who had fallen into the sea called out, perhaps asking to be lifted up by the sailors, pushed them away with oars or struck them with weapons.

I have not omitted this in order to make clear that the Jewish people themselves were a greater danger to one another than the enemy was, since they killed themselves—as though all things hostile to their destruction were not already enough: sky, enemy, sea, and rocks.

The bodies of four thousand five hundred dead were counted, cast up by the sea. The city was captured without a battle and destroyed from its foundations. Thus, in a short time, the Roman hand destroyed Joppa for the second time. Vespasian therefore rightly ordered that no pirate settlements should again be established there.

For this reason he left cavalry there and, though departing thence with a smaller number of infantry, left infantry there as well, so that the infantry might remain on the spot and prevent the band of pirates, accustomed to brigandage, from attempting anything. The cavalry, meanwhile, traversed the neighboring villages and towns of the region, so that everything might be utterly destroyed and they might not conspire toward any undertakings.

## CHAPTER XXI

While these events were taking place at Joppa, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, although they lived far away, were nevertheless not free from sharing in the disaster. When they heard what had been done by the Romans in Judaea, and especially when they learned that Josephus had been killed, at first they did not believe it, because no messenger had come to them from the region. Then they thought that the commander alone could not have fallen carelessly into the hands of the enemy.

In fact, no messenger had survived such a great disaster; and this very fact—because no informant remained—strengthened the report of complete destruction, that everything had perished and that nothing remained even to give information about what had happened.[¹⁵] [Note: “And by this very fact.” Earlier, the reading is “to the disaster”; below, “flowed” is transmitted for “remained.” ID.] A report remained, greater than any account could convey: while the silence itself held them in uncertainty and terror,[¹⁶] [Note: “Terrify.” ID.] everything they feared was believed. So far was the truth from being reported that things which had not happened were also added.

Rumor even asserted that Josephus had been killed, and this caused the greatest grief to everyone. But when they discovered that he was living among the Romans, they pursued him with such hatred that they detested the life of the man whose death they had first mourned, regarding it as evidence either of cowardice or of treachery. Hence their agitation against the Romans grew greater, so that they might avenge themselves upon Josephus.

The more their cause declined, the more fiercely they were inflamed for war. Where there should have been an end, there the beginning of evils was taken up. For adverse outcomes are lessons to the wise, teaching them to be more cautious so that the things which have already gone badly may not happen again; but to the foolish they are incentives to misery. The danger of their allies ought therefore to have been a reason for sobriety to the people of Jerusalem. But because they did not wish to understand so as to act rightly, it turned into their destruction (Ps. 35:4).

## CHAPTER XXII

Vespasian, however, both to use the delay to better advantage and to let the army rest for a little while from its labor, yielded to Agrippa’s request that he spend about twenty days in Caesarea Philippi, the city of Agrippa’s kingdom. At the same time, the weakened factions might recover from the frenzy of agitation and discord, since they ought to recognize that, if they turned back, they could be received through the intervention of the king, especially because such diligent bonds of service existed between the king and the Romans.

Finally, Tiberias, which was near Caesarea, did not reject the remedy; it recovered its health. For it too was seething with the grave illness of a populace divided against itself. Accordingly, Vespasian ordered three stronger divisions to be summoned and to proceed to Scythopolis, assigning his son directly to the undertaking. Scythopolis was the largest of the ten cities and was near Tiberias.

From there he ordered Valerianus to approach the walls with fifty cavalrymen, to urge peace, and to call those shut inside to faith in the alliance, so that the terror of the assembled army might strike those who were hostile, while the messenger of peace invited those who were willing. Valerianus dismounted from his horse near the walls; those who had approached with him did the same.

Judging them contemptible because of their small number, Jesus, the leader of the band of marauders, together with his men, who had dared to advance in the same manner, drove them from their position in a sudden sortie. At the same time, they killed men and seized the horses they had brought. They were madmen who did not understand that Valerianus had more wisely yielded to their insolence than seized the spoils of those who were offering peace.

Finally, the elders, offended by the atrocity of the deed, left the city and came to Vespasian to plead that the insolence of a few should not be charged against the whole population. Vespasian immediately sent Trajan to the city to investigate whether the people opposed the rashness of the plotters.

Trajan, reporting the people’s corresponding goodwill and the pleas of the elders, strengthened the credibility of the embassy. Thus forgiveness was granted to those who asked it, especially because Vespasian saw that the king was concerned for the condition of the entire city. Since the king’s good faith had been pledged, Vespasian willingly granted pardon for the offense, trusting that they would not dare anything of the kind again.

## CHAPTER XXIII

From there he marched against Taricheae with a carefully prepared and equipped army, because a great multitude had gathered in that city owing especially to the strength of its location. Josephus had surrounded it with a wall, except on the side where the waves of Lake Gennesaret washed a place inaccessible to infantry. Therefore, with vessels assembled, they were loudly preparing for a battle whose outcome could go either way.

If the land battle turned against them, they could flee to the ships; if they yielded in a naval engagement, they could return to the city and defend themselves behind the surrounding walls.[¹⁷] [Note: Perhaps “they fell.” GALLAND.] The defenses were similar in the city of Tiberias and at Taricheae. But the spirits at Taricheae were more enterprising; the walls at Tiberias were stronger.[¹⁸] [Note: “More experienced … wall.” BARR.] The fury of the people of Taricheae was also more ready, so that, if necessary, they would mingle everything together—naval battles with land battles, and land battles with naval warfare.

Finally, when they were surrounded and faced the opposing line, they dared more than their strength allowed. Yet their recklessness achieved nothing against the discipline of the Roman deployment or the courage of the veteran army. Before they suffered any destruction, they turned to flight and rushed to their ships.

Once gathered together, they fought as though in a dense battle line, as if the action were taking place on land. An innumerable multitude was also waiting for the enemy on the plain. When Vespasian learned this, he sent his son with picked cavalrymen. When Titus saw himself surrounded by immense forces, he reported to his father that the number of the enemy was greater than had been supposed. But he summoned those whom he had brought with him and infused them with a stimulus for battle by addressing them as follows:

## CHAPTER XXIV
Men, he said, it is fitting that, as you fight, you remember your Roman name and lineage—men whose hands no one who exists anywhere in the Roman world has escaped. For where did you bestow this name upon all the lands except by conquering? You must also remember the place in which you now stand and against whom you wage Roman war. For we are positioned at the very edge of the world. Yet, having traversed such vast stretches of land, you have seen nothing foreign. [Col. 2094C] For what is foreign to you, whose possession is the whole world? Whatever exists anywhere is your right; whatever the dwelling-place of all peoples contains is your possession.

[Note: “You were running well: who set in motion your triumphs, running throughout the whole world? Those whom Hasdrubal the Carthaginian did not set in motion [Col. 2094D] . . . . . these rebellious Judaea set in motion.” I would judge that this should indeed be read and punctuated in this way. GALLAND.]

He was running well who set in motion your triumphs, running throughout the whole world—triumphs which neither Hasdrubal the Carthaginian, nor Pyrrhus the Aeacid, nor Brennus leaning against the thresholds of the Capitol, nor the Persian hordes, nor the Egyptian phalanxes could set in motion. These were set in motion by rebellious Judaea, displaying an uneducated recklessness in warfare, more suited to quarrelling than to battle. Nor is there anything I fear in this; rather, I regard it as full of shame that you are exhausted by conquering. They, however, whenever they are defeated, have taken courage—[Note: “To become exhausted.” BARR.] you have been wearied by success, while they are made more stubborn by adversity.

Raise your spirits, therefore, Roman men, and, relying upon your ancestral valor, rise up against the enemy hordes. Nor should the number of the Jewish populace move you, since they are not deterred by so many tokens of your valor, which are far stronger than numbers. For among the Hebrews there is neither knowledge of military affairs, nor skill in battle, nor talent for command; no experience of discipline, no endurance for hardship. They bring into battle only contempt for death. Yet no one has ever defeated an enemy by dying, but by killing him.

They know weapons only in war; we train with weapons in peacetime, so that in war we may not experience the uncertain chances of battle. For outcomes are uncertain to the inexperienced; for veterans, [Col. 2095A] triumph is customary. What else do we do every day except ensure that battles are never unfamiliar to us? Each man trains at home as though in battle, so that in battle his practice may be a kind of rehearsal for combat. In short, no one would be wrong to assert that our exercises are wars without bloodshed, and our wars are exercises.

We advance into war fortified: the helmet shields the head on every side, the breastplate the chest, and the shield the whole body. Wherever the enemy may strike a Roman soldier, he cannot find an opening, since he sees him enclosed in iron. Such weapons are a burden to others, but to us they are a covering, because use makes them lighter. Our battle, then, is against unarmed and naked men.

Or are we afraid that we might be surrounded by numbers? First, cavalry is free in battle, and by retreating and pursuing [Note: “Battle.” BARR.] it rehearses the war. It circles even the largest battle-lines and withdraws across whatever distances it pleases. Then, in the actual infantry engagement, it is not so much the number of the many that decides the battle as the valor of the few. A multitude unaccustomed to discipline is itself an impediment: in prosperity, to victory; in adversity, to flight. Valor, however, endures and grows strong amid success, nor does it collapse entirely in adversity.

Moreover, habit of victory serves as an incentive for us to fight. Even if they fight for their country and children, that does not mean that they ought to be more ready than we are. For it is no less—indeed, I scarcely know whether it is not even more—for us to contend on behalf of ourselves than on behalf of our own people. We fight for ourselves, and when we fight for glory, we fight lest we prove less than what we are. Who, then, would doubt that it is more important to contend for glory than for safety?

For us, however, this war concerns the danger to our reputation, [Col. 2095C] lest the right we have won should perish. We also run the risk—conquerors of nations and masters of the world—of appearing equal to the Jews, whom we have set against ourselves as though they were our equals [Note: “As adversaries.” ID.], if we engage them only with an equal number. Our ancestors often routed great forces of the enemy with a small band. And what benefit do our daily exercises bring us? What benefit does long labor bring, if we come to battle as their equals?

We did indeed report their number to our father, because nothing else was permitted; but let him understand that we did not fear the danger, but reserved deference for the arbiter of war. We may anticipate the battle, hold the enemy, and seize victory while the reinforcements are arriving, lest those who come boast that the enemy was overcome less by our united strength than that we were protected by their valor.

With what face, then, shall we appear before our father if we have feared to begin the battle? With what shame shall I, a degenerate son, meet the eyes of so great a man—one who knows how to see his soldier only as a victor? How shall I prove myself his soldier and his son, when he has always been a triumphant commander, while I, defeated even in my own judgment—which is more grievous—have yielded to a Jewish enemy? What will happen to you when your commander is condemned—the commander whom your father, secure in his trust, has entrusted to you?

But I would rather have you give reasons concerning the commander’s valor than concerning cowardice. Let us therefore rush against the enemy; let us hurry, [Note: “Let us anticipate them.” ID.] let us crush [Col. 2096A] the enemy. I shall be the first to run into danger; follow me, so that you may guard the trust of our father and preserve what our father has committed to you. I do not demand companions in danger, but partners in victory.

Yet beware lest you seem to have reserved for others the palm of triumph offered to you, and to have snatched it away from yourselves. Certainly, if matters turn out otherwise, I would rather my father recognize me as his son by my wounds, if he does not recognize me in his soldiers.

Let us nevertheless suppose that our father is offended by our undertaking the battle. What, then, is more tolerable: to snatch victory away, or to abandon it? In snatching it away, haste is a mark of courage; in abandoning it, there is the guilt of cowardice. Let our father certainly condemn us as victors; I do not shrink from such a charge. I would rather be guilty while the state triumphs than innocent while it is harmed.

If only I might imitate Manlius Torquatus’ son, at least in the danger alone: his father ordered him to be struck down by the executioner, even though he was safe, because he had led the army against the enemy contrary to his father’s command. The young man stood amid the slain enemies, clothed in the triumphal decorations, secure beneath the executioner’s sword, because he considered it supremely blessed to die in victory. What could be more glorious than to end one’s life in triumph, rather than be preserved for the uncertain chances of affairs after a certain victory?

O crime of victory, to be desired by the wise! Would that we, too, might be charged with having won. Certainly, following that example, I alone shall be in danger, while you will triumph. And yet our father did not forbid us to fight; rather, he ordered us—those whom he sent to battle—to do so. Hence I judge that he will be more indignant if we yield to the Jews when we could have conquered than if we have fought.

## CHAPTER XXV

Having said this, he drove his horse first against the enemy, and the others followed with a great shout. They spread across the entire field, and for that reason seemed more numerous. Trajanus, too, sent by Vespasian with three hundred cavalrymen, arrived while Titus was already advancing.

The Jews could not resist for long, as they were thrown into confusion by the spears of the men and the neighing of the horses. Accordingly, some turned in different directions, while most made for the city. Titus sprang forward: he overtook some who were fleeing behind him and struck them down; he drove the scattered mass back from the walls by taking the route ahead of them, and, meeting those who were running back, cut off their flight.

Again some were struck down, while others escaped because the city provided them refuge; but [Note: “There too.” ID.] the battle was fiercer for those men as well. For those who had streamed in from the neighboring districts had initially preferred peace, but the arriving populace [Note: “It seems that *invitis* should be read.” GALLAND.] had extorted from them a desire for war against their will.

From this arose dissension and grave tumult within the city. Roused by the uproar, Titus turned to his soldiers:

“This is the moment, my most revered comrades, that I have been awaiting [Note: “That I was expecting.” BARR.]. The enemy are sowing tumult among themselves within the city; outside they are being slaughtered, inside they are fighting one another. Let us therefore hurry while they are still divided, lest perhaps, through fear of danger, they reconcile.”

He then mounted the horse from which he had dismounted, near the walls. Turning toward the lake, he made for the city across the water, and was the first to burst into it, followed afterward by the others [Note: “And the rest after him.” BARR.]. Immediately all who were inside scattered in flight: some were struck down, while others, climbing into boats, were drowned in the lake. Many people were killed inside.

Certainly, those who came from the countryside presented themselves to the Romans, asserting that they were free of guilt; Titus, in pious moderation, judged that they should be spared, pressing only the authors of the rebellion. He therefore sent a horseman to his father to announce the outcome of the victory.

Vespasian was delighted, especially by his son’s triumph, since Titus had accomplished the greatest part of the entire war being waged against Judaea. He hastened there and ordered the city to be watched more carefully, so that no one might escape, since all were liable to punishment. On the following day, however, on account of those who had taken refuge in small boats, he ordered rafts to be made. They were constructed without delay, since the neighboring forests and the large number of workmen made it possible to hasten the task.

## CHAPTER XXVI

The lake itself, like a broad bay enclosed by a kind of sea, extends for one hundred and forty stadia in length and spreads for forty in breadth, raising a breeze from its own waters as they ripple. Hence it is also called Gennesar, a Greek name meaning, as it were, “producing a breeze for itself.” Its water is fresh and suitable for drinking. It contains nothing thick or muddy from marshy wetness, since it is surrounded on every side by a sandy shore and is milder than the chill of a river or spring.

It is nevertheless colder than the surface of a tranquil marsh, precisely because the water does not lie spread out like a pool, but is more frequently stirred across the lake’s broader expanses by blowing breezes. Hence its draught is purer and gentler for drinking. If anyone wished to add human effort to nature’s gift, so that in summer he might suspend it and expose it to the night breezes, as the inhabitants do, he should judge it to be in no way inferior to snow for drinking.

Its kinds of fish are also superior to those elsewhere in taste and appearance.

The subject seems to require that we disclose the source of the Jordan, which we promised elsewhere [Note: “Clearly, Book I, chapter 35.” ID.]. For there had been doubt among earlier generations whether the river called the Jordan arose from Lake Gennesar. Philip, tetrarch of the region of Trachonitis, refuted this false belief and dispelled the error by throwing straw into Phiala, which the river boiled up at Panium. From this it is clear that the Jordan does not begin at Panium, but that its stream merely emerges there.

For its spring is not there, so that it began from that place in the manner of other rivers. Rather, it is conducted underground from Phiala in Trachonitis through subterranean channels, and there it again bursts forth like a spring, emerging and revealing itself. Phiala is in the land of Trachonitis, one hundred and twenty stadia distant from Caesarea.

The name Phiala was given by its appearance [Note: “Its form.” ID.], as though it expressed the shape of a wheel, because it is perpetually full of water, so that it is understood neither to overflow nor to diminish through any diversion. The water therefore flows downward according to a certain measure, and, when it reaches Panium, boils up again, as was demonstrated when the straw reappeared.

Thus the Jordan was revealed to rise again there, where men of earlier times had believed that it was born. Yet from the beginning Panium did not possess the same features, except for its natural beauty. The munificence of King Agrippa adorned the place with a more abundant and splendid approach. We are told that a cave, through which the Jordan raises itself, was built and embellished with astonishing beauty.

Hence it now begins not hidden or concealed through the hollow passages of the earth, but as a visible and open river flowing over the land. It pours into Lake Semechonitis and cuts through its marshes. From there, directing its course onward, it advances one hundred and twenty stadia without any intervening stream as far as the city called Julias. Afterwards it passes through the middle of the lake called Gennesar; then, wandering through extensive deserts, it is received by Lake Asphaltites and disappears into it.

Thus, after victoriously passing through two lakes, it comes to a halt in the third.

The region of Gennesar extends along the lake of the same name, from which it also took its name, possessing wonderful natural gifts and beauty. The fertility of the soil supplies spontaneous fruits, and the land, rich in woodland, naturally produces every kind of growth. By imitating nature through the skill of cultivation, it has bent its abundant fertility toward whatever uses it wished, so that there is nothing there which nature has denied, and nothing which cultivation has neglected. It is suited to everything and never foreign to any fruit.

Its climate is so temperate that it accommodates the diversity of all things that grow. There you may see both those nourished by cold spreading forth in abundance and those fostered by heat. There summer produce is mingled with winter produce at the same time: northern nuts and dates, which are known to grow only in hotter places [Col. 2098C]. Why should I speak of figs or apples, which a milder region of the sky nourishes? Yet they do not equal those earlier fruits. The former are the chief fruits of Palestine, and indeed cultivated fruits, and therefore more abundant; the latter are comparable, and, although far apart, you might call them close neighbors [Note: “It seems that *proximis* should be read.” ID.], engaged in a delightful rivalry between nature and the seasons.

The former, like a fertile mother, creates everything; the temperateness of the latter, like a good nurse, raises all things with gentle nourishment. Thus not only are varieties of fruit produced in abundance, but they are also preserved, so that some kinds do not fail for most of the year, while all the rest remain throughout the entire year until its end.

For grapes and figs that grow on grafted trees—fruits of a certain royal abundance—overflow for ten months without any failure. The remaining fruits of the branches, whether the violence of the countryside has protected them by their own natural means or human skill has produced them, do not know how to withdraw from their service, except when new fruits succeed them.

To this fertility of nature and temperateness of the air there is added the gift of a spring, which waters the aforesaid region with a kind of generative irrigation. It is called Capernaum. Some have not unreasonably judged it to be a branch of the Nile, not only because its irrigated fields are fertile, but also because it produces a fish such that one might think it the coracinus found in the lake at Alexandria from the influx of the Nile. The place, too, is named after the lake.

It extends thirty stadia in length and twenty in breadth.

Since we have spoken of the nature of the place, let us return to the completion of the battle. Having prepared the rafts according to his order, Vespasian placed a military force upon them to pursue those who had escaped the disaster by means of the boats.

What, then, could they do? They could find no place of safety on land; everything was surrounded by the enemy. There was no possibility of flight on the water, since the lake was enclosed and surrounded on every side by Romans. Nor was there any confidence of resistance in the small boats. For what could a few do against many as the rafts approached?

The rafts moved more slowly than the boats, but their attacks were more effective. Yet the only sounds heard were the clatter of shields and the rebounding of darts, while the men themselves suffered no wound. The Jews did not dare approach, and no one could safely bring a small boat nearer. At close range, a man could easily be pierced by spear-thrusts or his boat sunk.

If anyone attempted to swim away or emerge from the water, he was struck by an arrow and ended his miserable life in the waves. Nor could they resist for long, since they were being reduced in various ways. As many rafts gradually came together, the Romans forced the greatest number of boats toward the shore.

The Jews, hemmed in, either leapt back onto the land [Note: “They were leaping down.” BARR.] and were killed there by the Romans, or were cut down by those who pressed them from the rafts, or were crushed by the collision of the rafts, or threw themselves into the lake when the enemy leapt into their boats. You could see the waters mixed with blood and the lake filled with corpses. No one was spared, whoever happened to be encountered. The smell was heavy, the stench of the place most foul.

Six thousand Jews, in addition to those previously mentioned, and seven hundred were killed in that battle [Note: “Five hundred. Josephus, Book III, chapter 19.” GALLAND.].

Victorious, Vespasian returned to Taricheae. There he intended to distinguish the inhabitants of the region from those of the city, so that those who had not been the authors of the sedition might be spared. But the advice of many prevailed: they judged that so great a multitude remaining alive might revive renewed battles, was hostile to peace, and useless to the region—“for where would they stand, expelled from their country [Note: “Excluded?” BARR.]? By what means would they support themselves, deprived of everything, unless they lived by plunder?”

Vespasian therefore changed his decision and, instead of the hoped-for pardon, ordered them to leave through the gate facing Tiberias and make for that city. They readily believed what they desired. They began to leave, but when the route had been seized in advance, all the columns of departing Jews were blocked and led into the city’s stadium.

After Vespasian entered and examined the age and strength of all those whom he had ordered to be assembled, he selected six thousand of the stronger young men and sent them to Nero on the Isthmus. He ordered twelve hundred old and infirm men to be killed; he sold the remaining thirty thousand four hundred. All those found to have come from the territories of King Agrippa he gave to the king. The king, having received payment for them, likewise sent them into slavery.

In addition, the other peoples of the region of Trachonitis and Gaulanitis, together with the inhabitants of Joppa and Gadara, as instigators of war and disturbers of peace—abandoning their own possessions and invading those of others, and having violated peace by taking up arms—paid the just and deserved penalties for their crimes [Col. 2100C].

# BOOK FOUR

## CHAPTER ONE

After Taricheae had been for the most part destroyed, the Romans possessed the cities and territories of Galilee, except that Gamala, a city of the region of Gaulanitis, sustained the defiant spirit of its people, relying upon its rugged terrain. It is situated on a mountain, enclosed on the right and left by precipitous cliffs. It narrows toward the summit, is cut off in front by a deep cleft, and broadens somewhat toward the rear.

On that side too, the approach to the city is narrow and difficult, so that one might judge the path leading to it to resemble a camel’s tail. From the highest peak, a neck stretches out to an immense length, presenting the citadel like a head and raising it to a lofty height. At first it is narrow, as though the ground had been twisted into sloping bends and plunged into the depths; then, in the middle of the neck, it raises something like a mountain. The remaining parts are precipitous and impassable.

Hence many believe that it was originally called Camala, because it resembled the shape of a camel, but that through the corrupted usage of the inhabitants the name Gamala became attached to the city.

If you look at the buildings joined together, you might think the city suspended in the air, and especially imagine its northern part hanging down, while its southern side bends back slightly. Josephus had also added fortifications to this city. Relying upon them and upon the number of people who flocked there, they had mocked the siege of King Agrippa for seven months.

For both Gamala and Sotanis and Seleucia were parts of his kingdom. Seleucia lay beside that most pleasant and famous grove of Daphne in Syria, interwoven with cypress trees and bursting with springs. These springs pour nourishment from their abundant, milk-like breasts into the river flowing past the place, which they call the Lesser Jordan.

Yet Seleucia was a city; Sotanis was the upper, and Gamala the lower, part of Gaulanitis. For this reason, differing in their aims, those cities had chosen alliance with the Romans. Gamala, however, rebelled so stubbornly that when the king wished to address its people near the walls, he was wounded by a sling-stone.

The Romans, inflamed by this insult, began to press the siege more vigorously. Both sides fought with the greatest readiness, since the Jews also—believing that, if they were victorious, they would have no pardon because they had violated their own king when he was giving sound advice—fought with all their strength.

Agrippa was struck on the right elbow by a stone and withdrew from the battle; the Romans broke into the city. The enemy yielded to the missiles, and the wall to the battering-rams. Even those who were obstructing the engines could no longer resist. The wall, torn apart by the third battering-ram, opened a way for the besiegers against the besieged.

But this event, through the impatience of haste, brought the victors no small disaster. When they poured into the houses and searched them, or strove to carry off the spoils [Note: “So the printed editions read. But perhaps *praereptum ire* should be read.” GALLAND.], the houses, yielding under the weight and their foundations tottering, brought down ruin. Each neighboring structure was dashed against the next and became the cause of destruction.

Many Romans, caught in these collapses, encountered disaster amid victory. Most were buried beneath the fallen buildings; others, their bodies mangled, were scarcely preserved alive. Dust killed many; others, trapped in the narrow spaces, were cut down. From above, women, feeble old men, and those among the younger men who had taken refuge threw stones at those below or hurled whatever kinds of missiles came to hand.

Darkness covered everything, robbed them of sight, and confused their minds; ignorance, too, prevented them from finding an exit. Only with difficulty did they extricate themselves from the dangers and leave the city.

Meanwhile Vespasian, while pressing the enemy, had withdrawn into the interior of the city. Positioned amid the surrounding ranks of the enemy, he kindled the battle. For it was not fitting for so great a man merely to turn his back on the enemy, nor did he consider it safe.

He had sent his son Titus into Syria. Vespasian summoned up his renowned steadfastness, gathered himself for battle, and, locking shields with the few men present with him, stood undaunted, as though considering against whom he should hurl himself. The Jews, fearing his attack, began to press forward with less force, and each, fearing for himself, loosened the battle-line.

Thus Vespasian, facing the enemy, gradually withdrew his steps, appearing more like one fighting than one retreating. There Brutius fell with the ten men at the front [Note: “Called Ebucius by Josephus, Book IV, chapter 1.” BARR.], a man tested in many previous wars and, among the Jews, a soldier of recognized experience and proven courage [Note: “The old manuscript reads: ‘against the Jews.’ ID.].

A centurion, too, with ten other Syrians, performed a remarkable and memorable deed. For amid the confusion, when he saw the Romans being hard pressed, he withdrew into the hidden recesses of a certain house. There, while dining, when the Jews were discussing what plans they had made against the Romans, he killed them all in the dead of night and returned with the soldiers to the Roman army.

## CHAPTER II

When Vespasian observed that the army was sorrowful because of the loss of so many men—and especially because of the shame of having abandoned their commander, leaving him alone inside the enemy city—he consoled them with the greatest kindness, saying:

“If the fate of my danger is a source of shame to you, I had not advanced to war in such a way as to avoid dangers, but [Note: “To seize for myself.” ID.] to overcome them. But if you are troubled because many of our men were also killed, there is nothing remarkable in that. For when has there ever been a victory without bloodshed?

“Battles have their own outcomes. Although tested valor usually prevails in war, something nevertheless is often left to chance. But it is the mark of a prudent man to correct a fall in adversity and to maintain moderation in prosperity. On the contrary, it is characteristic of an inexperienced and untrained mind always to anticipate favorable outcomes, as though the contest were not against men; while it is the mark of weakness to lose confidence in the whole enterprise because of some setback, when everything that happens in war may suddenly be turned by the smallest moments.

“The truly outstanding man, therefore, is the one who amid adversity wrestles with sober fortune, overthrows his superior, and seeks to restore and correct his own lapses. But the careless man often falls because of his own impulses, and, rushing forward unwarily, collapses, brought down by his own momentum.

“If this often happens where valor stands alone, how much more in war, where armies of different kinds are locked in combat, where there is neither one plan nor a shared judgment? The unfavorable position, the difficult roughness of the ground, and the disadvantageous conditions of deciding a battle in a confined space placed the many against the few. The multitude itself was a burden to itself, while the few were less likely to be frustrated among the many.

“But such circumstances often intrude only for a moment. They do not arise from valor, but occur by chance. Therefore, comrades, there is nothing here that ought to distress you. The outcome was not turned by any weakness in your hands, nor by the courage of the Jews; the difficulty of the terrain hindered us from victory, while it merely delayed them.

“There is nothing that can be criticized except an ill-considered and [Note: ‘Disorderly.’ ID.] unorganized attack. For while you followed them to the higher parts of the city and rushed into [Col. 2102C] their houses, you yourselves entangled yourselves in danger. You entered their dwellings and accepted their perils. You held the city—who compelled you to proceed inward? The enemy ought to have descended to you, not you, rash in your pursuit of victory and forgetful of life and safety, to have pressed forward.

“Recover your courage, therefore, and draw upon your virtues not only for consolation but also, which is greater, for vengeance. You shall certainly have me leading the battle. Be ready in arms and spirit. Let danger make you stronger, not more fearful. It is easy to avenge an injury, if valor recognizes itself again.”

## CHAPTER III

With these words he kindled the soldiers’ courage. While they repaired the rampart, many withdrew from the siege by way of the precipitous terrain. For lack of provisions was already pressing upon them, and they believed that the weakened wall would yield to the engines.

Moreover, there was only one spring inside the city, and it too lay close to the walls. This circumstance placed them in the greatest fear, so that very many slipped away. Those who thought they should remain fought stubbornly.

Meanwhile the Romans undermined the tallest tower and brought it down with tremendous force. The city was shaken by this collapse, and everyone was thrown into confusion, fearing the ruins of the whole city. Hence Chares, sick in body, was overcome by the terror of so great a crash and died.

The Romans nevertheless held back from entering the opened city until Titus arrived. Roused by grief over his father’s danger, he rushed into the city with a few men and inflicted a great slaughter upon the Jews.

Only those positioned on the heights prevented the Romans from approaching by rolling down stones; they hurled spears and shot arrows. The stones, pushed by the Jews, rolled easily down the slope, and the missiles reached their targets; the arrows descended, not without danger to those whom they struck.

Against the higher parts of the mountain, the Romans’ throws were ineffective, their efforts fruitless, and their position itself dangerous. Suddenly, however, a storm of wind arose, turning back the Jews’ arrows and repelling their spears. Whatever the Roman army hurled was carried back against the enemy [Note: “Was borne back.” BARR.]. Thus, overwhelmed by the barriers of the elements themselves and by the whirlwinds of the winds, all those found there perished in the final destruction of the captured city [Col. 2103B].

Four thousand alone were killed by the Romans; we are told that five thousand died by falling from the heights. No age was granted pardon.

## CHAPTER IV

Giscala alone among the regions of Galilee had not yet turned the enemy against itself, because its inhabitants had gentler dispositions, being a rural population content with its own produce and contributing nothing to the war. But when many men joined together who made their living by banditry, even the aims of the gentler people were corrupted by depraved customs.

There was also a frivolous native named John, a plague to the people, second to none among the cunning in deceit, unequalled in wickedness. He had never lacked the desire to do harm, although for some time poverty had been an obstacle to exercising his iniquity. Yet I do not know how to decide [Col. 2103C] whether want concealed him or restrained him.

He was cunning in deceit, a craftsman of deception, skilled in lies, seeking trust and adding cruelty to carefully contrived schemes. He considered fraud a virtue and regarded it as elegance; he was ready to entrap even his closest friends; eager to conspire, fierce in daring, sharp in execution; a disturber in peace, a deserter in danger; accustomed to banditry, inexperienced in war. Though unable to carry things through, he nevertheless sowed the causes of preparing a dominion.

His restless spirit and ready audacity were nourished by increasing resources, which enabled him to unite a band of depraved men. When Vespasian learned that, through John’s faction, the people of the aforesaid city were being stirred to war, he sent his son Titus with one thousand cavalrymen, accompanied by whom he approached the city.

When he saw the walls crowded with people, Titus said that he was amazed that they followed the example of those whose destruction should have brought them to their senses in rebelling. Even if their first attempts had contained some presumption, what hope could the destruction of all hold out?

Certainly, at the beginning, hope of liberty might be pardoned; but perseverance in final and desperate circumstances is inexorable. For those who are moved neither by an example of humanity nor by earnest verbal admonition require weapons, not words.

You trust in your walls as though they protected you against Roman valor. What else can those shut inside display or put forward, surrounded as they are, except that they are bold in captivity? No one was permitted to speak. A band of plunderers had occupied the entire circuit of the walls, and John took care that no one should invite the Romans to a friendly conversation.

Therefore he forestalled the report of the conversation himself, saying that he was willing to undertake discussion of matters of common concern and did not refuse to hear proposals, whether perhaps Titus might advise what was useful or whether he ought to accept what was being reported. But he was prevented by the law of his country from discussing terms of peace, since a sacred day of the week still remained.

For just as taking up arms was forbidden, so too it was unlawful to deliberate about peace on festival days. To decide even by words concerning such a matter would be sacrilege for those compelled, and would not go unpunished for those who compelled them.

He asked permission for a single day, saying that so brief a delay could in no way be an impediment. For, with the enemy surrounding them, there was no free escape for those shut inside. They were being offered the choice of peace, and the equal nature of the alternative made fear unjustified. Meanwhile, he ought not to be pressed into deliberating about peace, since religious duty forbade him to violate the law of his country.

It was fitting, however, to respond to so generous an offer of peace: since the man who voluntarily offered peace beyond expectation should preserve even those who would escape, so that no one might perish and they might retain their own laws.

Titus judged that these words had been advanced without deceit, sounded the retreat, and recalled from the walls those whom he had brought with him. Thus John gained the opportunity to flee and, in the dead of night, departed with most of the people. Women also followed him as he left.

But the farther the men proceeded, the more women and children were left behind. The women, abandoned by their own people, stood fearfully watching the road. When they had already lost sight of their husbands, they imagined that the enemy was near and trembled at every sound. If anyone ran up, they turned back in misery, trembling as though they themselves were being pursued and chains were being placed upon them—as though those whom they feared were already present.

Titus, then, when the sun had already risen near the appointed time, proceeded toward the city with his army. The gates were opened. The people came out with rejoicing and welcomed the Romans with joy and eagerness. They rejoiced that the pestilent man was gone, that he had fled during the night, and that they had been given free opportunity. They begged for pardon, lest the flight of the man whom they could not hold without their own destruction should prove harmful to them.

Titus, content with postponing vengeance and with the swift completion of the affair, immediately sent many men to capture John, in case they might overtake him.

He himself entered the city and was content to afflict the disturbers of the peace with threats rather than punishment. He pardoned everyone, lest anyone, stirred either by hatred or by domestic disputes, should bring innocent people into disrepute and charge them with the atrocity of a most serious crime. For it is far more tolerable to leave an uncertain matter to the fear of a guilty conscience than to condemn an innocent person.

Fear often corrects the guilty; punishment inflicted upon the innocent, however, offers no means of correction.

John was therefore not found by those whom Titus had sent. But those who followed him—children and women—were found. Nearly two thousand were killed, while three thousand of the weaker age and sex, [Col. 2105A] once the appetite for killing had been satisfied, were assigned to captivity.

Titus granted the city a military guard. Thus all Galilee was brought under Roman power.

Mount Tabor also—thirty stadia in height, with a level summit extending for twenty-three stadia—was abandoned by some because of lack of water and surrendered by others to the Romans after requesting pardon. Yet by the valor and skill of Placidus also, to whom Vespasian had entrusted this task, the entire crowd of refugees, while following the retreating enemy and pressing hard upon him as he cleverly drew back, was surrounded in the middle of the plain, lost its refuge, and encountered destruction.

## CHAPTER V
Hitherto it has been permissible to wander about, while, avoiding the contagion of the sacred temple founded by our ancestors and of the sacred law, we occupy our pen with other cities; [Col. 2105B] but now it is time to undertake what happened at Jerusalem—not relying on ingenuity, but lest we seem to have denied the law of our homeland and the ancient worship the service of our grief. Even if there was in them a shadow rather than the truth, nevertheless a shadow indicates the traces of the truth. For a painting has the outlines of a shadow, but not its radiance; nor is it finished by the final touch, yet to those who look carefully it represents what is to come. Therefore the image delights less, but its charm allures more. Hence it pleased the arbiter of events to abolish the old and establish the new, so that those who, through the straits of unbelief, did not follow the images might follow the truth.

## CHAPTER VI

Fleeing, as we said above, from the regions of Galilee, John withdrew to the city of Jerusalem; [Col. 2105C] and, like a kind of pestilence, he infected the minds of many. The leaders of crimes from various regions flowed together there as though into a sewer. This was the chief cause of the city’s greater ruin: the depraved, bringing their crimes thither, thought that their flocking together there—where they believed they would be either safer or more insolent in accumulating crimes—was a service rendered to religion. They were therefore received indiscriminately, as though they had come to be defended by pious love for the temple. This was the first stain of the evils.

From this point the gentleness of the few was crushed by the insolence of the many; from this point they proceeded to slaughter, since the outsider showed less mercy; from this point they conspired to neglect the solemnities of the law and to transfer the priestly offices from good men to wicked ones. Since such men were strangers not only to pious worship but even to knowledge of the law, [Col. 2105D] they did not know what was holy.

First, men of royal lineage who resisted were bound, so that the others might yield through fear; then they were killed. To conceal the crime, they sent assassins into prison and falsely claimed that those whom they had killed without trial had been executed after being charged with treason. Thus everyone was overwhelmed by fear, since the powerful and innocent men Antipas, Lebias, and Phoras had been so easily crushed; no one now dared to resist.

From this they proceeded to appoint base and unworthy men as chief priests, so that those who had no qualification to earn the honor, having obtained the priesthood contrary to their merit, might be subjected to every outrage at the will of those who bestowed it. But when the priestly men opposed this—especially Ananus, older than the rest—they demanded that the chief priest be chosen by lot, so that no favor might confer the distinction of the highest office and the outcome of the lot might be regarded as entrusted to divine judgment.

In fact, they invoked an ancient custom by which those to be appointed to the chief priesthood were accustomed to be summoned to the lot; but they were plainly contriving an evasion of the law. For although the priestly law selected men for succession to the priesthood by lot, they placed forward, for appearance’s sake, one man from the priestly tribes, [Note: [Col. 2105D] Eniachium. BARR.] named Enachus, and ordered that the lot be cast.

Then a certain Phanis was chosen by lot, the son of Samuel, a gray-haired man for whom there was not merely no succession derived through the chief priests, but not even any knowledge of the priestly office, since he was occupied in the countryside. For that reason he did not even know that he had become chief priest. Finally, he was dragged from the fields, and, although reluctant, a different role was imposed upon him as though on a stage [Note: [Col. 2106D] “A foreign [or unsuitable] one.” ID.]; he was also clothed, according to the ancient custom, in the sacred garments. He was instructed at the moment about what he ought to do.

Thus the wickedness of the seditionists was exposed by the outcome of the lot, when the performance of so great a priesthood was reduced to an ignorant peasant. But to them the circumvention of the ancient solemnity was a joke; to the priests it was a grief. They lamented and groaned, weeping that the law was being mocked by the ruined men.

Nevertheless, relying on the authority of piety and on the indignation of the good, they gathered and attacked the disturbers. But since the latter were inferior both in cause and in numbers, they fled to the temple as to a citadel and established it for themselves like a fortress, to repel the multitude of the attacking people.

At first, stationed before the temple doors and in the vestibule itself, they fought against the people. If anyone was wounded, he sought the inner parts of the temple, pouring out his blood there upon the inner threshold; and their more grievous, bloodied wounds stained the pavements, while the exposed tissue of their open wounds was dressed with garments which they were not permitted to touch.

There was war within the city, war among citizens, war before the temple. The robbers did not even reverence this. When the people pressed them more insistently, they withdrew into the temple itself and immediately closed the doors.

By this obstruction Ananus was called back, lest he seem to be bringing war upon the temple and breaking through the temple doors consecrated by the religion of their ancestors. He checked the attack of the mob and stationed six thousand men in the porticoes, armed and maintaining a vigilant guard. Gradually, however, he softened his attitude in order to promote peace, chiefly so that the temple would not be polluted by the blood of citizens. He also advised that an embassy should be sent as an intermediary for peace, so that the civil war might be brought to an end.

John was added to carry out the embassy, a man of suspect loyalty and inflamed by the desire to seize power. An oath was demanded of him; he did not refuse, lest he suffer the penalty of perjury if he declined. He pretended [Col. 2107A] to favor the people, in order to deceive them.

What more is there to say? He went, prefaced his speech with a few words about peace, and then added much more to kindle war, saying that under the name of peace war lay concealed, that ambushes had been prepared, that Ananus was handing the city over to the Romans so that the ancient solemnity might be dissolved and the precepts of the law abolished, arranging everything in the opposite direction; and he directed the odium against the chief priest for what he himself was plotting.

Craftily, he also incited those whom he knew to be leaders and faction chiefs among the men who were shut up inside, asserting that they were facing death and that Ananus had specifically prepared their destruction. He said that he had come to expose the fraud. Help had to be sought promptly, before punishment was exacted from them.

What more is there to say? While standing in the middle as a representative of peace, he kindled war.

Men were chosen to invite the Idumaeans to battle: a volatile, restless, insolent people, ready for quarrels, delighted by changes of circumstance, heedless of danger, and headlong in battle. Thus they came without delay; twenty thousand men gathered, being people concerned with no cultivation of the land but prepared for brigandage.

Ananus could not remain unaware of the arrival of the Idumaeans. Finally, he ordered the gate to be closed, lest they enter with tumult; but he wanted them, if possible, to learn the truth and renounce the war.

## CHAPTER VII

The chief priests therefore climbed the wall and addressed the Idumaeans from the tower. They said that it seemed to them a great wonder that the Idumaeans had so quickly been ensnared by lies and were pursuing with weapons causes they did not yet understand; [Col. 2107C] they ought first to be arbiters of the matter rather than combatants in war, and above all to learn the merits of the case before taking up arms.

No injury had been inflicted upon men of their own race, worship, or solemnity more than upon the Idumaeans, yet they were being stirred up to join in such grave crimes. What else was being demanded of them except parricide against fellow citizens and sacrilege against the temple? Different aims and different customs do not usually come together. Similarity of character creates an alliance of wills, and related pursuits bind themselves together.

The most wicked men, who supported themselves by robbery, had presumed to summon the Idumaeans as their allies—men so utterly opposed to the purpose of those who called them that the latter had brought war upon their own country, while they had begged the Idumaeans to come as though to defend a foreign city.

You have nothing in common with robbers, you who are innocent; nothing in common with drunkards, you who are sober. If only that drunkenness were caused by wine, and not by madness. Once they have stuffed themselves with crimes, dissipating their own inheritances, they plunder what belongs to others; and what they have acquired wickedly, they squander still more wickedly and pour away even more ruinously. There is no end to plundering because there is no limit to their gluttony.

When they have drenched and filled themselves with wine, they belch up the excess of public affairs, so that they may again become drunk on our blood and mock the sacred religion that has always been held by you in veneration [Col. 2108A] and reverence.
