Therefore flee gatherings of parricides, abandon sacrilegious attempts, and leave the assemblies of robbers. You have been summoned to share in a crime; you have come to remedy the condition of your country.

We see before us a most distinguished people, whom it would have been fitting to come after being summoned by public deliberation, so that they might assist the most excellent city of the Jews—regarded as the capital of the entire nation—against its enemies.

But even if we failed to meet your request while we hoped for peace, and did not wish to trouble you prematurely [Note: [Col. 2108D] “We did not wish to trouble you prematurely.” ID.], since we were offering peace to those who were inciting war—nevertheless, since you have come as though by divine providence, deliberate for the common good and act as arbiters between both parties.

Seek the beginnings of the disturbance: who sounded the trumpet of war against the peaceful city; who shed the blood of its most distinguished citizens; on whose authority punishment was exacted from men who had not been convicted. Those who brought destruction upon us before the Romans—we were preparing war against them, and we were already enduring them as enemies.

Whose friendship with the Romans, then, is suspect? That of those who avenge themselves through the Romans, or that of those who repel the Romans? These things are certainly more grievous to us than Roman battles. By the Romans we die for liberty; by these men we are slaughtered as though for a crime.

Innocent men are falsely charged with treason, and after their death the accusation is fabricated, although inquiry normally precedes punishment, not punishment inquiry. What benefit is it to the dead to be acquitted when they are no longer indebted to any judgment?

Nevertheless, we have also received this fate: that our innocence be investigated after our slaughter. And gladly we plead before you both our own integrity and that of the dead, while you stand armed on behalf of our adversaries. Thus the slanderers have no evidence to offer that even before you they have the weaker case, since you believed them so quickly.

A good judge regrets finding himself surrounded by lies, and is more hostile to the deceiver than eager to believe him, because he considers it necessary to avenge the fact that he was rashly driven to believe falsehoods [Note: [Col. 2108D] Gualther reads *quo*. GALLAND.].

Therefore preserve for us a fair examination, and gather the truth not from a weave of words but from the sequence of events.

First of all, why would we betray our country to the Romans, whom we were able—and perhaps ought—to avoid provoking, lest we stir up the conquerors of all nations? But it is no longer for the present parties to deliberate about this. It belonged to an earlier time to choose what we should follow; now we must fall for liberty, [Col. 2108D] for it is better to die for one’s country.

Before the war it would have been more advantageous to prefer peace to death. But since war is upon our necks, many brothers have already been captured, others killed, grief comes from the dead and groaning from those bound: a free death must be chosen rather than a life of captivity.

Nevertheless, those who are dying have the opportunity to erase the disgrace of a false accusation of treason. Before you, Idumaeans, we plead our case. Let the guilty be produced; let the interpreters of the messengers be brought forward. If they have the men in custody, let them produce the avengers; if those who accuse do not have them in custody and are charging men with baseless suspicions they themselves have fabricated, they ought not to accuse what they cannot prove.

But because they do not dare to accuse, they wish to scatter suspicion among the populace; and therefore they rush into war so that they may not be summoned to judgment. In war, fury is satisfied; in peace, truth is examined.

We are here. We voluntarily offer ourselves first to punishment, provided that some accuser comes forward. Or, if resentment is directed against the people, inquire more carefully what was the purpose of the public assembly. Was it not to prepare battle lines equipped for war, or for each person to aid his country in the cause of liberty?

What had been resolved against those very robbers except that peace should be restored? Public indignation had been inflamed by individual grief, the blood of the innocent, the groaning of women, and the violation of ancestral statutes. The groaning of everyone resounded because each person feared that the same things might happen to him.

[Col. 2109B] Priesthoods were being conferred upon the most unworthy; they began to be demanded with shouts. Those men struck the people with stones and killed them with weapons; public grief burst into flame. They established refuges for robbers in the temple.

Thus the place of peace, revered even among foreign peoples, and the dwelling of holiness became an assembly of brigands. The place to which people gathered from every part of the world for the worship of a solemn festival is now a kind of den of wild beasts, soaked with human blood.

It is lawful for us to inquire into these matters, even while armed and without the formalities of war. Yet judgment has often been exercised amid weapons; justice has laid down the instruments of war and restrained the crowds by the verdict of equity.

You can turn these weapons to the defense of the city, though you took them up for its destruction. You may also enter without weapons, listen to everything, and inquire into everything. If you discover that anything was remitted even against an enemy, regard it as treason.

But if you are unwilling either to act as avengers or to serve as arbiters, why do you wonder that the gates are not opened to armed men? They are closed not against kinsmen but against weapons. Lay down the war, and the gates will open.

## CHAPTER VIII

When the priests had spoken these words—and especially Jesus, older than the others, though Ananus held the second place—the Idumaeans grew indignant that they had not immediately been admitted into the city.

Simon, one of the Idumaean leaders, said: “It is hardly surprising if citizens are savage and keep shut out those who have closed the gates against an allied nation and do not permit their companions and partners to enter. They speak to us from the wall and, as though we were adversaries, repel with walls those whom they regarded as friends.

Who would doubt that they are preparing to receive the Romans, and perhaps even crown the gates, when the Romans enter? What greater injury could there be? This city is accustomed to lie open to all peoples for the sake of worship and reverence; to us alone it is closed, as though to enemies. We alone are rejected; we alone are driven back.

They pretend to seek our judgment, although they have judged us not even worthy of the threshold of the city. Let them conceal what they have done against those men; we are witnesses and judges of our own wrongs.

We understand what those who are shut inside are suffering when we are ordered to lay down our arms. Can it be credible that the judgment of those whose loyalty is suspect should be awaited?

Let us therefore hasten to rescue those who are shut in, for whom the temple has become a prison, lest they be kept there until the Roman army arrives and be handed over as captives to Vespasian.

Let us remove the siege from the temple and drive away those most dreadful guards, who permit no one to go out even to relieve his bowels. If anyone wishes to bring food to those shut inside, he is prevented; if anyone wishes to leave, he is dragged away to death. The practice of religious worship has been turned into a crime.”

## CHAPTER IX

Hearing this, John yielded [Note: [Col. 2109D] The old manuscript reads “Jesus,” as in the preceding chapter and in Josephus, Book IV, chapter 7. BARR.], realizing that he was struggling in vain against the adverse will of God, since hostile battle lines were roaring both within and outside, and the city was being attacked from two sides.

The Idumaeans raged because they were excluded. Those stationed in the temple plotted how they might join the Idumaeans; the Idumaeans were troubled by the fear that the others might depart before accomplishing their purpose, while shame restrained them from turning back.

Already distrust had almost crept in when suddenly, during the night, an intolerable storm arose: a black tempest; the winds roared; the sky bristled; a great force of rain poured down [Note: [Col. 2109D] “Was poured forth.” ID.]; terrible flashes of lightning, immense thunder, and the bellowing of the earth made it seem as though the world were coming apart.

Who would believe that this harmed those inside the city more than those living outside it? Certainly the former were protected by roofs, while the latter were exposed to the rain. But fear of the injury terrified them more than the injury itself.

Finally, those who had no shelter, covering themselves with shields, remained at their posts and did not disperse. The others, each scattered around his own house, gave an opportunity for those inside the temple to open the gates.

Yet the people’s judgment was divided and uncertain. Some thought that the supreme God, angered at the Idumaeans because they had come armed against their associates, had stirred up the storms. Ananus and the more penetrating minds of the elders conjectured that the Idumaeans were being still more aroused by the wrong done to them, to the destruction of their allies.

Finally, more troubled than on other nights, Ananus yielded that night—not from bodily fatigue but rather from despair of spirit [Note: [Col. 2110D] “Overcome.” ID.]—to circumstances fluctuating against him and to the storms of the world working toward his destruction. He did not think the guards should be inspected, as though by doing so he were granting authority for each person to disperse according to his own judgment.

Those who had fled into the temple seized this opportunity. Rising, they cut through the bars of the gates. The crashing of the sky aided them, so that the sound of the locks and the tumult of those leaving would not be heard.

Then, coming to the wall, they opened the gate that was near the Idumaean camps.

That day would have been the last for the entire people if they had not thought that the signal should first be directed toward the temple before it was directed toward the city [Note: [Col. 2110D] “If they had not [given the signal] to the temple before [giving it] to the city,” etc. ID.].

But because those held shut inside the temple feared for themselves—lest, once the entry of the Idumaeans became known, the attack of the surrounding crowd should be turned against them and the dying people demand vengeance—they asked to be spared the slaughter first [Note: [Col. 2111D] “Those shut inside.” BARR.]. Then, once they had been freed, they would pour out against the people with united forces.

They turned toward those who had sent envoys to beg for assistance and safety, so that, as an unexpected reward for the breach, they might repay the authors of it with this favor.

When this plan succeeded, all of them poured out from the temple, as from a fortress, and, forming an extended battle line, slaughtered everyone they found throughout the streets—some asleep, others terrified.

Prayers were useless; tears were useless; the insignia of rank were useless; the favor of no merits availed anyone. They slaughtered everyone indiscriminately.

Finally, seeing the bestial savagery of their pursuers, since no one was spared, they hanged themselves, with an end more pitiable, as I think, than if they had been killed by an enemy. Voluntary death is attributed to savagery, and the knot of an ugly noose brings disgrace as well.

But what room was there for deliberation when fear of punishment was so great? Each person feared not death but the tortures before death, from which death would be a remedy.

Blood flowed everywhere, especially around the temple, because those who guarded the prisoners were gathered there. Eight thousand five hundred men were found to have been killed that day.

Then they turned toward the city and, just as though it were a flock of sheep, killed all the people they encountered. It was a pitiable spectacle: war was being waged within a city previously revered by all, and unjust destruction was being inflicted upon the poor and the weak.

The young and stronger men, whom they considered suitable for the faction, were indeed thrust into prison; but many, with great courage, preferred to endure every punishment rather than associate themselves with the ruined men.

There was no limit and no shame. Such was the fury of their savagery. Later, when in the course of time there seemed to be no more victims, they began to fabricate charges against those whom they wished to kill, so that they could bring the accused to trial—not to seek justice, but to inflame cruelty.

## CHAPTER X

There was in the city a man named Zacharias who hated the wicked and did not mingle with criminals. He was wealthy, and they thought that his abundance would either be effective in dissolving their faction or provide them with rich plunder. They therefore decided that he should be summoned on a charge of treason [Note: [Col. 2111D] “To be summoned.” ID.].

But, clear in conscience of such matters, he came forward with confidence, not only to refute the charges brought against him but also to establish that the accusers themselves were guilty of the greatest crimes. The case was heard before seventy men. They all acquitted him, because nothing resembling a crime had been produced.

But the others rushed in, threw Zacharias himself into the abyss, and disturbed the judges—not merely with insult but also with danger—so that, following their example, the others might thereafter beware of adopting firmness in judgment against their will.

Nevertheless, to ensure that no one would be acquitted, the very men who carried out their anger killed whomever they pleased without trial.

Gorgon was killed, a pleasing and amiable man. Niger Pereites, a warrior chosen among the defenders of Judaea to protect the common cause, so that he bore the insignia of valor even in the scars of his wounds, was dragged away to death. When he saw himself being led outside the city, he began to beg not for his life but for burial.

He did not even receive an answer appropriate to the mercy of so pitiable a request. Calumnies were fabricated: if anyone ransomed himself, he was innocent; whoever did not offer money was treated as though he were guilty.

## CHAPTER XI

While these things were happening at Jerusalem, Vespasian meanwhile was subduing other regions of the Jewish nation.

News reached him of the sedition at Jerusalem, of the deaths they had inflicted upon one another in domestic battles, and of the punishments citizens had exacted from citizens. Many urged him to go there, lest anything be taken away from the Roman triumph and from his own glory.

But he was a moderate and prudent man. He did not consider what seemed useful according to the convenience of the crowd, but what, according to a deeper policy, he judged advantageous to the common cause. He began to reply to those who advised him:

“The state is not always helped by battles; often renown is acquired and the debt owed to one’s country discharged even by laying down arms. What difference does it make how the enemy is defeated—by our sword or by his own? Except that, by his own sword, he is overthrown without Roman resentment.

“They cannot complain about us when they have wounded one another; at the same time, they show how justly they have made war upon us when they do not even spare themselves. This seems to be vengeance from heaven: those who have provoked the Romans are driven mad by fury.

“But if anyone says that something is being taken away from our glory, let him understand that a remedy accompanied by silence often outweighs a battle accompanied by danger.

“Indeed, our Maximus broke Hannibal more by delaying than by fighting. Although the Scipios subdued Africa, their victory was a common achievement of wars fought by many; to Maximus alone was granted the distinction of restoring the state by delay.

“It is therefore greater to have preserved the Roman empire than to have extended it. Yet let us weigh the merits of valor fairly. Even in war itself there are no fewer achievements of wisdom than distinctions of courage.

“Let them perish by their own weapons. Nothing is lost from our glory [Note: [Col. 2112D] ‘Nothing is diminished from the praise.’ ID.], and much is added to our victory. They do not know how to preserve their own people, whom we spare.

“Besides, if we begin to threaten them, perhaps they may come to their senses among themselves and be reconciled. I do not say this because I fear it, but I offer it against your opinion. Or, if the sedition continues, let them appear to have conquered themselves; let the Roman army have done nothing, let our hands have remained idle, and let the victory have been achieved not by our valor but by the enemy’s mutual destruction.

“Therefore this is the more prudent policy: that, while we are absent, they may rage toward their own destruction, so that no one may think that they have been worn down more by our forces than by their own factions. We shall approach at a better time, when a victor remains who can join our triumph.

“Certainly, let those who flee from their own people come to us; let those whom the plague of their countrymen has driven out find safety among us.”

## CHAPTER XII

Vespasian’s judgment did not deceive him. Those who could ransom themselves with money and thereby obtain release fled to the Romans.

All the roads and paths were filled with those fleeing. The rich were released; the poor were killed because they lacked money for ransom.

Many also feared ambushes and brigandage outside the city, especially the poor, who lacked an escort. Since the danger confronting them was equally present outside and inside, and dangerous in either place, most nevertheless thought that, because they hoped for burial in their native land, death among their own people was more bearable.

## CHAPTER XIII

When the greatest slaughter of the people had spread fear among everyone, it made all subject to the faction.

John was not content to exercise power jointly with the faction’s leaders; he began to aspire to tyranny and was indignant at having an equal. He therefore destroyed the arrangements of others, regarded nothing as valid except what pleased him, and gradually acquired bodyguards for himself.

Skilled in deceit, he circumvented whomever he wished by fraud, bound them through money, terrified them through power, and by these methods associated many with himself.

Yet there were also men who, even at the cost of danger, refused servitude, especially since they were accustomed to domination and could not endure slavery.

Thus three kinds of deadly calamity were established in one city: tyranny, war, and sedition. Each of these would destroy not merely one city but many.

Of the three, however, war was the lighter evil; and a just enemy seemed more tolerable than either a tyrant or a faction.

A fourth kind was added: assassins who, seeing the city seized by tyrannical disturbances or the tumult of sedition, ravaged everything nearby and carried everything away. They killed women and children who, because of the weakness of their sex or age, could not endure the labor of the journey.

Seven hundred were therefore killed. Grain was transported into the fortresses. They rushed upon fields, cities, and temples, carrying off booty; no opportunity for killing was overlooked. Under the appearance of a marching column they practiced brigandage [Note: [Col. 2113D] “They practiced it. Soon afterward they intensified it.” BARR.], more numerous than a band of robbers normally was.

The savagery of brigandage aggravated the war, without granting pardon for surrender or offering the mercy of acceptance.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 2113D]

Vespasian was therefore asked to come as a remedy, although his coming was feared as destruction.

He hastened to Gadara, where there were many wealthy people who, because of their patrimonies, feared the ambushes and attacks of the robbers more and more. For that reason they had secretly sent to Vespasian, asking him to approach them so that the city might be rescued from the robbers.

The Roman army arrived. When the Gadarenes saw it, they wished to flee but could not discover a way by which this could be done safely, lest the faction rise against those departing and destroy them all.

Nevertheless, the fact that Vespasian had been invited by the embassy of the Gadarenes did not escape notice. A leading citizen of the city named Dolesus, who knew of that embassy, was seized and killed. Having avenged the wrong, they left the city and withdrew to remote and more strongly fortified places.

Gadara was handed over to the Romans, and Vespasian was received with immense applause. He immediately sent Placidus to pursue those who had fled; he himself returned to Caesarea.

## CHAPTER XV

Placidus, having sent ahead five hundred cavalrymen, pursued the fugitives and forced them to withdraw into the nearest village. There, finding a picked body of young men, they took courage and rose up against the Romans.

This proved fatal to them. For when the cavalry surrounded them, those shut out from the village were slaughtered without any obstacle. While others withdrew in close formation, they were butchered before the thresholds of the gates.

A mound formed from the corpses of the slain rose to the height of the walls [Note: [Col. 2114D] “Was piled up.” ID.].

The Romans struck some with arrows and wounded others with various missiles. Finally, they stormed the fortress, and all there were killed except those who found an opportunity to escape.

Some of the fugitives magnified the fame of Roman valor in their reports, saying that the Romans seemed to possess bodies greater than human bodies and that no one could hope to resist the invincible.

As a result, everyone was terrified and immediately fled. Not only the neighboring and adjoining settlements but also the city of Jericho was abandoned. Because of the multitude of its inhabitants, Jericho had encouraged the hopes of the others.

With events proceeding according to his wishes, Placidus pursued them by cavalry as well. He struck down some in close formation and others scattered, pursuing them as far as the Jordan River.

He found a very large number obstructed at the riverbank, unable to cross, because at that time the river had perhaps swollen from the rains just mentioned or from melting snow.

When they saw that the Romans were present, they prepared themselves and crowded along the river’s edge. Necessity, having cut off the resource of flight, turned the remedy into their hands: they made a charge, and many hurled themselves upon the smaller number of cavalrymen.

The cavalry, using their familiar tactic and the ancient practice of military service, began to ride among them and cut apart the enemy wedge, break up their groups, press the exhausted, and pursue those who gave way.

Some were killed by the enemy’s sword, others by their own, since they had rushed together in a compact mass and collided with one another. Others plunged into the river and were submerged by the very force of their fall and by becoming entangled with one another.

Many, thinking that they could cross, entrusted themselves to the river. After advancing a short distance, some were swallowed by the force of the whirlpools, while others were swept away by the current.

If any who had learned to swim had made their way over the waters, they either clung to the shifting current, were caught among tree branches being carried down by the river, or, crushed by the trunks themselves, gave up their lives in the river.

Often, an unskilled swimmer, once he had seized someone who was swimming, held him so that he himself might escape as well; but, exhausting the man by gripping him in his arms, he caused both to sink, each becoming the other’s destruction.

If someone seemed likely to escape by being carried along by the favorable current [Col. 2115A] [Note: [Col. 2115D] “He was overwhelmed.” BARR.], arrows were shot at him. Suddenly falling backward, with the oars of his arms no longer moving, he died.

There were also those who did not know how to swim and, seeking a death free from suffering, climbed upon the raised banks and voluntarily threw themselves into the river.

Others entered along the sandy shore and were submerged when their feet sank. Many, slipping on smooth stones or stumbling in shallow places, staggered with unsteady steps and were overwhelmed by the pursuing waters.

Thirteen thousand were killed by the sword. An innumerable multitude was consumed by the river. A great quantity of booty was taken, consisting of flocks of sheep, camels, asses, and oxen.

Although the slaughter of human beings was immense, it was considered still greater because not only was the entire region filled with human corpses—for those seized wherever they had scattered and wandered were killed—but even the Jordan itself was blocked by the bodies of the dead and could no longer pursue its normal course.

The lake Asphaltites also changed its natural appearance through blood and the entrails of the dead; everything that the Jordan had swept along was carried into it.

Finally, it was estimated that ninety-two thousand two hundred Jews perished that day at the hands of only five hundred cavalrymen and three thousand infantry.

Advancing farther, Placidus also restored Abila, Juliade, and Betesmon, together with all the villages of that region as far as the lake Asphaltites, to Roman rule.

He also placed soldiers in boats, by whom all those who had taken refuge in the aforementioned lake were destroyed.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 2115C]

And so all these places as far as Machaerus were recovered. Vespasian, however, was waiting for the right moment to attack the metropolis of all Judaea with the Roman army. Meanwhile, while he was occupied with the affairs entrusted to him, news of a new disturbance began to filter in from the Gallic provinces: certain powerful men in the Roman military had defected from Nero.

When he learned this, he desired, after bringing the tumult of the wars in the East to an end, to relieve the danger posed by civil strife and by the whole Roman empire’s precarious situation. Thus, by means of news of success, he might either suppress or forestall every disturbance in Italy. As soon as the harsh winter had been moderated by the beginning of spring, he set out from Caesarea with the greater part of his army.

A city called Antipatris received him. Advancing from there, he burned the villages and killed those whom he found to be foreigners [Col. 2115D]. In particular, he ravaged whatever he encountered near Idumaea, because that people was restless and more friendly to war than to leisure or peace. He also seized two Idumaean villages, Ligarum and Capartorum, and their inhabitants, inflicting a great slaughter upon them. (Note [Col. 2115D]: In Josephus, book V, chapter 4, the reading is “Begabri Caphartophram” [Col. 2116D]. The old codex has “Ligarim and Coparcorem.” ID.) He killed more than ten thousand men, carried away a thousand prisoners, and expelled the remaining populace, so that he could establish a force of his own there, since the mountainous districts of that region were being harassed by brigandage.

He himself returned with the army to Amathus [Col. 2116A], which took its name from its hot waters, since the vapor of the waters is said to be called *Amathus* in the Syrian language. In Greek it is called *Thermae*, because it has a hot spring within its walls. From there he proceeded through Samaria, near Neapolis, toward Jericho. There Trajan met him, leading a considerable force composed of those peoples of the region of Peraea who, having been situated beyond the Jordan, had returned under Roman authority after their defeat.

When news arrived that the Roman army was approaching, most of the inhabitants of Jericho, seeing that the city was unsafe, withdrew into the mountains of the Jerusalem region. The entire crowd that remained was destroyed. It was not difficult to capture the city quickly, since it possessed no natural defenses and had been abandoned and left undefended by its inhabitants as they dispersed.

The city had been founded on a plain, above which rose [Col. 2116B] a broad mountain bare of vegetation. On the north, the land extends as far as the city of Scythopolis; on the south, it stretches toward the region of Sodom and the shores of the Asphaltite Lake. The soil is unhealthy and barren and therefore deserted by its inhabitants, because its natural sterility made it useless to cultivators.

Opposite this mountain, across the Jordan, is another mountain whose beginning rises from Juliadis and the northern region. It extends southward as far as the Sobaras, bordering Arabia Petraea; there too is a mountain which, according to ancient usage, is called “Iron.” Between these two mountains lies a plain which, because of its size and because it extends over a wide area (note: “is extended.” ID), the inhabitants traditionally called “the Great.” Its length is two hundred and thirty stadia [Col. 2116C], and its breadth one hundred and twenty. It begins at the village of Gennabar and ends at the Asphaltite Lake.

The Jordan cuts through its middle (note: “in the middle.” ID), not only without disturbing it, but also adding the beauty of green banks through the river’s alluvial deposits. The Asphaltite and Tiberias are adjoining lakes fed by a single spring, though their waters are of different qualities. The water of the one is excessively salty and useless; that of Tiberias is sweet and life-giving.

In summer, an oppressive vapor rises over the plain. As excessive dryness accumulates and the parched soil corrupts the air still further, it produces distressing illnesses among the inhabitants. Everything is dry except along the banks of the river. In the more distant parts, even the fruit of the trees languishes. The produce is more abundant, and the fruit of the palms more luxuriant, along the banks of the Jordan; elsewhere it is much thinner.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### [Col. 2116D]

There is also near the city of Jericho a plentiful spring, and one even more abundant for drinking and richer for irrigation. Joshua son of Nun, a Hebrew by nation and strong of hand, first wrested it from the Canaanite people. At first it was regarded as corrupted and sterile for reproduction, and it was unhealthy and of little use for those who drank from it.

Therefore the inhabitants asked the prophet Elisha—who was also Elijah’s disciple and in no way an unworthy successor to so great a master—to leave them a reward for their hospitality: namely, that he should visit the place and remedy the corruption of the waters. As the ancient Scripture of Kings teaches, he provided a remedy, ordering that a clay vessel with salt be brought to him. Taking it, he cast the salt into the spring and said: “I have healed these waters, and there shall no longer be death in them, nor shall they be barren.” And the waters were healed, “according to the word,” it says, “of the prophet Elisha” (4 Kings 2:21–22).

Thus, through the infusion of the blessed salt, the waters were tempered and the mouth of the spring opened; the channels of the waters were sanctified, so that the springs poured forth sweeter drink, all the bitterness of the waters became sweet, and the earth produced more abundant fruits. The best succession for the generation of offspring also supplied a plentiful abundance of descendants, and the life-giving water did not fail, since divine grace had breathed upon the faithful efforts of the righteous through the blessings of so great a prophet. (Note: “to whom.” BARR.)

At the prophet’s prayer, therefore, the response of the heavenly oracle changed the nature of the waters: it immediately drove away barrenness and infused fertility. There human generations began to multiply; the fruits of the earth and the sap of the waters, previously barren and bitter and accustomed to destroying the crops and twisting the sorrowful faces of those who drank them, infused fertility into the soil and sweetness into those who drank, so that land cultivated only briefly there yields more than land irrigated for a longer time elsewhere.

It is a new kind of grace: productivity is greater where use is less, and where someone has made greater use, the fruit is less. For this reason it waters more than other springs, because even a small quantity of it is abundant for producing fertility.

Finally, a plain surrounds it, extending seventy stadia in length and twenty [Col. 2117C] in breadth. There one may see the marvelous beauty of gardens, various kinds of palms, and such sweetness in the dates that one would think honey was flowing—honey in no way inferior to other kinds. There are also exceptionally fine swarms of bees; and no wonder, where they breathe in the fragrance of such different flowers and pour forth the sweet perfumes of paradise.

There opobalsam is produced. We use this expression with its added element because the farmers cut the branches only through the bark, on those places where the balsam is produced (note: “is generated.” ID), so that the liquid, dripping little by little through those openings, may gather. An opening is called *opē* (ὀπή) in Greek. There, they say, cypress and myrobalan grow, along with other products of this kind that are found nowhere else.

The water is like that of the other springs, though superior there: cold in summer and warm in winter. The air is milder, so that even in the depths of winter the inhabitants use linen garments as clothing [Col. 2117D].

## CHAPTER XVII

Now let us consider the character of the Asphaltite Lake. It is better to occupy our pen with descriptions of ancient places and with the marvels of the other elements than with the uprisings of the Jews. Those atrocities exasperate the mind; these things, when recounted, soothe the spirit and recall us to the knowledge of ancient history.

For us, whose talent is somewhat uncultivated, it is dear to retrace the footsteps of the fathers who came out of Egypt (note: “departing.” ID) and returned as far as the promised land, so that if our writings should perhaps come into someone’s hands, he may not read about us but reread the history of the fathers. It is sweet to dwell among the habitations of our ancestors, to review in memory the words and deeds of the ancients, and to cling to their grace.

But whether we describe the nature or the character of the waters, let us take care that our pen is not also thrown into that lake (note: “be cast out.” ID), about which there is a belief that whatever one might think should be submerged nevertheless springs back alive, and, however violently it is hurled down (note: “dashed against [it].” ID), is immediately cast out again.

The water itself is bitter and sterile, admitting none of the kinds of living creatures. It does not permit fish, nor birds accustomed to the water and delighted by diving, to plunge into it. They say that a lighted lamp floats upon the waters, but that, once the flame has been extinguished without any contact, it sinks; and that, even when something living has been submerged by force, it is difficult for it to remain in the depths.

Finally, they say that Vespasian ordered people ignorant of swimming to be thrown into the depths with their hands bound. All of them immediately floated back to the surface, as though lifted by some breath of wind and driven upward with great force.

Many people have believed numerous fabulous stories about this lake. Since we have not tested the truth of the matter, we have never thought it proper to report them. Nor have we wished to present as fact the claim that the water changes color three times a day and flashes in various ways under the sun’s rays, since the lake’s own water is darker than other waters and seems almost to display the appearance of something scorched. (Note: “water.” ID.) Certainly, if it too shines in the sun’s rays, there is nothing extraordinary to report as a miracle, since this is common to all waters.

It is certain that lumps of bitumen float upon the waters in a black liquid. Those whose duty it is approach them in boats and collect them. Bitumen is said to cling together in such a way that it cannot be cut apart with iron or with any other sharpened form of metal. It yields, however, to women’s blood, by which women undergoing menstruation are said to be relieved. At its contact, even urine—as those who have had experience of testing it assert—is reported to interrupt its cohesion. It is said to be useful for joining ships and, when mixed into medicines, beneficial to human bodies.

The length of the lake extends as far as Zoara in Arabia, for five hundred and eighty stadia; its breadth is one hundred and fifty stadia, reaching to the vicinity of Sodom. The Sodomites once inhabited an exceedingly fertile region, abundant in fruits and also adorned with splendid cities.

Now those places are deserted and scorched by fire. For although God had bestowed everything upon them as his gift—fields fertile in grain and countryside planted with vines and other fruit-bearing trees—they were ungrateful and did not keep before their eyes the power of the Most High God. They acted as though he saw nothing, foresaw nothing, and nothing could remain hidden from him or escape his notice. Thus they began to mingle all their deeds with the crimes of their excess and to pollute everything. They incurred divine displeasure, and, as the price of their crimes, fire descended from heaven and consumed that region.

Five cities were therefore burned, of which something like a shadow and outline can still be seen in the ashes. The lands burned; the waters burn, and the remnants of heavenly fire are visible in them and still remain. To the eye, the apples appear green and the clusters of grapes formed, so that those who look at them are made to desire eating them. If you pluck them, they split apart and dissolve into ash and raise smoke, as though they were still burning.

These facts, discovered concerning the territory of Sodom because of the punishment of the wicked, ought not to be consigned to silence. Once these matters have been recounted, there can be no doubt that a reward awaits the righteous.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Vespasian therefore filled all the nearest forts and fortified positions of the city of Jerusalem with a distributed force of the Roman army and its allies [Col. 2119B], so that the people might recognize that everything they had previously thought would join them in waging war against the Romans was now hostile to them.

Nevertheless, having assigned Lucius Annius to Gerasa, he captured the city by ambush. He also killed a thousand young men, whose escape was prevented by this preemptive action. Many prisoners were led away, and all their property was seized by the soldiers. By order of the commander, the possessions that were found were burned, and plunder was carried out at will.

The Romans ravaged the mountains and plains surrounding Jerusalem, while the city itself burned with war on every side. Nor were the people of Jerusalem free from awareness of their own dangers: all exits were closed, so that no one could escape the danger by flight. Inside there was internal evil; outside, everything was shut. They had neither the will to remain nor the opportunity to flee. And if any had hoped to obtain pardon from the Romans by defecting, their own people prevented them from leaving.

## CHAPTER XIX

Vespasian had returned to the city of Caesarea in order to gather all his forces there and then undertake the siege of the city of Jerusalem. News arrived that Nero had been killed after completing the thirteenth year of his reign, when he had already entered the eighth day of the following year.

He was worthy of such a punishment: he had violated loyalty through sacrilege, piety through parricide, and chastity through incest. He had also violated the very authority of the Roman empire, whose offices and affairs he had entrusted to the worst of his freedmen.

Since he himself kept faith with no one, he suspected everyone. For this reason he thought he should trust especially the utterly wicked Nymphidius and especially Gemellinus, whom their low condition had made dependent upon him. Yet even they eventually recoiled from his example of cruelty. Because he had killed everyone especially dear to him, they judged that they must be on their guard and wished to forestall what they feared.

Thus, conspiring with the others, they abandoned the parricide. For whom could he be expected to spare, when he had not spared his mother? Abandoned by all his own people, he fled the city with four of his freedmen. When he saw that the conspirators were pressing upon him and that an opposing force was approaching, he withdrew secretly to a suburban farm [Col. 2120A]. He was torn and lacerated by thorns as he feared being seen by anyone and betrayed.

Then, realizing that he was surrounded and wishing to avoid the infliction of severe punishments, he prepared for himself a certain wooden weapon (*maganum*, reading uncertain) and set it in his hands so that he might kill himself. Turning to his freedmen, he said: “What an artist dies!” (Note: “Thus.” BARR.—“I would change nothing, for the author may have written *itaque* [‘thus’] for *et ita* [‘and thus’].” Galland.)

Thus the most savage parricide met an end worthy of his deeds: he who had killed his mother and his own people did not spare himself. Truly he was a good artist of his own death, devising how he might perish in this way, lest even death itself should be free from his crime.

## CHAPTER XX

The rumor of Nero’s death had preceded the event, as is characteristic of human nature. Once it has received what it desired, it is satisfied not to inquire into the rest, but immediately to scatter whatever has pleased it and send it untested among the populace.

Not long afterward, however, it became known that Galba was in command of the Roman empire. Vespasian therefore wished to inquire into the new emperor’s judgment concerning the war against the Jews, and he sent his son Titus and King Agrippa.

Titus returned from Achaea after learning that Galba too, in the seventh month and seventh day of his assumed power, had been stripped of the insignia of office and had paid the penalty in the heart of the city, that is, in the Roman Forum, and that Otho had gained power through good fortune and imperial success.

Agrippa hastened to Rome in order to establish his influence with the new emperor. Titus thought the reverence owed to filial duty more important than the authority of the princeps. He judged that, if he proceeded onward without consulting his father (note: “if he should press onward.” BARR), his father would not approve it either.

Certainly the outcome showed that he had returned opportunely to his father [Col. 2120C], amid new circumstances whose direction was uncertain. Finally, Vespasian himself, anxious about the condition of the entire Roman empire and of his homeland, suspended the war and checked his advance (note: “advance.” ID), setting aside what was being done in Judaea because of his concern for the whole state and his dutiful solicitude for his country.

## CHAPTER XXI

Judaea, however, was not at rest. It was waging a more grievous war among its own people than against external enemies. Since the faction of John was intolerable, Simon rose up as well. He was inferior in moral depravity, but more confident in his bodily appearance for every kind of wicked undertaking, and accustomed through brigandage to the practice and testing of crimes.

He was a citizen of Gerasa, a vigorous young man (note: “in youth.” ID), whom the high priest Ananus [Col. 2120D] had struck down because of his criminal schemes and had forced to leave the region in which he lived, sending him off to other lands. But since he had no place among the peaceful and modest, he joined himself to a band of brigands. At first they too were suspicious of him, fearing that he might entrap them through faction; afterward he easily blended into their way of life.

With them he ravaged the areas bordering the fortifications, because they did not dare to seek anything farther away. They lay in ambush as though hiding in pits, attacking passersby without any open raid, content with what was almost domestic brigandage.

Simon, however, could not endure this limited ambition for long. In a short time he gathered a large force for himself by promising freedom to slaves, rewards to free men, and compensation to the desperate. As many flocked to him for the license to plunder, he dared to storm fortifications and seize the populations of cities, and he became terrifying to everyone.

He prepared for himself a refuge in a village called the Wall of Ajacis. (Note: Josephus, *Jewish War*, book V, chapter 7, calls this village Aim. BARR.) Already he was advancing surrounded by twenty thousand armed men when the people of Jerusalem, suddenly fearing his daily advances and judging that he would become their future enemy if he were allowed to grow stronger, thought that he must be cut down. They therefore attacked Simon in arms with a sudden sortie.

He was neither unwary nor unprepared for their ambush. He received the attackers, routed many of them, and forced others, defeated in battle, to retreat into the city.

## CHAPTER XXII

He also withdrew from an equal engagement with the Idumaeans, and, as though defeated because he had not won, was distressed. When another battle became necessary, he judged it more advantageous to test them by deceit and found a willing instrument for fraud.

When it became known what he was attempting, Jacob, one of the Idumaean leaders, shrewd and clever in such affairs, came secretly to Simon and offered to betray his homeland. To provide proof that he would deceive all the Idumaeans, and after requesting a reward for the future alliance so that he might be especially influential and trusted by Simon, he promised to betray them all.

Their agreement was sealed at a banquet in an atmosphere of fellowship and by enormous promises, and the pact between them was confirmed.

When Jacob returned to his own people, he first began to boast to a few of them that he had thoroughly investigated the strength of their adversaries: he had seen a powerful force, men experienced in war, and an enormous multitude, invincible in battle. He gradually introduced this sort of speech to the leaders (note: “to insert.” ID), and finally spread throughout all the ranks (note: “through all [the ranks].” ID.—Perhaps it should be read “through countless [men].” Galland) that Simon himself was exceedingly energetic: he had organized his army in royal fashion, maintained its ranks, distributed its units, and placed suitable commanders over them.

The Idumaeans, he said, ought to look to their own interests, so that they might experience such a man as a friend rather than an enemy. They could plainly see that he was superior in battle; they should withdraw without danger and avoid combat.

When he perceived that the enthusiasm of many had been inclined toward his view, he informed Simon that he should come out into the battle line, confident that the Idumaeans would be scattered. Simon did not delay. Jacob, like a standard-bearer with his men and apparently more eager for battle, saw the engagement being tested by light-armed troops. Before the forces came to hand-to-hand combat, he turned his horse and gave himself to flight. His men did the same.

In this way he turned and scattered all the battle lines and handed the victory to Simon without a battle.

Simon, having gained the triumph over so great a people, became more arrogant toward the others. He captured, sooner than expected, the ancient city of Hebron, famous for its inhabitants and rich in wealth. He found great plunder there and tore up its abundant produce.

For it is said to be the most ancient city not only of the cities of Palestine but also of all those founded in Egypt by the ancients [Col. 2122A]. Many even think that Memphis, which is regarded as the oldest, was founded later. Some also said that Abraham lived there after he had departed from Mesopotamia in Syria and set out for Egypt, and that his sons had a tomb there, built of the most beautiful marble and with exceptionally elegant workmanship, seven stadia from the city.

A great terebinth tree is said to have existed there from the creation of the world. Whether it still remains, however, is unknown to us.

From there he advanced, ravaging territories, storming cities, gathering peoples, and surrounded by forty thousand armed men. He emptied everything wherever he approached, whether as a friend or as an ally. What place could supply food for so great a multitude? Everything upon which such a number of warriors stood was trampled beneath the imprint of their feet as though beneath a pavement.

They not only carried off whatever produce existed, as though they had been devoured by locusts, but also left the ground crushed for the future, so that it refused to yield fruit.

John was terrified that Simon’s power was increasing, and the associates of his entire faction were shaken. They wanted Simon destroyed but did not dare to provoke him in war. Again they prepared an ambush. Lying in wait along the roads, they seized his wife with her entire female retinue and with the few men accompanying them.

They boasted as though they had achieved a complete victory and imagined that they held Simon himself captive, expecting him to beg them for mercy.

But he was hard and savage, moved by affection for no one and regarding nothing as sacred or dear. He was inflamed as though he had suffered an injury rather than lost a loved one, and he tortured those whom he found with punishments increasingly savage and severe.

He cut off the hands of many and sent them back to the enemy mutilated, so that they might announce his cruelty and convey his threat: unless his wife were quickly returned to him, he would overturn the walls and destroy the city. He threatened similarly to mutilate the hands and entrails of all who lived within the city unless they acted promptly for their own safety.

Terrified by this, they sent his wife to him. His fury was thereby calmed, and he allowed those shut inside the city a brief respite, so that he would not press the civil siege.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Not only had Galba been killed, but Otho too had been destroyed, while Vitellius’ commanders engaged in battle. The Gallic army had created Vitellius as emperor.

In the first engagement Otho appeared to be superior. When the battle was renewed the following day, Otho learned that the victory had fallen to Valens and Caecina, Vitellius’ companions, and that many of his own men had also been killed. Stationed at Brixia, he removed himself from mockery by voluntary death, having held power for only two days and three months.

Vitellius, therefore, victorious, proceeded toward Rome with the army that had survived on both sides.

## CHAPTER XXIV

At that time Vespasian, having set out from the city of Caesarea [Col. 2123A], was ravaging Judaea, subduing all the neighboring mountains and fortifications. He killed those who resisted; to those who begged he granted the pardon of life; he put his opponents to flight and established his own men.

The Roman commander Cerealis also traversed everything with the cavalry: he destroyed some, subjected others, and compelled the prisoners to form ranks. Everything around Jerusalem was burned, so that the Jews would have no refuge.

Thus, before the siege, every exit was closed to the Jews. They not only failed to provide for their own safety, but also fought among themselves in domestic conflict.

John was the tyrant within; Simon, the enemy outside the walls. Having recovered his wife and made a brief excursion, Simon ravaged Idumaea, returned stronger, and surrounded the walls of Jerusalem with the sound of arms.

John, stationed inside [Col. 2123B], trained his own people for war through vice, having granted authority to crimes. The passions for plunder, the desires for disgraceful deeds, the excesses of luxury, the scents of perfumes, and the curling of hair with curling irons were all in full force. They painted their eyes with antimony and put on women’s clothing. (Note: “they put on.” BARR.)

They pursued not only the adornment of women but also feminine softness and the indulgence of illicit lusts: men practicing women’s ways, making their voices effeminate, dissolving their sex through bodily looseness, cultivating their hair, whitening their faces, polishing their cheeks, and plucking their beards. Amid this dissolution they exercised an intolerable savagery of cruelty.

Finally, they walked with mincing steps. Suddenly, these momentary warriors drew hidden swords from beneath purple cloaks. Once they had bared them, they slashed to pieces whatever they encountered [Col. 2123C].

Anyone who had escaped Simon was killed by John if he had taken refuge inside the city; anyone who had fled from John was captured by Simon and sacrificed before the walls.

There was a bitter division. The Idumaeans sought to destroy John’s tyranny. They envied his power and hated his cruelty. They engaged his tyrant’s guards, drove them away, and pursued them as far as the royal palace, which had been built by a relative of the king of Adiabene.

They burst in after excluding the defenders and seized the temple, plundering the spoils of the tyranny, because John had stored the repository of his wealth there.

A serious fear arose that during the night the Idumaeans might enter the city from the temple, kill the populace with the sword, and destroy the city by fire. Terrified by this fear, and unable to endure one tyrant, they introduced another by common decision.

John had insinuated himself into tyranny by fraud. Simon, when asked, introduced his domination to the citizens and a tyrant to the city, as though he were providing a remedy for their safety. The high priest Matthias was sent to plead for his entrance.

But Simon did not decline to rule, with sufficient arrogance; and, as though burdened by it, he yielded to their entreaties, so that he might pour into the city with all his forces. They opened the gates with their own hands so that they might introduce a more dangerous man, while cursing the weaker one.

Simon therefore entered by common agreement but showed himself equally an enemy to everyone, pursuing with common hatred both those who had summoned him and those against whom his assistance had been requested.

John pressed him with his plots (note: “was pressed.” ID), and the city wavered. The contest between John and Simon was to determine which of them could do greater harm to his own people.

## CHAPTER XXV

During this period, the report of civil wars in the Roman army became stronger. The deaths of Galba and Otho and the accession of Vitellius had been disclosed; Vitellius was worse than those before him, as though all the dregs had settled at the bottom.

Veterans began to discuss these matters among themselves and to resent the fact that the Praetorian legions at Rome had seized such power. Although they had ceased to experience the dangers of war and did not even know the names of the peoples who were making war, they had nevertheless appointed an emperor of war and established him as the judge of Roman affairs in their own hands. (Note: “they establish.” ID.)

Then, following this example, the soldiers stationed in Gaul had aspired to give the empire to Vitellius, without consulting the Senate or the Roman people. Meanwhile, they themselves were treated like mercenaries, following the decisions of others: first to danger and last to honor; waging war for so long; receiving masters from their inferiors as their triumphs increased daily; and receiving not even useful masters, but the most cowardly, or men devoted to their bellies and their shameful pleasures.

They had to go to meet the wrong and remove it. They had a vigorous man in Vespasian, whom everyone ought to choose as emperor: mature in age for deliberation, stronger than younger men for battle. They had to act quickly, lest he be chosen by others first, and lest those with whom he had grown old in military service be despised while he triumphed.

When would there be a more suitable time for a worthy reward to be repaid for his labors? The Senate and Roman people would no longer tolerate the “Vitellian abyss,” the disgrace of private life—not to call him an emperor—remaining at the summit of empire, when Roman resources were insufficient for his expenditure. (Note: It seems one should read either “the Vitellian abyss” or “Vitellius, an abyss,” in the sense of Cicero, *Pro Sestio*, ch. 52: “You, gulph and ABYSS of patrimony, will revel at my peril?” The context confirms this restoration. Galland. Note: BARR.—But the received reading can stand if it is referred not to “is insufficient,” but to “expenditure.” Galland.)

Who could endure a tyrant ruling when the army possessed a governor worthy of the Roman empire? What peoples would submit themselves to luxury and surrender themselves to vices when the emperor’s laziness is an incitement to war, while firmness in the ruler of the state produces peace and courage against the enemy?

Who would not recognize in Vespasian, while still a private citizen, the dignity of kingship and the authority of the Roman empire, when so many military units and the entire stronger force of the Roman army stood ready for him?

What are we waiting for? Are we waiting for him, supported by our virtues, to owe his position as emperor to others, while we yield to others what lies within our own power? Certainly, if we do not wish to honor him, let us at least not diminish him. Let us not do him the injustice of rejecting him by our judgment as unworthy of the empire, while considering Vitellius worthy of it.

Finally, since his brother and his son Domitian were in Italy, there was certainly reason to fear that the man who ought long since to have been an ornament to his family might become a danger to it. Or, if they had begun—as we suppose—to press the tyrant, their rebellion, as brother and son, might become a charge against Vespasian, and we might begin to regard as guilty the man whom we had refused to see as emperor.

While the soldiers shouted these things among themselves, they approached Vespasian and begged him to take up the helm of the Roman empire.

He, however, refused and declared himself unworthy. An emperor had already been established, and civil war ought to be avoided. They pressed him more eagerly; he resisted more persistently.

Finally, armed men surrounded him with drawn swords and threatened him with death, pointing out that guilt would remain with them and that they would face grave danger if he refused. Thus he yielded to those who compelled him rather than voluntarily accepted what others customarily seek.

The soldiers pressed him; the commanders urged him. He assumed responsibility before honor and hurried to Egypt. He knew that the greatest strength of the Roman state was there, from which the grain supply was provided. He needed support if he won, or opposition to Vitellius if he thought the war should be prolonged. (Note: An entirely new word, set in opposition to *suffragium* [support]. See Gronovius, *Monobiblos*, ch. 21, p. 236. Galland.)

There were also there two orders of military men whom he hastened to attach to himself, so that the greatest city, surrounded by many natural defenses, might remain under his authority rather than another’s and might be sufficiently useful for either outcome of the war.

For this reason, since we judge that something should be said, however briefly, about the character of the region and especially about the metropolitan city itself—

## CHAPTER XXVI
Alexander founded the city of Alexandria, which, on account of his valor, received the surname “the Great Commander.” It lies between Egypt and the sea, as though a barrier placed between them; it is a city without a harbor, as are nearly all the cities of Egypt, and difficult to approach from outside, since it lies in the more remote parts of Asia. On the European side Egypt itself borders upon the arid land of Libya [Note: “Egypt.” BARR.]; its upper southern regions are bounded off from the Ethiopians by Syene and by the unnavigable cataracts of the Nile. On the east the Red Sea flows back as far as Clitro, a place at the very extremity of the world, which opens a navigable route to India. Thus enclosed on one side by the sun’s burning heat, and bounded on the other by the Indian and Egyptian seas, the land rests upon the mainland only by a single northern wall, the road that leads into Syria. Everything else is shut in on every side and fortified by nature; yet the northern region itself provides a divided defense and opens by a kind of double boundary, through which either foreign troops are transported across the seas to Egypt [Note: “Egyptian.” ID.], or freer access to the land is spread abroad.

The land extends to an immeasurable distance. For between Syene and Pelusium the entire length is two thousand stadia [Note: “Immense.” ID.], if the assertions are to be believed; and from Plinthine to Pelusium likewise three thousand six hundred stadia. It is a region unaccustomed to rain, yet not in need of rainfall, since the Nile’s irrigating waters supply it with spontaneous showers. [Col. 2126A] On both sides it has the Nile, the abundance of the sky, and the fertility of the earth: it moderates the fields, enriches the soil, and is equally useful to sailors and farmers. The former sail; the latter sow. The one travel around their own farms by boat; the other cultivate them by sowing with the plow, traveling without a wagon. You may see dwellings scattered throughout the whole land, which is divided by streams and raised, as it were, by certain lofty walls of navigable waters, since the dwellings wander amid the lands that the Nile surrounds. For the river is navigable as far as the city called Elephantine [Note: “Of the Elephants.” ID.]. Beyond it, the cataracts we have mentioned do not allow a vessel to proceed—not because of any lack of depth in the current, but because of the precipitous descent of the whole river and a kind of collapse of its waters.

The city’s harbor, like the approaches of most maritime places, is difficult to enter, and far more difficult than the others. It is broader, as though shaped like the human body, at the head itself and at the anchorage; narrower at the throat, where it receives the passage of the sea and ships, for which the harbor provides a kind of breathing space. Once someone has escaped the narrow entrance and the mouth of the harbor, the sea spreads out far and wide, like the remaining form of the body. On the right side of the harbor there is a small island, and on it a very large tower, which Greeks and Latins alike call the Pharos, from the practical use of the thing itself: it is visible from far away to sailors, so that, before they approach the harbor, especially at night, they may recognize by the blaze of its flames that the neighboring land is near [Note: “By a sign.” ID.], lest, deceived by the darkness, they strike the reefs or fail to find the boundary of the entrance.

There are therefore attendants there who, by placing beneath it torches and other piles of wood, keep a fire burning as a herald announcing the land and as a guide to the harbor’s jaws, showing the narrow passages of entry, the curves of the waves, and the bends of the entrance, lest a slender hull graze the rocks and strike hidden reefs at the very entrance. The straight course must therefore gradually bend, lest the ship, dashed against the rocks, encounter danger precisely where an escape from danger is expected. The approach to the harbor is narrow because on the right side it is constricted by the shore, and on the left by rocks, which block the harbor’s left side.

Around the island as well, masses of enormous size have been built and cast down, lest the foundations of the island fall under the continual rising force of the sea and be broken apart by its excessive violence. Hence, since the waves strike against one side of the island and run in the opposite direction between the jagged rocks and the constructed masses, that central channel is always turbulent, and because of its rough passage the voyage becomes dangerous for ships. The harbor is thirty stadia in breadth; its anchorage is safe, and its calm is extreme even in a storm, because, by means of the narrowness of the aforesaid entrance and the obstruction formed by the island, it drives the waves of the sea away from itself. Thus within, by a kind of compensation for the dangerous entrance, the harbor is extremely secure: for through those same narrow harbor-mouths the whole basin of the harbor is protected, withdrawn from storms, and calmed after the [Note: “Roarings.” ID.] blasts through which the entrance is made rough.

[Col. 2127A] Nor is it without good reason that the harbor has such protection and such magnitude, since it is necessary that goods useful to the whole world be brought into it. For innumerable peoples of those regions seek the commerce of the whole world for their own use, while the land, rich in grain and abundant in the other gifts and products of the earth, feeds and equips the entire world with grain and necessary merchandise.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

After Vespasian had settled his affairs in Alexandria, and after all who were engaged in military matters had united in support of his imperial authority, he felt secure about his absence and hastened his return to Syria. Yet he first instructed Tiberius Alexander, who was then governing Egypt, to win for him the allegiance of his army, which at that time was in the upper regions, and to support the necessity of the Roman Empire with whatever forces he could. Tiberius communicated by letter to the provincials and soldiers what had been imposed upon him, and all received it with joy; loyalty was promised, and favor poured forth.

Caesarea received Vespasian; from there he went to Berytus, with delegations from the cities streaming together in great joy. There Josephus was also ordered by the emperor to be released from his chains. Titus helped to have the chains broken rather than merely unlocked. If they were broken, it would be as though he had never been bound. His father approved the bringing of an ax and ordered the chains to be broken, so that the Jews might understand that pardon would not be denied to them either if they changed their course and asked for peace. At the same time, Vespasian was no longer reserving Josephus at another’s discretion, since the decisions concerning everything had been transferred to him.

## CHAPTER XXIX

They came to Antioch. There, after deliberation had been held about the point from which it would be best to cross to Italy—for he had considered everything in Egypt and Alexandria secure—speed was judged advisable. He therefore sent Mucianus with a large force of cavalry and infantry, so that he might precede the emperor’s arrival in Italy. Because fear of a lengthy voyage recalled him, Mucianus directed his route through Cappadocia and Phrygia. He also ordered Antonius, prefect of the third military division stationed in Mysia, to pour into the Italy assigned to him before the Vitellians could move.

For Vitellius, as though stupefied by drunkenness and sunk in sleep, thinking that he was conducting a banquet rather than an empire, slept while involved in such great affairs. [Col. 2127D] At last, scarcely awakened by the announcement of Antonius’s arrival, he sent Caecina with part of the army and entrusted the whole burden of his danger to another’s judgment, relying on Caecina’s strength because Caecina had defeated Otho’s forces.

Caecina encountered Antonius near the city of Cremona as he was approaching. He investigated everything and learned that a very powerful force was coming from different directions [Note: “From the opposite side.” BARR.], vigorous in war and practiced in triumphs. He saw that he himself could not contend against stronger forces, neither with equal strength nor with equal numbers. Calling the centurions together, he advised abandoning the war, because they were inferior in number and the emperor’s glory outweighed them. The reputation of a commander conducting the supreme enterprise was of great force in war. Vespasian had shone in the Gallic regions and in victories in Britain; Vespasian, girded with the laurels of the East, enjoyed the great advantage of his name. Vitellius, on the other hand, being nothing but dissolved in wine and continually belching up yesterday’s banquets amid his feasts, awaited nothing except that, when the enemy arrived [Note: “Had arrived.” ID.], he might perish drunk and without awareness of pain.

The soldiers’ courage was thereby increased by the glory of so great an emperor, while by the disgrace and shame of the other it was cast down. They must take care not to lose the reputation gained in the former war [Note: “Lest he should lose it.” ID.]. Although they had defeated Otho, who was Vitellius’s equal, they now had to deal with one who had encircled the whole world with his triumphs. They should forestall necessity by goodwill, choosing Vespasian as a fellow citizen rather than experiencing him as an enemy.

It is wretched to win a civil war; how much more wretched to be defeated, so that you appear as the enemy of your own people! The homeland remains for the victor; for the defeated it perishes—or, if it remains, it will remain only to bring hatred upon the crime, so that we seem to have brought war upon our fellow citizens for the sake of a tyrant. For the one who is defeated is no longer a citizen but a tyrant. Why should we join harmful hands? Let it be enough to have once won through crime, so that we may be ashamed of the person for whom we won. We had thought either that the emperor would remain sober or that, shaken by the weight of affairs, he would renounce perpetual sleep [Note: “Or even while in command.” ID.]. Why do we wait any longer? Our dangers are unwelcome to all our comrades-in-arms; our judgments have been censured and condemned by all peoples because of the crimes of the man chosen. Consider what sort of man he is, since even after victory he has been rejected.

We must surely first deliberate about the outcome of the war and then fight. If dangers overtake you, you deliberate in vain; once a decision has been approved, you will begin rightly. It was the duty of an anxious commander: everything had been examined by him; it was clear that Vespasian’s army was stronger; his loyalty to Vitellius had long since been proved. When he anticipated the outcome of the war, victory followed; when he distrusted it, defeat followed. It was plain what would happen. Nor was he afraid for his own death, but for the danger of the Roman army—and, what pains men more deeply, for the loss of the glory already won, so that those who were accustomed to win might appear defeated. He himself must take care lest it be judged that his victory in the earlier war had been due not to courage but to chance, and that his subsequent defeat had been due to cowardice.

## CHAPTER XXX

By these and similar speeches he brought the soldiers over to his opinion, so that they would go voluntarily with him to Antonius and surrender themselves to him. But the military populace is especially changeable: during the night most of them became troubled in their quarters, regretting their abandonment of Vitellius. They feared that, if he prevailed, there would be no room for pardon for those who had deserted their own emperor.

At daybreak they began first to confer with those they encountered, and then with everyone, about how they might correct their error. Drawing their swords, they attacked Caecina, wishing to avenge the wrong arising from their defection. But the centurions and chiliarchs intervened. Although they thought Caecina should not even be spared death, they nevertheless prepared to send him to Vitellius as a captive [Note: “Bound.” BARR.].

When Antonius learned this, he moved the men whom he had brought with him and attacked the deserters with weapons. On seeing the opposing column, they prepared for battle. But after daring to resist for a short time, when they turned to flee to Cremona, Antonius met them with his cavalry and anticipated every approach, so that the fugitives could not be received. He shut them in before the city and killed them. A very great multitude was slaughtered there; he pursued the rest into the city itself and destroyed them. Everything was plundered, and many inhabitants were killed for the sake of booty while defending their own property.

Thirty thousand two hundred men who belonged to Vitellius’s army were killed. Primus—for that was Antonius’s cognomen—lost four thousand five hundred Mysian soldiers, because the Vitellians, despairing of safety and wishing to avenge themselves, when they saw that they had been surrounded, did not yield victory to the Antonian forces without bloodshed on their own side.

Caecina was released from his chains and sent by Antonius to Vespasian. There he was consoled not only by the security of his life but also by the granting of rewards, which removed the stain of his treachery.

## CHAPTER XXXI

When Sabinus was lifted up by the news of this victory, wishing also to win commendation for himself before the emperor by forestalling Antonius’s arrival through either the destruction or expulsion of Vitellius—or, if Vitellius resisted, by having Antonius arrive, as it was already being reported that he would do at any moment—he gathered a military force from the units stationed at Rome to perform the duties of the watches. During the night he seized the Capitol.

Many of the nobles came to him during the day, among them Domitian, the son of Vespasian’s brother. Fearing that Vitellian vengeance might be diverted against him as Vespasian’s nephew, he found himself placed between two Vitellians and attacked the nearer one, being less concerned about the more distant one—for nearer dangers cause greater fear.

In anger, Vitellius sent Germans against the Capitol. Fierce by reason of the savagery of their nation and stronger in number at the same time, they surrounded Sabinus’s rebellious band. Almost all were killed. Domitian, however, together with many of the nobles, while the Germans were struggling toward the higher parts of the Capitol and were being driven back from the place by Sabinus and his companions, found an opportunity to flee. Or perhaps he was preserved for a public misfortune, as a future tyrant.

Vitellius tortured and killed Sabinus. All the gifts offered to the Capitol were plundered, and the temple was set on fire.

## CHAPTER XXXII

The next day Antonius arrived. The opposing side met him, and after three engagements had been fought around the city walls, all the Vitellians were routed and slaughtered.

Meanwhile Vitellius was feasting, lest he lose his lunch when he died, and, as is customary at the end, was stuffing himself with an excess of dishes for his final table. He buried himself in frequent cups of wine [Col. 2130A], so that he might lose awareness of either the disgrace or the danger that was approaching. He was dragged from the banquet, hauled through the crowd, mocked as he was dying, and subjected to insults that, because he was drunk, he did not feel.

He was killed in the middle of the city, pouring out wine and blood together and belching up his drunkenness. Had he lived longer, he would have squandered the resources of the Roman Empire on the expenses of luxury and the price of banquets. In the end, he ruled for eight months and five days. By then Rome had been exhausted by his gluttony. In addition, more than five hundred thousand of the slain were counted [Note: “More than fifty thousand, more correctly according to Josephus.” ID.].

## CHAPTER XXXIII

On the following day Mucianus and Antonius entered together with the army and scarcely succeeded in putting an end to the slaughter by the maddened soldiers. The soldiers were pursuing the Vitellians, who had presumed to establish the imperial government, and were searching the houses of private citizens. They were driven by such indignation that, when they found some people from the populace hiding out of fear, they struck them as though they were Vitellians before investigation could reveal the truth; so often the fury of the victors anticipated questioning.

Since Vespasian was absent, Mucianus placed Domitian in charge of public affairs, as though in the place of an interregnum [Note: “So that nothing blemish his good fortune.” ID.]. Domitian had not yet been completely possessed by a passion for disgraceful acts; he was still inexperienced in vices and a novice in crimes, as he was in power.

Vespasian, detained by winter and prevented by winds from crossing the sea, returned with his son to Alexandria. There, having learned of the victory and of the favor shown toward him by the Roman populace, he decided to hasten his departure, lest anything be changed in his absence. Yet he did not leave the war in Judaea unattended. He thought it should be entrusted to his son, as the partner and successor in his labors, so that he himself would not be absent from the Romans, nor Vespasian from the Jews, since his son would represent him.

Thus Titus, chosen to carry out his father’s triumph, was sent with a select force. He set out on foot and made for Nicopolis. That city is twenty-four stadia from Alexandria. From there, after the soldiers had been put aboard a fleet of larger ships, he sailed down the Nile as far as the city called Thonis [Note: According to Josephus, “Thmuis” should be written here. ID.]. From there he went on and lodged in a city named Thamna [Note: “The old manuscript reads Tanis, which agrees with Josephus.” ID.]. The second stopping-place for travelers was the city of Heraclea; the third was Pelusium. After spending two days at Pelusium because of the encampment, he traveled through the desert and reached the temple of Jupiter Cassius.

Next came Ostracine, a stopping-place lacking water. Nevertheless, through the diligence of its inhabitants, they had prepared a supply for themselves by constructing water channels. The Rhinocolurans received the advancing army [Note: “Rhinocolura.” ID.] with no small refreshment. The city of Raphaea [Note: “Josephus has Raphia.” ID.] met them; it is the first city of Syria for those traveling from Egypt. They came to Gaza, which was the fifth city for those arriving. From there they went to Ascalon, then to Jamnia [Note: “Thus we have corrected the text. The printed editions incorrectly read Gamnia.” GALLAND.], from which there is a crossing to Joppa, and finally they reached Caesarea.
