There it was necessary to remain for a short time, to gather also the force of soldiers that was still wintering there, since the severity of winter was already abating.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 2131]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 2131A]

In the first year of the imperial power conferred upon Vespasian, Judaea was being torn apart by harsh wars and internal seditions. Nor had it obtained any respite from its troubles during the winter, when the savagery of wars customarily rests. Indeed, a third tyrant, Eleazar, had arisen against it, as though he intended to correct the faults of his predecessors. He had joined in conspiracy with Judas, Simon son of Zeno, and Hezekiah, a young man of no little distinction, whom many others followed. After seizing the inner parts of the Temple and the entire surrounding area, they stationed weapons above the doors, on the front of the very entrance.

John, however, surpassed the conspirators in number and the faction in size, but was inferior in position. Yet he was by no means struck, but resisted those above him, though he was burdened by having enemies above his head. Simon, whom the people had brought in as their tyrant, held the upper parts of the city; the lower parts were also filled with his people.

The city was laboring under a threefold battle within itself: no interruption, no rest, no truce. Fighting took place at every moment. Many fell, countless were slaughtered; blood flowed, defiled everything, and filled the very thresholds of the Temple; corpses fell everywhere. Some were struck by arrows, others by missiles.

John stood between the other two: inferior to Eleazar, superior to Simon. By as much as he was surpassed by Eleazar, by that same amount he surpassed Simon. He occupied the middle position between them [Note: “In which.” BARR.], so that the more he was burdened by one, the more harm he himself did to the other. He was better supplied than the others with siege engines and varieties of missiles and thus matched them in war. Nevertheless, besides those who initiated the war, many priests too were killed and sacrificed among the very victims whom they had slaughtered.

Although a thick harvest of missiles fell upon everyone and battles raged everywhere, the priests nevertheless performed the ministry of sacrifice in due form. They did not abandon the duty entrusted to them; and because they were in the inner parts of the Temple, they were killed all the more severely, since blows driven by engines struck with greater force.

Many also who had come from the farthest parts of the world to pray, hoping for remedies and salvation, became involved in greater dangers the more closely they clung to the Temple. You could see foreigners lying together with citizens, priests together with profane men, the honorable with the shameful, the luxurious with the abstinent. With the blood of all mingled and flowing like a flood, the inner recesses of the Temple itself stood stagnant; all around, everything swelled with blood. Many, while attacking the defenders of opposing factions, slipped, were struck down by the frenzy, and sank into the blood [Note: “As though satisfied.” ID.].

Yet even so, the tyrants’ attendants were not frightened away from battle by the dangers. The greater the danger, the more fiercely the storm of madness raged. If destruction pressed more heavily upon one group, the others were summoned more violently, as though to victory, so that they might overthrow those already thrown into confusion.

Eleazar and Simon at least had the possibility of withdrawing and thereby recovering themselves through something like an interval of hours. John, however, was always in battle array and in combat at every moment. If those above him rested, the lower forces of Simon’s faction pressed him; if he had disturbed these, Eleazar attacked him. Yet John did not allow them to remain quiet either. When he had driven back some, he sprang upon others, ever-watchful in combat and no less tireless in cruelty.

When they spared their missiles, they hurled fire. Once the flames caught the roofs, they consumed the houses, which were filled with grain and other supplies of food intended to sustain a longer war; all were burned together. Greater fuel was given to the fire; burned timbers collapsed, and the roofs of lofty buildings fell.

Thus, by blood, fire, collapse, and famine, the sinews of the whole city were cut. [Col. 2132B] No place was free from danger; no time could be found for deliberation; there was no hope of conversion and no opportunity for flight. Everything was mournful, everything full of horror, everything full of savagery. Everywhere there was mourning, everywhere fear, everywhere the cries of women, the wailing of the old, the groans of the dying, and the despair of the living. You would have called those who remained pitiable and those who had died blessed.

## CHAPTER II

How were you deceived, O city, by your own people, you who once seemed blessed? How have you been conquered by your own arms, and how have your hands been turned against you—hands that once used to conquer without weapons and strike down the enemy without any battle, when angels fought for you and the waves of the sea served as your army, together with the clefts of the earth and the thunderings of heaven?

Rise now, Moses, and see your nation and the inheritance of the people entrusted to you perish by its own hands. Look upon that people of God, for whom the sea opened a pass as they walked, for whom heaven supplied food when they were hungry, who were shut in without the sea, besieged without Pharaoh, and famished without the barrenness of the earth.

Rise, Aaron, who once, when death was devouring many of the people because of the offense against almighty God, stood between the living and the dead; and death stopped, while the plague halted before your body and could not cross into the contagion of the living.

Rise also, Joshua son of Nun, who, while the priests sounded their trumpets, leveled the impregnable walls of Jericho; and see the people to whom you subjected foreigners, now themselves made subject and oppressed.

Rise, David, accustomed to drive away the exasperated spirit with the sweetness of your harp; and see how fury now rules and has blunted all the sweetness of your psalms in the minds of the depraved, while each of the leaders offers the whole people to death in order to extort freedom—the freedom for which you offered yourself to death.

Rise, Elisha, who brought the enemy into Samaria and made him a friend. Through you, in the Syrian camp, there resounded the crash of chariots, the voice of horsemen, and the voice of power. The enemy fled; the Jew escaped the siege. Where now are those merits? Where now are those deeds of the saints?

Nor is it surprising that they have lost the works of the prophets, since they denied the arbiter of the prophets. Therefore Judaea’s weapons are turned against you, and your prayers profit you nothing, because your faith accomplishes nothing. Therefore your people have risen against you, because your faithlessness has turned against you.

What remedy is sought where the author of the remedy is not reconciled? What did you think would happen when you crucified your Savior with your own hands, extinguished your life with your own hands, drove out your advocate with your own voices, and killed your helper by your own denunciations? Nothing except that you would also turn your own hands against yourself.

You have what you asked for. You snatched from yourself the governor of peace; you asked that the arbiter of life be killed; you demanded that Barabbas be granted to you, the man who had been sent to prison because of the insurrection that had occurred in the city and because of murder (Luke 23:19, 25).

Therefore salvation has withdrawn from you, peace has departed, rest has ceased; sedition has been given to you, destruction has been given to you. Recognize that today Barabbas lives for you and Jesus is dead. Therefore sedition reigns in you, and peace has been buried, so that you might perish more cruelly at the hands of your own people than if you had perished at the hands of foreigners.

What did the Roman people bring upon you, wretched city, by their weapons, compared with the evils that your own people brought? When you fought against the Romans, your own people did it. The Romans wanted peace; you declared war. What reason was there for you to provoke the stronger?

It was certainly a serious matter that a Gentile entered the Temple against the sacred law. But you were no longer God’s Temple, no longer God’s city, nor could you be, since you were a tomb of the dead—and especially of your own dead, whom you yourself had killed, not those whom you had lost to the enemy. For how could you be the dwelling-place of life when you were the habitation of death, a lodging-place of crimes, a den of robbers?

Ananus and Jesus, the chief priests, lay unburied within you. They who had once been clothed in priestly robes and had been objects of reverence even to foreigners lay there as shameful corpses, food for birds, prey for dogs, their limbs torn apart and scattered throughout the city [Note: “Dispersed.” BARR.]. It seemed that the appearance of ancient holiness lamented such an insult to the sacred name and the degradation of a once-glorious office.

But you yourself began this disgrace, you who killed the prophets in your midst and stoned the saints of the Lord. Zachariah lay lifeless before the Temple; he lay unburied. So this blood washes him.

What, moreover, was the cause of Ananus’s death except that he rebuked your people for not rising in defense of the Temple? He protested that liberty had been betrayed, courage abandoned, the remnants of the ancient rites trampled underfoot, and the altars defiled. He maintained that the people, now feeling nothing, should be abandoned to the use of lifeless images and marble statues [Note: “Mute.” ID.].

Many animals, after all, are accustomed either to return injury with vengeance, to feel an insult, to be provoked by a goad, or to avoid blows. Therefore one who neither rises up nor knows how to avoid what causes harm is like things that do not feel.

And in truth, where is that liberty of yours, for whose sake you once judged that you must yield neither to the Egyptians, nor to the Palestinians, nor to the Assyrians, and later not even to the Medes? Where is that faith of the Maccabees, which once, through a few men, routed the Babylonians, put the Persians to flight, and struck down Demetrius; which at last, through children and women, overcame the arms, swords, and fires of Antiochus, and preferred to die for the observance of the ancestral law [Note: The word “law,” missing from the printed editions, is supplied here. [Col. 2134D] GALLAND.] rather than obey the commands of a king?

Where is that most beautiful devotion of your fathers, that passion above all passions, by which they offered themselves to death not more for their children or wives than for the Temple of God? Formerly Aaron’s priestly staff also blossomed, cut from a wild root [Note: This word is absent from the manuscript. BARR.]. Now faith too is withered, piety has been buried, and every rivalry in virtue has departed.

Nor is it surprising that the people have withdrawn from God and follow the wicked spirit of contradiction, divided against themselves. For how could they preserve their own peace when they rejected the peace of God? “The peace of God is Christ, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14).

It is therefore deserved that from one people many have become enemies of one another, because they refused to follow Jesus, who unites the divided, and instead followed the spirit of fury, which divides those who were joined.

You were therefore paying the price of your faithlessness, Jerusalem, when you yourself destroyed your defenses with your own hands and pierced your own entrails with your own swords—so that the enemy showed pity while you killed, and he spared while you raged.

For you saw that God was fighting against you and acting on the side of the Romans, so that you yourself might inflict voluntary betrayal upon yourself. For this reason the Romans preferred to be spectators rather than executioners, lest, while your own entrails raged against one another, they should be thought to place their hands upon a contagion rather than upon an act of courage [Note: “Among the maddened.” ID.].

To the punishment for this unspeakable slaughter was added the impious savagery of cruelty: they denied burial to all who had been killed either in the Temple or around the streets of the city. No one had time to bury anyone, since they were occupied with war against one another and everyone was more concerned with striking than with burying.

Thus, in a kind of madness, they killed the duties of piety and grew savage in the service of impiety. Nothing had perished more completely amid such calamities than mercy, which alone is accustomed to lighten miseries and console hardships.

Those who had lost their relatives did not dare to bury them because of fear, since severe terror threatened from the leaders of the opposing faction. Those who had killed others were careful lest someone seize their victims for burial. It was therefore necessary for everyone to fear that what they wished to give to another they might take for themselves—or, worse still, that the use of a tomb which they had prepared for others might not be granted to them themselves.

In the Temple itself, therefore, instead of sweet-smelling ointments, fragrant incense, and the scents of various flowers, there was the oppressive stench of unburied corpses—corpses dissolved by rain, burned by fire, and heated by the sun. All the limbs of the slain citizens reeked with a dreadful odor. On one side, the decay of dismembered entrails; on the other, the stench of the burned—these filled all the senses and mouths of the living, so that they themselves were soon consumed by a more grievous disease and lamented that they had survived, by which they would perish under a harsher punishment.

They had been preserved for this purpose: to see, together with their homeland, the laws of nature themselves undone; the rights of the living denied, peace denied to citizens, burial denied to the dead; human and divine things alike stained and polluted; everything confused; mercy made a crime; cruelty treated as religion.

A fortress in the Temple, war at the threshold, smoke upon the altars: they were witnessing with their eyes what they had refused to believe would happen when the prophets foretold it.

Had not David said of them:

“They have polluted your holy temple;  
they have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven;  
they have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem,  
and there was no one to bury them” (Psalm 78:1, 3)?

At that time too the nations came into God’s inheritance to carry everything away; the Temple was polluted by the funerals of its own people; the corpses of the slain lay unburied as food for birds and ravenous beasts; blood was poured out so that it might stagnate in the Temple, and there was no one to bury the dead. Fury was transferred from the living to the dead, and from the dead to those who still lived.

Someone wished to bury a dead man? He himself was extinguished. The one who had killed the deceased transferred his anger to the gravedigger: he denied burial to the former and killed the latter. Then the one who had killed the gravedigger exercised even greater cruelty against the dead, stripping the corpse—already owing nothing, incapable of feeling punishment—of the final debt owed by nature.

What else could happen to those who did not receive the divine oracles? They mocked the prophets’ announcements and trampled upon every sacred law. They did not believe what was to come, although they themselves hastened its fulfillment.

There was an old and frequent saying that the city of Jerusalem would then perish and its holy places be burned when sedition assailed the law of war and domestic hands polluted the Temple of God. Yet they did not understand even this.

How often had the house of God been destroyed? How often had there been sedition, siege, and war? Yet that city never perished except when they crucified the true Temple of God with domestic hands.

And what was that Temple? Let them hear: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

For what else was it but sacrilege when they stretched out impious hands against the author of salvation, when they stoned him, beat him, rebuked him, and killed him?

Then truly divine fire consumed their sanctuaries. For the Temple burned by the Babylonians was later restored; destroyed by Pompey, it was rebuilt again. But once Jesus came, it was utterly burned, and when it was dissolved by the heat of the divine Spirit, it vanished.

It was fitting that we should precede this funeral of our ancestral solemnity with a more abundant lamentation, follow it as though in a funeral procession, and perform its rites according to the customs of our ancestors. But let us come to the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER III

Titus had returned to Judaea. After a few days had passed, so that the ranks of the military units might be replenished—units from which a selected force had been sent to Italy—he pressed on with the war, hastening to join his father lest he leave him alone to fight against the Vitellian forces.

He therefore set out with the army in great splendor. Everywhere there was desolation, and, with the column prepared, he watched suspiciously for ambushes, since he saw that he was superior in valor.

He came through the territory of Samaria. Gosna received him [Note: “Josephus has Gophna.” BARR.]; it had long since surrendered to the Romans. They came to Aulana, from which Jerusalem was no more than thirty stadia away.

From there, taking six hundred cavalry, he advanced and rode before the city. He also reconnoitered the position of the site, the character of the fortifications, the height of the walls, and the disposition of the populace, which was said to be oppressed by the weapons of robbers and surrounded by the support of factions. Thus, against its will, it submitted to the siege, lest it reveal its goodwill toward the Romans if freedom were granted.

Accordingly, Titus rode in splendid fashion with a few horsemen on the public embankment that led toward the city walls, and no one was seen to come forward. But when he turned his horse to the side in order to make the circuit of the walls, while the rest of the troop [Note: “The squadron.” ID.] followed its commander, many suddenly burst forth from a place called opposite the tomb of Helena. Leaping out, they seized the road in order to surround the larger part of the cavalry that was following Titus.

He himself had passed beyond the ambushers with only a few men, by the ambushers’ design, so that, abandoned by the others, he might more easily be overwhelmed. For it was not easy for him to return to his own men because of the multitude of enemies pressing upon him; nor could he proceed farther, since a ditch or rampart, together with the other obstacles of the terrain, prevented him and exposed him to danger on both sides.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 2136C] Titus, therefore, seeing that the means of safety lay in his own courage, and that there was no other way to open a path except by the sword—for the others had already turned their horses and withdrawn, while they themselves hoped to follow the emperor’s son—turned his horse and urged the others by shouting to follow him. He charged upon the enemy. This would seem impossible, unless it were known how much daring can accomplish in war, since it alone can serve as a wall for itself. Moreover, because the others were following behind him, the common rabble thought that it should be more concerned with its own danger than with pursuing the enemy. [Note: [Col. 2136D] “And if anyone.” ID.] But if anyone extended his hand to seize the horse, he was struck down.

In the end, only two of Titus’s companions were killed; with the rest, the emperor’s son returned to his own men. Nor does it seem at all doubtful that he—bareheaded and otherwise unarmed, since he had advanced on a sortie and was not prepared for battle—had put on neither helmet nor cuirass, and yet suffered no wound, although missiles were being hurled especially at him, because so great a man was being preserved for the destruction of that city. Indeed, indeed, “the heart of a king is in the hand of God” (Prov. 21:1).

Therefore, so that the Jews’ boldness should not increase through the success of their deceit and trickery, he advanced toward the city with the army and returned after nightfall. From a certain lookout point, from which the city and the immense size of the Temple could be seen, he pointed out to his men what kind of city they were at war with, and that they ought to be energetic and more cautious, since an innumerable population, prepared for deception, had to be conquered.

[Col. 2137A] He arranged which ranks should approach the walls. Those whom he knew were still exhausted from the night march he stationed at a distance, as if they were reserve troops. The advance proceeded gradually. When they reached the Mount of Olives, a valley lay between it and the city directly below it; its name was Cedron. When the Jews saw the army drawn up there from the walls—for it was six stadia away—they temporarily laid aside their factional zeal. With foreign enemies arriving, they set aside the contests of civil war under a domestic alliance. For fear often suppresses even bitter hatred.

Finally, the men of the factions urged one another to defend their country with united purpose, lest their dissension give the Romans a bloodless victory. Relying on their numbers, they thought that the enemy should be attacked suddenly, and in an unexpected sortie they threw the first ranks into confusion.

[Col. 2137B] But when the Romans, trained by long experience and by battles of many different kinds, had strengthened their courage and joined their ranks in their customary formation, [Note: [Col. 2137D] “Relying upon.” BARR.] they began to cut down the attackers, drive them back with their shields, and scatter them by throwing missiles—though not without general slaughter. The Jews had almost overwhelmed them, and the Roman line was wavering, when Titus, learning what had happened, arrived. He confronted the enemy, restored the battle, encouraged his own men, and raised the soldiers’ spirits, rebuking the Roman ranks for yielding victory to a confused multitude, not without the greatest disgrace of cowardice.

After the Jews had been repulsed—even those who pursued the Romans divided by the valley—he returned victorious to his own men. Confident in the support afforded by the higher ground against those below, should they attempt an engagement, the Roman army turned toward another area.

[Col. 2137C] [Note: [Col. 2137D] “As Caesar was departing.” ID.] When Caesar withdrew, the Jews poured out from the walls and attacked the enemy in a massive column, so that the soldiers, overwhelmed by the rush of the countless multitude, fled and took themselves to the higher parts of the mountains. With their flank exposed, even the others who preferred to fight began to flee.

Meanwhile Caesar stood in the midst of the people. Although many begged him not to expose himself to danger and, with the army scattered, to bear the whole peril alone—for he was lord of the world, and ought no longer to fight in the role of a soldier but as a commander, whose danger would mean the destruction of everyone—he did not yield. Putting military honor before safety, for him glorious death outweighed the disgrace of life, he presented his chest to the enemy. Those whom he had attacked were terrified, and he turned against others.

[Note: [Col. 2138D] “By appearance alone.” ID.] By the mere sight of him and by the glory of his exceptionally famous and spirited courage, [Col. 2137D] he threw the enemy into confusion. Those whom he approached therefore gave way, but Jews from other directions poured in ever more abundantly. They had almost surrounded Titus, except that many soldiers, seeing Caesar engaged in the midst of the battle, shouted aloud to the others, signaling that the emperor’s son must not be abandoned in danger.

Thus shame recalled and fear armed them all, lest they be branded with the disgrace of having deserted Caesar. Turning against the Jews, with every effort and all their courage they drove the disordered multitude into the valley; and it was not difficult to make those who were climbing fall back. Thus Titus twice recalled the fleeing military force from flight, freeing it equally from danger and disgrace, using courage in both cases, and finally shame. While avoiding cowardice, he inspired courage: first, lest Caesar be abandoned; afterward, so that the enemy might be repelled.

## CHAPTER V

After this, when the battle in the open had briefly subsided, an internal conflict followed. For, taking advantage of the Passover festival, John secretly arranged matters so that many people, as though going to the Temple for the sake of worship, were admitted as if they were allies; and thus he carried out his deception. They entered under the appearance of civilians but armed within. Casting aside their outer garments, they raised swords, their chests protected by armor, and prepared themselves for battle with defensive equipment.

Struck by this terror, those who were unarmed and were celebrating within the Temple rushed out, [Col. 2138B] and abandoned it empty. When John’s men followed them, slaughtering those whom they could catch and pursuing others beyond the circuit of the Temple, an opportunity was given to John and his associates to break in. Many people were killed there, so that even those who had offered no resistance were slaughtered on one pretext or another. Neither the tranquility of rest helped those who were quiet, nor silence those who kept still, nor patience those who gave way.

After John had seized the inner parts of the Temple, he also pressed Simon into a secondary position, setting Eleazar and the other leaders of the third faction in charge under himself.

## CHAPTER VI

For the third time Titus advanced against the enemy and led out the army. On arriving, he encountered a multitude of Jews gathered before the city, apparently wishing to surrender to the Romans, but behaving as though they were afraid. Suspecting a deception—and especially because he had recently seen them united among themselves and obstinate, and did not think it credible that they had suddenly changed—he warned the soldiers to beware of trickery and not to approach the walls rashly except according to his orders and in a compact formation, lest those who had left the city surround them from behind.

Suddenly a sound arose from the city, and a kind of senseless tumult broke out: some pretended to be voluntarily departing, while others resisted; some demanded that the gates be opened to them, while others ordered that they remain closed; some desired war, others peace.

The common soldiers rushed out to aid those who had asked for help from the walls. Many came out precipitately, without order or any proper method, as though they were going to meet the newcomers and bring them assistance. Their purpose was to give greater confidence to those who wished to break out, or fear to those who resisted, or an opportunity to escape to those caught among the opposing groups.

Those who had remained outside began to surround them from behind and press upon the surrounded men. The latter fled as though toward the wall, suspecting nothing from those who had pretended to offer peace. From there, too, stones and missiles were hurled, [Note: [Col. 2138D] “To cast down.” BARR.] and the pretended peace suddenly turned into battle.

Thereupon the Romans rushed back against the enemy. Although the Jews had attempted to surround the Roman soldiers who had advanced, they themselves were also afraid lest they be surrounded by the entire army. Thus, while guarding against the whole force, they almost lost from their grasp those whom they had thought already captured, though they had inflicted many wounds and were themselves wounded for the most part.

Nevertheless, they pursued the Romans as far as the tomb of Helena and, as is customary among those who insult their opponents, clashed their shields, mocking the Romans because they had now been surrounded by ambush twice.

## CHAPTER VII

Caesar, greatly angered, forbade those who were returning to mingle with the others and summoned an assembly. He said:

“Although Roman courage is great and surpasses that of the peoples of all nations, it is especially distinguished by orderly discipline and obedience to commands. That is the safeguard of military discipline. Nor is it surprising that the Jews weave deceptions and devise tricks, since they judge themselves inferior in courage. But just as it belongs to the weaker to rely upon ambushes, so it belongs to the stronger to take care that deception does not mock their courage.

“I therefore wonder that they are consistent with themselves in despair, whereas such conduct does not suit the Romans in the course of better fortunes. Thus it comes about that the success of their deceit is secure, while the exertion of our courage is uncertain. If the strength of the enemy were greater than his deception, it would be less shameful to be defeated. For to be conquered by equals or stronger opponents is free of disgrace.

“But when nothing harms us except the mere lack of restraint in fighting and a certain improper intemperance of our hands, what could be worse than for military discipline to be rejected in Caesar’s presence? I think that the laws of the army themselves deeply lament the disgrace of such great disorder, and that the commander laments greatly when he learns of these things—he who has always preferred to be obeyed by his own soldier rather than feared by the enemy.

“Obedience hastens the soldier’s success; fear of the enemy delays victory. What do you think a father will judge concerning his son whose authority is held in such contempt by the army? For judgment is being pronounced against the commander whose order is disregarded. There is no doubt that punishment has more often been inflicted upon those who fought the enemy against orders than upon those who advanced according to orders and yielded to courage. For the man who leaves the ranks is prescribed death by the laws.

“What, then, will happen when not one man but the army everywhere abandons its formation and disregards the commander’s established order? Recognize that you are soldiers of the Roman Empire, of the common people and the Senate, among whom even victory is a crime without the authority of an order.

“By this speech he terrified not only the officers of the soldiers but also the entire [Col. 2139D] army. For when he pressed the officers of the ranks especially hard, he seemed about to punish everyone. All therefore gathered around him and begged that the fault of the few who had first withdrawn be forgiven for the sake of all.

“Although Caesar was not quick to grant pardon for the offense, he was nevertheless willing to be persuaded to show mercy. He granted forgiveness to everyone, saying with great solemnity that he forgave them all, and that he had sufficiently punished everyone through the force of his rebuke. Punishment against individuals ought to proceed as far as action, but against a multitude only in words; against the former as far as penalty, against the latter as far as correction. For often, in good armies, errors in battle have provided the causes of future courage.” [Note: [Col. 2139D] “For courage.” ID.]

## CHAPTER VIII

After this Titus turned his anger against the enemy. Considering that, amid so many steep and precipitous places, the siege was dangerous, since the soldiers, caught off guard by sudden sorties, had nowhere to fall back, from which to rush against the enemy, or where to set up their siege engines, he ordered the precipices before the city to be filled in.

While this was being done, the Jews were still not free from their present dangers. They were afflicted by internal battle while the Romans were occupied in filling the precipices. No small force stood with Simon: ten thousand men, with fifty commanders; about five thousand Idumaeans also supported his faction. [Col. 2140B] Jacob and the younger Simon commanded those who supported Simon’s faction.

John, having seized the inner parts of the Temple by the deception mentioned above, was surrounded by six thousand armed men and stirred up the war. Two thousand more, together with four hundred other men, joined him later, after they had begun to come together with a common zeal for the defense of the city. Eleazar and Simon Arim, whom they had also previously employed, were their leaders.

While they contended with one another, their people were the spoil lying between the victors and, as though the prize of the contest, were transferred here and there according to the varying outcome. For a short time they had reached an agreement in the manner of a truce, but when awakened by the first Roman attack, they relapsed into their former disease, like an internal fever returning in sickly bowels when the external symptoms of disease had abated.

Outside there was usually war; within, sedition—now more serious because the sedition itself fed the war, and the war fed the sedition. Two men were contending for power; the people between them were not anxious about slavery but about not falling under the worse master.

## CHAPTER IX

Some powerful Canaanite founded the city of Jerusalem, whose name in his native language was said to mean “Righteous King.” He first called it Solyma; afterward he added the Temple, from which the city was called Jerusalem. From the beginning it had its inhabitants from the race of the Canaanites.

David was the first Hebrew to expel the Canaanites and establish his own people there. He built for himself a royal palace in the city. He also wished to build a Temple for God, but, prevented by an oracle, he left Solomon as his heir, so that he might build the Temple which David himself had desired.

Solomon therefore laid the foundations of the Temple. The other kings also added very much to the city’s adornment. Splendor aroused envy. Yet among all the works, the Temple surpassed them in the grandeur of its construction and in its gleaming marble. In it there was [Note: [Col. 2140D] This word is absent from the manuscript. ID.] a walkway, an extremely costly and large curtain, woven of scarlet, hyacinth, fine linen, and purple.

Such a variety of materials was not meaningless; rather, its appearance [Note: [Col. 2140D] “Mystery.” BARR.] signified the substance of hidden things, because the Temple belonged to him who, as creator of the elements, ruled heaven and air, earth and sea, and alone governed and directed everything.

Scarlet represents the fiery heavens; hyacinth, the air; fine linen, the earth, because it is born from it; purple, the sea, since it is dyed with marine shellfish. Thus you may derive two from color and two from origin.

Accordingly, the high priest customarily represented these four things in his clothing whenever there was the greatest solemnity of feast days, as though he were clothing the whole world and was about to intercede for the people in the likeness of the one who was to come as high priest, Jesus, who would take away the sin of the world.

The high priest covered his thighs internally with a linen covering, because above all else faith of mind is sought in a priest, as well as bodily chastity, which ought to gird up the intemperance of the flesh.

There were two sacred tabernacles, one inner and one outer. The priests always entered the outer one; into the inner one, which was called the second, only the high priest entered, and that only once, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sin of the people.

The Holy Spirit signified by this that Jesus would come, who alone would truly enter into the innermost chambers of the divine mysteries and know the secrets of the heavenly substance. He alone would reconcile the whole world to the Father by his blood, so that he might have mercy on both heavenly and earthly things.

Accordingly, after he came, he made peace through the blood of his cross among all things, whether in heaven or on earth (Col. 1:20).

Inside were the incense altar, the table, and the lamp. The incense altar signifies that the prayer of the high priest is directed to God the Father like incense (Ps. 140:2). The table signifies that Christ’s passion and the mysteries of the sacraments are upon it; hence David also says, “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. 22:5). Its twelve loaves signify the twelve apostles, witnesses of his passion and resurrection.

The lamp placed above the lampstand had formerly been beneath a bushel—that is, beneath the measure of the Law. Now it is beneath the fullness of grace, pouring forth abundant light with seven branches, because the Holy Spirit would illuminate the Temple of God with the power of the seven greatest gifts of grace. [Note: [Col. 2141D] “May illuminate.” BARR.]

The knowledge of the Trinity was therefore in the inner part of the Temple, which was called the Holy of Holies. There, once placed, Aaron’s staff blossomed, signifying that priestly grace would accomplish something greater in Christ after death, through which he redeemed the world.

In front of the Temple were fourteen steps. In the time of King Hezekiah, the shadow had ascended these steps, signifying that the end of his life was approaching. But, warned by an oracle, he prayed and obtained an extension of his life; this was shown by the fact that the sun returned over the same steps, signifying that as many years had been added back to his life.

## CHAPTER X

Since the city was fortified on every side by the works of many kings, and especially by those of Herod, who fortified the fortress called Antonia with the most magnificent construction and adorned it with the greatest splendor, Caesar went around searching from what side he could more easily enter the city.

After examining the circuit of the walls all the way around, he judged that the siege should be undertaken at the nearby mound where the high priest John lay buried. While he was examining it more carefully, one of his friends, Nicanor, who was zealously devoted to his duty, was struck by an arrow and fell.

He had approached more closely because he thought that future peace might make progress if he were given an opportunity for conversation; he was regarded as powerful and influential in testing the minds of his hearers.

Caesar was angered that the man who had offered salutary counsel had been killed by an unexpected wound. He drove the ranks into battle, and the war was inflamed by the hurling of various missiles, especially projectiles. Battering rams were brought forward, with which the strong walls were struck.

Disturbed by this, all those who had previously contended among themselves for domination came together in agreement. Given immunity for their earlier actions, they formed a single body, and, united by the pressure of danger, defended the city.

They also advanced onto the mounds and hurled fire upon the machines, intending to destroy the earthworks, burn the covered galleries, and set fire to the battering rams. They had almost burned up every kind of siege machine, unless many soldiers and allies, especially those from the quarter of the city of Alexandria, had bravely resisted.

Although they resisted vigorously, Caesar added the support of stronger cavalry. He himself also fought fiercely and struck down twelve defenders of the opposing line.

[Col. 2142C] Thus the remaining multitude, avoiding destruction, withdrew into the city, while the Roman works were saved from the fire.

In that battle John, the leader of the Idumaeans, fell. While he was before the walls and, having recognized a Roman soldier, entered into conversation with him, he was struck in the back by an arrow wound and immediately collapsed.

They say that an Arab, the most skilled of its javelin throwers, was responsible for his death. The Idumaeans were deeply grieved because they had lost a man both quick with his hands and sound in counsel.

## CHAPTER XI

On the following night it happened that three towers, which Titus had ordered to be raised above the earthwork so that the Jews might be struck by javelins either from equal or higher ground, suddenly collapsed without any force from the enemy.

At the sound, the entire Roman army was thrown into confusion, since they supposed that the enemy had destroyed the earthworks and cut down the towers. As the towers fell, they had caused great destruction over a wide area.

A pitiable disaster was almost committed: the victors were about to yield in flight to enemies who were uncertain because of the night. But the darkness and the collapse itself, raising a cloud of dust, prevented them from seeing, so that they did not know where to flee.

Each man asked the nearest person what had happened, but no one could establish the truth, because the nature of the event was equally unknown to everyone. At last Caesar, having learned what had occurred, ordered it to be made known that the sudden collapse had been caused by accident, not by any enemy sortie.

Thus the panic was calmed, and all the resources for capturing the city were placed in strength. Since the walls were extremely high, and most of them were covered with iron or bronze, and since their very height protected the enemy from missiles, the Romans brought forward battering-ram machines. By their repeated blows the strong walls were loosened. They began to rely upon lighter javelins and arrows in order to drive away the defenders and divert the obstacles that prevented them.

Thus, as the wall was gradually shaken, it gave way. For this reason the Jews called the battering ram itself “the great destroyer of cities.”

When part of the wall had been dismantled, the Jews abandoned the defenses of that wall, confident that they had two other inner walls, and withdrew to the second wall. As they fled, the Romans entered through the hollows of the wall and opened the gates. The entire army was thus admitted and almost demolished the outer wall, lest it obstruct those who were fighting—or, if circumstances went badly, serve as a barrier for those fleeing to it.

## CHAPTER XII

John and Simon, who had conspired together, divided the positions around the second wall. John fought with his men in the fortress called Antonia. Near it was the Temple portico, which extended toward the northern side. The place itself—where the fortress was later built under the name Antonia—lay between two northern porticoes and was called Brios.

Simon, meanwhile, had undertaken the defense of the city near John’s tomb. The Jews were fighting for their survival; the Romans, for victory.

Although courage gave them greater power for engagement, the position was nevertheless inferior for a siege. Since fighting from the wall burdened them, the Jews had the advantage of greater recklessness, while the Romans had sharper courage. Their commanders were present on both sides, and for this reason the contest grew greater, since each man was eager to prove his own dangers to his commanders.

Simon pressed his men by terror and fear. Titus appealed to the Romans especially through shame before him, since they considered it worse than death not to expose themselves to danger before Caesar, when he himself had so often not hesitated to offer himself to danger for the army.

They were armed by the habit of conquering and their ignorance of retreat. Above all, Titus was present as the judge of each man’s courage. From him they expected not merely a reward for bravery but, beyond everything, the richest prize: that, while he watched, they should perform some brave deed that would not displease him.

Moved by this incentive, Longinus, a man of the cavalry, saw the enemy crowds before the walls. As though indignant that they should challenge the Romans in battle and dare to come out on equal terms, he leaped from his horse and threw himself into the midst of the enemy.

He struck in the mouth one man who was preparing to meet him, [Note: [Col. 2143D] “In the mouth.” ID.] and at the same time took both his voice and his life. He pulled a weapon from the body of a fallen man and drove it into another, then withdrew victoriously to his own men.

We speak of the most distinguished men; many others imitated them on both sides, though in different ways. Despair gave the Jews boldness; desire for glory gave the Romans courage. The contempt of death was equal, though their spirits were unequal. For the Jews it was considered a consolation to die together with the enemy.

Titus hastened to finish the war, but without loss to his own men; indeed, if he could, he preferred to preserve the enemy themselves rather than destroy them. He gave the soldiers no other warning than that they should fight deliberately. That alone was true courage which was accompanied by foresight. Without deliberation, courage seemed to be recklessness, and nowhere was greater caution required than in victory.

For when a superior perishes together with an inferior, it is a triumph for the defeated. Care therefore had to be taken lest the outcome appear to have been accidental because he won, or the result of cowardice because he had failed to escape sharing the danger.

He therefore ordered the battering ram to be brought against the middle of the northern wall.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 2144B] Castor was there, a crafty man prepared for deception. After the others had been driven away by the archers’ missiles, he presented himself with nine companions in a new deception. [Note: [Col. 2144D] “Nine.” Josephus: ten. ID.] When he observed that, under the battering ram’s assault, the tower was being overturned and the wall was giving way and would easily collapse if the engine’s blow were repeated, he extended his hands and begged Caesar in a pitiful voice to spare the doomed city now, and not to think that it should be weakened for ultimate destruction.

Caesar judged that he was earnestly begging for mercy. Since he was about to grant it on the condition that surrender should precede, he ordered the blows of the engines to cease and the javelin throwers to hold back from battle. He gave Castor an opportunity to speak.

Castor pretended to descend, then as though to persuade his own men. Some, he claimed, wished to surrender; others resisted. Suddenly, as though indignant at being compelled, they struck themselves above their cuirasses and fell.

It was an astonishing spectacle. While the deception remained hidden, they thus prolonged the time. [Note: [Col. 2144D] “To delay.” ID.]

During this, one of the Roman soldiers struck Castor’s nostril with an arrow. Castor lamented and complained to Caesar and asked him to order someone to give him his right hand, saying that he would use it to escape.

Caesar entrusted the task to Josephus. But Josephus, who was on guard against the Jews’ ambushes, replied that he understood nothing sincere in Castor.

Nevertheless, Aeneas approached nearer to the wall and went to meet Castor in order to receive him as he came. Castor shouted at him to open his cloak so that he might catch the gold, and dropped a stone.

With watchful eyes Aeneas saw the stone in advance and escaped the fall with a swift leap of his body. Yet the huge collapse of the stone overwhelmed another man standing nearby.

When Caesar saw this, he pressed more vigorously toward the overthrow of the walls and ordered the engines to be driven forward with greater force. In response, fires were hurled to burn the machines. But when the wall had been loosened, Castor and his men threw themselves as though into the fire, disguising their trickery under the appearance of greatness of spirit in contempt of death, when in fact they were deceitfully seeking a means of escape for their lives.

## CHAPTER XIV

Only one wall remained—that is, the third—after the other two had been overthrown. Yet Caesar still exercised patience, since he had realized that whatever was destroyed would already be lost to him.

While he spared them and invited surrender without waiting for the army to advance, he rushed with a few men upon the second wall. The Jews, gathering their forces in the confined spaces, wounded many; many were also killed on both sides.

Then Caesar struck the resisting Jews from a distance with arrows. Among the tightly packed ranks, the missiles could nowhere be avoided; no blow fell without causing a wound.

The Jews therefore began to withdraw, and Titus recalled his men. Famine had already severely afflicted the city. Yet the Jews rejoiced as though they were the victors, because they had withdrawn inside the second wall, as though the Romans had been expelled. But they could neither repair what had fallen nor defend what was about to fall.

They nevertheless resisted for some time. The battle at the second wall lasted three days. On the fourth day, unable to withstand Roman courage, they withdrew inside the third wall.

In the meantime Caesar ordered the attack to be suspended, but commanded that the second wall be demolished. Since the greater part of the war still remained, he arranged that the soldiers should transport food for themselves, lest the victors be pressed by scarcity and afflicted by want.

For four days the soldiers carried grain for themselves. At the same time, it seemed a suitable moment for the Jews, if they wished to save themselves, to change their course. The people did indeed prefer this, but the leaders of the sedition considered the grave crimes they had committed against the populace. Since they hoped for no opportunity of pardon, they thought it lighter to perish with everyone than for the instigators alone to perish. [Note: [Col. 2145D] “They hoped.” BARR.]

On the fifth day, therefore, since the Jews brought no peaceful proposal, Caesar attacked the walls with a double formation. He ordered two earthworks to be raised: one against Antonia, the other against the wall that stood opposite John’s tomb.

By the latter he sought the destruction of the upper city; by the other, if he captured the fortress, he would easily also take possession of the Temple. Unless he brought it under his authority, he could not hold the city without danger.

Titus had divided the army into two formations. On the opposite side, John and Simon had likewise assigned themselves the duties of defense. John defended Antonia; Simon, with his armed men and the people of Idumaea, watched over the area near John’s tomb. From the higher position they frustrated by every means they could the efforts of the besiegers.

They had now become more practiced, taught by misfortune how to confront siege engines. They had also acquired for themselves several kinds of engines with which to destroy the Roman works and obstruct what had been begun.

When Caesar observed their reckless obstinacy, he wished to mingle speech with the military works, lest perhaps they should resist more stubbornly in despair of pardon, and perhaps might desist in hope of his promises.

He therefore began to urge them not to involve themselves in the destruction of a captured city, but to surrender it to his authority. It was already held by arms and, enclosed by the siege, was being pressed toward final destruction. He promised pardon to those who yielded, provided that they cared either for themselves or for their country, so that the whole city might not be demolished.

He also sent word to Josephus that he should address his fellow citizens in their native language, so that perhaps he himself might bend his countrymen and persuade them to renounce their own madness. [Note: [Col. 2145D] “If perhaps.” ID.]

Although Josephus knew the hatred of the Jews toward him, he nevertheless withdrew from the walls as far as an arrow’s shot, and yet close enough to be heard. In the language familiar to them, he continued an address intended to benefit his fellow citizens.

## CHAPTER XV
Before matters reached their final extremity, Hebrews, it had been the stubbornness of human nature to contend obstinately, while you thought that you would prove superior through your position and through the defenses of a well-known region. It is true that it would have been proper not to challenge the Romans, unconquerable in war, with weapons—Romans by whom those who had conquered you were themselves often defeated. Yet human imprudence has this failing amid prosperity, especially because the outcome of war is generally uncertain: and therefore each man entrusts himself to Fortune [Note: [Col. 2146D] *Sorti*, “to Fortune.” ID.], inferior though he may be in courage.

Finally, once the walls have been overcome, do you not think that the destruction of the temple as well must follow? Spare the shrines, spare the altars, spare the dwelling that was once heavenly [Col. 2146B]. For now God Himself has abandoned you, because you have abandoned the worship of piety. We have endured war in the midst of the temple; fires surround the temple and range about it. But the armed men standing around it are not of the kind they used to be. Nevertheless, while the Romans still have hands clean of sacrilege, they wish to spare you and not defile the sacred doors, nor abolish the ancient rites—if you will allow them. What more is being awaited? Two walls have been overthrown; the third remains, and it is itself weaker than the two that have fallen.

Or is divine protection hoped for, and help from the innermost sanctuary? But he who was defending us has gone over to the enemy, because the one whom we worshiped the Romans venerate, while we offended him. Who, moreover, does not know that God is with those who have subjected everything to themselves, except what is inaccessible because of excessive heat or cold? And therefore, outside the Roman empire, no one denies that God has at different times given the power over the same realms, beyond ordinary human use, to different peoples: first to the Egyptians, later to the Jews, and likewise that He was a helper to the Assyrians and Persians; afterward He turned to the Romans and remains with them. Finally, He has yielded all kingdoms to them and given the whole earth into their possession.

What have you to do with the conquerors of the whole earth, whom the secrets of the ocean and the furthest regions of India obey? Why should I add Britain, separated from the whole world by the intervening sea and brought by the Romans into the circle of the civilized world? Scotland trembles before them, though it owes nothing to the lands of the world; Saxony trembles, inaccessible through its marshes and enclosed by impassable regions. Although this seems to increase the burden of war, it too has often entered Roman triumphs as a captive. It is said to be a most powerful race of men, surpassing the others; nevertheless, it relies not on strength but on pirate vessels (*myoparones*) [Col. 2146D], prepared for flight rather than for battle.

But you reply that it is better to die than to lose freedom. When, Jews, did this opinion ever prevail among you? Or when among the Hebrews was servitude useful without being preferred to an unprofitable freedom? Jacob himself, the patriarch, brought the Hebrews down into Egypt so that they might not perish from hunger. The patriarchs descended, together with his twelve sons, those illustrious beginnings of our race. There was that Judas, distinguished in the lineage of the Jews, who gave his name to the people. There Joseph, exalted in a chariot and with horses, preferred to subject himself to authority in order to feed his own people rather than return to the freedom of his native origin. There Benjamin, piously detained by the stratagem of his brother, consented to the deception, because it was no crime to serve those more powerful. There their inheritance, when Moses summoned them, nevertheless desired to remain there. Thus even harsh servitude did not displease your fathers, since they preferred it to dangers.

You served the Egyptians—and would that you had served them only once! But you served them not only then, when by the rains of heavenly food you preferred the sustenance of servitude to its extremities; you also later descended into Egypt as defeated captives, when you were fleeing from the Assyrians. You served the Assyrians through many cycles of years, and that servitude was sweet. You served the Macedonians, Persians, Seleucids, and Palestinians [Note: [Col. 2147D] “That is, the Seleucids. Yet here one may doubt whether ‘Persians, Seleucids’ should be read as one continuous phrase, as though the former word contained the higher genus and the latter τὸ διοριστικόν, or distinguishing characteristic; or whether the words should instead be separated by a medial distinction. MAZOCH, cited work, p. 788.]. Do you alone consider the Romans burdensome, although those to whom you were subject also serve them?

Do you therefore owe these men hatred or gratitude, since they have made you equal with your masters? I regard this as vengeance on your behalf, not an insult, because they have avenged you upon those to whom you were subject. The Assyrian, who ruled all Asia, is pressed by servitude. The Egyptian plows for the Romans and strikes from his own land what that man reaps [Note: [Col. 2147D] “For them.” BARR.]. Macedonia, which had extended its empire as far as India after conquering Persia, recognizes masters whom it did not know and remembers in vain that it bestowed upon its kings the name of the Aeacids. Certainly it yielded on no other occasion than to the triumph of the Romans. Pyrrhus himself, bearing both the lineage and the name of the offspring of Achilles, was defeated in war and so subjected himself in his desire to obtain peace that he begged pardon.

What should I say about the Palestinians, whom the authority of a single governor restrains? Ungrateful men, is it not your own nobility to serve together with the Persians? For this is what it means: to serve with your kings and to have the greatest kingdom as a partner in subjection. But I ask: when were you free, you who now reject servitude? When, then, were you free? Or were you free when you ruled over others while you yourselves were under a king? You had God as your king; you rejected His kingdom, under which alone you were free, and you chose to serve human beings.

Why do you tear up the testaments of your fathers? An inheritance rebellious even against its fathers! You chose a king named Saul. After he was killed, a Palestinian people ruled over you. After a time David succeeded to the kingdom of the whole people, gentler indeed than his master, but nevertheless a master; and before David had come to rest, he too imposed a king upon the nation.

From Solomon onward the kingdom was again split in two, and its inheritance was divided through a long succession of dominion. To pass over the captivities: Cyrus restored many Jews to their own lands and sacred institutions. But your fathers, though they were worn down by the severe wars of the Persians, chose Roman alliance, although they were ennobled by the triumphs of the Maccabees.

Divine Scripture preserves the treaties of many embassies [Note: [Col. 2148D] “You see how our author calls the Maccabean books, in which those treaties are set out, divine Scripture. So too, above, in the prologue to this work, he calls the Maccabean books *theopneustos* (θεοπνεύστους), ‘God-inspired.’ MAZOCH, cited work, pp. 788, 852.]. You became friends of the Romans, you who had been servants of the Persians.

But again you preferred to have a king rather than a chief priest [Note: [Col. 2148D] “Priest.” BARR.], to whom the people might obey, when the cruelty of your own kings had become intolerable. After Herod’s death and Archelaus’s expulsion, you asked to be under the Roman Caesar. You handed yourselves over to Caesar, whom you all served in order to exchange one form of servitude for a better one.

For in the common condition of serving all alike, there is a certain freedom, since the obedience of servants is ennobled by the dignity of their rulers. Yet the Romans, founders of liberty, do not exact servitude, because they not only killed a cruel king but also refused to endure an arrogant one. Therefore among them the name of empire is august, because it increases its own people, not because it oppresses foreigners.

But granted that it is useful for you not to obey the Roman empire: let us see whether it is freedom, and whether it is not deadly. The Roman armies press upon you; the ruins of your homeland press upon you; the destruction of the temple presses upon you. Consider not what is useful but what is possible. For it is not the appearance of your wishes but the calculation of possibility that must be weighed.

The law of nature, infused equally into all human beings, birds, wild creatures, and beasts, is that each yields to the stronger: the bull to the lion; the deer to the bear; the leopard to the doe; the hawk to the eagle; the dove to the hawk; young bulls to the bull itself; flocks of sheep to the ram; the goat to the he-goat. So that no distinction based on different kinds may seem to intervene: you yield to those more powerful. Yet the Romans expel no one; you have expelled them. Indeed, they act so that not even the defeated may depart from their own lands: they preserved part of his kingdom for Antiochus.

And now what else is Caesar striving for except that your land not be abandoned, your region not be emptied, your city not be overthrown, and your temple not be burned? Victory is not given to everyone. Nature has given a few command over many, and many obedience to a few. Bulls rise above herds; rams above flocks. Preeminence belongs to the few, gentleness to the many. Put on gentleness yourselves; accept subjection, which even wild animals put on.

When Josephus said this, they abused him from the wall. They cursed the man advising what was useful. Many even hurled arrows, if they could injure him with death. But he, who could not bend the untamed by his speech, thought that they must also be confronted with testimonies from the Scriptures, especially since they were saying that God would not fail to protect His temple.

## CHAPTER XVI

Fools, is it only now that you hope divine help will come to you, when you have mixed everything with war, violated the altars, and demolished the defenses of the entire city? Fools, I say, and forgetful of your former sources of help: you have prepared shields and swords—and this against the Romans. You were not accustomed to conquer with such weapons. When did the victory of the Hebrews ever lie in spear and sword? Remember from where you originated and from whom you proceeded; remember how your fathers conquered their enemies.

Fools, whom have you deprived yourselves of as a helper while asking for foreign support? It was not through a multitude of people but through fear of God that our father Abraham [Note: [Col. 2149D] “An old manuscript: priest.” BARR.] entered Egypt. When he saw the chastity of his abducted wife held captive, he nevertheless refrained from war. He took up the weapons of pious prayer and brought in a defender who, while Abraham slept, conquered and restored his wife undefiled after defeating the enemy.

Sarah returned without weapons, bringing her husband a triumphal victory. Abraham slept, and Pharaoh was tormented. Sarah feared, and Pharaoh denied the crime. He expelled another man’s wife and, after condemning the crime, honored the chastity he had desired to despoil. Gold and silver were added to Sarah’s honor, so that they might condemn an intention untouched by the deed [Col. 2149B]. He asked father Abraham to pray to the Lord on behalf of his household. For his house was barren. Sarah returned richer, her honor safe; Abraham returned holier, having exchanged the reward of conjugal chastity for a remedy against sterility.

What should I say about his son Isaac? He too, relying on his father’s protection, did not lead out armed ranks against the arrogance of a powerful neighbor. Yet certainly he possessed a strong force of 318 household servants, which had defeated five kings in battle, stripped them of their spoils, and restored the captive Lot to Abraham, his uncle. He did not draw his sword from its sheath; instead he put on patience alone against those who envied him and displayed his innocence. Those who had announced that he must be exterminated came asking for peace; those who could not tolerate a neighbor sought friendship.

I tremble to recount so many marvels of our fathers. The holy Jacob, when his brother Esau threatened parricide, left his homeland, abandoned his parents, and carried with him as provisions nothing but prayer. Therefore, while he feared his brother’s ambushes in foreign places and lacked human companionship and aid, he found the counsel [Note: [Col. 2149D] “I would prefer ‘council,’ that is, a gathering or host, both from sacred history and from the author’s context.” GALLAND.] of angels. Led, as he says, to the camp of God, he wrestled with the Lord; and, as Scripture says: “He prevailed with God, although he considered himself unequal to men” (Gen. 32:28).

What else did Moses raise against the king of Egypt, his army, and his dragons, except a single staff? O mighty staff, which covered the heaven with darkness, flooded the earth with rains, and dried the waves of the sea! The Egyptians had surrounded the Hebrews. Moses prayed and did not fight. The sea was divided, and the people entered; Pharaoh followed. Moses, stationed amid the waves, prayed; Pharaoh was drowned with his people, and Moses sang (Exod. 15:4).

Who, considering these and similar events, would not marvel and understand that prayer gives us better weapons than strength? The former brings divine help to itself; the latter has only the body. Jesus son of Nave, the disciple and likewise successor of Moses, learned these weapons, which are not carnal but powerful with God. An imitator and equal of his teacher, he turned back the waters of the Jordan. When he saw the impregnable walls of the city of Jericho, he ordered the priests to sing and the people to shout. At this the walls suddenly fell, the city was burned, and all were killed except those whom the faith of Rahab the harlot protected from the destruction of the aforesaid city.

Gideon too chose three hundred men for war and ordered them not to carry weapons but mysteries: in the left hand they were to hold jars full of water, and in the right, torches. Struck with terror by this sight, the enemy immediately fled, and victory came to the Hebrews.

The care of sacred religion had been interrupted through the negligence of Eli the priest, and divine commands [Note: [Col. 2149D] “Were being deferred.” BARR.] were being neglected. When the Philistines [“Allophyles”] brought on a battle, the Hebrews were defeated, and even the ark of God was captured and surrendered to them without weapons. By this sign it became clear both that weapons do not conquer without religion and that religion can conquer without weapons.

King Hezekiah, when the Assyrian people had poured into the Jewish nation, had learned what insults against God were being hurled by the voice of Rabshakeh at the command of King Sennacherib and what ultimate disasters were being threatened against the people. He believed that words were not to be answered with words, nor weapons with weapons. Instead, rising, he clothed himself in sackcloth as in a shield; for a helmet he covered his head with ashes; for javelins he hurled prayer.

Prayer ascended; the angel descended. During the night we counted 185,000 Assyrian corpses, but we did not see the one who struck them.

I had passed over the five kings who, having undertaken war without consulting the Lord, began to be severely afflicted as they traveled through the desert because of the lack of water; thirst tormented both them and their horses. Necessity compelled them to restore the duty they had neglected. The king of Israel had been careless concerning the worship of God. Yet, when others advised him to seek the Lord’s prophet, he learned from those same men where Elisha was living and that he was not far away. They earnestly begged for the help of prayer and remedies for their necessity.

Although Elisha was offended with the king of Israel because that faithless man did not believe, he nevertheless promised both an abundance of water and the speed of victory. Water began to flow through the desert, and streams poured themselves spontaneously over the earth without any rain. The opposing forces rose. Their sleep, prolonged by the security of victory and relaxed concern, had weighed upon them. Suddenly they saw the waters gleaming red in the sunlight. Some thought that the kings’ peoples had fought among themselves and that the earth was wet with their blood. Therefore they rushed everywhere to seize the spoils, without order or restraint, each trying to outstrip the other. Thus, rushing into the midst of their enemies, they were surrounded, killed, and gave their own people a great slaughter.

Thus the holy prophet [Note: [Col. 2150D] “Saint.” ID.], having been entreated by our fathers, drove away both thirst and fear, and likewise brought help against hunger. For when Samaria was under siege and the king of Israel remained shut up within it, a severe famine pressed upon them, so that they did not abstain even from impious foods. The prophet was summoned because of the horror of such misery, and also because of the king’s messenger, who thought that the famine had grown worse through the prophet’s concealment. He replied: “On the following day you shall see both an abundance of grain and cheapness” (2 Kings 7:1).

To the messenger who did not believe, he said that the man himself, because he did not believe, would not see it, but that faith in the promises would not fail. Suddenly during the night, in the Syrian camp, the neighing of horses, the crashing of chariots, the rumbling of racing four-horse teams, and the clatter of weapons struck fear by their sound into the victors. They thought that numerous and powerful nations had come to the aid of the Hebrews, and they hurried to escape the danger they believed imminent. Night hastened their decision and increased their terror.

When the Assyrians fled, all the supplies they had seized were found in the camp on the following day. Abundance created cheapness, and cheapness fulfilled faith. Death deprived the unbelieving man himself of the benefit, but did not obstruct the public remedy.

It is therefore clear that many leaders of our fathers obtained victory without fighting at all, while others also proved superior in war—those to whom, when they sought counsel, the right to wage war had been granted by an oracle.

In the end, Amalek was defeated—but while Moses raised his hands. Jesus son of Nave conquered when he made the sun stand still. Gideon conquered when he tested those who would fight in the water. Samson conquered while he still preserved his hair undefiled. Samuel conquered when he proposed to set up a stone as a helper.

David triumphed when he joined Bathsheba—that is, “daughter of the Sabbath”—to his marriage through prophetic ministrations [Note: [Col. 2151D] “Mysteries.” ID. — “The holy Father has two such passages in his *Second Apology for David*, chapter 10, no. 51. ‘Finally,’ he says, ‘so that you may know that there is a mystery, interpret the names . . . BETHSABEE, DAUGHTER OF THE SABBATH,’ etc. [Col. 2152D] MAZOCH, cited work, p. 851.]. He also conquered in the civil war that he avoided being drawn into. He alone, though he could have initiated it, did not initiate it—for nothing is more disgraceful than civil war. Jonathan [Note: [Col. 2152D] “From the context, Jonathan seems to be the reading.” GALLAND.] too conquered in battle, but only after he had said to his despairing men, because they were inferior in number, that it made no difference whether they were few or many, since God makes a few who fear Him stronger than many (1 Kings 14:6).

A good man indeed in faith, if only he had persevered to the end. A woman too conquered with weapons because she preserved her faith in God. Saul, however, was defeated because he did not keep God’s command. Josiah was wounded because he advanced against the enemy contrary to the command. Otherwise he was holy, and therefore he was taken away so that he would not see the captivity due to our sins.

Nachao cried out: “I was not sent to you,” bearing witness to his faith; but association with a degenerate alliance overwhelmed him, just as it had previously overwhelmed Amaziah. In the end, a man of God had warned him to dismiss those whom he had hired for an alliance in war for one hundred talents of silver, if he wished to conquer. When he hesitated because he would lose so great a price, the prophet replied that the Lord had more from which He could even restore that silver to him. Trusting in this, he dismissed the hired auxiliaries and conquered with fewer men.

He did not even pay God the price of so great a victory [Note: [Col. 2152D] “Perhaps, ‘not even he.’” ID.]. Instead, immediately he offered sacrifices to the very idols he had captured as victor, as though he had conquered through their benefit, after reducing them to the spoil of captivity.

Zedekiah too, when the ruins of his homeland were already pressing upon him and he was being crushed by the enemy siege, was summoned by the prophet Jeremiah. He was told not to fear leaving the city and that he would be victorious if he obeyed the commands of heaven, or a captive if he thought it necessary to defend it. Through his faithlessness he deceived himself and his people.

The Jewish people had been carried away by the Assyrians into Babylon. Those who remained were considering transferring themselves to the Egyptians who had settled there. Through the prophet Jeremiah and the others, the Lord commanded them to be content with the rule of a single nation, lest doubled captivity increase their misery. But they set aside God’s oracles and became captives of two nations, although they had impatiently desired to escape the yoke of one nation. Thus they remained exiles in Egypt.

Those, however, who had been led away among the Assyrians, after the period of captivity that the Lord had appointed for the sins of the people had been completed, later, under the rule of Cyrus, obtained permission to return and came back with thanksgiving. The temple of God was renewed through the resources of the kings and the gifts of Cyrus, Darius, and the other Persians. Those very men who had destroyed it supplied the expense of restoring it; they also restored the rights of the priests and assisted the worship of religion.

But our people, while they competed among themselves for the priesthood and sought among the Parthians to have that honor conferred upon them, made religion a commodity. Why should we complain about the Babylonians? We have found our own people worse. The Babylonians returned to us every religious right [Note: [Col. 2152D] “This word is absent in some copies.” BARR.]; they restored the appointment of priests, while our own people sold it back to the Persians. They permitted the priestly bands to remain in our power; our own people made them tributary to the Babylonians.

What more should I add—the sanctuary stained with blood, the sacred thresholds soaked, the rooflines of the temple still standing half-ruined? God’s anger against us is less than our own contention. The former made us captives; the latter made us sacrilegious. The former scattered the Jews; the latter destroyed them.

Compare, if you please, the difference between our captivity and our rebellion. Our captivity spread the fellowship of our religion among the nations; our rebellion deprived even Jews of the favor of religion.

Who introduced the Romans into Judaea, except the rivalry of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus? Who introduced Sosius, except Herod? Who introduced Antony, except Sosius? Who implored Caesar to provide a king for himself, except you? Who else besides you expelled Antipater from the kingdom and placed freedom in the hands of Antipater?

And yet I do not accuse or deny that Florus acted criminally against you. But the complaint ought to have been brought to the Romans, not weapons employed against them. You rejected Nero, but Vespasian had succeeded him. By nature benevolent, he could have been still more benevolent out of personal inclination, because he had assumed command in Judaea. Or, if compassion did not move you, his valor certainly ought to have compelled you to look to your own interests.

But how could he not spare you, when he spared Joseph? For against whom should he have been more hostile than against me? Who built stronger defenses against the Romans? Who thought more earnestly that he must contend for his country [Note: [Col. 2152D] “Or, ‘that he must fight’? But I alter nothing. For among ancient authors *decerno* is sometimes used absolutely for ‘to fight.’ Nepos, *Hannibal* 4: ‘When he unexpectedly engaged this same enemy at Clastidium by the Po.’” GALLAND.]?

After you had come to favor the condition of warfare [Note: [Col. 2153D] “Of waging war.” BARR.], I did not approve the beginnings of the wars, but once they had been undertaken I did not abandon them. The ashes of the city of Jotapata bear witness to this: they sheltered me while I was still fighting, and I did not abandon the war until the city itself had been destroyed. I remained hidden as long as I could in the tomb of that overthrown city. I endured hunger so as not to surrender myself to the Romans. I sought ways of coming to you. But when I was discovered, I did not depart willingly; I preferred to perish with my people, but Caesar spared me. I preferred to face danger with you—not because I approved your plan, but because I chose to share danger with you.

Yet I give thanks to God that I did not fall into participation in so great a crime, lest I be considered an instigator of rebellions; or, since I could not become involved in these matters, lest I complete the parricide—or the death—that I could have avoided by my own hand [Note: [Col. 2153D] “You should think that nothing should be added or changed. Livy, book 4, chapter 41: ‘While I was avoiding this formidable enemy, I seem unexpectedly to have fallen into an engagement, or to have encountered him.’”].

Certainly, lest I see my most holy mother torn apart for my sake, and the limbs of my people scattered—things pitiable indeed, but nevertheless more tolerable to suffer than to have inflicted.

What, then, are you still awaiting? The standards of our ancestors? We do not possess such merits, nor such duties toward the worship of God. Nor do we possess the standards of the Romans, such as the treachery of the Assyrians, who, after receiving payment for their withdrawal, broke faith and thought that they should not retreat but press forward more fiercely.
