Indeed, if we gather from events that have occurred the movement of the divine judgment, it is certain that God is opposed to the Jews. In the end, the spring of Siloam, which had been dry before the war, and all the channels of the springs outside the city, whose flow had long ceased so that water was unavailable for our use except at a price, now return to their customary use and pour themselves out for Titus on his arrival. Abundant springs gush forth, and everything is filled with overflowing waters, so that they provide not only a lavish supply for the army to drink but also enough for the horses, soldiers, pack animals, and all the livestock. There is likewise no shortage of water for irrigating the gardens. You would think that the channels were flowing more generously as though the elements themselves were striving to aid the Roman victory.

We recognize the earlier prodigies, which also preceded the captivity of our city at that time: water ceased for the Jews but poured itself out for the enemy, lest thirst impede the siege.

Nor is it surprising if divine favor withdrew from the Jews, whom such great crimes have surrounded. Does a good man not avoid a dwelling full of horror? Does he not abandon his house if he learns that some crime has been committed in it? He shuns association with an unworthy habitation and curses the iniquities of those who dwell together there. Do we doubt, then, that the supreme and immaculate God abhors the contagion of such great crimes and turns away from the atrocity of murderous deeds, refusing to remain among bands of parricides—the God who commanded Dathan and Abiram to be separated from the innocent because they had challenged Moses and Aaron by usurping the priestly office, lest the pious either be defiled by association with the guilty or become involved in their punishment?

But why do I linger any longer in speeches, when everything around us is filled with horror and lamentation and the temple’s destruction is hastening? Who can watch this with his eyes, endure it with his senses, or tolerate it in his heart? O men harder than rocks, more rigid than iron, who, amid such prodigies of human affairs, still contend among yourselves over crime as though striving for a prize of virtue—and, what is more grievous, you yourselves destroy your homeland and increase its ruin!

Turn back at last; come to your senses at last; judge and see the beauty of the homeland that you have betrayed. What city, what temple, what dwelling places of the holy, what inner sanctuaries of sacred things, what works of the prophets are being torn open by your hands? Can anyone bring flames against these things, scatter fires, and feed the conflagration without being moved by any feeling? If rocks could feel, their hardness would dissolve.

Certainly even things without sensation often imitate the appearance of feeling amid the greatest bitterness of events [Note: [Col. 2154D] “They pretend.” BARR.], so that cliffs tremble and drops dripping with blood flow. Yet you remain unmoved, so that one wonders what better thing could remain afterward, what more worthy object you could reserve [Note: [Col. 2154D] “And thus, what else?” ID.].

Finally, if these things do not move you because greater matters are valued among the pious, at least have pity on your own relations. Place before your eyes the deaths of your children, whether by sword or hunger, and—more bitter than these—the servitude of your wives and daughters, for whom secure freedom will be available by a pact of surrender, or captive servitude through the destruction of the city [Note: [Col. 2154D] “Perhaps ‘captive servitude.’ Namely: ‘either secure freedom by a pact of surrender, or captive servitude through the destruction of the city.’ The former would arise from surrender, the latter from the city’s destruction.” GALLAND.].

Look to your interests while you may, lest after death you leave behind things more grievous than those you committed before death. Nor am I free from this danger. I know that my most holy mother, dear to me, and my wife, of no ignoble lineage and once belonging to a distinguished household, are endangered together with your people.

Perhaps you think that I urge these things because of my own family. Kill them, then, and take my blood as an additional reward. I shall gladly pay this price for your salvation, if after me you can come to your senses.

## CHAPTER XVII

When Josephus cried out these words with tears, he moved many of the people to flee to the Romans, selling what they possessed. Titus assigned each of them wherever he wished, so that the others too might be encouraged to surrender themselves to the Romans without fear.

Thus they streamed out whenever an opportunity to leave was found, secure of their safety if they came over to the Romans and unconcerned about servitude, since freedom would be preserved for them.

But those who followed John and Simon, the arbiters and instigators of the rebellion, feared the punishments for their crimes more than the hardships of war. Therefore they considered their refuges unsafe. Not only did they themselves not dare to leave, but they also set ambushes so that no one from the people would be permitted to depart from the city. They were more concerned to prevent their own people from escaping than to guard against the Romans’ entrance.

They were therefore held unwillingly; and if anyone was caught, he paid severe penalties. A slight suspicion became the gravest cause of death. Truth was sought not through evidence but through punishments. If any were wealthy, they were dragged to death on a fabricated charge of rebellion [Note: [Col. 2155D] “Treason.” BARR.]. If any were poor, because they had nothing with which to ransom themselves, they were exposed to death.

## CHAPTER XVIII
And now severe famine began to rage, while the sedition grew still more violent in its fury and madness. Grain could not be found, and no bread was available for public consumption. Wherever it was discovered that any existed, the house was immediately stormed. The master of the house was slaughtered as the keeper of grain that he had concealed. When no crops were found again, torture was inflicted, as though they had been hidden more carefully. Most people longed for the relief of death, whether famine afflicted them or cruelty [Col. 2155B] tormented them.

Finally, those who were older disdained to kill them, begrudging the gift of death to those whom famine, already a more ferocious executioner, had reduced to pitiable emaciation, their entrails consumed and their bare bones covered only by [Note: [Col. 2155D] Thin skin. ID.] thin skin. They breathed while half-dead, possessing only breath, and dragged along their feeble corpses. Whenever they saw vegetable refuse, whether accidentally dropped or thrown away as though it were dry, with bodies weakened, they licked the remnants lying on the ground with their mouths. Or whenever they saw grass growing between the walls, they tore it up and, with its miserable juice, sought to relieve their wretched hunger.

Those who were wealthier bought a measure of wheat with their entire fortune. What would they preserve that could not help them? The poorer bought barley, so that no one saw either seller or buyer. For this was punished as a crime more serious than any other. Nor did anyone wait for bread to be baked [Col. 2155C], lest death come first, or delay summon an informer. Those who possessed any grain, even the smallest quantity, hid themselves away and ate it uncooked. There was no table, no seat, no light, lest someone intrude and [Note: [Col. 2155D] Unexpectedly. ID.] catch them unawares. If there was any sound, the food was hidden; solitude was suspected, and gatherings were murderous. Hunger excludes every affection, and shame above all; for the hungry, modesty is a waste of life and a diminution of safety.

If a man who had a wife, children, or grandchildren possessed any food, he scarcely admitted it; women did the same. But if someone had a gentler disposition, as soon as food had been set out, it was torn from his hands. The food was pitiable, the meal tearful: children snatched it from their parents, parents from their children, and it was pulled from the very mouths of those who were eating. For many, another person’s vomit became food. No one felt horror at eating what was already decaying, nor shame at removing from his own people the last drops of life.

And even this spectacle of such an unhappy calamity was accompanied by fear: fear of being discovered. Thus it was carried out behind closed doors, lest someone arrive who might seek food from another’s mouth and, like a dog, lick another’s vomit with his own tongue. Yet even this was not without punishment, for wherever doors were barred, concealed food was suspected. The ministers of the seditions leapt upon them [Col. 2156A], stormed the closed houses, and demanded intolerable punishments of unprecedented cruelty. They did not even refrain from the shameful parts of the body. Punishment passed through those parts as well, where the sensation of punishment is more severe.

Many, when they saw the executioners already breaking in, seized the food that was ready, lest they themselves be deprived of their final provisions, or at least lest they avenge their impending death. And, as though the cruelty were not severe enough, those who seized food from the hungry were not themselves hungry. Through their plundering they had amassed the resources of others and fed upon what others had stored, while those who had gathered it themselves were starving and wasting away through fasting.

If some mother, moved by maternal affection and pitying an infant’s cries, wished to pour the juice of food into the child’s mouth from her own, she paid the penalty for her dutiful act: the child, hanging from her neck or clinging to her breasts, was pierced through together with her [Col. 2156B]. Many even thought it a favor to die and went out of the city to tear up herbs, graze upon roots, or strip bark from trees, if the greenery in them offered anything to relieve their hunger. When the Romans found them, they killed them.

But the person who had escaped the enemy fell at the very threshold of the gate, wasted by hunger and weak in the mouth, already deprived even of the functions of chewing. Those who returned were also met by a more deadly hand, which, with the bitterest crime, tore from the laps of the wretched what they had obtained at the greatest risk, without even leaving them a portion as payment for their danger. Thus they died under the greater assault of their own people than of the enemy. What even the enemy had spared, a fellow citizen took away.

Nor did seizing such food help them [Col. 2156C], since not long afterward [Note: [Col. 2156D] Burning. And shortly afterward, *inediis* should be read instead of *mediis*. BARR.] their green bodies swelled in the middle, and they were shaken by pain in their innermost organs; or, overcome by diarrhea, they collapsed as their strength was exhausted, regretting what they had desired: what had offered relief for a time became punishment. Then, by cooking green lizards and the cast-off skins of other kinds of snakes [Note: [Col. 2156D] Of the serpent kind. ID.], they added pestilence to their affliction.

For if they happened to find the carcasses of horses, they dragged them among themselves and fought a fierce battle over them; nor were the evils that were accumulating struck down even by the enemy. For when many, going out of the city with their children and wives, had withdrawn into the region where the deep hollow of precipitous ravines curved inward, the Romans led them away like captive [Note: [Col. 2156D] They led away. ID.] slaves and struck down especially those of younger age, as though they were the stronger, lest anyone perhaps dare to creep upon the combatants.

They watched so that, if anyone went farther into the outer spaces while carefully searching for food and investigating the roots of wild plants, he might be intercepted. Yet even with the enemy surrounding them, those whom hunger gave courage could not restrain themselves. The parents’ affection could not endure seeing their little children consumed by emaciation, their mouths stretched open in vain hunger—children whom they had taken as companions in danger, lest the leaders of the sedition kill them as hostages for their own flight. Hunger forced those for whom death by the sword was a blessing in comparison with starvation to go out [Col. 2157A].

The Romans, however, believing them contemptuous of death, intensified the forms of punishment [Note: [Col. 2157D] They increased them. Soon afterward, “affixing.” BARR.], first flogging them and then affixing them to the cross, inflicting this upon everyone they encountered, so that the sight of such tortures might restrain the boldness of the others from provoking them. Thus the suffering seemed pitiable to Titus, and the severity of so many disasters moved him. Innumerable people were captured; nearly five hundred were tortured each day, and they formed a mournful spectacle across the fields before the city, arranged so that they could be seen from the walls.

The Romans pitied them, but the Jews were not moved. The enemies showed compassion, while their associates did not yield; pity was more easily found among adversaries than among allies. Nevertheless, many were inflamed with indignation because, amid such great evils, they were becoming worse. One could see people afflicted in different ways, and such varied forms of punishment and shapes of torture, in such innumerable multitude, that there was now not enough space for crosses, nor crosses for bodies.

Inside, Simon raged and John roared; through their ministers they lay in wait for individuals. If anyone attempted to flee, he was dragged over the ground and torn apart. Those who had gone out were also tortured nearby [Note: [Col. 2157D] They were slaughtered. ID.], or the corpses of many who had been fastened to crosses were displayed to their relatives who had escaped. On the other side, they too had covered the wall with a kind of thicket of crosses, as though celebrating a triumph over their adversaries, whenever they discovered that any of their own people wished to flee to the Romans, so that fear of attempting it would seize the others.

No place was free from cruelty: captivity outside, hunger within, fear everywhere. Yet weapons were feared less than tortures, and it was lighter to be destroyed in the enemy’s tumult than by parricide. Nevertheless, Caesar did not cease inviting the leaders of the factions to hope for surrender. Having constructed siege ramps, he declared that the work would soon be completed; destruction threatened the city; they should take thought for themselves, so that they might gain safety and rescue the Temple from the flames.

To make this more readily believed, many Jews were sent to them with their hands cut off, lest they be thought to have passed over to the Romans by voluntary defection, and lest the Romans, regarding them as treacherous, refuse to trust them or kill them themselves. But they returned the persistent warning with grave insults: Caesar’s humanity seemed more deadly to them than his cruelty, since one deprived them of liberty while the other took away life. They preferred to die free rather than live as slaves. They had dedicated their lives [Col. 2157D] in the Temple. They would gain immortality if, burned together with the Temple, they died beside their ancestral altars and hearths.

Titus had accomplished nothing: he had taken away little and given more. In place of the Temple, paradise would come to them [Note: [Col. 2157D] It seems that *illoque*, that is, “and into paradise,” should be read: “they would be transferred.” GALLAND.]; and they, who had fought for the Temple of God, would be transferred there. Their only wish was not to see Roman triumphs with their own eyes or to submit their captive necks to the yoke. Their children were being consecrated, not killed, and their parents had been defenders of the heavenly sacraments [Col. 2158A].

Titus, all the more moved by this, ordered the engines to be brought forward at least to rescue those who were being held against their will.

## CHAPTER XIX

There was in the army the son of Antiochus of Commagene, who had come to share in the war. He was indeed an energetic young man, quick with his hands, but insufficiently prudent in judgment. Thinking that the discipline of the Roman army was too slow, and not considering the difficulty of the task, he hinted to Caesar that he was surprised the Romans were hesitating to bring down the wall.

Titus laughed and said, “It is a communal undertaking.”

At these words the young man rushed forth with those whom he had, armed in the Macedonian manner, kept especially ready for battle; for he had also come supported by others. The cohort called the Macedonian cohort was considered superior both in bodily strength and in its very height. As they approached, the battle intensified.

From the wall, those whom the extremity of danger pressed onward fought more eagerly; the success of the present engagement also encouraged them. Although those below were more frequently pierced by those above, and not all the missiles reached the men above, the king’s son, lively with youth, better protected by his armor and more compactly accompanied, avoided some blows and repelled others. His companions instructed him even when they advised him to beware, and therefore he remained unwounded.

But many of the Macedonian cohort, thinking it shameful to yield either to nature or to fortifications, fought with greater stubbornness and were wounded [Note: [Col. 2158D] “They were wounded.” Soon afterward, “Macedonian men.” BARR.]. Thus, after an unsuccessful attempt, they yielded to those above. They learned that, if Macedonian men wished to conquer, both Alexander’s eagerness for battle and the outcome of victory were necessary [Col. 2158C].

For when Alexander was besieging a city while the others delayed and the army lingered around the customary siege engines, he energetically placed ladders against the wall and climbed it. After driving away those who resisted from the wall, he threw himself alone into the city. There was no time for him to open the gates for himself without a companion, since danger pressed upon him; but his excessive courage and thirst for victory drove him forward against the enemy. The ranks gave way—but how many could he alone have struck down?

Then the enemy poured through the city’s various streets. If Alexander pressed into one direction, he gave the others an opportunity to surround him from behind. Thus the victor retraced his steps [Note: [Col. 2158D] His advance. ID.], lest he be surrounded by the populace. But they began to press together, and a tremendous force of weapons bristled over him. The helmet rang with clatter, and the shield resounded under the crash of stones.

And if the Macedonians, fearing for their commander, had not rushed in, the victor over innumerable nations would have been overwhelmed within a tiny city. His courage, then, was admirable: he leapt upon the wall, threw down the enemy, sprang alone into the city in a triumphant leap, and put the inhabitants to flight by his charge. Yet the outcome was also remarkable, and most necessary for the commander: although so many peoples were rushing upon him, so many arrows were being launched, and so many missiles were falling, there was no opening for a mortal wound [Col. 2159A].

Thus courage had brought danger, and eagerness would also have brought death if fortune had abandoned the combatant. The Macedonians entered through the breach in the gate. In this way rashness found victory, and fortune turned danger into glory.

Our own David, too, when he fought against giants [Note: [Col. 2159D] Intent upon the attack. BARR.], rushed against the enemy while he had a striker behind him; but Abishai, the king’s companion, forestalled the blow as he was balancing his weapon. Yet fortune saved Alexander, while grace saved the prophet.

## CHAPTER XX

When the son of Antiochus, king of Commagene, withdrew and recognized that the considered discipline of the Roman army arose not from fearfulness but from caution—that they were preparing to attack the wall with ramps [Col. 2159B], covered sheds, battering rams, and other engines—ramps were constructed by dividing the work among the units. Four principal ramps rose up; one of them was built directly opposite the fortification called Antonia and was carried across the middle of a pool called Struthion. A fifth unit had made this ramp thirty cubits high beside John’s tomb.

Opposite it, John, the leader of the seditions, dug a tunnel and suspended the Roman works. Since the Romans did not know what the Jews had devised in the concealed tunnel [Note: [Col. 2159D] What. ID.], the entire deception remained hidden: by placing an equal quantity of timber as supports beneath the tunnel, they had suspended the structures above it.

Therefore, when the opportunity appeared, they set fire to it. Once the fire had grown through the sulfur and pitch with which the timbers supporting the tunnel had been smeared, it easily consumed all the wood, and the collapse of the structures above followed. The Roman works suddenly fell with a tremendous crash [Col. 2159C]. Everything was filled with dust and smoke and covered in profound darkness, while the hidden cause produced even greater terror.

Then, when the other fuel with which the fire had initially been covered had been consumed, the unobstructed flames burst forth, exposing the trick. The Romans’ immediate fear of danger was reduced, but the loss of their labor left behind a heavy weariness. At the same time, the Jews’ taunts caused no small shame, and hope of preparing the remaining assault grew cold.

Two days later, on another section, when the wall was already being battered by a ram, Teptheus of Galilee, Magassalus, Jabenus, and Agyras, having seized torches, leapt upon the wall-engines [Col. 2159D]. Nothing more audacious, nothing more terrifying, emerged from the city against the enemy in that war. Bursting into the midst of the enemy, they did not tremble or draw back; but, as though lingering among the company of their friends, they did not think they should return until they had set fire to the siege machinery, although spears, arrows, and javelins were being hurled at them from every side.

There was a great rush of the Roman army to extinguish the fire; the Jews also shouted and strove to interpose obstacles so that aid could not come to the Romans. The Romans hurried to drag the battering rams away from the flames; the Jews continued to spread the fire. Thus, after everything that could burn had caught fire, the flames had surrounded the Romans, unless they had taken precautions promptly.

The Jews pressed on fiercely, and the very fact that their efforts in this sector had not been unsuccessful nourished their confidence in success. No longer content with the wall fortifications, they advanced farther, attacked the Roman guards themselves, and proceeded toward the fortress where the Romans had been stationed, which they had almost overturned by their own assault.

And unless the glory of the Roman name and the army’s ancient discipline—whose fear of the heavier punishment prevented them from abandoning such duties—had opposed their frenzy, the conquerors of cities would themselves have yielded their own fortifications. Thus the character of the battle and the practice of the siege were reversed. The Romans defended themselves with catapults and missiles of a faster kind [Col. 2160B], repelling the Jews with the very weapons by which they had previously been resisted.

Meanwhile Titus arrived, summoned by the shouting and called in as a remedy. The Romans immediately gained strength in Caesar’s presence, and shame nourished their courage. Titus shouted that it would be a grave disgrace to the Roman name if, with the situation reversed, they lost their own men when the enemy’s walls—walls they were to destroy—had already failed their defenders. The Jews distrusted their fortifications and relied only on rashness. If the Romans merely stood firm, victory would not be lacking.

Thus Titus, encouraging his men and fighting at the same time, steadied them and drove back the Jews. They were not only prepared in spirit for death but were also pressing forward with the very effort of their bodies, seeking to force the Romans from their position. The danger to Caesar was considerable amid the confusion, since friend could not be distinguished from enemy [Col. 2160C]. Titus moved about in the midst of it all: bold in youth and made more eager for battle by his desire for glory, he placed concern for his own safety after the completion of victory.

## CHAPTER XXI

After the enemy had nevertheless been driven back, the decision was uncertain. Some thought the ramps should be rebuilt and the wall-engines repaired; others advised withdrawing from the dangers of the siege. The material for repairs was lacking, and the danger was shared with many [Note: [Col. 2160D] “With the defeated.” Soon afterward, “those who had been exhausted.” ID.]. They judged it more prudent to enclose the city with a wall, so that famine might finish it once its supplies of food had failed.

This opinion prevailed: they should be enclosed so that they would have no free opportunity for sorties and would be worn down still further by despair of escape and lack of food. Accordingly, after the work was divided among the units [Note: [Col. 2160D] “By units.” ID.], the wall quickly rose, enclosing the entire city in a circuit.

Caesar assigned duties to his men so that they would not omit the watches even at night. During the first watch, he himself went around and attended to the duties of each guard-post. He assigned the second watch to Alexander. Finally, he entrusted the watches in turn to the tribunes, according to the ability he had discovered in each.

The wall was woven together with forts at intervals, and in these the soldiers stood guard. The sentries divided their sleep and their periods of watch equally among themselves. At every moment they went around the wall, each attending to his assigned duty over the prescribed stretches, moving from fort to fort. Night was filled by turns and by the succession of duties.

All hope of the Jews was cut off, and hunger, having enclosed them, poured into them and descended into the very marrow of the people. Everything resounded with the groans of those lamenting the punishment of a pitiable death [Col. 2161A]. The whole place was filled with corpses [Note: [Col. 2161D] All the paths were filled. BARR.]; and if one waited only a little, those whom one had found alive would perish within a moment.

Those who still breathed also bore the image of death, exhausted by emaciation. Drained by hunger and yellow with decay, they could scarcely raise their eyes, because their substance, consumed by fasting, supplied no vigor for natural movement. Only the shape of a human being remained; its use had perished. You saw images, but longed for human functions [Col. 2161B]. Dry skin clung to dry bones. If a slight movement revealed that someone was alive, the stench exposed him; the limbs were shriveled and the color so black that one might have thought it a shadow.

The miserable had not even enough strength to bury the dead, since everything had first been exhausted and they themselves were continually dying. And if recent food gave someone some strength, the heap of corpses removed hope and imposed impossibility. Many lingered in burying the bodies of their own people, but, unable to complete the duties of the final service, abandoned them when they too died.

They collapsed upon the dead whom they had undertaken to bury, so that the burden itself fell upon the person who had come to lift it; he needed for himself the service he was rendering to another. There was no room for grief amid the common disaster of all, except that the authors of so great a misery survived—and there was no time for complaint, even in the voices of their children, if they could still speak [Col. 2161C]. What would those who were already dying fear for themselves? Yet with their senses already mute, they looked upon the Temple as though vengeance for so dreadful an end were being demanded from it.

The tears for the final rites [Note: [Col. 2161D] Rites. ID.] had dried up, because the force of the evil had closed off every affection. The spirit had stiffened, every feeling was numb; they endured more than could be mourned. There was no longer enough earth for graves, since every place within the city that could serve as a tomb had been dug up.

Some attempted to proceed at night between the two walls through a new opening and the old city gate. Dangerous though these thefts were, affection for the dead persuaded them. Thus several often lay unburied for the sake of one, and they were deprived of the service of good works [Note: [Col. 2161D] The service of good deeds. ID.] that they had eagerly wished to perform for one person. Yet even where the enemy was absent, famine did its work.

Often the gravedigger preceded the person to be buried and, suddenly lifeless, was enclosed in the very tomb he had prepared for another. When he collapsed as he dug, he seemed, as though zealously completing his task, to claim the right for himself. Where earth was lacking, wooden boards were joined together so that the corpses of the dead might be enclosed in coffins. Many prepared such coffins for themselves with their own hands, lest this service fail; and they often voluntarily buried themselves in them, fearing that death might come first and that no gravedigger would remain.

Everything was silent with fear. Famine had taken away the voice. The city was full of death [Col. 2162A], yet there was no wailing at the funerals throughout the entire city. Although the capacity for feeling pain had perished, outrage did not cease.

Even amid such great evils there were people worse than all others, violators even of the dead. What shall I say of their lack of horror when they mocked the dead and brandished the edges of their swords against the corpses of the deceased? Some even tested the bodies of those still alive [Note: [Col. 2161D] “For piercing.” Another reading: “the living.” ID.] to see whether their weapons were sharp enough. Yet even this use was denied to many who begged for it, so that famine might consume the wretched for more grievous punishments.

Nevertheless, vengeance was not lacking for those who were dying. For what the living could not do, the dead avenged: they made their stench their avenger, using it to take revenge upon the robbers. Those who were raging savagely and seeking a remedy had put on a kind of appearance of piety [Col. 2162B], even those who were committing robbery, by ordering that the dead be buried from the public treasury. But when this could no longer be managed, they threw the remains of the dead from the wall into the deep ravines.

When Titus saw the precipitous caves full of corpses, with pus floating upon them from their torn entrails [Note: [Col. 2162D] “From the mangled.” ID.], he groaned deeply. Raising his hands to heaven, he testified that this should by no means be attributed to him, since he had wished to grant pardon if a surrender took place. He had waited for them to ask for peace and had been ready to preserve them unharmed if they would lay down their arms.

He therefore ordered the ramps to be laid down again, even though the forests were no longer nearby, because all the suburban groves and woodland had been cut down. The soldiers transported the timber, consoling their labor with the hope of victory. Yet the leaders of the seditions were not broken in spirit [Col. 2162C]. Simon raged and, not sated by the deaths of so many, did not yield; and because enemies were beginning to be lacking, he turned against his own allies.

## CHAPTER XXII
Finally, he also tortured Matthias, through whose agency he had been admitted into the city, and killed him, although he had been convicted of no crime in his presence, but merely accused of treason and suspected of a scheme which he had diligently and without any deceit believed should be quietly communicated for the benefit of the people, as to a trusted associate. He kept this deeply impressed upon his mind for some time; he no longer regarded him as a friend, but nourished his indignation while concealing the evidence. Therefore he ordered the man accused in his presence of having agreed and conspired with the Romans to be dragged away with his sons. [Note: The old manuscript reads “inexcruciatum” (“not tortured”). ID.] He was summoned, and no opportunity for defense was granted: he was condemned to execution before any examination, nor were his children spared, but were added to the punishment. [Note: “He is summoned.” ID.]

He begged not for an extension of life, but for the speed of death, in accordance with nature’s order: that he might be killed first, lest he should have to watch the slaughter of his sons, or survive the funerals of his children, himself soon to become a corpse. He did not obtain what filial affection itself demanded, even though he did not ask for it. This was what he asked to have repaid him as his reward: that he had opened the city to Simon. He was indeed guilty toward his country, but Simon’s advocate. Simon nevertheless owed him gratitude. How much more cruel was the man who spared neither a friend nor relaxed the punishment of the one who had secured his admission!

The father was led to execution with three sons; the fourth had escaped by flight. [Note: BARR reads “patriae” (“of the fatherland”) for “paternae” (“paternal”). ID reads “sumus” (“we are”) and “conserentibus” (“joining battle”).] He was placed in view of the Roman army, as though for an act of mockery, so that those whom he had wished to go out against might see his punishment. “Let your friends free you, if they can.” His sons too were brought out, and he was not permitted to give his children final kisses or receive them in one last embrace. He was not, however, deprived of the freedom of his paternal voice, and addressed his sons in a lamentable speech:

“I, my sons, brought the enemy upon you; I brought in the executioners when I asked Simon to enter the city. That day was for us the cause of this death, the cause of this parricidal spectacle. I deserved it, I confess, and I do not excuse my guilt: while I wished to restrain one man, I summoned a worse one. Simon was sought for our aid and turned against the fatherland for parricide; diligent counsels led to crime. We were guilty toward our country, we who sought a defender. We are rightly paying the penalty for our imprudence, but not for treachery. Simon himself absolves us while he destroys us: he declares that he was not granted to me, but sought with the fatherland in view, so that he might come to our aid against the savagery of John and bring in the Idumaeans as soon as he arrived.

“We thought that, when two men contended with one another, the people would be free. Who would believe me, that I had not brought this upon you through my own zeal, but had judged this the more tolerable of evils—unless you had killed me? But why do I speak as though I were excusing a crime? In my judgment I could have done nothing more grievous than place you upon our necks. But in that I shall have been guilty toward my country, not toward you. I may have owed death to my fellow citizens, but you owed me gratitude. I may have owed my country the punishment for treason, because I brought you in. When did I begin to be a traitor to you? If I had thought it necessary to flee, I would have looked to my own safety, not violated my bond with my country. Who does not flee an enemy—and an enemy within?

“But we thought you a citizen, and found an enemy. Summoned for our aid, what did you repay us? What had you promised beforehand, and into what were you afterward transformed? You entered to drive out the enemy, not to act as an enemy; to restrain his savage attack, not to provoke war; to prevent the slaughter of citizens, not to add yourself to it; to repel brigandage, not to commit brigandage yourself, but to help an innocent people.

“Why did you turn your weapons against us? Previously we were being attacked by brigandage; you brought war upon us. [Note: ID reads “appetebamur” (“we were attacked”).] Previously only a few were being dragged to death; you carried out a massacre of peoples. Who was a greater traitor to his country, who aided Roman arms more, than the man who destroyed the defenders of his country? Who more than the man who robbed so many citizens of their defense? Who more than the man who turned his sword from the enemy against his allies?

“The enemy outside the walls offered peace; you fought within the walls. He wished to lift the siege; you hastened the assault. He prevented the burning of our city; you cast flames upon the very roofs of the Temple. He granted a truce out of regard for our sacred rites; you extinguished the altars of God during the very days of the sacred festivals with the final destruction of the city and even with the blood of the priests. He had besieged the walls; you had besieged the Temple.

[Note: ID reads “coacervabo” (“I shall heap up”).—“Coacerbabo” (“I shall make more bitter”) seems preferable, for the author likes this expression. Above, book I, chapter 25, near the beginning: “That Hyrcanus and Antipater were encroaching upon others’ possessions, which had been . . . wrested from him, Antigonus might bitterly complain [COACERBARET] in a most grievous lament.” Thus the first edition; others perhaps less correctly think that “coacervaret” should be corrected, as does Barrensis here. The same reading, “coacerbabo,” is further supported by the simple “acerbo,” which the author uses frequently. Book II, chapter 9: “Lest you embitter one and summon another.” Likewise book IV, chapter 13: “They embittered the war without allowing surrender.” So also repeatedly elsewhere. GALLAND. BARR reads “exitia” (“destructions”) for “initia” (“beginnings”); ID reads “debitas” (“owed”), “qui” (“who”), and “librantis” (“poising”).]

“I shall heap up my crimes. I brought my hands against my country; I armed your fury; I impressed the beginnings of all these things upon this delirium of old age. I acknowledge the folly of my declining years. Let us lessen our shame by confession, since by denying the sin we cannot strip it away. Two of us, above all others, hastened the destruction of our country: I, through an error of counsel; you, through a deliberate purpose of parricide.

“Therefore, my country, I am paying the penalties I owe you; and for this very reason I thank Simon, that I shall not survive your ashes. Would that I were not to survive my sons! But, to increase the bitterness of your crime, Simon, I stand here as a spectator of the death of my children. I deserved it, I confess, because I could not bear to see John painted and chose you armed. O precipitous old age! We feared an image and desired a tyrant. I was your guarantor; I was your advocate; I carried out the embassy on your behalf. I asked you to be our master and brought in our executioner. Let us therefore look upon what we have done: John’s wax image terrified us, while Simon’s brigandage delighted us.

“Let the funeral procession be hastened. Let the executioner come. Let him strike the sons before their father’s eyes, and then the father upon the corpses of his sons. Let the wretched old man receive the executioner’s blow, the axe flashing above the necks of his pledges. What spectacle could be more disastrous, except the man who orders it?

“Cruel, criminal man, I do what you command; I do it, but unwillingly. Yet I have some consolation amid so great a calamity. I suffer whatever is most miserable because you have ordered it; I willingly undergo whatever is most monstrous, with you as judge. You have filled up the measure of the most savage crimes. At least let me address my children; let me bid my pledges a final farewell. [Note: Let there be some last opportunity for the eyes. ID.]

“Let there be a final place for kisses, which we share even with wild beasts. Let the wretched embrace of nature not be forbidden, an embrace which even chance may grant to the dead. What you have commanded for punishment, let it serve me for filial affection. I shall fall upon my own funerals and, while my body is still unburied, as though upon a mound formed by my own body, I shall gather them up, lest birds tear them apart or wild beasts devour them. I shall lick with my tongue the blood of my beloved children and cleanse my own blood, lest the beasts lick it. Perhaps filial affection and pity for nature itself will add this: that, dying in the tightest embrace, I may hold my children close, so that you cannot separate us, even if you wish to. Certainly, if you separate our bodies, you will not separate our souls.

“But we have already taken enough tears as provisions for the journey. Go before me, my sons, and prepare the way for your father, who will follow. If I can overtake you, I shall accompany you, and old age will be an obstacle there, so that I shall follow the living young men less quickly. Go ahead to your dwelling, so that you may receive your weary father in lasting hospitality. I myself wished to go before you, and I asked for it, but I did not obtain it. Yet because you are innocent, better dwellings will be prepared for you than if I, who summoned Simon, had gone ahead.

“That embassy burdens me, although it was entrusted to me by my fellow citizens and undertaken at the people’s request. [Note: ‘Undertaken.’ ID.] Go ahead, then, my sons, taking the heavenly path with a purer step.

“The mother of the Maccabees also preceded her sons. But they went to a reward, you to punishment. Yet that devout mother watched her sons die; rolling upon their blood, she saw the brothers embracing one another through the bond of nature, and she rejoiced in her triumph, which she won over the tyrant. The merits of the sufferers were different, but the savagery of the one giving the order was the same.

“Antiochus discovered this through Persian brutality; among the Persians, indeed, there are inventions of new punishments. You carried it out. Yet he preserved the mother to the end, to persuade her to accept the king’s will; you ordered the father to be preserved for the torture of paternal grief. Take courage, dearest sons: we suffer what the martyrs suffered. Simon has imposed what the barbarous persecutor invented and the tyrant commanded.

“Let us therefore depart willingly and flee the company of brigands. Indeed, when we have departed into that everlasting home, if someone should come to us and ask what that former people of God is doing, what shall we answer them? Especially if, since you are younger, Jonathan, whole in his prime of life, should meet you, and Saul should meet me, a sinner. [Note: BARR reads “quo” (“by which/because”); ID reads “decesserimus” (“we shall have departed”) and “maluit” (“he preferred”); BARR reads “nostra” (“our”) for “vestra” (“your”).] What, I say, shall we say except that the people once beloved, a new Judah, whom the sea fled before, for whom the sun stood still and the Jordan retreated; that people for whom the waves became a pathway, the air fruitful, and the earth heavenly, which—not like this earth of yours, which has assumed the appearance of corruption, but having received the grace of resurrection—now serves the Idumaeans and is subject to Simon, the prince of brigands, possessing neither secure servitude nor danger accompanied by freedom?

“What do we suppose those will answer who chose to perish in war rather than survive the freedom of their country? What also will Mattathias, the founder of the Maccabees, answer, who preferred to die while resting on the Sabbath in observance of the Law rather than live by fighting? [Note: ‘He preferred.’ ID.] If he hears how Simon not only carried out countless slaughters of citizens on the Sabbath, but compelled the priests of the Lord themselves to slaughter them on new moons and on all the holy days of festive celebration, how deeply will he groan?

“How greatly will Jeconiah grieve when he hears that Simon, after first overturning the city through seditions and violating the Temple’s ancient religion by the slaughter of citizens, though repeatedly urged to surrender himself so as to save the city from fire, preferred that everything perish in destruction—the city and Temple be burned and the entire people be killed—rather than lower the height of the domination he had seized! How much, I say, will Jeconiah grieve, although, in the time of pressing evils, he was less fortunate in his rule but better than his son?

“For the father, although in a pitiable condition, nevertheless with filial devotion preferred to be less fortunate for himself than for his country. Therefore, when the Babylonians were besieging the city, he went out with his family and surrendered himself to slavery, lest he see his country overthrown and the people of God captive. His son, however, was equal in misery but unequal in disposition: while fearing for himself, he brought both himself into exile and the city into destruction. Thus the one was unfortunate for his country and fortunate neither for himself, losing both his children and his eyes; the other was wiser, redeeming the captivity of his citizens with his own captivity.

“Finally, the outcome taught this lesson: the former, though older, died in the kingdom; the latter, though younger, died in servitude, although afterward the Babylonian king established him beside himself on the royal throne and granted him precedence in counsel, as a consolation amid his wretched calamity.

“Finally, my own lot is now more tolerable: to die after the slaughter of my children rather than live. Thus you may know how cruel is the man who slaughters sons before their father’s eyes. Even his royal gifts are worse than the wounds of filial affection. Either he ought not first to have inflicted such impious suffering, or he ought not afterward to have substituted such honors, as though any dignity could be redeemed by the loss of children or the slaughter of offspring compensated by any use of honor. No dignity, absolutely none, relieves such grief. No honor heals this wound, except death alone, which removes sensation and takes away remembrance.

“Hasten, then, executioner; yet delay while I look upon my children, while I see them before they die, lest someone, perhaps confused by the immaturity of his age, fear death when he is escaping a more savage tyrant. It is a benefit, my sons, to die, lest we see the captivity of our country. The wounds of the body are more tolerable than those of the mind. Now it is more tolerable for me to watch your deaths, which I was fleeing, than to watch the deaths of everyone together, than to see my country’s funeral pyre and the whole city become their tomb. Yet happier is the one who will have died than the one who has been kept alive.

“Most high God, may Simon not be laid low among the ranks of the innocent with his children; may he, captive, behold what he has brought about. No—far from it, far from it, I say; for whoever can imagine such a thing can endure it, and yet I do not pray this against him. Let him consider how great a crime it is, which the sufferer cannot even return by a wish; how bitter the vengeance, how savage the enormity of the crime committed, which the captive survivor wishes upon his country, because the mockeries of life are worse than the punishments of death.

“But let this be the end of my words. Hasten, executioner, while you carry the sword reddened with my sons’ blood. Strike the father, so that no one may cool the wound. [Note: ‘The wound.’ ID.] This alone is the medicine for one about to die; by this alone the blow of the sword and the pain of the wound are not felt. Strike me in the sight of the Roman army, as commanded, so that they may watch as avengers. Let the enemy show pity, since my ally shows none. Let the Romans judge, since Simon killed without judgment. They themselves are witnesses that I was not a traitor to my country but its defender, for they saw me fighting, not deserting. For my children, if I had been able, I would have driven away the enemy, not summoned him. And would that I had not summoned Simon either!”

Nor was any end put to such cruelty. His sons still lay unburied with their father; sacrilege was added to the parricidal spectacle. Ananias the priest was struck down, born of a distinguished family, although no one is more distinguished by the splendor of birth than by the office of religion. Through the former, nobility is sought; through the latter, it is not desired. Let an ancient lineage have for itself its various bundles of honors; priesthoods too have their own bundles, which are raised not by shoulders but by character, and lifted up not by the height of rods but by perseverance in labor, the loftiness of faith, and the summit of devotion.

The scribe Aristaeus, himself also of distinguished origin, was struck down; and with them fifteen others from the common people who excelled the rest—not that nobility makes an unjust death, but innocence. Eleven men were also seized in advance, who had conspired together, moved by the atrocity of his crimes; each fearing for himself what he saw being inflicted upon others, because Simon was faithless even to his friends and hope had been taken away, while famine ravaged everyone and the Romans were on the point of breaking in. Simon, disturbed when aid for defense was needed, and raging in the workshop of cruelty, was easily tempted by the opportunity for treachery, since one Judas among them had undertaken to guard the tower.

When this man summoned the Romans, promising that he would hand over the tower—some impatient that the treachery was proceeding so late, others doubtful because he had often prepared deceit while promising surrender—Simon forestalled him and exacted punishment from all his fellow conspirators. Their bodies too were thrown down from the wall.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Josephus’s father was kept confined, and no access to him was open. [Note: “To anyone.” BARR.] For this reason Josephus urged the Jews all the more earnestly to surrender, and recklessly advanced toward the wall, intending to free his country together with his father. At that point he was struck on the head by a stone and fell; he was almost overwhelmed by weapons hurled from above, had not men sent by Caesar arrived and rescued him from death under the protection of their shields.

When his mother learned of her son’s wound and was terrified by the voices of the brigands mocking him, she at once assumed both fear of his death and confidence in it. She also began to lament miserably:

“For these fruits of childbearing was I preserved, so that I should neither enjoy the service of a living son nor bury him when dead? My wish had been that he rather should give burial to his mother; that he should breathe out his final spirit in my hands; that he should warm the cold limbs of his failing mother; that he should gather her last breaths with his mouth; that he should close the eyes of the dying woman; that he should arrange the lips still breathing.

“But since I have been deprived of my wish, it would have been a consolation if I could at least have been present at the final moments of my dying son—a pitiable lot, indeed, but still tolerable—so that I might hold even the funeral of the one whom I had hoped to see survive.

“Yet let me at least watch my own funeral from the wall,” she said. “And if I may not touch him, would that no one should prevent me! But whom should I fear, deprived as I am of such a son? What should I dread, when death is a benefit to me? Would that they would all turn their weapons against me; would that they would all pierce me with the sword! What I could not do while alive, at least when dead I shall protect my son’s body with my clothing. One garment is enough for the burial of two. Perhaps one of the enemy will take pity, so that with my son’s cloak he may cover his mother’s eyes, and join eyes to eyes, hands to hands, mouth to mouth.”

Thus rushing toward the walls, she filled the very heavens with her pitiable lament. Her own people mocked her; the Romans wept. Among allies there was cruelty; among enemies, compassion.

“Strike me,” she said, “if there is any pity. I gave birth to the man whom you think should be persecuted. I gave him these unhappy breasts. Kill me, if you seek vengeance upon him.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

While she was lamenting, behold, Josephus came forward at his mother’s voice and began to mourn that he had escaped—he for whom it had once been sweet to die before his country and to fall for his country while offering salutary counsel. But now he was no longer contending for the safety of his parents, who, worn down by age and awaiting the final end of life in prison, would be freed if they died. Instead, he trembled for the altar, for the Temple, and for the city walls, still only half destroyed. He said that he had offered himself to the wound lest he see his country overthrown.

Moved by this lament, many judged that they should cross over to the Romans. By whatever route they could, they withdrew themselves from the ambushes of the brigands and from the guards who blocked their way. [Note: BARR reads “praetendendum” (“to be stretched before/obstructing”).] Titus indeed kept the mercy he had promised them, but another and more grievous misery befell them.

For when food was made available, what had previously been useful became a burden; and, their accustomed functions of eating having been lost, the work of digestion was idle. They had no strength in their teeth with which to chew food, no vigour in their arteries; they could not in any way gnaw bread. If they swallowed anything of a softer nourishment, they were strangled because the passages of their throats were already closed. The inward organs had stiffened; the channels for food were blocked. The veins of the liver, which draw in nourishment, had dried up. The function was gone, appetite accumulated, strength had failed, but desire remained.

The wretched men collapsed upon the food and practiced feeble bites like infants. Many, when they saw food, failed from the joy itself and died amid the nourishment they had longed for, finding consolation in their misery because they had fulfilled their wish. Yet the spectacle was pitiable, since more rose from food to danger than to health, so that nourishment itself caused harm. Their bodies were swollen by the unusual food rather than restored, and, as though suffering from a kind of dropsy, they paid the penalty with distended skin. [Note: “Of dropsy.” ID.]

If any still possessed the strength to eat, their appetite knew no limit; they stuffed themselves beyond measure with what they could not bear and burst apart, crammed with sudden food. What burden was not grievous to people for whom even the mere desire was grievous, so that seeing what they had desired became harmful? Incapable of controlling their impulses after the long famine, their natural senses too were oppressed; even the movement of joy weighed them down.

It is therefore no wonder if food is dangerous to those exhausted by suffering. Indeed, after a two-day fast, anything taken too greedily immediately becomes undigested. Hence it is customary for many to pour milk into weakened organs and, mixing it with honey, moderate the disorder of the humors irritated by fasting; by softer food they nourish the body’s collapse as though it were a kind of infancy.

Thus some of the Jews who had fled to the Romans were able to survive by regulating their food with a certain skill, until their flesh, unused to eating, returned to its proper functions. Yet even this did not benefit the wretched men; it became the cause of greater destruction. For when many of them, after taking food, cleansed their bowels, some expelled gold coins which they had swallowed while preparing their flight, lest, if caught—because the ambushers searched everything—they should suffer not only loss but danger; for it was considered a crime for anyone except the brigands to possess gold.

Afterward, therefore, the Jews gathered this gold from among the filth of the bowels in a pitiable spectacle. A certain Assyrian discovered it, and the rumor spread from one man to all. [Note: “From the Syrians.” See Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book VI, chapter 15. BARR.]

This class of people was headlong in avarice and ready for trickery, so that nothing was so atrocious that it would shun it, and nothing so shameful that it would blush at it, when money was at stake. From the Syrians the rumor spread to the Arabs, whose avarice was no less and whose barbaric savagery was closer to brutality, that the Jews were stuffed with gold. They plundered everyone they encountered who came out, contrary to right, contrary to the laws of surrender, contrary to Caesar’s promise that they were not to be killed. They cut into men still alive and, with bloody hands, ripped open the secrets of their bellies. They searched the bowels and sought gold amid their flowing excrement, no less shamefully than those whom hunger had driven to it—indeed, with even more savage cruelty.

Many bitter acts were committed in that conflict, but none more bitter than this. Finally, in a single night nearly two thousand men were cut open in this outrage. With their entrails divided, Syria counted its profits; Arabia reckoned the gains of its commerce, which, without the dangers of crossing the sea, they had converted into profit through this new invention of cruelty and regarded as merchandise.

This is something one can still find among such a class of people, and often among certain Egyptians as well: they conduct business by tending to funerals and sell the services of humanity for the profits of trade. Wretched hunger for gold! It considers nothing worth pursuing except what is profitable in the present, and nothing honorable if it is without money.

For a long time now, a grave desire to seek gain has taken root in human affections, and human life has become commerce: people live by buying and selling. The vice spread among countless people, so that the exchange of goods is now more tolerable than the exchange of morals and souls. The avarice of the Syrians infected the Roman army as well. Nothing passes more easily into another person than love of money and desire for possession, especially when it concerns the neighboring wealth in which one’s neighbor had abounded. No passion more effeminates the virtue of the spirit than desire for riches.

Finally, cleverness is praised and poverty is held disgraceful. This impeded the severity of vengeance, because countless people were found subject to such madness. Therefore Titus, who had proposed surrounding the Syrians and Arabs with the army, withdrew his decision out of consideration for their multitude. He granted pardon for the earlier offense and threatened punishment if it were committed again; with even harsher words he rebuked his own men, because, girded with gold and silver and glittering with precious weapons, they were not ashamed of their arms and so dishonored themselves with such great disgrace.

But he rebuked the Syrians and Arabs because, forgetful of the Roman name, they had devised things horrible even to speak of. They had come to share in the war, not to practice crimes. The Roman army required not only bodily courage but also strength of mind; it regarded not only bravery against the enemy but also obedience to discipline, so that a soldier should not be cruel, impious, or insolent, nor intent upon plunder rather than victory.

Such crimes, he said, were grave offenses in military service and were punished with great severity. Even amid arms, laws remained in force. Wars were better waged in good faith, and that faith was to be preserved even toward enemies. If it was owed to armed men, how much more to those who begged for mercy? Therefore they should beware of such crimes, lest they be deprived both of victory and of safety. He would no longer endure the criminal outrages by which they brought disgrace upon the Romans, being more a burden than a benefit.

Thus he restrained the avarice of the Syrians somewhat, but did not eradicate it, so that they avoided the judge rather than embraced the command. Finally, after first investigating whether Roman soldiers happened to be absent, they brought forth their detestable profit from the bowels of the wretched. Yet the outcome was not always the gain they expected, but only in a few cases, making their savagery all the more cruel. For many were killed not only for the sake of their wealth but also in the hope of profit, although the brigands themselves—and pirates more savage than brigands—refrain from brigandage when they do not sense that there is plunder. It belongs only to barbaric brutality to inflict harm for nothing. Even wild beasts pursue prey when they kill.

Outside there were bitter punishments; within, John was more brutal still.

## CHAPTER XXV

Finally, while such things were being done by the Syrians, even though others were recalled after the matter had been discovered, some nevertheless did not cease to defect. Among them was Manneus, son of Lazarus, who asserted that through one gate entrusted to him 115,000 corpses had been carried out, with another 880 funerals added, because he himself had undertaken the duty of guarding that place. This number, he said, had been gathered solely from those buried at public expense, apart from those whom their own people had buried. And what graves were there except those into which corpses were thrown from the wall?

After him, many men of no obscure standing, taking refuge with Titus, recalled that 600,000 dead had been counted as carried out through the gates. As for the corpses that could not be carried out because of the immeasurable multitude of the poor and that had been heaped together in the largest houses and in spaces belonging to various buildings, their number was beyond estimation.

And the advance of evils still continued, evils that had already surpassed the end of all those preceding them. The savage siege and grievous war still continued, though the Jews’ courage was now greater than their strength. Above all was the more terrible famine, which searched the bellies of animals that had voided their bowels and rummaged through the ancient dung of oxen, so that what was horrible to see became food for the hungry.

There was a pitiable heap of unburied bodies, and the earth itself, extending far around, was covered with corpses. Everything before the walls was filled with them: a dreadful sight, a heavy horror, a pestilential odor that distinguished neither victors nor vanquished, harmful to both alike and a greater impediment to the Romans, who were forced to trample the remains lying there with bloody footsteps. The earth itself was uncultivated, since everything that was needed for the soldiers and siege engines had been cut down and brought in.

For nearly thirteen miles around the city, the ground had been devastated far and wide, and the soil that once produced things lay bare. If afterward some stranger saw that entire orchard—where previously green groves, gardens breathing out flowers, various orchards, and suburban estates had presented a pleasing appearance—he groaned. The native inhabitant did not recognize it, and, having returned to the place of his birth while actually standing there, searched for his country.

## CHAPTER XXVI

After the embankments, covered ways, and other siege engines had been repaired, the fury of war was renewed, as though both sides had joined in their efforts to complete the work. The entire conflict was being decided at the risk of everything. For the Romans would have had to lift the siege if the embankments and battering rams were burned, since, because of the shortage of timber, the means for repairing them were not available. For the Jews, the destruction of their country would threaten them if they yielded by force, since the walls, shaken by repeated blows of the rams, would collapse.

The Jews therefore advanced with torches so fiercely that, as though the Roman army were about to give way, they scattered fire among the siege engines and attempted to break the siege. But their strength had already been exhausted by famine and their resources broken; their earlier successes failed them. Substance had failed, but boldness remained.

The Romans, on the other hand, felt greater shame at the thought that victory might be snatched from their hands by men who were drawing their final breath from hunger. When battle was joined, the leaders of the sedition were repulsed and, unequal to the struggle, retreated to the support of the walls.

But when John, attentive to the final means of defense, saw that the walls were uncertain and liable to collapse under repeated blows, he looked around and constructed an inner wall in the shape of the letter C. [Note: “Liable to fall.” BARR.]

The next day, when part of the wall had been shaken apart, the crash of the falling structure [Note: Perhaps “of the building”? GALLAND.] and the shout of the Roman army rang out together, as though the collapse of the wall had accomplished the destruction. But when the cry proclaiming the city fallen rang out, the appearance of a new wall reversed the situation and checked the Romans’ unexpected joy. [Note: “Resounded.” BARR. — “Extinguished.” ID.] The Jews’ courage revived because the danger had been postponed.

Then Caesar began to exhort the army to believe that this new wall should be attacked without any hesitation. Its recent construction revealed it to be weak and easily dismantled. They needed only to advance boldly; the fragments of the wall would make the ascent easy, so that the Romans fighting below would be brought level with the Jews contesting from the higher position. And because he saw them hesitating before the difficulty of the task, he gathered the strongest men around him and fired them for battle with the following speech:

## CHAPTER XXVII
It is known to everyone, most valiant comrades, that the ends of all things involve more difficulty than their beginnings, because the completion of an undertaking requires greater exertion. For as long as a ship runs freely over the open sea, even if the winds do not always blow from astern, the helmsman adjusts the hollows of the sails, and the strait is cleft without hindrance. But when one reaches the harbor, a favorable moderation of the breezes is necessary, and the ships’ entrance is confined within a narrow channel. Thus the concern over danger is greater when hope is near; and for builders, the beginnings of foundations are level, but the work of lofty summits is arduous. Often, too, at the very end of closing the work, the unfortunate craftsman is deprived of the reward of his labor, either buried by the collapse of the roof or deceived by an unstable foothold, so that he falls to the lower ground. What should I say of the farmer, for whom the labor of harvest is more arduous than that of sowing, and that of vintage than that of pruning—and for whom the dangers to be feared are always more serious when the fruits have ripened?

It is therefore nothing strange if danger still awaits us at the very harbor, as we complete our course: for we must climb by the narrower paths to the Antonia, so that, once our adversaries have been thrown down from it, we may seize the higher position and, stationed above the heads of the enemy, in a sense cut off their very breath. But this seems difficult to us, comrades—as though we had assembled for a game and not for war, in which men must either conquer or die. You ought to have offered excuses when you came to battle, to avenge the defeat of the Roman army and wash away the disgrace of a dishonored military force. If in Nero’s time you judged that the injury to the Roman name had to be avenged, what ought you to desire under the emperor Vespasian? Let us wash away the stain of the former reign, lest it cling to ours. Nero was thought to be going to remove it through Vespasian, but Vespasian has transferred it onto himself through Titus—unless we conquer. Our father has left us only the finishing touches required for victory. Are we therefore, after so many labors have been expended in vain, to retreat disgraced and unavenged, abandoning victory? As though it were not a lighter crime to withdraw from military service than to desert victory: the former is cowardice, the latter treachery.

But you think it dangerous to descend against the enemy and make the wall resound with arms—as though nature herself demanded of us something womanly rather than manly deeds, when for that very reason she infused us with the breath of life so that we might willingly pour it out again for glory. To what, then, except the greatest enterprises, should a warrior be exhorted by his commander? For exhortation to an ordinary task brings shame not only upon those assembled but also upon those who assemble, since it demands what is owed voluntarily: a soldier ought to offer that of his own accord.

And yet what excessive demand am I making of you? Is it not better to die through valor than to live in disgrace? A Jew has often rushed into the midst of Roman battle lines and fearlessly thrown himself among the enemy’s formations—not in hope of victory, but as a demonstration of courage and an exhibition of glory. Are you, against whom no one has yet stood with impunity by land or sea, for whom victory is no novelty and failure to win a crime—when you possess so many advantages for victory—not ashamed never even once to rush upon the enemy? Are you not ashamed to keep armed men idle and those standing ready for battle waiting with inactive spirits, so that hunger may fight on our behalf, and so that starvation may turn its own triumphs—rather than those won by our swords—into something we must blush for?

I ask again, are you not ashamed, vigorous comrades, conquerors of every nation, to hope for nothing from arms, nothing from your strength, but only from the siege—to wait until the enemy grows old through disease and dies in his own bed? And what victory can there be without battle? Everything is filled with corpses; misshapen spoils lie scattered, the bloodless remains of the dead—except those whom they themselves have slaughtered with their own hands. Why do we fear those whom hunger, fire, brigandage, and sedition have already destroyed? Why do we abandon divine benefits? For by whose will except God’s have they been made to turn their weapons against one another? They are also deprived of provisions, and there is no end to their domestic madness. I fear that we may now appear rebellious even against religious law, since we have so long preserved men who are faithless both to our religion and to their own.

But let it be so: let the war be fierce and frightening. Why should I soothe you with the promise that war is easy? Let victory be uncertain and danger certain. Am I not speaking to men who know, by human wisdom, that the courage of all living creatures is more ready in danger than in less intense struggles? Wild beasts themselves, when they see themselves surrounded by armed forces, rush upon them with greater force so as to open a path for themselves by violence. And a snake driven from its hiding place pours out more savage venom. There are even creatures harmless by nature that, in their own dangers, become stronger in inflicting harm. Stags have their weapons if someone comes against them, and they repel death with their horns. Wounded little bees have their stings as well.

But why should I speak of warrior-men among the Romans? When that Leonidas, born at Sparta, was about to fight against the innumerable army of the Persians, he said: “Let us take lunch on earth, for we shall dine in the underworld.” This saying had such force among the Greeks that not only did none of those three hundred Spartan men whom he commanded withdraw—except one alone, whom afterward no one accepted as a survivor—but neither did any of the others who had gone out to fight with them withdraw, except those whom Leonidas rejected as unworthy of so great a war.

What should I say of the Roman legions in their full strength? Cato, the champion of Roman eloquence and the sincere interpreter of truth, declared that they had advanced to war with exultation, all willingly fell where they thought they were to return, so that they would not change their resolve. Blessed are those of whom no one announced victory to the enemy by flight.

Yet among the three hundred Spartans one man escaped: they were fighting in a narrow pass so that they would not be surrounded. Of the Roman legions, no one chose life; all chose the inheritance of death. You are their descendants, if, with contempt for danger as a glorious disposition, you do not reject the lineage of courage. For what brave man does not know that he is mortal and that an end to living has been appointed for all?

How much better, then, to devote to one’s country what one owes to nature, and exchange necessity for glory; neither to drag out a life subject to the sighs of breathless old age, nor to fear the accidents of burning illness, when those worn down by age are plagued by daily vexations. Those who waste away through weakness, their strength and senses failing together, are, as many believe, assigned together with their bodies to the grave.

But there is no doubt that the souls of warriors and exceptionally brave men who have devoted themselves to death for their country, their children, and their religion—souls released by the sword from the bonds of this body—are received in heavenly dwellings by that pure, ethereal element, shining with the light of the stars, as into a lodging of supernal repose. To remain on earth, too, is a mark either of grace or of injury: oblivion conceals those wasted away by sickness, while glory follows those who have carried their breasts against the enemy, if death has overtaken them.

To these rewards I invite you, comrades, so that we may advance against the enemy whom we hold shut in. Let us climb the wall by means of the ruin of the stronger wall, which offers us a kind of ramp and is level with the lower wall. Whoever, carrying the standard of courage, climbs first onto the wall—or second, or third, or accompanies the others—will certainly not leave me without being rewarded with a rich gift, even though there is no greater reward than the glory of courage, which is often the safer course. For as soon as someone supremely confident in spirit and strength has climbed up, those who were resisting will flee, withdraw to the lower ground, or hide in hiding places. Thus what now constitutes the greatest danger will, if we seek it below, result without great effort in the completion of the battle once the enemy has been thrown down.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Titus had scarcely finished his speech when Sabinus, one of the men from Syria, presented himself. He was an outstanding warrior, and, standing before Caesar, he said that he was ready to obey the commands and to climb, if fortune should favor him in a manner pleasing to Caesar; but if success should fail him, nothing would happen to him beyond his expectation, since by his own judgment he had chosen to die for Caesar.

After saying this, he extended his left hand, raised his shield above his head, and brandished his sword with his right, rising up against the weapons with extraordinary force. Anyone who had not known him would have thought him contemptible on account of his slight build; yet suddenly he saw him advancing against the enemy, extending himself threateningly against both the enemy and the walls, as though already standing higher and fighting against those below, striking the wall with his hand.

Eleven eager men followed him in imitation, but they were unequal to following him to the end. The Jews resisted from the wall with javelins, stones, and arrows; whatever weapon each man’s hand found was hurled down upon Sabinus. Undaunted, he leaped at a swift run onto the ramp formed by the fragments, and, stationed at its summit, turned the enemy aside while each of those nearest him feared the danger. But as he balanced himself and raised himself toward the wall, directing himself against the enemy in confidence of victory, he slipped forward onto his face and fell with a tremendous crash.

The Jews, recalled by this, began to press the fallen man with missiles. Kneeling and protecting himself with his shield as long as he could, he defended himself against injury, and did not leave uninjured anyone he found near him. At last, however, overwhelmed by wounds, he laid down his life before he laid down the battle; he was neither thrown from his position nor knocked from the wall except as a dead man. Three others were also killed, and eight left half-dead, although the rest were rescued from destruction.

## CHAPTER XXIX

The death of Sabinus was not merely a source of terror to the others but also an incentive. The Roman soldiers who had been assigned guard duty, wishing to compensate by their accomplishment for having been forestalled by Sabinus’ zeal, formed a great and memorable plan, twenty in number. They would enlist a standard-bearer of the fifth rank, two men from the cavalry whom they considered the most ready, and one trumpeter; then, in the silence of the fifth hour of the night, they would raise themselves by way of the ramps made from the wall fragments to the higher ground, kill the guards, and seize the wall of the Antonia.

When this had been accomplished, the sound of the trumpet rang out more terrifyingly than usual, so that the Jews, exhausted by labor and released into sleep, would be thrown into sudden confusion, believing that everything was filled with enemies. They therefore began to flee before the truth could be established. For the uncertainty of danger and the darkness of the night prevented anyone from discovering how many they were.

When Caesar heard the blast, he ordered the army to arm itself. He himself, with picked men, was the first to climb the wall, an aid to his own men and an impediment to the enemy. Day broke, and Caesar, now visible from the wall, was encouraging his men. Some were lifted onto the wall by the hands of their comrades; others entered the city through the tunnel that John had dug to overthrow the Roman ramps.

Their own supports were turned to the destruction of the faithless men, and, shut in on every side, they withdrew into the temple. The Romans wished to rush in there as well, but were held back by the confined spaces and driven off by weapons. A serious battle took place in the vestibule, now fought not with javelins or arrows but with swords at close quarters: hand against wound, sword against sword, blow against blow. The striker was drenched with the blood of those he had struck, so that he himself seemed rather to have been struck.
