War-fury dominated the temple itself. The pavements floated with blood. The groans of the dying and the shouts of the victors resounded without order or measure. The hope of finishing the battle inflamed the Romans; the final destruction of their country deprived the Jews of fear of death. The Romans nourished their courage at the expense of glory; the Jews, through despair of safety, poured out all the provisions of their courage and reserved nothing.

## CHAPTER XXX

Julianus the centurion also undertook a most splendid deed. He was a man of exceptional excellence in arms, born in the province of Bithynia but accustomed to Roman discipline and trained in warfare, and distinguished by the service-pay of an honored military career. When he was standing near Caesar and saw the Romans driven back, because the Jews were superior in number and the Romans were still fewer, he suddenly rushed out from the Antonia and turned back those who were pursuing them. They did not dare resist, awed by the very appearance of so outstanding a man and by the proud authority of a courage surpassing human form, so that Caesar himself marveled.

O varied and uncertain, as it were, gamble of wars! Just as in a throw, so often through chance rather than courage, it plays with unexpected outcomes, providing new endings. Here too there were throws—not of dice, but of arrows, many kinds of weapons, and stones—by which the victor is often struck down by another’s wound. While he seizes another’s spoils, he himself is stripped: so it happened to Julianus, who was pressing upon the enemy from behind while killing others and restraining them within the enclosure. Made incautious by his very eagerness, and wearing shoes fixed with nails, as soldiers do, he did not notice the polished stone pavement, which he ought to have avoided. But, as though he were fighting securely in an open field, he slipped and fell, making a tremendous crash through his own downfall.

He could not rise after falling on the slippery ground. Yet, supporting himself on one knee, he drove back the enemy as he returned to the attack, so that he might strike those approaching and avoid, as far as possible, those hurling missiles. But exhausted and overwhelmed by the multitude, although alone—for no one dared to enter into such danger with him—he nevertheless fell bravely, neither contemptible nor unavenged.

I believe that he was not worthy of such an end, that so great a man’s courage should be deceived in this way. But prudence counts for very much in war: always cautious and watchful, it anticipates the accidents of uncertainty. He alone rushed out from the Antonia; he alone charged into the enemy ranks; he alone mingled with armed men; he alone forced the Jews to retreat into the temple. I fear that this harmed him all the more, because the faithless men were to be driven from the temple by God, and therefore his fall found no remedy.

Titus watched the victor with joy and the endangered man with immense pain. He wanted to help, but was far away. His own men called him back, because in the case of a soldier the danger belongs to one man, but in the case of a commander it belongs to everyone. The event taught Caesar what he ought to avoid rather than imitate.

At last the companions were so dismayed and the adversaries so elated that Julianus’ body fell into the power of the enemy, as though they still feared him even dead if he were restored to the Romans. After Julianus was killed, the others yielded with little difficulty. For the Romans had not yet climbed up in large numbers, and the Jews’ opportunity to kill him had increased their courage.

The most ready in that battle to repel the Romans were Alexa and Gitteus, conspirators of John, who served as champions of his faction; from Simon’s side there were also Melchio and James, leaders of the Idumeans and outstanding warriors; Arsimone and Judas, men of the third faction, also exerted themselves with equal force. With joined hands, they shut the Romans, who had been driven back, inside the Antonia.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Titus, on the contrary, judged the narrowness of the Antonia not a protection but an impediment to himself. He therefore ordered its fortification to be demolished completely, so that a path into the enemy might be opened for those about to engage them.

When he learned that the Jewish festival days were approaching, he ordered Josephus to interpret in Hebrew what he himself was going to say. What reason, he asked, could possibly persuade John to provoke the Romans? If he possessed confidence in his courage, he should choose another place for battle. He should advance there, provided only that he spared the city; that he did not contaminate the temple; that he did not obstruct the festival sacrifices; and that he left those whom he considered suitable for the service of the sacrifices. Let him display proof of his courage wherever he wished, outside the city and the temple. Caesar’s soldiers would not be lacking for the encounter. Titus was being forced against his will to destroy the entire city. He would wish to preserve its remnants, if John would allow it.

Torches threatened the temple—not because the Romans were eager to burn it, but because they wished to draw the instigators of the war out of it. If they believed themselves defeated, they should surrender; but if they hoped to be victorious, they should not retreat within enclosures but defend themselves in the fields, so that the temple might be rescued while the fires were already spreading and might be left free for purification.

While Josephus translated these words for the Jews, the common people listened in silence and approved inwardly, but feared to reveal their judgment. John replied that no sacrifice was more acceptable to God than to lay down one’s life for the altars, the hearths, and the temple—to offer men consecrated to God. Therefore, if necessary, he would gladly fall for freedom; nevertheless, he hoped that the city of God could not suffer destruction.

Titus replied: “Then rightly you preserve for God a pure city and a holy, undefiled temple by killing citizens, slaughtering the innocent, and destroying priests? Such crimes do not appease the divine powers; they offend them. Through the worship of sacrifices you have renounced your God. If someone denied you food, John, would you not seek him out? Your victims are not sacrificed to your God; his gifts are not returned to him. Human beings are slaughtered, and yet you still think that God will help you?

“Indeed, the events themselves teach this, and the piles of the slain and the heaps of your calamities bear witness. Who could see these things without groaning? Nor would I criticize you for fighting on behalf of your country if I did not wish to spare it, if I did not wish to preserve your country or your temple. Carthage was not worthy of such treatment, nor was the Hebrew Hannibal to be feared—he who had subdued the central part of the Roman world. Yet even Carthage was rebuilt, though it had endured the rebellious spirits of its citizens until its destruction.

“On my word, I promise you that all these things will remain safe for you; I offer you the pardon of safety—not as a reward for crime, but as the ransom of the city, so that through you I may redeem the condition of buildings destined to perish. Cease, I warn you, to disturb by your brigandage the purpose of Roman mercy. Jerusalem will not be spared from destruction out of fear, since Antioch, stronger in resources, has been preserved.

“Certainly your Jeconiah trusted even the Persians and, leaving the city, entrusted himself and his closest companions to barbarian fury, lest the city be destroyed on his account. You celebrate his memory, as your own writers assert—Josephus, his defender and the witness to the honor with which you commemorate the man who offered himself to captivity for his country. The barbarian Persian spared him, and I promise you impunity as well.

“Certainly Josephus also bore arms against the Romans. Trust the promise whose example we have already set before you. We give you Josephus as hostage for our pledge—indeed, we have already given him, since we preserved him. Let him speak to you in your native language and bind himself according to the custom you observe. I am not ashamed to seek a hostage and to offer a guarantor, lest I appear as a destroyer when I wish to spare.”

At this Josephus wept, begged John, mourned the condition of his country, and pleaded in tearful speech. He addressed him as a fellow citizen, but John was even more stubborn than the others. Josephus called upon the grace of almighty God, saying that John and his people would be safe, provided only that he ceased stirring up the Roman army to destroy the city.

When he could not bend him, Josephus said: “It is no wonder, John, if you persist all the way to the destruction of your country, since the divine defenses have already abandoned it. But it is astonishing that you do not believe it is destined to perish, when you have read the prophetic books in which the destruction of our country was announced to us, and its restored buildings again destined to be destroyed by the Roman army.

“For what else does Daniel proclaim? He was not prophesying what had already happened but what would happen afterward. What is the abomination of desolation that he proclaimed would occur when the Romans came, if not this very thing that now threatens us? What is that oracle so often recalled by us, announced by the Most High God: that the city would then perish completely, when a fellow citizen had been killed by the hands of its own citizens? Is this not what we now see being fulfilled? And perhaps, since it is no longer pleasing to defend the temple, it is pleasing that, stained by forbidden blood, it should be cleansed by fire.”

## CHAPTER XXXII

Josephus finished his speech, but John was moved by none of his tears and bent by none of his promises. God had long been driving the faithless minds onward, ever since they had stained themselves with their wicked act of parricide: nailing Christ Jesus to the cross.

He is the one whose death is the destruction of the Jews, born of Mary, who came to his own and his own did not receive him (John 1:11).

For when have the Jews not killed their own? Did they not kill Saul’s son, their own? The prophet Naboth was certainly stoned by his own people. Jezebel was a Jewess, and the Jews’ elders carried out her command. Ahab was a Jew, and he was responsible for Naboth’s death. How many other citizens have been killed by their fellow citizens, while the state nevertheless remained intact for a long time—even if it was later destroyed by the Babylonians after innumerable years, and afterward rebuilt?

This is the final destruction, after which the temple is irreparable, because by their crimes they turned away the temple’s guardian, the arbiter of its restoration.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

After Caesar’s speech and its repetition, the judgment of some was changed. Those who were able to withdraw went over to the Romans. Fear of the danger being threatened by the brigands recalled the others—and perhaps there was some inclination of mind to prevent more people from escaping the destruction that was to come.

Caesar received those who fled to him favorably. Among them were priestly men with their sons and other men of more distinguished families. He promised them the security of their lives and the right to retain their possessions, and sent them to a city called Gosna, so that no offense might arise from differences of custom and worship.

Those who remained in the city and resisted—whether because such a suspicion had arisen or because someone had devised a trick to prevent more people from slipping away—turned this into a charge warranting slaughter, so that those killed might be cast forth as an example. When Titus learned of this, he ordered those who had been recalled to go with Josephus closer to the walls, so that their own people might recognize them.

With tears and great lamentation, they mourned not their own fate but the destruction of their country and temple. They begged their fellow citizens to follow Caesar’s pledge, rescue the temple from the prepared fire, and understand that nothing had been prescribed against them contrary to the law, and that nothing had been taken away from their freedom. Let them themselves accept and experience the mercy of the Romans, whose unconquerable courage they had already experienced.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

While they were lamenting these things pitifully, their own people drove them away, and the battle was inflamed. The Jews rushed forward and, in their very recklessness, burst into the innermost sanctuaries. They occupied every recess and every secret place that was inaccessible to men excluded from the sacred rites.

The Romans also prepared for battle. Things forbidden by the fathers were violated out of the necessity of war, though with greater reverence for the Romans than for their own people. The Gentiles looked upon the temple with fear, while the Jews approached it with fury and recklessness; carrying hands wet with human blood, they themselves grasped the altars.

Titus, however, still persisting in his purpose, addressed John and declared that he was being forced against his will to the destruction of the city and temple. He said to him:

“What do those letters inscribed before the temple gates mean, John? Do they not signify that no one except a consecrated person ought to approach the temple? What do those enclosures before the temple mean? Is it not that they keep the sight of it from all foreigners and that knowledge of its secrets is open only to the initiated, whose view is unobstructed because their entrance is lawful?

“You exclude the sight of foreigners and compel their approach. You write that no outsider should enter and no foreigner go inside; yet you pour foreign blood within the temple and stain your altars with the blood alike of newcomers and citizens.

“I testify that it is not because of our intrusion but because of your transgression that you violate what belongs to you. I, an outsider, demand nothing. Rather, I solemnly assure you that, if you wish to withdraw, the temple will remain unharmed. No Roman will inflict hostile hands upon it, and none of your sacrifices will be violated.

“I will preserve the temple for you and for proselytes. The forms of sacred worship are different, but the practical use of the work is common. What belonged to worship has withdrawn from you; what belongs to the work has remained with the victors.”

## CHAPTER XXXV

When Caesar realized that not even these messages conveyed through Josephus could recall them—for the leaders of the faction thought that such frequent efforts to persuade them to desist arose from distrust rather than piety—he reluctantly returned to the battle out of necessity and ordered the Romans to be present.

But because the confined space was an impediment to such a great multitude, he assigned one thousand warriors to each of thirty chosen men. For the dense obstacles formed by the buildings could not accommodate the entire army.

He himself wished to descend at the same time, but his men called him back, lest in the narrow space, especially during the night, when it was necessary to counter the deceit of those lying in ambush, he should expose himself to some danger. He would accomplish more by being present as a spectator of the battle, since each man would judge that he ought to fight more eagerly under Caesar’s eyes.

Everything taking place around the temple could be seen from above, from the position of the Antonia, as though from a theater. Caesar yielded to this judgment and assigned Cerealis the task of arriving at the ninth hour of the night against the Jews who were stationed around the temple. He urged the others to press vigorously into the battle and promised that he would not fail to reward the merits of the fighters, as he examined the battle from above either as witness of anyone’s cowardice or as judge of his courage.

Cerealis arrived promptly at the appointed time, but found the guards awake. Battle was joined. Those stationed inside the temple were not sleeping, and when the men on watch engaged, the others easily prepared themselves for battle.

With his ranks assembled, the Roman pressed forward. The Jews, relying on their enclosures and narrow spaces so as not to be surrounded, ran in different directions. Thus the danger from their own men was more frequent, since they could not recognize one another in the darkness and were often pierced by their comrades while being mistaken for enemies. For who could distinguish at night whether he was meeting a comrade or an enemy? To ask was too late; caution was useful; anticipating the danger was prudent. It was a more tolerable outcome of guilt to err in striking another than to choose one’s own danger when the enemy was feared.

Thus throughout the night the Jews struggled with a twofold danger: what the enemy might inflict and where a comrade might make a mistake. By day the Roman was no less vigorous, urged silently by Titus, who watched the entire battle. The fighting continued fiercely until the fifth hour, while the Jews too resisted bravely, so that neither side yielded its position.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

While these battles were being fought between them, over the course of seven days everything was removed down to the foundations in the earth, and the road leading to the temple was made broader on the site where Herod had fortified the camp called the Antonia. This was done so that the soldiers would have room not only to move about but also to establish defenses and pile up ramps as far as the available ground required, from which even the highest summits of the temple might be struck.

As the Romans lingered more intently over this work and the Jews were pressed by hunger with increasing intolerability, they began to lie in wait for the Romans’ pack animals. If any soldier had released a horse to graze, or a mule needed for carrying a burden, they would seize and drive it away. Food was thus not only lost to the Romans but also sought as an occasion for outrage.

Caesar immediately removed the disgrace of this negligence by prescribing the punishment of death, but he did not suppress the fraud or obstinacy. Shut out from this necessary source of food, the starving men began to seek sustenance in herbs. They considered destroying the wall that Titus had built around the orchard, so that they would have freer opportunity to wander about, search for the roots of trees, and gather fodder. The circuit of the wall had enclosed them as though in a prison, and they now had no means of relieving their hunger.

They therefore crept out and, in a sudden sortie, attacked the men stationed toward the Mount of Olives. Those men did not fail in the duty assigned to them; they sounded the trumpet and summoned others from the remaining defenses of the camp and towers to join the battle.

The fighting was fiercer at the beginning, as shame drove one side and hunger the other with savage and necessary force. But as the Romans gathered, the Jews were driven back and turned toward the walls of their city.

Then one of the cavalry squadron, named Pedanius, spurred his horse forward, extended his right hand, and, leaning slightly, seized one of the fleeing Jews. He carried him captive to Caesar and, as the victor of a glorious capture, cast him alive at Caesar’s feet like a little hare dropped by an eagle or hawk. Titus was greatly pleased and dismissed him with praise and honor.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

The porticoes surrounding the temple were already burning. Everywhere there was mourning, everywhere death: outside, war; inside, war and fire besides.

Yet the Jews were not broken in spirit. They thought that whatever they did without deceit or insolence was perishing as an act of vengeance. Since they could no longer act otherwise, they challenged the Romans to hasten the destruction.

A certain Jonathes, small in body and even more deserving of contempt, was taunting the Romans beside the tomb of John, challenging anyone who wished to fight him hand-to-hand. Some disdained the man’s smallness; others were reluctant to fight someone whom they would immediately take captive; still others considered that it was dangerous to engage men who, at the extreme point of their safety, sought vengeance not through any courage but through sheer recklessness. There would be no glory if a man next to destruction were defeated, and great disgrace if someone through a fall or other mishap marred the common victory.

The exceedingly insolent man boasted and charged the victors with fear. He hurled insults, saying that the Romans relied not on their own strength but on the aid of others, and that the Jews were being defeated not by the warfare of enemies but by domestic seditions.

There was among the Roman soldiers a man named Pudens. Stung by these empty insults, he imprudently sought to protect his honor and neglected his safety. Made more incautious by his indignation, he exposed himself to a wound, fell to the ground, and brought shame upon his comrades. He also left Jonathes both the cause for his boast and the occasion of his death.

For Jonathes, delighted by the success of the contest and raising the display of his triumph, danced and exulted, brandishing his shield and sword in a kind of mock combat. By doing so he provoked the centurion Priscus into attacking him. Priscus could not tolerate the man’s proud and swollen boasting, and, while Jonathes was off guard, pierced him with an arrow.

Struck down, Jonathes taught that no one ought to insult another irrationally in battle, where the condition of victor and vanquished remains uncertain until the war is concluded.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

But in the inner city, when the inhabitants saw the enemy towering within the walls on the highest ramps and threatening all the fortifications, and feared that the danger was advancing inward like a wound in the body, they cut down the northern portico on the side where it adjoined the Antonia. They feared that through it the enemy might climb into the upper parts of the temple or that, from the higher ground, they might press upon those stationed below.

They also cut down everything nearby, lest the fires spreading through the buildings adjoining the temple consume the temple itself. Having cut off these structures, they burned them with fire. Thus they began first to do what they feared from the enemy.

They also prepared Solomon’s portico for a stratagem, filling the interior spaces beneath the arch of its highest roof with pitch and bitumen, which they concealed below the vault of the upper structure. Pretending that they wished to defend it, and frequently attacking the enemy, they provoked the Romans and drew them toward themselves.

The Romans brought up ladders and sought the top of the portico. The Jews gradually yielded the position because more Romans had climbed up. The Romans climbed in eagerly, though the more prudent suspected a trick and guarded against it. But the common soldiers, intent upon victory, hurried forward. Once the place seemed free of deceit, fire was brought to the inner vaults, with many men placed as though among nets. When the pitch, bitumen, and other fuel for the fire had been added, the flames spread through the entire portico.

The flames surrounded the victorious Romans, leaving them neither the possibility of resistance nor the opportunity for flight. They could not discover what to do. Titus watched his men in danger, angry that they had climbed without orders but pitying them because they were perishing as victors.

Many threw themselves down. But when they had escaped the fire, they died with broken legs and battered bodies. It was more pitiable if the wounded survived. Caesar wished to help but could not. Nevertheless, he encouraged those nearest him and shouted that they should aid his men.

Those voices, that grief of Caesar, were regarded by the dying as their final consolation. This was their provision for the journey; this was what consoled them as though by an exalted tomb and made them hasten toward death: that they would be buried in Caesar’s heart. Their lives would not perish, since the glory of those who died for Caesar would live on, leaving behind the inheritance of a triumph.

Thus some were surrounded by flames, others overtaken by them; and the enemy was close at hand, striking those who fled from the fire.

- [Col. 2174D] **Destitueretur**, “should be forsaken” (BARR.), is a variant for the reading concerning adverse success.
- [Col. 2175D] **Confectus**, “overcome, exhausted” (BARR.), is a variant reading.
- [Col. 2175D] **Tamen**, “nevertheless” (ID.), is a variant reading.
- [Col. 2176D] **Inferebant**, “were making their way in” (ID.), is a variant reading.

- [Col. 2177D–2178D] The old Roman codex reads: “would provoke the Romans to the destruction of the temple” (ID.).

## CHAPTER XXXIX
Nevertheless, Longinus, a man of outstanding courage, when the Jews challenged him to entrust himself to them with a promise of safety, preferred to run himself through with his sword rather than stain the courage characteristic of the Roman spirit with disgrace. Artorius, however, with considerable cleverness, shouted loudly for Lucius, saying: “You will be my heir if you catch me as I fall.” The pitiable man rushed to meet him as he fell and received into himself the death of the dying man. Truly a military testament—not written in ink but in blood; not on paper but on a sword’s edge. What he promised as an inheritance displayed remarkable ingenuity: he found a voluntary substitute for death.

Thus the colonnade was set alight as far as the tower which John had built above the gates of the royal palace when he was waging war against Simon—the palace that King Hezekiah had built for his residence. The Jews themselves had demolished the remaining part of it. On the following day, too, the entire northern colonnade was burned by the Romans as far as the eastern colonnade. For when the Jews themselves laid hands on their own buildings, they taught the Romans [Note: [Col. 2183D] “To spare those belonging to others.” BARR.] not to spare them.

By now the face of the temple was bare, and a savage famine raged among the people. They plotted against one another, each wondering from whom he might snatch food. Wherever there was a suspicion of food, there was war among members of the same household. They fought for food; their dearest ones were killed; the dead were searched, lest food should be concealed beneath their clothing. Some pretended to be dead, so that the living would not be suspected of possessing any food; yet even the living could neither carry on the duties of life nor pretend to be dead. Indeed, with open mouths like rabid dogs, catching breaths of air, they wandered here and there, led by want. Often, as though drunk, they returned to the same dwellings in order to search again what they had previously left empty.

And when they found no other consolation in famine, they stripped the leather from their shields, so that what had been their defenses might serve them as food. They chewed their shoes; nor did they feel shame at taking them from their feet, placing them in their mouths, and licking them with their tongues. Even the old straw that had once been thrown away was sought with no little diligence; and if anyone found it, he lent it at a high price.

## CHAPTER XL

What am I to undertake describing concerning the deed of Maria—a deed at which the mind of any barbarian or impious person would shudder?

She was one of the wealthier women of the region of Perea, which lies beyond the Jordan. When the horror of war arose, she had withdrawn with the others to the city of Jerusalem because it was safer; she had also brought there her wealth, which the leaders of the factions seized in competition with one another. Whatever food she had managed to obtain at a price was violently torn from her hands. She was harassed by the treacherous; she uttered dreadful curses; she wished to die, but could find no one to strike her. They preferred to insult and torment her longer rather than destroy her quickly. They thought that as long as she lived, there would be booty to take.

Everything had now failed, and, accustomed to luxuries, she could not soften the harshness of straw or the hardness of leather. Savage hunger penetrated into the innermost marrow, inflamed her humors, and drove her mind to frenzy. The woman had an infant whom she had borne. Awakened by his crying, and seeing herself and the little child wasting away, overcome by such enormities and unequal to so terrible a calamity, she lost control of her emotions. With the natural affection of a mother blotted out, she swallowed her grief and assumed madness.

Turning toward the little child, now having forgotten that she was a mother, and raging in spirit, she said:

“What shall I do to you, little one? What shall I do for you? Everything savage surrounds you: war, famine, fires, robbers, ruins. To whom shall I entrust you when I am dying, or to whom shall I leave you, so tiny? I had hoped that, if you grew up, you would nourish me as your mother, or bury me when I was dead. Certainly, if you died first, I would enclose you in a precious tomb with my own hands. What am I to do, wretched woman? I see no means of keeping either you or me alive. Everything has been snatched from us; for whom shall I preserve you? Or, at least, in what tomb shall I bury you, lest you become prey to dogs, birds, or wild beasts? Everything, I say, has been snatched from us.

“Yet you can still nourish your mother, my sweet child; your hands are fit for food. O your lovely entrails, your delightful limbs! Before hunger utterly consumes you, give back to your mother what you received. Return, my son, to that natural hidden place in which you drew breath; let that same dwelling be prepared as your tomb when you are dead. I myself shall embrace the child I bore; I myself shall kiss him. And whatever the impatience of love possesses, let the force of necessity possess as well, so that I myself may devour my own limbs—not with feigned bites, but with bites that leave their mark.

“Be food for me, then; frenzy for the robbers; and a tale for the world—the one thing still lacking from our calamities. What would you do, my son, if you too had a son? We have done what affection required; let us do what hunger advises. Yet your situation is the better, and has a certain appearance of filial affection: for it is more tolerable that you should give your mother food from your own entrails than that your mother should either kill or devour you.

“With these words, she turned her face away, plunged in her sword, and, cutting her son into pieces, placed him on the fire. She ate part and covered the rest, lest someone should come upon her. But the smell of the roasted flesh reached the leaders of the sedition. Immediately, following the odor, they entered the woman’s lodging, threatening to kill her because she had dared to eat while they themselves were fasting and to deprive them of food that she had found.

“But I have saved your portion for you,” she said. “I was neither greedy nor inhuman. Do not be angry: you have something to eat as well. From my own entrails I have prepared food for you. Sit down quickly; I shall set the table. You must marvel and [Note: [Col. 2185D] “Judge.” BARR.] judge my service, since you will find no woman’s affection like this one, a woman who would not deprive you even of the pleasure of her sweet child.”

As she spoke, she uncovered the burned limbs again and offered them to be eaten, encouraging them with words such as these:

“This is my meal; this is your portion. Look carefully, lest I have cheated you. Here is one of the child’s hands; here is one of his feet; here is half of the rest of his body. And lest you think it belongs to someone else, he is my son; lest you suppose it to be another’s work, I did it. I carefully divided for myself what I would eat and what I would reserve for you. Never were you sweeter to me, my son. I owe it to you that I am still alive. Your sweetness sustained my soul and prolonged the day of death for your wretched mother. You came to my aid in famine; you are the final gift of old age, the restrainer of those who struck me. They came to kill me; they have become my guests. They themselves will have what they owe you when they have taken part in my feast.

“But why do you draw back? Why do you shudder in spirit? Why do you not eat what I, your mother, have prepared? What satisfied your mother may also delight you. I am no longer hungry, since my son has fed me; I am fully satisfied, and know nothing of hunger. Taste and see, for my son is sweet. Do not become softer than your mother, weaker than a woman.

“But if you show compassion toward my wound and do not accept my sacrifice, and if you turn away from my burnt offering, I shall complete my sacrifice and eat what remains. Take care lest it be a reproach to you that a woman was found stronger than you, one who consumed the feast of men. I indeed prepared such a feast, but you made me, the mother, feast in this way. Passion held me, but necessity conquered.”

## CHAPTER XLI

Immediately the horror of so great a crime filled the entire city, and each person, as though the service of the parricidal banquet had been placed before his eyes, shuddered at it. After this, even the instigators of the sedition began to examine what foods they might seize, lest they find similar fare and consume it unwittingly. Everyone began to fear that he might live too long, and wished to die.

The enormity of this deed also reached the Romans. Many, terrified by the horror of it, fled to the enemy. When Caesar learned this, he cursed the contagion of that wretched land, raised his hands to heaven, and protested as follows:

“We came indeed to war, but we are not fighting with human beings. Against every frenzy of beasts and wild animals—why do I speak of sentient creatures?—we are waging war against every monstrousness of rocks. Wild animals love their offspring and nourish them even in famine; and those that feed upon the bodies of others abstain from the corpses of animals like themselves. This surpasses every form of savagery: that a mother should devour the limbs to which she gave birth.

“I am free of this contagion; to you I declare myself acquitted, whatever power you are in heaven. You know, you certainly know, that with the deepest affection I frequently offered peace, and—though I am not ashamed to say it—as the victor I begged for it. I wished to spare even the perpetrators of such great crimes and monstrosities, to spare the people, and to preserve the city. But what was I to do against those who resisted? What was I to do against those who raged against their own people?

“Although I had laid down my arms on many occasions, because they did not cease slaughtering their own people, I returned to the war in order to free those under siege, not to destroy them. They themselves often urged us from the walls to fight, lest they perish more grievously at the hands of their own people. What sort of citizens are these, for whom the enemy is a remedy?

“I had indeed heard of the intolerable ferocity of this people, who, by means of incredible beliefs, rouse themselves to every kind of insolence. They claim to derive their race from heaven; to have first assumed bodily form there; to have been inhabitants of heaven; to have descended to the worship of earthly things and from earth to return to heaven; to have crossed the seas on dry feet; to have made the waves of the sea flee before them; to have caused the waters of the Jordan to turn back and run toward their source; to have made the sun stand still so that they might defeat their enemies and night might not hinder them; that their own people were carried into heaven in fiery chariots; that the powers of heaven fought on their behalf; and that, while these powers were absent, the whole armies of their enemies were routed and victory was won while they slept.

“I had learned these things, but I thought they boasted of divine benefits bestowed upon them without extending their audacity so far as to suppose themselves incapable of being defeated even by the Romans. I therefore recognize that our battle is with people who believe themselves invincible, who boast that they survived the Flood, that they are heirs of the rivers, guests of the earth, travelers over the sea, riders of the ether; for whom water is a wall, air a road, heaven a dwelling; whom flames obey and bonds cannot hold.

“For the thirsty, the rock is opened and pours itself forth as drink. For the hungry, heaven is opened and food is sent; the camps are filled with the flesh of flying creatures, and man eats the bread of angels. Liquids are solidified, bitter things become sweet, the sun stands still, and darkness gives light. Finally, what more can there be, when such people can lack nothing in audacity? They claim that the dead live and the buried are raised again.

“There is widespread belief that these people have even conspired against the divine powers, and punishment bears witness to it. Even today the lands burn because of the impiety of their inhabitants; the earth’s chasms have swallowed many of them. How long, then, shall we remain in these places? Here we have seen the ruin of the earth; we have seen the Dead Sea; we have also seen the dead growths of the land, the dry soil, the empty shadows of green and fruitful plants—outwardly grace, inwardly ash. Who can doubt that we are in the underworld, where even the elements are dying?

“Indeed, even that which usually lives after death is dead among them—the compassion of nature and the reverence that survives the dead. For who does not love parents even after their death? Who does not love children who have been lost and preserve them in the place of dear pledges? Affection remains even if the pledge has died; the name of nature endures, and grace does not perish.

“But among these people a mother neither recognizes her living son, nor hears him when he calls, nor pities his cries. For the sake of a single hour’s accursed food, she laid parricidal [Note: [Col. 2187D] “Laid upon.” BARR.] hands upon her own child. But why do I accuse this as though it were something new, when they trace the beginnings of their race to the murder of a brother? When they proclaim the faith of Abraham himself, whom they call their father, the author of their discipline, and the founder of their worship, chiefly on the ground that he thought he should not spare his son, brought him to the altar like a victim, and did not hesitate to offer him as a burnt offering?

“I do not condemn devotion, but I ask about piety. They say that another of their people also made a vow, promising that, if victorious, he would sacrifice to his god whatever first met him on his return home. When he returned, his daughter met him, and he laid hands upon his daughter. And there are many other examples of this kind.

“What sort of nation is this, which assigns the killing of a human being to religion and considers parricide a sacrifice? What god could demand such a thing, or what priest could offer it? Finally, they say that the earlier man—Abraham, they [Note: [Col. 2187D] “He means Abraham.” ID.] claim—did not do this as one who was wiser, but wished to do it; whereas the other, as though [Note: [Col. 2187D] “Less prudent—namely Jephthah.” ID.] more deliberate, persisted.

“Let them have their rites, these hard-hearted people [Note: [Col. 2187D] “Hard people nonetheless.” ID.], among whom it is a discipline to kill their children. Unhappy city, in which there is such a workshop, such a [Note: [Col. 2187D] “Service.” ID.] mystery! May its ruins cover it and conceal its hateful [Note: [Col. 2187D] “Of the world itself.” ID.] contagion, lest the sun see it, lest the sphere of the stars behold it, lest the breath of the winds be stained. That purifying fire too will consume it.

“We think the feasts of Thyestes a fable; here we see the crime and behold a reality more terrible than tragedies. There the stronger sex was involved, and the offspring was another’s; here there is a woman for whom her own child became food. There, another’s deceit; here, her own will. He grieved; she mocked. She is a fitting food for such men, who by waging war obstinately brought their women to such a banquet.

“I believe that, afflicted by such bitter evils, they are already raving and have become mad, since they do not perceive these things. Therefore let us bring the war to an end more quickly, since they cannot be corrected; let us attack more vigorously, so that we may escape the waters of these regions, which are dying, and the lands that are collapsing.”

## CHAPTER XLII

After saying this, he ordered rams to be brought against the temple, but the repeated blows achieved nothing. Nevertheless, many, terrified, fled from the very leaders of the sedition to Caesar. Titus did not hesitate to receive them as men compelled by necessity rather than as men who had followed a promise; but good faith restrained his anger. He did not, however, place them in the position he had granted to earlier deserters, and he began to press his own men more vigorously, so that all the enemy might withdraw, overcome by fear.

But when they saw that the walls remained unharmed by the blows of the battering rams and continued to stand by their own mass, their boldness increased. Caesar, however, anticipating them by his ingenuity, ordered the silver-plated doors to be set on fire. When fire was applied, the silver began to flow away, and then gradually the wood also began to burn; thus the way into the inner colonnade was opened.

But Caesar, moved by pity, lest the temple be consumed when the nearby colonnades of the inner vestibule were caught up in the flames, called the commanders of the army into council and said that his contest was not with insensible things, nor was he waging war against buildings, which would benefit the victors if they were preserved unburned. The commanders, however, maintained that the strength of the walls and the fortification of the temple would provide the Jews with further encouragement, since insolence was pleasing to them; the roots of the rebellion had to be torn out completely, lest recklessness should again grow strong.

Caesar nevertheless postponed discussion of the matter until the following day. The Jews, however, thought they should throw themselves into the attack. But the Romans, locking their shields together, though fewer in number, withstood the first assault. The battle line was nevertheless wavering under the rush of the countless multitude. Therefore Caesar quickly arrived with cavalry, easily trampling down those whom he encountered and driving back the enemy column, relying on the fact that part of the vestibules was now open.

On the following day he arranged a larger force of his men to burst upon the enemy and set fire to the temple. This action would have rescued the city from the fire, had not the people’s madness called the enemy’s flames upon themselves. For Caesar ordered the fireballs to be extinguished, lest they obstruct those who were about to break in. When the Jews saw this, they lay in ambush for those who wished to extinguish the temple fires; after killing some of them, they inflamed the enemy.

One of the Romans found a half-burned piece of wood that had fallen from the pediment and, with the fire now fully established, brought it to the gate called the Golden Gate because its doors were plated with gold. The heat of the flames immediately melted the rigidity of the gold and exposed the wood, which, like an uncovered side, lay open to the fire. When the doors had been burned, the fire penetrated into the inner recesses of the temple. By now its vestibule doors were glowing.

All who had defended themselves behind the temple’s fortification were thrown into confusion and began immediately to tremble. A certain inclination of minds had already arisen that this was the day destined for the temple’s destruction, because on that very day it had once been burned when the Babylonians attacked, since it was the tenth day of the month of Joma [Note: [Col. 2187D] The old codex has “Loina.” Suidas testifies that “Lous” was called August by the Macedonians. BARR. — See also Dodwell, *On the Cycles of the Ancient Greeks and Romans*, Dissertation 9, [Col. 2188D] p. 397, where the Macedonian months are compared with the Hebrew months according to Josephus. In any case, Lous is July among the Macedonians. Yet Suidas should not be thought to have erred. The lexicographer must be understood to mean the Syro-Macedonians, whose year is known among scholars to precede the Macedonian month; consequently Λῶος, which is July for the Macedonians, is August for the Syro-Macedonians. On this matter Fabricius writes judiciously in the *Menologium*, pp. 43, 45. GALLAND.].

As the fire rose into the upper parts on the breath of the winds, it poured into the victors the joy and into the vanquished the grief appropriate to so great a disaster. A universal cry also arose; and not long afterward, the hostile destruction was made known to Caesar by a messenger. He rushed forward and, with as loud a voice as he could, ordered the fires to be extinguished. But amid the tumult there was no opportunity to be heard, nor any willingness to spare, since the Roman soldiers were burning with a desire for vengeance. Caesar’s well-known clemency removed their fear of disobedience, since they thought that no blame would attach to them when even the enemy was being spared.

Nevertheless, Titus recalled those whom he could by gesture and hand, and ordered some to restrain the soldiers’ attacks. But, with anger as their guide, the fire grew; the soldiers pressed the enemy, who had abandoned hope of safety and was now reckless of himself, expending his whole being upon danger. The common people, especially the lowest, were struck down wherever they were encountered, because they were protected by no weapons and were unable either to ward off a wound or turn it back.

## CHAPTER XLIII

Exhausted by his shouting, Caesar therefore withdrew, while the flames were still consuming the temple chambers. When these had been burned, the fire rushed furiously into the temple itself. At this sight, many were struck senseless; others threw themselves into the very fires [Note: [Col. 2189D] “Threw themselves.” ID.], since their eyes could not endure the spectacle and they wished to be preserved as survivors for the temple.

Titus came running back, wishing to survey what sort of building it was. Moved by admiration for it, he acknowledged that it surpassed all temples in workmanship. He marveled at the size of the stones, the brilliance of the metal, the grace of the construction, and the beauty of its appearance. Nor did he declare without reason that the place had enjoyed such renown that people came there from every region, because it was believed to be nothing less than the dwelling of the supreme God.

Honor added credibility to its religious standing, since even barbarian peoples venerated that temple; and robbers brought offerings to its religion [Note: [Col. 2190D] “Of the region.” ID.], although at that time its own people were plundering and scattering them, rushing upon everything that had been deposited by widows or orphans, as though they were taking vengeance upon the victors if anything from the booty were withheld from the Romans.

When they saw the temple also burning, they themselves set fire to the rest, so that no building might survive the destruction of the temple, considering it a matter of religious duty that everything should perish with the temple. Yet the Jews still did not lay aside their faithlessness; and this was the cause of a greater destruction. For when the minds of many were turning toward surrendering themselves to the Romans in an organized group, a certain false prophet began to proclaim, in the frenzy of his mind, that divine protection would not fail the temple. He summoned the people to himself as though to an oracle, asserting that he would at once drive back the enemy’s ranks and the flames from the temple in which he still remained.

Thus the wretched people, while disastrously believing false deceptions, were slaughtered like sheep, dishonored and unavenged. If they had wished to believe, they had clear signs of the impending destruction, by which they were warned, as though by unmistakable voices, that their end was near.

## CHAPTER XLIV

For nearly a year a comet had appeared above the temple itself, displaying everywhere a certain likeness of fire and a sword, and also announcing that the nation, the kingdom, and the city itself would be devastated by sword and fire. What could the likeness of a sword announce except war? What could fire announce except conflagration?

It was seen before the people separated themselves from the Romans. During the days of Passover, on the eighth day of the month Xanthicus, and on each night at about the ninth hour, the temple and its altar shone with such light as though it were day. The light remained for nearly half an hour each day. The common people interpreted this as an indication that the nation would be increased, and were thereby driven to believe that the time for recovering liberty had arrived. The wiser, on the contrary, thought that this kind of star usually announced war.

Let no one suppose that we have spoken in a manner alien to our own worship and discipline. First, because we are not asserting what seems true to us, but what happened, what opinions existed at that time, and what the prudent and the imprudent believed. Nor, when something has been said concerning the sect of the Jews, should it appear that we have written as though we were weaving their worship into the truth itself, rather than setting it forth in shadow and figure so that more perfect things might follow.

For we are also taught in the Gospel about signs among the stars: “There will be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars” (Luke 21:25). They also reported that, when a heifer was giving birth while standing at the altars for sacrifice, it gave birth to a lamb in the middle of the temple during the very festivals of the sacred rites mentioned above.

They also reported that the inner eastern gate, massive with solid bronze, which customarily required the labor of twenty men to close in the evening, and which had been secured with iron bars, opened of its own accord for several nights and was closed only with difficulty afterward by the guards. Many considered this also a sign of future blessings, since the gate would open for those who were about to enter.

The more discerning, however, said that the temple’s guard appeared to have been loosened, so that whatever was inside might be plundered by the enemy: worship would go out, devastation would enter; its renown would be emptied, and sacrifice would be destroyed. A reading teaches that this too was clearly signified before they crucified Christ Jesus.

Many days later, a figure of immeasurable size appeared, which very many people observed, as the books of the Jews made clear. Before sunset, there suddenly appeared in the clouds chariots and armed ranks by which the cities of the whole region of Judea and its surrounding territory seemed to be attacked.

During the solemnity of Pentecost, priests entered the inner parts of the temple at night to perform the customary sacrifices. They reported that they first felt a kind of movement and heard a sound; afterward they also heard a sudden voice crying out: “Let us depart from here.”

Jesus, son of Ananias, a peasant, four years before the Jewish people began the war, during the city’s complete peace and abundance, when the festival of Booths was being celebrated with solemn sacrifices, went up to the temple and began to cry out:

“A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem and against the temple, a voice against bridegrooms and brides, a voice against the whole people.”

He shouted this by night and by day. The leading men of the place, moved by it and shuddering at the terrifying sign of his voice, seized him and subjected him to many punishments, hoping that at least when afflicted by pain he would cease announcing things that were terrifying and full of portents.

But he was terrified neither by fear nor by blows or harsher threats. He neither altered his conduct nor his voice; with the same persistence in his prophecy and the same continuity of speech, without any interruption by entreaty, he remained fixed upon the same words, heedless of insult and unmoved in his purpose.

Since they did not consider this a superficial matter but thought it was being uttered, as it was, in a state of frenzy, they brought him before the judge of the place, who at that time was conducting public business there on behalf of the Romans. In order to investigate the truth, the judge tortured him with the most savage punishments. Ordering that the man be struck with lashes more violently the more he persisted, he sought to discover whether he had learned any more secret indications of the coming upheaval.

But he neither wept nor begged. At each blow he mourned not his own destruction but that of his homeland, crying: “Woe to Jerusalem.” When asked who he was, where he came from, or why he kept saying these things, he gave no answer. He continued only that lamentation for his homeland in pitiable mourning.

At last Albinus—for that was the man’s name—worn out, released him as though he were driven by a mad frenzy and did not understand what he was saying. But afterward he held no conversation with anyone, nor was he heard to say anything else. Instead, singing this as though it were a mournful and funeral song, he echoed it continually by day and by night: “Woe to Jerusalem.”

He did not insult the man who beat him, nor did he thank anyone who offered him food. His response to everyone was one and the same, filled with funeral wailing, especially during the solemnities of the sacrifices.

For seven years and five months the same sequence of words and the same sound of his voice continued. Thus, tireless throughout that long period, when the siege began he ceased crying out those same words, as though it was no longer necessary to announce what had now arrived.

But when the flames began to engulf the city and the temple together, he went around the wall and began to cry out again: “Woe to the city, the people, and the temple.” At last he added: “Woe also to me.” Struck by a sling [Note: [Col. 2191D] The old codex has *fundibalo*: more correctly so. BARR. — The first edition of Ascensius likewise has *fundibalo*; so too do the best manuscripts. That *fundibalus* is correctly derived from βάλλω (*ballō*, “to throw”) is shown both by the ancient Glosses, in which *fundibali* are λιθοβόλοι (“stone-throwers”), and by Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVIII, chapter 10. MAZOC. l.c., p. 795.], he gave up his spirit with the same cry.

It had also been written in ancient letters that the city itself, together with the temple, would perish when the temple had been made four-sided. Thus, whether they had forgotten or had been stunned by the necessity of the evils pressing upon them, when Antonia had been occupied they made the temple’s circuit four-sided.

Among these things, the most remarkable was that an equally ancient writing, which they called sacred, still contained the following prediction: at that time there would arise a man from their region who would assume sovereignty over the whole world. This belief drove them to such madness that they promised themselves not only liberty but also a kingdom.

Some thought that this referred to Vespasian; the wiser referred it to the Lord Jesus, who, born among them in the flesh from Mary [Note: [Col. 2192D] “Who was born among them.” BARR.], spread his kingdom throughout all the expanses of the earth. Although such events were arriving [Note: [Col. 2192D] “Giving warning … to beware.” ID.], they were unable to understand what had been divinely decreed.

## CHAPTER XLV

As the leaders of the sedition fled while the temple was being burned, the Romans placed their standards within the circuit of the temple itself and sacrificed opposite the eastern gate, proclaiming the emperor Titus with the loudest voices.

Meanwhile, a certain boy was in the place where the priests also were. They were being wasted by lack of water and by the heat of the neighboring fire, and were tormented by thirst. The boy asked one of the Roman guards to give him his right hand and offer him a drink. The soldier immediately extended it, moved equally by the boy’s age and his need. The little boy drank; and because it had been confidently entrusted to his innocent age, he seized the vessel of water and ran away, so that he might also provide the priests with an opportunity to drink.

The soldier wanted to follow but could not catch him. The boy relieved the priests’ thirst at the risk of his own safety. It was a good deception, since it harmed no one and came to the aid of necessity. In the end, the soldier himself admired the boy’s affection more than he condemned his trick, because, at that age, amid the destruction of the entire city and the common danger, he had not failed to perform whatever service he could out of reverence for the priests.

Not long afterward, the priests, exhausted by hunger and thirst, begged for life. Titus ordered them to be killed, replying that it was the mark of a degenerate spirit to wish to survive the temple and its service [Note: [Col. 2192D] “That they should survive the temple.” ID.].

## CHAPTER XLVI
But when John and Simon and the other leaders of the sedition [Col. 2192C] begged him to order the missiles and the din of weapons to cease for a little while, and to grant them permission to speak, saying that he should not shrink from clemency, he replied as follows after silence had been made:

“Too late, utterly wicked men, is the time for mercy, when nothing remains to be reserved, since already nothing has been left. I offered it to you, and you scorned it, and you regarded it as distrust, not clemency. But I was lamenting that innocent buildings were perishing through your crime; I was grieving that the ignoble multitude was being driven to death. I wanted to spare you, but you would not allow it. I suspended the battles, but you rushed into them. I offered peace, but you did not accept it. I addressed you repeatedly; I met with you again and again. I am not ashamed to say that, by pleading, I made you more insolent.

“What did you suppose? That the Roman battle-lines would yield to you, and that by your numbers you would surround the army of the conqueror of all the earth? What a small portion of the world has fought, since neither could your region contain the whole [army], nor did necessity permit it? For we have a greater concern with guarding the world than with enlarging it. Wherever we go, nothing is new, nothing foreign to us, since the whole earth is our possession. We thought that this brigandage, like a blemish on the body, should long be concealed; eventually we judged that it must be removed by severity, lest your disobedience and a certain darkness should obscure the splendor of Roman power.

[Col. 2193A] “You have experienced Roman valor, not by fighting but by dying. For we did not see your armies in the field, but on the wall, even though your fortifications did not help to protect your lives. What wall could resist those whom the ocean did not resist? Or what city enclosed by the defenses of walls would have been impregnable to our siege, when Roman arms have penetrated even Britain, surrounded by the wall of the roaring element?

“That precipitous mountain of water was laid beneath us. Your fathers, as Jewish stories relate, were surrounded by the wave of the Red Sea as they passed through it in the form of a wall; Roman strength broke through the wall of the Ocean. I do not begrudge you benefits belonging to others. Let the sea have seen you and fled, just as you fled when shut in by the enemy, because you could neither break through the enemy nor withstand him.

[Col. 2193B] “Our flight would have been a loss to us if the Ocean had fled. Before we reached the enemy, we had already fought the waves and conquered the raging sea. Britain received us, conquerors of the elements. What they trusted in, we subdued, so that the Ocean itself might contribute to the fullness of our triumph.

“But perhaps you relied on bodily strength. Are you stronger than the Germans, whom Roman valor led into slavery after they had been enclosed by the wall of the Alps? Nor are those things comparable to the rising hills of Mount Taurus, or to the Egyptian armies of Canopus, with whom you have experience of fighting. We have climbed above the clouds, and, descending from the clouds, have conquered peoples; we have opened an aerial road for all. We do not begrudge you a passage over the sea, provided that it is a passage for conquerors, while yours was for fugitives.

[Col. 2193C] “The mountains yielded to Roman valor; the rivers dried up, abandoning the course that nature had given them and bending into one which the conquerors commanded. Let your Jordan be turned back, as you say, and return to its source in order to open a road for you. The Roman maiden Cloelia did not need such a thing: after breaking her bonds, she escaped from the enemy and, carried along by the river, reached the Roman camp.

“Nor are we amazed by your fires, from which, you are accustomed to say, the Hebrew boys escaped while uttering the loftiest songs. Our Mucius, with no one compelling him, placed his hand in the flames and did not withdraw it until, victorious over the fire, he inspired his enemies with wonder at a courage that felt no flames.

“In the end, those who had hoped for triumph begged for peace. Or did those heavenly foods sustain you, and the nourishment of the rains stand against Roman valor? Yet you ought to have considered that Africa herself, the nourisher of the whole world, is subject to Roman strength. She serves us, although she feeds everyone; the hunger of all and the sustenance of the entire world are in our power. What nature gave to everyone, Roman valor made its own right.

[Col. 2193D] “It struck Hannibal himself and compelled him into exile—Hannibal, whom the whole world could not contain. Africa was too narrow for her citizens. Spain seemed unfit for staying; Gaul was cramped for the traveler; Italy was unworthy of a treaty of friendship and a partnership of alliance.

“[Note: [Col. 2193D] *Fulmina . . . fulminibus.* BARR. — Such a restoration seems to us insufficiently plausible. GALLAND.]

You may boast that rivers fought for you and heavenly powers battled on your behalf. We defeated Hannibal riding upon rivers and thundering amid the waves. The world was shaken by his storms, and he battered our walls with weapons. Nor was it necessary for our enemies to be destroyed while asleep, as your Assyrians were, but while fighting. Victory is not sought in dreams but in battle; there is no prize of valor where success is the gift of chance.

“Our enemies did not fall incautiously into our hands, deceived by the gleam of waters shining back at sunrise, while they supposed that we had been destroyed because of the appearance of spilled blood. Rather, knowingly and prepared for battle, they covered the fields of the earth with their bodies and filled them with their own blood.

“What courage placed you in such insolence? Did you not see those serving us who had once ruled over you? Egypt, which used to oppress you, pays us an annual tribute and opens a road as far as the regions of India, enabling us to go beyond the bounds of the world, seek another world, explore the hidden places of the sea and the farthest limits of the sun and Ocean, and add the inhabitants of another world to our rule.

[Col. 2194A] “What of the kingdom of Antiochus, who afflicted you with severe punishments? The very right of your religion had been taken away;

[Note: [Col. 2194D] *Eripuit* (“he took away”). BARR.]

we ourselves restored it to you, judging it more glorious to rule kings than to abolish a kingdom. The very seat of your masters, Antioch, did it not eagerly reject its own rulers and choose us as masters? Did you yourselves not flee to us in order to escape those masters? Did we not receive you and defend you against them?

[Note: [Col. 2194D] *Servavimus* (“we preserved [you]”). ID.]

[Col. 2194B] “We served you so that you might live according to your own laws; we gave you the power to devote yourselves to your own worship. We did not wish to know your sacred rites, but we honored them. Afterwards you thought that you should rebel.

“Pompey captured the Temple, but did not destroy it; he occupied the city, but preserved all its offerings intact. In return for this—O gratitude of an ally!—you repaid us by rebelling for a third time?

“Nero may have been contemptible, but Roman valor was not exhausted in one man. He had the soldier Vespasian, who had already recalled Gaul to peace: so brave in battle that through him even Nero conquered, and through him Nero was feared by his enemies; so faithful to his lord and emperor that he alone did not seek the imperial power, although he alone deserved it.

“But Cestius had injured you. A complaint ought to have been brought, not arms employed. Vespasian, my father, was sent. He could have poured himself upon the unprepared by surprise; he went around Galilee and burned distant places so that you might lay aside your insolence and ask pardon.

[Col. 2194C] “He displayed his valor; and, when he held everyone shut in, he went to Egypt in order to give you a pause for recovering your senses. Our absence made you more insolent, because you thought that we were occupied. But we are never so occupied as to be absent from the world. Even when absent, we are present; even when placed far away, we stand close by.

“For just as the soul gives life to all the members of the body through its own power, so Roman providence is present in every part of its empire and governs the entire Roman world as though it were present. For if that divine power has given individual souls the ability to govern the body, how much more has it supplied Roman vigor—the power by which, as though by a single body, our entire empire is animated—with a certain vital substance for protecting it!

[Col. 2195A] “You renewed the war that had been suspended. As my father was setting out for the city of Rome, which he had to recover from tyrants, he separated me from his company so that you would not lack an executor of his paternal benevolence. I came to the war with the appearance of one threatening, but with the disposition of one pleading.

“How often did I call out to the army from your walls? How often afterward did I withdraw it from the inner precincts of the Temple? How often did I restrain the fires? How often did I warn you? But you never listened.

“Now at last you beg me, as though anything remained—something such as has already been consumed—and yet I have kept the soldiers from slaughter, fire, and plunder. What do you want? Why do you still stand armed, as though you were going to give laws rather than receive them?

“If you seek surrender, lay down your arms. They are no longer to be feared by the victors, but are arrogant toward the defeated and full of insolence. You ask while armed, as though you had reason to doubt our good faith, or as though you were still challenging our valor and threatening war.

“The people has been destroyed; the Temple is burning; we hold the city. What else do you hope for except that your lives may be spared? Therefore lay down your arms as defeated men. I shall grant you life, even though you do not deserve it, because you were unwilling to preserve for yourselves what was yours.”

[Note: [Col. 2195D] *Vobiscum servare* (“to preserve with you”). BARR.]

Then they began to ask that, since they were bound by an oath never to surrender themselves to the Romans, they be granted permission to go out through the wall and proceed into the desert with their families, yielding the city to the Romans.

Titus was all the more provoked. “Are you even imposing conditions upon us?” he said. “Why not rather defend your homeland, stand by the Temple, rise up with all your strength, and keep the oath of death, since you have rejected life?” At the same time he ordered the Romans to rise up for the destruction of the enemy.

Very many began to be shaken by the greater indignation of the victors. Nevertheless, Zaraeus, the king’s sons, and their brothers, together with many from the common people, surrendered themselves. Nor did Titus, although aroused to anger, abandon his purpose at the sight of royal dignity; rather, he received the suppliants and gained only the profit of mercy—which is the greatest gain. For the authors of the sedition had plundered all the wealth of the royal household, so that nothing from it reached the Romans.

## CHAPTER XLVII

As soon as they had made a sudden attack and rushed into the palace, two of them assailed Roman soldiers and slaughtered one [Col. 2195D] infantryman. A cavalryman, however, asked to be led to Simon, claiming that he had something to disclose to the aforementioned leader of the sedition.

When he had been brought before him and began adding various empty statements, Simon ordered him to be killed. While the executioner delayed, the man—his eyes already covered with the bandage—escaped to the Romans. They, fighting at close quarters, received the fugitive; and when he had been brought before him, Titus, deeming him unworthy of death because he had been able to be captured alive by the enemy, ordered him to be stripped of his arms and released. He preserved for him what he had not lost through the enemy’s cowardice, but removed the military oath which, after being captured, he had betrayed and, as a deserter, dishonored.

That was a greater punishment for him. Among men, the disgrace of military service is more grievous than wounds inflicted by death.

[Col. 2196A] Nevertheless, the Jews were immediately repulsed and withdrew to the upper parts of the city, abandoning the defense of the Temple and the city. Great slaughter was inflicted upon those who remained behind, and the roads were filled with half-dead corpses.

Caesar ordered the siege engines to be brought up even against the upper parts. When the Idumaeans saw this, they chose men to send to Titus to ask for surrender. Learning of this, Simon anticipated them and intercepted the men chosen to request surrender.

But not long afterward the Idumaeans, although deprived of the assistance of their leaders, surrendered themselves to the Roman army, since they could no longer withstand the force of the attack. Thus hunger first, and finally despair of resisting, accomplished the surrender.

[Col. 2196B] The Romans, already exhausted by extensive slaughter, did not refuse mercy to their lives; and because of their eagerness to sell the captives into slavery, they were more ready to preserve them. Many were offered for sale, but there were few buyers, because the Romans disdained to keep Jews in slavery. Nor were there Jews remaining who could ransom their own people, since each person rejoiced simply to have escaped, even in poverty.

Thus they surrendered themselves everywhere, once fear had been removed. Since the brigands were gone, the Romans showed mercy.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

Finally, Jesus, one of the priests, son of Thebutus, surrendered himself. Having received a pledge of safety, he willingly handed over the vessels used in the priestly ministry: two lamps, tables, bowls, cups, and all the golden vessels, as well as the curtains and the garments [Col. 2196C] of the chief priests, together with the precious stones.

Phineas, the guardian of the treasury, was also captured. He displayed a large quantity of the priests’ purple cloth, scarlet cloth, and many other things that had been kept for use. Along with these he handed over cinnamon, cassia, many spices, incense, and numerous vessels used in the sacred rites. He also surrendered the sacred vestment, but under compulsion and fear; hence among his own people the deed was considered a venial offense.

Nevertheless, even if willingness was lacking, courage ought not to have been lacking. Although we often judge more severely than we are able to take precautions, if we ourselves were placed in such a necessity, we should nevertheless avoid the ministry of theft and the judgment of treason.

[Note: [Col. 2195D] *Facti* (“of the deed”). Soon afterward, *indicium* is found for *judicium* (“judgment”). ID.]

## CHAPTER XLIX

[Col. 2196D] The embankments had now been raised, and on the seventh day of the month they had begun to strike the upper wall with battering rams. The month is called Gorpiaeus [Col. 2196D]. The end had come.

[Note: [Col. 2196D] Alternatively, “Gorpiaeus,” which is called September by us, as Suidas explains. ID.]

The leaders of the factions themselves, who had been exulting amid the final dangers, were confused and terrified; they crawled on their knees before individuals, begging for help. One could see how pitiable that transformation was—from that terrible and arrogant height to this lowly and common degradation, into tears, weeping, and fear.

The wall of the upper city had not yet yielded, but they were already running among individuals, lamenting that no means of defense remained. [Col. 2197A] They thought that the enemy had entered. Many seemed to themselves to see the Romans already fighting from the upper positions: what they feared in their minds they imagined beforehand with their eyes, and the fear of their minds became an image before their sight.

Finally, believing with certainty that the enemy was already pressing upon their necks, although three towers—Mariamne, Phasaelus, and the Horse Tower—still remained, stronger than the others, they abandoned the upper parts and fled into underground passages or enclosed caves.

John, however, not long afterward, weakened by hunger and exhausted by fasting, surrendered himself to Caesar. Reserved for the triumph and bound with perpetual chains until his death, he escaped the executioner’s axe, but dragged out a breath of life rather than experiencing any pleasure in living.

Simon, meanwhile, remained hidden even amid the ruins of the burned city, concealing himself in underground chambers with a few of his more faithful companions. Caesar had already departed from the burned city, believing that Simon had either been consumed by fire, crushed by the ruins, or killed by some person.

[Col. 2197B] But as long as food was available, Simon burrowed farther inward in the excavated caves. When the food failed and no route of escape was open, he suddenly crept up to the surface, dressed in a white garment with a purple robe over it, in order to strike terror into those who saw him.

At first, while the Roman soldiers stood in astonishment, he ordered them to lead him to their commander. Rufus Terentius was in that place, whom Titus had left there as commander of the military force. When Rufus arrived and asked who he was, Simon first gave another answer; afterward he confessed that he was Simon.

From there he was sent to Caesar, and he too was reserved for the triumph. But because he had committed cruel acts against his fellow citizens and had not surrendered himself to Caesar, he was condemned to death after the triumphal procession.

[Col. 2197C] On the eighth day of the month Gorpiaeus the city was burned. Innumerable thousands were killed throughout the entire period of the siege—one million [“one hundred myriads,” as most assert], though these were Jews from everywhere, not all from the same region and place, since they had gathered there from all sides at the time of the festival of Passover.

Ninety-seven thousand captives were led away. Almost all the brigands were immediately killed. Those who were stronger were led in the triumph and afterward thrown to the beasts or subjected to other punishments in nearly every city through which Titus traveled, so that fear of the punishment of rebellion might be spread among all.

## CHAPTER L

[Col. 2197D] At the same time, the Alans, a fierce people long unknown to us, had been held back, along with other savage and untamed peoples of the interior, by the difficulty of the inland regions and by the barrier of the iron gate which Alexander the Great had placed upon the steep ridge of Mount Taurus. They inhabited Scythian Tanais and its neighboring regions and the Maeotian marshes, as though confined in a sort of prison by the ingenuity of the aforementioned king, so that they might cultivate their own lands and not invade those of others.

But whether because of the barrenness of the region—since the fertility hoped for by the greedy farmer did not correspond to the expected cultivation—or because of a desire for plunder, they approached the king of the Hyrcanians, who ruled those regions, whether by payment or by a promise of protection is uncertain [Col. 2198A], so that, once the gate had been opened, he would give them an opportunity to break out.

[Note: [Col. 2197D] An old manuscript has: “because of disagreement among the peoples among themselves.” ID.]

Having obtained this, they poured into the land of the Medes. After procuring swift horses and other equipment likewise fastened on their right side, they leapt onto them in turn whenever they wished and traversed nearly the entire region. First they threw everything into confusion and created the appearance of a larger multitude, against which no possibility of flight seemed available; then, after surrounding everyone, they inflicted as much slaughter as they wished and carried away the plunder.

The region was densely populated and rich in livestock, and, with no one resisting, it lay open to plunder. Pacorus himself, king of the Medes, withdrew into remote places, preferring to care for his safety rather than his kingdom. Thus his wife, children, and concubines, captured by the Alans, were later ransomed for one hundred talents.

[Col. 2198B] Nor was Tyridates, king of Armenia, free from danger. Made more cautious by another’s misfortune, he foresaw the disaster and wished, indeed manfully, to confront it, so that he might turn the enemy away from his borders.

While fighting, however, he became caught in a noose and would have fallen alive into the power of the enemy if he had not quickly cut through the awkward knot with a sharpened sword. For, under a certain insolent confidence in their own strength and a proud contempt for others, they pretended to conceal by such a trick both their customary practice of fighting familiar enemies from a distance and their ability to retreat. Throwing nooses and entangling the enemy is the Alans’ art and customary method of warfare.

[Note: [Col. 2198D] “The facility” (*facilitatem*). ID.]

## CHAPTER LI
