[Col. 2198C] Tyridates therefore fled, for him it was enough that he had escaped; but he left his kingdom to be devastated. As though they had received an injury because he had dared to engage them, they ravaged Armenia more violently than the kingdom of Media.

Thus enriched by the spoils of both kingdoms, they returned to their own country. When Titus learned of their invasion, he hastened to Antioch. Yet gradually, as befitted a triumphator, and concealing his purpose, he celebrated the spectacle of victory in each city.

Jews were killed in the arena wherever they went, torn apart by beasts, and displayed as the deserved punishment for rebellion. At Antioch, too, the gentile population persecuted them out of ancient hatred, because the kings of Persia had transferred to the synagogues the offerings they had claimed from the city of Jerusalem by right of victory, and had also bestowed other gifts upon the Antiochenes from their own resources.

Thus the accumulated wealth easily aroused envy. To pass over for the moment what rivals for the priesthood had done against the Maccabees [Col. 2198D], and how great a disaster the ambition of citizens had caused, as we have related above: later, Antiochus, born of no ignoble family but ruined in character, accused the Jews of conspiring to burn the city of Antioch with fire. He forced his own father, who was one of the leading Jews, and many others who had been accused, to their deaths through the violent action of the gentile multitude.

Nor did he rest, satisfied with that parricide and the slaughter of many. Later, when he found an opportunity [Col. 2199A], he used the pretext of the alleged conspiracy to attack the Jews again, claiming that a chance fire had burned the colonnades of the same city, its great square, and a very large part of its buildings. He would have quickly brought about the slaughter of everyone, had not the investigation been reserved for Titus upon his arrival, for fear that Caesar might be angered by the punishment of so many people. That circumstance brought safety to the Jews.

## CHAPTER LII

Many Jews also gathered at Masada, relying on the strength of its location. Titus considered it beneath an emperor to undertake its capture and entrusted the task to Syllae.

[Note: [Col. 2199D] An old codex has *Sileae*. Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book VII, chapter 38, has *Sylvae*. BARR.]

He had entrusted Syllae with supreme command of the Roman forces in those regions and with taking care that no further rebellion should arise. Titus himself hastened to Alexandria and from there crossed by ship to Rome.

Syllae energetically applied himself to the task assigned to him and broke down the wall of Masada with a battering ram. The defenders constructed an inner wall of wood, because wooden material used in such structures does not easily yield to blows from siege engines.

[Col. 2199B] But the Romans changed their method of warfare and hurled fire, which readily caught the wood and grew without any delay. Thus, as the blaze grew large, a great roar of flame was carried along. At first, the north wind drove it back from the side of the fortification, and it burned the Romans’ siege sheds more intensely.

Then, when the south wind arose, the fire turned back toward the fortress, so that the entire wooden structure of the wall was consumed as the material before it burned away. Since night had intervened, the Romans, confident of victory, withdrew into their camp, intending on the following day to conquer the defenders, now stripped and deprived of every means of protection.

But lest anyone escape, they surrounded the fortress with guards woven, as it were, into a continuous cordon.

## CHAPTER LIII
[Col. 2199C] Eleazar, the author of the disturbances, thus despairing of the situation and seeing that no means of defense remained, began a speech which, as a kind of epilogue, we have not omitted—lamentable as it is—closing the work in rhetorical fashion.

“What are we doing, descendants of Abraham, royal race, unconquerable through the power of priestly grace? Virtue is not judged by the outcome of victory, which is often uncertain, but by steadfastness of purpose. Hence it is clear that to overcome an enemy is a matter of fortune, but to change one’s mind is a mark of courage. I should rightly call you unconquerable, then, if no fear of death has yet conquered you.

“But your father Abraham did not establish you in this way. In his only son he taught that, if he were sacrificed for religion, it was not his death but his immortality that was to be expected. Why should I praise Josiah, than whom no one was a better interpreter of religion, a despiser of death, and an upholder of liberty? For though he had been placed upon that royal platform from which he might have postponed his death, nevertheless, because he saw that the people of Israel would be taken captive on account of their grave sins, he entered a foreign war and rejected life. Necho cried out: ‘I have not been sent against you, but against the king of Israel’ (2 Chronicles 35:21, 23). Yet Josiah did not withdraw until he had received the fatal blow of an arrow. Struck by that wound, he provides us with evidence as to whether merit or chance carries greater weight in war.

“Josiah, the restorer of the sacred rites of former times [Note: ‘Of the pious.’ ID.], was defeated; Necho, the most wicked of all men, conquered. But Josiah, though defeated, is now with the angels; Necho, though victorious, is in punishment. For who does not know that the reward of human beings is not placed in this life, but after the completion of this contest? Here we run so that there we may reach the palm; here is the contest, there the reward. Therefore there is no advantage here in a long life. In the end, Abel is killed early, while Cain survives: thus death belonged to innocence, and life to misery.

“From that time onward we have entered the same lot, so that living became wretched and dying blessed. For what is life except a prison for the soul, which is confined within this workhouse and clings to the fellowship of the flesh? It is shaken by the flesh’s weaknesses, afflicted by labor, crushed by anger, inflamed by desires, tormented by fury; [Col. 2200B] nor can it easily lift itself up, bound to the ground, compacted with dust, tightened by a fetter, and entangled in sinews.

“Yet it possesses no ordinary power: it gives life to the body and infuses strength of sensation into insensible matter; invisibly it bestows this upon each individual soul, governs the whole human being, and raises it beyond mortal frailty, so that it may apprehend the secrets of heaven and direct its mind toward the future. Thus, although it is situated within the body, it does not appear in the image and likeness of its Ruler; nor is it seen by bodily eyes. Neither its entrance nor its departure can be detected by any sight. It represents, in a certain way, the divine gift. When it enters, it infuses life; when it leaves the body, it produces death. Where the soul is, there is life; where it is absent, there is death. Whatever it visits, it awakens; whatever it leaves, is immediately dissolved and quickly withers. By the soul’s infusion, the dead rises again; by its departure, the living is deprived of life.

“Who, then, would doubt that an operation of immortality appears to be present in that whose power is to avert death? Yet the soul is a burden to itself, although it overflows for the use of others. What it gives to the body, it takes away from itself; for it is weighed down and, as it were, bent toward the earth together with this mortal body. Thus the life of the body is the death of the soul; and, conversely, the death of the body appears to be the soul’s freedom. For while we are in this body, our soul is enslaved—indeed, in a wretched slavery—in exile from paradise and wandering far from its Ruler.

“But when it has been released from the bonds of this flesh, it flies back to that pure, radiant, and higher place, appears before its Lord God, [Col. 2200D] enjoys the dwellings of the saints, and rejoices in the fellowship of the blessed. It no longer has any association with the dead, and has left behind its companionship with corpses [Note: Of the corpse. ID.]. Heavenly grace breathes upon it, and no agitation of human cares disturbs or harasses it.

“Rest shows us how much grace the soul recovers through the death of the body. For when the body is asleep, and its desires and all its movements are as though dead, we often converse with the saints; we receive those whom we have lost, so that the absent are present to us, the dead live, and all pain is stilled. Let us draw near and [Col. 2201A] converse with God; let us know the future. Let rest belong to the afflicted, and freedom to slaves.

“What we attain in death is therefore what we dream while sleeping; and what an image is in sleep, that in death is the experience of reality and the grace of freedom. Hence among certain peoples it is customary to accompany human births with tears and their deaths with rejoicing: they grieve that the former have been born for misery, but congratulate the latter on having returned to blessedness; they lament that the souls of the former have come into slavery, but rejoice that those of the latter have been released into freedom.

“The sages of the Indians, too, are said, when they have conceived a desire to die, to declare that they wish to depart, with no one raising an objection. Then, when the preparations for death have been completed, they joyfully leap upon the blazing pyre and bid farewell to those standing by. The women grieve, as though deprived of support, or grieve for the little children whom they are leaving behind; others bless them and do not begrudge them their haste toward better habitations, brighter places, and purer companionships.

“What more, then, can I say about you, when even among barbarian peoples death is a means of pursuing freedom? I have long known you well: you are prepared to live according to the customs of your ancestors, since you believe that you should serve neither the Romans nor any other nation, but God alone, who alone is the just and true Lord of all. The day has arrived that demands your will be proved by deeds, and that you not disgrace the glory of your former character by submitting, though born in freedom, to human domination.

“This is especially so since formerly you were permitted to serve without danger, whereas now you must endure harsh punishments along with slavery. If we offer ourselves as slaves to the Roman empire—Romans whom we were the first of all to provoke to war and whom we still hold at bay with our arms; if we did not surrender to the emperor when he offered peace, shall we surrender to Sulla when he threatens us with severity? O wretched men, for what hope of this life have we preserved ourselves? Granted that the enemy may forgive us: what will that profit us when God’s anger is manifest? Fires turned against us by the enemy, winds changing direction, flames driven back so that our defenses might be burned—who can live when God opposes him?

“There is no room for pardon, but a clear command to voluntary death. Why did night intervene, except so that the enemy might not forestall us [Note: Or: ‘lest.’ BARR.] and immediately break in once the wooden defense had burned, but so that time might be granted us to put one another to death, and we might be permitted to die with our children and relations? [Col. 2201D] Otherwise we would see panting old men and aged women dragged away by the Romans, and our dearest wives carried off for the victor’s lust. Let us die with our country, so that we may not survive to bear the disgrace and reproach of such dishonor.

“Where, then, shall we flee from the face of God, or where shall we go when the Lord of heaven is hostile to us? Even if the mountains fall upon us and hide us in hollow caves, how shall we avoid the indignation of such great power? Where shall we proceed where God is not, since he himself is everywhere?

“Are the examples by which we may learn that he who formerly presided over our nation has long been hostile to it because of our sins insignificant? Who could doubt this when he sees that our own hands have been turned against us, and that domestic sedition has destroyed more of us than war? I will not credit the Romans with having conquered us; nor do they themselves claim this, since they know that almost all of us have perished by our own weapons rather than by foreign ones.

“For what Roman weapons did the Jews living in Caesarea see? On their Sabbath, during the solemn observances of our sacred rites, a multitude of Caesarean Gentiles, suddenly seized and inflamed by a kind of madness sent down from above, destroyed twenty thousand and drove all the rest away, so as to empty the entire city. Did not madness indeed fill all Syria [Note: ‘Certain things.’ ID.], so that Jews and Gentiles settled in the same cities, previously bound to one another by the fellowship of residence, afterward clashed with arms, thereby preparing a path for the Romans’ future victory?

“For why should I speak of Scythopolis, where the Jews had first gathered in order to forestall the Gentile population, lest, following the example of the other cities, they plot anything against our people? Thus, when it would have been fitting for them to fight together against foreigners with united forces, the Jews instead resolved to fight against one another, so that some of them might battle their kinsmen and neighbors. Then, as the price of their labor and the blood they had shed, they were killed by the Gentiles—something they themselves had prevented the Gentiles from doing.

“The people of Damascus, without any cause, laid low eight thousand Jews [Note: Josephus reports eighteen thousand. ID.]. The people of Ascalon, two thousand five hundred. In the city called Ptolemais, two thousand were also slain.

“At Alexandria there had long been hatred between the Jews and the peoples of the nations, dating from the time when Alexander the Great had used the support of the Jews to subject the Egyptians. Hence, after the city was founded, privileges and dwellings were assigned equally to Jews and Egyptians, in different quarters so that their religious observances would not be mingled; for they wished to preserve their purifications without any contamination. From this arose frequent conflicts between them, quarrels, and appeals to judgment. Yet it is clear that none of the privileges granted by so great a king had been violated. Later, however, when a disturbance arose among the Gentiles, some Jews having been killed and others held for punishment, the Jewish population, stirred by the wrong, rose against the authors of the injustice. And when they were determined to avenge themselves more persistently upon their fellow citizens, a Roman army was brought in, which slaughtered sixty thousand Jews within the city.

“But why should I linger over lesser matters, when in the ruin of a single city we must lament the destruction of the whole world? Where is the great city Jerusalem? Where is beautiful Zion? Where is the marvelous temple? Where is that second tabernacle, the sanctuary of holiness, into which the high priest alone used to enter once a year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the people’s offense?

“It has been profaned by the nations; those who destroyed it dwell among the remnants of the city. Where, I ask, are you, city filled with peoples, revered by kings, acceptable to God, seat of grace? Your pavements were of marble, your walls shone with marble, your roofs gleamed with precious marble; your gates glittered with gold, while others shone with silver. All have been killed—both those who continually inhabited you and those who came to you from every part of the world—so that there can be no doubt that the whole world perished in you.

“Everything has been stripped bare; burned from the roofs and destroyed from the foundations. Your dwelling has become desolate, and there is no one to inhabit your tents. Does anyone still wish to live, and not regret having lived? Hard are the eyes that can see these things; pitiless the minds that can wish anyone to survive such suffering—not because disasters have ceased, but because there is now no rest.

“Where shall we turn our eyes, or what is there to behold with pleasure? The whole city is a tomb of the dead; ashes alone meet the gaze. The streets are empty of the living and filled with corpses. Wretched old men, their hair whitened with ash, sit in torn garments upon the remains of the dead, covering their naked bones in order to protect them from birds and beasts.

“A few women remain unharmed, whom the impious soldier has preserved for disgrace, not for life. Who, seeing these things and thinking about postponing death, would dare lift his eyes to heaven? Who could be so forgetful of his country, hostile to his own people, estranged from piety, deprived of tenderness—whose spirit could be so soft and effeminate? Who could be so fearful that he would not be ashamed to have been preserved for this?

“Would that we had died long ago, or, if life remained, that the light of our eyes had perished before we could behold the holy city destroyed by the hands of our enemies, and this temple, consecrated to God by our ancestors, so impiously consumed by flames, or see the priests lying slain in the temple!

“Let us therefore make amends for having survived these evils, so that we may appear not to have postponed death out of love of life, but out of devotion to courage. The enemy has surrounded the entire fortification; nothing remains except ourselves or our wives. They are already putting our children up for auction and competing among themselves over whose wife each will carry away—whether the women are to be distributed according to the rank of their offices and the order of their status, or whether the wretched women are to be forced to submit to lots [Note: ‘By lot.’ BARR.].

“For us too, extraordinary punishments are being prepared: the most refined tortures—not merely burning flames or various forms of slaughter by the blow of the victorious axe. After chains, prison, and the yoke, there will be a harsh punishment, though tolerable for men if disgrace were absent; but also limbs torn from the living, especially hands cut off [Col. 2203D]. And not without reason, since those hands failed in their duty when they could have helped themselves.

“We must also face the bites of wild beasts for the spectacle of the conquerors, a practice already celebrated in the various arenas of the cities. This ought either to make us ashamed by its example or move us to pity by its sight, lest we be preserved to fight either beasts or our brothers.

“What, then, are we waiting for? We are no longer free to escape what we fear. If we do not wish to kill our children out of mercy, or ourselves through courage, we shall necessarily be killed through disgrace by our brothers or relatives [Col. 2204A]. One course is urged by affection, the other demanded by the victors. If we do not wish to perform the service of piety, we shall be forced to undergo the spectacle of parricidal display.

“Let us therefore undertake what will benefit our children and wives. If we are weaker, let us take them away from future tortures; if we are stronger, let us overcome the compassion of parents and the affection we owe our relations. In this too let us conquer the enemy, when we deprive him of his prey. Courage demands this; shame counsels it. Not to fear death is courage.

“For we are all born for death, and we beget children for death; their death is assigned to nature, but captivity is assigned to disgrace. Therefore those whom we could not rescue from danger, let us rescue from humiliation. Take pity, then, fathers, on your children; husbands, on your wives; let us all take pity on the little ones—especially while we still possess the power to show pity—so that we may pity our own people and not appear both born and preserved for dishonor.

“For who could endure fathers being killed before the eyes of their children, or children in the sight of their parents? Old men exhausted by age being dragged either to death or, worse still, into slavery; women with disheveled hair being led before their husbands and violently dragged away to disgrace? To hear the voice of a wailing child calling for his father to come to the aid of one who asks, while you already hear in vain the bound hands [Note: ‘Having been bound.’ And shortly thereafter, ‘subjected.’ ID.] and the necks subjected to the yoke of captivity?

“Therefore, while our hands are still free, while we grasp the sword, let us undertake a deed that the victorious enemy will marvel at. Let our wives receive as the final gift of marital love, as though it were a dowry, an inheritance. We return these keys to them [Col. 2204C] with the new testimony of blood [Note: Of the Testament. ID.], so that they may be heirs of our freedom. They themselves encourage this—or at least deserve it—those who desire it; those who shrink from it must be compelled. Nor will the little children fear the sword, which because of their age they do not understand, but which they ought to receive from pious parents, so that they may truly become free.

“What could be more honorable for us as well? Even if we first burn the fortress, let us nevertheless preserve the grain, so that they may not think that hunger rather than devotion to courage compelled us to undertake the work of mutual slaughter. Let us give them food filled with blood; and if the flames consume it, the very smell of the burned grain will show the besiegers that what the besieged possessed in abundance has perished.

“After this, let each person offer himself to the wound, and, as he dies, protect his homeland, embracing it in a final embrace. Let our homeland, which was the dwelling place of our dignity, become the tomb of our freedom [Col. 2204D]; this mound is fitting for our funerals, so that we may be covered by the enclosure of courage.”

Inflamed by such a speech, the others held their drawn swords, kissed their wives, and embraced their children, weeping and at the same time hastening so that the enemy might not forestall them. “To you,” they said, “we give these pledges of our love, the final rewards of necessity.” And, having manfully restrained their affection [Note: An old codex reads: ‘They all stripped themselves of softness and excluded emotion.’ ID.], they excluded emotion and carried out the same acts. The fearless women offered themselves to the wound for the preservation of their chastity and themselves assumed the courage of their husbands.

After killing their relations and children [Col. 2205A], they chose strong men to complete the slaughter. Thus all nine hundred and sixty perished, together with the children and women [Note: Josephus reports two women. Some write that this occurred on 15 April, in the second year after the capture of Jerusalem, and in the year 74 from the birth of Christ. BARR.]. Only one woman survived: she had hidden her five children in an aqueduct [Col. 2206A] while the others were occupied with the final necessity. When the Romans arrived at dawn, she was awakened by their voices and became the informant about what had happened. Their possessions, however, had already been consumed by a fire they themselves had kindled.

[Col. 2205A]

## ANACEPHALAEOSIS OF THE HISTORY OF THE DESTRUCTION OF THE CITY OF JERUSALEM, THAT IS, A REPETITION OF ALMOST EVERYTHING SAID IN THE PRECEDING BOOKS

[Col. 2205]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 2205B]

In the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion, and in the first year of Vespasian’s reign, Judaea was being torn apart by fierce wars and domestic seditions. Jerusalem itself, their city [Note: A manuscript reads: ‘by a threefold war within itself.’ There were indeed three factions there: those of John, Simon, and Eleazar. Above, Book V, chapter 1. BARR.], was suffering from civil war. There was no interruption, no rest, no truce; fighting continued at every moment. Many fell, innumerable people were slaughtered. Blood defiled everything and filled the very thresholds of the temple; corpses fell everywhere. Some were struck by arrows, others by missiles. No place was free from danger; there was no hope of reconciliation, no possibility of escape. Everything was mournful and full of horror, full of savagery: mourning everywhere, fear everywhere; the cries of women, the wailing of old men, the groans of the dying, the despair of the living—so that one might call those who remained pitiable and those who died blessed.

“How have you been deceived by your own people, you who once seemed blessed? How have you been conquered by your own weapons, and your own hands turned against you—your hands that used to conquer without weapons and strike down the enemy without any battle, when angels fought for you and the waves of the sea served as your army, together with the openings of the earth and the thunderclaps of heaven?”

## CHAPTER TWO

“Rise now, Moses, and see your people and the inheritance of the people entrusted to you perishing by their own hands. Look upon that people of God for whom the passable sea opened when they advanced, for whom heaven supplied food when they hungered—shut in without a sea, besieged without Pharaoh, fasting without the barrenness of the earth.

“Rise, Aaron, who once, when death was devouring many of the people because of God’s anger, stood between the living and the dead; and death stopped, while the plague caught against the barrier of your body and could not pass to infect the living.

“Rise also, Joshua son of Nun, who leveled the impregnable walls of Jericho to the sound of trumpets, and see the people to whom you subjected foreign nations now themselves oppressed in submission.

“Rise, David, accustomed to drive away an enraged spirit by the sweetness of the lyre, and see how fury ruled and washed all the sweetness of your psalms from the minds of the lost [Note: ‘Of the delivered … has effaced.’ ID.], while each of the leaders brought the entire people to death in order to seize the freedom for which you yourself offered your life.

“Rise, Elisha, who brought an enemy into Samaria and made him a friend. Through you, in the camp of Syria, there resounded the crash of chariots, the sound of horsemen, and the voice of valor; the enemy fled, and the Jew escaped the siege. Where are now those merits, and where are now those works of the saints? Nor is it surprising if they have lost the works of the prophets [Note: ‘Have they lost?’ GALLAND.], since they denied the arbiter of the prophets.

“Therefore, Judaea, your weapons are turned against you [Note: ‘Your weapons.’ BARR.]; your prayers do you no good because your faith produces no effect. Therefore your people have been made hostile to you, because your faithlessness has turned against you. What remedy can be sought where the author of the remedy is not reconciled?

“What did you think would happen when you extinguished your own life with your own hands, when with your own voices you drove out your advocate, except that you would also lay hands upon yourself? You have what you asked for. You took away from yourself the Prince of peace; you asked that the arbiter of your life be killed and that Barabbas be granted to you, who had been sent to prison because of a sedition raised in the city and a murder (Luke 23:19). Therefore salvation withdrew from you, peace departed, and rest ceased. Sedition was given to you; destruction was given to you. Recognize that today Barabbas lives for you and Jesus is dead. Therefore sedition reigns in you and peace is buried, so that you may perish more cruelly at the hands of your own people before you perished at the hands of foreigners.”

## CHAPTER THREE

“How much evil did the Roman bring upon you with his weapons, wretched city, compared with what your own people brought upon you? Your own people made you fight the Romans. The Romans wanted peace; you declared war. What reason was there for you to provoke the stronger party?

“It was indeed a grave matter that a Gentile entered the temple against the sacred law; but it was no longer God’s temple. You were not God’s city, nor could you be, since you had become a tomb of the dead—especially of your own dead, whom you yourself had killed, not those whom you had lost to the enemy. For how could you be a dwelling place of life, when you were a habitation of death, a lodging place of crimes, a den of robbers?

“Ananus [Note: Above it reads ‘Ananus and Jesus.’ ID.] and John, the chief priests, lay unburied within you. Those who had once been clothed in priestly robes and had even been objects of reverence to foreigners lay there in disfigurement. Their corpses became food for birds and devouring dogs, torn limb from limb and scattered throughout the city, so that the appearance of ancient holiness seemed to lament such an insult to the sacred name and the deformity of a once-glorious office.

“But you yourself initiated this disgrace, you who killed prophets in your very midst, you who stoned the saints of the Lord. Zechariah lay lifeless before the temple; he lay unburied. Therefore your blood washes him.

“What, moreover, was the cause of Ananus’s death except that he rebuked your people because they did not rise up [Note: ‘Rise up.’ BARR.] in defense of the temple? He protested the lost freedom, the abandoned courage, the relics of the ancient rites trampled underfoot, and the altars defiled. He maintained that the people, defiled by the use of insensible images and statues and now feeling nothing in the manner of statues, should be abandoned [Note: Perhaps ‘of things that feel.’ GALLAND.]. Dumb animals are accustomed to exhibit, as it were, a return of vengeance: they feel injury, are provoked by the goad, and avoid blows. Whoever neither rises up nor knows how to avoid what causes harm is like those that do not feel.”

## CHAPTER FOUR

“And indeed, where is your freedom, for the sake of which you once thought you should yield neither to Egyptians, nor to Palestinians, nor to Assyrians, and later not even to the Medes? Where is that faith of the Maccabees, which once with a few men routed the Babylonians, put the Persians to flight, struck down Demetrius, and finally, through children and women, overcame the arms, swords, and fires of Antiochus? They preferred to die for the preservation of their ancestral religion rather than obey royal commands.

“Where is that devotion of the fathers, the most beautiful of all forms of suffering, by which they offered themselves to death not so much for their children or wives as for the temple of God? Formerly even the priestly staff flourished, cut from a wild root; now faith withers, piety lies buried, and all emulation of virtue has departed.

“It is no wonder that a people who departed from God and follow the wicked spirit of contradiction have been divided against themselves. For how could they preserve their own peace when they rejected the peace of God? The peace of God is Christ, who made both one (Ephesians 2:14). It is therefore just that members of one people should have become hostile to one another, because they refused to follow Jesus, who unites those divided, and instead followed the spirit of fury, which divides those united.”

## CHAPTER FIVE

[Col. 2207D]

“Thus, Jerusalem, you were paying the price of your faithlessness when you yourself destroyed your defenses with your own hands and pierced your own entrails with your own swords, so that the enemy pitied you while he spared you and you raged against yourself. You saw that God was fighting against you and acting on the Romans’ side, so that you might bring voluntary destruction upon yourself. For this reason the Romans preferred to be spectators rather than executioners, lest, while your own people raged against one another’s entrails, they should be judged to have applied the hand of contagion rather than courage.

“To this punishment of unspeakable slaughter was added an impious savagery of cruelty: they denied burial to all who had been killed either in the temple or around the city streets. No one had time to bury anyone, since they were occupied with fighting one another, and all were more concerned with striking than with burying. Thus, in a kind of madness, they killed the duties of piety and raged in the service of impiety; and amid such great calamities nothing had perished more completely than mercy, which alone usually lightens miseries and consoles hardships.

“Those who had lost their own people did not dare bury them because of fear, when grave terror pressed upon them from the leaders of the opposing factions. Those who had killed others guarded against strangers, lest someone seize the bodies for burial. Thus everyone had to fear that what they wished to grant to another might be taken for themselves—or, worse still, that they themselves might not obtain the burial they had prepared for another.”

## CHAPTER SIX

“Within the temple, therefore, instead of sweet-smelling ointments, fragrant incense, and the scents of various flowers, there was the foul stench of unburied corpses—corpses dissolved by rain, scorched by fire, and heated by the sun. Every limb of the slaughtered citizens reeked with a terrible odor. On one side, the rotting of disintegrated entrails; on the other, the stench of the burned bodies filled all the senses and mouths of the living, so that they themselves were soon consumed by a more grievous disease and groaned that they had survived, since they were perishing under a harsher punishment.

“They had been preserved for this: to see the laws of nature dissolved together with their homeland, justice denied to the living, peace to citizens, burial to the dead, and human and divine things alike stained and polluted, everything mingled together. Mercy was regarded as criminal, cruelty as a religious duty, a fortress in the temple, war at the threshold, and a funeral upon the altars. They saw with their eyes what they had refused to believe would happen when the prophets announced it.

“For David had said of these things: ‘They polluted your holy temple; they gave the bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven; they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them’ (Psalm 78:1–3).

“For at that time the nations came together into God’s inheritance to take everything away; the temple was polluted by the funerals of its own people; the corpses of the slain lay unburied as food for birds and ravenous beasts; blood was poured out so that it formed a pool in the temple; and there was no one to bury them. For fury was transferred from the living against the dead, and from the dead against those who still lived.

“Someone wished to bury a dead person, and he himself was killed. The man who had killed the deceased transferred his anger to the gravedigger and denied him burial. Then the one who had killed the gravedigger killed him in turn and exercised even greater cruelty toward the dead man, stripping him of the final debt owed by nature—though he already owed nothing, hated by them and incapable of feeling punishment.”

## CHAPTER SEVEN

“What else could happen to those who did not receive the divine oracles? They mocked the prophets’ announcements, [Col. 2209A] trampled every sacred law, and themselves hastened the fulfillment of what was foretold.

“For there was an ancient and frequently repeated saying that Jerusalem and its holy places would perish when the law of war was introduced by sedition and domestic hands defiled the temple of God. They did not understand even this. How often was the house of God destroyed? How often was there sedition? How often was there war? Yet that city never perished except when they crucified the Lord, truly the Temple of God, with their own hands.

“For this reason they also hear the words: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up’ (John 2:19). For what else was it but sacrilege when they stretched out impious hands against the author of salvation, stoned him, scourged him, seized him, and killed him?

“Then the divine fire truly destroyed their holy places. When the Babylonians burned them, they were restored. Later, when Pompey destroyed them, they were rebuilt again. But they were burned utterly when Jesus came, and the things of the divine Spirit, once dissolved, vanished.

“It was right that we should precede the funeral of the ancestral solemnity with a richer kind of lamentation, accompany it as though it were a funeral procession, and perform the rites according to the customs of our ancestors.”

## CHAPTER EIGHT

“But let us come to the full account of Jerusalem’s overthrow and the humiliation of the Jews. They deserved to be overthrown and held in contempt, since they had purchased Jesus, dearer than all other things, from a disciple for the price of thirty denarii—not in order to possess him as Lord, but to remove him from the land of the living as though he were wicked.

“Therefore, rightly expelled from their inheritance, scattered by the nations throughout the whole earth, and made more worthless than straw, they were driven out by those nations whom they had feared lest they take away their place and nation. And those who had purchased Jesus for thirty denarii in order to destroy him later justly saw thirty of their own people sold for one denarius as an object of mockery.

“Since almost all the Jews had unanimously consented to the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, almost all of them, gathered from every region for the feast of Unleavened Bread, were suddenly surrounded by war as vengeance approached. First, a deadly plague arose among them from the confinement of the place; then famine followed more swiftly.

“That the city could contain such a multitude of people was established by those who had been present under Cestius. For when Florus, wishing to report the number of the city’s men to Nero, who despised the nation, asked the high priests to count the multitude if they could in any way do so.

“When the festival called Passover had arrived—for at that time they slaughter the victims from the ninth hour until the eleventh—and since the meals are arranged by households of no fewer than ten persons, for it is not permitted to dine alone and many neighbors gather together, they counted 256,500 sacrificial victims [Note: Josephus says twenty per victim. BARR.]. If we reckon ten banqueters for each, this amounts to 2,565,000, or 2,700,000 [Note: The passage appears defective. Perhaps one should read ‘or seven hundred thousand,’ or ‘six hundred or seven hundred thousand.’ GALLAND.], all holy and pure.

“For lepers, people afflicted with vitiligo, men suffering from discharges—whom they call gonorrheics [Note: Gualtherus thinks that, following Josephus, one should read ‘gonorrheics.’ BARR.]—women polluted by menstrual blood, and others who were unclean were not permitted to take part in the sacrifices; nor indeed were foreigners, except those who had come for religious purposes.”

## CHAPTER NINE

“This great multitude was gathered from foreign lands. Yet at that time the entire nation was, as it were, enclosed by fate in a prison, and the city, packed with people, was besieged by war.

“Thus the number of those killed surpassed every human plague and every plague sent by God. The Romans killed some openly and captured others. For they searched the sewers and dug up the tombs, killing those whom they found. More than two thousand were discovered there. Some had killed themselves with their own hands, but more had killed one another with mutual wounds, while famine had seized others.

“They were paying the penalties for their crimes. After crucifying Jesus, the arbiter of divine things, they later persecuted his disciples as well. Yet many Jews, and very many Gentiles, believed in him, drawn by his moral teachings and by works flowing beyond human capacity. Not even his death put an end to their faith or devotion; rather, it increased their commitment.

“They also laid murderous hands upon him and led the author of life to Pilate to be killed. They began to press the reluctant judge urgently to condemn him. Yet Pilate is not thereby excused; the madness of the Jews is instead heaped up. For he ought not to have condemned one whom he had found guilty of no offense, nor should they have doubled sacrilege with parricide by having him condemned by those to whom he had offered himself to redeem and heal them.

“For although Pilate washed his hands, saying, ‘I am innocent of the blood of this just man; you will see to it’ (Matthew 27:24), nevertheless he is no less guilty. He recognized the glory of the Lord’s resurrection and, though unwillingly, tried to proclaim it, but in his faithlessness refused to believe it, as his own letter testifies, sent to Caesar in the following terms.”

## CHAPTER TEN
Pontius Pilate sends greetings to Claudius.

Recently an event occurred—and I myself verified it—that the Jews, through envy, have punished themselves and their descendants with a cruel condemnation. In the end, although their fathers had received the promise that their God would send them from heaven his Holy One, who would rightly be called their King, and had promised that he would send him to earth through a Virgin [Col. 2210D], the God of the Hebrews sent this man into Judaea while I was governor. When they saw that he had illuminated the blind, cleansed lepers, healed paralytics, driven demons out of people, even raised the dead, commanded the winds, walked with dry feet upon the waves of the sea, and performed many other deeds, and when the whole Jewish people declared him to be the Son of God, the Jewish leaders became envious of him. They seized him and handed him over to me, telling me one thing after another about him that was false, asserting that he was a magician [Col. 2211A] and acted contrary to their law.

I, however, believed that this was so, and after having him scourged I handed him over to their judgment. But they crucified him, and after he had been buried they placed guards over him. While my soldiers were guarding him, he rose on the third day. The wickedness of the Jews, however, flared up so greatly that they gave money to the guards and said: “Say that his disciples came and stole his body” (Matthew 28:13). But although they had received the money, they could not keep silent about what had happened. For they testified that they had seen him rise and that they had received money from the Jews.

## CHAPTER XI

We have entered upon these matters so that no one may tell a different story and think that the lies of the Jews ought to be believed. Concerning this, the perfidious Jews themselves bear witness, for Josephus, the writer of histories [Col. 2211B], says that at that time there was a wise man—“if indeed,” he says, “it is proper to call him a man”—a creator of marvelous works, who appeared alive to his disciples after the third day of his death, in accordance with the writings of the prophets. The prophets had foretold these and countless other things about him, full of miracles. From this the Christian assembly began, and it spread among every race of human beings; no nation of the Roman world remained that was left without knowledge of his worship.

If the Jews do not believe us, let them believe their own people. Josephus said this, and they themselves regard him as a very great authority. Yet, although he spoke the truth in this matter because of his fidelity to history—for he considered it wicked to deceive—he did not believe because of the hardness of his heart and the purpose of his perfidy. His lack of belief, however, does not prejudice the truth; rather, it added to the testimony [Col. 2211C], because he denied it neither as an unbeliever nor willingly. In this the eternal power of Christ Jesus shone forth: even the leaders of the synagogue, who had seized him for death, acknowledged him as God.

And truly, speaking as God, without respect of persons or any fear of death, he also announced the future destruction of the Temple; but the insult to the Temple did not move them. Since he reproved them for their crimes and sacrileges, anger blazed up against him, so that they killed the one whom no age could have overcome. For while others have deserved to accomplish by preaching what they accomplished [Note: “[By] praying.” And shortly afterward, “he commanded.” BARR.], this man possessed such power that he could obtain whatever he wished to be done.

## CHAPTER XII

On the eighth day of the month of September, therefore, the city was burned. Throughout the whole period, ten times one hundred thousand were slaughtered, according to the myriads, as most writers assert—Jews, that is, though not all from the same region or place, since they had gathered there from everywhere for the solemnity of Passover. Ninety-seven thousand captives were led away. Indeed, because of the enormous number of captives, they were so plentiful that thirty were sold by the Romans for a single coin under the auctioneer’s crown.

When the siege had been completed, Caesar Titus ordered the city and the Temple to be utterly demolished, so that the word of the Lord Jesus might be fulfilled: “Truly I say to you, not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed” (Matthew 24:2) [Col. 2212A]. Such, then, was the end of the siege of Jerusalem.

Some powerful man of the Canaanites founded this same city of Jerusalem, one who in his native language was called “Righteous King.” He first named it Salem; afterward he added the Temple [Note: “Perhaps added. What follows shortly seems to recommend restoration.” GALLAND.], and therefore the city was called Jerusalem. From the beginning, its inhabitants were of the Canaanite race.

David, the first Hebrew, expelled the Canaanites and established his own people there. He built himself a royal house in the city. He also wished to build a Temple for God, but, prevented by an oracle, he left Solomon as his heir, so that Solomon might build the Temple he himself had vowed to construct. Solomon therefore founded the Temple. The other kings also added very many things to the city’s adornment; envy arose from its magnificence.

## CHAPTER XIII

Among all its works, however, the Temple excelled in its immense construction and shining marble. It possessed a costly and very large curtain, woven with scarlet, hyacinth-blue, and fine linen—purple, not a useless material of such variety, but one whose appearance signified the mystery of hidden things. This was because it belonged to the Temple of the one who, as creator of the elements, ruled over heaven and air, earth and sea, and alone directed and governed all things.

Scarlet represents the fiery heaven; hyacinth-blue, the air; fine linen, the earth; and purple, the sea, since it is dyed with shellfish from the sea. Thus two are understood from their color and two from their origin.

Accordingly, the high priest customarily represented these four things in his clothing whenever the solemnity of the festival days was greatest, as though he were clothing the whole world, praying on behalf of the people. He did so in the figure of the one who was to come, Jesus the High Priest, to take away the sin of the world.

The high priest covered his thighs inwardly with a linen garment, because above all in a priest faith of mind and purity of body are sought—purity that ought to restrain the intemperance of the flesh.

There were two sacred tabernacles, one inner and one outer. The priests always entered the outer one; into the inner one, which was called the Holy Place, the high priest entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the people’s ignorance and sin.

The Holy Spirit signified by this the coming of Jesus, who alone would truly enter into the inner chambers of the divine mysteries and who alone knew the hidden substance of heaven. By his blood he would reconcile the Father to the whole world, so that he might have mercy on heavenly and earthly things alike. Accordingly, after he came, he reconciled all things through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or on earth (Colossians 1:20).

## CHAPTER XIV

Inside were the incense altar, the table, and the lamp.

The incense altar signifies that, like incense, the priestly prayer is directed especially toward God the Father (Psalm 140:2). The table signifies that Christ’s Passion and the mysteries of the sacraments are present upon it. Hence David says: “You have prepared a table before me” (Psalm 22:5). Its twelve loaves represent the twelve Apostles, witnesses of his Passion and resurrection [Col. 2213A].

The lamp, which is placed upon the lampstand, had formerly been under a bushel—that is, under the measure of the Law. Now, in the fullness of grace, it pours forth abundant light through its seven-branched form, because the Holy Spirit illuminates the Temple of God with the seven powers of the greatest gifts of grace.

The knowledge of the Trinity was therefore present in the inner part of the Temple, which was called the Holy of Holies. There Aaron’s rod, once placed there, blossomed. This signified that priestly grace would accomplish greater things in Christ after his death, through which he redeemed the world.

If the Jews had wished to believe, they had clear signs of the impending destruction, by which they were warned, as though by distinct voices, that their end was near. For nearly a year a comet burned above the Temple itself, resembling a hanging sword, announcing that devastation by sword and fire was destined for the people, the kingdom, and the city itself [Col. 2213B]. What does the likeness of a sword announce except war, and what does fire announce except conflagration? It was seen before the people separated themselves from the Romans.

During the days of Passover, on the eighth day of the eleventh month, every night at about the ninth hour, the Temple and its altar shone with such light that it seemed to be day. The light remained for nearly half an hour each day. The common people interpreted this as a sign that the nation was to be increased, and they were thereby encouraged as though the time for recovering liberty had arrived. The wiser, on the contrary, believed that this kind of star usually announced war.

## CHAPTER XV

So that no one may think that we have spoken of matters foreign to our worship and discipline, we first establish not what seems to us to be the case [Col. 2213C], but what happened, what opinions existed at that time, what the prudent thought, and what the imprudent thought. And when something has been said about the sect of the Jews, let it not appear that we have written of their worship as though it possessed the truth, but rather that we have set it forth as a shadow and figure, so that we might pursue more perfect things [Note: “Would follow.” GALLAND.].

For even in the Gospel we are instructed concerning the signs of the stars: “There will be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars” (Luke 21:25).

They also reported that a heifer gave birth while standing before the altars to be sacrificed, producing a lamb in the midst of the Temple during the very celebrations of the sacred rites mentioned above.

They further reported that the inner eastern gate, massive and heavy with solid bronze, which normally required the labor of twenty men to close in the evening after its iron bars had been fastened, was opened of its own accord for several nights and afterward closed only with difficulty by the guards [Col. 2213D]. Most interpreted this as a sign of future blessings, by which the gate would be opened for those who were about to enter. The more perceptive, however, said that the Temple’s protection appeared to have been loosened, so that whatever was inside might be plundered by the enemies; that the inner worship might depart and be emptied through devastation; and that the solemnity of the sacrifices might be destroyed. The reading teaches that this too was clearly signified before they crucified Christ Jesus.

Many days later, a figure of immeasurable size appeared, which very many people observed around them, as the books of the Jews have made known. Before sunset, chariots and armed battle-lines were suddenly seen in the clouds [Col. 2214A], by which the cities of the whole region of Judaea were to be attacked.

On the very solemnity of Pentecost, priests entering the inner parts of the Temple at night to perform the customary sacrifices reported that they first felt a certain movement and heard a sound; afterward they also heard a sudden voice crying: “Let us depart from here.”

## CHAPTER XVI

Jesus, son of Ananias, a rustic man, four years before the Jewish people began the war, while the city was in complete peace and prosperity and the solemn sacrifices of the Feast of Tabernacles were being celebrated, went up to the Temple and began to cry out:

“A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem, against the Temple, a voice against bridegrooms and brides [Col. 2214B], a voice against the whole people.”

He shouted this night and day. The leading men of the place, disturbed and terrified by the dreadful significance of his voice, seized him and inflicted many punishments upon him, hoping that at least when afflicted by pain he would cease announcing dreadful things full of portents.

But he was terrified neither by fear nor by blows or more severe threats. He changed neither his behavior nor his voice, but remained constant in the same proclamation and in the same sequence of words, without any interruption for entreaty. He disregarded the injury and remained unmoved in spirit.

Since they did not regard this as a superficial matter but believed that it was being expressed in a state of mental exaltation, they brought him before the judge of the place, who at that time was conducting public business there on behalf of the Romans. In order to investigate the truth, the judge tortured him with the most savage punishments [Col. 2214C]. The more he persisted, the more vehemently the judge ordered the man to be beaten with whips, so that, if he had discovered any more secret indications of the coming disturbance, he might reveal them.

But he neither wept nor pleaded. With every blow he lamented mournfully not his own destruction but that of his country, saying: “Woe to Jerusalem.”

Nor, when asked who he was, where he came from, or why he kept saying the same things, did he give an answer. He merely continued that lament for his country with miserable mourning.

At last Albinus—for that was the man’s name—worn out, released him as though he were driven by a mad frenzy and did not understand what he was saying. But afterward he neither conversed with anyone nor was he heard to say anything else. Like a mournful and funeral song, he continually repeated day and night: “Woe to Jerusalem.” He did not insult the man who beat him, nor did he thank the one who gave him food. To everyone there was one and the same response, filled with funeral wailing, especially during the solemn celebrations of the sacrifices.

For seven years and five months the same sequence of words and the same sound of voice continued. He remained tireless for so long. When the siege began, he stopped shouting the same things, as though the proclamation ought to cease once the events foretold had arrived.

But when the flames began to envelop both the city and the Temple, he went around the wall and began shouting again: “Woe to the city, and to the people, and to the Temple.” Finally [Col. 2215A] he added: “Woe also to me!” And with a sling-stone’s blow he gave up his spirit while uttering the same cry [Note: The printed editions read “with a slinger’s blow.” For this correction, see what we noted above at Book V, chapter 44. GALLAND.].

## CHAPTER XVII

It was also written in ancient books that the city, together with the Temple, would perish when the Temple had been made four-sided. Thus, whether they had forgotten or had been stunned by the necessity of the disasters overtaking them, when the Antonia had been occupied they made a four-sided circuit around the Temple [Note: The printed editions incorrectly read “failed.” Otherwise, this passage above, in Book V, chapter 44, at the end, reads: “they made a four-sided circuit of the Temple.” GALLAND.].

Among these things, the most remarkable was that an equally ancient writing—which they called sacred—continued to bear this statement impressed upon it: at that time a man would arise from their region who would assume dominion over the whole world.

This belief drove them into such madness that they promised themselves not only liberty but also a kingdom. Some thought that this referred to Vespasian; the wiser referred it to the Lord Jesus [Col. 2215B], who, born according to the flesh from Mary, spread his kingdom throughout the whole world.

Although such great warnings remained, they could not avoid what had been divinely decreed [Note: “Warning.” BARR.]. For, recognizing that God’s wrath was manifest against them, they refused to seek any remedy that might bring consolation. Such was the clouding of their guilt that it covered the eyes of their minds.

## CHAPTER XVIII

When their affairs had reached despair, Eleazar, the author of the disturbances, among other words expressing distrust, thus lamented his abandonment by God:

“O wretched men, for what hope of this life are we being preserved? Granted that the enemy should forgive us: what will it profit us when God’s anger is clear? Fires turned against us by the enemy, the blasts of the winds changed, flames driven back, so that our resources might be destroyed [Col. 2215C]. Who can live when God opposes him? There is no place for pardon, but the command of voluntary death is manifest.

“For what purpose did night intervene, except so that the enemy might not anticipate us and immediately break in after the defenses of the wall had been burned, but so that time might be left for us to practice mutual slaughter, and so that we might be permitted to die with our children and relatives rather than see breathless old men and old women dragged away by the Romans and our beloved wives carried off for the victor’s lust?

“Let us die with our country, lest we survive to endure the reproach of such disgrace. Where, then, shall we flee from the face of God, or where shall we go when the Lord of heaven is angered against us? If mountains fall upon us and hide us in hollow caves, how shall we nevertheless avoid the indignation of such great power? Where shall we advance, so that God will not be there, since he himself is everywhere?

“Are these insignificant examples by which we are taught that the one who formerly ruled has long been hostile to our nation because of our sins? Who could doubt this, when he sees that our own hands have turned against us, and that domestic sedition has destroyed more of us than war has?”

## CHAPTER XIX

I will not grant the Romans the credit of having conquered, nor do they themselves claim it, since they know that almost all of us perished by our own weapons rather than by foreign ones.

The Jews living in Caesarea saw the arms of the Romans. On the day of rest, the Sabbath, during the solemn observances of our sacred rites, a multitude of Caesarean Gentiles, suddenly inflamed by a certain impulse and by madness sent down from above, destroyed twenty thousand and drove all the rest away, so that they emptied the entire city [Col. 2216A].

Did not the whole of Syria become filled with madness, so that Jews and Gentiles living in the same cities, previously bound to one another by their residence there, later clashed with weapons, thereby preparing the path to future victory for the Romans?

For what should I say about Scythopolis? The Jews had first hastened there to forestall the Gentile population, lest it contrive anything against our people after the example of the other cities. Thus, although it would have been proper for them to join forces and fight against foreigners, the Jews instead fought against one another, so that some of them took up arms against their own relatives [Col. 2216B] and neighbors.

Then, as the price for their labor and the blood they had expended, they were killed by the Gentiles—something they themselves had prevented from being done among the Gentiles.

The people of Damascus, without any cause, struck down eight thousand Jews. The people of Ascalon [Note: “Josephus says eighteen thousand.” ID.] killed two thousand five hundred. In the city called Ptolemais, two thousand were also killed.

At Alexandria there had long been hatred between the Jews and the peoples of the nations, dating from the time when Alexander the Great had used the assistance of the Jews to subjugate the Egyptians. Therefore, when the city was founded, privileges and separate dwellings were assigned equally to Jews and Egyptians, so that the worship of those who wished to preserve their purifications without any contamination might not be mixed with that of others.

From this arose frequent conflicts between them, disputes, and appeals to judgment. Yet it is clear that nothing had been violated of the benefits granted by so great a king [Col. 2216C]. Later, when a disturbance arose among the Gentiles and some Jews were killed while others were held for punishment, the Jewish people, moved by the injury, rose against the authors of the injury. When they wished to avenge their fellow citizens with greater persistence, a Roman army was brought in, and it slaughtered sixty thousand Jews within the city.

## CHAPTER XX

But why should I linger over lesser matters, when we must lament the destruction of the whole world in the ruin of one city?

Where is the great city of Jerusalem? Where is beautiful Zion? Where is the wondrous Temple? Where is the sanctuary of holiness corresponding to that tabernacle, into which the high priest alone used to enter once a year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sin of the people? [Col. 2216D]

It has been profaned by the Gentiles. Those who destroyed the city dwell among its remains.

Where, I ask, are you, city filled with peoples, venerable to kings, acceptable to God, seat of grace? Your pavements were of marble; your walls gleamed with marble; your roofs shone with precious marble. Some of your gates glittered with gold, others gleamed with silver.

All have been killed: both those who continually inhabited you and those who gathered to you from every part of the world, so that there can be no doubt that the whole world perished in you.

Everything has been stripped bare; your roofs have been burned, your foundations demolished [Col. 2217A]. Your dwelling has become desolate; there is no one to dwell in your tents. Does anyone still desire to live, and not regret having lived?

Hard must be the eyes that can see these things; unfeeling the minds that can wish to survive such sufferings—not because the catastrophe has ceased, but because now there is no rest.

Where shall we turn our eyes, or what decision could bring delight? The whole city is a tomb of the dead. For those who look toward the sun, ashes meet their gaze. The roads are empty of the living and filled with corpses.

Wretched old men, their white hair covered with ashes and their garments torn, sit upon the remains of the dead, covering naked bones in order to protect them from birds and beasts.

A few women have survived unharmed, whom the impious soldier preserved for dishonor, not for life.

Who, seeing these things and thinking about postponing death, would dare to raise his eyes to heaven? Who could be so forgetful of his country, hostile to his own people, alien to compassion, deprived of tenderness, whose spirit could be so soft and half-manly?

Who could be so fearful that he would not be ashamed to have been preserved for this? Would that we had perished long ago, or, if life were to remain, that the light of our eyes had first been extinguished before we looked upon the holy city destroyed by the hands of enemies and saw this Temple, consecrated to God by our ancestors, so impiously burned with flames, or the priests lying slain in the Temple!

## CHAPTER XXI

Let us therefore make amends for having survived these evils, so that we may appear not to have delayed death out of love of life but through an intention toward virtue.

The enemy has surrounded every fortification. Nothing remains except either us or our wives [Col. 2217C]. They are already putting our children up for auction and competing among themselves over whose wife each may carry away. Will the women be distributed according to the rank of their dignities and persons, or compelled to undergo the misery assigned by lot [Note: “Restore ‘sortitus’; Barrensis has it above, in Book V, chapter 53, near the end.” GALLAND.]?

Prodigies of punishment and the most elaborate tortures are also being prepared for us: not only burning flames or various deaths by the blow of the victorious axe—after chains, prison, and the yoke, a harsh punishment, though tolerable for men if it is free from mockery—but also limbs torn from the living, especially severed hands.

And not without reason, because they failed in their duty when they could have helped themselves.

There is also the prospect of being bitten by wild beasts for the entertainment of the victors, a spectacle already being celebrated in the various arenas of the cities. Either the example ought to make us ashamed, or the sight ought to be marvelous, that we are being preserved either to fight beasts or to fight our brothers [Col. 2217D].

## CHAPTER XXII

Eleazar brought forward many other things of this kind, full of distrust and despair.

From all these events, and from the events themselves, the Jews clearly recognized that God was angry with them. Yet they did not glorify God or give thanks, but “became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Romans 1:21).

They hated the one who had come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24); hating him, they crucified him, and they attempted to nullify the glory of his resurrection. For if they had not recognized him, they would not have become so guilty.

Hence the Lord himself says of them: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15:22–24).

For they recognized him only in part [the text is uncertain; BARR. proposes *ex parte*], as even the demons did when they said: “We know that you are the Son of God” (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:33). They saw marvelous things and heard things still more marvelous, but they did not recognize the truth of the matter, because, hard of heart, they refused to believe.

For if they had truly recognized him as believers, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory, as Paul says (1 Corinthians 2:8).

Hence the Prophet says: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel does not know me” (Isaiah 1:3).

What is signified by the ox except every holy preacher, laboring in the seed of the word of God? What is signified by the donkey except the brutish people of the nations? Hearing the preaching of any shepherd, it immediately ran to the Lord’s manger, so that it might cling to the nourishment of God’s word.

## CHAPTER XXIII

It is fitting that Israel was expelled from the promised land after forty-two years of Christ’s visitation, because Israel is said to have been brought into it after forty years from the departure out of Egypt. In those years it received the two stone tablets of the Decalogue a second time, through which a two-year period is prefigured, appointed to complete the number for the overthrow [probably *eversionis*].

During those years, too, the elevation of the bronze serpent must especially be noted. By looking upon it, each dying person was restored to life.

For just as during that period they were nourished by manna, received through Moses the mediator the Law written on stone tablets, and those at the point of death who did not look upon the elevated serpent perished, so, during this period of destruction, those who refused to draw life-giving nourishment from the true manna—of which it had been said, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven,” and so forth (John 6:51)—and who refused to follow the true mediator, Christ Jesus, of whom it had been foretold, “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as you hear me. Whoever does not hear him shall be exterminated from his people” (Deuteronomy 18:15–18), and who declined to follow his laws, written in himself as in the true rock, refusing at the moment of that most wretched destruction to believe that he had been raised up upon the cross and had risen from the dead, were expelled from the promised land and perished [Col. 2218D].

Thus that people which sat in darkness and dwelt in the region of the shadow of death (Isaiah 9:2), seeing the eternal light of the resurrection, may enter into it with its fullness; and thus “the remnant of Israel may be saved” (Romans 9:2), so that from the two walls one Church may be joined together in the resurrection upon that cornerstone which makes both one (Ephesians 2:14), our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 2219]

## List of Manuscripts and Printed Editions Used for the Exacting Revision and Correction of Those Works of Saint Ambrose Contained in This First Volume

[Col. 2223]

### Books on the Six Days of Creation

They were collated with the following manuscripts:

Vatican manuscripts, or variant readings excerpted from the Vatican Library; the Corbie manuscript, now at Saint-Germain, written in Lombard script and apparently about 800 years old; a second Corbie manuscript, now likewise at Saint-Germain, but written by a more recent hand; a third Saint-Germain manuscript, also of considerable antiquity; the Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, about 700 years old; a second Colbert manuscript, no more than 400 years old; two Victorine manuscripts, likewise little more than 400 years old; one Royal manuscript, of still more recent date; one Dionysian manuscript, apparently about 500 years old; one Chartres manuscript, namely from the monastery of Saint Peter in the Valley, written in Lombard script more than 800 years ago. [Col. 2224] One Bigot manuscript, apparently more than 600 years old; one Jumièges manuscript, about 500 years old; one Benignian manuscript, that is, from the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, elegant and apparently 800 years old; one Remigian manuscript, that is, from the monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims, likewise 800 years old; and one Le Mans manuscript, or from the monastery of Saint Vincent at Le Mans, written at a date not much later than that of the preceding manuscripts.

They were also collated with the following editions:

The commonly used edition of Amerbach, Basel, 1492; that of Erasmus, published by Claude Chevallon, Paris, 1529; that of Jean Gillot, published by Guillaume Merlin, etc., Paris, 1568; that of Cardinal Felice Peretti da Montalto, published by Domenico Basa at Rome, 1579; and editions of the same cardinal printed at Paris in 1603, 1614, 1642, and 1661. [Col. 2225] Since nearly all the treatises in this volume have been corrected against essentially the same editions, we shall henceforth omit a separate account of their recension.

### The Book on Paradise

It was collated with the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings mentioned above; one Clairmont manuscript, or from the College of Louis the Great, 800 years old; the Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 800 years old; another Colbert manuscript, about 500 years old; one Bigot manuscript, nearly 600 years old; one Laudun manuscript, or from the regular canons of Saint-Laud at Rouen, at most 300 years old; one Jumièges manuscript, about 600 years old; one Michaelian manuscript, or from the monastery of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea, of the same age; one Rheims manuscript, or from the Church of Blessed Mary at Rheims. Since Archbishop Hincmar gave it to that church, there is no doubt that it was written more than 800 years ago; one Remigian manuscript, about 400 years old; one manuscript from Saint-Thierry, or from the monastery of Saint-Thierry near Rheims, 500 years old; one Benignian manuscript, 800 years old; and one Tournai manuscript, or from the monastery of Saint Martin at Tournai, likewise 500 years old.

### The Books on Cain and Abel

They were corrected against the following manuscripts:

Two Vatican manuscripts of excellent quality; one Benignian manuscript, 800 years old; one manuscript from Fleury, or from the monastery of Saint Benedict on the Loire, written by an ancient hand; and one Laudun manuscript, indeed more recent, but sufficiently accurate.

### The Book on Noah and the Ark

It was revised against the following manuscripts:

Two Vatican manuscripts, as above; one Corbie manuscript, now at Saint-Germain, about 800 years old; one Colbert manuscript, about 500 years old; one Mazarin manuscript from the Royal Library, not particularly ancient but written with the greatest accuracy; one Tournai manuscript, 500 years old; one Longpont manuscript, or from the Cistercian monastery of Longpont, likewise about 500 years old; and one Vallis-Clara manuscript, or from the Cistercian monastery of Vallis Clara, likewise of the same age.

### The Books on Abraham

They were collated with the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the Vatican readings, as above; one Corbie manuscript, now at Saint-Germain, 800 years old; one Colbert manuscript, about 500 years old; one Mazarin manuscript, now Royal, no more than 300 years old; another Royal manuscript, very incomplete and not of particularly remote antiquity; one Vallis-Clara manuscript, approximately 500 years old; one Longpont manuscript, of nearly the same antiquity; one manuscript from Saint-Thierry, likewise about 500 years old; and one Tournai manuscript, also of approximately equal age to the preceding manuscripts.

### The Book on Isaac and the Soul

It was corrected against the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts mentioned above; one Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 800 years old; another Colbert manuscript, slightly less than 500 years old; one Bigot manuscript, also about 600 years old; one Ebrulphian manuscript, or from the monastery of Saint Ebrulfus, of only slightly more recent date; one Remigian manuscript, at least 400 years old; one manuscript from Saint-Thierry, 500 years old; one Tournai manuscript, likewise 500 years old; one Longpont manuscript and one Vallis-Clara manuscript, of the same antiquity; and one Joyacian manuscript, that is, from the Cistercian monastery of Joyaco, more than 400 years old.

### The Book on the Good of Death

It was collated with the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, as above; one Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 800 years old; another Colbert manuscript, nearly 500 years old; two Royal manuscripts, more than 400 years old; one Bigot manuscript, about 600 years old; one Pratellian manuscript, or from the monastery of Saint Peter at Pratellis, likewise 600 years old; one Michaelian manuscript, of almost the same age; one Albinian manuscript, that is, from the monastery of Saint Albinus at Angers, of good antiquity; one Le Mans manuscript, of the same quality; one Fleury manuscript, of no less antiquity; [Col. 2226] one Remigian manuscript, about 400 years old; one manuscript from Saint-Thierry, more than 500 years old; and one manuscript each from Tournai, Longpont, Vallis Clara, and Joyaco—all of them of nearly the same antiquity.

### On Jacob and the Blessed Life

It was revised against the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings, as above; one Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 800 years old; another Colbert manuscript, nearly 500 years old; one Victorine manuscript, of slightly greater antiquity; one Bigot manuscript, more than 600 years old; one Remigian manuscript, at least 400 years old; one manuscript from Saint-Thierry, 500 years old; one Tournai manuscript, approximately of the same age; and one each from Longpont, Vallis Clara, and Joyaco, likewise about 500 years old.

### On Flight from the World

It was corrected against the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings mentioned above; one Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 800 years old; another Colbert manuscript, nearly 700 years old; a third and fourth Colbert manuscript, about 500 years old; one Victorine manuscript, more than 600 years old; one Bigot manuscript, at least 600 years old; one Pratellian manuscript, likewise about 600 years old; one Fécamp manuscript, 500 years old; one Ebrulphian manuscript, of no lesser age; one Albinian manuscript, of excellent quality; one Remigian manuscript, about 400 years old; one manuscript from Saint-Thierry, 500 years old; one Tournai manuscript, of equal age; one Alnetian manuscript, that is, from the Cistercian monastery of Blessed Mary at Aulne, about 500 years old; and one Vallis-Clara manuscript, likewise of the same age.

### On Joseph the Patriarch

It was collated with the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings mentioned above; one Corbie manuscript, now at Saint-Germain, 800 years old; another Saint-Germain manuscript, 400 years old; one Colbert manuscript, about 500 years old; one manuscript from the monastery of Saint Bernard at Paris, likewise at least 500 years old; one Ebrulphian, one Michaelian, and one Albinian manuscript, of the same age; one Benignian manuscript, 800 years old; one manuscript from Laon, or from the distinguished Church of Laon, 700 years old; and one each from Saint-Thierry, Tournai, and Vallis Clara, about 500 years old.

### On the Blessing of the Patriarchs

It was corrected against the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings mentioned above; one Corbie manuscript, now at Saint-Germain, 800 years old; another Saint-Germain manuscript, 400 years old; one Royal manuscript; one manuscript from Saint Bernard; one Ebrulphian; one Michaelian; one Albinian; and one manuscript from Saint-Thierry, all about 500 years old; one Tournai manuscript, 500 years old; one Laudun manuscript, 700 years old; and one Benignian manuscript, 800 years old.

### On Elijah and Fasting

It was collated with the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings mentioned above; one Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 1,000 years old; another Colbert manuscript, about 500 years old; one Saint-Germain manuscript, 500 years old; one Victorine manuscript, of the same age; one Michaelian manuscript, about 600 years old; one manuscript from Laon, nearly 700 years old; one Tournai manuscript, 500 years old; and one Vallis-Lucentian manuscript, or from the Cistercian monastery of Vallis Lucens, of the same age.

### On Naboth the Jezreelite

It was revised against the following manuscripts:
