The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings mentioned above; one Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 1,000 years old; a second Thuane manuscript, now also at Colbert, but more recent; a third Colbert manuscript, more than 500 years old; a fourth Colbert manuscript, of the same age; one Clairmont manuscript, 800 years old; one Mazarin manuscript, now Royal, 300 years old; one Dionysian manuscript, 500 years old; one Pratellian manuscript, more than 600 years old; one Jumièges manuscript, of only slightly more recent date; one Laudun manuscript, but more recent; [Col. 2227] one Michaelian manuscript, about 600 years old; two Albinian manuscripts, of the same or comparable age; one Vendôme manuscript, that is, from the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity at Vendôme, about 700 years old; one Rheims manuscript given by Hincmar, and therefore at least 800 years old; one Remigian manuscript, of fairly good quality; one manuscript from Laon, about 700 years old; one from Saint-Thierry, more than 500 years old; one Benignian manuscript, 800 years old; one Tournai manuscript, 500 years old; one Pontigny manuscript, or from the Cistercian monastery of Pontigny, about 500 years old; and one Carolian manuscript, or from the Cistercian monastery of Carolilocus, likewise of no lesser age.

### The Book on Tobit and the Books on the Appeals of Job and David

They were collated with the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings, as above; one Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 1,000 years old; another Colbert manuscript; one Victorine manuscript; one Dionysian manuscript; and one Tournai manuscript, all about 500 years old; and one manuscript from Laon, 700 years old. We have not separated these treatises from one another because they are contained in the same manuscripts.

### The First Apology of David

It was collated with the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings, as above; one Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 1,000 years old; two other Colbert manuscripts, about 500 years old; one Royal manuscript, about 500 years old; one Mazarin manuscript, now Royal, 300 years old; one Corbie manuscript, now at Saint-Germain, 800 years old; one Victorine manuscript, about 500 years old; one Dionysian manuscript, of the same or comparable age; one Audoenian manuscript, or from the monastery of Saint Ouen at Rouen, 600 years old; two Albinian manuscripts of better quality; one Le Mans manuscript of good antiquity; one manuscript from Laon, about 700 years old; one Remigian manuscript, 400 years old; one from Saint-Thierry, about 500 years old; one Benignian manuscript, 800 years old; and one Tournai manuscript, about 500 years old.

### The Second Apology

It was corrected against the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings mentioned above; one Royal manuscript, about 500 years old; one Mazarin manuscript, 300 years old; two Colbert manuscripts; one Victorine manuscript; and one Dionysian manuscript, all about 500 years old; one Laudun manuscript, about 700 years old; and one manuscript from Saint-Thierry, about 500 years old.

### Expositions on Twelve Psalms

They were collated with the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, as above; one Royal manuscript, 600 years old; one Thuane manuscript, now at Colbert, 500 years old; another Colbert manuscript and one Victorine manuscript, of the same age; one Remigian manuscript, 400 years old; and one manuscript each from Vallis Clara and Longpont, 500 years old.

### Exposition on Psalm CXVII

It was revised against the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings, as above; one Royal manuscript, approximately 500 years old; two Sorbonne manuscripts, about the same age; two Navarrese manuscripts, also not greatly different in age; one German manuscript, about 400 years old; one Colbert manuscript, likewise 400 years old; one Audoenian manuscript, about 500 years old; one Jumièges manuscript, about 400 years old; one Fécamp manuscript, about 600 years old; one Ebrulphian manuscript, of the same or comparable age; one Vendôme manuscript, nearly as old; one Rheims manuscript, of somewhat inferior quality; one Remigian manuscript, about 500 years old; one manuscript from Saint-Thierry, about 500 years old; and one Laetian manuscript, that is, from the monastery of Laetiacum in Hainaut, whose age or script we were unable to determine.

### Exposition on Luke

It was corrected against the following manuscripts:

The Vatican manuscripts, or the variant readings mentioned above; one Corbie manuscript, now at Saint-Germain, 950 years old; five Colbert manuscripts, 600, 500, and 400 years old; one Victorine manuscript, about 400 years old; one manuscript from Saint Bernard, about 500 years old; one Royal manuscript, about 200 or 300 years old; one Clairmont manuscript, of the same age; one Jumièges manuscript, 600 years old; one Pratellian manuscript, 700 years old; one Turin manuscript, 600 years old; one Michaelian manuscript, about 700 years old; one Albinian manuscript, about 500 years old; one Chartres manuscript, of no more recent age; one Rheims manuscript, 700 or 800 years old; one Remigian manuscript, of the same antiquity; and one Sorbonne manuscript, 300 years old.

## Volume Back Matter

[Col. 2227C]

# Index of Subjects and Opinions

[Col. 2227]

**N.B.** This Index employs a twofold numerical notation: the first, corresponding to the larger type, indicates the columns of the Benedictine edition in which the text is continuously inserted; the later numbers [the source breaks off].

## A
## INDEX OF SUBJECTS AND STATEMENTS

**A**

**AARON**, a figure of Christ, 861, 8. Why he did not enter the Promised Land, 1245, 20.

**ABEL**, a figure of Christ, 862, 12; and of the Church and Christian people, 185, 5. Why he was preferred to Cain, 187, 11. Why his sacrifice was more pleasing to God, 768, 7. He offered God not what was second-rate but what was first, not what was scanty but what was rich, 202, 402. Why he is called a shepherd, whereas Cain is called a worker of the soil, 195, 24. Both of them signified two mutually opposed sects, 184, 4. Through them the progress of human wisdom is represented, 187, 10.

**ABNEGATION.** His spirit departs from that man, and he is present with Christ, who denies himself in order to cling to Him, 370, 47; 1104, 5.

**ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION**, what it is, 1507, 15. What it is according to the Jews, ibid.

**ABRAM**, why, after his name was changed, he was called Abraham, 292, 27. Philosophy could not equal him in its aspirations, 282, 3. He makes the disputations of the philosophers rich—those who would form their precepts from his conduct, [Col. 2228] 322, 23. Why Moses proposed him to us for imitation, 281, 2. How great Abraham’s devotion was in carrying out God’s commands, 282, 3. How great his hospitality, 294, 32. When he had advanced to ninety-nine years, why is he called a boy? 298, 25. How God tested him, 304, 66 and following. Approved faithful by the Lord’s testing, 148, 9. He was often led astray by the false appearance of good things, but was not wholly bent away, 315, 6. Whether, when he received a son from the maidservant, he committed adultery, 209, 22 and following. He is tested as a strong man, encouraged as a faithful man, challenged as a just man, 283, 3. He became humbler through triumph, 287, 16. Because he despised everything for God’s sake, he receives everything from Him multiplied, 285, 9. What is celebrated as a great saying among the words of the wise, ἕπου Θεῷ—that is, “Follow God”—he himself fulfilled, 283, 4. Abraham, departing from the observation of the stars, saw God, 317, 9. How he saw the Lord, 1267, 6. The Lord appeared to him, revealing the Passion of His body, 307, 78. In the inward secret of his mind he paid homage to the perfect Trinity in each of the Persons, [Col. 2229] 197, 30. How he prophesied the coming Sun of righteousness, 317, 11. He prophesied what he did not know, 306, 71. Why Matthew chose Abraham and David above all as the ancestors of Christ, 1316, 6 and following. The gathering of the nations and the most holy assembly of the Church were first promised to Abraham by divine oracle, ibid. His offspring was spread through the inheritance of faith, 289, 21. Who are Abraham’s seed and are received among his children? 805, 61. He not only believed in the multitude of peoples believing in Christ, but also that the splendor of heavenly grace and the resurrection of immortal life would be handed down to the offspring of the Church, 333, 48. Why the just are said to rest in Abraham’s bosom, 846, 11.

**ABSINTHIUM.** Whoever is anointed with the herb cooked with oil is not touched by gnats.

**ABSTINENCE** recalled mankind to paradise, 538, 7. An elegant comparison of the abstinence of rich and poor, 569, 16. The rich fast in order to commit crime, 577, 44 and 45. Abstinence is required of those who undertake the contest of purification, 885, 1.

**ABYSS** is called a multitude and depth of waters, 19, 32.

**ACHAB.** See **AVARICE**.

**HAWKS** are by no means to be accused of cruelty toward their own young, 103, 59.

**BETWEEN A RESIDENT, AN INHABITANT, AND A SOJOURNER**, the distinction, 857, 36.

**ACCUSER.** Everyone is a more serious accuser of himself, and each person himself pronounces an inescapable sentence against himself, 959, 13. You cannot flee from yourself as your accuser, when your own conscience summons you, 977, 10. It does not seem absurd that the one who accuses himself on behalf of another should be just, 1050, 21.

**ACTION AND INTENTION**, what each is and how they differ, 1268, 8 and 9. For human actions there is a corresponding quality of reward, 1481, 47.

**ADAM** is called “man” in the Latin interpretation, 979, 15. He was made outside paradise, whereas the woman was made within paradise: what this teaches us, 153, 24. Adam in paradise was interpreted as an earthly νοῦς (*mind*), 149, 11. He received the figure of Christ, 1333, 49. He is called the mind, Eve the sense, and the serpent pleasure, 313, 1. Bodily pleasure took the form of the serpent; the woman is the symbol of our sense, and Adam of the mind, 179, 73. Adam and Eve are types of soul and body, as well as of Christ and the Church, 1352, 66. How Adam was placed in paradise to work and guard it, 154, 25. What sleep God cast upon him, 167, 50. Why untamed beasts and the birds of heaven were brought to him, but not domesticated cattle, 167, 49. Whether God, who is good, could have created Adam as a transgressor, 161, 40 and following. Whether He rightly forbade him knowledge of good and evil, 156, 30. Why He gave him a command which He knew he would certainly not keep, 160, 38 and following. What food was forbidden to Adam, 163, 42. The command not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is examined, 154, 26. Why God said to Adam, “You shall surely die,” and not simply, “You shall die,” 163, 43. How one who had not tasted death could fear death, 155, 28 and 29. From where death came upon him, 159, 35 and following. By what deception Adam was cast down, 738, 3; 753, 33. Adam’s threefold sin, 1343, 33. He would not have descended from paradise unless he had been deceived by pleasure, 418, 3. He fell through the sin of pride, 1046, 8. He wished to know what did him no good to know, 1064, 24. He fell not through his own fault but through the fault of his wife, 174, 62. Why the serpent assailed him with feminine allurements rather than with its own poisons, 1163, 28. He fell more grievously in paradise than he would have fallen on earth, 776, 26. How Adam and Eve came to know that they were naked, 174, 63. How they made coverings for themselves, and what these signify, 175, 64 and following. The fault committed made them bodily beings from spiritual ones, 1108, 14. Whether Adam, as guilty of sin, could have been condemned by God, 157, 31 and following. Why he is reproved before the woman, who had sinned first, 177, 70. The difference between his condemnation and that of the serpent, 180, 75 and following. Why the serpent is condemned first, the woman second, and the man third, 179, 73. Why God, after the sin, placed Adam opposite paradise, 168, 52. It was not a change of place but of character that made him an exile from his nature, 1427, 73. He was expelled from paradise and banished to a fortress, so that he might do penance, 787, 21. The fortress in which Adam was banished held the heirs of all his posterity in perpetual exile, 1215, 23. See **EVE**.

Why Adam fell into those inextricable snares by which all his inheritance is strangled, 1208, 47. Through his fault death belongs to all, 1352, 67. We were all in him, and in him all perished, 1467, 234. We had been expelled from the Lord’s paradise, from which Adam, conscious of his sin, turned his face away from the Lord, 650, 32. See **ORIGINAL SIN**.

Comparison of Adam with Christ, 1336, 7. Adam’s ruin emptied us, but Christ’s grace filled us, 953, 23. The evil succession of Eve was devouring the whole man; Christ’s glorious inheritance set the whole man free, 1155, 41. To our peril Adam satisfied his hunger for the knowledge of good and evil; for our benefit Christ took upon Himself hunger, 1335, 6. The whole human race would have perished in Adam unless the Samaritan, descending, had healed his bitter wounds, 1428, 73. Christ reclaimed the spoils which the devil had seized in Adam, 1241, 11. See **CHRIST**.

**ADOLESCENCE** alone is weak in strength, infirm in judgment, burning with vice, disdainful of admonitions, and alluring through pleasures, 633, 21. The movements of our adolescence are calmed by the faithful station of old age, 188, 11. Adolescents are recalled from vice more by fear than by reason, 504, 58.

**ADRIATIC SEA.** The other seas mingle with it, 38, 13.

**SOJOURNER.** Who can truly be called a sojourner and a pilgrim on earth? 1003, 31.

**ADVERSITY AND TRIBULATION** are in a certain sense graces, 1207, 40 and following. Tribulations are good when they are characteristic of the just, who endure them not for their merits but for their devotion, 925, 92. Everything grievous that a person suffers on earth is not necessarily endured because of his sins, 653, 2; 657, 11 and following. We do not enter tribulations without God’s judgment, 1197, 8. What is adversity to the just, except an exercise of faith, a distinction of patience, a glorious training in virtue, and a confession filled with victory? 1146, 16. Faith that is not exercised quickly grows weak, and when idle is tested by frequent hardships, 1111, 21. It benefits you that there are many persecutors, 1234, 43. Scourgings are remedies of salvation for the just, 1112, 26. Those who have fallen through the course of prosperity and the enjoyment of favorable circumstances are corrected by adversity, 900, 30. We have no confidence in pleasures; we have confidence in sufferings, 1304, 70. In adversity life is blessed, even if it is inundated by many dangers, 454, 27 and following. Afflictions are crowns for the strong man, but infirmities for the weak, 319, 13. Whoever is not broken in tribulation and follows the law is blessed, 754, 34. Outstanding examples of some who were blessed in adversity, 473, 39 and following. See **MARTYRS**.

This is the first virtue: not to be broken by adversity and not to be lifted up by prosperity, 753, 31 and following. He is to be praised as a good governor of himself who is not lifted up by prosperity and not broken by adversity, 1070, 39. The just man should neither be cast down by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity, 1244, 18. See **PROSPERITY**. In adversity the just man is not broken, 1084, 17. He is struck by the waves of worldly cares but is not overthrown, 318, 11. The just are tested by worldly afflictions but are not estranged from keeping the heavenly commandments, 320, 21. The Lord does not wish to break us through humility into despair, but only to correction, 1115, 5. Whoever hopes for better things is never broken by lesser ones, 1045, 6. Why the things regarded as adversities should be endured patiently, 685, 30. The sufferings which Christ accepted for His servants, let us undergo for the Lord, 829, 32. When we are shaken by adversity, meditation on the law should be ours, 1122, 28. The faithful soldier does not ask that persecutions cease, but asks to be helped amid persecutions, 1110, 21. When the mind is pressed by adversity, then it implores divine help, 1086, 1. God is always present with His just when they are carried into various adversities, and according to what law, 1243, 16. God is always good to the just, even in adversity, 662, 3. In distress the just man blesses the Lord with a more grateful affection, 954, 25. By various examples it is shown that the just praise God’s justice in adversity, 1196, 6 and following. It is a magnificent thing if, subjected to injuries, insults, illness, and poverty, you praise God’s judgment, 1098, 33. It is a great thing to cling to Christ when some storm troubles you, 1054, 34. Desolation is followed by humility, humility by patience, patience by testing, and testing by consolation, 1087, 4. The greater the tribulations, the richer the consolation is reserved, 1099, 36. In misery, one kind of consolation is to be free from guilt, 629, 10. Scourgings after death are of no benefit, 665, 8. In this life neither prosperity remains nor adversity lasts long, 748, 24. See **PERSECUTION** and **TRIBULATION**.

**TOWARD ADVERSARIES**, the promised faith must be kept, 687, 36. No one is a heavier adversary than a domestic one; no one is a more harmful enemy than he whom the power of the heavenly substance supports, 885, 1. Before anything else, the adversary must be driven from the hidden and secret places of your heart, 928, 4.

**ADULTERY** is a grave offense and an injury to nature, 87, 19. Even a barbarian recognizes that the crime of adultery must be avoided, 258, 8. Whatever is committed with a woman who is not a lawful wife is condemned under the charge of adultery, 291, 25. How severely God punishes adultery, 284, 7; 302, 59 and 60. Among irrational animals, adulteries procured by human beings are censured, 82, 9.

**ADULTERESSES** have three darts: the eyes, words, and persistence in making approaches, 492, 23.

**EGYPTIANS** circumcised females as well as males, 348, 78.

**EMULATION**, in good and in evil, is found in Scripture, 778, 4 and following. In Scripture, “rival” is used for one who is crooked and envious, 781, 71. Sub-emulation possesses cunning; emulation possesses simplicity, 781, 10.

**AENON** is said to mean “the eye of punishments,” 816, 3.

**EQUINOX**, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April according to the Romans, or, as others think, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, 253, 60. Ἀὴρ (*aēr*), a Greek word, is called *ver* in Latin, “spring,” 263, 84. Whether the air is accustomed to change at the rising of the moon, 76, 30.

**AGE.** Every age is generous toward Christ, 1293, 36. Strength of spirit excludes the weakness of age, 801, 52.

**ETHIOPIA** is designated in the Latin interpretation as rejected and lowly, 151, 16.

**HUMAN AFFECTIONS**, although holy, often change, 1119, 18. All human power lies in affection, 1060, 15. The eye goes astray wherever affection goes astray, 406, 40.

**ACAR** is said to mean “dwelling,” and why, 345, 72; also “sojourner” and “resident,” 194, 23.

**LAMB.** Although a little lamb may be among many thousands of sheep, it recognizes its mother’s voice, and she that of her young, 122, 25.

**LAMB, PASCHAL**, was a figure of Christ, 297, 40. What our ancestors prefigured by eating the lamb, 902, 36.

**FIELDS.** The beauty of fields in full growth is described, 46, 36.

**FARMER.** To be a farmer is one thing, and to be a worker of the soil another, 271, 107.

**AIN**, the letter—that is, “eye” or “spring,” 1170, 1.

**WARS OF THE ALANS**, 1506, 10.

**LAKE ALBANUS** is not mingled with the waves, 39, 16.

**GAMBLING** has its own laws, which the statutes of the courts do not dissolve, 603, 38.

**ALLEGORY** exists when one thing is done and another is represented, 292, 28.

**ALLELUIA**, that is, “praise God,” 973, 3.

**ALEPH**, the first letter, whose interpretation is “teaching,” 973, 1.

**GARLIC.** People enjoy it, 123, 28. It should be taken as medicine, not as food, ibid.

**BITTER THINGS** are not inflicted by God in order to harm, but in order to correct, 1084, 16.

**TO BE LOVED.** He who loves everyone demands to be loved, 1032, 45. It is a moral principle that we should see, above others, those whom we love, 503, 56. The goads of love quickly pierce hearts unless the reins of desire are loosened, 503, 37. See **CHARITY** and **LOVE**.

**AMBITIOUS MAN.** He who makes earthly things supremely important seems to worship the devil, 192, 16. Ambition often makes criminals of those who are pleased by no other vices, 1340, 31. By what remedy the weapon of ambition may be blunted, 1343, 34. See **RICH** and **PRIDE**.

**AMBROSE.** The anniversary of his priestly ordination is celebrated each year, 1489, 73. He rejoiced that the just lived long and grieved when they died, 211, 12. He compiled much about the deeds of Elijah in the frequent discourse of various books, 537, 5. He undertook the labor of treating the subject not to display his talent, but to instruct his people, 35, 7.

**AMEN.** Why it is repeated so often in the Gospel of John, 882, 36. This is the harmony when a Psalm is answered in the Church: “Amen” is said, 1468, 238.

**AMIANTHUS** is not easily consumed by any fire, 541, 19.

**AMINADAB** signifies “father of good pleasure,” 993, 33.

**ALMONDS.** How farmers treat them so that they become sweet from bitter, 55, 56.

**AMPHISCIANS**, who they are, 73, 23.

**ANANIAS** lied to himself: he could have offered less without deceit, 769, 9. Delivered over to eternal death, he brought everyone to devotion to the faith through a salutary fear, 1197, 7.

**NATURE OF THE ANGELS** is more divine and remains free from bodily injury, 1440, 126. Angels are nothing without zeal, and they lose the prerogative of their substance, 1199, 14. Although they began at some point, they already existed when this world was made, 9, 17. They praise the Lord before the beginning of the world itself, 737, 2. The angels’ marvelous power, 300, 53. God granted them so much that they have the power to give life, 1356, 79. How quickly he renounces sin who considers that all things are full of angels, 976, 9. It is not in our power to see an angel, but it is in his power to appear, 1275, 26. Guardian angels are good, 1055, 36. The Lord sends them for the defense of those who are to become heirs of the heavenly promises, 976, 9. Each person ought either to seek the patronage of the angels or to fear offending them, 1462, 210. Angels need God’s mercy in a manner different from human beings, 1066, 29; 1077, 58. The archangel himself could not abstain from sin, 1352, 76. By what error the angels were cast down from their virtue and grace, 677, 4. A light fault in an angel is judged by a more severe judgment, 1066, 29. Job’s praise of an inferior substance is the condemnation of the angel who was cast down from a higher state, 824, 21. How empty is the pomp of angelic boasting, 770, 11. Where the evil angels and the devil are, 1077, 58. They are held captive and restrained by earthly allurements, 1078, 58. They do not belong to the common right of God’s indulgence and the remission of sins, 1077, 58. See **DEVIL**.

**SOUL.** What the human soul is, 266, 92. What kind it is, 357, 4. Aristotle said that it is ἐντελέχεια (*entelecheia*, actuality), 266, 92. Critias and his disciples said that it is blood, ibid. Many philosophers held that it is fire, ibid. It is a philosophical fiction that the souls of human beings and beasts alike are common, 408, 45. According to the natural philosophers it is called earth, 323, 26. The soul is not made of mud or earth; it is a magnificent work inspired by God’s creative act, 1089, 10. It is not corporeal, 405, 38. It is incorporeal, immaterial, and marvelous, 1091, 15 and following. The doctrine of the soul’s incorruption is established, 222, 36 and following; 405, 38, 41 and following. The soul is the better part of the human being, 127, 39. The whole person is in it, 129, 43, etc. It is called by the name “human being,” 130, 45. It is made in the image of God, whereas the body is made in the likeness of beasts, 129, 42, 43 and following; 760, 48. The soul lives where it is clothed with nothing mortal, nothing weak, and nothing deserving punishment, 1253, 24. The mind is nourished by knowledge of things, 1446, 148. Nothing else makes a rational soul live except the address of God, 1045, 7. Certain ages seem to belong to it, 1041, 30. What its first fruits are, 205, 1.

There are three affections of the soul in the body: rational, appetitive, and irascible, 1444, 139. The irrational part is divided into seven sections, 242, 40. Its four movements, and what they are, 335, 54. The heats and ardors of souls are greater than those of bodies, 1209, 1. The soul’s steps are its advances, 1137, 14. How they are to be directed, 1144, 12. Its first progress is explained, 359, 8 and following; its second, 360, 11 and following; its third, 367, 38 and following; and its fourth, 371, 50 and following. What the soul’s beauty and grace are, 231, 10; 382, 78; and 1188, 15; and its strength, 216, 22; and its greatness, 1276, 31. The Word of God inscribes in the soul either the gifts of nature or of grace, 902, 80. Although the soul has no sex, it represents the functions of both sexes: it marries, conceives, and gives birth, 204, 47. The soul of the just is the bride of the Word, 1035, 8. What kind of bridegroom the soul has, 1361, 24. No one fails to consider the union either of soul and Spirit or of Christ and the Church blessed, 1256, 36. What can please Christ the bridegroom except peace of mind, purity of heart, and love of the mind? 1361, 23. What its offspring are, and how promptly they should be produced, 205, 1. The more intensely the soul desires to cling to Christ, the more it fails, 1104, 4. The soul that is to receive the Word must be such that it dies to the world and is buried with Christ, 373, 53. When it clings to the good, invisible and immortal God, it becomes like Him, 406, 41. It concentrates on divine things and flees earthly things, 358, 6. It despises visible and sensory things and ascends to eternal realities, 360, 11. The souls of the just are compared with eagles, 1484, 55.

The soul is a chariot that has good or bad horses, 378, 65. It is God’s chariot, 993, 34. Why philosophers have expressed the chariot contests of souls in their books, 379, 67. Adorned with the flowers of virtues, it is a garden, or it contains paradise budding within itself, 398, 19. It is a city fortified by Christ and besieged by the devil, 131, 49. It is a wall, and in what way, 1256, 37. In the human soul there are two sects, 184, 4. From it come good and evil, ibid. What division of its parts it suffers, 337, 57. Its twofold nakedness, 272, 112 and 113. What its rust is, 1270, 14. It wastes away when sin is diminished; it grows fat when sins accumulate, and for what reason, 856, 34. Its death creeps in through the effect of crime, when the devil tempts and the flesh persuades, 1357, 63. Once it has clung to desires, it can hardly fly back to the heights from which it descended without God’s wrath, 1352, 65. Care must be taken that it not be glued to this body, 406, 40. Let our soul not become flesh, but rather let our flesh become soul, 1011, 7. It would never be overcome by the body unless it were first tempted by the devil, 1351, 62. The soul’s flesh consists of carnal thoughts, 1168, 37.

How the soul is healed, 252, 59. How it turns away from and rejects sin, 1445, 144 and following. Although the disagreement between flesh and soul had, through the transgression of the first human being, become part of nature, nevertheless through the Savior’s cross they were brought into harmonious fellowship, 1444, 141. In Scripture, “souls” is used for hands and for human beings, 871, 11.

**ANNA** is presented in such a way that she is clearly believed worthy to announce that the Redeemer of all had come, 1301, 62.

**YEAR.** What is a solar year? 74, 24. What is a lunar year according to the Hebrews and Romans? 74, 24. In what month it begins, 253, 60; 258, 71. More than six thousand years are reckoned from the creation of the world, 1412, 7.

**GEESE.** Their sentries saved the Roman Capitol from the Gallic enemy, 97, 44.

**ANTICHRIST** will come from the tribe of Dan, 523, 32. He rises from the abyss in order to wage war against Elijah, Enoch, and John, 930, 10. Arius, or Sabellius—in fact, all who mislead us through a false interpretation—are Antichrists, 1508, 21. Where the Antichrist is, there are the days of the half-year, 888, 8. The Jews will believe in him, [Col. 2233] 896, 19.

**APELLES**, the author from whom many used to propose questions concerning Holy Scripture, 155, 28.

**BEES.** Their marvelous nature in producing offspring, constructing honeycombs, gathering honey, establishing a king, and showing loyalty toward him, 106, 67 and following. Their song, 109, 76. When covered with oil they die; with vinegar they revive, ibid.

**APOLLINARIANS** are censured because they say that Christ assumed a body but not a soul, 868, 26.

**APOLLO PYTHIUS** was not the author of the saying “Know yourself,” but it was taken from Moses, 986, 13.

**APOSTLES** are the more excellent and active members of Christ, 948, 10. Why Christ chose not the wise, nor the rich, nor the noble, but sinners and tax collectors, 1366, 44. Christ sent them to sow faith—men who would not compel but teach, and would not exercise power but exalt the teaching of humility, 1424, 59. The Romans’ internal wars were brought to an end, with the result that the Apostles were sent throughout the whole world, 934, 21. They are Christ’s censors, through whom the world was acquired, 1293, 36. They are the pillars of the Church, 1030, 38. In them were the merits of the prophets, 1417, 27. They saw the Lord not only according to the body but also according to the Word, 1267, 5. They are good flowers, having poured forth the fragrance of their various writings and works, 1040, 25. The Apostles, whom the Lord cleansed from every stain of sin, were not afterward darkened by any blemish, 520, 25. The Lord gave them the authority that had previously belonged to His judgment, so that sins might be remitted through the equity of release and not remain bound for a long time when they were soon to be released, 858, 37. Why they commanded demons not in their own name but in Christ’s, 1341, 26. Why the instruments of the apostolic ministry are fishing nets, 1354, 72. The Apostles are the hours; Christ is the day, 1464, 222.

**TO APPEAR**, who is said to do so, 1274, 24.

**WATER** is divided into three kinds: sea, rivers, and lakes, 336, 55. How the gathering of the waters could have taken place, 35, 8 and following. Where all their overflow was diverted, 39, 14 and 15. How they can be above the heavens, 26, 9 and following. The marvelous diversity of waters, 57, 62. Water knows how to gather, fear, and flee when God commands, 33, 1 and 2. Praise of water, 1514, 48.

**EAGLE.** Whether it feeds its young, 104, 60. How it tests them, ibid. and 1212, 13. Aquila and Symmachus, who could not perceive the unity of the Father and the Son, nevertheless confessed it several times in their speech, 155, 27.

**TREES.** Their origin, 51, 47. Their diversity, fruitfulness, age, and sex, 54, 54; 61, 71. Their uses, 59, 65. How their sap differs from one another, 58, 63.

**ARK.** Noah’s ark is compared with the ark of the covenant, 234, 16. In its construction the human form of the body is represented, 232, 13; 248, 50.

**RAINBOW.** Why God placed His bow in the cloud, 790, 27.

**ANIMALS** exist on account of human beings: some for utility, others for pleasure, and others for enjoyment, 239, 33. Those harmful on land are harmless in water, 81, 6. See **BEASTS**.

**HERON**, fearing rain, flies above the clouds, 97, 43.

**DRY LAND** signifies a certain kind of earth, and what kind, 39, 17. Why the earth was called dry land, 40, 19.

**RAM.** Why it is compared with the air, 334, 50. It is a figure of the divine Word, 335, 52. The ram sacrificed by Abraham was a figure of Christ, 307, 77.

**COUNCIL OF ARIMINUM.** The authors of treacherous transgression, while following the emperor’s favor, lost God’s favor, 1372, 71.

**ARISTOTLE.** His view concerning superfluous narrators, 1110, 19. He posits two principles of things, matter and form, and a third with them called the operative principle, 2, 2. What he thought about the eternity of the world, 2, 3. See **ARIANS**.

**ARIUS** is a moth, and for what reason, 1207, 13. The martyrs confessed as God’s Son the one for whom they offered their blood; against him the Arians raised a question concerning origin, 1294, 37. By excluding one from participation in divine operation, they introduce several, and grant servants the prerogative they deny the Son, 128, 40. What they deny Christ they will not deny the Antichrist, 1509, 21. We recognize that they have fallen into treachery: they abandoned the Apostle and follow Aristotle, 1249, 10. They differ little from the Jews, 715, 26. They arrive at the assertion of the Manichaeans, 732, 70 and following. The divinity of the Son is proved against them, 1314, 95. They humble and cast down their own soul, 847, 12. With royal support they threaten cruel punishments unless the church is handed over to them, 786, 19. They seek partnership with royal power in order to attack the truth of the Church with military arms, 1474, 17.

**ARMS.** Their weapons wound the weak, and no one can use arms well who does not know how to bear them, 1334, 50.

**ARMENIANS AND GOTHS** believed the preaching of the Gospel, 1507, 14.

**RUIN OF ARROGANCE** is evil, 1005, 35. You have learned to follow humility rather than arrogance, and to pursue diligence rather than power, [Col. 2234] 196, 27. See **RICH** and **PRIDE**.

**ARTERIES.** Many think that the heart is the beginning of the arteries and of innate heat, 137, 61. An artery contains less blood and much more spirit, 266, 92.

**ARTS.** Some are practical, others theoretical, 9, 17.

**REEDS AND CANES**, who are compared with them, 1380, 104.

**ASCIANS**, who they are, 73, 23.

**ASER** signifies “riches” in the Latin interpretation, 524, 38. His blessing is explained, ibid.

**ASS.** What the lazy ass teaches us, 117, 11. In the she-ass the people of the Gentiles are represented, now subjected to Christ, 305, 71; 1296, 43.

**ASSYRIANS**, that is, “those who direct,” 151, 17.

**CUNNING** fears everything and does not trust its own counsels, 963, 21. It must be spiritual if it is to preserve salvation and know no deceit, 781, 10.

**ATHLETES.** Their various contests and names, 801, 55. Who are called boys, youths, and men? 800, 52. Abstinence is necessary for them, 885, 1. A good athlete displays his limbs in order to demonstrate the discipline of his way of life, 1228, 21. On the final day he receives the lot of the crown, 113, 1. When is he considered defeated in the contest? 799, 51. His fall is properly called a ruin, ibid. Ambrose, as a boy, saw an athlete who, after knocking down his opponent, struck his forehead with his heel—because he had insulted him, 876, 24. God’s athlete is trained and tested by adversity, 284, 16. We are athletes and are driven forward; some fall, and most are knocked down, 800, 51.

**ATOMS.** The combination of stronger atoms does not provide the cause of continuous endurance, 4, 7.

**HEARING.** The duty of listening is the foundation of everything, 1158, 3. One must be silent when one does not find a prepared listener, 916, 70.

**AUGUSTUS.** The Roman Empire was transferred to him after the weariness of civil wars, 934, 21.

**EARS.** Why they project more prominently, and the inward curving of their interiors, 138, 62; 235, 19. Their useful function is as necessary as their appearance is beautiful, 235, 19.

**GOLD** is commended not so much for its own sake as because of the punishment it brings upon human beings, 581, 55. See **AVARICE**.

**AVARICE** distributes the rights of possessions, which God had willed to be common to all, 1064, 22. It avoids sharing with the multitude, 99, 47. The abundance of favorable circumstances is a great enticement to wrongdoing: it lifts a person into pride and pours forgetfulness of the Creator into him, 659, 16. How there is a snare in gold, birdlime in silver, a bond in an estate, and a nail in love, 397, 16. Desire for gold is the source of treachery, and sacrileges are commonly generated by devotion to avarice, 681, 16. Avarice breaks faith and does not keep the simplicity of words, 755, 37. It is true that avarice appears to be the cause of our poverty, 1439, 124. It is a vain outpouring, 576, 42. How great human avarice is, 90, 26. It is censured, 92, 30. Envy of wealth makes the lands unsafe and incites many to robbery, 557, 70. The insatiable avarice of merchants is censured, 557, 70 and following. How frequent shipwrecks rightly accuse it, ibid. Avarice is inflamed by profit, not extinguished, 567, 4. The more it takes away, the more it believes itself poor, 193, 21. There is no limit to robbery where there is no measure in desire, ibid. The fever of love is no less than that of labor: our fever is avarice, our fever is lust, 1351, 63. The fire of carnal desire is vain, 852, 23. Why the languor of avarice is evil, 750, 28. Robbery is subordinate to it, 1183, 45. In the story of Ahab and Jezebel the avarice of the rich is described, 576, 42. See **WEALTH**.

The goods of the avaricious are not true goods, 951, 17. He knows how to call nothing good except what is profitable, 574, 36. Sterility alone is profitable to him, 574, 35. For the avaricious, every profit is a loss to virtue and fuel for desire, 89, 23. How what we think is profit in money is loss to the soul, 1026, 26. Those who value money more highly than religion sell Christ for money, 880, 32. Rare is the person who prefers God’s law to gold and silver, 1085, 21. How justly God punishes the avaricious rich man, 578, 48. While we want more, we lose even what is less, 1147, 21. He whose desires the world cannot contain is in need of the whole world, 579, 50. However far he extends the dimensions of his house, he is confined within the narrow limits of his own judgment, 1042, 33. He is the guardian, not the master, of his possessions when he buries them in the earth, 582, 58. What is more miserable than to be tormented by guarding things whose abundance brings no benefit? 391, 4. Devouring others, he too is devoured by others, 84, 13 and 14. Let your eyes not be the eyes of a wolf, lying in wait for prey, 1171, 8. How every avaricious person is both a slave and a beggar, 490, 20. Beware lest you bury your heart alive in the earth, 466, 23. What else is the mind of the avaricious except metal? 661, 21. All the greedy, all the avaricious, possess Gehazi’s leprosy together with his riches, 1349, 54. See **RICH**.

**AVERNUS**, a sea, 39, 15. [Col. 2235]

**BIRDS.** Various kinds are described, 98, 47 and 48. Their different feet, and why they differ, 108, 74. Why none are without the function of feet, 98, 46. The kinship of fish and birds, 98, 45.

**B**
BABYLON, that is, confusion, 278, 128.

BATHS. At Rome, formerly sons did not bathe with their parents, especially when they had reached puberty, 274, 116.

BARRABAS means in Latin “son of the father,” 1526, 102.

BASILISK. It is said to kill whatever animal it sees first; if it is first seen by a human being, it is killed, 1095, 24.

BAPTISM OF JOHN is the eye of supplications; the baptism of Christ is the eye of thanksgivings, 816, 3. What distinction there is between the two baptisms, 1175, 19, and 1307, 79. John baptized with water, Christ with the Spirit, 1535, 140. The Lord was baptized, not wishing to be cleansed, but to cleanse the waters, so that they might possess the right of baptism, 1308, 83. Water begins first and completes the mysteries, 1514, 48. The sacraments of the altar are not received before baptism, 1533, 135. The baptized person renounces the devil and his works, 7, 14. He also renounces the world, 1502, 36. He justifies God, because he confesses his own sins, 1204, 30. In baptism there is confession and forgiveness of sins, 1348, 3. The baptized person descended naked into the Jordan, 966, 32. He also descends into Christ’s death and ascends into his resurrection, 819, 10. Although baptized over his whole body, he is afterward cleansed by spiritual food and drink, 1178, 29. He does not offer sacrifice unless he enters the eighth day, 972, 2. The garment with which the Lord clothed us when we emerged from the sacred font must be preserved, 1361, 25.

BAPTISM. There is one baptism of the Church, with which catechumens must be baptized, 997, 14. It is administered by the priests of the Church, ibid., 15. It is to be conferred upon every age, 349, 81. Nor should it ever be repeated, 1491, 78. What Christ accomplishes through the sacrament of baptism, 806, 63. In it all righteousness is fulfilled, 689, 44, and 980, 17. Sin is washed away, 42, 23; 210, 10; 561, 83; 1031, 42, and 1476, 24. For while water washes the body, sins are cleansed by the Spirit in the soul, 1307, 79. Even in the font itself, the sanctification of divinity breathes upon it, 1307, 79. A person receives the sevenfold Spirit, 652, 36. Those who delay receiving baptism are censured, 561, 83 and following; 1464, 221. The Red Sea was a figure of baptism, 689, 43. Likewise the transformation of the river Jordan, 1278, 37. Elijah also displayed its type, 562, 48. The baptism of suffering is that by which each person is cleansed with his own blood, 997, 14. Who should be baptized in milk, 1176, 21. See SACRAMENTS.

BATHUEL is said to mean “wisdom”; in the Latin interpretation, however, it signifies “daughter of God,” 426, 20.

BEATITUDE is not placed in riches, authority, or honors; nor in nobility of birth, elegance, or beauty; nor in bodily health, 743, 15. Here it is found to be neither great nor genuine, 1166, 30. For those things that are to come are more excellent, 1152, 33. The teaching of Aristotle and the Peripatetics, and the Pythagorean doctrine concerning beatitude, were first recognized by Abraham, 345, 70. Whatever is perfect is blessed, 456, 34. All beatitude comes from God, 1028, 32. It consists solely in possession of the true and the good, 455, 32; 1058, 7. The beatitude of eternal life is described, 411, 52 and following. Who sees God, 787, 21. Although there are many good things, there is nevertheless one eternal life, 1342, 30. In perfect beatitude there is everything, 410, 49. Why Christ proposed the beatitude of eternal life, 742, 13. Likewise, why there are different rewards, 1224, 9. What the dwelling places of souls are after death until the final day of judgment, 407, 45 and following. In what order their joy has been arranged, 408, 48. In the resurrection we shall be transformed into the state of a simple creature, 1458, 194. The recompense is the kingdom of heaven and the habitation of paradise, 1157, 46. Its acquisition is not to be attributed to our merits, 1166, 30. No age is too weak for the kingdom of God, 1462, 213. Nor is any sex excluded, 743, 14. It is closed to no one except the person whom the profession of his own voice has excluded, 1459, 200. Weakness cannot impede beatitude, 472, 34. The thief, a minister of the devil, reached the place from which the devil himself had been cast down, 864, 17. It seems difficult to human beings to purchase hope at the cost of dangers and to exchange the loss of present things for the gain of the future age, 1421, 1. How the heavenly kingdom is seized, 1382, 112 and following. Why Saint Luke set down only four beatitudes of the Lord, but Saint Matthew eight, 1367, 49; 1370, 62.

WARRIOR. Courage is necessary in more difficult places, 229, 5. The contests of wars are false madnesses, 866, 4.

LAKE BENACUS is not mingled with the waves, 39, 16.

A blessing is invoked in place of a curse, 578, 46.

[Col. 2236]

A blessing is the votive bestowal of sanctification and graces, 515, 7. When the priest gives a blessing, the people respond “Amen,” and why, 882, 36.

OUR BENEFITS are not to be publicized, but kept private, 1356, 5. In an equal benefit, the one who began first is preferred, 230, 6; 1373, 74. Divine benefits are always full and overflowing, 1276, 29. They are bestowed not upon those who sleep, but upon those who keep watch, 1347, 49.

BENJAMIN is a type of the Apostle Paul, 530, 57 and following; 1038, 17. His blessing is expounded, 530, 57 and following.

BERSABEE is called “daughter of the sabbath,” or “full daughter,” or “well of the oath,” 726, 51. Why she was not omitted from the genealogies of the Lord, 1328, 39.

BEASTS. Why God formed shorter necks for some animals and longer necks for others, 124, 30. Why he granted horns to many of them, 893, 15. By smell alone they know how to distinguish harmful things from beneficial ones, 120, 21. They do not know the hatreds of stepmothers, 121, 22. See ANIMALS.

BETH. The letter is explained as “confusion,” 981, 1.

BETHEL, that is, “house of God,” 284, 6.

BITUMEN possesses a powerful natural capacity for binding, 234, 14.

GOOD. What is the nature of the good, 376, 60. What is not evil is also good, 389, 1. What is the order of goods? 327, 33. From where philosophers derived that good which they assert to be the highest, 412, 55. From where the Epicureans derived the claim that pleasure is the highest good, 351, 85. They are refuted, 314, 3. God alone is the highest good, 382, 78 and 79. What is truly good is incorruptible, 314, 3. We understand that what is good is naturally a precept, 161, 39. What is good is written by the Spirit of the living God; what is defective, however, is written with an iron stylus, 731, 66. What is good and ought to be done is harmonious and adherent; what is shameful, however, is discordant, 154, 26. Our good should not arise from necessity, nor with grief and sorrow, but voluntarily, 1243, 36. Whatever good happens to us, let us attribute it to God’s justice, 183, 2; 1075, 52. God brings about what is good, not what is evil: he brings about glory and leaves punishment, 179, 74. It is divine that good things are promised; it is ours that they are changed, 230, 6. In the performance of the good there is reward, 744, 17. Many things in this age seem good and pleasant, but are not, 1080, 6. According to the judgment of a certain philosopher, four things ought to be present in a good man—and what they are, 325, 29.

GOODNESS is a fruit of the Holy Spirit, 782, 12. There is no complaint where goodness of mind and goodness of deed are in agreement, 1272, 19. Popular goodness abounds toward others but is more restricted toward oneself, 1261, 2.

OXEN know, when rain is imminent, to remain by the mangers; gathering fair weather through their natural sense, they look outside, 120, 20.

BOXWOOD is useful for forming the letters of the alphabet, 54, 53.

C
CADAVERA: The corpses of the dead were once customarily burned with torches, 833, 41.

CAESAR defeated Pompey the Great and his younger son, 934, 21.

CAESARIES: Reverenced in old men, venerated in priests, terrifying in warriors, becoming in young men, adorned in women, pleasing in children, 135, 56. Its usefulness and beauty, 235, 21.

CAIN is called “acquisition,” and why, 184, 3. The twofold defect in his sacrifice, 195, 25 and following. The other defect, 214, 18. Justice was lacking, 216, 21. Why he chose a barren field for fratricide, 218, 26. Why God asked him where his brother was, 218, 17 and following. Why he received a sign so that no one would kill him, 769, 7. Why vengeance was not immediately taken against him, 223, 38. Why he was released without a prescribed punishment, 177, 71. The longevity granted to him was a punishment, 222, 37. From whom he feared being killed, 221, 33. Cain was a figure of the parricidal Synagogue and Jewish people, 185, 5.

CALCEAMENTA: Footwear is customarily made from the hide of a dead animal, 1423, 57.

CALICES: Two cups, one of death and the other of life, 822, 17.

CALUMNIA: Calumny is more serious, temptation lighter, 1190, 24 and following. Against slanderers and sinners, the just man is content with his own judgment; but he reserves the judgment of his merits for Christ, 847, 13. Why those attacked by false accusations ought not to be troubled, 493, 27.

CANCRI: The crab’s cunning in capturing the oyster, 88, 22.

CANIS: A dog, lacking reason, uses its keen faculty of perception to acquire for itself the power of reason, 221, 23. With a dog’s blood every disease of wild animals is cured, 123, 26. Dogs train the human affections to show gratitude, 119, 17. At Antioch a dog pointed out the soldier who had killed his master, 122, 24. Those who customarily enumerate the origins of dogs are reproved, 580, 54.

CANTICA: The Song of Songs contains three kinds of wisdom: moral, natural, and mystical, 365, 27 and following. How much the two songs of Moses illuminate his books, 739, 5.

CANTORES: Why Solomon appointed singers for himself, 1052, 26.

CANTUS: The singing of the Church, 34, 5. Of men, women, virgins, and little children, 42, 23; 741, 9. Those who contend in singing or playing stringed instruments have a share in the crown on the last day, 118, 1.

CANERE: What does it mean to sing inwardly? 742, 12. God delights in a song—not only in being praised, but also in being reconciled, 739, 5.

CAPH: Why the letter *kaph* signifies “they are bent down,” 1103, 7.

CAPRAE: Whence the name derives, 334, 50. For goats and sheep food is medicine, 48, 40. Sensing weapons armed with poisons, they apply herbs as a remedy to the wound, ibid.

CAPREA: The doe expels arrows from its wound with dittany, 123, 26. The leopard heals itself with the blood of a wild doe, 123, 26. It avoids garlic, ibid., 28.

CAPTIVITAS: This is truly to be mourned: captivity that appears to have been deprived of the freedom of eternal hope, 1172, 9.

CAPUT: It is demonstrated that the head is the most excellent of all the members, 135, 55 and following; 234, 17; 236, 23. From it the course of the veins, the passages of the breath, and the forces of the blood are conveyed into all parts of the body, 1221, 1. Why the bones of the head are covered with thicker hair, 141, 73. Why those condemned for some crime are banished from the head [beheaded], 1222, 1.

CARO: In Scripture, “flesh” is used for the earthly human being, 132, 32. It cannot be made according to the image of God, 130, 45. Our flesh is earth, which the wicked work and the good cultivate—and how, 271, 108. Not flesh but the affections are responsible for guilt; flesh, however, is the servant of the will, 448, 11. Infused with the serpent’s fraud and poison, flesh became the flesh of sin and the flesh of death, 817, 5. The nature of the flesh resists discipline because it obeys pleasure, 230, 7. It is always boiling over and is itself a storm, 232, 12; 634, 23. It is the goad of the mind, and its passions are our stings of remorse, 318, 13. We cannot be servants both of the flesh and of God, 373, 54. To walk according to the flesh is sin—and why, 817, 5. Flesh and blood, and spiritual wickedness, are overcome by patience, bodily self-restraint, and moderation of spirit, 801, 56. Unless the perception of the flesh dies, no one can bear the fruit of eternal life, 420, 8. No enemy is more burdensome to a person than the person himself and the weakness of his own flesh, 650, 30. The swelling of our flesh must be chastened, 847, 12. Although it may seem that not the condition of the flesh but guilt humbles us, nevertheless the flesh too is humbled in many ways, 918, 75. If the strength of the flesh has failed, the strength of the mind has prevailed, 832, 40. Let flesh become an appendage of the soul, 1444, 141. The frailty of human flesh is elegantly described, 44, 30. The grass and flower of the field are figures of human flesh, 44, 29. The flesh of weakness is a bed of pain, 871, 12. That the weakness of the flesh is not to be feared, and why, 826, 26; 830, 33. Those whose works are carnal we call children of the flesh, 231, 9. People who devote themselves to adorning their flesh are like giants, 230, 8. God had cursed the flesh of transgressors, but it is blessed in Christ, 1033, 2. The flesh of the sinful human being was a vessel of the devil; afterward it became a chosen vessel, 1240, 11.

CARTHAGINEM: Carthage was founded by the Tyrians, 557, 72.

CASPIUM mare: The Caspian, Cretan, and Northern seas, 38, 12.

CASTITAS: Where there is a conscience of chastity, the countenance is freer, 994, 6. Chastity habitually abolishes all the passions of the body, 151, 26. The praise of chastity is greater in a young man than in an old man, 504, 58. In the path of chastity there is a good step, 1188, 15. The gates of the Church are gates of chastity, 1407, 99. The Church is the house of chastity, 1040, 26. How greatly the practice of chastity has advanced through the Gospel, 1039, 21; 1113, 28. Modesty separates us from beasts and joins us to angels, 963, 21. How deservedly those free from lust are compared with angels, 1011, 8. On the islands, those who choose to hide themselves from the world for the sake of their purpose of continence renounce themselves, 41, 23.

CATECHUMENUS: By what method a catechumen should be instructed, 1410, 107. How he ought to take care not to learn wrongly from Photinus, Arius, and Sabellius, 172, 58.

CEDRUS: Cedar is suitable for suspending the roof’s ridges, 54, 53. The use of cedar boards is chosen for raising the gables of roofs and for shaping the elements of letters, 1256, 38. By the appearance of the cedar, the glory of the ancestors who were righteous is proclaimed, 1015, 20.

CEREBRUM: Why the brain is softer than the other parts, 138, 61. It is the beginning of the nerves and of every voluntary movement, 137, 61.

[Col. 2238]

CERVIS: For deer, it is poison instead of food, 48, 40. They are healed with olive branches, 47, 37. Their course is straighter, that of the fox more winding, 981, 2. How great their simplicity is, 638, 2.

CERTAMEN: Those entering the purifying contest require a discipline of life, 885, 1. In the chariot race, how great is the skill of the Greek horses, 690, 46. In the circus there is a base and contemptible rivalry, a foul and misshapen ugliness of disputes. The enthusiasms of the circus are false madness, 860, 4. Those who hasten to different spectacles of circus games and theaters are reproved, 1026, 27. A serious contest exists within a person, so that he fights against himself and battles his desires, 1234, 46. The struggle of one who fights within is more difficult than that of one who fights outside, 711, 15. Why it usually happens that we are crowned in more difficult and harsher contests, 929, 8. What must be done by one who has enrolled in Christ’s contest, 560, 79.

CETE: Immense kinds of fish, where they live, 91, 28. They are said to be seen in the depths of the Atlantic Ocean, 93, 32.

CETHURA: In Latin, the name signifies “fragrant,” 194, 32.

CHALDAEORUM: The Chaldeans’ opinion concerning the upper world, 316, 9. We understand that they are more intent than others upon empty superstition, 290, 22. They investigate the courses of the stars out of a vain zeal for superstition and sow the impious errors of paganism, 747, 22. The Chaldeans’, that is, the mathematicians’, science concerning human birth is useless, harmful, impossible, and impious, 67, 12. They are considered more skilled in numbers, 1297, 47.

CHAM: The name signifies “heat,” 270, 106; 276, 120. It was not Ham, who had sinned, but his son whom Noah condemned to servitude—and why, 274, 120. Ham deserved to have a wicked son because he had been wicked toward his father, 270, 105; 273, 114.

CHAMAELEON: The chameleon is said to counterfeit different appearances through varying heat, 109, 77.

CHANAAN: The name means the same as “their confusion,” 270, 106; 276, 120.

CHANANAEA: The Canaanite woman was the first to come forth from the nations of the Gentiles, and through her persistent entreaty she deserved to receive from the Lord such a testimony, 907, 49. She calls Christ back as he passes by, begs him when he is silent, worships him when he makes excuses, and bows before him when he refuses, 1383, 113.

CHARITAS: Hope precedes charity; salvation follows, 1245, 22. Since hope and faith are in charity, there is no doubt that charity is the greater, 1183, 44. Charity is greater than all things, 1542, 176. How good is the fire of charity, 1131, 2. Good charity and good piety: both belong to God, and both are God, 846, 10. If we love our parents, how much more ought we to love the creator and author of our parents—and of ourselves, 421, 10. Truly he loves God who preserves his commandments without sadness and without fear, by willing devotion rather than under compulsion, 1131, 4. Whoever follows Christ is not led to perfection by a reward; rather, he is brought to the reward by being perfected, 672, 28. Charity is raised up in the Old Testament and raised again in the New, 1023, 20. The wings of charity are wings of fire, by which it inflames the ardor of love, 1217, 29. Charity has its nail; it has its sword, by which the soul is wounded, 1169, 39. There are no stronger or heavier bonds than those of charity, 1155, 39. The wounds of charity are good, 723, 44. It is good to be wounded by the arrow of charity, 1023, 17. Why the zeal of charity is harsh, 1169, 9. Charity has death, charity has zeal, and charity has wings of fire, 381, 77. Blessed is the man who wastes away in the love of God, 1236, 52. Charity kills guilt and all sins, 1169, 39. Great charity remits sins, 692, 49 and 50. Charity excludes every disturbance, 1079, 2; 1243, 16. It binds us to those above and grafts us into heaven, 53, 57. Whether on the left or on the right, the dwelling of charity is good, 1023, 19. Whoever loves fulfills the commandments of the Law willingly; whoever fears observes them unwillingly, 951, 30; 1131, 3. Love of the mind is greater than the grace of speech, 846, 10. The righteous person regards his brother’s distress as his own, 870, 6. Through acts of piety and charity we should obtain a blessing for ourselves from the dying, 404, 36. Whoever loves must preserve an enduring disposition of charity in every condition of life, 752, 30. Those who appear in the Church to be weak, poor, foolish, and even sinners need more abundant honor and must be supported with greater assistance, 1076, 54. In what sense Christ commands us to hate parents and love enemies, 1162, 15 and following. Going beyond the oracle of the Law and the summit of philosophy, he extended the duty of piety and charity even toward those who had injured him, 1373, 73 and following. Christians are not permitted not to love even their enemies, 1100, 41; 1130, 57. Whoever has not spared others will deprive himself of the hope of forgiveness, 221, 34. How good it is to endure abuse without returning it, 1037, 14. See ENEMY.

CHRISTUS: Christ is the Messiah, 365, 26. That the Word could assume flesh, 717, 29 and following. Why he was necessary in order to undo Adam’s sin, 1039, 22. From nature itself God sent beforehand many examples by which he might prove and establish the beauty and truth of the Incarnation he was to assume, 105, 65. It is demonstrated by argument that Christ was awaited in Adam and the other patriarchs, 860, 6 and following. Isaac, offered by his father, is a figure of Christ, 862, 12. So too Jacob, 467, 25. And Judah, 679, 11. His blessing is applied to Christ himself, 518, 16 and following. He was likewise represented in Joseph, 679, 12; in Moses’ rod, 1001, 24; in the pillar of cloud, 1019, 3; in the bronze serpent, 1073, 15. David was a type of Christ, 686, 12, 14; 682, 120; 1202, 25. Why Luke thought Christ’s generation should be referred to God, 1318, 11. The root is the family of the Jews, the branch is Mary, and the flower is Christ, 1289, 24. Why, according to Luke, the successions from Abraham to Christ are more numerous, but according to Matthew fewer and through other ancestors, 1318, 14 and following. Why Matthew thought Christ’s genealogy should be traced through Solomon, whereas Luke traced it through Nathan, 1318, 13. In Christ’s genealogy there can be more successions but fewer generations, 1331, 45. How Christ belonged to a true and royal line if the Prophet had foretold that no one descended from Jeconiah would reign, 1329, 42 and following. Why Matthew counted many sinners among the ancestors of the Lord’s line, while Luke avoided doing so, 1327, 36; 1332, 46. Ahab and Jeconiah are numbered among his ancestors so that, as he was to redeem all human beings, he might begin the benefit with his own ancestors, 718, 33.

When and how Christ existed, what he was, what he had done, what he was doing, where he was, whither he came, how he came, at what time, and for what reason, 1295, 40. Christ’s flesh was the Virgin’s offspring, 682, 22. For although he was born of a Virgin and of the Holy Spirit, he is nevertheless the Son of a human being, because the Virgin was human, 864, 18. The Jews, who thought he would come through a woman, do not believe that he came through a virgin, 1307, 78. In Christ, flesh is the dispensation which he assumed under the title of compassion and by right of mercy, in order to redeem the captive, cleanse the defiled, and raise the dead, 875, 20. How he came into the world with a kind of leap, 365, 31. He came in the sign, he came in the Law, he came in the body, 1450, 166. Christ’s flesh is born for us; the Word is given, 754, 33. He was created so that he might show me the eternal ways by which a human being could return to God’s kingdom, 1025, 25. He was born for us who believe—not for Jews, heretics, or Manichaeans, 754, 33. He came to be the ruin of unbelievers but the resurrection of the just and faithful, 776, 28. He came quickly for the Jews, opportunely for the Gentiles; quickly for those perishing, suitably for those who would believe, 1181, 38. Where is he born, if not in your heart and in your breast? 1294, 34. If the shadow of the apostles healed, how much more does Christ’s flesh, which touches them, defend people from death, 879, 30. It was a shadow that healed, and now it protects the whole world, 1210, 5, 6. Why Christ’s flesh is the temple of God, 942, 16. His body is a great temple and wondrous altar, 1002, 26. At his birth Christ was proved to be God by no ordinary signs, 1296, 43. Every age, both sexes, and the miracles of the events confirm the faith of the Lord’s birth, 1301, 58 and following. To investigate when and how he was born, and how great he is, is more an obstacle of questioning than a benefit of edification, 1406, 93. I am not permitted to know the sequence of Christ’s generation, yet I am not permitted not to know the faith of his generation, 1406, 93. Do not nourish Christ as though he were a little child, but know that he is to be worshiped as true and perfect God, 940, 11.

Christ alone is the complete image of God, 1514, 49. He is God from God, equal from the Equal, 767, 4. He proceeded from the Father’s innermost and incomprehensible substance and is always in the Father, 527, 51. Christ’s willing is accomplishing, 411, 54. Truly great is he whose power filled the world, who is everywhere and will always be, 1286, 13. Christ did not begin from the Virgin, for he was speaking before the Virgin, 1346, 44. Why, according to his divinity, he is the beginning and end of all things, 8, 15. Those who did not believe Christ to be the Son of God did not believe him to be the Virgin’s son either, 1267, 6. Scripture itself speaks of Jesus as God and human being, perfect in both, 1346, 45. In the one name of Christ there is an expression of both divinity and Incarnation, and faith in the Passion, 1405, 93. Christ is not one person from the Father and another from the Virgin, 767, 4. He did not lay aside what he was, but preserved it, 965, 27. Whoever recognizes Christ without faith in his divinity or without the sacrament of his body is a moth, 1270, 13. Whoever denied that he was human denied that he was God, 1438, 120. He is the one who was born of the Virgin, the one who performed miracles among the people, the one who died for our sins and rose from the dead: if you withdraw any one of these, you have withdrawn your salvation, 1401, 101. Christ’s flesh could bring neither loss nor increase to his divinity, 717, 29. The prerogative of great virtues was reserved for him alone, 655, 6. He is a true prophet, and how, 1075, 53. He knows the end of time not through human nature but through divine nature, 1478, 34. He knows it for himself; he does not know it for me, 1479, 35. Christ’s flesh, as though enclosed by the wall-like brightness of divinity, possessed the heavenly protection of grace, 1020, 7. Christ always possesses charity in his substance, as he possesses kingship, 369, 46. God is Father to him by proper generation, to us by voluntary adoption; to him by grace, to us by nature, 1540, 167. He was human according to the flesh, but beyond human according to his operation, 919, 76. The kingdom he possesses belongs not to human bodily power but to divine power, 1528, 113. Those who say that Christ assumed human flesh but deny that he assumed human affection are greatly mistaken, 956, 5. When he assumed a body, he had to undergo everything belonging to a body; but divinity does not know alteration through these affections, 1442, 133. With the delight of divinity set aside, he is truly affected by the weariness of my weakness, 1516, 56 and following. He was in the midst of sufferings as victor over weaknesses, not conquered by weaknesses, 956, 6. He descended to our wounds so that, through a kind of familiarity and abundance of himself, he might make us sharers in heavenly nature, 1366, 46. He assumed many affections and duties in order to teach how we ought to conduct ourselves in them, 1230, 33. He was afflicted by miseries in order to make blessed those who were placed in misery, 829, 32. In Christ, obedience, humility, and death belonged not to divinity but to the body, 720, 39. He is said to have prayed not for assistance but for an example, 1357, 10. How Christ’s soul was troubled by fear, 642, 11. In Christ there could be no cause by which he might receive the wound of any sin, 839, 53. Christ alone never deviates, 315, 6; 679, 10. The flesh with which Christ clothed himself had been clean from every sin, 696, 59. Born of a Virgin, he owed nothing to woman’s inheritance, 1039, 23. It was fitting that he who was not going to possess the sin of bodily falling should feel no natural contamination of generation, 695, 57. Why, although he knows everything, he does not know sin is clearly demonstrated, 830, 34. How Christ in his flesh assumed the likeness of sinful flesh and became sin for us, 811, 5, 6. The assumption of sins in him is an act of mercy, not a crime, 817, 6. He alone was not captured by the vanity of this age and carnal pride, 187, 10. He prays not to intercede for himself but to obtain something for me, 1365, 42. In Christ one thing is expressed according to the unity of divinity, and another is spoken according to the human affection, 862, 16.

Luke thought himself sufficiently rich if he had claimed the Lord’s manger for himself out of everything, 1296, 43. In what sense Christ had an artisan as his father on earth, 1313, 2. He honored Joseph and Mary not by a debt of nature but by a duty of piety, 784, 16; 1302, 65; 1490, 74. His subjection is instruction in human virtue, not a diminution of divine power, 957, 8. It is not a manifestation of weakness but an operation of power; it is more the agent of a temporary dispensation than enslaved to perpetual servitude, 957, 6. Once the servitude of his own body had been laid aside, ibid., 7. Christ would have lost the benefit of his work had humility not received it, 1227, 18. Why he presented himself as the author of humility, 1515, 51. The lower his humility, the more divine his providence, 1312, 91. He gives the form of humility, 1375, 84. He humbled himself so that you might learn what humility is, 929, 76. He bent himself to every service so completely that he did not disdain even the service of a reader, 1346, 45. Christ’s servitude, poverty, and suffering, 767, 2 and following. Christ redeemed the world in poverty and contempt, 1205, 34. Therefore he came here poor, so that the devil would have nothing to take away, 1344, 39. How he was rich in poverty, 869, 5. How great is he in riches, who by his poverty made all the rich rich, 524, 33. Christ’s poverty enriches, his fringe heals, his hunger satisfies, his death gives life, and his burial raises up, 524, 38. His poverty is my inheritance, and the Lord’s weakness is my strength, 1295, 41.

Christ was led into the desert by counsel, mystery, and example, 1338, 14. Let us follow his footprints from the desert so that we may return to paradise, 1338, 12. Christ allowed himself to be tempted by the devil so that in him we might conquer all things, 1335, 4. He deceives in order to conquer; he conquers in order to deceive, 1339, 19. He deceived the devil and the prince of this world, 1283, 3. He exposed himself to many temptations so that he would not pass over any of our contests with temptation, 755, 38. He alone could be appointed our guide against the allurements of the world and the tricks of the devil, 1336, 9. What belongs to you is that Christ suffers the beasts; what belongs to him is that he is proclaimed by angels, 1298, 52. The Lord’s hunger is a pious deception, 1338, 16. Blessed is his thirst, because he thirsted for us, 960, 14.

Christ was baptized in the Jordan when he instituted the form of the saving washing, 642, 14. God is proved by no work more than by the mystery of his baptism, 1312, 91. Three things in Christ chiefly contribute to the use of human salvation: namely, the sacrament of baptism, the desert, and fasting, 1335, 4. A comparison of Christ with John, 1285, 10. Why Christ ate with sinners, 1285, 10. He sought not gymnasia filled with choirs of wise men but a simple populace, 1299, 53. Why he appeared between Moses and Elijah, 522, 30. Why, in the Passion, he could be seized by a few, although at one time he was not seized by the people, 1349, 56. When we read that Jesus was seized, let us beware of thinking that he was seized according to his divinity, 1519, 68. Attacked by calumnies, he offered a triumphant silence, 1190, 24. Although he could avenge himself, he preferred to complain rather than take revenge, 1231, 35. Christ wishes to be considered of little worth so that he may be purchased by everyone, 1391, 31. Christ’s wounds exhaled no stench of repentance but every fragrance of grace, 828, 32. How he was abandoned by the Father, 900, 31; 980, 19. The Lord’s concern for your salvation was so great that he almost endangered his own while winning you, 453, 25. Christ called his enemies to grace—those whom God’s eye saw and loved, 826, 26. He did not allow even his enemies to be wounded, 1519, 71.

Christ alone was chosen as worthy of such a death that he might take away the sin of the world, 682, 22. Why he was chosen for this by the Father, 1410, 109. Even the saints did not believe that Christ would die, 1379, 98. He could have avoided death but did not wish to, 1333, 47. He died once for all collectively, and dies once for each individual—not repeatedly, 1207, 42. He is both testator and heir, 1500, 27. How, as a triumphant victor, he ascended his cross as though it were a chariot, 1527, 109. Where the place of the cross was, 1528, 114. He suffered at the Venerarium, 938, 5. Christ’s Passion was an image of the heavenly kingdom, 1156, 43. Let us return love to Christ as a debt, charity as a gift, and gratitude as the price of his blood, 1390, 26. In him, once divinity had been separated from death, it did not undergo partnership with bodily sufferings, 1391, 32. Why Christ was struck only after death, 1533, 135. Water came forth from Christ’s wound so that we might drink salvation, 829, 32. A comparison of Christ’s burial with Moses’ burial, 186, 9. How the first day on which Christ died is to be reckoned, 915, 69. How after his death he was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, 630, 14. Christ suffered because he took pleasure in doing good, not because he sought an increase of glory from his suffering, 672, 28. He was crucified for our faith; he was crucified for our desires, 1378, 96. He assumed the servitude of death in order to grant you the freedom of eternal life, 1207, 42. Christ’s blood is purple, which stains the souls of the saints and makes them kings, 1190, 20. The blood and Passion of Christ are the crown of the great contest and the splendid gift of his betrothal, 370, 46. The Lord’s cross is a precipice to unbelievers but life to believers, 1158, 4. This is the glory of faith: truly to understand Christ’s cross, 1410, 107. Christ’s cross restored paradise to us—and why? 766, 3. In it we have rested and laid down our sins, 1461, 208. On the Lord’s wood we sail safely and securely, 941, 13. The Lord’s cross abolishes and conceals all errors, 683, 24. The true cross of the Lord does not consume the merits of others but makes them fruitful, 1114, 29. We are in the shadow, protected by the covering of Christ’s cross, 999, 19. There is a certain spiritual nail that fastens the flesh to the gibbet of the Lord’s cross, 1168, 37.

Christ descended into hell so that those who were there might be released from everlasting bonds, 922, 84. Christ was born by his own authority, died by his own will, slept by his own power, and himself is the author of his resurrection, 519, 20. Where testimony to the resurrection is brought forward, the services of servants lend their support; where the glory of the rising Lord is displayed, the splendor of the servants is hidden, 926, 2. Christ is Lord because he redeemed his servants; God because he raised himself, 893, 14. His divinity is life, eternity is life, flesh is life, Passion is life, death is life, and resurrection is the life of all things, 793, 36. The first and greatest foundation of faith is to believe in Christ’s resurrection, 509, 80. Christ penetrated closed and impassable places not through bodily nature but through the quality of his resurrected body, 1540, 170. Christ leaps from heaven into the Virgin, from the womb into the manger, from the manger into the Jordan, from the Jordan onto the cross, from the cross into the tomb, and from the tomb into heaven, 1034, 6. He ascended above all the heavens to God’s seat—and how, 849, 17. God descended, humanity ascended: the Word became flesh so that flesh might place for itself the throne of the Word at God’s right hand, 996, 8. He returned with the majesty of his nature to the place from which he had come, 1333, 47. Why he preferred to carry the wounds received for us into heaven, 1540, 171.

Christ is the end of the Law, and his death solves the riddles of the prophets, 910, 57. Why he is the end of the Law and the fullness of charity, 783, 16. He is the end of the ways, the end of righteousnesses, and the end of testimonies, 1024, 22. He is the end of our hope, the fullness and completion of all things, and the sum of every virtue, 867, 1. Everything must be referred to Christ, 891, 12. Christ is the head of all things, 961, 18. He was the head of the old Synagogue, which Moses founded, 912, 62. He is the head who rises up in all of us through each individual member, 827, 29. When he is removed, the members cannot live, 1222, 2. He was sought once in his own body and is sought frequently in that body which is the Church, 961, 16. The prerogative of calling the Churches was reserved for Christ alone, 312, 92. He alone is the Bridegroom of the Church, 520, 22. Christ washed the world with his blood; its sin could not have been abolished in any other way, 942, 17. He is the remission of sins, the redemption of captives, and the assistance of those who labor, 1184, 1. It would not have benefited us for him to be born unless it had benefited us to be redeemed by him, 1295, 41; 1160, 10. He contributed more to my redemption than to my creation, 1181, 40; 1227, 19. He redeemed us; the adversary sells us. The adversary auctions us to death; Christ redeems us for salvation, 1436, 114. The adversary consigns us at a cheaper price; Christ redeemed us at a great price, 1437, 117. Why he alone redeemed humanity, 949, 13. He assumed the cause and place of humanity, 671, 27. He began the benefit of redemption with his own ancestors, 1327, 36. Nothing seems more beyond human possibility than that Christ should have offered himself wholly for the world, 1379, 102.

Christ is redemption and likewise mercy, 942, 17. Christ is our hope and patience; he himself became our redemption, he himself is our expectation, 854, 28. God is more precious to the religious person; the Redeemer is more precious to the sinner, 488, 14. Christ’s solid gifts reach each individual: everyone possesses them, and no one is defrauded, 1155, 41. What is more proper to Christ than to stand as advocate for peoples before the Father, offer his death for all, repel death, and restore life to those who are perishing? 861, 8.

How good a physician Christ is, 816, 4. With him there is no postponement of healing; he customarily heals by a word, not by iron, 1209, 2. His speech is medicine, 1428, 75. So too is knowledge of him, 884, 39. Christ’s will is common to all, 1003, 29. He was born for all, came for all, suffered for all, and rose for all, 1077, 57. Whether you come late, at night, or at any hour, you will find Jesus ready to receive you, 1534, 138. Where grace is to be given, Christ is present; where severity is to be exercised, only ministers are present—Jesus is absent, 299, 50. What is severe in others is sweet in Christ, 1032, 43. Those whom he binds he frees, and those whom he constrains he absolves, 933, 17. He fails no one and abounds for all; we are the ones who fail, 1384, 116. Christ, the true light, shines for everyone, but he does not wish to rush upon the importunate or force the unwilling, 1117, 13; 1401, 74 and following. He rejects neither those who are willing, binds no unwilling person, resists none who cast him out, and is absent from none who ask, 663, 4; 1349, 56. No one can take him away from you unless you yourself take yourself away from him, 1360, 20; 1395, 50. For unbelievers he sleeps; for the faithful he keeps watch, 899, 26. He sleeps in the negligent and is awakened in the saints, 1024, 20.

How Christ is to be sought, 1055, 36; 1207, 41 and following; 1538, 161. He always wishes to be sought and more frequently found, 1119, 17. He deigns frequently to meet those who seek him and to condescend to them in order to raise them up, 369, 44. He wishes to be anticipated as the Sun of righteousness and, in order to be anticipated, waits, 1217, 30. How quickly the door of our heart should be opened to him who knocks, 1118, 14 and following. Christ must be followed in all things, and each person ought to imitate him according to his ability, 841, 1.
