The crowd does not follow him to the heights and does not ascend to lofty places, 1366, 46. Whoever follows Jesus possesses his reward within himself, 454, 28. Christ’s perfection and fullness are the portion of his servants, 1257, 42. Christ brings increases of grace with him when he comes, 1034, 6. There is no greater salvation than to be with Christ and to cling to him through a certain unity of body, 861, 11; 1393, 42. Whoever receives Christ within as a dwelling is fed with the greatest delights of overflowing pleasures, 1359, 16 and 19. He does not fast, 1360, 22. Where Christ is, there is life; there is the kingdom, 1530, 121. No one can perish if Christ has not been taken away from him, 1222, 2. Whoever hears his voice will not fear shipwreck, 1334, 2. How Christ ought to be held, 368, 43. He alone is the one whom no one ought to abandon and no one ought to change, 1399, 67. Whoever separates himself from him is an exile from his homeland and a citizen of the world, 1462, 214. Who can conceive and give birth to him? 1509, 24 and following. Who can touch him? 1539, 165. Whoever does not hold Christ’s head should at least hold his feet, 387, 15 and following. Let us always speak of him, and how this should be done, 807, 65. Who is an imitator of Christ? 817, 5 and 6. Who are his participants and companions? 1075, 53. What will we be through participation in his glory, whose reproach makes us glorious? 1031, 41. What is an insult under others is glory under Christ, 933, 17. The best condition is to be under Christ, under whom both servitude is precious and freedom glorious, 448, 11. His yoke does not crush necks but honors them, 562, 83.

Christ is the perfect way, 1026, 26. Moses led the Jewish people through the desert; Christ leads them through lilies, 374, 56. How we ought to entrust our journey to the guidance of the Lord Jesus, 1019, 5; 1022, 13 and following. He is the way that leads to the destination, the truth that confirms, and the life that is restored through him, 1411, 54. To know Christ is eternal life, 1420, 38. Why Christ is truly the light of all, 833, 41. Christ is fittingly the day in the mystery, whose twelve apostles are the hours, 1464, 222. It is day for those among whom Christ is present; it is night for those to whom he denies himself, 1054, 33. Before Christ’s coming there was winter; after his coming there are flowers, 366, 35; 1040, 25. Why Christ is called the hand of God, 1252, 22. He is called the Word, the pen, and the scribe, 1380, 105. He is the true Levite—and why? 210, 11. He is the true shepherd; those who did not wish to be fed by him, death will devour, 952, 21. Christ’s food is virtue; Christ’s food is strength, 1401, 74. By his power you go out from the borders of Egypt and arrive in the promised land, ibid., 75. All will hunger whom he has not fed, 499, 42. Christ is the grain of wheat and the mustard seed, 1454, 182 and following. How he was the vine and the grape, 520, 24. He is a lamb for us but a kid for the Jews, 489, 18. How aptly he is compared with a deer, 638, 2 and following. According to the mystery of the Incarnation, he is a star, 1297, 45. Why he is a rock, 859, 2. A great and small mountain, 644, 17. The good torrent that ceased for the Jews so that it might overflow for us, 774, 20. He is the bed of the saints, on which all hearts wearied by worldly battles rest, 369, 45. Christ’s flesh is the reclining place of the Church, 1015, 19. How Christ is a seal on the forehead, in the heart, and on the arm, 380, 75. Great is his grace, for he has given nearly all his names to his disciples, 1407, 97.

CHRISTIANI: Because we did not have a name on earth, we received one from heaven, so that we might be called Christ’s people, 780, 7. A Christian has his own dignity, and among Christ’s people there are different orders of honors, 1250, 14. How great is the magnificence of Christian men, 1344, 36. When I say “Christian,” I mean “perfect,” 1130, 51. How most things among Christians are formed after the pattern of the ancient Jews, with corresponding types and classes and causes, 1265, 1. Christians did not fail in the midst of their riches because of their simplicity; the Jews were in need amid their riches, 797, 44. How they possess the spoils of the Jews, 1240, 11 and following. We are sheep: let us seek pasture. We are drachmas: let us possess our value. We are children: let us hasten to the Father, 1462, 211. A son of God through the washing, a friend through virtue, a hired servant through labor, and a slave through fear, 1466, 228. What are the battles of Christian men? 1506, 11. Nothing loose or soft befits Christ’s soldier, 856, 23. He ought to offer everything in order to be raised with Christ, 825, 23. Christians who impose harsher commandments are reproved, 1029, 37. How rightly Christians are compared with a vineyard, 1500, 29 and following.

CIBUS: Why human food was created after the fodder of beasts, 43, 28. Whether the Lord commanded that one should eat more vegetables than meat, 265, 89. In diet—
Simple herbs and vegetable foods, or fruit: everyone ought to be content with these, 43, 28. It is a certain law of nature to seek only as much as suffices for nourishment, and to reckon one’s patrimony only in terms of food, 90, 26. It is unbecoming to worry about food for one who is serving in the kingdom, 1441, 130. Food is our only natural medicine, 56, 57. Food is medicine for sheep and goats, 48, 40.

**CICADAS:** By the songs of cicadas in midsummer, the trees burst open—and why? 109, 76.

**STORK:** In Roman usage, the stork is called a pious bird, 102, 52. From it the name ἀντιπελάργησις (*antipelargēsis*, repayment of filial care) was derived, ibid. The piety of storks toward their parents, 101, 55. How they depart and are led away by crows, 101, 53. They announce the beginning of spring, 120, 20.

**CIRCUMCISION:** The commandment of circumcision is explained, 347, 78 and following. Bodily circumcision is a figure of spiritual circumcision, 293, 29. What is prescribed by the term “circumcision,” 292, 27. Circumcision purified; the law sanctified; grace justified, 1450, 166. Why it is no longer observed today, 293, 29. Why Ishmael was circumcised in the thirteenth year of his age, 352, 91. Among the Egyptians not only males but also females were circumcised, 348, 78.

**CLERIC:** A cleric ought to display works not only of office but also of virtue, 1418, 29. The clergy for the most part went astray; the priest changed his opinion; the rich sided with the earthly king: the people preserved their own faith, 1189, 17. See **PRIEST**.

**COCCUM:** “Scarlet” (*coccum*) was placed in the Exodus in place of fire, 1201, 22.

**HEAVEN:** Why it is so called, 30, 15. What its quality and substance are, 10, 21; 12, 23. It is an intelligible οὐσία (*ousia*, substance), whereas earth is visible or sensible substance, 332, 46. Philosophers assert that the ether is composed of a certain fifth οὐσία (*ousia*), 338, 58. This opinion is refuted, 13, 23 and 24. Plato asserts that it is a winged chariot, 335, 54. Those who think that the causes of crimes are conveyed by a certain necessity of birth set their mouth against heaven, 666, 12. Heaven is many times larger than earth, so that by comparison with heaven earth has been reckoned by most people as a mere point, 761, 49. That there are several heavens, 24, 5 and 6. [Col. 2244] Who believed that the revolutions of the heavens produce an indescribable harmony, 336, 54; 738, 2. Their opinion is refuted, 24, 6 and 7. There was a place for vices in heaven, 1117, 12. Why it is called holy, 1121, 25. He is called “heaven” who practices the life of the angels by guarding his integrity, 1117, 12. The heavenly element ought to be an image of your life, 1116, 8, 9. How a person ascends into heaven through various stages, 829, 17.

**EVIL THOUGHT:** One must confront evil thought and desire, 1067, 34. There is no mind or soul that does not also receive the savage impulses of evil thoughts, 251, 57. Thoughts, rather than sudden intrusions, are to be held responsible for crime, 746, 21. When you have driven out vain thoughts, God will give you possession of an empty heart and mind, 203, 44. Do everything thoughtfully, so that you will not regret your deed, 1067, 32 and following.

**PERFECT KNOWLEDGE:** It is not perfect knowledge to know what you should do while being ignorant of the order in which it should be done, 1012, 12.

**KNOWING:** To know oneself: how and how greatly useful this is, 986, 13 and following. You will then forget the Lord when you have forgotten yourself, 196, 26. No one can fully understand what he has received unless he remembers what he was before, 1125, 35. To know does not consist in mere superficial knowledge, but in carrying out the things that ought to be done, 157, 30.

**EYE-SALVE:** A remedy for diseases of the eyes, 1000, 22.

**SNAKE:** When pressed by danger, it hides its head, 1222, 2. It flees from the stag and kills the lion, 48, 40.

**DOVE:** A type of the peace of the Church, 1312, 92.

**ENTRUSTED AND DEPOSITED:** They call “entrusted” and “deposited” what we have committed to someone for the purpose of safekeeping, 614, 67.

**COMPARISONS:** The nature, not the appearance, of comparisons must be considered, 1453, 176.

**DESIRE:** “Desire” is spoken both of good and of evil, 832, 38. Rivers of desires and evil passions burst forth from the flesh as from a fountain and overflow widely, 232, 12. Desire anticipates reason, but reason resists desire, 445, 3. Reason can soften desire but cannot eradicate it, 443, 1 and following. Evil desires must be confronted quickly, 978, 12; 1027, 29.

**CONFESSION:** God awaits the voice of your confession, 782, 14; 1465, 225. If you stumble in anything, God looks to you to acknowledge your error, 1523, 90. While the disease of sins is concealed, it grows hot; when exposed by confession, it evaporates, 840, 57. True grief and confession of the inner heart occur when all those things are enumerated by which the hidden entrails of the mind are pierced with the bitterest feeling, 834, 42. The wound of sin seeks a physician; the physician demands confession, 872, 14. Sin is poison; accusation of sin is the remedy, 829, 11. No one can be justified from sin unless the sin has first been confessed, 178, 71. How one who accuses himself, although he is a sinner, begins to be righteous, 1012, 11. Whoever declares his iniquities to God is justified, 199, 34; 559, 75; 996, 10. Condemnation of present things is absolution concerning future things, 820, 13. Confession of sin is a shortening of punishments, 219, 27. In confession there is pardon, and in condemning one’s own sin there is justice, 854, 30. A modest confession greatly benefits the accused, and by shame we lighten the punishment that we cannot escape by a defense, 821, 14. The invention of a crime, not its confession, is shameful, 1328, 38. God’s justification consists in this: that even when we have done something good, we nevertheless always confess our sins to God, 1166, 30. God is accustomed not only to forgive the faults of those who confess, but also to bestow rewards on those who amend, 732, 68. By confessing his sins, the righteous deprives the adversary of a voice, 769, 8. You must not only renounce sins, but also erase every memory of your former conduct, 1481, 44. See **THE KEYS OF THE CHURCH**. The confession of faith is the price of immortality for us, 1354, 74. Where the violets of confessors are found, 1441, 128.

**SHAME:** The shame that you undergo for Christ’s name is good, 916, 68.

**MARRIAGE:** How great are the bonds of marriage? 86, 18. Divine law has turned marital affection into a part of nature, 1163, 17. Why people ought neither to despise marriage nor join unequal partners to themselves, 288, 19. Marriage is not censured, but chastity is called to greater honor, 1458, 196. A husband is not a master but a husband; he has not taken a maidservant but a wife, 87, 19. The conduct of married partners must be endured, 86, 18. They should rise together at night for prayer, 309, 84. They are taught that unions of minds are more religious than unions of bodies, 1392, 26. See **MATRIMONY** and **WIFE**.

**HEMLOCK:** Harmful to life, 47, 38. By it the frenzies of lust generally withered, 48, 39.

**CONSCIENCE:** No pleasure is better than that which comes from an amended conscience, 351, 85. The conscience of a good deed is a reward to a devout mind, 332, 47.

**CONSCIENCE BEFORE GOD:** Conscience reveals itself before God, and a person’s thought either condemns or acquits itself before him, 920, 79. An innocent conscience does not fear the judge of justice and the rewarder of merits, 983, 7. A good conscience is one that, when examined, is approved, 1004, 33. Alien words cannot fasten a crime upon someone whose own conscience has not received it, 847, 13. A good conscience does not need a defense of words: supported by its own testimony, it is itself its own judge, 847, 13. Eloquence itself falls silent if the conscience is sick, 1041, 27.

**COUNSELS:** We then consider counsels more salutary when they appear to have been examined through more deliberate reflection, 981, 1.

**CONSOLATION:** The first consolation, in order, is that God does not forget to show mercy, 1195, 3. The second consolation is that, through various punishments on account of our sins, we come to forgiveness, ibid. Consolation ought to be gentle, not harsh, 834, 42. We have often seen disputes arise over consolations, 834, 42.

**CONSULS:** Consuls are entered in the records of a sale, 1294, 39.

**CONVERSION:** No one is converted except the one who is converted by his own will, 752, 30. Blessed is the person who has been able to restore himself after a fall, 677, 6. It is greater to have withdrawn oneself from vices than never to have known the vices themselves at close range, 1247, 3. Whoever is corrected rises with virtue, 855, 33. It can happen that things which are sometimes displeasing may be amended with grace, 326, 31. Nothing is more pleasing to God than the conversion of the soul, 905, 45. The Lord knows how to change his judgment if you know how to amend your offense, 1292, 33. The judgment of the Word of God is that forgiveness be granted to the converted—provided that the conversion has been properly made, 1066, 30. How great is the power of complete amendment, 1247, 4. It is no ordinary virtue to pass from wickedness to good conduct, from earthly things to eternal things, and to change the habits of a carnal life, 939, 7. If we know how to chastise ourselves, we strike down the aerial powers, 1123, 28.

**BANQUET:** A certain elaborate and lavishly prepared banquet, 115, 5. Revelries are to be avoided, 561, 81.

**HEART:** The heart gives signs of salvation when it recognizes the causes of its own disturbance, 832, 39. What the voice of the heart is, 1211, 8 and following. Let the heart cry out first, so that speech may be heard by God, 1212, 12. Although God sees all the secrets of the heart, it is nevertheless good for each person to open and pour out his soul before him, 1246, 24. Whoever has lost the cry of the heart has also lost that of the tongue, 1280, 41. What it means to pour out one’s heart, 966, 30. If your heart is not idle, your time is not idle, 747, 24. Whoever burns within the heart is consumed in the body, 711, 13. If the heart is agitated, it indicates great danger, 832, 38. How great a gift it is to be pure of heart, 698, 64. The heart must be cleansed, and how, 1101, 45 and following. How the veil that remains over the eyes of the heart is removed, 1000, 22. Sometimes it is better to be naked in body than veiled in heart, 724, 46. The heart has two chambers, 233, 14.

**CORAL:** A plant in the sea; if transferred into the air, it hardens into the firmness of stone, 93, 33.

**CORE:** The duties of the sons of Core, 935, 1.

**LEATHER:** Suitable for a bag and for footwear, 1423, 57.

**CROW:** Calls for rain in a full voice, 96, 39. The love of crows for their young, 103, 58.

**CROWN:** It is sought by struggling, not by resisting; by effort, not by opposition, 772, 17. There is no crown unless there has been a struggle in a difficult contest, 1213, 19. A crown is fitting not for those decked with flowers but for those covered with dust; victory adorns not those softened by pleasures but those hardened by the labor of training, 1196, 5. The more numerous the contests, the more excellent the crown of virtues, 1264, 6; 1344, 37. The crown was customarily given to contestants only on the final day, 133, 1. The clearer the merit of the one crowned, the more abundant the justice of the one who crowns, 1145, 16.

**BODY:** The form of the human body surpasses that of other creatures, 135, 54. Its structure is like that of the world, ibid., 55. The individual members of the human body provide such service that they also furnish beauty, 235, 18 and following. The human body is enclosed by skin so that it may be protected from cold and heat, 248, 50. It is woven together like a nest, 233, 14. Why it is called a “womb,” 1108, 14. When we suffer bodily impressions, why we are accustomed to cry out, 1210, 7. How many occupations the needs of this body bring upon us, by which the vigor of the soul is hindered and its attention recalled, 394, 12. Bodily strength is increased by frequent exercise, but when unexercised it diminishes and declines, 216, 22. Even when the saints bear a body, they are nevertheless not in the flesh but in the spirit, 1062, 18. Many are situated in the body who are pilgrims away from the body and present with God, 1010, 2; 1167, 31. The soul of the righteous uses the body as an instrument or organ, 400, 25; 401, 27. Good kings are those who can make themselves rulers of their own body, 939, 7; 1151, 30. The use of our body is a serious enemy to us, 401, 26; 1112, 24. That soul is blessed which no hostile battles of the body can conquer, 376, 61. Bodily pleasures are the food of evils, 376, 61. A person devoted to bodily allurements dishonors himself, 117, 10. Bodily weakness is sobriety of mind, 18, 31. Our body is this tabernacle of testimony, 1144, 11.

**REPROOF:** Reproof belongs to one who loves, not to one who curses; to goodness, not to cruelty, 1081, 7. Reproof is instruction, 822, 19. Christ’s medicine is reproof, 840, 56. Whoever wishes to be healed does not fear being reproved; but he does not wish to be reproved in anger, rather by the word of God, 823, 19. The order of fraternal reproof, 1067, 32. Discipline, or reproof, is burdensome unless it possesses knowledge, 1082, 10. How the wise person should strive to correct others, 255, 66. A serious shame and embarrassment arise when one is reproved by an inferior, 728, 56. Friendly reproof accomplishes more than turbulent accusation, 1475, 21. Every discipline or reproof, although it has bitterness for a time, nevertheless afterward customarily bears peaceful fruits, 1082, 10.

**CORRECT:** To correct one’s resolve and change it for the better is not fickleness but virtue, 1184, 45. Correction after the Lord’s Passion is necessary, 1424, 60.

**RAVEN:** Many consider it, as it were, an announcer of future things, 254, 62.

**QUAILS:** They feed on hellebore, 48, 39.

**CREATURE:** At its beginning, creation followed God’s command and made use of the law, 36, 8. We must not condemn anything in creatures if some things appear difficult for us to understand, 147, 7.

**CRIMES:** Let us redeem our crimes through good works, the price of faith, and mercy, 210, 10. See **SINS**.

**CRITIAS:** He believed that blood was the soul, 266, 92.

**CRUELTY:** Many are deceived by vices that flatter, while harsh and excessively severe cruelty turns very many away from itself, 1183, 45.

**GUILT:** Guilt has no substance, 905, 44. It entered this world like a guest, alien and foreign to our nature, 728, 59. Malice is the source of sin; guilt is the fall produced by weakness, 1165, 25. A holy man mourns guilt more than misery, 1194, 36. Guilt is within, and virtue also is within, 731, 66. Your own guilt accuses and exposes you, 579, 51; 731, 66. Guilt increases when it is exposed but not guarded against, 449, 13. Guilt that is restrained by shame is more tolerable than guilt proclaimed with insolence, 302, 59; 719, 34. Innocence had made me arrogant; guilt made me submissive, 452, 21. See **MALICE** and **SIN**.

**DESIRES:** The causes of desires are the pleasure of the flesh, the appearance of glory, and eagerness for power, 1343, 35. The abandonment of desires and vanity is an addition to truth, 436, 47. When desires have been restrained, virtues and good works can germinate, 260, 77. The end of temptations is the end of desires, 1343, 35.

**CYPRESS:** It never loses its greenness, 1015, 21. It is suitable for adorning ceilings and gables, 54, 53.

**GOOD GUARDIAN:** The presence of a good guardian is more frequent where the walls are more fragile, 229, 5.

**SWAN:** Why does it have a longer neck? 108, 75.

# D

**DALETH** means in Latin “fear,” or “birth,” 1009, 1. Why many are condemned and few crowned, 870, 6. **DAN** is interpreted as “judgment,” 523, 34; 877, 25. His blessing is explained, 522, 32–33. He was a figure of Antichrist, 877, 25.

**DANUBE** cuts through the peoples of the western regions belonging to the Barbarians and the Romans, 28, 12.

**DARIUS** the Mede wished to connect the Red Sea with the Egyptian sea, 37, 10.

**DAVID.** The Hebrews call him “the exalted one”; the Latins interpret the name as “the humbled one,” 720, 39. The Lord Himself rejoiced to be called his son, 676, 3. Those who said that he was the Son of God and the Christ are criticized, 713, 22 and following. David was a great teacher of moral conduct, 971, 1. His courage became the victory of all, 684, 26. In him piety was greater than the bodily strength with which he fought, 1008, 46. God’s grace was greater in him than in Solomon, 843, 4. Why he danced before the ark, 1385, 5. His clemency of character, gentleness of piety, and fervent devotion, 1162, 15. How patient he was of insult and suffering, 685, 30. He spared his enemy and preferred to preserve his innocence rather than his life, 768, 7. He had learned from Christ to be a good father, 1150, 27. Why Absalom first called him “the boy” and afterward “the son,” 1190, 23. By a rationally prepared remedy he outwitted irrational desire, 445, 3. What he required from the Lord as a servant, soldier, and called one, 1044, 4. Much more admirable is the one who overcame power than the one who overcame love, 710, 9.

David thirsted for the blood of Christ, not for the element of water that was in the pool of Bethlehem, 686, 35. He saw the sacraments of the new law, 695, 58. He saw the future remission of all sins [Col. 2247], foresaw the splendor of grace through the washing of regeneration and the infusion of the Holy Spirit, 683, 24. With devout faith he celebrated the Lord’s resurrection, which was to occur many ages later, 819, 79. What David himself did not know, the lesser prophet Nathan understood, 1119, 18.

Why David was not free from sin, 687, 36; 718, 33. He seems to have tasted sin in order to teach how sin could be abolished, 815, 1. How effectively he taught us to repent of our sins, 815, 1. How quickly, after confessing his sin, he groaned in the sorrow of guilt, 677, 5. By confessing his own iniquity, he was justified in himself, 1051, 22. How he asked that his sin be erased, 820, 14. The Gentiles wrongly object that he sang of his murders and adulteries, 709, 6 and following. He was distinguished by nothing more than this: he judged that the adultery he had committed had to be washed away by the tears of repentance, 1327, 37 and following. David sinned, as kings commonly do; but he repented and wept, as kings commonly do not, 681, 15; 709, 7. In choosing the punishment for his sin he followed reason; in sorrow, piety, 822, 16. By what works he covered his sin, 883 and following. He loved the Lord so much that, through excessive charity, he covered and concealed every sin, 683, 25. Although it had been abolished by repentance, he was nevertheless under suspicion, lest his disgrace perhaps still remain, 1031, 40.

David’s deed with Uriah’s wife was a mystery in its figurative aspect, but a sin in its historical aspect: guilt came through the human being, the sacraments through the Word, 1326, 38. The mysteries prefigured under that same adultery are disclosed, 720, 37 and following; 725, 50 and following. God has already judged concerning his holiness and righteousness, 676, 3. He was a figure of Christ, 122, 25; 182, 20; 686, 12 and 14; 703, 81 and 1241, 11. What his entering the house of Achimelech, where he asked for five loaves, signifies, 1364, 35 and following.

**DEBT.** When it is paid, not the amount but the intention of the one making the payment is considered, 217, 23.

**DECORUM.** Whatever is good is proper; whatever is improper is evil, 375, 60.

**DEFENSE** is not arrogance when no special distinction of honor is claimed, but a fearful hardship is driven away, 1172, 10. The better cause is the one that is not defended but proved, 1525, 97. Let those seek defense who fear defeat, 1525, 97.

**DELIGHT** is natural, 738, 2. It is the greatest incentive both to virtue and to error, 737, 1. It is the first origin of sin, 179, 73. When the mind’s vigor has been relaxed, it pours itself forth, 357, 2. Through Adam’s error it covered and, as it were, concealed our body, 259, 72. A grave and unjust struggle against the delights of present things, 748, 25. In a small delight there is perpetual bitterness, 634, 22.

**OFFENSE** is less than injustice or iniquity, 690, 45; 692, 49.

**DEMOCRITUS.** Antiquity accorded him very great authority concerning physical matters, 2, 3.

**TEETH.** Their usefulness, 139, 66; 236, 22.

**DEPOSIT.** Something is deposited and entrusted when we commit it to someone for safekeeping, 614, 67.

**DESERT.** In the desert there are very many temptations, difficult striving toward virtue, and an easy fall into error, 1336, 8.

**DESIRES.** It is human to extend our desires beyond ourselves, 1192, 28. All our desire must be established before the Lord, 831, 38.

**DESPAIR.** One must never despair, and why, 826, 26. If someone has lighter passions, he should not entirely despair of divine grace, 269, 102. See **HOPE**.

**DESPISE.** Why we ought to despise no one, 1226, 17.

**DEVOTION.** In carrying out God’s commands, devotion is first in order among the virtues and the foundation of the others, 282, 3. It itself remains forever, 1006, 41. The mind feasts on the nourishment of devotion, 1053, 29. Religious devotion is free from ambition, 1343, 34. It is the good companion of humility, 1148, 23. Three duties of devotion are defined in us: faith is required, zeal is desired, and deeds are sought, 194, 22. Late devotion has no praise, 1214, 19.

**GOD.** God the Maker is revealed by His works, 421, 10. Whoever thinks that he can comprehend God from the corruptible things of the world is made foolish, 5, 9. What glory is greater than to pour the knowledge of divinity into the hearts of nations? 894, 16. When God says, “I am who I am,” He expressed the reality, not a name, 896, 19. He is one, not one among a number, 1487, 65. Wealthy Philosophy made several gods for itself; the poor Church knows one God, 1474, 17. Being belongs to the one who always is, 1521, 80. For always to be is divine, 128, 41. He has neither a beginning of days nor an end, 5, 9. God is spirit, 127, 40. He has nothing corporeal in His substance, 914, 65; 1456, 188. There can be no corporeal representation of the incorporeal God, 9, 18. It cannot be disproved that the Persons of the Trinity were seen in whatever form the will chose, not one formed by nature, 1274, 25. He is not seen by bodily eyes, 1207, 41.

[Col. 2248] It is proper to God to be good, 1083, 15. God is good in His entirety; man in part, 1487, 65. God’s goodness has overflowed beyond our merit, 761, 50. How He is good to all, 663, 4. God’s goodness is toward all, but severity toward a few, 1081, 7. God’s hand is the fullness of goodness; His face is the illumination of the mind, 924, 88. God, remaining in Himself, gives to others but receives nothing into Himself from others, 382, 78. He suffers neither decline nor diminution, nor does He admit increase, 186, 8; 874, 20. God is present everywhere and to everyone: how is He nearer to some? 1219, 39 and following. Although God is immeasurable, He holds the measure of all things, 197, 30. Nothing is immeasurable to God, who comprehends all things by a certain measure of His knowledge, 850, 20. What kind of walking God has, 176, 68.

Since God is unchangeable, why is He said to become angry? 231, 9. He does not think as human beings do, as though some new decision should come to Him, 231, 9. The incomprehensible splendor of divinity weighs upon the senses of our body, 1415, 17. God’s judgments are inscrutable, but the judgments of His mouth are not inscrutable, 992, 29–30. Human desires do not grasp His plan, 1366, 43. The Spirit of God is not comprehended by human opinion, but descends unexpectedly, as it were, through some occurrence, 1528, 115. How praiseworthy is the desire to see the divine countenance? 1062, 19. Nothing exists beyond God’s knowledge, 1906, 28. To God all things that will be are present, and what is hidden is manifest, 770, 11. How the number of hairs is known to God, 1436, 112. Whoever knows the Lord is known by the Lord, 791, 31. Knowledge of God is a matter of His favor, not of vision, 792, 33. God’s will is immovable, whereas human beings are changeable, and why, 961, 18.

For God, law is will, and the right to give, 838, 51. The divine will is the foundation of all things, 12, 22. God’s will is power, 1355, 3. God’s will is the measure of things: His word is the completion of the work and the origin of nature, 24, 4. It is the power of nature, 26, 10. God’s word is His will; God’s work is nature, 19, 33. What can the one who can do all things not do, except what He does not will to be able to do? 1231, 37. What is God’s activity like? 179, 74. God’s voice is effective in nature, 36, 8. That God is the creator of the world and of the Flood, 243, 42. Christ and the Spirit are the hands by which God created the human being, 1092, 17. God’s first voice, imparted to each creature as it was brought forth, is the law of nature, which has remained upon the earth for all ages and provides the ordinance of future succession, 42, 26; 49, 43. What He commands, He does, 37, 9. He does not labor over the greatest things and does not disdain the smallest, 80, 5. He is wonderful in both, 126, 37.

God’s providence toward human beings, 89, 25. Some philosophers wrongly denied it, 268, 100. God, whose servant it is a virtue to be, has Himself permitted us to call Him Father, 518, 17. If it is right to honor and love parents, how much more must love and honor be offered to the Father of all? 345, 69; 463, 20. God alone is the true teacher, 1078, 59. He does not wish to share dominion with others, 1122, 27. How great is God’s love toward us, 452, 24 and following; 729, 62 and following. How His mercy fills the earth, 1077, 57. Human mercy is toward one’s neighbor; the Lord’s mercy is toward all flesh, 1230, 29. Your life is not in your abundance but in God’s mercy, 1140, 28. The sight of God is our salvation, and in His face lies our help, 932, 15. Where God’s help is, there is certain assistance for salvation, 1151, 30; 1166, 29. Those whom God looks upon He illuminates, 697, 61; 792, 33.

He gives quickly, 198, 31. He is not slow to reward: He promises quickly and gives generously; and why? 288, 18. The petitioner’s vow is slower than the reward of the one who gives, 822, 18. The gifts of God who gives are more abundant than the wages of the one who works, 892, 12. God gives nothing imperfect, 196, 28. He gives His own gifts without any loss in giving, and enjoys more fully what we use, 240, 35. It belongs to divine mercy that He be the cause of death for no one and consider all worthy of redemption, 898, 25. He wishes all things to be saved, 760, 48. If He does not enter into you, the fault belongs not to the one who does not enter but to the one who does not open, 1220, 40. He wishes all whom He formed and created to be His own; He even seeks those who flee and does not wish the hidden to perish, 865, 20. He is accustomed to gather the scattered, seek the abandoned, and collect the forsaken, 984, 9.

God abandons or rejects no one except the one who thinks he must withdraw himself from His sight, 672, 29; 802, 57; 1167, 31. Nothing is more grievous than for one who has gone astray to be abandoned by God, 221, 32. How grievous it is to be cast away from God’s face, 672, 30; 699, 67. What it means to be rejected by God, 989 and following. Each person joins himself to God through his pursuits, or separates himself from Him, 1167, 31. God is abandoned through depraved conduct and the deformity of vices, 1167, 31. Those who hated God were abandoned; those who were going to love Him were chosen, 1495, 1. God blinded the Jewish people not through harshness but through foreknowledge, and not through malice but through fairness and justice, 1191, 27.

[Col. 2249] There are two principal kinds of virtue in God: one by which He forgives, the other by which He avenges, 212, 15. God’s mercy is joined with judgment, and judgment with mercy, 1232, 40 and following. God is called “God” because He is merciful, and “Lord” because He avenges, 246, 47. He generously bestows mercy and dispenses judgment together with compassion, 619, 86. He is severe in reproving but gentle in correcting, 886, 3. His severity returns to goodness, 1081, 7. He is accustomed to approve and increase His work rather than diminish or condemn it, 1200, 19. Although He becomes angry, He forgives; although He strikes, He heals; although He hands the flesh over to destruction, He saves the spirit, 826, 26.

When God is angry with the guilty, He delays; when He has mercy, He hastens to absolve. He restrains in order to correct, admonishes in order to amend, and anticipates in order to forgive, 822, 17. He is angry at our sins but does not forget mercy; He threatens punishment but does not permit destruction. He moderates vengeance and recalls severity, 245, 45. How merciful and devout He is, whether He shows mercy or takes vengeance, 1081, 7; 1453, 175. In rewarding gifts He keeps His promises; in exacting punishments He adheres to the prescribed measure, 822, 17. The Lord’s strong hand, just as it strikes severely, so quickly heals; strong for the wound, it is also strong for the remedy, 855, 33. The one who is ready to forgive does not wish to take vengeance, 423, 14. He condemns no one first; each person is the author of his own punishment, 1394, 46. How great is the Lord’s patience, that He does not immediately punish the sinner! 298, 46. God’s patience does not prejudice the truth, 667, 14. We ought to ask God for mercy rather than implore justice, 1179, 32. We merit it by faith, zeal, and works, 194, 23. We must flee first to God rather than to human supports, 202, 40. The Lord keeps His promises even toward the undeserving, 588, 73.

God’s possession alone bears the fruits of perpetual grace, 211, 11. The Lord has set before you, as your portion, gold, honors, nobility, and Himself: choose whichever you think best, 1060, 13. We must prefer God to all things, 285, 9. For the one whose portion is God, nothing should matter except God, 420, 7. He is the possessor of all nature, 1057, 5. No one is alone when God is present to him, 845, 9. No one is absent from God except the one who has made himself absent, 787, 20. One who stands with God cannot fear falling, 285, 9; 1136, 17. Let us live for God, for whom it is glorious to die, 1058, 7. Let us cling to God through vows, a pure conscience, and a spirit of charity, 209, 9. How we draw near to God through Christ, 1248, 8. How rare is the one who can say to God, “I am Yours,” 1125, 37 and following. With God as guide, every labor is lightened, every obstacle removed, and incentives supplied, 799, 50. The one whose right hand God holds with His own hand is guided well, 671, 27.

It is good to seek the Lord, but sometimes this turns into evil, 1342, 31. What it means for a person to walk in his own ways and in the ways of God, 1012, 10. How God is justified, 1384, 2. How He is magnified, 1290, 27. Whoever does not show reverence to God will not render obedience to nature, 219, 28. These are the chief virtues: to express God as an image expresses its archetype, to love Him as a son loves his father, and to worship Him as a subject worships a king, 422, 11.

How God speaks, 176, 69. When God speaks once, how can several things be heard? 967, 33. Why He is said to swear, 203, 43. How He becomes angry, 822, 19. What God’s entering and departing are like, 899, 29. By God’s hand we understand the power of punishing, 823, 20. Why God is described as both light and fire, 1066, 27. The Lord’s fire is eternal light, 1442, 132. It usually illuminates rather than burns, 66, 9.

There is nothing more grievous that you can do than to sin against God, 1435, 106. Whatever appears to be done as an injury to God is the most bitter of all things, 759, 47. No enemy is more grievous to all than the one who harms the author of all, 1200, 18. Our own advantage must be rejected when there is an injury to divinity, 1485, 60.

**DEVIL.** His nature is not evil, but his works are unjust, 1350, 61. Why he will not remain forever, 1394, 46. By what deception he was deceived, 1337, 11. Through pride he lost the grace of his nature, 1046, 8. The devil’s judgment is delayed, and why, 1228, 23. The Lord does not wish the holy to share a common judgment with the devil’s associates, 1228, 22. By what punishment he is punished, 433, 40–41.

That the devil was in the earthly paradise under the figure of a serpent, 148, 9. This should neither be criticized nor doubted, 149, 10. Nevertheless, most denied it, 149, 11. What the devil envied in the human being, 169, 54. His malice easily detects what is hidden, 1285, 3. That his very malice benefits human beings toward salvation, 148, 9. The devil is a wicked teacher who mixes falsehoods with truths, 1408, 102. He is first introduced as having spoken the name “Jesus the Nazarene” in Luke’s Gospel; and in Genesis he was the first to name God to the human being, 1350, 60.

Just as the saints are members of Christ, so the impious are members of the devil, 776, 27; 919, 9. The devil is a most savage king, 908, 54. Everything subject to his power must be avoided, and why, 1342, 30. He is the author of all crimes, 844, 6; 1173, 12. Who is as much your enemy as the prince of this world and his associates? 901, 33. He is the mountain that cast itself into Judas’s heart, 929, 9. He rejoiced because he had taken an apostle away from Christ; but in the conversion of the thief he lost more than he had taken away, 864, 17. Is it surprising that he can weigh human beings down, when by his obstinate spirit he does not yield even to God? 1174, 15.

He seeks companions in guilt in order to deliver those made liable to punishment, 978, 13; 1447, 150. He imitates the partridge, which seizes and hatches the eggs of others, 118, 13. He borrowed what he did not possess and does not wish to return what he received, 797, 46. God permits the devil to exercise power over human beings so that the good may be tested and the wicked punished, 1395, 49. He received permission to tempt, but not the capacity to overthrow, 149, 10; 1437, 115. His temptations must be understood so that, instructed and prepared, we may beware, 172, 58. His various temptations are set forth, 170, 55. Anger, fury, slaughter, and weapons are the devil’s arms, 801, 56. You must be especially wary of his flattery, 1343, 34. He tempts as an adversary and defends as a servant, 825, 25.

The devil can harm no one unless that person has cast himself into his power, 1340, 25. He holds no one bound under the yoke of slavery unless that person has first sold himself to him for the price of sins, 447, 10. The devil’s snare does not catch you unless its bait has first caught you, 1153, 37. The devil quickly shuts the door of our heart if he finds it open, 649, 28. If we do not crush the devil, the fault is ours, 1110, 18; 1344, 36. Against him one must use not loudness of voice but greatness of heart, 1211, 8. He is conquered not by your merit but by hatred of himself, 1418, 29. The devil is set against Christ by antithesis, 1436, 114; 1437, 117. Christ wished to deceive the prince of the world in Himself and to triumph over him in His disciples, 1005, 34. How blessed is the person in whom the devil found nothing that he could recognize as his own, 466, 24. In Him alone, who committed no sin, he found nothing, 374, 55.

**DIALECTIC** flows with an abundance of words; piety preserves the fear of God, 791, 28.

**Διὰ παντὸς** means both “through all time” and “through everything,” 1024, 21.

**DAY.** The meaning of “day” varies, 244, 43. A day is a portion of time, not its beginning, 10, 20. The period of one day is measured by twenty-four hours, 22, 37. The Lord’s Day has preeminence from the order of number and holiness from the Lord’s resurrection, 936, 1. Although God made all the days, this day nevertheless received preeminence among the others in the divine work, because on it every sin was removed, 887, 6. Christ is the Day, 1054, 33; 1464, 222. For those with whom Christ is present it is always day, and the sun never sets, 1122, 26. What the evil days are, 792, 32.

**DIGESTION.** How it occurs, 141, 71; 238, 28.

**DIGNITY.** Every worldly dignity lies subject to the devil’s power: useful for a fragile life and empty of fruit, 1341, 28.

**LOVE.** The difference between affection and love, 1542, 177. Where love is perfect, there is security, 1353, 70. See **CHARITY**.

**DILIGENCE** is a support for the gifted, 316, 8. Diligence and faith hold the higher place, 831, 35. It is not enough to do what is right unless you also hasten what you do, 295, 33. God condemns efforts that are late, 1537, 162. Good diligence joined with wisdom, and discovery joined with natural talent, 448, 50. The candidate for the heavenly kingdom ought to be an active soldier, 462, 10. We cannot shape our nature, but we can shape our diligence, 808, 66. God is more present to the diligent and absent from the negligent, 1499, 23.

**FLOOD.** It began and ended in spring, 246, 48; 252, 60. Why in Noah’s six-hundredth year, ibid. In what manner the Flood lasted forty days, 244. How the five human senses are prefigured by the fifteen cubits of water by which the Flood rose above the mountains, 248, 52. Why the grace of fertility was not lacking after the coming Flood, 229, 6. Whether the olive leaf brought by the dove existed before the Flood or arose during the Flood, 256, 68–69; 259, 74. The raven and the dove sent from the ark signified wickedness and virtue, 254, 64. The Flood was restrained by the power of the divine Spirit, 251, 58.

**Διορατικόν.** What it is, 335, 54.

**DISCIPLINE.** How discipline, wisdom, and understanding differ from one another, 886, 3. The fullness of perfect discipline does not allow the mind to be consumed by the devouring vapor of lusts, 211, 11. Christ gave nearly all His names to His disciples, 1407, 97.

**DISCORDANT PEOPLE.** No spaces can be sufficient for them; for the peaceful and tranquil, even narrow spaces abound, 323, 26.

**DISTINCTION** is better than confusion in every matter, 215, 21.

**RICH.** From where the term “rich” is derived, 572, 28. Who is truly rich, 582, 60. To be rich means to have what is sufficient for one’s desire, 320, 20; 361, 11. The just person is rich, 1534, 139. Who is richer than the one who is rich in the Lord? 782, 12. If the rich keep God’s commands, what seemed impossible becomes possible for them, 988, 18. Not all rich people are greedy, 1493, 86. Why the rich person is sometimes just, while the poor person is a sinner, and why, 962, 18. It is contrary to nature for the rich person to be merciful, 1488, 70.

[Col. 2251] The rich have closed ears, blunted by the sound of bronze; money resounds to them more than divine words, 1058, 9. How great is the rich person’s hardness toward the poor? 565, 1; 581, 56 and following. The rich person envies the poor person even his burial, 578, 46. Avarice strangles the poor person in this age, but the rich person is suffocated forever by his own snares, 1028, 31. The grief and anguish of a certain poor parent whom a rich man was forcing to sell his son are described with great elegance, 570, 21 and following. The rich person’s deadly hunger, and still more deadly luxury, 570, 20. How far and wide the rich spread their desires, 276, 125; 286, 12. How many rich people judge that God is not sufficient for them, 1125, 37. How rare on earth is the person who can say, “The Lord is my portion,” 1056, 3.

The elements were given to all in common; the ornaments of the world are equally open to rich and poor, 134, 52. How great are the insolence and swelling pride of the rich, 1473, 14. Ostentation of usefulness and abundance of worldly possessions usually inflate human beings, unless they are ashamed that what belongs to others is praised more than what belongs to themselves, 1139, 28. The rich person disdains what is his own as though it were worthless, but desires what belongs to another as though it were most precious, 568, 9. How restless he is, 573, 29. The richer they are in abundance, the poorer the rich are, 566, 4 and following. They regard whatever belongs to another as their own loss, 568, 11 and following. They are more wretched than the poor, 573, 31. The condition of slaves is more tolerable than that of the rich, 572, 28. Wealth is captive; poverty is free, 579, 51. The rich serve a wretched slavery, 579, 52. They are not possessors of riches but are possessed by their own riches, 583, 63. The rich person is rightly charged with folly, 575, 38. He is like dust before the face of the wind, 759, 46. As a cedar is broken, 812, 77. An excellent example of a particularly filthy rich man, 569, 18. The rich person should not disdain the needy, nor the poor envy the rich, and why, 947, 5. There is no distinction among the corpses of the dead, except perhaps that the bodies of the rich, swollen with luxury, stink more heavily, 133, 57.

**RICHES.** From where the term is derived, 339, 60. Riches are foreign to us: they are neither born with us nor pass away with us, 1469, 246. It is not riches that are condemned, but the riches of sinners, 790, 27. Wealth does not prejudice faith, provided that we know how to use it in works, 880, 31. Riches are impediments among the wicked but aids to virtue among the good, 1493, 85. Not all poverty is holy, nor are riches criminal, 1473, 13. The heavenly judgment condemns not those who possess riches but those who do not know how to use them, 1371, 69.

Praise of riches is not praise of human beings but of the metals in which human beings are punished, 580, 54. Why the succession of flowing worldly advantages and the abundance of riches are granted to the impious, 668, 21. Riches come to the impious by chance, not through any merit, nor are the profits of a treasury rewards of virtue, 668, 17; 784, 17. How useless riches are, 572, 27. They cannot bring salvation, 1120, 21. On the road to the kingdom of God, do not seek wealth or inheritance, 853, 27; 1481, 44.

If you wish to be a god to sinners, a terror to kings, and an object of reverence to others, despise the things of the world and strive to prefer the reproach of the Lord’s Passion to all riches, 1061, 15. It is the mark of an excellent mind to be content with its own limits, not to be lifted up by an abundance of riches and by possessions flowing according to the grace of pleasures, 321, 1. Flee the riches of the sinner, lest he find a place from which he can wound you, 789, 24; 853, 27. Riches are the devil’s snare, which he set for the Savior and by which he strangled the apostle Judas, 1153, 36. How great it is to despise riches—and how rare this very thing is, 1060, 15. Why do we spare an inheritance that even the devil himself judges worthless in comparison with salvation? 825, 23. You see that riches flow in, but you do not see that they flow past, 966, 32. How the riches of the world pass away like the dream of one awakening, 628, 8–9. See **ABSTINENCE** and **AVARICE**.

**DIVORCE.** See **WIFE**.

**TEACHERS.** The distinction between teachers and those who teach, 1134, 12. The varieties of teachers, 1161, 14. Teachers who demand from others what they themselves cannot imitate, and to whom they may be compared, 1435, 105. He whom Wisdom itself taught rightly understood above all teachers, 1134, 11.

**TEACHING.** Understanding produces teaching, not memory, 1093, 19. All moral teaching is pleasant, 971, 1. The person who is good through devotion to knowledge will be better if he seeks the grace to carry out rational and moral teaching, 992, 31. A good life without teaching possesses grace; teaching without life does not possess integrity, 973, 1. Life must be sought before teaching, ibid. Teaching cannot receive a reward where it does not possess the grace of innocence, 975, 6. Teaching of an undefiled life gives old age its excellence, 1135, 13. Why teaching is called leaven, 1457, 191. Whoever errs in doctrine has not chosen the way of truth, 1016, 25. When the impious hear certain learned people, they are accustomed to avoid them because of their teaching, 1096, 27.

**DOEG** is a type of Judas, 1364, 37.

**DECEIT** is good when plunder is irreproachable, 462, 10.

[Col. 2252] **LORDS.** The one who does not have one lord has many, 1496, 6.

**GIVE.** No one can give what he does not have, 526, 45.

**UNTIL.** What it signifies in Scripture, 254, 63.

**DOTHAN** signifies “defection,” 486, 11.

**DRAGON.** It binds the elephant, whose collapse is the victor’s death, 48, 40.

**HARSH.** Let no one think that what is just is harsh, 1146, 16.

**LEADERS.** With bad leaders one quickly goes astray, 440, 55.

# E
## E

**DRUNKENNESS** has two forms, 272, 11; 275, 18. There is drunkenness of sin, and there is also drunkenness of grace, 554, 61. The good drunkenness of the spiritual table, 1138, 24. The good drunkenness of the saving cup, 773, 19; 1239, 4. It makes people sober; it produces joy, not staggering, 192, 19. It is the guardian of chastity, 193, 20. How ridiculous and hateful drunkenness is among ordinary people is set forth in an elegant description, 548, 42; 553, 60 and following. And especially among military men, 549, 46 and following. Also among women, 555, 66. The protestations and toasts of drinkers, 554, 62. A certain monstrous manner of drinking is censured, 555, 64. The effects of drunkenness, 192, 18. How great are the evils of drunkenness and wine, 539, 10 and following; 542, 23 and following; 551, 52 and following; 553, 59 and following; 556, 68. Lust is aroused through the eyes, but kindled by drunkenness, 712, 18. Drunkenness must be avoided, through which we cannot guard against crimes, 301, 57. Wine has greater force than poison, 551, 52. As continence is the mother of faith, so drunkenness is the mother of faithlessness, 548, 41. More secret matters are often extorted through wine, 554, 63. A banquet of one day is the price of your life, 1126, 39. Drunken men are compared with ships, 557, 72. An example of a drunken young man converted to philosophy, 548, 45.

**CHURCH**: betrothed in the beginnings of the world in paradise, prefigured in the Flood, announced through the Law, called through the prophets, it long awaited the beauty of the Gospel, 974, 4. Rebecca is a type of the Church, 461, 9. And that widow to whom Elijah was sent, 1347, 50. And Mary, 1284, 7. And the woman in the Gospel, 1456, 187. And the woman who entered the Pharisee’s house, 1095, 25. The Church rightly assumes the appearance of a sinful woman, 1388, 21. The Lord saves a woman in her type, 1453, 175. It is represented by the moon, 517, 13. The Lord’s Church is one, and its assembly is one, 33, 2, 3. Christ deigned to gather all nations into one body of the Church, 761, 50. All are called, and all are redeemed by Christ, 946, 4. No one was called to the Church before Christ called the peoples of the nations, 1495, 5. The Lord gathered it for himself from sinners, 938, 5. Christ gathered it for himself through humility and through the cross, 1147, 20. The assembly of the Church was first promised to Abraham, 1316, 7. The kingdom of the Church was granted in predestination before that of the Synagogue, 462, 10. All are called to the Church, but first the people of the Synagogue, then those of the nations, 1121, 24. In seeking for himself a Church from a people that was not a people, God preferred it to that ancient and royal people, the Jews, 780, 7. Among the nations there was falsehood; truth withdrew from the Jews and came to the Church, 1119, 19. The Church is free; the Synagogue has been cast out, 1324, 29. It seized the kingdom of the Synagogue, 1383, 115. It returned the money of charity that it had received from the Lord, but the Synagogue did not return it, 797, 44. The heel of Christ is the Synagogue; the beauty and glory of his face is the Church, 948, 11. Christ desired the appearance of his Church and prepared to take her as his wife, 724, 48. Christ saw her naked, and he saw and loved her, 722, 41 and 42. The assembly of the nations, previously untamed in its conduct, began to be the bride of Christ, 993, 32. As the beloved and the beloved hastened toward each other, the spiritual union of Christ and the Church was celebrated, 1257, 40. She married Christ, 1328, 38. No one doubts that the sacrament of Christ and the Church is spiritual, 826, 27. Christ is the husband, the Church is the wife: a wife in charity, a virgin in integrity, 1472, 9. The Church is life made in Christ, from his rib, and raised again in him, 794, 37. Hence she is the mother of the living, 1310, 86 and following. As a virgin she conceived us from the Spirit; as a virgin she gives us birth without a groan, 1284, 7. In her there are bitter and grievous pains until Christ is formed in us, 940, 10. Why she appears barren in this world, 345, 72. The Church loves and never changes her affection toward her Christ, 72, 22. No one can love God as much as the Church, 1388, 22. All her hope is in Christ, 519, 22. Her beauty excels in hearing and in works, 358, 7. What she is and how great she is, 1190, 21. She is called charity, and by loving God she has received his name, ibid. She is called “radiant” (*actinosa*), and why, 643, 16. How she is without blemish, 1271, 17. She is beautiful in imitation of Christ, and entirely cleansed of every sin in her footwear, 1189, 16. She is a crown of glory, 1160, 11. She is the body of Christ, 1161, 12; 1168, 35. She consists of two things: either that you do not know how to sin, or that you cease to sin, 1433, 96.

[Col. 2253] The Church is the pillar and foundation of truth, 470, 34. Her kingdom will remain forever—and why? 1431, 91. God founded and extended her forever, 942, 17. The Church is founded in tribulations, in storms and tempests, in anxieties and sorrow, in adverse circumstances, and is prepared amid rivers, 946, 4. She was founded upon the seas and prepared upon the rivers, 34, 6. She dwells beside the waves and is not shaken by the waves; she is more ready to give help than exposed to danger, 521, 27. Her various waves and storms, 227, 1. She is struck by the waves of worldly cares but is not overthrown; she is beaten but not shaken, 1318, 11. Christ is attacked in her, 961, 16. The Church of the Lord is not conquered by her persecutions, but tested by them, 889, 9. Many test her, but cannot harm her, 78, 33. Her frequent persecutions have produced for us titles and victories of martyrdom, 995, 7. She has falls and frequent risings, but she grew through her falls, 78, 32. She can be overshadowed, 65, 7. Why the Lord is accustomed to give thanks to the Father on her behalf, 1403, 83. In the night of the world, let the Church show you the way, 776, 26. Faith is found on her finger, 1378, 97. The Church of God shines above all assemblies, 1020, 7. She alone, and no other assembly, can say: “I hold all your commandments; I know those of the Old and New Testament,” 1255, 33. In her there is rejoicing; in heresy and paganism, weeping and sorrow, 33, 3. In her everyone has an ear; outside her they do not, 1519, 69. He rightly squandered his inheritance who withdrew from her, 1462, 213. If there is any church that rejects the faith and does not possess the foundations of apostolic preaching, it must be abandoned, 1399, 68. We are sometimes admonished not to reject those who have been separated from our faith and fellowship, 55, 55. How the less honorable members of the Church sometimes obtain greater honor, 236, 25. What the beginning of the newly born Church was like, 1298, 50. She is there where the priestly rod and grace flourish, 377, 64. From one Church several churches are derived, 1354, 78. Each is indeed filled with the Spirit and with grace; nevertheless they are joined according to the likeness of the temporal priest, 1284, 7. We who have undertaken the priestly ministry must bravely endure bodily sufferings not only for ourselves but also for the Church of the Lord, 829, 32. A voice must be raised for Christ when wolves attack the Church’s sheepfold, 119, 27.

**The keys of the Church.** We have received the Holy Spirit, who not only forgives our sins but also makes us his priests, so that we may forgive the sins of others, 1092, 19. The power of forgiving sins was reserved for the Gospel, 858, 37, 38. God also forgives sins through those to whom he grants the power of forgiving, 1358, 13. Sins are forgiven through the word of God, whose interpreter and, in a certain sense, executor is the Levite; they are also forgiven through the office of the priest and the sacred ministry, 212, 15. God is the Father, Christ the shepherd, the woman the Church: Christ carries you in his body, the Church seeks you, the Father receives you; as a shepherd he carries you back, as a mother she searches for you, as a father he clothes you; the first is mercy, the second intercession, the third reconciliation: the redeemer comes to the aid, the Church intercedes, the author reconciles, 1461, 208. The Church has curtains with which she covers sins and shadows guilt, 34, 5. If you distrust forgiveness for grave sins, bring forward sinners; bring forward the Church, which may pray for you, and in consideration of which the Lord may forgive what he could deny you, 1357, 11. If you have gone astray after baptism, let the Church weep for you; let her herself lament your sins, and let her weep greatly, 819, 10; 1377, 91. Let the Church pray for you, and let the people shed tears, 1465, 225. Most people used to be held back from the pursuit of conversion because they thought that in the Church sins were without forgiveness in proportion as the commandments were holier, 1183, 43. After penance, we ought to favor the forgiveness of sins, 1467, 236. Forgiveness should neither be difficult nor indulgence lax, 1475, 21. One must not always punish those who have sinned, and for what reason, 1417, 27. In the Church, where it is especially fitting to show mercy, the form of justice must be especially carefully maintained toward sinners, 1065, 26. Ease of forgiveness gives an incentive to wrongdoing, ibid. It is better for the many to be freed by the condemnation of one or another than for more people to be endangered by the acquittal of two, 1198, 11. The Church does not know how to publish her laws, 420, 8. Those who did not attend church are censured, 1184, 45. “Hasten early, and bring to the Church the first fruits of your devout vow; afterward, if worldly necessity calls, you will proceed securely to your affairs,” 1218, 32. How delightful it is to begin the day with hymns and songs, with the beatitudes that you read in the Gospel, 1218, 32. There are many days on which one must come to the Church immediately at midday, sing hymns, and celebrate the offering, 1073, 48. Every day, whether going beforehand to church or devoting ourselves to prayers at home, let us begin from God and end in him, 322, 22. Rain was granted through the prayers of the supplicating Church, 76, 30.

The Church is the tabernacle of the righteous, 318, 11. She is a house whose abundance overflows with graces; the Holy Spirit is a torrent of delight, 773, 19. Her bedroom is the body of Christ, 979, 16. For the devout, the Church is a house; for the devout, heaven is a homeland, 951, 18. She is the city of God, 1168, 35. Fortified through Christ, besieged by the devil, 131, 49. She is a wall with twelve apostolic gates, 1256, 37. Her towers are priests, 131, 49. She is the city of God, 1168, 35. The walls of Jerusalem are her assemblies, founded throughout the whole world, 702, 83. Her gates are gates of chastity and justice, 1407, 99. She began to be in gardens after Christ suffered in gardens, 1258, 45. She is frequently compared with a garden, 1534, 139. And with a flock of goats, 1177, 22. Why she is also called heaven, the world, and the globe of the earth, 1121, 25. She is an image of heavenly things, 641, 9.

**ECHENEIS** stops a huge ship, 93, 31.

**ECHINUS** the earthly creature is enclosed against ambushes by its spines, 120, 20. It fortifies for itself two ways of breathing, and why, ibid. The echinus foretells an approaching storm, 89, 24.

**EDOM**, that is, “earthly” and “crafty,” 1223, 6.

**ELEAZARUS**: how blessed he was in steadfastly enduring torments, 474, 40, 41.

**AMBER** (*electrum*) is the tear of a shrub, 58, 63. Why certain tiny animals are found in electrum, ibid.

**ELECTION.** There is no opportunity for retreat left to one who is given the choice of choosing, 286, 11.

**ALMSGIVING.** Whoever gives alms pays what is owed; he does not give what is not owed, 580, 53. A rich man ought to distribute alms to the poor from his own goods, 574, 36 and following; 579, 52 and following; 582, 58 and following; 586, 67. How just it is to sprinkle something from your goods upon the poor, 1064, 22. Make support for mercy out of the instrument of avarice; make the grace of sincerity out of the allurements of corruption, 559, 76. What good is it to pity a poor person unless you give him sustenance? 1128, 44. Money is worthless when hoarded, precious when scattered, 825, 24. By giving to the poor, let us acquire for ourselves the grace of angels and of the other saints, 1469, 245. Many who gave their possessions to the poor, having been enriched, ought not to demand from the Lord a worldly reward of this kind, 1059, 11. Nothing is more grievous than for us to look down upon our poor brothers with a proud eye, 1005, 37.

**ELEMENTS**: why they are called in Greek *stoicheia* (στοιχεῖα), 40, 18. There are four from which all things are composed, 10, 20. Why God did not create them before giving them suitable adornments, 15, 27. What their qualities are, by which they are mixed with one another, 40, 18. What has been composed from them must necessarily be dissolved, 12, 23.

**ELEPHANT**: why it has a projecting trunk, 124, 31. Its limbs are described, ibid. How it is captured, ibid. How it renders great service to the Persians in warfare, 125, 33. It is said to live for three hundred years and more, ibid., 34. That formidable creature is formidable to bulls, yet fears a mouse, 126, 37. When it is cheated of its reward, its vengeance, 555, 65.

**ELIJAH** and **ELISHA**, in order to cross the waters of the Jordan, first crossed the torrents of the passions of our mind by the step of the mind, 1243, 16. Elijah possessed great virtue and grace, and in what respect, 1278, 36. He was not fleeing from a woman but from the world and worldly allurements, 431, 34. He is compared with Christ, 1406, 96.

**ELIZABETH** was from the tribe of Judah, 1315, 5.

**ELISHA**, who left nothing for himself, abounded for the peoples, 115, 6. He did not think that God was absent from him, but sought his presence in his benefits, 833, 40. See **ELIJAH**.

**ELOQUENCE** of two wise men from among the Gentiles, compared with snow and bees, 1414, 15. Although buying and selling may seem to be a somewhat equal contract, each person nevertheless sells what is cheaper to himself and buys what pleases him, 904, 41.

**EMPIRICISTS**: from where they received their name, *empeirikoi* (Ἐμπειρικοί), 815, 1.

**ENGADDI** is called “temptation” in Latin, 995, 8. It is a place in Judaea where balsam is produced, ibid.

**ENNON**: they interpreted it as “the eye of the proud,” 1170, 2.

**ENOCH** is called in Latin “the grace of God,” 152, 19. It is a clear sign of the Lord’s piety and divinity, 1333, 48.

**ENOS** means “man” in Chaldean and in Latin, 356, 1.

**EUPITHMETIKON** (Ἐυπιθμήτικον): what it is, 335, 54.

**EPOU THEŌ** (Ἐπου θεῷ, “Follow God”): what it means, 283, 4.

**HORSE**: it scents war from a distance and is roused by the sound of the trumpet, 89, 25. We see it stirred by popular enthusiasm, rejoicing in applause, and delighted by the trainer’s blandishments, 206, 3. The difference between the driver and the rider of a horse, 584, 64, 65. Those who are accustomed to boast of the nobility of their horses as though they were consuls are censured, 580, 54. River horses, or hippopotamuses, in the Nile, 80, 4.

**ERROR**: there is none where there is a simple affection of piety and every faithful understanding, 817, 6. He is worthy of a heavier punishment who has deceived someone weak, foolish, and imprudent by persuading him into error or by agitating his heart, 1245, 19.

**ISAIAH**: how he saw the Lord, 1267, 6. The devil’s words to a certain prophet, perhaps Isaiah, 1124, 32. The saw divided the structure of his body more easily than it bent his faith, 1500, 25.

**ESAU** and **JACOB** represented the Jewish and Christian peoples, 1223, 6. Esau was a type of wickedness, 184, 4.

[Col. 2255] **EUCHARIST.** Christ is shown to offer his body through the priests; his word sanctifies the sacrifice that is offered, 853, 25. He gave the bread that the priest himself consecrates daily with his words, 524, 38. At the Church’s banquet he both serves and is served, 192, 19. “Food and drink are served to me daily; he gives it to everyone, gives it daily, gives it always,” 1202, 27 and 28. It has been demonstrated that our Lord is food, a feast, or nourishment for those who eat, 902, 36. Do not doubt that an angel is present when the sacrifice is offered, 1275, 28. When should the offering and sacrifice be celebrated, by which Christ fills the hungry with the feasts of his body? 1073, 48. The venerable communion of the sacred offering, 1420, 43. It is food for refreshment; it is food of blood, 1483, 51. You pluck the rose—that is, the blood of the Lord’s body, 1140, 2. Come to the food of the Lord’s body, to that cup by which the devotion of the faithful is inebriated; the body does not stagger but rises again, 1166, 28. The more solid food is the body of Christ; the stronger drink is the blood of Christ, 1400, 71. Whoever has not brought peace and charity to the altars of Christ will be sent into darkness, 1460, 204. No one receives Christ’s food unless he has first been healed, 1400, 70. Holy fasts lead us to the Eucharistic table, 545, 33. It is the remission of sins, 525, 39. We eat the body of Christ so that we may be participants in eternal life, 1514, 49. Spiritual banquets are accustomed not to harm those who are filled but to benefit them, 1251, 19. Every unclean person must be separated from the altars of Christ, 561, 82.

**EUNOMIAN** says that the Son is unlike the Father, 45, 32. The fruit of the degenerate Eunomian root is worse, 32, 21.

**EUPHRATES**: most think that it is named *apo tou euphrainesthai* (ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐφραίνεσθαι), that is, “from rejoicing,” 152, 18. In Latin it is called “fertility” and “abundance of fruits,” 151, 18. It flows toward Babylon, 755, 36.

**EURIPI** stand calm at the rising of the moon as long as it is without light, 76, 30.

**EVE**: why she was made not from the same earth as Adam but from his rib, 166, 48. In paradise, the senses—Greek *aisthēsis* (αἴσθησις)—were a figure, 149, 11. How the devil attacked her, 170, 56. The seductive ambition for the promised honor deceived her, 1343, 34. From woman vice began and falsehood commenced, 171, 56. By giving Adam what she had tasted, she repeated the sin, 158, 33. She entangled the serpent but did not free herself, 978, 13. If she had had burning torches, she would never have entangled us in the little cords of her transgression, 149, 11. We would have conquered if she had kept silent, 843, 3. After she confessed her offense, a gentler and beneficial sentence followed her, 178, 72. What her punishment was and what it signifies, 178, 72. Most people think she should be excused because, loving her husband, she feared being separated from him, 159, 34.

**EVANGELISTS** wrote the Gospel without any effort, with the divine Spirit supplying the richness of words and all events, 1266, 3. They did not speak by their own power, nor did they all say everything identically; rather, the grace of the Holy Spirit granted them what each was to say concerning the works of the Lord Jesus, 616, 73. Although they possess all things in all respects, nevertheless each contains the fullness of particular virtues, 1264, 8; 1403, 81. In what they differ from one another, 1529, 118; 1532, 129 and following. Their judgments do not conflict when the mystery is in agreement, 1527, 107. It is not credible that they could have said things contrary to one another, 1313, 1. It is fair that the one who merited being an Evangelist should be cleared of suspicion either of negligence or of falsehood, 1541, 172. What the one who evangelizes the kingdom of God ought to be like, 1398, 65. Many wished to write a Gospel, but only four have been accepted, 1269, 10. Some have thought that the four forms of living creatures read in the Apocalypse are to be understood as the four books of the Gospel, 1264, 7. There is only one Gospel, although there are four books, 883, 38. Although the Church possesses the four books of the Gospel, she overflows with Evangelists throughout the whole world, 1265, 1. There is truly natural wisdom in the Gospel according to John; Matthew wrote more morally; Mark more rationally, 1262, 3. In nearly all Gospel passages a spiritual sense is at work, 1442, 134. Luke wrote the Gospel in a historical style, and for what reason, 1261, 1, 4 and 7. How the Alexandrians and Egyptians read the beginning of the Gospel of John, 393, 35. The Gospel contains all truth, 1206, 37. It excludes the imperfection of philosophy, 325, 30. It is not only a teaching of faith but also a school of morals, 1230, 33. In the New Testament we have learned the commands of new virtues and drawn in new ways of life, 859, 3. How we ought to approach it, 912, 61. Let its likeness be present in your deeds, 1255, 34. In the Gospel is the perfection of goodness; in the Law, instruction in equity, 1515, 53. In the goodness of the Gospel, God’s judgments are taught better than in the severity of the Law, 1084, 16. The shadow is in the Law, the image in the Gospel, the truth in heavenly things, 852, 25. In it the shadow of the Law no longer grows dark for us, but the truth shines forth, 859, 2. The Law announces Christ through hidden mysteries but does not show him face to face as the Gospel does, 1061, 16. The Law is, as it were, a figure for us; the Gospel, as it were, the light and seal of truth, 910, 58. Christ is a helper through the Law, a protector through the Gospel, 1164, 23. The Gospel works the restoration of the dead Law in later generations, 913, 63. What God announced through the prophets, he manifested and fulfilled in the Gospel, 1186, 7. The Gospel shines like a lamp on the way in shadow—that is, in the world, 643, 14. How it is a sea, 86, 17. Evangelical preaching is a wedding shoe, 1308, 81. There is power in that preaching, 1107, 12. Wealthy heresy composed many Gospels; poor faith held only this Gospel, the one it had, 1474, 17. Although heresies have many Gospels, they do not have one, 1265, 2. The pseudo-Gospel according to Thomas, Matthias, the Twelve, and Basilides, 1265, 2. Gospels corrupted by heretics, 1261, 2.

**EVILATH** is the land in which there is good gold, and the carbuncle and prasinus stone, 755, 36.

**EXAMPLE.** For most people, the sight of a righteous person is a warning to correction; for the more perfect, however, it is a source of joy, 1094, 22. It is considered better to resemble a few than many, 185, 5.

**EXERCISE** increases bodily strength, 216, 22.

**ARMY**: how armies complete a march, 1018, 2.

**EXHORTATION** is used for consolation, and consolation for exhortation, in the Apostle, 1098, 34.

**ESTEEM** is our price, 963, 21.

**EXILE**: the restraints of prison in this world are harsher than exile, 1228, 23.

## F

**HUNGER** will afflict all whom Christ has not fed, 449, 42. Divine reading brings forgetfulness of hunger, 1339, 20.

**FATAL DECREE** is not binding, 232, 5.

**FEVER**: if it burns intensely, the physician is accustomed to deny the drink itself to those who are thirsty, 785, 18.

**FERTILITY** of the earth is attributed not to the sun but to divine favor, 64, 6. That which is fertile is seemly; that which is infertile is unseemly, 376, 60.

**FELIX, NABOR, AND VICTOR**, our martyrs, are the mustard seed, 1453, 178.

**BITTERNESS OF GALL** is found useful for human salvation, 148, 8.

**LENDING AT INTEREST** is ancient, but it is an ancient sin, 620, 88. The inhumanity of moneylenders is elegantly described and chastised, 793, 9 and following. They are compared with Judas and the devil, ibid., 12 and following. Also with the Echidna and other serpents, 604, 41. They sell children for their fathers’ debts, 600, 29. They used to forbid a debtor’s corpse to be carried to burial, 602, 36, 37. Their inhumanity in exacting interest even from gamblers, 602, 38 and following. The various names they use, 604, 40. How insatiable their greed is, 597, 31; 605, 43 and following. They are compared with the sea, 605, 44. And so is their money, 596, 16. How wickedly they plunder unwary young men, 597, 23 and following. Both the moneylender and the debtor are sinners, 609, 54. Those are censured who, having received money from a moneylender, miserably consume it through their own lack of restraint, 597, 17 and following; 600, 30. Whoever binds himself to a moneylender sells himself—not for money, but for guilt, 601, 32.

**INTEREST** can be good, and lending at interest praiseworthy: lend to God in the hand of the poor, 610, 55, 56. Whoever has more with which to lend is the more righteous, 611, 59 and following. See **USURY**.

**FENNEL**: by feeding on it, the serpent drives away the blindness it has acquired, 119, 19.

**HAY**: how is it made? 42, 26. It was produced before the sun, ibid., 27. How we ought to be like hay, 45, 31.

**CAUSE OF FERTILITY** comes from heaven, 30, 16.

**ON THE LEAVES OF THE FIG TREE**, 57, 60.

**FAITH** comes before the letter; grace comes before the Law, 1321, 21. Just as faith begins from the Old Testament, so it is fulfilled in the New, 1379, 99. Christ restored us to the way of our ancestors and to the ancient simplicity of faith, 1323, 26. It is one thing to believe in God’s commandments, another to believe the commandments, 1082, 12. Our faith is the Word of God, 1433, 98. The truth is the foundation of faith, 1237, 56. Christ’s deeds are the bulwarks of faith, 1042, 33. How shameful it is to believe human witnesses about another person but not to believe God’s oracles about himself, 289, 21. If good men said it, we would consider it wrong to believe them; therefore one must believe when God speaks, 1353, 71. The birth of faith is a good pain, through which Christ is formed and born in the Church, 776, 28. Why it is good for faith to precede reason, 289, 21. God willed that it should be born through certain stages, 15, 27. How great a protection our faith, by which we live, is for us, 861, 11. By what it ought to be nourished, 215, 19, 20. It is formed not in the forensic language of wisdom but in the power of God, 1107, 12. Why no one should offer the excuse that he believes late, 346, 74. According to the devotion of the believer, spiritual light is poured into each person, 1511, 37. Those who believed with more spontaneous faith are better than those who believed because of promised benefits, 1356, 5. “Behold, he loves the freedom of faith who gave freedom,” 1032, 45. Faith is worn down, pressed, sown—and how, 1453, 179 and following. There is a religious violence of faith and a criminal sluggishness, 1469, 1. A perfect man is required with regard to faith, 1334, 50. Faith separates us from comparison with irrational animals, 1222, 2. Above all things, it ought to commend us to God, 208, 8. It is the stable foundation of all virtues, 868, 4. And their root, 219, 28. The root of faith is hope, 1165, 27. From faith comes charity; from charity, hope; and again they pour themselves back into one another in a certain holy circuit, 1478, 30. Faith precedes devotion, 509, 81. Virtues without faith are leaves: they seem to flourish but cannot be useful, 757, 41. And works are vain, 1435, 103. Where true faith is, there is the grace of true light, 1075, 51. Christ illumines with the brightness of faith, the glory of his resurrection, and the power of divine works, 1186, 8. Faith made the wise, 1177, 24. Whatever the soul believes, it both conceives and gives birth to the Word of God, and recognizes his works, 1290, 26. Christ is touched by faith; Christ is seen by faith, 883, 39; 1003, 29; 1397, 57; 1357, 156. Our voice is faith, 1280, 42. Its cry is great, 1211, 8. For those who believe in the Lord, consolation is in the Lord’s mercy, 1194, 2. Faith presents us to God, 787, 20. Faith is what obtains gifts; humility is what commends what has been offered to God, 585, 67. Is anything more precious than faith? 825, 24. It is your price, by which divine mysteries are bought, 500, 45. It is our price, which acquired all human beings for Christ, 963, 21. It diminishes sin, 698, 63. It will aid toward forgiveness even if there has been some offense in one’s works, 1254, 26. It can cleanse from every sin, 1480, 42. Every sin is washed away through the mysteries of faith, 1518, 66. If you preserve it, even if you have died like a serpent, you too will rise again, 818, 8. God preferred human salvation to be sought through faith rather than works, and for what reason, 893, 14. God requires not bare tears but faith, 1539, 162. If anyone does not believe in Christ, he deprives himself of the universal benefit, 1077, 57. For one who does not possess the warmth of faith, it would have been more tolerable not to have received faith than to have neglected it, 990, 24. Faith alone marks each person, 1293, 36. The faith of the common people is generally more steadfast than that of the rich and priests, 1189, 17. Where faith is small, there is disturbance, 1353, 70. It must not be split but remain solid, 1529, 119. All are adulterers who desire to adulterate the truth of faith and wisdom, 1472, 9. For the devout, a lapse of love does not impede faith, 1379, 98.
