Let faith be the guide before you on your journey, 1143, 11. It is our door, which, if strong, secures the whole house, 1118, 14. There is no truer homeland than faith, 1184, 2. The crumbs are, as it were, certain doctrines of faith, 1474, 15. The wealth of faith is never exhausted, 1462, 212. It is not burdened by age, ibid., 213. Heaven and earth will pass away, but faith remains, 849, 17. The faith of believers is primary; confession is its execution, 834, 4. Perfect confession of Christ seeks both devotion of spirit and profession of voice, 1235, 49. The confessor’s veiled reply is not enough; there must be an open confession, 1522, 87. The garment of faith consists of the proclamation of heavenly things and the blood of the Lord’s passion, 617, 77. When the case of religion was being tried, faith ought to have occupied the judgment seat, and faithlessness to have been set up as the accused, 467, 25. Faith is owed first as a pledge, 1270, 12. It is a moral rule for everyone that those who demand faith should establish faith, 1288, 19.

**SON**: the generation of the Son from the Father has no temporal beginning, 1213, 17. In God he is another person, but one in power, 1487, 66. He is the Only-begotten, not one among those begotten, 1487, 65. He alone is the image of God, possessing such likeness to the Father that he has unity of divinity and fullness, 128, 41. He is the face of the Father, 1192, 28. By nature, as consubstantial with the Father, all things are rightly proper to the Son; they are not bestowed by grace as a gift, 1426, 67. He is the wisdom of God by nature, not by progress, 1383, 1. He knows the thoughts of hearts, as does the Father, 200, 37. The Father’s equal suffers no injury because he is sent, 1503, 1. Although sent, he is not inferior because the Father sends him, 1302, 65. Why he does nothing from himself, 1230, 32. The Son of God was hidden in the Law, veiled in the prophets, and completed in the preaching of the Gospel, 1456, 188. Before he was born from the Virgin, he was seen, 1274, 24. Although he assumed what he was not, he nevertheless did not cease to be what he was, 730, 64. Although I may not know how he was born, I must not fail to know that he was born, 1353, 71. Why he assumed flesh and death, 435, 44. He became an angel to angels and a prophet to prophets, 773, 18. How he is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, 288, 16. He thought that he should claim nothing for himself from this world, 340, 62. See **CHRIST**, **TRINITY**.

**CHILDREN** are the rewards of marriage, 1282, 2; 1509, 22. It is no small gift of God to give children—propagators of the race and heirs of succession—and why? 1276, 30. It was considered disgraceful not to have children, and this was punished by the authority of civil laws, 1320, 18. It is a shame for women not to have the rewards of marriage, for whom this alone is the reason for marrying, 1282, 45. As we are about to depart from this body, we take pleasure in the final touch of our dear pledges and are consoled by this provision for the journey, 510, 83. Love of children has often recalled many from completing martyrdom, 1163, 18. Why a father disciplines his son more harshly than a master does a servant, 1145, 15. How greatly children ought to honor their parents so that they may possess the inheritance of the final blessing, 513, 1. Sacred Scripture frequently declares works to be children, 657, 14. The seed of the saints is greater in faith than in generation, 1330, 44.

**END**: what it is, 955, 1. The true end is one that will not be the end of one person but of all, 849, 17. Whatever has a beginning also has an end; and for whatever an end is given, it is clear that a beginning has been given, 6, 10.

**FIRMAMENT**: from where it received its name, 31, 16. Whether it is the same as heaven, 25, 8; 30, 15. Why God commanded it to exist between water and water, 787, 21.

**VARIETIES OF LEAVES**, 57, 61. And remedies are made from the same leaves, 47, 37.

**THE SPRING** that watered paradise: what was it? 149, 12.

**ANTS**: their industry should be imitated, 118, 16.

**FORTITUDE** pierces every resistance and clings to no obstacles, 151, 17. Those who endure the numbness of wounds more than their pain do not possess the glory of fortitude, 1516, 56. As faith is the incentive of fortitude, so fortitude is the support of faith, 1437, 118. What its effects are, 1371, 67.

**BROTHERS**: we are all generated by one and the same mother, 267, 94. By a certain right of kinship we are all joined together like brothers, and we ought to love one another as though born from the same womb, 323, 28. Among brothers, inheritance ought to be divided not by an intervening judge but by piety acting as arbiter, 1439, 122.

**FRAUDULENT** people must be avoided, 88, 21.

**FOREHEAD** reveals the disposition of the mind through its appearance, 136, 58.

**VARIETIES OF FRUITS**, 58, 62.

**COOT** nourishes with its own young the eaglet abandoned by the eagle, 104, 61. It senses the disturbance of the sea, 97, 43.

**ROPES**: what they are called, 1499, 21. They are used by those who measure the boundaries of fields and mark off the extents of properties, 1070, 40.

## G
GAD: the blessing is explained, 524, 35ff.

ROOSTERS: their crowing is shown to be not only pleasant but also useful, 112, 88.

GANGES: flows against India, 150, 14.

JOY: is a fruit of the Holy Spirit, 700, 12; 1237, 54.

GROANING: what kind is good, and that it is the first gift of the Holy Spirit, 831, 37.

ASTROLOGERS: set their mouths toward heaven—and in what manner? 666, 12.

GENTILES: seemed to seek their god in caves and the dwellings of caverns, 935, 24. How greatly the benefits Christ bestowed on his own differ from those which the gods bestowed on the Gentiles, 1404, 88. By what method those who are called from the Gentiles to the Church are to be instructed, 1408, 104ff. How they ought to read the sacred Scriptures, 172, 58. They maintain with Christians the exchange of greetings and similar services, 1425, 62. The Lord does not forbid us to dine with them, 1359, 18. The field bought with the price of death benefited them for burial, 960, 13. Their case is more tolerable than that of the Jews, 990, 24. Those who came into the Church under Christian emperors and pretended to be Christians are rebuked, 1235, 49. Many of them have mercy and sobriety, but they have no fruit because they have no faith, 757, 41. See FAITH and MARRIAGE.

KIND: it appears immortal, but the individual persons are mortal, 314, 4.

GEON: the Nile circles the land of Egypt or Ethiopia, 150, 14. It signifies a certain cleft in the earth, 151, 26.

THE FEAST DAY OF GERVASIUS AND PROTASIUS, 1037, 16.

GIANTS: who they were in the time of Noah, 230, 7ff. Fables introduce them as wishing to fight against the heavenly powers, 278, 127.

GIMEL: the third letter according to the Hebrews; in Latin it is called “retribution,” 993, 1.

GLORY: it is good to be subject to Christ, 1224, 7. It is not the portion of a single crown but the reward of all crowns, 1161, 11. If Christ’s reproach is glory, how great is his glory! 1031, 41. The glory of the world does not descend with the sinner, but the glory of virtue rises with the innocent, 953, 24.

GOMORRAH AND SODOM: in their native language the Chaldeans called them “blindness” and “barrenness,” 257, 69.

THE WARS OF THE GOTHS, 1516, 10.

GRACE: God’s grace must be acknowledged, but nature must not be ignored, 1478, 31. In what the spirit of life and the spirit of grace differ, 1277, 33. We have a great adversary who cannot be defeated by us without God’s favor, [Col. 2259] 1327, 37. No one without the true Jesus can grasp the uncertain and hidden things of wisdom, 944, 20. It is not in our power to direct our journey according to our own will, 783, 15. Everywhere the Lord’s power cooperates with human efforts, so that no one can begin anything without the Lord, 1309, 84. No one can be perfect and safe without God’s favor, 980, 17. Since the hereditary bond of iniquity has clung to human minds, the help of the liberator is necessary, 1015, 22. God gave grace and restored nature, 1156, 42. Nature is the work of the Creator; grace is the gift of the Redeemer, 505, 63. Whatever holy thing you have conceived is God’s gift, God’s inspiration, God’s grace, 204, 45. Every creature, whatever good it possesses, received it from Christ, 1166, 30. That God should be honored by a holy person is God’s grace, 1269, 10. God calls those whom he deems worthy and makes religious whom he wills, 1417, 27. Grace is commended by the privilege of eternal action and by the graciousness of heavenly protection, 632, 18. The medicine of salvation is sought for the wound, grace for health, 982, 3. Heavenly teaching can change vicious affections, and divine action can pour the practices of piety into sacrilegious hearts, 701, 76. Where grace is concerned, we are saved not by the merit of works or the justification of virtues, but by the generosity of the giver and the choice of the redeemer, 906, 47. It is dull-hearted not to attribute the good one does to the author of grace, 196, 25ff. The righteous refer to God the author whatever good they have obtained, 199, 34. Whoever attributes everything to grace will possess the promised land, 891, 12. David does not think it a matter of his own virtue but of heavenly grace if he is not abandoned by Christ, 839, 55. Every soul is called to Christ’s grace, 930, 12. So that it may be redeemed from guilt without payment, 945, 2. Christ’s manifest mercy is proclaimed toward all, since those who perish perish through their own negligence, while those who are saved are delivered by Christ’s judgment, 221, 11. The Lord calls even the thoughtless whom he has mercy upon, 1419, 33. Christ brings with him the increase of grace when he comes, 1038, 6. God’s grace makes us more blessed than our own innocence, 837, 47. Whoever has the spirit of grace lacks nothing, 1277, 35. The Law has measure, but grace is overflowing, 909, 56. The Law is within measure; grace exceeds measure, 1434, 98. The fervor of eternal grace excludes the fervor of worldly grace, 1241, 10. Spiritual grace cleansed us from every stain of excess, 1177, 24. Without our labor, not from works but from faith, God forgave us sins by his grace, 885, 1. God shines upon the righteous through grace and upon the unrighteous through mercy: granting the former the reward of their merits and forgiving the latter their sins, 984, 9. Those who perish through their own sin are freed by the Lord’s mercy, 1229, 29. Grace differs according to our merits, but the mercy of the divine work is the same, 1461, 208. The good Lord demands earnest effort and supplies strength, 1400, 72. The grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow workings, 1288, 19. You yourself are the author either of your injury or of your grace; divine action makes no mistake, 919, 77. Let the one who can bear the fruit of grace do so; let the one who owes it bear the fruit of repentance, 1306, 76. God often abandons those whom he wishes to be tested, but he abandons completely those whom he forsakes, 980, 18. See CHRIST and GOD.

GRATITUDE: Virtue knows no measure of grace; not content merely to return what it has received, it wishes to heap up what it has taken, 1373, 74. In exchanges of thanks it is not enough to return what one has received; one must enhance what one returns, 217, 23. Both the one who returns thanks possesses grace, and the one who possesses it repays it by the very fact that he possesses it, 1389, 25. Human beings learn from dogs how to return a favor, 119, 17. A steadfast memory of God’s benefits must persevere in gratitude, and obedience must not be lacking, 197, 30. Neither by day, nor by night, nor at any time ought we to cease giving thanks, 1075, 52.

GRATIAN, THE EMPEROR: abandoned and betrayed by his own, 961, 17. Surrounded by calumnies and deceit, 963, 21ff. Burial is denied him, ibid., 24.

CRANES: their vigilance in guarding and their order while flying, 99, 50–51.

GLUTTONY: expelled the ruler from paradise; abstinence recalled the wanderer to paradise, 538, 7. What disturbances it usually brings into a household, 542, 24. Those who serve the belly and the throat walk in the womb, 179, 74. See DRUNKENNESS.

THE USEFULNESS OF THE THROAT, 140, 69. A person’s throat is an open tomb, in which deadly treachery and dead words are buried, 1535, 141.

## H

THE HEIR: for the human heir, the description of a co-heir is a loss, but Christ’s inheritance is undivided, 1155, 41.

HERESIES: while all attack one another, they recoil upon themselves, 732, 69. Like Eve, they test the firmness of faith with feminine feeling, 1459, 200.

HERETICS: are assailants of the faith and enemies of the truth, 1132, 6. Whoever does not possess the truth of faith has a false imitation, [Col. 2260] 658, 15. The deadly doctrine of heretics consists of false insanities, 860, 4. Mani, Marcion, Sabellius, Arius, and Photinus are nothing other than brothers of the Jews, 1473, 13. A heretic arguing about the Lord’s generation according to worldly usage is rich in words and poor in strength, 1372, 70. Christ is not present in these disputations, 1110, 20. Many of them wish to claim bodily continence, so that they may obtain credibility for their assertion through the testimony of sober flesh, 248, 49. We ought to be circumspect in answering heretics or Jews, 1502, 34. Let no heretic deceive you because he can produce certain examples from the holy Scriptures, 1340, 26. He can assail what is imperfect; he cannot overthrow what is perfect, 1114, 29. How grievous his bites are, 1422, 51. His treachery belongs to the Midianites, 1198, 11. Heretics are compared with wolves, 1037, 16; 1421, 48ff.; and with foxes, 1418, 31; 1421, 47. Understand all heretics and schismatics to be separated from the kingdom of God and from the Church, 1432, 95.

HALCYON: where does it live, and for how many days does it raise and feed its young? 96, 40ff. Sailors call these days of anticipated calm “halcyon days” (Halcyonidas), ibid.

HARMONY: what it is, 1470, 3.

HE: this letter signifies in Latin “is” or “I live,” 1018, 1.

HELLEBORE: the ailments of a sick body are often relieved by it, 48, 39.

THE HEPTATEUCH: what it signifies, 1241, 12.

THE JUICES OF HERBS: wholesome, 47, 37. It is the physicians’ task to know their powers, 56, 57.

HEROD: although related by no kinship to the Jews, he fraudulently seized the kingdom by a false claim, 1329, 41. In him all the impious are signified, 1525, 99.

HERODIAS: sought iniquity through wicked arts in the killing of John the Baptist, 771, 13.

HETH: in Latin interpretation it is called “terror,” 1056, 1.

HIPPOCRATES: did not accept Critias’s opinion concerning the soul, 266, 92.

THE SWALLOW: its diligence, industry, and devotion toward its young, 102, 56–57. It remedies their blindness, ibid.

HUMAN BEING: why the Greek word ἄνθρωπος (anthrōpos) is so called, 130, 46. What a human being is and in what part especially he consists, 357, 3. He consists of soul, body, and spirit, 207, 6. He is God’s creature, the most excellent of all things on earth, 341, 63. He is God’s most precious work, 1088, 6ff. He possesses something the angels do not, 1091, 14. There are two generations of the human being: one according to the image of God, the other according to the formation from the clay of the earth, 263, 86. The Word is not “according to the image,” but the image of God; the human being is not the image, but is “according to the image of God,” 1064, 23; 1091, 16. God established him above all earthly things, 264, 86. Whoever remembers that he was created in the image and likeness of God does not wish what is corruptible and earthly to be his own, 886, 4. Virtue makes him glorious, faith makes him rare, and the image makes him precious, 1089, 10. God created him for incorruption, but human beings, departing from nature’s gift, made themselves subject to death, 760, 48. Why did God approve him only after the woman had been made? 165, 46–47. Why is God said to have rested after creating him? 142, 76. The nature of things would have vanished unless, by divine providence, one to use them had been added, 1088, 6. Why does God permit a few things to exist that harm the human being? 93, 31. A human being ought to know himself, 127, 39; 132, 50. This saying was spoken not by the Pythian Apollo but by Solomon, ibid. Before the Law, human beings did not know that they could be dissolved through the corruption of clay and had been formed from hardened mud, 1137, 20. They ought always to attend to themselves: why, and how? 133, 50ff. We cannot know ourselves more fully unless we first know what the nature of all living creatures is, 114, 3. In comparison with the angels, the human being seems to be a dumb beast, 670, 26. Whoever has not understood is compared with beasts; whoever understands is compared with angels, 952, 20. He is compared with good and bad fish, 85, 15. He is a bird that ought to fly from earth into heaven, 1154, 38ff. Why, when he was destroyed, were the other irrational creatures also destroyed? 231, 10; 239, 31ff. In what respects does he surpass or fall below the other living creatures? 850, 20; 1213, 14. A human being must beware lest he be bent down like cattle, 117, 10. His great duty is to be born more for the world than for himself, 1088, 6. Who are called “square” human beings? 233, 13. In the human being there are two minds and two laws, 1479, 49ff. The petitions of the outer and inner human being are not identical, nor are they all approved by Christ, 782, 13. How the Lord joined both to one another through unity of will, 807, 64. The inner human being was crucified, buried, and raised again in Christ, 794, 37. For us the old human being, once stripped off, causes less labor than when put back on, 851, 22.

THE PENALTY OF MURDER, 267, 94ff. Those who shed human blood kill God’s work, 131, 48.

HONOR: consists not only in honoring but also in generosity, 1490, 75. Often worldly honor departs before it has arrived, 1341, 28. Where someone is thought to be honored and exalted, there you may understand that, like the courses of rivers, he has passed by more quickly than he came, [Col. 2261] 795, 39.

THE GARDEN: that which Plato elsewhere called Jupiter’s garden and elsewhere the garden of the mind—where did he derive it from? 398, 19.

HOSPITALITY: is commended, and all are shown to be bound to it, 295, 34ff. The religious observance of hospitality provides a venerable form of the commandment, 1398, 66. The laws of hospitality must be preserved, 101, 54. So great is the grace of hospitality that we willingly transfer the dangers of others onto ourselves, 1364, 35. To be hospitable in expectation of being repaid is an attitude of greed, 1458, 195.

TO RESIST AN ENEMY: to resist the enemy shut up within you is more than to resist one who is kept at a distance, 468, 29. Within yourself you have a war against yourself, 1070, 39. Virtue must be honored even in an enemy, 687, 36.

HUMILITY: failed in paradise; therefore it came from heaven, 1024, 32. It arose from guilt, 1083, 14. It found praise for virtue even in Christ, 1146, 19. We learned it not only from Christ’s speech but also from his action, 1228, 20—and how, 1157, 46. Why did he present himself as its author? 1515, 51. It is despised in this world but approved by God’s judgment, 1006, 41. It is good, especially when voluntary devotion is joined to it, 1148, 23. See CHRIST.

Nothing is more precious than humility, 1089, 10. Nothing is more exalted, 1480, 40. It is a great thing in all circumstances to maintain the measure of humility, 1147, 20. The righteous glory in it, 1224, 7. The holier someone is, the humbler he is, 646, 22. Grace shines forth more brightly in the humble, 1020, 7. Power deceives; humility does not abandon, 2146, 19. It brings no loss, 1227, 18. By desiring nothing, one attains everything one disdains, 1147, 20. The whole aim of our striving is that we be humble and follow the truth, 1222, 3. It is not remarkable in old age, but it is rare and wondrous in the young, 1204, 31. When we are humbled, we recognize our sins, and by that very humility we cleanse our offenses, 1097, 30. When humility has been filled out, sin is dissolved, 1087, 4. While the humble are subjected to and oppressed by the rich, they are exalted and suddenly shine forth, 795, 39. Humility is not defined by the pursuit of every kind of honor, 1515, 51. It is not always a virtue, but may also belong to affliction, 1122, 28. For many, crime humbles them unto ruin, 919, 76. There is the humility of labor and weariness, and there is also the humility of virtue and purpose, 1226, 15. Even if it belongs to disturbance rather than virtue, it often generates virtue, 1083, 14.

THE HUNS, OR CHUNNI: their peoples obey only the laws of chance, 603, 39. They are subject to moneylenders, ibid. They wage war by every means, ibid. The Chunni rose against the Alans, the Alans against the Goths, the Goths against the Taifali and the Sarmatians, 1506, 10.

WINTER: it is winter for us when the sun lingers in the southern regions—and why? 72, 21.

HYMNS: God is truly praised in them, and in them there is remission of sins, 973, 3. In the morning hymns are spoken and psalms are sung, 552, 55. Let us not cease concerning the praises of God, whether by speaking a hymn or by singing the divine glory at every moment, 897, 23.

## I

THE ANIMAL SEEN BY THE JAUNDICED: and the usefulness of its horn, 1094, 23.

JEDITHUN: was a prophet and sang psalms with his six sons, 955, 3.

IDOLATRY: the serpent was its author in paradise, 174, 61. It is the error of the Gentiles to venerate pieces of wood, 1064, 23. They worship wood because they think it is the image of God, 1095, 25. The Church knows empty ideas and vain figures of images no more, but knows the true substance of the Trinity, 429, 27. The error of the nations, by which they attributed divine honor to the sun alone, was refuted by God, 43, 27. By venerating metals and stones, the Gentiles drew upon themselves a similar rigidity of stupor, 1132, 5; 1305, 75.

IGNORANCE AND DESIRE: are illnesses of the soul, 376, 60.

FIRE AND WATER: why their nature is necessary, 28, 12. The Lord came to send fire upon the earth, to illuminate the souls of all, kindle zeal, and burn away guilt, 848, 15. God’s utterance is fiery in three ways: either because it cleanses, or because it kindles, or because it illuminates, 1201, 21. Divine fire cleanses the mind and consumes error, 1200, 20. It diminishes sin and feeds upon guilt with its own heat, 848, 15. It burns in order to correct the sinner’s conscience; it does not consume in order to destroy, 1200, 20.

THE FIRE ASSIGNED TO THE DEVIL AND HIS ANGELS: what is it? 998, 17. There is neither any bodily gnashing of teeth nor any perpetual fire of bodily flames, 1460, 204. All who desire to return to paradise, whether John or Peter, must be tested through fire, 1225, 12ff. How the righteous and sinners will pass through fire, 789, 26. In the repayment of merits, fire illuminates the righteous and consumes the impious, 66, 10. Sinners seek the abyss, where there is the darkness of shadows, 787, 21.

EMPERORS: in establishing laws they ought to be stricter, but in imposing punishments merciful, 823, 19. You, emperor, rescue by signing a pardon the one being led to death, and you have dissolved your own sins, 1071, 42. Those who are closer to the emperor obtain a greater share of imperial favor, 1370, 61. In cities the images of good rulers endure, while the images of tyrants are destroyed, 670, 24. Whoever crowns the emperor’s image certainly honors the one whose image he has crowned; and whoever despises the statue seems to have committed an injury against the emperor, 1095, 25. The emperor’s daughter was summoned to sacrifice for the purpose of transporting the Greek armies, 1410, 108.

IMPIETY: is contrary to nature, 759, 47. It is a kind of mother of sins, 217, 25. The first commands of the prophet David are to flee impiety, not remain in sin, and meditate on the Law, 772, 17.

THE IMPIOUS: even if they seem to live, they are more wretched than all the dead, 220, 31. They delight in the errors of others, 273, 115. How miserable their portion is, 660, 21. They are members of the devil, 819, 9. Why God turns away from their prayers, 220, 31. Their success is no small temptation for the righteous, 1047, 10ff. How incredible is the speed of their extinction! 669, 22. In the good, the heavenly image always remains; in the impious, it is erased and cast down, 669, 24. How their journey perishes while their substance is preserved, 765, 58. Their names are written where they chose to live, 951, 19. The punishment of the impious is no small one: not to possess the rest of death, 660, 18.

WICKEDNESS: increases through use and practice, 240, 34.

THE WICKED: is so called who wishes to destroy uprightness by his malice, 956, 17. He is constricted within himself, strangled by the snares of his own malice, 1042, 32. He is troubled more by present things than by future ones, 220, 32.

THE IMPUDENT MAN: a description of a certain one, 320, 10. See GREED, LUST, INCONTINENCE.

IMPUNITY: nourishes boldness, 240, 34.

INCONTINENCE: of human beings is rebuked, 92, 30.

THE USE OF INDICTIONS, 253, 60.

THE INDIAN OCEAN: is higher than the Egyptian sea, 37, 10.

INDIFFERENT THINGS: do not possess the strength of vigorous virtue, but they increase and spread its grace, 229, 5. They have harmed many, 276, 122.

THE UNDERWORLD. See FIRE.

WEAKNESS: is the workshop of virtue and more useful than grace, 796, 42. Let no one test the weak or cast down the infirm—and why? 1486, 61.

NATURAL TALENT: use it so that you may look toward heavenly things and not seek earthly ones, 1028, 31.

THE UNGRATEFUL PERSON: is one who expects the debt of gratitude to be demanded from him, 260, 78. In prosperous circumstances forgetfulness of a benefit quickly creeps in, 495, 33.

LOVING ENEMIES: in what sense Christ commands it, 1100, 41; 1162, 15ff. Nothing can offend the person whose custom it is to forgive, 1476, 24. The righteous remain silent and pray against the insolent, 845, 9–10. How the righteous prefer to accuse themselves rather than deform another—even one by whom they suffer injury, 1049, 18ff. The purpose of the righteous is far more perfect and powerful than all others: to intervene for persecutors and excuse sinners, 1051, 23. It is a good shield for the triumphant to defend an enemy whom one could strike, 846, 11. See CHARITY, INJURY.

INIQUITY: shamelessly seizes what does not belong to it and does not revere its author, 259, 75. It is greater that iniquity itself be erased than that sin be removed, 698, 62. Iniquity has such laws that it hates innocence and loves crime, 1526, 102. Where iniquity prevails, it is recalled by no exchange of good works, 906, 46. Iniquity is forgiven through the washing, while sin is covered by good deeds, 692, 49. The punishment of iniquity is postponed by the addition of bitter interest, 820, 13.

THE UNJUST PERSON: who should be called unjust, 950, 17.

INJURY: must be endured with equanimity, 1525, 97. One must not repay those who lie in ambush with an equivalent injury, 1150, 28. God wishes his disciples to be patient under injuries and not readily strike back, much less strike, 1087, 3. The times of injuries are contests of temptation and examinations of testing, 685, 30. It is one thing to call oneself worthy of a reward and another to call oneself unworthy of an injury, 1171, 10. See CHARITY, ENEMY.

INJUSTICE: flee it, for it makes those still living into the dead, 1242, 13. The soul of the unjust does not cry out as one living, because it is dead to God, 1211, 8. The unjust person is useless to others and harmful to himself, 768, 6. Whatever he says is iniquity, which is referred back to its author, 768, 6.

INNOCENCE: is later in time than wickedness but older in the nobility of its merits, 188, 11–12. Every sin is servile; innocence is free, 490, 20. It itself sees God, 814, 81. The defense of innocence consists not in a loud voice or in the advocacy of a forensic plea, but in integrity of conscience, 1231, 35. Innocence does not love to defend itself with many words, 617, 78. When its fruit is brought forth, 806, 63.

THE INNOCENT: harms no one and sins against no one, 881, 35. In the Innocents, although infancy is without the use of reason, it nevertheless confesses the God for whom it is killed, [Col. 2263] 1298, 49.

DISOBEDIENCE: was the cause of death, 159, 35. Whoever transgresses God’s command is stripped and made naked, and becomes contemptible to himself, 175, 65.

THE FOOLISH PERSON: is one who has bad judgment, 950, 17.

INSTRUCTION: has such power that it conquers nature, 205, 3.

UNDERSTANDING: how understanding, wisdom, and discipline differ, 886, 7. Understanding is God’s gift, 1093, 19; 1180, 34. Our precious treasure is understanding, 1115, 4. The fullness of virtue is the beginning of understanding, 1208, 45ff. There is understanding leading to death, just as there is prudence leading to destruction, 1249, 9.

INTEMPERANCE: kindles lust, generates indigestion, and creates corruption, 238, 29.

THE INTEMPERATE: are judged contemptible in their own estimation, 446, 6.

THE INTESTINES: why their coils are intertwined, 140, 61; 237, 28. Their double covering, 237, 29.

ENVY: quickly follows prosperity, 303, 65. It corrupts nature’s gentleness through the thickening of malice, 1085, 19. How it is to be appeased, 319, 15; 463, 14; 465, 21. How greatly the Lord rejects the envious, 1346, 46ff.

THE INVISIBLE: what it is, 42, 25.

ANGER: how serious a passion it is, 785, 18. It is a grave teacher of sin, ibid. Where there is anger and grievous sadness, the Word does not remain there, 1119, 18. For the powerful, anger is burdensome; for the wicked, depravity; for the righteous, the weakness of their condition, 632, 16. How greatly it must be guarded against, 508, 78. It is excellent to temper emotion through deliberation; and restraining anger is considered no less a virtue than not becoming angry at all, 1368, 54. Where there is the fullness of charity, there is no anger, 1417, 28.

THE RAINBOW: why it signifies future rain, 269, 103. Which bow God placed in the clouds, and why, ibid.

ISAAC: in Latin signifies “laughter,” 355, 1. He prophesies by speech, not by knowledge, 306, 74. Why he is read as having been gathered to his own kindred rather than to the people, 185, 6. In him there is a figure of Christ’s generation and passion, 186, 7; 288, 20; 305, 71–72; 355, 1; 862, 12. See CHRIST.

ISSACHAR: the blessing is mystically explained concerning Christ, 522, 30–31.

THE PEOPLES OF ITALY: their heat is tempered by tranquil peace, 1501, 32.

## J
## J

**JACOB.** Why he is introduced as a shepherd of sheep, 195, 24. He bore the figure of goodness, 184, 4. Placed amid the greatest dangers, he did not lose but rather acquired the blessedness of life, 459, 1 and following. By self-restraint and faith he overcame the traces of human passions, 194, 23. How perfect he was, 459, 3 and following. He foresaw Christ on earth, 464, 15. And the Church shining in Christ, 472, 34. How blessed he was at the very moment of death, 471, 35 and following.

**JAMES.** The first to ascend the priestly throne, 1413, 9.

**BOASTING.** No one ought to boast, 123, 91; 1418, 29. Boasting deceives even the strong, 1341, 27. It is insolent even in one who is upright and just, 832, 38. It is empty, 1226, 15. While people desire to boast of the glory of their virtue, they withdraw from the place of their merits, 1340, 21. Let there be no boasting about pre-eminence, but contention in humility, 1515, 51. Boasting is a companion of those who turn away from the truth, 327, 33. If boasting must be avoided, how much more must no one boast of false things as though they were true, 191, 16.

**DARTS.** They are often hurled back against those who have thrown them, 789, 25.

**JAPHETH.** He is called “breadth,” 276, 124.

**LIVER.** It is stretched by honey and its bitterness is tempered by food, 547, 39.

**FASTING.** Its origin and antiquity, 537, 6 and following. Just as the human race had lost grace through desire for the forbidden fruit, so its strength had to be restored through fasting, 867, 1. Christ fasted so that you might not depart from the commandment, 1285, 10.

**FASTING.** What it ought to be, 545, 34 and following. Boasting must be avoided in fasting, 547, 40. A prescribed fast must not be broken before the end of the day, 1073, 46. How great is the power of fasting, 123, 28; 536, 2 and following; 540, 541; 544, 29 and following; 545, 35; 547, 40. It is burdensome to no one, 542, 23. It is the seasoning of food, 544, 32. It is a good covering, 665, 10. It commends us, 1361, 23. Fast, if you wish to conquer the allurements of the flesh, 1340, 24. Fasting is the slayer of sin, 547, 37–38. By the fast of forty days, and by more frequent prayers, let us lessen the punishments of our sins, 244, 44. If anyone wishes to obtain the fruit of the resurrection, he must not be a transgressor of the mystical fast, 1338, 15.

**JEPHTHAH.** He was overcome by his own vow, 681, 16.

**JERICHO.** What it signifies, 1427, 73.

**JERUSALEM.** Having been conquered in triumph by the Roman army, it blazed with the fire that was kindled there, 1242, 14. One must stand in Jerusalem and flee from Babylon, 749, 26.

**JESUS SON OF NUN.** A figure of Christ, 944, 21. He commanded the heavenly lights, not by his own power but through the mystery of Christ, 714, 24. The likeness of the sacred name delivered him, 1203, 29. See CHRIST.

[Col. 2264]

**JETHRO.** He is called “superfluous,” 195, 24.

**JEZEBEL.** That is, “outpouring of vanity,” 431, 34.

**JOACHIM.** The one called Joachim in the Books of Kings is named Jeconiah by Jeremiah, 1328, 40. There were two Joachims, that is, two Jeconiahs, 1331, 46.

**JOHN.** He did not yet have the spirit of life, but he had the spirit of grace, 1277, 33. He was anointed like a good athlete and trained in his mother’s womb, 1291, 29. He did not know the hindrances of infancy, ibid., 30. His birth was ennobled not only by his parents but also by his ancestors, 1271, 15. Why he received the name “Voice,” 802, 57. He is compared with Christ, 1285, 10; 1406, 96. Greater than all the prophets, but among those born of women, not of a virgin, 1382, 110. His comparison with Elijah is elegant, 1278, 36. Whether he did not believe that the Christ whom he had believed would come would also die, 1378, 98. Whoever speaks of John prophesies Christ, 1292, 32. When belief is given to him, it is given to Christ, 1278, 37. He saw the hidden things of the heart, 1307, 78. Born as a forerunner, he died as a forerunner, 1279, 38. He is a type of the Law, 725, 48; 1303, 68; 1377, 94. He received the role of the Jewish people, 1308, 81. In Christ’s forerunner I ought to recognize nothing more than the building-up of the Church that was arising, 1305, 75.

**THE SOUL OF JOHN.** Darkened by vice, but already made beautiful through the washing, 984, 8. He was a young man who corrected his way in his youth, 983, 7. He touched greater and higher things, 1541, 172. Some doubted concerning his death, 1225, 12. He died, 1411, 4 and following. Even in the death of the body the order of his life was not interrupted, 1412, 4. See EVANGELISTS.

**JOB.** The malice of the devil made the virtue and patience of the holy man more illustrious, 148, 9; 1145, 16. He was stronger when sick than when healthy, 654, 3. How many afflictions were heaped together at once so that he might perish, 1123, 29. Why, placed in temptation, he spoke mysteries, 1345, 40. The hand of the Lord took everything away from him and restored everything, 855, 33. His praise is the condemnation of the Angel, 824, 21.

**JOD.** In Latin meaning it is called “confession,” or “desolation,” 1086, 1.

**JONAH.** Water corrected him whom earthly things had led astray, 94, 35; 922, 83; 1433, 97.

**JORDAN.** The name signifies “descent,” 327, 34; 422, 12; 642, 14.

**JOSEPH.** A figure of Christ, 267, 25; 679, 12; 893 and following; 905, 43 and following. Even in his dreams he was a type of Christ, 485, 7–8. And he was sent to his brothers, 486, 9 and following. And he was sold, 487, 14; 490, 20. And likewise in the other actions of his life, 498 and following. The mysteries of Christ were prefigured in him, 526, 47 and following. How bravely he endured hardships and bitter trials, 1123, 31. He was a mirror of chastity, 483, 1–2; 1332, 47. His chastity is commended, 491, 22 and following. For the sake of chastity he underwent martyrdom, 493, 26. His chastity would never have come to our remembrance if the wife of that lord had not tested his feelings, 148, 9. Guilt did not seize him, prison did not enclose him, Egypt did not discolor him, 1003, 27. His temptation is the consecration of his virtue, 1345, 42. The individual parts of his blessing are explained, 526, 46 and following. Joseph had the crown of chastity, Paul that of justice, Peter that of faith, 1161, 11.

**JOSEPH.** Why Joseph’s genealogy rather than Mary’s is described in the Gospel, 1314, 3. He could not violate the temple of the Holy Spirit, the womb of the mystery, or the mother of the Lord, 1284, 6. The Lord, placed on the cross, made clear that he had not had relations with Mary his wife, 1283, 4.

**JUDAH.** A type of Christ, 518, 16; 679, 11. And of the Lord’s Passion, 1332, 47. The tribes of Judah and Levi were joined by the intermingling of their lineage, 518, 16.

**JUDAS.** Why Christ gave a command to Judas, who was about to transgress, or chose him though he was to betray him, 161, 39. By what reasoning he was chosen not through lack of foresight but through providence, 1366, 45. He was just when he was joined to the number of the apostles, 940, 9. He was contemplating selling Christ, but the great grace of the Lord and certain consolations of paternal compassion were calling him back, 844, 6. The wretched man perished at the meal at which others were saved, 607, 47. The thief saw the Lord’s kingdom in his own cross, which Judas could not see at Christ’s banquet, 864, 17. He went out from Christ’s banquet to the devil’s brigandage; he went out from the grace of sanctification into the snare of death, 873, 17. He could not endure the Lord’s patience, though he betrayed his majesty, 863, 17. The servant betrays the Lord, the disciple his teacher, the chosen man his author, 1518, 63. Some think he should be excused, but wrongly, 875, 21. He had received the office of sanctifying others, 876, 22. With his own mouth he led himself to death, 769, 8. He sought avarice and found sacrilege, 771, 14. He was a figure of the unbelieving Jewish people, 880, 32.

**THE JEWISH PEOPLE.** At what times they had kings, 1319, 16. It was a gift of the Jewish people to discern spirits, so that it might know whom it ought to include among the prophets, 1265, 1. The ten tribes of the Jews were led away to the Assyrians, while the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, as though guilty of the graver crime, passed into Babylon, 755, 37. Although those who were led away into Babylon [Col. 2265] seemed to have been subjected because of their sins, they were nevertheless regarded as much better than the nations, 908, 53. At some point the torrent of spiritual outpouring ceased among the Jewish people, 774, 20. Why their offering and sacrifice ceased after Christ’s coming, 861, 10. God took away from them the prophets, took away the sacred rites, took away the voice, 1279, 40. They persecute Christ with hostile hatred, although, if they were converted, he did not deny them a remedy, 862, 14. They are no longer excusable, 630, 13. Their hardness is rebuked, 257, 70; 1532, 128. They possess chastity and great diligence in reading, but they are without fruit, and why, 757, 41. The thief recognized Christ in his own sufferings, whom the Jews did not recognize in his benefactions, 864, 17. They will be punished more severely than the Gentiles, and why, 1486, 64. They are from the father the devil, not by succession of flesh but by succession of crime, 1349, 54. Worse than their teacher the devil, 1350, 61. Why the sign of Jonah is summoned to rebuke their unbelief, 946, 25. All Jewish matters are like parables, that is, like figures requiring interpretation, 909, 55–56. A Jew believes not in the truth but in the shadow, 1221, 43. He is ignorant of the spiritual Law, 1131, 4. He interprets its words bodily, 175, 66; 1242, 12. He does not keep the Law in his heart, 1025, 24. Why among the Jews there is not the law of God, 1206, 36. They seem to have believed neither the psalms nor the prophetic lamentations, 1358, 5. The Jewish people are rich, Christians poor, 728, 57. The Apostle shows that the Jew has rightly been separated from the body of the Church, 1065, 27. God sold the Jewish people, who were of lesser worth, and purchased the Christian people, who were of greater worth: the former was sold into sin, the latter bought with blood, 904, 42. Through their offense salvation came to the Gentiles, 908, 53. Through zeal for faith the people of the Gentiles acquired eternal life for itself, which the Jewish people lost through its negligence and sloth, 1198, 13. Israel’s guilt benefited the Gentiles; the faith of the Gentiles freed the Israelite people, 966, 29. The Jews ought not to despair of pardon if they wish to do penance, 1433, 97 and following. Even if they do not wish to be healed, God reserves for them the grace of return, 666, 12. See CHURCH.

**JUDGE.** A good judge ought not to obey his own will but to uphold what belongs to the laws, 1231, 36 and following. He must yield neither to envy nor to fear, 1525, 99. How the providence of the divine judgment teaches him greatness of spirit and patience, 223, 38. He who is not permitted in many cases to refrain from the sword can nevertheless remit penalties, 838, 51. The practice of secular discipline has established that everyone should praise his own judge, 1083, 15.

**JUDGMENT.** The end of judgment is justice: in one case the guardianship of truth, in the other the fruit of equity, 1173, 14. In judging, care must be taken that the punishment not be greater than the guilt, 709, 5. Human judgments are terrifying even to sinners; how much more are divine judgments to be feared, 1049, 17. This judgment is grave, when the Lord demands that judgment be passed against a man concerning himself, 811, 72. God’s judgments assist the holy and sinners, but in different ways, 1253, 26. See GOD.

**THE JUDGMENT.** What Christ’s final judgment will be, 762, 52. His first coming was for the redemption of sins, his second for the restraint of offenses, 1058, 17. Why the Lord will come in fire, 1442, 132. God does not wish the judgment of the holy and of the devil’s companions to be one and the same, 1228, 22. There is a threefold order of people who must be present at Christ’s final judgment, 764, 56. In Christ’s judgment no innocent person will be endangered, and no criminal will escape, 1172, 10. In God’s judgment the same person is partly saved and partly condemned, 1238, 58. Why the holy person comes to judgment while the impious person does not, 1229, 24. Those who rise for judgment have hope of pardon, 1032, 44. The impious do not rise for judgment but, as though judgment had already been rendered, are punished, 1413, 9. Why the impious and unbelieving who did not believe in Christ are not to be judged at the final judgment, 761, 51. After the end of this life the soul remains suspended in uncertainty concerning the future judgment, 209, 9. The day of judgment is at hand: if you do not wish to be seized, fear and flee every day, 1479, 39. To judge another is a grave matter, 1230, 31. Often, in judging, the sin of the judgment is greater than the sin of the person judged, 709, 5. The form of judgment that you yourself decide ought to be imposed on another must necessarily return upon you, 1229, 26.

**YOKE.** Christ’s yoke is easy if you think of the ornaments of your neck as adornments, not burdens, 994, 6. Why we ought to take up not only the yoke of the Word but also to take it up in youth, 982, 3. Who bears that yoke from his youth, 1080, 3; 1214, 19.

**TO SWEAR.** It is an indication of knowledge and a testimony of conscience, 1145, 14. How dangerous an oath is, 1521, 82. Who can swear, 1145, 14. The custom of swearing with the Gospels touched, 964, 25.

**JUSTICE.** Philosophy divided it into three parts, 1373, 76. It is a common virtue, 1291, 30. It is the parent and fruitful source of the other virtues, 153, 22. It alone embraces all the virtues, 344, 68. Where justice is, there is harmony among the other virtues, 152, 18. No virtue seems to bear more abundant fruits, 151, 18. No possession can be richer, 825, 25.

[Col. 2266]

It alone was born more for others than for itself, 227, 2; 768, 7; 1174, 14. The work of justice is to preserve the measure appropriate to each person’s merit, 1385, 6. That is true justice which is extended even to enemies, 1205, 35. God alone has the power to possess justice perpetually and in all things, 1205, 35. What hunger for justice is, 1369, 56. We cannot know what the form of justice is unless we know what the image of iniquity is, 765, 1. As God’s justice is great, so his vengeance is severe, 669, 22. See GOD.

**JUSTIFICATION.** It is derived from justice, 131, 46. It is the work of justice, 1084, 16. The Lord’s justifications in hymns, songs, and psalms, 1052, 25.

**THE JUST.** Whatever is just is never harsh, 1147, 17. What is just can be made unjustly, 1272, 18.

**THE JUST MAN.** To see a just man is precious, 1095, 25. He is the image and glory of God, and why, 425, 17. Who is truly just, 1195, 5. This is the form of the just man: to fear and dread nothing except the loss of virtue, 457, 38. To be just before God is perfect praise, 1272, 18. Why many seem just to human beings but few to God; why they are one way to human beings and another way to God, 241, 37; 1272, 18. Why God knows the just but does not know the unjust, 791, 31. The just man alone remains forever, 240, 35. There is perpetual life for the just, but none for the wicked, 223, 37. The life of the just has fullness, while the days of the impious are empty, 1291, 29. The life of the just is peaceful, while the unjust is full of restlessness and disturbance, 468, 28. The possession of the just is to be pleasing to God; for fools there is no rank, 322, 22. How he possesses the earth, 797, 45. All things pass away from him, 813, 79. What is set before the just and what their methods of action are, 1048, 14–15. He ought to stand before the eyes of the Lord like a soldier in the presence of his commander and like one placed on duty, 749, 27. He is his own enclosure and his own ever-watchful guardian, 844, 6. Here are the snares by which, even if he is not entangled, he is nevertheless hindered, 640, 6. He notices his own frailty more than the unjust person does, 633, 20. If he encounters a stumbling-block and falls, he should maintain sobriety, practice repentance, and often restore himself, 800, 51. What belongs to frailty falls; what belongs to justice rises again, 799, 51. When he falls, the strong will tremble, 940, 9. When his mind begins to cleanse itself, 254, 62. God spares the just person who sins as a result of the frailty of his condition; he punishes the unjust as one who detests an ungrateful person, 811, 73. He is not acquitted by another’s sentence but by his own life, 964, 25. God does not judge him, 811, 73. He hears even the dead, 220, 31. When the divine hand touches the just, it heals them rather than wounding them, 791, 30. Neither does the sinner escape the punishment of his wickedness, nor is the just person deprived of the rewards of his equity, 1048, 15. Although he is abandoned in this world, he is not abandoned by the Lord, 802, 58. Why, 810, 70. He remains before God even if he is condemned by human beings, 327, 36. In the Lord’s power, the help of the just is not ruin, 629, 11.

**THE JUST MAN.** How he always speaks of the works of God, 1008, 46. He blesses the Lord when he labors; the sinner when he indulges himself, 1146, 16. The life of the just is fruitful for others and sweet for himself, 768, 6. How great a wall he is for his homeland, 299, 48. How much the number of the just benefits the salvation of peoples, 211, 12. The life of the just rebukes the sinner, whom it condemns by silent authority greater than if it spoke with a clear voice, 788, 23. Why people more readily follow the way of sinners than that of the just, 748, 25. The remnants of the just are virtues; the remnants of the impious are wickedness and the sin of unbelief, 814, 82.

**YOUTH.** It is freer for love, more heedless toward falling, more fragile toward weakness, and harder to correct, 1183, 45. Young men are accustomed to boast of luxury, pleasures, and desires for adultery, 262, 81. A younger person ought to know himself so that he may correct his way, 987, 15 and following. Some are old in youth, and others young in old age, 803, 59.

## K

**KOPH.** That is, “completion,” or “look,” 1209, 1.

## L

**LABAN.** He is called “white” in Latin, 428, 26. Or “whitened,” 466, 24.

**LABOR.** Labor is common to human beings and every creature, and why, 452, 24. We were created for labor and redeemed for rest, 1146, 19. The labor of the soul is greater than that of the flesh, 829, 33. Ignorance is the cause of labor, 668, 19. Only for the human being is the course of life prescribed in labor, and for what reason, 1264, 6. The ways of the Lord are full of labor; therefore the ruined flee from them, 159, 16. No virtue exists without labor, because labor is the progress of virtue, 209, 8. Although it is not pleasant in relation to grace, it is nevertheless fruitful in relation to reward, 188, 12; 209, 8 and following. Its fruit is noble, 1264, 6. Through it we advance so that we may recover what has been allotted to us, 156, 29; 1381, 108. In the divine portion there are groans and labors, 1060, 13. Continuous labor turns away desire, 100, 52.

**TEARS.** Their commendation, 112, 89. How useful they are, [Col. 2267] 1192, 31 and following; 1523, 89 and following. Whoever is a sinner should mourn and rebuke himself so that he may become just, 1194, 1; 1369, 55. Tears are accustomed to undertake an embassy on behalf of sins, 819, 10; 831, 38. They can not only wash away our sin but also water the track of the heavenly Word, 1388, 18. Let tears wash away the sin that shame prevents one from confessing with the voice, 1523, 88. The person who commits things that ought to be mourned does not know how to weep, 1054, 32. The tears themselves are not bitter, but the feeling of the person who shed them was bitter, 831, 37.

**LAKE.** Larius, Benacus, and Albanus are not mingled with the waves of the sea, 39, 16.

**JOY.** It quickly pours error into the mind, 753, 32. Whoever clothes himself in joy through knowledge of reason is established in perpetual rejoicing, 1098, 33.

**LAMED.** That is, “heart,” or “to a servant,” 1114, 1. Why more was exacted from him than from Cain, 224, 38.

**LARIUS.** See LAKE.

**TO PRAISE.** To praise God is to commend one’s vow and fulfill it, 199, 34. To rest in the praise of God is not an idle act of good work, 1365, 39. How the just person ought at all times to be attentive to the praises of God, 1053, 30. While we are in sin, how can we fully praise God, 1253, 25.

**PRAISES.** One’s own praises must be avoided, 1478, 32.

**LAUREL.** The heads of victors are crowned with it, 54, 53.

**READING.** It should be daily exercise for us, so that no encounter with temptations can disturb us, 1124, 33. Frequent reading performs the office of instruction, 1100, 39. Attentive to the nourishment of divine reading, he neglects the hunger of the body, 1339, 20. We read certain things so that they may not be read: not so that we may retain them, but so that we may reject them, 1265, 2.

**READER.** Christ did not disdain the office of reader, 1346, 45.

**BED.** Christ is the bed of the saints, 369, 45.

**LION.** At the sound of a roaring lion many animals, struck with terror, collapse, 118, 14. The lion rejects yesterday’s food and turns away from the very leftovers of his meal, 118, 14. He fears the rooster, especially a white one, 123, 26. He is tormented by the small sting of a scorpion, 126, 37. The dog is beaten so that the lion may be afraid; and he who is provoked by his own injury is restrained by another’s, 206, 3. When sick, the lion devours a monkey so that he may be healed, 123, 26.

**LEOPARD.** It heals itself with the blood of a doe, 123, 28.

**LEPIDUS AND SERTORIUS.** Rebels against Roman power, 934, 21.

**HARES.** They become white in winter and return to their own color in summer, 109, 77. They mate, raise their young, and give birth continuously, 605, 43.

**LITTLE HARE.** It is formidable in the sea, 93, 31.

**LEVI.** His blessing is explained, 516, 10 and following. Christ appears to derive his lineage from the tribe of Levi according to the assumption of the body, 517, 14. From it also came the chief priests who killed Christ, 517, 13.

**LEVITES.** The name signifies “received for me,” or “he himself for me,” 210, 11; 1056, 4. Why the Levites are called firstborn, 208, 7. Why Moses called them firstborn and redeemers of the others, 212, 13. By the holiness of their life and by prayer they washed away the sins of the people, 210, 11.

**LAW.** It is twofold, natural and written, 123, 15. The law of nature is greater than the prescription of laws, 285, 8. In the heart of the just, the law is unwritten but natural, 810, 68. Not only the person who does not know the law, but also the one who does not act according to the law, is deprived of the law, 1164, 21. Who is said to incur the anger of the laws, 823, 19. The one who is lord of the law does not obey the law but makes the law, 1356, 7. How the law of God is truth, 1205, 36. The Law must first be loved, and second meditated upon, 751, 30. The old Law was given not only to the Hebrew but also called the foreigner, 424, 15. Whether it was beneficial for the old Law to be promulgated, 451, 20 and following. In what sense the ancient Law was good and useful, 1323, 26 and following. How the commandment of the Law was good even though it produces death, 449, 13 and following. The Law is the author of good, sending us toward grace, 1392, 35. The Law instructs not only in the duty of acting but also corrects the feeling of the secret mind, 1048, 13. In the Law are commandments, justifications, testimonies of justice, and precepts, 1125, 34. The way of the Law; to stand in the ways of the Law, 1024, 22. The radiance of the Law is not in the letter but in spiritual understanding, 1191, 26. Those who interpreted the Law bodily do not keep it but transgress it, 1061, 15. What is handed down for us to follow is not the empty content of the Law but its solid usefulness, 1364, 32. Whoever separates himself from the Law separates himself from eternal life and from Christ, 1219, 35. Who keeps the Law of God in all things, 1041, 30. The one who loves fulfills the precepts of the Law willingly; the one who fears does so unwillingly, 715, 30. The Law announces Christ beforehand, 1181, 39. It is the shadow of Christ, 1021, 10. The entire sequence of the old Law was a type of what was to come, 1299, 56. What mysteries the old Law foretold, 1377, 94. The Law is both the herald of the Church and the repentance of grace, 1303, 68. Although there is justice in the Law, it is not through the Law, 1360, 21. The Law examines merits; grace considers faith, 892, 12. According to the truth, no one is justified unto perfection in the Law, 1125, 34. Why the old Law was not sufficiently complete, 346, 74; [Col. 2268] 644, 18. The help of the Law would have been weak unless Jesus himself had come to earth, 891, 11. The Law does not have remission of sins; but what is lacking in it is completed in the Gospel, 1389, 23. The letter is servile; grace is free, 463, 13. What difference there is between those who contend for the Law and those who contend for grace, 1359, 17. Moses broke the first tablets of the Law for the Jews so that the later ones might remain for Christians, 245, 45. The Word in the womb, the Law in silence; the Word is brought forth, the Law is fulfilled; but the fulfillment of the Law is the explanation of the Word, 1280, 42. The understanding of the Law vanished and became spiritual, 629, 12. The bodily interpretation of the Law died when Christ revealed its spiritual grace, 1061, 16. At the head of the Synagogue the Law is dead, but its spiritual understanding is established, 1159, 8. Christ, who is its end, is not the defect but the fullness of the Law, 910, 57; 1206, 37. What does the Law profit if you do not know the end of the Law, if you do not know the mystery, if you do not recognize the sacraments, 1132, 6; 1427, 70.

**LEAH.** A figure of the Synagogue, 1226, 24.

**FREE.** He alone is free who does everything wisely and lives in such a way as he wishes, 463, 12. We are not constrained to obey by servile necessity but by the will’s free choice, whether we incline toward virtue or toward guilt, 443, 1. Christ heals those who are willing; he does not bind the unwilling, 663, 4; 1117, 13; 1349, 56. Freedom under Christ is glorious, and servitude precious, 448, 11.

**LIBERALITY.** Its grace returns to the giver, 575, 37. The more diligent the liberality, the less excusable the obstinacy, 1499, 23.

**FREEDMAN.** What difference is there between a freedman and a free man, 448, 12.

**LUST.** Its agitations are in the loins and are usually aroused by the devil, 829, 33. A person, like one placed on a ship, ought to turn away the eyes of the soul so that they do not see the bilge-water of lusts, 1028, 33. A certain licentious and exceptionally lustful youth is rebuked, 828, 30. Whoever is subject to lust is a slave, 490, 20.

**SPLEEN.** It has a fruitful proximity to the liver, and why, 140, 71.

**TREE.** The tree of the knowledge of good and evil truly existed in paradise, and there is nothing blameworthy in this, 147, 8. Earthly trees are said not to give fruit but to bear it; the tree of life and wisdom gives fruit, that is, bestows and grants it, 756, 40. Whether the tree of life seems to contribute more to life than the breath of God, 155, 28–29. Why God neither permitted the tree of the knowledge of good and evil to be touched nor prohibited it, 171, 57. Whether God prohibited Adam only from eating the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, but not from combining it with other fruits, 173, 59.

**LILIES.** Their greenness is hidden, not lost, 1440, 127.

**TONGUE.** Its usefulness, 138, 65; 139, 67. How we can and ought always to speak the things that belong to God, 808, 66 and following. Talkativeness is the shipwreck of innocence and virtue, and an incitement to falling away and sin, 791, 28. The person is to be praised who wishes first to know what ought to be said before expressing what he thinks, 982, 5.

**LETTERS.** The strokes of letters can be erased without damage to the books: the ink is erased, but the wood remains, 245, 45.

**LOCUSTS.** They are healed by olive leaves, 47, 37. They are food for the prophets and a figure of the Gentile people, 1304, 71. The *σελευκίς* (*seleucis*) devours it, 110, 83.

**THE RATIONAL FACULTY (λογιστικόν).** What it is in a human being, 335, 54.

**DARNEL.** Darnel and tares do not come from the seed of wheat but have a particular kind of their own, 49, 44.

**LOT.** In Latin interpretation he is called “declension” or “departure,” 287, 14; 315, 6; 323, 25; 327, 35. How great his hospitality was, 299, 51. His piety toward his kinsmen is commended, 300, 54. He is burned by the flames of women, whom the sulfurous flame did not burn, 1112, 25.

**LUKE.** The Evangelist is praised by the Apostle, 1269, 11. He followed each event historically, 1543, 186. He believed himself sufficiently rich if he could claim the Lord’s manger for himself, 1296, 43. See EVANGELISTS.

**LUCRINE SEA.** 39, 15.

**WRESTLER.** If he fixes his knee or slips with his foot, he is considered defeated, 799, 51.

**LIGHT.** The light of day is one thing, and the light of the sun, moon, and stars another, 65, 8. From what else should the word of God in Scripture have begun except from light, 19, 33.

**MOON.** Why it is called the great luminary, and from what its greatness may be proved, 74, 25. The sphere of the moon is seen equally by everyone, ibid. How it is in the power of the night, ibid. It undergoes a diminution of light, not of body, 65, 7. Certain signs are gathered from the sun and moon, but not signs of births, 67, 12 and following. If the fourth day of the moon is clear, people judge that it gives a prediction of fair weather for the remaining days until the month is complete, 78, 34. The brains of animals, the moist parts of sea creatures, and the inner parts of trees are emptied or filled according to the moon’s progress, 76, 29. It is ridiculous that people generally believe the moon can be drawn down by magical incantations, 78, 33. The moon represents the mystery of Christ and the Church, [Col. 2269] 77, 32. The moon’s change teaches the instability of things, 77, 31.

**WOLF.** If it sees a human being first, it takes away his voice; if it realizes that it has been seen first, it lays aside its ferocity, 123, 26; 1095, 24; 1421, 48. It flees the leaves of squill, 123, 9.

**NIGHTINGALE.** It usually signals the beginning of the rising day, 96, 30. Why, while brooding over its eggs, it consoles the sleepless night with the sweetness of its song, 111, 83.

**LIGHT.** It is what commends the other furnishings of a house, 19, 33. There is a harmful, uncertain light, 72, 22.

**LUXURY.** How great is human luxury, 91, 26. It possesses neither faith nor observance of discipline; it is the seedbed and origin of vices, 556, 69. If the flesh dies to luxury and lack of restraint, then it resumes true life, 652, 36. For the luxurious person, deprivation of pleasures is a punishment, 1474, 18. For the luxurious, the house is a tomb, and for what reason, 951, 18.

**LUXURY.** The luxury of women is rebuked, 571, 25–26.

## Maccabees

The seven brothers of the Maccabees—how blessed and steadfast they were amid torments, 475, 42 ff.

## Teacher

The true teacher is God alone, 1078, 59; 1122, 27.

## Magi

The Magi traced their origin to Balaam and were devoted to magical arts, 1297, 47–48. Why they brought Eastern spoils to Christ’s cradle, 1334, 49. They offered gold to the king, frankincense to God, and myrrh to the deceased, 1296, 44. Why they came by one route and returned by another, 1297, 46.

## Pomegranates

Pomegranates generally flower quickly and cannot bear fruit unless they are cultivated, 55, 56. The Church is compared with them, ibid.

## Malice

Malice is nothing, 428, 24. What is it except the absence of goodness? 376, 60. It is not substantial but accidental, 16, 28. It arose from us; it was not created by God, 17, 30 ff. It is the source of sin, 1165, 25, and the cause of faithlessness, 1435, 110. The devil presides over it, Christ over the virtues, 831, 35. Why God judged that it should meanwhile be restrained rather than abolished, 434, 43. Simplicity dissolves malice, and virtue dissolves guilt, 254, 64. The departure of malice brings about the entrance of virtue; and by the same zeal with which crime is excluded, innocence is joined to us, 213, 16. See GUILT.

## Evils

There are no evils except those that entangle the mind in crime and bind the conscience, 18, 31. God did not create evil; our own merits discovered it for themselves, 1479, 36. Evils arose from good things, 376, 60. We naturally understand that what is evil must be avoided, 161, 39. Knowledge of evil can often benefit us, 172, 58. First what is evil creeps in; afterward what is good is recognized, 187, 10. The incentive to evil is usually either anger or desire, 159, 34. Evil is never corrected by evil, nor is a wound healed by a wound; rather, it is aggravated, 618, 82. What we consider evil is generally not evil in every respect but useful for the common good, 148, 8.

## Commandment

How extensive is God’s commandment, 1129, 49 ff. Just as there is a Holy of Holies, so there is a commandment of commandments, 1025, 23. Why God commanded that his commandments be guarded with such strictness, 978, 14. Why God ratified his statutes, with heaven and earth as witnesses, 1213, 15. To command too much is a matter of providence and caution, 1197, 9. God ought not to have given the weak perfect commandments that they could not bear, 1175, 18. The righteous receive commandments; the servant, orders, 246, 47. Although a person has been cleansed from sin, he must labor to observe the precepts of life and not depart from the heavenly commandments, 450, 15. To keep a commandment is generally a matter of necessity and fear; to love it is a matter of charity, 1237, 55; 1246, 23. How precious it is to keep the Lord’s commandment and to know the mystery of the commandment itself, 975, 7. Whoever carries out God’s commandments justifies God, 1009, 47. Observance of God’s commandments increases the grace of his very nature, 976, 9. If anyone keeps one commandment but transgresses another, it benefits him nothing, 979, 15.

## Mandrakes

Male and female mandrakes, 1216, 24. Sleep is induced by means of them, 48, 39.

## Manichaeus

Manichaeus assigns to himself another author besides God, 45, 32. The Manichaeans are refuted when they say that there is one God of the Old Testament and another of the New, 732, 70 ff. The Manichaean heresy does not accept the prophets, 1255, 33. Manichaeus and Valentinus are refuted because they say that Christ is not the son of David and did not assume flesh, 716, 27 ff. He does not walk in the way, 976, 8.

## Manna

Manna was a shadow of the Eucharistic bread, 1203, 27.

## Gentleness

Gentleness is pleasing to all; it heals the inner wounds of souls, 945, 1. Piety is the mistress of cruelty, and gentleness prevails over harsh impulses, 462, 11. It was necessary before the Lord’s Passion, 1424, 60. Who is gentle? 787, 22.

## Hands

The usefulness of the hands, 140, 69. The hand, the reconciler of divine grace, is brought to the sacred altars; through it we offer and receive the heavenly sacraments, 140, 69.

## Mara

Mara—that is, bitterness, 1019, 5. [Col. 2270]

## Marcionite

The Marcionite does not accept the Law, 1131, 4. Hence the plagues of Marcion, Valentinus, and the Manichaeans, 17, 30.

## Sea

Why is the sea good? 41, 21–22. It is shown to surpass the lands, 94, 34–35. There are more things in the sea than on land, 80, 5. Why does it not easily overflow the lands? 27, 12. Why does it have salty and bitter water? 29, 14. The seas are enclosed within limits imposed upon them, 37, 10. The Lord made the sea not for navigation but for the beauty of the element, 557, 70. No one can sail the sea fearlessly unless he has first sailed on rivers, 294, 30.

Different seas and their names, 38, 12–13. The various gulfs of the sea, 38, 13. The Adriatic lies within the Tyrrhenian; the remaining seas mingle with the Adriatic, ibid. The British Sea, 39, 15. The Caspian, Cretan, and Northern Seas, 39, 12. The Lucrine and Avernan Seas in Italy, 39, 15. The Sea of Tiberias in Palestine, 39, 15. The Red Sea in the Indian Sea, 37, 10. The Egyptian Sesostris wished to connect the Red Sea with the Egyptian sea, 37, 11. A continuous wave from the Indian Sea to the shore of Gades, and from there into the Red Sea, encloses the world, 38, 13.

## Mary

Mary flowed from the tribe of David, 1316, 5. She was no less than was fitting for the Mother of God, 1532, 132. She was a virgin by grace, wholly undefiled by every stain of sin, 1255, 30. Her humility, devotion, faith, and modesty, 1287, 17 ff. She was a virgin in conduct, modesty, prophecy, and mystery, 1284, 8. She was no less chaste in speech than in body, 1299, 54. According to Eve’s inheritance she was a cloud; according to the integrity of virginity she was light, 1019, 3. Her virginity has the fullest testimony, 1533, 133. It was not intercourse with a man that opened the secrets of the virginal womb; rather, the Holy Spirit poured undefiled seed into an inviolate womb, 1300, 56. Although Scripture frequently calls Mary a wife, it indicates not the loss of virginity but the attestation of marriage and the celebration of the wedding, 1283, 5. Why was she especially chosen to bear Christ, since she was betrothed to a man? 1281, 1. Her virginity is preserved both intact in modesty and inviolate in reputation, 1281, 1. The Lord preferred that some should doubt his own origin rather than his mother’s modesty, 1281, 1. Mary’s presence instructed John while he was still in the womb, 373, 53. Christ does not deny her as his mother—not, as certain heretics seek to ensnare us, 1392, 38. She did not labor to give birth to Christ; she gave birth to him, 941, 11. We do not easily find any woman who prophesied more abundantly than the Lord’s mother, 1293, 35. She is a type of the Church, 1533, 134. Let Mary’s soul be in each person, so that it may magnify the Lord; let Mary’s spirit be in each person, so that it may rejoice in God, 1290, 26.

## Marys

There were several Marys and several Magdalenes among the Evangelists, 1537, 154. Whether there was only one woman named Mary who anointed Jesus, 1386, 12. Mary, Martha’s sister, anointed Jesus’ feet, 1269, 9. Why Mary was the first to see the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, 296, 39.

## Marius

Marius fought against Cinna, and Roman blood was shed on both sides, 934, 21.

## Martyr

The martyr suffers persecution freely—and for what reason? 1240, 7. The martyrs excluded fear of punishments through love of martyrdom, 1079, 2. What a voice the martyr has who is not ashamed of Christ, 1042, 33. Take away persecutions, and there are no martyrs, 1146, 17. Take away the contests of the martyrs, and you have taken away the crowns; take away the torments, and you have taken away the beatitudes, 1345, 41. The death of the martyrs is powerful: it abolishes prior guilt, 381, 76. Faith is the beginning of a Christian, but the fullness of the Christian is righteousness in the passion of the martyrs, 1238, 57. The martyr’s trembling must be equated with the confidence of a steadfast man, 1240, 8. The martyrs succeed dead kings in the eternal kingdom, honored by heavenly grace, 1507, 13. In heaven the martyr will show us the crown of his scar, 1540, 171. Where the roses of the martyrs are to be sought, 1441, 128. Those who wear cups down at the tombs of martyrs are reproved, 554, 62. Many martyrs of Christ are hidden every day, confessing Jesus as Lord, 1234, 47 ff. The time for martyrdom is when divine things must be preferred to every affection arising from family ties, 1163, 20.

## Mother

Mothers ought to nurse their own children, 303, 63. What maternal affection and filial reverence ought to provide, 1533, 132.

## Prime Matter

Prime matter is called *hyle* (ὕλη) by the Platonists, and is said by them to be uncreated, 1, 1. It is not eternal but created, 13, 25; 23, 2. It was not, as the philosophers wish, discovered, but made, 1404, 85.

## Methuselah

The years of Methuselah are counted beyond the Flood, 1332, 48.

## Marriage

Christians ought not to be joined in marriage to pagans, Jews, or heretics, 309, 84. Christian women are not joined to pagans according to God’s judgment, 1470, 2 ff. Most pagans, wishing to take Christian wives—something denied them by Christian parents—pretended for a time to profess faith in Christ, 1235, 48. It is not in keeping with virginal modesty to choose a husband; a girl ought to await the judgment of her parents, 3011, 91. If a younger widow wishes to marry, she ought to leave the choice of a husband to her parents, 312, 91. Whoever seeks the pleasures of marriage should not seek someone superior in wealth, whom marital necessities cannot maintain, [Col. 2271] 284, 6. In a wife one should seek neither gold, silver, nor possessions, but the grace of a good character, 309, 85. Marriage is joined by God’s command so that heresy may be destroyed, 1276, 30. Whoever condemns weddings is expelled from the Church, 1337, 10. Why does the man who has taken a wife fasten upon himself the bonds of the mind? 1004, 32. There are appointed times for marriage and for the begetting of children, 1280, 43. If a righteous man discovers his spouse’s disgrace, he must show himself free from bloodshed in regard to homicide and chaste in regard to adultery, 1283, 5. See MARRIAGE.

The bridegroom of the soul is the Word of God, to whom the soul is joined by a certain lawful covenant of marriage, 398, 20. A good marriage occurs when the soul marries the Word and the flesh marries the spirit, 1386, 9.

## Mattilaeus

Persia was opened to Mattilaeus, 934, 21.

## Matthias

The lot fell upon Matthias, lest the apostles’ election appear to diverge from the command of the ancient Law, 1274, 23.

## Maximus

The emperor Maximus, harsher than Pilate, denied Gratian burial, 965, 26.

## Medicine

Medicine took its origin from a wound, 815, 1. That medicine is older which is accustomed to heal with herbs and juices, 56, 57. The beginning of medicine is to cut into the causes of disease, 252, 59. For burning wounds it customarily applies gentler medicines by which it may ease the pain, 834, 42. The precepts of medicine are contrary to those devoted to divine knowledge, 1253, 23. Few profess medicine, although many claim to know some of its remedies, 778, 3.

## Physicians

Why are physicians so called? 815, 1. Who are called the children of physicians? 778, 3. Christ is physician and medicine, 816, 4; 884, 39; 1209, 2; 1428, 75. This physician is not from the earth: he heals every sickness and makes whole entire peoples, 1001, 23. The wise man is himself his own physician, 848, 15.

## Meditation

Meditation on Scripture is especially necessary for priests, 1100, 39. Let us exercise ourselves in its unceasing use—and why? 1123, 28. Why one must meditate on the Law all day, 1133, 7. Whoever seeks God’s salvation meditates on the Law day and night, 1253, 23. For the one who meditates on the Law, it is always day and light without decline, 1133, 7. Through meditation on the heavenly commandments, practice in good works grows strong, 1043, 35. For the person whose meditation is the law of God, mercies are always at hand, so that he may live forever, 1099, 39.

## Honey

The uses of honey, 107, 70. It generally harms diseased internal organs, 1138, 25.

## Melchizedek

Melchizedek, preceding grace, displayed the figure of the holy sacrifice, 1321, 21.

## Men

“Men” signifies the inner parts, or things arising from them, 1130, 1.

## Falsehood

Every falsehood has thirst; truth has abundance, 960, 14.

## Mind

According to the opinion of most people, the human mind is situated in the head, 234, 17. It is divided into the rational and the irrational, 314, 2. It is the governing part of the soul and the soul’s virtue, 407, 44. What is the food of the mind? 537, 5. It is nourished by discoveries of wisdom, 318, 11. A sober mind restrains all passions, governs the senses, and directs speech, 241, 38. Sobriety of mind is medicine for the body, 242, 38. Why is the good mind compared with gold? 320, 20. How does one depart from one’s land and kindred? 313, 2. When does one descend into Egypt, or ascend from there? 318, 13. When does winter occur in the mind? 723, 43.

## Month

When we designate a month as consisting of thirty days, we also designate nights, 244, 43. The ancients were accustomed to observe the months from the beginning of the moon, 895, 18. The first month is March, the second April, 253, 60.

## Mercenary

A wage must be paid to the mercenary, 621, 91–92. It is not arrogant insolence but an innocent conscience to seek one’s wage from the person whom one has served, 994, 3. To kill a person is to deny him the support owed for his life, 622, 92.

## Reward

Reward more easily follows one who does not await it, 1263, 4. Preserve your reward for the future, and consider the reproaches of this age as increases to your reward, 1244, 18.

Why are divers called *mergi*? 97, 43.

## Merits

Where merits differ, rewards differ, 508, 76. Those who are released through commendation of their merits are relieved by the payment of punishments, 1194, 2. The ordering of heavenly decrees concerning human beings proceeds not according to our merits but according to God’s mercy, 1233, 42.

## Mesopotamia

Mesopotamia is so called because it lies between the two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, 150, 14.

## Military Service

Stipends were established for military service so that, while expenses were being sought, a robber might not rage unchecked, 1306, 76–77. What should be distributed to soldiers after victories? 288, 17. See KING.

What a Christian soldier ought to be, 856, 35. What wars such a soldier must endure, 1506, 11. Those who serve the kingdom should not concern themselves with food, 1441, 130.

## Miracle

A miracle occurs in the elements; a lesson in the mysteries, 1353, 69. Before the Gospel, miracles were either rare or nonexistent, 1379, 101.

## Misery

Misery that cannot be excused—nothing is more intolerable, 597, 20. Let no one call a person miserable who is righteous, 829, 32. [Col. 2272]

## Mercy

Mercy is the fullness of the virtues, 1306, 77. Prudence is good, but mercy is sweet: few attain the former, while the latter reaches everyone, 339, 10. Mercy is a portion of justice, 1064, 21. There is just mercy and unjust mercy, 1065, 25 ff. Mercy must begin from the domestic duty of piety, 1491, 79. Kinship does not make one’s neighbor; mercy does, 429, 84. One must extend one’s hands to works of mercy, 1365, 40. Pursue mercy, so that you may deserve grace, 1374, 78. The oil of mercy heals the sick, 1141, 7. Our price is mercy, which redeems us from death, 963, 21. Be merciful, so that you may remain invulnerable—or so that you may be able to heal yourself if you are wounded, 789, 24. Whatever you confer upon another, you pay to yourself; whatever proceeds from you returns to you; and whatever good you do benefits you, 1090, 10. Mercy is not accustomed to judge according to merits but to assist necessities: to help the poor, not to investigate their justice, 576, 40. Mercy is owed to all the needy, but especially when hardship casts some of the rich and noble into the lowest condition, 1185, 6. Mercy alone follows us; as the guide preceding us to the heavenly dwellings, it acquires eternal tabernacles for the dead through the paltry interest of money, 1439, 122. In the fortieth Psalm and in the Gospel, mercy is crowned, 745, 19. See ALMSGIVING.

The mercy of God. See GOD.

## Moderation

Moderation is natural: whatever exceeds measure is considered superfluous, 554, 61.

## Necklaces

*Moduli* are called precious ornaments that are customarily hung around matrons’ necks, 1189, 18.

## Monasteries

Some who had left the monasteries are reproved, 799, 50.

## Moral Interpretation

The moral meanings come first, the mystical second: in the former there is life, in the latter knowledge, 973, 2. Although the honey of moral words stings, it does not injure, 1138, 25. See SCRIPTURE.

## Morals
