Sobriety of mind is a bodily disease, 18, 31. Great maturity of character must be cultivated, so that it may overcome nature, 1204, 31. What is your burial mound except evil habits? But Christ frees you from it, 1371, 91.

## Death

Among the Greeks, death is called *teleutē* (τελευτή), “completion” or “end”; in the Scriptures it is called sleep, 404, 34. There are three kinds of death, 390, 33; 1419, 35 ff. Death is a kind of separation of soul and body, 186, 8; 222, 35; 392, 8; 404, 33. Why does God allow us to depart from this age? 341, 64. Whether death is evil, 389–390; 402, 30. It harms no one—if only life did not harm anyone, 1242, 13. It is more a flight from sin than a loss for the dying, 961, 17. Its bitterness belongs not to death but to guilt, 404, 33. Christ ascended the cross to teach that death is not to be feared, 1025, 25. Death is not terrifying, since it is the end of nature, not a punishment, 1436, 110. Death itself is not terrifying, but fear and opinion concerning death are, 403, 31. If you are strong, despise death; if you are weak, flee and follow Christ, who is life, 1411, 1. Bodily death is not to be feared by the brave, desired by the wise, and sought by the miserable, 1419, 36. Death is altogether good, 395, 15. Why is the dead preferred to the living, and the one not yet born to the dead? 1195, 3. An honorable death is the redemption even of a discolored life, or the support of an innocent one, 839, 52. It is a testimony of life, 404, 35. Through death life is not taken away but transferred to better things, 222, 35. Through life there is passage to death; through death, return to life, 403, 32. For the righteous, death is the end not of nature but of guilt, 962, 19. For the righteous, death is a harbor of rest; for the guilty, a shipwreck, 403, 31. Death alone is rest for a man, 395, 12. Where there is faith in the resurrection, death is not an image of death but of rest, 1398, 62. The Lord turned the sleep of death into the grace of pleasure, 1358, 14. Death either enjoys the good of its own rest or suffers from another’s evil, 395, 13. The one who dies in order to rise again is nearer to salvation than the one who lives in order to die, 839, 52. Death is the fullness of service, the sum of reward, and the grace of dismissal, 404, 35. Death tests, and life tests, 1244, 18. Bodily death should be tasted by taking a sip; the life of the soul should be held as a possession, 1411, 2. To die in Christ is arduous and glorious, 920, 79. It is more glorious to die for Christ than to reign in this age, 392, 8. Some philosophers argued that release harms the wicked, while death benefits them, 1195, 3. It was an ancient opinion that whoever bound himself on earth would depart from the body still bound, 858, 37. Legions and great peoples have often been freed through the offered deaths of certain individuals, 1410, 108.

## Motion

Motion contrary to nature makes the body subject to corruption, 12, 23.

## Moses

Moses received his name from the waters, 3, 6. Why he was endowed with God’s name, 186, 7. He was a figure of the coming Teacher, 186, 7. And so was his staff, 1001, 24. He was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and in every discipline of worldly prudence, 3, 6. He withdrew into the solitude of Ethiopia, and why, ibid. He placed the empty and usurping teaching of philosophy after the reasoning of truth—and why? 116, 8. Why did he feed Jethro’s sheep? 195, 24. He spoke with a weak voice, yet was heard by God more than all others, 1211, 8. Every day he cries out in the Church, and the Jews alone do not hear him, 1211, 8. [Col. 2273]

Moses prayed; Christ acted, 1203, 29. Moses thought it possible for God to make what is incorporeal comprehensible to bodily eyes, 1061, 17; 1192, 28. He did not see the whole fullness of divinity, 924, 89. Why did he not enter the promised land? 1245, 20. Why was he always engaged in battle? ibid. Whether he died, 186, 8.

## Woman

A woman is considered more suited to domestic services, just as a man is to public duties, 167, 50. What assiduous care women ought to show toward pregnant relatives! 1288, 20. A woman erases the image of God if she smears her face with artificial whiteness and covers it with acquired redness, 131, 47. Whether girls ought to wear earrings, 311, 89. Sexual relations with a young man and the appearance of youth are dangerous for women, 1533, 134. One must avoid a wanton woman’s encounter in every way, 711, 14. A woman may seem cheap to you in price but is powerful in vice, 711, 12. Although woman was the first to sin, she ought not therefore to have been excluded from the work of divine operation, since she was to bear redemption for herself, 166, 47. Why did she first receive the mystery of the resurrection? 1520, 74; 1537, 157. Just as sin began with women, so good things also begin with women, 1290, 28.

## Many Words

How sin enters through excessive speech, 200, 36. See TONGUE, SILENCE.

## World

Plato considers the world incorruptible and neither created nor made, 1, 1. Aristotle assumes that it always has been and always will be, 2, 3. What did the other philosophers think about it? 1, 1 ff. Although its shape is spherical, it is not eternal, 5, 10–11. Some assert that it subsists of its own accord, 9, 18. At the beginning of spring heaven and earth were made—and why? 7, 13. God created the world without any delay, 4, 8; 8, 16. The world is a specimen and an emblem of divine activity, 8, 17. He who created the world protects the inhabitants of the world, 1209, 2. How did the four cardinal virtues, as it were, enclose the ages of this world? 152, 17 ff. Why will the globe of the earth someday be dissolved? 560, 78.

The world and the age must be fled, 417 ff. What that flight means, 425, 17; 433, 38; 816, 2. How we may flee well, 439, 55. How we can flee in spirit even though we are retained there in body, 435, 45. Why we ought to flee the world, 428, 25; 432, 37, and how swiftly, 430, 32. Where one must flee, 432, 36. You now owe nothing to the world, since you once renounced it, 340, 56. Flee the sea of the age, and you will not fear shipwreck, 1343, 32. To have fled the world is more a matter of grace than of having entered it, 658, 15. The flight from the age is glorious, 426, 19. How blessed it is, ibid., 20. I avoid the world as something fetid, guard against it as a plague, and leave it as something harmful, 1410, 107. If you flee this world, it too will flee from you, 813, 79. Examples are presented of those who rightly fled the age, 438, 51 ff. Whoever wishes to be saved must rise above the world, 418, 4. Like an eagle, our soul must transcend the world and direct its flight toward heaven, 396, 16. He wanted his disciples to be above the world, 1161, 11. Learn to be under Christ so that you may be above the world, 1497, 11. Beyond the world there is rest; beyond the world, the fruit of rest, 1402, 80. Eternal things cannot follow unless earthly things have come to an end, 672, 29.

David frequently discussed the vanity of the world, 661, 1. In the world everything considered magnificent is empty; there, whoever thinks himself to be something is nothing and indeed does not exist at all, 428, 25. Everything in this world is nothing, 661, 21. This is the land of captivity, the other is the land of freedom; this is the land of sin, the other of eternal rest; this is earthly, the other heavenly, 796, 41. How those who pursue temporal things resemble Lot’s wife, 900, 32–33. He had rightly failed whose substance was the food of the age, 682, 20. We are engaged in a struggle with the age, 784, 17. How many bonds there are in this age, 1004, 32. How many and how great are the snares in this world, 1336, 10. The age is slippery; we quickly slip, 791, 31. Whoever delights in this world is subject to the passions of the senses, 426, 20. How great is the malice in this world, 433, 38–39. Without divine help, human beings cannot flee earthly enticements and desires, 417, 1 ff. The globe of the earth is full of remedies because it is full of snares, 977, 12. What remedies has God provided against worldly vices and the shipwrecks of the age? 421, 9–10. For the one to whom the world is failing, Christ is eternal, 1506, 8. Whoever is a member of God’s household is an exile from the world; whoever dwells in heaven is a stranger on earth, 1053, 28. Whoever despises worldly things will deserve eternal things, 1367, 50. Whoever conquers this age becomes a pillar of God, 1030, 38. Whoever passes from this age sees a great vision, 798, 47. The conquerors of the age are preferred to princes, 1507, 12. Blessed is the one who has kept himself from the company of the faithless, 459, 2. Who are the dead of the age? 811, 72. For whom has the world been crucified? 1392, 34. Whoever is bound to God is released from the world, 1155, 39.

## Moray Eels

What the mixture of the moray eel with the viper teaches us, 86, 18.

## Purple Shellfish

The shellfish that provide the royal insignia are marine creatures, 94, 33.

## Borrowers

Those who take loans are reproved, 618, 80 ff.

## Tamarisks

In the tamarisks there is a figure of wicked cunning, 60, 69. [Col. 2274]

## Mystery

Every mystery ought to remain hidden, lest it be rashly disclosed to profane ears, 296, 38. The teaching of the mysteries must be kept under restraint, 200, 35. Care must be taken lest the mysteries of the Creed or of the Lord’s Prayer be made public, ibid., 37. Whoever thinks that the secret mysteries entrusted to him ought to be divulged to the unworthy sins against God, 990 ff. By remaining silent, the faithful interpreter of the mysteries proclaims Christ more fully, 1014, 18. Christ alone opened the human ear to the knowledge of mysteries, 968, 35. What took place in a figure was not counted as a crime against the patriarchs, 293, 28. Mystical meanings surpass moral ones, 757, 42. See SCRIPTURE.

## N

### Naaman

Naaman declared the salvation that was to come to the nations, 1347, 50.

### Naason

Naason—that is, “serpentine,” 993, 33. He is a figure of Christ, ibid., 34.

### Naboth

Naboth is counted among the saints—and for what reason? 786, 19. Although we have received no prophetic word from him, we have nevertheless received a prophetic deed, 1500, 25.

### Nostrils

The usefulness of the nostrils, 138, 63; 235, 20. Flat nostrils seem contrary to nature, 235, 20.

### Nature

Nature is the better teacher of truth, 121, 20. Its testimony is stronger than an argument of doctrine, 120, 21. It is the interpreter of the imperial command, 88, 22. Once the commandment of the divine Word has been given, it has grown permanently into nature, 116, 9.

### Necessity

Necessity, which imposes obedience against one’s will, generally brings distaste, 100, 52. Where necessity has been decreed, industry is dishonored, 71, 19. Necessity corrects the one whom piety ought to have urged, 421, 10. Those who attribute their sin to some necessity arising from a decree or from their own action seem to accuse God, 219, 27.

### Nimrod

Nimrod is called an Ethiopian by interpretation, 278, 128. He was the beginning of the Babylonian kingdom, 2778, 128.

### Naphtali

The blessing of Naphtali is explained, 525, 41.

### Nerves

The nerves are, as it were, the organs of the individual senses, 237, 61. Their beginning is the brain, ibid.

### Nile

The Nile was called Egypt and Gihon, 344, 68. It throws itself from the highest mountains into the Cataracts and, by the magnitude of its roar, deafens the ears of the inhabitants, 25, 7. Having poured out its river, it forms a stagnant lake throughout Egypt, 28, 12. At what time and why does it overflow? 247, 48.

### Snow

When snow falls, a more abundant wheat harvest than usual follows, 1415, 16.

### Nobility

When the nobility of one’s lineage is endangered, one’s condition is more shameful, 580, 54. The grace of virtue is greater than that of nobility, 718, 33.

### Harmful Person

What harms individuals benefits the community, 148, 9. See HUMAN BEING.

### Owl

Since the owl sees only in darkness, whom does it symbolize among the wise of the world? 111, 86.

### Noah

Noah is called *just* or *rest* in Latin, 227, 2. His household was rightly preserved in the Flood, 241, 36. His obedience is praised, 246, 47. How he discovered that the waters had receded, 256, 68. How he appears, like Adam, to have worked the earth, 271, 107. What his sleeping and nakedness symbolized, 860, 6. He was a type of Christ, 1332, 48. See WINE.

### Name

A name is that by which each person is properly identified, something not shared with the others, 896, 19. The merits of the saints have this quality: they receive a name from God, 1292, 31. Know yourself, 1088, 10. See KNOWLEDGE, HUMAN BEING.

### Novatian

Novatian is characterized by falling away, we by remission; he by impenitence, we by grace, 858, 37.

### Night

The shadow of the earth makes night, 67, 11.

### Cloud

The pillar of cloud is a type of Christ, 1019, 3.

### Naked

No one is naked except the one whom guilt has stripped naked, 493, 25. What you are ashamed of—being naked—was taught to you by guilt, not by nature, 967, 32.

### Number

When a number is added, what previously existed is removed, 183, 3. The second number is not complete because it is divided, 242, 39. The number three is mystical, 1278, 36; 1291, 29. It is salutary and suitable for those about to sacrifice, 305, 69. The perfection of the gift belongs to the number four, 342, 65. How vain it is to fear it, 78, 34. The seventh is clean, complete, and sacred, 242, 39. A virgin is signified by it, ibid. The numbers of the week are always virginal, 349, 80. In them the universe is sometimes comprehended, 1433, 95. The number is one of rest, 1043, 1. Seven groups of twelve and two groups of forty seem to designate a sacred number, 1301, 62. The perfection of the eighth number, 972, 2. In it there is the fullness of the resurrection, 1452, 173. See OCTAVE. The seventeenth, fortieth, and fiftieth are mystical, 1319, 16; 1338, 15. In fifty there is the number of the Jubilee, the number of remission, in which the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven, 276, 123; 688, 42.

### Nun

Nun—that is, “unique” or “their pasture,” 1140, 1.

### Weddings

Weddings are so called because, out of modesty, girls used to veil themselves, 312, 93. See MARRIAGE, MATRIMONY.

### Nod

What is a nod? 1279, 41.

## O
## O

**OBEDIENCE** is the foundation of all virtues, 1375, 82. [Col. 2275] It arises from the same source as humility and finds its completion in it, 720, 39. Disobedience arose in Paradise; therefore obedience descended with the Savior, 1204, 32. Christ had especially to restore obedience—and for what reason? 955, 4. Christ, the teacher of obedience, instructs us by his own example in the precepts of virtue, 1365, 42. How we ought to carry out God’s commandment, 311, 90. If you add anything to or subtract anything from a commandment, it seems to be a kind of transgression, 171, 56. Those who despise God’s commandments are reproved, 33, 1; 91, 29. Whoever does not show reverence to God does not render the obedience of nature, 219, 28.

**OUR OFFERING** cannot be pleasing to God unless our inward parts are cleansed, 205, 46. God is not appeased by gifts that are offered, but by the disposition of the one who offers them, 214, 18. We ought to offer what is undefiled, in which the affection of the one offering shines forth, 261, 79. In what way ought you to offer yourself to Christ? 1237, 55. The firstfruits of the soul ought above all to be offered, 202, 41 ff. This is truly the primitive sacrifice: when each person offers himself as a victim and begins with himself, so that afterward he may be able to offer his gift, 215, 19.

**OCEAN:** its ebb and flow, 76, 30.

**EIGHTH:** just as it is the perfection of our hope, so the eighth is the summit of virtues, 1367, 49. Why are many psalms entitled “For the Eighth”? 1412, 6. See **NUMBER**.

**EYES:** their usefulness, 136, 59; and their beauty, 235, 18. They are situated in a most suitable place, 137, 60. Sight is considered superior to all the bodily senses, 253, 61. Its weakness, 75, 26. Its pain is healed by a salve, 1000, 22. Why do we turn the eyes away when we become angry with someone? 1187, 77. What is approved by sight is worth more than what is praised in speech, 20, 34. From the sight of the eyes either good or adversity is produced, 1170, 6. Hence we are often tempted, 1170, 3. The eye’s function is to look; it is your responsibility to beware of what you see, 1170, 2. Which are the eyes of the mind? 1105, 7 ff. They themselves illuminate the whole human body, 919, 77.

**ODOR:** why does a pleasing odor linger longer than speech resounds or an appearance is visible? 138, 63. It is the messenger of fruits, 194, 23.

**OLIVE TREE:** locusts are healed by its leaves, 47, 37.

**OIL:** this material light is nourished by oil, and the darkness of shadows is driven away, 256, 67.

**OPIUM:** it became familiar through nearly daily use—and why? 48, 39.

**REPROACH:** it is more beneficial to endure it than to refute it, 855, 31.

**GOOD WORKS:** nature itself is their teacher, 424, 15. It is characteristic of good works that they do not need an external commendation, 20, 34. As the lily shines, so the works of the saints gleam, 1020, 7. How our works may not pass away with the passing world, 436, 46. It is necessary to direct your works toward God, so that his favor may breathe upon you, 209, 9. Nothing should readily be undertaken as a work except what we have examined and tested with the greatest care, 174, 62. A person is required both to seek new things through his works and to preserve what he has acquired, 154, 25. Fasting devoid of good works and virtues is more pitiable, 1463, 215. Works that cannot produce true fruit and good progress must be abandoned, 209, 9.

**PRAYER:** how, when, and for what should one pray? 201, 38; 1243, 15; 1365 ff. How frequently we are commanded to pray, 1430, 87 ff. Prayer ought to be continuous and unceasing, and for what reason, 216, 22. How one should always pray, 1213, 18; 1218, 33. One should pray especially at night and in the morning, 1213, 17; 1215, 22; 1217, 30 ff. The day is not sufficient for supplication; one must rise at night, and at midnight, 1072, 45. Let us devote the greater part of it to reading and prayers, 1053, 31. Woe is me if I do not rise at midnight to confess to God, 1306, 76. Whoever prays is redeemed, provided that he devoutly applies himself to prayers and is constant in prayer, anticipates the day, and frequents the night, 808, 65. Do you not know that each day you owe the firstfruits of your heart and voice to God? 1215, 22. When the human mind is troubled and the harsh and difficult struggles wear us down, the Lord’s help must be sought, 772, 18. What virtues are required in prayer? 215, 21. What is the prayer of the righteous like? 994, 4. What is that renowned prayer and groaning which God does not despise? 831, 35. It is the cry of the heart’s inward affection, which is heard from heaven, 1186, 9. With God it is not words but thoughts that speak, 200, 37. Humility commends prayer, 194, 34 ff. By praying, it draws divine aid to itself, 1173, 11. Whoever meditates on the Lord’s ordinances is always humbled, 1166, 30. By bending the knees, offence against the Lord is mitigated and grace is summoned, 141, 74. If we pray with speech, let us also sympathize with the mind, 1026, 26. A good life makes prayer fly and gives spiritual wings to prayers, by which the prayer of the saints is lifted up to God, 1247, 5 ff. The prayer of the faithful grows rich when nourished by apostolic food, 216, 22. Prayer must not be publicized, 200, 35–36. When you pray, ask for great things—that is, things eternal, divine, and heavenly, 1212, 11. God does not hear anything except what he considers worthy of his benefits, 1212, 11. The Lord always grants more than is asked, 1530, 121. For whom should one pray? 201, 39. Why does God often not grant what is asked in prayer? 1431, 90. When the Lord wishes to forgive, he gives the grace and confidence to make supplication, 821, 15. [Col. 2276]

**THE DIGNITIES OF PRAYER**, 1250, 15. It is food for the mind, 1445, 142. It is a good shield against weakness, 846, 11. Those who are more perfect draw near to God; but righteous men of the next order are content if their prayer draws near, 1248, 7. The adversary frequently pours worldly thoughts even upon those who are praying, 1252, 20. Supplication is praiseworthy in a sinner, 832, 38.

**TO BE IGNORANT OF THE ORDER OF DOING SOMETHING**, even if you know what you are doing, is not perfect knowledge, 1012, 12.

**OREB** signifies drying up, 431, 34.

**OREGANO:** the tortoise drives away poison with it, 119, 19.

**ORIGEN** carefully examined the interpretations of many people concerning Scripture, 1014, 16. He was devoted to ecclesiastical office, 336, 54. He granted very much to the philosophical tradition, ibid. He asserted the harmony of the stars, 336, 54.

**STAIN OF ORIGIN** cannot be an impediment to virtue, 1327, 36. See **ADAM**, **SIN**.

**MOUTH:** its usefulness, 138, 65; 140, 68; 236, 22.

**KISS** is a pledge of devotion and love, 139, 68; 359, 8; 863, 17; 1388, 20; 1462, 212.

**DOOR:** why is the opening through which the excess of food is expelled located at the rear? 141, 72; 236, 24.

**LEISURE:** leisure is dangerous to a virtue that feels secure, 1112, 25.

**SHEEP:** why does it tear at grass insatiably at the approach of winter? 120, 20.

**Οὐρανός**—that is, “heaven”: whence does it receive this name? 108, 73.

## P
## P

**PADUS.** The Po, a dependable importer of maritime supplies with Italian resources, 28, 12.

**PAEDAGOGI.** The terrifying scourges of pedagogues are beneficial, 126, 38.

**Πάλη**, in Greek, is *lucta* in Latin, that is, wrestling, 801, 56.

**PALMS.** How we ought to be like them, 61, 71.

**VINE LEAVES**, 57, 60.

**BREAD.** He for whom the Holy Spirit is rest and perfection does not need the bread of angels and the water of refreshment, 805, 61. The multiplication of the five loaves signifies the author and creator of the whole material nature, 1404, 85.

**PARADISE.** Who and what the earthly paradise is, where it is, and what human being God placed in it, 145, 1 ff. Why it is said to be toward the East, and not opposite the East, 153, 23. What the four rivers flowing from it are, and what they signify, 150, 14 ff. How beasts, cattle, and birds are said to have been in it, 167, 51. How some interpret it mystically, ibid. Paradise is the true home that first received the human being, lost not by right but by deceit, 1358, 14. The grace of paradise is not sought in one day, nor in two or a few months, but is always sought, and sought in all things, 1024, 21. The just are often caught up into it, and how, 168, 53. Why the ascent to the third heaven is necessary for a person to be caught up into paradise, 168, 53. See **BEATITUDE**.

**LEOPARD.** By the variety of its coloring it reveals the soul’s varied movements, 118, 15.

**PARENTS.** Affection toward children ought to be equal, 460, 5 ff.; 484, 5, 6. The dissolution of children is attributed to the father’s negligence, 404, 35. The impiety of parents toward their children is censured, 103, 58 and 61. Hatred of fathers toward sons, and of sons toward parents, is censured, 121, 22. How much we owe our parents, 1302, 66. You are forbidden both not to love your parents and to prefer them to God, 1443, 136. Piety toward divine religion must be preferred to the ties of kinship with parents, 1420, 41; 1459, 21. The first degree of piety is to honor one’s parents, 1489, 74. They must be supported in necessity, ibid. and following. The stork is an example of piety toward parents, 101, 55. Christ honored His parents not by the obligation of nature but by the duty of piety, 1490, 74. A father is not to be mocked but revered, 275, 118. Scripture teaches that parents ought to be praised, and why, 1271, 15. The disgrace of ancestors cannot be a dishonor to their descendants, 718, 33. Both father in son and son in father are reproved, 273, 114.

**PASSOVER.** Why it is called the Lord’s Passover, 198, 31. It is celebrated every year in spring, 7, 14. It ought to be celebrated by the chaste and sanctified, 151, 16. From Passover until Pentecost there is freedom from fasting; praise is offered to God and the Alleluia is sung, 688, 42. See **PENTECOST**.

**PASSIONS.** It is difficult to find a soul free from passions, 209, 8. Innocent affections are good passions, 264, 88. Every affection except the enticement of disordered pleasure is indeed a passion, but a good passion, 264, 88. When vicious passions move the mind, corruption is produced; when they arouse the pursuit of virtues, there is progress in discipline, 249, 53. Intemperance is a kind of source of bodily passions, 327, 34. Pleasure and pain are, as it were, the natural leaders of the passions, and the others follow them, 445, 5. Our flesh is tossed and fluctuates as though on the open sea amid various passions, 248, 51. We must first conquer the passions of our own body, 889, 9. Great shipwrecks occur when the storm and tempest of the mind, body, and all the senses are stirred together, 247, 49 [Col. 2277]. How can there be security where different passions are fighting, 1188, 14? Every passion is servile, 463, 12. All passions are nails, 397, 16. Endurance of passions is a rare and difficult virtue, 1129, 49. The hiding places of the passions: whoever falls into them is submerged and does not emerge, 34, 4. When the soul is exhausted by turbulent and stormy passions, once they cease it regains virtue, 254, 63. Each person presides over himself with a kind of royal authority: if he restrains bodily luxury within himself and reduces his flesh to servitude, 362, 16. A stronger mind possesses the ruling virtue that commands the bodily senses rather than obeying them, 321, 19. The pursuit of learning and attention to discipline can moderate every disorder of the passions, 55, 56. When bodily passions have been cut away, the just person remains in the body almost incorporeal, 250, 55. It is a great thing for someone to be tranquil within himself and in harmony with himself, 468, 29. That belongs to a kind of immortal person, 195, 24.

**SHEPHERDS.** Why shepherds of sheep were an abomination to the Egyptians, 195, 24.

**HOUSEHOLDERS.** Duties toward their servants, 308, 83.

**PATIENCE.** It is an indication of humility, 1087, 3. If hope is taken away, patience cannot be perpetual, 1165, 27. See **INJURY**.

**PATRIARCHS.** Coming before the Law and freed from the bonds of prescriptions, they shone forth with the free and similar grace of the Gospel for us, 1321, 21. The patriarchs instruct you not only by teaching but also by erring, 301, 58.

**PAUL.** Benjamin prefigured Paul, 500, 44 ff.; 530, 57 ff.; 1038, 17. Paul’s blindness is Christ’s weeping, 504, 59. The persecutor fell and the preacher of the Gospel rose, 855, 33. See Paul yesterday persecuting, today believing, tomorrow preaching, 1511, 32. Paul was chosen as teacher of the nations, 826, 28. His calling is the Church’s firmness, 365, 31. He took care, as far as he could, not to sin after receiving the sacraments of baptism, 1031, 40. He glories not in knowledge but in ignorance: he denies what belongs to knowledge; he confesses what belongs to charity; he exalts what is alien and denies what is his own, 795, 40. He saw eternal things when he began not to see bodily things, 1105, 8. How did he hear those things which afterward he was not permitted to speak, 795, 41? His free preaching for Christ stripped the Jewish people and cut away all their privilege, 505, 64. How was he tested in every contest, 801, 56? He uses words that are natural rather than popular or technical, 424, 16. Those whom he reproved he wanted to grieve until repentance, not to plunge into deeper sorrow, 1049, 18. How rightly he lent the Lord’s money at interest, 796, 43. On his account the thirteenth tribe was sanctified, 513, 2.

**POVERTY.** It is intermediate: both good and evil people can be poor, 1368, 53. Not all poverty is holy, nor are riches criminal, 1473, 13. It is not the punishment of sin, 668, 17. No one ought to complain about it, 102, 57. What poverty is good and not to be avoided, 728, 57. Poverty is blessed if it knows its own goods in truth, 89, 23. It benefits a person and exercises the body without oppressing it, 133, 51. It is good if it proceeds from piety and is undertaken as an exercise of the virtues, 925, 91. It is more readily acceptable to God than a treasure, 1006, 37. If poverty is blessed and heaven is open to it, let us disregard earthly riches and avoid bodily excess, 925, 91. Poverty is glorious, and why, 1423, 55. Are there trials in poverty and riches, 134, 53; 1069, 37 ff.? The disgrace of want often breaks saints whom fear of death had not broken, 1153, 35.

**THE POOR.** In what way are the poor superior to the rich, 134, 52? Let no one mock the poor, and why, 1486, 61. Whoever mocks the poor provokes the one who made him, 1095, 26. Does that poor man seem worthy of mockery and execration who nevertheless has a portion in heaven, 1058, 8? How unjustly, often within the very Church, the just person who distributed his possessions to the poor is despised, 1244, 18. Christ’s poverty. See **CHRIST**. Who is the mystical poor man, 797, 44? There is a good poverty in one’s character, 869, 5. Be poor in spirit and you will be rich whatever your income, 194, 21.

**PEACE.** There is one peace that contains an occasion of offense, and another that does not, 664, 6. It is the end of the whole of virtue, and of bodily strength itself: when the war has been completed, it restores peace, 1244, 17. Christ gave peace by calming the wars of souls, 788, 22. Where there is peace, and much peace, there the cross of Christ is not a reproach but salvation, 1245, 21. Begin peace with yourself, so that you may bring peace to others, 1369, 59. The leisure of peace is sometimes dangerous, 1111, 22. Those seeking peace are accustomed to carry before them an olive branch, 256, 67.

**TO SIN.** To sin is to deviate from what is according to nature, 759, 47. Sin is transgression of the divine law and disobedience to heavenly commandments, 161, 39. Before we are born, we are stained by contagion; and before we enjoy the light, we receive the injury of our very origin, 694, 56. Unless the Lord forgives, no one can be saved whom the inheritance of a harmful condition has itself bound to guilt, 854, 28. Through the succession of nature there is also a succession of guilt transmitted from one person to all, 732, 71 [Col. 2278]. Adam transmitted the inheritance of vice down to us, 918, 75. In him the whole human condition was stripped bare through the succession of nature, subject not only to guilt but also to misery, 721, 41. Our iniquity is one thing, and that of our heel another: in the heel Adam was wounded by the serpent’s tooth, and through his wound left the human race an inherited condition subject to succession, 947, 8. From this it is shown that sin proceeded, as though the body and soul were its parents, while bodily nature is tested and the unsound soul suffers with it, 1445, 143. The flesh was sin, inasmuch as it had been condemned by hereditary sin, 1039, 21. The condition drew vice with it; guilt infected nature, 712, 19. The kingdom of sin is the kingdom of death, which long prevailed throughout the whole world, 932, 16. God preferred that there should be more whom He could save and to whom He could grant forgiveness of sin than a single Adam free from guilt, 166, 57.

Whether a person can be without sin, 1271, 17. No one is without sin, 681, 15; 683, 24. To deny this is sacrilege; to confess it to God is a remedy for impunity, 1254, 27. How it is evident that we are all under sin, 693, 53. A person may not be struck by one particular wound—for example, injustice, intemperance, or unchastity—but he remains open to the other wounds, 839, 53. Such are sins generally that, if you avoid one, you fall into another, 1183, 45. You are not required never to commit sin, but not to remain in sin by taking up a lasting residence there, 746, 22. It is not a virtue to be unable to sin, but to be unwilling, 1485, 57. To have fallen into guilt belongs to nature; to erase it belongs to virtue, 681, 15. No time ought to be empty of protection, because no time is empty of guilt, 349, 81. Why do we often find serious sins among illustrious and blessed men, 1327, 37? How useful the falls of saints are, 1523, 89. Some are sinners of heaven, others sinners of earth; who these are, 168, 34. There are three kinds of sinners: of thought, of action, and of persistence, 745, 20. Voluntary and accidental sins, 998, 17. Mortal sins, 701, 77; 1407, 99. Whoever has committed graver sins easily slips into the others, 217, 25. Sins that are grave and manifest are plunged down without any doubt; lighter sins, however, are often lifted up by good works, 906, 46. If you carry grave sins from here, you will not have rest there, 816, 2. To have sinned belongs to the human condition; to act impiously is the poison of treachery and a most wicked mind, 632, 17. He is unpardonable who has labored to find the evil he was seeking, 770, 12. It is worse to live for sin than to die in sin, 402, 28. No one dies more grievously than one who lives in sin, 240, 34. You yourself are the cause of your wickedness and the instigator of your crimes, 18, 31. Even a tiny spark of sin, if kindled by fuel of some vice, raises a serious conflagration, 749, 26. A bodily fall ought not to be counted as vice unless the mind inclines toward guilt, 274, 115. The author of sin is not the flesh but the affection, 448, 11. Truly pitiable is the condition in which a person is compelled to give an account of a sin he cannot avoid, 634, 22. Whoever bears the image of God ought to be without sin, 811, 73. See **GUILT**.

For sinners the law is absent; if it were present, they would not offend, 189, 14. We recognize our offenses more after we have sinned, and why, 177, 70? While we are in the desire to sin, the eyes of the mind are darkened by a kind of smoke of iniquity, so that they do not see the deformity of what they desire, 319, 16. Many, because of excessive iniquities, do not accept consciousness of sin, 180, 75. The memory of offenses burdens the conscience unless medicine is sought, 840, 57. The soul has no peace through the virtues when our sins rush before our eyes, 826, 28. Our sin always confronts us like a wicked exactor, or like a dishonest moneylender approaching his debtor, 769, 8. We are guilty without an accuser; we are tortured without a torturer; bound without chains; sold without a seller, 827, 28. God sees the person who is thinking of sinning, 977, 12. God, the angels, the devil, and his ministers see the sinner, 978, 13. Just as God regards the good deeds of the just, so He detects the hidden deeds of sinners, 826, 26. How miserable is the condition of the person who thinks his sins can deceive God’s knowledge, 627, 6. You would fear—not merely to do but even to speak or think—what is wicked if you believed God to be present to you, 976, 10 ff. The more hidden an iniquity is thought to be, the more frequent it usually becomes, 1048, 13. The robber flees the day as though it were a witness to his crime; the adulterer blushes at the light as though it were conscious of his adultery; the parricide flees the fruitfulness of the earth, 218, 26. Sins earn for God a reason for forgetting, so that He may blot out those whom He has found unworthy of His visitation, 646, 22. No one is far from God except one whom his own crimes have banished, 586, 68. No one belongs to Christ except one who is free from crime, 1127, 41. Why Christ does not enter the souls of sinners, 830, 35. Whoever follows guilt departs from Christ, 486, 10. A person is not rejected by the Lord; he rejects himself, 898, 25. Salvation does not flee sinners; they themselves flee salvation, 1229, 27. We cannot live for God unless we die to sin, 510, 83. As though by a father’s right, God is accustomed to disown degenerate children, 645, 20.

Most people glory in their own falls and think that things which are crimes are marks of praise; in this they must be judged worse than dumb animals, 690, 46 [Col. 2279]. They are more detestable because, when they commit such great crimes, they do not feel shame, 1100, 41. How evil are those for whom virtues are a disgrace and sins a praise, 751, 29? Among most people innocence is regarded as cowardice, and guilt as praise, 262, 81. Most people profess injustice as praise, 775, 25. How the sinner attempts to excuse himself by producing examples from the divine Scriptures, 175, 65. There is still a remedy for healing in that sinner who hears the word of God and hides himself, 177, 70. Nothing causes greater pain than the guilt of sin, 228, 2. Our guilt is a more serious adversary for us, 827, 28. Why does every guilt, as though by an adversary’s force, usually cast the mind from its place and move it from its proper state, 962, 19? As many sins, as many vices, so many kings, 1236, 50. Inveterate habit of sinning has such power that it excludes nature and is found incurable, 749, 27. What else is sin except a burden that weighs down the traveler of this age, 628, 7? How can one who has violated divine things refrain from human offenses, or be good to human beings who has injured God, 217, 25? How great is the worthlessness of offenses, 1437, 117. There are people who, while alive, are surrounded by a tomb and filled with the dead, 763, 55. How great a folly it is to provoke the divine majesty, 780, 8. Through sin a person loses the name of human being and becomes a serpent, mule, and beast, 1090, 11. A sinner cannot praise God, 1253, 25. Sin is compared to a horse, 330, 43, and to a killing frost, 1108, 15. How sins are punished, 213, 15. Sins follow the just; they do not precede them. They precede the unjust, 683, 24. Because of human crime even the elements themselves are condemned, 218, 26. The imperfect soul desires only to escape the judgment of sin; the perfect soul seeks to acquire the reward of the heavenly kingdom, 1176, 19. The unjust are winnowed like chaff, the just like wheat, 659, 17. When we sin, we are handed over to the adversary for reproach, so that on the day of judgment he may accuse and betray us as an enemy, 854, 30. Every sin is the enemy’s seed, 943, 20. The guilty, even unwillingly, attain an end belonging not to nature but to guilt, 222, 35. Why, when condemning sin, God delayed vengeance against its author, 433, 39? Great sins are removed by great medicine, 559, 75. How their ropes and bonds are loosened, 1071, 40 ff. Bent beneath involuntary vices, let us appease God for ourselves; let us follow what He commands and avoid what He forbids. Let there be eagerness to appease the divinity, obedience in following the commandment, and caution against transgressing what is forbidden, 422, 12. Let the sinner acknowledge his guilt, the impious groan, and the just person not exalt himself, 633, 19. Guilt is pardonable when confession of offenses follows it, 177, 71. The person who confesses his own sin is justified, 199, 34. How does the person who confesses his sin justify the Lord, 693, 53 ff.? It belongs to a good mind to feel the wound of sin, 691, 47. Not to feel the bitterness of the wound is an incurable sickness, 691, 47. It is not knowledge of wickedness but participation in crime that is condemned, 648, 27. Why Christ ate with sinners, 1285, 10. It is not absurd that criminals should live together with the pious, and the stained with the consecrated, 212, 14. See **CONFESSION** and **PENANCE**.

The Trinity forgives sins, 1369, 55. Only the one who does not know his own wounds can heal them, 1362, 27. How good and ready God is to forgive sins, 1292, 33. The Lord’s mercy in releasing sins is extraordinarily great, 243, 42. God is not accustomed to undo or renew sins that He has once forgiven, 848, 14. Those whom God redeemed from sin He increases in reward, 713, 20. Sin is forgiven by grace, erased by the blood of the cross, and covered by charity, 697, 62. Let justice remit iniquities, fortitude fear, and temperance impurities, so that the remission of sins may become perpetual, 1016, 26. See **THE KEYS OF THE CHURCH**. What fruit can be sweeter than the remission of sins, 1021, 12? Who should rejoice in the absolution of their crimes, 402, 29? It is good to be condemned in sin and scourged for an offense, 177, 71. We often see some who had formerly been negligent Christians become more diligent after committing a sin, and ordinarily become perfect through repentance for it, 819, 11. Blessed is the fall that is repaired for the better, 865, 20. Whoever is without sin is subject to Christ, and why, 784, 16? Whoever has stripped himself of the service of offenses possesses authority, not servitude, 321, 19. The kings from the seed of Abraham are those who do not serve sin, 347, 77. Whoever returns to the Lord restores himself to himself; whoever departs from Christ disowns himself, 1463, 220. Unless sin has been forgiven here, we shall not have rest; if there is no rest, there will be no eternal life; if there is no eternal life, we shall not exist, 858, 38.

**BREAST.** It is like a kind of sanctuary of wisdom, 236, 23.

**MONEY.** Money acquired wrongly stains body and soul, 1348, 53. In monetary lawsuits, when the price has been returned, the legal claim is discharged, 1524, 94. See **AVARICE**.

**FEET.** Their usefulness, 141, 74. Why a human being has only two, ibid. Although their steps seem narrower, they become broader when we walk, 236, 23.

**PENTECOST.** It marks the beginning of the eighth week, 1476, 25. Our ancestors handed down to us that all fifty days of Pentecost should be celebrated as Passover; all the days are like the Lord’s Day, 1476, 25.

The partridge, stealing and brooding another’s eggs, wastes its labor, 117, 13.

**PERFECTION.** In what perfection and completion consist, 375, 59. The person who lacks nothing is perfect; the person who has nothing remaining is just, 465, 21. The perfect person does not know the inconveniences of this body or the adversities of the world, 455, 32. It belongs to a perfect mind to take nothing from earthly or bodily things, 331, 46. The perfect person does not know wickedness or deceit, 814, 81. Whence perfection came before Christ’s advent, 286, 12. In a perfect person there is a twofold virtue, namely intention and action, 1268, 8. It belongs to the perfect not to turn aside; to the prudent, not to turn aside completely, 315, 6. It belongs not to the perfect person to await, but to have awaited, 859, 1. Perfect virtue possesses the tranquility and stability of rest, 468, 28. Perfect virtue remains always amid adversities and pleasures; adversities diminish nothing of its perfection, nor do pleasures add anything to its perfection, 456, 35 ff. Here life is not perfect but in shadow, 1029, 35. Christ sleeps for the fearful but keeps watch for the perfect, 1353, 68.

**PERFECT THINGS.** They are not sought in beginnings; rather, from beginnings one reaches what is perfect, 1409, 105. The end of our discipline and studies is perfection, 668, 20. Perfect things are one at the end, 1416, 21.

**TREACHERY.** It can confess but cannot believe, 1358, 12. Its weapons are more serious than those of battle, 1200, 18. Its cause is twofold: either wickedness or fear, 1435, 110.

**PERSIANS.** By not obeying the king’s laws, they carry out upon themselves the sentence of their own death, 107, 68.

**PERSECUTION.** It occurs so that faith may shine, virtue excel, and the inner mind be made manifest to all, 824, 21. Many seek Christ in leisure and do not find Him; they find Him in persecutions, and find Him quickly, 368, 41. Whoever flees the persecutor also rejects Christ the defender, 1236, 51. The Christian people were established through endurance of injuries and the experience of dangers, and the Church gained increase, 907, 37. There are far more inner persecutors than others, and they are more serious, 1234, 45 ff. See **ADVERSITIES**, **CHURCH**, and **MARTYRS**.

**THOSE WHO PERSEVERE.** The same furnace is golden for those who persevere that it is iron for the fragile, 1225, 11. It is not within human power, but belongs to the merciful God, that you may complete what you have begun, 1098, 35.

**PESTILENCE.** It first infects irrational creatures, especially dogs, horses, oxen, and those that seem to live among human beings, 239, 31. The plague of oxen, human beings, and other livestock, 1506, 10. Pestilence in regions is brought to an end by the death of one particular person, 1410, 108.

**PETER.** Peter totters on the sea but does not fall, 94, 35. What Peter’s ship signifies, 1352, 68. The ship that has Peter is not troubled; the one that has Judas is troubled, 1353, 70. Where Peter is, there is the Church; where the Church is, there is no death but eternal life, 879, 30. Peter’s hook does not kill but consecrates, 85, 16. Peter was rightly reproved by Christ because he dared to claim constancy without considering his vulnerable nature, 940, 9. The speech of Peter when he was tottering is more trustworthy than the teaching of many, 932, 15. His error is the teaching of the just, and his tottering is the rock of all, 1522, 84. As Eve led Adam astray, so a woman wrongly led Peter in, 1520, 75. Peter’s denial is weighed, 1520, 74 ff. What he seemed to have denied with his voice, he confessed with tears, 932, 15. He erased his fall by his confession of charity, 684, 25. Peter’s having been able to sin was so extraordinary that his sin could not even be grasped by the Evangelists, 1520, 78. Jesus looked at Peter, and immediately the error departed, 112, 88; 699, 68. When Christ first looked at Peter, He saw and enlightened him, 699, 68. Why Peter was asked three times about his love, 692, 50. The priest is rightly chosen who has bound himself threefold with the spirit of divine charity, 894, 16. Why was he placed over the Church after having been tempted by the devil, 904, 40? Christ left him to us as a kind of substitute for His love, 1542, 176. Christ gave Peter so much glory through the cross that he honored Christ with reversed footsteps, 1245, 21. Why he asked to be suspended with his feet inverted, 626, 2.

**PHARAOH.** In what sense he preferred to be the devil’s portion rather than God’s, 1061, 15. By punishing Pharaoh, God sought not the increase of His own praise but the increase of our correction, 1197, 7.

**PHARES.** It is interpreted as “division,” 914, 65; 1322, 24. Phares and Zara prefigured a twofold life and a double service under the Law and the Gospel, 1321, 21 ff.

**PHARISEES.** Why they were so called, 1322, 24. They were divided from the truth, 1160, 9. They do not, even in a small point or moment, transfer themselves to the spiritual understanding of the Law, 914, 65. They refer nothing to the inner person, but everything to the outer and earthly person, 914, 66 [Col. 2281].

**PHE.** In Latin it signifies “I have erred,” or “I have opened my mouth,” 1184, 1.

**PHILOSOPHY.** Is there a twofold species, 335, 52? It seeks what belongs to others while not knowing what belongs to itself, 1249, 9. It seeks divinity in statues, 765, 1. It made many gods, 1274, 17. How much it transferred from the sacred books, 407, 45; 410, 51. It is not the concern of holy people to describe the axis of heaven and the spaces of the elements in the philosophical manner, 1120, 30.

**PHILOSOPHERS.** Their method of reasoning, 121, 23. They used fewer Latin and customary expressions, so that they might use their own, 1296, 42. Most boast of their art in ornate language, 1426, 66. They are rich in speech, poor in faith, and excluded from truth, 790, 27. Whence their opinion concerning the highest good was taken, 412, 55. In philosophical speech there is the vanity of the world, 1107, 12. What the supreme master of philosophy, as they call him, replied when he was accused and questioned, 1172, 11.

**PHISON.** According to the Hebrews it is called “change of mouth,” and why, 151, 153; 755, 36. Its beauty and fertility, ibid.

**PHOENIX.** How long it lives in Arabia, and how it dies and rises again, 110, 79; 1212, 13.

**PHOENICE, TYRE, AND SIDON.** They are neighboring cities, 556, 70.

**PHOTINUS.** Photinus says that Christ is the son of David, not of God, 715, 26. Christ says, “I will,” because of Photinus; He commands because of Arius; He touches because of Mani, 1356, 4. Photinus is a moth, and why, 1270, 13.

**PHOTINIAN.** The Photinian says that Christ did not yet exist at the creation of the world, 45, 32.

**PAINTER.** A painter ought to represent shadows, 66, 11.

**PIETY.** How great a virtue piety is, 1208, 45. Piety is first owed to God, second to parents, 746, 20. The measure of order does not outweigh piety, 471, 33. The receptacles in which the hidden mysteries of piety are held ought to be pure, 927, 3. Just as, through the unity and fullness of divinity, God the Father is wholly in the Son and the Son in the Father, so through intention and the affection of piety the whole human being is in Christ, 794, 37. Sometimes the devil compels a person to become impious through excessive piety, 1337, 10. See **GOD** and **PARENTS**.

**PLEDGE.** They call a pledge what has been received in exchange for borrowed money, 614, 67. What is the pledge that the Law commands to be returned, 611, 57; 614, 67 ff. See **USURY**.

**PILATE.** He was a type of all judges who would condemn those whom they considered innocent, 1525, 101.

**PINE.** With a drop of pine resin, the fox heals itself, 119, 19. In the pine there is great power of God, 60, 68.

**FISH.** Their creation, 79, 1 ff. Their various kinds are enumerated, 80, 5. How respiration occurs in them, 83, 10, 11. Why they have dense and sharp teeth, 84, 12. They lick the earth and seek their prey from it, 80, 3. They feed on herbs and small worms, 84, 13. Why, when removed from the water, they cannot live, 83, 10. Fish have several methods of reproduction, 82, 7, 8. They know nothing of adulterous contamination, 82, 9. Their exceptional piety toward their offspring, 82, 7. The relationship of parent and children, 83, 10. Some bring their offspring back into the womb in order to protect them, 82, 7. The solemn migration of certain fish for the sake of nurturing their offspring, 91, 29, 30. They have dwelling places assigned to them, 90, 26. The smaller is devoured by the larger, and again the larger by the stronger, 84, 13. See **TÝMALLUS**.

**PLANETS.** Why they are so called, 69, 15.

**PLANTS.** All plants have seed, or something possessing the power of seed, 59, 66.

**PLATO.** The father of philosophy, 328, 37. He established three principles of all things: God, the exemplar, and uncreated matter, I, 1. He proposed a fictitious and shadowy *πολιτεία*—“constitution” or “republic”—and why, 281, 2. He went to Egypt for the sake of learning, to become acquainted with the sayings of the prophets, 1195, 4. From there he transferred a dialogue that he wrote about virtue, ibid. He could read the writings of Moses, 236, 24. He transferred material from our books into his own, 438, 50. What he thought about the harmony of the stars, 336, 54. What Plato’s garden was like, 398, 19.

**RAIN.** It is poured from the sea onto the lands, 41, 22. It is granted through the prayers of the Church, 41, 22.

**PUNISHMENT.** The punishment of the guilty is a kind of absolution from offenses, 1228, 22. Whoever fears punishment should preserve grace, 1041, 28. Punishment corrects and reforms the person who has gone astray, 1195, 3.

**PENANCE.** Christ is the teacher of penance, 827, 29. To amend the future belongs to human attention; to condemn the past belongs to divine power, 1247, 3. It is the human being’s task to perform penance for offenses; it is God’s gift to fulfill the grace of the mystery, 1307, 79. To do penance is of no benefit unless it is done as it ought to be, 815, 1. Penance must be carried out in prayers and supplications, with sorrow and tears, 842, 59. The complete definition of penance is the recollection of offenses, and how, 815, 2. The sinner always recognizes his guilt too slowly, 176, 68. Whoever does penance removes the shame of confessing his crime, 1080, 5. Whoever does not acknowledge his error is insane, raving, and senseless, 691, 47 [Col. 2282]. Shame diminishes guilt; self-defense increases it. By remaining silent we correct ourselves; through contentiousness we fall, 217, 24. Neither honors nor embarrassment before friends should be considered when penance must be done, 838, 51. Whoever does penance ought not to be troubled if someone brings his sin against him, 820, 13. He ought to offer himself to punishment and meet the divine indignation, ibid. The fall of a serious weakness is not grievous if there is not also a deliberate determination of the will not to rise from it, 837, 47. To perform penance is true medicine, 816, 4. The water of tears, the water of penance, is the second cup by which you restore yourself after the first, 819, 11. God is easily reconciled when He is earnestly entreated, 1465, 224. Judgments are sweet for the person doing penance, 1032, 43. Penance is laborious; grace is sweet, 851, 22. Penance seeks patience, and patience moderates great offenses, 836, 46. Penance erases an offense; wisdom guards against it, 1433, 96. How the person who repents of sin is freed from punishment and penalty, 212, 13? Whoever has done penance flees the coming wrath, 816, 2. Those who postpone it until death are censured, 1464, 221. Ambrose wrote two books on penance, 815, 1.

**FRUITS.** Their variety, 56, 58 and 59.

**PONTUS.** Sweeter than the rest of the sea’s gulf, 92, 29.

**PEOPLE.** What it declares mystically, 54, 53.

**POSSESSOR.** No one can be a possessor who does not receive the fruit, 1370, 61. What you possess is more valuable than what you still hope for, 471, 32.

**OCTOPUSES.** Their cunning in capturing prey, 88, 21.

**POWERS.** Their ordering is from God; ambition for power is from evil, 1341, 29 ff. Power is not evil, but the person who uses power badly is, ibid. It is a law of nature that those who possess the greatest power should be more lenient in punishing, 107, 68. Often it is a sign of greater authority not to restrain offenders than to take vengeance, 1016, 24. Continuous and prolonged power produces insolence, 100, 52. It is a serious matter to use power in such a way that you fall under someone else’s power, 1455, 186. Evil power is the power to make permissible what is not permissible, 1232, 38. All power of the age is a dream, not reality, 495, 30.

**DRINK.** What drink is necessary for a human being, 272, 110.

**HERALDS.** Who is led away by the heralds’ cry, 44, 30?

**PRECIPICE.** Falling from the highest places is called a precipice; a fall on level ground is called a slip, 776, 26.

**REWARD.** The more excellent the reward, the more earnest the duty, 1374, 78. See **WAGES**.

**PRESUMPTION.** Why no one should easily presume, 123, 24. No one ought to rely on his own virtue, 1327, 37.

**TRANSGRESSOR.** In Greek, *apostata*, “apostate,” from departing; in Latin, *transgressor*, “transgressor”—and why, 1167, 32.

**PRESBYTER.** Give the presbyter what earthly abundance you have, so that you may receive from him the spiritual thing you lack, 1491, 79.

**FIRSTFRUITS.** They are judged not by time but by holiness, 207, 7. What the firstfruits of our senses are that we ought to offer to God, 206, 5, 6.

**FIRSTBORN.** Every firstborn is holy, 529, 55. The saints are called firstborn, 8, 15. Not every firstborn is holy; but everything holy is also firstborn, 208, 7.

**PRINCES.** Only their heads cast in bronze, and their faces fashioned from bronze or marble, are worshiped by human beings, 136, 57. The power to command is an incentive to sin, 710, 12. See **EMPEROR** and **KING**.

**PRINCIPLES.** Various kinds of principles, 6, 12.

**PROGRESS.** What the course of our life ought to be, 180, 76. The beginning of progress toward virtue is to abstain from sin, 744, 18.

**PROPHECY.** Prophecy is the announcement of the future, 515, 7. It is fulfilled not only by miracles of events but also by the exactness of words, 1289, 24.

**PROPHETS.** They were called seers because of their inner eyes, 1105, 8. The Lord spoke in them, and therefore they could not err, 1509, 22. They did not prophesy continually, but when the grace of the spirit of prophecy infused itself into them, 1119, 18. Placed in an ecstasy of mind, they prophesied, filled with the Spirit of God, 860, 5. And how, 339, 61. Why, in order to prophesy, they commanded someone skilled in singing psalms to sing, 1052, 26. For them future things were present things, 807, 64; 1077, 57; 1122, 27. Things that were to come were revealed to them by the Spirit as though present, 559, 77. No one can be a prophet unless he has prophesied about the Son of God, 1413, 10. God’s truth must be gathered from the prophets’ oracles, 772, 18. Why we sometimes avoid the words used by the prophets, 558, 73. The life of the prophets is according to the Gospel, 1322, 23. Their food is the fulfillment of the divine will, 1304, 72.

**PRIVATE PROPERTY.** While claiming private possessions, we have lost what is common; and nothing is truly private where nothing is perpetual, 1439, 124.

**PROSPERITY.** The success of sinners makes us waver, 776, 27. God’s foreknowledge and providence are proved all the more by the fact that a person placed in sin abounds in the success of worldly prosperity, 667, 14. Prosperity has often overthrown many whom harsh punishments had not broken, 1124, 31. See **ADVERSITY**.

**PROVIDENCE.** The supports of divine providence would not be lacking to human beings if we wished to preserve God’s justice, 1213, 14. See **GOD**.

**PRUDENCE.** What its effects are, 1371, 66. The prudent and self-controlled possess virtue and the soul, 316, 7.

**SINGING PSALMS.** Its twofold duty, 884, 41.

**PSALMS.** The order of the Psalms does not correspond to the order of events, and for what reason, 688, 41 ff. The Psalms entitled “For the end” are either about Christ or belong to Christ Himself, 955, 1. Many are written “For the eighth,” 1367, 49, and “For the winepresses,” 1500, 24. How great the power of prophecy is in the Psalms, 740, 8. Although the body of all the Psalms is one, nevertheless within it there flourishes a natural, mystical, and moral …
sense, 777, 2. The praises and virtues of the Psalms, 740, 9 ff. What psalm is not a medicine for a sinful conscience? 815, 1. A person ought not to end the day without the celebration of the Psalms, 95, 36. Psalm XXI concerns the Passion of Christ, 1185, 3. The thirty-third is moral, but the thirty-sixth is more expansive and sweeter, 777, 2. The title of the thirty-fifth psalm is explained, 765, 2. The thirty-seventh has greater power to stir repentance, 815, 1. In the thirty-ninth the New Testament is announced, 859, 1. The fortieth is inscribed as spoken in the person of the Savior, 745, 19. In the fortieth, exhortation to virtue is given rather than suppression of error, 745, 19. From the fiftieth we learn how repentance ought to be practiced, 689, 42. What is the title of the seventy-second? 661, 2. Why the seventy-fifth is entitled “for the Assyrian,” 1447, 153. In the eighty-fourth the coming of the Lord Jesus is prophesied more clearly, 1033, 2 and 3. The hundred and tenth and the hundred and eleventh are asserted to have been composed in meter, 973, 3. In CXVII the Passion of the Lord is described, 973, 3; 975, 7. Why CXVIII is arranged according to the letters of the Hebrews, 991, 1; 1140, 1. It is composed concerning the person of Christ, 994, 2; 1092, 17; 1140, 10. How greatly its ethical teaching excels, 971, 1. It wholly forms the perfection of the human being, 1131, 3; 1246, 1.

PSALTERIUM [PSALTER]: It appears to be divided into five books—and how? 882, 37 ff. The Book of Psalms, corrected according to the Hebrews, among the Greeks, 1056, 2. In it lies the progress of all people, and a kind of medicine for human salvation, 739, 7. The Psalter is good when the life of faith accords with it, the flesh aspires to the soul, and the will to virtue, 947, 7.

PUDICITIA [CHASTITY]: Bodily chastity and spiritual grace are the true sacrifice of Christ, 104, 62. See CASTITAS.

PUDOR [SHAME]: It is generally our corrector, 1100, 41. Whoever is ashamed of what he has done does not afterward know how to commit anything of the kind for which he would likewise be ashamed, 691, 48. Fear is a weak guardian of perseverance, but shame is a good teacher of duty, 1475, 21. The saints have great concern for modesty, so that often there is modesty in their very desires, 1280, 43. Modesty excuses the guilty person; shame accuses its own author, 1012, 11. How great the modesty of women ought to be, 297, 42.

PUELLA [GIRL]: A sacred girl is consecrated by a devout veil, 1038, 20.

PUERITIA [CHILDHOOD]: Christ taught us that childhood is a virtue, 800, 52. In childhood there is a certain venerable old age of character, and in old age an innocent childhood, 1485, 58. It is said proverbially: “He handles a sword like a child,” 1334, 50. We say “boys” when we mean little servants, 308, 82.

PUERPERIUM [CHILDBIRTH]: A man cannot be present at childbirth, 68, 14.

PULCHRITUDO [BEAUTY]: What is true beauty? 32, 21.

PULMO [LUNG]: Why is it softer? 140, 70.

PUPILLA [PUPIL]: The pupil of the eye is protected by a kind of extremely secure natural rampart, 137, 60.

PURPURA [PURPLE]: Purple adorns the banquets of kings and dyes their garments, 81, 6. It is worshiped in kings, ibid. It is made from water, ibid. The brilliance of purple is produced by infusions of various juices from various sources, 690, 45.

PUTEI [WELLS]: What do the wells dug by Isaac signify? 363, 20 ff.

PYTHAGORAS [PYTHAGORAS]: The inventor of the name “philosophy,” 328, 37. For this reason he established the practice that his disciples should keep silent for five years, so that through so much silence they might learn to speak, 982, 5. He asserts that there is one world, whereas others assert innumerable worlds, 1, 2, 3. The Pythagorean confession, 349, 80. David and Isaiah are older than the Pythagoreans, 983, 5.

## Q

**QUADRAGESIMA** is fasted throughout all the days except Saturday and Sunday, 545, 34. See **FASTING**. The fortieth day, through the Lord’s resurrection, is now considered not the first but the last, 244, 44.

## R

**ROOTS** that have no roots are destroyed, like vegetables or hay, 786, 19.

**RAPHIDIN**, that is, “breadth of judgment,” 1019, 5. [Col. 2284]

**REASON**, where it is present, leaves nothing superfluous, 316, 8. How it resists desires, 443, 1 ff.; 445, 3. This exercise of right reason, which the Greeks call *λογισμός* (*logismos*), by which the mind intent upon wisdom is strengthened, 446, 6.

**REBECCA** was a figure of the Church, and in what way, 310, 87–88; 311, 90; 1013, 14.

**REDEMPTION.** See **CHRIST** and **GOD**.

**KINGDOM** must not be seized, even if it is owed; rather, it must be awaited, so that it may be bestowed at its proper time, 684, 27.

**RELIGION** takes precedence over duties of piety, 1446, 146. No regard for royal power is to be had where obedience is rendered to religion, 685, 28. Where religion is holier, there the faith of truth is fuller, 1145, 14.

**RELICS** are what remains of a human being from a dead body, from its remains, 814, 81.

**WE ARE RENEWED** through the regeneration of the bath; we are renewed through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; and we shall also be renewed through the resurrection, 652, 35. When wickedness is poured out, new grace is received, by which each person is renewed, 966, 30. Whoever is renewed is always in the light, 921, 81.

**REPTILES** are called not only snakes but also fish, 80, 4.

The letter **RES**, according to the Latin interpretation, means “head” or “primacy,” 1221, 1.

**RESIN** joins broken marble together, 489, 17.

**RESPIRATION**: how does it occur in a human being? 83, 11.

**RESPONSES** of the psalms, 42, 23.

The condition of the ancient **REPUBLIC** is described, 100, 52. Its customs and laws, 106, 66.

Two kinds of **RESURRECTION**, 763, 54. To command the dead to rise again belongs to divine power alone, 1350, 59. This is much more divine than forgiving sins, 1358, 13. It is natural for all living creatures to be born and die; God granted human beings this special grace, that the dead might live again, 874, 20. Resurrection cannot easily be understood except by those more perfect and more firmly grounded, 1540, 166. We are taught to believe in the resurrection by examples, 109, 78–79.

**THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD**: why it was given, 396, 15. It will restore us to the grace of the simple creature, 1458, 194. After the resurrection the righteous will be changed into incorruption, while the reality of the body remains, 762, 51. Resurrection is that by which all the bonds of the enemy are loosed and every triumph is abolished, 881, 34. In the Revelations, why one should not glory at all, but in weaknesses, 796, 42.

**A KING**, even if he possesses the laws in his power, is nevertheless more subject to God, 1179, 33. Power does not release justice; justice releases power. Nor is a king released from the laws; rather, he releases the laws by his own example, 710, 8. Kings are summoned under no laws to punishment, 692, 51. Although a king is absolved from the laws, he is nevertheless answerable to his own conscience, 701, 77. Christians ought to be subject to the higher powers, lest anyone think that the constitution of an earthly king may be dissolved, 1354, 73. If you have riches, you are liable to Caesar, 1502, 35. It is the duty of virtue that, even through dangers, willing soldiers obey royal command, 686, 34. They are forbidden to present themselves to the emperor and judges, 1063, 19. The fall of kings is the punishment of peoples, 727, 56. An insult must not rashly be offered to kings, whether by God’s prophets or by priests, if there are no more serious sins for which they ought to be reproved. But where the sins are more serious, the priest does not seem to be permitted to spare the offender, so that he may be corrected by just reproofs, 835, 43. He is a king who is not ashamed to be reproved in his actions and rebuked in words, 1043, 34. The true king is one who has not learned to be subject to disgraceful acts, in whom the enticement of guilt and error could not reign, 939, 7. And the one who governs his own body well, 939, 7.

**RAHAB**: in type, a prostitute; in mystery, the Church, 1322, 23; 1480, 40. She ought to teach you how Christ is to be followed, 825, 24.

The **RHINE**, a wall of the Roman Empire to be remembered against savage nations, 228, 12.

The **RHÔNE**, driven on by a swift current, cleaves the straits of the Tyrrhenian sea, 28, 12.

**DEW** is more abundant when the night is clearer, under the moon and through the night, 75, 29.

The **WHEEL** first came into being without thorns, 51, 48. It is set before us as a mirror of human life, ibid.

**REUBEN**: what blessing did he signify in its mysteries? 1515, 8–9.

The leaves of the **BRAMBLE** kill a snake, 47, 3.

The **RED SEA**, 37, 10. See **SEA**.

**RUTH**: why she is mentioned in Christ’s genealogy, 1324, 30 ff.

## S

The day of the **SABBATH** was later in the order of days, but earlier in the sanctification of the Law, 935, 1. The Sabbath belongs not only to days but also to months, years, generations, and the world itself, 1475, 23. What the Sabbath called *δευτερόπρωτον* (*deuteroproton*) is, 936, 1. The second day of the week is the Lord’s Day, 935, 1. Perpetual Sabbaths are festivals of the eternal resurrection, 1363, 30. Why the works of the Lord’s healing began on the Sabbath, 1350, 58.

**SABELLIUS** is a moth, and why, 1270, 13. The Sabellian is refuted who says that the Son of God and the Father are the same person, 715, 26.

The **PRIESTHOOD** is great in the Word of God, 424, 16. Priests offer sacrifice for the people; although weak in merit, they are nevertheless honorable through the sacrifice, 853, 25. After Christ came, they began to offer themselves as victims, 715, 25. When the priest blesses, the people respond: “Amen,” 882, 36. How the high priest, the presbyter, and the minister of the sacred altar ought diligently to perform the office they have undertaken, 989, 23; 1441, 131. What zeal ought they to have? 1198, 11. “You who are a priest, rescue the one being led to death, and you will have atoned for your sins,” 1071, 42. The minister of the sacred altar who flees from his own people is an exile from the world and renounces everything, 420, 7. Now priests teach the lessons of chastity, 517, 12. We reject marriage after the manner of angels, 859, 3. The good in me comes through the mercy and grace of Christ and through the ministry of the priesthood, 1225, 13. There are many simple priests of the Lord, poor in speech but exalted in abstinence and virtue, 790, 28. When people are rebuked by priests, they aggravate their sin by wishing to deny or defend it, 677, 6. The towers of the Church are the priests, who possess an abundance both of the word concerning natural matters and of discipline concerning morals, 132, 49. The flock is the people, the night is the age, and the shepherds are the priests, 1298, 50. See **THE KEYS OF THE CHURCH**.

**PRIESTS** are all the children of the Church, and for what reason, 1364, 33; 1484, 53. We ought to imitate the priestly life, 1364, 33.

If there was great power in the **FIGURE OF THE SACRAMENTS**, how much greater is their mercy in the reality? 689, 43. Then the day shines more brightly when we celebrate the sacraments, 502, 52. The divine sacraments are good pastures, 1140, 2. Some are in the place of pastures, others in the privilege of the sacraments, 773, 19. The Church is furnished with two rivers: the bath of grace and the tears of repentance, 310, 87. Who ought not to take part in the heavenly sacraments? 1466, 232.

What kind of **SACRIFICE** is acceptable? 214, 17. When is it full and perfect? 208, 8. Four kinds by which sacrifices were commended, 214, 19. A sacrifice is commended both by speed and by grace, 195, 25; 197, 29 ff. Whoever sacrifices must believe in the one light of the Trinity, 197, 30. In sacrifices, a sweet odor is the Church’s, 1029, 34. We ought to bring everything prepared for the sacrifice, and not delegate it to others, 305, 68.

The letter **SADE**, according to the Latin interpretation, means “consolation,” 1194, 1.

The **SECULAR PERSON** has many masters, whose vile slave he is, 1126, 39.

The **WORLD** is subject to secular wickedness, 812, 76. If you pass beyond secular things, you will pass over to paradise, 812, 77. See **WORLD**.

British **SALTS** are healthful as food for the body and exceedingly agreeable as drink, 93, 33.

**SALIM** is said to mean “ascending,” 816, 3.

What does the **WILLOW** signify mystically? 54, 53.

Did **SOLOMON** ask for wisdom and in it find even all the things he had not asked for? 926, 93. He built a temple for God, but did not preserve the temple of his own body, 712, 16. Why did he appoint singers in it? 1052, 26. He whose wisdom is celebrated through all the ages became foolish because he loved his wife too much, 1163, 18. Perhaps he therefore went so seriously astray, so that people would not err and believe that the promise of the future Messiah had flowed to him, 1317, 9. The Jewish populace believes that Solomon came in place of Christ, 680, 13. The Jews are refuted who called him the Son of God and Christ, 713, 22 ff.

**DANCING** in honor of God is considered praiseworthy, 1052, 27. The mysteries revealed concerning the resurrection do not accord with the reproaches exacted for dancing, 1386, 8.

Our **SALVATION** must be entrusted to God alone, and why? 814, 83. Every time is suitable for salvation, 1181, 38.

The name **SAMARITAN** signifies “guardian,” 1428, 74. See **SCRIPTURE**.

The letter **SAMECH**, that is, “hear,” or “firmament,” 1157, 1.

**SAMSON** strangled the lion, but could not strangle his love, 711, 16.

The life of the **SAINTS** is a standard of living for others, 483, 1. They were not of a superior nature but of superior observance; they did not fail to know vices but corrected them, 484, 4. Through the Lord’s providence, sins slipped upon the saints, and why? 677, 4, 7; 680, 13. The saints are members of Christ, 819, 9. They are mountains of spices to which Christ flees, 1258, 44. They are called heaven, 1121, 25. They give thanks to their author because they have nothing for which to repent of having been in this world, 322, 22. This is the reward and life of the saints: that they redeemed others, 507, 71. The Lord forgives some on account of the merits of others, 1357, 11. All the saints will pass through fire, 997, 14 ff. See **FIRE**.

**BLOOD** is hot and fiery, 266, 93.

The threefold discipline of **WISDOM**: *θεωρητική* (*theoretike*), *πρακτική* (*praktike*), *λογική* (*logike*), 992, 31. Philosophers distinguish three kinds of wisdom: natural, moral, and rational, 1261, 2. How wisdom, understanding, and discipline differ, 886, 7. The spirit of wisdom is poured into all according to their capacity, but into all who are faithful, 808, 65. Wisdom is lofty of mind, 847, 12. A feeble mind cannot bear its radiance, 319, 16. The more wisdom is sought, the deeper it is judged to be, 906, 48. It must be stored in the hidden place of the heart, 925, 1. It certainly exists in the height of human thought, 1177, 24. It must be sought where there is tranquility of mind and the peace that surpasses all understanding, 662, 22. The highest end of wisdom is that we be tranquil in mind, 1244, 17. What is the beginning of wisdom except renouncing the world? 1029, 36. Do not rebuke or judge as idle those whom you see studying wisdom, 1430, 85. It does not distinguish abilities but wills: the one is more capable who is nearer in affection and closest in discipline, 947, 6. Better is the foolishness that has eyes to see its breasts than the wisdom that does not, 828, 31.

The **WISE PERSON** is defined by the Sophists as “a good man skilled in speaking”; and from where did they derive this? 347, 75. When you see a wise person, recognize that the glory of the Lord has descended upon him, 1191, 26. The wise person is assessed in three things: sense, speech, and mind, 320, 20. A wise man is subject to the law voluntarily, not by necessity, 751, 30. What the vigilance of a wise man ought to be like, 346, 76. How his mind should walk backward, that is, look upon past things, 274, 117 ff. His mind ought to be hospitable, 352, 92. When he diminishes, he adds, 436, 47. How he may take pleasure in bodily health and other prosperous things, 455, 33 ff. He conceals his own injury, 928, 4. The saying of the Seven Sages, “Follow God,” is taken from our writings, 315, 5.

**SARAH** is called in Greek *ἄρχουσα* (*archousa*), “she who rules”: Sarah, *ἀρχὴ ἐμή* (*arche eme*), that is, “my power,” or “the beginning of my authority,” or “of my kingship,” 351, 85. She was a type of the Church, 294, 31; 296, 38.

**SATAN** fell from heaven to earth, where temptations are ordinarily harsher, 1117, 10. See **DEVIL**.

How terrible was the envy of **SAUL**, who directed an error of speech toward the destruction of an innocent man, 781, 9. His fall is a terror to others, 940, 19.

Those whom **SCANDALS** harass are not only the little ones but also the least, 1244, 19. We must not supply the wicked with goads for rivalry against us, 780, 9 ff. Why there is no scandal for those who love, 1245, 20.

The **SCARUS** alone among fish chews the cud, 84, 12.

The **STAGE** of a human being, 44, 30. The entertainments of the stage soften the mind, 34, 5.

Why God wished the **KNOWLEDGE OF GOOD AND EVIL** to exist in human beings, 148, 8. Avoid seeking what one is not permitted to know, 1415, 18. It is burdensome to know what you can neither carry out nor avoid, 160, 36. “What I have read, I venture to affirm; what I have not read, I reverently leave to those who know,” 1225, 14. No food is sweeter than knowledge and learning, 490, 19.

The letter **SCIN**, that is, “above the wound,” 1238, 1.

The **SCRIBES** descended from the tribe of Simeon, 517, 13.

The first book of the **SACRED SCRIPTURES** of the Old Testament is Genesis, 1177, 25. The Samaritans follow only the five books of Moses, while the Synagogue principally follows seven, 1503, 38. The Old Testament is the foundation of faith, 1474, 19. Christ’s discourse is the Old and New Testament, 754, 33. The New Testament was in the Old Testament and ran within it, through which it was announced, 1017, 28. How those who do not accept the Old Testament should be refuted, 160, 38. Heretics who do not accept the law of the Old Testament cannot hold to Christ, and why, 1024, 23. Many things were not idly added by the Seventy to the Hebrew reading. The Church follows the opinions of the Seventy more closely, 1082, 13. In copying the Greek text of Scripture, a scribe could have erred, 1193, 35. An ancient copyist of the psalms could have made a mistake, 1254, 27. An interpreter of Scripture or an ancient copyist could have erred, 1013, 15. Frequent translation of the meaning of Scripture from Hebrew into Greek and from Greek into Latin is accustomed to weaken it, 837, 49.

In the Old Testament there are three kinds of wisdom: natural, moral, and rational, 1261, 2. Every divine Scripture is either natural, mystical, or moral, 777, 1. The letter that kills lies; the spirit that gives life is truthful, 1206, 36. The former bears a curse; the latter brings a blessing, 914, 67. The Jew, while following the letter of the Scriptures, has died, 813, 80. The Church has two eyes: one that sees mystical things, the other moral things, 1176, 20. The mystical sense is sharper, the moral sweeter, 1105, 7. The mystical discourse of the heavenly Scriptures is like stronger food, while the persuasive ethical discourse is sweet and softer, 1138, 24. Solomon expressed the moral subject more fully in the Book of Proverbs, the natural in Ecclesiastes, and the mystical in the Song of Songs, 364, 23; 974, 3; 1262, 2.

There is much obscurity in the prophetic Scriptures, and how they can be understood, 1078, 59. God’s truth must be gathered from them, 772, 18. In them there is usually not one figure only but many, so that one discourse may contain several forms, 1483, 52. We must examine not the sequence of words but the weight of the subject matter, 1486, 63. We must not easily criticize in them anything that we cannot understand, 147, 7. How Christ enlightens us when we think about something difficult in the Scriptures, 1035, 9. They commonly set past events in place of future or present ones, 304, 67.

The traditions of the Scriptures are the body of Christ, 1391, 33. The Lord’s money is divine Scripture, 1498, 18. Let it be your road, 1143, 11. It builds everyone up, 946, 4. Whoever exercises his mind in the divine Scriptures or in counsels ought to exercise it longer, 1013, 13. Let us spend the whole day and night practicing in a certain arena of the heavenly Scriptures, 1123, 28. Why we ought to wear out and polish their words through long use, 216, 22. It is a fire kindled by meditation on those heavenly writings, 848, 15.
